en: Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

I pay homage to the Teacher who has extinguished all darkness in every respect and has pulled sentient beings out from the mire of birth and death; I shall now expound this treatise, the Abhidharmakośa.
The Commentary states:
Those who intend to compose a treatise must necessarily have a lineage of transmission; it is the principle that one should first pay homage to the Honored One whom they revere.

Thus, the Master of the Sūtras (Śāstrakāra) observed that all those in the world are deluded by false teachers and heterodox doctrines, whereas his own teacher has forever transcended all darkness, established teachings that are not in vain, and occupies the station of a Great Teacher. Having achieved supreme and uncommon virtues, [the Master] sought to induce profound and pure faith in him as a condition for correctly propagating the teachings he established. Therefore, he first praised and paid homage to the Buddha, the Bhagavān, whose merits in self-benefit and benefiting others are perfected, using this as an auspicious omen to signal the commencement of the treatise.
In this regard, because the Blessed One is fully endowed with both the qualities of wisdom and abandonment, his self-benefit is perfected;
because he is replete with the quality of grace, his benefit for others is perfected. Why is this so?
Because all darkness regarding every mode of existence is eternally extinguished, the perfection of the virtue of wisdom is attained;
because darkness regarding all objective spheres is also eternally extinguished, the perfection of the virtue of abandonment is attained;
and because the hand of correct teaching pulls sentient beings out of the mire of birth and death, the perfection of the virtue of beneficence is attained.

Although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have dispelled all darkness, they are still unable to extinguish it in every respect; therefore, they do not achieve the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Because they have not attained the various forms of non-knowledge and do not exercise the wisdom that acts [upon them], and because they lack the wisdom that accords with their mental dispositions and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are unable to rescue and deliver sentient beings in accordance with reality.
Because their virtues for self-benefit and benefitting others were not yet perfected, those who possessed noble qualities were not called "Masters.

Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has perfected these two virtues; he rescues all sentient beings without error, achieves rare and vast renown, and occupies the most exalted station. Thus, he alone is titled the Great Master (*śāstṛ*). Therefore, I first praise and pay homage to the virtues of the Great Master in order to introduce this treatise, the *Abhidharmakośa*.
What is the Abhidharma?
The verse says:
Pure wisdom along with its attendants is called Abhidharma, as well as the wisdom and treatises that can attain it.
The commentary states:
"Wisdom" (prajñā) has the meaning of discerning phenomena;
"purity" (viśuddhi) has the meaning of being untainted (anāsrava).
The various outflows (*āsrava*) are called "stains" (*mala*); because the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is free from these stains, it is called "pure wisdom" (*viśuddhaprajñā*).
On what basis is it known that this untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) is named *Abhidharma*?
It is because the Blessed One permitted the inquiries of Śakra and others.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"I possess the profound Abhidharma and Vinaya; you may ask whatever questions you wish.

This means that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was invited to inquire at his pleasure regarding the Noble Path and the fruits of the Noble Path; the same applies to the invitation for those of the Vatsa lineage to inquire as they please.
Furthermore, for what reason is only untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) designated as the Abhidharma?
It is because, having directly realized (*abhisamaya*) the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) by means of it, one no longer becomes deluded.
Is it not the case that direct realization is not accomplished by wisdom alone?
In that case, the Abhidharma (Dharma-prakāśa) should not consist of wisdom alone.
Indeed, it is not wisdom alone; rather, it includes the associated factors (sānucara).
What are these associated factors?

This refers to the mental factors—such as form, feeling, perception, and so forth—that arise in accordance with wisdom, as well as the mind itself; this is a general description of the concomitants of pure wisdom.
Why, then, are the untainted five aggregates called Abhidharma, yet the concomitants such as feeling and so forth are not specifically designated as Abhidharma?

Because wisdom possesses the capacity within all three types of clear realization—namely, those consisting of vision and so forth—arising and other factors, as well as form, constitute the objective basis (*vastu*) and nothing else;

whereas feeling and the others pertain exclusively to the clear realization that takes the objective basis as its object, for feeling and the others each have their own specific functions, such as experiencing (*anubhava*).
If it is wisdom (*prajñā*) that is able to see, it should be called *abhidharma*; how could feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] be called *abhidharma*, since they are like the blind?
This is because they cannot discern the Four Noble Truths.

For within the direct realization of the characteristics of suffering and so forth, its vision (*darśana*)—that is, its clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*)—is most preeminent, as it functions through the discernment (*pravicaya*) of the various truths.

Although sensation and the other [mental factors] function together with pure wisdom (*viśuddha-prajñā*), it is the power of wisdom that sustains them as they direct themselves toward their respective objects; therefore, among the factors of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they are not the most preeminent.
Consequently, the attainment of the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*) is designated as the ultimate Abhidharma.
Is there a conventional *abhidharma* that is taught as being the ultimate (*paramārtha*)? Yes;
it refers to the various forms of wisdom (*prajñā*) and treatises by which this [ultimate] is attained.

This means that the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*) which is attained can only be acquired through those various wisdoms—namely, the superior mundane wisdoms of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī*), reflection (*cintā-mayī*), and hearing (*śruta-mayī*), along with their attendants (*sānucara*). Without such wisdom and its attendants, it is impossible to realize the untainted faculty of wisdom. Because these serve as the means for attaining it, they share the name "Abhidharma" (the Dharma of Non-outflow Wisdom), just as the means of loving-kindness (*maitrī-upāya*) is also called "loving-kindness" and so forth.

One is able to obtain the various treatises, namely that fundamental Abhidharma; because it is the supreme provision for untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), it is also called "Abhidharma" (the Higher Dharma).
Just as the maturation of karma (*karma-vipāka*) is so named, the provisions for outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth are likewise termed "outflows" and so on.

The aforementioned statements regarding wisdom also refer to that which is acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*). Apart from this innate wisdom, there would be no one capable of reciting and upholding the teachings of the Abhidharma.
Since it is only through innate wisdom that one can correctly recite and uphold the Dharma of the Sūtras and so forth, that [wisdom] is also designated as *abhidharma*.
Is it not the case that this treatise is also called Abhidharma because it is the supreme provision for untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*)?
For what reason, then, is it specifically named Abhidharma?
The *Abhidharmakośa* verse states:
"Because it encompasses that ultimate truth and because it relies upon it, this work is established with the name *Abhidharmakośa*.
The commentary states:
This is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) and *bahuvrīhi* (exocentric) compounds.
"Treasury" (*piṭaka*) means that which is solid and substantial, like the core of a tree.
All meanings of solidity and substance found within the Abhidharma treatises are subsumed under this term.
Because it is the treasury of that [Abhidharma], it is called the "Abhidharmapiṭaka," which is to say, the solid and substantial meaning of the Abhidharma.
"Abhidharma" (Treasury) or "basis" is like a sheath for a sword; that is to say, the Abhidharma is the basis for this treatise.

Because this treatise was composed by drawing upon the meaning of that Abhidharma, it takes that Abhidharma as its treasury and is thus called the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treasury of Abhidharma). This signifies that the Abhidharma serves as the basis [for this work].
For what reason is this Abhidharma, upon which the present treatise relies, taught?
And who was it that first taught it?
Although one should not ask these questions regarding the person who taught the Dharma, for in the Buddha’s teaching, one relies on the Dharma and not on the person.
As for the desire to necessarily take human beings as the measure, this and the previous question shall now be answered collectively.
The verse says:
"If one sets aside the analytical knowledge of phenomena (pravicaya-dharma), there is truly no other superior means capable of extinguishing all afflictions."
"Because of afflictions, the world drifts in the ocean of existence; for this reason, the Buddha taught the Abhidharma.
The Commentary says:
Since there is no superior means other than the discernment of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) capable of extinguishing the afflictions that draw the world into suffering, the Blessed One said:
If there is even a single dharma that has not been realized or fully known, I do not say that one can rightly bring an end to suffering.
Because the afflictions have not yet been extinguished in the world, one wanders in the cycle of birth and death within the ocean of the three realms of existence.
In order to cause those in the world to cultivate the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and thereby extinguish all afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said:

"For this reason, the Buddha taught the Abhidharma. If the Buddha had not taught it, even the great śrāvakas such as Śāriputra would have been incapable of correctly discerning the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the root Abhidharma upon which this treatise relies is certainly the word of the Buddha.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) refers to tradition as evidence that he himself does not believe the Abhidharma was spoken by the Buddha.
For what reason does he disbelieve it?
Because it is traditionally heard that the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra and others composed it, and because [the Buddha] did not state that the Abhidharma (*abhidharma*) was his basis (*āśraya*).
As the Blessed One told Ānanda:
"From now on, you all should rely upon the measure of the Sūtras, for the meanings and tenets of the various Abhidharma schools differ.
This is not correct.

Because the great śrāvakas compiled [the teachings] in accordance with the Buddha’s holy instructions, the Abhidharma is authorized by the Buddha and is also called "the word of the Buddha" (buddhavacana); for it accords with the wisdom that thoroughly understands the causes and effects of both affliction and purification, just like the various sūtras.
If that which is permitted by the Buddha were not called the Buddha’s teaching, then one would have to discard immeasurable sūtras.

Furthermore, if it were said that what is not based [on the Buddha] is not the Buddha’s word, then the Vinaya Piṭaka would not be the Buddha’s teaching, because at the time of his parinirvāṇa, he did not exhort [the disciples] to rely upon it.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because one also exhorts the bhikṣus to rely upon the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, then one must consequently admit that the extensive *Vinaya* was not spoken by the Buddha, and thus would not be an authoritative standard.

If the Vinaya is the Buddha’s word because it is an extensive commentary on the Sūtra of the Precepts (Prātimokṣa), then why do you specifically doubt that the Abhidharma, which is an extensive commentary on the Sūtras, is not the Buddha’s word?
Furthermore, the aggregate of wisdom (prajñā-skandha) together with its attendants and superior requisites is called the Abhidharma.
Among the four reliances (pratisaraṇa), it is stated that wisdom is the reliance, but not that words are the reliance; otherwise, there would be the fault of logical inconsistency.
Furthermore, they claim that the Sūtras alone are not the definitive basis, yet they ultimately fail to state that the Abhidharma and Vinaya possess a distinct status as bases.
Moreover, one must necessarily admit that the Abhidharma is a differentiation of the Sūtras; therefore, it constitutes a valid basis.
Alternatively, the *geya* and other [genres] should also not be the basis, because the Blessed One exhorted reliance on the *sūtra* alone.
Furthermore, what meaning does the term "basis" (*āśraya*) intend to reveal here?
If it reveals the sense of "valid authority" (*pramāṇa*), this is logically not necessarily the case.
How is it that the World-Honored One previously spoke of four criteria of authority (*pramāṇa*), yet now speaks only of the sūtras as the criterion?
Or rather, at the earlier time, he should have relied on speaking of only one, because the other three—dharma and so forth—are subsumed within the sūtras.

Since you have already been refuted regarding your reliance on a person (*pudgala*), and since your current exhortation to rely on the specific distinctions of the Sūtras would now be redundant, your present statement regarding "reliance" must clarify a distinct meaning.

Namely: "Until now, your mind has belonged to me; this was relying upon a *pudgala*. From this day forward, having no other basis, you should rely solely upon the Sūtras and not allow them to be forgotten."
Furthermore, the term "sūtra" used here refers collectively to all the holy teachings of the Tathāgatas.
Were it not so, teachings such as the *geya* (verses) would not be authoritative bases [for practice].

Yet, the specific exhortation to rely on the *Prātimokṣa* is intended to engender a sense of reverence for the precepts; for one should not seek the underlying meaning of that *Vinaya-sūtra*, but should instead practice with devotion exactly as it is stated. Since those who violate the grave precepts cannot be restored, there is thus a repeated exhortation to rely [on the *Prātimokṣa*] in order to maintain the precepts firmly.
Therefore, the statement "relying on the sūtras" does not mean relying solely on the sūtras as the authority.

Furthermore, when [the Buddha] exhorted Ānanda to rely on the *sūtrapramāṇa* (the authority of the sūtras), he was in fact exhorting him to rely on the Abhidharma; because this [Abhidharma] is the authority for the sūtras, it is called *sūtrapramāṇa*.

This refers to the definitions found in all the various sūtras; for the Abhidharma can resolve the meaning of these sūtras by distinguishing between those of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and those of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).

Because the name "Abhidharma" signifies that which can comprehensively encompass all the words of the principles of the Noble Teachings without contradiction, those sūtras that accord with these principles are called sūtras of definitive meaning.

That which contradicts this principle is called "provisional meaning" (*neyārtha*). Since that which is provisional may fearfully violate the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one should seek its intended meaning by relying on correct reasoning and authoritative teaching.

If it were otherwise, then as previously stated regarding relying solely on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), one should now likewise do so; one should merely exhort reliance on the sūtras and should not speak of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As for the claim that the Abhidharma teachings of the various schools are not the word of the Buddha because their doctrinal tenets differ, the same should apply to the Sūtras, since we observe differences in both wording and meaning among the Sūtras of the various schools.

Because the sūtras differ, their tenets vary; that is to say, there are certain schools that recite the *Saptabhava-sūtra*, and in their Abhidharma they establish the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), as well as establishing the gradual realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*) and so forth.
The *Saṃgītiparyāya* and other such sūtras praised for their study are not recited within the Sarvāstivāda school;
likewise, numerous sūtras such as the *Karatalopama* were never previously recited in other schools.

Although there are many sūtras recited in common across various schools, their names and phrases differ from one another; for instance, some sūtras state that you, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, shall attain perfect enlightenment in a future age, or speak of karma that is neither black nor white, and the ripening of karma that is neither black nor white. Thus, there are immeasurable names and phrases that vary among the different schools. Therefore, one should not conclude that the Abhidharma is not the word of the Buddha simply because its meanings and tenets differ [from other sources].
The Abhidharma is certainly the word of the Buddha, because the Buddha himself upheld the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
As the Blessed One said:
"It is extremely rare to find one who has grown old and become decrepit yet still goes forth as a monk and upholds my Tripiṭaka."

If it is argued that this statement refers to the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*, the reasoning is necessarily incorrect; for that is merely a specific classification of the Sūtras, and there is nowhere stated that it should be maintained separately.

There are indeed places where it is stated that one upholds the *sūtras*, the *vinaya*, and the *mātṛkā*, yet there is no other place where it is said that one upholds the *kṣudraka-piṭaka*. Furthermore, it cannot be asserted that the *kṣudraka-piṭaka* is identical to the *mātṛkā*, because they have distinct explanations.
As the Great Venerable Kāśyapa said:
"What is the designation for the *mātṛkā*?

It refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the eightfold noble path, the four right endeavors, the four bases of spiritual power, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), emptiness-of-emptiness, wishlessness-of-wishlessness, signlessness-of-signlessness, the various [knowledges] at the conclusion of clear realization, the various conventional knowledges, the meditative absorptions practiced in alternation, the knowledge of the absence of contention, the knowledge of the vow of wisdom, the knowledge of the ultimate concentration, the dharmas such as calm abiding and insight, as well as the *dharmaskandha* established through the compendium of diverse categories."
All such categories as these are collectively termed *mātṛkā*; they cannot be found in their entirety within the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*.
Therefore, to claim that the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka* constitutes the third [piṭaka] is not a sound teaching.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"One should diligently train in the Abhidharma and the Abhivinaya.
Thus, we know that the Buddha taught the Abhidharma.
If that were so, would the Abhidharma-piṭaka not constitute a fourth [piṭaka]?
No, because it is accepted that the Vinaya-piṭaka itself is the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
All discursive paths associated with the most excellent and superior ethical discipline (*śīla*) are called *Abhivinaya*, because they can directly confront the *Vinaya*.

All discursive paths associated with the profound nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena are called *Abhidharma*, because they can directly confront the nature and characteristics of phenomena.
Alternatively, those sūtras which are called *dharma* are [the basis], while the treatises that manifest and definitively resolve their meaning are called *Abhidharma*.
The *Prātimokṣa* is the original name for the *Vinaya*, while that which specifically manifests and extensively analyzes the *nidāna* (origins) is called *Abhivinaya*.
Therefore, what has been stated does not constitute a valid objection.

Furthermore, the Buddha’s holy teaching is comprised within three aggregates (*piṭaka*); just as with the Sūtra and Vinaya collections, the Abhidharma must necessarily be included within the collection of authoritative measures (*pramāṇa*).
The *Saddharmavipralopa-sūtra* also states:
“The Abhidharma and Vinaya, The essential texts and meanings within the Āgamas—
There will be disciples who do not transmit them, Fearing that upon hearing them, their peers might look down on them.”
Furthermore, it is said that this Dharma, this Vinaya, and the teaching of this Great Master are themselves the Abhidharma.

One observes in the Sūtras instances where a preceding term is present, yet at times that referent is expressed apart from that preceding term; for example, as in "the Perfectly Awakened One" (samyaksaṃbuddha) being referred to simply as "Awakened" (buddha), or "superior morality" (adhiśīla) being spoken of merely as "morality" (śīla), or various forms of desire and greed being referred to simply as "greed" (rāga) and so forth. Therefore, one knows that this Dharma is indeed the Abhidharma.

In some instances, the Blessed One has also used the term "Dharma" as a skillful means to refer to the Abhidharma; that is to say, if there is a teaching that accords with the Sūtras, elucidates the Vinaya, and does not contradict the nature of reality (dharmatā), one should follow such principles and instructions.
One should know with certainty that the Abhidharma is truly the word of the Buddha.

The sin of slandering the True Dharma is profound and utterly terrifying; let not those who cherish themselves engage in the evil practice of speaking ill of it by claiming that the Abhidharma was not spoken by the Buddha.
The refutation of the opposing arguments is concluded.
As stated above, it was for the sake of causing the world to cultivate the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) that the Buddha taught the Abhidharma.
What, then, are those phenomena that are to be discerned?
The verse says:
Contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena— With the exception of the Path,
all remaining conditioned phenomena Are called "contaminated" because the outflows increase in accordance with them.
The untainted refers to the Truth of the Path and the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena—namely, space and the two types of cessation. Among these, space is non-obstructive;
analytical cessation refers to disjunction from fetters, which is distinct for each specific object of bondage.
When that which is to arise is ultimately obstructed, one separately attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The treatise says:
All phenomena (*dharma*) are, in brief, of two kinds: first, those with outflows (*sāsrava*), and second, those without outflows (*anāsrava*).
This is the general statement; next, it shall be explained in detail.
With the exception of the Noble Truth of the Path, all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). What, then, are these?
This refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ*), from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
As it is said: "What is called the aggregate of clinging to form?
It is contaminated form that accords with the various clingings," and so on, in detail, up to consciousness, which is likewise.
For what reason are the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*)?
Because within them, the outflows (*āsava*) increase accordingly.
Among the various afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the designation "outflow" is established because they cause the defiled mind to constantly leak [impurities].

Because they are associated with the outflows (*āsrava*), and because the outflows increase in accordance with their objects, they are called "increasing in accordance with the outflows" (*āsrava-anuśayana*).
The meaning of this "increase in accordance" (*anuśaya*) will be discussed in detail later.
By this, those [factors] belonging to different realms or stages, as well as those that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, are already excluded.

Since the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) within the sphere of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are outflows (*sāsrava*), they do not mutually increase one another; therefore, these two names are not established in opposition to each other.
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*)?
As the Blessed One said:

"Dharmas with outflows (sāsrava) refer to all forms (rūpa) that accord with grasping (upādāna) and serve to increase the sense of grasping at existence; this is explained in detail up to and including consciousness (vijñāna), which is likewise."
That which is contrary to this is untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma.
Such, in brief, are the characteristics of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted.
To provide a detailed analysis, it is further stated as follows:

This refers to the arising and growth of present greed, hatred, or delusion toward all forms—past, future, or present—or toward any of the various secondary afflictions (upakleśa) among the mental factors (caitta-dharma), and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, for what purpose was this said?
It was to distinguish and analyze those factors conducive to the various types of grasping (*upādāna*).

If that were so, one should have stated only that they "give rise to" afflictions such as craving, or each of the other secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) individually; it would not be a general statement capable of providing specific discernment.

In order to allow for the distinct identification of each meaning, it is stated that not all afflictions can manifest simultaneously; therefore, they are spoken of collectively, or else [referred to] individually according to each specific secondary affliction (*upakleśa*).

Furthermore, the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are subtle; at the stage of their active manifestation, they cannot always be discerned. In contrast, the modes of activity of anger (*krodha*) and the like are coarse and manifest, making them easy to recognize; therefore, only these are mentioned collectively.
The remaining secondary afflictions that fall within the mundane are termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*); being comprised by the mundane, they are said to "fall within the mundane.
This means that they abide in the world and do not transcend it; the name "mundane" (*loka*) is established based on the essence of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"I shall now proclaim for you the world and the origin of the world.
It further states:
"One observes that the arising of the world does not exist within the world; this is what is meant by 'non-existence,' and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, how is it known that all things fallen into the world are termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*)?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"I shall explain to you the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas.

Contaminated dharmas refer to all that exists: the eye, all forms, all visual consciousness, all visual contact, and whatever internal feelings—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—are produced conditioned by visual contact; and so on, up to the mundane mind, mundane dharmas, mundane mental consciousness, and mundane mental contact."
To speak at length, up to what is called "contaminated phenomena" (*sāsrava-dharma*).

As for "uncontaminated phenomena" (*anāsrava-dharma*), this refers to supramundane mind, supramundane mental objects, and supramundane mental consciousness; to speak at length, up to what is called "uncontaminated phenomena."
Based on these authoritative scriptures and through correct reasoning, the characteristics of contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena are established;

they cannot be arbitrarily determined. The Dārṣṭāntikas, contradicting both reason and scripture, falsely assert that all form (*rūpa*) and so forth existing within the body of a non-sentient being who is free from faults are called uncontaminated phenomena.
This must certainly not be so, for it contradicts the sūtras. As a sūtra says:
"Regarding all forms—past, future, and present—that give rise to or produce current greed, hatred, or delusion," and so forth, as explained at length.

If the form and other elements within the body of one who is not counted among sentient beings and is free from faults can still give rise to and increase the greed and other afflictions of sentient beings, how can they be untainted (*anāsrava*)? Why is this so?

Because [beings such as] Aṅgulimāla, Ulūka, and Kāśyapa gave rise to outflows (āsrava) such as greed, hatred, and delusion based upon the body of the World-Honored One, they are reckoned by way of their words;

it is not the seventh case in the sense of being an object (*viṣaya*), but rather the seventh case in the sense of a locus (*āśraya*). Just as oil is the locus of the sesame seed, it is called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) because it is the locus of the outflows.

This is unreasonable, because it asserts that the present arises based on the past and future; yet, one has never relied upon the past or future to give rise to present greed and other afflictions. Therefore, that position is certainly not tenable.
Furthermore, the aforementioned sutra states:
"Or, among each of the various other secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there are mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) that are not secondary afflictions;

there are also those that are not mental factors. To distinguish these, it further specifies "mental factors"; thus, we know that the repeated mention of "mental factors" (*caitasika-dharma*) is intended to indicate the locative case (*saptamī vibhakti*) signifying the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).

Furthermore, cessation and the path should be the basis for the absence of knowledge; as it is said that ignorance has the nature of being non-knowledge regarding suffering and so forth, because the seventh case (locative) is used here in the word "regarding" (*at*).
If these [form and so forth] are not admitted as bases for verbal expression, why do you stubbornly insist that they must necessarily be bases?

Therefore, the arising of delusion and other afflictions with respect to form and so forth does not require them to be definitive bases for the outflows (*āsrava*) in order to be termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, all sounds would necessarily be untainted (*anāsrava*), because sound is certainly not the basis for the outflows (*āsrava*);
yet one should not maintain that sound is definitively untainted, for the Sūtra states that the substance of sound is defiled (*saṃkliṣṭa*).
It is not a reasonable statement to say that the untainted (*anāsrava*) is called "afflicted" (*saṃkleśa*).
Furthermore, the wholesome consciousness within the bodies of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) would consequently become untainted, as it is not a basis for the outflows (*āsrava*).

If it is argued that [the consciousnesses] are "with outflows" (sāsrava) because they are pursued by the divisions of the outflows, then all consciousnesses of those in training (śaikṣa) would necessarily be with outflows.
Furthermore, since visible forms, excrement, urine, wine, and so forth are not bases for the outflows, they would all consequently be without outflows (anāsrava).
Furthermore, it is contrary to correct reasoning that the body of an Arhat is untainted (anāsrava);
therefore, the Sūtra states:
"All suffering whatsoever has grasping as its condition."
Nevertheless, the body of an Arhat is certainly suffering; thus the Sūtra says:
"When an Arhat’s life comes to an end, He gives rise to deep and great joy, Just like casting off a vessel of poison, Or like being cured of many diseases."
The Dārṣṭāntikas say: "Life is defined as the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) projected by prior karma.
If this were untainted (anāsrava), the Noble Ones would not regard it as being like a vessel of poison."
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"All Arhats constantly feel shame and revulsion toward themselves, and they reproach and disparage their own bodies.
Since a Noble One should not feel shame, revulsion, reproach, or disparagement toward any untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena, the body of an Arhat must necessarily be tainted (*sāsrava*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Obscured by ignorance and bound by craving, both the fool and the wise alike experience the body of existence (*bhava-śarīra*).

If one were to claim that the body produced by ignorance ceases, while a body induced by other forms of knowledge continues to arise, then the wise would have no body of existence produced by ignorance and craving; this would contradict the teaching of the Sūtra.

Furthermore, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) would necessarily possess fruits; if the body of an Arhat did not exist—being a body as loathsome as a disease or poison—to claim that it is not subsumed within the three realms of existence (tridhātu), who but a Dārṣṭāntika would hold such a view?
Furthermore, since the dharmas such as the eye possess both faults and the absence of faults, and their essential natures and characteristics are identical, one should not hold them to be distinct.

Moreover, according to the Dārṣṭāntikas, the eyes and other faculties within the bodies of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are likewise not the basis for the outflows (*āsrava*), because they maintain that the five consciousnesses are free from affliction (*kliṣṭa*).
If an Arhat lacks the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*), would this not contradict the Sūtra?
For it is said that he contemplates his own five aggregates of grasping as being like an abscess or a disease.
Furthermore, according to their tradition, external phenomena that do not belong to the category of sentient beings are suffering, yet they are not the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

One should maintain that there is the latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*) which is not itself attachment, that the eye is not the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), and that feeling (*vedanā*) is not the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). As a sūtra states:
"The feeling that arises simultaneously with contact is called the aggregate of feeling."
Therefore, all forms of suffering should be the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), as stated in the Sūtra:
"If one is deluded or hesitant regarding various sufferings or the origin of suffering, this constitutes doubt regarding the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origin."
Having thus demonstrated that the tenets of the Dārṣṭāntika school lack ultimate truth, one might ask:
Is there any authoritative scripture (āgama) that validates their position?
They claim that there indeed is.
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"Being free from greed, hatred, and delusion, one is then free from all outflows (*āsrava*).

It further says that there are six matters of the mind being stunted and obscured (*cittakhila-cittanivaraṇa*), namely: the matter of the mind being stunted and obscured by various forms (*rūpa*) that are with outflows and with grasping (*sāsrava-sopādāna*), and the same applies to sounds and so forth.

He says: since it has been stated that there are various forms (*rūpa*) that are tainted (*sāsrava*) and subject to grasping (*sopādāna*), one knows that there are distinct untainted (*anāsrava*) forms; this applies extensively even to contact (*sparśa*).
That [opponent] relies on a figurative inference (*arthāpatti*) to falsely construct this calculation.
However, within the Noble Teachings, one should not give rise to various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) by relying on such figurative inferential methods. As it is said in the Sūtra:
"All feelings whatsoever that arise from contact are entirely extinguished."
One should also infer by implication that there are other sensations not produced from contact;
yet this should not be accepted.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
Mahākāśyapa has no mental attachment toward the households of donors;
by the same principle, it should be understood that other arhats do have mental attachment toward the households of donors.
Furthermore, in that sūtra, the meaning cannot be inferred, as the word "if" (yadi) is absent because it was not stated.

That is to say, regarding the statement, "If there are contaminated and grasping forms and mental obstructions," it merely says, "There are contaminated and grasping forms and mental obstructions. This reveals the fault of form itself rather than serving to distinguish form; therefore, that school likewise lacks authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*).
Although that Elder has mistakenly cited a scriptural passage stating:
"If bhikṣus possess outflows and grasping, they will not attain parinirvāṇa in this present life," and has further cited another scriptural passage:
“The True Brahmā is free from all taints (*āsrava*), unstained by the world;
he is called the Solitary Realizer (*pratyekabuddha*) Bhagavān, sovereign and free from all taints.
This does not correspond at all to that meaning.

I also do not admit that Arhats and others possess out-flowing grasping (*sāsrava-upādāna*); for although the eyes and other faculties are termed "out-flowing" and "conducive to grasping," they are not themselves the "grasping" or the "out-flows.
Furthermore, the Sūtra does not state that Arhats and others lack factors conducive to grasping or are free from all out-flows.
"Speech is also unstained" means that because all afflictions regarding all worldly objects have been severed.

According to the sūtras, greed and so forth are termed "stains"; thus, because one has eternally abandoned greed and the like toward all things grasped within the world and all realms of existence, it is called "unstained."
By this, one may explain the statement in other sūtras where the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Arhats and others have already attained dissociation from all worldly things; though they move within the world, they are able to subdue it and are not defiled by the world."
This means that regarding all worldly, outflow-tainted matters, they are not bound by any afflictions.
Therefore it is said:
"Arhats and others have already attained dissociation from all worlds; though they move within the world, they are able to subdue it and are not defiled by the world."

The intended meaning of this sutra is that although Arhats and others remain within the world, they nonetheless achieve accomplishment; because they have attained the antidote to the world, they subdue the defilements of worldly afflictions.
Therefore, that school possesses no authoritative teaching whatsoever.
Furthermore, their adherence to this view relies on the method of etymological interpretation, asserting that what coexists with the outflows (*āsrava*) is called "with-outflow" (*sāsrava*).
This explanation is irrational, because it establishes a definition that is inconsistent [with the actual nature of the phenomenon].
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Regarding all things possessing form, whether past, future, or present, one gives rise to present craving, or anger, or pride," and so forth, as explained at length.
How could going, coming, and the present arise simultaneously?
Furthermore, the Dārṣṭāntikas are merely stirring empty space; for among the eighteen elements, the first fifteen are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*), as stated in the Sūtras.
As the Sūtra says:
"Contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) are all that exists as eye, all that exists as form, and all that exists as eye-consciousness; and so on, up to body, tangibles, and body-consciousness."
All that has been said reveals the meaning without exception.
They say, "We do not recite this sutra.
However, one cannot achieve what is desired merely by not reciting the sutra; if you wish to achieve what is desired, you should diligently recite the sutra.
Furthermore, since they do not regard all sūtras as authoritative, how can they be called Sautrāntikas?

That is to say, when they see a sūtra contradicting the tenets of their own cherished school, they either reject it outright or alter the text according to their own views, claiming that the original wording was lost during oral transmission.
Alternatively, some may not accept any of it at all; for instance, sūtras such as the *Anupūrvasūtra* all state that these [teachings] are not included within the noble scriptures (*ārya-śāsana*).

Those who uphold the Abhidharma truly cherish their own school and have fabricated and inserted these into the Āgamas. Consequently, they turn their backs on immeasurable sūtras and, transgressing the words of the Noble Ones, give rise to many divergent tenets. I shall gradually demonstrate this in this treatise.
Having already explained the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the causes of the contaminated, what is the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
It refers to the Noble Truth of the Path and the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
There is another interpretation which states:
It is called "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*) because it belongs to the same category as the outflows, just as one speaks of a particular clan.
Furthermore, another explanation states:
it is called "with-outflows" because it is defiled by the outflows, just as food that is poisoned.
Some offer this explanation:
they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) because they are abandoned together with the outflows; it is like when Śakra, Lord of the Devas, fell along with his *tāḍaka* drum.
There are many such etymological interpretations of this kind.
That which is contrary to those is called untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
The Noble Truth of the Path refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*), such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, that are not tainted.

The three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are space (*ākāśa*) and the two types of cessation (*nirodha*), namely, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
These three types of unconditioned phenomena, beginning with space, as well as the noble truth of the path, are termed "untainted" (anāsrava) for these reasons.
The noble truth of the path has already been mentioned previously; it shall be discussed in detail later.
Among the three unconditioned phenomena briefly explained, space has non-obstruction as its sole nature; because all phenomena appear most clearly within it, it is called "space."

This takes non-obstruction as its characteristic, because all primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) aggregates are entirely incapable of being completely covered or obstructed by it.
Alternatively, it is neither that which is obstructed nor that which obstructs; therefore, it is said that non-obstruction is its characteristic.
Space has already been explained.

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) has the nature of dissociation (*visamyoga*). It is called "deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) because it consists of the individual discernment of each of the Four Noble Truths.
Its nature is a specific form of wholesome wisdom (*kuśala-prajñā-viśeṣa*); since nirvāṇa as dissociation is the fruit of this [wisdom], it is termed "cessation through deliberation."
Some say that all phenomena to be abandoned share one and the same analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The Abhidharmikas reply:

[This is not so], for it varies according to the specific objects of bondage. If all phenomena to be abandoned shared one and the same analytical cessation, then when the extinction of the afflictions to be abandoned by the *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* is realized, would the extinction of the other afflictions also be realized?
If it were already realized, then cultivating further remedies would be useless;
if it were not realized, then one object would realize only a portion of itself and not the rest, which contradicts reason because it entails the fallacy of having parts.
Therefore, one must necessarily conclude that the state of dissociation (visamyoga) corresponds in measure to the objects of bondage; this does not contradict correct reasoning.
The analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) has already been explained. Non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is obtained through the permanent obstruction of future arising.

Discrimination (*pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to the wisdom accomplished through diligent application in accordance with reality. That which permanently obstructs the arising of future phenomena by means of this wisdom is called non-discrimination cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

For example, when the eye and the mind are focused exclusively on a single visible form, regarding the remaining forms and all sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles that perish moment by moment, one attains non-discrimination cessation with respect to those portions of the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). This is because the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) and a portion of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna-kāya*) can never arise again with respect to objects already ceased, as they take only simultaneous objects as their conditions.
Because its function of arising is dependent upon a simultaneous basis and conditions;

if a dharma can obstruct the function of another dharma’s arising, this [obstructing] dharma—apart from wisdom—certainly hinders that dharma, causing it to remain in the future and never arise again, whereby it attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This dharma truly exists; it shall be established later in accordance with the sequence of reasoning in the original text.
It was previously stated that, excluding the Path, all other conditioned dharmas are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
What is meant by "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*)?
This should now be explained.
The verse says:
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena— namely the five aggregates such as form—
are also called "paths of the world," "bases of speech," "possessing departure," "possessing objects," and so forth.
The treatise says:
They are called *skandhas* because they are concealed, accumulated, and suppressed by various calamities such as old age, illness, and death.
To distinguish them from the five aggregates of morality (*śīla-skandha*) and so forth, the terms "form" (*rūpa*) and so on are used.

While the five aggregates of morality cannot fully encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), the five aggregates beginning with form do fully encompass them; therefore, these alone are specifically mentioned here.

That which is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) is so named because it is produced by the collective gathering of various conditions. Since that which is yet to come has not yet arisen, how can it be called conditioned?
It is also termed "conditioned" because it belongs to that same category.
Just as firewood, even while in its unburnt state, is still called "firewood" because it belongs to that same category;

or rather, there is no error in establishing a name based on what has been or what will be, just as lutes and harps are said to "possess sound," or as one speaks of "milk-giving breasts" or "lotus ponds."
All phenomena that are non-arising do not transcend that category, and are therefore called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Regarding these conditioned phenomena, in various sūtras the Blessed One has designated them by names such as "paths of the world" (*lokamārga*) according to their specific meanings.

What, then, is that? It refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), which are also called "paths of time" (*adhvan*). This is because the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; because they flow through the paths of the future, present, and past; and because those phenomena that do not arise lack the necessary conditions.
Although they do not arise [as such], there is no error in establishing these names because they belong to that same category. Some say:
they are called "paths of the world" (*adhvan*) because they are swallowed by impermanence, or they are called "bases of name" (*nāma-āśraya*).
"Speech" refers to vocal sound, or that which is capable of speaking; this is a specific differentiation within the continuity of vocal sounds.
"Basis" refers to the meaning associated with names, which fully encompasses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are three bases for speech; there are neither four nor five.
By this, one can properly reconcile the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, which states that the bases for speech are subsumed within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Is it not also the case that [the meaning] arises based on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Why, then, is that meaning not established as a basis for expression (*vyañjanāśraya*)?
Because there is no logical possibility for that meaning to coexist with the name (*nāman*).
As it is said regarding the basis of expression: it refers to the meaning that coexists with the name.
If meaning and name could be spoken of simultaneously, they would be established as the basis of speech (*vāgvastu*).

However, because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) meaning and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) name cannot be spoken of simultaneously, and because there is no principle for their coexistence—given that the mundane and the supramundane lack the logic of being simultaneous—they are not established as the basis of speech.
Alternatively, because this [cessation] is extinguished, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is established; thus the Sūtra says:
"The cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*) is called cessation.
Cessation is not the basis for verbal expression; the basis for verbal expression is the aggregates.
Furthermore, another explanation states:

If, in a given case, three factors can be established as the basis for speech—namely, the basis of meaning, the basis of words, and the basis of both—the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) consists solely of meaning; therefore, it is not the basis for speech.
Some say: It is also based [on the aggregates], but lacks verbal expression.

Alternatively, it is called "detachment" (*viveka*); because one eternally abandons *nirvāṇa* while sinking into the cycle of rebirths within the various realms of existence, it is termed "detachment," which signifies the cessation of the constant transmigration through those realms.
If one has already attained [the fruit] and will certainly not return, this state possesses detachment; therefore, it is called "possessing detachment.

Just as one who possesses wealth is called "wealthy," so too does the conditioned possess the sense of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*). Since all conditioned phenomena are like rafts, the Noble Path itself must also be relinquished.
As stated in the sūtra:
"Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas.
Or it is called "possessing a basis" (*savastuka*).
"Phenomenon" (vastu) refers to that which is the support or the locus; this is the meaning of "cause.
An effect depends upon its cause because it arises from the cause, just as a child depends upon its mother.
Alternatively, an effect abides in its cause because it can cover the cause, just as a person sits upon a bed.
It is because it is obscured by its fruit; because cause and fruit exist sequentially; and because of their subtle and coarse natures.
Because this possesses an object, it is called "possessing an object" (*savastuka*), as illustrated by the previous example.
These are exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); such categories as these describe the various synonyms for conditioned phenomena.
Regarding these aforementioned conditioned phenomena, the verse says:
"Those with outflows (*sāsrava*) are called 'appropriation-aggregates' (*upādānaskandha*), And are also said to be 'with contention' (*saraṇa*)."
As well as suffering, its origin, the world, the bases of views, and the three realms of existence.
The commentary says:
Has it not already been stated that, with the exception of the Noble Truth of the Path, all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*)?
Why is this stated again here?

Although it has already been explained previously, it is stated again in order to clarify their specific designations and concepts, or to establish the definitive meaning of those designations and concepts.

It was previously stated that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are called aggregates (*skandha*); now it is stated that those which are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are called "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*). By implication, those which are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are simply called aggregates.

Within the context of the various outflows, the designation "clinging" (*upādāna*) is established because they are able to grasp at the three realms of existence, or because they are able to maintain the karma that leads to future existence; therefore, they are called "clinging."

The aggregates arise from grasping (*upādāna*) or are capable of producing grasping; therefore, they are called "aggregates of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*), like fire from grass or chaff, or like trees with flowers and fruit.

Furthermore, these contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are also called "contentious" (*saraṇa*); this is because the term "contention" (*raṇa*) is applied to the afflictions (*kleśa*) insofar as they disturb the wholesome side and cause harm to oneself and others.
The aggregates coexist with conflict, or they arise together with the aggregates of conflict; therefore, they are called "with conflict" (*saraṇa*).
Here, the meaning is to show that neither the aggregates nor the conflict can arise if even one of them is missing.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates other designations for contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*).

That is to say, they may be called "suffering" (*duḥkha*), namely the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), because they are the basis for all forms of oppression and because their intrinsic nature is coarse and unstable.
It is called "origination" (*samudaya*) because that very category can act as a cause and because it can accumulate [suffering].
It is called "the world" (*loka*) because it is subject to destruction.
As the Blessed One said:
Because its nature is subject to destruction, it is called "the world" (*loka*).
If that were so, the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) would also be worldly.

It is not so; for while there is no second instance of destruction [in the case of the Path], the nature of destruction in the Truth of the Path is indeterminate, whereas the nature of destruction in the world is determinate.

Alternatively, it is called a "station of views" (*diṭṭhāyatana*), because the five views, such as the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth, abide therein and increase along with their latent tendencies (*anusaya*).
Is it not the case that all defiled afflictions (*āsrava*) increase along with them?
Is it not the case that all views have already been stated to be subsumed under outflows (*āsrava*), grasping (*upādāna*), and contention (*raṇa*)?

Although this is logically sound, those views, regarding all types of tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) at all times and in all aspects, lack any distinction; for they are characterized by firm attachment, immovability, and the increase of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Because their essence and function increase and flourish, and in order to manifest that these outflows (*āsrava*) are capable of producing these various bases of views (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna*), they should be stated repeatedly.
This is not the case for attachment (*rāga*), delusion (*moha*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*); for while those [factors] such as attachment exist in all types of objects, they do not exist at all times;
whereas delusion exists at all times and is not without differentiation.
Because doubt is undifferentiated yet not firmly adhered to, the outflows (*āsrava*) are not said to exist in that state.
Alternatively, it is called the "three realms of existence" (*trai-dhātuka*), because they are the cause of existence, the basis of existence, and are subsumed within the three realms of existence.

The word "etc. is used to include those termed "defiled" and so forth; such categories as these are outflowing (*sāsrava*) phenomena, which are designated by various names according to their specific meanings.
As stated above, the five aggregates (*skandha*), beginning with form (*rūpa*), are called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); what, then, is the aggregate of form?
The verse says:
"Form consists only of the five faculties, the five objects, and the unmanifest.
The commentary says:
"Form" refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Regarding the "five faculties," they are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties.
Regarding the "five objects," they are the objects of form, sound, odor, taste, and the tangible.
"Those comprised by and within the range of the eye and so forth, as well as the unmanifest," refers to the form included in the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).
"Only" means that only these—the ten spheres and a small portion of one sphere as thus revealed—are designated as the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
What are the characteristics of these various forms?
The verse says:
That consciousness relies upon pure matter; These are called the five faculties, such as the eye.
The commentary states:
"That" refers to the previously mentioned five faculties, namely the eye and so forth;
"consciousness" refers to the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.

The "basis" refers to the bases of the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness; it has pure matter (*rūpaprasāda*) as its essence, and this very pure matter is termed the visual faculty and so forth.
Therefore, the Blessed One stated in the sūtras that the defining characteristic of the visual faculty and so forth is pure matter.
This treatise also states:
"What is the eye-faculty?
Its nature is pure matter that serves as the basis for visual consciousness," and so forth, as explained in detail.

In the various holy teachings, consciousnesses are distinguished by their faculties (*indriya*), not by their objects (*viṣaya*); therefore, we know that those words indicate the faculty and not the object.
Some say: "That [word] refers to the object and not the faculty," yet there is no mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that takes visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth as its object.

If consciousnesses such as those of name-and-form were [the sense organs], then those consciousnesses would incur the fault of being called "eye" and so forth, because they are distinguished by the term "pure matter" (rūpaprasāda).

If that were the case, the word "matter" (rūpa) would become redundant, since the meaning—that those consciousnesses depend on the pure [matter] named the eye-faculty and so forth—would already be established.
Since that which is the support of consciousness is pure and non-material (*arūpa*), the term "material" (*rūpa*) must be employed to distinguish it from that.
If you claim that the term "material" is stated in the *Sūtra*, this may be so for the *Sūtra*; however, it does not state a specific distinction regarding the support of consciousness.
If it is argued that this statement is from the root treatise itself, that too is equally doubtful; one should consider both possibilities together:

if this interpretation were intended to dispel a difficulty, the word "matter" (*rūpa*) would have to be included; furthermore, if the term "basis of consciousness" (*vijñānāśraya*) were analyzed as a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*), then pure faith (*śraddhā*) would also have to be called an eye-faculty and so forth.
Therefore, the term "form" (*rūpa*) is included to exclude this interpretation.

There is not a single phenomenon that, while having consciousness as its support, is pure such that it could serve as the basis for this interpretation. Thus, the word "form" is extremely useful; by means of this, the statement in the root treatise is explained.

Furthermore, within this context, the preceding term "eye" is used for the purpose of exclusion; although those [other four] sense organs all have pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) as their essential nature, they do not serve as the support for visual consciousness. Therefore, those four organs are not subsumed under the faculty of the eye.

The subsequent statement is intended to exclude the immediately preceding support; for although that [preceding mind] also serves as a support for visual consciousness, it does not have pure matter (*rūpa*) as its intrinsic nature, and thus that mental faculty (*manas*) is not subsumed under the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).

Alternatively, the former statement reveals the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) eye, while the latter statement is intended to reveal the *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous) eye; the same applies to the other sense-faculties.
If this were so, since there is no distinction in the characteristic of pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*), they would not constitute five [faculties].
Not so; for their functional capacities differ.
How is it known that their capacities are distinct?
Because the support for consciousness of uncommon objects is fixed.
Furthermore, because their causes are distinct, we observe that there are differences between the effects, just as in the case of the sounds of the lute, the harp, the flute, and the pipe.

Now, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the causes for the eye, the ear, and so forth, each have their own distinctions; because these causes are distinct, the essential nature of the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) of the eye and the other faculties also possesses distinctions.
Although their substances are distinct, because their causes are not different, it would follow that their resultant pure matter (*rūpa*) should likewise have no distinction.

This objection is not valid; for although they share the same characteristic, we observe them to be different, just as there are distinctions between the internal and external primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

If it is argued that, just as with sound, although the causes differ, they are subsumed in a single location because their characteristics are one—and that the same should apply to the five sense organs such as the eye—there is no such fault; for although the causes of sound differ, it serves as the object for a single consciousness.
They are subsumed under a single location because the five faculties, such as the eye, serve as the bases for their respective classes of objects and consciousnesses;
furthermore, since they are manifested by their distinct functional roles as individual supports, it is not appropriate for all the faculties to be subsumed within a single location.

Furthermore, just as consciousness and sensation, though both share the common characteristics of discerning and experiencing respectively, are distinguished as six types of consciousness and three types of sensation due to their differing causes, so it is here:
although these differ as six and three, they are subsumed under a single category because their essential nature is the same.

If it were argued that the eye and other [faculties] should likewise be subsumed under a single location, then for what reason would feeling (*vedanā*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) occupy the same location?
Therefore, they are not subsumed under a single location; this demonstrates that their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) exist as distinct entities.
Although their specific characteristics differ, they are subsumed within the same location.
Having already analyzed the characteristics of the eye and so forth, the characteristics of visible form and so forth shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Visible form consists of two or twenty types; sound has only eight kinds;
taste has six and fragrance four; touch has eleven as its nature.
The treatise says:
Regarding the statement "form is twofold," this refers to two types of meaning, namely, color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna).
Among these, there are twelve kinds of color-form and eight kinds of shape-form; thus, they may be twenty in total.
The manifestation of the twelve refers to blue, yellow, red, white, clouds, smoke, dust, mist, shadow, glare, light, and darkness.
Among these twelve, the four types beginning with blue are the primary manifest colors (*varṇa*), while the eight types beginning with clouds are their specific varieties (*viśeṣa*).
Those meanings that are obscure shall now be briefly explained.
When the vapors of the earth rise upward, they are called mist (*nīhāra*).
When it arises obstructing light, that within which other forms can still be seen is called a shadow (*chāyā*); the opposite of this is darkness (*andhakāra*).
The radiance of the sun is called light (*āloka*).
The flames of the moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, precious gems, lightning, and so forth, are called "luminosity.
As for the eight types of shape and color, they are: long, short, square, round, high, low, regular, and irregular.
Among these, "regular" (samyak) refers to an even shape; an uneven shape is called "irregular" (asamyak).
Other forms are easy to understand and are therefore not explained here. Some say:

There are twenty-one kinds of visible form (*rūpa*). Space (*ākāśa*) is the first; the second is the single category of manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*), which is itself a differentiation of the visible form belonging to the space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*).

Among manifest colors, blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, light, brightness, and darkness can be known solely by their manifestation. Among shapes (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), that which is the nature of bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karma*) can be understood solely by its shape. As for the remaining forms, both shape and manifest color can be understood.
As for how a single entity could have two natures:
this is not what our school maintains, and therefore there is no such fault.
This shall be further examined in the *Karmaprajñapti* (Chapter on the Exposition of Karma).
The sense base of form has already been explained; now the sense base of sound shall be explained.
It is called "sound" because it is capable of summoning [others], or it is designated as "sound" simply as a vocal resonance.
The sacred teaching of the Sugata all states this:
Sound is the objective sphere apprehended by the auditory faculty; it is of the nature of derived matter produced from the four great elements.

This sound is of eight types: first, there are four based on the distinction between those caused by the great elements that are appropriated (*upātta*) or unappropriated (*anupātta*), and those belonging to the category of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*) or not belonging to the category of sentient beings (*asattva-saṃkhyāta*); these are further divided into eight by the distinction between those that are agreeable (*manojña*) and those that are disagreeable (*amanojña*).

Appropriated primary elements (mahābhūta) refer to those belonging to the category of sentient beings in the present life, such as those that are nurtured, outflowing, or maturation-born; the opposite of these is termed non-appropriated.

Among these, sound that has appropriated primary elements as its cause is of two kinds: namely, that produced by the application [of effort] of sentient beings, and that which arises otherwise without depending on application.
Furthermore, that which is produced by the application of effort (*prayoga*) among sentient beings is of two kinds:
first, that produced by the application of the hands and so forth; second, that which has the nature of vocal informative action (*vāg-vijñapti-karman*).
This vocal informative karma is further of two kinds: that which arises dependent on names, and that which does not depend on names.
That which arises dependent on names is further of two kinds:
first, the determinate (vijñapti), and second, the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
The two types that do not depend on names are likewise so.
There is the distinction of sound characterized by having appropriated great elements as its cause;
there is also the sound characterized by having non-appropriated great elements as its cause, which is likewise of two types.

The first arises from the application of sentient beings; the second is produced by the agitation of the elements. The former refers to sounds such as those of conch shells, bells, and drums; the latter refers to those emitted by wind, forests, rivers, and the like.
Those sounds belonging to the category of sentient beings include the voices and hand-claps of people; other sounds belong to the category of non-sentient beings.
Among these various sounds, those that produce joy in hearers are called "agreeable sounds," while those contrary to this are called "disagreeable."

Among these eight, only the first two are logically appropriate, because sound—which is comprised of the great elements (mahābhūta) that serve as its cause—is categorized as either sentient or non-sentient, and as either appropriated or non-appropriated.
One should likewise be able to speak of distinctions such as "agreeable" and so forth regarding visible forms (*rūpa*) and the other [objects]; why then is this mentioned only in the case of sound?

Visible forms and the others should also be said to have both appropriated (*upātta*) and non-appropriated (*anupātta*) primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause; this is indeed how it should be stated. However, because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the sphere of sound is difficult to discern, it is described as being of two kinds solely with respect to its causes.
Visible form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects] are not like this; therefore, they are not mentioned.
Since the definition of sound as included in the *Abhidharma-kośa* does not differ [from that of the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*], these eight types of sound should not be established.

Is it not the case that there are sounds produced with great elements (*mahābhūta*)—both those that are appropriated (*upātta*) and those that are unappropriated—as their cause, such as the sound produced by the conjunction of a hand and a drum?

There is no such sound, because the two [types of] great elements each produce their own distinct results, and it would entail the fallacy that two sets of great elements could not share a single result as a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Although there is a mutual impact between the two sets of four great elements—those that are appropriated and those that are non-appropriated—they each act as causes to produce their own respective sounds; since those sounds each rely upon their own specific substrata, they do not constitute a single tripartite entity.

Although two sounds may arise due to the mutual impact of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of a hand—which is appropriated (*upātta*)—and a drum—which is unappropriated (*anupātta*), these sounds mutually obscure one another such that one or the other is perceived; their distinct characteristics are not easily discernible. Therefore, the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) consists of only two types.
The sphere of sound has already been explained; now the sphere of taste shall be explained.
The reason for departing from the sequential order is to demonstrate that there is no fixed rule regarding the arising of consciousness with respect to those objects.
"Taste" refers to that which is consumed; it carries the sense of being something to be tasted.
This [taste] is of six kinds, distinguished by the differences of sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and bland.
Having explained the sense-base of taste, the sense-base of odor shall now be explained.
Odor refers to that which is smelled; it is of four kinds, because there are distinctions between pleasant odors, unpleasant odors, and those that are neither [equal nor unequal].
Regarding "equal" and "unequal": they differ because the physical bases (*āśraya*) upon which increase and decrease depend are distinct.
Some say they differ because of the distinction between being weak and being intense.
The present treatise states:
There are three kinds of odors—pleasant odor, unpleasant odor, and neutral odor.

That which can nourish the sense faculties and the primary elements is called pleasant odor; that which is contrary to this is called unpleasant odor; that which lacks the functions of the former two is called neutral odor.

That which arises through the predominance of various meritorious karmas is called "exquisite fragrance"; that which arises through the predominance of various sinful karmas is called "unpleasant fragrance"; and that which arises solely through the power of the four great elements is called "neutral fragrance."

Although this is a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), it also possesses distinctions; therefore, while it is produced by the power of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it is also subsumed under the dominant fruits of sentient beings.
Having explained the sphere of odor (*gandhāyatana*), the sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) shall now be explained.

Tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) refers to that which is touched; it has eleven as its nature, meaning that its substance consists of these eleven real entities: namely, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the seven derived tangibles—smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, and thirst.
If that were so, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) would necessarily become an object of touch.
Since this [faculty] can touch that [object], the latter must certainly be touched by the former; therefore, some say:
"The body-faculty can only be a toucher and not an object of touch, just as the eye-faculty can only see and not be seen."
Furthermore, there are those who say:

"There is not even the slightest dharma that can touch another dharma; rather, when the basis (āśraya) and the object (ālambana) arise in immediate succession, the designation 'contact' (sparśa) is established.
If this consciousness is able to apprehend that object, it is metaphorically said to 'touch' that object."
Since an object is not the support for consciousness, it cannot be that which contacts;
for this very reason, only earth and the other elements are designated as "the tangible," whereas their associated forms and so forth are certainly not the tangible.
The intention here is to clarify that body-consciousness arises based on the body-faculty without taking those objects as its cognitive domain.
If those forms and so forth were not tangible, how could the form and other qualities of flowers and such things undergo transformation and decay when touched by the body?

Because that which serves as the basis is impaired, we observe that when the basis undergoes benefit or harm, the dependent [qualities] likewise undergo benefit or harm; this is not the case for the opposite.

For example, when a location is moistened and nourished by sweet rain, the crops and forests flourish and grow lush; yet when it is oppressed by scorching heat, the opposite occurs. Thus, one knows that when the great elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as the basis are impaired, it is the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) and so forth that undergoes transformation and decay, and nothing else.
This point shall be discussed in detail later.
Among these, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) will be explained next;
for now, the characteristics of smoothness, roughness, and so forth should be briefly explained.

Because smoothness itself is the nature [of the element], it is called "the nature of smoothness" (*ślakṣṇatva*), just as because distinctness itself is the nature, it is called "the nature of distinctness.

Regarding the etymological explanation: it is called "smooth" (*ślakṣṇa*) because it can be touched and rubbed; this signifies being soft, warm, and capable of being grasped. Because it possesses the function of roughness (*karkaśa*), it is called "possessing roughness," just as one who has hair is said to "have hair."
Because roughness is itself its nature, it is called "the nature of roughness.
This is a synonym for force, coarseness, and hardness; because it can exert suppression, it is called "heavy," which signifies the capacity to accomplish the subjugation of others.
Because weight itself is its nature, it is called "the nature of weight.
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
it is called "heavy" because it causes a scale to sink when placed upon it; it is called "light" because it is easily moved or shifted.
It is observed in the world that although material objects may be large in form, they are easily moved because they possess lightness;
since lightness is their very nature, it is called "the nature of lightness" (*laghutva*). The *Vibhāṣā* states:
It is called "light" because it does not cause that which is preeminent to fall.
It is called "cold" because, being oppressed by it, one desires warmth to arise; furthermore, it is called "cold" because it causes condensation and makes things easily discernible.
This refers to the meaning that their impairment and benefit can be quickly known: the desire for food is called hunger, and the desire for drink is called thirst.
One might ask: since desire is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*), does it not contradict the definition of contact (*sparśa*)?
Because the name of the effect is established within the cause, there is no fault of contradiction.
It is as when one says "the river is pleasant" or "the steps are pleasant," or that "food is the life of humans" and "grass is the life of livestock."
Other qualities not yet mentioned—such as rigidity (*staimitya*), strength (*bala*), and weakness (*daurbalya*)—are subsumed within these [categories] and therefore are not explained separately.

Rigidity is not distinct from smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*); strength is simply roughness (*karkaśatva*) and heaviness (*gurutva*); and weakness resides within softness (*mṛdutva*), warmth (*uṣṇatva*), and lightness (*laghutva*).
In this way, the remaining types of tangibles are included within these eleven according to their respective natures.
For what reason do smoothness and the others differ from one another?
It is because of the differences in the increase or decrease of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which they depend.
