Due to the increase of the water and fire elements, the quality of smoothness arises; due to the increase of the earth and wind elements, the quality of roughness arises; due to the increase of the earth and water elements, the quality of heaviness arises; and due to the increase of the fire and wind elements, the quality of lightness arises.

Therefore, at the time of death, the heavy nature within the body increases excessively; because the water and wind elements increase, cold arises, and for this reason, it is also said that the resulting state of suffocation occurs.
If this is so, why is it said that it is not devoid of smoothness?
As each [quality] increases incrementally, there is no fault in this.
Alternatively, "stupefaction" (mūrchā) is a specific differentiation of smoothness (ślakṣṇatva), not merely the nature of smoothness itself;
one should understand that this cause also possesses such differentiation.

Therefore, the quality of smoothness may arise due to the increase of the water and wind elements, or it may be produced due to the increase of the water and fire elements; thus, there is no contradiction between these two statements.
Because the wind element increases, hunger arises; because the fire element increases, thirst arises. The remaining [elements] should all be explained accordingly as appropriate.
That such derived matter exists with a distinct substantial nature apart from the primary elements will be discussed extensively later.
*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Two.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Part Two: The Second Exposition on the Fundamental Matters, Chapter One, Part Two. Within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) have already been explained; now, that which remains—the unmanifest (*avijñapti*)—shall be discussed.
The verse says:
Whether the mind is distracted or non-existent, Flowing along as pure or impure,
And being of the nature derived from the primary elements— For these reasons, it is called the unmanifest (avijñapti).
The treatise states:
Regarding the phrase "disturbed mind, mindless state, etc.," the word "etc. refers to both categories, namely the undisturbed mind and the state of possessing mind.
An unwholesome or neutral mind is termed "disturbed," while other minds are termed "undisturbed."
The attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation are termed "mindless" because they are capable of extinguishing the mind.
Although there are other resultant states that are likewise mindless, unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) does not flow along with them; therefore, the term "mindless" does not include them.
It is called "flowing along" because it continues in a similar succession through the three natures, as well as during states with mind and without mind.
Regarding "pure" and "impure," these refer to the wholesome and the unwholesome.
When wholesome minds and so forth arise, they give rise to pure non-informative matter (*avijñapti*); this similar succession is termed either restraint (*saṃvara*) or non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).

Unwholesome minds and so forth give rise to what is called "impure non-informative matter" (*avijñapti*); this similar continuity is termed "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*) or "neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint.
If it is an indeterminate mind, it likewise functions as two kinds of momentary origination; for this reason, these are called the two types of originating minds.
However, for both pure and impure non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), the concomitant mind may not be similar [to the motivating mind];
yet if it is pure non-informative matter, or if there is no mind at all, the two—the cause and the motivation—are each similar.

Having already explained that the outflows of purity and impurity follow [the mind] in states such as the distracted mind and the mindless state, it was further stated that these are "derived from the primary elements" (*mahābhūta*). However, since there are other acquisitions of purity and impurity that also follow [the mind], the term "derived matter" (*upādāyarūpa*) is used to distinguish them.
In this context, "creator" (kāraka) signifies the meaning of "cause. How is this known?
As it is said in a sutra:
The phrase "form creates the view of self" means that the view of self arises on account of form.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "it is by this that the unmanifest is explained": because it is a pure or impure form that flows continuously through various states originated by wholesome or unwholesome mental factors, it is called "unmanifest" (avijñapti) because—although similar to manifest action—it does not communicate or make itself known to others.

In order to clarify the causes and conditions for establishing such a name, it is said, "by this it is stated," which indicates that this is the intention of another master, as the Master of the Sūtra (Śrīlāta) does not accept such a type of unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa).

In brief, that unimpeded wholesome or unwholesome matter which arises based on the distinctions of bodily and vocal manifest karma, as well as the distinctions of wholesome and unwholesome minds, is called the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).

Now, it is said that the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) was unable to fully explain the characteristics of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) within this verse, because he defined it as "that which flows along" (*anuvartana*).
He himself explains:

"That which is a similar continuity is called 'flowing along'; the first moment cannot be called a continuity, lest there be the fault of over-extension. Therefore, it is certain that the non-informative matter of the first moment does not fall within the characteristics described here.
Furthermore, since a continuum (*saṃtati*) is conventional and not real, and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) would likewise not be real, this would contradict the tenets of the Abhidharma school.
Moreover, because that which is produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) does not flow on continuously during states of distraction or mindlessness, it should not be considered unmanifest.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because [the non-informative] exists within the state of having a mind (*sacittaka*) as it follows the flow [of the primary action], then pure and impure informative actions (*vijñapti-karman*) would also possess the characteristic of the non-informative (*avijñapti*).
Furthermore, the claim that the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the state of being without mind (*acittaka*) is useless, as this has already been subsumed by what precedes.
The phrase "disturbed mind and so forth" already includes all other states of consciousness; what, then, does the second "and so forth" include?

The Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika) should reflect on this. If it is argued that the latter "and so forth" includes the non-disturbed mind while the former is redundant, this cannot be correct, for there is no room for such inclusion. How could the latter "and so forth" possibly include the non-disturbed mind?

The refutation states that reasoning arises in relation to similar instances; since it proceeds by way of non-arising and so forth, and because reasoning does not extend to other cases, it does not constitute a complete inclusion.
Alternatively, the statement regarding a distracted mind would become useless.

Furthermore, one should specify that it is only the pure (*śubha*) non-informative (*avijñapti*) that flows continuously during the state of mindlessness, and not others; yet even in his own commentary, he does not make such a distinction.
Therefore, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) should reflect upon this principle: how can he define the characteristics of non-informative matter without falling into error?
That which arises from volition and other mental states, as well as that which is unmanifest (avijñapti) even in the absence of mind,
being non-obstructive and of a derivative nature— this is called non-manifest form (avijñaptirūpa).
Non-manifest form has thus been explained.
Regarding what is here called "derived from the great elements" (mahābhūta), what are the great elements?
The verse says:
The great elements are the four realms, namely earth, water, fire, and wind.
They are able to accomplish the functions of supporting and so forth, having the natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion.
The treatise says:
For what reason are these great elements (mahābhūta) called "elements" (dhātu)?
Because it is the source from which all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) arise,

and because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) themselves also arise from [other] primary elements— the sources of such arising are designated by the world as "elements" (*dhātu*), just as gold-bearing ore is given the name "gold element" (*suvarṇadhātu*).
Alternatively, they are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they are the source from which various kinds of suffering arise, as illustrated by the previous analogy. Others say:

they are called "elements" because they can maintain the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as well as the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*); thus, these various elements are also termed "great elements."
Why is it called a "seed" (*bīja*)?
Why is it termed "great"?
When various derivative forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) arise in their distinct varieties, they are able to give rise to their respective categories; therefore, it is called a "seed."
Some say: Because the karma of sentient beings is predominant, birth and death have never been non-existent since beginningless time; therefore, it is called a "seed.
Alternatively, when a phenomenon appears, it is termed "existence" (*bhava*); because it grows and develops this nature of existence, it is called a "seed."
This means the sense of having the nature of dharmas that grow and develop, or the sense of growing and developing the bodies of sentient beings.
Alternatively, it is called "seed" (*bīja*) because it can manifest the ten types of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), for it is by this power that they are manifested.
If that were so, there would be the fault of a great error, because all causes and conditions would have utility at the very moment the effect arises. [Reply:
There is no such great error, because they do indeed possess great utility.

Regarding the term "great function" (*mahāvyāpāra*): it refers to the four kinds of superior functions that exist within the fundamental matters of all sentient beings. Based upon these, consciousness and space are established; thus they may be called the "fundament of sentient beings. Furthermore, they are termed "great" (*mahat*) to distinguish them from other [factors].
Furthermore, among the matters that deceive and delude foolish people, these four are the most preeminent; therefore, they are called "great.
Just as among deceitful thieves, those whose deeds are superior are distinguished from the rest and thus termed "great deceivers" and "great thieves."
Thus, among these four causal conditions, they are called "great" (*mahābhūta*) because they are superior, which distinguishes them from others without any logical fault.
Some say: these four serve as the universal support for all other forms (*rūpa*); they are called "great" because they are extensive.
Some say: Because solidity and the other [qualities] are present within all aggregates of form and so forth, they are called "great" (mahābhūta).

In aggregates where wind predominates, there is an absence of visible form and so on; in aggregates where fire predominates, there is an absence of taste and so on. In all aggregates of the form realm, fragrance and odor are absent. Within aggregates of blue and so forth, there is an absence of yellow and so on; within aggregates of smoothness and so forth, there is an absence of roughness and so on. Since sound and the like are not fixed [in their presence], only these four are designated as the great elements.
For what reason is space not designated as a great element (*mahābhūta*)?
Because the characteristics of a great element are not established therein.
The designation "great element" is established for that which can cause benefit or harm; since space is not so, it is not a great element.
Is it not because space possesses the capacity for containment that it can be diminished or increased?
In reality, space has no functional utility of containment; it is not the case that when material forms aggregate, space opens up and makes way according to the locations they occupy.
How does it provide space?
Because it is non-obstructive, it does not hinder the existence of other things.
Thus, space has no function of either diminishing or augmenting.
If that is so, with what intention was it said:
"Because it can accommodate and receive [other things], it is called space"?

The meaning of this statement is as follows: because space exists, it allows resistant forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*) to interpenetrate one another. Since the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*) shares some slight resemblance to the characteristic of space, this location is conventionally designated by the name "space."

The space element (*ākāśadhātu*) consists of apertures such as the throat, which enables sentient beings to swallow food and drink, as well as to perform functions such as transformation and excretion.
Since it lacks the capacity to cause harm or benefit, space is certainly not a primary element (*mahābhūta*).
Furthermore, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are neither unitary nor permanent; their individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are manifold, and their distinct effects are immeasurable.

Space (*ākāśa*), by its very nature, is unitary and permanent, its characteristics are without differentiation, and it possesses no effects whatsoever. It is not the case that a distinct effect arises from a non-distinct cause; therefore, space is not designated as a primary element.

If it is argued that because other causes possess distinctions, they can assist space in producing distinct effects, then these distinct causes themselves are capable of producing those distinct effects; what need is there to insist upon this space as a cause?
Some say: Because the nature of space is eternal, there is no distinction in its characteristics across the stages of the arising and ceasing of phenomena;
earth and the other elements are not so, and therefore their phenomena differ.

We observe that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) undergo a transformation of their characteristics within their various states, such as the seed and so forth, before arising as sprouts and the like;

however, unconditioned space (*ākāśāsaṃskṛta*) is not like this. Because its nature and characteristics are eternal, it possesses no activity whatsoever. Since it cannot produce anything, it is not a primary element.
Furthermore, within this context, because the two terms "great" (*mahat*) and "seed" (*bīja*) are both present, only four meanings are established;
for while space possesses the quality of being great, it lacks the meaning of being a seed, as "seed" and "productive capacity" (*janana-śakti*) are distinct designations.
Some say: Space also lacks the status of a "great" element because its essence is not matter (*rūpa*).
Since derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) and other conditioned non-material phenomena possess the capacity to produce [matter], they are seeds and not "great" elements.

As previously stated, because the two meanings of the primary elements (mahābhūta) are mutually unestablished, and because the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) cannot be produced if even one of them is missing, the primary elements are exactly four, neither more nor less.
The *Vibhāṣā* masters speak thus:
"If [the faculties] were fewer, they would lack capacity; if more, they would be redundant. Therefore, there are only four, like the legs of a bed or seat. Others say:
The primary elements (mahābhūta) are naturally only four. Some say:

regarding derived matter (upādāyarūpa), the primary elements require only the four functions of supporting, cohering, maturing, and growing; whether they were fewer or more than these, they would lack capacity and utility.
How is it known that these four great elements are always inseparable?
This should be understood from the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra* and the *Mahābhūta-sūtra*.
Furthermore, it stands to reason that this must be so. What is the reasoning?

It is because within stones and the like, the three activities of cohesion, heat-production, and falling are currently observable; therefore, we know that water, fire, and wind are constantly inseparable therein.

Since within all waters one can perceive the three activities of maintaining, gathering, and possessing warmth, as well as flowing and moving, it is known that earth, fire, and wind are constantly inseparable from them.

Within the flames, the three activities of supporting and gathering, striking, and moving are currently observable; therefore, it is known that earth, water, and wind are constantly inseparable therein.

Within the aggregate of wind, there are presently observable functions capable of sustaining and giving rise to the three tactile sensations of cold, warmth, and touch; therefore, we know that earth, water, and fire are constantly inseparable from it.
Furthermore, how are these four elements known?
Because they constantly follow one another due to these causes and conditions, and because they are able to accomplish the functions of supporting and so forth.
That is to say, the elements of earth and the others successively accomplish the four kinds of activities: supporting, cohesion, maturation, and growth.

For this reason, when the four activities—such as supporting and so forth—are observed within a collection of matter, one knows that therein the elements such as earth and the others exist in mutual inseparability, constantly following one another.
Are the four functions, such as "sustaining" and so forth, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the elements (*dhātu*) themselves? No. Why is this so?
These four elements, in their respective order, have solidity, moisture, heat, and motion as their intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
It should be understood that here, "nature" (*svabhāva*) is mentioned to reveal the "substance" (*dravya*), in order to clarify that substance and nature are not mutually separate.
How should one understand that the four elements, such as earth and the rest, possess distinct characteristics—such as solidity—and distinct functions—such as supporting?
Furthermore, how is it known that the characteristics and functions of these four elements are not different, while their specific natures are being examined for distinction?
Because we do not perceive any distinction in the activities of the characteristics [of solidity and so forth].

Since we do not see any difference in the activities of solidity, upholding, and so on, we counter-interrogate you for the sake of verification: do you say that apart from the characteristics of solidity and so forth, there exists separately and distinctly an activity of upholding and so forth?

However, the functions such as supporting and the characteristics such as solidity are neither different from nor identical to one another. Solidity and so forth are the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of earth and the other elements, as they have nothing else upon which to depend.

In contrast, the functional activities such as supporting have distinct objects of observation for their designation; therefore, this "function of supporting" is not predicated of the specific characteristic itself.
One must not claim that all phenomena are called "earth" because they possess the function of supporting, for this would lead to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, it should be understood that the characteristic of solidity (*khakkhaṭalakṣaṇa*) within the earth element has no other object of observation; it is only when observing something distinct that is supported that one speaks of the function of supporting.
The moist characteristic of the water element has no other object of observation; that which is subsumed under the distinct observation is said to be its function of encompassing.
The warm characteristic of the fire element has no other object of observation; that which is ripened by the distinct observation is said to be its function of ripening.
The wind element has no distinct object of observation other than its characteristic of motion; rather, it observes that which is being nourished, such as the *kalala* and so forth.
Alternatively, sprouts and the like are said to be the "nourishing karma," where "nourishing" means either increasing in intensity or flowing and projecting [growth].
Motion refers to that which can induce the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) to arise in succession and reach another location.
Therefore, the activities such as supporting and so forth are not identical to the characteristics such as solidity and so forth. Some say:
Because the three times and the single time are distinct, one knows that the meaning of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "activity" (*karman*) is different.
Some say: earth and so forth have the activity of supporting and so forth, while the earth element and so forth have characteristics such as solidity and so forth.
This argument is incorrect, because there is no distinction between wind and the wind-element; thus, length and motion would have to be one and the same.

If the wind-element has motion as its intrinsic nature, why do both the Sūtra and the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* state that the wind-element is the nature of lightness and so forth that moves, and further describe lightness itself as a derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*)?
To say that motion is wind and lightness is derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) is to manifest their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
To state that lightness is wind is to indicate the cause by means of the effect, because it is the effect of wind.
Is it not the case that the fire element is also a cause of lightness, since it is said that fire and wind increase lightness?

Although this statement exists, fire is not determinative; if the increase of fire serves as the cause for the nature of lightness, then in that place there must necessarily be an increase in the wind element.

Alternatively, there may be lightness caused by an increase in the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*), yet within it there is no increase in the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*), such as when the flowers of reeds and the like are tossed upward by their lightness.
If the fire element were increased therein, a sensation of heat (*uṣṇa-spraṣṭavya*) should be perceivable within them.
Because this wind element universally serves as the cause of lightness, "lightness" is specifically cited to uniquely manifest the wind element.

However, since the characteristics of earth and the other elements are easily understood, it is unnecessary to mention effects such as heaviness; this is done to highlight that motion is difficult to discern in contrast to the three [characteristics] of solidity and so forth.
Are the elements such as earth and so forth identical to earth and so forth? No. Why is this so?
The verse says:
Earth refers to color and shape; names are established according to worldly convention.
Water and fire are likewise; wind is both an element and so too [a conventional designation].
The treatise says:
The term "earth" expresses only the spheres of visible form and shape.
Since earth is not composed of four spheres in total, why is it said that only visible form and shape constitute earth?

Although odor, taste, and the tangible element are present herein, this statement is made in accordance with worldly convention; for when people in the world point out the earth, they do so by indicating its visible form and color.

If that is so, when worldly people indicate things such as clothing, they do so by means of manifest form (*varṇa-saṃsthāna*), as when they speak of "clothing," "white," or "long. Yet you admit that the four bases (*catvāri āyatanāni*) constitute the nature of clothing and the like; the same should apply to earth. Why, then, is it said that [earth] is only form?
Furthermore, people in the world also designate the name "earth" for odors and so forth, saying:
"I am now smelling earth," "I am tasting earth," or "I am touching earth.
Although this is the case, it is the visible form (varṇa-saṃsthāna) that can effectively represent the earth, water, and fire.

Why is this so? It is because the world does not commonly say that one smells water, nor does it commonly say that one smells or tastes fire. Although it is said that one touches earth and so forth, these refer directly to the elements of earth and so on; therefore, although odors and other qualities exist within earth, they are specifically mentioned because their manifest color and shape are predominant.
Furthermore, visible form and shape indicate that there is no difference between the two realms or the various stages; therefore, they are mentioned specifically.

If that were so, then because visible form and shape also indicate clothing and the like, as well as superior fragrances and so forth, they should likewise be mentioned specifically [in those contexts].

The conceptual designations arising in the world are not fixed; therefore, the Abhidharmikas follow these worldly conceptual designations to demonstrate the distinctions between earth, clothing, and so forth.

Furthermore, no real entity is universally established by the world; rather, all that is commonly established by the world is conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*). Thus, regarding conventional phenomena, one should speak according to the specific conceptual designations arising in the world. For this reason, there is no fault in metaphorically describing fragrance and other qualities as "earth."
Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of form as it represents the stage [of existence], it is stated thus:
because the conceptual names used by worldly people are not fixed, one cannot take a single example and assume that all others are identical.

It has already been stated that clothing and so forth have four bases as their nature; one should understand that all other composite phenomena (*saṃgraha-dharma*) are likewise to be known accordingly.
Within objects such as clothing, there are also [characteristics] such as arising (*jāti*); those objects should therefore have five bases as their nature.
Although it is not the case that they do not exist, worldly people do not give rise to the conceptualization or designation of "clothing" and so forth with respect to them.
If that were so, the sense-base of sound (*śabdāyatana*) should be called "clothing" and so forth, because worldly people speak of hearing the "sound of clothing" and the like.
Although sound also exists, it is not continuous; since visible form and the other [sensory objects] exist at all times, only four are mentioned.
Just as earth has only manifest color and shape as its essence, so too do water and fire, in accordance with worldly convention.
In the world, water is perceived as blue, long, and so forth; therefore, its manifest color and shape are said to be the intrinsic nature of water.
Having perceived the tactile characteristics of flowing water, people in the world then say: "Water flows here."
However, this flowing substance is not actually water by nature, because the objects of the five sense organs, such as the eye, are distinct;
nor is it visible color (*varṇa-rūpa*), because it can be touched by the body;
furthermore, it is not shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), because it is not included among the eight types of form.
Since there is no distinct locus of visible form apart from its manifest appearance and shape, how is it that one perceives the characteristics of flowing water through touch?

When a mass of waters is impelled by the force of the wind, it arises in various locations in a continuous succession; it is with respect to this that the world gives rise to the notion and the name "flowing."

When these various waters arise in different locations, their manifest form is seen by the eye and their intervening moist nature is touched by the body. Therefore, when the manifest form and the moist nature are struck by the force of the wind and pushed one against another as they arise in different locations, this is called "fluidity. Apart from these, there is no separate substance of flow; thus, flowing water and the like are conventional designations and not ultimately real.

Because fire is perceived in the world as being red, long, and so forth, its manifest color and shape are said to be its intrinsic nature; furthermore, when these very qualities of color and touch undergo transformation, they are termed flames and embers.
This is a conventional designation and not a reality, because no single substantial entity is apprehended by the body or the eye.

Having already explained the distinction between the elements such as earth and their respective spheres (*dhātu*), since the world establishes the name "wind" for that which moves, there is no difference between wind and the wind-sphere; by this principle, it is said that wind is itself the sphere.

Is it not the case that people in the world also conceive the notion of wind with respect to manifest color and shape, since they commonly demonstrate to one another "black winds" and "whirlwind masses"?
To resolve this objection, the word "also" (api) is stated.
This is the distinction between the earth and its element, as all the masters of antiquity have said:
"Because the earth is mixed therein, it appears thus.
To clarify that the wind is itself the wind-element, he speaks again of "that" (*tat*); "that" (*tat*) serves to define it precisely.

Between these two explanations, the former is superior because there is no distinction between the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality) and the *aśubha* (foulness), and because foulness takes only the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) as its object.
The verse says:
In this context, the faculties and their objects Are said to be the ten bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
The treatise states:

It has already been explained that the substantial entities of the sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) constitute the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Within this context, these same faculties and objects are also designated as the ten bases (*āyatana*) and the ten elements (*dhātu*).
In the system of the bases (*āyatanamukha*), they are established as the ten bases, namely, the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*) and so forth.
Within the classification of the *dhātus*, ten *dhātus* are established, namely the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and so forth.
Having already established the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and established it as a sense-field (*āyatana*) and element (*dhātu*),
for what reason is this aggregate of form called "form" (*rūpa*)?
In the noble teaching of the Sugata, it is said that form (*rūpa*) is so called because it undergoes transformation and decay.

The intended meaning of this statement is as follows: it is called "transformation and decay" (*vipariṇāma*) because it is the cause of painful feeling, because it involves contact (*sparśana*), and because it is subject to change; it is designated as "form" precisely by virtue of this transformation and decay.
Regarding the cause of painful feeling: when form undergoes transformation and decay, it can give rise to painful feeling.

As stated in the *Arthavargīya*: "For those who pursue various desires, Constantly giving rise to expectations, If those desires are not fulfilled, The distress and ruin are like being struck by an arrow."

Regarding "that which is subject to contact": when the hand or other [limbs] touch it, the form (rūpa) undergoes transformation and decay; this is the sense of being "resistant" (sapratigha) and subject to transformation. Regarding "that which is subject to alteration":

just as the bodies of cattle, sheep, and so forth can be altered, this refers to the sense of being subject to transformation and exchange. It is called "transformation and decay" (vipariṇāma) because it is subject to such alteration.
In what sense can material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) be subject to transformation?
It is because they arise as different characteristics that they are said to undergo transformation.
Alternatively, they are called "form" (*rūpa*) because they can manifest past habitual karma, as stated in the Sūtra:
"O Māṇava! This refers to karma habitually practiced in previous lives that can bring about an unwholesome physical form, namely, excessive anger and resentment.
Or, because it can express what exists within the inner mind, it is called 'form' (rūpa), as stated in the Sūtra:"
"Venerable one!
Your faculties are now serene and joyful; you have surely realized the Deathless.

For does this not explain that the term 'form' (*rūpa*) is defined solely with respect to the category of sentient beings who possess views? It is because only this [category] can manifest the karma accumulated in the past and the internal mind."
If that were so, then non-sentient matter that is not visible would all fail to be "matter" (rūpa).
There is no such fault, because this definition applies only within the context of material aggregates; it does not mean that all forms of matter are capable of signifying.
Furthermore, since there is nothing capable of representation among all non-material aggregates, this etymological explanation is logically established, as the Sūtra says:
"Karma is the cause of birth."

This teaching states that all births are caused by karma, but it does not say that all karma is a cause of birth; therefore, one should not now object that because karma is not a cause of birth, it must therefore not be karma.
If it were not so, even the terminology of the Sugata could be challenged, for not all form (*rūpa*) is subject to transformation and decay.
The Blessed One spoke these words— “it is called form because it is subject to transformation and decay”— referring specifically to form that possesses resistance and obstruction (*sapratigha*).
Furthermore, he spoke thus:
"Who is it that undergoes transformation and decay?
It is through the touch of the hand that it immediately undergoes transformation and decay," and so on, as explained at length.
He further said:
"There is no evil karma that those who indulge in desire do not commit.

It is not that noble ones (*ārya*) do not indulge in desire at all, yet they ultimately do not perform actions that invite rebirth in the miserable realms (*apāya*); therefore, we know that such statements refer exclusively to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*)."
This should also be accepted as such and cannot be challenged.
Alternatively, all matter (*rūpa*) is capable of indicating past habitual karma, for even the matter of insentient beings is universally admitted to be the fruit of past karma.
How is "invisible form" (anidarśana-rūpa) indicated?
Because it is not separate from "visible form" (sanidarśana-rūpa); there is no visible form apart from the invisible.
Since visible and invisible forms share a single karmic fruit, by this means the meaning of the invisible is established through its indication.

Furthermore, it would follow as an error that non-sensory objects (*arūpa*) and so forth would also constitute matter (*rūpa*), because although they arise from karma, they do not exist constantly; even if they did exist constantly, they would be difficult to perceive due to their subtlety.

Since matter born of maturation (*vipākaja-rūpa*) does not arise immediately following volition (*cetanā*) and does not persist accordingly, only various forms of matter have the capacity to indicate past habitual karma.
If that were so, since sound is not produced as a result of maturation (*vipākaja*), it would follow that it is not matter (*rūpa*).
Although it is not produced by karma, it can nevertheless manifest karma previously cultivated, just as in the case of the examples cited, such as the *sāleyya* and others.

Furthermore, the cause for the arising of sound exists constantly even during the state of mindless meditative absorption (acittaka-samāpatti); therefore, there is no contradiction with the definition of matter (*rūpa*) as explained.
Some say: it is called matter because it is subject to transformation and resistance (*rūpaṇa*).
If that is so, how can atoms (paramāṇu) possess the quality of resistance?
No single atom exists in isolation in the present; rather, because they exist in an accumulated state, the meaning of resistance is established. Some say:

There are also atoms that exist in isolation; yet, although they possess resistance and obstruction (*bādhanā*), they do not give rise to consciousness, because the five consciousnesses require a collection [of atoms] as their support and object. This is just as when an atom is established: although it lacks spatial dimensions and lacks tactile contact, it is nevertheless admitted that the atom has the functional capacity for resistance (*sapratigha*), opposition (*sāntarāya*), and obstruction (*āvṛti*).

One should know that the meaning of "changeable and obstructive" (*rūpaṇa*) is likewise: because those [factors] that have already ceased or not yet arisen belong to that same category, they are like the "homogeneous eye" (*tatsabhāga-cakṣus*), which is like firewood that has been consumed.
Furthermore, it is as the world says:
one is called a "horse" because of galloping or running swiftly, yet this does not apply to all horses.
Although it lacks those specific qualities, because it resembles them, the meaning of "category" (jāti) is established.

It is merely by following a partial resemblance that a name and concept are established; this case is likewise. By this principle, one explains that even dharmas that will never arise are called "form" (rūpa) because they abide in the characteristic of form.

Furthermore, it is as when people in the world speak of what has not yet occurred as if it were already so, saying: "If fire were to suddenly break out now, it would burn down the village and its outskirts, leaving nothing remaining.

It is also like when people in the world speak retrospectively of what has already ceased, saying: "In the past, fire broke out and burned down the village and its outskirts, leaving nothing remaining."

It is not that those things which have not yet functioned or whose function has already ceased can actually burn; nevertheless, it is also logical to speak of them as such because they share the same characteristics.

The same principle should apply to dharmas that are definitely not destined to arise: even if they were to arise, they would likewise possess resistance (*pratighāta*). Therefore, the definition of *rūpa* (form) as "that which possesses resistance" is established.
Although this is so regarding the past and future, how is it with non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)?
One explanation states:
because informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) possesses resistance and obstruction, non-informative matter also receives the designation "matter" by following suit.
This is unreasonable; for matter that follows the mind (*cittānuvartin*) does not arise from informative action (*vijñapti*), as it would otherwise not be matter.

Here, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) erroneously establishes the opponent's position, stating: "Just as when a tree moves, its shadow also moves," thereby committing the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): "Just as when the tree ceases, the shadow must necessarily cease, so too when informative matter (*vijñaptirūpa*) ceases, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) should cease."
However, this is not analogous to that [example], because what is established is different.

That is to say, while it is established that the basis possesses resistance and therefore is also called "matter" (rūpa), when speaking of this example, it is stated that the basis of the unmanifest (avijñapti) is precisely the four great elements (mahābhūta).
It is not the case that the unmanifest (avijñapti) does not follow along when those primary elements (mahābhūta) are not fully accomplished; therefore, there is no such fault in this context.

Furthermore, the contrary [position] suffers from the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika), meaning it is not certain that this arises from that, or that when that ceases, this also necessarily ceases. For example, when a father, a craftsman, or a seed ceases, their son, a palace, or a sprout do not necessarily cease accordingly.

Furthermore, it is like the basis of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*): although that basis ceases and is no longer accomplished, the subsequently produced knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) continues to function until the cessation of the continuity of the aggregates.
It is also like the basis co-arising with the untainted (*anāsrava*): when one is born into a higher realm, although that basis has ceased, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) continues to function.

If that which is supported by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is called "form" (*rūpa*) because the primary elements possess resistance and transformation, then the five sense organs (*indriya*), which serve as the supports for the five consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness, should also be called "form," since they likewise possess resistance and transformation.
Some explain this as follows:
"There is no such fault.

When the unmanifest (avijñapti) evolves in dependence upon the primary elements (mahābhūta), it is like a shadow depending on a tree or light depending on a jewel; however, when the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, depend upon the eye and so forth, it is not thus, because [the sense organs] can only serve as auxiliary conditions for their arising."

The Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) states that this [comparison]—like the statement that a shadow depends on a tree or light depends on a jewel—is not intended to conform to the Vaibhāṣika doctrine, because it is accepted that the atoms of visible color (*varṇa-paramāṇu*) such as shadows each depend individually upon their own primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
This is not a statement from the *Vibhāṣā* of our own treatise, nor does it contradict the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*.
The intent of this statement is to say that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of shadows and so forth have the primary elements of trees and so forth as their support.
Why is this so? Because when the primary elements (mahābhūta) such as shadows arise, abide, and undergo transformation, they all follow those [elements].
This term "shadow-light" intends to express a collective aggregate and does not refer solely to visible color (varṇa), just as the terms "tree" or "jewel" do not refer to a single quality alone.

Therefore, the atoms of shadow-color and so forth arise depending upon the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the shadow and so forth; furthermore, the primary elements of the shadow and so forth arise depending upon the primary elements of the tree and so forth. Consequently, there is no inconsistency in this regard.
The Master of the Sūtras further states:

Even if one grants that shadows and light depend upon trees and jewels, the unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) is not like those [phenomena] in its dependence, because it is maintained that although the primary elements (mahābhūta) which serve as its basis may perish, the unmanifest form does not necessarily perish along with them.
This objection does not concern the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*, for it is accepted that both the supported and the support perish together.
If the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as the support for the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) should cease, the supported unmanifest never fails to cease as well.

The unmanifest (avijñapti) of the first moment may perish together with its basis, the primary elements (mahābhūta); but as for the unmanifest of the second moment and subsequent moments, how can it be?
If the primary elements of the second moment and so forth do not exist, how could that unmanifest matter (avijñaptirūpa) possibly exist in the present?
Although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are not absent within this state, those primary elements are not the support for this [mind], because they are not its generative cause.
How marvelous is such a thorough understanding of the Abhidharma!

Is it not the case that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are not only the generative causes (*janakahetu*) of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) and serve as its supports, but are also accepted as its supports by virtue of being four other types of causes?

If the unmanifest (avijñapti) that depends upon them were not to cease even after its supporting primary elements (mahābhūta) have ceased, then when an Ārya is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), the untainted (anāsrava) unmanifest would—since it is admitted to be possessed—necessarily manifest.
However, once the primary elements upon which it depends for both arising and subsistence have ceased, the untainted unmanifest, though still possessed, does not function.

Therefore, it is known that for those who practice the unmanifest (avijñapti) in the desire realm, it necessarily depends on the non-extinction of the primary elements (mahābhūta) upon which it relies. If this were not so, how could that be the case?
For this reason, all the masters have made this statement:
All derived matter has two kinds of bases: first, the basis of origination; second, the basis of functional transformation.

When a noble one is born in the formless realm, by virtue of the basis of functional transformation, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are absent; therefore, although the untainted unmanifest (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-avijñapti*) is still possessed, it does not manifest.
This confusion has arisen because they have not followed the masters of Abhidharma who provide unerring explanations.

However, although the five sense organs that serve as the bases for visual consciousness and the others possess the quality of transformation and resistance (*rūpaṇa*), they do not constitute "form" (*rūpa*) because their specific categories are distinct.

There are types of consciousness that do not depend upon form; only the five groups of sensory consciousness arise in dependence on form, whereas all six consciousnesses take the mind as their support, which is also obtainable within the formless realm.

Furthermore, in the lower realms, the functions of the mental faculty (manas) are observable in states such as sleep, dreaming, and meditative absorption, whereas the functions of the five sense faculties are not.
Moreover, it is logically untenable that the intrinsic nature of the six consciousnesses—being of a single category of phenomena—should be both material and non-material.

There is no non-manifest form (*avijñapti*) that does not arise in dependence upon matter; therefore, because its basis possesses resistance (*sapratigha*), the dependent non-manifest form may also be designated as "matter.
Furthermore, the term "matter" is established based on a partial classification, just as the names "ox" or "peacock" are applied.
It is not that there is no distinction; thus, one should not raise an objection.
Having explained the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the aggregates of sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Feeling has the nature of experiencing; perception has the nature of grasping images;

the four remaining aggregates are called the aggregate of formations. Thus, these three—feeling and the others—along with unmanifest form and the unconditioned, are termed the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) and the constituent of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
The treatise states:
That which arises in accordance with contact and experiences what is pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral contact is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
"Experiencing" has the meaning of being able to utilize [the object].
This, moreover, is of three kinds: namely, pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
That which benefits the body and mind is called pleasure; that which harms the body and mind is called pain; [and that which neither benefits nor harms is called neither-pain-nor-pleasure].
That which is experienced but is neither painful nor pleasant is called "neither-painful-nor-pleasant," just as something may be neither black nor white.
Furthermore, how is it known that this has a distinct substantial entity? Some say:

Because they perform three distinct functions—namely, increasing, decreasing, and being contrary to both—the faculties (*indriya*), the great elements (*mahābhūta*), and their associated factors—it is known that there are three distinct entities.
Alternatively, some say:
because they increase the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of greed, hatred, and delusion respectively, it is known that there are three distinct entities.
Although ignorance increases in accordance with all feelings, it is described according to its specific characteristics by way of its objects and its association.

Furthermore, although ignorance is associated with all three feelings while greed and hatred are each associated with two, this statement is made because they manifest most frequently through their respective associations.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this statement was made because [the afflictions] resemble the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of greed, hatred, and delusion. Other masters say:

When the Abhidharma states that greed increases (*anuśete*) within pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), it does not mean that pleasant feeling alone can give rise to greed; rather, it means that greed arises in accordance with pleasant feeling. It should be understood that the same applies to hatred and delusion in relation to the other two feelings.
To state the matter directly: based on both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*), one knows that the third feeling is certainly not non-existent.
As for scripture, it is as stated: "Because of the abandonment of pleasure and the abandonment of suffering, there remains herein only that which is neither painful nor pleasant."
As for the principle: a mind devoid of feeling (*vedanā*) necessarily does not arise, because a mind devoid of suffering and pleasure can be observed in the present.
How do we know that a mind devoid of feeling necessarily does not arise?
It is because it is so stated in all the sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact, which arises together with feeling, perception, and volition.
Thus, up to: with the mind and mental objects as conditions, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact, which arises together with feeling, perception, and volition."
Since the seventh consciousness does not arise apart from feeling, we know that a third type of feeling definitely exists.
Furthermore, it is taught that feelings are, in brief, of two kinds:
first, appropriating feeling (*upādāna-vedanā*); second, intrinsic feeling (*svabhāva-vedanā*).
Appropriating feeling refers to that which is able to experience its own respective object.
Feeling as intrinsic nature refers to that which is able to experience its own respective contact.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
There are contacts conducive to pleasant feeling, contacts conducive to painful feeling, and contacts conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
These refer to the meaning of contact as that which is experienced by pleasant feeling and the others.
It is difficult to discern the distinguishing characteristics between the feeling that experiences the object and the mental factors that share the same objective field, as stated in the Sūtra:
He fully experiences and receives it.
This term "experiencing and receiving" appears to be stated in reliance upon wisdom; therefore, that sutra further states immediately thereafter:
"I do not receive further existence; I know this as it truly is."

Although sensation (*vedanā*) is also able to experience objects, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is difficult to discern; therefore, sensation has contact (*sparśa*) as its experienced object as its own nature. This is its unique distinction, which is easily understood as being different from other [mental factors].

Thus, these various feelings (*vedanā*) and mental factors (*citta-dharma*), because they share the same object of cognition (*ālambana*) yet differ in their mode of experiencing (*anubhava*), have distinct objects of cognition and distinct objects of experience. Consequently, regarding contact (*sparśa*) and feeling: at the time when contact serves as that which is experienced by feeling, it is not the object of cognition;
at the time when it serves as the object of cognition, it is not that which is experienced. Therefore, the object of cognition and the object of experience are distinct.
By means of this, one thoroughly understands such textual passages:
"When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is that one is experiencing a pleasant feeling," and so forth, as explained at length.

The intended meaning here is that one is able to discern the distinctions between the three feelings through non-erroneous, investigative wisdom—recognizing what is not pleasant as suffering, what is not suffering as pleasant, and what is neither suffering nor pleasant as being distinct from both—and the same applies to the others.
In this context, feeling does not have the nature of being experienced as its own essence, because that is precisely what constitutes the nature of feeling itself.
Rather, it experiences the object of perception (*ālambana*) along with other phenomena, for everything is experienced by the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
There is an Āgama that can manifest this principle, as stated in the Sūtra:

"Conditioned by various elements (dhātu) arise various contacts (sparśa); conditioned by various contacts arise various sensations (vedanā); conditioned by various sensations arise various cravings (tṛṣṇā)."

Regarding "various realms" (*nānā-dhātu*): this refers to the fact that there are distinctions among the various natures and characteristics of the sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
Why, then, is it not stated that there are various feelings (*vedanā*) based on various realms?
Furthermore, why does it not say that various cravings arise conditioned by various realms?
This too is subject to the same doubt; therefore, both should be explained together.
It is the natural order of things (*dharmatā*) that they are established in this sequence, and thus there is no fault.

In the world, it is directly observed that when a subsequent fruit arises from a prior seed, there is a distinction in the fruit due to distinctions in the flower, milk, and so forth; thus, the fixed relationship between cause and effect is established through their successive production.

The relationship between simultaneous cause and effect should likewise be established as certain; therefore, although feelings (vedanā) also have the elements (dhātu) as their cause, they take contact (sparśa) as their proximate cause.

Just as fire is produced by the friction of two pieces of wood with wind acting as the proximate condition, so too, when these three factors combine to produce feeling, contact serves as the proximate condition.

Therefore, it is established by reason that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of feeling (*vedanā*) consists in the experiencing of contact (*sparśa*), rather than the experiencing of an object (*ālambana*).
This feeling is generally categorized as threefold according to its temporal periods, and is specifically divided into six types based on the support (*āśraya*) of contact.
The aggregate of feeling has already been explained.

The third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), has the apprehension of images as its essence. That is to say, with respect to all objects of cognition—such as forms established according to their original nature as blue or long; sounds such as those of lutes or conch shells; odors such as those of lotuses; tastes such as bitter or pungent; tangibles such as smooth or rough; and phenomena such as arising and ceasing—it apprehends them according to their respective characteristics. Therefore, it is called perception.
Therefore, this aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is named according to its specific qualities; it is called "perception" because it is able to apprehend mental images (nimitta).
Its general and particular categories—three, six, and three respectively—should be understood in the same manner as those of feeling (vedanā).
The aggregate of perception has now been explained.

The fourth aggregate is that of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It consists of the remaining four types of formations; that is, with the exception of the three previously mentioned—form, feeling, and perception—and excluding consciousness, which will be discussed as the fourth, all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are called the aggregate of formations.
These are associated and dissociated, such as volition (*cetanā*) and acquisition (*prāpti*), respectively.
The *Sūtra* speaks only of the "six groups of volition" because of their preeminence.
Why is this so? Volition is the nature of karma;
as the cause that brings about its fruit, its power is the strongest. Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"That which can create outflows and conditioned phenomena is called the aggregate of formations and grasping."

If it is claimed that only these [mental factors] are called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), this is logically untenable; for since other formations such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are not included therein, they would consequently not be subsumed under any aggregate.
If one asks what fault lies in this, it would follow that there could be no knowledge of or abandonment of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
If that were so, what fault would there be?
It would contradict the holy teaching.
As the Blessed One said:
If one has not attained or known even a single dharma, I say that one cannot bring an end to suffering; the same applies to what has not been abandoned or extinguished.

If it is argued that other formations—such as space and non-analytical cessation—are free from this fault, that is also logically untenable, because they serve to increase the grasping at a self, and the grasping at a self is capable of obstructing the dharma that brings about the exhaustion of suffering.
That Elder says: "The aggregate of formations consists solely of volition; other factors such as attention (*manasikāra*) are merely specific varieties of volition.
He further states:
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) and the other formations cannot be separated from volition (*cetanā*), nor can a distinct substance of volition be found apart from these other formations.

Therefore, although this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is not a single entity, it is subsumed under the single factor of volition; thus, although the Sūtra mentions only volition, it does not contradict reason.
Furthermore, how is it known that all formations such as attention (*manasikāra*) have volition (*cetanā*) as their essential nature?

Because the Blessed One stated in the sūtras that the six groups of volition constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), and because he designated craving, hatred, and so forth as mental action (*manaskarman*).
The karma that is neither black nor white and has no ripening fruit is that which can exhaust all karma; this is because the Noble Path is described here by the term "volition" (*cetanā*).

Furthermore, since the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are described as "white-white ripening karma," it would be incorrect to describe a distinct phenomenon using a different name. Moreover, it is not the case that stating "one is one" constitutes an erroneous statement.
The Blessed Ones never speak erroneously;
although the doctrine of the Sthaviras is stated in this way, it is not logically tenable, for what is established earlier and later is mutually contradictory.

It is said that while it was previously stated that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists solely of volition (*cetanā*), it was later stated that the aggregate of formations is not a single entity.
How can a single volition be anything other than a single entity?
For it is taught that the aggregate of formations consists exclusively of the six types of volition.
The claim that the essence of attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth is volition (*cetanā*) is logically untenable, because the manner in which the Dharma is taught varies.

It is observed in the sūtras that the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dharma exhibits various differences: sometimes he mentions the first [term] to include the subsequent ones; sometimes he mentions the last to include the first; sometimes he mentions both the first and the last to include those in between; and sometimes he mentions the middle to include both the first and the last.
In which sūtras is the first mentioned as a means of including the subsequent?

These include the sūtras on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), nutriment (*āhāra*), *gopālakas*, the dharmas of non-falling back (*avinipātadharman*), and the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).
Dhyāna consists of the four meditative concentrations (samādhi) cultivated through practice.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"If one cultivates the first dhyāna, one attains abiding in happiness in the present life."

It is not that others cannot attain abiding in happiness in the present life; rather, this statement is made by citing the first to include the subsequent. Thus, there is no deficiency in what the Tathāgata has taught.
Regarding "food," it is said in the *Caturāhāra-sūtra*:
"The first is material food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), which is both coarse and subtle."
It is not that the other three nutriments lack the distinction between coarse and subtle; rather, this statement is made by citing the first to include the subsequent ones.
Regarding "Gopālaka," it refers to what that sutra says: one does not fully understand form, but not the other four aggregates.
Having already understood this, [the author] makes this statement by citing the first instance to include the subsequent ones.
Regarding the "dharmas of non-retrogression," that sutra states:
"A person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry does not fall into the evil destinies."
It is not that other noble ones fall into the evil destinies; rather, this statement is made by mentioning the first to include the subsequent.
Regarding the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), it is said in that sūtra that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the truth of origination.
It is not that other defiled phenomena are not included within the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); rather, this statement is made by citing the first to encompass the subsequent ones.
This will be demonstrated separately during the investigation of the Truths.
All such immeasurable sūtras cite the initial member to include those that follow; therefore, there is no deficiency in what the Tathāgata has taught.
In which sūtras is the latter mentioned as including the former?
They are the sūtras concerning the acquisition of self-existence (*ātmabhāvapratilambha*), the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), and the praise of fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Regarding the acquisition of self-existence, it is said in the *Catuḥpratilambha-sūtra*:
Those born in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception cannot harm themselves nor can others harm them.
This applies to all gods of the form and formless realms who cannot harm themselves nor can others harm them; this statement is made by mentioning the last to include the first.
Regarding the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the *Saptavijñānasthiti-sūtra* states as follows:
"There are sentient beings with form who are uniform in body but diverse in perception, such as the Ābhāsvara devas; this is the third station of consciousness."

It is not that the Parīttābha and Apramāṇābha heavens do not also possess "a single perception despite having different bodies"; rather, this statement is made by citing the latter to include the former.
Regarding the praise of the field of merit, that sutra says:
"If one constantly cultivates the merit of sublime giving toward an Arhat..."
"Constantly for all the devas, they offer praise and present auspicious omens.

This does not mean that those who previously practiced the merit of sublime giving did not receive the praise and presentation of auspiciousness by the devas and others; rather, this statement is made by citing the latter to encompass the former.

If it is claimed that the first three [types of noble ones] may also be called *arhat* because they are worthy of offerings, then this sūtra would not be of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), for the name *arhat* primarily refers to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
In which sūtras are the intermediate sections subsumed by citing only the beginning and the end?
These refer to sūtras such as those praising renunciation and those on the clear realizations (*avetyaprasāda*).
Regarding the praise of renunciation, that sūtra states:

“Those who have gone forth from the household life and are able to realize the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) as well as the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*), these are said to have accomplished much.

It is not that those who have not gone forth from the household life realizing the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*) and the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*) do not accomplish much; rather, this statement is made by citing the beginning and the end to encompass what lies between.
Regarding the praise of verified purity (*avetyaprasāda*),
that sutra states: "Those who, toward the Tathāgata, Abide in sublime, unshakable faith,
And possess pure and virtuous ethical discipline, Shall always encounter auspicious fortune."

It is not that one who dwells with unwavering faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha fails to encounter auspiciousness; rather, this statement is made by citing the beginning and the end to encompass what lies in between.
In which sūtras, then, is the middle cited to encompass both the beginning and the end?
As the Sūtra states:
"If one cultivates the fourth dhyāna, it is called the attainment of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
It is not that all seven bases are incapable of exhausting the outflows; rather, this statement is made by citing the middle term to encompass both the beginning and the end.
In all such immeasurable sūtras, the middle is cited to encompass both the beginning and the end; therefore, there is no deficiency in what the Tathāgata has taught.
As it is with all sūtras, so it should be with this one as well.
Although the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is a collection of many factors, there is no fault in mentioning only the first one, volition (*cetanā*).

Why is it that, at the outset, attention (*manasikāra*) and other such formative forces of conditioned phenomena are not mentioned? It is because volition is the most preeminent, just as the mind is able to lead, just as the three bases must be present, and just as the two types of cultivation are practiced.
Regarding the mind’s capacity to lead, as the sūtra says:
"The mind leads the world.
While it is not that factors such as feeling and perception do not exist therein, this statement is made because the mind is preeminent.
Three bases manifest; as the Sūtra says:
"Because faith manifests toward three bases, one can generate much merit.
This does not mean that factors such as non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view are absent therein; rather, because faith is predominant, it is described in this way.
Regarding the cultivation of two dharmas, as stated in the sūtras:
"Two dharmas should be cultivated, namely śamatha and vipaśyanā.
All wholesome conditioned dharmas should be cultivated; however, because śamatha and vipaśyanā are preeminent, they are spoken of in this way.
In these and other such sūtras, the most excellent dharmas are invariably presented at the beginning; this case should be understood in the same way.

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has left many teachings that are incomplete in various places, such as those concerning stūpas, the destinations of the virtuous, the liberation of the mind, and the severance of fetters.
Regarding the stūpa, as stated in the sūtras:
"A stūpa should be erected for three types of persons.
By this principle, it should not be that a stūpa is erected for an ordinary worldling (pṛthagjana).
For one who has not yet seen the truths, it should be understood that this sutra is a teaching with further implications (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).
Regarding the "destinations of the noble person" (*satpuruṣagati*), as stated in the *Sūtra*:
there are seven destinations of the noble person, namely, those who proceed toward the fruit of arhatship, which is nirvāṇa.
It should be understood that this sutra is an incomplete teaching (*sāvasesa-vacana*), for other noble ones are not born into the destinies of non-noble persons.
Regarding "liberation of mind," as stated in the Sūtra:
"Having attained arhatship, his mind is liberated from the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*)."
However, in reality, one is liberated from all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); it should be understood that this sūtra is an incomplete statement (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).
Regarding the "severing of fetters," the sūtras state:
"By permanently severing the three fetters, one realizes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*)."

It should be understood that this sutra is a statement made with intentional brevity (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*), for it does not mean that all afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya-kleśa*) have not been permanently severed.
Sūtras such as these speak in terms of what is predominant; this case is likewise so, because the functional capacity (*kāritra*) for producing conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is predominant.
Why is it said that these [factors] can create conditioned phenomena?
It is because they possess the superior capacity to project and produce effects.
Although the effect exists primordially, it is produced only in part; since these factors can accordingly project it, they are established as "creators."
That Elder said: "To create conditioned phenomena means that volition (*cetanā*) is able to create conditioned phenomena that previously did not exist.
It is like the weaver who says:"
"I take these threads and weave them into garments;
this too should be so.
Such an assertion is necessarily illogical, because there is a difference between that which has a basis and that which lacks a basis.
His intention is that volition (*cetanā*) is like a weaver, while conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are like garments; however, there is no analogy for the threads upon which those garments depend.
If one were to admit that future conditioned entities possess even a slight degree of functional efficacy, then the meaning of "creation" would be established.
The Elder [Vasumitra] uses the analogy of a thread to demonstrate that the future exists; however, this established analogy may be verbally sound but devoid of meaning.
The masters of the Abhidharma state that for a phenomenon existing as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*), which was previously non-existent and now exists, this analogy is appropriate;
if one maintains that even a substantial entity (*dravyasat*) was previously non-existent, then such an analogy certainly should not be established.

Furthermore, they should explain the distinct characteristics of the conventional and the real; if there were a difference, there would be no analogy, and if there were no difference, it would be like a flower in the sky.

To claim that desire, hatred, and so forth are mental karma (*manas-karman*)—and thereby to know that volition (*cetanā*), such as attention (*manasikāra*), constitutes its essence—is also logically untenable.

Although the essence of greed, hatred, and wrong view is not itself karma, they are also called karma because they are the provisions for karma; just as other provisions are also designated by the names of those [provisions] themselves.
As the Sīla-sūtra says:
"The sight of the noble ones is joy; the river steps are joy."
Because it is the provision for happiness, it is also called "happiness.
Furthermore, as stated in the Sūtra:
"If the faculty of the eye is neither disciplined nor guarded, this factor will bring about an undesirable maturation."

Although the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is itself a dharma that does not possess maturation (*avipāka*), because it serves as the requisite for unwholesome maturation, it is also said to be able to induce undesirable maturation.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:
"The five factors of decline, such as fondness for idle talk (*abhilāpa-prasaṅga*)."
The actual factors of decline refer to the various afflictions (*kleśa*), because they lead to the decline of the fruits [of practice].
Discursive talk and the like are their provisions, and are thus also called factors of decline.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:
“Fools, attached to desire, give rise to strife; the sages are without strife because they have abandoned desire.
Therefore, one should eliminate all desire and wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.”
"By being attached to sensory objects, various conflicts arise; though the objects themselves are not desire, they are called 'desire' because they are the provisions for desire.
Therefore, a sutra says:
'The wonderful objects of the world are not true desire; true desire is the greed of human conceptualization.'"
Furthermore, as stated in the Sūtra:
"The latent tendencies increase with respect to form.
Form itself is not a latent tendency; rather, it is the provision (*sambhāra*) for them, and thus it is described in the same manner as they.
Furthermore, as it is said in a sutra:
"Women are the defilement of the holy life; women afflict and harm sentient beings.
In reality, women are not the defilement; rather, it is greed and so forth that are the defilements. Because they serve as the provisions for those defilements, women are also called "defilement."

Furthermore, while the sūtras proclaim seven outflows (*āsrava*), in reality there are only two; the others are not themselves outflows, but are called "outflows" because they are the provisions for the outflows.

By such sūtras as these, it is logically established that greed, hatred, and so forth are called "mental action" (*manas-karman*) because they are the provisions for mental action, rather than being the substance of the action itself.

It is not correct to claim that the action which is neither black nor white and has no ripening (avipāka) is able to exhaust all karma because it is designated by the name "volition" (cetanā), as this refers to the Noble Path;
nor is it reasonable to maintain that the nature of attention (manasikāra) and so forth consists of volition, for there is no such fault in applying names such as "perception" (saṃjñā) to these.
As a sutra states:
"Cultivating the perception of impermanence can eliminate craving for sense-desires, as well as craving for the realms of form and formlessness.
Therein, the term "perception" (*saṃjñā*) is used to designate the various noble paths (*āryamārga*).
Since it is already admitted that the Noble Path is not a differentiation of perception (*saṃjñā*), this case should be understood in the same way; thus, there is no fault.
Furthermore, it is said that the mind associated with feeling (*vedanā*) can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, a Sūtra states:
"By cultivating the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*), one relies on a mind free from greed to destroy the nest."
Since the Noble Path is not a distinction within the category of feeling, this case should likewise be understood as such; thus, there is no error.
Some, having heard the Sūtra state that "karma binds sentient beings," claim that all karma is capable of binding.
In order to dispel such perverse attachments, it is said that this karma of volition (*cetanā-karman*) can exhaust all [other] karmas.

Furthermore, this statement is made to manifest the superiority of this karma; for the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are described as "white-with-white-ripening" (*śukla-śuklavipāka*) karma.

Regarding the claim that the nature of *manasikāra* (attention) and so forth is volition (*cetanā*), this is not correct, because it does not investigate the fact that the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth have the five aggregates or four aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
As the Sūtra says:
"Whatever therein is form or feeling," and so on at length, "up to what is called the meditative absorption."

For the Dārṣṭāntikas, karma does not possess the nature of matter; rather, because they wish to show that among all karmas, those that induce maturation have the strongest power, they describe all wholesome phenomena consisting of the five aggregates as "karma" in this context.
Furthermore, just as feeling, perception, and consciousness are here described as "karma" despite their essence not being volition (*cetanā*),
so too should mental attention (*manasikāra*) and other such factors be described as "karma," even though their essence is not volition.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates are subsumed under distinct aggregates, this would establish that what is obtained is being described by a different name for a different phenomenon.

Once this is established, the argument stated above—that greed, hatred, and so forth are called "mental action" (*manas-karman*) and are therefore identical to volition (*cetanā*)—is logically untenable.
It is directly perceived and established that distinct entities such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth are designated by the name "action" (*karman*); the same should apply to others.
By this, the reason stated subsequently is refuted, for it is not the case that distinct phenomena must be designated by distinct names.
Furthermore, one observes that different names are used to describe different phenomena;

for example, it is said that "one who is able to practice gives gifts such as incense. The essence of giving is volition (*cetanā*), not the incense itself.
