However, because volition is awakened by means of incense and other such objects, different names are used to describe different phenomena. It is not the case that stating one thing is the same as another constitutes erroneous speech; for the Blessed Ones (*bhagavat*) never utter erroneous words.

The claim that the essence of *manasikāra* (attention) and so forth is volition (*cetanā*) is also logically untenable. This is because [the teaching] is stated according to what is predominant; because the relationship between names and their referents is not fixed; because the inclinations of the sentient beings to be converted differ; and because sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) are actually extant. It is not that the Blessed One spoke these words erroneously.

If the essence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) were established as being merely volition (*cetanā*), it would reveal that the Blessed One’s statement is erroneous; for one would have to admit that the Blessed One asserts a single dharma-essence to be multiple, and conversely, asserts what is not a single essence to be one.
If it is said that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is not composed of a single entity, this demonstrates that the Blessed One’s words are free from error.
Therefore, that [opponent's] reason has words but lacks logic.

Furthermore, what they have established contradicts inference (*anumāna*); namely, that the essence of the aggregate of formations is not merely volition (*cetanā*), because it is established as a general designation, just like the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) or the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
If it were otherwise, it should be designated merely as "name" (*nāman*), because it would constitute a single dharma, just like the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).

The intention here is to show that, just as the sixth category—the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)—is established as a collective designation, it subsumes eleven bases (*āyatana*) and seventeen elements (*dhātu*) without including multiple individual dharmas.

Since the term "formations" (*saṃskāra*) is established as a general designation, it subsumes the four aggregates but does not subsume all formations; therefore, one knows that the essence of the aggregate of formations is not merely volition (*cetanā*).

If that were so, it should have been mentioned last, like those [other aggregates]. This will be demonstrated in its proper sequence among the mental factors (*caitasika*); since it would not be convenient here in the text, let us leave it for now.

Furthermore, because the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is illustrated by the metaphor of the plantain tree, one knows that the essence of the aggregate of formations is not merely volition (*cetanā*).
As it is said that the aggregate of formations is like a plantain tree, this demonstrates that the essence of the aggregate of formations is composed of many constituent factors.

Furthermore, because the sūtras speak of "conjunction" (*samprayoga*), one knows that the essential nature of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is not merely volition (*cetanā*). As a sūtra states:
"Vision is associated with the faculties of faith, realization, and wisdom."
If faith and wisdom were both identical to volition (*cetanā*), then the essence of volition would be associated with itself;
however, it is logically untenable to admit that a thing is associated with its own self-nature.

Furthermore, mental attention (*manasikāra*) and the other [mental factors] should not be considered mere distinctions of volition, because in the sūtras, volition is mentioned separately from mental attention and the rest.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"He perceives thus, and he intends thus.
If that wrong view were identical to intention (*cetanā*), then this point should be stated as follows:
When one thinks in such a way, one thinks accordingly; or when one sees in such a way, one sees accordingly.
If one were to speak thus, what difference would there be in meaning?
Furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra:
He possesses such faith, aspiration, diligence, pliancy, mindfulness, wisdom, volition, and equanimity; these are called "superior practices" (*viśeṣa-carita*).
If volition were identical to the practices such as faith, then having already mentioned faith and the others, why would volition be mentioned again?
Furthermore, since these various factors appear to function simultaneously, how can multiple entities arise from a single volition (*cetanā*)?
Regarding this, the Sthavira offers the following explanation:
"In order to include the other formations (*saṃskāra*) that arise at this time, he mentions volition once again."
The faith and other qualities mentioned previously were taught to manifest the superior practices arising at this stage, such as the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and the four modes of practice.
This means that although "view" among the five corruptions is itself an affliction, it is mentioned separately once again because of its preeminence.
Regarding the four types of practitioners, as stated in the Sūtra:
"One cultivates the sublime conduct and right view of body, speech, and mind, and abandons the evil conduct and wrong view of body, speech, and mind.

It is not that right and wrong views are not subsumed under the sublime or evil conduct of the mind; rather, they are mentioned separately because they are preeminent. This [case] should be understood in the same way.
This is logically untenable; for faith and the other [faculties] should also be subsumed under volition (*cetanā*), and thus should not be mentioned separately.
But was it not already stated that faith and the others are mentioned to show the superior practices (*viśeṣa-caryā*) arising at this time?

Although it has already been stated, this is nonetheless unreasonable: for a single dharma to arise simultaneously with multiple entities, such as feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā), is illogical.

Because it is illogical, it is not the case that within the single category of a dharma such as feeling, distinct types like pleasure or smallness can arise simultaneously. Therefore, that explanation does not belong to the tenets of the Buddha’s teaching.
Furthermore, if one were not to direct the mind toward those respective points, what is taught in various sūtras would be incomplete.
As the Blessed One said:
"The training, the untrained, and the śaikṣa and aśaikṣa [disciples] possess morality, concentration, wisdom, and liberation."
Since this sūtra does not mention "volition" (cetanā), it would follow that other factors such as "attention" (manasikāra) are omitted;
if you argue that the listener already knows them, then the mention of "wisdom" (prajñā) and so forth would likewise be useless.
Therefore, that explanation is certainly untenable; the analogy is also irrational because those held by various views are difficult to liberate.
To demonstrate that the bondage of various views is firm and strong, the faults are explained both collectively and individually in relation to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Among the unwholesome mental actions, wrong view is the most grave; to demonstrate that it surpasses greed and hatred, it is logically necessary to explain its abandonment through both general and specific antidotes.
Since volition is not seen to have a superior function over faith and the other faculties, for what reason is this volition explained both generally and specifically?
Therefore, that analogy does not correspond to the principle [it illustrates].
As previously refuted,

if one maintains that volition (*cetanā*) has faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the reasoning for explaining volition and faith, etc., both collectively and individually, cannot be established.

The analogy he establishes for "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is extremely dissimilar; it is not the case that all afflictions and all unwholesome mental actions have "view" as their essential nature (*svabhāva*). How, then, can one take the fact that "view" is spoken of both collectively and individually as a precedent to claim that "volition" (*cetanā*) should likewise be spoken of collectively and individually?

Furthermore, even if it were granted that those factors such as attention (*manasikāra*) are all of the nature of volition (*cetanā*), the volition established here is not the same as wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). It is established within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-sphere (*dharmāyatana*), as either a predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) or an efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), consisting of analytical wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyāprajñā*) and the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is because, apart from attention and so forth, there is no other significant volition [of this kind].
Furthermore, what is the purpose of this specific explanation within the sutra? As the sutra states:

"If there is that which is felt, there is that which is perceived; if there is that which is perceived, there is that which is conceptualized; if there is that which is conceptualized, there is that which is sought."
Since that school admits that *vitarka* (initial inquiry) is itself *cetanā* (volition), they cite *vitarka* as the vehicle.
To this, the Sthavira says:
"This sutra does not refer to a vehicle."

If one does not posit vitarka (applied thought), then doubt and cetanā (volition) would be identical to manasikāra (attention) and chanda (desire); this should not be doubted, because their characteristics are different.
[Objection: If their substance is indeed cetanā, how can their characteristics be different?
If that were so, the mention of *vitarka* (applied thought) would be useless, because they maintain that its characteristic is identical [to that of *cetanā*].
Furthermore, since you already admit that *manasikāra* (attention) and the like are simply *cetanā*, what fault is there in suspecting that *cetanā* is likewise identical to them?
Therefore, those words are entirely devoid of meaning.

Furthermore, regarding their claim that mental factors such as attention (*manasikāra*) cannot be known apart from thought (*citta*) and thus do not exist separately: one should diligently seek the knowledge of their separate existence. How can one allow that because they are not perceived, attention and the other factors must all lack a nature distinct from the essence of thought?

Furthermore, as you repeatedly state that perception (*saṃjñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) proceed in dependence upon formations (*saṃskāra*) and conditions (*pratyaya*) in a manner that is similar, even though you cannot demonstrate the distinction between their two characteristics, your own school nevertheless admits that their substance (*svabhāva*) is distinct from volition (*cetanā*), attention (*manasikāra*), and so forth. It should be the same in this case: even if you do not know what their substance is, how does that prevent it from being distinct?
If the essence of attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth were distinct from volition (*cetanā*), why would no sūtra state them as belonging to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*)?

Since they are also called "formations," their inclusion in the aggregates is already established by that designation; for instance, when *vitarka* and *vicāra* are mentioned, it is said that "formations" are being mentioned; when faith, desire, and so forth are mentioned, it is said that "predominant formations" (*adhipatisaṃskāra*) are being mentioned; and when the various life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*) are mentioned, it is said that "vital formations" (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*) are being mentioned.
It is not that the essential nature of these factors is not subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), for they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), just like form (*rūpa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).

No sūtra states that they are subsumed under any other aggregate; yet, since there are sūtras that state they are "formations" (*saṃskāra*), how could one of sharp faculties claim they are not included in the aggregate of formations?
Furthermore, although other causes for future existence apart from craving are said to be "origination," they are not called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Yet you should not admit that they are not subsumed under the [Four] Truths, for all phenomena consisting of cause and effect are subsumed within the Truths.
The same should apply to mental attention (*manasikāra*) and other formations; although they are called "formations," they are not designated as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Yet you should not admit that they are not included within the aggregates, for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are subsumed under the aggregates.

The Blessed One, for the sake of excellence, spoke only of volition (*cetanā*), yet this does not mean that other factors such as attention (*manasikāra*) are not included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Furthermore, it should not be said that the Blessed One speaks with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) when there is no underlying reason.

The other factors apart from volition (*cetanā*) that are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) have already been discussed previously; their logical establishment is absolute. Is this not, then, a case of the Buddha’s intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*)?

Furthermore, while it is logically real that there are other factors besides volition included within the aggregate of formations, why is only volition mentioned? What is the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) here?
If there were no underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*), one would be slandering the Blessed One by claiming that he does not act in accordance with wisdom;
if there is an underlying intention, then the basis for the Buddha’s cryptic speech is established of its own accord.
Therefore, it is well-established in meaning that the four remaining types of formations are called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), as this accords with both reason and scripture.
Thus, because this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) does not exhaust all bases of existence, it is described in its entirety as being of three types according to the [three] time periods.
Just as the essence of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) was previously analyzed, it is then established by way of the two doors of the bases (*āyatana*) and the elements (*dhātu*).
Having thus explained the essential nature of the three aggregates—feeling, perception, and formations—they should likewise be established as bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).

That is to say, these three aggregates, along with non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and the three types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), constitute seven dharmas which, within the classification of bases, are established as the *dharmāyatana*, and within the classification of elements, are established as the *dharmadhātu*.
*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Two.
*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Three.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Chapter Three: The Third Part of the First Chapter on the Exposition of the Fundamental Entities. Having already explained the intrinsic nature, bases, and elements of the four aggregates.
The fifth aggregate, consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), as well as its nature, bases, and elements, shall now be elucidated.
The verse says:
"Consciousness is the individual discernment [of objects]; this is also called the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*)."
And it should be understood that there are seven elements; the six consciousnesses, when they transform, become the mind-element (*manas*).
The treatise says:
"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to discernment (*vijñapti*), which means the general grasping of the characteristics of an object.
Each [consciousness] grasps the specific characteristics of its respective object; this is called "individual discernment.

This means that although many objects such as form and so forth may appear before the visual consciousness, it grasps only form and not sound or other objects; it grasps only blue and so forth, and not what is designated as "blue" and so on; nor does it grasp what is agreeable or disagreeable, nor male or female, nor a person or a tree stump, nor gain or loss, and so forth.
Just as that visual consciousness apprehends only the general characteristics of its own object, so too should the other consciousnesses be understood accordingly.
Other masters say:
"Whoever metaphorically designates an 'agent' with respect to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does so in order to preclude the notion that there is a cognizer existing apart from consciousness."
Furthermore, where else can one see that the "agent" is merely a conventional designation applied to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)?
For we observe that a shadow is said to be "moving"; even though it lacks actual motion, it is said to move when it arises in successive locations without interruption.

Consciousness is also like this: when it arises in a continuous succession across different objects, although there is no physical movement, it is nonetheless said to "cognize" because it is capable of apprehending its object; thus, there is no fault.
How is this known to be so?
Because it is observed elsewhere that the existence of an agent is denied.
As the Blessed One told Potaliputra:
I never say that there is one who can fully comprehend it.
Furthermore, some say:
"The momentary [dharma] is called the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the continuity is called the agent."
That which is established by my own intention shall be further demonstrated within the discussion on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This consciousness is generally described as threefold according to its temporal periods, and is divided into six types based on its respective supporting faculties (*indriya*).

It should be understood that this very aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) mentioned above is established as the sense-base of mind (mana-āyatana) within the system of bases (āyatana-mukha), and as seven elements (dhātu) within the system of elements (dhātu-mukha).
The word "and" (ca) indicates that what was originally one is analyzed into two systems, thereby defining the distinct bases and elements of each individual consciousness.
What are the seven elements?
They are the six consciousnesses and the mind, namely, from the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element.

These very six consciousnesses, when they transition, become the mind-element (*manodhātu*). One should understand that this distinct establishment of the categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) exhaustively encompasses all phenomena without exception.
In this regard, one should reflect:

if the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is precisely what is called the seven mind-elements (*manodhātu*), and it was previously stated that the aggregate of consciousness is divided into six based on its respective supporting faculties (*indriya*),
then apart from these six consciousnesses, what dharma is now designated as the mind-element?
There is no other dharma;
within this very context, the verse says:
"By means of the six groups of consciousness themselves, that which has ceased without interval constitutes the mind (manas)."
The treatise states:
It is precisely because the six groups of consciousness, having ceased without interval, can give rise to subsequent consciousness that they are called the "mental element" (*manodhātu*).
Since there is a difference in temporal phase, there is no fault in establishing it as distinct.
Just as a fruit is established as the seed of its father, if that were so,
the essence of the *dhātus* would consist of only seventeen or only twelve, because they mutually subsume one another.
For what reason, then, are eighteen *dhātus* established?
The verse says:
Because it establishes the basis for the sixth [consciousness], the eighteen elements (dhātus) should be known.
The commentary says:
Just as the five consciousness-elements have the five distinct elements of the eye and so forth as their supports, the sixth mental consciousness has no separate support.
Just as consciousness cannot arise apart from its object, it is likewise the case that apart from its support, consciousness cannot be produced.
To establish this basis, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is taught.
Thus, one should know that there are six each of bases, supported faculties, and objects, whereby the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) are formed.
How can that which has already ceased be called the basis for present consciousness?
This manifest consciousness arises due to its proximity to conditions.
Just as visual consciousness arises only by depending on the eye despite the presence of visible forms,
so too does this consciousness arise only after depending on the immediately preceding thought that has just ceased— the manas— despite the existence of the objective realm.

Therefore, the aforementioned term "immediately preceding cessation" is intended to exclude the mind that ceases with an interval; for although one previously heard of [the teaching] and avoided it, [the subsequent cognition] had not yet arisen.
Consequently, the six consciousnesses that have already ceased without interval serve as the support for the present consciousness and are thus designated as the *manodhātu* (mind-element).

Alternatively, while the present consciousness is currently functioning as its support (*āśraya*), the past [consciousness] has already become an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), for it is also capable of taking up its fruit in the present.

Although [the present mind] arises in dependence upon that [past mind], it does not conform to it; therefore, a mind is not called a mental factor (*caitta*) in relation to another mind, because the categories of mental factors necessarily conform to the mind.

Having already explained the aggregates (*skandha*), the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*), one should now investigate their inclusive meaning within this context:

the aggregates collectively encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); the aggregates of clinging encompass only all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*); and the bases and elements collectively encompass all phenomena (*dharma*) without exception.
The five aggregates and the unconditioned are called "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*).
Having thus distinguished their individual inclusion, one should now analyze their collective inclusion.
The verse says:
All phenomena are subsumed by a single aggregate, sense-base, and element;
they are subsumed by their own nature and not by others, because they are devoid of other-natures.
The Commentary says:
One aggregate is form; one base is the mind; one element is phenomena. These three collectively subsume the five aggregates and the unconditioned.
"Collectively" (tong) has the sense of "gathering" (ji).
The general statement is made so that one may understand there are three categories in total, rather than assuming there is only one for each.
Other schools maintain that "inclusion" (saṃgraha) means including others, because it is stated in various places that "the remainder includes the remainder."

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the three aggregates subsume the eightfold noble path: if they were to subsume by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*) would subsume only right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and not right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) or right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*);
the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*) would subsume only right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), and would not subsume right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*).
Since it is not stated thus in the sūtras, one might conclude that all dharmas are comprised solely of the nature of others.
This position is incorrect, as there is no definitive reason for it.

If they were comprised of the nature of others, by what cause would it be determined that the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*) comprises only right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) and right effort (*samyak-vīrya*), but does not comprise right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), or any other factors?

If it is argued that this inclusion also has a fixed cause—namely, right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) and right effort (*samyak-vīrya*)—then their nature is fierce and sharp, which involves the factors of wisdom (*prajñā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and concentration (*samādhi*);
yet, the characteristic of wisdom is incompatible [with them], and mindfulness involves the characteristic of concentration, not thought and the others.

If that were so, it would follow that [the category] contains only its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because you do not admit that it contains phenomena with different characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*).

Since there are no phenomena whatsoever that do not possess different characteristics when compared to one another, if you were to admit that they contain one another based on even a partial similarity of characteristics, you would have to admit that every phenomenon contains all phenomena.
Is it not the case that while a factor may be associated with another nature, it is not associated with every other nature?
Likewise, one must admit that while a factor may be subsumed by another nature, it is not subsumed by every other nature.

This should not be taken as an analogy. For that which is associated (*saṃprayukta*) consists solely of dharmas with objects (*sālambana*); they exist in relation to one another as distinct entities, yet they function together upon a single object, sharing the same time, basis, mental aspect (*ākāra*), and category. This is what is meant by "association," and therefore it does not apply to all [dharmas].
Regarding their mutual inclusion, this applies to all phenomena; what fixed cause is there such that this includes only those and not other phenomena?
Therefore, it should follow that everything includes all phenomena.

When various material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are compared with one another, there is not a single instance where they lack the sense of mutual similarity through shared conditions; however, this is not the case for their mutual inclusion (*saṃgraha*).
If [the sense bases] were to include the nature of others, why would the eye and so forth not include the ear and so forth?
The same would apply to their mutual relations, such as acquisition (*prāpti*) and the like.
If that were so, for what reason does the Sūtra state this:

In this context, they are metaphorically described as being "comprised" because they are mutually concordant; that is to say, right thought and right effort both belong to the category of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), as they are concordant with right view;
and mindfulness belongs to the category of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), as it is concordant with right concentration.
This is a metaphorical designation for inclusion (*saṃgraha*).

If that is so, then as it is said in various sūtras: "The five faculties, such as faith, are included within the faculty of wisdom"; "I gather my followers through the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*"); and "the central pillar of a pavilion includes all the other building materials."
The world also speaks of "gathering" in such cases as: a pair of bolts gathering the door-panels, the rim of a wheel gathering the spokes, and thread gathering the cloth.
What is the meaning of this?

All such instances are spoken of with a figurative intention (*abhiprāya*); that is to say, based on the intention of employing skillful means to attract [things together], prevent their dispersal, and maintain them, they are figuratively said to be "gathered."
The statements cited as scriptural evidence regarding the inclusion of other-natures (*parabhāva*) are merely provisional; for they depend upon others for their establishment.
Since their inclusion depends on causes for their establishment, their meaning is identical to non-inclusion.

Furthermore, if one were to admit that a dharma necessarily includes other-natures, then at the moment a single dharma arises, all dharmas should arise, and at the moment a single dharma ceases, all dharmas should cease. In that case, undesirable faults would only increase.
If a single category were abandoned when one category is abandoned, then the cultivation of superior remedies would be rendered useless.

Because they perceive such various faults, the masters of our own school maintain that [the categories] are subsumed by their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This formulation—that they are "subsumed by their intrinsic nature"—is the ultimate statement, for it does not depend on anything else;
this subsumption, which does not depend on causes, is the true subsumption, because all phenomena are always subsumed by their intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, how is it known that [a phenomenon] does not include the nature of another?
Because all phenomena are devoid of the nature of others.

That is to say, the nature of the eye-faculty is devoid of the nature of the ear and so forth; since they are devoid of one another, to claim that "this includes that" is logically impossible. Therefore, we know that all phenomena include only their own nature.

In this way, the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya) comprises only the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), because its nature consists of the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana), the eye-element (cakṣur-dhātu), the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya), the truth of origination (samudaya-satya), and so forth;
it does not comprise the other aggregates, as the other bases, elements, and so forth lack that nature.
In this manner, other dharmas should be considered accordingly.
One should reflect upon the meaning of their inclusion within the nature of causes (*hetu-svabhāva*).
To which realm (*dhātu*) do the male and female faculties (*puruṣa-strī-indriya*) belong?
For what reason do you suddenly give rise to doubt regarding this?
A different school states:
"Because it is not the body-faculty (kāyendriya), it is not included within the body-element (kāyadhātu)."
Therefore, doubt may arise.
One should abandon this doubt, for while [the sense-faculties] are definitively subsumed within the body-element (*kāyadhātu*), they are distinct from the function of the body.
How could their elements be the same?
Because their type, object, and consciousness are identical, they are subsumed under a single element (*dhātu*).
Regarding "identity of type": this is because the two organs—the male and female—are identical in terms of the bodily category.
From the identity of their objects, one knows that their types are identical.
The male and female organs take tactile contact as their object, identical to that of the body.
Contact within the eyes, nose, and throat is perceived upon swallowing; other locations are not so. How could these three differ from the body-faculty?
Their objects are the same because they are manifested by the same consciousness, for all of them serve as the basis for body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
Because their predominance (*adhipatya*) differs, they are established as distinct faculties.

That is to say, although the male and female [faculties] share the same category, object, and consciousness as the body faculty, and thus occupy the same locus and realm, they are established as two separate faculties because there is a distinction in their nature of predominance.
Just as the eleven faculties, though they occupy the same locations and realms, are established as distinct faculties because their predominant functions differ—
whereas the faculties of the eye, ear, and nose each rely on two locations— by what reason do the number of their elements (*dhātu*) not become multiple?
Because two are combined into one, there are only eighteen.
For what reason are two combined into a single element (*dhātu*)?
The verse says:
Because their type, object, and consciousness are identical, although there are two locations, the essence of the element is one.
The treatise says:
Although the sense organs of the eye, ear, and nose each have two locations, because their type and other factors are identical, they are combined into a single element.
Regarding "similarity of type," it is because they share the same nature of the eye.
Regarding "similarity of object," it is because they share the same object of form (*rūpa*).
Regarding "similarity of consciousness," it is because they serve as the basis for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
The same applies to the ears and nose; therefore, they are established as a single element (*dhātu*).
Since the substance of the element is one, for what reason are there two bases (*āyatana*)?
The verse says:
Nevertheless, in order to make [the body] dignified and beautiful, each sense organ, such as the eye, arises in two locations.
The Commentary says:
Because the physical form of the supporting body must be dignified and beautiful, although the essence of the element (*dhātu*) is one, it arises in two places.
If the locations of the eye and ear faculties were each to produce only one [organ], and the nose had no two nostrils, the body would not be dignified.
This explanation is incorrect; for camels, cats, owls, and the like are thus ugly—how could they possess dignity?
Therefore, the various sense faculties are of distinct types; they arise through such specific arrangements and distinctions, which depend upon causes and conditions.

When there are obstacles to these specific causes and conditions, they may not arise as pairs, just as in the case of the body faculty, where the head, neck, abdomen, back, hands, feet, and other parts are arranged according to their distinct types. One should not harbor doubts or difficulties regarding this.

They too depend upon causes and conditions; thus, due to the presence of obstructing or distinct causes and conditions, there are deficiencies in the limbs of snakes and other such beings. Furthermore, it is observed that the tongues of those species do not arise from a single cause. Therefore, the specific arrangement of the various sense organs arises in dependence upon causes and conditions, and is not for the purpose of adorning the body.
If that is so, why is it said that the sense organs, such as the eyes, each arise in two locations for the sake of physical beauty?
This has a different meaning; it is not for the purpose of adorning the body.

We observe in the world that even when something is preeminent and perfected in its function, it is described as "beautiful. If the sense organs such as the eyes were each lacking in one location, the functions of seeing, hearing, and smelling would all be unclear. Since the clear functions arise only when each exists in both locations, this statement regarding "beauty" is precisely intended to mean that it serves to enhance the excellence of their functioning.
Having already explained the inclusion of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), their meaning shall now be explained.
Regarding the objects of knowledge, the aggregates include the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while the bases and elements also include all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.

Why is this so? Within the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), they are sometimes called aggregates (*skandha*), sometimes bases (*āyatana*), and sometimes elements (*dhātu*), due to the distinct meanings of these three categories.
What are these distinct meanings?
The verse says:
Accumulation, arising-gate, and lineage—these are the meanings of aggregate (*skandha*), sense-field (*āyatana*), and element (*dhātu*).
The commentary says:
The meaning of accumulation is the meaning of *skandha* (aggregate); the meaning of gateway for arising is the meaning of *āyatana* (base); the meaning of lineage is the meaning of *dhātu* (element).
For what reason is it known that the meaning of a collection is the meaning of *skandha*?
This is because it is stated in the sūtras. As a sūtra says:

"Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all such forms, when briefly gathered into a single aggregate, are called the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)."
In this sūtra, the meaning of "accumulation" (rāśi) is revealed as *skandha*.
For what reason is it known that the meaning of "entrance" (*mukha*) is *āyatana*?
It is by virtue of its etymological derivation (*nirukti*).
"Base" (*āyatana*) refers to a gateway for arising; because the mind and mental factors arise and grow therein, it is called a "base," which signifies its function as that which enables their growth.
As the Sūtra says:
"Brahmin, you should know that with the eye as a gateway, one sees only forms."
This sutra establishes only six categories for the meaning of the "gate of proof," yet there are twelve gates for the mind and mental factors; thus the Sūtra says:
"With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact occurs, and simultaneously with it, feeling, perception, and volition arise."

In this manner, up to the point where the mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*) serve as conditions to give rise to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the triad of their conjunction (*trikasamnipāta*) gives rise to contact (*sparśa*), along with sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). Other masters say:
"Because the mind and its associates grow and arise in dependence upon these [bases], they are called 'bases' (*āyatana*)."
For what reason is it known that the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*) is "element" (*dhātu*)?
Because its meaning is similar to that of a worldly clan or lineage.
For example, when there are many varieties within a single mountain—such as realgar, orpiment, red ochre, and *añjana*—it is called a "multitude of elements" (*bahudhātu*).
In this way, within a single body or a single continuum, there are eighteen classes of dharmas, which are called the eighteen *dhātus*.
Just as in a mountain there are various ores that serve as the source for the production of substances such as realgar, which are termed "classes" (*gotra*).
Thus, herein, the fundamental sources from which mind and mental factors arise are designated as "lineage" (*gotra*).

If this were so, the meanings of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) would become confused, for both would share the same meaning of being the fundamental sources from which mind and mental factors arise.
Based on this, the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*) should be explained differently.
Just as realgar and other minerals are called a "lineage" because their essential natures differ when compared with one another,
so too the eye and other faculties are called a "lineage" because their essential natures differ when compared with one another.
If that were so, since the mind-element (manodhātu) has no distinct substantial nature from the six consciousnesses, it would not be a separate element.
This objection is not valid, because the substantial natures of the support (āśraya) and the supported (āśrita) are distinct.
Some say: because the distinctions in the establishment of time-periods. Others say:
Sixth, the mind comes first; the six [sense bases] do not precede the mind, and thus there is a profound difference.

Although the essential nature of all the elements (dhātus) extends across the three periods of time, distinct names are established according to their specific positions. It is for this reason that it is said that the six [bases] come first and the mind comes after.
Regarding the future mind, since its temporal status has not yet been differentiated, how can one say that the six [consciousnesses] come first and the mind comes later?
Furthermore, if the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is explained as a "collection," then the aggregate would not be real, because a collection is merely conventional.

This objection is not valid, because the statement establishing the meaning is made with respect to that which serves as the basis for the aggregate; it is not the case that the aggregate itself is the meaning.
Meaning is a specific designation for a real entity (*dravya*), whereas an aggregate is not a real entity.

This commentary reveals that the sūtra possesses a profound meaning: just as with a collection of words, apart from the basis of the collection, no separate, substantially existent entity of a "collection" can be found;

likewise, apart from the aggregates (skandhas) such as form and so forth, one should not seek a substantially existent self-entity elsewhere, because the term "self" is merely a conventional designation applied to the continuity of the aggregates, just like a worldly collection.
If the self does not truly exist, yet the aggregates were to truly exist, what meaning would the Sūtras convey?

Lest those to be trained, upon knowing that the dharmas such as form possess immeasurable distinctions across the three times and various categories—each being an aggregate—should conclude that the aggregates are infinite, and thus become discouraged and withdraw, thinking: "How can I possibly fully know and eternally abandon these infinite aggregates?"
To encourage them [to practice], although the aggregates are infinite, they are described collectively as one because they share the same characteristics.
Furthermore, all foolish worldlings give rise to the notion of a unified whole regarding the many aggregates, thereby manifesting the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*).

It is for the purpose of causing them to eliminate the notion of a unified whole that it is taught that within a single aggregate there are many constituent parts; it is not intended to demonstrate that the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, are composites of multiple dharmas and are therefore merely conventional and not real.
Furthermore, a single atom is comprised of the three time periods; when analyzed by wisdom, it is condensed into a single aggregate.

Although an aggregate (*skandha*) is indeed a collection, its reality as a substantial entity is established; the same applies to other phenomena. Therefore, the aggregates are not merely nominal designations.

Furthermore, since the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) is also applied to each individual distinct phenomenon, the aggregates are certainly not merely nominal designations. For example, it is said that feeling (*vedanā*) arising simultaneously [with other factors] is called the aggregate of feeling, and perception (*saṃjñā*) is called the aggregate of perception; the rest is as stated in the Sūtra.
Because they arise in combination at all times, although the aggregates (*skandha*) are distinct, the sense of a "collection" is established.

Other masters say that the meaning of "aggregate" is the sense of being "divisible into parts," because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possess the three temporal divisions of past, future, and present.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrāntika) judges this interpretation to deviate from the sūtra; however, I now maintain that this is not so, for it does not contradict reason.
How could the two meanings of "base" (*āyatana*) and "element" (*dhātu*) not deviate from the sūtra, yet be accepted therein as correct? Furthermore, what reasoning is there [for your position]?

In seeking scriptural evidence for the meaning of "aggregates" (skandha), you insistently demand proof from the sūtras, yet regarding the meanings of "bases" (āyatana) and "elements" (dhātu), you rely solely on logical explanation and utterly refuse to seek scriptural authority.
Observing these remarks, it appears you are acting out of partisan bias; therefore, one should follow the principle that there is no contradiction with reason.
Why is this? Because the Blessed One has taught three types of explanations regarding the objects of knowledge through such categories as the aggregates (*skandha*).
The verse says:
Because of the threefold nature of delusion, faculties, and inclinations, the aggregates, bases, and elements are taught as three.
The Commentary says:

Although the intention of the Sugata is extremely difficult to discern, if one seeks it through reasoning, it appears to be thus: because the disciples possess three types each of delusion, faculties, and inclinations, the Sugata taught the three kinds of dharma-gates—the aggregates, bases, and elements—in accordance with them.
"Joy" refers to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*); "three" means three for each.

There are three types of delusion among those beings to be converted: there are those who are deluded regarding mental factors and grasp them collectively as a self; those who are deluded regarding form alone; and those who are deluded regarding both form and mind.
The faculties are also of three kinds: sharp, medium, and dull.
Interest is likewise of three kinds: extensive, concise, and intermediate.
Because of these distinctions among the beings to be converted, the Sugata taught the three categories of aggregates, bases, and elements in their respective order.

The Master of the Sūtra has explained only a portion of what is taught here; namely, because there are three distinct stages: the stage of having already transcended mental attention (*manasikāra*), the stage of having already mastered the practice, and the stage of first undertaking the task;
because there are three distinct faults: conceiving the pride of "I," adhering to the notion of "mine," and being deluded regarding the basis and conditions of consciousness;
and because there are three different maladies: arrogance and indolence arising from relying on one's life, wealth, and lineage.
Based on these reasons, the Blessed One taught the three categories—the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu)—in their respective order.
That Elder stated:

"The aggregates are taught to clarify the characteristic of the distinct aspects of the grasped as a unified whole; the bases are taught to clarify the characteristic of the distinction between the object and the subject; and the elements are taught to clarify the characteristic of the distinction between the object, the subject, and the consciousness produced therefrom."
Furthermore, regarding the section on the "bases" (*āyatana*), how can one universally establish the characteristics of the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*)?
This is because, within this context, the five sense organs such as the eye and the mental organ (*manas*) are not explained as being of the nature of the object.

However, although all phenomena (*dharma*) are objects of the mental faculty (*manas*), this [definition] does not provide a comprehensive account of the objects of the mind when establishing the system of the bases (*āyatana*). It merely states that seven phenomena constitute the objects of the mind; as the Sūtra says:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that 'dharmas' refers to the external base (*bāhyam āyatanam*), which consists of those phenomena not subsumed within the other eleven bases."

Furthermore, since it is taught in various places that dharmas serve as the objects of the mental faculty (*manas*), the statement that "bases" (*āyatana*) do not universally establish the characteristics of object and subject seems incorrect. Regarding this, some further state:

"As the Sūtra says, 'With the mind and dharmas as conditions, mental consciousness arises,' this implies that all dharmas are objects of the mind. This is merely words; it lacks both logical reasoning and scriptural authority.
If this were necessarily the case, how could one speak of establishing a definitive distinction between the characteristics of the locus?
Furthermore, since it would not universally establish both the object and the subject, the fault would be the same as before.
Moreover, the Venerable Elder said:
Since there are no phenomena that are not the objects of the mind, all are subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

If this were so, one should establish only a single sphere of mental objects, because all phenomena are objects of the mind; however, this is merely a verbal assertion, as there is no authoritative evidence for it.

Furthermore, regarding what was said: although they are in fact a single location, eleven others are established based on their distinct characteristics within that one. That is to say, the first, the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), is also called the dharma-base (*dharma-āyatana*); continuing in this way up to the mind-base (*manas-āyatana*), which is also called the dharma-base; whereas the final dharma-base is called only the dharma-base.
If that were so, it would contradict the *Sūtra on the Sequence of the Bases*, which states:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that 'dharmas' refers to the external base (*bāhyāyatana*), which consists of those phenomena not subsumed within the other eleven bases."
Furthermore, in various places it is taught that "dharmas" constitute the objective sphere (ālambana) of the mind;

nowhere, however, is it stated that the eleven bases beginning with the eye are themselves called the "dharma-base" (dharmāyatana). Therefore, one cannot claim that although they are all [part of] the dharma-base...

However, in that sutra, the term "dharma-sphere" (dharmāyatana) is used to refer to those phenomena not included within the other eleven spheres; therefore, that statement is merely their own speculative construction.
Furthermore, although they establish both objects and subjects, it is extremely confused.
What confusion is there in the five sense-faculties grasping their own respective objects and the mental faculty taking all things as its object?
To have the subject take the object as its object, and for the object to become the subject—is this not indeed confusion?
Because they do not understand what herein constitutes the subject (*viṣayin*) and what constitutes the object (*viṣaya*), they are utterly confused.

In this sūtra, I perceive the following intent: the teaching of "place" (*sthāna*) is intended to clarify the distinction between the non-confused basis (*āśraya*) and the object (*viṣaya*), as well as the subject (*viṣayin*).
What is the purpose of this?
It is for the sake of abandoning the grasping at a self.
Those who maintain the doctrine of a self falsely claim:
"I am the seer," and so on, up to "the knower"—this self is the locus of pleasure and the like.
This sutra demonstrates that there are multiple dharmas performing functions; it reveals that there is no single dharma named "the seer" or even "the locus."
For this reason, although all phenomena are objects of the mind, they are not its specific objects.
Only that which is exclusively an object is established as an "object of the mind" (*ālambana*), and only in relation to this is the mind established as the "subject" (*ālambaka*).

Let it not be thought that this refers to a different conception of "self. There are certain dharmas whose locus has as its essence only the object; there are also those which possess an object but are not supports.
Alternatively, these may be established as one with the mind (manas) as possessing an object; since they are dependent [upon it], there is no fault.
Although the eye and the other [faculties], as well as the mind, possess the sense of being "unshared objects" (asādhāraṇa-viṣaya) for the mental faculty, they are not exclusively objects;
whereas the five bases such as form, although they are exclusively objects, lack the sense of being unshared objects for the mental faculty.

The five faculties, such as the eye, have no other objects; thus, the objects such as visible form are called "unshared. It is in relation to these objects that the term "possessor of the object" (viṣayin) is applied.
Herein, the word "base" (āyatana) refers to the six bases of support, namely the eye and so forth, while it refers to the six bases of objective reference, namely visible form and so forth.
This is designated as a "base" (*āyatana*) because it manifests as the condition for the growth of distinct phenomena;
it is precisely according to this principle that the name "base" is explained, meaning it is called a base because it is capable of producing the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Therefore, the statement regarding the "bases" (āyatana) is established to provide unmixed objects and subjects, which are non-confused and functionally effective.
I perceive this intended meaning in this sutra.
One who discerns phenomena should further investigate this:
For what reason, among all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), are two distinct factors established as the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) and perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"The Blessed One has established them through his thorough mastery of phenomena; one should not subject him to questioning."
Alternatively, it is said that there is a reason [for this distinction]. The verse states:

Because they are the roots of contention and the causes of birth and death, And for the sake of the sequential order, Among all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), Feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established as separate aggregates (*skandha*).
The treatise states:
Briefly, there are two kinds of roots of worldly strife: namely, attachment to sensual desires and being fettered by craving for them; and attachment to views and being fettered by craving for them.

In the beginning, [craving] arises from sensation (*vedanā*), and in the end, it is produced by perception (*saṃjñā*); through the power of relishing sensation, one becomes attached to various desires, and through the power of inverted perception, one becomes attached to various views.

Furthermore, among the phenomena of birth and death, sensation and perception constitute the most predominant causes: because of indulgence in pleasant sensation and because of clinging to inverted perception.
For those who act out of craving and views, the cycle of birth and death proceeds by means of these two causes, as will be explained later.
Because of this sequential causality, one should understand that feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established separately as aggregates (*skandha*).
Their sequential causes will be explained immediately following.

Furthermore, these two—feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*)—serve as the fundamental roots for the arising of the two types of defilements, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*); they each individually manifest the name of a "station of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*); and the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is established based on the extinction of these two.

Since there are many such categories of causes, why is it that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is said to be included within the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), but not subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*)?
The verse states:
The aggregates do not include the unconditioned, Because the meaning is incompatible.
The Treatise says:

If one were to assert that the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) constitute an aggregate (*skandha*), whether by including them within the [five] aggregates or by positing them as a sixth, in all cases this would be unreasonable, because it contradicts the meaning [of the term].
Why is this so? Because those [unconditioned phenomena] are neither form (*rūpa*) nor even consciousness (*vijñāna*), they do not exist within the five [aggregates].

"Aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of a collection; since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)—unlike form and the others—do not possess such categorical distinctions as past and so forth that could be briefly summarized into a single collection called the "aggregate of the unconditioned," they do not constitute a sixth [aggregate].

Furthermore, because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are contrary to the meaning of being the basis for inversion and the means for its abandonment, they are not established as aggregates (*skandha*).

To explain: the mention of the contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) reveals the basis for inversion, while the mention of the uncontaminated aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) reveals the means for abandonment. Unconditioned phenomena possess neither of these two meanings; since they do not correspond to these meanings, they are not established as aggregates.

Some say: Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*), it cannot be called an aggregate, just as a worldly jar that has been broken is no longer called a jar.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) objects, saying:

In that case, it would follow as a logical error regarding the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*): namely, that when the bases and elements cease, they should no longer be bases and elements, which would contradict your own tenet that sentient beings conceive of a self entirely within the category of the aggregates (*skandha*).

In the state of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, the aggregates (*skandha*) cease all at once; this is not the case for the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), as they do not arise in their entirety. It is only because the arising of the aggregates is grasped that one conventionally designates it as "birth.
If the cessation of the aggregates were also established as being the aggregates, then the remaining aggregates would have to persist even after *parinirvāṇa*.
Sentient beings fear that the aggregates (*skandha*) possess many faults and afflictions; they should therefore not conceive the notion of security regarding *nirvāṇa*.

It is not the case that the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) as a whole possess many faults; thus, the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder) still follows within the bases and elements. Therefore, the aggregates should not be treated as equivalent to those [bases and elements] in establishing their nature.

Furthermore, the meaning of the term "cessation" (*nirodha*) here does not intend to indicate simple annihilation, because the intrinsic natures of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are not of the nature of annihilation.

The intended meaning of this statement is that where the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) are entirely absent, it is called the "cessation of the aggregates. Since the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack any sense of accumulation whatsoever, they can be termed the "cessation of the aggregates"; however, the sense of "gate" (*mukha*) or "class" (*gotra*) is likewise absent there, so they should not be treated as analogous cases.
This commentary accords well with the meaning of the verse.
Since the Blessed One’s arising of the teaching is preceded by awakened wisdom (*buddhi*), upon what basis did he explain the aggregates (*skandha*) in this particular order?
The verse says:
According to their coarseness, defilement, vessel-like nature, and the distinctions of the realms, they are established in this order.
The treatise says:

The five aggregates are established in this sequence because of their relative coarseness, their degree of defilement, their analogy as a vessel and its contents, and the distinctions among the realms.

Regarding the establishment [of the aggregates] according to their coarseness: among the five, the most coarse is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Because it possesses resistance and obstruction, because it is the basis for the five consciousnesses, and because it is the object of the six consciousnesses, it is mentioned first among the five.

Among these four, the most coarse is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); because its mode of activity and function are easily understood despite its lack of physical form, it is mentioned first among the four.

Among these three, the most coarse is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); because its mode of activity in grasping the characteristics of male, female, and so forth is easily understood, it is mentioned first among the three.

Among these two [aggregates], the coarse one is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); because the manifestations of craving and so forth arise with distinct characteristics and are easily understood, it is mentioned first among the two.
The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is the most subtle, and therefore it is mentioned last.

Regarding establishment based on defilement: since beginningless saṃsāra, men and women have mutually felt defiled attachment toward one another’s bodies; because this is manifested through form and so forth, "form" (rūpa) is mentioned first.
Thus, because craving for form arises from indulging in the flavor of feeling (*vedanā*), feeling is explained next.
Because this indulgence in the flavor of feeling arises from the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), perception is explained next.
Because this inversion of perception arises through the power of the afflictions (*kleśa*), the formations (*saṃskāra*) are explained next.
Because the power of these afflictions depends on the production of consciousness that brings about future existence, consciousness is mentioned last.
Regarding "like a vessel" and so forth: form is like a vessel, because it is the basis for feeling.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is like food and drink, for it increases or diminishes the body of sentient beings.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is similar to seasoning, because by grasping at the equality between enemies and friends, it assists in the arising of feeling.
The formations are like a cook, because they produce the ripening of the desirable and undesirable through the power of the karmic afflictions such as volition and craving.

Consciousness is likened to the eater, because it is the predominant master within the fundamental state of sentient beings, and because it is the primary leader for the arising of sensation and the other [mental factors].
It is precisely for this reason that, among the formations conducive to merit such as feeling and perception, only consciousness is specifically described as being "conducive to merit.
Furthermore, it is by virtue of this same principle that it is said that "formations are the condition for consciousness."
Furthermore, because of this, he said to Ānanda:
"If consciousness were not present, it would not enter the mother's womb.
Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure."
Among the co-arising factors such as feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā), these sūtras merely designate the primary consciousness (vijñāna).
Regarding the distinctions according to realms: within the desire realm (kāmadhātu), form (rūpa) is preeminent, because all sense faculties and their objects consist of form.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), feeling (*vedanā*) is supreme, because all superior and sublime feelings can be fully obtained therein.
Among the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), perception (*saṃjñā*) is most supreme, because the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) is clearest in those stages.
The state of existence within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is the most excellent among all states of existence, because the volition therein can produce the greatest fruit.
This is precisely the station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), wherein consciousness dwells.
To illustrate this according to the sequence of a field and its seed in the world, the order of the aggregates (*skandha*) is thus established.

By virtue of these five aggregates, there is no fault of increase or decrease; that is, for these reasons of sequential order, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established separately among the mental factors (*caitta*).

This means that within the mental factors, feeling and perception are coarse, give rise to defilement, share the same category of nutriment, and assist [the mind] in the same way; because they are powerful in two realms, they are established as separate aggregates.

Having followed the root verses, we have thus explained the fourfold causes for the sequence according to the gate of transition (*pravṛtti-mukha*). Now, according to the gate of return (*nivṛtti-mukha*), one further type shall be explained: namely, that there are two essential gates for entering the Buddha-dharma.

First is the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); second is mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*). Since the gate of impurity contemplates derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and the gate of mindfulness of breathing contemplates the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), matter (*rūpa*) is mentioned first because it is the object of these essential gates.

By means of this power of observation, one analyzes the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) through their momentary and atomic distinctions; when observing in this way, because the body attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), the mind experiences joy, and therefore feeling (*vedanā*) is explained next.

Since the conjunction of sensation with the body invariably results in either benefit or harm, and it is logically impossible for such benefit or harm to pertain to a "self," through this contemplative understanding, the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*) is extinguished and the notion of phenomena (*dharma-saṃjñā*) arises; therefore, the notion is explained next.
Because of this perception, one realizes that there are only phenomena (*dharma*), and thus afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise; therefore, "formations" (*saṃskāra*) are explained next.
Once afflictions have subsided, the mind abides in pliancy and becomes capable; therefore, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is explained next.
The sequential order has already been explained; the reverse order should now be discussed, but I shall desist for fear of excessive prolixity.
Thus, the sequence of the aggregates (*skandha*) has been explained.

Within the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), one should first analyze and explain the sequence of the six faculties (*indriya*); from this, the sequence of their respective objects and consciousnesses can be understood.
For what reason do the eye and the other [faculties] follow this specific order?
The verse says:
The objects of the first five are exclusively present; The objects of four are exclusively derived matter.
The others function with distance, speed, and clarity, or according to their respective order.
The treatise says:
Among the six sense faculties, the first five—eye and so forth—perceive only present objects; therefore, they are mentioned first.

The mental objects (*ālambana*) are indeterminate; they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) across the three periods of time, and one may apprehend only one, or two, three, or four of them. For this reason, they are explained later.
As for those whose objects are determinate, their application is free from confusion and their characteristics are distinct; therefore, they are explained first.
Regarding the "objects being indeterminate": because their application is disordered and their characteristics are not distinct, they are explained later.

As for the so-called four objects, those that are exclusively derived matter (bhautika) carry over from the previous section; among the five [types of objects], the first four objects are exclusively derived matter, and therefore they are explained first.
The body and its objects are not fixed, as both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) serve as its objects; therefore, it is mentioned last.

At times the body-faculty perceives only the primary elements, at times it perceives only derived matter, and at times it perceives both. For this reason, some say that body-consciousness most frequently arises in dependence on five types of tangibles: namely, the four primary elements and any one of the qualities such as smoothness.

Some say that [the faculties] have as many as eleven conditions; others say there are four, as previously stated, according to their respective applications of distance, speed, and clarity; for this reason, they are mentioned first.
That is to say, because the faculties of the eye and ear apprehend distant objects, they are mentioned before the other two.

Among the two [faculties], the function of the eye is explained first because it reaches further; for example, when a distant grove is struck by wind and so forth, one perceives its swaying but does not hear the sound.
Furthermore, the function of the eye is more rapid; one first sees from afar a person striking a bell or drum, and only afterwards hears the sound.

The two faculties of nose and tongue both function with objects that are not distant; the nose is mentioned first because its operation is more rapid and clear. For example, when facing various fragrant foods and drinks, the nose first smells the aroma, and the tongue subsequently tastes the flavor.
Thus, for the time being, the sequence of the faculties has been explained by distinguishing between those whose objects are fixed or unfixed, and those whose functions are remote, swift, or clear;
alternatively, the sequence of the faculties is explained according to their arrangement from top to bottom within the body, following their respective locations of support.
It is traditionally said:
among the parts of the body, the sense-base of the eye is the most superior and is manifest on the face; therefore, it is mentioned first.
The bases of the ear, nose, and tongue faculties follow in descending order.
The body occupies many lower positions;
the mind has no fixed location, yet that which arises in dependence upon the five sense organs is discussed last.

Is it not a matter of factual reality that the atoms of the olfactory faculty reside within the nasal cavity and do not dwell beneath the eyes? As it is said, the three faculties are arranged horizontally in rows without variation in height, like a floral crown.
In reality, it should indeed be so; however, the Master of the Sūtra (the author of the *Abhidharmakośa*) provisionally explains it in this way by taking the sense faculties as their bases.
Perhaps because the Master’s statement appears to allow for alternative interpretations, I shall now provide a verse here:
The functions of the first five arise first; The functions of the five [faculties] are distant in the first two.
Regarding the three functions, the first two are explained clearly, or they follow the sequential order of their respective locations.

Among the six sense faculties, the first five—eye and so forth—exert their function prior to the objects such as form; the mental faculty (*manas*) arises only afterwards. Therefore, they are mentioned first.
As stated in the original treatise:

"The five objects, such as form and so forth, are first perceived by the five consciousnesses and subsequently cognized by the mental consciousness. One should know that both serve as the support for their respective consciousnesses and grasp their own objects; these are all the functions of the eye and the other sense organs."
Among the five faculties, the first two have a remote function because their objects do not come into contact with them; therefore, they are mentioned first.
Between these two, the function of the eye is even more remote than that of the ear, as demonstrated by the preceding examples; for this reason, it is mentioned first.
Regarding the functions of the three organs beginning with the nose, the first two are more distinct; therefore, the nose comes first, followed by the tongue, and then the body.
For instance, while the nose can perceive subtle odors, the tongue is not so capable regarding tastes such as sweet or bitter.
Just as the tongue can perceive subtle flavors, the body does not do so regarding cold and warmth.
The sequential explanation according to their respective locations is no different from what was stated previously.

If objects such as visible forms are first perceived by the five consciousnesses and subsequently known by the mental consciousness, how is it that one can perceive visible forms and so forth within a dream?
Other masters say:
"In a dream, one recollects objects previously experienced;
were it otherwise, those born blind would also perceive visible forms within their dreams."

Some say: In dreams, one does not necessarily recollect objects previously experienced, because the appearances of those objects manifest clearly and are grasped distinctly; this is unlike the state of waking, where one recollects and discerns previously experienced objects as if colors and other forms were manifest and clearly graspable within the dream itself. Furthermore, when recollecting past objects during the dream state, there is no superior quality that exceeds that of the waking state.

Because this recollection of previously experienced objects manifests with such clarity that it surpasses [the clarity of] the waking state, one is therefore able to apprehend within a dream forms and other objects not previously experienced.
However, as for the fact that one sometimes can recall past objects while in the state of dreaming, this is not a true dream, because one cannot clearly apprehend the characteristics of the object.
If that is so, for what reason can one born blind not apprehend color during the state of dreaming?
Who says that one born blind cannot perceive color during the state of dreaming?

If you claim that what is remembered in a dream must necessarily be an object previously experienced and not one never before experienced, then one must admit that the person born blind perceives color in a dream, because they have seen color in other previous lives.
Furthermore, it is not only previously experienced things that are seen in dreams, as stated in other passages; therefore, the same should apply to the dreams of those born blind.

As for what the *Mūla-śāstra* says—that the five objects such as form are first perceived by the five consciousnesses and subsequently known by the mental consciousness—this is stated according to what is possible, and is not necessarily so in all cases.
The claim that, regarding objects such as visible form, the eye and other [faculties] function first and the mental consciousness arises later, is not necessarily fixed.
This is because the *Mūla-śāstra* states that the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, serve as one another's equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Herein, for the time being, this is explained in terms of the sequential perception of visible forms and so forth during the non-dreaming, non-meditative state. By this, the form apprehended in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) has already been explained.
Those who dwell in seclusion all say:

"The blue and other colors within concentration are visible forms; it cannot be said that these forms in concentration are of a different class from those previously perceived by the visual consciousness, because they appear clearly within this concentration."

This matter of the meditative state is produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) generated by that meditation; it is pure, distinct, and unobstructed, like the matter of the space-element (ākāśadhātu).
Thus has the sequence of the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu) been explained.
Within this context, one should further investigate:
for what reason, although the substance of all ten bases (*āyatana*) is matter (*rūpa*), is the name "matter-base" established for only one of them?
Furthermore, although the substance of all twelve bases is phenomena (*dharma*), why is the name "phenomena-base" established for only one of them?
The verse says:
To distinguish it as most excellent, To include many superior dharmas,
One location is named "form," And one is named the "dharma-base."
The treatise states:
Although all twelve bases (*āyatana*) and ten material phenomena (*rūpa*) are *dharma*, they are differentiated such that one [of them] is established as a general name.
What is meant by "differentiation" refers to their respective distinct bases.
If material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) were identical because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the same, then their designations as bases (*āyatana*) would necessarily be either two or one.

Since disciples, by means of these general names, would only understand them collectively and fail to discern their specific characteristics, the Tathāgata established distinct conventional names for the various differences between objects (*viṣaya*) and subjects (*viṣayin*). Thus, he established distinct designations for the meanings of sound and so forth, as well as for the eye and so forth, upon the basis of form (*rūpa*).
Since the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) has no other distinct meaning or name, its general name is itself its specific name, just as in the case of the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇahetu*).
When various specific names are established, they are intended to manifest a specific meaning;
since this [name] manifests a specific meaning, it is itself the specific name. The same applies to the sense-sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Regarding the term "most excellent," it is due to two causes and conditions that the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is most excellent among the sense bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) alone:
first, because it is visible (*sanidarśana*), it can be demonstrated as having distinctions such as being "here" or "there";
second, because it is resistant (*sapratigha*), it undergoes transformation and destruction when touched by hands and the like.

Furthermore, because it is manifold, because it is the object of the three eyes, because the world collectively designates the name "form" (*rūpa*) for this [object], and because the great masters of treatises do not designate the name "form" for sound and so forth, only this one is called "form."
Within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), because it subsumes a multitude of phenomena such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth, a general designation should be established.
If this general designation were absent, how could one subsume many distinct phenomena with diverse characteristics into a single category?
Furthermore, within this context, "name" refers to categories (*nāmakāya*), while "dharmas" refers to all phenomena; thus, the name "dharma" is established. These include:

the dharma of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), the dharma of the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), the dharma of knowledge (*jñāna*), the dharma of recollection (*anusmṛti*), the dharma of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*), the dharma of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the dharma of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the dharma of the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*) and the Refuge in the Dharma.
