This is not the case; for if matter and the like are not separated from the faculties, although they are not the [direct] supports, they are nonetheless closely associated with the mind and its factors. Therefore, this fault does not arise.
The *Vibhāṣā* states:

If material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are oppressive, disruptive, or destructive, they can produce suffering; that which is contrary to this can produce pleasure. That which is comprised within one's own body is termed "appropriated" (*sopādāna*).
Other masters say:

If sentient beings grasp at something as their own self, and they employ all means, at all times and in all places, to protect it from conditions such as grass, ash, fire, thorns, frost, and hail, then that which is comprised within one's own body is called "appropriated" (*upātta*).
If that were so, it would contradict what is stated in the sūtras. Thus, a sūtra says:
"That place where consciousness is stored as its appropriation and where consciousness follows and encompasses it is called 'appropriated' (sopādāna)."
Although this statement exists, it is not contradictory; there are briefly two kinds of appropriated phenomena (*upātta-dharma*):
first, those which are grasped as "mine" by craving and the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which are termed appropriated;
second, those which, acting as causes, are able to produce suffering and pleasure, which are termed appropriated.
The continuity of the various states of the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) induced by past karma is called the second [link].
Within this, there is craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); these are immediately severed and extinguished when right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) arises.

The continuity of maturation (*vipāka-santati*) is not yet severed even for those whose outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted; therefore, if a phenomenon, once it has been appropriated (*upātta*), continues to function without being relinquished until *parinirvāṇa*, such a phenomenon is exclusively termed "appropriated" (*sopādāna*).
This is the distinction between the two meanings of sūtra and śāstra.
Having thus explained what is appropriated (*upātta*) and so forth,
among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are of the nature of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and how many are of the nature of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)?
How many are accumulative, and how many are non-accumulative?
The verse says:
Within the element of tangibility there are two; the remaining nine are derived from matter.
One part of the dharmas is likewise; ten material elements are accumulative.
The treatise says:
the element of tangibility (spraṣṭavyadhātu) comprises two types: first, the primary elements (mahābhūta), and second, the derived elements (bhautika).
These two are explained as before in the commentary on the eleven types of contact (*spraṣṭavya*).
Regarding this, the Elder Alpaśruta stated:
"There is no derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) within the sphere of the tangible."
Why is this so? It is because it is a specific configuration of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

That is to say, the sequential arrangement of the primary elements within a composite aggregate of gold, silver, crystal, mica, diamond, plantain, refined silk, and so forth, is designated as the tactile sensation of smoothness.
In contrast, that which exists within a composite aggregate is described as the tactile quality of roughness (*karkaśa-spraṣṭavya*).
The remaining [qualities] are likewise, as appropriate, merely specific arrangements of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Furthermore, because the eye is also capable of cognizing them, it means that by relying on the eye, one perceives the shape, magnitude, and color-form of the primary elements; one is also able to cognize objects such as smoothness and roughness. Therefore, it is known that smoothness and the other qualities are not distinct from the primary elements.
This statement is incorrect, as it contradicts the sacred teaching.
As stated in the Sūtra:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that 'contact' refers to the external sense-base (bāhyāyatana); it consists of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements, being material, invisible, and resistant."
Since he does not admit its existence, such a sūtra should not be rejected, for it was included in the compilation.
Furthermore, as it does not contradict other sūtras nor violate reason, it should be established as authoritative.

He [the opponent] claims that this sūtra was not included in the compilation because it deviates from the general summary verse (*uddāna*), just as it is said that the *Anupada-sūtra* was established as a separate category because it was composed differently.

If that were so, then one would have to discard all the sūtras of the Noble Teachings that contradict the tenets of one's own school; for instance, it is said that the two types of *śūnyatā* sūtras were established as separate categories because they were composed differently, yet they too deviate from the general summary verse.
Such categories as these mutually refute one another.

If it is argued that this sutra was not spoken by the Noble One because it contradicts other sutras—since the *dharmāyatana* is not stated to include formless phenomena—as in the *Śāriputra-daśottara-sūtra*, which states only:
"There are ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*)."

Therefore, we know that this sūtra was not included in the formal compilation; rather, it was composed and inserted into the Āgama by the Abhidharma masters who were fond of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
If that is so, would the Abhidharma masters not likewise have been able to say:
"The Dārṣṭāntika masters, out of hatred for non-informative matter, composed and inserted [this] into the *Daśottara-sūtra*"?
In this way, as they successively contradict and deny one another, they bring about the ruin and disorder of all the sūtras.
However, because the *Daśottara-sūtra* intends to reveal ten kinds of phenomena that should be fully known (*parijñeya*), it simply states that there are ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*).
Since these eleven [factors] are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering, and since the Truth of Suffering is exclusively that which should be fully known (*parijñeya*), there is no contradiction.

Because the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) possesses both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) natures, it should likewise be cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*), just like the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*). Therefore, why does the *Ekottarika-āgama* (The Scripture of the Incremental Increase) speak only of factors that should be fully known among those ten? Is it not also the case that they should be permanently abandoned (*prahātavya*)?
This objection is not valid, because the established truths differ.
Furthermore, in that sutra, Śāriputra certainly intends to state that it is not the case that all phenomena are subject to exhaustion.

Indeed, that same sutra further speaks of ten kinds of phenomena that should be permanently abandoned—namely, the five internal and five external factors conducive to the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). It is not that there are no other phenomena that are also to be permanently abandoned; therefore, this [interpretation] does not contradict other sutras.

Thus, the Elder’s assertion that there is no derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) within the sense-field of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*) certainly contradicts this *Prakaraṇapāda* Sūtra; the wise should understand this.
As for the claim that [tangibility] is merely a differentiation of the shape of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), this does not state a valid reason.
How is this known with certainty?

It is because the specific distinctions in the dimensions and configurations of the primary elements (mahābhūta) are what are termed "smoothness" and so forth; there are no smoothnesses or the like that exist separately from the primary elements, nor are they anything other than the particular arrangements of those primary elements.
The primary elements themselves are not what is apprehended by the eye; rather, that which is apprehended by the eye consists of color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna).
How, then, can it be said that [shape] is simply a particularity of shape among the primary elements?
Is it not the case that even in the dark, the body can perceive differences in shape and dimension?
If this were so, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) would have to be perceived by two sense faculties, because you assert that shape and dimension are themselves the primary elements.
By this, the second reason—that the eye can also cognize those [qualities]—is refuted.

Furthermore, as for the claim that "depending on the eye, one can also cognize smoothness and so forth, along with the color-form and dimensions of the primary elements (mahābhūta) as they are perceived," what is the meaning of these words?

If you claim that the eye perceives the shape and dimension (*saṃsthāna*) of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and since you maintain that shape and dimension are not distinct from the primary elements, you must admit that the eye faculty can perceive the primary elements themselves.

If you claim that the eye faculty perceives color-form (*varṇa*) and the shape and dimension of the primary elements are known by inference based on this, then how can you exclude smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*) and other qualities from being distinct from the primary elements?

Since one infers smoothness and so forth by seeing their color-form, these terms refer to the primary elements themselves; what reason is there, then, for saying that smoothness and so forth are not distinct from the primary elements?
This is nothing but empty talk and lacks any real meaning.
Furthermore, one should say that solidity is simply a specific arrangement of the other three great elements, just as smoothness or roughness are;

for others could likewise conceive it in this way—that the specific arrangement of the other three great elements is what is called solidity, and no distinct solidity exists apart from those three that can be apprehended.
Since there is no distinct cause, one should not maintain a separate apprehension; therefore, the meaning of that statement lacks any functional capacity.
Furthermore, because one perceives bitterness or acidity upon smelling an odor, one should say that the essence of bitterness or acidity is not distinct from the odor itself.

Furthermore, since characteristics such as smoothness differ from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), there must be a distinct nature apart from the primary elements. That is to say, the nature of smoothness is not identical to the nature of solidity, because smoothness is not present in all instances of solidity; for example, while earth is solid and its solidity is never separated [from it], smoothness is not.
If that were so, then smoothness would not be inseparable from solidity, nor would it be identical to moisture, for not all moist places possess smoothness;
nor would it be identical to heat, for not all hot places possess smoothness;
nor would it be identical to motion, for smoothness cannot be perceived in things such as the breath.
From this, it is known that smoothness is not a primary element (*mahābhūta*);
yet it is not non-existent either, because it is perceptible as a real entity (*dravya*) just like other phenomena, and because it can serve as a condition for the arising of reflected images.

If it is claimed that there is only a distinction in arrangement and no substantial entity, this is also logically untenable; for a distinction in arrangement must have a basis, and the nature of that basis is precisely smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*).
Alternatively, one should only perceive the specific arrangement [of the parts], and not also cognize the quality of smoothness therein.
Furthermore, the Sūtra employs a skillful means to state that such a quality of smoothness exists, as the Sūtra says:
"The skin of the Tathāgata is exceedingly fine and smooth; no dust or impurities adhere to his body."

Furthermore, although there are sūtras that mention the nature of smoothness and others that do not, there has never been a sūtra that negates its existence; moreover, it does not contradict correct reasoning. Thus, the thesis that the nature of smoothness is substantially real is established.

Furthermore, if the nature of smoothness were not distinct from the four great elements and lacked a separate substantial entity, it would be merely nominal and not real; in that case, the body-consciousness should not perceive it, because body-consciousness perceives only objects that are ultimate realities (*paramārtha*).

Furthermore, if it were devoid of conceptual differentiation, the perception of smoothness would not exist; just as there are distinct perceptions regarding each individual entity among the great elements when they are free from conceptual differentiation, one says that body-consciousness takes the actual entities of the great elements as its object, rather than taking a conventional phenomenon as its object.
The nature of smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*) is likewise; since it is apprehended by the body, it cannot be said to be merely conventional rather than real.
Furthermore, because it does not exist within each of the individual primary elements (*mahābhūta*), the nature of smoothness exists separately from the primary elements.
By this reasoning, it is also generally established that there exists a nature of roughness and so forth distinct from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The specific distinctions therein shall be further demonstrated.
The Venerable Sthavira says:
There is no distinct derivative entity called "lightness" or "heaviness"; rather, it is the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) themselves—whether few or many—that are designated as light or heavy.

Furthermore, since the nature of lightness and heaviness is established through mutual dependence, they do not possess a real substantial essence. That is to say, a single object is designated as "light" in relation to this and "heavy" in relation to that; this is not the case for qualities such as solidity, which are not established through mutual dependence.
Furthermore, because lightness is said to be the characteristic of the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*), lightness itself is wind.
As the treatise states:
"What is called the wind element?"
It refers to the nature of lightness and mobility.
The Blessed One also said:
"The various natures of lightness and mobility are called the internal and external wind elements."
This statement is incorrect, because it was previously stated that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are distinct from this [characteristic], as they do not possess its nature.

If you claim that the nature of lightness is the wind element (*vāyudhātu*) simply because you fail to understand the meaning of the sūtras and treatises, then you must explain which primary element constitutes the nature of heaviness?

If it is asserted in this school that there is a further increase of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which constitutes heaviness, and that this heaviness is identical to those primary elements, this is logically untenable, because the characteristics of heaviness differ from those of earth and water.
Furthermore, because [the qualities] are present within every composite aggregate, there should be no distinction between them.
If you argue that there is no fault because they exist in varying degrees—more or less—then weight would not be distinct from solidity or moisture.
Furthermore, since you admit that the combination [of atoms] constitutes heaviness, bodily consciousness should not take those [atoms] as its object.

Moreover, because you admit that heaviness exists within the aggregated mass of many great elements (mahābhūta), it would follow that heaviness must exist in every such aggregated mass, as there is no fixed cause [to distinguish them].

If it is said that the specific aggregation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) can act as a causal condition to produce heaviness separately, then there is no such fault, for this is what is actually perceived in the world.

Furthermore, as for the claim that lightness and heaviness are not substantially existent because they are established through mutual dependence, this is not a sound argument. It is like the relationship between cause and effect: lightness and heaviness are likewise.
For instance, when a single object is designated as a "cause" in relation to something else, it is not the same thing that is designated as an "effect" in relation to that very same thing;
and when it is designated as an "effect" in relation to another thing, it is not the same thing that is designated as a "cause" in relation to that very same thing.
In this way, a single object is designated as "light" in relation to one thing, yet it is not designated as "heavy" in relation to that same thing;
it is designated as "heavy" in relation to another thing, yet it is not designated as "light" in relation to that same thing.
Since cause and effect are real, how could this be merely provisional?
Therefore, it is only the designating expressions that are mutually dependent and indeterminate, not the essence of the designated reality which undergoes alteration.
This is also like the case of "this shore" and "that shore," or the nature of lightness and heaviness.
That is to say, one establishes the name "the other shore" for that object, but this does not cause the essence of this shore to change;
nor does one establish the name "this shore" for that object, which would cause the essence of the other shore to change.
When a single entity undergoes a continuous succession, it is designated as "this shore" or "that shore" in relation to its respective limits.
The same applies to lightness and heaviness; their essence is not indeterminate.
Furthermore, just as with black and white, so it is with lightness and heaviness.

This means that a single entity is designated as "black" in relation to this and "white" in relation to that; yet it is not the case that there is no distinct substantial entity for the manifest color. Therefore, dependence upon mutual relation is not an unreal reason.

If it is argued that when many things are depended upon, they are collectively designated as having a single nature—such as a "jar" or a "forest"—and that this is merely conventional and not real, then the same must apply here [to the single nature of the mind]; thus, it is not real.
How do you know this to be so?
One should state the reason for this.
However, this is not a valid reason, as it entails a logical fault.

If you argue that solidity and so forth are not established through mutual dependence, whereas this [conceptualization] is established through mutual dependence and is therefore not real, then the verbal designations "solidity" and so forth are likewise established through mutual dependence—since the name "solid" is established in dependence upon non-solid objects—and thus solidity is not unreal; the same should apply here as well.
If it is argued that this is not so, because one has never observed the hard being described as the wet due to their dissimilarity, this is not incorrect;
for the causal factors upon which they depend are invariably determined, and thus their meanings are similar.
However, that which is called "moist" does not depend on something else for its designation as "hard," because there is no other dependent cause [for it].
It is in dependence upon non-hard objects that this is designated as "hard"; it has never been designated as "non-hard" in dependence upon those [objects].
The same applies to lightness and heaviness; thus, their meanings are analogous.

Although at times heaviness is predicated of a light aggregate, this does not mean that its nature as light is abandoned through such predication. Rather, due to other conditions, a different designating term arises, while the substance itself undergoes no alteration.
As has already been argued above, therefore, mutual dependence is not an unreal cause.

Alternatively, even all solid objects are established as distinct categories through mutual dependence; that is to say, what is called "solid" may be designated as "superiorly solid" or "extremely solid," and within these, the term "solid" is also spoken of as "not solid."

Since their principles are identical, you ought to feel joy; yet you cannot cause joy [in this matter], because lightness and heaviness—both being either solid or non-solid—would have to become one and the same thing.

Furthermore, the substantial existence of the natures of lightness and heaviness, distinct from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), is established; however, one should not say that they are indeterminate due to mutual dependence, for if so, they would likewise have to become a single entity.
Just as black and white, though mutually dependent and opposed, differ in category and are not one;
even if one were to say that although black and white differ in category, it has never been said that white is black or black is white.
This is also not the case, for we observe such a statement in the world.
Although the designation is not fixed, the essence does not change, as has already been stated previously; therefore, their essences are distinct.

Furthermore, as you have stated, a minute fire is cold; there exists a subtle mass of warmth which, in relation to this, is termed "cold," and in relation to that, is termed "warm. Although the names are not fixed, the substance itself is real.

This should also be understood as follows: there are certain aggregates of matter in which the subtle atoms of lightness are numerous and the subtle atoms of heaviness are few; such an aggregate is designated as "light.
Conversely, those aggregates in which this is reversed are designated as "heavy."
The principle that the two natures of lightness and heaviness are identical in substance yet distinct in character is evident; for what reason, then, is this not accepted?

As for the claim that because lightness is spoken of in relation to the wind element, lightness is therefore identical to wind—this is also incorrect, as this point has already been explained within the analysis of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Regarding the three qualities beginning with solidity (*khara*), movement (*īraṇā*) is the most difficult to discern; therefore, the light effect is cited to reveal the wind cause (*vāyu-hetu*).
Although all four primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are causes of lightness, this statement is made because wind is predominant [in that respect].
Although fire increases, it is not determinate;
furthermore, lightness and motion are mutually compatible and similar, which is why the treatise and the sūtra state:
"Lightness and so forth have the nature of motion."
If one were to definitively grasp the meaning solely according to the literal words, then that same sutra states:
"Hair, body hair, nails, and so forth are called the internal earth element.
Would it then follow that hair, body hair, and the rest are exclusively the earth element?
Therefore, those words have a specific underlying intention; one should not hold that they negate the creation of light matter (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, there is a verse in the Āgama which says:
"Heavy and solid within the body, Like a heavy ship sinking in the sea."
Therefore, heaviness must substantially exist as a real entity, just like solidity.
Other masters say that the nature of lightness has the non-existence of heaviness as its essence.
This is also not the case; for while heaviness is absent in space and the like, lightness ought to be present there.
Furthermore, heaviness is not entirely absent in firewood and the like, as lightness is also found therein.
If it were not so, then when cast into water, it should not float.
Furthermore, existence and non-existence cannot coexist as simultaneous properties.

Nor should one say that it floats because of its "vastness," for vastness is a property of shape (*saṃsthāna*) and not of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*); if it were so, then vast objects such as stones would also have to float.

Furthermore, this nature of lightness is the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); therefore, its substance is not non-existent. That is to say, because of pliancy, one who cultivates meditative concentration experiences a sensation of lightness in the body; thus, one should not maintain that [this sensation] is non-existent or that it is not the fruit of pliancy.

If it were argued that something is called a "result" merely because it causes the body to be free from heavy contact, this reasoning is also incorrect; for lightness is itself a cause for the nourishment and growth of the body.
One should not claim that its absence can also nourish, for if that were so, the body would be nourished even in the absence of *prasrabdhi* (serenity).

If you claim that pliancy can eliminate heavy contact and that only the arising of the primary elements (mahābhūta) is called "nourishment" (puṣṭi), then one should say that the cessation of other primary elements by pliancy and the arising of other primary elements is what constitutes nourishment.
What is the purpose of establishing heaviness?

If the nature of heaviness were like that of lightness—meaning it did not exist as a distinct entity—then it would be identical to the position held by the Sthavira; however, this is unreasonable, because the two characteristics of lightness and heaviness do not exist within the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

If one maintains that the nature of lightness has as its substance a small portion of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), then one should maintain that when pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) manifests, only a small amount of the primary elements arises. Why?
Because pliancy arises in opposition to the primary elements; if they are in opposition, even a small amount [of them] should not arise.
If they were not mutually exclusive, what would obstruct the non-arising of the many?
Therefore, lightness (*praśrabdhi*) should not be the fruit of pliancy.
Furthermore, lightness does not have heaviness as its unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta-svabhāva*), because their categories differ, just like the nature of heaviness itself.
Furthermore, the Āgamas speak of lightness and heaviness, as it is said therein:
"Just as when there are iron balls or iron sheets, if fire is present, they become extremely hot."
At that time, there arises that which is extremely soft, extremely light, and extremely pliant, the opposite of this [previous state].
My body likewise becomes extremely rigid, extremely heavy, and extremely unpliant;
yet if there is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), then there is lightness and pliancy, making it capable of practicing abandonment.
Contrary to this, even if there is heaviness (*gurutva*), it lacks the function of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and is unfit for cultivation and abandonment.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Four;
*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter One, Part Five: The Fivefold Exposition of the Fundamental Matters. Furthermore, the Elder said:
When the fire element is slight or not intensified, it is termed "cold. Why is this?
Because in that case, either the sun is absent or it is far removed, and thus coldness arises.
Furthermore, just as when extreme heat arises, it is not that some distinct derivative tangible arises, but rather it is universally admitted that only the fire element increases;
so too, when the heat diminishes, there should likewise be no distinct derivative tangible produced, and it should be admitted that only the fire element decreases.

If cold were something distinct, one would also have to admit the existence of a distinct derived tangible that is neither warm nor cold; therefore, it is certain that there is no such thing as a derived tangible that is cold. Rather, what is called "cold" is simply the state where the fire element is minimal or not predominant.
We observe that those afflicted by the sensation of cold are able to find relief when the fire element increases.

If it were the case that an increase in the cause of affliction necessarily leads to further affliction, what wise person would hold such a view—that one who has been harmed by a small fire should throw themselves into a great fire?
If it is argued that there is harm because of a deficiency of fire, this is necessarily illogical, for there must certainly be other causes capable of causing harm.
That is to say, because the fire is slight, other increased cold elements are able to cause harm; it is not due to the fire itself.

Based on this, it is argued that to claim cold is a "beneficial" factor by virtue of being a minor cause implies that if the cause were increased, the resulting benefit would likewise increase; therefore, that treatise is not logically sound.

Furthermore, their claim that when heat increases or decreases, there is no produced entity and that it is merely fire itself, is also unreasonable; for we observe that two phenomena are mutually contradictory, such that when one phenomenon increases, the other decreases.

Just as when the path capable of abandoning [defilements] and the defilements to be abandoned [coexist], no distinct defilement arises when the path increases; likewise, no distinct defilement arises during the stage of regression from the path.

Furthermore, because the conditions for the arising of cold differ—namely, that within a conglomeration where the water and wind elements are predominant, the cause for the arising of cold exists rather than the fire element—one should not raise an objection based on the predominance of the fire element.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that the fire element becomes slightly cold, the fire within a mass of snow is extremely subtle and minimal; it should not be the case that the cold there is extremely abundant.
One should not say, as if the fire element were gradually diminishing.
In this way, it is logical that the fire element increases further and further;
for since they maintain that cold fire has no distinct substance, one cannot claim that a small amount of gold is therefore not gold.

Therefore, there exists a distinct entity different from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), which increases in its substance when the fire element (*tejodhātu*) diminishes; this derived tangible (*upādāyarūpa-spraṣṭavya*) is called "cold.

Some maintain the position that the increase of the primary elements produces the tangible of cold, and that this tangible of cold is identical to those primary elements. This reasoning is also incorrect, because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of cold differ from those of water and wind.

Furthermore, if it were established by two substances, its essence would have to be provisional (*prajñapti*), and it would consequently not be an object of tactile consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), because it would lack a distinct nature apart from coldness and warmth.

To argue that this is no different from the case of "no-distinct-coldness" is logically incorrect; for that [latter] is simply a specific state (*avasthā*) within the categories of coldness and so forth, distinguished by degrees such as mild or intense.
Other masters claim that cold and so forth have only heat as their unconditioned essence (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is also not correct, because their categories (*jāti*) differ; just as with heat and so forth, it is impossible for a non-existent phenomenon to possess a different category.

Alternatively, the functions of earth and so forth should be considered unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) in nature; for one could also say that what is merely water and so forth is called the "earth element" and so on. Therefore, what [the opponent] has stated does not refute that cold touch is a cause of derived matter (bhautika-rūpa).

Furthermore, because cold can serve as a condition for the arising of perception, it cannot be said that the fire element is simply non-existent where heat is absent; otherwise, there would have to be a mass of matter entirely devoid of fire, which is illogical given that existence and non-existence cannot coexist in such a manner.

Since fire must necessarily exist within all aggregates of matter (*rūpa-skandha*), cold-tangible objects (*śīta-spraṣṭavya*) would consequently be non-existent; therefore, we know that cold-tangible objects exist separately from fire.
Furthermore, the substance of all cold-tangible objects is truly existent, for their characteristics are distinct and can be presently perceived, just like heat and so forth.
Furthermore, because it is spoken of as "warmth" (*uṣman*) in the sūtras, its substance must necessarily exist; thus the sūtra says:

"I am able to endure both cold and warmth. If at that time the cold and warmth are balanced and appropriate, one is then able to bring [the practice] to maturity, realize, and achieve it; this is not the case when it is extremely cold or extremely warm.
If extreme cold or heat prevents one from performing activities, it follows that the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) of cold must truly exist.
Furthermore, the Venerable Sthavira says:
"The two types, hunger and thirst, are not derived matter, because their nature is that of longing."
This reasoning is also incorrect, because these two are names for the effect applied to the cause.
Due to a specific type of contact that afflicts the body, there arises a desire for food and drink; since this is the cause of hunger and thirst, it is called "hunger" and "thirst."
As for what was said regarding pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), it refers to the nature of physical lightness; it is called "pliancy" because it is the fruit of pliancy.

If that were so, this cause [of pliancy] should have heat as its nature, because the heat of the fire element can digest and assimilate food and drink, thereby giving rise to the desire for food and drink.
This statement is unreasonable; the two desires for food and drink would then have to be derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), because fire is their cause.
Furthermore, the fire element cannot be the cause of these two desires, for if it were, they would have to arise at all times.

We clearly observe that the two types of desire do not exist at all times; how then can it be that, according to your own school, although the primary elements (mahābhūta) which serve as the basis for the derivative tangible (upādāyarūpa) that causes desire are never absent, this derivative tangible itself is not always present?
This example is not applicable, because the desire for [tangible] objects arises in dependence upon the production of contact through the strengthening of the wind and fire elements.
If it is argued that the two types of desire should likewise be so, this is also illogical, as previously stated, because those two desires must be of the nature of derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).

If it is argued that just as the great elements (*mahābhūta*) which are contacted give rise to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), yet body-consciousness is not of the nature of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), so too should desire be;

this is not analogous. Consciousness does not necessarily arise only when the great elements are intensified, whereas desire is not like this, as it arises from intensification. Therefore, that body-consciousness does not depend on the great elements.
Whether they arise as equal or superior, their differentiation occurs only in accordance with their basis and not through their own distinctiveness.
They arise with the body and tangibles as conditions; this is not the case for the two [mental] desires, just as it is with derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
They arise due to the predominance of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Since they arise in accordance with the specific variations of the primary elements, for what reason are they obstructed such that they are not considered derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)?

If wind and fire are intense, the two desires increase; if wind and fire are subtle, the two desires decrease. Since they vary according to the intensity or subtlety of the primary elements, for what reason do these two desires not possess the nature of derived matter?

If it is argued that although the two types of desire arise from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), they do not depend upon them and are therefore not derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)—that is, desire depends on the mind and not on the primary elements—then this objection should not be raised to force their classification as derived matter.
If that were so, this desire would not need to depend on the increase of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) in order to arise.
One does not observe a body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) that arises in accordance with the specific variations of the primary elements without depending upon them;
rather, one observes only that body-consciousness takes the primary elements as its condition, arising through mere contact whenever they are equal or predominant.

If those two desires were thus, they should arise at all times without depending on a cause for their intensification; consequently, the difficulty previously stated—that the two desires would always arise and be difficult to stabilize or dispel—would follow.

Furthermore, although the elements of wind and fire may sometimes increase, the two desires for food and drink do not manifest; therefore, we know that these two desires do not arise due to the non-manifestation of their causes.
At that time, by what cause do those [two] causes fail to arise?
Because the supporting body possesses defects, or because it is obstructed by other conditions, the two types of desire do not arise.

Is it not precisely for this reason that they do not arise? Why then must one separately postulate that the tangible object (*spraṣṭavya*) produced by volition (*abhisamskāra*) is the cause of desire?
This cannot be so, because desire and body-consciousness would arise simultaneously; thus, even when there is an obstruction, consciousness would be able to arise while desire could not.
What logic is there for this?
When mental factors arise, they are necessarily bound to and dependent upon the mind; thus, these three—the mind, its object, and the consciousness—are always present together.
Furthermore, because that aspiration is subsumed within the stage of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna), it arises simultaneously with all classes of mind.
If the primary cause for the arising of desire is present at that time yet desire does not arise, it must be because other necessary conditions for its arising are lacking.
These other conditions refer to the derived tangible objects (*upādāya-spraṣṭavya*).
Therefore, apart from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), hunger and thirst do not exist as substantial entities; they have derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) as their nature.

Furthermore, one should not say that the obstructive contact produced by the primary elements is itself what obstructs the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), lest it follow that the obstruction produced by the mind and so forth is itself what obstructs the derived contact, for there would be no difference in their causes.

Let us cease this extensive dispute; one must certainly believe that there exist two distinct entities of hunger and thirst, which have the nature of derivative tangible objects (*upādāya-spraṣṭavya*).
Now, one should reflect upon this:
when the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) increase within a mass of matter (*rūpa-kalāpa*), do they constitute its essence (*svabhāva*) or its function (*vṛtti*)?
For what reason is one further exhorted to engage in such deliberation?
It is because one wishes to eliminate unreal faults.
As the Master of the Sūtras himself states in a certain passage of his own treatise:
This is the fault inherent in that school’s position.
That school refers to the Vaibhāṣikas,

who maintain that although all primary elements (mahābhūta) within a composite are equal in substance, there are some composites in which a particular function is predominant, just as it is with the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta).

Furthermore, regarding the taste of salt within a perceived lump [of food], I have not yet ascertained the intended meaning of this passage in the Sūtra. Specifically, who exactly is being referred to as a Vaibhāṣika?
If it is claimed to be the great masters who excellently explain the Abhidharma, they do not hold such a view.

He explains that the great elements (mahābhūta) are predominant by virtue of their essential nature; within the various aggregates of matter—such as stone, water, flame, and wind—the characteristics of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion are respectively predominant, because each individual aggregate is perceived as such.
If the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) within various aggregates were equal in substance, one should not perceive only one of them therein.

Furthermore, the designation of names such as "earth" based on worldly convention would be entirely without cause, being a mere empty verbal expression, since all material aggregates are identical in their shape and color.
If one maintains that the essence of solidity and so forth is uniform and without distinction, on what basis could distinct perceptions of "earth" and so forth arise?
If it is argued that this is due to their functions, the reasoning is necessarily untenable, because function is not distinct from the entity itself.
If activity were real, then it would increase the substance, because the real is identical to the substance.
If activity were unreal, it would likewise increase the substance, because it is not different from the substance.
There is no lack of practical utility, nor is there an increase in a separate substance; by this, the aforementioned mind and mental factors are explained.
Regarding the analogy of salt within a lump: since the function—namely, the sensation of salt and so forth—is identical to the substance itself, it is an increase in the substance-function.
In general, it is thus; however, there is a distinction: because the great elements possess resistance and are capable of accumulation, their spatial distinctions can be clearly discerned.
Sensation and the other [derived aggregates] are non-obstructive and cannot be accumulated; they differ only in terms of their functions and the variations in the intensity of their cognition.

Therefore, while the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) can be accumulated and are described as increasing in terms of their substance, the mind and mental factors are described as varying in intensity and subtlety in terms of their functional distinctions.
Is it not the case that material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) also increase in their functional efficacy?

For example, when vinegar is mixed with water, a potent medicine with poison, or salt with water, although the number of components in each case is the same, their functions differ. How, then, can you say that matter increases only in terms of its substantial entity (*dravya*)?

This is not contradictory, for although the atoms of contact between the vinegar and the water are equal, their tastes differ: the atoms of the taste of vinegar are more numerous, while the atoms of the taste of water are fewer; thus, the superiority of the vinegar's taste results from the increase in its substance.
Within various aggregates, because substances such as taste are predominant, they are said to be "predominant in function.
This is because categories such as excellent medicines and poisons differ according to the principles of dependent origination; such is the nature of their essential types.

Therefore, although they are few, they are able to subdue the many; it is not that a distinct function arises from a different ontological category. Thus, the insistence on the increase of function is a false conception.

Alternatively, just as with the categories of substance (*dravya*), so it is with the categories of type (*prakāra*); therefore, it is said that mind and the like increase only in terms of their functional application.
In terms of their essential nature (*tattva*), they are said to increase; that is, all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), for example, because they are established by depending on many bases.

Furthermore, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are said to increase in terms of their essential nature, because they are perceived in actuality, and because of both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*).

This means that when the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) increase, their substance (*dravya*) is directly perceivable, whereas their function (*kāritra*) and activity (*karman*) are not, because they possess accumulation and obstruction.
Regarding the scriptural authority (*āgama*), it is as stated in the *Bījopama-sūtra*:
"If there were an earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) without a water element (*ab-dhātu*), it would not aggregate, for there would be nothing to hold it together."
Each of these points is explained in detail as in the sutra.
The intent of this sutra is to state that there is no aggregate of matter entirely devoid of the water element; if it were entirely devoid of it, it would not be a cohesive combination.
However, there are cases where [the great elements] cannot encompass other aggregates of matter and cause them to coalesce, because they are too few.
The remaining realms should be understood by applying this same explanation.

As for the principle: if "increase" were spoken of in terms of the function alone rather than the accumulation of substance, then there would have to be an increase in function even upon a single atom (*paramāṇu*) of either the great elements or derived matter.

Just as in the case of a single dharma-substance such as sensation (*vedanā*), at times its activity increases so that it alone can serve as an object, for what reason do atoms (*paramāṇu*), when dwelling individually and separately,
fail to serve as objects for the arising of the five groups of consciousness?

Furthermore, regarding those atoms whose activity is predominant, their characteristics would be coarse and manifest, and thus they could not be considered atoms; therefore, for all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), increase is spoken of in terms of their substance, because they are accumulative and possess obstructive resistance (*sapratigha*).
For all non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*), which are non-accumulative and lack obstructive resistance, increase is spoken of in terms of their activity.
This principle having been established, it cannot be shaken.
Yet the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) states:

"The Vaibhāṣikas claim that although all primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are equally present in their essence within every aggregate, there may be some aggregates in which the function of a particular element is preponderant. This statement was made because he did not understand our school's tenets.
Furthermore, it should now be explained:

for what reason are solidity and the other [characteristics] the supports of matter (*rūpa*), and not the other [elements] such as matter itself? Because these [solidity and the rest] pervade all locations.

This means that within all aggregates, the four characteristics such as earth and so forth are universally present, whereas this is not the case for form and so forth. By virtue of this, the three meanings of earth and so forth are established:
first, the meaning of support; second, the meaning of production; and third, the meaning of vastness.

Furthermore, because it is pursued by form and the other [aggregates], we observe in the world that when objects such as jars or basins are matured by fire, transformations of form and the others can be perceived; and because there are distinctions in striking, tapping, or stroking, transformations of sound arise.
In other [elements] such as visible form, this is not the case.
Therefore, solidity and so forth are accompanied by visible form and the rest; they are the support of visible form, but not of the other [elements] such as visible form.
Furthermore, because they can destroy other material objects, visible form and the rest lack the capacity for destruction when supported by earth.
If that were so, then observing intense colors such as snow for a long time should not destroy the sense faculty.
This is not the case, because it is the basis of those colors that destroys the basis of the faculty.

Since one perceives the arising of suffering when looking at them in the dark, we know that only the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are destroyed, not the faculty; for if the faculty were destroyed, one would not perceive the arising of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
Furthermore, derived matter (*rūpa*) cannot destroy the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), because it is not an object of touch.
Therefore, since the primary elements alone are capable of destroying other material things, they are the support of derived matter, and not derived matter or the like.
Some say: "Because they possess the nature of being tangible as solidity and so forth, they can serve as a basis.
This statement is irrational, because coldness and the like would then necessarily become primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
However, because tactile sensations such as coldness are not all-pervasive, they do not constitute great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Is it not the case that there is no sensation of cold within heat, and likewise no sensation of heat within cold? If so, heat should be like cold in not being a great element.
This objection is not valid, because coldness exists within warmth; it is merely imperceptible due to being covered by the latter.
If that were so, the tactile quality of coldness would have to be as pervasive as warmth.

This is not the case, because the function of coldness is absent within warmth, whereas the function of warmth can be perceived within coldness, but the function of coldness cannot be perceived within warmth.
The objection that "coldness is as pervasive as warmth" should be set aside.
What is the function of warmth?
It is the capacity to bring things to maturity.
Have you not seen that cold can also bring about maturation? Just as an object does not rot or decay because of warmth, the cause of its not decaying is called "that which brings about maturation";
cold is likewise, and should therefore be the same as warmth.

This is also not the case; for water and wind elements may temporarily congeal when they are predominant, and it is because of their function as heat that they mature therein. Therefore, one should not say that [the elements] serve as a support by virtue of having the nature of tangibles such as solidity, for if so, coldness and the like would also have to constitute the nature of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
However, that sensation of cold is a derived form (upādāya-rūpa), because it is the fruit of the four great elements resulting from the predominance of the water and wind elements.
Furthermore, the substance of that sensation of cold is not a primary element (mahābhūta), because the four definitive functions of supporting, cohesion, maturing, and growth cannot be found therein.
Is it not because cold, snow, and so forth possess a superior efficacy through their congealing?
This statement is irrational, for it is when the water and wind elements are predominant that they produce the cold sensation which gives rise to those effects.
Furthermore, it is precisely because of heat that substances such as sugarcane juice can be solidified.
If you claim that cold is the result of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), then since cold and heat are mutually contradictory, they should not coexist; how, then, could cold arise from heat?

Just as solidity and moisture do not contradict one another because they share a single objective basis, so it is with water and fire; since they share a single objective basis, there is no logical reason for them to be opposed.

For example, when cold water is poured over quicklime, heat is produced from that coldness; this case should be understood in the same way. Because the primary elements (mahābhūtas) share a single objective basis, they remain in constant conjunction despite their mutually contradictory natures.
Cold is a fruit produced in proximity to water and wind; the earth element is entirely non-contradictory with them.
Although the nature of fire is contradictory, it does not cause harm, because they share a single fruit; thus, what prevents their conjunction?

Furthermore, because one observes that those elements increase, one posits distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*) within the aggregates; since those elements are the causes capable of producing all derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), they are termed "primary elements."
It is not because cold increases that a distinct primary element (mahābhūta) is established within the aggregates; therefore, it is not a primary element.
However, because heat increases, within the aggregates the notion of one primary element ceases and the notion of another primary element arises.
Cold is not like this; therefore, there is a distinction between the two natures of the cold and the warm as the supported and the support.
Is it not evident that through the increase of cold, the water element solidifies, and the world likewise applies various names such as ice, snow, and hail to this?
This objection is like the previous explanation regarding how the elements of water and wind, when intensified, produce the result of a cold sensation.

Alternatively, ice, snow, and hail are merely different names for water; grass, wood, and the like are not given the different name "fire. Therefore, the logic of that objection is certainly inconsistent.
Therefore, the sensation of cold is exclusively of a derivative nature; by this, the element of tangibility (spraṣṭavyadhātu) is established as having two aspects.

The remaining nine material elements are exclusively derivative, namely: the five sense organs, and the objects of form, sound, odor, and taste. A portion of the element of mental objects (dharmadhātu) is likewise exclusively derivative.
What does this mean? It means that because unmanifest karma arises in dependence upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it is called "derived" (*upādāya*).
However, the term "sound" is used to demonstrate that there is certainly no single element whose nature consists solely of primary elements.

The remaining seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and one portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), excluding non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*), are established by implication as being neither of the two types [of derived matter].
The Dārṣṭāntika masters maintain this view, stating:
"All derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is not distinct from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)."
Why is this so? Because it is stated in the sūtras.
As it is said:
What is called the internal earth element?
It refers to whatever is internal, individual, solid, and of a solid nature within the fleshy mass of the eye, closely grasped [as one's own], and so forth, as explained at length.
If the various sense-faculties existed separately from the primary elements, one should not speak of the nature of the primary elements in relation to those faculties.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that all persons consist of nothing other than the six elements."

Since it has already been established that the six [bases] are the real entities (vastu) upon which the conventional designation of a "sentient being" depends, we know that the derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) of the eyes and so forth, as well as visible forms and so forth, are not distinct from the primary elements (mahābhūta).
If derived matter were distinct from the various primary elements, for what purpose would this sūtra not have stated so?
That statement is unreasonable, for it fails to comprehend the profound intent of the sūtra.
The sūtra cited previously made that assertion in accordance with worldly designations and conceptions;

that is to say, worldly people give rise to the designation "eye" with respect to the physical mass of flesh that is the eye, and this designation "eye" arises based upon the primary elements (mahābhūta) and so forth that serve as the support for the eye.
Regarding the "flesh-ball of the eye," this is said in general to consist of all that is derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta) and is not separate from the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya).
If it were otherwise, this sutra would have stated only: "within the eye, each distinct [part]," and so forth, or "the quality of solidity," and so forth.
Since the "eye of wisdom" has already been refuted, it is unnecessary to speak of the term "flesh-ball" therein.
Furthermore, the word "eye" is used in the locative sense of cause (*hetu-saptamī*), whereas the term "within the flesh-ball" is used in the locative sense of support (*āśraya-saptamī*).

From this it is known that all that arises from the eye is subsumed under the cause consisting of the primary elements (mahābhūta) derived from the sense-organ (indriya) of the eye; these are not separate from the great elements.

Within the fleshy mass produced by the eye, whatever exists internally and individually is called the internal earth element (pṛthivīdhātu). This demonstrates the productive cause (janakahetu) and the supporting cause (niśrayahetu) for the eye and so forth, such as the earth element; by repeating the locative case (saptamī-vibhakti) twice, all that is the eye and the great elements upon which the fleshy mass depends are subsumed.

The reason the cited sūtra later mentions only the six elements and does not speak of others is due to a specific underlying intention: namely, that at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), the eye and other [faculties] do not yet exist.
Although the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is present in this stage, it is still unable to perceive tactile objects such as cold.
If a phenomenon possesses an intrinsic nature but has not yet performed its function, it should not be established among those things that have utility.

Furthermore, only the six elements constitute the fundamental entities that possess utility for sentient beings, because they are constantly functional from the moment of the mind at rebirth-linking until the final moment of the mind at death.
What is the function of consciousness for one abiding in the meditative attainment of cessation?

That past consciousness can act as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the future; by means of this, the future fruit is determined to arise. This is the function of that consciousness.
If that were so, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) should also have a function, because the function of its homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) has never been absent.
This objection is not valid, because there is a distinction between being definitively accomplished and being definitively accomplished [in a specific way].
This means that although the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) may not be fully accomplished, it still possesses the function of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) that yields its fruit;

whereas it is certain that the substance of that consciousness cannot be unaccomplished while acting as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for a future fruit. Therefore, the status of consciousness and the body-faculty are not equivalent.

Furthermore, the function of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is not that of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); rather, its function as the basis for the arising of consciousness is its function as a body-faculty.

For one who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the function of the final consciousness that will necessarily arise upon emerging from it is the function of the preceding consciousness.
Therefore, it is logically established that only the six elements constitute the fundamental substantial bases for all sentient beings.
Alternatively, the space element may be cited here to represent all derived matter; thus, citing this sutra does not preclude the existence of derived matter.
The space element (ākāśadhātu) truly exists as a derived form (upādāyarūpa), for this has already been established previously.

Furthermore, if one maintains that derived form is not distinct from the primary elements (mahābhūta), then it would follow that all forms and so forth share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristics of solidity and so on.

If that were so, there would be no distinction between the objects of the five faculties, such as the eye; this would contradict what is stated in the sūtras regarding the distinct objects of the eye and the other faculties.
How can it be maintained that the objective spheres, such as form, all possess the same characteristic, namely, the characteristic of solidity and so forth?
However, it is not the case that all objects are the domain of all sense faculties; this [position] cannot satisfy the minds of the wise.

If one were to argue that there is no such fault because the five objects, such as visible form, are said to share a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being derived matter (upādāya-rūpa)—[the response would be as follows].

As for the claim that there is no fault in the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) sharing the same characteristics—namely, the characteristics of solidity and so forth—that is also not the case, because it is not admitted that the nature of derived matter possesses a distinct ontological essence.

Furthermore, the sense organs such as the eye apprehend specific, determinate characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) regarding their respective objects such as visible form, rather than indeterminate, general characteristics. Why is this so?

Because this school does not admit that derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) possesses a distinct substantial entity (*dravya-svabhāva*) for its nature, as is the case with the characteristics of solidity and so forth; therefore, one cannot claim that—just as it is said of visible form and the rest—that although they share the same self-nature (*svabhāva*) of being derived matter, the distinction between the objects of the eye organ and the others is nonetheless established.

Thus, although visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth share the same specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as hardness and other such qualities, they are established as distinct objects for the sense faculties such as the eye.

Furthermore, the sense faculties such as the eye apprehend the determinate specific characteristics of their respective objects like visible form, rather than their general characteristics. This is to avoid the great logical fallacy that, because the general characteristics of the sense faculties and their objects like visible form would be identical, those objects would also be apprehended by all five sense faculties.

Furthermore, since dharmas such as sensation (vedanā) and objects such as form (rūpa) share the same characteristic—namely, the aspect of mental activity (ākāra)—sensation and the like should also be apprehended by the eye and the other sense organs.

Therefore, one must certainly admit that form and the other objects possess distinct categories of unique characteristics; for this reason, although each individual sense organ can apprehend multiple aspects, there is no fault of confusion among the objects of the five organs, because their categories are distinct.

If it is argued that just as those five faculties, such as the eye, though sharing the same characteristic—namely, the characteristic of clarity and purity—are each able to apprehend their respective objects, so too color-form and the other [objects], though sharing the same characteristic—namely, the characteristic of solidity and so forth—are each the distinct domains of the eye and the other [faculties].
This is also not the case, because other phenomena also possess the characteristic of clarity and purity.
If the characteristic of clarity and purity were the specific characteristic of the sense organs such as the eye, then one should not admit that other phenomena also possess this characteristic.

Nevertheless, the characteristic of clarity is also admitted to exist; therefore, clarity is not a distinctive characteristic of the eye and other sense faculties, whereas solidity, moisture, and so forth are their distinctive characteristics.

If one maintains that the characteristics of form and so forth are identical in both cases, yet asserts that the eye faculty perceives only the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) and not the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), there is no distinct reason or evidence for this.
Alternatively, although the eye and other faculties share the same purity of nature, their functional capacities differ; therefore, they apprehend their respective objects separately.
Regarding the difference in functional capacity: it arises from the distinction among causes.

Although the eye and other faculties are alike in being effects of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the proportions of these elements vary; since the causes differ, the functional capacities of their effects differ. It is by virtue of this that the principle of the distinct apprehension of objects is established.

Furthermore, one should not claim that the distinctions among form and so forth also arise from the different increases or decreases of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); for if that were the case, there would be the fault that atoms (*paramāṇu*) could not be established.
Therefore, this defense of yours is logically untenable.
Furthermore, how does that venerable one establish the distinction between the object (*ālambana*) and the subject (*ālambaka*)?

For instance, when a person touches their own body, since they maintain that the body and the touch are of a single characteristic and are mutually indistinguishable within a single moment, whom could one designate as the object?
What constitutes the objective field (*viṣaya*)?
If there is a distinction, the definition of the categories is established.

That which is touched by the characteristics of solidity and so forth is called the object; that which is contrary to this is called the sensory faculty (*indriya*). This is because it is admitted that there is a distinction between the nature of the body and the nature of tangibility.
If there were no distinction, then there would be no established differentiation between the object (*ālambana*) and the subject (*ālambaka*), which would contradict both reason and scripture.

If it is argued that, although the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses a single characteristic, there is no contradiction in establishing it as both object and subject within a single moment, this reasoning is also incorrect; for while the mental consciousness serves as an object, it is at all times established as a subject. Therefore, such a fault does not exist.

However, the primary elements (mahābhūta) such as solidity, which are the objects of the body faculty, have never at any time been established as having an object; therefore, that attempted rebuttal by analogy is fundamentally inconsistent.
If one were to grant that the primary elements such as solidity, which are the objects of the body faculty, are also "possessors of an object" (viṣayin), what fault would there be?

The *manas* (mind) should be established as a single location; in that case, there would be no definitive establishment of this as the *kāyāyatana* (body-base) and this as the *spraṣṭavyāyatana* (tangible-base).
One must explain what fixed principle exists therein to determine that this is exclusively an object (*viṣaya*) and that this is exclusively a subject possessing an object (*viṣayin*).
Therefore, their fundamental tenets are confused and difficult to distinguish.

Furthermore, if form and so forth were identical to the great elements (*mahābhūta*), then their claim that each individual atom (*paramāṇu*) of blue color is either the four great elements or is only one [element] would entail faults in both cases.

However, although the sense-spheres such as form share the common designation "form," they possess distinct characteristics of nature, such as blue, masculine, fragrance, sweetness, and coldness; because these five objects differ from one another in this way, the five faculties, such as the eye, do not have the fault of having a common object.

If the fundamental elements (mahābhūta) were distinct in their nature and characteristics, yet identical in essence to the blue atom (paramāṇu), then since they would not be different, the fourfold nature [of the elements] could not be established.

Furthermore, if the blue atom consisted of only one fundamental element, then the four fundamental elements would necessarily be mutually separated, because a single aggregate would then contain only one fundamental element.

This would contradict and harm such sūtras as the *Bījopama-sūtra* (The Simile of the Seed), for it is not reasonable that distinct natures and characteristics of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) should result in non-distinction.
If one claims that a single mass of blue color arises because one [element] increases, one must explain which element increases to make it blue?
If one were to claim it is the earth element, then ponds, rivers, and oceans should not possess a blue color.
If one were to claim it is the water element, then jade, blue stones, and the like should not be intensely blue.
If one were to claim it is the fire element, then the blazing fires of the world should not be intensely red.
If one were to claim that it is the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*), then color should not be unobtainable within the wind.

If it is said that blue color is distinct from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) yet exists as a real entity that conforms to the increase of a single element—such that many of the four great elements each produce blue color which combines to form a single aggregate—this would not contradict reason; therefore, there is derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) that is distinct from the primary elements.
Furthermore, there is authoritative scripture that clearly establishes this, as stated in a sutra:
"All forms whatsoever are comprised within the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements."
Furthermore, what reasoning is there to know that the derived [matter] designated by speech is distinct from the primary elements and has its own specific objective referent?
Yet the Sūtra states:
"There are some foolish persons who, through the six bases of contact, experience pleasure or pain upon encountering various objects; or, in some cases, it is produced by those [objects]."
One cannot conclude from this statement regarding "derived" (*bhautika*) matter that there exists a separate seventh sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
This is not a definitive proof, for there are instances where such a term "derived" is used even when referring to things that possess distinct natures.
As it was said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"That which is produced by the view of self—by what is it produced?
It is said: "It is produced by form," and so on, as explained at length.

If one sees that in other instances where something is produced, there is no distinct referent, and thus concludes that this case is likewise so, then there would necessarily be a view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) having form as its essence; this would entail the fault of contradicting one's own tenets.

Furthermore, one should not entertain doubts regarding this sutra’s statement that [derived matter] is produced from the primary elements (mahābhūta) on the grounds that the nature of the phenomena referred to by the term "produced" might be either different or non-different [from the primary elements], since other sūtras definitively establish their difference.
As stated in the Sūtra:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that 'eye' refers to the internal sense-base (āyatana), which is derived from the four great elements (mahābhūta) and consists of translucent matter (rūpa-prasāda); it is visible, yet non-apparent, and possesses resistance. This is explained at length for the 'body-base' as well."

"O Bhikṣus, you should know that 'form' refers to the external sense base (āyatana) which is derived from the four great elements (mahābhūta), possessing form, being visible, and being resistant. 'Sound' refers to the external sense base derived from the four great elements, possessing form, being invisible, and being resistant. The two bases of odor and taste are likewise explained in detail. 'Tangible objects' refer to the external sense base consisting of the four great elements and what is derived from the four great elements, possessing form, being invisible, and being resistant."

In this context, it is clearly explained that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are subsumed solely within one part of the sense-field of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), while all other material sense-fields are not primary elements. Therefore, we know for certain that the terms "primary" and "derived" (*upādāya*) function here as they do in the *Ahaṃkāra-sūtra*, where "the derived self" refers to something distinct [from the primary elements]. It is certainly not the case that, as in the *Ṣaṭsparśāyatana-sūtra*, one particular derived element lacks a distinct referent.
Therefore, it is established that a portion of the nine material dharmas within the dharma-realm is produced by something other than the four great elements.
Thus has the nature of the great elements been explained.
Among the eighteen realms, the ten material realms—consisting of the five sense organs and the five objects—are capable of accumulation, because their substance as atoms can be gathered together.
By logical extension, the other eight [elements] are not accumulative, because their substance is not composed of atoms and thus cannot be aggregated.
Having thus explained what is accumulative and so forth,
among the eighteen elements, how many are capable of cutting and how many are objects to be cut?
How many are the burners and how many are the burned?
How many are the weighers and how many are the weighed?
These six categories should now be answered collectively.
The verse says:
It is held that only the four external elements can both cut and be cut;
they are also what is burned and what weighs. They are also what burns and what is weighed; [regarding these] there is dispute.
The treatise states:
Visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility constitute the axe, the firewood, and so forth; these are what are termed "the cutter" and "the cut.
The term "only" (kevala) serves as a restrictive definition, intended to clarify that cutting and the like are definitively comprised of the four external elements and nothing else.
The inclusion of the word "and" (ca) is intended to show that both the agent of cutting and the object of cutting are common to all four elements.
One might ask: since conditioned phenomena are momentary by nature, does it not follow that they entirely lack the status of being either the agent or the object of cutting?

Although this is the principle, the various aggregates of matter arise in continuous succession, and distinct conditions separate them so that they each arise in succession; therefore, it is not the case that there is no "that which cuts" or "that which is cut."

Regarding this meaning of being "cut": it does not apply to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the other [faculties], for the various material faculties cannot be made into two distinct continuities by being separated through different conditions; this is because once a limb is severed from the body, that part no longer possesses the faculty.
Furthermore, the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the others are also not capable of cutting, because they possess a pure and subtle nature, like the light of a precious gem.
These meanings are expressed solely by words; just as the entities that can cut and are cut consist only of the four external elements.
The nature of that which is burned and that which weighs is likewise: namely, only the four external elements are designated as "the burned" and "the weigher.
Because the physical sense organs, such as the body, possess a subtle and refined character, they are not either of these two things, just like the light of a jewel.
Sound does not arise in a continuous stream alongside [the object] like visible form and the other [sensory objects], because it is interrupted; thus, none of the six criteria apply.
Regarding the burner and the weighed object, there are differing disputes.
That is to say, some maintain:
The nature of that which burns and that which is weighed is also as previously stated: they consist solely of the four external elements.
Alternatively, some say that only the fire element can be called "that which burns," while "that which is weighed" refers exclusively to heaviness.
Having thus explained the agent and object of cutting and so forth,

among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are born of maturation (*vipākaja*), how many are nurtured (*aupacayika*), how many are of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*), how many possess substantial reality (*dravyasat*), and how many are momentary (*ekakṣaṇika*)?
These five questions should now be answered collectively.
The verse says:
The five internal [bases] possess both maturation and nutriment; Sound does not arise from maturation.
The eight unimpeded [knowledges] are of the nature of outflow and also of the nature of maturation;
the remaining three are substantially only dharmas; and in terms of moments, only the latter three [are momentary].
The Treatise says:

The five internal [bases] refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. They consist of both that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and that which is nurtured (*aupacayika*); their nature as "outflow" (*naiṣyandika*) is excluded, and for this reason they are not so designated. [Objection:

Is it not the case that the five elements of the eye and so forth, having arisen previously, must certainly be said to act as causes for the eyes and other faculties that arise later or have not yet arisen? If this were so, these eyes and others would possess an outflow-nature, because a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) produces an outflow-result (*naiṣyandika-phala*).
For what reason, then, is it said that they exclude "outflow-nature" (*niṣyanda-svabhāva*)?

It is not said that the eyes and so forth lack outflow-nature altogether; rather, since their nature as being produced by nourishment (*puṣṭi*) or maturation (*vipāka*) is such that there is no distinct outflow-nature, it must be excluded.

Just as there is a distinct "nourished" (aupacayika) arising that differs from "retribution-born" (vipākaja), and a distinct "nourished" arising that differs from "retribution-born," there is no separate "outflowing" (naiṣyandika) apart from these two; however, in order to distinguish different categories, the general discussion is set aside to treat the specific case.
