Chapter One, Part Six: The Analysis of the Fundamental Matters. Thus has been explained the attainment of accomplishment and so forth.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are internal and how many are external?
The verse says:
Twelve are internal, such as the eye and so forth; The six, such as visible form and so forth, are external.
The treatise says:
The six sense organs and the six consciousnesses—these twelve are called "internal. The "external" refers to the remaining six objects, such as form and so forth.
That which serves as the basis for the notion of "self" is called internal; everything else is external.
Since the self-entity (*ātman*) does not exist, how could there be anything internal or external?
It is not that pure morality (*śīla*) does not exist; rather, there is a basis for pure morality. Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtrakāra*) provides the following explanation:
"Because it is the basis for the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), the mind is metaphorically designated as 'self'."
Therefore, a sutra says:
"By well-taming oneself, the wise attain birth in heaven.
Elsewhere, the Blessed One spoke of taming the mind, as a sutra states:
"One should well subdue the mind; a subdued mind can lead to happiness.
Therefore, it is only with respect to the mind that we metaphorically designate "self.
Because the eyes and so forth are its immediate supports, they are called "internal."
Form and so forth are called "external" because they are remote from being the objects of this [consciousness].
If that were the case, the six consciousnesses should not be called "internal," for as long as they have not yet reached the state of the mind (manas), they do not serve as the support for the mind.

When reaching the state of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), it does not lose its nature as the six consciousness-elements; nor, when not yet having reached the state of the mind-element, does it transcend the characteristic of the mind.

If it were otherwise, the mind-element would exist only in the past and the six consciousnesses only in the present and future, which would contradict your own school’s tenet that all eighteen elements (*dhātus*) pervade all three periods of time.

Furthermore, if the six consciousnesses of the future and present lacked the characteristic of the mental element (*manodhātu*), they would likewise not be established even when reaching the state of the past mental element, because characteristics do not undergo alteration across the three periods of time.
This explanation is not correct; it must now be addressed.

For what reason, among those mental states and mental factors that share a single arising, a single abiding, a single cessation, and a single fruit, is the mind designated as "internal" while the mental factors are designated as "external"?

Is it not the case that the mind, as the basis for mental factors (*caitta*), should be called "internal" because it is the nature of the supported (*āśrita*) and is extremely intimate with its basis?

Furthermore, while the eye and so forth do not always serve as the basis for visual consciousness and so forth, there has never been an instance where the mind does not serve as the nature of the basis for mental factors; therefore, only the mental factors should be designated as "internal."

Alternatively, what special principle is there here such that those which serve as the basis for the conventional notion of "self" are established as "internal," while those which depend upon them are not?
Therefore, what they have said lacks any profound underlying logic.
Furthermore, only a small portion of the mind is the basis for the grasping at a self, whereas all bases of the mind are termed "internal. Therefore, one should not provide such an explanation:
that because it is the support for the grasping at a self, the mind is metaphorically designated as the "self."
Furthermore, because a small portion of the mind is the basis for greed and so forth, all minds would consequently become defiled.
Or, because a small portion of the mind is the basis for vitarka and vicāra, all [minds] would consequently be accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Since this is not the case, how could that be so?
For no distinct causes and conditions can be found.
Furthermore, how could it possibly exclude the nature of the self-grasping that relies upon the mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth?
Because the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) takes the five aggregates of clinging as its object,
that interpretation is certainly not logical. If so,
for what reason is the mind said to be the self?
Because it always functions with mastery over its own object.
"Self" (ātman) refers to that which always functions with mastery over its own object; since the mind never at any time fails to function upon its own object, all minds are termed "self."

Nor do the mental factors (caitta) receive the name "self," because the mind (manas) is their chief, because the Sūtras state that it proceeds alone, and because they must depend upon the mind to function with respect to objects.
Just as, although all mental factors (*caitta*) are likewise subdued, one speaks of "subduing the mind" only with reference to its predominance;
so too it is said of the "self": it is only the mind and not the mental factors.
If a phenomenon provides a unique benefit to this mind that resembles a self, it is termed "internal."
Contrary to this, other dharmas are termed "external"; therefore, there is no fault of mental concomitants (caitta) being internal.
Furthermore, although mental concomitants arise, abide, and so forth simultaneously with the mind, the mind alone is designated as "internal" in relation to the mind.
Regarding those that are not mental factors (*caitta*), they function as the nature of the support (*āśraya*) for one another across different classes of mind, because they never abandon it.
On the other hand, all mental factors, when compared to the mind of a different class, must necessarily be separated from it, because they possess the nature of being supported (*āśrita*).
That is to say, if a wholesome mind takes a wholesome, afflicted, or neutral mind as its basis, it does not abandon them; the same applies to afflicted and neutral minds.

If a virtuous mental factor, in relation to that defiled or neutral mind, relinquishes its status as the supported nature (*āśrita-svabhāva*), and likewise for a defiled or neutral factor in relation to others, then the mind, in relation to the mind, functions as the supporting nature (*āśraya-svabhāva*) without any intervening distinction; thus it is designated as "internal.
Mental factors, however, in relation to the mind, function as the supported nature and possess an intervening distinction; therefore, they do not receive the designation "internal."
Furthermore, among the mental factors (*caitta*), when compared to their corresponding primary mind (*citta*), they function as its supports (*āśraya*) to a greater or lesser extent.
The primary mind, however, does not function as a support for them in this same way; for this reason, the designation "internal" (*ādhyātmika*) applies to the mind but not to the mental factors.
If that were so, the great dharmas (mahābhūmika-dharmas) should also receive the designation "internal.

This is not the case, because it would destroy the classification of mental factors (*caitta*), just as among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) there are those who do not fall into the category of [wholesome] dharmas.

Furthermore, other masters explain the term "internal" based on etymological reasoning (*nirukti*), stating: "Because the self (*ātman*) exercises a predominant influence over them, they are called internal."
I maintain that the self-substance (*ātman*) possesses a predominant efficacy (*adhipatya*) with respect to other phenomena.
As the venerable Kumāralāta stated in this verse:
"If there were no distinct predominant efficacy In the nails, fingers, or the tip of the tongue..."
"Moving, touching, and tasting delicacies—its functions should not differ.

Within the various aggregates of form, such as color, fragrance, taste, and touch, either the body-faculty alone exercises a predominant function, and so it is explained at length up to the eye-faculty.
The mind also exercises predominant influence over other [factors]; therefore, all twelve [bases] receive the designation "internal.
If that were so, since one also observes that the specific natures of feeling and the others exercise predominant influence over other [factors], then all dharmas should be designated as "internal."

Since, according to the school of the Elder (Sthavira), all phenomena are subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), how does that school establish the distinction between internal and external?
They say it is "as in other cases. How is it "as in other cases"?
That which serves as the basis for the six consciousnesses is established as internal, while that which does not serve as the basis for the six consciousnesses is established as external.
Now, that which serves as a basis belongs exclusively to the category of sentient beings and is both intimate and unique; matter and so forth are not so determined.
Just as with those forms and so forth,

although they too are included among sentient beings, are proximate, and are not shared [with others], yet because they are not the basis [for consciousness], they are established as external and not as internal.

Thus, although the eye and so forth are included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), because they serve as the bases for sensation and the like, they are established as internal and not external; the remaining portion of the sphere of mental objects is designated solely as external.

Furthermore, although the eye and other faculties both pertain to the two divisions [internal and external], their internal and external natures are not mutually contradictory; therefore, one should not maintain that this constitutes a difficulty.

That is to say, when they serve as the support (*āśraya*) for visual consciousness and the like, they are established as having an internal nature; when they serve as the objective sphere (*ālambana*) for mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they are established as having an external nature.

That [opponent] claims that the faculty of mind (manas-indriya), while being included within the internal bases (ādhyātmikāyatana), is also included within the external bases (bāhyāyatana) because it is the object of the mental consciousness (mano-vijñāna).
Such categories and expressions as these are merely following one's own whims and are unable to refute the fault.
This resembles inference but lacks authentic scriptural authority. Why is this so?
Because it contradicts the sūtras.
As stated in the Sūtra:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that 'dharmas' refers to the external sense base (*bāhyāyatana*), which consists of those dharmas not included within the other eleven bases; they are invisible and non-obstructive.

Now, according to this sūtra, it is not the case that all dharmas are subsumed under the *dharmāyatana*, because this sūtra specifically excludes from the *dharmāyatana* those dharmas that are already included within the other eleven bases.

Nor is it the case that only those distinct dharmas they [the opponents] grasp are called the *dharmāyatana*, because in this sūtra, unlike the case of the *manāyatana*, it does not speak of formless [entities].

In their own school, they maintain that only the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) are called the distinct *dharmāyatana*, and within these, there is no form.
If this sūtra were to teach the locus of phenomena based on those distinct dharmas, then just as it states they are "invisible and non-resistant," it would likewise have stated they are "formless.

For this reason, within this sūtra, there is a repeated and extensive negation of any dharma other than the loci of the eye and so forth—namely, that such a dharma is not subsumed within the eleven loci and is invisible and non-resistant.

If form consisted only of that which is visible and resistant, with no other form remaining, and one intended simply to explain the distinct category of the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), one should have said merely: "Dharma refers to the external base not subsumed under the mind-base (manāyatana) and is also formless."
Consequently, this distinct category of *dharmāyatana*—which is not included within the [other] eleven [bases] and is invisible and non-resistant—is established.
Alternatively, one should say that what is invisible and non-resistant but not included within the *manāyatana* is also formless (*arūpa*), because the term "formless" is not explicitly stated here.

Furthermore, because it excludes the eye and other sense bases from being subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), it is established that there exists a distinct category of form within the sphere of phenomena.
What is this form? It is called unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*).
This shall be examined together in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
How is it that others may understand that although the sense bases such as the eye are objects of the mind (*manas*), they are exclusively internal?
Therefore, in this sutra, the inclusion within a general number and their specific distinctions are excluded in order to reveal the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

This means that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, observing future generations, foresaw that there would be those who call themselves disciples of the Śākya (Śākyaputrīya) and would maintain that all phenomena (dharmas) are the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
To refute them, he spoke with clarity and precision, saying: "The sphere of mental objects consists of this alone; it is not all phenomena."

Therefore, it is only with respect to the characteristics of the *dharmāyatana* (the sphere of mental objects) that one speaks of its not being subsumed under the other eleven spheres; for since there is no sense of mutual inclusion among the eye and the other [senses], such a statement is not made regarding the spheres of the eye and so forth.
Furthermore, because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can take all phenomena as its objects, one must ensure that not all phenomena are thereby subsumed within the *dharmāyatana*.
Therefore, it is refuted in this manner within this context.

Furthermore, the position held by that Venerable Elder—that the eye and so forth possess both internal and external natures—must necessarily fail to be established; for nowhere has it been stated that when the eye and so forth serve as the support (*āśraya*) for visual consciousness and the like, they are established as internal, and when they serve as the objective sphere (*ālambana*) for mental consciousness, they are established as external.
By this, the mental faculty (*manas*) cited [as an example] is immediately refuted, for it has never been stated [in scripture] to be like the eye and other faculties.
How can you call yourself a master of resolving difficulties while remaining utterly ignorant of the method for establishing a homologous example (*sapakṣa*)?
Since this is already the case, why cite the distant as an example?
To establish that the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya) possesses the nature of pervading both the internal and external, one should instead cite the nearby ear as the analogous instance;
likewise, to establish that the auditory faculty (śrotra-indriya) possesses the nature of pervading both the internal and external, one should also cite the nearby eye as the analogous instance.
The Elder stated that the nature of the eye and so forth as being both internal and external must necessarily be established, just as the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that whatever eyes there are—whether past, future, or present; whether internal or external—and so forth, up to the detailed explanation—the same applies to the mind."
If that were so, it would entail the fault of over-extension, as stated in the Sūtra:
"One dwells contemplating the body within the internal body," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, as another Sūtra says:
"Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; whether internal or external," and so forth, as explained at length.

Since there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) within form and the other aggregates, the Sūtra should not have used the phrase "whatever there may be. Furthermore, how could there be an "internal" aspect within feeling, perception, and mental formations?
Furthermore, you yourself previously stated that whatever serves as the support for the six consciousnesses is established as "internal.

Since you have granted this, it follows that form and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth—which are not the supports of consciousness—should be called exclusively "external. Why, then, does the Sūtra speak of them as "internal"?
Just as form, sensation, and so forth, although spoken of with the term "internal," are not internal bases but are subsumed solely under the external bases;
likewise, the eye and so forth, although spoken of with the term "external," are not the dharma-base but are subsumed solely under the internal bases.
If that is so, what is the intended meaning of the sutra?
We shall together investigate the intention of this sutra.
Your previous statement is, moreover, unreasonable; I shall now explain the intended meaning of this sutra.
That is to say, the eye and so forth, which serve as the bases for consciousness, are called "internal," while form and so forth, which are the objects of cognition, are called "external.
There is no dispute regarding this.

Furthermore, just as the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)—whether already arisen, currently arising, or yet to arise—is called "internal" because it is the support for consciousness, that which is contrary to this is called "external"; this applies likewise to the mental faculty (*manas*) and its internal and external aspects. Moreover, if an object such as form functions within the same body as the support of consciousness, it is called "internal," and that which is contrary to this is called "external."
Thus, establishing the internal and external in terms of location and the physical basis does not contradict the holy teachings and accords with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, the position established by the Venerable [Vasumitra] that the eye and other faculties possess the nature of being both internal and external is certainly untenable. It is not merely untenable; its definitions are also confused, because he maintains that the nature of being internal or external consists in the eye and other faculties serving as the bases and objects for consciousness, which results in a confusion of their defining characteristics.
That is to say, when the mental consciousness arises taking the mind that serves as its support as its object, where should this mind be said to reside?
It cannot be said to be internal, because it is the object of the mental consciousness;
nor can it be said to be external, because it is the support of the mental consciousness.

It should not be categorized as either internal or external, because this is not stated in the sūtras. No sūtra has ever stated that such a mental faculty (manas-indriya) is internal, external, or both internal and external. [Objection:
Is it not said that there is a mind that is both internal and external?
This is explained as "internal" and "external" with respect to the body upon which they depend.
If it were explained otherwise, the internal nature of feelings and so forth would not be established.

Furthermore, one would not possess all three modes of observation regarding the mind, because there would be no possibility for abiding in the contemplation of the mind while the mind is exclusively external.
According to that [position], when the mind serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*) for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is designated as "external";
this very same [mind] is designated as "internal," because the mind always serves as the support (*āśraya*) for consciousness.
If it is granted that when the eye and other [senses] serve as objects for mental consciousness, they too are merely "internal," what fault would there be?
It is not the case that those eyes and others do not sometimes function as the support (*āśraya*) for the consciousnesses produced by themselves.
Thus, the Elder’s establishment of the internal and external gates contradicts the sūtras and fails to avoid confusion.
Only that established by me and the great masters of the Abhidharma accords with the sūtras, is fully accomplished, and is free from the fault of confusion.
Having already explained the internal and external [bases],
among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and how many are "counter-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*)?
The verse says:
The dharma-element is of one type; the remaining two are of two types, depending on whether they perform their own function or not.
The commentary states:
regarding the "dharma of the same type," this refers to the single dharma-element, which is exclusively of the same type.
Now, one should first distinguish the characteristics of the objective field (ālambana) and its homogeneity (sabhāgatā).

If an object is definitively the focal object (ālambana) of consciousness—for instance, as the dharma-dhātu is definitively the focal object of that mental consciousness—it is because it is not shared [with other cognitions].

Among these, that which has already arisen, is currently arising, or is destined to arise as consciousness is called the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) object-condition, because the mind is able to universally take all objects as its domain.

Within the objects of the three times and the non-temporal realm, there is not a single element of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in which infinite mental consciousnesses have not already arisen, are not currently arising, or will not arise; for two moments of mental consciousness are capable of universally taking all phenomena as their objects. Therefore, the dharma-realm is always termed "homogeneous."
Regarding "the remaining two," this refers to the other seventeen elements (*dhātus*), all of which possess both the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and the "counter-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
What are these termed "homogeneous" and "counter-homogeneous"?
They are defined as those that perform their own function and those that do not perform their own function.
If they perform their own specific function, they are called "homogeneous" (sabhāga); if they do not perform their own specific function, they are called "non-homogeneous" (tat-sabhāga).
How is it that the eye and other faculties are described as being either homogeneous or non-homogeneous?
Furthermore, the "homogeneous" (sabhāga) eye is said to be of three kinds: that which has seen, is seeing, or will see visible forms within the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
The "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) eye is said to be of four kinds: those that are the opposite of the aforementioned, as well as those that are of a nature not to arise (anutpattidharma).

The masters of the West maintain that there are five types of *sabhāga* (homogeneous) eyes; that is, they further divide those of the "non-arising" category (*anutpatti-dharma*) into two, based on the distinction between those with consciousness (*savijñāna*) and those without consciousness (*avijñāna*).
As it is with the eye, so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, and body; each should be described according to its own object and its own function.

Regarding the mental element (*manodhātu*), there are three types of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) states, namely: that which has already cognized, that which is currently cognizing, and that which will cognize an object.
The mind of that same class (sabhāga) is of only one kind, namely, that which is of a nature not to arise (anutpattidharma).
Regarding the visual objects of the form realm (rūpadhātu), it is said there are three kinds: those already seen, those currently being seen, and those yet to be seen by the eye.
Those of the same class (*sabhāga*) are said to be of four kinds: namely, those that are the opposite of this [the *tatsabhāga*], and those that are non-arising (*anutpattidharman*).
This is explained in detail up to the element of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), which is likewise; for each, one should explain its specific function in relation to its own respective faculty.

The six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are established as two categories based on whether they have arisen or not; this is as explained in the case of the element of mind (*manodhātu*).
If the eye is "functioning" (*sabhāga*) with respect to one [object], it is functioning with respect to all others;
if it is "non-functioning" (*tatsabhāga*) with respect to one, it is non-functioning with respect to all others.
To speak at length, this applies even to the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
Form (*rūpa*), however, is not like this: for one who sees it, it is "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*); for one who does not see it, it is "of that same class" (*tatsabhāga*).
There may be various forms residing on mountains such as Mount Meru and others that are of the same class (*sabhāga*) for all sentient beings;
yet those possessing the divine eye do not perceive them because they serve no purpose.

There are certain forms that are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) only with respect to a single sentient being, such as when one observes in private what has been, is being, or will be seen by oneself alone.

There are also certain forms that are called "homogeneous" with respect to hundreds or thousands of sentient beings, such as the forms of the moon, dancing, or wrestling, which are observed in common.

Furthermore, for what reason is it said that the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) aspects of the eye differ from [the homogeneous and partially homogeneous aspects of] visible form?
It is possible for many sentient beings to see a single visible form together; however, there is no utility in two sentient beings observing with a single eye.
Sound is explained in the same manner as visible form, because it is a common object of experience (*sādhāraṇa-viṣaya*).
As for the three—odor, taste, and tangible—their explanation follows that of the internal spheres (*ādhyātmika-dhātu*), because they are not common objects.

Nevertheless, according to conventional designations and conceptual notions (*prajñapti-saṃjñā*) used in the world, people say, "I and others smell this fragrance together," "we taste this flavor together," or "we perceive this tangible together. In what sense, then, are these "common" (*sabhāga*)?
Regarding the meaning of "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*): "part" (*bhāga*) refers to mutual interaction; because they share this same part, it is called "homogeneity.
What is meant by "mutual interaction"?
It refers to the mutual interaction between the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness; that is to say, the sense of successive conformity.
Alternatively, "part" (*bhāga*) refers to the mutual interaction of their respective functions;
therefore, it was previously stated that if they perform their own function, they are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).

Alternatively, "part" refers to the contact (*sparśa*) that arises, because it is produced through the interaction of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness. Since they all equally possess this "part," they are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*); that is, they equally possess the function and equally possess contact.

That which is the opposite of this is called "having a counterpart" (sabhāga). Because it is not "having a counterpart" (asabhāga) yet shares a commonality in kind with that "having a counterpart," it is named "having a counterpart.
In what way does it share a commonality in kind with that?

This means that because this and that share identical characteristics such as views, occupy the same location and realm, and serve as mutual causes, are mutually related, and mutually induce one another, they are identical in terms of their generic category.
The *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *tatsabhāga* (partially homogeneous) have already been explained.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and how many are not to be abandoned (*aheya*)?
The verse says:

Fifteen are abandoned only by cultivation; the last three realms are common to all three [types of abandonment]. Those that are non-defiled are not born from the six [sense-bases]; those in the form realm are certainly not abandoned by insight. The Treatise says: The fifteen [factors]—the five views, doubt, and the ten afflictions associated with them—are abandoned only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). The final three realms—the ignorance of the form realm, the ignorance of the formless realm, and the ignorance associated with the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—are common to all three types of abandonment: they may be abandoned through insight, through cultivation, or through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Those factors that are non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*) are not abandoned through the path of insight, as they do not arise from the six sense-bases (*ṣad-āyatana*). Furthermore, those factors belonging to the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) are certainly not abandoned by insight alone, because they are associated with the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), which are incompatible with the coarse nature of the path of insight.
The fifteen elements refer to the ten material elements and the five consciousness elements.
"Exclusively abandoned by cultivation" means that these fifteen elements are abandoned solely through the path of cultivation.

The final three elements refer to the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), as they are mentioned last among the six triads.
Regarding "pervading the three," this means that each of these three realms subsequently pervades three types [of abandonment].

Among these, the eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the mental states and mental factors associated with them, as well as their various acquisitions (*prāpti*) and all co-existent factors such as their arising and so forth, are all abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
All remaining contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
All uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava*) are not to be abandoned.

Regarding this, some say that when the first moment of the noble path (*ārya-mārga*) arises, all states of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) are forever rendered unaccomplished; therefore, this state is also abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
The Sūtra states:

"The Stream-enterer attains the state of one who does not fall. This does not mean that by failing to permanently sever the bodily, vocal, and mental karma that invites rebirth in the miserable destinies, one merely obtains the designation of "one who does not fall" because those [karmas] have been exhausted.
Furthermore, it is said:
"I have exhausted the hells," and so forth, as explained at length.
"Exhausted" (kṣīṇa) has the meaning of "severed" (prahīṇa).
Just as an Arhat declares of himself:

"My births are exhausted," so too are the defiled bodily and vocal actions that lead to rebirth in the evil destinies abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), for they are all utterly incompatible with the Path of Insight (*darśana-mārga*).
To refute this assertion, it is further stated that what is non-defiled and not produced by the six [consciousnesses] is certainly not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
This nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is comprised within the category of non-defiled neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*) phenomena.
If this [state] were defiled, then an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm who has already abandoned sensual craving would no longer be an ordinary being.

Furthermore, since the attainment of this state depends upon and belongs to the body of birth, one should not, while born in one realm or level, establish the nature of an ordinary being belonging to another realm or level.
If this were wholesome, then one who has severed the roots of goodness would not be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Therefore, it is subsumed under the category of non-defiled neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*) nature.
Since it is non-defiled, it is not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*); if it were abandoned by insight, it would have to be abandoned by the stages of patience (*kṣānti*).

If [the non-defiled] were abandoned by patience (*kṣānti*), it would still have to be possessed at the very moment patience arises; in that case, even an *ārya* would be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Furthermore, that which is non-defiled is certainly not abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), because it is only designated as "abandoned" when the afflictions taking it as their object are ultimately severed.
Furthermore, it is neither "born from the six" nor is it "abandoned by insight.
"The six" refers to the sense-base of the mind (*manāyatana*).

That which arises differently from these is called "not born from the six"; this means it arises from the five faculties, such as the eye, namely the five consciousnesses and so forth, because they function externally by taking objects such as visible form as their conditions, and thus they are not abandoned by insight.

Furthermore, as for all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), whether defiled or undefiled, they are not abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*); rather, like undefiled phenomena, they are only designated as "abandoned" at the time when the afflictions taking them as objects are ultimately severed.
What is the meaning of "abandonment"?
Briefly, there are two kinds:
first, abandonment through detachment from bondage; second, abandonment through detachment from objects.
Regarding abandonment through detachment from bondage, as the Sūtra says:
"When there is no internal eye-fetter, one knows as it truly is: 'I have no internal eye-fetter.
Regarding abandonment through detachment from objects, as the Sūtra says:
"O bhikṣus, if you can eliminate desire and greed regarding the eye, this is called the 'permanent abandonment' of the eye.
The great masters of the Abhidharma, following that sequence, establish two kinds of abandonment: first, abandonment by intrinsic nature (svabhāva-prahāṇa);
second, abandonment of the object (ālambana-prahāṇa)."

If a phenomenon is a fetter (*saṃyojana*) and shares the same fruit (*eka-phala*), it is said to be "abandoned by its own nature" (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*) when its antidote arises; because of that abandonment, one attains dissociation (*visamyoga*) from the objective basis (*ālambana-vastu*).
However, it is not necessarily the case that [the defilement] becomes non-existent with respect to that [basis]; this is called "abandonment of the object" (*ālambana-prahāṇa*).

In this context, all contaminated form, as well as non-defiled contaminated formless states and their various acquisitions (*prāpti*) and other derivative phenomena such as arising, are bound by the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through seeing and through cultivation.

When these various fetters are gradually abandoned in this manner, for each distinct category, the attainment of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) arises; at that time, those fetters and their associated results are all said to be "abandoned."

Regarding those tainted forms (*rūpa*) and untainted-tainted formless states (*ārūpya*), as well as their various acquisitions (*prāpti*) and associated factors such as arising (*jāti*), the acquisitions of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*) have not yet arisen at that time; therefore, they are not yet termed "abandoned," because those dharmas are abandoned solely by the final path of immediate succession (*anantarya-mārga*) of their respective stages.

The various paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) cannot effect the sequential abandonment of defilements according to the distinctions between the stages; how then could they sever those dharmas such as form?

For one who has seen the Noble Truths, the dharmas of the miserable realms (*apāya*) have already attained non-arising because their conditions are deficient; yet, because the afflictions (*kleśa*) that take them as objects have not been completely severed, they are still not said to be "severed."
If a dharma has not been abandoned, yet has already been attained as non-arisen or is unaccomplished, what difference is there between this and that which has already been abandoned?
Abandonment refers to the attainment of dissociation through the path of antidotes; it does not mean merely being non-arisen or unaccomplished.
Furthermore, it is not because something does not arise that it is called "severed," for this is not necessarily the case. Why is this so?
Because there are instances where something has already been severed yet still arises, such as the maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*) within that body, according to their respective conditions.
There are some that have already been abandoned and have attained non-arising, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth.

There are also some that have not yet been abandoned but have already attained non-arising, such as all past and future dharmas that do not arise within the continuum of a noble one (*ārya*) who has not yet abandoned defilement, including craving-for-existence (*bhavarāga*) and others.

If those who have attained patience regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) still give rise to such things as false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), even though they have not yet been abandoned, this does not mean that these factors are not [previously] established, just as it is with other phenomena.
Accordingly, they are nonetheless termed "abandoned" (*prahīṇa*).
Furthermore, it is not fixed. Why is this so?

There are cases where [a factor] has already been abandoned yet is still possessed, such as the non-defiled dharmas within that body; whereas for those defiled dharmas that correspond to them, once they have been abandoned, one certainly does not possess them.

Alternatively, there are defiled phenomena which, although not yet abandoned, are not possessed [by one]; for example, when one who has not yet abandoned desire attains the "heat" stage (*uṣmagata*) and the corresponding morality, the various transgressions of that morality are relinquished even though they have not yet been abandoned, because they are to be abandoned by the final path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The nine grades of non-vocal and non-physical karma are not gradually abandoned, because the faults of those who are defiled are also slight.
Regarding such categories, some may be possessed even when not yet abandoned, as is the case with other dharmas according to their respective applications.
Other masters say:

"The two types of karma—bodily and vocal—that bring about rebirth in the miserable realms (*apāya*) and so forth are not abandoned by insight (*na dṛṣṭiheya*), because they are directly originated by [afflictions] that are themselves not abandoned by insight. Regarding this, others raise an objection:
It is observed that the karma produced by one category [of affliction] can only be permanently severed by the arising of the path belonging to another category;
therefore, their statement is certainly unreasonable.
This objection is not valid, for it should be considered with careful scrutiny.
Furthermore, one observes that when afflictions of a certain category arise from their own immediate causes, the path of that same category can immediately and permanently sever them.
Why not cite this to prove that principle?
If what is abandoned by insight were to arise from its own immediate cause, it should nevertheless not be regarded as being fixed within that specific category.

As for the determination of the categories (*pakṣa*), they are distinguished by the power of non-universal afflictions (*akliṣṭa-kleśa*); therefore, although there are thirteen distinct categories, five gates are taught as the definitive categories.
From this it is proven that the two types of karma—of body and speech—if they are directly originated by a specific category [of affliction], are abandoned simultaneously with that category.
Since these karmas are not directly originated by the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), they are not themselves abandoned through seeing.
Therefore, that statement is not unreasonable.
Yet the Sūtra says:
"The bodily, vocal, and mental actions performed by those with wrong views are all themselves wrong."

This is not contradictory; for the sūtra merely states that the three types of karma arise from those who hold wrong views, rather than stating that the three types of karma are produced by wrong views themselves.

Alternatively, this statement is made because one initiates these karmas by taking as their cause and motivating factor the afflictions such as greed—which are abandoned through cultivation—that arise from wrong views.

However, because the afflictions such as greed, which are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), can act as the immediate cause (*āsanna-hetu*) arising in each moment to initiate this karma, it is said that the two types of karma—of body and speech—are exclusively abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, a sūtra states regarding a stream-enterer:
"I have exhausted the hells and so forth.
This statement refers to the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) with respect to those realms; because they will never arise again, it is termed "exhausted."
Regarding this, there is an objection:
If future dharmas that will never again arise are called "exhausted," what is the characteristic of these non-arising dharmas?
They should be like past dharmas, termed "non-extinguished" dharmas.
However, since at that time the entity does not yet exist at all, how can it be said that it is a phenomenon subject to arising or a phenomenon not subject to arising?
One should reflect upon this:
can such an objection be raised regarding whether a phenomenon exists or does not exist in the future?
Furthermore, one should interrogate the Blessed One’s words as they were spoken:
"One prevents unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising.
And he also said:
This cessation means that [the defilements] do not continue further.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The cessation of all outflows (āsrava) is termed 'abandonment'."
These statements should also be challenged:
since at that time there was no entity whatsoever, how could one speak of non-arising, non-continuation, and negation?
Alternatively, this may be the opposite; therefore, what has been stated—that because it will never arise again it is called "exhaustion" (kṣaya)—is not unreasonable.
Furthermore, just as there is a distinction in meaning between the term "severance" (prahāṇa) and other terms, so too is it with the term "exhaustion"; they cannot be treated as identical.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"One is able to sever the aggregate of wealth, whether it be small or great.
It further says:
It is capable of severing such acts as killing;
this case should be treated similarly, and cannot be used as a precedent.
Furthermore, although the Sūtra states that a person who has fully realized the Truths (dṛṣṭisatya-paripūrṇa-pudgala) never intentionally takes the life of a living being, and so forth at length.
This also cannot prove that physical karma is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), because this sūtra states that Arhats are the same in this regard.
However, this statement in the sūtra is made because for a beginner, there is certainly no persistent underlying intention (*āśaya*) toward grave evil.
Since all Arhats have severed those proximate causes and their respective types are exhausted, this statement was made.
Therefore, various sūtras do not serve as proof for that [opposed] meaning.

By this, it is established by reason that what is undefiled, what is not born of the six [consciousnesses], and matter (*rūpa*) are certainly not abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). This principle is fully proven.
Having thus explained what is abandoned by seeing and so forth,
among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are "seeing" (*darśana*) and how many are not?
The verse says:
A portion of the eye and the dharma-element are said to be the eight kinds of seeing;
the wisdom co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not seeing, because it does not judge.
It is the eye, when functioning as its own counterpart (sabhāga), that sees forms, and not the consciousness which depends upon it.
It is traditionally taught that [the eye] cannot see because it is obstructed by various forms.
The treatise says:
The eye is entirely seeing; one part of the dharma-dhātu—namely, the eight kinds—is seeing; all others are not seeing.
What are these eight?

They are the five defiled views, beginning with the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), mundane right view, the right view of those in training (*śaikṣa*), and the right view of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), these eight are "views," while the remainder are not.

Among all phenomena (*dharmas*), only two possess the nature of seeing (*darśana*). Within the category of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), only the eye possesses the nature of seeing. Among immaterial phenomena (*arūpadharma*), that which has clear and sharp modes of activity (*ākāra*), which functions as an internal door (*antar-mukha*) to investigate objects, and which is wisdom (*prajñā*), possesses the nature of seeing, and nothing else does.
Regarding the characteristic of the eye herein, it has already been explained as before.
It is commonly understood in the world that because it observes and illuminates forms, because it is the opposite of darkness, and because its function is clear and sharp, the eye is called "seeing."
The five defiled views will be explained in their characteristics within the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa* (Chapter on Latent Tendencies).
Worldly right view refers to the superior wisdom that is wholesome, contaminated (*sāsrava*), and associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Right view of one in training refers to all untainted wisdom within the person of one in training.
Right view of one beyond training refers to the definitive untainted wisdom within the person of one beyond training.
The single term "right view" fully encompasses three types.

These three are distinguished separately in order to clarify the differences between the views of the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, this reveals that [the path] arises through gradual cultivation.

For example, during the night when there is no moonlight or other illumination, one wanders through perilous terrain amidst clouds and mist; whatever forms and images one perceives are nothing but distortions. The observation of dharmas by the five defiled views is likewise so.

For example, when there is the light of the moon and such during the night, one travels through dangerous and obstructed places with all darkness dispelled; the forms and images seen therein are somewhat clear and pure. The observation of phenomena through right view in the world is likewise.

For example, when during the day clouds rise up and obscure the solar disk, yet one travels over level ground, the forms and images seen gradually become clearer and more distinct; so too it is with the vision of the Dharma for those in training who possess right view.

For example, when the midday sun spreads its brilliance during the day, the mist and fog are cleared away and one travels over level ground; the forms and images seen are most extremely bright and pure. The observation of dharmas by the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is likewise.

As the practitioner gradually cultivates practice and wisdom arises, the various forms of delusion and darkness within their own mind are removed; in this way and that way, the correct view regarding all objects of focus gradually increases in clarity and purity, becoming distinct. It is not that the objects of focus themselves are pure or impure; rather, because of the presence or absence of defilements and obstructions in one’s own self-awakening wisdom, it is said that the objects of focus are pure or impure.
These various views, in general, comprise five categories:

first, the indeterminate category; second, the defiled category; third, the wholesome-with-outflows category; fourth, the category of those in training (śaikṣa); and fifth, the category of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Among the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) categories, the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is seeing; however, the ear and other faculties, as well as all unobscured-indeterminate wisdom (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-prajñā*), are entirely not seeing.

Among the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) categories, the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) are seeing; all other defiled wisdom is entirely not seeing—namely, wisdom co-arising with greed, hatred, pride, non-associated ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*), and doubt—and other defiled phenomena are likewise all not seeing.
Among the categories of those in training (*śaikṣa*), there is no wisdom that is not vision; however, the remaining [factors] are not vision.

Among the categories of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), as well as the remainder, are not vision; all other wisdom of those beyond training is entirely vision.
Among the categories of wholesome *sāsrava* [phenomena], only the wholesome wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is "view" (*dṛṣṭi*);
all others are not view. Other masters state that even the wholesome, *sāsrava* wisdom associated with the mental consciousness may also not be view.
This refers to the wisdom induced by the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), the wisdom that initiates manifest action (*vijñapti*), and the wisdom at the time of death.
Furthermore, within this category of wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) states, the wisdom co-arising with the five sensory consciousnesses is also not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
For what reason is this so?
Are all the types of wisdom that have been excluded not views?
Because they do not involve decisive judgment (*niścaya*).
Only that which possesses the characteristics of wisdom as previously described constitutes the essence of "view" (dṛṣṭi).

That is to say, it is wisdom that operates within the formless realm, whose mode of activity is clear and sharp, which investigates its objects, and which functions through the internal door; this alone is "view," and nothing else.
Only this wisdom characterized by investigation possesses the capacity for decisive judgment, because it functions by deliberating upon its object of focus.
The wisdom that is excluded [from being "view"] lacks the capacity for decisive judgment through deliberation regarding its object; therefore, it is not a view.
Regarding the term "decisive determination" (*niścaya*): it refers to the process where, preceded by deliberation regarding an object, one reaches a final, definitive discernment.
If that is so, since the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) lacks this characteristic, it should not be called "seeing."

Has it not already been stated that because the world collectively understands that the eye observes visible forms, because it is the opposite of darkness, and because its function is clear and sharp, the eye is also called "seeing"?
The Sūtra also says:
"The eye sees various visible forms."
If it were the eye that sees, why would it not simultaneously perceive all objects?
There is no such fault, for we maintain that only a portion of the eye is capable of seeing visible forms.
What is this "portion"?
This refers to the "homogeneous" (sabhāga) eye.
The characteristics of the homogeneous eye have already been explained previously; it becomes homogeneous only when sustained by consciousness.
Since not all sense organs are simultaneously sustained by their respective individual consciousnesses, there is no such fault.
If that were so, then the consciousness which depends upon it would be the "seeing" and not the eye, because seeing occurs only when visual consciousness arises.
This is not the case; rather, it is through the sustaining power of visual consciousness that a superior function arises, just as a superior fire arises depending on the power of fuel.

If the function of seeing color were a phenomenon produced by consciousness, then this function of seeing color should arise independently of the eye; for it is through the nourishment provided by consciousness to the co-nascent great elements that the superior sense organ is produced, enabling it to see various forms. Therefore, one should not say that it is the consciousness, as the supported, that sees.
What wise person would speak thus:

"Whatever causes and conditions can produce a discernment, that discernment is identical to those causes and conditions; since consciousness is the cause of seeing, it is not itself the essence of seeing"?
On what grounds is it definitively known that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is not "seeing"?

Because there is neither logical reasoning (*yukti*) nor scriptural authority (*āgama*). Regarding the absence of logical reasoning: it is because [visual consciousness] would be no different from the consciousnesses of the ear and so forth.
What distinction is there between visual consciousness and the other consciousnesses, such as those of the ear and so forth, such that visual consciousness alone is called "seeing"?
Therefore, it is not reasonable to say that consciousness itself is the essence of seeing.

If you argue that it differs from the other consciousnesses because of the difference in its supporting faculty (indriya), this is logically untenable; for while consciousness may acquire the name "visual consciousness" simply due to the difference in its support, it does not thereby become the act of seeing.
It is not the case that because their bases differ, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) undergoes alteration and transforms into the essence of views.

Just as fire produced from grass, wood, cow dung, or chaff differs in name though its nature of heat remains the same, so too, when the various consciousnesses are compared, there is no difference in their essential category.
To say that seeing depends exclusively on visual consciousness and nothing else is a statement made according to popular sentiment rather than correct reasoning.
If it were the case that something becomes "seeing" simply because it takes form as its object, then the mental consciousness that takes form as its object would also have to be considered seeing.
The argument that it constitutes "seeing" solely because it takes present form as its object is also unreasonable, for there is no distinguishing cause.

It is universally established that wisdom taking objects of the three periods of time as its objects is "seeing"; by the same logic, consciousness taking past and future forms as its objects should also constitute "seeing."
If there were a consciousness of the past or future that takes present visible forms as its object, one would have to admit that those who are blind could perceive present visible forms.

If you claim that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not of the nature of seeing, then you must also admit that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is likewise not of the nature of seeing; for it is impossible that within a single category, a portion is of the nature of seeing while another portion is not.
There is no contradiction in principle.
How could one class [of phenomena] be partly wholesome and partly unwholesome?
This case should be understood in the same way.
This should not be taken as an analogy, because their substantial entities (*dravya*) and their meanings (*artha*) differ.

Although the various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are identical in terms of their substantial category, they possess distinctions in their categories of meaning, such as being wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth, just like the substance and meaning of fire.

Within the categories of the essential nature of consciousness that discriminates objective aspects, there are distinctions between pure and impure types of meaning, which are termed wholesome and unwholesome.
However, one cannot conclude that because there are distinctions in the types of meaning, there must likewise be distinctions in the essential nature itself.

Just as fire, although it may vary in intensity—whether fierce or feeble—and differ in its conditions—whether with smoke or without smoke—remains identical in its essential nature, being without discrimination and having heat as its intrinsic nature.

Thus, although these various consciousnesses are identical in their essential nature as they discern objective phenomena, they differ according to distinctions in their categories, such as being wholesome and so forth.
Therefore, the example cited does not constitute a valid rebuttal.

If it is argued that although the essential natures of the various consciousnesses are identical, there are distinctions among their objects (artha) such as "seeing" and so forth, this reasoning is incorrect. This is because the distinct characteristics of the essential natures of these dharmas are directly perceived; they should not be grasped as being distinctions among objects, for [the nature of seeing] is not like [wholesomeness and so forth], which pervades all dharmas such as the various consciousnesses.
Thus, it has been shown that there is no causal basis for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) to constitute seeing, as this is logically impossible.

As for its absence in the scriptural teachings, it means that there is no authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*) stating that visual consciousness sees, which would allow listeners to develop understanding; rather, in various sūtras, it is found that "seeing" refers to the eye and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, it is said that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is what sees, not the eye; this contradicts worldly convention.
In the world, one is called "blind" simply because they lack eyes, not because they lack visual consciousness.
That is to say, blindness results solely from the non-attainment of the eye, and does not depend on whether visual consciousness is attained or not.
It is not the case that those born in the second dhyāna or above—who, when visual consciousness is not manifest, possess the eye but lack consciousness—could be called "blind.

Furthermore, if those who are blind were to produce visual consciousness despite being deficient in the eye-faculty, they would not be called "blind," nor should they be called "those without vision."
If you say that because visual consciousness does not manifest before one, one is called "blind" despite possessing the faculty,
then all those in the world who possess eyes should also be called "blind" during states when consciousness does not arise.

Furthermore, if the visual consciousness possesses a distinguishing characteristic that differentiates it from other consciousnesses and thereby allows it to be designated as "seeing," then this distinguishing characteristic itself must be seeing.

If this visual consciousness lacks such a distinguishing characteristic to differentiate it from others, yet one still claims that the visual consciousness—and not the others—is seeing, then that would be like the decrees issued by a wicked king.
Is it not just as with wisdom? This is also the case here.

For example, while all forms of wisdom have the characteristic of discerning phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), sometimes they are both views (*dṛṣṭi*) and discernment, and at other times they are not views but are merely discernment.

Thus, these various consciousnesses take the apprehension of objects as their characteristic; at times they are both seeing and discerning, and at other times they are not seeing but are only discerning.
By this, the objection raised by others is explained:
"If consciousness is able to see, what else is there that discerns?"
This is because you grant that there is no distinction between "view" (*darśana*) and "cognition" (*vijñāna*).
Such an analogy is fundamentally inconsistent in principle.
It is by means of a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) that wisdom is designated as "view," and this specific characteristic is itself the act of seeing.
It is not that the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) causes consciousness to be called "seeing," because this specific characteristic is itself the faculty of seeing.

If the specific characteristic were itself the act of seeing, then the sense of "seeing" would belong to the eye, which serves as its support; for consciousness merely acquires a distinct name by virtue of its support.

Alternatively, one should explain what specific characteristic this concentration possesses that distinguishes it; apart from its supporting faculty (*āśrayendriya*), what other factor is present in visual consciousness alone that is absent in auditory consciousness and the others?
Furthermore, regarding their statement that "just as seeing is [distinct from] wisdom, so too is the consciousness of seeing": [this is untenable].

If you concede that there is no distinction [between them], you must also concede that the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is itself wisdom (*prajñā*), for it is commonly accepted within the context of association (*samprayoga*) that its essence is exclusively wisdom.

Furthermore, if you maintain that there is no difference between seeing and consciousness, then seeing should be identical to all forms of consciousness, and consciousness should be identical to seeing; by what cause, then, would one who is blind or asleep not see?
If it is claimed that there is no visual consciousness at that time, this is also not the case, because their essential natures are identical.
In what way does its nature differ from that of other consciousnesses, such that while others lack the capacity for seeing, this alone possesses the capacity to see?
Such rescues as these have already been extensively refuted above.
Alternatively, a single dharma would have to possess two essences: one essence capable of cognizing and another essence capable of seeing.
If you grant that it can see even though it is not of the nature of seeing, then your own tenet falls into the fault of over-extension.

If you argue that this is also the case because it is not contradictory for wisdom (*prajñā*) to be able to see and to discern, [we reply: it is not so, because there is no distinction between seeing and wisdom; do you not see that consciousness (*vijñāna*) likewise lacks any distinction?

If that were so, those with eyes should not differ from the blind; for what reason is one who lacks eyes said to be "blind" because they lack the accomplishment of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), yet one who possesses eyes is not called "blind" when other consciousnesses are present? Such faults have already been discussed at length previously; therefore, it is certain that visual consciousness is not seeing.
Furthermore, there are other masters who establish, by a different reasoning, that visual consciousness is certainly not "seeing," on the grounds that it cannot perceive obstructed forms.
However, the intention of the Sūtra’s author did not accept that reason; therefore, he marked it as a "traditional report" (kila) within the verse.
That is to say, it is traditionally taught that one cannot perceive forms obstructed by walls and the like when they are directly perceived.
If it were consciousness that sees, then since consciousness is non-obstructive, walls and such would not hinder it, and one should therefore see the forms behind the obstruction.
He then retorts: "If visual consciousness does not arise with respect to that obstructed color, how can it see, since the consciousness has not arisen? This objection is irrational;

for even if one were to grant that visual consciousness could arise with respect to that [obstructed object], it still could not see it, because it was previously stated that there is no distinction between [visual] consciousnesses in this regard.
Therefore, the argument that "visual consciousness does not arise with respect to obstructed forms, and since consciousness does not arise, how can there be seeing? is not a valid answer.
Furthermore, one should not say that visual consciousness does not arise with respect to obstructed forms, for such a principle is logically untenable.

To address this objection: if one maintains that visual consciousness possesses the function of seeing visible forms, then because consciousness is non-obstructive (*anāvaraṇa*), it should likewise arise even with respect to obscured forms.

If it is argued that, just as the function of consciousness in discerning forms cannot arise with respect to obscured forms, this is also logically untenable; for it is accepted that visual consciousness operates upon the same object as the obstructive eye.

If you say that my statement is also the same as this, you should not hold such a view; for it is logically untenable to deny that the seeing of forms by the eye constitutes the objective domain of the eye.
Furthermore, for what reason do you say: "Since consciousness does not arise, how can there be seeing?"
Birth is itself seeing, and seeing is itself birth.
If one says that consciousness does not arise, how could it see?
This is equivalent to saying that since consciousness does not arise, how could it be born?
Or it may be said: "Since consciousness does not see, how could it possibly see?
Should one not raise a general objection here:
'Why does it not arise?'"
Why is it not seen?

Furthermore, if one holds the view that all causes and conditions arise solely from the preceding moment and that nothing arises simultaneously, then consciousness—whether arising or not arising—would be unable to see.
According to their own tenets, this too is not a valid answer.
Furthermore, visual consciousness arises even when obstructed by objects such as lapis lazuli or mica; why then do you say that visual consciousness does not arise with respect to an obscured color?

If you claim that visual consciousness arises therein because there is no obstruction to light, then you must admit that the possibility of visual consciousness arising with respect to an obstructed object is established; thus, your previous statement contradicts what you yourself have admitted.

Furthermore, it is observed in the world that visual consciousness arises even when separated from light; for example, a person can see various dark forms, and nocturnal birds and beasts can also see objects obscured by darkness, not because they desire to observe darkness while waiting for light.

If you claim that the nature of objective phenomena must be such, then nocturnal birds and beasts should be like humans; their consciousness would likewise not arise when obstructed by darkness. One cannot argue that the nature of the same dark color changes depending on whether it is encountered by a human or an animal.
If it is argued that the nature of the various realms of existence (*gati*) must be so, it is not so, because the various realms are the result of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
For instance, cats, wildcats, dogs, and others perceive various forms with defiled minds even in total darkness.
Only the eye that is of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*) is subsumed within the category of the realms of rebirth (*gati*); therefore, one may form such a conception regarding it.
It is the natural law of maturation that, among the various realms of rebirth, there may be cases where the eye is able to apprehend forms obscured by darkness.
If it is argued that the eyes of nocturnal birds and beasts are able to see because they are always accompanied by light, this reasoning is also incorrect, for such light cannot be apprehended.

If one claims it cannot be apprehended because it is subtle, then the illuminating function should be absent regarding distant objects, and visual consciousness would consequently fail to arise therein.

Therefore, the argument that "since visual consciousness does not arise with respect to obstructed forms, how can one see them? is not a reasoned answer; it is merely what those who lack discernment find pleasing.
If that is so, for those who maintain that the eye-faculty itself sees, why does it not apprehend objects obstructed by a barrier?

Because the eye is subject to resistance (*sapratigha*), it lacks the capacity to see obstructed forms; furthermore, since consciousness and its support (the sense-faculty) operate upon the same object, [consciousness] cannot arise [with respect to such forms].
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) further raises an objection, saying:

"Does the eye not perceive its object only when it comes into contact with it, as is the case with the body-faculty? If so, why do you say that because it is 'resistant' (sapratigha), it does not see that [distant] object?
This objection is not valid, for it fails to understand the meaning of "resistance" as it was explained.
Why is this so? It is not merely because this [definition] states that the eye is a phenomenon characterized by resistance through obstruction (*sapratigha*).
Since it only apprehends objects that are in contact and not those that are not in contact, it cannot apprehend forms that are obstructed.

In this context, it is also stated according to the meaning of "resistance by way of object" (*viṣayapratighāta*): if [a sense faculty] is obstructed with respect to a certain object, it does not exercise its function even toward other objects where there is no obstruction, let alone toward those where there is an obstruction.
All cognitive faculties (*viṣayin*) must be such that they cannot simultaneously apprehend all their respective objects.

If this is so, then visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is likewise possessed of resistance (*sapratigha*); it should not be said that its lack of capacity to see obstructed forms is due solely to the eye being possessed of resistance, nor should it be said that consciousness does not arise with respect to them because it functions upon the same object as its basis (*āśraya*), for you yourself have stated that "all cognitive faculties must be such."
This example is not applicable, as it fails to understand the intended meaning.

According to my interpretation, because the eye possesses the nature of resistance regarding its object (*viṣayapratighātitva*), and because visible form possesses the nature of resistance through obstruction (*āvaraṇapratighātitva*), the visual function does not arise with respect to a form that is obstructed.

Although the mind (*manas*) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are determined in terms of their respective supports (*āśraya*) and supported (*āśrita*), they are not determined in terms of their activity regarding a single object; these two types [of consciousness] cannot apprehend a single object at one and the same time.

The objective sphere apprehended by the eye-faculty, which serves as its basis, is precisely that which is apprehended by the eye-consciousness, which depends upon it; furthermore, they must necessarily be simultaneous. Therefore, regarding an obstructed object, just as the function of the eye is blocked, so too is the function of the consciousness. For this reason, it is said that because the consciousness and its basis operate upon the same object, one may say that eye-consciousness does not arise with respect to that [obstructed] object.
If you grant that consciousness has the capacity for seeing, for what reason does it not arise?

Is it not the case that the eye is subject to objective resistance (*viṣayapratighāta*), yet when obstructed by objects such as lapis lazuli, it is still able to exercise its function toward what is thus screened?

For what reason is it said that if something is obstructed with respect to a certain object, it will not exert its function even toward other objects where there is no obstruction, let alone toward those where there is obstruction?
Did we not state previously that they are not apprehended simultaneously?
When one apprehends the lapis lazuli, one does not apprehend what it obstructs;
when one apprehends what it obstructs, one does not apprehend the lapis lazuli.
Since they are not apprehended simultaneously, there is no fault of contradiction.
If that is so, for what reason is the eye unable to apprehend obstructed forms such as walls?
It is not because, as you claim, light is absent therein.
Why is this so? Because it is observed in the world that one can perceive objects even when separated from light.
Since you claim they are not the same, for what reason would [the eye] fail to perceive them?
All accumulated forms possess the nature of obstruction;
for example, light and darkness act as obstructions differently.
Although darkness and light occupy the same spatial location, a person obstructed by darkness cannot perceive [objects], whereas a person obstructed by light can perceive forms.
Nocturnal birds and beasts, although they can perceive objects obscured by darkness, cannot perceive those obscured by walls and the like.
Similarly, although they can perceive objects obscured by glass and the like, they cannot perceive those obscured by walls and the like.
For this reason, the visual faculty sees only such things as walls, but does not see the various forms obstructed by those walls, because accumulated matter possesses the nature of obstruction.
Such is the natural law of phenomena; it cannot be further scrutinized or challenged.

There are sense organs that, although capable of apprehending objects with which they do not come into contact, cannot apprehend other such non-contacting objects because they possess limited resistance;
and there are sense organs that, although capable of apprehending objects with which they do come into contact, are unable to apprehend certain other contacting objects.
Regarding what the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) says:

"How could the eye, like the body-faculty, only apprehend when in contact with its object? Since it possesses resistance (*sapratigha*), why does it not see that [distant object]? To this, one should pose the following challenge:
"If the faculty can apprehend an object without being in contact with it, then it should be able to apprehend all objects that are not in contact."
If it were to grasp by way of contact, then everything that is in contact would necessarily be grasped.
If this were not the case, the statement [of its nature] would be rendered useless.

Therefore, it is said that because the eye possesses resistance (*sapratigha*), it lacks the capacity to see obstructed forms; since consciousness and its support (the sense organ) operate upon the same object, one may say that visual consciousness does not arise with respect to them.
If it is granted that consciousness perceives, for what reason does it not arise?
Thus, this establishment and refutation are logically fully established.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Six.
Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle Seven.
