translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.

7. The Seventh Section of the First Chapter on Explaining the Original Matters: If the eye is that which sees, for what reason did the World-Honored One say it is a "gate" and not say it is "that which can see"?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"O Brahmin, you should know that the eye serves as a door solely for the purpose of seeing forms.
It is not logical to say that the act of seeing is itself the door; rather, one may only say that seeing is obtained by means of the door.

This sūtra does not definitively prove that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is itself the seeing, for it does not state that visual consciousness sees visible forms solely by means of the eye as its gateway.
Other masters maintain that it is wisdom (*prajñā*) that sees visible forms by means of the eye as its gateway.
One should abandon stubborn adherence and together carefully examine and seek the intended meaning of this sūtra.

According to our own school’s interpretation, because foolish people are blinded by ignorance and lack a true guide, they either cling to causes such as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or atoms (*paramāṇu*), or they cling to the idea that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise without a cause. Alternatively, they claim that if all conditioned phenomena were to perish moment by moment, the entire world would simultaneously undergo total destruction; thus, through these false conceptualizations and speculations, they imagine that conditioned phenomena either endure for a temporary duration or are ultimately eternal.

Therefore, the World-Honored One, in order to reveal the successive causality of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), taught such sūtras with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*): that although they perish moment by moment from beginningless time, they are neither destroyed nor severed; that not every effect arises from a single cause, yet conditioned phenomena do not arise without a cause. He taught that "the eye serves as the gate solely for the seeing of forms," and so on extensively until, "the mind serves as the gate solely for the cognizing of phenomena."
"Door" has the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*). There are two kinds of conditions: those of the same category and those of different categories.

Here, for the time being, we speak of conditions of the same category; regarding the eye serving as the door for the seeing of forms, this means that when a subsequent eye arises, the preceding eye serves as its condition.
The statement that "seeing form" indicates the arising of its function; this should be understood to apply likewise up to the sphere of the mind (*manāyatana*).

Furthermore, this sutra is intended to show that each of the [senses], such as the eye, possesses two functions: first, the ability to serve as a gateway, and second, the ability to apprehend an object.

Regarding that which can act as a gateway: for instance, the eye faculty acts as a basis, enabling the mind and mental factors to engage their respective objects through their individual modes of activity.
Regarding that which can apprehend an object: for instance, the eye faculty functions solely to see visible forms.
If it were otherwise, there would be a contradiction in meaning alone, for all minds and mental factors would have to be exclusively seeing.
However, all minds and mental factors take the eye as their gateway; yet you maintain that the essence of seeing is exclusively mind and not the [mental] factors.

Furthermore, the various mental factors such as feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā) have distinct functions, such as experiencing, grasping images, and volitional formation; they should not be considered mere seeing.
Since it is stated that there is "mere seeing," it is clearly understood to be the eye, because this visual faculty alone is capable of seeing.
Thus, the function of the eye is briefly twofold: first, it serves as a gateway; second, it is capable of seeing forms.
This should be understood accordingly for the other sense bases up to the mind base.
Therefore, my school’s position does not incur the fault of contradicting the sūtras.

Furthermore, this sūtra has another meaning: namely, that the means of seeing (*darśana-upāya*) is metaphorically designated as a "gate" (*mukha*), because worldly convention uses the term "gate" to refer to a means.
As it is said in the world:
"Relying on this gate, I shall certainly obtain the wealth and treasures of my desire."
This is precisely what I rely upon as the meaning of this expedient means.
The World-Honored One also told the householder Hasta:
"You should gather the assembly in accordance with the Dharma by relying on this gateway."
This means that the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) serve as the skillful means for gathering [beings].
Here, it is stated that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) serves as the skillful means for seeing; for the eye is able to see forms because it is sustained by consciousness.
Since consciousness is the skillful means for seeing and the basis of seeing for the visual faculty, it is metaphorically designated as "the eye."

This means that consciousness serves as the instrument by which the eye is able to see forms; just as in other sūtras, at the stage of discerning form, the name "consciousness" is metaphorically applied to the substance of the eye-faculty because the eye is the nature of the support for consciousness and is its proximate condition.
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"forms cognized by the eye.

Here, too, it is the same: at the stage of observing and illuminating form, consciousness is designated as the "eye" because it is the proximate condition and the support; thus, the name "eye" is applied metaphorically to the essence of visual consciousness, which does not contradict the Sūtra.

In order to cause non-Buddhists to abandon their grasping at a self that maintains the faculties and leads them to erroneously grasp at objects, this is a provisional designation; it is intended to make those brahmins understand that consciousness maintains the faculties and can apprehend its own objects, rather than a self maintaining them.

If that were so, one should state that it is visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) alone that acts as the gateway for seeing visible forms, and one should not mention "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). This is lest those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) should cling to the notion that "the self sees," interpreting what they grasp as a self to be designated by the term "consciousness," for among the worldlings, many commonly cling to consciousness as being the self.
If it is said to be the eye, one knows that the eye is the support (*āśraya*) for visual consciousness; it is certainly not the self (*ātman*).
The essence of the self is eternally abiding and must lack any support;
upon hearing that there is a support, the conception of a self ceases.
Furthermore, to avoid other faults, one should not speak of "consciousness" (vijñāna). For the Sūtra will state:
"With the mind as the gate, it is solely for the sake of cognizing phenomena.
If one were to speak of consciousness, one would necessarily have to specify that it is the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) that serves as the gate.

If one were to make such a claim, it would not accord with reason, because it is consciousness itself (*manovijñāna*) that can cognize all phenomena, and not some other "cognizing consciousness" acting as a means.

Would it not be said that the mind (*manas*) also incurs this same fault? For example, when it is said that the eye is the "door," it is understood that the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is the means for seeing.
Thus, when it is said that "the mind (manas) serves as the gate," one should understand that this refers to the mental consciousness (mano-vijñāna) as a means for comprehension.
Although "mind" is mentioned, there is no such error;
for upon hearing the name "mind," one should understand it solely as the mental faculty (manas), not as the mental consciousness.
Why is this so? Because the eye-faculty has utility, as it arises simultaneously with consciousness.
Since visual consciousness acts as the instrument for seeing for the eye, the name "eye" may be applied to this consciousness.

The mind-faculty (manas) is useless because it is past; since the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) and the mind do not act as a mutual expedient, the mind is not designated as "mind" in relation to the mental consciousness.
Rather, the mind serves as the expedient for the mental consciousness to cognize phenomena, for it is only by depending on the mind-faculty that the mental consciousness can cognize phenomena.
Therefore, if it is said that the eye serves as the gate, the wise should understand that consciousness is designated as the "eye" for the purpose of abandoning the grasping at a self.

When one reaches the sixth [sense-base], it is said that the mind (*manas*) serves as the gate; the wise should understand that the mind itself lacks the function of discernment, and thus the mind serves as the means (*upāya*) by which the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to discern.
Furthermore, this sutra states that there are two kinds of eyes: namely, the "non-concordant" (tat-sabhāga) and the "concordant" (sabhāga).
Although the non-concordant eye cannot see forms, it can serve as a gateway to induce the concordant eye to arise and see forms.
Within a single lifetime, one must first obtain the eye of that same class (*sabhāga*), and only thereafter does it induce the arising of the eye of that same class.
As it is with the eye, so it is for the body, up to and including the tactile faculty.
There are two kinds of mental attention: first, that which is ineffective; second, that which is effective.
Although ineffective mental attention cannot comprehend phenomena, it can serve as a gateway to induce effective mental attention, thereby enabling the comprehension of phenomena.
Since mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the mind (*manas*), and the mind is mental consciousness, there is no fault in saying that the mind is capable of cognizing.
Such arguments used to explain this sūtra mean that it should not be cited as a definitive proof to establish that seeing is the eye and that cognition is consciousness.
Furthermore, the Sūtra-master says:
"As for the statement in the Sūtra that 'the eye can see forms,' it is said to be able to see because it is the basis of seeing.
For what reason does the Sūtra-master give rise to this interpretation?
As that sutra states:
"It is the mind (*manas*) that cognizes phenomena (*dharma*); it is not the mind that cognizes, because [the mind] is past.
Since the mind is the support for consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is said to 'cognize. The eye is likewise."
This does not constitute a valid proof, because the manas and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) belong to the same category.
Since the characteristic of the mental consciousness is itself the manas, there is no contradiction in saying that the manas can cognize objects.
As the Sūtra says:
"Due to the violence and evil of the mind, whatever one does or says is nothing but unwholesome.
One should not say that such bodily and vocal karma is produced by means of a past mind.
This is because the present mind is violent and evil, giving rise to unwholesome karma of both body and speech.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"The outflows that would arise from desire do not arise, because the mind is free from defilement."

It is not the case that a non-turbid mental concentration can give rise to a non-turbid mental consciousness; therefore, one should not say [the distinction] is stated by way of the support (*āśraya*).
Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
"The mind leads the world."
How could this be a statement regarding mental factors (caitta) in reference to the mind (citta)?
Therefore, one cannot cite that scriptural passage to prove that the expression "the eye sees" refers to the consciousness (vijñāna) which is its support.

Furthermore, regarding the statement in this sutra that "the eye sees forms," one must not insist that it means the visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) sees; for nowhere is it definitively stated that consciousness sees, whereas it is stated in various places that the eye sees, and as previously mentioned, other teachers maintain that wisdom (prajñā) sees.

However, regarding this sūtra’s statement that "the mental consciousness cognizes dharmas," there is no fault in explaining it in terms of its support (āśraya). This is because there are instances where it is definitively stated that "consciousness cognizes," whereas there is no instance where it is definitively stated that "the mind (manas) cognizes"; thus, within this meaning, there is no conflicting interpretation.
Furthermore, the Sūtra-master says:
"Or, one may speak of the action of the dependent by way of its basis, as when people in the world speak of the sound of a bed or a seat.
For what reason does the Sūtra-master give rise to this fixed adherence?
Other words and other interpretations cannot be without a cause.

If it is argued that there is a cause because consciousness perceives visible forms by relying on the power of the eye, this does not constitute a valid reason, for the cause by which consciousness perceives visible forms is not universally established.

In our own school’s tenet, we maintain that consciousness is able to sustain the eye-faculty, which serves as its basis, thereby enabling it to see forms; therefore, the reason [stated by the opponent] that "consciousness sees" is not established.
Furthermore, no other sūtra definitively states that consciousness sees.
Is it not as when one speaks of the sound of a bed or a seat? This usage is tenable because it is universally established.
That the sound and the bed or seat are established as distinct entities is universally acknowledged.

Therefore, upon hearing this expression, one understands that the activity of the dependent (the sound) is being described by means of its support (the bed or seat), just as is commonly accepted in the world regarding the existence of real objects.

Regarding other metaphorical designations (*prajñapti*), it is not universally established that there is a consciousness which perceives [them] as such; therefore, one should not give rise to such a dogmatic adherence.

If that is so, then even "seeing with the eye" is not universally established. Why, then, do you say only that "consciousness possesses seeing by means of the eye," rather than saying that "visual consciousness sees form based upon the eye"?
That visual perception is established as a matter of common experience has already been stated previously.

Since there is no distinction among the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and so forth, whereas there is a distinction among the faculties of the eye, ear, and so forth, it is not the case that a functional eye arises independently of consciousness; therefore, it is said that the visual faculty possesses the capacity to see by being sustained by consciousness.
The faults in the view that consciousness sees have already been fully discussed; therefore, one should not say that it is by means of visual consciousness that one sees.

However, when the Sūtra speaks of "forms cognized by the eye," this refers to the activity of the dependent (consciousness) as designated by its support (the sense organ), because it is universally established that the eye and consciousness are distinct.

Now, we hear that the function of consciousness resides in the eye-faculty; this is known as describing the activity of the dependent (the consciousness) by way of its basis (the faculty). By this, one can also explain the statement in other sūtras: "that which the eye delights in."
Other masters say:
"The longing of the eye-faculty for the eye-consciousness cannot be established, because it lacks conceptualization;
only when there is conceptualization can longing be established."

It should be understood that herein, the conceptualizing mental consciousness induced by visual consciousness is metaphorically designated as "eye" because it arises through the mediation of the eye; like the mental applications (*manopavicāra*), it possesses conceptualization and can give rise to longing.
Therefore, one cannot cite the function of the supported [the eye] to prove that the supporter [the eye] does not see; for it is established by both reason and scripture that the eye can see forms.

Thus, we have first demonstrated that the theory maintaining that consciousness sees is inconsistent with correct principle; by this, the theory maintaining that wisdom sees is also refuted, as its faults are equal.

Furthermore, if the discernment associated with visual consciousness were what sees, then the discernment associated with other consciousnesses should also see; consequently, all objects would become visible.
Moreover, since all sense faculties serve as the bases for seeing, they would all necessarily become eyes.
Furthermore, what is the reason for maintaining that only the wisdom associated with visual consciousness sees, and not other forms of wisdom?
Moreover, as previously stated regarding the blind and the non-blind, all other objections and difficulties should be extensively applied, as appropriate, to the theory that wisdom sees.
Since the theories that consciousness or wisdom sees have both been refuted, it follows by extension that the eye-faculty itself is capable of seeing.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing—these four characteristics are each distinct and do not overlap. Thus, there is no confusion between them.

If one maintains that consciousness and so forth are the seers, then as previously stated, because there would be no distinction between them, seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing would become confused.
However, this school asserts:

it is the visual consciousness that sustains the faculty, enabling it to have the function of seeing; it is not the visual consciousness itself that sees. The same applies to hearing and so forth, according to their respective cases.
Furthermore, it is the eye that sees, not the visual consciousness and so forth, because the evidence from sūtras, śāstras, worldly convention, and reasoning is clear.
Regarding the sūtras, the *sūtras* state in various places that "the eye sees forms."
Furthermore, a verse says:
"Two eyes and two ears, because of the abundance of seeing and hearing.
Moreover, a sutra states:
My disciples are like the eyes of the world, for they guide the world so that it may abide in the True Dharma.
If the eye were not seeing, the disciples of the World-Honored One would not be able to provide guidance, being the same as those who possess worldly eyes.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The five faculties, such as the eye and so forth, each have their own respective range and each have their own respective object.
Because such statements are extremely clear.
"Śāstra" refers to the *Mūla-abhidharma* and the *Vibhāṣā*.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
"The two eyes see visible forms."
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* also states this: "The eye has seen, is seeing, and will see.
Many such statements as these are found there; the *Vibhāṣā* likewise makes this same assertion.

If that which is apprehended by the eye is called "the seen," it is stated as "that which is experienced by visual consciousness" in order to demonstrate that the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) eye possesses the capacity for seeing; that is, visual consciousness maintains the eye-faculty so that it may have an object of apprehension, and this is what is meant by the term "seeing."
"Worldly convention" refers to the common consensus of the world that one who lacks the eye-faculty is called "blind.
"Reasoning" refers to the fact that the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and so forth are each distinct, and thus they are not identical to consciousness and the like.
The scriptures, treatises, worldly logic, and reason are thus clear in proving that it is exclusively the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) that is definitively capable of seeing.
Nevertheless, following their own dogmatic attachments, the Dārṣṭāntika masters have falsely raised objections against this point, saying: "Why do you gather here to clutch at empty space?"
Visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye, visible forms, and so forth. Among these, which is the agent and which is the object in the act of seeing?
There are only dharmas as cause and effect; in reality, there is no functional activity.
To conform to worldly convention, we employ conventional designations, calling the eye "that which sees" and consciousness "that which cognizes."
The wise should not be attached to these.
This means that one should not stubbornly cling to the regional terminology spoken by the Buddha, nor should one insistently pursue worldly designations and concepts.
This statement does not accord with the sacred teachings or correct reasoning, nor can it refute the nature of visual perception.

Although all conditioned phenomena arise from conditions, we speak of the distinct characteristics and functions of various dharmas; that is to say, although conditioned dharmas arise equally from conditions, they do not lose their own fixed characteristics and functions. Therefore, while the Blessed One taught that dharmas arise from conditions, he also taught that earth and the other elements possess distinct characteristics and functions.

Just as the earth element and others, though produced from conditions, possess their own specific characteristics such as solidity as previously described, and also possess determinate functions such as supporting,
so too the eye, visible forms, visual consciousness, and the rest, though produced from conditions, must necessarily possess various distinct, determinate characteristics and functions.
Due to these distinctions of definitive characteristics and functions, the eye is designated solely as "eye," not as form or consciousness;
form is designated solely as "form," not as consciousness or eye;
and consciousness is designated solely as "consciousness," not as eye or form.
Although within this there is no single, real entity possessing the functions of seeing, being seen, or cognizing, it may nonetheless be designated as "the seer," "the seen," or "the cognizer.

Furthermore, within this principle that there is no such single, real entity possessing these functions, just as one may say that eye-consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms, so too is it said that the "eye-seeing" arises conditioned by visible forms and consciousness.
Within such phenomena that lack any collective, real characteristic or function, there appears, in accordance with worldly convention, what seems to be a collective, real characteristic or function.
Regarding this collective, real characteristic or function, the Blessed One exhorts those who possess wisdom to eliminate their attachment, and thus he spoke these words:
"One should not stubbornly cling to regional terminology; one should not insistently pursue conventional designations and concepts."

This means that one should not stubbornly cling to the verbal expressions arising from the worldly attachment to a real, universal essence that possesses the characteristic of seeing, for such a characteristic does not exist.

Furthermore, one should not insistently seek the names and concepts arising from the worldly attachment to a real, universal agency that performs the function of seeing, for such a function does not exist.

Just as it is with the characteristics, functions, and so forth, one should understand that the same applies to the rest; one must not, on account of the absence of a universal substantial characteristic or function, transcend conventional designations and terminology, nor dwell exclusively in accordance with the ultimate truth, nor cling to the notion that distinct practical functions do not exist.

Therefore, one must certainly not contradict the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), but rather conform to conventional designations (*saṃvṛti*). By this, one merely negates the world’s persistent and firm attachment to a collective, real nature and function; it does not mean that one also negates the persistent and firm attachment to the distinct natures and functions of phenomena in their ultimate sense. This is because the natures and functions of all phenomena arising through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) each truly exist, yet it is not the case that every cause produces every effect.
Therefore, in our school, we maintain that the eye can see based on both truths; thus, there is no fault in either case.
The Blessed One also allows for an agent and an action, as the Sūtra says:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that because it cognizes and cognizes, it is called consciousness."

Although the *Potaliputra Sūtra* states, "I never say there is one who cognizes," it does not entirely negate the agent and the activity; such a statement was made because [the Buddha] intended to exclude only a small portion.
I shall further elaborate upon dependent origination through reflection in [the section on] "Reflection.
Thus, by abiding in the correct principles of the Noble Teaching and seeking definitive discernment through reflection, one sees with the eye of wisdom what others do not.
Yet, they falsely raise objections against this, repudiating conventional reasoning and disparaging the ultimate tenet; it is certain that such empty-handed grasping belongs solely to them.
Furthermore, what does the cited scripture actually establish?

Does the statement here that the eye is not the essence of seeing, nor that it is said that the eye sees, imply that one accepts—just as the non-Buddhists do—that all phenomena possess a single, real, universal nature and function?
Furthermore, the cause and effect spoken of by them would necessarily be non-existent, because they do not admit that dharmas possess distinct characteristics and functions;
it is only when there are distinct characteristics and functions for each dharma that one can speak of the differentiation between cause and effect.
If one grants that phenomena possess distinct characteristics and functions, then such a repudiation is rendered futile.
Conversely, if one claims that there are no general or specific functions whatsoever, this contradicts the principles of both conventional and ultimate truth.

Since you have already conceded that cause and effect as well as the two truths are not non-existent, you must likewise concede that all phenomena possess both conventional and ultimate utility; therefore, the principle that the eyes and other faculties apprehend their respective objects is established.
That is to say, they are capable of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and cognizing; thus, the general characteristic of the function of "seeing" is already established.
Now, one should further consider the distinct characteristics of seeing and using: regarding the visible form that is seen, is it seen by one eye or by two eyes?
For what reason should this be considered once again?
Is it not universally established that if one eye is closed, the other eye can still see? Thus, the principle that both eyes are capable of seeing form is already proven.
Although this principle is established, it remains undecided whether the two eyes see form sequentially or simultaneously.
To ascertain this with certainty, one should further investigate.

If that were so, it should be stated that when one of the two eyes is closed or one eye is impaired, it does not cause the other eye to lose its capacity for vision; therefore, we know that even a single eye is capable of seeing forms.
If those two eyes are unimpaired and both open, then the two eye-faculties see forms simultaneously.
While the principle of one eye seeing form is manifest and easily established, the simultaneous seeing by both is difficult to establish; therefore, it must be analyzed and explained.
The verse says:
Or [it sees] with both eyes simultaneously, because the perception of form is distinct.
The commentary says:
At times, both eyes are able to see forms simultaneously.
On what basis is this known for certain?
Because the vision is distinct and clear.
Because when one eye is closed, the perception of the continuity of forms is not distinct, whereas when both eyes are open, that same form is perceived distinctly.
If the two visual organs were to perceive sequentially, then even with both eyes open, there would be only a single perception.
Just as when one eye is closed, the perception of forms is not clear, it should likewise be so when both eyes are open;
and just as when both eyes are open, the perception of forms is distinct, it should likewise be so when one eye is closed.
Since this is not the case, we know with certainty that there are times when both eyes see simultaneously, because their nature is one.
Even if there were hundreds or thousands of eyes, they would still give rise to a single consciousness; how much more so when there are only two?
Other schools maintain that because the locations [of the two eyes] are separated, when the eye sees forms, it is only one [eye] acting and not both. Furthermore,

when observing an arrow or similar object with one eye, because one can discern its curved or straight characteristics with precision and because the visual process is so rapid, a mind of overweening pride (*abhimāna*) leads one to claim, "I am seeing with both eyes simultaneously."
This argument is unreasonable.
Why? Is it not evident that when the entire body is submerged in water that is either cold or warm, the sense-faculty of the body and its various limbs simultaneously perceive the touch?
In this way, although the two eye-spheres are separated by distance, there is no logical contradiction in their seeing visible forms simultaneously.

Although the locations of the two visual faculties are distinct, they are subsumed under a single faculty because they are of the same kind; thus, a single visual consciousness arises based on both eyes. Therefore, it is accepted that seeing occurs simultaneously through both without any fault.
However, due to a distinct cause, it is by means of only one eye that one can definitively discern whether an arrow or other object is curved or straight.

As for this "distinct cause," it is because the atoms of the eye are arranged laterally like the flowers of the *kustumburu* plant; thus, when an object is directly present before it, it is seen with clarity, whereas when not directly present, it is not perceived.

When observing the straight or crooked characteristics of an arrow or similar object, if the arrow is placed between the two eyes, it does not appear directly before both eyes; rather, they glare at one another, and the vision is not clear or precise.
If one were to place an arrow or similar object before only one eye, the other eye would look on from the side and fail to perceive it clearly; therefore, one closes one eye.
When using one eye for such tasks as aiming an arrow, that single eye observes directly without visual confusion, making it easy to discern whether the line is straight or crooked.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the two eyes do not see simultaneously because their locations are separated, this is also incorrect. For example, when a person’s two hands both touch cold and warmth, although the locations are separated, consciousness arises simultaneously;
the same should apply to the eyes—why then could they not see simultaneously?
Furthermore, if one eye were obstructed by a cataract, a single consciousness should not arise simultaneously from both eyes.

Moreover, as for their claim that one perceives with both eyes at once due to the rapid succession [of cognitions] leading to overweening pride (*abhimāna*), this is actually the capacity to see, not overweening pride.

Furthermore, although the function of seeing with both eyes is rapid, if at one time consciousness were produced by only one eye and the other eye could not assist in producing that consciousness, then there would be no difference in the clarity or dimness of the perceived color when opening both eyes versus closing one; this is because the consciousness within the single eye would necessarily be empty [of visual content].
By this, the position asserted by the Sthavira is also refuted. He says:
"The two eyes function sequentially with respect to their objects; thus, vision is clear.

Alternatively, when one eye is closed or impaired, even if the other is open, there is no mutual substitution. The consciousness produced therein relies on only a single gateway; because it shifts so rapidly, vision is not distinct."

This argument is also incorrect. According to your position, when the two eyes alternate moment by moment, one eye would always be vacant and unable to see color, while the other eye would constantly be able to see color; consequently, there should be no difference in the clarity or dimness of vision between a person with two eyes and one with only one. Therefore, what you have said fails to provide satisfaction.

Furthermore, if one eye were closed or impaired, visual consciousness would always function through only a single gateway, and thus the perceived forms would not be clear; however, when both eyes are unimpaired and open, a single visual consciousness functions through two gateways, and by this means, the principle that what is seen is clear is established.
If it is claimed that when both eyes are open and unimpaired, the eye-consciousness functions through a single gateway at that time, this is what was previously stated.

Alternatively, when one eye is closed or impaired, even though the other eye is open, there is no mutual substitution; the consciousness produced therein relies on only a single gateway, and because it functions so rapidly, vision is not clear.

To say that [the distinction between clarity and dullness] is rendered useless and that there is no alternative explanation is also illogical, because there is indeed an alternation between preceding and succeeding moments.

Furthermore, the consciousness of the first moment would have to be clear, and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would consequently have to be perpetually obscure; therefore, their claim certainly lacks any causal basis for the distinctions between clarity and dullness in the perception of forms.
Furthermore, they should explain this: when visual consciousness arises, the conditions for both the left and right eyes are equally present.
Why, then, do they not simultaneously produce consciousness together?

For those who argue that the two eyes produce consciousness sequentially, there is no causal factor at the time the conditions are complete that would cause the function of producing consciousness to belong first to the left rather than the right, or vice versa.

Furthermore, according to the tenets of the Sthavira school, when the entire body is submerged in cold or warm water, the atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*) are capable of producing consciousness throughout.
However, when the body-faculty is impaired internally or externally, although bodily consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) arises, it is not clear.
Therefore, one should know that when body-consciousness arises with clarity, it necessarily does so by virtue of its basis being broad and pervasive.
A body and its objects, extending for many hundreds of *yojana*s, appear before it entirely, such that from top to bottom, they all arise simultaneously as a single consciousness.
For what reason do you not allow that two eyes, situated no great distance apart and both having their objects present before them, simultaneously produce a single consciousness?

Examining your intention now, there is no other cause or condition; you merely wish to willfully contradict the tenets of the great treatises of the Abhidharma masters, displaying your own cleverness among the dull and ignorant.
The Abhidharmikas say:
It is logically certain that there are no *sarvatraga-sabhāga* (universally homogeneous) atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*).

When the body is enveloped and oppressed by thirteen masses of fire, although there are still immeasurable atoms of the body-faculty, they are not *sabhāga* (functioning) because they do not produce body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
If consciousness were to arise universally [throughout the body], the body should disintegrate.
Regarding this, the Sthavira says: "This point should be challenged as follows:
Is it because the body-consciousness does not arise universally that the body he has received does not disintegrate?"
Is it because they are sustained by the power of past karma?
Furthermore, as for all the injuries to their physical forms, are they caused by bodily consciousness or by being burned by fire?
Furthermore, since fierce fires pervade and press upon that body, for what reason does the tactile consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) not arise everywhere?
Moreover, where the consciousness arises, the body ought to disintegrate.
Such objections are all unreasonable, because karma must depend on conditions to be able to sustain the body.

It is said that by the power of karma, the atoms of the body-sense faculty (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*) within that body do not produce consciousness everywhere; for if they were to produce consciousness everywhere, the body would immediately disintegrate.
Why, then, does he not accept such a principle?
Furthermore, it is by virtue of this that the distinction between the superior and inferior power of karmic forces is established.
Regarding the lightness or heaviness of the suffering experienced by those sentient beings born there, it is because their karma is not equal.
That is to say, among those who possess bodies of identical size, those whose sense organs consist of fewer atoms will experience intense and piercing feelings of suffering.
If the atoms of the sense faculties within that same body are more numerous, then a weak sensation of suffering arises.
If it is argued that the superior or inferior nature of the resultant suffering (vipāka) is simply the natural law (dharmatā) of karma, what need is there for those [atoms]?
This objection is not valid, for there would otherwise be no distinction between the superior and inferior suffering experienced by a single body at different times.

If it is argued that this fault does not apply because the power of a single karma produces results of painful sensation with varying degrees of superiority and inferiority within one life due to the multiplicity of completing karmas (*pūrṇa-karman*), this reasoning is also incorrect; for when multiple karmas ripen, there is no fixed cause for their arising sequentially in such a manner.
If it is claimed that [suffering] arises when conditions coincide, then the principle that the power of karma depends upon conditions is established.

Although karma is capable of summoning the fruit of ripened suffering, it is only when the body, contact, and body-consciousness meet as conditions that body-consciousness arises; and it is only simultaneous with body-consciousness that the sensation of suffering arises. Therefore, the power of karma necessarily depends upon conditions to be realized.

There are non-sentient phenomena (*asattvadharmāḥ*) that can also act as conditions to produce painful feelings (*duḥkhavedanā*), yet these are not maturation (*vipāka*). If one were to claim that such conditions are also the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) of karmic power, then since a dominant fruit is not a maturation, it need not be continuous; its excellence or inferiority is not fixed.
Thus, it is impossible for karma not to depend on conditions for its accomplishment; this principle is difficult to transcend.

Therefore, what I have stated—that the power of karma causes the atoms of the body-faculty within that body not to produce consciousness everywhere, lest the production of consciousness everywhere cause the body to disintegrate—is a principle that is thoroughly established.

Regarding the statement that whatever harm occurs to the body's form is caused by the tactile consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) acting as fire to burn it—I say that this harm is certainly due to the tactile consciousness.
If there were no conscious awareness, how could external fire possibly [cause such harm]?
When pleasing objects do not appear before one, pleasant feelings do not arise and the body receives no benefit.
All those who are wise say this:
it is only by encountering external conditions that internal objects are awakened, giving rise to the mind and mental factors, which then bring either harm or benefit to the self.
If there were no painful sensation arising simultaneously with consciousness, what could cause harm to that body?
Therefore, the position they maintain is certainly not logical.

As for their claim that "a fierce fire pervades and oppresses the entire body, yet why does the bodily consciousness not arise everywhere?"—the Sthavira should likewise face this same issue: he must explain why, when the objects of both eyes appear simultaneously, visual consciousness arises from only one eye-organ and not from both.
Furthermore, as previously stated:
what was stated previously?

It means that by the power of karma, the atoms of the body-sense faculty (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*) within that body do not produce consciousness everywhere; for were they to produce consciousness everywhere, the body would immediately disintegrate.
Regarding the statement that "the body should perish where consciousness arises," on what basis is it definitively known that their bodies do not perish?
For instance, in the Reviving (Saṃjīva) and other hells, the bodily parts perish as soon as consciousness arises in those locations, yet they are not completely destroyed.
If the entire [body] were to perish, it would have to undergo death and rebirth repeatedly.
Therefore, one should know that many parts of the body simultaneously give rise to a single consciousness.
Thus, although the eye-faculty exists in two locations, it can simultaneously give rise to a single consciousness.
How is it that a single eye-consciousness evolves in dependence upon two eye-faculties?
It is because consciousness has no form and no place of abiding.
Because the mode of its transformation based on two [faculties] is difficult to definitively describe, how is it known that consciousness has no abiding place?
It is because a single consciousness transforms in dependence upon multiple faculties.

That is to say, if visual consciousness had an abiding place, since there are two eye-faculties but only one visual consciousness, the consciousness would have to transform in dependence upon only one eye; consequently, one would see forms with only one eye and not with both, or else there would simultaneously be two visual consciousnesses transforming in dependence on two faculties within a single continuum.
Since both of these positions are thus untenable, it follows that the mind and mental factors certainly have no place of abiding.

If it is argued that a single consciousness abides in two eye-loci at one time, this too is irrational, because it would entail the faults of having parts and being intermingled, thereby contradicting its unity.

That is to say, if a single consciousness were to abide in both eyes at one time, it would necessarily have parts: the part abiding in the left eye would not abide in the right, and the part abiding in the right eye would not abide in the left.

Furthermore, there would be a confusion [of the sense bases], because the eye-consciousness between the two eyes would also abide in dependence upon the body-faculty; thus, the body-consciousness would also become eye-consciousness.
Moreover, it could not be a single entity; if there were no eye-consciousness between the two eyes, how could it constitute a single unity given that there would be an interruption?

If this were so, it would follow that a single visual consciousness does not reside in each of the two eyes simultaneously; therefore, one should not admit that a single visual consciousness resides in the locations of both eyes at one time.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that visual consciousness dwells within the eye, how could it dwell there?
Would its substance and characteristics interpenetrate like oil dwelling in sesame seeds,
or would they rely on one another as distinct entities like fruit dwelling in a vessel?
However, both of these positions are unreasonable.
If it were as in the former case, since the eye and visual consciousness would have distinct natures, they would necessarily become one.
If it were as in the latter case, the principle that partless phenomena can combine as separate entities is not established.
If the mind and mental factors have no place of abiding, how can it be said that they cognize various forms by relying upon the eye-faculty, and are therefore called "eye-consciousness"?
Furthermore, if eye-consciousness does not abide within the eye, how could the eye-faculty function as its supporting basis (*āśraya*)?

This criticism is unreasonable. Because the eye serves as the specific, proximate arising-condition for visual consciousness, it is designated as its "support" (*āśraya*) and its "nature as support" (*āśrayatva*).
One cannot say that because something depends on another, it must therefore abide within it; for instance, a minister is said to depend on a king, and people are said to depend on wealth and food.

If it is argued that visual consciousness resides within the eye because it undergoes impairment or benefit according to its supporting faculty (indriya), this reasoning is also incorrect; for we observe that objects such as shadows, light, and reflections do not reside [in their supports], even though they undergo impairment or benefit according to those supports.

This means that although reflections and the like do not reside within trees and such objects, when those trees and so forth undergo benefit or harm, the reflections likewise undergo benefit or harm accordingly;

furthermore, one observes that in the great ocean, the water increases or decreases in accordance with the waning or waxing of the moon, yet the great ocean does not reside within the moon. Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) you have established suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
If that were so, why can visual consciousness not apprehend the physical mass of the eye, eye-salve, an applicator stick, the eyelids, or cataracts which serve as the support for the eye?
Even if one grants that visual consciousness resides within the eye-faculty, it cannot apprehend these because they are situated in extreme proximity to it.

Since it has been conceded that visual consciousness does not abide in its object, just as it does not abide in the sense organ, why should it not likewise be able to apprehend the physical mass of the eye-flesh and so forth?
This is not the case, because the dependent consciousness and its supporting organ function with respect to the same object.
Furthermore, although extremely distant forms and the locus of consciousness do not touch one another, they cannot be apprehended.

If it were the case that the eye-ball and so forth could not be apprehended by consciousness because they are in immediate proximity to their respective sense organs, then all forms that are not in immediate proximity to their respective sense organs should be able to be apprehended; therefore, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that visual consciousness apprehends its object.

If an object of apprehension cannot be perceived when it is either extremely near or extremely distant from its supporting sense organ, then visual consciousness must have a location rather than being without a location;
only then can one say that this consciousness is extremely near to or extremely distant from the color-form that is its object of apprehension.

This is also not the case, because proximity and distance are spoken of in reference to the sense organs that serve as their bases, or because they are spoken of in reference to the immediately preceding causes of their arising.

The eye is the immediately preceding cause for the arising of visual consciousness; since consciousness grasps the eye-organ as its "self," it is in reference to this very cause that there is said to be proximity and distance.
Alternatively, because visual consciousness functions within the body, there is no fault in speaking of "near" and "far" with respect to the body.
On this principle, the body is called a "conscious body," for consciousness grasps the body as its own internal possession; thus, it is known that visual consciousness functions within the body.
Some say: "Mind and mental factors must necessarily have a locus of abiding, for we observe that all effects abide in the locus of their causes.

That is to say, we see that all effects produced in the world do not fail to abide in the locus of their productive causes; just as the *kalala* abides in the locus of semen and blood, so too do sprouts and the like abide in the loci of their causes, such as seeds."
Since the eye-faculty is the cause for the arising of visual consciousness, visual consciousness must necessarily abide in the location of the eye-faculty.
If it is argued that it is like sound, which also exists apart from its source, this defense is untenable, because sound never exists apart from its supporting basis.

This statement is unreasonable. Just as there is a difference in the continuity of things such as excrement and soil, it is not the case that [the eye and visual consciousness] have an identical continuity like seeds and the like.

Because they differ in their essential natures (*dravya-bheda*), the eye and visual consciousness differ in their continuity, just like excrement and soil. Although sprouts and the like differ in their locations because they differ in their essential natures as causes, visual consciousness is likewise not located in the locus of the eye. It is not the case that, like sprouts and the like, it could be said to reside therein because its continuity with its cause—the seed—is non-different.
Furthermore, because consciousness does not abide in the locations of form and so forth.
Just as color, light, space, and mental attention can act as causes for the arising of visual consciousness, yet when the consciousness arises, it does not abide in those locations.
The eye should be understood in the same way: although it is a cause for consciousness, when consciousness arises, it does not abide in that [eye].

Is this not just as the eye, though equally a cause for consciousness along with visible forms and other factors, is such that when visual consciousness arises, it relies solely upon the eye and not upon visible forms and so forth?

In this way, although the eye-faculty and visible forms alike serve as causes for consciousness, when visual consciousness arises, it should reside only in the eye and not in visible forms and so forth.

For what reason do you now fail to accept this principle: that although the eye-faculty and visible forms differ in being the support (*āśraya*) or non-support for the consciousness they produce, they both equally function as the causal nature for the continuity of that distinct class of visual consciousness?

Thus, although the eye-faculty and other [faculties] differ from the object—such as visible form—in their relationship to the consciousness they produce (being its support versus not being its support), they equally function as the consciousness itself and are not the cause upon which it resides.
From this it is known that mental states and mental factors certainly have no place of residence; this meaning is fully established.

Therefore, as previously stated, because consciousness has no form or color and no fixed location, its mode of operation based on these two [bases] is difficult to define with certainty; this must logically be so.
Regarding what has been explained thus far: when the eye and other sense faculties correctly apprehend their respective objects, do they reach them or not?
For what reason do you still harbor doubts regarding this?
It is because two different explanations are seen within the sūtras.
As the Blessed One said:
The visual faculty of sentient beings is obstructed by agreeable and disagreeable forms.
It is not that they do not reach one another; thus, the meaning of "obstruction" is established.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
With his divine eye, he observes sentient beings— extensively described as being either far or near.
Since distance and proximity cannot be established for an object that is already present before one,
a doubt arises again because of these two [contradictory] statements.

The meaning of "the sense faculty and its object reaching one another" (*prāpti*) is not fixed. If it is defined in terms of functional capacity, then "reaching" means arriving at the object, and thus all sense faculties would only apprehend objects that have been reached.
If it is defined in terms of essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), then "reaching" means being without an interval (*nirantara*).
The verse says:
The faculties of eye, ear, and mind, and their objects, are not in contact; these three are contradictory [to the others].
The commentary says:
The visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) perceives only non-attained objects (*aprāpta-viṣaya*), because it perceives both distant and near objects simultaneously.

If the eye were to reach its object, it would entail movement; yet Devadatta and others, who possess the quality of movement, cannot reach two directions—both distant and near—at one and the same time. Therefore, the visual faculty perceives non-attained objects.

If it is argued that, like a lamp, [the visual faculty] reaches both distant and near objects simultaneously because that is its nature, this argument is incorrect because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).

That is to say, if someone were to claim: "For example, just as a bright lamp reaches and illuminates two directions—distant and near—simultaneously, so too does the visual faculty reach and apprehend two objects—distant and near—simultaneously, because it shares the same nature of luminous fire as that lamp."
This reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because the nature of the eye as fire-light is not universally established (*aprasiddha*).

Furthermore, the eye ought not to have the nature of fire-light, because one seeks illumination when desiring to see in the dark; it is not the case that a lamp, when wishing to illuminate a jar, a garment, or other objects, requires the assistance of a separate source of light in order to illuminate them.

If it is argued that because the fire-light within the eye is small, one must seek the assistance of a great light to see, this too is unreasonable; for we observe that a small light is overwhelmed by a great one, and thus the eye would ultimately be unable to see forms.
Furthermore, the analogy of a bright lamp is not the same as that of the eye, because it cannot illuminate objects that are immediately adjacent and without interval.
That is to say, just as a bright lamp can both burn and illuminate objects that are extremely close to it, such as its own oil and wick; [the eye cannot do so].
The eye is not like this, for it cannot see objects that are extremely close, such as eye-salve.

Furthermore, just as a bright lamp illuminates all objects—whether distant or near—without interval or partiality, the eye is not so; for it may see mountains and the like while skipping over intervening forms such as trees and forests.
By this analogy of the lamp, it differs from the eye.

Since the reason previously established—that the eye perceives both distant and near objects simultaneously—proves that the eye perceives only non-contacted objects (*aprāptaviṣaya*), this principle remains unshakable.

Furthermore, the eye should not reach its object in order to apprehend it, because it cannot apprehend an object that is immediately adjacent; because it can also apprehend forms obstructed by substances such as rock crystal (*sphaṭika*); and because there is doubt regarding what is seen.
If [the sense organ] perceives by reaching the object, why is there any hesitation?
It is not reasonable to hesitate regarding that which has already been reached.
Furthermore, this is because one has not yet clearly discerned the difference between a person and a tree stump.
Since it is said that [the eye] reaches that [object], one would clearly perceive its vertical dimension but not its specific distinctions; what is the cause for this?
Furthermore, the eye has no capacity to reach distant objects;
it is impossible for the eye, while remaining here, to travel across many thousands of *yojana*s to reach the sphere of the moon.
The argument that "because the eye possesses luminosity, this fault does not apply" is likewise unreasonable.
Since it is not established by consensus that the eye possesses the luminosity of fire,
and since the nature of the eye is not fire, how could it possess the luminosity of fire?

The auditory faculty likewise apprehends only non-contiguous objects, because the distinctions of direction and distance—such as north, south, and so forth—can be discerned; that is to say, one can discern the differences in the sounds of near and far directions, such as north and south.
If sound must reach the auditory faculty before it can be heard, then it should be like taste and other objects; yet this is not the case for any of them.
Is it not true that the olfactory faculty also perceives the distinctions of fragrance—whether near or far—only after it has apprehended them?
Although [the nose] perceives, it does so only by turning toward the direction [of the object]; it apprehends fragrance clearly and then infers its specific distinctions.

The eyes and ears, however, perceive and hear objects across distances and directions without requiring such turning, and are thus able to cognize them; therefore, they are not of the same category as the olfactory faculty in apprehending its object.

Furthermore, because the perception of sounds—whether near or distant—is characterized by being either clear or unclear, if one could only hear them once they have reached the ear, all perceptions should necessarily be clear.
Moreover, there is a distinction between the certain determination and the hesitation involved in perceiving sounds that are near versus those that are distant.

If one hears [the sound] only when it has arrived, then since there is no distinction between [the arriving and non-arriving states], one should be as certain regarding all distant sounds as one is when they are near.
Conversely, if one is hesitant regarding distant sounds, one should not have certainty regarding any nearby sounds.
Based on these proofs, [the mind] does not reach its object when it hears.
The mental faculty (*manas*) likewise perceives only non-contiguous objects (*aprāptaviṣaya*), because it does not perceive co-existent or associated phenomena (*sahabhū-saṃprayuktadharma*).

If one were to argue that, just as the nose—though unable to grasp its own simultaneously arising fragrance—nevertheless grasps a contiguous object, so too is the case for the mind, this reasoning is necessarily incorrect.

Since it is an established principle that the nose can only apprehend odors produced externally by sensory contact or arising internally through innate conditions, just as it is said that only internal food can perform the function of food, it cannot perform the function of food at a time when it is not being apprehended.
Furthermore, because they lack form, there can be no reaching [of the object].
Therefore, the sense-faculties apprehend objects that are not reached.

If it were argued that the three faculties are able to apprehend objects that are not reached, this would logically be untenable, for they would then have to be able to apprehend all things—regardless of location or time—that are not reached by them.
That is to say, if the three faculties apprehend non-contiguous objects because they are alike in being non-contiguous,

then why can they not apprehend all things that are not reached— such as those situated at the furthest distances above or below, those separated by obstructions, or those already ceased or yet to arise?
Furthermore, since those three faculties have not yet arisen or have already ceased, how is it that they cannot apprehend [their objects]?
Moreover, when facing one direction, why can one not see the objects of other directions? This objection is not valid.

For example, just as a magnet is able to attract iron, so too a magnet, though it can attract various pieces of iron that do not reach it, cannot attract iron that is separated by an obstacle extending for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, nor can it attract iron that has already ceased or not yet arisen, nor iron that does not face it—even if it does not reach it. Likewise, [the faculties] cannot attract what has not yet arisen or what has already ceased.

Furthermore, just as mirrors and the like produce images, it means that although mirrors and such can produce images of objects even when those objects do not reach them, they cannot produce images of all things that are extremely distant, obstructed by barriers, already ceased, not yet arisen, or not facing the mirror; nor can they produce images of things that have not yet arisen or have already ceased.
The same applies to the eye and other [senses], so this should not be raised as an objection.
Therefore, that objection does not cause the three faculties to lose their capacity to apprehend objects that are not in contact.
Some say that the ear can apprehend objects in contact, because sound proceeds in a continuous stream and enters the ear, and furthermore, because one can hear sounds within the ear itself.

This argument is irrational, because as soon as the hand grasps the bell, the sound ceases immediately. If the sound were to arrive at the ear through a continuous series, then while the hand grasps the bell, the sound based on that bell might indeed cease; however, the series produced from it and transmitted through the intervening space, being separated from its source, would not cease, and thus this sound should still be audible.

However, when a bell is struck, one directly perceives that all other sounds from bells suddenly cease and become entirely inaudible; it is not that the others can be made to cease while this one remains, for as this one ceases, the others likewise cease.
Because they are not heard, the others are likewise not heard.

If it is argued that when a lamp goes out, both the near and distant light are extinguished, this is also not the case, because there is a distinction between their functioning simultaneously or non-simultaneously, and because they are not identical in their continuity. That is to say, we clearly perceive the lamp and its light functioning together; as soon as the flame of the lamp is extinguished, the light is no longer seen.

Sound is not like that, for they maintain that it proceeds in a continuous succession away from its substance and enters the ear; thus, they must necessarily admit that when the sound is heard upon reaching the ear, the initial sound attached to the substance has long since ceased and perished.
If it were not so, the state of a śrāvaka initially produced would still persist, thereby losing its momentary nature (*kṣaṇikatva*).
Therefore, sound is not the same as that lamp-light.

Furthermore, the continuity of the lamp and the light are distinct; just as the mind and mental factors arise together from the same conditions, when those conditions are impaired, both cease simultaneously.
Sound is not like that; its continuity is without difference, just as the continuity of consciousness arises from non-common conditions.
Within the continuity of sound, although the preceding sound has ceased, the subsequent sound still arises—why then is it not heard?
Therefore, the sound produced by depending upon a substance serves as the condition for the arising of auditory consciousness.
If it were otherwise, one would only hear sound once it has reached the ear; consequently, there would be no distinction between perceiving sounds that are near or far.

However, as for that which one can hear within the ear, it is not like odors and so forth, which are adjacent to the nose and other faculties; although it occurs within the ear, it is nonetheless a non-contiguous object (*aprāptaviṣaya*).

Because words press against the ear, making syllables and phrases difficult to discern, those who wish to listen attentively block such painful pressure; therefore, the ear perceives only non-contiguous objects.
Now it should be investigated:
for what reason is the eye unable to apprehend the color of jars, garments, and so forth in the dark— is it because their substance does not exist,
or because they are not within its range?
Is it because the causes for apprehension are absent?
Or is it that apprehension does not occur because the causes for obstruction are present?
Furthermore, it is not the case that forms in the dark are unapprehendable because they lack substantial existence, for those with the divine eye (divyacakṣus) are able to perceive them directly.
Furthermore, it is not the case that color-form (*rūpa*) in darkness cannot be apprehended because it is not an object; for its causes, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), are currently perceptible.

Moreover, even if illuminated by a luminous spell (*vidyā*), it should not be apprehended [as such], because atoms (*paramāṇu*) and other forms within the light are not objects that the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) can see.

Although it is said that this color in darkness cannot be apprehended because it is a different class of color from that which exists in light— just as there is color in the intermediate state (antarābhava)—
this is not reasonable.
Why is this so? Because one should not grasp that contact which accompanies [the object]; furthermore, when holding up a light to illuminate it, no distinct color is seen.

Alternatively, darkness and light would have to become the causes for its destruction and arising respectively, and form would also have to possess a heterogeneous nature; yet we observe that those who have previously experienced a certain type of object recognize it as being that very same thing even when touching it in the dark.
Furthermore, because colors such as red-dyed garments seen in the dark do not appear different when brought into the light,
this proves that they are not a distinct category of color.
If this is so, for what reason is the color of darkness not perceived?
The Dārṣṭāntika masters assert this:
"Because of the absence of light, which is a contributing cause for grasping.
What function does light perform in this context?
This means that there is a benefit consisting in the capacity to apprehend the sense faculty (*indriya*), just as one who eats dry flour does not obtain its flavor.
Furthermore, it is said that visible form exists within the range of visibility.

If this were so, light would only be able to provide benefit to the object and not to the faculty; for instance, when the body dwells in darkness, one perceives forms in a luminous place. This is established both by the analogy of dry flour cited above and by the scriptural authority (*āgama*) quoted therein.

Furthermore, as for the statement that "form is in a visible location," the intention is not to say that form exists within light; rather, it means that the object resides within the range of the sense faculty's power and its location, because that sutra explains at length that this extends even to the point where "phenomena reside in a knowable location."

Furthermore, if you argue that the substance of objects such as jars or garments already exists in the dark, yet cannot be perceived because they lack the auxiliary causes for perception, and that they can subsequently be perceived when encountering auxiliary causes such as light which makes those colors manifest—then you must likewise admit that the substance of wind already exists in space, yet cannot be perceived because it lacks the auxiliary causes for perception, and that it can only be perceived after encountering auxiliary causes such as fans which make that wind manifest.
Furthermore, one should also admit that the mutual friction of two pieces of wood is the cause for the perception of fire, rather than the production of a separate fire.
However, this should not be admitted, as it entails logical faults.
Those who maintain the doctrine of a self (*ātman*) should likewise be able to say:
The essence of the self exists prior [to perception], yet because it lacks the sense organs capable of apprehension, it cannot apprehend.
Therefore, darkness and color are not auxiliary causes for apprehension; rather, it is because light is absent that the eye cannot apprehend.
If that is so, for what reason is it not apprehended?
It is because the causes that obstruct its apprehension exist. What are these?
This refers to the fact that when various forms are obstructed by darkness, clouds, smoke, dust, and so forth, the eye cannot perceive them; this is established by analogy with well-known cases.

Since light is the opposite of these obstructions and serves as the cause for perception, it is only by depending on that light that one can apprehend form; therefore, light is also said to be a cause for the arising of consciousness.

Furthermore, just as lapis lazuli and a wall differ in their capacity to obstruct based on the perceiver, so too do darkness and light differ in kind; thus, there is a distinction in their essential natures as being obstructive or non-obstructive.

As has already been argued above, is it not also the case that [cognition] fails to apprehend due to the absence of auxiliary causes? For even when a real object exists, cognition does not arise if the faculty of vision, its functional capacity, and attention are absent.
Although this is the case, doubt may still arise.
That is to say: just as one does not perceive color in the dark, it is likewise with light.
Consequently, it remains unknown whether the non-perception is due to the absence of the object seen, or due to the absence of light.

It is universally established that clouds and the like obstruct visible form so that it is not seen; furthermore, since darkness as an obstruction is itself perceived, there is no doubt that in the dark, the eye cannot apprehend form due to the obstruction of darkness.
As it is said: "Extremely distant forms cannot be perceived because of their distance.
Furthermore, it is also said:
Extremely distant forms cannot be apprehended because they lack proximity;
between these two explanations, the former is superior, for it possesses substantial reality and does not give rise to doubt.

Thus it should be understood: because there is the obstruction of darkness and because there is no light, all forms present in the dark are necessarily not perceived due to that obstruction of darkness.
Because light acts as the cause for the apprehension of objects by counteracting these obstacles, it is only when depending upon that light that the eye can apprehend visible forms.
What has been stated is necessarily so according to reason.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Seven.

8. Chapter One, Part Eight: Explaining the Fundamental Bases. It has already been stated that three faculties apprehend objects not in contact with themselves.
The remaining three—the nose and so forth—are the opposite of the aforementioned; that is, the nose, tongue, and body apprehend only objects in contact.
How is it known that the nose perceives only odors that have reached it? Some say:
because when one stops breathing, one does not smell odors.
This reason is insufficient to establish the point.
Even if one were able to smell fragrances when there is a cessation [of contact], how could this prove that the nose perceives only those odors that have reached it?
For atoms do not touch one another.
Why do they not touch?
If the atoms were to touch one another in their entirety, there would be the fault of the substantial bodies intermingling;
if they touched only in part, they would incur the loss of being partless.
Therefore, this reason—that the nose perceives only odors that reach the sense organ—is insufficient to prove [the existence of atoms].
Indeed, there are times when one can perceive the fragrance of breath even though it does not come into contact [with the nose]; how, then, could the meaning of "reaching" be established?
Since that objection stands, how is this reason to be understood?
Now, examining the ultimate meaning, it is said that an object can only be apprehended when it arises in close proximity to the sense faculty.

By this principle, it is taught that the nose, tongue, and body perceive only objects with which they are in contact (*prāptaviṣaya*). This is just as it is said that the eye cannot see colors that are in contact with it, such as the eyelid or a stick.

It is not necessary for the eyelids and so forth to actually touch the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) in order to be designated as "reached" (*prāpta*); rather, when the eyelids and so forth arise in proximity to the faculty, they are immediately termed "reached.
Because such reached forms cannot be seen, it is said that the eye faculty perceives objects that are not reached (*aprāptaviṣaya*).
Just as the eye and other sense organs perceive objects that are not in direct contact with them, yet they cannot perceive extremely distant objects;

so too it is with the nose and the others: although they perceive objects in contact, they cannot perceive objects that are extremely close. However, because odors and so forth arise in proximity to these organs, there is no fault in saying that these three organs perceive objects in contact.
The atoms of the sense organs, such as the nose, and their objects, such as odors, do not mutually touch one another, because they are not of the nature of the tangible.
Furthermore, since they possess the quality of resistance through obstruction (*pratighāta-sapratighatva*), if they were to touch, it would entail logical error.
To clarify this point, it should further be investigated.
Suppose someone were to raise an objection:
"If atoms do not touch one another, how can striking them produce sound?"
How could this be the same as the position of the followers of Ulūka (the Vaiśeṣikas), who claim that sound is produced only through the conjunction of qualities?
Yet they raise such an objection.
However, since the principle of conjunction does not hold when things meet, one should not admit that sound is produced by the conjunction of qualities.
If that is so, how can sound be produced?

Within this true and noble teaching and its principles, the terms "separation" and "conjunction" as well as "striking" depend solely upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). That is to say, when two sets of preeminent primary elements arise through separation or conjunction, they receive those names; at this stage, these primary elements are the cause for the production of sound, and the sound co-arising with them is the object of the auditory faculty.
What fault is there in this?
If they do not admit it, neither do I. Furthermore, there is a logical reason:
since atoms do not touch one another, how could the meaning of the conjunction of their respective primary elements (mahābhūta) be established?
When they arise in immediate proximity, they are already termed "joined"; why wait for them to actually touch before they receive the name "joined"?
Furthermore, you should not hesitate over this point: these primary elements (mahābhūta) certainly do not touch one another.
Why is this so? Because it is that which is touched (*spraṣṭavya*), not that which touches (*spraṣṭṛ*).

Among all the aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*), only the element of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) is called "that which is touched," and only the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*) is called "that which touches. Beyond this, the meaning of "touch" should not be further contemplated.

If it is claimed that what is touched is also capable of touching, then one must admit that the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is also that which is touched; in that case, the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*) would become confused.
However, since there is no such confusion, the distinction between object and subject is established.

If it is argued that there is no fault of confusion between these two because the objects and bases of tactile consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) are distinct, how can it be that this does not result in confusion?
For if the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) were also an object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), for what reason would it not become the object of tactile consciousness?

If you admit that the element of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) can also perform the function of touching, for what reason does it not serve as the support (*āśraya*) for body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*)?
Furthermore, if atoms (*paramāṇu*) definitely do not touch one another, then the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* should not state:
"That which is non-contact serves as the cause for the arising of contact," referring to the moment when separated objects are in the process of coming together.
Contact as a cause gives rise to non-contact, namely when objects that were in conjunction are in the process of separating;
contact as a cause gives rise to contact, namely when objects that were separated come together again;
and non-contact as a cause gives rise to non-contact, namely the continuous succession of similar types of motile dust particles.

The Vaibhāṣika school definitively does not admit the principle that atoms (paramāṇu) can mutually touch one another; one should know that their statement possesses a specific underlying intention. For instance, they speak of a collection of many atoms in a mote of dust, stating in their treatise that "that which is non-contact arises with non-contact as its cause. Therefore, it is clear that their statement certainly has a distinct intended meaning.
What is the specific intention [behind this]?
It means that the term "contact" (sparśa) is used with reference to a combination [of factors].
The Vaibhāṣika masters all maintain this view:
However, it is solely through the sustaining power of the wind element that the atoms are held together so as not to disperse.

When a composite form arises due to the conjunction of various conditions, it is said that what was previously a non-contact cause gives rise to contact; this means that the cause of dispersion produces the state of aggregation.
Is it not the case that there are atoms which do not aggregate, but only aggregate when waiting for conditions? If so, then everything would have to be produced as contact with contact as its cause.
To this some say: there are also atoms that do not aggregate; therefore, this fault does not apply.
Some say: Because it is in relation to coarse composite matter that the term "non-tangible" (*asaṃspṛśya*) is established for subtle composites.
