Therefore, the statement that "that which is produced from a cause of non-tangibility is tangible" means that what is produced from a subtle aggregate is a coarse aggregate; thus, there is no error in their meaning.

Because of the convergence of various conditions, aggregated matter is maintained; when the wind element ceases, the opposite occurs, and dispersed matter arises. Thus, at this stage, it is said that the cause of contact gives rise to non-contact; this means that the cause of a coarse aggregate gives rise to a subtle aggregate.

Because of the convergence of various conditions, the aggregate of form is maintained; the wind element does not extinguish these coarse aggregates of form, which may either produce their own kind or transform to produce coarser forms. This is said to mean that contact is the cause for the arising of contact, and that coarse aggregates are the cause for the arising of coarse aggregates.

By this principle, the various motes of dust moving in space are able to sustain the coarse; the wind element does not arise, and the subtle aggregations continue in succession without transforming into the coarse. This is called "that which is not produced by contact arises from that which is not contact," meaning that the cause of the subtle aggregation produces the subtle aggregation.
This refers to the specific intention behind those statements.
Furthermore, the term "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*) is also applied to that which is non-material (*arūpa*), as stated in the Sūtra:
"When emerging from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), how many contacts will one experience?"

When three types of contact occur—namely, the immovable contact (*āniñjya-sparśa*), the contact of nothingness (*ākiṃcanya-sparśa*), and the signless contact (*animitta-sparśa*)—it is not the case that there is any calculable sense of actual mutual contact within them. Therefore, the principle that these respective great elements (*mahābhūta*) certainly do not touch one another is fully established.
If you grant that they touch one another, what further fault would there be?
Was it not previously stated that if the atoms were to touch in their entirety, there would be the fault of the substantial entities intermingling;
yet if they touched in only a single part, they would incur the loss of being partless.
However, that Elder further states regarding this:
"The substance of atoms is itself spatial extension (digbhāga).
How can there be a substance while claiming it has no spatial extension?"

This statement is irrational. If you grant that atoms have no further subdivisions and yet possess spatial dimensions because they possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then all formless phenomena (*arūpadharma*), since they likewise possess intrinsic nature and lack [spatial] differentiation, should also possess spatial dimensions.

If it is argued that because formless phenomena lack the meaning of aggregation, they should not be called "spatial parts," this too is irrational, for it is also taught that formless phenomena possess location and possess aggregation.
Furthermore, the position that matter possesses conjunction is also irrational, for it would result in [matter] becoming a single entity; that which is a single substance cannot be called "conjoined.
Moreover, the Sthavira says:
"Because both types of atoms are partless, there is no distinction in their locations."
This is also unreasonable, for that treatise itself states:
"Some say that atoms do not obstruct one another in their location.

This thesis is flawed, as it contradicts the scriptural teaching of "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*). For what reason, then, does it further state that because both types of atoms lack parts, there is no distinction in their place of residence?

Furthermore, regarding what was said: it is precisely for this reason that it is accepted that they are spoken of as being inseparable based on occupying the same location; moreover, it is stated that at least five atoms may occupy the same location without mutual obstruction.
All of this is unreasonable.
If five atoms were permitted to occupy the same location, what would act as an obstruction to prevent hundreds of thousands of koṭis from doing the same?
In that case, a single atom’s location would have to contain all existing atoms, and thus the entire world would be the size of a single atom.

Alternatively, one would have to deny that five minimal atoms can occupy the same location without mutual obstruction, because the space occupied by a collection of many atoms is broad; therefore, one must admit that atoms possess parts.
Perhaps the meaning is that atoms neither touch nor are separated from one another; otherwise, it would be impossible for a single atom to exist alone in the present without being aggregated.

As has already been argued previously, therefore, within every composite aggregate, all [elements] are present according to their respective capacities; it is for this reason that the term "non-separation" (*avinirbhāga*) is employed. This does not mean they are called "non-separate" because they occupy the same location; rather, since they are partless (*niravayava*), the sense of "not touching" (*aspraṣṭavya*) is established.
If that is so, how can the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the tangible-object element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) function as the toucher and the touched?
Since it has already been established that atoms do not touch one another, we must now consider together the meaning of "toucher" and "touched."
If you claim that our school accepts contact because we have already admitted the contact between the sense-faculty and the object, what further point is there to consider?
You alone should reflect upon this matter.
This is not reasonable, for those who maintain the doctrine of contact should likewise reflect upon this same point.

If the nose and tongue were also to come into contact with the atoms of their respective objects, for what reason would you not admit that these sense-faculties and their atomic objects are the "touched" (spraṣṭavya) and the "toucher" (spraṣṭṛ)?

If you do not admit that both touch the atoms of their own objects, yet you still designate them as "taking an object through contact" (*prāptaviṣaya*) just like the body-faculty, then this case is exactly the same as that principle.
Alternatively, there should be mutual contact within non-material phenomena, because of the three types of contact previously cited.
Therefore, one should here collectively investigate the intended meaning of "contact" as taught in the sūtras.

However, as I previously stated, it is because an object must arise in proximity to its sense faculty to be apprehended that it is called "apprehending the reached object" (*prāptaviṣaya-grahaṇa*); now, the contact between the faculty and the object should be understood accordingly, for they are extremely close.

Is it not the case that since all the faculties of nose, tongue, and body apprehend objects that reach them without distinction, then the faculty of touch should also pertain to the nose and tongue, and the objects touched should likewise include odors and tastes?
This is also unreasonable, because although they are equally proximate, there are distinctions among them.
For example, although the eyelids and so forth share the common designation of "reaching," there are nonetheless distinctions among them.

The eyelids and so forth do not attain the designation of "reaching" (prāpti), for if they did, there would be no distinction between all things that reach [an object]; this is because the eyelid, the probe, the medicinal ointment, and the cataract differ in their degree of proximity to the eye faculty, ranging from slight to intermediate.
Furthermore, just as the eye and other [senses] are alike in apprehending non-contacted objects, yet there are no distinctions among those non-contacted objects;
so too it is with the nose and other [senses], which are alike in apprehending contacted objects, and thus there ought to be distinctions among those contacted objects.

Furthermore, regarding smoothness, roughness, and so forth, the world collectively gives rise to the conceptual designation "the tangible" (*spraṣṭavya*); in relation to that body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), it is called "the tangenter" (*spraṣṭṛ*). Therefore, there is no fault.
Some say: in reality, there is neither a tangenter nor the tangible; however, because they appear as if they exist, the name "contact" (*sparśa*) is established as a conventional designation.
Alternatively, one might seek further reasoning therein; however, one should not admit that the object and the body-faculty actually come into contact with one another.

As previously stated, this would result in a confusion between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*). Therefore, following this correct principle, one should explain that the designations "the toucher" and "the touched" arise from their causal conditions.
Other masters say:

Although individual atoms do not touch one another, there is no fault in the fact that composite matter does touch; it is by this that sounds are produced through striking. Just as individual atoms lack resistance and changeability, yet composite matter possesses resistance and changeability without being non-existent.
This is not reasonable, for there is no composite matter apart from atoms;
if one were to touch a composite, one would necessarily touch the atoms, and thus one would have to admit that atoms themselves touch.
Therefore, what was stated previously is superior in terms of reasoning.
Furthermore, the Sthavira said:
"If this touches that, then that necessarily touches this."
Once that which is touched has been formed, there is no logical contradiction in its being touched by other contacts;
if it were otherwise, atoms would not mutually support one another and thus could not coalesce.

If it is claimed that this "upholding" is the power of the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*), how could the wind element be like a hand holding something up, such that it upholds the atoms so they do not scatter or fall?
This objection is irrational; for instance, the water mandala is upheld by the wind mandala so that it does not scatter or fall, yet how could the wind mandala be like a hand holding something up?
Just as they are supported by that, so too should this be.

If one were to say, "I grant that atoms touch one another, and because they touch, they support one another," then the objection regarding the difficulty of holding [a vessel] with the hands would be rendered futile.

Regarding what you have said—that atoms touch one another and are arranged in succession so as to be able to support one another—I also say that they are able to support one another through being arranged in close proximity by the power of the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*). Therefore, one should not say that if this were otherwise, atoms would lack mutual support and thus could not combine;

for contrary to your claim, atoms do indeed possess mutual support because they form a composite. Furthermore, even without touching, they can still support one another, just as the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*), though not touched, can support the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) and cause it to arise and manifest before one.
Furthermore, as for what he said—
that if this touches that, then that necessarily touches this, and since it has thus become the "touched," there is no logical contradiction in the remaining cases of touching and being touched—
this was stated by him without careful reflection.

As previously stated, the object and the body-faculty do not actually touch one another; for otherwise, there would be the fault of the confusion between the object and the faculty, it would contradict reason for either the whole or a part of the body to be touched, and because all resistant phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*) are comprised within the category of obstructive resistance (*āvaraṇa-pratigha*).
Since spatial locations are mutually exclusive and cannot interpenetrate, they ought not to touch one another, for they lack constituent parts.

It is not the case that they touch only a single part, because [atoms] are indivisible; nor can they touch as a whole, for if many atoms were to occupy the same location, the fault would be as previously stated.
How can it be said that "if this touches that, then that must touch this," and so forth, as explained at length?
Furthermore, according to this same principle, one could also say:
"if this sees that, then that must see this. Since it has been established as being seen, there is no logical contradiction in the remaining cases of the seer and the seen.
If this one hears that, then that one must certainly hear this; since it has already been established as something heard, there is no logical contradiction in others hearing what is heard by them.
Since that is not the case for the former, how could it be so for the latter?

If the element of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) does not itself come into contact [with other tangibles], how can the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) act upon one another by mutually supporting or harming each other?
Must they necessarily come into contact to be able to cause harm or benefit, or otherwise? How could it be so?
If this were necessarily the case, how could the eyes be harmed by looking at the sun or snow,
and how could they be benefited by looking at the lunar disc?
It would follow that the eyes do not reach the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the sun and so forth.

Furthermore, you do not admit that there are primary elements (mahābhūta) coexisting with that light, because you maintain that light arises dependent upon the primary elements of the solar and lunar disks.
For that Elder himself has stated:
"The primary elements and the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) are for the most part inseparable."
There are also some cases where separation is attained, namely the light of the sun, moon, lamps, and jewels, as well as the fragrance of solitary wandering scents detached from flowers.

Following this line of inquiry, since the body-faculty (kāyendriya) perceives only objects that reach it, and because heat is currently perceived by the body within sunlight, how do you know that the sunlight depends solely on the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the solar orb and not upon the primary elements of the body-faculty located nearby?

If, at a certain location, the body perceives the heat of the sun and approaches that place, and the eyes see the sunlight, one should know that this light is not separate from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); therefore, it is only by being in close proximity to the primary elements as conditions that they can cause harm or benefit.
It has already been established that the primary elements (mahābhūta) are proximate, yet neither extremely distant nor in direct contact.
For instance, although the tangible does not touch the body-faculty (kāyendriya), it can nevertheless act as a cause for the benefit or injury of the body.

If it is argued that what is touched causes benefit or harm to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) relies, then how does this apply to snow, sunlight, and so forth in relation to the eye?

Even if one grants that what is touched causes benefit or harm to the primary elements upon which the body-faculty relies, one would still not grant that the primary elements upon which the body relies can cause benefit or harm to the body-faculty while remaining untouched by it. Would this not establish the principle of benefit and harm through the mutual proximity of the primary elements, even though they do not actually touch one another, because they act as causes for one another?

Therefore, one should not say: "If the tangible element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) also does not touch [other tangibles], how can the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) relate to one another by mutually supporting or harming each other?"
However, the Bhadanta says:
"All atoms do not actually touch one another; it is only because they are without interval that the name 'contact' is metaphorically applied.
In this context, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika), wishing to manifest the excellence of that Bhadanta’s view, spoke as follows: "The intention of this Bhadanta should be found pleasing."

If it were otherwise, these atoms would necessarily have intervals between them; since their interiors would be empty, what would obstruct their movement such that they could be considered "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*)?

Now, the intention of the Venerable One [Vasumitra] is stated as follows: it is neither acceptable nor objectionable, but one must simply investigate how they can be without interval yet not touch one another.
Because the underlying principle has not yet been clarified, the intended meaning is difficult to discern.

If one were to say that the atoms are entirely without interstices yet do not interpenetrate, they would necessarily possess parts; for it is not permissible for them to occupy the same location while remaining without interstices.
Since it is already granted that there is an interval, why do they not touch?
Therefore, the term "interval" (*antara*) simply serves to definitively indicate the sense of proximity.

Here, the word "definitive" (*niyata*) may indicate the sense of certainty; because there is certainly a gap, it is called "definitive-interval" (*niyatāntara*), just as something with certain heat is called "definitively hot" (*niyatoṣṇa*). Thus, the principle that there is certainly a gap is established.

Alternatively, it may indicate the absence of something, meaning that it does not exist therein; for example, because they are separated by the color of tangible atoms (*paramāṇu*), they are called "uninterrupted" (*nirantara*). Likewise, when great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise in close proximity as atoms, this is metaphorically designated as "contact."

If one provides this explanation, then the Venerable’s statement that all atoms do not actually touch one another, but that the designation "contact" is applied only by way of their being contiguous, possesses profound significance.

It is precisely by virtue of the power of obstructive resistance (*pratighāta*) that something is admitted to be resistant, insofar as it can obstruct the movement [of others]; it is not by admitting that they occupy a common location and are mutually accommodated that one can say they possess obstructive resistance.
Is it because they share the same location that you object to their abiding without intervals while permitting gaps between them, yet deny that there is movement toward one another?
There is no cause for fear; such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Those things that possess resistance (*sapratigha*) must necessarily occupy different locations; otherwise, if they shared a single location, they would become partless (*niravayava*). Therefore, the principle of their abiding without intervals is certainly untenable.
Although there may be slight gaps in between, the power of resistance obstructs their movement.
What are these gaps? Other masters say:
This is a form that lacks tangibility.
Furthermore, some say: it does not exist at all.
The Master of the Sūtras further states:
"Moreover, if it is admitted that atoms possess spatial dimensions (dig-bhāga), then whether they touch or do not touch, they must both have parts.
If they lack spatial dimensions, even if one admits that they touch, there would be no fault; however, this statement is irrational."
"Having parts" (*sāvayava*) and "having spatial divisions" (*digbhāga*) differ in name but are identical in meaning.

Since the assertion that atoms have no parts has already excluded the possibility of spatial divisions, how can you again give rise to doubt by asking: "If one grants that atoms have spatial divisions, then since they lack such divisions, how could they be touched?"
Furthermore, there are faults in both cases—whether the contact occurs with the entire body or with only a portion—as has already been fully discussed.
How, then, can you say:
"If there are no spatial parts (digbhāga), even if we grant that they touch, this fault does not arise"?
Therefore, it is said that there is no intervening space even as small as an atom of matter; thus it is called "uninterrupted" (*nirantara*).

When such great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise in close proximity, this is metaphorically designated as "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*); this meaning is established. It is not the case that the sense of being "impinging" (*sapratigha*) and "partless" (*niravayava*) is established by virtue of having a common locus of residence or by residing without an interval.

Now one should investigate: do the sense organs, such as the eye, perceive their respective objects only when the object is of equal size, appearing as a mountain or the like due to rapid movement—just as a whirling firebrand appears as a circle?
Do they apprehend their own objects by taking [objects] of equal or unequal magnitude?
The verse says:
One should know that the three beginning with the nose apprehend only objects of equal magnitude.
The Commentary states:
Regarding the three faculties previously mentioned—the nose and so forth—that reach their objects, it should be understood that they can only apprehend objects of equal dimension.

For example, just as the atoms of the faculties of the nose, tongue, and body are of an extremely minute measure, the atoms of the objects—odor, taste, and the tangible—are likewise; for the consciousnesses of the nose and so forth arise from the conjunction of these corresponding factors.

Is it not the case that the atoms of the three faculties, such as the nose, sometimes cannot apprehend odors and so forth in their entirety? Why, then, is it said that they apprehend only objects of equal magnitude?
It is because the atoms of these three faculties do not apprehend objects such as odors that exceed their own size; therefore, it is said that they can only apprehend objects of equal magnitude.

This does not mean that some atoms of the three faculties are incapable of apprehending some of the three types of objects; rather, they apprehend according to the extent to which the minute particles of the object reach the sense faculty.
Those sense organs are subtle and yet capable of producing functional activity; the eyes and ears are not fixed.
That is to say, regarding the eye and its objects: at times it perceives what is small, as when seeing the tip of a hair;
at times it perceives what is large, as when momentarily opening one's eyes and seeing a great mountain and so forth.
Sometimes they apprehend equality, as when one sees grapes, wild jujubes, or other fruits.
The faculty of hearing likewise apprehends the smallness or greatness of the measure of sounds such as mosquitoes, thunder, or lute music.
Since the mental faculty lacks material obstruction, its distinctions of shape and magnitude cannot be discerned.
In the verse, the term "should be known" (*jñeya*) should be understood as also exhorting one to understand this meaning.
Now, taking advantage of this opportunity, we should further investigate: how are the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the various faculties, such as the eye, arranged and differentiated?

Although it is difficult to establish [its existence] because it is invisible, one must certainly explain its specific arrangement, as it possesses resistance, occupies spatial locations, and arises through aggregation.

The atoms of the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya-paramāṇu) reside upon the pupil of the eye, facing their respective objects and arranged side-by-side; they are covered by a transparent membrane, like a cumin flower, which prevents them from dispersing.
Some say that they abide in a manner like a mass of accumulated spheres; because their substance is transparent, they do not obstruct one another, like an autumnal spring or pond.
The atoms of the auditory faculty reside within the ear cavity, arranged in a circular fashion like rolled birch bark.
The atoms of the olfactory faculty reside within the nasal bridge, facing backward and downward like a pair of fingernails.
These first three faculties are arranged horizontally in rows without any variation in height, like a floral garland on a crown.
The atoms of the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya-paramāṇu*) are distributed across the tongue, shaped like a half-moon.
In the center of the tongue's surface, an area the size of a hair-tip is not pervaded by these atoms of the tongue-faculty.
The atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) are distributed throughout the entire body, corresponding in measure to the shape of the body itself.
The atoms of the female faculty (*strīndriya*) are shaped like the head of a drum.
The atoms of the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) are shaped like a thumb-nail.

The atoms of the eye-faculty are sometimes all of the same class (sabhāga), sometimes all of the corresponding class (tatsabhāga), and sometimes some are of the corresponding class while the rest are of the same class; this applies likewise up to the atoms of the tongue-faculty.

Regarding the atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*), it is certain that not all of them are "functioning" (*sabhāga*); even within the most intensely heated *Naraka* hell, where fierce flames envelop the body, there still remain infinite atoms of the body-faculty that are "non-functioning" (*tatsabhāga*).
Therefore, it is said as follows:

Even if consciousness were to arise from every [atom], the body would necessarily disintegrate, because no single atom of a sense faculty or an object can serve as the support (*āśraya*) or the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) capable of producing body-consciousness; for the five consciousnesses are determined to require the accumulation of multiple atoms before they can constitute the nature of a support or an object-condition.
How are the supports of the six consciousnesses established?

Is it the case that, just as the five consciousnesses take only the present as their object while the mental consciousness takes all three times and the non-temporal as its objects, the supports of these consciousnesses are likewise so?
Not so. Why is this? The verse says:
The latter relies solely on the past; the five consciousnesses rely either simultaneously or [on the past].
The treatise says:

Because the six groups of consciousness, having ceased immediately prior, are all termed "mind" (*manas*), this serves as the supporting faculty (*āśraya-indriya*) for mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*); therefore, mental consciousness relies solely on the past, whereas the support for the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, is either simultaneous or [the past].

Some say that this also refers to the past; that is to say, while the five [faculties] such as the eye are the simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*), the past support is the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
Thus, each of the five consciousnesses has two supports, whereas the sixth mental consciousness has only one.
To clarify the distinctions in meaning within the verse, one should further ask:
if something is the nature of the support (*āśraya*) for visual consciousness, is it also the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for that same visual consciousness?
If something is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for visual consciousness, is it also the nature of the support (*āśraya*) for that visual consciousness?
One should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first alternative refers to the co-nascent eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
The second phrase refers to the mental factors (caitta-dharma) of the dharma-element that have ceased without interval.
The third phrase refers to the past faculty of mind (manas).

The fourth phrase refers to everything except those elements already mentioned; this applies likewise to the body-consciousness (kāya-vijñāna), where each should be explained according to its own respective faculty.

The response for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) should follow the pattern of the preceding statement: that which is the nature of the support (*āśraya*) for the mental consciousness is necessarily its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

However, there are cases where something is the immediately preceding condition for the mental consciousness but does not serve as its support; this refers to the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) that have ceased in the immediate past.
Furthermore, regarding the five consciousness-elements (*vijñānadhātu*), just as their supporting bases— the sense organs— necessarily exist in the past and present,
is it the same for their objects of perception (*ālambana-viṣaya*), or is there a difference?
There is certainly a distinction: that which has already ceased and that which has not yet arisen are not objects of the five consciousnesses. Why is this?
Because [the five consciousnesses] function with a single object identical to their support (*āśraya*), whereas they do not function toward a support when the object is not present.
To those who maintain that the objects of the five consciousnesses exist only in the past, one should say:
"If this were so, would it not follow that only what has arisen previously serves as a condition, while those factors arising simultaneously with the consciousness are all non-conditions?"
Furthermore, regarding matter that has already ceased, they maintain that its substance is non-existent and arises merely as an object apprehended by the conceptualizing mind;
moreover, one must necessarily admit that the sense organs which serve as its basis also exist in the past and are capable of producing present consciousness.
Thus, all those statements are unreasonable.
Setting aside for a moment the basis [of consciousness] and the objects of other types of cognition,
how is it that the object of visual consciousness is only the past, yet it does not perceive all past forms?
Because there is no difference between that which ceases after an interval of a hundred years and that which ceases immediately.
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the former] takes its own cause as its basis—

claiming that matter which ceases immediately is the cause of present consciousness, whereas matter which ceases after a hundred years lacks the status of a cause— this is also not the case, because there is no difference in their causes.
Only that which has ceased immediately prior is the cause of present consciousness, not that which ceased a hundred years ago.
What evidence is there for this?
Just as those forms that ceased a hundred years ago have no relation whatsoever to present visual consciousness, so too must it be with forms that have ceased immediately prior.
Since there is no difference [between the two], why should this alone be the cause?
Even compared to a hundred years ago, there is a difference, because when visual consciousness is about to arise, this visible form serves as its condition.
If that were so, the object of visual consciousness would not be past, because consciousness exists in the future while taking a present object as its condition.

Furthermore, one cannot say that [consciousness] at one time takes an object at another time as its condition; apart from functioning as an object, what other kind of condition would it serve for visual consciousness?
When visual consciousness arises, the form that ceased long ago and the form that ceased recently are no different; why then does the former not serve as a condition?
For you maintain that both what has ceased long ago and what has ceased recently lack substantial reality, and thus there is no distinction between them.

Furthermore, the principle that what has long since ceased or what has recently ceased can function as a causal condition is in both cases untenable; for the objects of the present are distinct in their continuity, and they do not constitute a single resultant nature devoid of differentiation.
Furthermore, you should explain how the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body are said to apprehend objects that have reached them (*prāptaviṣaya*),
given that the past and future are defined as "distant. Moreover,
if the five consciousnesses were to take only the past as their object, how could there be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding them?
If it is argued that there is a direct perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa-buddhi*) regarding one's own feelings— such as the thought, "I have previously experienced such suffering or pleasure"—
this defense is not tenable, because the moments of time differ between the feeling itself and the cognition that apprehends it.

This refers to the feelings that have previously arisen within one's own continuum, which are experienced at one time and cognized at another. The time of experiencing refers to the time of benefit or harm; at that moment, these feelings have not yet become objects of cognition.

This means that when a feeling (*vedanā*) co-arising with a consciousness that cognizes another object is actually present, it is capable of producing benefit or harm; this stage of benefiting or harming is called the "time of experiencing" (*anubhava-kāla*).
This is because the feeling, as its own nature (*svabhāva*), experiences the contact (*sparśa*) that accompanies it, since it arises as its own essence;
and because the consciousness and other factors experience the aspect of that benefit or harm, since they arise as their own essence.
Only when this [object] has ceased in the past can it serve as an object for the arising of present recollection; this stage of recollection is termed the "time of cognitive awareness.
By this principle, [this occurs] only with respect to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Because there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the objects previously experienced, the validity of direct perception is established with respect to one's own experience. There are three types of direct perception, distinguished by their specific natures:
that which relies on the sense faculties (*indriya*), that which is receptive (*anubhava*), and that which is cognitive (*avabodha*).

Since it is already admitted that past forms and so forth have never been apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can it be said that there is a direct perceptual awareness of them as one has of one's own body, while for the bodies of others there is no such personal experience?
If there were no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of what is apprehended by direct perception, one could not have the cognition that "I previously experienced such suffering or pleasure.

Since the knowledge that takes that experience as its object is not itself a cognition of direct perception, likewise, when visible forms and so forth are not directly perceived by their own respective sense organs, there should be no cognition of direct perception stating "I previously experienced such forms," and the knowledge that takes those objects as its domain should not be a cognition of direct perception.

Furthermore, if the five present objects such as visible form were not apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then—just as with the cognition arising from an object that is a future feeling which was never previously experienced through direct perception—one would certainly not think, "I have previously experienced such suffering or pleasure. By analogy, since the cognition arising from past objects such as visible form does not depend on what was previously apprehended through the senses via direct perception, one likewise should not think, "I have previously experienced such visible forms and so forth."
Just as in the case of painful sensations and the like, only after they have been experienced through direct perception (pratyakṣa) does a direct perceptual cognition apprehending them arise;
likewise, only after forms and so forth have been experienced through direct perception based on the sense faculties does a direct perceptual cognition apprehending them arise.
Because it is currently being experienced, one must certainly accept this.
If, at the time of experiencing feeling (*vedanā*), it does not take feeling as its object, and if, when taking feeling as its object, it does not experience feeling, why did the Blessed One say:
"When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it really is that one is experiencing a pleasant feeling," and so forth, in detail?
There is no contradiction here.

What has been stated refers to the time of investigation, not the time of direct experience; it is spoken thus because it demonstrates that the practitioner is free from delusion regarding the feelings of pleasure and so forth, which were previously experienced and obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, there should be no perceptual cognition regarding objects that have never previously been experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For this reason, the five consciousnesses take only present objects as their domain, because they necessarily take what is co-arisen (*sahaja*) as their objective support (*ālambana*).
Since the sūtra states:
"With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises," and so forth in detail,
for what reason does consciousness arise by depending upon two conditions, yet the name "support" (āśraya) is applied to the sense faculty and not to the object?
The verse says:
Because consciousness varies according to the transformation of the faculties, the eyes and so forth are called "bases" (āśraya).
The commentary says:

The eye and so forth are themselves the six elements of the eye and so forth; because the sense organs such as the eye undergo transformation, the various consciousnesses likewise transform and differ.

Since they become clear or dim according to the increase or decrease of the respective organs, it is not the transformation of form and other objects that causes the consciousness to differ, for consciousness follows the organ and does not follow the object. Therefore, the designation "based on" applies only to the eye and the other [organs], and not to the others.

If that is so, the mental consciousness also shifts in accordance with the body; for when the body is afflicted by disorders such as wind-disease, the mental consciousness becomes disturbed, whereas when the body is clear and at ease, the mental consciousness is tranquil. For what reason, then, does that mental consciousness not take the body as its support?
There is no such fault, because [the mental consciousness] follows its own basis (*āśraya*).

That is to say, when wind-disorders and the like afflict the body, a body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) associated with painful sensation arises; this body-consciousness is termed a "disturbed mental element" (*manodhātu*). When this [body-consciousness], together with the painful sensation, ceases, it serves as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) for the arising of a disturbed mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Conversely, when [the conditions] are contrary to this, the mental consciousness is tranquil. Therefore, the mental consciousness follows its own basis.

Is it not the case that an untainted consciousness can arise immediately after a tainted mental element (*manodhātu*), and so forth? If such differences exist, how can it be said that mental consciousness follows its own support (*āśraya*)?

It is not on the basis of categories such as tainted or untainted that it is called "following its own support," but rather on the basis of distinctions in intensity, clarity, or dullness. For example, when a wholesome, unwholesome, or obscured eye-consciousness arises from an unobscured-neutral eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), it is still termed "eye-consciousness following its own support."
This case should also be understood in the same way; therefore, the dependent does not necessarily conform to the ontological nature of all that upon which it depends.
If it were otherwise, it would follow that the dependent does not conform to its support.

For what reason is that which is cognized an object (*viṣaya*) rather than a faculty (*indriya*), yet the name "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is established in accordance with the faculty and not the object?
The verse says:
Because of those [faculties] and because of their uncommon cause, Consciousness is designated according to the faculty.
The Commentary states:

That is to say, because it was previously stated that the eye and so forth are called "bases" (*āśraya*), the designation of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) follows the sense organ rather than the object, as the base is predominant.

Furthermore, regarding what is "unshared": the eye is the exclusive basis for its own visual consciousness, whereas visible form is also commonly apprehended by the visual consciousnesses of other bodies as well as by the mental consciousnesses of oneself and others; this should be understood to apply likewise up to the body and tangible objects.
Is it not the case that because the objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are not shared [with the other five], it should be called "dharma-consciousness"?

This objection is irrational, because the names "general" (*sāmānya*) and "particular" (*viśeṣa*) applied to "dharmas" are shared but not universal, and because the objects [of the mental consciousness] do not possess the two aforementioned causes.
That which is called "dharma" in its general sense does not refer solely to the specific name *dharmadhātu*, nor does it universally encompass all consciousnesses.

Furthermore, although the specific *dharmadhātu* is not shared with others, it is not of the nature of a faculty (*indriya*) that serves as the support for mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Therefore, when a phenomenon is both the support of a consciousness and unique to it, the consciousness is designated according to that phenomenon;

this is not the case for form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Consequently, one does not designate them as "form-consciousness" and so on, just as one does not call them "drum-sound-consciousness" or "barley-sprout-consciousness."
Furthermore, this verse has another meaning: it refers to the fact that [the sense organs] are followed by the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth;
and regarding "unshared," it means that the eye and so forth are unshared.

That is to say, there may be one instance of a material form producing four instances of eye-consciousness, but there is never a single instance of an eye-faculty producing two instances of eye-consciousness, much less one capable of producing four instances of consciousness.

In this way, because the bodies, eyes, and [other faculties] of different realms, destinies, and species each produce their own distinct consciousnesses, they are called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*); this is explained in detail up to the body being likewise.

Is it not the case that the mental faculty (*manas*) of one sentient being also produces the mental consciousness of another sentient being? It is not that it does not produce it at all, but rather that it does not do so simultaneously.
Since two mental states do not arise simultaneously and a single consciousness cannot be like matter (rūpa) and so forth, it is said that there are not two [consciousnesses], much less four.

Thus, because the eye and other faculties are followed by their respective consciousnesses, and because consciousness arises separately according to the distinctions of birth, realm, and destiny, for these two reasons, [the sense bases] follow the faculties and not the objects.
Some say: "The faculties and consciousnesses are both internal in nature, whereas the objects are exclusively external; therefore, [the designation] follows the faculties. Others say:
Since both the sense faculties and consciousnesses belong to the category of sentient beings, whereas objects such as visible forms are not fixed [as sentient], the teaching follows the faculties.
Although visual consciousness arises only through the conjunction of various conditions, why does the sūtra mention only the eye and visible form?

Because it is the basis (*āśraya*) and the object (*ālambana*) of visual consciousness, whereas other factors, though they may serve as conditions for the arising of visual consciousness, are neither its basis nor its object.

Furthermore, because it is an immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for visual consciousness—would it not be the case that empty space and light, which can produce mental attention (*manaskāra*), are also immediate conditions for visual consciousness?
Because the two conditions—the eye and visible form—are extremely proximate to the arising of visual consciousness, they differ from space, light, and so forth.
Furthermore, the arising of visual consciousness necessarily depends upon the power of its support (the eye) and its object (form), as well as their unique status.

When visual consciousness arises, it necessarily relies upon the eye and visible forms as its basis and object; other dharmas are not so fixed. That is to say, the consciousness of nocturnal creatures arises without depending on light, the consciousness of aquatic creatures is produced without awaiting space, and the same applies to humans regarding obstructed colors such as lapis lazuli or rock crystal; furthermore, the celestial eye produces consciousness without requiring either space or light.

If it is argued that the arising of visual consciousness necessarily depends on light—since one must be near both light and form, and since one perceives form only when either the primary light or the secondary light serves as the requisite condition—and furthermore, that the production of visual consciousness necessarily depends on space, because space pervades all places; [then we respond as follows:]
All of this is irrational: if the eye depends on light, it must depend on great light to illuminate forms before they can be seen.
Since the eyes of cats, wildcats, and the like do not possess great light, how could they see?

Furthermore, there are people whose eyes lack clarity yet can see forms at night; this greatly contradicts your position. As it is said: "There are people who, even in the darkness, are able to perceive forms without depending on light."

If space were to pervade all places, then because it is without obstruction, it should also be able to apprehend obstructed forms such as walls and so forth, and be able to produce mental attention (*manasikāra*).
It would universally serve as a co-nascent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*) for the six consciousnesses; however, the eye and visible form are not co-nascent.
Therefore, the sūtras mention only the eye and visible forms;

alternatively, they speak according to what is appropriate for those being taught, as in the *Hastipadopama-sūtra* and other sūtras, where all conditions such as mental attention (*manasikāra*) are fully explained.

Regarding the stage (*bhūmi*) of the body, the eye, the visible object, and the visual consciousness as they abide together: when the eye sees a visible object, are the stages of the body, the eye, the object, and the consciousness the same or different?
One should say that these four are either different or the same.

As for what is meant by "the same": it refers to one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who, with an eye of their own level, sees a visible object of their own level; in this case, all four belong to the same level.

When born in the first dhyāna, one sees forms of that same level with the eye of that same level; all these factors belong to the same stage. It is not the case that when born in other stages there are four factors belonging to the same stage.

As for what is different: if one born in the desire realm sees a form of the desire realm with an eye of the first dhyāna, the body and the form belong to the desire realm, while the eye and the consciousness belong to the first dhyāna.
If one sees a form of the first dhyāna, the body belongs to the desire realm, while the [eye and] consciousness belong to the first dhyāna.

If one sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the second dhyāna, the body and the forms belong to the desire realm, the eye belongs to the second dhyāna, and the consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna.
When seeing forms of the first dhyāna, the body belongs to the desire realm, the eye belongs to the second dhyāna, and both the form and the consciousness belong to the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna, the body belongs to the desire realm, both the eye and the forms belong to the second dhyāna, and the consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna.
In this same manner, it should be understood according to reason when one sees forms of a lower stage or forms of one's own stage with an eye belonging to the third or fourth dhyāna levels.
In this way, if one is born in the stages of the four dhyānas, there are differences regarding these four matters, which should be reflected upon according to reason.
The other realms should likewise be analyzed in this manner.
Now, I shall briefly explain the characteristics of this determination.
The verse says:
The eye is not inferior to the body; color and consciousness are not superior to the eye.
Color is in every respect [inferior or equal] to consciousness; the same applies to the two [color and consciousness] in relation to the body.
As it is with the eye, so it is with the ear; the next three [faculties] belong to their own level;
body-consciousness belongs to its own level or a lower level; one should know that the mental faculty is not fixed.
The treatise says:

The body, the eye, and visible forms all pertain to five stages—that is, they exist within the desire realm and the four dhyānas. Eye-consciousness exists only in the desire realm and the first dhyāna. Among these, the eye-faculty, relative to the stage where the body is born, is either equal to or superior to it, but never inferior;
visible forms and consciousness, relative to the eye, are equal to or inferior to it, but never superior.
The eye-faculty of a lower stage is habituated to seeing coarse forms; it lacks the capacity to see the subtle forms of higher stages.
Furthermore, the eye-faculty of a lower stage possesses no superior function.

Since the higher stages possess their own distinct and superior eye-faculties, and since the eye-consciousness of the lower stage exists within its own level, the eye-faculty of a lower stage cannot serve as the support for a consciousness of a higher stage.

Regarding form in relation to consciousness, it extends equally across the same level, the higher levels, or the lower levels. Regarding form and consciousness in relation to the body, they are like form in relation to consciousness; that is, they extend to their own level, or to the higher or lower levels.

Regarding consciousness in relation to the body, that which extends to its own level occurs only when one is born in the desire realm or the first dhyāna; that which extends to a higher level occurs only when one is born in the desire realm; and that which extends to a lower level occurs only when one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna levels.

Regarding visible forms in relation to the body: those from one's own level or lower levels are seen by eyes of a higher level; those from a higher level are seen only by eyes of that same higher level.

Furthermore, with eyes of one's own level, one sees only visible forms of one's own level or lower levels; with eyes of a higher level, one sees visible forms of one's own level, as well as those above and below.
The detailed exposition of the ear-element (*śrotra-dhātu*) should be understood as being like that of the eye.
That is to say: the ear is not inferior to the body; sound and consciousness are not superior to the ear.
Regarding sound, it is in all respects [either equal to or inferior to] both consciousness and the body; the same applies to the body.
As appropriate, this is explained in detail as in the commentary on the eye.
The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body are all entirely of their own level (*svabhūmika*), because for the most part they are the same.

This is because the two consciousnesses of smell and taste belong only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and because the nose and tongue perceive only objects that have reached them (*prāptaviṣaya*).

Regarding the specific distinctions therein: the body and the tangible object must belong to the same level (*bhūmi*), because [the tactile consciousness] perceives objects that are in direct contact.
As for the consciousness in relation to the tangible object and the body, it may be of its own level or of a lower level.
"Of its own level" means, for example, when one is born in the Desire Realm or the First Dhyāna; "of a lower level" refers to when one is born in the three higher Dhyanas.

It should be understood that the four factors of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) are not fixed: namely, the mind is sometimes in the same stage as the body, consciousness, and mental objects, and sometimes in a higher or lower stage. The body exists only in five stages; the [other] three exist in all stages; and they arise only in the five stages.
When the mind (manas) and its consciousness take dharmas of their own level as objects, it is said that the mind and the [other] three [aggregates] abide in the same level.
As for the case where the mind-element (manodhātu) sometimes belongs to a higher level, this refers to when one is dwelling in meditative concentration (dhyāna).

If one is born in the desire realm and gives rise to a consciousness of the desire realm immediately after the first dhyāna to cognize dharmas of the desire realm, the mental faculty belongs to the higher stage while the three [other aggregates] belong to the lower stage.

Alternatively, when the consciousnesses belonging to the first, second, or third dhyānas arise immediately after the second, third, or fourth dhyānas respectively, they cognize the dharmas belonging to the first, second, or third dhyānas; in these cases, the mental faculty (manas) belongs to a higher stage, while the three [consciousnesses] belong to lower stages.
In this way, when one is born into the first dhyāna or other higher realms and subsequently descends from above to below, it should be understood according to the same principle.

At the time of taking birth, the mind of a higher stage does not rely upon a body of a lower stage; for it is absolutely impossible for a body-root of a lower stage to remain without having ceased while one undergoes rebirth in a higher stage, and furthermore, it is certainly never the case that one passes away while abiding in a mind belonging to a different stage.
Thus it should be understood: there is no mental faculty (*manas*) of a lower stage that relies upon a body of a higher stage.

However, it is not contrary to reason for a mental faculty of a higher stage to rely upon a body of a lower stage. That is to say, when one first takes rebirth in the Desire Realm or the Form Realm immediately following the mental element (*manodhātu*) of a higher stage, the mind belongs to the higher stage while the body and consciousness belong to the lower stage; the phenomena (*dharma*) cognized by them may belong to its own stage, to a higher stage, or to the unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
In this way, it should be understood that it is not contrary to reason for the mental faculty (*manas*) of a lower stage to experience the body of a higher stage.

Likewise, when one is traversing meditative absorption, it is not contrary to reason for there to be a mental faculty of a lower stage depending upon a body of a higher stage; that is to say, when born in a higher stage, one first gives rise to the consciousness-body and the mind of transformation belonging to a lower stage.
The same should be explained extensively regarding the phenomena of consciousness.
Furthermore, one should investigate:

if an eye of the desire realm sees a form of the desire realm, or if an eye of the form realm sees forms of both realms, at that time, by how many kinds of eye-consciousness can those forms be cognized?
Furthermore, how many types of conceptualization arise therein?
To prevent confusion regarding this thesis, I shall first provide a general summary and subsequently offer a detailed explanation.

It should be understood that, for the time being, we shall distinguish between the conceptualization of calculation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) and the indeterminate conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), as these two occur throughout all stages; with respect to these two types, all visual consciousness is devoid of conceptualization.
Furthermore, wholesome discrimination can take as its object all levels—its own, those above, and those below;
defiled discrimination takes as its object its own level and those above;
and neutral discrimination takes as its object its own level and those below.
In whatever place one is born, as long as one has not yet abandoned craving for that place, one possesses all three types of conceptualization belonging to that level;
if one has abandoned craving for that place, there remain only two types of conceptualization belonging to that level, namely, with the exception of the defiled type.

One born in another stage does not have a wholesome eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) of the first dhyāna manifest before them, because such consciousness is necessarily bound to the stage in which one is born.
Furthermore, even when born in the first dhyāna, one cannot give rise to a wholesome eye-consciousness by relying on an eye-faculty belonging to another stage.

One born in another stage cannot give rise to the manifestation of non-obscured-neutral conceptualization belonging to another stage, because this [conceptualization] is also necessarily bound to the stage of birth.

It is not the intention here that only the conceptualization arising within a single lifetime is being discussed; for if it were said to be only that which arises in one lifetime, then upon being born in a higher stage, there would certainly be no conceptualization of a lower stage, since those three types of conceptualization of the lower stage could not possibly manifest during that particular birth.
Furthermore, the discrimination of the higher stages should be exclusively wholesome and not indeterminate, for the reasons already stated previously.
Generally speaking, all other births may possess them in their entirety.
Having thus provided a general analysis, we shall now proceed to explain them individually.

When one who has severed the roots of goodness sees a form with the eye, that form is cognized by an eye-consciousness that is defiled and non-obscured-neutral; regarding this, three kinds of conceptualization arise, namely: wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured-neutral.

When one whose roots of goodness are not severed and who has not yet abandoned craving sees a form with the eye, that form is cognized by three kinds of visual consciousness, and regarding it, three kinds of conceptualization arise.

If ordinary beings born in the desire realm have already abandoned craving for the desire realm but have not yet abandoned craving for the first dhyāna, when they see various forms with the eye of the desire realm, these forms are cognized by an eye-consciousness that is either wholesome or non-obscured-neutral.

Regarding this, there further arises discrimination of the desire realm: for one of the "receding" type (*parihāṇadharman*), all three types are present; for one of the "non-receding" type (*aparihāṇadharman*), only two types are present, namely excluding the defiled. This is because when one sees the forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna, those forms are cognized solely by an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding this, one should understand that the conceptualizations of the desire realm arise again as previously described.

Furthermore, two kinds of conceptualization belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna arise here; that is to say, excluding the defiled, when one sees the forms of that stage with the eye of the first dhyāna, these forms are cognized solely by an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
Regarding this, there further arise distinctions within the desire realm: for those of the "receding" type (*parihāṇadharman*), there are two kinds, namely excluding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
for those of the "non-receding" type (*aparihāṇadharman*), there is only the wholesome (*kuśala*).

Furthermore, regarding the three types of conceptualization belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna: when one who has abandoned craving for the first dhyāna but has not yet abandoned craving for the second dhyāna sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the second dhyāna, these forms are cognized solely by an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding this, there further arises discrimination pertaining to the desire realm: for one of the "nature of falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*), all three types are present;
for one of the "nature of non-falling away" (*aparihāṇadharman*), only two types exist, namely, with the exception of the defiled.
Regarding this, the initial distinction of the first dhyāna arises: for one of the "subject to regression" (parihāṇadharman) type, there are two kinds, namely excluding the defiled;
for one of the "not subject to regression" (aparihāṇadharman) type, there is only the wholesome.

Furthermore, regarding this, two types of discrimination arise within the stage of the second dhyāna; that is to say, excluding the defiled, when one sees the forms of the first dhyāna with the eye of the second dhyāna, these forms are cognized solely by an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
Regarding this, there further arises discrimination within the desire realm: for one of the "receding" type (*parihāṇadharman*), there are two kinds, namely excluding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
for one of the "non-receding" type (*aparihāṇadharman*), it is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).

Regarding this, there further arises a twofold distinction of the first dhyāna: for one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), all three types are present; for one of the "nature of non-falling away" (aparihāṇadharman), it is exclusively wholesome.
Regarding this, there further arises a twofold distinction of the second dhyāna stage, namely, with the exception of the defiled (kliṣṭa).
When one sees the forms of the second dhyāna with the eye of the second dhyāna, these forms are cognized solely by an eye-consciousness that is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding this, if a further conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of the desire realm arises, there are two types for one subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*): namely, excluding the neutral;
whereas for one not subject to regression (*aparihāṇadharman*), there is only the wholesome (*kuśala*).
The conceptualizations arising from the stage of the first dhyāna should also be understood in this same way.
Furthermore, regarding the three types of conceptualization arising from the stage of the second dhyāna, one should provide a detailed explanation according to the principles set forth here.

One who has already abandoned craving for the second dhyāna but not yet abandoned craving for the third dhyāna; one who has already abandoned craving for the third dhyāna but not yet abandoned craving for the fourth dhyāna; and one who has already abandoned craving for the fourth dhyāna—these should be analyzed accordingly.

Just as it was explained regarding ordinary beings born in the desire realm, so too should it be explained in detail, as appropriate, for those born in the four dhyāna stages and for noble ones born within the five stages.

However, there is a distinction: for all noble ones, whether subject to regression or not, there are no defiled conceptualizations directed toward higher [realms], because the universal [defilements] of other stages have already been abandoned, and because the merits of the path of seeing are necessarily free from regression.
Following this methodological approach, one should likewise investigate the auditory consciousness that hears sounds and its associated conceptualizations.
Having concluded this digression, we should now address the main subject.
We shall now proceed with careful analysis:

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), which ones are cognized by how many of the six consciousnesses? How many are permanent and how many are impermanent? How many are faculties (*indriya*) and how many are not faculties?
The verse says:
Five external [elements] are cognized by two [consciousnesses]; The element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) that is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is permanent.
One portion of the dharmas is faculties, as are the twelve internal bases.
The treatise says:

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the five elements beginning with form (*rūpa*) are, respectively, the objects of the five consciousnesses beginning with visual consciousness; furthermore, they are all collectively the objects of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Thus, these five elements are each cognized by two types of consciousness among the six consciousnesses.

By this analogy, it should be understood that the remaining thirteen elements are all cognized solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), as they are not the objects of the fivefold body of sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*).

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), there is not a single element that is entirely permanent; only a portion of the dharma-element, namely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), is permanent. By this principle, it is understood that all other elements consist of impermanent phenomena.

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), a portion of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the twelve internal [elements] constitute the faculties (*indriya*), and nothing else. That is to say, the five feeling faculties, the five faculties beginning with faith, the life faculty in its entirety, and a partial portion of each of the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) are subsumed within the element of phenomena.
The five faculties, beginning with the eye, are subsumed under their respective names.
The female faculty and the male faculty are subsumed as a portion of the body element (*kāyadhātu*), as will be explained later.

The mental faculty (*manas*) is generally subsumed within the seven mind elements (*cittadhātu*); the latter three [faculties] are partially subsumed within the mind element (*manodhātu*) and the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
By logical extension, the remaining five elements—form and so forth—and a portion of the dharma-element are all non-faculties by nature.

Regarding the twenty-two faculties as taught in the Sūtra, they are: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, mind faculty, female faculty, male faculty, life faculty, pleasure faculty, pain faculty, joy faculty, grief faculty, equanimity faculty, faith faculty, energy faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
In the Sūtras, the sequence of the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is established; therefore, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is taught immediately after the body faculty (*kāya-indriya*).

However, the great masters of the Abhidharma transpose this mental faculty and place it after the life faculty (*jīvita-indriya*), because they teach according to the order of the objects of cognition (*ālambana*) and because it is easier to clarify the various classifications through the gates [of analysis].
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Eight.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Nine.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Two: Distinguishing the Differences. Section One: Distinguishing the Differences, Part Two of One. Thus, having already enumerated the faculties according to their elements, one should now further investigate herein:
For what reason did the Blessed One specifically designate them by the name "faculties" (*indriya*)?

The entire internal sphere (*ādhyātmika-dhātu*) and a portion of the dharma-sphere (*dharma-dhātu*) are designated as faculties (*indriya*) by virtue of their predominance (*adhipatya*), because they attain predominance over their respective objects.
This meaning of predominance makes manifest the meaning of "sphere" (*dhātu*).

The term *dhātu* (element) refers either to the "earth" (*iti*) or the "endurance" (*kṣānti*) element. "Supreme sovereignty" is the meaning of the earth element; "brilliant illumination" is the meaning of the endurance element.

Only that which is intensely blazing and manifest is called a "faculty" (*indriya*). This term generally indicates the twenty-two faculties, which exercise a predominant influence over their respective aggregates.

Since all phenomena possess their own distinct predominant influence when compared to one another, they should all be called "faculties" (*indriya*). However, because this [specific faculty] is the most predominant, its designation as a distinct entity is established, just as the lion king, the village headman, and the universal monarch are so designated due to their supreme predominance over beasts, villages, and the four continents, respectively.
This is "extremely predominant" (*aty-adhipati*); with respect to whom is it predominant?
The verse says:
It is traditionally taught that five are predominant over four, and the four faculties are predominant over two kinds.
Among the five [faculties] and the eight [faculties] of defilement and purity, each acts as a predominant factor in its own respective domain.
The treatise says:
It is not the case that all faculties collectively constitute the ultimate predominance with respect to a single matter.

Each of the five faculties, such as the eye, exercises a predominant influence over four matters: first, the adornment of the body; second, the guidance and nourishment of the body; third, the production of consciousness and so forth; and fourth, their unique functions.
Adorning the body refers to the fact that if any one of the five sense faculties is lacking, the body becomes unsightly.
Sustaining and nourishing the body refers to avoiding dangers and difficulties through seeing and hearing, as well as being able to consume solid food.
Fragrance, odor, and touch—all three constitute edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). As a verse says:
"Just as a person with clear vision Is able to avoid present dangers, So too, those who possess wisdom in this world Are able to distance themselves from future suffering and evil."
The learned can know the Dharma; The learned can leave behind evil;
The learned abandon what is meaningless; The learned attain Nirvana. "The body subsists through food;
Life depends on food for its existence. Once fed, it causes the mind—"
"Appropriate pleasure and tranquility.

Regarding "the arising of consciousness and so forth," this refers to the production of the five sensory consciousnesses and their associated mental factors, which vary in clarity or dullness according to the sense faculties upon which they rely.
Regarding "their unique function," this refers to the apprehension of their respective objects, such as seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching distinct objects.
Some say: The eye and ear possess predominant efficacy, respectively, in protecting the physical body and the Dharma-body; the two preceding verses serve as proof for this.

Some say: Both the eye and the ear are able to protect the two bodies—the body of birth and the Dharma-body—because the eye and the ear each serve as a predominant condition for associating with virtuous persons and hearing the true Dharma.
The female and male faculties each exercise predominant influence over two matters.
First, regarding the predominance of the two—the female and male faculties—it is twofold: first, the differentiation of sentient beings; second, the differentiation of their individual distinctions.

Regarding the difference in sentient beings: at the beginning of the kalpa, the forms and types of sentient beings were all identical; only after the two sexual organs had arisen did the distinctions between female and male forms appear.
Regarding the difference in differentiation: this refers to the variations in the arrangement of movement, speech, breasts, topknots, and so forth.

Some say: They are called "differentiated sentient beings" because there are distinctions in their courage and timidity; they are called "differentiated by distinction" because there are distinctions in their clothing and ornaments. Others say:

This [state] possesses sovereign power over both the defiled and purified categories; therefore, it is said that with respect to the two types of feeling, because one undertakes non-restraint, gives rise to immediate retributive karma (*ānantarya-karma*), and severs the roots of goodness, it is called possessing sovereign power over the defiled category;
and because one is able to undertake restraint, enter the Path, attain the fruits, and become free from desire, it is called possessing sovereign power over the purified category.
The bodies of *śaṇḍha* (eunuchs) and others do not possess such qualities.

Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) having predominance over these two: it is because of this that the faculties and their distinctions are designated; for when this exists, that exists, and when this is absent, that is absent.

Alternatively, it is because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is required in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) for the continuity and maintenance of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), since only through it is there a determination regarding the place of rebirth.
This is because when one gives rise to a wholesome or defiled mind of that same level, or gives rise to another mind, it does not constitute death.
The mental faculty (*manas*) exercises sovereignty over two aspects: namely, the ability to link to a subsequent existence (*pratisaṃdhi*) and the capacity for autonomous functioning.
Regarding the linking to a subsequent existence, as the Blessed One said to Ānanda:
"If consciousness were not to enter the mother’s womb, would the semen and blood be able to form the *kalala*?"
"No, World-Honored One! ...
[and so on, as extensively explained] ..."
Regarding "acting with mastery," as the Sūtra says:
"The mind leads the world; The mind thoroughly encompasses it.
Thus, this single dharma, the mind, Acts with mastery over all."
Some say: Because the faculty of mind (*manas*) possesses sovereign power (*ādhipatya*) over both the defiled and purified categories, it is said to "pertain to both. As the Sūtra says:
"Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is purified, sentient beings are purified."

The five sensations, such as pleasure, and the eight faculties, such as faith, possess predominant power within the realms of defilement and purification. That is to say, the five [sensations] beginning with pleasure have predominance over defilement, because they serve as the basis for the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) such as craving.

Some say: This [feeling] exercises sovereignty over both the defiled and purified categories, because it is taught as the basis for worldly attachment (*gardha*) and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*). For it is stated in the Sūtras:
"Because of pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated" (*sukhād dhi cittaṃ samādhīyate*), and "Suffering is the basis for faith" (*duḥkhaṃ śraddhāyā āśrayaḥ*), and so forth.
The eight faculties, beginning with faith, exercise sovereignty over purification, as stated in the Sūtra:

"My noble disciples possess the ramparts and moats of faith, the power of diligence, and the defense of mindfulness; their minds are concentrated and liberated, with wisdom as their sword," and so forth, as explained at length.
Since this [category] includes the latter three faculties,
they certainly possess predominance (*adhipatya*) with respect to the pure class (*śukla-pakṣa*).
Regarding this, the first tradition states:
The pleasure [of the eye] is explained last. Some say:

"That which can guide and nourish the body is not the function of the eye and so forth, but is the predominance of consciousness; for it is only by means of the various consciousnesses discerning objects that are either adverse or favorable that one is able to avoid dangers and receive solid food."

Furthermore, they argue that the unique capacity to perceive visible forms and so forth is not distinct from consciousness; therefore, with respect to the eyes and other sense organs, such a non-common function cannot be established as a separate predominant activity. Consequently, it is not by virtue of this that the eyes and other organs constitute faculties (*indriya*).
If that is so, how is it? The verse says:
Because they exercise sovereignty over the cognition of their respective objects, The six faculties are established in total.
Based on the body, two faculties are established: female and male, because they are predominant with respect to the physical form, its defilement, and its purification.
It should be known that life, the five sensations, and faith and the others are established as faculties.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the faculty of "complete knowledge" (ājñendriya) are likewise;
in the attainment of successive paths and in [the attainment of] nirvāṇa and so forth, they exercise predominance.
The commentary says:

That which cognizes its own respective objects refers to the group of six consciousnesses. The five faculties, such as the eye, possess predominant efficacy regarding the consciousnesses that can discern their respective individual objects; the sixth faculty, the mind, possesses predominant efficacy regarding the consciousness that can discern all objects. Therefore, each of the six, beginning with the eye, is established as a faculty (*indriya*).

However, even in the absence of an object, the status of the sense-faculties would still be undermined; for the eye and other faculties serve as the common causes for the consciousness that cognizes all objects, and it is only by following the state of these faculties that consciousness becomes clear or dim.
This explanation is unreasonable, for it would follow that the sense-faculties of "homogeneity" (sabhāga) would not be faculties.
Is this fault not also present in your own position?
We do not incur this error, because we maintain that they possess predominance (adhipatya) with respect to the adornment of the body.
