Furthermore, it is not the case that all [eye-faculties] serve as the universal cause for the consciousness that cognizes all forms, because the eye-faculties perish moment by moment and because the consciousnesses that cognize various forms do not arise simultaneously.
If it is argued that there is no distinction in the category (*jāti*) of the eye, then visible form (*rūpa*) should likewise be the same, because there would be no difference in their categories.

If it is claimed that there is a distinction between the categories of blue and yellow, then the eye should also be so, because there are different categories such as those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and those nurtured by food (*aupacayika*).

The claim that consciousness merely follows the sense organs in being clear or dim is also not a valid reason; for it is only after the substance of consciousness has arisen that it can possess clarity or dimness according to the organ. Since the dominant power (adhipati-bala) and so forth are required to bring what has not yet arisen into existence, if even one of these conditions is lacking, consciousness will not arise.

Alternatively, because consciousness varies in clarity or dullness according to the sense organ, the function of guiding and nourishing the body should be attributed to the organ. If the activity of the eye is predominant, it gives rise to a superior consciousness capable of avoiding dangers and thus guides and nourishes the body;

if the activity of the eye is weak, it gives rise to an inferior consciousness that fails to perceive dangers, causing the body to fall. Therefore, the guidance and nourishment of the body reside in the organ, not in the consciousness.
Furthermore, what slight difference is there here?

In the previous section, it was already established that the eye and other faculties give rise to the visual consciousness and its associated mental factors; in this present section, that point is merely abbreviated. Since it is not something you have not already seen, why should it be cause for rejoicing?
Since there is no distinct meaning [in this], it should not be stated again.

Furthermore, as for your claim that the functions of seeing form and so forth are not different from consciousness, this is also incorrect, because the notion that consciousness can see and so forth has already been refuted previously.
This means that the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is not the entity that sees, because it is no different in kind from the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) and the others.
Such objections are explained in detail as previously stated.
Furthermore, it is said that two faculties are established based on the body because they possess predominance (*ādhipatya*) over the states of femininity and masculinity.
This means that among females, the female faculty (*strī-indriya*) is predominant, while among males, the male faculty (*puruṣa-indriya*) is predominant.

As for those who possess both female and male characteristics (*ubhayavyañjana*), this refers to those whose physical forms, voices, activities, and inclinations differ according to both the female and male types.
The essential nature of the female and male faculties is not separate from the body faculty, for these names are established based on a specific portion of the body.

This particular location differs slightly from other parts of the body faculty in that it is a portion of the body faculty of the desire realm capable of serving as the basis for the arising of unwholesome body-consciousness associated with greed; therefore, they are established separately from the body faculty as two distinct faculties.

Although the body-faculty exists during the initial stage of a kalpa and so forth, there is no differentiation such as female or male physical forms; therefore, these two faculties should be established separately from it.

This also does not transcend the meaning of the previous section, for it was previously stated that these two faculties possess predominance regarding the differentiation of sentient beings and the differentiation of their specific types.

Furthermore, it is said that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the five feeling faculties (*vedanendriya*), faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth, are established as faculties because they possess predominant influence (*adhipatya*) respectively in the maintenance of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) and in the processes of defilement and purification; since this is no different from the previous category, it should not be restated.

It is further stated that the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are likewise so; they possess a predominant efficacy (*adhipati-bala*) in the attainment of subsequent paths, nirvāṇa, and so forth.

That is to say, the first faculty possesses a predominant efficacy in the attainment of the second; this second faculty possesses a predominant efficacy in the attainment of the third; and this third faculty possesses a predominant efficacy in the attainment of nirvāṇa, because it is not possible to realize those [attainments] apart from these faculties.
Nor is it different from what was stated previously, so there is no need for a redundant explanation; this is because they possess predominance (*adhipatya*) with respect to purity.

Furthermore, the Master of the Sūtras’ (*Sūtrakāra*) interpretation of the term "also" (*api*) as indicating that each [of the faculties] individually can function as a faculty is likewise unreasonable, for such a doubt should not even arise.

Because the specific meaning has already been established by the superior statements regarding the attainment of successive paths, nirvāṇa, and so forth, one should not further give rise to doubt therein.

If it is argued that doubt should arise because there is no distinction in their essential nature, this is also illogical; for the three stages of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning are each distinct and do not mutually subsume one another, and thus doubt cannot be produced.
If one should harbor doubts, they are resolved by the fact that each subsequent [category] has already been distinguished; why then trouble oneself with this further illustration?

Although they are identical in being of the nature of nine faculties and thus without difference in essence, there is a distinction in their dominant power (*adhipati-bala*); how, then, could such doubts be permitted?
It should be one faculty that is neither the female nor the male faculty, because this doubt arises upon seeing this.

Now, the explanation of those words has another meaning: it is intended to show that apart from the nine [faculties], there are no three distinct faculties. Just as the female and male faculties are established separately from the body faculty, yet apart from the substance of the body faculty, there are no two distinct faculties.

The same applies to the three faculties (*indriya*): although they are established based on the distinct meanings of the nine faculties, there are no three faculties existing separately apart from those nine; this explanation is logical.
Furthermore, the Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika) explains that the word "etc. (*ādi*) is intended to indicate that there are other alternative formulations (*paryāya*).
What is the alternative formulation?

It means that within the cessation of afflictions abandoned through seeing and those abandoned through cultivation, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) possess predominant efficacy, respectively.

This is also not the case; if only the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) were designated as "predominant," then those included within the paths of preparation, liberation, and advancement within the paths of seeing and cultivation would not be called faculties.

If all four paths were equally predominant, then the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and so forth, would have to be included among the first faculties, because they possess predominance over the cessation of the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).

It is already known that the faculty of "already-known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) should be included as the third; however, [the previous explanation] contains many faults and is not a sound interpretation. Now, I shall explain those statements through a different perspective: The first faculty is established because the untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) possesses sovereign power (*ādhipatya*) in first attaining the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the principles of the Truths (*satya*), where such realization had not previously occurred.

The second faculty is established because, once untainted wisdom has attained direct realization, it possesses sovereign power in the gradual and permanent abandonment of remaining afflictions (*kleśa*), wherein the aspiration for further application (*prayoga*) is not yet fully satisfied.

The third faculty is established because, when untainted wisdom is already free from afflictions, it possesses sovereign power regarding the various untainted abidings in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

Because wisdom is the foremost and possesses the three types of clear observation (*abhisamaya*), it is specifically designated as a faculty (*indriya*), while the other eight serve as its auxiliaries.

In reality, however, the faculties established here should also pertain to both [the path of seeing and the path of cultivation]. Is it not the case that within this context, "patience" (*kṣānti*) has already attained clear observation regarding the principles of the truths, and the seven cognitions (*jñāna*) constitute a repeated clear observation therein; thus, patience would not be included in the first faculty?
Furthermore, because it is separated from patience, it would not be included in the second; consequently, this path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) should not be called a faculty.

If it is argued that since the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) also possesses the principle of the truths—because what was previously not yet realized is now realized—then the established faculties would become confused.

This is not a fault, because there is a distinction between the realization through vision (*darśana-abhisamaya*) and the realization through knowledge (*jñāna-abhisamaya*). It is just as when worldly wisdom has already attained realization regarding the noble truths, one still says that the untainted [wisdom] has "previously not yet realized" and now "attains realization."

Furthermore, although the aggregate of suffering is a single entity, its aspects (ākāra) differ, and thus there are distinct clear realizations (abhisamaya). For one who has not yet reached a definitive certainty regarding the principles of the truths, there is only the clear realization of vision; only when one has attained such certainty can it be called the clear realization of knowledge and vision. Therefore, those seven knowledges are also termed "attaining clear realization now" after having previously lacked it.

However, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) does not share this same fault; for although it is identical to the seven knowledges in a single moment, its subsequent continuities are all distinct. Thus, as many subsequent moments are termed the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*), they do not belong to the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Since there are moments of the seven knowledges (*jñāna*) in which one repeatedly performs the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the principles of the Truths, these should not be treated as analogous to those [other moments].

However, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth, just like the first moment, continue in the same manner; they are all capable of maintaining the acquisitions of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) from the afflictions destroyed by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), thereby ensuring their continuity.
The Master of the Sūtras should not be held to this same [fault], for there is no such error here.

Furthermore, although the Knowledge of the Path (mārgajñāna) has not attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding its observed objects in a single moment, it has already attained clear realization regarding the objects of the path across immeasurable moments; thus, because the few are subsumed by the many, it is termed "clear realization" with respect to all objects, thereby constituting the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*).

Just as one cannot be said to have crossed the great ocean or Mount Sumeru if one has not yet crossed even the distance of a single mustard seed, it is likewise appropriate to say that one has not yet attained deliverance from those [afflictions].
The masters of the West maintain that the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) is also subsumed under the faculty of "that which is yet to be known" (*ājñātavyendriya*).
If one follows their explanation, this fault does not exist at all;
therefore, what I have said is free from the two aforementioned defects.

If something is established as a faculty (indriya) because it possesses predominant influence, then among the afflictions belonging to the categories of craving and views, the two factors of feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā) also possess predominant influence; therefore, perception should likewise be established as a faculty, just like feeling.
Furthermore, the various afflictions possess a predominant influence over things such as the destruction of the wholesome factors; thus, they ought to constitute the essence of faculties (*indriya*).
Moreover, faculties are established on the basis of being preeminent. Since among all phenomena Nirvāṇa is the most preeminent, for what reason is Nirvāṇa not established as a faculty?

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, the vocal organ, the hands, the feet, and the anus are also established as faculties (*indriya*), because they possess predominance (*ādhipatya*) over speech, locomotion, and the act of excretion.

Such matters as these should not be established as faculties (*indriya*), because the characteristics of what is accepted as a faculty are as follows. The verse says: The basis of the mind, its differentiation, its maintenance, and its defilement; The commentary explains: The basis of the mind refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Its differentiation refers to the male and female faculties (*strīpuruṣendriya*). Its maintenance refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Its defilement refers to the five faculties of sensation (*pañca-vedanendriya*). Furthermore, the purification of this [defilement] refers to the five faculties beginning with faith (*pañca-śraddhādīndriya*). Since these characteristics are absent in the other factors, they are not established as faculties. Furthermore, the faculties are established based on their predominance (*prādhānya*) in these respective functions. For example, the eye and so forth are predominant in the apprehension of their respective objects; the male and female faculties are predominant in the differentiation of the body; the life-faculty is predominant in the maintenance of the continuity of the aggregates; the five faculties of sensation are predominant in the experience of the results of karma; and the five faculties beginning with faith are predominant in the attainment of nirvana. Therefore, it is established that there are precisely twenty-two faculties. As for the phrase "the basis of the mind," it means that the mind relies upon them. Because they are the support (*āśraya*) of the mind, they are called the "faculties. The term "basis" (*āśraya*) is used here in the sense of support, just as one speaks of the "basis" of a painting or the "basis" of a reflection. It is not used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), for even though the mental factors (*caitta*) rely upon the mind, they are not established as faculties. Nor is it used in the sense of a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), for although the primary elements (*bhūta*) are the support of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), they are not established as faculties. Thus, it is established that the six sense bases are the basis of the mind. Regarding the phrase "its differentiation," it means that based on the male and female faculties, the bodies of sentient beings are differentiated. If these two did not exist, there would be no distinction between male and female. Therefore, these two are established as faculties. Regarding the phrase "its maintenance," it means that based on the life-faculty, the continuity of the aggregates is maintained. If this did not exist, the aggregates would cease immediately after birth. Therefore, this is established as a faculty. Regarding the phrase "its defilement," it means that based on the five faculties of sensation, the mind becomes defiled. If these did not exist, the mind would not be defiled by attachment and so forth. Therefore, these are established as faculties. Furthermore, the purification of this [defilement] refers to the five faculties beginning with faith. Based on these, one attains nirvana. If these did not exist, one would not attain nirvana. Therefore, these are established as faculties. Consequently, it is established that there are exactly twenty-two faculties. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "Because of predominance in the apprehension of objects, in the differentiation of the body, in the maintenance of the aggregates, in the experience of the results of karma, and in the attainment of nirvana, there are twenty-two faculties. This concludes the section on the faculties. Next is the section on the truths (*satya*). The verse says: "The truths are suffering and origination, cessation and the path. The commentary explains: There are four truths: the truth of suffering, the truth of origination, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. Among these, the first two are worldly truths (*saṃvṛtisatya*), while the latter two are ultimate truths (*paramārthasatya*). As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "The first two are conventional truths; the latter two are ultimate truths. This concludes the section on the truths. Next is the section on the aggregates (*skandha*). The verse says: "The aggregates are form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. The commentary explains: There are five aggregates: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. Among these, the first four are material, while the last is immaterial. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "The first four are material; the last is immaterial. This concludes the section on the aggregates. Next is the section on the elements (*dhātu*). The verse says: "The elements are eighteen. The commentary explains: There are eighteen elements: the six internal elements (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), the six external elements (form, sound, odor, taste, tangible, and phenomena), and the six consciousness elements (eye-consciousness through mind-consciousness). As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "The elements are eighteen. This concludes the section on the elements. Next is the section on the sense-bases (*āyatana*). The verse says: "The sense-bases are twelve. The commentary explains: There are twelve sense-bases: the six internal sense-bases (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) and the six external sense-bases (form, sound, odor, taste, tangible, and phenomena). As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "The sense-bases are twelve. This concludes the section on the sense-bases. Next is the section on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The verse says: "Dependent origination has twelve links. The commentary explains: Dependent origination consists of twelve links: ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "Dependent origination has twelve links. This concludes the section on dependent origination. Next is the section on the faculties (*indriya*). The verse says: "The faculties are twenty-two. The commentary explains: There are twenty-two faculties: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, female, male, life, the five sensations (pleasure, pain, joy, grief, and equanimity), and the five beginning with faith (faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom), as well as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "The faculties are twenty-two. This concludes the section on the faculties. Next is the section on the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). The verse says: "The absorptions are four. The commentary explains: There are four meditative absorptions: the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas. These are distinguished by the abandonment of the five hindrances, the application of the five factors, the abandonment of the five factors, and the application of the four factors, respectively. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "The absorptions are four. This concludes the section on the meditative absorptions. Next is the section on the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). The verse says: "The formless attainments are four. The commentary explains: There are four formless attainments: the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "The formless attainments are four. This concludes the section on the formless attainments. Next is the section on the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). The verse says: "The immeasurables are four. The commentary explains: There are four immeasurables: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "The immeasurables are four. This concludes the section on the immeasurables. Next is the section on the liberations (*vimokṣa*). The verse says: "The liberations are eight. The commentary explains: There are eight liberations: the liberation of one possessing form seeing forms, the liberation of one not perceiving internal forms seeing external forms, the liberation of pure form, the four formless liberations, and the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "The liberations are eight. This concludes the section on the liberations. Next is the section on the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). The
This is the equipment, this is the purification; it is by virtue of these measures that the faculties are established.
The treatise says:
That upon which the mind depends consists of the six faculties, such as the eye; these six internal bases are the foundation of sentient beings.
The differentiation of these characteristics occurs by means of the female and male faculties; their continued existence throughout this single lifetime occurs by means of the life faculty;
their defilement occurs by means of the five feeling faculties;
and the accumulation of their purification occurs by means of the five faculties beginning with faith.
This [attainment] is purified by means of the final three faculties.
Since the purpose for establishing these faculties is fully accomplished by this, one should not further establish perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth as faculties.
Among all afflictions, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the most grave; therefore, only feeling (*vedanā*) is established as a faculty in relation to it.
Regarding those for whom craving is predominant: this is because the sūtras state that craving is the cause of the arising of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). As a sūtra says:
"With craving as cause, the six sense bases arise."

Furthermore, one should consider that conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is not itself the cause for the arising of afflictions; rather, once other causes have produced inverted views, conceptualization falsely discriminates and maintains them so that they continue in succession, and cannot be severed or destroyed except through the application of the correct antidote.
Therefore, it is said that this perception serves as the cause for that [craving].

Feeling is the cause of craving and applies to both types [of craving]; yet feeling is established as a distinct root because it is a predominant fault and a cause of affliction, and because it functions as a cause for both types [of craving].
Other masters say:

Perception (*saṃjñā*) is not established as a faculty because it is overwhelmed by other factors; that is to say, wholesome perceptions are overwhelmed by right wisdom, while defiled perceptions are overwhelmed by inversion.
Because they are not predominant (*adhipati*), they are not established as faculties (*indriya*).
Furthermore, although the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are also not predominant, sensation (*vedanā*) is predominant among them;
therefore, it alone can be established as an faculty. Alternatively, it is because sensation either diminishes the wholesome factors (*kuśalapakṣa*) or destroys the matter of the fruit of happiness.
How can that which is inferior, base, and defiled be established as a faculty (*indriya*)?
For a faculty is a phenomenon of preeminence within the world.

Furthermore, although *nirvāṇa* is superior among all phenomena, it is not established as a faculty because it extinguishes the faculties; this is like the destruction of various jars, wherein the destruction itself is not the substance of the jar.
Furthermore, the vocal organs and so forth are also not designated as faculties (*indriya*), because they would result in the grave fault of being indeterminate and disordered.
Regarding the fault of indeterminacy: which vocal organ would be established as the faculty of speech?
That which is capable of producing vocal sounds is called the "instrument of speech," and this is the tongue.

If that were the case, then mental investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*), as well as the various winds that initiate vocal action, should also be established as faculties, since they too are capable of producing speech.

This means that vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), and so forth, give rise to vocal sounds by depending on conditions such as the lips, teeth, palate, and throat; they do not depend on the tongue alone, for there would otherwise be no distinguishing cause.
Furthermore, vitarka, vicāra, and so forth, are the predominant causes for the production of vocal sounds.

Moreover, since the hands, armpits, wind instruments, stringed instruments, breath, and so forth can all serve as causes for producing vocal sounds, one should not establish the tongue alone as the faculty of speech (*vāgindriya*).
If it is argued that because the cognition of form also depends on language, the eye should not be established as a faculty (indriya) in its own right, this reasoning is necessarily incorrect.
For those born blind, although they hear descriptions of form, they do not perceive the distinct characteristics of blue and so forth.
The hands should not be designated as faculties (indriya) with respect to grasping, because the mouth and other organs are also capable of grasping objects.
The feet should not be designated as faculties with respect to locomotion, because classes of beings such as snakes and fish possess locomotion without the use of feet.
The organ of excretion should not be called a "faculty" (indriya) because it is capable of relinquishing; for the mouth and other organs are likewise capable of relinquishing.

Regarding the fault of confusion: the faculties established by that [opponent] would become confused, because the mouth is capable of both grasping and relinquishing, and because the hands and feet both possess the functions of grasping and moving. Such are the faults of confusion and the like.
Furthermore, such an extreme error would mean that the faculties established by him would have no limit.

If the tongue-faculty were distinct from the speech-faculty, one should likewise admit that the nose-faculty is distinct from the breath-faculty, because the tongue can speak while the nose passes the breath.

If something were established as a faculty simply because it has some slight efficacy with respect to another, then the throat, teeth, lips, stomach, and so forth should also be established as faculties, since they possess predominance over such functions as swallowing, chewing, and containing food.
Alternatively, since all causes exercise sovereign influence (*adhipatya*) over the production of their own respective effects, they should all be established as faculties (*indriya*).

Thus, the followers of Kapila act like children at play; one should not accept their [designation of] speech organs and so forth as faculties, for there is no fixed, unmixed, and supreme predominance in them.
Furthermore, other masters provide a distinct definition of the characteristics of the faculties (*indriya*).
The verse says:
"Alternatively, they are the basis for the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*), as well as [the bases] for arising, abiding, and experiencing."
The first fourteen are established [as faculties]; the same applies to the latter regarding cessation.
The commentary states:

Some say this indicates the tenet of other masters (*apara-ācārya*). They establish the faculties based on what constitutes the most preeminent basis for the forward progression (*pravṛtti*) and the reversal (*nivṛtti*) of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), because these possess sovereignty (*adhipatya*) over arising, abiding, and experience.

The continuous succession of birth and death is the meaning of "transmigration" (*saṃsāra*). The basis for this transmigration refers to the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*), because the eye and the other [senses] are definitively their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Birth occurs by taking the two sexual organs as conditions, for it is through them that birth is obtained.
Abiding depends on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), as it is the cause for the non-interruption of that continuity.
Experience depends on sensation (*vedanā*), because the five sensations act as conditions for the occurrence of benefit or harm.

Within the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*), fourteen faculties are established based on these four types of predominant functions; likewise, within the state of cessation (*nivṛtti*), the remaining eight faculties are established based on these same four predominant functions.

The cessation of birth and death is the meaning of "returning to extinction" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); this refers to the ultimate severance of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). The basis for attaining this consists of the five [faculties] beginning with faith, because they are the most excellent causes for the growth of all roots of virtue.
The first untainted faculty (*anāsrava-indriya*) is able to produce this attainment, because it is produced for the first time within the group of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*).
The subsequent untainted faculty causes this attainment to endure, because it arises in a continuous succession over a long period of time.

Subsequently, the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) cause one to attain the enjoyment of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*), because they are what manifest that state.

Neither karma nor afflictions are established as faculties, for they are not the productive causes of the six internal bases (*ādhyātmika-ṣaḍāyatana*), and because each of them individually lacks the specific capacity [to produce them].

If that were so, the eye and other [faculties] would also not be faculties; the mental faculty (*manas*), joy (*sukha*), pleasure (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) would not be uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);

and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) would not be contaminated (*sāsrava*). While such a point might hold true if one speaks in terms of predominant influence, one should not form a fixed attachment to this [interpretation]. Since the various karmas and afflictions lack a fixed, unique, and predominant function, they are not established as faculties.
The meaning of the faculties (*indriya*) and the reasons for their establishment have already been explained; now the individual nature of each faculty shall be discussed.
Among these, the characteristics of the faculties from the eye up to the male faculty have already been analyzed in the preceding chapter.
That is to say, those consciousnesses rely upon five kinds of pure matter (rūpa-prasāda), which are designated as the faculties of the eye and so forth.
The two faculties of female and male are established based on specific distinctions within a portion of the body faculty.
Because the essence of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is dissociated from thought (viprayukta), it shall be analyzed in detail among the dissociated factors.
Since the essence of faith and the other [faculties] consists of mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), they shall be analyzed in detail among the mental factors.
As for the five feelings, such as pleasure, and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), there is no other place where they are discussed; therefore, they should now be explained.
The verse says:
Displeasure of the body is called suffering; that same [displeasure] when pleasurable is called happiness.
Furthermore, the mental pleasure of the three dhyānas is likewise so named; in other stages, this is termed joy.
Displeasure of mind is called *daurmanasya* (sorrow); the intermediate state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is undifferentiated from the two [preceding states].
Based on the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, three faculties are established according to the nine stages.
The treatise says:
"Bodily" refers to bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*), so called because it arises in dependence upon the body; that is, sensation associated with the five consciousnesses.

"Displeasurable" has the meaning of affliction and harm; among the sensations experienced together with the five consciousnesses, those that are capable of afflicting and harming are termed the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).

What is called "pleasurable" (*sukha*) has the meaning of "beneficial. That which is experienced as beneficial internally by the five consciousnesses, occurring together with contact (*sparśa*), is termed the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Within the first dhyāna, the three consciousnesses are accompanied by pleasure; these are also included herein because they belong to the same category.
In the third dhyāna, that feeling associated with the mental consciousness which is capable of providing benefit is also called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Since there is no other body of consciousness in that stage, this very joy associated with the mind is established as the faculty of pleasure.

The pleasant sensation that arises simultaneously with the mental consciousness is of two kinds; in the third dhyāna it is called "pleasure" (*sukha*), because in that stage one is free from craving for joy (*prīti*).
Excluding the third dhyāna, in the three lower stages it is called the faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*), because there is still craving for joy present.

The meaning of these two mental states—joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*)—is identical in that they both consist of mental satisfaction and benefit; in what way do their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ such that they are divided into joy and bliss?
It is because there is a distinction in the way their modes of activity proceed.
When mental satisfaction proceeds with a mode of activity characterized by tranquility, it is termed the faculty of bliss (*sukhendriya*).
If there is a mental state that is joyful and characterized by coarse, active movement, it is called the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
Alternatively, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) involves a superior degree of benefit, whereas the benefit conferred by the faculty of joy is not like this.
Because of this pleasure of the third dhyāna stage, the noble ones describe it as a point of attachment.
The sensation that accompanies the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and is capable of causing affliction is a lack of mental satisfaction; it is called the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

Having established four feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*) based on the distinctions between the characteristics of experience—namely, whether they are pleasant or unpleasant for the body and mind—it is said that there is no distinction between the "intermediate equanimity" and the two [other feelings] in this context.
"Intermediate" means that which is neither pleasant nor unpleasant; it is precisely this absence of suffering and pleasure that is termed the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Regarding the feelings within body and mind, what feeling does this meditative concentration possess?
It should be said that this feeling pervades both body and mind.
For what reason are suffering and pleasure each divided into two [roots], while neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is established as only a single root?
This is because there is no distinction between [the experience of] body and mind.
That is to say, mental pleasure and pain are for the most part restless, whereas pleasure and pain in the body are characterized by stability.
As for neither-pain-nor-pleasure, whether in the body or in the mind, their mode of activity (*ākāra*) is without difference, as it consists solely of stability.

Furthermore, mental suffering and pleasure arise largely from conceptual discrimination, whereas this is not the case for physical sensation, as it occurs in accordance with the power of the objective field.
This is also true for Arhats and others; their equanimity (*upekṣā*) is free from conceptual discrimination in both body and mind, arising spontaneously through the mode of abiding in the Middle Way.
Furthermore, painful and pleasant sensations, whether residing in the body or the mind, differ in their modes of manifestation toward enemies and friends;
neutral sensations, whether residing in the body or the mind, do not differ in their modes of manifestation toward objects that are neither [pleasant nor unpleasant].
Therefore, suffering and pleasure are each divided into two [roots], while neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is established as only one root.
Having already explained the essential nature of the various feeling-faculties such as pleasure, the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) shall now be explained.
It is not possible to describe their essential natures individually; rather, they should be established collectively based on the nine faculties within the three paths.

These nine—namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*)—are themselves the three untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties within the three paths.

This means that when one is on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the nine factors beginning with the mental faculty (*manas*) constitute the essence of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), because they function with the mode of activity of intending to know what is as yet unknown.

If one is on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), those same nine factors beginning with the mental faculty constitute the essence of the second faculty, the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*); for the purpose of abandoning the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one repeatedly realizes the objects already known.

In the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), the nine factors beginning with the mind constitute the essence of the third faculty, the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*). It is called "knowing" (*jña*) because one knows that one has already known; it is called "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvin*) because knowing has become one's nature through cultivation, or because one is able to protect that knowledge.
Nine faculties are associated to constitute this state; therefore, the eight [faculties] beginning with volition also receive this name.

Thus, although there are twenty-two names for these faculties, their actual substance consists of only seventeen: the two faculties of female and male are subsumed within the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), and the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) are subsumed within nine faculties.
Having thus explained that the essential natures of the faculties differ, we shall now analyze their distinctions according to various categories and meanings.
Among these twenty-two faculties, how many are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without-outflows (*anāsrava*)?
The verse says:

Only the last three are exclusively untainted (anāsrava); it should be known that the material faculties, the life-faculty, and the faculties of grief and suffering are exclusively tainted (sāsrava); the remaining nine faculties pertain to both.
The Commentary states:
Regarding the final three faculties mentioned immediately prior, their essence is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); this carries the meaning of being "without defilement" (*vimala*).
"Defilement" (*mala*) and "taint" (*āsrava*) differ in name but are identical in essence.
The seven material faculties, the life-faculty, and the faculties of grief and suffering are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the "seven material [faculties]": these are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, female, and male faculties, as they are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Regarding the two types of the nine faculties: those previously mentioned as the three untainted faculties that subsume the nine faculties beginning with the mental faculty (manas) are called untainted; the remaining nine faculties beginning with the mental faculty are called tainted.
Other masters say:
"The five faculties, such as faith and the rest, are also exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), because the sutra speaks only of those possessed by the noble ones (*ārya*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:"
If one were entirely devoid of these five faculties, such as faith, I would say that such a person abides in the category of external worldlings (*bāhyapṛthagjanapakṣa*).
This is not a valid proof, for this statement was made with reference to the untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).
How is this known to be so?
Because this statement was made after first establishing the distinctions among the various noble stages based on the five untainted faculties, such as faith.
"Completely lacking these" refers precisely to the meaning of the previously mentioned untainted faculties, such as faith.
If it were not so, one should only say that there are no faculties such as faith, and one should not speak of "this.
Alternatively, there are briefly two types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*):
first, the internal, meaning those who have not severed their roots of goodness; second, the external, meaning those whose roots of goodness have already been severed.
This was stated with reference to external worldlings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*). If one entirely lacks these five faculties, such as faith, I say that they abide in the category of external worldlings.
Is there a sūtra that serves as proof that these five faculties, beginning with faith, can be both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted?
There is also. How so? It is as the Blessed One said:

"If I had not yet truly known these five faculties, such as faith, in terms of their arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape; if I had not yet transcended this world of gods, humans, Māras, and Brahmās; and if I had not yet realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment," and so forth, as extensively explained.
The non-outflow (anāsrava) dharmas should be examined in this same sequence.

Furthermore, it is said that before the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma, he first surveyed the world universally with his Buddha-eye and saw that there were sentient beings dwelling in the world, whether newly born or fully grown, possessing the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior faculties.
If there were already those possessing untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) in the world before the Wheel of Dharma was turned, the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world would be in vain.

If you offer a divergent interpretation of these two cited sūtras, I shall further refute it with a superior analysis in accordance with reason; therefore, the faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) certainly pertain to both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted.
Thus, having already explained the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*),
[we now consider] among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are maturation (*vipāka*) and how many are not maturation?
The verse says:

Life-faculty is exclusively maturation; sorrow and the final eight are not. The material faculties, the mind-faculty, and the remaining four feelings each pertain to both [types]. The commentary says: The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is exclusively of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*). Sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and the last eight faculties are not. The five material faculties, the mind-faculty (*manas*), and the remaining four feelings—namely, pleasure, pain, joy, and equanimity—each pertain to both maturation and non-maturation. Furthermore, among these various faculties, it is indistinguishable that only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is definitely a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
How could this life-faculty not be distinguishable? For the life-faculty that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*) is not a result of maturation.

Likewise, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is also a result of maturation (*vipāka*), because it is the fruit of the volition (*cetanā*) directed toward the Saṅgha or an individual by a bhikṣu who has attained the ultimate meditative absorption (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*) and the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*).
"May all my karmas that are capable of inducing the maturation of wealth be transformed so as to induce the fruit of the maturation of longevity," for this is stated in the *Mūla-śāstra*.

Others say: "By means of the power of the ultimate meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*), he draws forth the lifespan induced by previously accumulated karma conducive to indeterminate experience (*aniyata-vedanīya-karman*) from a former life, causing it to be experienced in the present."

Furthermore, there are those who wish to claim that the power of the meditative concentration of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*) draws forth the remaining maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of karma from previous births; yet the Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika) states that it is by the power of this superior concentration that the momentum for the duration of the faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)—which have never before existed—is drawn forth. According to this view, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not a maturation, whereas the others are.
This statement is unreasonable.

Why is this so? For instance, that [opponent] asserts that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is merely the momentum (*vega*) of the duration of the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), as will be refuted later.
Even if one were to grant this, it would be unreasonable to maintain that they are of the nature of *aupacayika* (nutritive) or any other such category.
First of all, they should not be maintained as being of the nature of *aupacayika*, because they serve to protect the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).

Since the maturation (*vipāka*) to be prevented has already been exhausted, it is not logical that there should be nourishment (*aupacayika*) alone once the continuity of maturation has been severed, as this would lead to the fallacy of over-extension.

Nor should one maintain that these [faculties] are of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*), because the eyes and so forth have no distinct nature of outflow, because the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is not the outflow-result of the wholesome (*kuśala*), and furthermore, because it would entail the fault of the realms (*dhātu*) becoming confused.

Furthermore, one should not maintain that this is of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*), because it is certainly not a cause of maturation in the desire realm, and because they themselves admit such a fact.
However, what they have said is so confused that it is difficult to scrutinize; regardless of what name you assign to that phenomenon, how can you say that this life-force is not maturation?
The Venerable Dharmatrāta states that this life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is also not a maturation (*vipāka*).
Thus, his treatise says: "There are thirteen faculties that pertain to both types.
This contradicts our own treatise, which states: "One faculty is neither karma nor the maturation of karma; nine faculties are neither karma nor the maturation of karma; twelve are indeterminate."
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the subsequent eight faculties, beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), are all not maturation (*vipāka*), because they are determinate (*vyākṛta*).

When the Sūtra speaks of karma that is "conducive to the experience of sorrow" (*daurmanasyavedanīya-karman*), there is no fault in this expression, as it refers to being conducive [to sorrow] by way of association (*samprayoga*) with feeling; it is just as when one says there is contact conducive to the experience of pleasure (*sukhavedanīya-sparśa*), and so forth.
For what reason is it definitively asserted that sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*), while this [other mental factor] is a maturation?
Because it is not logical. Why is it not logical?
Because those who are free from desire and greed do not follow [the maturation], the case of maturation is not so.

Even if one were to grant that it does follow, it would have to be like the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), such that Arhats and others could also be known to possess it; yet in reality they do not, as it is precluded by the Sūtra.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Even upon seeing the Great Master in the state of parinirvāṇa, there is no sorrow and so forth.
Furthermore, because it serves no purpose, the wholesome does not function; it cannot provide benefit, just like the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
By what mark is it known that there is indeterminate joy (*avyākṛta-prīti*)?
At that time, although external signs are absent, internal conceptualization arises; or rather, while wholesome joy may manifest, unwholesome roots of grief (*daurmanasya*) cannot possibly arise.

One should understand the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state by analogy with the wholesome (*kuśala*) characteristics; however, indeterminate joy (*prīti*) does not contradict the path of detachment (*vairāgya-mārga*).
Furthermore, the Āgamas provide scriptural proof that such joy exists, as the Sūtra says:
"They still experience the maturation (*vipāka*) of joy."

Since it is not stated that the black category (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*) possesses the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), we know that the faculty of grief transcends the nature of maturation (*vipāka-dharma*).
It is established by implication that the remaining faculties pertain to both categories;
that is to say, each of the twelve—the seven material faculties, the mental faculty (*manas*), and the four sensations (*vedanā*) excluding grief—pervades both classes.
Regarding the seven material faculties (*rūpīndriya*), those that are nurtured (*aupacayika*) are not maturation (*vipāka*); all others are maturation.

As for the mental faculty (*manas*) and the four sensations (*vedanā*), those that are wholesome (*kuśala*), afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), or belong to the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and supernormal transformation (*nairmāṇika*), are also not maturation as appropriate; all others are maturation.
Having thus explained these [categories] such as maturation (*vipāka*),
among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many have maturation and how many are without maturation?
The verse says:

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) definitely has maturation (*vipāka*); the first eight and the last three have none. The mental faculty (*manas*), the remaining [faculties], and those associated with feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth—each of these may belong to both categories. The treatise says: [The verse: Doubt definitely has maturation; The first eight and the last three have none. The mental faculty and the rest, along with feeling and so forth, Each and every one is common to both. The commentary states: Among the twenty-two faculties, doubt definitely possesses maturation, because it is an unwholesome state. The first eight—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, female, and male faculties—do not possess maturation, because they are exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*). The last three—the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of equanimity, and the faculty of mental joy—are also neutral and thus do not possess maturation. As for the mental faculty, the remaining four feelings (suffering, grief, pleasure, and equanimity), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), each of these may be either wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; therefore, each is common to both categories of having or not having maturation. Thus it is said: "Each and every one is common to both. This concludes the explanation of the faculties. Now, regarding the classification of the faculties as internal or external: there are six internal faculties and twelve external ones. What are the six internal? The treatise says: [The verse: Six are internal; the others are external. The six consciousnesses arise based upon them. The commentary states: Among the twenty-two faculties, six are internal: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental faculties. The remaining sixteen are external. Why are these six called internal? Because the six consciousnesses arise depending upon them as their bases. Furthermore, the six consciousnesses are designated as "internal" based on the internal sense-bases (*āyatana*). Since the six consciousnesses are internal, the six faculties that serve as their bases are also designated as internal. The remaining faculties are external because they are the objects of the six consciousnesses. Regarding the classification of the faculties as appropriated (*upātta*) or non-appropriated (*anupātta*): there are eleven appropriated faculties and eleven non-appropriated. What are the eleven appropriated? The treatise says: [The verse: Eleven are appropriated; the others are both. The ten material faculties and the life faculty are appropriated. The commentary states: Among the twenty-two faculties, eleven are appropriated: the ten material faculties (the five sensory organs and their five objects) and the life faculty. These are called "appropriated" because they are grasped by the mind and mental factors, and because they serve as the basis for the continuity of the aggregates. The remaining eleven—the mental faculty and the ten mental factors—are non-appropriated, as they are not material and cannot be grasped by the physical body. However, the mental faculty and the other mental factors are also sometimes called "appropriated" in the sense that they are associated with the appropriated aggregates. Therefore, it is said: "The others are both. This concludes the explanation of the appropriated and non-appropriated faculties. Now, regarding the classification of the faculties as defiled (*sāsrava*) or undefiled (*anāsrava*): there are eighteen defiled faculties and four undefiled. What are the eighteen defiled? The treatise says: [The verse: Eighteen are with outflows (*sāsrava*); Four are without outflows (*anāsrava*). The mental faculty, the three feelings, And the three faculties of faith and so forth. The commentary states: Among the twenty-two faculties, eighteen are with outflows: the seven material faculties (the five sensory organs plus the female and male faculties), the five faculties of feeling, and the six consciousnesses. The remaining four—the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of equanimity, the faculty of mental joy, and the faculty of equanimity—are both with and without outflows. Specifically, when these four are associated with the outflows, they are with outflows; when they are dissociated from the outflows, they are without outflows. The mental faculty, the three feelings (pleasure, suffering, and equanimity), and the three faculties beginning with faith (faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom) are all capable of being both with and without outflows. When they are associated with the outflows, they are with outflows; when they are dissociated from the outflows, they are without outflows. Therefore, it is said: "The mental faculty, the three feelings, and the three faculties of faith and so forth" are both with and without outflows. This concludes the explanation of the defiled and undefiled faculties. Now, regarding the classification of the faculties as belonging to the three realms: there are nineteen faculties belonging to the desire realm, thirteen belonging to the form realm, and two belonging to the formless realm. What are the nineteen belonging to the desire realm? The treatise says: [The verse: Nineteen belong to the desire realm; Thirteen belong to the form realm. Two belong to the formless realm; The others are excluded from all three. The commentary states: Among the twenty-two faculties, nineteen belong to the desire realm: the seven material faculties, the five faculties of feeling, the five consciousnesses, and the male and female faculties. Thirteen belong to the form realm: the seven material faculties (excluding the female and male faculties), the five faculties of feeling, the mental faculty, and the faculty of equanimity. Two belong to the formless realm: the mental faculty and the faculty of equanimity. The remaining nine—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, pleasure, mental joy, and the three faculties beginning with faith—are excluded from all three realms. This concludes the explanation of the faculties belonging to the three realms. Now, regarding the classification of the faculties as roots of existence (*bhavarāga-mūla*) or roots of liberation (*mokṣa-mūla*): there are three roots of existence and three roots of liberation. What are the three roots of existence? The treatise says: [The verse: Three are roots of existence; Three are roots of liberation. The three unwholesome roots are the roots of existence; The three wholesome roots are the roots of liberation. The commentary states: The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—are called the roots of existence because they cause one to remain bound within the cycle of birth and death. The three wholesome roots—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—are called the roots of liberation because they lead one toward the cessation of suffering. This concludes the explanation of the roots of existence and liberation. Now, regarding the classification of the faculties as faculties of power (*bala*) or faculties of weakness (*durbala*): there are five faculties of power and five faculties of weakness. What are the five faculties of power? The treatise says: [The verse: Five are faculties of power; Five are faculties of weakness. The five faculties beginning with faith are faculties of power; The five faculties beginning with faith are also faculties of weakness. The commentary states: The five faculties beginning with faith are called faculties of power when they are strong and firm, capable of overcoming the obstacles of the afflictions. They are called faculties of weakness when they are weak and feeble, unable to overcome the obstacles of the afflictions. This concludes the explanation of the faculties of power and weakness. Now, regarding the classification of the faculties as faculties of knowledge (*jñāna*) or faculties of ignorance (*ajñāna*): there are three faculties of knowledge and three faculties of ignorance. What are the three faculties of knowledge? The treatise says: [The verse: Three are faculties of knowledge; Three are faculties of ignorance. The faculty of knowing "I shall come to know the unknown," The faculty of complete knowledge, and the faculty of final knowledge—these are the faculties of knowledge. The faculty of knowing "I shall come to know the unknown," The faculty of complete knowledge, and the faculty of final knowledge—these are the faculties of ignorance. The commentary states: The faculty of knowing "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of complete knowledge (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) are called faculties of knowledge because they represent the progressive stages of realizing the Dharma. The faculty of knowing "I shall come to know the unknown" refers to the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), where one realizes the truths previously unknown. The faculty of complete knowledge refers to the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), where one has already realized the truths and continues to cultivate them. The faculty of final knowledge refers to the stage of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), where one has fully realized the truths and attained liberation. These are called faculties of knowledge. The faculty of knowing "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of complete knowledge, and the faculty of final knowledge are also called faculties of ignorance
Regarding the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) as debated previously, one should know that it necessarily has maturation (*vipāka*).

The word "necessarily" (*niyata*) is intended to indicate that it exists and is not non-existent; it excludes its being a non-maturing cause (*avipākahetu*), because it is neither neutral (*avyākṛta*) nor untainted (*anāsrava*).

This is not intended to demonstrate that only this faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) possesses maturation (*vipāka*), lest there be the error of implying that all other faculties are entirely without maturation; rather, it merely demonstrates that grief alone necessarily possesses maturation.

To explain by skipping the sequence is to demonstrate that whether taken collectively or individually, both the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) lack any ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*); this is unlike the case here where determinate (*vyākṛta*) and tainted (*sāsrava*) factors must be taken collectively to constitute a ripening cause. Therefore, explaining by skipping the sequence is profoundly useful.

The first eight faculties, beginning with the eye, and the final three—these eleven faculties are definitely without maturation (*vipāka*), because the eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and the three are untainted (*anāsrava*).

It is established by implication that all others pertain to both categories; namely, the mind faculty, the remaining four feelings, and "faith and so forth"—the term "and so forth" including the four faculties such as diligence—all eleven of these pertain to both types.

The faculties of mental volition (*manas*), joy (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are, when unwholesome or wholesome with outflows (*sāsrava*), subject to maturation (*savipāka*); when neutral (*avyākṛta*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are without maturation.
As for the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), when it is wholesome or unwholesome, it is subject to maturation; when neutral, it is without maturation.
If the five faculties beginning with faith are contaminated (*sāsrava*), they possess maturation (*savipāka*); if they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they lack maturation (*avipāka*).
Thus has been explained [the distinction between] those with maturation and so forth.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
The verse says:
Only the last eight faculties are exclusively wholesome; the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasya*) pertains to both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
the mind faculty and the remaining sensations (*vedanā*) belong to all three types; and the first eight are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The Commentary states:

The five faculties, beginning with faith, as well as the three untainted faculties, are exclusively wholesome. Although they appear later in the sequence, they are placed at the beginning here for the sake of following the immediate context.

The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) pertains exclusively to the nature of the wholesome and the unwholesome; the mental faculty (*manas*) and the four faculties of feeling (*vedanā*) all pertain to all three natures; and the eight faculties beginning with the eye (*cakṣus*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Thus has the classification of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so forth been explained.

Among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
The verse says:
In the desire, form, and formless realms, respectively, the last three are excluded.
Together with the female faculty, the male faculty, the faculties of sorrow and suffering, as well as the remaining faculties of form, joy, and pleasure.
The treatise says:

Excluding the last three untainted faculties from the desire realm—because those three faculties are exclusively non-bound—it should be understood by analogy that there are nineteen other faculties bound to the desire realm.

In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as previously stated, one excludes the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and further excludes the four faculties of male, female, sorrow, and suffering. By this analogy, it should be understood that fifteen faculties also pertain to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

As for the exclusion of the male and female faculties: because those in the form realm have already abandoned the dharma of sexual desire, there is no cause remaining for them to experience these two faculties.
Some say: "It is because this body is ugly.
This explanation is incorrect, for the concealment of the private parts is not a matter of ugliness; thus, the previous explanation is superior.

Nevertheless, the Buddha places them within the category of males; as the sūtra states, there is no possibility or occasion for a female body to become a Brahmā, whereas there is the possibility and occasion for a male to become one, because his power in being free from desire is fierce and resembles the function of a male.
As it is said in praise of the Great Brahmā King:
"The Great Brahmā is like a true man (*puruṣa*); Whatever was to be attained has already been attained;
Through the power of the path that transcends desire, He is therefore called a 'true man'."

Regarding the exclusion of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*): because there is no occurrence of harm within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and because suffering is the maturation (*vipāka*) of harmful karma.
Some say it is because their bodies are extremely pure and subtle.

Regarding the exclusion of the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*): it is because that realm lacks any characteristic of opposition, and furthermore, because the continuum is moistened by *śamatha*.
Some say: the form realm possesses the knowledge of being free from desire, whereas sorrow is the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of ignorance.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as previously stated, one excludes the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), the female and male faculties, the faculties of sorrow and suffering, and furthermore, the five material faculties along with the faculties of joy and pleasure; by this principle, it should be understood that the remaining eight faculties are associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Having thus explained those factors bound to the desire realm and so forth,

among the twenty-two faculties, how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
The verse says:
The mental faculty and the three feelings pertain to all three [categories]; sorrow is abandoned by insight and cultivation;
nine are abandoned only by cultivation; five are abandoned by cultivation, while the others are neither.
The Commentary states:
Mental joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) each pertain to all three [categories of abandonment].
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) pertains only to what is abandoned through seeing and cultivation, because it is not untainted (*anāsrava*).

The seven faculties of feeling—namely, the feelings of pleasure, pain, and the three types of equanimity—are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they possess form, are non-defiled, are not produced by the six [consciousnesses], and are not untainted (*anāsrava*).

The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are either abandoned through cultivation or are not to be abandoned at all, as they encompass both the wholesome-tainted (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The final three faculties are exclusively non-abandonable (*aprahātavya*), because they are all untainted (*anāsrava*) and faultless phenomena (*dharma*).
Is it not the case that the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) is also abandonable? As a sutra states:
One should understand that the Noble Path is like a boat or a raft; even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is non-Dharma.

This is not "abandoned" in the sense of being severed by the two paths of seeing and cultivation; rather, it is called "abandoned" because it is relinquished upon entering the state of the Nirvāṇa-realm without remainder.

Having already explained the distinctions among the categories of the various gates, we shall now discuss the initial acquisition of the various faculties (*indriya*) that constitute maturation (*vipāka*). How many maturational faculties are acquired at first, and in which realm are they first acquired?
One must ask about the initial acquisition of maturational faculties in order to exclude the possibility that rebirth can be continued by an undefiled mind (*akliṣṭa-citta*).
The verse says:
For those born from desire-realm wombs, eggs, or moisture, two faculties are first acquired as maturation;
for the miraculously born, six, seven, or eight; in the form realm, six; and in the higher realms, only the life faculty.
The Treatise says:
At the initial stage of taking birth through the womb, egg, or moisture-born modes, one acquires only two ripening faculties (*vipāka-indriya*), namely the body faculty and the life faculty.
The practitioners of contemplation say:

At this initial stage of birth, one also possesses the seeds of the eye and other faculties; however, only the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is capable of producing its own consciousness, whereas the eye and others are not. Therefore, only these two are mentioned.
Or, as in the case of those born blind and others who lack the eye-faculty and so forth at the moment of rebirth, there would be only these two [faculties].
This statement is unreasonable. Why is that?

Because the five consciousnesses do not exist at the moment of initial rebirth, the mention of birth from a womb, egg, or moisture excludes miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), as the sense faculties of those born miraculously arise instantaneously.
This discussion concerns maturation (*vipāka*); it does not refer to the mental faculty or equanimity, because at that time they are necessarily defiled and thus not maturation.
At that time, one also acquires the faculties such as faith and so forth, because they are not of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).

The stage of the *kalala* is not mentioned here; although at that stage one acquires dharmas produced by maturation, such as form and so forth, their essence is not that of a faculty, and therefore they are not mentioned.

At the initial stage of apparitional birth (*upapāduka*), one acquires six, seven, or eight faculties. Those without gender acquire six, as at the beginning of a kalpa; these six are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life-faculties.
Those with one gender acquire seven, such as the various devas and so forth.
Those with both sexual organs obtain eight; it is possible for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) in the miserable destinies (*durgati*) to possess both organs.
Those in the first stage of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) obtain six, as explained in the case of those born by transformation in the desire realm who lack organs.

"The upper [realms] possess only the life-faculty" refers to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); because their birth and its accompaniments are superior, they are called "upper," and therein, at the beginning, one obtains only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) which is of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).
From this it is proven that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) truly exists.
If it did not exist, by acquiring which faculty could one be said to "be born" in the formless realm?
It cannot be called the birth of the fruit of karma through being wholesome or defiled, for such states have not yet been received [in that realm] and might still arise [there].
Furthermore, a resultant consciousness (*vipāka-citta*) lacks the capacity for continuity, as it is only admitted that defiled consciousnesses can continue.
For those who maintain that the past and future do not exist, at such a time, the resultant consciousnesses of all three periods would be non-existent.
Since retribution (*vipāka*) does not exist, upon what could "arising" (*jāti*) be said to depend?
Although you may rush about with false conceptualizations to establish your own position, you must necessarily admit that there is a real dharma upon which arising depends.
Having explained the initial acquisition of the maturation faculties (*vipākendriya*), one should now explain the final faculties that are extinguished.
At the time of death in which realm do how many faculties cease last?
The verse says:
At the moment of death, the various faculties cease; in the formless realm, three; in the form realm, eight.
In the desire realm, nineteen, eighteen, or eight [faculties] cease; in the gradual [death], four cease, and for the virtuous, five increase.
The treatise says:
This explains, for the time being, how many faculties cease at the moment of death when the mind is defiled or indeterminate.

This means that when one is about to die in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the three faculties of life, mind, and equanimity cease last; for in the formless realm, there is only the feeling of equanimity and no others.
Furthermore, the term "formless" excludes the presence of form therein.
Other masters say:

Since that [formless realm] possesses form, if one does not assert the existence of a substantial entity called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), how could the cessation of maturation (*vipāka*) therein be termed "death in the formless realm"?
If it were argued that it is called death because the four aggregates of maturation cease, then one would also have to call it death when a wholesome or defiled mind is present.
If it is said that the maturation experienced in that stage has not yet been exhausted, how could there be a time for its exhaustion without further experience?
When a wholesome or defiled mind is present, what kind of karmic maturation should be said to be experienced by that [mind]?
That which is not manifest cannot be called "feeling" (*vedanā*).

If it is argued that it is called "feeling" because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of that maturation (*vipāka*) constantly persist therein, this reasoning is also incorrect, for the habitual tendencies you maintain are not universally established (*asiddha*).
Because this would lead to an excessive error: although the maturation (*vipāka*) may be exhausted, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) would still persist.
Just as with the habitual tendencies of karma, there would be no end to the time of death.
If the maturation were exhausted without habitual tendencies, then karma likewise should not have any remaining habitual tendencies.

If it is argued that the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) are related to the manifest maturation (*vipāka*) in the same way as my acquisition [of a body], then just as my acquisition does not give rise to further maturation once it has arisen, the predispositions would likewise cease to exist.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the maturation is experienced simply because the predispositions for maturation continue to evolve, for the nature of the two is not identical.
Furthermore, the principle of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) as you conceive them is untenable; this shall be extensively debated later.

Therefore, one must certainly admit that from the mind at rebirth until the mind at death, there exists a distinct, real dharma called "maturation" (*vipāka*), which continues to evolve in a constant stream. When that [stream] is severed, it is termed "death in the formless realm."

At the time of death in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), eight faculties cease last: namely, the five beginning with the eye, plus the first three [mental] faculties. This is because the faculties of those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) are never deficient at birth or death.

At the time of sudden death in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), nineteen, eighteen, or eight faculties cease: for those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), ten cease—namely, the female and male organs plus the eight previously mentioned;
for those with one sexual organ (*ekavyañjana*), nine cease; and for those without sexual organs (*avyañjana*), eight cease.
When dying gradually, the four faculties of body, life, mind, and equanimity are the last to cease; these four necessarily do not cease one after another.

If one dies with a wholesome mind within the three realms, the number of faculties increases by five in every stage, because a wholesome mind must possess the faculties of faith and so forth. That is to say, in the formless realm, the number increases to eight faculties, and so on up to nine in the desire realm at the final moment of gradual death.
Furthermore, one should investigate:
among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are capable of realizing which fruit of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*)?
Although the fruits of asceticism can also be attained through factors that are not faculties, since this discussion concerns the faculties, we inquire only about them.
The verse says:
