Nine attain the two extreme fruits; seven, eight, or nine attain the two intermediate fruits;
eleven attain arhatship; these are stated according to what is possible based on a single [type of] basis.
The treatise says:
The "extremes" refer to the fruits of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and Arhat; the "middle" refers to the fruits of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Furthermore, the fruit of Stream-enterer is attained by means of nine faculties: namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*), and the first two untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*), such as faith and so forth. Since this fruit and its corresponding path (*mārga*) are subsumed within the stage of the Not-yet-arrived (*anāgamya*), there is only equanimity present.
How is this obtained through the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātendriya*)?
It is because the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) arises simultaneously with the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
If that is so, for what reason is it said that only the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) is able to obtain the fruit of disjunction?
Only this [path] can sever [the defilements], whereby the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) arises, because it is able to obstruct the acquisition [of those defilements].

For this reason, it is said that the acquisition of dissociation from those [defilements] is exclusively the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the virile fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
If that is so, what function does the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) have with respect to the fruit and its acquisition?
For dissociation from the defilements and the acquisition [of that dissociation] are brought about by the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga), as this [path of liberation] is not their fruit.

Some say: Because the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is a subordinate member of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), that which is accomplished by the path of uninterrupted transition is itself termed the accomplishment of the path of liberation; it is like the deeds performed by a minister being designated as the deeds of the king.
The masters of the West say:
"The path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) can realize the acquisition of disjunction (visamyoga-prāpti).
This statement is incorrect, because disjunction would then have to be the fruit of that path.
This shall be extensively analyzed later; for now, it is briefly explained.

Although the path of liberation is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) with respect to the fruits of śrāmaṇya, it is nonetheless their associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); therefore, there is no fault in saying that it "attains" those fruits, because the essence of śrāmaṇya arises through mutual dependence.
Who could possibly obstruct the fact that these states stand in mutual relation as the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*)?
If it is argued that the same should apply to the preparatory (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and superior-progress (*viśeṣa*) stages, we grant this and see no fault.

Alternatively, the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*) may also serve as a homogeneous cause for attaining the fruit of stream-entry; this refers to the occasion when one transforms the faculties, as in the case of an arhat.
From the perspective of what is possible, there is no fault in such a statement.

The fruit of Arhatship is also attained through nine faculties: namely, the mental faculty, faith and the others [the five spiritual faculties], the two untainted faculties [of knowledge and vision], and any one from among the sensations of pleasure, joy, or equanimity.
Since this fruit and its path (the stage of approach) are subsumed within all nine stages, one takes any one of the three types of sensation accordingly.

The middle two fruits each involve attainment through seven, eight, or nine faculties, due to the distinctions between realization through the mundane and supramundane paths, as well as gradual and leap-over realization.

First, regarding the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) realized through the gradual path: if attained by means of the mundane path, it is acquired through seven faculties—namely, the mental faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the five faculties of faith and so forth;
if attained by means of the supramundane path, it is acquired through eight faculties—namely, those same seven faculties with the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) as the eighth.
Regarding those who attain transcendence by being doubly detached from sensual desire, just as the fruit of stream-entry is attained by means of nine faculties,
it should be known that the attainment of the fruit of non-returner is likewise.
Although this is the general rule, there is a distinction based on the difference in the levels (bhūmi) upon which those who attain transcendence through complete detachment from sensual desire rely.

Regarding the sequential realization according to one of the three types of feeling: if one enters the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) during the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), it is attained through eight faculties when relying on the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), with joy (*saumanasya*) as the eighth;
when relying on the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), it is attained through nine faculties.
The ninth [root] has already been established; if an Arhat were also to attain [the fruit] by means of nine faculties, it would contradict the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
For that treatise asks:
"By how many faculties does one attain Arhatship?"
Answer: Because there are eleven [factors].
Since the three feelings certainly do not arise simultaneously, it is attained by means of nine [factors] alone.
The statement regarding eleven faculties is made based on what is possible.

That is to say, it is possible for a single individual (pudgala) to repeatedly fall away from the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), and then to repeatedly regain [the faculties] through the sensations of pleasure, joy, and equanimity.

The Non-returner (anāgāmin) does not incur this same fault, because for him there is no possibility of attaining the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) through gradual progression, and for him there is no possibility of falling away from the leap-over attainment (*vyutkrāntaka*).
Furthermore, one should investigate:
which faculties are possessed?
Among those faculties, how many are necessarily possessed?
The verse says:
One necessarily possesses life, mind, and equanimity; each of these is necessarily possessed as a triad.
If one possesses the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), one necessarily possesses four;
if one possesses the eye-faculty and so forth, as well as the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one necessarily possesses five faculties.
If one possesses the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), one necessarily possesses seven.
If female or male faculties, as well as sorrow, are acquired, faith and the others each become eight;
the two untainted [faculties] become eleven, and the first untainted [faculty] becomes thirteen.
The Treatise says:

Among the faculties of life, intention, and equanimity, one is necessarily accomplished; those who possess them are definitely endowed with these three faculties. There is no deficiency in the accomplishment of these three, as they are universally present across all stages and bases.
The five faculties beginning with faith pervade all stages (*bhūmi*) but do not pervade all bases (*āśraya*);
the remaining fourteen faculties pervade neither.
Therefore, the life-faculty and others are necessarily established as three [faculties], while the remainder may or may not be established.
How are the four faculties, beginning with the eye, accomplished?
They are fully present in those born in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) and partially present in those born in the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
The body faculty (kāyendriya) is present in its entirety among those born in both the Desire and Form Realms.
The female and male faculties arise in a small portion of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) arises in the desire realm, the three lower dhyānas, and for noble ones born in the higher realms.
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) arises in the desire realm, the two lower dhyānas, and for noble ones born in the higher realms.
The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is definitely accomplished in all stages of birth within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is definitely accomplished by those who have not yet abandoned desire and greed. As for the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhādi-pañcendriya*), they are definitely accomplished in those states where one has not severed the roots of goodness, and where the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) have already been attained and not yet lost.
Apart from these states, in all other positions, these are definitely not accomplished.

If one possesses the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), one necessarily possesses four: namely, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣendriya*), and the pleasure-faculty.

If one possesses the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), one also necessarily possesses four: namely, the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the equanimity-faculty, and the body-faculty. As for the remaining faculties, they may or may not be possessed, as should be considered according to what was stated previously.
If one possesses the eye faculty, one necessarily possesses five: namely, the life, mind, equanimity, body, and eye faculties.
It should be understood that for the ear, nose, and tongue faculties, there are likewise five; the first four are as with the eye, and the fifth is the respective faculty itself.

If one possesses the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one necessarily possesses five: namely, the life-faculty, the mental faculty, the equanimity faculty, the pleasure faculty, and the joy faculty.
When born in the second dhyāna but not yet free from craving for it, one possesses only the defiled feeling of pleasure belonging to the third [dhyāna].
If one possesses the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya), one necessarily possesses seven: namely, the faculties of body, life, mind, and four sensations, excluding that of grief.
If one possesses the female faculty (strīndriya), one necessarily possesses eight: the seven as described for the faculty of suffering, with the eighth being the female faculty.
The male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) is also eightfold: seven are as explained for suffering, and the eighth is its own root.
The faculties of faith and so forth are also eightfold, namely: life, mind, equanimity, and the five faculties beginning with faith.
If both the female and male faculties are present, they necessarily constitute fifteen.

If one possesses the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), one necessarily accomplishes eleven: namely, the life-faculty, the mental faculty, the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity, the five faculties beginning with faith, and the faculty of one who has already known.
It is the same for the faculty of one who has full knowledge (*ājñendriya*); one accomplishes eleven, including its own faculty and the others.

If one possesses the faculty of "I do not yet know" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), one necessarily accomplishes thirteen faculties: namely, the body, life, mind, suffering, pleasure, joy, equanimity, the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and the faculty of "I do not yet know.
It is traditionally taught that at the stage of gradual death, because of a profound mental revulsion toward birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one is able to enter the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Having thus explained the states and the definite accomplishment of the *pudgala*,
it shall now be explained how many faculties (*indriya*) are definitely accomplished by those who possess the very minimum.
The verse says:
At minimum, eight [factors] are present when there is no wholesome [state]: the faculties of feeling, body, life, and mind;
for a fool born in the formless realm, the wholesome, life, mind, and equanimity are present.
The Commentary says:
One who has already severed the roots of goodness is said to be "without goodness.
If such a person possesses the absolute minimum of eight faculties— namely, the five feeling faculties, the body faculty, the life faculty, and the mind faculty— it is because,
according to the process of gradual death, only the body faculty remains.
The "fool" refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), because they have not yet seen the Truths.

Such a person born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also possesses eight faculties: namely, the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), as well as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind-faculty (*manas*), and the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣā*). This is due to the fixed number [of faculties] and because they are described as being "fools."
Good words do not apply indiscriminately to the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
Among those who possess the maximum number [of faculties], how many faculties do they accomplish?
The verse says:

At most, nineteen are acquired; for those with both sexual organs, the three purities are excluded. For noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire, two purities and one organ are excluded. The commentary says: *The maximum number of faculties acquired is nineteen. This excludes the three types of pure faculties (the faculty of perfect knowledge of what has been known, the faculty of perfect knowledge, and the faculty of final knowledge) in the case of those possessing both sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana). Furthermore, in the case of noble ones (ārya) who have not yet abandoned desire, two pure faculties and one sexual organ are excluded.*
Those who possess both sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana) are endowed with the faculties such as the eye; excluding the three untainted (anāsrava) faculties, they possess the remaining nineteen.
The untainted are called "pure" (śuddha) because they are free from the two bonds.

If a noble one in training (śaikṣa) has not yet abandoned desire-attachment, even when possessing the maximum number of faculties, they likewise possess nineteen—excluding the two untainted faculties and excluding one of the sexual organs.
The two untainted [faculties] refer to either one of the first two faculties preceding the faculty of one who has already fully known.
Regarding the phrase "one gender," it means there is neither the possession of both genders nor the absence of gender, because they have attained the noble dharmas.
*Abhidharmasamuccayaviniścayaśāstra*, Fascicle Nine.
*Abhidharmasamuccayaviniścayaśāstra*, Fascicle Ten.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Two: Distinguishing the Differences, Part Two of Two. Having already analyzed the elements (*dhātu*), the various formations (*saṃskāra*) that arise simultaneously with the faculties (*indriya*) have been extensively discussed.
Now, one should reflect upon this:
for what reason are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) investigated as arising together?
It is in order to dispel false doctrines and to reveal the correct principle.
That is to say, some maintain that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise spontaneously without cause;
others maintain that conditioned phenomena arise due to a single cause;
and still others maintain that conditioned phenomena arise from causes such as primordial nature (*svabhāva*) or other unbalanced factors.
Furthermore, there are those who hold the view that when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise, they do so solely by taking what has previously arisen as their cause.
In order to refute these various heterodox positions and to reveal the correct principle of arising, one should engage in careful investigation.
In this context, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are briefly of two kinds:
first, those with form (*rūpin*), and second, those without form (*arūpin*).
Those without form are of three kinds:
First, mind; second, mental factors; third, formations dissociated from mind.
Regarding those with form, there are two types:
first, aggregates of atoms; second, that which is not an aggregate of atoms.
Initially, the aggregation of atoms is of two kinds:
first, those bound to the desire realm; second, those bound to the form realm.
Initially, those bound to the desire realm are further of two kinds:
There are two types of aggregates: those without sense-faculties (*anindriya*) and those with sense-faculties (*sendriya*).
Herein, we shall first analyze the matter of the aggregate of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The verse says:
The subtle aggregate of desire, being without sound, consists of eight entities when lacking the sense-faculties;
it consists of nine entities when possessing the body-faculty; and it consists of ten entities when possessing the remaining faculties.
The treatise says:
The final, most subtle division within resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*), which can no longer be further analyzed, is called the atom (*paramāṇu*).

This means that this atom cannot be further divided into multiple parts by any other form or by the faculty of discernment; it is thus described as the minimum of form. Because it has no further parts, it is designated by the name "minimum."
Just as a single *kṣaṇa* is the shortest unit of time, which cannot be further divided into half a *kṣaṇa*, so too,
when a multitude of atoms are combined with one another such that they are certainly not separated, this is called an "atom-aggregate" (*paramāṇu-saṃcaya*).
This occurs in the desire realm; where there is no sound and no sense faculties, eight entities arise together, with none of them lacking any other.
What are these eight entities?
They are the four great elements and the four derived forms: visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
If this sound were to exist [independently], it would constitute nine entities.

It is not mentioned [separately] because it is shown to arise from the mutual impact of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and is not like form (*rūpa*) and other [derived phenomena] which exist at all times.
In the case of an aggregate of atoms that possesses roots but lacks sound, there are nine or ten co-arising entities.
In an aggregate possessing the body-root (*kāyendriya*), nine entities arise together: eight as previously described, with the body as the ninth.
There are other groups of faculties that arise together as ten entities; nine of these are the same as those of the body, with the addition of one such as the eye.
The eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are never separated from the body, because they function in dependence upon it.
These four faculties, however, arise in mutual separation, because their locations are distinct.
If sound arises within this aggregate of possessed faculties, it becomes ten or eleven [elements] when the produced sound is added.
Because these have appropriated primary elements (mahābhūta) as their cause, they arise inseparable from the various faculties.
The reasons for this are not stated here; they should be understood as previously explained.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), with the exception of the two objects—odor and taste—the rest is the same as in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); therefore, it is not discussed separately.

If it is argued that there is a fault because the term "objects" (*vastu*)—whether based on their substance (*dravya*) or their location (*sthāna*)—would result in being too few or too many, there is no such fault, because the distinction is made between the supported (*āśrita*) and the support (*āśraya*), and between their substance and their location.
That is to say, the objective basis (*āśraya-vastu*) is explained in terms of its substance (*dravya*), while the subjective basis (*āśrita-vastu*) is explained in terms of its locus (*sthāna*).
Alternatively, there is no fault in explaining it solely in terms of substance, because herein it is stated that they arise simultaneously with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The essence of shape, color, and so forth does not exist determinately, because they are absent within light and other such phenomena.
Alternatively, they exist only as bases; however, in order to refute various misconceptions, the primary elements (mahābhūtas) are explained separately.

Regarding those who engage in much slander: this refers to those who either slanderously claim that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) have no distinct intrinsic nature; or again, slanderously claim that there is no distinct substance of derived matter within the sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*); or again, slanderously claim that not every aggregate possesses all [elements]; or again, slanderously claim that their number is not fixed.
By explaining the primary elements individually, all such slanders are eliminated.

If it is argued that because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) each produce their own derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), there should be many [derived matters], this reasoning is incorrect, for it is spoken of in terms of categories.
It has already been stated that material phenomena necessarily arise together.
The co-arising of formless [phenomena] shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Mind and mental factors necessarily arise together; so too do the various formations, characteristics, or acquisitions.
The treatise says:
Mind and mental factors necessarily arise together; if one is absent at any given moment, the others never arise.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are precisely these conditioned things, namely, those with form (*rūpin*) and those without form (*arūpin*).

The phrase "necessarily concomitant" (sahabhū) from the preceding section should apply here as well; that is to say, when material and other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise, they necessarily arise together with the four characteristics, such as arising (*jāti*).
As for the mention of "or acquisition" (*prāpti*), it means that among all conditioned phenomena, only those pertaining to sentient beings arise together with acquisition.
Some say this indicates that [the definition] does not apply universally to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Among the four types of conditioned things previously mentioned, matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) have already been extensively analyzed as explained in the preceding chapter.
However, mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) and so forth have not yet been extensively analyzed; therefore, we shall now first analyze the various mental factors in detail.
The verse says:
Mental factors are, for now, fivefold, distinguished by the universal ground and other categories.
The commentary says:
The mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are, for now, divided into five categories, because the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) and the others differ from one another.

What are these? First, the universal mental factors; second, the wholesome universal mental factors; third, the universal mental factors of affliction; fourth, the unwholesome universal mental factors; and fifth, the minor afflictive mental factors.
"Ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to a place of abiding or a sphere of activity; if something serves as the abode or the field of activity for another, that thing is said to be the "ground" of that dharma.
Since this ground is the mind—the ground of all great dharmas—it is called the "Universal Ground" (*mahābhūmi*).
Among these, those factors that belong to the universal ground are called "universal mental factors" (mahābhūmikadharma).
This is because they arise universally in conjunction with all types of minds.
Mind is not a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*), because it does not arise simultaneously with [other] mental factors.
What are those factors?
The verse says:
Feeling, perception, volition, contact, and desire; wisdom, mindfulness, and attention;
resolve and concentration—these are present in all states of mind.
The commentary says:
That which, with respect to the body as its basis, can benefit, harm, or be neutral toward it, and which experiences pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral contact, is called feeling (*vedanā*).
That which establishes and grasps the causes for the differentiated characteristics of objects, such as male and female, is called perception (*saṃjñā*).

That which causes the mind to engage in the performance of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate, thereby bringing about that which is excellent, inferior, or neutral, is called volition (*cetanā*).
Because of the existence of volition, it causes the mind to have a dynamic activity toward its objects, just as the power of a magnet can cause iron to have movement.

Contact (*sparśa*) is so called because it arises from the conjunction of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness; it serves as the cause for feeling (*vedanā*) and consists of the mutual encounter between them.
Desire (*chanda*) is so called because it is the longing for and grasping of an object.
The discernment of the characteristics of objects—whether they are correct or erroneous—is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
The cause for clear recollection of an object without forgetfulness is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).
That which draws forth the mind and mental factors, causing them to be alert toward their objects, is called attention (*manasikāra*); this is what is referred to in the world as "paying heed."
The confirmation of an object is called *adhimokṣa* (resolute conviction). Other masters say:

"Superior" (*adhi*) means preeminent, and "conviction" (*mokṣa*) means liberation; this [faculty] enables the mind to operate with unimpeded mastery toward its object, just as superior morality and so forth cause the mind to be undistracted when apprehending its focal object.
The cause for not being dispersed is called *samādhi*. That Elder says:

"There are no such ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) as are reckoned; there are only three, because the Sūtra speaks of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) as arising together."
Is it not the case that those sūtras also speak of contact? As that sūtra says:
"The coming together of the three is contact.
Although the sūtra speaks of the existence of contact, it does not state that it has a separate substantial entity; thus that sūtra says:
Thus, the gathering and conjunction of these three factors is called contact (*sparśa*).
Therefore, there is no such thing as the nature of the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) as you have conceived it.
This statement is unreasonable, because according to that sutra, the meaning implies the existence of contact, and thus the principle is established.

In that sutra, the Buddha did not define the characteristic of contact (*sparśa*); rather, he spoke of the assembly of conditions that give rise to contact. That is to say, when the sutra refers to "contact," it means that contact is conditioned by contact; this is not the actual characteristic of contact. It is that which is produced from the conjunction [of conditions] that is called actual contact.
How is it known that he does not speak of the characteristic of contact (*sparśa-lakṣaṇa*), but rather speaks of the conditions for contact?
Because other sūtras separately state that the eye and so forth are the conditions for contact.

That is to say, there is a sūtra which says that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are the condition for contact, and in a verse it is said that two are the conditions for contact; therefore, we know that the conjunction of the three is the condition for contact, not contact itself.

One should not say that these three serve as mutual conditions for one another, for all three are conditioned by contact and possess the characteristic of contact; this is because while the eye and visible form are conditions for visual consciousness, visual consciousness is not a condition for the eye and visible form.

Even if it were granted that these three factors serve as mutual conditions, since contact possesses conditions but is not itself those conditions, there ought to exist a distinct, truly existent characteristic of contact produced apart from the conditions of the triadic conjunction of the eye and so forth.
Regarding the three proximate conditions that can give rise to contact, the name "contact" is applied metaphorically; it is not the actual characteristic of contact.
That the eye and form act as conditions for contact means they function as its basis and its object, respectively.
Regarding the statement that visual consciousness and contact can act as conditions for one another, this means they function as a single effect because they are not separate from their basis.
Therefore, the name "contact" is applied to them metaphorically.

However, the claim that the eye and other faculties stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect such that their conjunction is called contact is also unreasonable, as its meaning cannot be established.

It is not that in their own school the principle of mutual causality among co-arising factors is not admitted; rather, it cannot be established because one exists while the other does not, because their continuities are distinct, and because they do not share a single fruit.

Even if it were granted that these three factors serve as mutual causes and effects, one should not say that they act as conditions for contact (*sparśa*), because in their own school, contact is not admitted to be a real entity.

It is observed that only what exists can serve as a condition for what exists, as in the cases of sensation (*vedanā*) for craving (*tṛṣṇā*), or the eye and visible forms for consciousness (*vijñāna*).

However, it is taught that the eye and so forth serve as conditions for contact (*sparśa*). Since the conditions are substantially real, the result must likewise be so; thus, one knows by inference that there exists a distinct, substantial contact.

Since you admit that these three factors mutually serve as cause and effect and name this "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*), you should also admit that from this conjunction of the three, contact arises as something distinct. It is for this reason that it is said: "The six sense bases are the condition for contact."

The gāthās also state that these two serve as conditions for contact; otherwise, since there would be no real dharma to be designated as "conjunction," it would merely be a conventional designation applied to these three [factors].
Furthermore, those three factors do not serve as mutual conditions for one another and thus lack the sense of conjunction; how, then, can they be established as the condition for contact (*sparśa*)?

If it is argued that this is like saying that color and other qualities are the conditions for objects such as jars and garments—yet there are no jars or garments apart from color and the rest—then the same logic should apply here as well.

If that were so, then feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] would not be distinct entities. Just as it is said that feeling and the rest have the eye and visible form as conditions, feeling and the others likewise should not exist apart from the eye and so forth.

If you argue that the characteristic of contact (*sparśa*) is not manifest—meaning that while the specific characteristics of feeling and the others are clearly manifest, no such distinct characteristic of contact can be apprehended, and its existence is known only through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—then there is no separate essence of contact apart from the threefold conjunction.
This is also not the case; the substance of tangibility (spraṣṭavya) truly exists because it possesses function, just like the sense organs such as the eye.
That is to say, although the sense organs such as the eye are not directly perceived, their own substance is known to exist because they are capable of apprehending objects.

Furthermore, just as volition (*cetanā*) and other such factors, though not directly perceived, are known to exist through mental construction—namely, by virtue of their functional activity in accomplishing mental karma (*manas-karma*) and so forth—one knows that they possess a substantial essence (*svabhāva*) by means of this very activity.
If mental factors (*caitta*) were directly perceptible, there would be no one who could grasp them as being identical to the mind;
the same would apply to contact (*sparśa*). Although it is not directly perceived, its existence as a distinct entity is known because it possesses functional efficacy.

Furthermore, I have never seen it stated in any of the holy teachings that a phenomenon lacking intrinsic nature (avastuka) possesses a distinct function; rather, the expression "possessing a function" is used only with respect to phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (savastuka).
Since it is stated that contact (sparśa) possesses a function, we know that this contact has a distinct intrinsic nature of its own.

If it is argued that the specific distinctions among the six bases, such as the eye and so forth, are themselves capable of producing sensation (*vedanā*) without a separate function of contact (*sparśa*), meaning that the internal base and the external object together produce consciousness, and their mutual causality and conjunction is termed "contact," which then produces sensation—and therefore there is no separate function of contact within this process—[we respond as follows].

This statement is unreasonable, for it has already been explained previously; furthermore, it would render the repeated statements in the Sūtra purposeless, and it would entail the fault that craving and so forth would be identical to feeling and so forth.

This means that it has already been stated previously that, within that school's own system, it is not the case that simultaneous arising is not permitted for things to act as mutual causes and effects; thus, the logical point could be established.
Furthermore, the Sūtra’s repeated statement that "contact is the coming together of the three" would otherwise become redundant.

That is to say, the Sūtra first states that visual consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions; by this, the nature of the eye and so forth, as well as their causal relationship, are already established.

Furthermore, because it subsequently mentions that feeling, perception, and volition arise simultaneously, it clearly demonstrates that those [mental factors] are produced through the conjunction of the causes and conditions of the eye and so forth.

In that case, the repeated mention of the "contact of the threefold conjunction" would certainly be useless, because the causal relationship of the eye and so forth has already been established by what was previously stated.

Would it not be the case that if one were to say that contact is a distinct entity produced from the conjunction of the causes and effects such as the eye, then the expression "threefold conjunction" would likewise be rendered useless?

The Sūtra should simply state that visual consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions; it subsequently mentions the co-arising of feeling, perception, and volition because the principle of the sequential relationship between cause and effect regarding the eye and so forth has already been established thereby.
It is not so; this statement has another meaning.
We do not say that the expression "the conjunction of the three" is intended to establish the sense of cause and effect regarding the eye and the other factors.
If that is the case, what meaning does this statement establish?

This is specifically intended to establish the meaning that contact exists as a distinct entity. That is to say, when the eye, the object (form), and consciousness arise simultaneously, the eye does not depend on the other two, nor does the form.
Since the arising of consciousness necessarily relies upon both a support (āśraya) and an object (ālambana), the arising of visual consciousness must depend on the other two.
When the various mental factors arise, they likewise depend upon a support and an object; however, that support is of two kinds:
first, the combined support, which is consciousness; second, the separated support, which is the eye.

Alternatively, consciousness is its intimate basis of support, the eye faculty is its basis of attachment, and the object of cognition is its apprehended object; therefore, when it arises, it necessarily depends upon these three factors.

Regarding the statement that "eye-consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms": this means that the eye and visible forms, in conjunction, act as conditions for the arising of eye-consciousness; that is to say, they function together as conditions simultaneously, neither increasing nor decreasing.

Furthermore, the subsequent sutra states that "contact is the conjunction of the three," meaning that with the conjunction of the eye, form, and consciousness as conditions, eye-contact arises; this also signifies the sense of these factors acting together as conditions simultaneously, neither increasing nor decreasing.

If it is claimed that the term "conjunction" (saṃnipāta) means "acting together as conditions," then the essence of contact (sparśa) would have to be a composite of three dharmas; what other substantial entity could there be that is "contact"?

This too is irrational, because the triad of eye, form, and consciousness lacks the sense of acting as conditions for one another. Nevertheless, since it is said that all [three] act together as conditions, it is established by this that the essence of contact exists as a distinct entity.
If that were so, one should simply say that contact arises from the conjunction of the three. It is not so;
rather, the fifth case-ending is employed to prevent doubt regarding its arising at a later time.
If it were stated otherwise, one would suspect that it arises subsequently.
It should be as stated in the Sūtra:
"Because King Mandhātṛ gave rise to an evil thought, he fell simultaneously.
If that is so, for what reason does the sūtra state only that the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are the condition for contact (sparśa)?

Feeling and the other [mental factors] also take that [contact] as their condition; otherwise, for what reason would the Sūtra state only that contact is the condition for feeling, given that feeling is also a condition for the arising of contact?
Since this is so, that must also be so; I shall explain this for you when discussing dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Thus, following the correct principles of the Abhidharma, I have explained the phrases in the Sūtra as meaningful expressions, unlike the Elder’s arbitrary interpretation of the term "conjunction of the three" (*trikasamnipāta*), which is devoid of meaning.

Furthermore, if one holds that feeling arises in dependence on the conjunction of contact, and consequently asserts that contact is simply a differentiation of the six sense bases, then by the same logic, when grasping arises in dependence on the conjunction of craving, one should assert that craving is simply a differentiation of feeling.
Since this is not the case, how could that be so?

Alternatively, one should state a distinct cause for that [contact]; since it has already been established that contact possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one should not claim that contact is simply the conjunction of the three.
Furthermore, contact (*sparśa*) exists as a real entity, because the Sūtra describes it as a mental factor (*caitasika*), just like feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).

That is to say, the Blessed One, in the Sūtras, states that contact has the nature of a mental factor; for there can be no non-existent dharma designated as a mental factor. Therefore, like feeling and the others, contact must exist as a reality.
As stated in a verse:
"Taking the eye and visible forms as conditions, The various mental factors arise:
Consciousness, contact, sensation, and perception, Along with volitional formations, which comprise the causes of existence."
The Elder explained the meaning of this verse as follows:

"That which is called a mental factor (caitta) does not exist separately from consciousness (vijñāna), because it is taught in a sequential order, because the term 'consciousness' is used, and because it is never dissociated from consciousness."

Regarding the meaning of "successive order," it refers to the sequence of arising: namely, from the eye and visible form, consciousness and contact arise; from these, the various mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) subsequently arise.
Those such as feeling (*vedanā*) that arise simultaneously [with consciousness] are called mental factors, whereas contact (*sparśa*) is not a mental factor.
Regarding the mention of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): it is because consciousness is explicitly mentioned here that contact (*sparśa*) is the mind itself, not a mental factor (*caitta*).

As for "not separate from consciousness": it means that contact can exist without being separate from consciousness; since there is no sense of a prior conjunction [of factors] before consciousness, it is merely designated as a mental factor while lacking a distinct substantial entity.
Regarding the three proofs currently presented, the reasoning in each case is untenable.
First, the argument concerning the sequential order is inconsistent with reason, because it does not state that consciousness arises between the eye and its object.
Furthermore, it asserts that from the eye and the object, consciousness and contact arise, and from these, mental factors such as sensation subsequently arise.
If that is so, what other mental factors (caitta-dharma) are produced from two conditions?
In the Sūtras, the Blessed One has clearly and explicitly taught that all mental factors arise from two conditions and not from a third.
Among these, we maintain that the mental factors (*caitta*) also arise from two conditions and do not belong to a third.

The Elder (*Sthavira*), however, gives rise to a divergent conceptualization therein, asserting that the mental factors exist only in the third category; this is either to disparage the Tathāgata or a failure to comprehend the meaning of the sūtras.
Next, it is argued that the mention of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is also illogical; for how could one see that when consciousness is mentioned, mental factors (*caitta*) are thereby excluded?

This verse does not treat consciousness alone; however, one cannot conclude that because the term "mental factors" does not belong to consciousness, [the verse] is therefore not about feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [factors] either.
One might argue that feelings (*vedanā*) and other such phenomena are likewise not mental factors (*caitta*).
Why? Because we observe that the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is used here [in the definition of the aggregate of consciousness].
Although the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is used, if one accepts that feeling (*vedanā*) and the others are mental factors (*caitta*), then contact (*sparśa*) should be treated in the same way.

As for the later statement—that contact cannot exist apart from consciousness because the sense of "conjunction" (*sannipāta*) is necessarily absent prior to consciousness—and the claim that mental factors are merely nominal designations lacking a separate substance, this is also unreasonable, because the term "contact" is spoken by way of the category of mental factors.

It was previously stated that mental factors arise from two conditions; now, following that same principle, the characteristics of contact and so forth are enumerated. Since these are not the preceding consciousness itself, how could they lack a distinct substance?
They must, like feeling and the other [mental factors], certainly possess a separate intrinsic nature.
Although contact (*sparśa*) does not actually arise apart from consciousness (*vijñāna*), one should not say that its essence is identical to consciousness.

For when consciousness arises, it likewise does not arise apart from contact, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and other mental factors (*caitasika*); thus, it too would have to be of the nature of mental factors and would only be designated "mind" by way of convention.
Since the mind is not so [independent], how could contact be otherwise?
Furthermore, because its meaning cannot be established apart from words, it is said that the name "contact" is merely a conventional designation based upon consciousness.
As for the claim that it is not separate [from consciousness], this is not proven.

If "not being separate from speech" means "having that as its cause," then consciousness is likewise not separate from mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*); thus, as previously stated, it should be merely a conventional designation for "mind.

If you claim that this objection is equally invalid—namely, that because consciousness is not separate from mental factors such as sensation, it must be identical to sensation and so forth, and thus merely a conventional designation for "mind"—[we reply: [this is not the case].
This too is unreasonable, because it is already established by consensus. For a sūtra states:
"The mind arises together with mental factors such as feeling; they are not separate from one another.
Furthermore, the meaning of a verse confirms this established consensus, stating that various mental factors arise in dependence upon both the eye and visible form.
Is it that only mental factors (*caitta*) are produced by the two conditions? No; how then could consciousness (*vijñāna*) also be produced?

Consciousness is itself the mind (*citta*). By this, it is established that the two conditions of the eye and visible form can produce all mental states and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), not merely the mind alone.

Although it has already been stated in general that all mental factors (*caitta*) arise from two conditions, it has not yet been specifically revealed which ones these are; therefore, "contact" (*sparśa*) is mentioned again.
Contact is the cause of sensation (*vedanā*), and for this reason, it is explained first.

Based on those two conditions, the mental factors (caitta) arise first, and only afterwards does consciousness (vijñāna) arise; otherwise, why would it further state that they are "simultaneous," which has the meaning of arising together?
Regarding the various mental factors—the word "various" being a plural term—one has already mentioned contact (sparśa); what are the others?

Therefore, it is said that they are subsumed under feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and the formations (*saṃskāra*). This demonstrates that feeling and the others necessarily arise simultaneously with the preceding consciousness and contact.
As for "subsumed under the formations," this refers to all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
If it were not so, one should have spoken only of "volition" (*cetanā*), rather than saying "all," because volition is a single entity.
For what purpose, then, is the phrase "having causes" (*sahetuka*) further stated?

It is to include those factors that coexist with the preceding [volition] and are inseparable from it; for these arise simultaneously with it and take it as their cause, rather than depending on the eye and visible forms, since this [volition] lacks a physical support (*āśraya*) and an objective referent (*ālambana*).
Some offer this explanation:
"This statement regarding 'having a cause' (sahetu) indicates that both mind and mental factors arise from conditions.
This explanation is incorrect, because it would render redundant what was previously stated—that [consciousness] is produced by the two conditions of the eye and visible form.
There is another alternative explanation:
the phrase "having a cause" (sahetu) reveals that the mind and mental factors have a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
What is a homogeneous cause?
This means that the preceding, homogeneous eye and visible forms are called "conditions" (pratyaya) because they are not of the same class as those [subsequent moments];
however, because the preceding, homogeneous [factors] are like seeds, they are called "causes" (hetu).
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"The eye gives rise to consciousness; because it is a proximate condition, it is also called a cause.
Since all mental factors (caitta-dharma) also arise with the eye-faculty as their condition, they are likewise said to possess a cause.
Since the former [verse] concerns conditions (*pratyaya*) and the latter concerns causes (*hetu*), there is no fault of redundancy.

Having thus correctly explained the meaning of the *gāthā*, it was previously stated that this objection is likewise unestablished; namely, that if consciousness were not separate from mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*), it would follow that consciousness is merely a provisional designation for sensation and the like.

That statement is irrational, because it is taught herein that the mind and mental factors arise simultaneously; this demonstrates that when consciousness arises, it is not separate from contact and the other factors.
Therefore, although it is true that contact does not actually exist apart from consciousness at the time of its arising, one should not say that contact has consciousness as its very essence.

Since consciousness, when arising, does not exist apart from contact, feeling, perception, and so forth, the mind itself must also have mental factors as its nature; it is merely designated by the conventional name "mind," and this principle is thoroughly established.

Regarding those words of theirs—namely, that contact can exist without being separate from consciousness because there is no sense of conjunction prior to consciousness, and that mental factors (caitta) are merely nominal designations without a distinct substance—this is nothing more than empty talk; it is entirely unreasonable.

Since those three proofs do not accord with reason, the previous statement—that the substance of contact (*sparśa*) truly exists because it is taught in the sūtras as a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*), just like feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*)—is thoroughly established. Therefore, one should believe and know that there exists a real contact distinct from the triad of sense faculty, object, and consciousness.
Furthermore, contact (sparśa) truly exists, because the Sūtra states that it is subsumed under the category of nutriment (āhāra), just like consciousness (vijñāna) and the others.
Regarding this, the Sthavira further asserts:
"Among the four nutriments, contact does not necessarily have the mere conjunction of the three [bases, objects, and consciousness] as its essence."

Why is this so? The nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) ought to have that which is touched as its substance; however, among the six objects, there is nothing corresponding to "that which is touched" such that it could serve as a basis for the arising of feeling (*vedanā*). Therefore, there is nothing else upon which it depends to produce feeling.
This means that contact is the most powerful among all causes for bodily sensations—such as those of superior cold, heat, or being sawn—and is therefore established separately as a nutriment.
By way of this door of contact, it is logically possible to become detached from all three types of sensation.
That statement arises merely from one's own conceptual construction; furthermore, since the conjunction of the three is certainly not contact (*spraṣṭavya*), how could it be nutriment?
Or perhaps it is something else?
What is the basis for this doubt such that you say "it is not necessarily so"? You should simply set aside your hesitation and judge with certainty that it is not.
If it were like edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), what further fault would there be?
That is to say, just as edible food is not established by a single factor, yet is designated as "one" despite being composed of many factors, so too is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*):
it is formed by the conjunction of the three. What fault is there in this?

This analogy is unreasonable, because each individual [sense organ] also possesses the nature of solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); it is not the case that the eye and so forth, taken individually and separately, can be called the substance of the contact-nourishment (*sparśa-āhāra*) formed by the triad.

Furthermore, since all phenomena are subsumed within the categories of sense-faculties, objects, and consciousness without exception, the three types of nutriment—such as edible food and the rest—should all be included within the category of contact (*sparśa*). Consequently, there would be only one type of nutriment; the Blessed One should not have taught in the sūtras that there are four kinds of nutriment.

If consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*) were subsumed within the faculties and consciousness, and if the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) and mental volition-food (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*) were not distinct from their objects, then having already explained the food of contact (*sparśāhāra*), the subsequent mention of the other three would render the Blessed One’s words purposeless.
Therefore, the wise should not accept the statement that the conjunction of the three is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).
Furthermore, it is also illogical to claim that the object of contact constitutes the essence of the nutriment of contact.
Within the context of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), it has already been stated that tangibles constitute its essence.
Furthermore, the logical principle that three types of sensation (*vedanā*) are abandoned at the time of abandoning that [edible food] would not be established.

This is because tangible objects are already included within edible food, as the nature of edible food is constituted by the combination of three bases; if the nutriment of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*) were identical to the nutriment of tangibles, there would then be only three [nutriments].

Furthermore, it is said that when the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) is attained, the three types of feeling (*vedanā*) are permanently severed; yet, it is at the time of attaining detachment from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) that all feelings are completely severed. It is not the case that the sense of permanent severance regarding feelings occurs at the time of attaining detachment from the objects of contact.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the sequence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the "feeling conditioned by contact" (*sparśapratyayā vedanā*) mentioned therein should be the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*); when that contact is severed, all feelings should be severed, rather than being severed because the objects of contact are severed.
Nowhere in the various holy teachings is it ever stated that the tangible serves as a condition for feeling; therefore, when feeling is severed, it is not due to the tangible.
Furthermore, the claim that the tangible can produce feeling without depending on anything else is deeply laughable.

Since it is granted that the tangible object perishes and enters the past at the moment it ceases, and that feeling only arises in the third moment, then at the time when feeling arises, the tangible object has already ceased and its substance is separated by a temporal interval; what generative function could it possibly have?

According to that doctrinal position, consciousness only arises when there is no interval between the sense faculty and its object; likewise, feeling only arises when there is no interval from consciousness.
When bodily feeling arises, the body and the tangible object have already ceased to exist, and since time has long since passed, how could they serve as its cause?

Furthermore, at the moment consciousness arises, bodily contact has already ceased; since it lacks even the causal function of being an object for the immediately succeeding consciousness, how much less could it possess such a function for the bodily sensation that arises at a later time, separated by an interval?

If it is argued that feeling arises only because the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness exists beforehand as cause and effect, and therefore the faculty and object also possess a reciprocal capacity to produce [feeling] at the very moment feeling arises;

In this way, there would be an excessive logical error: namely, that contact could only arise because name-and-form and the six sense bases must first exist as its causes and conditions; thus, one should say that "name-and-form is the condition for contact.
Alternatively, one should say that "the six sense bases are the condition for feeling," because they are functional at the time feeling arises.

Although those who propound the theory of the dependent origination of specific states admit that feeling arises with the six sense bases as its condition, they have never stated that the six sense bases are conditioned by feeling.
Even if it were granted that the contact [with the object] can produce feeling, how could one say that nothing further is required?
If those feelings were produced without depending on the sense faculties and consciousness, why would they not also arise within wood, stone, and the like?
If those feelings must depend on conditions such as the sense faculties and consciousness to arise, then it is the same for other objects; why, then, are they not so described?

Since among the six objects there is nothing like the tangible that can produce feeling independently of anything else, what distinction is there between this and the other objects such that it alone is praised as the cause for the arising of feeling?

Since it is certain that there is never a moment when the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness are in conjunction and yet feeling does not arise, what they have asserted lacks any rational basis and arises solely from the conceptual constructions of their own minds.

Furthermore, how could that venerable one say that one becomes weary of an inferior realm and thereby becomes detached from the defilements of a sublime realm, yet cannot become weary of others and thereby become detached from other defilements?
Otherwise, it would follow that detachment from one set of defilements results in liberation from others; for no distinct cause for such a distinction can be found.
Precisely for this reason, the dharma-knowledge of suffering and its origin cannot simultaneously abandon the craving for the form and formless realms.

Since superior contacts such as cold, heat, and being sawn apart do not exist in the higher realms, it is known that the mind takes the contacts belonging to the desire realm as the nature of the nutriment of contact.
Therefore, the claim that one can become detached from all three types of feeling through the gateway of contact cannot be established logically.

Furthermore, a sūtra states that when the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) is severed, the three feelings are permanently severed; thus, we know that the Buddha taught that contact and the three feelings are severed simultaneously and forever.

Since the sūtra does not state that the three feelings are to be severed *after* the nutriment of contact has been severed, one should not say that one will be able to become detached from all three feelings by severing contact alone, for it is said that when contact is severed, the feelings are also severed.

It is not the case that when one attains detachment from the desire realm, one simultaneously attains detachment from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); therefore, we know there is a distinct dharma called contact (*sparśa*), which is the proximate cause of feeling (*vedanā*). When the Peak of Existence is severed, this contact is then severed; because of its severance, the three types of feeling are permanently severed, after which there is nothing further to be done.
Therefore, it is established by reason that among the mental factors (caitta), there must certainly exist a real contact (sparśa) called the nutriment of contact (sparśāhāra).
To prove that the essence of this contact is substantially existent, the masters of antiquity have also set forth many reasons.
The Elder harbors overweening pride therein, claiming that he himself can explain such causes.
I shall now offer praise and censure regarding his virtues and faults.
What are the causes established by the ancient masters?
That is to say, they all claim:

"Contact (sparśa) must truly exist, because there are distinct statements regarding the existence of cause and effect, defilement and purification, and their respective severance; it is just like feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and so forth."

Regarding the statement here that cause and effect exist, it means that this contact is said to have the six sense bases as its cause and sensation as its effect; it does not mean that conventional phenomena can be said to possess ultimate (paramārtha) cause and effect.
Regarding the statements concerning defilement and the departure from defilement, the Buddha spoke these words in the *Mahāṣaḍāyatanika-sūtra*:
"If one does not see the eye as it truly is and does not know it as it truly is, then various defilements arise within the eye."
Thus, if one gives rise to various defilements regarding form, eye-consciousness, and eye-contact—and so on, in detail, up to mind-contact—one becomes defiled.
Conversely, by being the opposite of this, one attains freedom from defilement.
It is not that defilement or purification can be predicated of conventional phenomena.
As for the statement regarding their distinctness, it refers to what the Buddha said in the *Ṣaṭṣaṭka-sūtra*:
"There are six internal bases, six external bases, six groups of consciousness, six groups of contact, six groups of feeling, and six groups of craving, each being distinct."

In this sūtra, contact (*sparśa*) is taught as existing separately from the sense-faculties (*indriya*), the objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); it cannot be said that it is merely a designation (*prajñapti*) or that it is explained as being distinct from its respective bases.
Regarding the statement that there is "severance," it refers to what the sūtra says:
"When the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) is severed, the three types of feeling (*vedanā*) are forever severed."
It is not by seeing conventional phenomena that one is said to have "seeing according to reality," nor is it because the Noble Path abides in its object of focus.

As for the statement regarding "distinctive speech," this refers to the fact that even within the entities that serve as the basis for conventional designations (*prajñapti-dharma*), there are individual distinct verbal expressions, such as saying, "I see a jar, a garment, color, and so forth.
This case should be understood in the same way; thus, one should speak of eighteen types of contact (*spraṣṭavya-kāya*).
However, since this is not the case, we know that the essence of contact (*sparśa*) is not identical to the threefold conjunction (*trikasamnipāta*).
The statement by the Venerable Sthavira that "the name 'contact' refers to the threefold conjunction" is likewise not contradictory to this principle.
Why is this so? Because names, forms, and so forth also possess the meaning described above.
Within the contact resulting from the conjunction of causes and conditions such as the eye and its objects, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the aforementioned principles.

Regarding the statement that there is cause and effect as previously explained: it refers to the contact resulting from the conjunction of causes and effects such as the eye and so forth. Here, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are the cause and feeling (*vedanā*) is the result; for apart from the internal six sense bases, the triadic harmony does not exist, and because pleasure, pain, and so forth arise from this triadic harmony.

Regarding the statement that there is defilement (*saṃkleśa*), the term "defilement" refers to the fact that the contact of the three [faculties, objects, and consciousness] serves as the cause for sensation (*vedanā*); through the application of seeking, various defilements arise, and at that time, one wishes for the arising of one's own consciousness.

To distinguish the specific modes of experience within this gateway, the supporting faculties and the objects apprehended are presented; by seeing and knowing these things as they truly are, one attains freedom from defilement.

The statement that they are distinct means that one analyzes how the combined nature of causes and conditions—such as the eye and so forth—serves as the origin of sensation (*vedanā*), from which craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises; it does not mean that all eyes and forms are causes of visual consciousness, nor that all visual consciousnesses are effects of eyes and forms.

Furthermore, it is like the burden and the bearer of the burden: although there is no bearer apart from the burden of the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), they are nonetheless explained separately in the sūtras.
This case should be understood in the same way.
The statement that there is "cutting off" refers to the cutting off of afflictions (*saṃkleśa*).

Previously, it was stated that the pursuit of skillful means gives rise to various afflictions; now, it is stated that the cutting off of those afflictions is precisely what is called "contact of cutting off."

Because it is designated based on its observed objects, it is called "seeing as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-darśana*) and is said to be the objective support (*ālambana*) for the abiding of the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).

Regarding the statement that there is a distinction: this refers to the fact that contact (*sparśa*) is the conjunction of the three [faculties, object, and consciousness], and not a single unified entity; thus, unlike a jar or similar things, it cannot be described as having multiple parts (*aneka-avayava*) within a single whole, such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

There is also the meaning expressed by this statement: namely, that just as the factors such as name-and-form and the six sense bases are not established by a single dharma, and although they do not exist substantially, they nonetheless possess the various meanings described above.
This case should also be understood in the same way; therefore, there is no fault. Thus, in all such instances, the reasoning is untenable.

Furthermore, their claim that the conjunction of causes and conditions—such as the eye and so forth—is designated as "contact" has already been refuted. As was previously stated, within their own system, it cannot be established that simultaneous arising entities can function as mutual cause and effect, and so on.
Such a position will be further refuted later.
Moreover, what is the purpose of the causal conjunction of the eye, visible forms, and so forth, with respect to sensation?
It has already been argued that it is not merely the conjunction of cause and effect that can produce something.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that the eye and visible forms act as causes to produce results such as sensation (*vedanā*).

If this is so, then these causes and effects should either jointly produce consciousness (*vijñāna*) and serve as conditions for contact (*sparśa*), or else a distinction should be made within this context.
If it is argued that such a statement does not exist—namely, that while the Blessed One said, "With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises;

the meeting of these three is contact"—but nowhere did he say that with the eye and visible forms as causes, results such as feeling arise, and thus one might claim that consciousness and contact are produced by the conjunction of cause and effect in this way, and therefore such a statement should not be made—this too is irrational, because there is indeed a passage where it is stated. For this very sutra speaks of their arising together with feeling and so forth; the term "arising together" (sahaja) signifies that they originate simultaneously with consciousness and the rest, which shall be established later.

However, regarding that sūtra’s statement that visual consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions: because consciousness is the basis for sensation and the other [mental factors], and its functional activity is predominant, the Blessed One—fearing that there might be attachment to the idea that the conditions of the eye and visible forms produce only visual consciousness—therefore stated in this sūtra that the eye and visible forms act as causes to produce effects such as sensation.

Furthermore, a verse from the Gāthās states that the two conditions of the eye and visible forms give rise to various mental factors (*caitta*); this serves as sufficient clear evidence that the conditions of the eye and forms do not merely produce consciousness (*vijñāna*).

To maintain that contact (*sparśa*) arises and produces feeling (*vedanā*) solely because the causes and effects—such as the eye and so forth—conjoin is logically untenable, for a provisional phenomenon (*prajñapti-dharma*) lacks causal efficacy and is indeterminate.

The claim that the contact resulting from the conjunction of causes and conditions—such as the eye and so forth—has the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as its cause, and that there is no "triple concurrence" (*trikasamnipāta*) apart from these internal six bases, is also logically untenable.

Is it not the case that the triple concurrence would likewise not exist if either the object or consciousness were absent? Furthermore, it is not the case that all provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) are formed by the combination of three things; rather, a provisional phenomenon can still exist even if one of its constituent elements is missing from among its supports, just like the letter *ī*.

Regarding the statement that contact (*sparśa*) is a real mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*): although it arises in dependence upon the sense faculties, objects, and consciousness, the internal six bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) possess the most predominant power of production; because they are the superior causes of production and its support, they are mentioned specifically.
It is precisely by virtue of such a distinguished basis that the designation "six contacts"—namely, eye-contact and so forth—is applied.
Since a provisional phenomenon lacks functional efficacy, how could it produce the fruit of sensation?

To say that contact (*sparśa*)—arising from the conjunction of the three—is the cause of feeling (*vedanā*), and then to further claim that the pursuit of means gives rise to affliction (*saṃkleśa*), is redundant, as this has already been explained separately.
That is to say, it was previously stated that various afflictions arise within the eye, the form, and the visual consciousness; apart from these three factors, what other "contact" could there be?

Thereafter, the term "eye-contact" is stated again. If it is claimed that this repetition refers to the nature of the causal conjunction of the three factors—the eye and so forth—then one should not have spoken merely of "eye-contact," for visual consciousness and visible form do not depend solely upon that [conjunction].

Since the triad of eye, form, and visual consciousness are equally without distinction in their nature as the basis for contact, what is the reason for speaking only of "eye-contact" and not of "form-contact" or "visual-consciousness-contact"?

Furthermore, according to your own tenet, the eye-consciousness arises from the eye and visible form, and only subsequently does sensation arise; thus, the eye-consciousness serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for sensation. Since the proximate basis (*āśraya*) is neither the eye nor the visible form, it should properly be called "contact of consciousness" (*vijñāna-sparśa*). Why, then, do you conversely call it "eye-contact" (*cakṣuḥ-sparśa*)?

If it is argued that existence and non-existence follow a fixed relationship—namely, that where those six bases such as the eye exist, there exists contact such as visual contact, and where they do not exist, contact does not exist, just as those born blind lack visual contact and so forth.
As this sūtra states:
"The six sense bases are the condition for contact.
This is because contact is said to exist when there is the conjunction of a faculty, a form, and consciousness; it does not exist in the absence of a faculty.

This is also not the case; for although one may possess the six bases such as the eye and so forth, there are times when the various consciousnesses do not arise, and thus contact does not exist—as in the states of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) or the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). In those states, there is no mind, as will be established later.

Therefore, if it were determined that [mental factors] necessarily follow the presence or absence of their bases, then the name "contact" (*sparśa*) should apply solely to consciousness (*vijñāna*) based on that principle.
Furthermore, regarding the term "mental factor" (*caitta*), one should reflect upon this:

if contact were strictly dependent on the presence or absence of the sense faculties (*indriya*), it would have to be called a "faculty-factor" (*indriya-caitta*) rather than a "mental-factor" (*citta-caitta*).

Furthermore, regarding those born blind and others who abide in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*) within the state of possessing mind: since they already possess the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), what else could be lacking? Why do bodily contact (*kāyaspraṣṭavya*) and bodily consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) not arise?

It is not that bodily contact does not exist because bodily consciousness does not arise; rather, one observes that while the body-faculty exists, bodily contact is absent. One should know that such contact follows the presence or absence of consciousness. Contact is produced by consciousness, not by the faculty or the object, because consciousness is the dominant cause; therefore, it should be explained in accordance with consciousness.

However, since various sūtras speak of "eye-contact" and so forth, we know that there exists a distinct entity of contact which is a mental factor (caitta); it is designated according to its basis, such as the eye and so forth, just as the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth are named according to their bases.

This principle is fully established; therefore, one should not say that the nature of the six contacts, such as eye-contact and so forth, is the conjunction of their respective causes and effects, such as the eye and so forth.

If you argue that—just as there is a distinct "contact" which, though arising in dependence upon consciousness, is called "eye-contact"—so too it is with the self, this reasoning is incorrect. This is because the name "contact" is applied based on its predominant cause or its basis, or because intermediate terms have been elided, or because it refers to the support, namely the eye.

Furthermore, a sūtra states that "defilements arise with respect to the eye, with respect to forms, and within eye-consciousness. By this, it has already been explained that the triad of eye, form, and consciousness possesses a nature of causal conjunction, because they are taught in sequence according to their respective characteristics of mutual dependence.
If it were otherwise, one should have taught the six faculties, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses in their respective order.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of this statement in the Sūtra: "That which gives rise to defilement within eye-contact"?

If it is claimed that these words reveal the meaning of the arising of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) from the nature of the conjunction of cause and effect in the eye and so forth, this interpretation is irrational; for by the sequential mention of the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness, that [meaning] has already been revealed.

Alternatively, since the sūtras state that various defilements arise within visual consciousness, this already establishes that the triad of eye, form, and consciousness possesses a nature of causal conjunction; for there is no consciousness without a faculty and an object, and thus when defilement arises in consciousness, it occurs precisely through the conjunction of these three.
Is it not true that we previously stated that not all visual consciousnesses are the results of the eye and visible forms?
Although such words were spoken before, they lack actual meaning; therefore, this does not constitute a valid defense.
That [consciousness] which lacks the eye as its basis is not the result of the eye and visible forms, because [the opponent] maintains that only present phenomena exist.
Alternatively, one must explain what that consciousness is.

If it were the case that at certain times consciousness does not exist as a result because the eye and visible forms are absent, then the nature of cause and effect would ultimately be non-existent, for you maintain that they do not coexist.

Since all visual consciousnesses are the results of both the eye and visible forms, the statement regarding the arising of defilement within visual consciousness already establishes that the triad of eye, form, and consciousness possesses a nature of combined cause and effect; why then is it necessary to state this again?

This is because you have failed to properly evaluate the characteristics of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and instead have arbitrarily interpreted the meaning of the Buddha’s sūtras according to your own personal sentiments, resulting in this confusion. Therefore, you should apply yourselves even more diligently to seeking an unerring understanding of the characteristics of the nature of phenomena.

Regarding the statement that at that time one wishes for the arising of one's own consciousness, in order to distinguish the specific modes of apprehension within this gateway, the supporting faculty and the apprehended object are cited. While it may be acceptable for it to be the consciousness, the faculty and the object must be considered:
how do these two cause the differentiation of sensation?
As previously argued, when that sensation arises, the substance of the sense organ and its object has already ceased, as they lack the functional capacity for arising.
Since defilement thus entails these faults, the state of being free from defilement is likewise untenable.
