Having thus explained the characteristics of acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*),
what is the "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*)?
The verse says:
"Equal portions among sentient beings.
The treatise says:

There is a distinct, real entity called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*), which refers to the mutual similarity among various sentient beings; the fundamental treatise calls this the "generic similarity" (*nikāyasabhāga*).

The mutual causes for the similarity in physical form, sensory faculties, functional activities, food and drink, and so forth among all classes of sentient beings born into a single realm, as well as the causes for their reciprocal desires and inclinations, are termed the "homogeneity of the group" (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Just as the karma, mind, and primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of a fresh and pure color are all its causes, so it is with the body and its form.

It is not merely due to karma that the physical form manifests; rather, it is a fruit induced by a corresponding karma, because there are differences in the functions of the sense faculties (*indriya*), as well as in food, drink, and so forth.

If it is argued that this distinction arises because there are distinctions among the completing karmas (*pūrṇakarma*), such reasoning is untenable. For there may be bodily forms that arise solely from similar projecting karmas (*ākṣepaka-karma*), yet they differ in their karmic functions and so forth due to distinctions within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
If the physical body and so forth were solely the fruit of karma, then activities such as abandoning or engaging in whatever actions one desires would be impossible.
In this context, "similarity" refers to the mutual correspondence between the physical body, its karmic functions, and one's inclinations.
"Part" (*bhāga*) has the meaning of "cause. Because there is a distinct, substantial entity that serves as the common cause for these [beings], it is called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*).
Such homogeneity, the Blessed One taught, applies only to sentient beings and not to things such as grass or trees.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"This is the generic similarity (*nikāyasabhāga*) of these devas; this is the generic similarity of these humans," and so forth, as explained at length.
Depending on the distinctions of realms, destinies, births, locations, bodies, and so on, there are immeasurable varieties of sentient beings' generic similarities.

Furthermore, there is the dharma of homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*): namely, the homogeneous character of the aggregates, bases, and elements is relinquished when an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) enters the state of non-ordinary birth; the homogeneous character of sentient beings is relinquished when one enters *nirvāṇa*.
Is it not the case that the nature of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) is itself the commonality of worldlings (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*)? This cannot be so, because their functions differ.
That is to say, the cause for the mutual similarity of their physical forms, activities, and inclinations is termed "commonality" (*sabhāgatā*).
If it is contrary to the attainment of the noble path and serves as the cause for being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is called "the state of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*).

At the moment of entering the state free from birth (*niyāma*), one both relinquishes and acquires the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*); regarding the state of being an ordinary person, one relinquishes it and does not acquire it again.
How is it known that the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is non-material?
It is because there exists a functional capacity to produce a category of things that is not distinct [from itself]; by seeing its fruit, one knows that it exists.
This is like seeing the fruit obtained from present karma and thereby knowing that there was karma performed in a previous life.
Furthermore, because practitioners of meditation realize this through direct perception,
why not accept the existence of a "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) for insentient things?
One should not raise such an objection, for it would entail a great fault.

You also admit that there are destinies such as those of humans and devas, and modes of birth such as the womb and the egg; why then do you not also admit that mangoes and the like have destinies and modes of birth such as mung beans and the like?
Furthermore, because the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, never stated such a thing.
One should merely investigate why the Blessed One spoke of "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) only with respect to sentient beings and not with respect to grass and the like.
Furthermore, how is it known that such homogeneity exists as a real entity?

Furthermore, I understand it in this way: because those grasses and so forth lack mutual functional activity or desire that is similar to one another, it is not said that there exists a distinct *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) among them.
Furthermore, because grass and other such things arise only by depending upon sentient beings, the term "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) is applied exclusively to sentient beings.
Moreover, this phenomenon arises due to both prior karma and present effort; since these two conditions are entirely absent in the case of grass and similar entities, they lack homogeneity.
Precisely by virtue of this fact, it is proven that there exists a substantial entity (*dravya*).

Furthermore, although images made of wood, plaster, lacquer, carving, or painting, and their actual physical forms, possess color and shape that are mutually similar, they are nonetheless said to be one and the same reality.

Therefore, it is not the case that one merely perceives a resemblance and immediately declares it to be real; rather, it is only with respect to distinct categories of similar things that the term "real" arises. Thus, we know that these distinct dharmas truly exist.
This is a true statement, for it arises from this dharma.
Furthermore, because it was previously stated.
How was it previously stated?

That is to say, one perceives that the physical form is a fruit induced by karma that is mutually similar, because there are differences in the functions of the sense faculties, as well as in food, drink, and so forth.
Since these various *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous groups) differ from one another, how could there arise a cognition and designation of non-difference regarding them without a further *sabhāga*?

Because the various *sabhāga* (homogeneous) factors serve as the cause for things of the same class and so forth, they function as the cause for the mutual application of similar cognitions and designations among those of the same class.

For example, although the eyes, ears, and so forth are established as having the nature of matter (*rūpa*) only by being derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), the nature of matter is established even though the primary elements themselves are not derived from other primary elements.
This should clarify and establish the categories of "universal" (sāmānya) and "particularity" (viśeṣa) as maintained by the Vaiśeṣikas.
If the Vaiśeṣikas maintain these two categories, their essence would not be unitary, they would be momentarily impermanent, and they would lack any basis for their successive differentiation.
Even if it were the same as that [position], there would still be no great fault.

We do not require the followers of the Buddha (Śākyaputrīya) to abandon their view—that the sense faculties such as the eye can travel toward objects such as form—and instead adopt some other interpretation.
Therefore, that which he has objected is merely partisan speech; those seeking correct reasoning should not accept it.
Having already explained *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity), what is *asaṃjñin* (the state of non-perception)?
The verse says:
In the state of non-conception, within non-conception, the mind and mental factors cease;
it is a karmic maturation and its inhabitants dwell in the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) heaven.
The treatise says:

If one is born among the sentient beings of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), there is a dharma that can cause the cessation of the mind and mental factors; this is called "non-conception" (*asaṃjñi*).
It is a real entity that can obstruct future mind and mental factors so that they do not arise for a time, just as a dam blocks a river.

This dharma is exclusively the maturation (vipāka) induced by the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti); for within that heaven of non-conceptualizing beings (asaṃjñisattva), both the state of non-conception and the form (rūpa) are solely the maturation induced by that attainment of non-conception.

This meditative absorption lacks the power to project the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because both the homogeneous character and the life-faculty are results produced solely by the fourth dhyāna accompanied by mind (*sacittaka*).

The remaining aggregates in that state are a shared maturation (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*), because within the realm of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva-deva*), there is mental activity for a long duration both prior to entering the state of non-perception and after emerging from it.
However, because the state of being without mind lasts for an extremely long duration, it is collectively termed the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva).
Where do these sentient beings of no-thought reside? They reside in the Heaven of Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala).
This refers to a lofty and superior abode within the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala), similar to the intermediate dhyāna, which is called the Heaven of Non-conception (Asaṃjñisattva).

They take their past karma as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for sustenance; that is, by means of past karma, they are drawn toward a commonality of type (*nikāyasabhāga*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and so forth. Furthermore, because they are drawn and assisted by the mind at the moment of rebirth (*pratisandhicitta*) and the mind that immediately enters the fruit of non-conception, they likewise possess past contact (*sparśa*) and other factors as their sustaining nutriment.
In the state of mindlessness, there is only past contact and so forth as nutriment, while none exist at all in the present.
In the state of mindfulness, both types are present, because those sentient beings arise from perception.

Having passed away from that place, they will certainly be reborn in the desire realm and nowhere else; for the power of the lifespan induced by their prior cultivation of meditative practice has been exhausted, and they are unable to cultivate further meditation there—just as an arrow shot into the air falls once its momentum is spent.
If sentient beings are to be born in those places, they must necessarily possess karma of the desire realm to be experienced in subsequent lives;
just as those who are to be born in Uttarakuru must necessarily possess karma for rebirth in the heavens.
The attainment of non-conception has already been explained.
What are the two meditative attainments?
They are the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation.
First, regarding the nature of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*):
The verse says:
"Thus, the attainment of non-conception / Is sought by those in the final dhyāna / As a means of liberation."
Wholesome, it is experienced only in the next life; non-noble ones attain it for one lifetime.
The commentary says:
As previously stated, there is a phenomenon that can cause the cessation of the mind and mental factors, which is termed "non-conception" (*asaṃjñika*).
Furthermore, there is another distinct dharma that can cause the cessation of the mind and mental factors; this is called the "attainment of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

The use of the term "attainment" (*samāpatti*) indicates that this state is identical to the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*) in its cessation of the mind and mental factors; it is called an "attainment" because it is correctly accomplished or thoroughly accomplished.
Other masters say:
It is called "concentration" (*samādhi*) because it causes the mental factors to proceed in accordance with reality, and because it causes the primary elements of the mind to proceed in equilibrium.

As for the "non-conceptual state," it is either concentration that is non-conceptual, or the absence of conception within concentration; thus it is named the "attainment of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), because this attainment arises through the repudiation of conception.
Ordinary worldlings are unable to weary of or destroy sensation, because they enter meditative absorption through attachment to sensation.
In which stage does this concentration reside?
It resides in the final dhyāna; that is, it is in the fourth dhyāna and not elsewhere.
This should not be said.
Why? Because this concentration can certainly bring about the maturation (vipāka) of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñika).

It has already been stated that the realm of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva) resides within the Heaven of Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala). Now it must be explained that the Heaven of Vast Fruit exists within the final dhyāna; however, could one cultivate its cause in other stages?

This objection is not valid, for it has never been so stated; nowhere has it been said that the state of non-conceptual absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is the cause of the realm of non-conceptualization.

Is it not the case that the previous verse stated that non-conception (*asaṃjñin*) is a maturation (*vipāka*), and in its commentary it was explained as the fruit of the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)?
This is not so; such a statement was never made in the verse, and it is only now being asserted.
Why is this meditative absorption called the "absorption of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana-samādhi*)?
It is because they cultivate this absorption seeking liberation.

They cling to non-perception (*asaṃjñi*) as true liberation and hold the absorption of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) to be the path of transcendence; thus, they cultivate this absorption in order to realize non-perception.

Since no noble being (ārya) clings to that which is with outflows (sāsrava) as true liberation or true transcendence, this meditative absorption is called the "absorption of ordinary beings" (pṛthagjana-samādhi).

Because it was previously stated that the state of non-conception (asaṃjñin) is a result of maturation (vipāka), its inclusion within the category of the indeterminate (avyākṛta) is established without needing to be explicitly stated.

Now, since the attainment of non-conception is invariably wholesome, would it not be self-evident that it is subsumed under the nature of wholesomeness because it is a cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*), and thus need not be explicitly stated?
Does this [attainment] act as a cause within the realm of the non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) to summon the maturation of the five aggregates?
Not so; for it has not yet been stated in the verse.
Furthermore, who could possibly exclude the defiled-neutral?
If that were the case, one should have said "purely wholesome" here.

It is not so; for there exists the realization of the meaning apart from words. This should be explained according to the previous discussion on the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Alternatively, by simply saying "wholesome" (*kuśala*), it is already indicated that it is nothing else.
Since this certainty is of the nature of a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), to what kind of feeling (*vedanā*) does it correspond?

It is experienced only in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), and not experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), or as indeterminate (*aniyata-vedanīya*).
A certain class of masters maintains this fixed position, but according to reason, it should be experienced both in the next life and indeterminately.

Why is this so? One who has accomplished this meditative absorption may also enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*); once having entered that state, this absorption will certainly never manifest again.

It is with reference to its actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) that the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is called the "absorption of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana-samāpatti*), not with reference to its possession (*prāpti*).

Furthermore, it is admitted that this meditative absorption is accessible to those outside of this Dharma and to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), but not to noble ones (*ārya*); for all noble ones, regarding the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), do not delight in entering it, viewing it as if it were a deep pit.

Since the verse already mentions the term "seeking liberation," it clearly indicates that this meditative absorption belongs exclusively to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); furthermore, to state again that it does not belong to noble ones (*ārya*) would be redundant.
When this [absorption] is first attained, how many time periods (*adhvan*) are acquired?
In these various stages, just as with the prātimokṣa vows, it is acquired anew in each moment because it has not been previously attained.
At the time of the first moment, one does not acquire the past [vows], because there is no mind [at that point]; nor does one cultivate the future [vows].
Therefore, when first acquired, it is acquired as belonging to only one time-period, namely the present.
From the second moment onwards until one has emerged [from the attainment], it also becomes past; once one has emerged, until it is relinquished, it exists only as past.
Just as with the divine eye and ear, there is no cultivation of them in the future; they are acquired solely through application (*prayoga*), not through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).
Next, what are the characteristics of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?
The verse says:
The attainment of cessation is likewise; it is for the sake of peaceful dwelling and belongs to the Peak of Existence.
It is wholesome, associated with two types of feeling, and is indeterminate. It is attained by noble ones through application.
One does not attain Buddhahood prior [to this], because it occurs within thirty-four moments of thought.
The Commentary says:
As was the case with the previously mentioned attainment of non-perception, so it is with the attainment of cessation.

That is to say, just as for one who has already become detached from the craving of the third dhyāna, there is a state that can cause the cessation of the mind and mental factors, which is called the attainment of non-conception;

likewise, for one who has already become detached from the craving of the sphere of nothingness, there is a state that can cause the cessation of the mind and mental factors, which is called the attainment of cessation.

Regarding the distinguishing characteristics of these two meditative attainments: the former, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), is entered upon by first applying the mental attention to the perception of renunciation, as one seeks liberation through the repudiation of perception.

Now, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is entered upon by first applying the mental attention of the perception of stillness, out of a desire for tranquil abiding and a distaste for agitation.

Whereas the aforementioned attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) belongs to the borderland of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), this attainment of cessation belongs to the borderland of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because the body born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is drawn forth by the most supreme karma, it is called the "Summit of Existence" (*bhavāgra*).
Alternatively, it is called the "Summit of Existence" because it is the ultimate limit; just as the very end of a tree is called the "top" of the tree.
Only in this stage (the fourth dhyāna) is there the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
For what reason is this attainment absent in the lower stages?
Because one can only attain this supreme liberation by becoming weary of all states of mind and by severing the final state of consciousness.
This liberation is established by way of two conditions:
first, because of the aversion toward all mental states; and second, because of the temporary cessation of the final mental state.

If this meditative absorption were present in a lower stage, it would not constitute an aversion toward all types of mind, as one would still be unable to feel aversion toward the minds of the higher stages.

Nor can it be called the "severance of the mind at the limit," because the minds of the higher stages have not yet been severed; rather, it should be called the "aversion to a portion of all minds," and it should also be called the "severance of the mind at the middle."

Among the three natures, this attainment of cessation, as previously stated, is exclusively wholesome; it is neither defiled nor neutral. This is because the noble ones do not take up a defiled or neutral state as a peaceful abode out of their aversion to and fear of mental distraction.

The previously mentioned attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) conduces to feeling experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*) or at an indefinite time (*aniyata-vedanīya*); the present attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), however, conduces to feeling experienced in the next life, in subsequent lives, or at an indefinite time.

That is to say, with respect to its maturation (*vipāka*), it may be conducive to feeling experienced in the next life, or conducive to feeling experienced in subsequent lives, or at an indefinite time, or it may not be experienced at all.
This means that if one has arisen in this meditative attainment from a lower stage and does not give rise to a higher stage, one then enters parinirvāṇa.

This attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) can bring about the maturation of the four aggregates of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra); the aforementioned attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñisamāpatti), however, is attained only by ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).

This attainment of cessation is attained only by noble ones (*ārya*); ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are unable to give rise to the attainment of cessation because they have not yet abandoned the obstacles to arising in the attainment of cessation that pertain to their own level.

As long as one has not transcended the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) pertaining to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one is absolutely incapable of arising in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); since no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) can transcend these afflictions of the Peak of Existence, only noble ones (*ārya*) attain the meditative attainment of cessation.
Other masters say:

Because ordinary beings fear annihilation, and because noble ones enter into this through their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in the nirvāṇa of the present life, only noble ones attain it, not ordinary beings.

That explanation is unreasonable, for it applies equally to the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); in both cases, the mind is interrupted, and there is no difference in the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) toward nirvāṇa.
Regarding this, some say:
"In the fourth dhyāna, the mind and mental factors are coarse, yet because they still possess a basis (*āśraya*), one does not fear their interruption."

That too is unreasonable; for one cultivates the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) in order to extinguish the mind, and cultivates it with the perception of renunciation in pursuit of liberation. To fear the extinction of the mind is contrary to correct principle.

Since one cultivates the attainment of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) with the thought of renunciation, one should likewise enter it through the resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) of nirvāṇa; therefore, that [previous] explanation is not a valid reason.
Do all noble ones (ārya) who attain the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) necessarily attain such an attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti)?

One should say that it is not obtained [by detachment]. This is because this concentration is certainly not obtained through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*). By what, then, is it obtained?
It is obtained through application (*prayoga*), for it must be realized through application.
Just as when the attainment of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is first realized, one attains only the present and not the past;
nor does one cultivate the future, because cultivation can only occur through the power of the mind.
The second moment and those following, until it is relinquished, also constitute the past.
Does the World-Honored One also attain [this] through preparatory effort (*prayoga*)? No.
How so? It is attained at the time of attaining Buddhahood.

That is to say, it is attained by the World-Honored One at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). Would it not then be the case that even the knowledge of exhaustion is not called "attained" at the time of attaining Buddhoadhood, let alone the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?

When Bodhisattvas abide in the vajra-like samādhi, they are said to have attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), because that which constitutes its essence is attained at the moment it arises.

At the time of attaining Buddhahood, it should be stated that the knowledge of exhaustion manifests without the need for preparatory effort (*prayoga*), because when a mere aspiration momentarily arises, all perfect qualities manifest in accordance with that aspiration.

The merits inherent within the Buddha’s body are not obtained at the moment of attaining Buddhahood; how, then, could it be said that the Buddha attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) at the time of his attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?

Because the Bodhisattva had already permanently abandoned all defilements of the afflictions (*kleśa*), the merits within the Buddha’s body were able to arise; therefore, it is said that all the merits possessed by the Tathāgata are obtained through the removal of defilement (*vairāgyalābhika*).
Therefore, what they have said also contains errors.
To provide an appropriate explanation for them: it is a case of using a distant term to refer to something proximate;

or, because one will certainly attain Buddhahood at the time of the Vajra-like Samādhi, it is also called "attaining Buddhahood," as one is certain to achieve Buddhahood in the immediately succeeding moment.
Setting aside this matter for a moment:
how could the World-Honored One have attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) at the time he had not yet arisen from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?

Because he was supremely perfected and liberated through both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), because he had permanently abandoned the hindrance of concentration (*samāpattyāvaraṇa*), because he had relinquished non-attainment, and because he possessed mastery over the arising of the attainment of cessation, he was established as one liberated in both ways, just like those who had already arisen from it.
The masters of the West (Paścātya) say:
"During the stage of training (śaikṣa), a bodhisattva first gives rise to this meditative absorption and subsequently attains bodhi.
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr say:
It is not the case that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises only after one has previously entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
For what reason is it known that this [Eastern] country had not previously produced it?
Why, then, is the origin [of such a claim] in the Western [country] not questioned?
Furthermore, we of Kaśmīra maintain that enlightenment is attained in thirty-four moments of thought (*citta-kṣaṇa*).

This is because it is certain that Bodhisattvas first become free from attachment to the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) before entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); they no longer need to abandon the afflictions of the lower stages, and thus attain Great Enlightenment in thirty-four moments.
Within the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya), there are sixteen moments of mindfulness;

when one is free from craving for the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), there are eighteen moments of mindfulness—namely, nine paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and nine paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) for the abandonment of the nine grades of afflictions of the Peak of Existence.
Thus, these eighteen, added to the previous sixteen, total thirty-four.
Since there is no room for a dissimilar state of mind to arise during this interval, it is certain that the attainment of cessation cannot arise at the preceding stage.

If one were to arise in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) during the preceding stage, one would indeed transgress the resolve regarding the time limit; however, because Bodhisattvas are determined never to transgress their essential resolve, it is in fact the case that Bodhisattvas do not transgress their resolve.
Nevertheless, this does not mean they do not transgress the untainted noble path (*anāsravamārga*).
If that is so, how is it that his resolute intention (*cittābhiprāya*) is not transgressed?
It is because he has made this firm resolve: "Until I have attained the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*), I shall never break this cross-legged posture.
He certainly does not transgress such a resolute intention, for he brings all matters to completion during that single sitting alone.
Is it not because he has already transgressed the intention to give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) noble path?

How could a Bodhisattva, for the sake of exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*), cultivate the two paths of seeing and meditation never before attained, and—desiring to uproot the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) to be abandoned by insight and to eliminate the enemy of the afflictions of the Peak of Existence to be abandoned by cultivation—make a solemn vow and sit in the full lotus posture?

Before the task is yet complete, one abandons within that state the essential, expected path of untainted treatment (*anāsrava-pratipakṣa-mārga*), which is precious from time immemorial and capable of deceiving the world; instead, for the sake of attaining a common and easily obtained meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one causes delay.
Thus, because awakening is perfectly attained through thirty-four moments of thought, it does not have preceding [moments] as its cause; as stated in the Sūtra:

"When emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation, one shall experience three contacts, namely: the contact of the imperturbable, the contact of nothingness, and the contact of the signless."
What are these three contacts, and how are they contacted?

Some say that there are the three contacts of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*) associated with the mind arising from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); one contacts these three contacts respectively at the time of emerging from the attainment of cessation.
Other masters say:

The contact associated with the mind in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is called "unmoving contact" (*āniñjya-sparśa*), because these two exclusively cultivate the perception of consciousness and space.
The contact associated with the mind in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is called "contact of nothingness" (*ākiṃcanya-sparśa*), because there is no longer anything previously existing.

Contact associated with the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called "signless contact" (*animitta-sparśa*), because the characteristics of perception and non-perception are not distinct.
For this very reason, the four formless attainments are described as "attainments of conceptualization" (*saṃjñā-samāpatti*).
The mind arising from the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) may be either contaminated (sāsrava) or uncontaminated (anāsrava).

At the time of emerging from the attainment of cessation, one may enter the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna/samāpatti) either in reverse order or by skipping stages (vyutkrāntaka), for it is possible for such a mind emerging from the attainment of cessation to manifest before one.
Furthermore, other masters state as follows:
This refers exclusively to the untainted (*anāsrava*).

When the mind that takes *nirvāṇa* as its object arises from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is said to "contact the three contacts"; because it is untainted, it is called "immovable" (*āniñjya*).
Because it is subsumed under the stage of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it is called "nothingness.
Because it takes nirvāṇa as its object, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).
Although it has already been explained that these two meditative attainments have many common and differing characteristics, there are further similarities and differences among them.
The verse says:
The two meditative attainments depend on the desire and form realms; the attainment of cessation first occurs among humans.
The commentary says:

Regarding the two attainments, they refer to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Both of these arise based upon the two realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and form (*rūpadhātu*).
However, concerning this, some say:
"The attainment of non-perception occurs only within the lower three dhyānas and not in the fourth, lest the cause and the fruit be too closely proximate."

Some say: One also enters the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) in the fourth dhyāna, with the exception of the Heaven of No-Conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), because one who is born in that heaven experiences its fruit.
Other masters say:

One enters the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), not in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); otherwise, it would contradict the treatise (*śāstra*).
As the *Mūla-śāstra* states:
"There may be that which is the existence of form (*rūpa-bhava*), yet this existence does not consist of the five aggregates (*skandha*)."

This refers to sentient beings of the form realm, or those born in the heavens of those with perception, who abide in a mind of a different category—whether they have entered the attainment of non-perception, the attainment of cessation, or are born in the heaven of non-perception.
Having already attained entry into the state of non-conception, this is called "form-existence" (rūpabhava), yet this existence does not consist of the five aggregates.
From this it is proven that both of these meditative attainments arise based upon the realms of desire and form; this is termed their common characteristic.

Regarding what is called "distinctive characteristics": it refers to the attainment of the non-percipient absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), which can first arise in both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

As for the first arising of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), it occurs only among humans; that is, the attainment of cessation can first be cultivated and achieved only among humans.
It exists only among humans, because there are those who can explain it and interpret it, and because they possess the power of intense preparatory application (*prayoga*).

There are those who, having first attained it among humans, subsequently fall away from it before being reborn in the form realm; there, relying on a body in the form realm, they again cultivate and give rise to it. It cannot be entered in the formless realm, as there is no physical basis (*āśraya*) for it.

The life-faculty necessarily functions in dependence upon both form and mind. If one were to enter the meditative absorption of cessation in the formless realm, both form and mind would be absent, and thus the life-faculty should be severed.
Since the aggregates exist by depending upon one another in succession, there is no sentient being who possesses only a single aggregate.
Furthermore, because the mind and mental factors are inseparable, there is no sentient being who possesses only three aggregates.
On what basis is this known?
It is because there is falling back from the attainment of cessation, according to the meaning of the *Udāyi-sūtra*.
The Sūtra says:
"Venerable One!

There are bhikṣus who, having previously in this place been endowed with pure śīla, endowed with samādhi, and endowed with prajñā, are able to repeatedly enter and emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; such a thing is possible."
One should know this as it truly is: that person, either in the present life or at the time of death, will be unable to apply themselves diligently so as to bring their liberation to fulfillment.

Upon the dissolution of this body, they will transcend the heavens of those who subsist on physical food and, according to their merit, receive a mind-made body among the gods of "receiving" (*āhāra-vaśitā*). Having been born there, it is also possible for them to repeatedly enter and emerge from the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).

One should know this as it truly is: the Buddha taught that this body of the *manomaya-kāya* devas is the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*) within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), existing only at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
If one who has attained this attainment were never to fall away from it, they should not be able to go to take birth in the realm of form.

Thus, the distinct characteristics of the two meditative attainments have been explained in detail through six categories: namely, differences in their levels (*bhūmi*), preparatory application (*prayoga*), continuity (*saṃtati*), maturation (*vipāka*), experience (*vedanīya*), and initial arising (*prathama-utpāda*).

Chapter Five: Distinguishing Differences, Part Two, Section Five. Now it should be considered:

since in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are entirely extinguished, for what reason is it described specifically as the "attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-samāpatti*)?
One enters this meditative absorption because one feels aversion toward those two;
that is to say, perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) serve as the basis for the defilements of views and craving, and are therefore specifically objects of aversion.

These two factors possess many faults and afflictions, as has already been analyzed at length within the discussion of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); thus, through specific aversion toward them, one enters the absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Other masters say:
Regarding all associated dharmas, whether their arising or ceasing, or their acquisition or abandonment, such matters as these do not occur except simultaneously.
Nevertheless, the teachers of the Dharma employ skillful means according to the occasion, explaining them through various distinct approaches.

The Abhidharma relies solely on correct reasoning to analyze the nature, characteristics, and categories of all phenomena, and to adjudicate the provisional and ultimate intentions of the various sūtras, so as not to cause one to dogmatically cling to the literal meaning to the exclusion of others; by this means, one should understand the underlying intentions of the sūtras.
As it is said that in this meditative absorption consciousness does not depart from the body, one should know that mental factors likewise do not depart.
As it is said that in this meditative absorption all mental formations (*saṃskāra*) cease, one should know that the mind (*citta*) therein must also cease.
This discourse on the shadow-like nature of phenomena is found in other sūtras as well.
For instance, it is said that the perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas has heedfulness as its root; furthermore, another sūtra tells Ānanda:
"Unsurpassed enlightenment is attained through diligence."
As it is said that wisdom can destroy the afflictions, another sutra further states:
"Cultivating the perception of impermanence can sever sensual desire," and so forth, as explained at length.
The Dārṣṭāntikas (Exemplificationists) speak as follows:

In the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), only feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are extinguished; for there is a distinction between those who have no mind and those who have entered the attainment of cessation, as evidenced by the fact that one may die while in the attainment of cessation. Furthermore, the Sūtra states that when entering the attainment of cessation, consciousness does not depart from the body, and it also says that vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are mutually inseparable.
This statement is unreasonable, because all minds arise and cease simultaneously with feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā).
What authoritative scripture (āgama) proves that this point is established?
As it is said in a sutra:

With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three is contact, which gives rise to sensation, perception, and volition simultaneously. This continues in the same manner up to the mind and mental phenomena as conditions giving rise to mind-consciousness and so forth.
Nowhere has it been stated that there is a seventh consciousness which could be maintained as existing apart from feeling and perception.
Furthermore, because the basis (*āśraya*) within this meditative absorption ceases, that which depends upon it (*āśrita*) also ceases.
It is not that mental factors (*caitta*) can arise independently without a basis; therefore, in this state, all minds and mental factors cease entirely.

If it is argued that the term "simultaneous" (*saha*) here signifies arising without interval—just as Mandhātṛ fell at the same time because an evil thought arose, or as the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is cultivated simultaneously with impurity—then this case should be understood in the same way.
This is logically impossible, as there is a distinction [between them].

Regarding Māndhātṛ and others, the sūtras state that they both arose simultaneously; however, in reality, this should be understood as signifying immediate succession (*ānantarya*), because an unwholesome action and its unpleasant fruit must certainly not arise at the same time.
Furthermore, because that sūtra speaks of a "fifth turning," as it says:
"King Mandhātṛ fell simultaneously because an evil thought arose.
This indicates the meaning that he fell at a later time.
Because the factors of enlightenment regarding impurity differ in nature—being either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—they do not arise simultaneously.
This sūtra’s use of the term "together" (*saha*) indicates that they arise at the same time.
Since this does not contradict either the sacred teachings or correct reasoning, the statement here means "together," rather than "immediately following."
Furthermore, to maintain that the term "concomitant" (*saha*) indicates immediate succession (*anantaram utpādaḥ*) involves the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). As stated in the Sūtra:
"The clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Truths is concomitant with pleasure and concomitant with joy.
One cannot further maintain that this is identical to the *Mandhātṛ* and other sūtras, which would imply that the clear realization of the Four Truths arises only immediately after pleasure and joy.
Furthermore, as stated in the sūtras:
"A mind with attachment" (*sarāga-citta*) is so called because it is concomitant with attachment.

One should not maintain that a mind arising immediately after attachment is what is termed "a mind with attachment," for such a view would entail the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the term "concomitant" (*saha*) indicates the sense of simultaneity.
Furthermore, because feeling, perception, and so forth depend upon the mind, they are called mental factors (*caitta*).
If they were separated from their support, these feelings, perceptions, and so forth would not be able to arise.

If it is argued that the mind serves as their "equal-and-immediate condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) and thus constitutes their support, then the mind itself—since it too arises immediately following a preceding mind—should likewise be called a mental factor.
Furthermore, since mental factors arise immediately after the mind, the mental factors would also have to be established as a basis (*āśraya*).
Such points will be discussed more extensively in the section on the six causes (*ṣadhetu*).
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"When entering the attainment of cessation, all mental formations (saṃskāras) cease.
Therefore, we know that the attainment of cessation does not merely cease these two factors of feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā).

Furthermore, regarding the continuity of consciousness, if it were not to cease temporarily within this meditative absorption, it must necessarily possess a basis (*āśraya*) and an object (*ālambana*) with which the consciousness is conjoined; for consciousness does not arise apart from its basis and its object.

Since the threefold conjunction exists, there must necessarily be contact; and since feeling, perception, and volition arise simultaneously with contact, then within the meditative attainment of cessation, the two factors of feeling and perception should likewise not be extinguished.

If it is argued that although the Sūtra states that feeling conditions craving, yet for an Arhat, despite the presence of various feelings, these do not serve as conditions for craving; then contact should likewise be understood in this way, such that not all contact gives rise to feeling and the like.
This analogy does not hold, because there is a distinction.
The Sūtra itself specifies: "If the various feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance serve as conditions, craving arises.
Since Arhats lack contact associated with ignorance, craving does not arise in them despite the presence of feeling.
There has never been a case where contact (*sparśa*) arises without producing feeling (*vedanā*); therefore, wherever there is contact, feeling and the other [mental factors] necessarily arise.

Other masters claim that within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), although the substance of consciousness exists, there is no contact; however, it is unclear what they intend by "contact" in this context.

However, all consciousnesses necessarily arise in dependence upon a support (āśraya) and an object (ālambana). The Buddha taught that the conjunction of these three factors—the support, the object, and the consciousness—is contact (sparśa); with contact as a condition, sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and so forth arise.
To concede that the threefold conjunction exists within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) yet claim that contact (*sparśa*) is absent is nothing but empty words.

Furthermore, if it were held that only the mind exists within the attainment of cessation, there would be no volition (*cetanā*), because it is taught that all mental formations (*manasikāra*) are entirely extinguished within this attainment.
If the mind were without volition (*cetanā*), it would be without deliberation; a mind devoid of deliberation is likewise not admitted, for all mental activities arise from volition.
Since volition does not exist, the mind must certainly be non-existent as well.
Sentient beings who lack consciousness must logically exist, for they possess life-force (*jīvita*) and other such factors, which distinguishes them from those whose life has ended.
The possession of both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) by sentient beings is not determinate; if the mind were invariably present, then form would likewise be so.
Since there are times when form is absent, the mind should be understood as such too; therefore, that which possesses life-force is designated a "sentient being."

However, life must necessarily depend on either form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*). To cite the scriptural teaching that "consciousness does not depart from the body," there is no contradiction even in the case of the mindless meditative absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*), because consciousness will inevitably arise again within this very supporting body; therefore, it is said that it does not depart.
This refers to the continuous flow of consciousness within a single stream of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), which is not ultimately severed.
It is like a demonic affliction that, for a time, does not manifest; because it has not been permanently eliminated, one is still said to be "not free" from it.

The statement that life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are inseparable does not contradict the states of meditative absorption or the mindless states (*acittaka*), because that statement was made only with reference to a limited scope.

Since in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) there is no warmth at all, yet life-force and consciousness are not absent, it follows that in these meditative absorptions there is no consciousness at all, yet life-force and warmth are not absent.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no form whatsoever; this shall be discussed in detail later.
Therefore, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) must necessarily be without mind.

Nevertheless, that the mind arises again after the meditative absorption is because it is drawn forth and sustained by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) of the mind prior to the absorption, and further, because it is induced by the force of the resolve made during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
Is the essence of the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) conventional or real?
It should be said that the essence of this attainment is real and not conventional, because it is capable of obstructing the mind and preventing it from arising.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) cites an alternative interpretation, saying:

Because the preceding meditative mind is capable of acting as an obstruction; that is to say, the preceding meditative mind arises in opposition to other states of mind, and by its arising, it causes other minds to cease functioning for a time.

This [state] induces a basis for the mind that is contrary [to its usual mode], causing the continuum to persist; thus, it is only the state of non-functioning that is conventionally designated as "meditative absorption" (samādhi), having no separate substantial reality.

Since this is merely a conventional designation for the stage of non-functioning, it exists neither before entry nor after emergence; therefore, it is said to be subsumed under the category of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta).
Alternatively, it is the very basis itself that, being induced by a concentrated mind, arises in such a manner; this is conventionally designated as "concentration.
If this is so, from what does the subsequent mind arise?

They claim that this [consciousness] arises based on the body endowed with sense faculties (*sendriya-kāya*), because the body endowed with sense faculties and the mind serve as seeds for one another in turn.
How can such a principle be tenable?
For it would follow that consciousnesses of all objects would arise simultaneously at all times.

Regarding the statement that subsequent minds arise depending on preceding minds: because there is no second immediately antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), even though there may be simultaneous objective supports and objects, there is no arising of consciousnesses for all objects at once.

If one maintains that consciousness arises depending only on the presence of the sense-faculties and the body, without depending on causes and conditions of its own kind, then for all states and all objects, what factor acts as an obstruction so that consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously?
I have heard that there are other masters who give rise to such a view, maintaining that multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously within a single body;
observing that you, Venerable Sir, seem to have inherited this tradition, I therefore speak these words in order to accord with their tenet.

If it is argued that what has been stated—that subsequent consciousness arises depending on the presence of the faculty-endowed body rather than depending on a preceding mind—is said with reference to the state of being without mind; for since the seeds of mind exist within the faculty-endowed body, [subsequent consciousness] arises solely from them and does not depend on a preceding mind.
To claim that [the mind] does not arise from those [seeds] during the state of consciousness is also unreasonable, as there would be no distinction between cause and effect.
Furthermore, when various consciousnesses arise during the state of consciousness, they would have to depend even more upon the seeds of the sense-faculties and the body.

Why is this so? Within the body endowed with sense faculties during the state of mindlessness, there exist seeds of minds that are contrary to other minds; because these [seeds] suppress and subdue the seeds of other minds within the body endowed with sense faculties, those [other seeds] should lack the superior power to give rise to further minds.

If it is argued that in this state there exist within the body endowed with sense faculties seeds of immeasurable minds that do not contradict [the current mind], and that by the superior power of these [seeds] other minds arise, then the same should apply during states where a mind is present; why, then, would [those minds] not arise without depending on a body endowed with sense faculties?
Furthermore, suppose there were someone who maintains that sprouts such as rice and barley do not depend on seeds of their own kind as a cause, but arise solely through conditions such as the earth—
what intelligent person would not laugh at hearing such a claim?
Furthermore, you maintain that the essence of the attainment of cessation is merely nominal; yet it remains unknown what dharma serves as the basis for that nominality.
A nominal dharma cannot exist apart from its nominal basis.
Moreover, if its essence is non-existent because it does not function, how can it be said to be subsumed under conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*)?
This [intrinsic nature] is absent in its prior and subsequent states as well as in the present, because an existent nature cannot be apprehended at any time.
To say that it exists and is subsumed under conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is merely empty talk; it possesses no meaning whatsoever.

If it is argued that even a provisional concentration (*prajñapti-samādhi*) has a basis—namely, that the body which serves as its basis is induced by the concentrated mind to arise in such a manner, and is thus provisionally designated as "concentration"—then this concentration would necessarily be categorized as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
An indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharma cannot be said to be wholesome; therefore, it must arise solely in dependence upon the mind.

It is not the power of a preceding concentrated mind that can obstruct other minds. From this, one knows that apart from the preceding mind, there must exist a distinct dharma capable of obstructing the mind.

By virtue of this dharma, although the causal conditions for mind exist during the state of non-mentation, the mind does not arise; this distinct dharma is called the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Its essence is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and is substantial rather than nominal.

Because the practitioner of meditation has been impelled by the power of their prior resolve and aspiration, the force of the attainment of cessation gradually diminishes until it reaches the state of total exhaustion; then, with the mental factors of unobstructed intention serving as conditions, the mental consciousness arises once again.
By applying this principle of interpretation accordingly, the same applies to the previously mentioned attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*).
Having thus analyzed these two attainments,
what is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
The verse says:
The essence of the life-faculty is longevity; it is able to sustain warmth and consciousness.
The commentary says:
The essence of life is itself longevity; therefore, the fundamental treatise states:
"What is the life-faculty?
It refers to the longevity of the three realms."
Although its synonyms are thus stated, its essential nature remains unexplained; one should further specify which phenomenon is called "life-force" (*āyus*).
It is said that there is a distinct phenomenon capable of sustaining warmth and consciousness, which is designated as life-force.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"When life, warmth, and consciousness— these three factors— abandon the body,
the abandoned body lies prostrate, like a piece of wood without thought or awareness."
"Therefore, there exists a distinct dharma capable of sustaining warmth and consciousness, which serves as the cause for their continuous abiding; this is called 'life-force' (āyus).
If that is so, by what dharma is this life-force itself sustained?"

I say that this life-span (*āyus*) is able to sustain [heat and consciousness] because it is exclusively the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of karma, and because it persists throughout the course of a single lifetime.

Heat (*uṣman*) is not exclusively the maturation fruit of karma; as for consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is neither. Although there are instances where it persists throughout a lifetime, it is not invariably the maturation of karma; therefore, one cannot say that consciousness is sustained by karma. For this reason, it is said that life-span is able to sustain heat and consciousness.

Within the flow of consciousness that is not produced by non-karmic causes, karma possesses only a slight capacity to maintain its functional efficacy; within a single homogeneous continuum, the ripening-consciousness (vipākaja-vijñāna) is interrupted and then resumes again, sustained by the power of the life-force (jīvitendriya).
Furthermore, how is it known that vitality (*āyus*) can sustain heat (*uṣman*)?
It is because heat exists only where there is vitality; yet we also observe that those who lack heat still possess vitality. Therefore, we know that the essence of vitality is not sustained by heat.
Is it not the case that one may see warmth even where there is no life-force (*āyus*)?
Although such warmth is indeed seen, it is not what is being discussed here; for this discussion concerns the warmth that co-exists with the life-force and consciousness.

From this, it is known that there exists a distinct, substantial dharma whose power is able to sustain the warmth belonging to the category of sentient beings and is able to sustain consciousness; this is called "life-force."
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras further states:
"Now, I do not say that the essence of life (*jīvita*) is entirely non-existent; I merely say that the essence of life is not a separate, substantial entity (*dravya*).
If that is so, what dharma is designated as the essence of life?"
This refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)—as projected by karma according to their respective realms—as well as the force of duration upon which they depend.

Because the continuity of the six sense bases and the force of duration upon which they depend is determined by karma, they abide for a specific period of time according to that projection; therefore, this force of duration is designated as the essence of life (*jīvita*).

Just as there is a force (*śakti*) projected by a grain seed that persists until the time of ripening, or as there is a force projected by a released arrow that persists until it comes to rest, so too the substance of life-force (*āyus*) is substantially real, as established in the [Abhidharma] treatises on the sense bases (*āyatana*).

Regarding this, one should simply inquire into the intention of the Sūtra: if, in a certain location, there is no internal fifth base of form (*rūpāyatana*) produced by karma as its maturation (*vipāka*), and at times in that location there is also no sixth base of mind (*manāyatana*) produced by karma—specifically during states where defiled consciousness arises over a long period, or during the continuous flow of wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousness—then what could be called "life-force" in the absence of the force of maturation projected by karma?

If, in a certain state, there is the maturation of karma that proceeds continuously from the moment of birth until the stage of death, one may say that in this state there exists a momentum for the duration of abiding projected by karma; because its continuity is determined, it is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Since this [state] lacks the force of momentum for the duration of its stay that is projected by karma and thus does not proceed in constant, uninterrupted succession, how can it be said that it possesses the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
Such being the case, what phenomenon is designated as the "force of momentum for the duration of its stay projected by karma"?
Since there is no momentum (*vega*) that draws [the continuum] and causes it to abide for a specific duration, to whom does this determination of continuity belong?
Since such a determination of continuity does not exist, on what basis can one say that the essence of life (*āyus*) consists in abiding for a certain length of time as required?
Therefore, regarding this point, the Master of the Sūtras has constructed many words that express nothing at all.

Furthermore, the examples he cites lack the power to prove his case: just as the continuity induced by a seed proceeds without interruption until the time of ripening, and the continuity induced by a discharged arrow proceeds without interruption until the time it comes to rest—both of which possess a momentum (*saṃskāra*) that persists until those respective times.

Since that which is not the maturation of karma continues in an uninterrupted succession at all times, one may say that even when the karma has ceased, there remains a "projected momentum" (*sthiti-śakti*) within the continuum; this continuum is determined, and it persists for as long as the duration to which it corresponds.
Therefore, the examples cited lack the power to prove [your point].
Consequently, the essence of life (*jīvita*) is a distinct entity that can sustain warmth and consciousness, and is thus called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Furthermore, this life-faculty does not function solely in dependence upon the body, for the life-faculty exists even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
It does not depend solely on the mind, because life exists even in states devoid of mind.
If that is so, upon what does the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) depend for its operation?
It depends on the projecting karma of previous lives and on the present homogeneous group (nikāyasabhāga); the homogeneous group, in turn, functions in the same manner as the life-faculty.
Now, one should further consider this:
when those who die do so, is it because their lifespan has been exhausted, or is there another cause?
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:
There are those who die because their lifespan is exhausted, but not because their merit is exhausted.
This is elaborated in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the first permutation: it is due to the exhaustion of the karmic force that produced the maturation (*vipāka*) of the lifespan.
The second phrase refers to the exhaustion of the karmic power that brings about the fruits of wealth and happiness.
The third phrase refers to the simultaneous exhaustion of both types of karma capable of producing those fruits.
The fourth phrase refers to the inability to avoid or escape from untimely and calamitous conditions.
One should not further say that it is because of the relinquishing of the life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*), for this meaning is already subsumed within the first phrase.

In the state where the life-span is exhausted, the exhaustion of merit (*puṇya*) no longer has any efficacy regarding death; therefore, when both are exhausted simultaneously, death occurs, and this is called "death due to the simultaneous exhaustion of both."
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
Should this life-span be said to proceed in accordance with the continuity [of the aggregates],
or should it be said to abide as soon as it arises?

Sentient beings bound by desire who have not entered the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) should be said to possess a life-span that proceeds in accordance with the continuity [of the aggregates].

Those who have entered the attainment of non-conception, those who have entered the attainment of cessation, and all sentient beings of the form and formless realms should be said to possess a life-span that remains fixed once it has arisen.
What is the meaning of those statements?
If the supporting body is subject to injury, and life-force is injured accordingly, this is called the first type: that which proceeds in accordance with the continuum (*saṃtāna*).
If the supporting body is not subject to injury and remains as it arose, this is called the second type: that which remains once arisen (*sakṛdutpanna*).
The former [passage] reveals the presence of obstacles, while the latter reveals their absence; by this, it is established that untimely death exists.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"There are four ways of obtaining a physical basis (*ātmabhāva*): namely, there is one who obtains a physical basis such that he can only harm himself and cannot be harmed by others."
This is explained in detail through four permutations.

Regarding those who can only harm themselves and not be harmed by others: this refers to those born in the *Krīḍā-pramoṣaka* (Heaven of Forgetfulness through Play) and the *Mano-manasikāra-kupita* (Heaven of Anger of the Mind) within the Desire Realm. Because they habitually indulge excessively in play, their bodies become exhausted and their mental faculties become lost.
Furthermore, because they give rise to intense fury and look at one another with hearts full of resentment, they perish there and not elsewhere.
This should also be explained in the case of those who practice the relinquishing of life, for they do so by abandoning their own lives rather than through the agency of others.

Those who can only be killed by others and not by themselves are those dwelling within an egg, as well as those in the fetal stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, *peśī*, *ghana*, and *praśākhā*, because they lack the capacity to cause harm to themselves.
Those who can be harmed by both [killing and weapons] are the majority of other sentient beings in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Those who cannot be harmed by either are all sentient beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as well as certain sentient beings in the desire realm, such as: those in the hells (*naraka*), those in Uttarakuru, those correctly abiding in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrīsamādhi*), the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and the absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*); royal seers (*rājarṣi*), messengers of the Buddha; Dāmilas, Udras, and Kṛmis as prophesied by the Buddha; the householder’s son Yaśas; Kumārajīva; the Bodhisattva in his final birth and the mother of that Bodhisattva while she is pregnant with him; and all universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and the mothers of those universal monarchs while they are pregnant with them.
If that is so, why does the Sūtra say:
"Venerable Sir,
what kind of personal existence (ātmabhāva) obtained by sentient beings cannot be harmed by oneself nor harmed by another?"
Śāriputra refers here to sentient beings born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Because it mentions the latter first and thereby includes the former, it is like other sūtras which mention the beginning to include the end; as it is said in a sūtra:
"In the first dhyāna, there is the bliss born of seclusion."
This mentions the first [stage], implying that the subsequent stages also possess this bliss.
This sūtra is likewise: it mentions the latter to imply the former.

Alternatively, excluding those at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), sentient beings born in the other formless absorptions (*ārūpya-dhyāna*) are also capable of only self-harm, just like the gods of the *Lalitavistara* (Playful Forgetfulness) and the *Manopahata* (Mind-Afflicted) in the desire realm.
They too, by the power of giving rise to such types of afflictions, pass away from that state.

Alternatively, the self-body obtained within other formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) can be destroyed by the noble path (*ārya-mārga*) of its own level, and it can also be destroyed by the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of a higher level.
In the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), both types of harm are absent from above; therefore, it is said to be "neither harmed by either.
But is it not the case that the Peak of Existence is also harmed by the noble paths (*āryamārga*) of other stages, and thus should be called "harmed by another"?
If one follows this explanation, the principle should also apply here.
However, what is stated now is that the higher stages are intended by the other [meaning], because the term "other" (para) is also applied to denote something superior.
Alternatively, one might say that something is called "another" only when it lacks sovereign power over it; since higher stages possess sovereign power over lower stages, they are not termed "others.
However, one should raise this objection here:

if the Buddha’s intention were to define "killing oneself or another" as the severing of afflictions within one's own or another's path, then he should not have stated that death occurs because of killing oneself or another. Death or non-death would not be determined by whether or not afflictions are severed, but rather by the act of killing itself.
Furthermore, this does not accord with the reasoning of the previous explanation, namely that those in the hells (*naraka*) and so forth are not killed by themselves or others.
Nevertheless, since that Venerable One had already understood the meaning of being killed by oneself or others as previously stated, he spoke these words again in order to clarify another point:
"O Mahāsthavira!"
"Do those sentient beings pass away from that place?
"Śāriputra, if those sentient beings have not severed their afflictions, they do indeed pass away."
Having already severed the afflictions, he attained parinirvāṇa right there.
For what reason did the Venerable One, relying on his final acquired body, again question the Blessed One?
Because they neither harm themselves nor others, some develop a persistent overestimation of their status regarding them; in order to cause them to abandon this, he asks again:
"Those sentient beings," and so forth, as explained at length.
What is the difference between the formations of vitality (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) and the formations of life-span (*jīvita-saṃskāra*)?
If the life-span of phenomena that have arisen is called the formations of vitality, the life-span of phenomena that have not arisen is said to be the formations of life-span.
Some say as follows:
That which is not to be relinquished is called the life-force (*jīvitasaṃskāra*); that which is to be relinquished is called the vitality-force (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*).
Furthermore, some say:
that which is the fruit of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) is called the life-force, while that which is the fruit of prior karma is called the vitality-force.
Furthermore, there are those who say:

that which arises with clarity (*vidyā*) as its predominant condition is called the formations of vitality (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), while that which arises with ignorance (*avidyā*) as its predominant condition is called the formations of life-span (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
Alternatively, there are those who say:

That which is obtained through the continuum of one who is free from craving is called the formations of vitality (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*); that which is also obtained through the continuum of one who possesses craving is called the formations of life (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
This is the distinction between the formations of vitality and the formations of life.
The life-faculty has already been explained.
What are the characteristics (lakṣaṇas)?
The verse says:
The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) refer to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), whose nature is first abiding, then changing, and finally ceasing.
The commentary states:
These four kinds are the characteristics of the conditioned; because they manifest that nature, they receive the name "characteristics."

Regarding that which "arises" herein: it refers to a distinct dharma that serves as the unobstructed, predominant cause at the stage when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise, because it is capable of inducing and drawing them forth.
As for "inducing and drawing forth," it means that at the time those [phenomena] arise, this dharma acts as their predominant condition (*pratyaya*).

Although all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that arise may be termed "birth" (*jāti*), this specific designation of "birth" is established solely based on the unobstructed, predominant cause for the state of arising of those conditioned phenomena.

"Abiding" (*sthiti*) refers to a distinct entity (*dharma*) which is the unobstructed, predominant cause that leads already-arisen and as-yet-undestroyed conditioned phenomena toward their own results.
"Differentiation" (*visabhāga*) refers to a distinct dharma that serves as the cause for the subsequent moment of a continuity of formations to differ from its predecessor.
"Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to a distinct dharma that serves as the predominant cause for the destruction of co-arisen formations.
"Nature" (*svabhāva*) has the meaning of essence (*ātman*).

Is it not stated in the Sūtras that there are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned, among which "stability" (sthiti) acts as a virtuous friend capable of sustaining the conditioned? Why, then, is it not mentioned?
Since the Sūtra does not mention it, there must be a specific reason; you should provide an explanation for this.
If there were characteristics that expressed only the conditioned, this sūtra would indeed state them.
However, this characteristic of abiding does not express only the conditioned, because unconditioned phenomena also abide in themselves.

Alternatively, because this [treatise] fully reveals both the merits and the faults of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it speaks of four kinds; whereas in the *sūtras*, because they reveal only the faults of the conditioned, they speak of only three.

Alternatively, just as other sūtras state only that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are subject to arising and ceasing and are not without difference, so too this sūtra does not lack an abiding essence;
it speaks only of the existence of the three [marks] because it observes a minor cause.
Therefore, there is no contradiction between the four [noble truths] and the three [realms].
For what reason is it said that there are only three?
Because the state of abiding pertains to both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) categories; thus, one must avoid causing those to be converted to give rise to such doubts.
Because the conditioned and the unconditioned are mutually similar, although "abiding" exists, only three [characteristics] are mentioned.
Alternatively, "abiding" is already implicitly stated within this sūtra, because it directly mentions three without using the word "only";
otherwise, it would have had to state that there are "only three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned."
Alternatively, in this sūtra, "abiding" (*sthiti*) and "alteration" (*anyathātva*) are explained together; otherwise, the mention of "abiding" would be rendered useless.

The purpose of explaining them together is to show that the abiding of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) necessarily entails alteration, whereas unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) possess abiding but lack alteration; thus, they are distinguished from the conditioned.

In this sūtra, the mention of "abiding and change" (sthity-anyathātva) does not indicate that abiding is itself change; rather, it indicates that conditioned phenomena possess arising and cessation, as well as abiding and change.
If one were to claim that the abiding of unconditioned phenomena is not established, this would be unreasonable, for it must necessarily be established.

Since it must be established that there are three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and by this very fact the existence of a "subsistence" (*sthiti*) for the unconditioned is established, it is certain that there are only four conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
Since these characteristics of arising and so forth are themselves conditioned, they should each have their own separate four characteristics of arising and so forth.
If there were further characteristics, it would lead to an infinite regress, because those [characteristics] would themselves possess further characteristics such as birth and so forth.
While we indeed admit that there are further [characteristics], they do not entail an infinite regress. Why is this?
The verse says:
These [conditioned phenomena] possess "arising-of-arising" and so forth, which have efficacy with respect to eight and one.
The commentary says:

In this context, some say that the term "existence" (*bhava*) also serves to reveal its definition; the intent is to show that this existence consists of only four [primary characteristics] and no others. These refer to the four primary characteristics previously mentioned.

As for "arising-of-arising" (*jāti-jāti*) and so forth, these refer to the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), namely: the arising-of-arising up to the cessation-of-cessation (*nirodha-nirodha*).
