By this, the *Vibhāṣā* commentary is also validated, which states that the claim "there is no abiding" was spoken with the underlying intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) regarding the time after a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), and does not mean that there is no abiding whatsoever.

Regarding what they have said—that this [interpretation] is merely their own arbitrary conceptualization and speculation that conforms to the Sūtras of the Sugata, for those Sūtras never state that there is "abiding"—I now say:

such individuals have either not read this Sūtra, or they have dismissed it as invalid based on their own biased sentiments, or their minds have been clouded by partisan attachment; thus, although they have repeatedly examined the text, they have failed to grasp its meaning.
May those who seek the truth please investigate this:

who among them clings to their own arbitrary interpretations of the Buddha’s sūtras, asserting that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have even a momentary duration, and who rejects these sūtras as invalid authority?

However, since the Bhagavān previously stated in a sūtra that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have no duration at the moment of their cessation, he feared that teachers of the Dārṣṭāntika school in future generations might misinterpret that scriptural passage to deny even momentary duration; therefore, he further taught this *Tālapatropama-sūtra* (the Sūtra on the Simile of the Clapping Hands) to demonstrate that conditioned phenomena do possess a temporary duration.
He could not accept this statement of the Great Master and further rebuked him, saying:

"For what reason do you only allow that it was spoken with the underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) of referring to the subsequent moment, yet do not say it was spoken with the underlying intention of referring to the subsequent homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*)?"
What is the difference between this [homogeneous character] and a moment?
This objection is irrational, because there is a distinction.

A momentary duration has a simultaneous cause, whereas such a cause does not exist for the duration of the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*); therefore, this objection does not accord with correct reasoning.
He further rebuked him, saying:

"If it is by the power of duration that conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) can remain for a short time, why does this same power not cause all conditioned things to remain for as long as a thousand koṭis of moments?"
For what reason would the cause for the abiding of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in a single moment not cause them to abide for a thousand *koṭi* moments?
This too is irrational, because even apart from the cause of production, [the opponent] does not admit that conditioned phenomena arise.
For what reason does the cause that produces a single moment of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) not immediately produce a thousand *koṭis* of moments?
The logic of this principle should apply equally whether one advances or retreats.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
One should know that pleasant feeling is pleasant both in its arising and its abiding.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"One should know that form and so forth have arising and have abiding."
If it is claimed that this sūtra speaks in terms of a continuum (*saṃtāna*), this is not consistent with correct reasoning, because the meaning cannot be established.
That is to say, if one does not admit that a moment (*kṣaṇa*) has duration, how can the meaning of the continuity of a continuum be established?
Since a continuum must necessarily be established based upon moments, such a characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) is thoroughly established by both reason and scripture.
Yet, the Dārṣṭāntikas stubbornly claim it does not exist; one wonders what grievance they have harbored against duration that they cannot accept this principle, even though it is so manifest.
Another raises an objection:
"If the characteristic of impermanence exists as a distinct entity apart from the nature of impermanence, why does the characteristic of suffering not exist separately from suffering?
Such an objection based on analogy is logically untenable.
If it is argued that the nature of impermanence exists by virtue of the characteristic of impermanence, one might raise an objection based on this statement, saying:
"The nature of suffering should likewise exist by virtue of the characteristic of suffering.

However, while the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) is indeed impermanent, they cease only by taking the characteristic of cessation as their condition; just as the nature of conditioned phenomena is impermanent, yet they arise only by depending on the condition of arising.
Regarding this nature of suffering, even if there were further characteristics of suffering to serve as conditions, what further purpose would they serve?
Therefore, the logical objection raised by way of analogy is not established.
By this, the objection concerning emptiness and selflessness is already refuted.
Furthermore, the characteristic of impermanence is also the characteristic of suffering, because its essence is impermanent and because it is so taught in the *Duḥkha-sūtra*.
Moreover, that [position] should likewise encounter this objection:

if a produced phenomenon must depend on a distinct productive condition in order to arise, then one must also admit that a phenomenon which is suffering must depend on a distinct condition of suffering in order to become suffering.
Alternatively, the phenomena that arise would have to arise spontaneously, independent of the conditions for their arising, just as suffering and so forth do.
Furthermore, this was already stated previously.
What was stated previously?
If, according to your view, that which exists at certain times must depend upon other dharmas and their arising activity to be established as existing,
then in our school, since all things exist at all times, the nature of dharmas does not depend upon causes and conditions.

Since suffering lacks a self and so forth, it should possess a nature [of cessation]; and since cessation, like arising, must depend upon other factors, we know that there exists a distinct internal cause capable of effecting cessation. That which is apart from the phenomenon to be ceased is termed the characteristic of impermanence (*anityatā-lakṣaṇa*).

If it is claimed that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have no distinct cause for their cessation, then arising (*utpāda*) should likewise exist without depending on a cause; for both of these are factors distinct from the entity itself.
Alternatively, one must explain the cause for the distinction between these two.

If it is argued that there is indeed a distinction between these two—namely, that the arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) necessarily depends on causes, as we observe differences in the speed of their arising—and that if the cessation of conditioned phenomena also depended on causes, there would likewise have to be differences in the speed of their cessation; [this objection is addressed as follows:]...
If cessation were as slow or fast as it was at the time of arising, it would contradict the tenet that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇabhanga*).
Therefore, one should know that they perish spontaneously without a cause; this entails no such fault, because a cause of cessation must necessarily coexist with the phenomenon itself.

There is no difference in time; the cause of arising and the formations may be simultaneous or non-simultaneous, for even if separated by an interval of time, it still acts as a cause. Thus, when the various formations arise, there may be slowness or speed.

If the cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were not dependent on causes, they would have to perish at the very moment of their arising; or else, there would be no perishing even in subsequent stages, since you maintain that both the prior and subsequent states are equally causeless.

If you argue that since the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have not yet arisen at this stage, how can it be difficult to establish that they possess cessation, then you must admit that arising is the cause of cessation, because only when arising is observed does cessation occur.
Since it has already been granted that the cessation of all conditioned phenomena necessarily depends upon their arising, how can it be said that they cease without a cause?
Furthermore, the existence of a cause for cessation is established by the authoritative teaching (*āgama*), as a sūtra states:
"Because this phenomenon ceases, that phenomenon also ceases."
Furthermore, it is said:
"In this way, all that exists has a cause.
Thus, one knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) cease by means of a cause.

Furthermore, all conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) serve as causes for one another: it is only by virtue of arising that cessation can occur; it is only by virtue of the existence of the factor of cessation that arising can occur; it is only by virtue of duration that change occurs; and it is only by virtue of change that duration can undergo transition.
Furthermore, there is another objection:
"Since the cause for abiding does not exist, phenomena perish spontaneously; what need is there for a cause of cessation?

This objection is irrational. For those who maintain that only prior arising constitutes the cause, at the very time the cause exists, the effect has not yet arisen, because they hold that the future entity is non-existent.
At the stage when the subsequent effect arises, the preceding cause has already ceased; although there is no persisting cause, what prevents there being persistence?
Therefore, what they have stated does not mean that there is no cause for cessation.

Furthermore, it was previously established that the characteristic of persistence acts as a cause: once conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have arisen, they persist for a single moment. How, then, can you further claim that persistence is without a cause?

If it is argued that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perish spontaneously because they necessarily cease after a single moment, then if there were no characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), what would cause them to become non-existent? That which has arisen must perish precisely due to the characteristic of cessation; therefore, the characteristic of cessation exists as a distinct entity apart from the conditioned phenomenon itself.
Furthermore, one should not maintain that the essence of the characteristic of cessation is non-existent, for as stated in the sūtra cited previously:
"The arising of conditioned phenomena can be known, and their cessation and the alteration of their duration can also be known."
It is not that one should be exhorted to understand a non-existent thing, for all things that can be understood are merely different names for what exists.

Furthermore, just as there must necessarily be a specific capacity for production that causes a produced phenomenon to reach the state of having been produced, so too must there necessarily be a specific capacity for cessation that causes a ceased phenomenon to reach the state of having been ceased; therefore, the meaning of cessation is established as being distinct from production.
Furthermore, that Elder (Sthavira) spoke as follows:

"Just as although there are no distinct entities such as 'existence-ness,' 'oneness,' 'length-ness,' 'shortness-ness,' 'conjunction-ness,' or 'disjunction-ness' upon which they depend, one can nevertheless establish the existence of phenomena such as 'being existent,' 'long,' 'short,' 'conjoined,' or 'separated'; so too it is with 'abiding' and the rest—they have no distinct objects of dependence."

This statement would result in the fault of contradicting one's own tenet, for that school itself admits that there exist dharmas such as length, shortness, conjunction, and disjunction, which are established in dependence upon others.

They maintain that all dharmas rely upon causes and conditions, being non-existent previously and existing now; therefore, all dharmas possess an existent nature in dependence upon others, rather than being without anything upon which they depend.
In your school, it is held that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are originally non-existent and now exist; their existence-nature (*sattva-svabhāva*) is established only by depending on arising.
The Abhidharmikas, however, assert that the existence-nature of all phenomena exists at all times, without depending on causes and conditions.
Therefore, what he has stated contradicts his own tenet.
Since the negation of other similar categories is established only through one [aspect], it likewise depends upon another aspect for its establishment.

Length and shortness are established through mutual dependence, or they are established in dependence upon the arrangement of atoms; thus, they do not exist inherently but must necessarily depend on others for their formation.
Conjunction and disjunction likewise depend upon distinct entities; therefore, everything exists in dependence upon something else, and no designation can be established without such dependence.

Furthermore, the causes for the arising of phenomena should also be refuted by this same principle: if a nature such as "existence" were established without dependence, then arising should be the same;
however, such a thing does not exist. Thus, all the various states of conditioned phenomena are established in dependence upon different causes and conditions, and do not exist spontaneously.
Therefore, it is thoroughly established that each moment of the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) exists as a distinct reality.

The position maintained by the Dārṣṭāntika masters—that the characteristics of the conditioned, such as arising and so forth, exist as a conventional continuity—does not accord with correct reasoning and contradicts the sūtras.
Only our own school accords with the sūtras and conforms to reason; therefore, the wise should diligently study and practice this.
The characteristics of conditioned phenomena have already been analyzed in detail.
What, then, is the meaning of the categories such as "name-bodies" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth?
The verse says:
The so-called "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are collectively explained as concepts, phrases, and phonemes.
The commentary states:
"And so forth" includes the phrase-body (*padakāya*) and the phoneme-body (*vyañjanakāya*), because the *Mūla-śāstra* speaks of the name-body, phrase-body, and phoneme-body.

The general designation for all perceptions (*saṃjñā*) is the group of names (*nāmakāya*); the general designation for all phrases (*pada*) is the group of phrases (*padakāya*); and the general designation for all syllables (*vyañjana*) is the group of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*).
The term "general designation" (*uddeśa*) carries the sense of a collective assembly, because the verbal root *ud-śās* is used in the sense of a collective assembly.
"Perception" (saṃjñā) refers to the conceptualization, grasping, and conventional establishment of phenomena.
That which is produced by words— namely, [concepts] such as "eye," "ear," "bottle," "garment," or "chariot"—
is precisely what constitutes the "body of perception" (saṃjñākāya), which is to say, the "body of names" (nāmakāya), such as "eye," "ear," and so forth.
"Chapter" (*pariccheda*) refers to "discursive exposition. The *Lokāyata* (Worldly Treatise) commentator explains:

this exposition is inexhaustible; bearing distinct chapters, it is capable of ultimately expounding the intended meaning, namely that merit brings about the maturation of pleasant results, and so forth.
In this way, the body of chapters (*varga-kāya*) is itself the body of phrases (*pada-kāya*), as it is said:
“Merit brings about a pleasant ripening; Whatever one desires is fulfilled as wished;
And together with the swift realization of the foremost, There is the eternal peace of *nirvāṇa*.”
Regarding such phrases as these:

"syllables" refers to characters such as *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, and so forth; such "bodies of syllables" (*akṣara-kāya*) are themselves "bodies of phonemes" (*vyañjana-kāya*), which refers to [consonants] such as *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and so forth.
Other masters say that the root treatise states:
"What is a 'multitude of names' (*nāmakāya*)?
It refers to names, names, and things."

It is not that those masters intended to debate whether names and so forth possess the characteristic of being substantially real, yet they initiated their inquiry based on a provisional combination; therefore, when they ask about "name-bodies" and so forth, they must certainly be asking about the substantial nature of names and so forth. In the process of investigating the substantial nature of names and so forth, what purpose is served by examining their provisional combination?

Furthermore, regarding the distinctions among the three characteristics, such as "name" (*nāman*) and so forth: that which is manifested by sound and which manifests the meaning, having been collectively established as a definitive means of expression (*vācaka*), displays the intrinsic nature of the object of knowledge as it is intended to be understood—like an echo or a reflection; this characteristic is "name."
If one can analytically discern the categories of meaning—both extensive and concise—within the objects of knowledge, this characteristic is the *pada* (phrase).

When the sound of the speaker has already ceased, that which still causes one to maintain mindfulness, holds [the meaning] without confusion, and transmits it to others, this characteristic is the *vyañjana* (syllable).
In this context, "name" (nāman) refers to that which follows and converges.
Just as a vocal sound converges toward its object, so too do names follow and pursue their respective intrinsic natures (svabhāva), invoking them.
A phrase (*pada*) is that which can differentiate the meaning of what is spoken; that is to say, it can analyze and distinguish the various categories of meaning.
A syllable (*vyañjana*) is that which is capable of manifesting something, because by means of this and depending upon this, that is manifested.

This is precisely what constitutes a "syllable" (*akṣara*): it means that which causes mindfulness to be fixed so as not to be lost; or, by virtue of being sustained by it, one is rendered free from doubt; or, it is capable of maintaining that [object] and transmitting it to another.
Therefore, it is said:

"Just as the signs of the objects of the preparatory means serve as a staircase for the objects realized within meditative concentration (dhyāna), so too do phonemes with respect to names, phrases, and meanings."
Other masters say: Because characters such as *a* and *i* can manifest phrases (*pada*) and sentences (*nāman*), they are called "syllables" (*vyañjana*).
These same characters, whether individually or collectively, can express intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), and are therefore called "names" (*nāman*).
This very combination, which is capable of ultimately defining the various categories of meaning, is called a "phrase" (pada).
In this way, the three types [of phonemes, words, and phrases] would have to become a single entity, and furthermore, they would not be real; therefore, they cannot be relied upon.
Furthermore, there are other masters who manifest the three categories [of name, phrase, and phoneme] within a single locus.
For example, as it is said: "O Desire, I know your origin.

In this instance, each individual syllable is designated as a phoneme (*vyañjana*); "Desire" (*kāma*) is the name (*nāman*); and the whole is designated as the phrase (*pada*). Thus, these constitute the collective exposition of the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).

This also does not avoid the faults previously mentioned; therefore, the three characteristics of "name" (*nāman*) and so forth stated at the outset are superior, as they are suitable for investigation.
Is it not the case that in the Sūtras, the four formless aggregates—feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—are collectively designated as "name"?
This treatise also states:

"The bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are included within form (*rūpa*); the remainder of the sphere of mental objects are all termed 'subsumed' [under non-form].
Why, then, is it said here that they are "named"?
It has, however, as its nature the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra-skandha*).
Both the sūtras and the treatises, in order to subsume all dharmas within a concise framework, categorize them into two types: those whose essence is form are collectively termed "form" (*rūpa*);
[those whose essence is non-form are collectively termed "non-form"].
All other non-material phenomena are collectively termed "name" (*nāman*), because within the collection of non-material factors, "name" is subsumed.
Since the general term is used here for the specific, it is called "name.

In this context, "name" refers specifically to that which can manifest the meaning of what is expressed; therefore, its nature consists solely of the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Is meaning expressible or inexpressible?
According to reality, one should say that meaning is inexpressible.
If this is so, for what reason is it that understanding [a word] such as "cause" as the meaning "cause" is not a mistaken understanding?
Furthermore, it would contradict the Sūtra:
"I shall briefly explain for you the essential points of the Dharma;
there are both the meaning and the phrasing. There is no such fault [in our position], because [the distinction between meaning and phrasing] is established as a mere designation (*prajñapti*).

This refers to the people at the beginning of the eon who, regarding various objects, collectively established various distinct conceptual names; through this tradition, their understanding of these names and concepts remains free from error.
Furthermore, as it is said:
"Speech can produce names, and names can manifest meanings.
Yet, while the sūtras speak of "elegant phrasing and profound meaning," they never state that there exists a separate entity called "phrasing" apart from the meaning itself.
Even if one were to grant this, there would be no fault, for the Blessed One’s teaching possesses both complete phrasing and meaning.
That is to say, the Blessed One’s instruction is able to correctly and clearly manifest immeasurable gateways of meaning; because its phrasing is perfect and without omission, he spoke thus.

Furthermore, all phenomena of the three periods of time each possess names corresponding to those three periods. That is to say, regarding past phenomena, the Buddhas of the past have already revealed them using past names;
the Buddhas of the future will likewise reveal them using future names;
and the Buddhas of the present are currently revealing them using present names.
The future and the present should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, among all phenomena, there is nothing that lacks a name; if there were, it would entail the fallacy of being something that is not an object of cognition (*ajñeya*).
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke these words:
"Name can overshadow everything; there is nothing that surpasses name.
Therefore, this single dharma is said to follow its own sovereign course. Other masters say:
Meanings are few while names are many, because within a single meaning there are many names.
Others further state:
names are few while meanings are many; for names are comprised only by a small portion of one *dhātu* (the *nāma-dhātu*), whereas meanings fully encompass all eighteen *dhātus*.

Furthermore, there are those who say that names are mutually more or fewer in number: that is, with respect to the meaning of "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*), names are many while meanings are few; whereas according to the meaning of "establishing the teaching," meanings are few while names are many—because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, establishes boundless names for each and every phenomenon (*dharma*) in accordance with its various meanings.
Just as greed is called "craving," "fire," "snake," "creeper," "thirst," "net," "poison," "spring," "river," "long," "broad," "needle," "thread," and so forth—all such [designations apply].
Regarding this, the Sūtra Master (Sautrāntika) says:

"Since these three have speech as their nature, they take sound as their substance and are subsumed under the self-nature of form (*rūpa*); how then can they be said to be formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*)?"
This criticism is unreasonable.
Why is this so? Because it is known through both scripture and reasoning that [the self] exists as something distinct.
The teaching refers to the statement in the Sūtra:
"the power of speech and the power of syllables.
If the syllable were identical to speech, what would be the purpose of mentioning them separately?
Furthermore, it is said:
"One should uphold the words and phrases of the True Dharma.
It is also stated:
Rely on the meaning, not on the letter.
Furthermore, it is said that the cause [of a verse] is the *chanda* syllables; *chanda* refers to the substance consisting of words measured according to the proportions for composing stanzas.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"One knows the phenomena (dharma) and one knows their meaning (artha).
"Phenomena" refers to names and so forth; "meaning" refers to that which is expressed.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The phrasing and meaning are skillful.
It also says:
One should recite the True Dharma using well-spoken phrases; if one recites the True Dharma using poorly spoken phrases, its meaning will be difficult to understand.
Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata has attained rare and marvelous collections of names, phrases, and syllables.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The various resolute understandings of these phrases and sentences are extremely rare.

Based on such teachings, one knows that there exist distinct collections of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and syllables (*vyañjanakāya*) capable of expressing various meanings, which—just like vocal sounds—are real entities rather than mere designations.

The principle is that it is observed that at times one perceives sound but not the syllables, and at other times one perceives the syllables but not the sound; therefore, we know their essences are distinct.
That which occurs when one perceives sound but not the syllables refers to cases where, although one hears the sound, one does not comprehend its meaning.
We observe that there are people who, upon merely hearing someone else’s words, further inquire: "What did you say?

This failure to understand the meaning of the heard sound is entirely due to not having grasped the articulated phonemes (*vyañjana*); how then can one maintain that the phoneme is no different from the sound?
There are times when one obtains the word but not the sound; this refers to understanding the meaning without hearing the sound.
It is observed that some people, without hearing another's speech, perceive what is being said by observing the movement of the lips and so forth.
The fact that one can attain the definitive meaning without hearing the sound is entirely due to having personally mastered the articulated syllables (*vyañjana*).
Based on this logical proof, the syllable must necessarily differ from the sound.
Furthermore, we observe in the world that people recite mantras while concealing their voices; thus, we know that the mantra-syllables are distinct from the mantra-sounds.
Furthermore, one observes that in the world there are two debaters whose speech sounds similar, yet one is defeated and the other victorious;
this cause of victory and defeat must exist apart from sound.
Moreover, because the spheres of the two unimpeded knowledges—of phenomena (*dharma*) and of expression (*nirukti*)—are distinct, it is known that syllables are separate from sound.
Therefore, sound is merely vocal expression, and its characteristics possess no distinction.
Its various inflections necessarily depend upon [the phonemes] ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, and so forth.

It is essential that speech-sounds give rise to syllables; the combination of these syllables in sequence produces names (*nāman*), and once these names have arisen, they are able to manifest meaning. Based on this successive process, one makes such statements as these.
Speech is able to produce names, and names are able to manifest meanings; therefore, it is established as a fundamental principle that the sound and the name are distinct.

One should know that herein, sound is the speaker and the phoneme (vyañjana) is that which is spoken, while the meaning is neither of the two. In this way, the establishment [of these categories] is free from confusion.
In this regard, the Master of the Sūtras further states:
"Not every sound is designated as 'speech' (vāk); rather, it is only such sounds by means of which a meaning can be understood that are designated as speech."
This means that among all meanings, those capable of expressing them have already been established by speakers as the definitive means of expression (*vācaka-pramāṇa*).

If the meaning of a sentence is manifested by names, and this function of manifestation is already accomplished solely through sounds (*ghoṣa*), why must one gratuitously postulate the existence of a separate, substantial name?
What is called the definitive authority of the signifier (*vācaka-pramāṇa*)?
Is it not the case that when a conventional designation (*saṃjñā-nāman*) is established together regarding an object, this is precisely what is called the definitive authority of the signifier?
That is to say, among various objects, the speakers first collectively establish such syllables, which are definitively able to signify such objects through successive transmission.
Because such syllables are established through common consensus, such names are produced based on these syllables; these names constitute the definitive means of expression (*vyavahāra-pramāṇa*).

When those who speak are about to utter words, they must first contemplate this definitive standard. Consequently, whether speaking for oneself or for others, one is able to understand the meaning revealed by the speech.

Therefore, it is not that sound alone can manifest meaning; rather, speech produces syllables (*vyañjana*), syllables in turn produce names (*nāman*), and only then can a name express the intended meaning.
Just as speech produces syllables and syllables produce names, one should likewise consider the principle by which phrases (*pada*) are produced.
In this regard, the Master of the Sūtras further states:
"Moreover, it is not yet understood how this name is produced by speech—is it manifested by speech, or is it generated by speech?"
If [names] were produced by speech, then because speech has the nature of sound, all sounds should be able to produce names.
If it is argued that there is a distinction among the sounds that produce names, then these [distinctions] alone would suffice to manifest the meaning; why wait for a separate name?
If it were manifested by speech, then since speech is of the nature of sound, all sounds should be able to manifest names.
If you claim that there is a distinction among sounds that manifests names, this alone would suffice to manifest the meaning; why then wait for a separate "name"?
The objection regarding the claim that sound is capable of signifying meaning applies equally here.
That is to say, if the essence of sound itself were able to manifest meaning, then all sounds would necessarily be capable of manifestation.
If it is argued that there is a distinction among those sounds capable of manifestation, then such a distinction must be the name itself.
Therefore, the logical inference presented does not constitute an error or a valid objection.
However, the speaker first holds the name they intend to use within their mind; only then do they deliberate:
"I shall initiate such and such speech to proclaim such and such meaning for others."
Consequently, at a later time, speech is produced following from volition; based on speech, syllables are produced; syllables, in turn, produce names; and only then do names manifest the meaning.
By means of this sequential principle, it is said that speech produces names and names are able to manifest meaning; such an establishment is logically necessary.

If one does not first place the name within the mind prior to the aggregates, then even if speech is uttered, it would lack definitive expression and would not cause others to generate an understanding of the meaning.
Furthermore, the Sūtra Master says:

"Alternatively, one should maintain that there exists a distinct entity of 'text' (vyañjana), and that the collection of these constitutes the 'bodies' of names and so forth; to further maintain that there are other [entities] would be useless."

This is also unreasonable, because there are no passages that function simultaneously; because, for this reason, the principle of a collective synthesis cannot be established; and because it is not the case that the meaning is not revealed within each individual passage.

Or, just as when trees and other great composite formations arise, it is not that shadows do not arise separately based upon them; although the shadow is manifested through convention (*prajñapti*), its substance is not conventional.

In the same way, these various texts should also be understood as names and phrases arising separately from a collection; although those names and phrases are manifested through convention, their substance is not conventional.
This is well stated, for the principle is thoroughly established.
If that were so, then all conventional phenomena (prajñaptidharma) should be able to be established as having an intrinsic nature (svabhāva). There is no such fault; why is this?

Since names also exist within a single syllable, there is no provisionally existent phenomenon that could disturb the formation of a single real entity; therefore, the provisional and the name are not analogous in meaning.
Since a name can also be obtained within a single syllable, how can one know that this name exists apart from the syllable?

In this way, a single syllable, like a meaningless syllable, has nothing to be expressed; it is only by depending on this as a condition that a distinct name arises, which is then able to signify a meaning.
However, because they are extremely close, their distinct characteristics are difficult to discern, just as it is difficult to distinguish between two colors of light on a wall.
If it is granted that sound itself can manifest meaning without there being separate entities such as names (nāman), what fault would there be?
Is it not a fault to contradict and undermine the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa)?
There is no sound that can be apprehended by the mind alone; syllables (vyañjana) and so forth are not like this, and therefore their essential natures are different.

However, there are instances where sounds are produced based on a common convention and one listens with attention, yet understands only the sound while failing to understand the meaning; subsequently, by means of this very [sound], one comes to understand it. It is not that the preceding cognition of the sound failed to understand the meaning, such that the subsequent cognition alone is able to understand the meaning through it. Therefore, we know that names and so forth exist separately from the sounds; the former mental state did not grasp the signified object because it had not yet attained [the name], whereas the latter mental state is only then able to understand the meaning once it has attained it.
If it is argued that this is not so, because the subsequent mind still understands the meaning by means of obtaining a specific quality of sound,
and this specific quality of sound is not distinct from sound itself—
this too is incorrect, because the principle that the convention of the signifier is identical to the specific quality of sound is not established.

If the convention established as the expressive designator were merely a particularity of sound, then it should be cognizable even without a shared convention, just like the particularities of color; for the distinction between the two colors blue and yellow does not require a shared convention before it is cognized.

Although no prior conventional designation for differentiation was established between the two colors, because the specific characteristics of blue and yellow are not distinct from color itself, once they have been apprehended by the visual consciousness, the mental consciousness is then able to differentiate between them through subsequent conceptualization.
Furthermore, it is logically untenable to establish a convention upon a convention; therefore, one should not say that [the sound] can express the convention.

Although it is not distinct from the sound itself, for one who has not previously established a convention, even though the sound is perceived, it cannot yet be discerned because it further depends on the establishment of another convention. This constitutes its distinctive characteristic when compared to other sounds.

Furthermore, if the convention established for the referent were merely a particularity of the sound itself, then one should have already understood all the distinctions between meaningful sounds and meaningless sounds even before the convention was mutually established; that is, one should have known that this particularity exists in one sound but is absent in other sounds.

Previously, when no conventional agreement regarding distinctions had been established, although the meaning was not understood upon hearing two sounds, one should nevertheless be able to discern the characteristics of the distinction between sounds that possess a conventional agreement and those that do not, just as one discerns the distinction between two colors.

Thus, we know that there exist distinct entities called the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*); these arise dependent upon sound and are capable of clearly manifesting meaning.
However, regarding this, the Sthavira further states:
"With mental action as the precursor, the specific arrangement of syllables within the temporal sequence of the produced sounds constitutes the names and so forth."
It is logically impossible for this [sound] to have a self-nature (svabhāva) that exists apart from sound itself.

Thus, by means of the preceding reasoning and scriptural authority, it should be made clear that the Sthavira’s statement is devoid of substance; it is not merely by his fabricated terminology that he can establish that sound is the very essence of names and so forth.

If it were possible to establish that sound is identical to its name and so forth merely through such fabricated verbal expressions, then one should likewise be able to establish that all phenomena whose distinct existence is universally acknowledged lack any distinct intrinsic nature.
That is to say, the very nature of moisture, when accumulated and congealed, is called the nature of solidity;
that same nature of solidity, when dispersed and dissolved, is called the nature of moisture;
and that same nature of solidity and moisture, when separated from cold, is called the nature of heat.
That is to say, when the aforementioned three natures undergo slight transformation, they are termed "mobile nature" (*calatva*).
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) cognized by visual consciousness is subsumed within the sense-base of odor (*gandhāyatana*);

likewise, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that possess objects of perception are termed "mind and mental factors" (*cittacaitta*). In this manner, all such [categories] should be established as valid.

Furthermore, since the meanings can also be understood through the manifest characteristics of fragrance, touch, and so forth, one should not establish that the collections of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) have sound as their essence. Therefore, in my teaching, there exist the three—names and so forth—which are distinct from sound and are capable of manifesting the underlying principles and meanings.
If one can correctly demonstrate even a small portion of what is incorrect, I should accept and adopt it; for the true meaning cannot be overturned merely by the empty words they have fabricated.
Furthermore, although they claim:

"As the Blessed One said that speech arises from vitarka and vicāra, and that speech does not arise without vitarka and vicāra, because sound produces sound, the three—name (nāman), phrase (pada), and syllable (vyañjana)—have no distinct substantial entities," this too is without fault, just as in the case of giving and so forth.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One experiences pleasure through giving.
This case should be understood in the same way: that which has speech as its cause is called "speech."
Furthermore, just as causes such as contact are themselves also called "contact" and so forth,

so too, although they claim that the groups of names, phrases, and syllables (nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya) are not universally known and are thus formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), when I am about to produce speech regarding them, since they are not universally known, upon what could that speech rely for its production?
This is also unreasonable, because in the world, even without the power of discrimination, there can still be cognitive engagement.
As it is said in the world:
"burnt by vegetables" or "rotted by mud."
Although that [consciousness] does not directly apprehend [the object], it is nonetheless capable of being an objective support;
this case should be understood in the same way. It is also like when one perceives light with the eye and yet says, "I do not clearly perceive the form."
Furthermore, when making the sound of clapping one's hands together, one says "making a sound" rather than "making a clap.
Likewise, those lacking wisdom merely say:
"By abandoning desire, one abandons excrement and urine."

As for the actual meaning: by abandoning desire, the birth-fluids emerge through the impure path; this can arouse the wind-mind, and the mind in turn arouses the wind, whereby the wind then effects the abandonment.

In this way, it is not that there is no cognition of names and so forth capable of discerning their meanings; rather, they cannot be known because the characteristics of the cognition of names and so forth are subtle.

Although an unsettled mind cannot distinguish, "This is the cognition of sound," "This is the cognition of names," or "This is the cognition of meaning," they are nonetheless not non-existent. Therefore, when carefully examining the distinct characteristics of all phenomena, the verbal expressions arising from the coarse minds of worldly beings are insufficient as proof.
Furthermore, ordinary people in the world cannot even know the domain traversed by their own introspective wisdom; therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has expounded it according to reality.
All those who grasp at a self, when they observe and perceive it, do so entirely with respect to the five aggregates of clinging.

Thus, if worldly people cannot even comprehend coarse and superficial matters unless they have heard them explained, how much less could they understand the subtle and profound sets of names, phrases, and syllables (nāma-kāya, pada-kāya, vyañjana-kāya) included within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*) without being shown? Therefore, what they say is certainly irrational.
Furthermore, the Sūtra-master says:
"Since momentary sounds cannot be accumulated, and no single phenomenon arises gradually part by part, how can the arising [of a word] be produced by speech?"
Furthermore, he explains it himself:
"How do they depend on the past moments of informative action (*vijñapti*)?
It is the final moment of informative action that can produce the non-informative (*avijñapti*)."
Furthermore, he raises a self-refutation:
"If that were so, then since the name (*nāman*) arises from the sound at the final moment, one should be able to understand the meaning by hearing only the final sound.

If one holds this position—that speech (*vāk*) produces the phoneme (*vyañjana*), the phoneme in turn produces the name, and only then does the name manifest the meaning—then the fault and objection herein should be the same as those stated previously, because the phonemes of successive moments cannot be accumulated.
If you claim that speech *manifests* (vyañjaka) names, this should be treated as an error, analogous to the case of [speech] producing [names].
Furthermore, whether it be that speech manifests or produces the phonemes (*vyañjana*), neither position is tenable when applied to names, just as in the case of speech itself.

This objection contradicts the tenet you yourself uphold; for you assert that the past and future lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and that sounds of successive moments cannot arise simultaneously. How, then, could phonemes constitute a word, or words constitute a sentence?
If each preceding moment successively assists the next until the final moment constitutes the phoneme, name, or phrase, then one should understand the meaning upon hearing only the final moment;
yet there is no mutual assistance, because past and future moments do not exist [simultaneously].
Since it is constantly a single thought-moment, how could they mutually assist one another?

Since there is no mutual assistance, the preceding and succeeding moments would be identical; thus, the subsequent moment would be like the initial thought-moment and should be unable to signify its object.
If hearing [the sound] later is the same as hearing it initially, it would follow that it is of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
Therefore, the position held by them—that sound itself is the expressive sign (*vācaka*) because the preceding and succeeding moments mutually support one another—is logically untenable.
In our school, all three time periods exist and are not non-existent; thus, the subsequent [moment] depends upon the preceding one to produce the name (*nāman*) and so forth.

Although names and so forth arise only at the final moment, one cannot comprehend their meaning merely by hearing them, because the sounds produced do not possess the complete auditory conditions for the conventional agreements regarding names and so forth that were previously established.
However, there are those who attain understanding upon hearing even a single sound; this is due to the force of habitual cultivation (*abhyāsa*).
By means of this, one may infer the rest; therefore, the Sūtra Master (Sthiramati) stated that [the opponent's view] is refuted and not [our own].
The *Vibhāṣā* states that each of the three—name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and phoneme (*vyañjana*)—has three types.
Regarding what is called "the three kinds," these are: name (*nāman*), name-body (*nāmakāya*), and multiple-name-body (*nāmakāyabahutva*).
The same applies to phrases (*pada*) and syllables (*vyañjana*).
A name has many states: it may arise from a single syllable, or from two syllables, or from many syllables.
Regarding "arising from a single syllable": when a single syllable is uttered, it can only be called a name (*nāman*); when two syllables are uttered, it is called a name-group (*nāmakāya*).
Alternatively, it is said that when three syllables are uttered, it is called a multiple-name-group (*bahunāmakāya*).
Some say: It is only when four syllables are uttered that one can speak of a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*).
As for that which arises from two syllables, when those two syllables are uttered, there can only be a "name" (*nāman*); [it cannot yet be called a name-group].
When four syllables are spoken, it is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*).
Alternatively, it is said that when six syllables are spoken, it is called a "multiple name-body" (*bahunāmakāya*).
Some say: It is only when eight syllables are uttered that one speaks of a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*).
Within the production of multiple syllables, when three syllables are produced, there is merely a "name" (*nāman*); it is only when six syllables are uttered that one speaks of a "name-group."
Some state: "When nine syllables are uttered, that is what is called a 'multitude of names' (nāmakāya). Others state:
When the twelve syllables are spoken, they are then called a "multitude of name-bodies" (*nāmakāya*).
Taking this as the gateway, one should explain the arising of other multitudes of syllables, name-bodies, and multitude-bodies according to reason.
Phrases (*pada*) also have multiple categories, namely: intermediate phrases, initial phrases, final phrases, short phrases, and long phrases.
If eight syllables form a name, it is called an intermediate phrase, because it is neither long nor short.

This refers to the thirty-two syllables situated in the middle, which give rise to four lines; these four lines constitute a *śloka*, and the literary compositions of the sūtras and śāstras frequently rely upon this numerical standard.
If a phrase consists of six syllables or more, it is termed an initial clause; if it consists of twenty-six syllables or fewer, it is termed a subsequent clause.
If it consists of fewer than six syllables, it is termed a short clause; if it exceeds twenty-six syllables, it is termed a long clause.
Furthermore, based on the intermediate case, three types are distinguished: when eight syllables are spoken, there is merely a *pada*; when sixteen syllables are spoken, it is called a *padakāya*.
Or, it is said that when twenty-four syllables are spoken, it is called a *bahupadakāya*.
Some say: it is only when thirty-two syllables are spoken that one refers to a "multitude of phrases" (*padakāya*).
Since a phoneme (*vyañjana*) is identical to a syllable (*akṣara*), there is only a single position.
When one syllable (*akṣara*) is spoken, there is merely a phoneme (*vyañjana*); when two syllables are spoken, it is called a "body of phonemes" (*vyañjanakāya*).
Alternatively, it is said that when three syllables are spoken, it is called a "multitude of bodies of phonemes" (*bahuvyañjanakāya*).
Some say: "It is only when four syllables are spoken that one may call it a 'multisyllabic word-group' (vyañjanakāya).
For this reason, one should state as follows:

When a single syllable is spoken, there is a name, but no body of names and no body of multiple names; there are no phrases, no body of phrases, and no body of multiple phrases; there is a phoneme, but no body of phonemes and no body of multiple phonemes.

When two syllables are spoken, there is a name and a name-body, but no multi-name-body; there are no phrases or the other two [categories]; there is a phoneme and a phoneme-body, but no multi-phoneme-body.
When four syllables are spoken, there are the three [factors] beginning with name, there are no three [factors] beginning with phrase, and there are the three [factors] beginning with phoneme.

When eight syllables are spoken, there are the three [factors] beginning with name; there is a phrase, but there is neither a phrase-body nor a multi-phrase-body; and there are the three [factors] beginning with phoneme.

When sixteen syllables are spoken, there are the three categories of name (*nāman*) and so forth; there is a phrase (*pada*), there is a phrase-body (*padakāya*), but there is no multiple-phrase-body; and there are the three categories of phoneme (*vyañjana*) and so forth.
When thirty-two syllables are spoken, each of the three—name, phrase, and phoneme—possesses its own three types.
Taking this as the gateway, the rest should be explained according to reason.
Having briefly analyzed these three, one should further investigate:
to which realm are such things as names (nāman) bound?
Is it included among the category of sentient beings or not?
Is it born of maturation (*vipākaja*), is it nurtured by growth (*aupacayika*), or is it of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*)?
Are they wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral?
All of these should be analyzed.
The verse says:
They are comprised within sentient beings of the desire and form realms; they are of the nature of outflow and are neutral.
The commentary states:
These three, beginning with "name" (nāman), are exclusively bound to the two realms of desire and form.

Regarding the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), some say it exists only in the stage of the first dhyāna, while others say it also extends through the three higher dhyānas; this distinction arises from whether one follows the verbal expression or the actual bodily basis (*āśraya*) to which it is bound.

If one speaks of these three as being bound according to the speech, when one is born in the desire realm and utters speech of the desire realm, the name-body (*nāmakāya*) and so forth of that speech are all bound to the desire realm.
The meaning expressed by that speech, however, may be bound to any of the three realms or may be unbound.

Furthermore, when one produces speech belonging to the first dhyāna, that speech and its names, etc., are bound to the level of the first dhyāna, while the body is bound to the desire realm; the meaning is as previously explained.
Likewise, if one born in the level of the first *dhyāna* produces speech belonging to two levels, it should be considered accordingly.
If one born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stage utters speech belonging to two stages, this should also be understood according to reason.

If it is said that these three [name, phrase, and syllable] are bound to the same stage as the body, this means that for one born in the desire realm or in the four dhyānas, name and so forth are each bound to their own respective stage, while speech may be bound to either its own stage or another stage; the meaning is as previously explained.
Furthermore, the three beginning with "name" (nāman) are comprised within the category of sentient beings, because non-sentient conditioned phenomena do not establish them.
That which establishes [them] is the speaker, not the meaning that is manifested; moreover, it establishes only the present, not the past or future.
Furthermore, the three beginning with "name" (nāman) are exclusively of the nature of outflow (niṣyanda), being neither nurtured (aupacayika) nor born of maturation (vipākaja).
As for the statement that name and the others arise from karma, this is because they are the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) produced by karma.

Furthermore, since the name and the other two [factors] are comprised solely within the category of non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) nature, when one who has severed the roots of goodness speaks of wholesome dharmas, although they acquire the names and so forth of wholesome factors, they do not actually possess wholesome dharmas.
Those who are free from sensual desire do not produce unwholesome states;
those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa) do not produce defiled states, because they produce the expressive names and so forth, which are not the expressed dharmas themselves.
As explained above, the remaining meanings concerning the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) that have not yet been discussed shall now be briefly analyzed.
The verse says:
"Similarly, the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*), as well as the formless realms (*ārūpya*) and maturation (*vipāka*)."
The acquisition (*prāpti*) and the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) pertain to all three categories; however, the non-acquisition is not the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of meditative concentration.
The Commentary states:

The phrase "likewise" is used to show that, like the sets of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) pertains to the desire and form realms, to sentient beings, and is an outflow, unobscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The inclusion of the term "and" (ca) regarding "formless" (ārūpya) indicates that it is not restricted solely to the desire and form realms;
the inclusion of the term "and" regarding "maturation" (vipāka) indicates that it is not restricted solely to outflowing (niṣyanda) results.
Thus, in terms of realm (dhātu), it pertains to all three; in terms of category (jāti), it pertains to both meanings.
What is maturation? It refers to the generic similarity (*nikāyasabhāga*) of rebirth in realms such as the hells, and among modes of birth such as the egg-born. What is outflowing?

This refers to all types of homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*), such as those pertaining to realms, stages, locations, castes, lineages, śramaṇas, brahmins, learners (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Other masters state:

among the various types of homogeneity, that which is projected by past karma is the homogeneity of maturation (*vipākaja-sabhāgatā*); that which arises from present application is the homogeneity of outflow (*naiṣyandika-sabhāgatā*); and both acquisition (*prāpti*) and the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) pertain to all three—namely, the momentary (*kṣaṇika*), the outflowing, and the maturational.
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are exclusively *niṣyanda* (outflow).

The word "exclusively" is used to clarify that they are not *vipāka* (maturation) or other types of results. As for the remaining factors that ought to have been mentioned but were not—namely, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*)—they are as previously explained; furthermore, the remaining meanings can be understood by analogy with what has already been stated.

This means that because it is taught that "attainment" (*prāpti*) and so forth are merely "accomplishment" (*siddhi*), they are included within the category of sentient beings; this meaning can be inferred accordingly. Furthermore, because it is taught that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) possess "arising" (*jāti*) and so forth, one can infer by analogy that these characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) apply to both sentient and non-sentient things. All other meanings have already been clarified as appropriate to each case; therefore, there is no need for further elaboration here.
The Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle Fourteen (Fascicle Fifteen).
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Seven: Distinguishing the Differences, Part Two, Section Seven. Having thus already explained the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).

Introduction: When a producing characteristic (*janaka-lakṣaṇa*) produces that which is produced (*janyadharma*), it does not do so apart from the conjunction of other causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*). Among these, what dharma is designated as a "cause-condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*)?
Briefly, there are six kinds of causes; what are the six?
The verse says: The efficient cause, the co-existent cause, the homogeneous cause, the associated cause, the pervasive cause,
and the ripening cause— these six alone are accepted as causes.
The treatise states:

This treatise maintains that causes are only of six kinds, neither more nor less: first, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); second, the coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); third, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); fourth, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*); fifth, the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*); and sixth, the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The nature of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) pervades all phenomena; therefore, it is explained first.
The nature of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); thus, it is placed second.

The remaining causes, such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and others, each include only a small portion within the category of the conditioned according to their respective applicability; they are explained in sequence for the sake of linguistic convenience.
Because phenomena depend upon them for their arising, they are called "causes. Since these six causes were not taught by the Buddha, how can this treatise establish such terminology on its own?
There is certainly no doctrine that was not spoken by the Great Master which the Abhidharma would venture to propound.
It does not appear in the sūtras because it is obscured;
however, since its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) can be apprehended, it must certainly exist.
Furthermore, in various sūtras, the Blessed One employs skillful means (*upāya*) to provide alternative explanations according to the capacities of those to be converted.
The masters of the Abhidharma, seeing a small portion of its characteristics, knew that it must certainly exist; for it was clearly compiled, and thus some have said:

"The meaning of these six causes was taught in the *Ekottarika-āgama* and the *Ṣaḍvarga-āgama*, but as a long time passed, the text became lost. The Venerable Kātyāyanīputra and others sought the characteristics of all phenomena through uninterrupted contemplation, and they were mysteriously moved by celestial beings who appeared and bestowed [the text] upon them—just as the gods bestowed the *Vatsasūtra*. This principle is necessarily so."

Although the meaning of the four conditions is fully set forth in this scriptural collection, there are those in other collections who do not recite it, because much has been lost over the long passage of time.
Since we observe that other sūtras contain some omissions, we know that this [sūtra] likewise does not present the matter in its entirety.
Furthermore, because the meaning of the six causes is explained scattered throughout various parts of the sūtras, it must certainly exist as a reality.
That is to say, as it is stated in the Sūtra:
"With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
Furthermore, as it is stated in another Sūtra:
Two causes and two conditions can give rise to right view.

Such factors as these constitute the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); for all phenomena possess the sense of being efficient causes toward others, and this cause is established because it produces [the effect] without obstruction.
As stated in a sutra:
"There are three path-factors that are accompanied by right view.
Furthermore, as another sutra states:
The conjunction of the three is contact (*sparśa*), which arises simultaneously with feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).

All such factors as these constitute the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perform a single function at the same time by way of mutual concomitance, this cause is established.
As it is said:
"Such a person is endowed with both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.

It should be understood that for such a person, while wholesome dharmas have disappeared and unwholesome dharmas have appeared, there still exist accompanying roots of goodness that have not been severed."
Because they have not been severed, there remains the possibility for further roots of goodness to arise from these roots of goodness.
Furthermore, it is said: "O Bhikṣus!"

If one frequently engages in vitarka and vicāra regarding various objects, the mind will frequently enter into those very objects; with ignorance as the cause, various defiled attachments arise, whereas with clarity as the cause, one becomes free from all defiled attachments.
All such factors as these are homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*). Past and present homogeneous dharmas are established as this cause because they draw forth their own effects.
As the Sūtra says:
"View is the root, associated with faith, realization, and wisdom."
Furthermore, as a sutra states:

"If there is discernment (*vijñapti*), there is cognition (*vijñāna*); it is only when one is in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that cognition is according to reality, not when one is not in concentration.

Such instances constitute the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*). Mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are associated because they perform a single function together; this cause is established on the basis of their collectively apprehending a single object.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"For those with wrong views, whatever bodily, verbal, and mental actions they perform, and whatever aspirations they have, are all in accordance with their views; all such formations belong to that same category, and thus all these dharmas are capable of bringing about results that are not desirable, not pleasant, and disagreeable."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
When any of the various views arise, they all take the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their root.
If this view arises, it cannot tolerate anything; this view can give rise to both craving and aversion.

All such factors as these constitute the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*). This cause is established because doubt, views, and ignorance—along with their associated and co-existent factors—that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin in the past and present, are able to give rise to all defiled phenomena of both similar and dissimilar types.

Because one category [of karma] can serve as the cause for producing results belonging to five categories, the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) is established in addition to the similar-type cause (sabhāga-hetu).
As the Sūtra states:
"If the action performed is wholesome and impure, and is produced through cultivation, one will experience its various maturations upon being born in that place."
Furthermore, as a sutra states:
"All intentional karmas that are performed and accumulated will certainly bring about maturation (*vipāka*).

Such factors as these are the causes of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*). All unwholesome and wholesome *sāsrava* (outflowing) dharmas are established as this cause because they bring about results of a different category.
These six causes have been taught by the Buddha in various places; however, those who harbor aversion and turn their backs on the Dharma fail to perceive them due to delusion.

Furthermore, in many sūtras, the Blessed One has taught the principles of simultaneous arising (*sahabhū-hetu*) and prior arising (*pūrva-janma-hetu*). One should understand that the meanings of the first two causes correspond respectively to the statements: "When this exists, that exists" (*asmin satīdaṃ bhavati*) and "From the arising of this, that arises" (*asyotpādād idam utpadyate*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One clearly explained the meaning of two kinds of causes within the sūtras, stating:
"Those who are dull-witted and dwell in ignorance perform even meritorious formations because of that ignorance."
This sūtra thus demonstrates that there is a cause from a previous life.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"With the eye and visible forms as conditions... [and so on,] up to: with the mind and mental phenomena as conditions, there arises an attention produced by delusion, which is defiled and turbid."
In this context, the delusion of the fool is ignorance (*avidyā*);
his longing is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); and the manifestation of craving is karma (*karman*).
This sūtra demonstrates that there is a co-arising cause, for it states within a single moment of mind that there are factors which serve as causes for one another in succession.
The sequence of ultimate meanings shall now be further determined.
Having briefly presented the causes, they shall now be explained in detail.
First, what is the characteristic of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)?
The verse says:
"Excluding itself, all else is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
The commentary says:
This efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is briefly of two kinds: first, that which possesses the power to produce; second, that which merely does not obstruct.

When all phenomena arise, with the exception of their own self-nature, all phenomena serve as their efficient cause because they do not act as obstructions during their arising; among these, a small portion possess the power to produce.

Furthermore, for instance, when a single visual consciousness arises, it takes the eye, which serves as its support, as its basis-cause (*āśraya-hetu*); it takes the perceived form, which serves as its object, as its establishing-cause (*pratisthā-hetu*); it takes the visual consciousness itself and so forth, which function like seeds, as its non-interruption-cause (*anuccheda-hetu*); it takes the associated mental factors as its sustaining-cause (*parigraha-hetu*); it takes the co-existent factors as its assisting-companion-cause (*sahāya-hetu*); and it takes the auditory faculty and so forth as its abiding-support-cause (*pratiṣṭhā-hetu*).
These are collectively designated as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). Among them, one part is called the "powerful cause" because it possesses the superior capacity to produce [the effect];
the remaining parts are called "powerless causes" because they merely abide without acting as obstacles.

Although other types of causes can also function as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the efficient cause has no further distinct designation; it is like the case where the general term for the sense-spheres of form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth serves as their specific names.
Why, then, is a thing's own self not its own efficient cause?
This is because the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) does not exist with respect to its own self-nature (*svabhāva*).
That is to say, the meaning of the efficient cause is "non-obstruction," yet a thing itself is always an obstruction to itself.
Furthermore, if all phenomena did not depend upon their own self-nature, they would necessarily be eternally established, as there would be no basis for their diminution or other modifications.
Other masters say:
If a self-nature were to have itself as its cause, then ignorance would take ignorance as its object, and so on, up to old age and death taking old age and death as their objects.
If this very thing were the cause of itself within a single moment, it would contradict the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Other masters say:

"Because a thing does not perceive its own utility within itself, it is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), just as, for example, a fingertip, a blade edge, or the eye [cannot act upon themselves]."

If, with the exception of its own self-nature, all other phenomena serve as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for this one phenomenon, then how could it be consistent with reason that even an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*) serves as the efficient cause for the Noble Path?

Furthermore, it is only at the moment of arising that [a phenomenon], by abiding without obstruction, can function as a cause; it should not be so in other states. It would not accord with correct reasoning for something to sometimes act as a cause for another and sometimes not.
At the stage when the Noble Path arises, that [non-obstruction] is necessarily its cause; therefore, it is not the case that it lacks a cause at other times.
If, regarding the arising of this [Path], something is capable of acting as an obstacle but does not do so, it may be established as a cause.
However, regarding that which has no obstructive function toward this [result] in the present life: even if it does not act as an obstruction, how can it be considered a cause?
It is because all phenomena possess obstructive power in relation to one another that they can serve as causes.
This means that where this one dharma exists, there is no possibility for a second to exist;
and even if this dharma were to exist elsewhere, there too it would be impossible for any other dharma to exist.
In this way, do not all these phenomena mutually act as obstructions?
Yet, because they do not so obstruct, they may all be established as *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient causes).
Even formless phenomena possess fixed conditions such as temporal dependence; therefore, they too possess the power of obstruction when considered in relation to one another.

Furthermore, when one phenomenon arises among all phenomena, just as there is no obstruction from other phenomena that possess desire, it is said that a phenomenon cannot arise due to two conditions: first, the absence of a concordant cause; second, the presence of an adverse condition.
When all phenomena arise, they necessarily depend upon specific causes and conditions of superior power, as well as the absence of other obstructing factors.

Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), phenomena arise because the productive cause exists and the obstructive cause is absent; therefore, it is solely by virtue of non-obstruction that all phenomena are designated as "efficient causes" (*kāraṇahetu*). This does not mean that a force capable of obstructing fails to do so.

Regarding the statement that "one who possesses the power of non-obstruction does not act as an obstruction," there is a slight distinction in the state of non-obstruction; for both possess the power of non-obstruction and equally lack any superior efficacy.
By this, all objections have already been dispelled.
If all phenomena are capable of acting as causes because they abide without obstruction, for what reason do all phenomena not arise simultaneously?
And when one person commits an act of killing, for what reason do all others not likewise incur the karma of killing, just like the killer?
It is only because there is no obstruction that they are said to be causes; they lack any superior efficacy.
How could contact with ashes, thorns, and the like be the cause of pleasant feeling?
It is not that contact with ashes and so forth is the cause of pleasant feeling; rather, it is the cause of that cause, meaning it belongs to the same category.
Painful sensation can serve as a cause for pleasant sensation; since painful sensation arises from contact with ash and the like, it is therefore a "cause-of-cause.
In this manner, regarding the mutual relationship between views and so forth, one should explain how even those possessing slight functional capacity are all causes.
Based on the brief indication of the principles regarding contact and sensation provided above, the remaining cases may be understood by analogy; there is no need for extensive elaboration.

Therefore, with respect to the fruit it produces, the *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient cause) is not merely non-obstructive, but also possesses a generative power. Nevertheless, because it lacks the direct cause (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the causal motivation (*samutthāna-pratyaya*), all phenomena cannot arise simultaneously, unlike the case where all those who kill necessarily incur the karma of killing.
Past dharmas act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the other two time periods; those dharmas of the two periods, in turn, are the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) of the past.
Future dharmas act as the efficient cause for the other two periods by virtue of non-obstruction.

Since those dharmas of the two periods [past and present] do not exist simultaneously with or subsequent to [the future], they do not serve as sovereign fruits (*adhipatiphala*) for the future; because a fruit must be appropriated by its cause, there are thus only two causes [that can produce such a fruit].
Based solely on the absence of obstruction, it is admitted that [the efficient cause] extends across all three time periods.
Present dharmas act as efficient causes for dharmas of the other two periods; within those two periods, only future dharmas serve as the effects of present [causes].

Conditioned phenomena are both cause and effect; conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are neither cause nor effect; unconditioned phenomena are neither cause nor effect; and unconditioned and conditioned phenomena are causes but not effects.

For this reason, it is said: the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is for the most part not the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*), because while all phenomena are efficient causes, only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are sovereign fruits.
Having thus explained the characteristics of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
what are the characteristics of the second [cause], the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)?
The verse says:
Coexistent factors are mutual fruits, as are the primary elements and their characteristics,
and the mind and its concomitants.
The treatise says:

If phenomena are mutually the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) of one another, those phenomena are also mutually the *sahabhū-hetu* (coexistent cause), because they arise by mutually assisting one another.
What are their characteristics?

Just as the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are mutually co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another, even though some possess an increase in substance while others do not, all three and one act as mutual causes for one another; for a self-essence (*svabhāva*) should not depend upon itself, nor should it depend upon a substance of the same kind (*sajātīya*).

Each of the primary elements (mahābhūta) depends solely upon the other three; it is only when the four primary elements aggregate as distinct categories that they possess the functional capacity to produce derived matter (upādāyarūpa).

Likewise, the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa) and that which is characterized (lakṣya), as well as the mind (citta) and its concomitants (cittānuparivartin), also serve as mutual causes for one another.
This is indeed the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), which, by being mutual effects, encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as appropriate.

The definition of the cause stated here is too narrow; for it should be said that the mental concomitants (*citta-anuvartin*) and the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are each mutually co-existent causes. Furthermore, one should not say that only those things which are mutual effects constitute the co-existent cause.
The primary dharma and its secondary characteristics (lakṣaṇānulakṣaṇa) are not mutual effects, yet they function as causes.
This constitutes the characteristic of being a cause; this [point] should be further analyzed.
For this reason, the statement regarding the characteristics should be examined.
Since the *Mūlaśāstra* states that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) may have a single fruit and serve as simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*), there is no fault in this.

However, it has never been seen stated in the *Mūlaśāstra* that matter which follows the mind (*cittānuvartirūpa*) acts as a cause for the mind; therefore, one should investigate the intention of the author of this treatise regarding this point.

Some masters say: This is a statement made with intentional omission; it reveals a fault in the treatise rather than establishing a proof, because a fault in a treatise is defined as a deficiency or omission in its meaning.
Other masters further say:

In this context, the author of the treatise does not intend to provide a full exposition of the characteristics of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); rather, he merely seeks to refute the tenets held by other schools.
