Specifically, in order to refute the attachment to the view that "there is only mind," he states that mental factors (*caitta*) exist apart from the mind.

Furthermore, in order to refute the attachment that karma consists solely of volition (*cetanā*) and that there is no such thing as non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*), he further states that there are bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind.

Again, in order to refute the attachment that the characteristics of birth and so forth are not substantially real entities, he further states that there are formations dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow the mind.

Is it not the case that you have already fully explained the characteristics of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), thereby further establishing the existence of distinct mental factors (*caitta*), bodily and vocal non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), and the characteristics of arising (*jāti*) and so forth?
Furthermore, since the characteristics of the co-existent cause have never been fully explained in other passages, to fail to explain them here would result in an omission.
Therefore, one should reflect as follows:

"In this context, I perceive this intended meaning: if a phenomenon necessarily arises simultaneously with the mind, pervading all states of mind and functioning in dependence upon the mind, then that phenomenon and its supporting mind are said to be *sahabhū-hetu* (simultaneous causes) in relation to one another."
The various mental factors (caitta-dharma) do not necessarily arise together; they may be few or many, as is observed in actual experience.
Furthermore, bodily and vocal actions are not present in all states of mind, for there are instances where neither is present when the mind is indeterminate (aniyata).

The characteristics such as arising and so forth all evolve in dependence upon the mind and do not depend upon one another; for arising and the rest all take the dharma as their primary factor and mutually support one another.
For this reason, it is not said that they are causes for one another.

Furthermore, herein, it is intended to show that only dissimilar types are taught as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), whereas it is established by implication that similar types act as mutual causes.
Moreover, it is to demonstrate that bodily and vocal actions depend solely upon the mind and not upon intimation (*vijñapti*), and for this reason, they are not stated to be causes of the mind.
Furthermore, the intention of that Great Virtuous One is difficult to discern; even those possessed of wisdom have not yet fully understood it. Consequently, some here form this view:

"Only the mind can serve as the co-existent cause for the matter that evolves concomitantly with the mind, but matter cannot [be the cause] for the mind. This is because matter arises from the mind and originates dependent upon the mind, just as a king and his ministers [relate]; the superior does not depend on the inferior."
This calculation is irrational, because the minister and the king possess mutual power in their roles of defense and support.
What is the nature of the dharmas that follow the mind?
The verse says:
The two types of mental factors (*caitta*) and their characteristics, as well as those of the mind itself,
are the phenomena that follow and revolve with the mind (*cittānuvartin*).
The treatise says:

All factors associated with the mind—namely, the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the untainted (*anāsrava*) states, the two types of restraint (*saṃvara*), as well as the characteristics such as arising of those factors and of the mind itself—are all called "factors that follow the mind" (*cittānuvartaka-dharma*).
For what reason are their secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) not mentioned?
The reason for this omission shall be explained later in due course.
For what cause are these factors termed "conforming to the mind" (*cittānuvartin*)?
The verse says:
"By way of time, fruit, wholesomeness, and so forth.
The commentary says:
Briefly stated, it is called "concomitant with the mind" (cittānuvartin) due to ten conditions, such as time, fruit, and so forth, including virtue.
First, regarding time: this means that it arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the mind, and belongs to the same temporal period.
"By way of result, etc. means that this [mental factor] shares the same result, outflow, and maturation as the mind.
"By way of being wholesome, etc. means that this shares the same nature—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—as the mind.
Is it not the case that by merely stating that a single lifetime abides and ceases, one already knows that it likewise falls within a single world-period (*adhvan*)?
Although one thus knows it falls within a single world-period, one has still not yet fully understood whether this dharma and the mind exist in the past or the future.
Nor are they mutually dissociated.
Alternatively, in order to demonstrate that these are dharmas that do not arise, it is further stated that "they fall within a single time period.
If this were so, one should simply have said "falling within a single time period."
If it were not so, one would not be made to know that [the result] necessarily falls within a single lifetime.

Furthermore, since both outflowing (*niṣyanda*) and ripening (*vipāka*) results are also subsumed under the category of "one result," why are outflowing and ripening results mentioned separately from "one result"?

It is indeed so. In this context, when it says "one fruit," it refers only to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*). But does this statement not apply generally, such that it would also include the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*)?
Although this is also subsumed under the category of "speech," it is not what is being elucidated here.

Furthermore, there are four types of *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruits of human effort): simultaneous, immediate, subsequent, and non-arising. This [text] clarifies that it is not a fruit co-existent with its cause, in order to refute the exclusive attachment to the view that the *puruṣakāra-phala* exists within a composite aggregate (*saṃghāta*) that arises simultaneously with its cause. Since the members of such a composite aggregate are mutually fruits of one another, and because a thing itself cannot be its own *puruṣakāra-phala*, this demonstrates that it is not that [composite] which arises simultaneously.

Within the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), there is the sense of being a single fruit; for this reason, the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) are mentioned separately.
One should know that in this context, "single time" and "single fruit" differ in their meaning: the former indicates simultaneity, while the latter indicates commonality.

Among these, even the most minimal mental king (citta-rāja) acts as a co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) for fifty-eight factors; that is to say, the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma), their forty primary characteristics (mūla-lakṣaṇa), and the eight primary and secondary characteristics of the mind—these are called the fifty-eight factors.
Among the fifty-eight [factors], excluding the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) of mind, the remaining fifty-four are co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the mind.
For what reason are the secondary characteristics of mind not co-existent causes for the mind?

Because the mind does not arise by virtue of their power, because the mind and they do not stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect, and because they possess efficacy toward a single dharma;
furthermore, because they do not share the same fruit as the mind-king (*cittarāja*), and because within the aggregate, the majority of factors are not their fruits.
Precisely because of these many stated reasons, according to their respective characteristics, they are not called "mental concomitants" (cittānuvartaka-dharma).
If that is so, how can the mind serve as a co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) for them?

Because the [mental] states such as arising and so forth undergo transformation in accordance with the mind-king (*cittarāja*), should one not understand that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their arising and so forth likewise take the mind as their co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*)? That is to say, just as derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is not the result of arising and so forth, yet arising and so forth are not non-co-existent causes for the primary elements, this case should be understood in the same way.
The reasoning in such examples is inconsistent; for that which is a successive fruit—whether one or many—is not the fruit of those [elements].

It is not the case that derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is subsumed under any single fruit among the successive fruits of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). How could it be permissible to claim that derived matter is not a fruit of the primary elements' arising and so forth? To use this as an analogy constitutes a fallacy.
Furthermore, it is as previously stated.
What was stated previously?
That the mind cannot arise by virtue of that power.
However, since the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) arise through their mutual influence, this fault does not apply.
Other masters say:

among the fifty-eight factors, only fourteen can serve as causes for the mind—namely, the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) together with the four primary characteristics of the mind. The characteristics such as arising and so forth do not have the power to serve as causes for the mind, unlike the primary characteristics that follow the mind.
If that were so, it would contradict the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, which states:

"There may be a truth of suffering that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but is not itself the cause of the view of a self-identity—namely, all other defiled truths of suffering, excluding the future view of a self-identity and its associated factors, as well as their arising, aging, duration, and impermanence."

There are some who hold that the truth of suffering has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause and also serves as the cause for the view of a self-identity; these are the factors excluded [from the category of "associated"]. They argue:
"We do not recite those [factors] and their associated dharmas, because one should only recite and uphold the treatises after having first analyzed them according to their underlying principles."

Otherwise, the definition of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) would be undermined, or one would have to admit that even the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are co-existent causes of the mind.
Furthermore, some say:
"All factors gathered together are mutually co-existent causes for one another, because within such a collection, if even one factor is missing, the remaining phenomena will not arise."
Among these various explanations, the first is the best.
Furthermore, within this co-arising assemblage, there are those that are primary movers (pravartaka) rather than secondary followers (anuvartaka), namely the mind-king (citta-rāja);
and there are those that are exclusively secondary followers, namely matter (rūpa) and the formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).

There are those that are both the primary mover (*pravartaka*) and the concomitant mover (*anuvartaka*, *anuvartin*), namely the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), because they follow the mind in their movement and because they can move the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
There are two cases where neither is the case, namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
How can there be the principle of cause and effect within a collection of dharmas that arise simultaneously?
For what reason is it known that such [causality] does not exist?

Since dharmas arising simultaneously have not yet arisen at the stage immediately preceding their birth, they should all equally be non-existent; how, then, can one speak of a producer and a produced?
Furthermore, it is said that where there is a cause, there is an effect.
If dharmas in the future were able to arise [independently], there would be the fallacy that all dharmas would arise at all times.
Moreover, regarding simultaneously arising dharmas, there is no definitive proof for which is the cause and which is the effect, just as with the two horns of an ox.
Furthermore, in worldly matters where seeds and sprouts are universally established as causes and effects arising in succession, such simultaneous causality has never been observed.
Therefore, it must now be explained how the principle of cause and effect can exist within a collection of dharmas that arise together.
Now, we shall first explain the characteristics of cause and effect, so that one may understand the existence of simultaneously arising causes and effects.

That is to say, among the various characteristics of causes briefly mentioned above, the Blessed One has stated in many sūtras: "When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises."
The opposite of this—neither existing nor arising—is what is called the general characteristic of cause and effect.
Herein, the former [passage] clarifies the meaning of the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), while the subsequent text further clarifies the meaning of the previously arisen cause (*pūrvaja-hetu*).
If that is so, there would certainly be no co-arising cause; for the Blessed One taught that "this being, that exists," and since the future does not exist, how could it serve as a cause?
This objection is not valid, because there is no multiplicity [of dharmas] and because the future is not non-existent; this shall be discussed in detail later.
Furthermore, this sūtra proves the existence of the future, or else that [opponent] should state a sūtra whose meaning does not contradict reason.
Regarding this, the Elder (Sthavira) explains the meaning of the Sūtra as follows:
"When this exists, that exists" means that the causal continuity must first exist, and only then does the resultant continuity abide.
Which arises first?
Which, having arisen, abides?
To answer this, it is further stated: "Because this arises, that arises."
This demonstrates that because the arising of the cause precedes it, the subsequent arising of the effect continues in succession.
Thus, the Sthavira merely follows his own whims to falsely interpret the Buddha’s sūtras in order to support his own position.
Such an interpretation of the Buddha’s sutras lacks a definitive reason that can serve as proof.

That is to say, what definitive reason serves as proof for the statement "when this exists, that exists"? It is said merely with reference to the continuity of cause and effect, not with reference to each individual momentary cause and effect.
That for every single moment of cause there is a corresponding single moment of fruit accords with correct reasoning;
it is not the case that the continuity of the fruit arises only after the continuity of the cause has ceased, for that would contradict correct reasoning.
Furthermore, what he has stated lacks any superior reasoning; it is not an explanation preceded by insight, nor can it elucidate the profound meaning of the sūtra.
If he argues that because momentary cause and effect are difficult to perceive, he speaks instead of continuous cause and effect, this too is incorrect, as such a thing is impossible.

This means that it is impossible for a causal continuum to arise from a resultant moment without an intervening gap, nor is it possible for a resultant continuum to arise from a causal moment without an intervening gap.

If it were as that [other] explanation suggests, it would imply that the Blessed One’s teaching was not rational, or else that this sutra was not spoken with reference to the causality of the continuum.
Such an explanation makes the meaning of dependent origination difficult to comprehend; therefore, they ought to provide another interpretation for the meaning of this sutra.
Furthermore, by what reasoning is it definitively determined that the former sutra speaks in terms of a continuum (*saṃtāna*), while the latter does not?
The latter sutra should also be explained in this way:
"Because this arises, that arises" means that first there is a causal continuum, and subsequently a resultant continuum comes to abide.

In that school’s doctrine, there is no distinction between the meaning of "arising" (*utpāda*) and "being about to arise" (*utpatsyamāna*), just as there is no difference between the time when something is about to be born and the time when it is about to emerge.
Furthermore, regarding the question you have raised:
which comes first, the agent of arising?

To claim that "that which has already arisen abides" is also illogical, because the two modes—the preceding and the succeeding—do not depend upon one another, and the referents dependent upon each mode differ.

It is not the case that the previously stated principle, "dependent on this, that exists," requires the subsequent statement, "because this arises, that arises," for its meaning to be understood. This is because the previous statement, "dependent on this, that exists," does not require the inquiry, "what arises, such that that arises? nor does it require the subsequent explanation, "because the cause arises, the effect arises," for the former meaning to be fully realized.

Just as it will be explained later that "because this arises, that arises," which requires the inquiry "what arises so that that arises? and further requires a specific explanation that "because the cause arises, the effect arises" for the meaning to be clear;

likewise, the previously stated principle that "dependent on this, that exists" also requires the inquiry "dependent on what does that exist? and further requires a specific explanation that "dependent on the cause, the effect exists" for the meaning to be clear.

Therefore, since that which is depended upon before and after is distinct in each case, my explanation—that the first sūtra reveals the meaning of the co-arising cause (*sahaja-hetu*) and the subsequent sūtra further reveals the meaning of the previously arisen cause (*pūrvaja-hetu*)—is logically established.
He further explains the meaning of this sūtra through another method:
"The preceding sūtra is intended to reveal that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) have causes, while the subsequent sūtra is intended to refute the attachment to a permanent cause.
This too is irrational, because it is established that both methods apply to the subsequent sūtra as well.
This means that because the Sūtra speaks only of "this arising" and "that arising," both matters are established together.

By stating that cause and effect arise in succession, it reveals that formations (*saṃskāra*) have causes, thereby refuting theories of causelessness. Because of the term "arising," it reveals that the cause is impermanent, which likewise serves to refute theories that posit a permanent cause, for no eternally abiding phenomenon can ever undergo arising.
Since both matters are established by the latter explanation, the former sūtra would then be rendered useless.
As it is not the case that the Bhagavān teaches useless sūtras, we know that the two sūtras are not to be interpreted according to that [former] explanation.

Even if one were to accept such an interpretation of the preceding sutra, it would not contradict the meaning of the co-nascent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); that is to say, based precisely upon this co-nascent cause being present, it is able to bring about the presence of its co-nascent effect.
Does this not demonstrate that conditioned phenomena have causes, thereby refuting the theory of causelessness?

As will be stated later, "because this arises, that arises," this demonstrates that the cause is impermanent and thus refutes the theory of an eternal cause, without contradicting the teaching of prior arising as the cause.

Thus, the previously stated principle that "this being, that exists" (asmin satīdaṃ bhavati) serves to demonstrate that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) have causes; it also refutes those who propound causelessness (ahetuvāda), yet it does not contradict or undermine the teaching of simultaneous arising as a cause.
Furthermore, since the cause of a prior birth exists only when it is currently present and does not exist in the future, there would be nothing at all that could arise.
Since that school itself asserts that the future does not exist, and thus nothing can arise, how could the Sugata have clearly taught that "this being, that comes to be"?
Thus, there is this statement:
"This is a qualified statement; the meaning of what is stated exists and is currently established as such.
Therefore, that statement of his is also a qualified statement."
The object that is said to exist must also be presently existent, because no cause for its being distinct from this [present existence] can be found.
Such a corroborative example (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta) is fully established for both parties, just as when one says: "that form is in the state of currently ceasing."
Furthermore, there has never been a case where, regarding something universally established as non-existent, one makes a specific distinction and says that it exists;
how then can one make a specific distinction regarding a future non-entity and say that it exists, while within that same specific distinction, also say that it does not exist?
What has been stated thus contradicts correct reasoning.
Furthermore, since you admit that future dharmas possess causes, their substance must exist even though they lack functional activity.
If you do not admit that the future possesses causes, you must concede that it is absolutely non-existent, like a rabbit's horn.
Since you admit that causes exist, you must also necessarily admit that future entities exist, as they differ from absolute non-existence.
There are many types of meanings for what is called "non-existent":
the unarisen, the ceased, the absolutely non-existent, and mutual non-existence.

The statement that [dharmas] in the first two periods (the future and the present) are "non-existent" refers only to the absence of their activity; therefore, dharmas in the future period do not lack their substantial essence entirely. Thus, they can possess the sense of being "that which produces" and "that which is produced. Although activity is absent at the precise moment of arising, they still possess the functional capacity to produce the dharma that is to be produced.
Furthermore, I do not admit that either unarisen causes or already-arisen causes are true agents, because phenomena possess no true agency.
True agency refers to the capacity of causes and conditions to constantly produce their respective effects.
This notion of a "true causal operation" (tattvika-kāritra) is not accepted by the Buddha.

Rather, the arising of all phenomena is mutually dependent; if any factor is lacking, the others do not arise. This does not mean that one thing's non-arising constitutes the sense of another thing's arising.
Based on this measure, this is stated to be the cause; since the functional capacity of this cause does not exist at all times, there is no fault of all phenomena arising at all times.
Furthermore, I do not maintain that co-nascent causes alone, without depending on other causes, can produce phenomena; therefore, there is no fault of all phenomena arising at all times.
Furthermore, as for those who assert that only the previously arisen cause exists, how could they alone claim to be free from such faults?
Since that previously arisen cause would exist at all times, it follows that all phenomena should arise at all times.
Whatever cause is asserted to be capable of producing phenomena, all such [causes] can be subject to these same logical difficulties.

However, as for those who falsely cling to the theory of the *anugata-dhātu* (the pervasive element), they maintain that there is always present an infinite number of causes for the production of phenomena; would this not uniquely bring upon your own school the fault of all phenomena being produced instantaneously at all times?

If you maintain that although only the preceding cause produces an effect, it can do so only by depending on other conditions, why do you not also allow that this co-arising cause can likewise produce phenomena only by depending on other conditions, just as you maintain that only the preceding cause can produce all phenomena?
However, they do not arise constantly; the same applies to the future, so this should not be raised as an objection.

To claim that for simultaneously arising phenomena there is no definitive proof of cause and effect—comparing them, for instance, to two horns—is entirely unreasonable, because we observe that when one of two horns is destroyed, the other does not necessarily follow suit.
If the destruction of one follows the destruction of another, they may be compared as being produced by mutual influence, like the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Furthermore, I do not admit that all co-arising phenomena possess the relationship of being mutual causes and effects; which ones, then, do you admit?
This principle applies only when there is a single common fruit or a reciprocal fruit, or when one phenomenon arises through the power of another.

Such a relationship of cause and effect exists among simultaneously arising phenomena; however, this is not the case for the two horns of an ox as described above. Therefore, they cannot be cited as a valid example by way of shared properties (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Furthermore, the Abhidharmikas do not maintain that there is a definitive rule for co-arising factors to be mutually effects, such that one is exclusively the cause and the other is exclusively the effect;
rather, they maintain that within such a composite assemblage, all members are both causes and effects in relation to one another. Therefore, one should not demand a fixed causal determination.

Furthermore, just as those who maintain that only preceding [moments] are causes admit that some preceding moments are not causes— meaning it is not the case that all preceding moments lack causality— so too,
those who maintain that simultaneous [moments] are causes admit that some simultaneous [moments] are not causes— meaning it is not the case that all simultaneous moments lack causality.

Furthermore, there is another analogy that proves the cause of simultaneous arising; therefore, the reason established by the opponent suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is because it is observed in the world that a lamp and its light arise simultaneously, yet they stand in a relationship of cause and effect.
Furthermore, by what reason is it proven that the lamp is the cause of light?
It is because light undergoes variations—increasing or decreasing, remaining still or moving—in accordance with the lamp.
Moreover, those who desire light take up the lamp, and those who loathe light destroy the lamp.
I also allow that light arises dependent upon a lamp; however, I do not allow that it arises simultaneously with that lamp.

Why is this? Because light and lamp arise together, it is impossible for the light to wait for the lamp before it is produced; it is not logical for dharmas that arise simultaneously to be mutually dependent.

Just as a thing does not arise from itself by depending upon itself, but rather the subsequent moment of light arises immediately after due to the preceding lamp serving as its condition, this [example] should not be cited as an analogy.
This too is unreasonable, because when a lamp first arises, it is impossible to find a lamp that is devoid of light.
That is to say, one has never seen a case where a lamp exists at a time when there is no light; therefore, [your position] is unreasonable.
If it is argued that [the object] cannot be apprehended because the duration is too brief, this is also not the case, for it is not universally established (*prasiddha*).

If there were even a slight instance of the lamp of ignorance that is universally established in the world, and someone were to question why it cannot be apprehended, one might reasonably answer: "It cannot be apprehended because the duration is too brief."
However, since the lamp of even the slightest ignorance is universally established in the world, one should not say that it is impossible to perceive [the lamp] due to the brevity of time.

If you admit that the lamp and its light always arise simultaneously, then you should not say that the lamp is the cause of the light, because both the lamp and the light would be produced from a single cause.
That is to say, since oil, the wick, and so forth serve as the causes for the lamp, they should likewise serve as the causes for the light.
Thus, since these two arise from the same cause, just as the lamp does not arise dependent upon the light, the light should likewise not arise dependent upon the lamp.

Furthermore, there is an analogy showing that things do not arise through mutual dependence: for example, the three factors—the sesame seed, its husk, and the person handling it—combine and arise from a single cause; they are not reciprocal causes, as this is universally established in the world.
The same applies to the lamp and its light: because they arise from a single cause, it is logically impossible for the light to take the lamp as its simultaneous cause.

The lamp and its light cannot arise from one and the same cause; just as when the husk, the kernel, and the oil are present within a sesame seed, one does not see the husk, the kernel, and the oil arising together from a single cause such that they could stand in a relationship of cause and effect.

There are two kinds of lamps: those perceived directly before one's eyes and those that follow as causes. These serve as evidence for the existence of cause and effect; therefore, it cannot be said that they arise from a single identical cause.

Furthermore, it is universally established that there is a distinction among the causes of various phenomena that arise simultaneously with a preceding factor. That is to say, when a single type of factor precedes, the various co-arising phenomena within the sprout—namely its color, odor, taste, and tangibility—have distinct causes.

Since color, fragrance, taste, and tangibility all arise simultaneously within a single sprout, yet each has its own distinct cause, we know that the lamp and its light, which also arise simultaneously, must likewise not be produced by a single cause.

If the lamp and its light were produced from a single cause, then when an object were used to cover the lamp, the light—just like the lamp—should not cease its continuity; and since the lamp would be like the light, it too should not arise.
In the case of sesame seeds, the husks and the human fat do not arise from a single cause; even when one of these conditions is obstructed and fails to arise, the other can still be produced.
This is not the case with a lamp and its light; therefore, their causes are different.
If it is argued that the substance of the lamp and its light are not distinct, this does not contradict our [position on] co-arising causes.

Furthermore, because the flame and the light are not of the same nature (*dharmatā*), their substances are different; they function as cause and effect due to the previously mentioned reasons such as concomitance.
Therefore, the analogy of the lamp and its light is fully established in meaning.

Furthermore, since one is seen to enter the meditative absorption of cessation while feeling aversion toward the two dharmas of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), mental factors such as volition (*cetanā*) likewise cannot arise, just as sensation and perception do not; this is because it is taught that within this absorption, mental formations (*manasaḥ saṃskārāḥ*) have ceased.

Based on this, by analogy with the observation that volition (*cetanā*) and other mental factors arise in association with feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), we know that for all phenomena, there exists a co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) external to their previously arisen causes.
However, the Sthavira says:

"Mental factors such as volition cannot arise within the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) because they share the same causes for the arising of feeling and perception; it is not because they arise through being mutual causes (*anyonya-hetu*)."
What is meant by the cause common to both?

If it is argued that this is "contact" (sparśa), then it should exist in this state, because they maintain that mental activity (citta-pravṛtti) exists within the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
If this [consciousness] is the basis, it exists in this state as well, because all mental factors arise in dependence upon consciousness.
Since the common cause is present, why do those [mental factors] not arise?
Furthermore, one would have to abandon the theory that [mental factors] arise sequentially; for you admit that contact (*sparśa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) serve as their causes.

Consequently, it should not be argued that volition (*cetanā*) and other factors do not arise simply because they share the same causes for the arising of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).

Furthermore, because we observe that although causes may be identical, they do not necessarily arise simultaneously, we know that those which must arise together are certainly mutually dependent as causes.
That is to say, because consciousness arises from the eye and visible forms that have previously existed, an immeasurable number of visual consciousnesses can all potentially arise.

Although the causes for the arising of these [consciousnesses] are the same, they do not arise simultaneously because they do not arise by acting as mutual causes for one another; rather, it is only from a preceding consciousness that a subsequent consciousness arises, and not from a subsequent consciousness that a preceding consciousness arises.
From this verification it is known that although the causes for arising may be common, those that do not depend upon one another do not necessarily arise simultaneously;
if they necessarily arise simultaneously, they must certainly arise through mutual dependence.
By this, the principle of simultaneous causality is fully established.

Furthermore, it was previously stated that within a sprout, form and other factors arise simultaneously, each with its own distinct cause; therefore, one should know that although their originating causes differ, they still possess the principle of arising sequentially and simultaneously.
Therefore, whether [factors] arise together or do not arise together is not necessarily determined by whether their causes are identical or different.
Furthermore, it is taught that mind and mental factors arise from the same cause, and it is also taught that there is a causal relationship between them at the very moment they arise together.
This means that it is taught that mental factors (*caitta*) and visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) arise with the same causes, namely the eye and visible form; therefore, the Sūtra states:
"With both the eye and visible form as conditions, various mental factors arise."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
Thus, these two sūtras state that the mind and mental factors arise from the same causes.
Furthermore, it is taught that all mental factors (caitta-dharma) arising simultaneously depend upon the mind for their production; thus, the Sūtra says:

"Whether it be perception (saṃjñā) or volition (cetanā), all mental factors are of the same nature as the mind, they rely upon the mind, they are bound to the mind, and they function in dependence upon the mind."

It is not the case that mental factors do not arise simultaneously with the mind; for there is the sense of being dependent upon and following the mind, since that which is non-existent and that which exists cannot constitute the relationship of the supported and the support.
This meaning shall be further explained later.
Therefore, it is certain that there exists a co-nascent cause (*sahaja-hetu*).

Furthermore, if the co-nascent cause were definitively non-existent, it would be impossible to establish the relationship between the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).

That is to say, if the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), such as the eye, arise solely in dependence upon previously arisen primary elements, then since the primary elements and the eye would share the same set of primary elements as their cause, for what reason is the derived matter exclusively the eye and not the primary elements themselves?
Furthermore, this would contradict the Sūtra, wherein the Blessed One addressed those who go naked, saying:
"I never say that for one who undergoes manifold sufferings, suffering arises without cause and without condition."
If one maintains that all phenomena possess only antecedent causes and lack simultaneous causes, then one must admit that suffering does not arise at the time when its causal conditions are present;
for by the time suffering arises, its causal conditions would already have ceased to exist. This would contradict what was previously stated in the sūtra.
Furthermore, this would contradict the correct principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), as stated in the Sūtra:
"With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises.

In that case, the eye and forms of the preceding moment would not be the support (*āśraya*) or the object (*ālambana*) of the subsequent visual consciousness; yet, since they exist at one time and do not exist at another, they are not absolutely non-existent, and thus it can be said that these [preceding factors] are indeed the support and the object.

This case should also be understood in the same way: when that visual consciousness arises, the eye and the visible object have already ceased; therefore, the visual consciousness would arise spontaneously without the power of an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because there can be no basis (*āśraya*) for a non-existent dharma, and because visual consciousness takes only a present object as its condition.

If the eye, visible forms, and visual consciousness did not arise simultaneously, then the eye and visible forms would not be conditions for visual consciousness; or else, the ear, sounds, and so forth would also be conditions for visual consciousness, since they would equally lack any connection with visual consciousness.

If the Bhagavān were to teach that visual consciousness arises solely with the eye and visible forms of a preceding life as its conditions, then he should have taught that visual consciousness takes only consciousness as its condition; for [consciousness] is a strong condition of its own kind, like a seed, and because a preceding consciousness serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for a subsequent consciousness.

Since it is not stated that consciousness is a condition for visual consciousness, we know that in this context only the simultaneously arising eye-faculty and visible object are said to be the conditions for visual consciousness. Because two consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously within a single body, consciousness is not stated to be a condition for visual consciousness.

If it is argued that this passage speaks only of the unique conditions (*asādhāraṇa-pratyaya*) of visual consciousness, then since the preceding moments of the eye and visible forms—and likewise the ear and sounds—are not factors belonging to visual consciousness, there is no difference in their status; why then are only the eye and visible forms considered unique conditions, while the ear and sounds are not?

Furthermore, it must necessarily be so, because the sixth consciousness lacks a distinct, simultaneously arising basis (*āśraya*) and object (*ālambana*). It is taught that consciousness arises only by taking the previously arisen mind (*manas*) as its basis and object, unlike the other [sensory] consciousnesses.
Furthermore, the various consciousnesses do not take only what has previously arisen as their object, because a sūtra states:
"With the mind and mental phenomena as conditions, mental consciousness arises. This is because mental consciousness takes all three time periods as well as unconditioned phenomena as its objects.
By this, it is definitively established that the condition of co-arising exists; this principle is thoroughly proven.
Furthermore, this sutra states:
"The coming together of the three is contact."
Because it is clearly established as a realization:
if visual consciousness has arisen and the eye and visible objects have already ceased, with what does the visual consciousness then come into conjunction?

If one were to say that the five types of contact are like mental contact, this is also not the case, because the power of mental consciousness is strong and it universally comes into conjunction with all phenomena.

Although the mental consciousness and its object do not arise simultaneously, it is not the case that their essence lacks the meaning of conjunction, for in our school, the three time periods and the three unconditioned phenomena are all substantially existent;
in your school, however, since only phenomena of the present time exist, the meaning of conjunction cannot be established.
Furthermore, for those who reject the notion of co-emergent causes (*sahaja-hetu*), from what cause would the first untainted phenomenon (*anāsrava-dharma*) arise?
For such a prior cause has never previously existed.

If it is argued that the pure realm (*viśuddha-dhātu*) exists primordially, then since the cause is eternally present, by virtue of what obstacle has the fruit of the untainted phenomenon never yet arisen?
If you say that it further relies on the assistance of other conditions, then why is that which it relies upon not itself considered the cause?
Furthermore, one should pointlessly raise such an objection as to why one does not instead maintain that [the effect arises from] Īśvara and so forth.

If it is argued that one must wait for a transformation within the continuum, this reasoning is also incorrect, because there are faults whether [the continuum] is different from or identical to the pure realm (*viśuddhadhātu*).

That is to say, if they were different, the same objection as before would apply: why does this very transformation not serve as the cause? How, then, can you still maintain that the pure realm is the seed?
Alternatively, one should raise this objection as being in vain:
"If it is like taking a purgative and then having a deity descend to cause its effect,
if you say [the mind] is one, then since its prior and subsequent states are identical, it should ultimately lack the function of producing untainted (anāsrava) results."
However, since there is no cause for that difference between the prior and subsequent states, it cannot possess such differences spontaneously without a cause.

If one were to say it is like a seed that undergoes transformation upon depending on conditions—wherein a homogeneous seed, through the gathering and assistance of auxiliary conditions such as soil and so forth, may continue in succession and only achieves its transformational difference after waiting for the proper time—[then this would be acceptable].

If the uncontaminated seeds of the pure realm that you maintain exist as contaminated, then maintaining them is futile; for a contaminated phenomenon cannot serve as the seed of an uncontaminated one, nor can an uncontaminated phenomenon serve as the seed of a contaminated one.
If it were untainted (*anāsrava*), how could one who has fundamentally accomplished the noble path (*āryamārga*) fall into the evil destinies?
Could one who has accomplished the noble path still be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?
It is not the case that the noble path does not arise within the state of an ordinary person, for at such a time one may indeed be designated as an ordinary person.

If you argue that this fault does not apply because [the afflictions] are few, then they cannot serve as the cause for the arising of the antidote to those firmly accumulated afflictions from beginningless time.
Furthermore, there is no need for further laborious analogies, as the Sūtras have already refuted what they maintain.
As the Blessed One said:
"I truly do not see even a hair’s tip of white dharma remaining in Devadatta," and so forth at length.
The Blessed One himself stated that the roots and seeds of white dharma within Devadatta’s body have been extracted without remainder; therefore, this sutra further states:

There are accompanying wholesome roots that have not yet been severed; because they have not been severed, it remains possible for further wholesome roots to arise from them. At a later time, however, all of those will be severed.

Now it should be explained: apart from severing those roots of goodness, what further factor remains that has not been completely uprooted, such that one lacks a sense of conscientious regard and is unable to believe and accept the meaning taught within the Buddha’s dispensation?

It cannot be maintained that because a pure realm (*viśuddhadhātu*) exists within a great mass of wood, it likewise exists within the bodies of sentient beings; for this would entail the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Just as a great mass of wood may be rendered pure or defiled according to another's desire, so too should sentient beings be admitted to become either pure or defiled according to another's will. Furthermore, once the noble dharmas have arisen from the uncontaminated seeds of the pure realm, one would then have to admit that they could again become ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) according to another's desire.
Furthermore, one must also maintain that those Arhats of the *parihāṇadharman* lineage possess the seeds of afflictions;
it will be established later that there is falling away from the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Moreover, the Sthavira says:

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) definitely lack a co-nascent cause (*sahaja-hetu*). For if they were to arise, they would have to do so without a cause; furthermore, it would follow that one type of phenomenon could arise from another type.
This is because, at the stage immediately preceding their arising, co-nascent factors cannot act as the productive cause for one another, as they themselves have not yet arisen.
Furthermore, one would have to seek two distinct causes for those two [factors], since both arise by means of those two causes.
This argument is irrational because there is no evidence for it.
Since this is what you yourself accept—namely, that among co-arising dharmas at the stage immediately preceding their arising, one is not the cause of the other—no proof for a cause has been stated.
Is it not already stated that [a cause] is so because it has not yet arisen?
This too is equally doubtful: by what reason is it proven that a phenomenon which has not yet arisen cannot function as a cause?
Furthermore, how is it that they perversely allow a non-substantial phenomenon to be a cause, while denying this status to a substantial phenomenon?

If you claim that the entity of that which has not yet arisen does not exist, then if the entity does not exist, do not claim that it has a cause; for one cannot say that things such as a rabbit’s horns, which are absolutely non-existent, have a cause—this case should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, you do not admit that rabbit horns are non-existent.
Moreover, according to our school, existence is manifold, as there are distinctions between essence and function, and between the provisional and the real.
Although [the future] exists, its capacity to project a result has not yet arisen; therefore, it is said to be "unborn."
Since its essence is not non-existent, how can it lack the status of being a cause?
To fail to state the evidence for [its causality] while yet insisting that what has not yet arisen cannot be a condition for the arising of dharmas is contrary to correct principle.

If one holds that something cannot function as a cause because it has not yet arisen, but can function as a cause once it has arisen, then one must concede that past dharmas necessarily possess the nature of being causes.
If that were so, the adherence to the existence of a "concomitant realm" (anubandha-dhātu) would be in vain, or else the concomitant realm would exist without a cause.

If it is argued that the past serves as a successive cause (pāramparya-hetu), this is mere empty talk devoid of any real meaning; for how can something that has no substantial entity whatsoever be established as a successive cause?
The wise should observe this blind faction: they erroneously grasp non-existent dharmas as causes, while they deny the causal significance within existent dharmas.

If it is claimed that the past is a cause, yet that which is not past is not a cause, then the future should likewise be the same. Just as past dharmas are not successive causes because their substance does not exist, so too the future should not be a successive effect because its substance does not exist.

Furthermore, "successive transmission" is a term for continuity; it is not logical that this very dharma should continue within itself. Since there is no past or future and only the present exists, there must certainly be no cause for successive transmission.

However, regarding what has been stated, one must further seek the two distinct causes for those two; for I have already conceded that when both arise together, it is because I allow that mental states and their concomitants all arise from preceding homogeneous causes of their own kind, as well as being produced by simultaneous heterogeneous causes.
Why, then, do you laboriously raise objections regarding this?
Therefore, the Elder has no grounds whatsoever to prove that the principle of simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) does not exist.

Furthermore, his assertions—that only a single moment possesses the nature of having a support (*āśrayatva*), and that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dharma*) possess simultaneous causes—are difficult to comprehend and are irrational statements.
Although it is difficult to discern, its existence as an object is not non-existent, just like the nature of the support (*āśraya*).
That is to say, although the nature of the support is difficult to discern within a single moment, the mind and mental factors do not lack a support in that momentary eye-faculty and so forth.
Furthermore, although the fruits of various karmas are difficult to discern within a single moment, their production through induction is not non-existent.
This co-nascent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) should be understood in the same way.
Consequently, all that the Venerable has stated is not well-said, as it contradicts both scripture and reasoning.
Because it is certain that there exists a co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) by virtue of this, the principle of the co-arising cause is thoroughly established.

Chapter 8: The Eighth Part of the Second [Chapter], "Discriminating Differences. Thus has the characteristic of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) been explained.
What are the characteristics of the third [cause], the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)?
The verse says:
The homogeneous cause consists of similar factors; It belongs to its own category and level, and must have arisen previously.
The Path proceeds through the nine stages; only those that are equal or superior serve as its fruit.
The same applies to those produced by application, such as those accomplished through hearing and reflection.
The treatise says:
That which can nourish or produce various results of uniform outflow (niṣyanda-phala), whether distant or proximate, is called the similar cause (sabhāga-hetu).
It should be understood that this cause consists only of similar dharmas acting upon similar dharmas, not upon dissimilar ones.
Just as wholesome aggregates serve as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for one another, it should be understood that the same applies to defiled and neutral aggregates.
Other masters say:
among the pure-neutral aggregates, five are effects of matter, while four are not causes of matter, because their nature is inferior.
Other masters say:
"The five [mental aggregates] are the results of the four [material aggregates], but the material aggregate is not a cause for the four, because its power is inferior.
Other masters say:
Form and the four aggregates do not serve as causes for one another in their mutual relationship, because they are inferior and of different categories.
If explained in terms of stages, other masters state:
the *kalala* stage can serve as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for all ten stages.

In the nine stages beginning with *arbuda*, each stage—excluding its predecessor—acts as a cause for those that follow; however, from the perspective of a subsequent stage looking back at a preceding one, there is only the sense of being an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
If this were so, then the color of the initial *kalala* would have no cause, and the color of the final stage of old age would have no effect; therefore, such a principle is untenable.
Furthermore, there are masters who say:
each of the ten stages of the preceding birth acts as a homogeneous cause for the corresponding color of each of the ten stages of the subsequent birth.
Following this principle, it should be stated accordingly that all external elements likewise act as homogeneous causes for their own respective categories.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"All material forms (*rūpa*) definitely lack a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); they arise and grow solely through the assistance provided by the conjunction of various conditions.

Since we currently observe sprouts growing from within the mud excavated from beneath the earth, it is not the case that seeds previously existed underground; from what, then, do these sprouts arise?"
Therefore, it is known that material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) have no homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
Their position contradicts what is stated in the *Mūla-śāstra*, which says:
"Past primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are the causes, conditions, and so forth, for future primary elements."
He says: "My statement is not in contradiction with this, because there are both proximate and remote conditions; they are described as 'cause' and 'dominant condition' respectively.
This is a deceptive fabrication made to evade the difficulty; though it appears to follow the literal text, it actually contradicts reason.
Furthermore, it is not accepted that form (*rūpa*) possesses a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), as this would contradict both reason and scripture.

However, regarding the case where a sprout grows from mud excavated from beneath the earth, there was previously a seed there; yet, due to the absence of the conditions for conjunction, the sprout and so forth had not yet arisen.
Now, through the conjunction of conditions, the sprout and so forth are produced.
If that mud could arise without a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it would either arise as everything or not arise at all, because there would be no determinate cause.
Can it then be said that all similar things are homogeneous causes for similar phenomena?

Not so. Why? Because [a dharma] of its own category and its own level serves as a cause only for that which is of its own category and its own level; therefore, it is said to be "of its own category and its own level."
"Category" refers to the five categories, namely: those abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to those abandoned through cultivation.
"Level" refers to the nine levels, namely: the desire realm as one, and the four dhyānas and four formless attainments as eight.

Among these, that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm serves as a homogeneous cause for that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm; and so on, up to that which is abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm serving as a cause for that which is abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
As it was stated regarding the five categories of what is to be abandoned in the desire realm, so it should be stated accordingly for each of the four stages of the dhyānas and the formless realms.
Does this apply to all [categories]?
Not so; it is that which has arisen previously.

That is to say, only those dharmas that have arisen previously serve as homogeneous causes for subsequent similar dharmas—whether already arisen or yet to arise. This is called the complete definition of a homogeneous cause.

To state only that a preceding birth is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for a subsequent birth is deficient in meaning, because it fails to state that it is a homogeneous cause for what has not yet arisen.
To state only that the past is a homogeneous cause for the future and the present, etc., is likewise deficient in meaning, because it fails to state that causes and effects exist within the past.

If it is as previously stated, this comprehensively includes the meaning of the preceding and succeeding dharmas taught in the root treatise, as well as the principle that the past serves as the cause for the present and future, while the present serves only as the cause for the future.
Why is there no similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future?
Because in that [future] state, the meaning of sequential order—prior and posterior—does not exist.

Is it not the case that when all phenomena are in the process of arising, they have already been able to eliminate all obstacles; thus, in relation to those yet to arise, could they not be said to be "prior"?
Furthermore, the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) should also not exist in the future, because there is no temporal sequence between the retributive fruit and its retributive cause.

A homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is established based on a temporal sequence; it does not exist at the very moment of arising. Since [the future entity] has already passed beyond the subsequent stage and lacks functional activity, it is like other future phenomena.

The past consists only of what precedes; the future consists only of what follows; and the present encompasses both preceding and succeeding [moments], as these are fixed according to the [three] time periods (*adhvan*).
Although all dharmas of the past are indeed prior, their status as preceding or succeeding is already determined at the moment they take up their effects.

A future dharma, at the very moment it is arising, cannot be established as having a distinct activity prior to or subsequent to others; it is only upon reaching the present state of having already arisen that it can be distinguished from the future as a subsequent stage, taking that [future] as its fruit through its own activity.
If that were so, then the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) should likewise not exist in the future; yet this [homogeneous cause] and that [retributive cause] are not of the same nature.

Why is this? This homogeneous cause is indistinguishable from its resultant flow (*niṣyanda-phala*) in terms of being wholesome and so forth; if there were no sequence of priority and posteriority, they would have to serve as causes for one another.
Since they would mutually serve as causes and mutually serve as effects, the notion that they mutually function as cause and effect contradicts reason.

Since there is no principle capable of precluding their mutual status as effects, one would have to admit that an effect exists prior to its cause, and that two minds can simultaneously function as causes for one another; this would, however, contradict the text of the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.

The retributive cause (vipāka-hetu) differs from its fruit in characteristics; thus, although it is devoid of temporal sequence [of preceding and succeeding], there is no such fault as mentioned above.

Therefore, while the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) is established according to its stage and does not exist in the future, the retributive cause is established according to its characteristics and is not non-existent in the future.
If the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) does not exist in the future, would it not follow that the meaning of "cause" is something that previously did not exist but now exists?

There is no fault, because this is admitted; [the distinction] is based on states (*avasthā*), not on substance (*dravya*). Because of the combined activity, the fruit is a fruit of state, not a fruit of substance. This combined activity is the convergence of the specific causes and conditions of a phenomenon (*dharma-viśeṣa-pratyaya-sāmagrī*), whereby the phenomenon proceeds through different states.

The functioning of dharmas across different states does not occur apart from their essence; yet, this functioning across states is also not identical to that essence. Thus, these different states arise from other different states.
Since causes that produce homogeneous effects are termed "different states," the fruit produced by the collective operation of these states is a state-fruit, not an essence-fruit.
While there is no error in principle, there is a contradiction in the phrasing, as stated in the original treatise:
"If a dharma serves as a cause for another dharma, there is no time when this dharma is not its cause."
Is it not the case that the past and present serve as causes for those [dharmas], whereas the future does not? If so, would this not contradict the aforementioned statement?

There is no such fault of contradiction, because this was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣya*), referring to the universal causes of the three time periods—namely, the co-existent (*sahabhū*), associated (*samprayukta*), and maturation (*vipāka*) causes.
Other masters explain:
Although this treatise is composed based on all six causes, there is no fault.
Since future dharmas lack both similar-type and pervasive causes, how can it be said that there is no time when they are not a cause?
Although the future does not exist [in a substantial sense], this intention is to say that while it can serve as a cause, at the time when it no longer exists, it is not a cause.

Furthermore, this future must necessarily exist; that is to say, when a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is in the process of arising, it is certain to function as a cause by eliminating all obstacles.
Based on this, it is said in secret that there is no time when [a dharma] is not a cause.
However, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) says:
"That is not a good explanation, because a future dharma is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) prior to its state of actual arising, but only becomes one afterwards."
Such objections have already been resolved previously; that is to say, it is not because there is a sequence of before and after within the future.
When it is said that there is no time that is not a cause across the three periods of time, the intention is to show that there is no fourth period beyond these.
If that were so, the same should apply to the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
However, the treatise does not permit this; therefore, the treatise states:
"When this dharma has not yet reached the state of having already arisen, it is not an equal-and-immediate condition."
There is no such fault. Why is this?

The equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is based on the power of opening and making way; it does not possess the capacity to open and make way during the stage of actual arising. It must exist at the time when [the dharma] has already arisen that there is the power of opening and making way; once it has reached the state of having already ceased, it is termed "already opened and made way."

As for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it is like the nature of a seed: while abiding in the state of the "seed-nature" during the stage of being about to arise, it reaches the moment of having already arisen and is then able to actually grasp its fruit; therefore, this cause is not of the same category as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Other masters explain:
Immediately after [the moment of] "presently arising," this homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) necessarily takes up its own fruit;

however, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is not so determined, as it only takes up its own fruit at the stage when it has already ceased. Therefore, one cannot speak [of it] based on the time of "presently arising."
The *Vibhāṣā* commentary presents two modes of exposition:
as it is stated in that [text], so it should be here;
as it is stated here, so it should be there.
However, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) says:
"What merit is gained by composing it in this manner?
It merely demonstrates that the author of the treatise is not skilled in composition."
There is no such fault; rather, it serves to further demonstrate that the author of the treatise is skillful in composition.
That is to say, he is able to reveal that among his various compositions, some possess an implicit meaning (*sāvaśeṣārtha*) while others possess an explicit meaning (*niravaśeṣārtha*).
Why is it necessary to demonstrate that there is a further underlying intention in the text?
For such texts with a further intention exist everywhere;
where they exist will be explained subsequently.
If this is how one skillfully reconciles the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, how then should one reconcile the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*?
As that treatise states:

"There may be a truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) which has the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but is not itself the cause of the view of a self-entity—namely, all other afflicted truths of suffering, excluding the future view of a self-entity and the truths of suffering associated with it."
There may be a truth of suffering that has the view of a self-identity as its cause and also serves as the cause for the view of a self-identity; this refers to the aforementioned excluded factors.
This is an error of the reciter, as these words do not appear in the text.
That treatise merely states:
"Excluding the future *satkāyadṛṣṭi*-associated *duḥkhasatya*, there is no [such thing]" and uses the phrase "and that.
Even if such a statement were made, one should know, by inference from the meaning, that it is erroneous.
How should one interpret the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*?
It states that all phenomena are determined by four factors: namely, cause, fruit, support, and object.

One should know that regarding those texts, the causes refer to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), and the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*); the fruits refer to the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
The "basis" refers to the six faculties, such as the eye;
the "object" refers to the six spheres, such as visible form.
Furthermore, how should one interpret the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*?
As it is said:
What are the phenomena that do not have mind as their cause?

They are the first untainted mind of a person who has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), as well as the first untainted mind of other ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are certain to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth.

However, since all future untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) of that ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) do not have [prior] mind as their cause, why is it said that only his first untainted mind [is so described]?
Some offer this explanation:
that passage does not intend to define the meaning of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
What are they? Only two types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are distinguished: those possessing the nature for parinirvāṇa and those lacking the nature for parinirvāṇa.
Although the text does not explicitly mention those lacking the nature for nirvāṇa, it is understood through the logic of the argument that they exist.

That is to say, since it has already been stated that there are certain other ordinary beings who will definitely enter the state of rightness and departure from corruption (*samyaktva-niyāma*), by this same principle it follows that there are also other ordinary beings who will definitely not enter the state of rightness and departure from corruption.
Other masters explain:
That passage also analyzes the meaning of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). However, it speaks only of cases where a mind is ultimately not caused by a non-mind.

Although for those who have not yet entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) are indeed not caused by a non-mind, once they enter that state, only the very first untainted mind is a phenomenon caused by a non-mind; all subsequent minds are without exception caused by a mind.
How should the *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra* be interpreted?
As that treatise states:

"Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with past defiled visual consciousness, they may, in relation to this [present] mind, either (1) be able to act as a cause but not be subject to increase (*anuśerate*), or (2) be subject to increase but not be able to act as a cause, or (3) be both able to act as a cause and subject to increase, or (4) neither be able to act as a cause nor be subject to increase."

Furthermore, regarding those that can serve as causes but do not increase through association: this refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are of the same class or are universal (sarvatraga) and precede this mind; specifically, those latent dispositions which do not take this mind as their object, or which, even if they did, have been abandoned, as well as the associated latent dispositions that have already been abandoned.

Regarding those that increase through association but cannot act as causes: this refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) which, being of the same class or universal (sarvatraga), follow after this mind; such latent dispositions, when not yet abandoned, take this [mind] as their object and can act as its cause.

Regarding "also those that increase by association": this refers to those proclivities (anuśaya) which, being of the same class and universal (sarvatraga), existed prior to this mind; specifically, those proclivities that take this [mind] as their object and have not yet been abandoned, as well as the proclivities associated with it that have not yet been abandoned.

That which cannot serve as a cause and is also not subject to increase by way of association refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are of the same class or are universal (sarvatraga) occurring after this mind; specifically, those latent dispositions which do not take this [mind] as their object, or which, though they once did, have been abandoned; or other objects; or other latent dispositions; or universal latent dispositions belonging to a different realm (dhātu).
Just as that past defiled visual consciousness is, so too is future defiled visual consciousness.
While the logic of the four alternatives for the past may be tenable, how can the four alternatives be established for the future?
Some offer this explanation:
regarding the future, three propositions should be established; however, that which increases [the defilements] by following along cannot function as a cause, because it lacks a subsequent [moment].

Nevertheless, the statement that "the future is like the past" indicates that at the moment of arising, it necessarily enters the present. In relation to other [dharmas] that have not yet arisen, it can be designated as "prior," and in contrast to these, others may be called "subsequent."
Other masters explain:

This statement regarding the future also involves four alternatives; it does not mean that there are [latent dispositions] existing in the future that arise after the mind, as is the case with the past.

That is to say, there are similar-type and universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in the future world which, with respect to those future defiled visual consciousnesses, have been objectified but are not yet abandoned; these are what increase through association (*anuśerate*), but they do not act as causes.

Regarding the statement that "homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) belong only to their own level," on what basis is this definitively stated? It is definitively stated with reference to the contaminated (sāsrava).

If it concerns the uncontaminated path (anāsrava-mārga), each stage, when considered in relation to the others, serves as a cause for all nine levels—namely, the four dhyānas, the three formless attainments (ārūpya), the threshold concentration (anāgamya), and the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara)—which are called the nine levels.
The remaining states that lack meditative concentration (*asamāhita*) are not sharp enough; therefore, none of them can give rise to the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-ārya-mārga*).
The truths of the path (*mārga-satya*) throughout the nine stages serve as mutual causes for one another. Why is this so?
Because this is not bound to a specific level (*bhūmi*), nor is it grasped as "mine" by the craving (*tṛṣṇā*) of any particular level.
Therefore, although the Truths of the Path (*mārgasatya*) differ in their levels, they serve as causes for one another because they belong to the same category.
However, not everything serves as a cause for everything.
For what does it serve as a cause?
It serves as the cause for results that are equal or superior; because it arises from application (*prayoga*), it does not serve as a cause for inferior results.

Regarding the noble paths (āryamārga) based on the first dhyāna, there are those based on the first dhyāna up to those based on the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana); it should be understood that the same applies to the paths based on the second dhyāna and so forth.

Among these, a path based on its own level or a higher level exists, whereas one based on a lower level does not. That is to say, a noble path based on the first dhyāna serves as a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) for noble paths based on all nine dhyānas and nine levels.

That is to say, this [noble path] based on the first dhyāna functions solely as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for paths based on the first dhyāna, and does not function as a cause for paths based on higher [dhyānas], because their nature is inferior.

A noble path based on the second dhyāna—and by extension, one based on the first dhyāna—serves as a homogeneous cause for noble paths based on the remaining nine stages, excluding those based on the first dhyāna itself.
That is to say, this [noble path] based on the first two dhyānas takes only the noble paths of the nine stages as its similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and not those based on higher stages.

The noble path based on the first dhyāna that relies on the third dhyāna takes as its similar cause the noble paths of the nine stages based on the other dhyānas, excluding those based on the first two.
That is to say, this [path] takes only the noble paths based on the first, second, third, and ninth stages as its homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and not those based on higher stages.

Furthermore, if it is a noble path based on the first dhyāna or the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it serves as a homogeneous cause only for the noble paths based on these nine stages, including the sphere of nothingness itself.
Thus, these paths common to all [nine stages] take the noble paths of the nine stages as their homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).

For example, just as the noble path of the first dhyāna takes the noble paths of the other [eight] dhyānas as its causes, so too should one extensively analyze and discern how the noble paths of the remaining stages likewise depend upon those of the nine stages, as appropriate.

Furthermore, while the various paths of the untainted (*anāsrava*) are subsumed within a single stage (*bhūmi*), it is not the case that all serve as causes for all; they function as causes that are equal or superior, not as inferior causes.

For example, a previously arisen patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for a future patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering; this is what is meant by "equal."

Furthermore, this very patience (*kṣānti*) can also serve as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the subsequent states, from the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*);

thus it is called "superior. This is explained in detail up to the point that all already-arisen knowledges of non-arising serve only as homogeneous causes for their own equal class, as there is nothing superior to them.

Furthermore, the various paths that have already arisen—the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning—act as similar causes for three, two, and one [subsequent paths] respectively; it is also not contrary to reason that they serve as causes for one another in turn.
How can a superior uncontaminated path arising later serve as a homogeneous cause for an inferior uncontaminated path arising earlier without contradicting reason?
Who says that a later, superior [path] is the cause of an earlier, inferior one?

What logical obstacle prevents the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) of a dull-facultied lineage (mṛdvindriya-gotra) from having been previously cultivated in a prior life from serving as a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for the path of seeing (darśanamārga) of a sharp-facultied lineage (tīkṣṇendriya-gotra) that is certain not to arise within one’s own continuum in the future?
All sentient beings, each with their own distinct continuum, are by the very nature of things established as having six types of spiritual lineages (*gotra*).

It should be understood that the same applies to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) in relation to what precedes them; however, there is a distinction: namely, that the path of one beyond training arising in a previous life can serve as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) arising later in one's own continuum, because it is possible for one who has fallen away from the state beyond training to be reborn into a state of sharp faculties within the path of cultivation.
If that were so, it would contradict the original treatise, which states:
