"The faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*) takes the faculty of one who knows and the faculty of one who shall come to know (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), but not as its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) or its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); the same applies to the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) with respect to those two faculties."
There is no contradiction here, as there is an underlying intention (*abhiprāya*), as previously explained in succession.
Such passages with an underlying intention exist everywhere; these very ones are such cases, and therefore one should demonstrate the passages containing that underlying intention.
What further meaning is intended here in this passage?

It means that, with reference to the faculty of "already-known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*)—which is comprised within such a nature of faculties arising later—it is implicitly stated in relation to the faculty of "not-yet-known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) comprised within such a nature of faculties arising earlier:

[the former] acts as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), but not as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) or an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because it is inferior and arises later.

This passage speaks only of those untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) that have already performed their function and proceed in dependence upon a continuum, as when it is said that the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) are "useful.

If this were so, since sentient beings are established by the nature of things (*dharmatā*) within their respective individual continua according to the three vehicles of enlightenment (*triyāna-bodhi*), it would follow that the path of the Śrāvaka vehicle could serve as the cause for the Pratyekabuddha or Buddha vehicles, and the path of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle could serve as the cause for the Buddha vehicle.
There is no such fault, because their natures are extremely remote from one another.
For one who has already ascended the path of the Śrāvaka, it is impossible for them to further give rise to the path of another vehicle.

If that were so, then once one has ascended the path of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or the path of those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), it would be impossible for them to further give rise to these paths; consequently, a previously arisen path of those who follow by faith would not serve as a cause for a path of those who follow by dharma that will never arise again in the future.
Nor is there this fault, because a path of dull faculties can indeed be transformed into a path of sharp faculties.

That is to say, by means of that very continuum of aggregates belonging to one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), it is possible to subsequently attain a continuum of aggregates belonging to one who follows by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).

However, it is not the case that from a continuum of aggregates that has already ascended the Śrāvaka vehicle, one can subsequently attain a path belonging to the continuum of aggregates of the Pratyekabuddha or Buddha vehicles.
Based on this principle, it is said: although such a case does not exist, one may still engage in conventional conceptualization.

If there were anyone who emerged from meditative absorption during the Path of Seeing, even those following the path of faith (śraddhānusārin) could subsequently attain the faculties of those following the Dharma (dharmānusārin); however, since there is no such possibility of emerging [from the Path of Seeing], the distinction between the faculties and that of the vehicles (yāna) are not the same.
For this reason it is said: paths of dull faculties serve as homogeneous causes for both dull and sharp faculties; however, a path of sharp faculties serves only as a cause for sharp-faculty paths.

For example, the paths of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), and those liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) serve, respectively, as homogeneous causes for six, four, and two [subsequent paths].

Likewise, the paths of those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and those liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*) serve, respectively, as homogeneous causes for three, two, and one [subsequent paths].
This should also be understood, as before, as being indeterminate: how can the paths of the higher stages be called "equal" or "superior" when they serve as causes for the lower stages?
It is by virtue of the increase of the cause and by virtue of the faculties (*indriya*).
Is it only the Noble Path that serves as a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for what is equal or superior? No, it is not so. How then?
Other mundane dharmas produced through application also serve as causes for those that are equal or superior, but not for those that are inferior.
What is the nature of these dharmas produced through application?
They are those consisting of what is heard (*śrutamaya*) and what is reflected upon (*cintāmaya*), and so forth.

The term "and so forth" includes those produced by cultivation and the like. The merits arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation are called "produced by them" because they are generated through preparatory application (*prayoga*); thus, they serve as causes only for that which is equal or superior, not for that which is inferior.

For example, dharmas consisting of hearing-accomplished wisdom (śrutamaya) bound to the desire realm can serve as homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) for dharmas consisting of hearing- and reflection-accomplished wisdom within their own realm, but they are not causes for those consisting of cultivation-accomplished wisdom (bhāvanāmaya), because such [cultivation-accomplished wisdom] does not exist in the desire realm.

Dharmas produced by reflection (*cintā-maya*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for those produced by reflection, but not for those produced by hearing (*śruta-maya*), because the latter are inferior.

If dharmas produced by hearing belonging to the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are able to serve as homogeneous causes for those produced by hearing and cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) within their own realm, they do not serve as causes for those produced by reflection, because such [dharmas] do not exist in the realm of form.

Dharmas produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) only for dharmas produced by cultivation within their own realm, and not for those produced by hearing (*śruta-maya*), because the latter are inferior.

Dharmas produced by cultivation associated with the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) serve as homogeneous causes only for dharmas produced by cultivation within their own realm, and not for those produced by hearing or reflection (*cintā-maya*), because such [dharmas] do not exist there and because [those produced by hearing and reflection] are inferior.
Other masters say: "Dharmas produced by reflection (*cintā-maya*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for those produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).
But is it not the case that in the desire realm there are dharmas produced by reflection, yet none produced by cultivation?"
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are factors produced by cultivation (bhāvanā-maya) but none produced by reflection (cintā-maya).

However, worldly dharmas serve as homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) only for their own realm; the previous statement that they are causes for their own category and own stage was based on the fact that they are contaminated (sāsrava).
How is it that they explain volition (*cetanā*) as the cause of cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?
Some offer this explanation:

although there are roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in the desire realm that are comprised within superior skillful means and are produced by reflection (*cintāmaya*), they are extremely tranquil; because they resemble wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*), they are termed "produced by cultivation."
There is no fault in explaining that volition (*cetanā*) is the cause for those [dharmas].
Other masters explain:

the dharmas accomplished through volition (*cetanāmayī*) belonging to the desire realm, which are cultivated at the time of attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), are called "accomplished through cultivation" (*bhāvanāmayī*) because they are the fruit of an Arhat’s wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāprajñā*) and resemble that wisdom of cultivation.
There is no fault in stating that reflection (*cintā*) serves as the cause for those [dharmas].
These dharmas accomplished through hearing, reflection, and cultivation each have nine grades, namely: the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) and so forth.

If the lowest-of-the-low grade serves as the cause for all nine grades, the lowest-middle grade serves as the cause for eight, and so on, until the highest-of-the-high grade serves as the cause only for the highest-of-the-high grade, because the preceding inferior grades are excluded.
Wholesome dharmas acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for wholesome dharmas produced through effort (*prāyogika*);
however, wholesome dharmas produced through effort do not serve as causes for those acquired at birth, because the latter are inferior.

Furthermore, wholesome dharmas acquired at birth are also divided into nine grades; all of them stand in relation to one another as mutual causes, since it is possible for each subsequent grade to manifest after any preceding one.
Other masters say: "Because one attains all [maturations] within a single moment of meditative concentration.
However, because there are nine grades of manifesting maturation that can be established as distinct, the nine grades of the defiled should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, because there are nine grades of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), one may establish nine distinct grades.

There are four types of non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states: those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those of deportment (*airyāpathika*), those of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and those associated with the mind of transformation (*nairmāṇika*). In their respective order, these can serve as causes for four, three, two, and one [subsequent state].
Other masters say:
"All [factors] are mutually causes for one another because they share the same bondage.
This explanation is unreasonable; otherwise, the four factors—heat and so forth—of the first dhyāna would also be mutual causes for one another.

Furthermore, the transformative mind of the desire realm has four dhyānas as its fruits; however, a higher dhyāna is not the cause for a lower dhyāna fruit, nor is it obtained through the cause of preparatory effort (*prayoga*), lest one should exert effort and yet gain nothing.
For this reason, it is asked: Is there any already-arisen untainted dharma (*anāsrava-dharma*) that is not the cause of an untainted dharma in its unarisen state? Yes;

for example, the category of the already-arisen *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering) is [not the cause] of those dharmas belonging to its own lineage (*sva-gotra*) that are of the category of the *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering) and have not yet arisen in the future. This continues in the same manner up to the already-arisen *vajropama-samādhi* (diamond-like concentration), which is [not the cause] of the various untainted dharmas of its own lineage that are of a lower stage and have not yet arisen.

Furthermore, all superior [dharmas] serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for all inferior [dharmas] by way of their preparatory application (*prayoga-dharma*), and the resulting fruits are either equal or superior.
Is there any instance where the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) previously acquired within a single continuum are not the cause for those that arise later?

There is [such a case]: namely, when the category of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) has already arisen after the category of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) in the future; for a fruit can never exist prior to its cause, and furthermore, there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future.
Is there any case where previously arisen untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas are not the cause of subsequently arisen untainted dharmas? Yes;

for example, a superior previously arisen untainted dharma is not the cause of an inferior subsequently arisen untainted dharma. This is as when the attainment (*prāpti*) of the previously arisen *duḥkhe-dharmajñāna* is not the cause of the subsequently arisen attainment of *duḥkhe-dharmakṣānti*, because although the latter arises later, it is inferior.
In this way, one should understand that for all acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various noble paths, the former is superior and the latter is inferior; this should be known by analogy.

Here, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) answers the question by asserting that when one falls from a higher fruit, a lower fruit manifests; however, this is not definitive, because even after falling from a higher fruit, it is possible for one to refine the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) so that a superior, untainted [fruit] manifests in the present.
One should distinguish this from that.

However, the causal efficacy of this homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) with respect to its fruit is inexhaustible; it is not like the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu), whose causal efficacy with respect to its fruit is necessarily finite.
Since Arhats receive homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) yet enter *nirvāṇa* before their fruits have been fully exhausted, it follows that a homogeneous cause does not necessarily produce its fruit.
That is to say, even when a homogeneous cause exists, due to the presence of obstacles, the fruit may arise at another time or may never arise at all.
Therefore, regarding this matter, some raise the following question:
"Does the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) also take up its fruit?
In response, the general answer is given:
Those who bestow a fruit must necessarily be able to take up that fruit. Why is this?
Because it is logically untenable to bestow something without taking it up.

There are cases where [a dharma] can take up a fruit but cannot give one; this refers to the final aggregates of an Arhat. Although the preceding aggregates are capable of giving a fruit, they enter parinirvāṇa before having exhausted them.

Furthermore, regarding activities such as listening, reciting, and analytical reflection, although the preparatory efforts and auxiliary conditions encountered are identical, one observes differences in the accumulation of roots of virtue; therefore, it is known that the function of the cause does not pertain solely to this present life.
However, the statement that "wholesome roots arise by the power of the wholesome roots accompanying them" is made on the basis of their actual possession (*samanvāgama*).

The intended meaning of this statement is as follows: although both those who possess [the roots] and those who do not can produce a fruit due to the cause, the power to produce the fruit is stronger in those who possess them;
yet, despite the difference in strength, they are equal in their status as causes.
Furthermore, although both proximate and remote causes may be fully accomplished, there is still a distinction of superiority and inferiority regarding the production of the fruit.
If wholesome roots were produced solely by following along with those [remote] wholesome roots, then once the wholesome roots had been severed, they would never again be able to reconnect.
Therefore, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is inexhaustible in its functional utility regarding the bestowal of its fruit, whereas the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is not.
Where has such a doctrinal point ever been stated?
Is it not said, within the analysis of the characteristics of these causes, that "the future and present take the past as their cause, and the past and present take the future as their cause"?
Furthermore, for what reason do the mind and mental factors at the moment an Arhat passes away completely obstruct the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
This is because, while they are admitted to have the nature of homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*), these two [the final mind and its concomitants] and their effects are not simultaneous.
The equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) functions by the power of opening up space.

At the moment of the final passing away of all Arhats, there are no subsequent mind-moments or mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arising in immediate succession; because the causes and conditions for their arising are incomplete, there is no equal-and-immediate fruit to be opened up. Consequently, they lack the power to open up space, and thus the definition of the final dharma as an equal-and-immediate condition is excluded.

However, causes and effects of the same kind (sabhāga-hetu) apply to both proximate and remote instances; furthermore, there is no limit to the results they project, yet it is not certain that the results thus projected will necessarily arise. Therefore, one cannot analogously establish the nature of a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for a subsequent state based on the analogy of the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya), which precludes such a status for later stages.
There is another explanation which states:
One must certainly admit that the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is established only with respect to its immediate fruit (*anantara-phala*).

Furthermore, one should not say that when wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral minds arise in succession, the subsequent mind does not arise because the preceding moment acts as its homogeneous cause; for we observe in the world that seeds, sprouts, stalks, leaves, buds, flowers, and fruits—objects that are dissimilar to one another—arise in succession, each following the other immediately without any interval, with the preceding state serving as the cause.
Furthermore, it is as irrational as claiming that hair or horns can produce *pú* and *wěi* reeds;
for we observe in the present that when either the wholesome or the unwholesome increases, the other necessarily decreases.
Moreover, if the antidotes and their respective objects of abandonment were both to increase through cultivation, then there would never be any possibility of liberation from suffering.
Furthermore, as one practices the antidotes to that which is to be abandoned, those antidotes should increase;
thus, there would be no case where an antidote fails to be established. Such faults as these cannot be avoided by them.

Moreover, we observe in the world that once one has mastered the knowledge of scripts, treatises, crafts, and so forth, even if contrary conditions arise in the interim, when it manifests again in a subsequent state, it does so with the preceding similar continuity as its cause. Therefore, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) can indeed be separated by intervals.

The analogies of the seed and the sprout are incapable of proving [the point], because external things arise in a fixed sequence and abide accordingly, whereas internal phenomena do not; therefore, these analogies are ineffective.

For instance, immediately following a seed, a sprout necessarily arises, and not stems or leaves; however, immediately following a virtuous mind, one does not observe that such a [specific] mind necessarily arises.
Furthermore, a stalk may arise immediately after a sprout, but a sprout cannot arise immediately after a stalk;
thus, the sequence in which wholesome and unwholesome minds arise is not fixed.
Moreover, while external objects are determined by time and circumstance, internal phenomena are not; therefore, the analogy lacks validity.

This means that due to the excellence of the power of functional capacity, diligent effort, instruction, and so forth, the virtuous mind of a practitioner of meditation continues in succession for a long duration, whereas the unwholesome mind of those habituated to desire continues in succession for a long duration; since this is not the case for sprouts, stalks, and the like, whose timing is indefinite, there is a distinction between the internal and the external.
Furthermore, in the case of rice and similar things, which possess the same neutral nature (*avyākṛta*) throughout their successive production, the status of being a cause is possible;
however, in the case of the mind and its associates, which differ in nature—such as being wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth—throughout their successive production, they cannot serve as an analogy.
To claim that *pú* and *wěi* grasses grow from hair and horns is a worldly convention that contradicts reason.
If one allows that things arise from one another without distinguishing between the same and the different, why would two [causes] not each produce two [effects]?

However, just as hair, horns, excrement, warmth, and so forth serve only as favorable conditions for the growth of reeds and cattails, a similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) can function as a cause—whether with an interval or without an interval—only with respect to its own kind.
Having thus explained the characteristics of the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
what are the characteristics of the fourth, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*)?
The verse says:
The associated cause is determined by the fact that mind and mental factors share the same basis.
The treatise states:
Only mind and mental factors are associated causes.
Is it not the case that, because there is no qualification here, the time, object, and aspect would also be associated even if they were distinct?

Even if one were to provide a qualifying statement that these three are identical, then in the case of different bodies sharing the same instruction, they should also be said to be associated; therefore, it is said that they share the same basis (*sāmāśraya*).

To generally refute this objection, it is said that mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) must necessarily share the same basis (*āśraya*) in order to function as mutual *saṃprayuktaka-hetu* (associated causes).

Here, the term "same" indicates that the basis is one and the same; that is, if visual consciousness takes the eye-faculty of this very moment as its basis, the associated sensations (*vedanā*) and other factors likewise take that same eye-faculty as their basis. It should be understood that this applies similarly up to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its associated factors, which share the same basis in the mind-faculty (*manas*).
Now, one should reflect upon this:
since the nature of the bases for the faculties such as the eye and ear is the same, for what reason is it said that the consciousnesses which depend upon them have distinct bases?
Why trouble yourself with such a question?
Although the nature of the supports for the various consciousnesses is the same, they are distinguished by their different categories.
If this is so, why is it understood that the term "common support" refers exclusively to the sense of simultaneous, momentary support?
The statement that visual consciousness and the others share a single basis does not mean that all visual consciousnesses share a single basis in the sense of a long-term generic support.
Furthermore, because their immediate supports are identical in kind, the visual consciousnesses and so forth would have to be considered associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) of one another.
The Blessed One also spoke of the various faculties as the bases for the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth by way of their commonality of kind; thus the Sūtra says:
"Having seen a form with the eye, one gives rise to sorrow, joy, or equanimity."
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"With the eye as its door, it functions solely for the purpose of seeing forms.

These [passages] all refer to those of the same category that share a common basis; therefore, the verse should be qualified in this way: namely, that the mind and mental factors arise simultaneously and share the same basis.
Therefore, that commentary itself subsumes two meanings, stating: "If visual consciousness takes this momentary eye-faculty as its support," and so forth at length.
Since the verse lacks the term "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*), how can it be known that these "common supports" are not of the same duration, but rather belong to a single moment?

If you argue that there is no fault because it is included within the commentary, then the composed verse should not have mentioned "having a common basis" (*sāśraya*), but should instead have stated only that the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) is definitively the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Furthermore, the term "associated" (*samprayukta*) is sufficient to preclude all such objections; for association cannot exist between things that differ in time or basis.
It is simply said that they are associated; by this, one knows that at all times, their bases, modes of activity, objects, and entities are identical.

If they were based on different times, had different modes of activity, or different objects, they would not be associated; thus, it is not the case that a single category of entity arises simultaneously with many entities.
Since they are associated together, what is the distinction between the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*)?

First, that which is an associated cause is also a co-existent cause; however, there are co-existent causes that are not associated causes, namely: the derivative matter (*anuvartaka-rūpa*) such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth, and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
If an associated cause is necessarily a co-existent cause, then what is the difference in meaning between these two causes here?
That which is not an associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) is indeed a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), because the meanings of these two causes differ.

Nevertheless, a single dharma may be both an associated cause and a co-existent cause; the distinction in meaning is that the sense of inseparability is the associated cause, while the sense of having a common result (*eka-phala*) is the co-existent cause.

Furthermore, those factors that arise and abide simultaneously through mutual power are the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); if they mutually take the same object through mutual power, they are the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
Other masters say:
the co-existent cause is established by the principle of being mutual effects, just as traveling companions rely on one another to traverse a perilous road together.

The associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) is established on the basis of five kinds of equality; it is just as when traveling companions share the same food and perform the same tasks together, such that if even one among them is missing, they are no longer associated. Therefore, the meaning of being mutual causes is fully established.
Having thus explained the characteristics of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*),
what are the characteristics of the fifth, the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)?
The verse says:
The universal [cause] refers to those previously arisen [factors]; it serves as the cause for defilement within the same level.
The treatise states:

As for the universal cause, it refers to previously arisen universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) and their associated factors, which act as the universal cause for all subsequent defiled dharmas—whether of their own category or another category—within the same level.
What are the dharmas called "pervasive" (sarvatraga)?
They shall be analyzed in detail in the Chapter on Latent Dispositions (anuśaya).
These are established separately because the power of their causal influence operates beyond that of the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).

Furthermore, because they also serve as causes for the defiled dharmas of other categories (*nikāya*), it is through this power that the afflictions of other categories and their attendants (*pārṣada*) are likewise produced and grow.
Within the afflictions comprised within one's own category, what is the distinction between the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)?
Since the view of a self-body gives rise to various forms of craving, and various forms of craving can also give rise to the view of a self-body, how can their distinct characteristics be known?

There is also a distinction between these two causes within our own school: namely, because of the grasping at a self, it is able to cause various forms of craving to arise, becoming firm, expansive, and intense.

Because the view of self universally takes all objects of craving as its objective support, craving causes the view of self to arise with firmness; however, it cannot cause it to increase, expand, or blaze intensely, because craving cannot universally take the objects of the view of self as its objective support.

Because all pervasive afflictions, when viewed in relation to one another, are each capable of universally taking their respective objects as their cognitive domain, every single pervasive affliction is able to cause the others to arise, becoming firm, expansive, and intense.
Therefore, these two causes are not without distinction.
If a single moment of a single category can serve as both a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), what is the difference between them?

Although they simultaneously produce two types of outflowing results (*niṣyanda-phala*), the results of their own respective categories are more abundant than those of others; thus, there is indeed a distinction between these two causes.
For what reason and in what manner does one's own school flourish?
It is because it is nurtured by two causal factors: because these serve as its proximate causes of production, they cause it to expand and become intense.
If both produce only their own category (*sva-nikāya*), how do these two causes differ?
There is no universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) that produces only its own category.
This is because when a universal dharma manifests, it simultaneously possesses the power to grasp the results of all five categories.
Furthermore, their distinctions have already been explained as before. Other masters say:

"A portion of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) is the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), and a portion of the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)."

That teacher’s intention is to say that the meaning of the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is identical to that of the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); however, this is not logical, because other categories [of phenomena] would also have to be similar-type causes. Consequently, even those that are not pervasive causes would become similar-type causes in relation to other categories, and thus all causes would become confused.
Although the various causes lack individual substantial entities, the meanings of these causes do not intermingle with one another.

If a pervasive factor (*sarvatraga-dharma*) can serve as the cause for defiled phenomena of all five categories, then it follows that those abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) should serve as the cause for all defiled phenomena; this is precisely what our own tenet asserts, and thus it should not be considered a difficulty.
Therefore, the *Prakaraṇapāda* states as follows:
"What are the phenomena that have as their cause those things abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
They are all defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) and the maturation (*vipāka*) produced by phenomena abandoned by insight."
What are the phenomena that have the indeterminate as their cause?
They are all conditioned indeterminate phenomena and unwholesome phenomena.

Or there may be a portion of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but is not itself the cause of the view of a self-identity; this is explained in detail up to: excluding the future view of a self-identity and its associated factors, as well as their arising, aging, duration, and impermanence, all other defiled portions of the Truth of Suffering [are such phenomena].
If that were so, it would contradict the *Prajñaptiśāstra*, which asks:
"Is there any phenomenon that is unwholesome and has only unwholesome states as its cause?"

It is said: Yes, there is. This refers to the initial arising of a defiled volition (*kliṣṭa-cetanā*) by a noble one (*ārya*) who has fallen away from the state of being free from desire (*vītarāga*). It is based on causes that have not yet been abandoned that this [scriptural] statement was made in secret.

Although these defiled volitions possess both unwholesome (*akuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) causes, the neutral causes have already been permanently severed. Since all afflictions to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) have been abandoned when the noble one falls away, and since there is absolutely no falling away from the Path of Insight (*darśana-mārga*), and because all defiled-neutral states of the desire realm are abandoned through insight, it is only the unwholesome cause that remains accomplished upon falling away. Thus, they are described as "not yet abandoned," and therefore there is no fault.

If dharmas that have already been abandoned can also function as causes, for what reason do the noble persons (*ārya-pudgala*) never manifest craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*), intense anger (*pratigha-samyojana*), or the various types of conceit (*māna*)?
Since the view of nihilism, false views, and the view of a self-identity have all been abandoned, and since craving and the other [defilements] arise proximately to them in their respective order,
how can they serve as causes at this present stage?

It is not that they only now become causes; rather, while in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the defiled dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation have already used those to be abandoned by seeing as their universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Since there is no time when a dharma is not a cause for another dharma of which it is a cause, it can be said to remain a cause even though it has been abandoned.

It should be understood that herein, past and present universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) act as the cause for the five categories; they can take the five categories as their objects and are also subject to increase (anuśerate) by the five categories.

Regarding those associated dharmas, with the exception of the increase of the concomitants and so forth, and further excluding the five categories of objects that serve as their cognitive conditions (*ālambana*), the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of those various dharmas do not constitute a universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*). This is because they exist either before or after [the primary dharma], because their natures are remote, and because they do not share a single fruit.
There are pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are not pervasive causes, namely, the pervasive latent dispositions of the future.
There are pervasive causes that are not pervasive latent dispositions, namely, those dharmas with a single fruit that are past or present pervasive latent dispositions.
There are those that are both [past and present], namely the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the past and present.
There are those that are neither, namely all other dharmas.
Regarding this, some raise the following objection:

If it is argued that views, doubt, and ignorance are called "pervasive causes" (*sarvatraga-hetu*) because they produce heterogeneous effects and are distinct from others, thus being termed "pervasive," this function is not unique to them alone. For instance, the latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*), through its clinging to objects, serves as the root of all misconduct. Just as wrong view causes the latent tendency of attachment to cling intensely to various objects, so too does attachment cause wrong view to become intense and expand within its own objective referent, even leading to the severing of the roots of virtue.

Just as when one has slandered cessation and the path through wrong view, one brings forth the latent tendency of craving to delight in birth and death; so too, once one has delighted in birth and death through craving, one is able to bring forth wrong view to slander cessation and the path.

Therefore, it is logically untenable to maintain that only views (*dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) function as universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) producing fruits across the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*), while other afflictions such as craving (*rāga*) do not.
This objection is not valid, because the functional roles of these causes differ.

Non-pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) collectively constitute only the virile fruit (puruṣakāra-phala) and the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala) of all defiled dharmas belonging to the five categories, because they can successively act as equivalent immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya) to cause them to arise, and because they do not obstruct their arising.

The universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) also take the defiled phenomena of all five categories as their outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*); how is it that these differ from those [non-universal ones] such that this is so?

Because universal latent dispositions universally take all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as their objects, their power is firm, intense, and expansive; as soon as they have arisen, they are able to induce fruits of both similar and dissimilar types.
Non-universal latent dispositions are not like this, for their objective range is narrow and their functional capacity is inferior.

Although the latent tendency of greed (*rāgānuśaya*) clings to its objects, it also serves as an indirect cause for wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), even leading to the severing of all roots of goodness; yet it does not momentarily arise and suddenly induce the five categories of defiled phenomena in oneself and others as its outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).

Once the latent tendency of craving (*rāgānuśaya*) has produced attachment to birth and death, it can induce wrong views that slander cessation and the path; since these are mutually induced within this same category and not from a different category, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, because the meaning is extremely profound and difficult to comprehend, its infinite distinctions are not easily understood.

That is to say, within all phenomena there is absolutely no real agent or action; yet it is nevertheless taught that there are immeasurable kinds of causes capable of bringing about various results. Regarding these results, this is the proximate cause and this is the remote cause; this cause brings them into being and this cause causes their cessation; this cause makes them exist and this cause does not harm them; this cause is the attractor and this cause is the support; this cause is like an associate and this cause is like a seed; this cause is like food and drink and this cause is like medicine.
The distinctions among these causal meanings are boundless, and constitute the sphere of experience solely for the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Having thus analyzed the characteristics of the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*),
what are the characteristics of the sixth, the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*)?
The verse says:
The retributive cause consists of the unwholesome, as well as the wholesome that is exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The commentary says:
Only unwholesome states and wholesome states with outflows (*sāsrava*) are retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*), because they are phenomena that constitute retribution (*vipāka-dharma*).
Since this cause, according to its respective capacity, can bring about a retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*), it is called a retributive cause.
In this context, what is the meaning of "cause"?
It refers to the fact that dharmas conforming to karma can differentiate sentient beings; thus, the Sūtra says:
"The superior and inferior, high and low, among the various classes of sentient beings are differentiated by their karma."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Karma is the cause of birth.
In the verse, the word "and" (ca) indicates that although this cause and its fruit differ in their essential nature and characteristics, they are not confused in their categories.

The word "only" (eva) is used to exclude the sense that the essence of the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) encompasses all types of causes. That is to say, there are other masters who claim that all effects are termed "ripening" (vipāka); they too would have to admit that the essence of the ripening cause encompasses all causes.
The word "only" (kevalam) is used to prevent one from following the arbitrary speculations of other masters.
For what reason, moreover, do they maintain that all results are termed "maturation" (vipāka)?
Because it is stated in the Sūtra:
What is the karmic maturation (*vipāka*) of this great radiance?
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"The karmic maturations resulting from two kinds of food offerings are equal and identical."
Furthermore, it is said:
craving is the maturation of feeling.
It is also stated:
If the Tathāgata had not spoken these words, then this assembly would not have experienced such a karmic maturation.
Furthermore, he asked:
"What is the karmic maturation of this dream?"
Furthermore, people in the world also speak of food and so forth as being the maturation (*vipāka*) of happiness;
such instances are indeed numerous.
These various uses of the term "maturation" are all metaphorical designations, just as the eye is called a "field of merit," or as "love" is called an "ocean," or "fire" is called a "mother."
How do we know that the preceding [passage] was also spoken by way of analogy?
If it were not so, all untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena would have maturation (*vipāka*).

However, various sūtras negate the possibility of maturation for untainted phenomena, stating that untainted volition (*cetanā*) is neither black nor white and is an action without maturation (*avipāka-karman*) capable of exhausting all karma.

Therefore, when it is said that the outflow (*niṣyanda*) induced by untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) is called "maturation" (*vipāka*), although such a conventional designation is established based on their conceptual calculations, there is no difference in meaning.
Furthermore, within the various sūtras there are also such metaphorical designations; for example, a short human lifespan is described as the "outflow fruit" (*niṣyanda-phala*) of killing.

This contradicts the statement that "equal outflow" refers to the dominant [cause], because it would be illogical for unwholesome karma and non-obscured neutral states to be considered equal outflow fruits.
For what reason is it definitively known that only unwholesome dharmas and wholesome contaminated dharmas are ripening causes?
Because it is stated in the sūtras.
Specifically, the sūtras state:

there is black karma with black ripening; there is white karma with white ripening; there is black-and-white karma with black-and-white ripening; and there is non-black, non-white karma that can exhaust all karmas.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"It is directly perceived that one experiences the agreeable maturation or the experience of lamentation as maturation, due to wholesome or unwholesome [actions].
It also says:
"I have encountered harm through bodily karma and so forth," meaning that when painful sensations arise, one experiences their ripening as suffering.
Again, he says:
"I have encountered benefit through bodily karma and so forth," meaning that when pleasant sensations arise, one experiences their ripening as pleasure.
There are many such proofs of this kind.

Furthermore, just as the meanings of the two causes—homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—do not overlap, the two fruits—outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*)—should likewise not be confused with one another.

Although all results of maturation (*vipāka*) do not transcend those of outflow (*niṣyanda*), the result of maturation is not itself a result of outflow; therefore, one knows that the results of maturation and outflow are distinct.
The Buddha, observing what was appropriate for those to be converted to hear, taught the Dharma with specific distinctions;

whereas the Abhidharma, relying on ultimate reality, definitively adjudicates all phenomena. Thus, the result of maturation does not subsume all results, because the Sūtra states that there are three types of results of karma.
If all fruits were exclusively maturation fruits (*vipāka-phala*), the Sūtra should not have spoken of both "fruits" and "maturation.
If one maintains that all fruits are maturation fruits, one must also admit that all causes are maturation causes; for the Sūtra states that all karmas are productive causes (*janaka-hetu*).

Just as the eye, ear, and so forth have past karma as their cause, and all that arises from causes must likewise stem from past karma, it follows that the Sūtra’s statement that ignorance is the cause from which greed, hatred, and delusion arise would be contradicted.
Furthermore, there are sūtras that state:
"Due to causes and conditions, sentient beings become addicted and defiled.
All such cases should be attributed to past karma; what fault would there be in accepting this?
Just as various bodies are the fruits of past karma, so too are the differences in the manifestation of afflictions.
If this were the case, one would be identical to those who hold the heterodox view of disconnection (*visaṃyoga*), and would not be a disciple of the Buddha.
Setting aside for now such digressions that dispel ignorance, we should now correctly analyze the fundamental characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
For what reason do untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas not bring about maturation (*vipāka*)?
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
Because it lacks the moisture of craving, it is like a genuine seed that has not been watered and nourished.
Furthermore, since untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are not bound to any level of existence (*bhūmi*), how could they possibly summon a retribution (*vipāka*) that is bound to such a level?
For what reason do neutral states not bring about maturation?
Because their power is weak, like a rotten seed.
Other wholesome and unwholesome states can bring about maturation, like various sound and intact seeds moistened by water.
However, the term "vipāka-hetu" (ripening cause) may be analyzed as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), as the Sūtra says:
"the eye born of ripening" (*vipākaja-cakṣus*).
Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound), as the Sūtra states: [“the eye that is a ripening”].
Regarding the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma, the meaning has been explained as previously discussed.
As for the term "maturation," it refers either to ripening apart from its cause or ripening differently from its cause; these two aspects pertain to the fruit.
Alternatively, when the karma that has been created reaches the time of its fruition, it transforms and becomes capable of ripening; this is one sense of "cause" (*hetu*).
However, the Master of the Sūtras (Śrīlāta) states:
"The Vaibhāṣika masters offer this explanation: 'ripening as a different category' is the meaning of *vipāka*."

To say that the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) ripens only as a different category [of result], while the co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) and so forth ripen only as the same category, and that the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) alone—being both of the same and different categories—is therefore uniquely called the "retributive cause," and so forth at length, is all unreasonable; for the Vaibhāṣika masters do not definitively maintain that everything obtained from the six causes is termed "ripening" (*vipāka*).
If this is granted, there is no fault even if one uses "result" as a synonym for it.
This ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is generally said to be of two types:
first, that which is capable of projecting (*ākṣepa*).
Second, regarding the fulfillment [of the result]:
Furthermore, the commonality of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) cannot be projected by the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) alone.
How is this known to be so?
Because it is stated in the sūtras. As the sūtra states:
"Karma is the cause of birth."
Furthermore, it is said:
"Karma causes one to revolve in the cycle of birth and death.
It is also stated:
Karmic power can distinguish sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The inferior realm is induced by volitional karma."
One should know that the inferior realm (*hīnadhātu*) is precisely the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇapāda* states:
"All life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*) are the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma, yet they are not themselves karma."
Regarding the statement that "non-associated formations have no such karma," various commentators explain this passage from the *Prakaraṇapāda* as follows:

"All life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*) are indeed maturation (*vipāka*); because they possess the most predominant power in bringing about maturation, it is with this underlying intention that this statement was made."
Does this explanation not further refute the existence of a drawing power in the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), since karma is the predominant cause for maturation (*vipāka*)?

Life-force (*jīvita*) and the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) are preeminent maturations; it is only by admitting that karma alone draws forth life-force and the homogeneous character that one can say that the power of karma in drawing forth maturation is most supreme.

It should not be otherwise; for when karma draws forth a life-span and a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), even that which is not itself karmic in nature can likewise induce a ripened result (*vipāka*).
If one were to maintain that what is non-karmic can also draw forth a superior ripened result, then one could not say that the power of karma is supreme in inducing ripened results.
Therefore, that interpretation is certainly not reasonable.

It is not the case that bodily and vocal actions, which follow the mind, are necessarily unable to project the life-force and the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*); for if this were so, it would contradict both the sūtras and correct reasoning.
The Sūtra states:
"The inferior realm is induced by volition.
This explains that the life-force (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) of the desire realm are produced solely by mental karma, not by bodily or vocal karma.

The numerous atoms of bodily and vocal informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) are produced by a single moment of mind; among them, only one atom projects the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), for it is illogical that others should possess this capacity.
If it were admitted that they arise simultaneously and together produce a single effect, then they would have to be simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another.

However, it is not accepted in our school’s tenets that resistant derived matter (*sapratigha-upādāya-rūpa*) serves as a simultaneous cause for another, because such matter is not produced through mutual power.

Furthermore, it is not the case that individual atoms sequentially draw forth the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*), because they arise from a single mind; nor is there any fault in the fact that a single arising mind lacks distinct functional capacities to separately project subsequent [moments].

The same fault applies to those [actions] that are ripening-karmas (*vipākakarman*), because within a single lifetime they are each capable of individually producing the full fruits of form, odor, taste, and so forth.

Based on this, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is also explained in the same way: because its substance consists of many abstentions (*virati*) arising from a single mind, and it is not admitted that these [abstentions] act as simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*) for one another.
If there were no non-concomitant causes among obstructive derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), the mention of the term "obstructive" would be useless.
This statement is made to indicate that all obstructive derived matter is not a concomitant cause;
however, there exists obstructive-less derived matter that can serve as a concomitant cause, and thus it cannot be treated in the same manner as the former.
If the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—bound to the desire realm were unable to project [rebirth], it would contradict the sūtras, which state:
"If one cultivates, practices, or frequently practices killing, one will be born in hell," and so forth at length.
Furthermore, this contradicts the *Mūla-śāstra*, which states:
"Among these three types of unwholesome conduct, which offense is the greatest?

It is the false speech that facilitates the schism of the Saṃgha; this karma brings about the maturation of a lifespan of one kalpa in the Avīci Hell. This lifespan is definitively taught to be the "projected fruit" (*ākṣepaka-phala*).
This explanation is stated to clarify that the volition which acts as the producer is coarse and easy to understand; thus, there is no contradiction.

Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are times when a single aggregate (*skandha*) serves as a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers, for example, to the acquisition of a dharma (*prāpti*) together with its arising (*jāti*) and so forth.
Sometimes two aggregates serve as ripening causes (vipāka-hetu) to collectively produce a single fruit, namely, wholesome or unwholesome form (rūpa) along with its arising and so forth.

Sometimes four aggregates serve as ripening causes to collectively produce a single fruit, namely, wholesome or unwholesome mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) along with their arising and so forth.

Because there is no concomitant matter (*anuvartaka-rūpa*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are no five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that serve as a maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit.
Other masters say:

"In the desire realm, there are also five aggregates that serve as causes to collectively produce a single fruit; namely, the manifest and unmanifest matter (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*) of the same moment, along with the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) that give rise to them."
That argument is incorrect, because the bodily and vocal actions produced differ from their respective productive karmas in terms of their maturation (*vipāka*).
Since the producer and the produced do not necessarily occur at the same time, the fruits they induce do not necessarily arise simultaneously.

As for the claim that the producer and the produced should be a single fruit because they are capable of taking up a fruit at one and the same time, this reasoning is also incorrect; for although the producer and the produced may coincide in time, their fruits are distinct.
Although manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) arise in the same moment, there is still a difference in the results they produce.

Furthermore, while manifest actions consist of many atoms (*paramāṇu*), non-manifest action likewise consists of many instances of abstention (*virati*); yet even though they necessarily arise simultaneously, their results differ. How much more so, then, could the mind and mental factors that produce them—being non-concomitant with matter (*rūpa*)—possibly take on a single result together?
Therefore, what he has stated is certainly not logical.

Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are times when a single aggregate (*skandha*) acts as a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers to the acquisition of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-prāpti*), the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and their respective births and so forth.

Sometimes two aggregates act as ripening causes (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers, for example, to the wholesome informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) of the first dhyāna along with its arising and other characteristics.
There are no informative actions in the second dhyāna and above, because there is no capacity to initiate them.

Sometimes four aggregates function as a maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; that is to say, when there is no concomitant matter (*anuvartaka-rūpa*), consisting of wholesome mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) along with their [characteristics] such as arising (*jāti*).
There are six such minds, which will be explained later.

Sometimes the five aggregates act as a collective ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to produce a single fruit; this refers to the concomitant matter (*anuvartaka-rūpa*), all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), and their [characteristics] such as arising (*jāti*).

Within the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), sometimes a single aggregate acts as a ripening cause to produce a single fruit; this refers to the attainment of recollection (*pūrva-janma-smṛti-labdhi*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and their [characteristics] such as arising.
Sometimes four aggregates function as a single ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to produce one fruit; this refers to all wholesome mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Thus, there are nine ripening causes in total; that is, within the three realms, there are respectively three, three, and two types according to their sequential order.
There is karma that brings about the maturation of only one sphere (*āyatana*), namely, the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), such as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth.
If it brings about the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*), it necessarily brings about two spheres, namely, mind and mental objects.
If one experiences the sense-base of tangibles, it should be known that there are likewise two: namely, tangibles and mental objects (*dharma*).
If one experiences the sense-base of visible forms, one necessarily experiences three bases: namely, visible forms, tangibles, and mental objects.
If one experiences odors or tastes, it should be known that there are likewise three [bases]: namely, each [of those two] individually, together with the tangible and the mental object (dharma).
If one experiences the body-base, one necessarily experiences four bases: namely, the body-base, the form-base, the tangible-base, and the mental-object-base.
If one experiences the sense base of the eye, one necessarily experiences five bases: namely, the eye, the body, visible forms, the tangible, and the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*).

One should know that experiencing the ear, nose, or tongue likewise involves five bases: namely, each [sense organ] as one, along with the body, visible forms, the tangible, and the mental-object base.
There are karmas capable of inducing six, seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven bases (*āyatana*).
Since sound is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*), it is not discussed here; this is because karma may have either few or many fruits.

Just as external seeds produce fruits that are either few or many—for instance, the seeds of the lotus and others yield various distinct fruits such as roots, sprouts, stalks, flowers, pericarps, filaments, and leaves—whereas the seeds of the grape and other such plants do not.

The species of *pāṭala* trees have many roots, trunks, branches, twigs, flowers, leaves, and various kinds of fruits; there are also various species of water and land plants and trees that have only a single trunk, such as the *śara* grass and others.
Alternatively, there may be growth consisting only of leaves without stems and so forth; such is the nature of seeds, and one should not question it.

There is karma of a single moment that has maturation over many moments, but there is no karma of many moments that has maturation in a single moment, lest the fruit be less than the labor expended and thus diminish the cause.

There is karma of one lifetime with maturation in three lifetimes, but there is no karma of three lifetimes with maturation in one lifetime; this is the natural law regarding the power that draws forth maturation.
Furthermore, the fruit of maturation does not coexist with the karma, because the fruit is not experienced at the very moment the karma is created.
Furthermore, karma that is present does not ripen into its fruit immediately, because the principle governing the gates of karmic reception is determinate.
Nor does it ripen without interval, because it is induced by the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) in the subsequent moment.
Because at the very moment it arises, its power is difficult to restrain.
Furthermore, since a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) produces a fruit of a different category, it must depend upon a continuity (*saṃtati*) in order to bring it about.
Having explained the six causes, the determination of their temporal status shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
"The universal and the similar [causes] / Belong to the three times and have three [results] in the three times.
The commentary says:
The pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and homogeneous (*sabhāga*) causes exist only in the past and present; they do not exist in the future, for the reasoning is as previously explained.
The three causes—associated (*samprayuktaka*), co-existent (*sahabhū*), and retributive (*vipāka*)—are entirely present throughout all three time periods.

Since the verse does not specify the temporal locus of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), it should be understood by implication that it extends across the three time periods as well as the non-temporal;
for its specific temporal division cannot be definitively stated.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 16; *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 17.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Nine: Distinguishing the Differences, Part Two, Section Nine. Having already distinguished the characteristics and temporal determinations of the six causes, one must now establish the designation of "cause" in relation to their effects.
What is called the fruit that corresponds to its cause?
The verse says:
Fruits are conditioned phenomena and disjunction; The unconditioned has neither cause nor fruit.
The treatise says:
There are five kinds of fruits, which shall be explained in detail later; for now, we shall briefly indicate the conditioned and the dissociated.
As stated in the root treatise:
What are the resultant phenomena (*phala-dharma*)? They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
But since analytical cessation is admitted to be a result, must it not necessarily have a cause?
That which lacks a cause cannot be said to be a fruit, for such a thing has never been observed.
I also accept that the Path is the cause for realization, because the Sūtra describes it as the fruit of śrāmaṇya.
Within these six causes, from which cause is this [attainment] derived?
I say that this fruit is not derived from the six causes, because the six causes previously mentioned are what depend upon for its production.
If that is so, one must admit that this cause of attainment (*prāpti-hetu*) exists as a seventh cause, distinct from the preceding six.
What our school accepts is exactly as you have stated. Is it not the case that in your own school there is such a recitation: "Nirvāṇa is a fruit, yet it has no cause"?
Although such a recitation exists, there is no error in its meaning.
That is to say, in the world, when a desired undertaking is accomplished through exertion of effort, people collectively designate it by the name "result.
Death is an extreme source of affliction for a person; therefore, among all things, non-death is what a person most desires.
That which is thus desired is called a "fruit" because it is realized through the functional power of the Path.

As for the statement that there is no cause, it is because the Path is not any of the six causes with respect to the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) that has been attained.
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is, with respect to the Path, not a fruit that is produced, but a fruit that is realized;
the Path, with respect to cessation through deliberation, is not a cause that produces it, but a cause that realizes it.
Therefore, the Path and Cessation stand in mutual opposition; it cannot be definitively stated whether they are cause and effect, or right and wrong.
If the Path were the cause for the realization of Cessation, then Cessation alone should be the fruit of the Path.
Who says that the fruit of the Path is definitely not the acquisition (*prāpti*) of cessation?
For the Path serves as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the acquisition of cessation, or it is also said to be its simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

However, this [acquisition] is not the fruit truly sought by the Noble Ones (*ārya*). This is because the Noble Ones cultivate the Noble Path with the cessation they have attained held within their mental continuum; thus, the superior fruit of the Path is solely the cessation attained, not the acquisition of that cessation. This is because the Noble Ones do not cultivate the Noble Path seeking after conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

Therefore, in the sūtras, the Blessed One spoke of the fruits of śrāmaṇya as being solely the abandonment [of defilements] through that which is not the path, rather than merely the realization of the path.
This does not mean that the cultivation of the path is useless; for at the moment one attains the first thought-moment of the path, what was to be accomplished has already been achieved.
If you admit that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is an efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), you must admit that nirvāṇa has a dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
However, one does not admit that analytical cessation possesses the capacity to produce the arising of the eye and other faculties in the same way that sound and other phenomena do.

This means that during the stage of the actual arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena do not act as obstructions; therefore, all phenomena can serve as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
However, within the category of conditioned phenomena, only those that are past or present possess the functions of grasping and giving, and are thus said to have results.
Future phenomena and unconditioned phenomena do not function in such a manner; therefore, they do not possess results.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
"All causes and conditions that can produce consciousness are impermanent."
Although unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are causes and conditions, they cannot produce [an effect]; therefore, the Buddha did not speak of them [in this context].
As previously analyzed regarding the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), there are briefly two types of efficient causes:

first, those possessing the power to produce; second, those that merely do not obstruct. Thus, while unconditioned phenomena serve as a cause by way of non-obstruction, they do not possess an effect because they cannot produce one.
Does not the Sūtra state:
"With the mind and mental objects as conditions, mental consciousness arises"?
For what reason, then, is the unconditioned, though included within mental objects, unable to produce [consciousness]?
Based on the capacity for manifold production, the *Abhidharmakośa* makes this statement; what prevents a small portion from being incapable of producing?
Alternatively, even the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) could produce consciousness, yet consciousness is not its fruit, because it has been stated previously that [the unconditioned] is not a producer.
This would then imply impermanence, since that [unconditioned] is said to be able to produce future existence-consciousness.

By this principle, just as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are established in terms of cause and effect, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not; therefore, it is logically established that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is a cause without an effect, and an effect without a cause.

In this regard, many types of people revile *nirvāṇa*, and the causes for their reviling are manifold and diverse. I shall now primarily refute the grounds for the Master of the Sūtras' (Sautrāntika) reviling, while incidentally refuting other teachers as well, in order to establish *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*; by means of this, I shall also discuss the other two unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

In this context, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) cites the Sautrāntika doctrine that all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack substantial reality, because they do not exist as distinct, real entities in the manner that form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth do.

However, as for what the Sūtras state, they define space solely by the absence of anything tangible; that is to say, when one encounters nothing tangible in the darkness, one then says: "This is space."

When the seeds that give rise to already-arisen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have been extinguished, and by the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) the remainder no longer arises, this is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

When, apart from the power of discernment, the remainder no longer arises due to the deficiency of conditions, it is called "cessation not through discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), such as the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) of one who dies prematurely within the remainder of their *nikāya-sabhāga*.
All of these are irrational, as there is no evidence to prove them.

Furthermore, regarding what you said—that space is defined solely by the absence of tangibility—I also accept that the name "space" refers to the absence of tangibility, because space is indeed intangible.
To say that space is merely the absence of tangibility and does not exist as a separate entity—what is the proof for this?
It is already established that when there is no object encountered through touch in the darkness, one then says: "This is space."
Does this reason not prove that [space] does not exist? It is not merely by using what has been stated as a reason that one can prove that space definitely does not exist.
For they merely state: "This is space; it is not something that can be contacted."
How do we know that "space" is designated only in reference to the absence of tangibility?
It is like the common worldly expression:
"This pleasure is not suffering."
Is it that only the absence of suffering is designated as "happiness"?
If you say this is not so—claiming that the two sensations of suffering and happiness differ because one causes harm while the other provides benefit—then this analogy is inconsistent.

For this space performs no function whatsoever that could be comparable to happiness; thus, the previous argument would become redundant, since you now seek to prove its non-existence solely on the grounds that space performs no function at all.

Furthermore, it cannot be established that the absence of tactile contact is the definitive reason for asserting that space exists; to use this as proof that the essence of space is merely the absence of anything tangible would mean that the Master of the Sūtras has no valid reason here to prove that space definitively exists.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Space is unconditioned because it performs a function; thus it is not unlike pleasure.
As the Blessed One said:
Wind relies upon space; while it is without activity, it has a support, yet there is no conscious grasping involved.
Furthermore, the characteristic of luminous color is the mark of space.
Therefore, one knows that the substance of space truly exists.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"However, by relying upon light, space becomes manifest.
From this, it is definitively established that the characteristic of space is what is called "light"; for this reason, the Sūtra further speaks these words.
This means that the Buddha first stated that wind relies upon space, and subsequently stated that space has no basis of reliance, so as to prevent that brahmin from giving rise to such a doubt:
"How can it be known for certain that space exists?"
However, because the World-Honored One stated that wind depends upon space, he spoke these further words to dispel that doubt:
"If space were non-existent, what would light depend upon?
Light possesses color, visibility, and resistance."
If space did not exist, who could provide containment?
Therefore, when the World-Honored One said that "space is manifested by means of light," he meant that the manifestation of the color of light serves as the characteristic of space as a real entity.
However, that Elder, failing to understand the intended meaning of this sūtra, falsely raised this objection:
"If space is made manifest by means of light, then space should be subsumed under the category of material phenomena (rūpadharma)."
If one questions thus: "From where does this [space] come?
Furthermore, the essence of space should not be non-existent, because it is described in the sūtras in the same manner as the mind. As a sūtra says:
Space is colorless, invisible, and non-obstructive; upon what, then, could it depend?
Such specific designations cannot apply to the self, nor to things such as the horns of a rabbit.
In this context, that commentary provides this statement in response to the question asked.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"I am well-tamed."
"I am the support"—if one were to speak these words in response to a question, such a statement should not be made; rather, one should say:
"Brahmin! Space has no substance; upon what could it possibly depend?"

Furthermore, one should not say that space is manifested by relying on light, nor should one say it can be understood in terms of a prior limit (*pūrvānta*), nor that it can be found in terms of an agent (*kartṛ*); rather, one should answer such questions according to reality.
If one speaks of what does not exist as if it did exist, such speech becomes meaningless and useless.
Furthermore, the analogy cited lacks the power to prove [your point], because it was taught that "I" and "the basis of the I" refer to the mind.
This has already been extensively examined and analyzed regarding its internal meaning.
If terms such as "formless" (arūpa) and so forth lacked any real referent, what would the analogy you have cited establish?
Furthermore, regarding what they have said:
"If the essence of space possessed even a slight degree of substantial reality, then because space is eternal, obstructed matter would never arise;
or else one must admit that it is included within the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), as the Vātsīputrīyas do."
He spoke thus because he failed to reflect carefully.

For according to his own tenet, it is not that the essence of space is obstructed by other obstructive matter; rather, when other matter arises, space opens up and makes way for it, which results in the fallacy of its being impermanent. This is because, according to what he maintains, space truly cannot accommodate other obstructive matter.
However, because this space has the nature of providing room and is not of the nature of matter (*rūpa*), there is no need for it to open or make way.

Since the essence of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is obstructive matter, when other matter arises, it stands to reason that it must open and make way; thus, the space-element is a subtle and light form of matter which, though not obstructing others, is itself obstructed by them, and is therefore subsumed under the category of impermanent, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

Since the characteristic of space neither obstructs other things nor is itself obstructed by them, how could it be categorized as impermanent or conditioned at the moment when material phenomena arise?
Space coexists with matter without contradiction; therefore, throughout all stages, it neither arises nor ceases.

However, as for the presence of obstructions within walls and the like, this is because obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*) occupies those spaces, thereby blocking others; it is not because space (*ākāśa*) or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are absent there.

The matter of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu-rūpa*) is subtle, thin, light, and wondrous, and thus cannot obstruct other matter; when it is displaced by other coarse and heavy matter, it immediately yields the way.
All resistant material phenomena (*sapratigha-rūpa-dharma*) should be understood in this way: where one occupies a space, a second cannot possibly exist there.
Since space (*ākāśa*) is non-resistant (*apratigha*), it differs from the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*); how, then, could it be subject to the same fallacy of impermanence as the latter?
Furthermore, as for what they have said—
that if the essence of space were a truly existent entity, it would necessarily be conditioned because it would be indistinguishable from the element of space—
this is mere empty talk devoid of actual reasoning, for the Blessed One himself has stated that there is a distinction between them.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Space is without form, invisible, and non-obstructive.
It further states:
When the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*) is abandoned through detachment from the defilements of form (*rūparāga*), it is abandoned simultaneously with four [other elements].

If the realm of space were not distinct from empty space (*ākāśa*), then since empty space is without form, invisible, and non-obstructive, the realm of space should likewise be so; it should, therefore, be said to be abandoned at the time of detachment from the defilements of the formless (*ārūpya*), just as the realm of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) is described.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that the space-element (ākāśadhātu) constitutes a conventional person (pudgala), and it also says that space is manifested by means of light.
If the space-element were identical to space itself, and if light itself were the space-element, how could the Sūtra state that "it is light that manifests space"? It would not be logical.
