Thus we know there is a distinction.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"Of all dharmas—whether conditioned or unconditioned—that which is free from defilement is the foremost."

However, within this sutra, there are two types of dharmas. It cannot be said that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not exist as a dharma, for if it lacked a substantial nature (*svabhāva*), it could not constitute the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

As for the various unconditioned [factors], they manifest that their substance is manifold; thus, there are both space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Only by being free from defilement can [non-analytical cessation] be established as manifold, and apart from these, no other unconditioned factors exist.
For this reason, the space element is not identical to empty space.
The Elder (Sthavira), failing to reflect, stated that there is no distinction between the two. Other masters say:
"There is no separate space, because there is no cognition of 'space' regarding obstructed matter.
This statement is irrational; for it is precisely by this very reason that one can prove that space exists as a distinct entity.

Since there exists a distinct entity of space (*ākāśa*) within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), which is characterized by the absence of resistance, it can serve as an object-condition (*ālambana*) for the arising of the cognition of space;
for if there were no such object-condition, that cognition would not arise.
Therefore, their assertion is nothing but empty words.
Furthermore, it may also be said that there is no distinct obstructive matter within space, because the cognition of matter arises [therein].
However, this does not prove the non-existence of matter; therefore, it cannot prove that space is non-existent.

If it is argued that all material forms (*rūpa*) possess an essence that can be known, then emptiness (*śūnyatā*) should likewise be so; for it can be known through inference (*anumāna*). That is to say, although the eyes and other [faculties] are not directly perceived, they are known to possess an essence by virtue of their functional utility.
Since this space also possesses function, its substantial existence is known through inference.
Its function is as previously described; therefore, space exists as a distinct, real entity.
Furthermore, regarding that which was said:

Regarding the claim that "the state in which the seeds for the arising of already-arisen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have been extinguished, such that they do not arise again due to the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*),

is called 'cessation through discernment' (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)," this cessation through discernment is logically untenable as well, because there is no distinction between it and the non-arising of phenomena due to the absence of conditions (*pratyaya-vaikalya*).

Regarding the two types of non-arising—through the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) and through the absence of conditions (*apratisaṃkhyā*)—if one investigates them minutely, what difference is there between them?
Furthermore, since there is also non-arising apart from the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), would it not follow that the cultivation of the path is rendered useless?

This is not useless, for by the power of cultivating the path, one can extinguish the seeds of future latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that have not yet arisen and those already produced; because these seeds are extinguished, the afflictions and suffering of future lives are prevented from arising.
If you claim this is not so, by what power could that [non-arising] be attained?

As for the "seeds" (bīja) asserted by the Dārṣṭāntika masters, their roots have already been uprooted without remainder during the previous investigation into the existence or non-existence of possession (prāpti); from where, then, could these seeds arise again now?

If the seeds are not non-existent, and these latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not arise again either due to the absence of conditions or because their seeds are destroyed by the power of analytical discernment (pratisaṃkhyā), what is the difference between these two?
Furthermore, regarding phenomena that do not arise, just as those of the past will never arise again, what need is there to abandon them?

Even if the seeds have not been severed, since the phenomena produced from them will certainly not arise again—just as if they were already severed—the diligent cultivation of the path of abandonment would be rendered useless.

Is it not the case that in your own school as well, regarding dharmas for which non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) has already been attained, one must further apply diligent skillful means to cultivate the path capable of abandoning them in order to abandon that [attainment]?

Our school may indeed hold this view; for since we teach that the afflictions and suffering of the three time periods are abandoned in general, and that one separately realizes *nirvāṇa* through various dharmas that do not arise, these [dharmas] must still be abandoned because they would otherwise obstruct the attainment of *nirvāṇa*, just like those of the past.

Your school is not so, for you maintain that Nirvana consists solely in the non-arising of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and suffering; thus, although the seeds have not yet been extinguished, there is a state of "as if already extinguished" wherein they never arise again. Since this non-arising is itself the essence of Nirvana, how does it differ from what follows?
Upon careful investigation, no distinction is found between them.
Therefore, in our school, it is said that the essence of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained by severing the afflictions and suffering of the three periods of time;

whereas cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained solely by the non-arising of future conditioned phenomena due to the deficiency of their conditions. It is by virtue of this that the characteristics of these two cessations do not become confused.
Furthermore, what he has stated contradicts the sūtras. A sūtra says:
"If the five faculties are cultivated, practiced, and frequently cultivated, they can bring about the eternal severance of all suffering of the past, future, and present."
This essence of permanent abandonment is itself nirvāṇa; it possesses the sense of non-arising only with respect to the future, not with respect to the past or present. Is this not contradictory?
Although there is this textual passage, it does not contradict the meaning.
The intention of this sutra is to state that because the afflictions conditioned by past and present suffering have been severed, it is called the "severance of all sufferings.
As the Blessed One said:
"You should sever craving for form; when craving is severed, it is then called the 'severance of form' and the 'thorough knowledge of form,'" and so on at length.
The principle that past and present suffering is abandoned should likewise apply here. Alternatively, there may be a specific intended meaning within this sūtra:

"past afflictions" refers to afflictions arising in past lives, and "present afflictions" refers to afflictions arising in the present life. Thus, because the afflictions arising in these two periods serve to produce future afflictions, they induce seeds within the present continuum; when these seeds are severed, those [afflictions] are also said to be severed. This is just as when the maturation (vipāka) is exhausted, one also says that the karma is exhausted.
Future sufferings and all afflictions, because they lack seeds, will never arise; this is what is called "abandonment.
If it were otherwise, for what reason would it be necessary to abandon those of the past and present?
It is not the case that one must exert effort to cause [defilements] to cease when they have already ceased or are currently ceasing;
all such claims are merely empty words.

Furthermore, this refutes the first interpretation of the sūtra’s meaning: namely, that when the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) abandons defilements, there are no past or present defilements capable of being taken as objects, which could then be abandoned by it.
Yet the Sūtra states:
"By cultivating the five faculties, one abandons past and present suffering.
At that time, would those afflictions be in the future or in the present?
It is certainly impossible to maintain that this grasping exists in the past, for since it has already ceased and no longer exists, how could it still need to be abandoned?
If it were in the future, such grasping would not exist; being like a flower in the sky, what object of perception could there be?
If it were present, there would be two minds existing simultaneously, which is irrational due to the fault of concurrent occurrence.
If one claims that the seed exists, the seed itself cannot be established.

Even if one were to grant that [the afflictions] are established, it would still be unreasonable; for the essence of mind and mental factors does not lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*). How, then, could it be said that they take past and present suffering as their object?
Nor should they be reckoned as uncontaminated minds (*anāsrava-citta*), because uncontaminated minds are not afflictions.

Furthermore, since [the object] is not something to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*), how can you maintain that by abandoning it, one also says that the afflictions (*kleśa*) directed toward the two periods of past and present are abandoned?
Now, let me ask you: what past or present afflictions do you claim are abandoned in this state?
Therefore, what you have said is entirely devoid of real meaning.
Furthermore, regarding the afflictions that arise conditioned by [factors] transcending the world, the cultivation of the five faculties should be unable to sever them. Why is this so?
Because the Sūtra does not state this.

You maintain that the Sūtra’s statement regarding the abandonment of past and present [afflictions] refers to the abandonment of past and present afflictions that take [the object] as their cognitive support; therefore, the statement regarding the abandonment of future [afflictions] should be understood in the same way.
Does not the Sūtra state:
"By cultivating the five faculties, one abandons future suffering"?
Since the term "suffering" is used in a general sense, it also includes that which takes [suffering] as its object.
"Detached from worldly afflictions"—is this not like that scripture regarding "empty flowers," which lacks any basis and is explained according to one's own whims?

The World-Honored One spoke in general terms that the cultivation of the five faculties can sever all suffering of the past, future, and present; for what reason do you insist on interpreting these words regarding the severance of the past and present as meaning that the severance applies to the past and present afflictions that take those [objects] as their cognitive objects?

If you maintain that this statement regarding the "cutting off of the future" means the cutting off of the substance (*svabhāva*) of future suffering, you must certainly explain the phrase "cutting off the future.

If it were merely the cutting off of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that take the future as their object, then one would be unable to cut off those afflictions that arise taking that which is beyond time (*adhvaviprayukta*) as their object, even through the cultivation of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

If you definitively interpret the statement regarding the abandonment of future [suffering] as meaning that it abandons the substance of future suffering, and thus includes the afflictions that take it as their object and exist apart from the [three] time periods,
then— since the term "future suffering" is general— it should likewise include the afflictions of the past and present that take it as their object.
If that were so, the Sūtra should not have stated separately that one can sever past and present suffering.

By this reasoning, it is established that the Sūtra’s mention of severing past and present [suffering] refers only to the severance of the substance (*dravya*) of suffering; thus, we know that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is proven to sever the suffering of all three time periods, and is not established as having merely the non-arising of future proclivities (*anuśaya*) and suffering as its essence.

Furthermore, the scriptural citations you have adduced are also inconsistent; for it is not logically tenable that the cessation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) directed toward past and present suffering constitutes the cessation of all suffering (*sarva-duḥkha-prahāṇa*).
Likewise, the claim that the cessation of craving (*rāga*) entails the cessation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth is also logically untenable, as the same fault applies as before.
How is it called "abandonment"?
You should reflect on this yourself.

Furthermore, the aggregates such as form are not called "abandoned" solely because craving is abandoned; for the aggregates such as form are also the objects of anger, pride, and so forth, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also abandoned simultaneously with craving. Therefore, one should not definitively state that form and the others are abandoned merely by virtue of the abandonment of their subjective perceivers.

In this way, the statement regarding the abandonment of past and present [afflictions] should also be explained; it does not refer solely to the abandonment of the afflictions that serve as the objective conditions.
Therefore, the scriptural citations he adduces accord with our own school, whereas they do not accord with the principles of his own school.

By this, the latter interpretation of that scripture—which claims that the term "seed" has no real referent and that it is based on this [non-existent seed] that cessation is taught—is also refuted; how could such a meaning possibly be established?

Furthermore, the analogy cited is not one of like nature (*sādharmya*), because karma and its maturation (*vipāka*) possess distinct entities; since the status of a "seed" cannot be established apart from the afflictions (*kleśa*), how can one say that by severing those seeds, one severs past and present suffering?
Therefore, that [position] is without merit and merely constructs empty words.
Furthermore, to claim that non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the essence of *nirvāṇa* is utterly irrational, as it entails the fault of impermanence (*anityatva*).

The Abhidharma states that there are cases where noble ones (*ārya*), having already severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), may still fall back and be reborn; this principle is firm and will be extensively debated later.
Therefore, what they have stated is not something that the wise would find acceptable.
Furthermore, since their own school admits that the future does not exist, how can they maintain that what is already non-existent becomes even more non-existent?
That "what previously existed later ceases to exist" is a fact universally established in the world.
Furthermore, how can that which the proponents of that treatise maintain—nirvāṇa as mere non-arising—be called "attained"?

It is called the attainment of nirvāṇa because, through the attainment of the antidote, one realizes a basis for the body that is ultimately incompatible with the arising of future afflictions and further existence. Thus it is termed "attainment."
If that were so, as soon as one attains the first moment of the noble path, one should attain nirvāṇa regarding the afflictions to be abandoned.
At that time, one would have already attained the basis of the body which is ultimately incompatible with those afflictions that are to arise and are to be abandoned by this path.

If one were to abide in this way, then upon later training in the path, one would already be an Arhat (aśaikṣa), because one would already possess the physical basis that is the opposite of what is to be remedied by that path.
While abiding in these paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), what liberation-path has yet to be realized that remains to be sought?
If one has already attained *nirvāṇa*, what further use is there for cultivation?
This objection does not hold, because at the first moment of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśabīja*) are extinguished simultaneously [with the path].

According to your own tenets, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the various afflictions cannot be called the "acquisition of an affliction that is about to arise" unless the seeds of the afflictions have been permanently extinguished; for subsequently, there would be a body that is fundamentally incompatible [with such arising].

Furthermore, it is not the case that the seeds of all afflictions have already been permanently extinguished before the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) has arisen; therefore, when one abides in subsequent training on the path, there is no fault of having already become an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*).
If that were so, those beyond training (aśaikṣa) would still possess afflictions. Why?
Because if the first moment of the Noble Path does not contradict the seeds of affliction, then subsequent moments should likewise be the same, as there is no distinction between them.

However, this "attainment" (*prāpti*) cannot serve as a valid analogy, because we admit that its substance is distinct [from the dharma it attains], and because it arises at a later time as a specific differentiation of the noble path (*āryamārga*).
That is to say, I maintain that attainment exists as a separate, real entity; it does not contradict "patience" (*kṣānti*), yet it is incompatible with "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Why is this so? Because wisdom and the acquisition of afflictions are mutually exclusive, yet they arise simultaneously.

In your own school, you maintain that the "seeds of affliction" are merely the transformation of the continuum that serves as the basis for afflictions, and you define nirvana as the absolute non-arising of afflictions; what, then, is the ontological substance of these phenomena?
What dharma does it not contradict?
With what is it in contradiction?
Furthermore, at the time when the initial noble path is about to arise, it is the stage when the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is about to perish.

When the first Path of the Noble Ones arises, one abandons the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Apart from that, what distinct seeds of affliction could there be that would not contradict the first Path of the Noble Ones, yet subsequently contradict the path of non-distinction?
Therefore, your tenet is not well-established.
Furthermore, if nirvāṇa were entirely without essence, how could the sūtra state:
"Among all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, this is the foremost"?
How can a name for a phenomenon (*dharma*) be established for that which has no substantial entity?
How can one speak of superiority among that which is non-existent?

We observe that among all phenomena possessing their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), one may speak of superiority or inferiority in relation to one another; however, we have never seen it said that rabbit horns or flowers in the sky are established as superior or inferior in relation to one another. Therefore, it is certain that *nirvāṇa* exists separately and possesses its own specific characteristic; thus, it is called a "phenomenon" (*dharma*).
Because its essence is superior to other phenomena, the sense that the essence of nirvāṇa is substantially existent is established.
Furthermore, the Blessed One definitively taught it to exist, as stated in a sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there definitely exists non-arising."
If this did not exist, the manifold sufferings of birth and death would have no end.
It is because of its existence that there is non-arising, and so forth, as explained at length.
I do not say that nirvāṇa is entirely non-existent; rather, it exists in the manner that I have described.

As it is said regarding this sound: that which existed previously does not exist, and that which will exist later does not exist; yet, because one cannot say that what is non-existent is existent, the meaning of its existence is established.
One should know that the same applies to the statement that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) exist: although they do not exist [in a substantial sense], they may still be praised as existing.
Therefore, the ultimate absence of all calamities and misfortunes is called nirvāṇa; this is the most excellent among all that exists and does not exist.

To cause those to be converted to give rise to deep aspiration and joy, it should be praised as the foremost; it is not the case that by speaking thus, the sense of nirvāṇa being an existing entity is established.
Why is this so? Because the two modes of existence—nominal and real—are mutually incompatible, and because no other type of existence has ever been taught.

Although it is said that this sound "existed previously but does not exist now" or "will exist later but does not exist now," one must carefully determine: is this statement of "existence" made with respect to an entity that is ultimately non-existent, or is this statement of "existence" made precisely with respect to an existent thing, establishing it by excluding other possibilities?
If there were some distinct entity existing prior to or subsequent to a sound that could obstruct it, one might say "it does not exist" in the sense that this sound does not exist within that entity.

All instances of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) necessarily depend upon the existence [of something else] for their expression. If, however, one speaks of "existence" regarding an entity that is absolutely non-existent (*atyantābhāva*), how would that not contradict reason?

There is no entity called "nirvāṇa" belonging to you that could serve as a locus for the cessation of suffering; rather, it is precisely because such an entity does not exist that it is described as "non-existent. Therefore, the analogy you have established is incapable of proving your point.
Furthermore, one should not cite conventional discourse to deny the ultimate truth (paramārtha) in order to support one's own position.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) does not approve of such an interpretation here, for he states that it is impossible to negate existence, and thus the meaning of "existence" is established.

If one does not even rejoice in the conventional existence of verbal expressions, how could one say that unconditioned phenomena possess verbal expressions? Therefore, it must certainly be the case that verbal expressions cannot be based upon that which is ultimately non-existent when they are spoken.

However, since that ultimate nirvāṇa is neither existent nor provisional, neither false nor real, and there is nothing else that could be admitted as existing, why is it so extremely profound and obscure for the Dārṣṭāntikas to posit the existence of *dharmatā*?

Furthermore, nowhere has it ever been seen that among non-existent things there can be distinctions of superior or inferior; nor do the wise ever praise or disparage among what is non-existent. Yet, it is said:
"Though it is non-existent, it may still be praised."
This is merely words.
How can you further claim that because all calamities and misfortunes ultimately do not exist, it is called nirvāṇa, and that among existence and non-existence, this is the most supreme?

This means that one perceives superiority and inferiority only within phenomena (*dharma*) that possess substantial existence (*sattva*), not within those lacking substantial existence; therefore, what they say relies solely on false attachment.

Is it not the case that because there are distinctions among existent phenomena, non-existence (*abhāva*) must also have distinctions corresponding to them, just as with form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), and so forth?
It is not the case that they are non-existent yet distinct; this too is incorrect, because neither identity nor difference between the non-existent and the existent can be established.

That is to say, if this non-existence were to possess distinctions, would it be due to its sharing the same characteristics as existence, or due to its having characteristics different from existence?
If it were identical [to non-existence], it would necessarily be existence;
if it were distinct [from non-existence], one should specify what characteristic of form constitutes its being non-existent.
Is it not the case that non-existence itself is this very characteristic?

If that were so, since both form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) are non-existent (*abhāva*), what difference is there between them such that one says that form and the others are non-existent yet distinct from one another?
For example, although form and sound are equally existent, they possess various distinctions in their characteristics;
this is not the case for the non-existent, because it lacks any distinct essence (*svabhāva*).
Based on what has been stated, there are things that, though non-existent, may still be praised; this is explained at length, showing that such claims are merely empty words devoid of actual meaning.
Therefore, superiority and inferiority can only be established regarding what exists; regarding what does not exist, there can certainly be no superiority or inferiority.

Since the Blessed One has stated that nirvāṇa, which is free from defilement, is the most excellent among all phenomena, it must be established as having substantial existence, just like form and other such things.
Furthermore, if the essence of nirvāṇa were non-existent, how could it cause those to be trained to feel weary of cyclic existence and aspire toward liberation?
Because there are no characteristics of superiority or inferiority within non-existence.
Furthermore, it would follow that the Great Sage’s deluded disciples would regard non-existence as being like existence, as some have taught.
Moreover, if one were to give rise to the view that denies nirvāṇa, it would follow that this constitutes right view and an unerring understanding.

If it is argued that this view is false because it does not realize that nirvāṇa is merely the non-existence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), then the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) would necessarily become a correct view, since it too takes as its object only the non-existence of conditioned phenomena.

If it is argued that this view is not correct because the absence of [the self] in mere formations (*saṃskāra*) is not an expedient means for liberation, this is not so; for the view that there is no [self] in formations is not itself called the "view of annihilation" (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), as it is a different kind of view.
However, since all views of annihilation merely take the non-existence of conditioned formations as their object, they cannot prevent the fault of failing to establish right view.
Furthermore, if one gives rise to views such as "peaceful" regarding the object of cessation, these should not be considered right view, because they do not constitute a true understanding.
In that which is not non-existent, there is neither tranquility nor non-tranquility, just as the son of a barren woman is neither brave nor cowardly.

We observe that in illness there is no separate state of health, and in various afflictions there is no separate state of bliss; likewise, within the state where conditioned distinctions do not exist, there must separately exist the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, if nirvāṇa lacked substantial reality, how could it be subsumed under the Noble Truths?
How could that which has no substance be called a "truth" rather than a "falsehood"?
Moreover, what is the meaning of the term "Noble Truth"?
Is it not the case that these words pertain to the meaning of non-erroneousness? For in the vision of the Noble Ones, both existence and non-existence are entirely free from inversion.
That is to say, regarding suffering, the Noble Ones see only suffering; regarding what does not exist within suffering, they see only its non-existence.
What contradiction does this pose to the meaning of the Noble Truths?
There is indeed a contradiction here: namely, that wisdom (*prajñā*) necessarily does not arise in the absence of an object (*ālambana*).
Yet, you claim that noble wisdom perceives what is non-existent as its object; what error could be more perverse than this!
This point shall be analyzed in the discussion of the past and the future.
How can it be that while [the cessation] is ultimately devoid of names and concepts and non-existent, one may nevertheless say, "This is the cessation of suffering," without contradicting reason?
Since we directly perceive that the designation "this" or "that" arises only with respect to what exists, how could such a designation arise with respect to what does not exist?
Furthermore, if it were non-existent, how could it constitute a third truth?
Regarding this, the Sūtra Master (Sautrāntika) offers a flippant reply:
"Because the noble vision and the teaching [of the third fruit] occur immediately after the second, it is established as the third.
This reply is irrational.
The intention of the current objection is this: if cognition necessarily does not arise in the absence of an object, how can one perceive the unconditioned as the third truth?
Furthermore, if it lacks substantial reality and consists of nothing but empty words, for what reason is it designated as the third Noble Truth?

Furthermore, if the cessation of suffering were merely the non-existence of suffering, then one should speak only of the path that remedies suffering; for by speaking of the path, the non-existence of the suffering it remedies is already made manifest.
If it does not cause [suffering] to cease, how can it be called the "remedy"?

Since this treatise relies on the path of cultivation (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) for the purpose of bringing about the non-existence of suffering, the cessation of that suffering is already implicitly revealed by the teaching of the path; why, then, would one speak of the cessation of suffering separately from the path that abandons it?

Therefore, if nirvāṇa were nothing other than the path that abandons suffering and lacked a distinct substantial entity, it would be a mere empty word. What use would there be in designating it as the third noble truth?
Furthermore, you ought to explain what fault you perceive in the position that establishes *nirvāṇa* as a real entity (*dravyasat*), such that you do not accept it?
However, to assert that *nirvāṇa* is a distinct real thing does not contradict even a single point of the purposeful meaning within the Buddha’s holy teaching.
Although they claim: "If one asserts that [the self] exists substantially, one falls into the error of adhering to false conceptualization, which is a fault," this is not logical;
for even to conceptualize something as ultimately non-existent is called 'existence,' and is therefore equally false.

Furthermore, they have other false conceptualizations, namely that future phenomena are non-existent and yet further non-existent, which they reckon as *nirvāṇa*; the faults of this are as previously explained.

Moreover, they conceive that there exists a seed of affliction within phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), which is neither identical to nor separate from them; although it is like a person (*pudgala*) or an axe, it nevertheless possesses the functional capacity to produce obstacles to the Path and so forth.

Such categories as these involve the grasping at non-existence as existence and are false conceptual constructions; since you have long been habituated to them and hold them as your own tenets, why do you now repudiate them?
Although you have made this statement by means of another’s words, it would seem to protect the Vaibhāṣika school;

yet, upon closer examination, the Master of the Sūtras appears to be generally weary of and opposed to the Vaibhāṣika school, wishing to rely on the analogy of a flower in the sky to negate that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Now, for the time being, let us set aside the negation of nirvāṇa and employ it as a corroborative example (dṛṣṭānta) to prove that other things do not exist.

If you truly wish to protect the Vaibhāṣika school, your discourse should not align with those who advocate the doctrine of the destruction of phenomena (*dharmakṣaya-vāda*). Do not defile your own mind with the dust and impurities of the evil views found in their treatises; rather, you should bathe yourself in the waters of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) of this school.

Furthermore, it is said that nirvana cannot be apprehended as a substantial entity (*bhāva*), unlike form (*rūpa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), nor can it be apprehended as a function (*kāritra*), like the eye (*cakṣus*) and the ear (*śrotra*).

This is indeed the case; for nirvana truly cannot have its substance or function apprehended in the manner of form and feeling, or the eye and the ear. Nevertheless, there exists a substance and function of nirvana that can be known as distinct from those [of conditioned phenomena].
Conditioned phenomena such as form rely upon their own continuums; their essence and function are coarse and manifest, making them easy to comprehend.

However, that nirvāṇa does not rely upon a continuum; its essence and function are subtle and hidden, making them difficult to comprehend. Only when the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) is directly present for a practitioner who possesses diligent and superior insight can one realize the true essence and function of nirvāṇa.
Having emerged from contemplation, he uttered these words:
"How marvelous is Nirvāṇa—cessation, tranquility, excellence, and detachment!

It is not that those who are blind fail to perceive blue and yellow; rather, it is as if one were to claim that even those with clear vision do not see forms. Furthermore, whether you admit it or not, if you grant that Nirvāṇa can be called "existent," then you must necessarily grant that its essence is truly not non-existent, for existence cannot be established apart from a real entity.
Furthermore, characteristics are identical with their substance; since nirvāṇa possesses characteristics such as cessation and tranquility, the existence of its substance is established.
Moreover, regarding what was said:
"If cessation were something separate, how could one establish the use of the sixth case (genitive) for 'the cessation of that thing'?"

Because cessation and the entity are not mutually related, as they do not stand to one another in the relationship of cause and effect, the sixth [case-ending] can only be established in the sense of negating that entity; for "cessation" is defined as the non-existence of that entity.

That statement is irrational, because the relationship between phenomena does not consist solely of cause and effect, nor does it consist solely of the absence of a distinct entity; how, then, can the cessation of those phenomena be established?
It should be understood that the two types of cessation belong to two distinct minds, because these two minds are capable of obstructing the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those [defilements].
Furthermore, the acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) necessarily depends on two paths:

first, the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) ceases simultaneously with the acquisition of the afflictions; second, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises simultaneously with the acquisition of analytical cessation.

When the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a defilement has not yet been extinguished, the acquisition of its dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) reaches the stage of having arisen; thus, when the acquisition of each respective defilement is extinguished, the acquisition of the corresponding analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) arises. Therefore, it is said that this specific cessation belongs to that specific entity.
This meaning has already been clarified in the sūtras, where it is said:
"Venerable One!
Regarding the statement 'cessation, cessation,' by what cessation does one say 'it ceases'?"
It is said to be "extinguished" because of the extinction of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*).
If there were no separate extinction [of suffering], the Sūtra should have simply asked:
"Of what is this the extinction?"
This refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*). In what sense is it said that [Nirvana] is "extinction" because of the extinction of the five aggregates of clinging?

One should understand that when the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is extinguished, it is called the "extinction of the afflictions. I do not at all admit that the extinction of these very sufferings is itself named Nirvana; rather, because I admit the extinction of suffering, it is only when one attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) separately from the path of suffering that it is called Nirvana.

If cessation were non-existent as a distinct entity, the aforementioned fault would follow: namely, that an Arhat would still possess afflictions, or else that one abiding in the path of training would already be free of them, because there would be no distinction between the two states at a later time.
In this regard, the Master of the Sūtras further states:
"On what basis is this cessation [of perception and feeling] (nirodhasamāpatti) exclusively associated with this acquisition (prāpti)?
Is this not a frivolous fabrication intended to evade the difficulty?"
If there were no fixed cause for the disjunction from and the acquisition of the same category of defilements, what fault would there be?
Since the power of a single path brings about the total destruction of all fetters and the total acquisition of disjunction, what need is there for a fixed cause?

Either it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that the relationship between the means and the result is inherent, or the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*) is the specific cause for this certainty, because it is by means of the path that the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyogaprāpti*) is induced; it is not the case that the cessation of the afflictions abandoned by one path of abandonment is obtained through another path.

Therefore, you should rejoice that the analytical cessations (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained through the same path of abandonment are not of a single substance; for what certain cause is there to say that one belongs to greed and another belongs to hatred?
If there were no fixed assignment [of acquisitions], what fault would there be?

That is to say, within a single category, all that is to be destroyed is severed by a single path; since the disjunction (visamyoga) thus obtained shares one and the same acquisition (*prāpti*), what need is there for a fixed cause?
Or as previously stated.
What was stated previously?

It is that by virtue of their natural, non-erroneous connection, greed and the like have been naturally and determinately connected to cessation from the very beginning; thus, at the moment the path of abandonment arises, one can realize them collectively. Therefore, there is no lack of a definitive cause, nor is there any fault.

If one were to claim otherwise, it would contradict the holy teaching (*āgama*). There is indeed a holy teaching that reveals that *nirvāṇa* has solely non-existence as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Thus, a *sūtra* states: "All suffering is abandoned without remainder; each is relinquished, exhausted, detached from passion, ceased, stilled, and forever vanished. No further suffering continues, is grasped, or arises. This is supreme tranquility, this is supreme excellence—namely, the relinquishing of all bases and the exhaustion, detachment from passion, cessation, and extinction of all craving; this is called *nirvāṇa*."
Furthermore, if one asserts that the essence of nirvāṇa is merely non-existence, it serves as an excellent explanation for the scriptural metaphorical statement:
"Just as the extinction of a lamp’s flame, so too is the liberation of the mind."
He says: "This teaching is like the nirvāṇa of a lamp; it is merely the cessation of the lamp's flame, with no other entity existing.
Likewise, when the Blessed One’s mind attained liberation, it was merely the extinction of the aggregates, with nothing further remaining."
The masters of the Abhidharma have already mastered this teaching, stating that there are two ways of explaining the meaning of the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanirodha*):
first, that there is no separate substantial entity apart from the suffering itself; and second, that there is a separate substantial entity apart from the suffering itself.
The Buddha, observing that the inclinations of those to be converted differ, has thus taught these two kinds of cessation.
That is to say, in some places he teaches that there is no separate entity, as in the two types of sūtras cited above.
Furthermore, there are places where it is taught that they possess distinct entities, as the Sūtra says:
"There definitely exists non-arising.
And another Sūtra states:
There are instances where there is detachment.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"I perceive that there truly exists the category of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), namely, nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"It is called cessation because of the cessation of the five aggregates of clinging.
Instances of this kind are indeed numerous; therefore, my own tenet does not contradict the sacred teachings.

Furthermore, regarding the lamp-flame's *nirvāṇa* mentioned in the sūtras, since the characteristic of impermanence exists as something distinct from the lamp itself, how does this analogy contradict the intended meaning?
Alternatively, although the *nirvāṇa* of the lamp has no separate essence, it is not non-existent, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) possess the nature of impermanence.
Its essence is not non-existent; therefore, there is no fault in speaking on the basis of this.

Furthermore, the sūtra cited here cannot prove that the essence of nirvāṇa is exclusively non-existent, for this sūtra speaks only with reference to the moment of entering parinirvāṇa without remainder.
This means that in this state, all other remaining bases are abandoned without remainder and individually relinquished, and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, there is no contradiction. Other masters say:
Regarding the term "non-arising" (*anutpāda*): it is called "non-arising" because it relies upon this non-birth (*ajāti*).
Concerning this, the Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika) states:

"We see that this seventh case ending (*saptamī-vibhakti*) has no power whatsoever to prove the existence of cessation (*nirodha*). With what intention, then, is it said that [cessation] 'relies upon this non-birth'?"
If, according to this statement, it refers to the meaning of "already existing," then [suffering] should never have arisen in the first place, because nirvāṇa is eternal.

If, according to this statement, it refers to the meaning of "already attained," then one must reckon that it depends on the attainment of the Path; thus, you should accept that it is solely by depending on the Path, or by the attainment of the Path, that suffering is prevented from arising.

We observe that this seventh case construction (the locative) possesses great power in proving the existence of cessation (*nirodha*), because both the path (*mārga*) and its attainment (*prāpti*) depend upon cessation.
It is only because nirvāṇa exists that one seeks the path and its attainment;
if it did not exist, what would be the purpose of seeking it?

Furthermore, the non-arising of suffering does not occur solely through the Path; it may also occur because one has already attained a superior state at the time of attaining *adhimātra-kṣānti* (supreme patience), whereby suffering no longer arises.
Moreover, suffering also does not arise due to the deficiency of conditions; this should be considered *nirvāṇa*, as has been stated previously.
If it is argued that this is because the seeds have not yet been extinguished, this has already been refuted as before.
How was it refuted previously?
Although the seeds have not yet been extinguished, they are as if already extinguished and will ultimately never arise; how does this differ from what follows?

Furthermore, if suffering does not arise either by means of the Path or by means of its attainment, then at the very first moment of the Path, delusion and suffering would already be absent; the fault here is as previously stated.
Consequently, while abiding in the path of training (*śaikṣamārga*), afflictions would necessarily be non-existent.
If it is argued that this is because the seeds of the afflictions have not yet been destroyed, why would the seeds not be destroyed when the path of their antidote arises?
For they are directly opposed to one another, like darkness and light.
Furthermore, it is only at the stage when the attainment of nirvāṇa is actually arising that the afflictions and suffering which are to be remedied are designated as "permanently destroyed."
Therefore, that master says:
it is based on this non-arising that one speaks of "non-arising.
The seventh case (locative) possesses great power in establishing the existence of cessation (*nirodha*).

If it is argued that, were this so, the cultivation of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) would be useless, this reasoning is also incorrect, because nirvāṇa is precisely the fruit of this path.
If the afflictions and suffering to be abandoned by the first moment [of the path] are already termed "permanently extinguished," then what is the fruit of that path?
Therefore, the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) does not possess the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyoga-phala), because it arises simultaneously with the acquisition of cessation (nirodha-prāpti).
Thus, having refuted the Master of the Sūtras’ (Sautrāntika) denial of the cause, it is established that the essence of nirvāṇa is substantially real.
Other masters say:
"Nirvāṇa is not substantially real because it is neither cause nor effect, like a rabbit's horn and the like.

All things that are substantially real are proven by their causes and effects; since nirvāṇa is not subsumed under the nature of cause or effect, there is certainly no evidence to prove its existence. Therefore, nirvāṇa is definitely not substantially real."

That statement is irrational; for it has already been established that unconditioned space (*ākāśa-asamskrta*) exists as a real entity and is not of the nature of cause and effect, and this [unmanifest form] should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, there is merely a verbal claim:
"In that school's tenet, this is admitted to be of the nature of cause and effect, but it is not a real entity."

That is to say, those who maintain the doctrine that nirvāṇa is non-existent admit that the future is the effect and the past is the cause, yet they do not admit that the past and future possess a real ontological nature; therefore, the nature of cause and effect does not prove the existence of causes [in the past and future].

If one asserts that the past and future exist substantially, then one must also assert that the essence of nirvāṇa is both a fruit and a cause; for nirvāṇa is admitted to be a fruit of śramaṇaship, and it serves as a non-obstructive cause for dharmas currently arising.
The practitioner of the path of cultivation acts for the sake of accomplishing nirvāṇa; thus, "that which is accomplished" is called the fruit, and that which is accomplished is the fruit.
Alternatively, one should explain what it means for something to be "accomplished" yet not a fruit.
How could there be an entity that is eternal and yet be both cause and effect?
This should not be criticized; rather, one should instead reproach oneself: how can there be a cause that possesses a fruit while existing as a substantial entity?
For instance, when a single moment arises independently of a homogeneous cause, there is no logical possibility for a similar example to be found anywhere.
Other masters say:
"Although nirvāṇa exists, it is conventional and not real.
This is also incorrect, because the substantial basis upon which the convention depends cannot be found.

If it is claimed that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the provisional basis for nirvāṇa, this is also unreasonable, because [conditioned phenomena] would then necessarily possess the nature of being abandoned, defiled, tainted (*sāsrava*), and impermanent.

A provisional analytical cessation cannot be apprehended apart from its basis; although it takes the abandoned defiled, out-flowing, and impermanent as its basis, it is itself not something to be abandoned.

Being untainted (*anāsrava*), stainless (*vimala*), and eternally abiding (*nitya*) by nature, and because it is diametrically opposed [to the defiled], it should not take that [defiled basis] as its support, just as light and darkness cannot coexist; furthermore, a conventional phenomenon (*prajñaptidharma*) has never been seen to contradict its own support.
Furthermore, since you admit that nirvāṇa is the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), how can it be said that conditioned phenomena serve as its basis?
For we have never seen it clearly stated that darkness has light as its basis.
Moreover, at the time when the conditioned phenomena exist, their cessation has not yet occurred.
When one who has not yet abandoned desire possesses greed and so forth, it should not be admitted that for such a person there is the cessation of greed and so forth.
It is only when greed and so forth are absent that one realizes nirvāṇa.
Therefore, what they have said does not accord with correct reasoning.
Others further say:
"Cognition must necessarily have an object, yet nirvāṇa lacks reality. They speak thus:
It is logically impossible that the wisdom taking *nirvāṇa* as its object should have "names" (*nāman*) as its objective domain;
for if it did, the two views—the false and the correct—would necessarily become mutually constitutive.
That is to say, if correct view were to realize that *nirvāṇa* is quiescent and eternally abiding, it would become a "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), because all names are impermanent.

If those with false views were to denigrate *nirvāṇa* by claiming it is impermanent, they would actually be establishing right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), because their understanding would accord with the true nature of reality.
Those who assert that *nirvāṇa* has no essence never admit that the name itself is non-existent;
likewise, those who assert that *nirvāṇa* has an essence never admit that the name itself is *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, what they say also contradicts correct reasoning.
Furthermore, the Elder said:
As the Blessed One stated, "The meaning of these words is exceedingly difficult to perceive: namely, that all bases are forever relinquished, which is peaceful, sublime, and even Nirvana."
If such is nirvāṇa, how is it difficult to see?
It is because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is extremely difficult to perceive.
How can that which is non-existent have an intrinsic nature that can be described?
This is because they themselves hold that nirvāṇa is not substantially existent.

If it is argued that although analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not substantially existent, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*) is substantially existent; therefore, the extinction attained by being separated from that [view] is called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, a sutra states:
"In this way, the realm of cessation (nirodhadhātu) is manifested by taking the view of a self-identity (satkāya) as its object.

This contradicts correct reasoning; since the posited realm of cessation is neither identical to nor distinct from the view of a self-identity, how can it be said that cessation possesses intrinsic nature (svabhāva)?
If there were an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how could you further claim that cessation is not substantially existent?

Since you already admit that nirvāṇa is not substantially existent, it must lack intrinsic nature; why then do you use these contradictory statements, written for the sake of deceiving those of little wisdom who believe in such things?
Furthermore, the Sūtra states only this:
"In this way, the realm of cessation (nirodhadhātu) is made manifest by taking the view of a self-identity (satkāya) as its object.
How can it be definitively known that cessation is not a real entity, while only the view of a self-identity is a real thing?

However, it is universally established in the world that those things which are said to be manifested by depending on others are all substantially existent entities, such as light being manifested by depending on darkness and so forth.

There is no instance whatsoever where something is manifested by depending on a substantially existent entity while itself not being substantially existent; this is a matter of universal consensus. Therefore, the *satkāya* (the "perishing collection") is a substantially existent entity.

This means that cessation is not real; it is merely a conventional expression. Those who explain the manifestation of the cessation of the *satkāya* (the view of a self-identity) do so because they establish this [cessation] based on the cessation of that [view].
It is said to be "cessation" because of the cessation of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), as it is clearly stated in other sūtras.

Furthermore, regarding what he has said: although there are statements in various sūtras concerning the three realms, the three nirvāṇa realms, the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*), the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*), the realm of cessation (*nirodha-dhātu*), that which has arising and that which is without arising, and the noble truth of the cessation of suffering—I now clearly understand these to be the state of peace.
All such [categories] as these are likewise not contradictory, because they are established by taking the *satkāya* (the transitory collection) as their object.

This too is stated merely in passing; even if the three realms and so forth are established by taking the *satkāya* as their object, since there is no evidence to prove it, how can one definitively know that their essence is not substantially existent?

Furthermore, it is argued that because [an object] is manifested through its relation to this or that, it must be a substantially existent entity; thus, it is established as a proven fact that a non-entity cannot be manifested by another, just as light and so forth cannot be manifested by conditions such as darkness.

Furthermore, what he said—that the *sūtra* speaks of the existence of a "sphere of cessation" (*nirodhadhātu*)—is also not contradictory, because it is taught by way of being conditioned upon the departure from the body of existence (*bhavakāya*).
Nor is there any contradiction in the existence of "non-arising," for it is established as not functioning within actual arising; thus, it is indeed arising.

The claim that the meaning of "the continuity is severed" is also illogical; for as stated above, that which is manifested by another is substantially existent, because the natures of arising and non-arising are distinct, and that which does not exist should not be described as existing.
Apart from the provisional and the real, there is nothing else that exists.
If one maintains that non-arising is neither provisional nor real existence, it should not be called "existence," as has already been stated previously.

There are two meanings regarding the cessation of the continuity of arising: namely, being distinct from the body of existence and being distinct from non-existence; these should be understood according to the two meanings of the cessation of suffering mentioned above.
How can it be definitively stated that only the non-arising of what has arisen is called the "cessation of the continuum," rather than there being a distinct entity?
If one were to admit a distinct entity, the statement regarding its arising or non-arising could be established as having meaning;
however, if there is no distinct entity, it should not be termed "existent," and the faults previously mentioned would apply.

Furthermore, the Blessed One should have stated in the sūtras only that "existence does not arise," and he should not have used the expression "this existence is unarisen. The World-Honored One should not make erroneous statements regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); since he asserts that both what is real and what is unreal exist, this is an erroneous statement.
Is its essence unreal because that which is unarisen is spoken of as being existent as if it were arisen?
Or is its essence real because that which is unarisen is spoken of as being existent as if it were arisen?
Because this causes such deluded and erroneous thoughts to arise.

Furthermore, when the continuum is severed, it is non-existent before the Path has arisen; once the Path has arisen, it exists; and when one regresses from the Path, it becomes non-existent again. Since the various noble ones (āryas) can regress and give rise to afflictions, the severance of the continuum would consequently not be unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Furthermore, the claim that nirvāṇa is non-arising because it is not substantially existent is also logically untenable, as it merely posits a thesis without providing a supporting reason.
By what reason is this proven?
Because it is not substantially existent, nirvāṇa is without arising; yet this absence of arising does not mean its essence is substantially existent by virtue of being eternal.

Furthermore, if one were to admit that the non-substantial is what realizes the absence of arising, then all conventional phenomena would likewise be without arising, and conventional phenomena would themselves be non-arising.

If that is so, since your own school does not admit that momentary real dharmas arise, and since a continuum is merely conventional and likewise lacks arising, then for you both arising and ceasing are entirely non-existent in reality.
How unexpected it is that you, who once loathed the flowers in the sky, have now come to produce various distinctions among those very flowers!
Furthermore, as for what you have said, it is as stated in the sūtras:
"All phenomena (dharmas) refer to the twelve bases (āyatanas)."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"These twelve bases are all characterized by conceptual proliferation and are all impermanent.
Another sutra further states:
The eye, forms, and eye-consciousness—and so on, in detail, up to the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness—are all impermanent.
If you claim that nirvāṇa is real and permanent, the Blessed One ought to have made a distinction regarding this.

What has been stated above is not a result of careful investigation, for it assumes that everything exists exactly as it is expressed in words, which would entail the presence of affliction (*paridāha*).
As that sūtra states:
"These twelve bases (*āyatana*) are all characterized by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and are all impermanent."
All [the twelve bases] possess the heat and affliction of craving; they are not the essence of the noble paths, nor are they subsumed within the [unconditioned] base.
Furthermore, since that [Nirvana] definitely lacks the heat and affliction of greed and so forth, why is it not distinguished [from the others]?

However, that sutra speaks with intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) based solely on the essence of the twelve bases that are with outflows (*sāsrava*), stating that "these twelve bases all possess heat and affliction. It further states, based on this very point, that they all possess conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and are all impermanent. One should not, on account of this, slander the essence of Nirvana by claiming it does not truly exist.

Therefore, it must certainly be admitted that there exists an essential nature of *nirvāṇa* distinct from suffering, its origin, and the path; thus, the meaning of its being eternal and real is established.
Now, one should investigate the nature of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) states the following definition:

"That which does not arise further due to the absence of conditions, apart from the power of analytical discernment, is called non-analytical cessation, such as the remaining aggregates of one who dies prematurely within a given *nikāya-sabhāga*."
Furthermore, one should interrogate them: what is meant by "deficiency of conditions"?

If the conditions for the arising of a phenomenon are not in harmony, yet there is no lack of the phenomenon's own essence even when they are not in harmony, how could this [deficiency] act as an obstruction to prevent the phenomenon from arising?
Is it not the case that when conditions are lacking, one says the conditions are incomplete? What dharma could there be in such a state?
The fault here is the same as before.
If you claim that the lack of conditions means the conditions themselves do not exist, this is also unreasonable; for that which does not exist cannot obstruct the arising of existence.

Based on this certainty, it is not merely the absence of conditions that is called "cessation not through deliberation" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). Rather, there exists a distinct dharma which, by virtue of the absence of conditions, possesses the superior capacity to obstruct a dharma that would otherwise arise, rendering it never to arise again; this is termed "cessation not through deliberation."

If there were no distinct dharma capable of acting as an obstacle, such that dharmas simply do not arise due to the deficiency of conditions, then when one later encounters the convergence of those very same types of conditions, the previously non-arisen dharma should now arise once again.

Is it not just as we allow for the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) through the absence of conditions, yet do not maintain that one loses this non-analytical cessation when encountering the convergence of conditions of that same type?
Likewise, we maintain only that phenomena do not arise due to the absence of conditions, and not that those phenomena resume arising when encountering the convergence of conditions of that same type.
The examples cited are not equivalent, because existence and non-existence differ.
That is to say, through the deficiency of conditions, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which prevents a factor that is capable of arising from ever arising again.

This continues until the attainment of nirvāṇa, where a fixed continuity is established; even if one were to encounter the convergence of conditions of that same kind, there would be no way to relinquish what has already been attained.

Now, as for the deficiency of conditions, this merely means that the conditions are absent; there is no non-existent dharma capable of acting as an obstruction to what exists. Later, when one encounters the convergence of those same types of conditions, what dharma could possibly prevent it from arising again?
However, if a phenomenon were to abide within the state of non-arising, there would necessarily be no principle by which that phenomenon could ever arise again.
Therefore, there must certainly exist a factor capable of permanently obstructing the conditions; it is not merely the absence of conditions that causes it never to arise.

Is it not the case that the principle of dependent origination is naturally such that "dependent on this, that arises; in the absence of this, that is absent; through the cessation of this, that ceases"? To calculate non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) [as a distinct entity] would therefore be in vain.
What is the intended meaning of this statement?
It expresses that phenomena do not arise solely because of the deficiency of conditions.
Since no definitive expression is seen here, how can it be known that [phenomena do not arise] solely because of the deficiency of conditions?
Since no other cause for non-arising is mentioned, we know that non-arising occurs solely through the absence of conditions.

No other cause for non-arising is stated here because that [non-arising] is attained merely through the absence of conditions; it is the attainment of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Is it that this very absence of conditions (*pratyaya-vaikalya*) serves as the cause?
No; for that which is non-existent lacks the functional capacity to serve as a cause.
Rather, during the state of the absence of conditions, the mind abides in such a way that it attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Thus, this cessation is obtained precisely because of that mind, not due to a deficiency of conditions.

Furthermore, according to the principle of dependent origination as explained, one can definitively ascertain the existence of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), for the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "Because feeling ceases, craving ceases."
How is it proven that non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) exists? It is because the term "cessation" here does not refer to any other form of cessation.

To begin with, it cannot be the cessation of impermanence (anityatā-nirodha), for one observes that craving arises at the very moment feeling ceases; nor can that which has not yet reached the stage of having arisen be subject to cessation by the characteristic of impermanence.
Furthermore, that [cessation] cannot be described as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because it is said that feeling is abandoned through the abandonment of craving.
As the Blessed One said:
"You should abandon desire for feelings; through the abandonment of desire, these feelings are then abandoned."
In this sūtra, the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of sensation (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is explained to clarify that their abandonment necessarily occurs simultaneously.

In the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, both sequential and non-sequential cessation are taught; all members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-aṅga*) may be termed analytical cessation, as they share the same antidote.

By this principle, one should understand that there exists a non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) apart from impermanent cessation (*anityatā-nirodha*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). It is attained through the absence of the conditions for the arising of craving; it is with reference to this that it is taught in an esoteric sense that "with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases."
Furthermore, a sutra states that there are two types of arhats; by this, one may infer the existence of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). As the sūtra says:
"Briefly stated, there are two kinds of arhats, namely: those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and those not subject to falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*)."
All Arhats have severed all afflictions without remainder, yet there are those who attain the knowledge of non-arising and those who do not.
From this, one may infer by analogy that there must necessarily be a distinct dharma.
If one attains it, the afflictions abide within the state of non-arising;
one attains the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and this dharma is the very essence of analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one does not attain it, the afflictions may arise, whereby there is retrogression and the absence of the knowledge of non-arising.
Since afflictions do not arise due to the excellence of the faculties (*indriya*), what is the use of postulating this entity of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
Based on what meaning is the name "excellence of the faculties" spoken?

If this refers merely to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), then its intention is to say that afflictions do not arise because one has attained the excellence of the faculty consisting of the knowledge of non-arising.
This further should be considered:
since all Arhats have severed their afflictions, for what reason is there attainment and non-attainment of this superior faculty of wisdom?

If it is argued that "superior" refers to the name of the *parihāṇadharman* (one subject to falling away), this is also illogical, because even one who has attained this faculty still possesses the possibility of falling back and giving rise to afflictions.

This refers to one of the nature of falling back (*parihāṇadharman*), who, having attained superior faculties up to the stage of being capable of reaching [the goal] (*prativedhanādharman*), may still encounter conditions that cause them to fall back and remain in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), giving rise to various afflictions (*kleśa*).

If, upon attaining superior faculties, no afflictions arise, and they transform their nature of falling back to attain the faculty of reflection (*cetana-dharman*), they should no longer give rise to any afflictions whatsoever.

However, this is not the case; from this we know that there are Arhats who attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) because the conditions for the arising of various afflictions are absent, and by the power of this [cessation], they are able to obstruct the afflictions so that they never arise again.

If it were possible for one who has attained the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) to fall away, then all [the aforementioned cases] would be valid; however, since falling away is not established, none of them are so.
That the possibility of falling away must exist will be examined later.

Furthermore, within the designation of the "first dharma" (agra-dharma), the plural particle (*bahuvacana*) indicates that there are many unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). This proves that among the unconditioned, there exists non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), for only by adding this to the previous two types can they constitute a plurality; beyond these, no other unconditioned phenomena exist.

Furthermore, although "cessation" (*nirodha*) and "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) differ in name, they are identical in essence; for the Sūtra states that the Stream-enterer has exhausted the three evil destinies. Thus, we know there exists a distinct entity of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because this exhaustion is certainly not subsumed under any other form of cessation.

This refers to what is stated in the sūtras: "The stream-enterer has exhausted hell, has exhausted the animal realm, and has exhausted the realm of hungry ghosts," and so forth, as explained at length.

It is not that he has already been able to sever [the rebirths in] all miserable destinies (*durgati*), because he has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Rather, the miserable destinies are only designated as "severed" at the time when one has ultimately abandoned craving for the desire realm.
Some say: "The afflictions that take the various evil destinies as their objects can still arise in a stream-enterer; therefore, they are not yet said to be abandoned.
This reason is not valid, because even though the objects have been abandoned, the afflictions that take them as objects can still arise.
Nor does the term "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) indicate impermanence or cessation, because that which is exhausted has not yet arisen.

From this it is proven that there must certainly exist a distinct dharma called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); by attaining this dharma, one ensures that the various miserable realms (*apāya*) will never arise again.
If one maintains that [a phenomenon] simply does not arise because its conditions for arising are absent, the fault is as previously stated.
However, the Venerable Elder (Sthavira) says:

"The designation 'non-analytical cessation' (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) has never been mentioned in the various holy teachings; it is merely a false conceptualization and a groundless imputation of existence. Since it is not taught by the Noble Ones, it cannot be trusted or relied upon."
This is also not the case, for it has been taught by the Sage.

Furthermore, those things they cling to, such as the "ancient pervasive element" (*pūrvānuśaya-dhātu*) and so forth, are entirely useless—like the speech of a mute person in a dream—and serve only to entice those who lack wisdom and inspire in them a sense of delight.
Who among the noble ones has spoken such words?
In what sacred teaching can even a fragment [of this] be found?
Therefore, O Elder, do not measure another's doctrine by the standard of your own; this too is not the teaching of the Noble Ones.

Is it not the case that within various sacred teachings, apart from the two kinds of cessation—analytical and non-analytical impermanence—it is stated in many places that there exists such terms as "cessation" (*nirodha*)? How can the Sthavira fail to accept this?
The Abhidharmikas state:

there are those who claim that through the five factors, one may also attain cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) in the future; in order to distinguish them and facilitate easy understanding, the word "non-" (*a-*) is added to the term "deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) in this treatise.

The proponent’s intention is as follows: the Blessed One stated that certain phenomena, not preceded by analytical discernment (*apratisaṃkhyā*), will never arise again in the future due to the absence of necessary conditions.
One should understand that this is precisely the essence of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); how, then, can it be claimed that this was not spoken by the Noble One?
Furthermore, other masters maintain that non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained due to other factors, rather than through the deficiency of conditions.
While the sense organs and their objects serve as the conditions for the arising of various consciousnesses,

when a single organ and the mental faculty (manas) are focused upon a single object, although the conditions— the organs and objects— of other consciousnesses are fully present, those respective consciousnesses cannot arise.
How could there be a deficiency in the roots and objects that serve as the conditions for their arising?

Yet, although the roots and objects are present, the consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously; therefore, we know this occurs solely through the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

If it is argued that this is due to the absence of the second and subsequent equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), then by what cause is that second and subsequent equal-and-immediate condition absent?
Is it not the case that because the various consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, they lack the second condition, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
Furthermore, for what reason do the consciousnesses not arise together?
Because there would be logical faults; one must certainly not say that the various consciousnesses arise simultaneously.
If one asserts that they arise simultaneously, there would be faults such as the simultaneous arising of both defilement and purity.
These faults could only exist if simultaneous arising were already established;
how could the prior existence of these faults serve as the reason for their not arising simultaneously?
However, since consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, there is no such fault;
for it is because one attains non-analytical cessation that consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.
Such assertions as these are all unreasonable.
If one were to attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) not through the absence of conditions, then having attained it, one would be liable to fall away from it again.
For although multiple consciousnesses cannot arise simultaneously, they may still arise sequentially at a later time.

If, based on the five consciousnesses, one were to say that because the objects of perception have already ceased and passed away, the various consciousnesses capable of arising are never produced again, this would be the same as the previous case: due to the deficiency of conditions, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained, causing them to never arise again.
From this it should be understood that what was stated previously is correct; therefore, the thesis that non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is substantially existent is established.
However, when the treatise states that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are "without a basis" (*avastuka*), this means they are "without a cause" (*ahetuka*).
Why is this so? There are five kinds of entities (*vastu*):
first, the entity as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vastu*), as it is said in a certain passage:
If one has already attained this matter, one accomplishes that matter.
Regarding the two types of objective referents (*ālambana-vastu*), as it is said in a certain passage:
"All phenomena are known by wisdom according to their respective matters."
Third, the matter of that which is bound: as it is said in some passages, "If one is bound to this matter by the fetter of attachment, is one also bound to this matter by the fetter of aversion?
Fourth, the matter of the cause: as it is said in some passages:
What are the phenomena that possess a basis?
They refer to all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma).
Regarding the five bases included therein, as it is said in a certain passage:

Because there are matters concerning fields, matters concerning dwellings, and matters concerning wives and children, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states, based on the fourth [category], that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is "without matter" (*avastuka*); it does not state that the unconditioned is "without matter" based on the first [category], which is the matter of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Seventeen;
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Eighteen.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Ten: The Tenfold Discrimination of Differences, Part Two of Ten. Having completed the ancillary discussion on the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*), that which was originally intended to be elucidated shall now be explained.

Regarding the five fruits to be discussed—namely, the fruit of maturation (*vipāka*), the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda*), the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and the dominant fruit (*adhipati*)—one should state which fruit is obtained from which of the six causes.
The verse says:
The subsequent cause has the ripened fruit; The preceding cause has the dominant fruit.
