The similar and pervasive causes have the outflowing fruit; The simultaneous and associated causes have the fruit of human effort.
The Commentary states:

Among the five fruits, the third—the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*)—is not obtained through a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*); therefore, it is not discussed here. For now, we shall analyze how the six causes obtain the remaining four fruits.
Regarding the "subsequent cause," this refers to the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), because it is mentioned last among the verses on causes.
The first ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is that which is obtained from this cause. Some say:
"Since maturation arises from maturation, it should not be called 'without maturation' (avipāka).
This statement is irrational, because the meanings of being produced by two causes—homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and maturation cause (*vipākahetu*)—are distinct.
This means that the preceding maturation (*vipāka*) acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) to produce the subsequent maturation as its outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Thus, the subsequent maturation is established by prior karma; that which establishes the various karmas is called the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*), and the maturation that is established is the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
The two causes differ in essence, and the two fruits are distinguished in meaning; since the categories of cause and fruit are distinct, there is no fault of mutual confusion.

However, as for the essence of ripening (*vipāka*), it is like cooked food and drink: it lacks any superior capacity to produce further ripening. Therefore, only unwholesome states and wholesome states associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) are ripening causes, and they are termed "having ripening."
Regarding the "prior cause," this refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because it is mentioned first among the verses on causes.
Regarding the "subsequent dominant fruit" (*adhipati-phala*), this is the fruit obtained from that cause.
A fruit that is dominant is called a "dominant fruit."
If it exists merely by being unobstructed, what kind of sovereign power (*adhipatya*) does it possess?
Is it not precisely because it exists as unobstructed that it is said to have sovereign power? Why trouble yourself with such an inquiry?

Furthermore, this was already explained previously in the discussion of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*): the efficient cause also possesses a superior force. For instance, when visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so forth are in the process of arising, the ear and other faculties possess an indirect sovereign force; for once one has heard [the teaching], there arises the desire to see.

When various objects arise within the receptacle world, the karma of sentient beings possesses predominant power (*adhipati-bala*). Furthermore, even with respect to unwholesome karma, there is a predominant generative function regarding pleasant fruits, and with respect to wholesome karma, there is likewise a predominant generative function regarding unpleasant fruits; these instances of predominance should be understood as they apply.
The homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) obtain the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*); because the fruit resembles its cause, it is called "outflow.
Since the characteristics of the fruits of these two causes are similar, although there are two causes, their fruit is one.

Co-existent and associated dharmas obtain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); there is no separate human effort apart from the substance of the person. That which is obtained by this [person] is called the fruit of human effort.
To what dharma does this term "human effort" refer?
Regarding the functional capacities inherent in all phenomena, this accords with the subsequent verse which states:
"If something arises through the power of another, that result is termed 'human effort' (*puruṣakāra*)."

However, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) maintains that this term "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) refers directly to the functional activity (*kāritra*) possessed by all phenomena; if so, he should have stated:
"It is called human effort because it collectively draws forth a single fruit."

If that were the case, then only those [factors] that are immediate or separated would have a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), while there would be none among those that arise simultaneously; for it is not possible for all factors arising simultaneously to obtain a single fruit of human effort together, since a self-essence does not arise through its own power.
Nor can it be said that each [cause] separately draws forth its own fruit, lest the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) be rendered non-uniform in its result.

In this context, the meanings of "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*), "human power" (*puruṣabala*), "human capacity" (*puruṣasāmarthya*), and "the human's functional sphere" (*puruṣaprabhāva*) are not distinct; because the efficacy of all phenomena is like human effort, it is termed "human effort," just as a valiant man is called a "lion" because he resembles a lion.

Are not the results produced immediately after the two causes—homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and pervasive (*sarvatraga*)—also results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*)? Furthermore, while all dharmas produced immediately after those two causes may or may not be results of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), they are all invariably designated as results of human effort. Why, then, is it said that only the simultaneous (*sahabhū*) and associated (*samprayukta*) [causes] obtain the result of human effort, and not the homogeneous and pervasive causes?

Only these two causes are fully capable of producing both the co-nascent (*sahaja*) and the immediate (*anantara*) results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); the former two causes are not, and for this reason they are not mentioned.

A result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) is merely similar to its own cause; since results of similar type (*sabhāga*) and pervasive (*sarvatraga*) are likewise merely similar, those two results are designated solely as "outflow.
The others are not outflows, as they are not obtained by those two causes.

Furthermore, regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), the sense of "simultaneous" is predominant; for it is only the simultaneous and associated causes that are uniquely able to obtain the simultaneous fruit of human effort, and thus these alone are specifically mentioned.

Moreover, although the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) can also obtain the various fruits of human effort that arise immediately after it, it does not necessarily obtain them all, because the final aggregates of an Arhat do not have a fruit of human effort arising immediately thereafter.
The two causes—the co-existent and the associated—necessarily obtain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); therefore, they are specifically mentioned.
Other masters say:

"The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and others also have the capacity to obtain the fruit of human effort; however, this is not the case for the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), because it lacks both the simultaneous and the immediate fruits of human effort."
Other masters say:
This retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) also possesses a remote *puruṣakāra-phala* (human effort fruit) that is separated by an interval, just like the harvest obtained by a farmer.
Having already established the certainty of the mutual relationship between causes and fruits, we shall now properly analyze the distinctions among the characteristics of the fruits.
What are the characteristics of the results, such as the maturation result (*vipākaphala*)?
The verse says:
The maturation result consists of neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, which belong to sentient beings and arise from determinate (*abhisaṃskāra*) karma.
The outflowing fruit resembles its own cause; disconnection results from the exhaustion [of defilements] by wisdom.
If something arises through the power of another, that result is called "virile.
With the exception of preceding conditioned phenomena, all conditioned phenomena are "dominant" results.
The treatise says:
Only among non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena is there a fruition result (*vipākaphala*).
If that were so, then even those not included within the category of sentient beings would have to be fruition results.
The term "sentient being" (sattva) is used to exclude those [other phenomena], because only within sentient beings does maturation (vipāka) exist.
If that were so, then among those things counted as sentient beings, nurtured (aupacayika) and outflowing (naiṣyandika) states would also have to be considered maturation.

Furthermore, to distinguish it from those [other types of causes], it is said that they are "born of the determinate" (*vijñapti-ja*). All unwholesome states and wholesome *sāsrava* states are called "determinate" because they can determine a maturation (*vipāka*); the maturation arises only at a later time from them.
It is not the case that what arises simultaneously or immediately [after] them is called "born of the determinate."
This is what is called the characteristic of the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*).

But would it not be the case that maturation itself also takes the substance of a prior maturation fruit as its homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), since it is the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of that prior maturation? If so, one should also say that it arises from the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and is of the nature of an outflow; why then do you say it arises from the determinate (*vyākṛta*)?
There is no such fault regarding that which is not of the nature of a uniform outflow (*niṣyanda*).

While the substance of a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) is confused by the characteristics of its homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), it is not confused by the characteristics of its ripening cause (*vipākahetu*); therefore, it is said to arise solely from the determinate (*vijñapti*).
From this, it should be understood by analogy that [the non-sentient] is not of the nature of an outflow, because an outflow fruit resembles its cause and thus involves confusion;
whereas a ripening fruit differs from its cause and is free from such confusion. Since things not included among sentient beings are also produced from karma, why are they not called ripening fruits?
This should not be challenged, because only the fruit obtained from non-common karma is termed *vipāka* (maturation). Why?
Because non-sentient things are not fruits obtained solely from non-common karma, since non-sentient phenomena can be commonly enjoyed by others.
Is it not the case that the non-sentient environment inhabited by Mahābrahmā is the fruit of distinct karma, and thus should also be called "karmic maturation" (*vipāka*)?
Why then do you say it is not? Some say:
"The dwelling place of Mahābrahmā arises through the sovereign power (*adhipati*) of the karma of all the Mahābrahmās."
Others further say:
"Since the dwelling place of Mahābrahmā remains unbroken in its continuity, it is logical that others may experience it within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); therefore, it is not non-common.
How can a single object be the collective result of the karma of immeasurable sentient beings?"
Has it not already been stated that the remainder may be enjoyed in common?
If it were a non-sentient fruit produced by non-common karma, it would necessarily arise and perish simultaneously with its maturation (vipāka).
Furthermore, it is observed in the world that when a sovereign dies, the kingdom over which he ruled continues to exist.
If the kingdom were produced solely by the karma of the sovereign and not through the collective karma of other sentient beings, then others would be unable to enjoy or utilize it.

Furthermore, if insentient things were produced by the distinct karma of individual sentient beings, then the houses, gardens, ponds, cities, mountains, and rivers occupied by each and every sentient being's body would all be entirely different from one another.
But in reality this is not so; therefore, we know that a single object is the collective result of the karma of immeasurable sentient beings. [Objection:

Since the substance of karma is manifold, it should be unable to produce a non-manifold fruit. How, then, can it be said that the many karmas of immeasurable sentient beings collectively produce a single non-sentient object?
There is no such fault, for example, because a sprout and so forth are established as a single entity when observed in relation to its own kind of cause.

That is to say, although a sprout arises through the power of causes such as earth, water, time, human effort, and manure, it is established as one when observed in relation to its own kind of cause; it is not established as many when observed in relation to causes such as the earth.
In this way, insentient things, because they are observed to have their own causes, constitute a single entity; it is not by observing their immeasurable karmas that their substance becomes manifold.

Furthermore, we see in the world that various kinds of fruits do not arise from various kinds of karmas; why then do you not allow that various kinds of karmas can produce non-various kinds of fruits?
What causal function does karma have regarding the non-sentient fruits it produces?
Karma acts as the *kāraṇahetu* (efficient cause) toward those fruits, as has already been explained.
Having thus explained the characteristics of the *vipākaphala* (maturation fruit), the characteristics of the *niṣyandaphala* (outflow fruit) shall now be explained.

A phenomenon that resembles its own cause is called a "result of outflow" (*niṣyandaphala*); that is to say, it resembles two causes: the similar-type cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*).
Just as a similar-type cause may be wholesome, defiled, or neutral, the characteristics of its result of outflow are likewise the same.
Just as the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is exclusively defiled, so too are the characteristics of its outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Is it not the case that the simultaneously arising fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) also resembles its own cause? How, then, can it be said that only a phenomenon resembling its own cause is called an outflowing fruit?

The outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) does not resemble its own cause, whereas the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) differs from its own cause; therefore, that which resembles its own cause is called the outflowing fruit, and there is certainly no risk of confusing it with the fruit of human effort.

Is it not also the case that there are causes of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), such as the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), which, while belonging to a different category (*nikāya*), takes dharmas of a different category as its outflow fruit?

Because they are both defiled and thus similar in nature, the outflow of another category is not dissimilar to the cause of its own category; yet, since the nature of their "virile fruit" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) also differs, they are not necessarily identical to their causes.

Other masters explain the phrase "resembling its own cause" as follows: the effect and the cause possess two kinds of similarity—first, similarity in terms of substantial category (*dravya-jāti*), and second, similarity in terms of essential category (*svabhāva-jāti*).
By "substantial category," they mean [mental factors] such as sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
Regarding "nature and category," this refers to such things as the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

Even when they are of the same nature and category within the co-arising result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), their individual entities must necessarily differ, because they are results of human effort such as being experienced (*vedanīya*) or not being experienced (*avedanīya*), and so forth.

If, among the results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) arising subsequently, there may be differences in both their substantial nature (*dravya-jāti*) and their generic category (*nikāya-sabhāga*), one cannot say that the result necessarily resembles its cause.

Although the nature of a result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) must resemble its cause, and within that category there are cases where the substance also resembles the cause, it is only the result of outflow that is invariably similar to its own specific cause; therefore, the expression "resembling the cause" does not suffer from the fault of ambiguity.
If the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) also obtains an outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), why not admit that it is simply called a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)?

In relation to its own category of fruits, it is indeed a homogeneous cause; however, when viewed from the perspective of other categories, it is exclusively a universal cause and not a homogeneous one.
However, non-pervasive dharmas are, according to their respective natures and categories, exclusively homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) when compared to their own category.
As for pervasive dharmas, when compared to other categories, those belonging to the defiled class are exclusively universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

From the perspective of its own category, this [cause] possesses both causal conditions; therefore, although the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) does obtain a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), it cannot be admitted that it is called a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Having thus explained the characteristics of the result of uniform outflow, the characteristics of the result of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*) shall now be explained.
The exhaustion of phenomena through wisdom is called the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).

It is called "exhaustion" because it is cessation; it is called "wisdom" because it is discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*). Thus, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is designated as the fruit of dissociation. Because one realizes this cessation by means of discernment as its cause, thereby becoming free from all fetters, it is called a "fruit."
Having thus already explained the characteristics of the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*), the characteristics of the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) shall now be explained.
If a dharma is produced by the power of another, that dharma is called the fruit of human effort; this is of four types:
co-arising, immediate, separated, and non-arising, as previously stated.
"Simultaneous arising" (sahaja) refers to that which arises at the same time through the power of being mutual causes for one another.

"Immediate succession" (anantara) refers to that which arises at the subsequent moment through the power of the preceding thought-moment as its cause, such as when the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) gives rise to the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti).
"Separated by an interval" refers to that which arises through the power of a causal force transmitted across a distant period of time, such as farmers [producing fruit] from grain or wheat.
"Non-arising" refers to nirvāṇa, because it is attained through the power of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Since this [result] is not produced, how can it be said that it is called a "virile fruit" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) because it is produced by that power?
We observe that the term "produced" is also applied to "attainment" (*prāpti*); for example, when one says, "my wealth has been produced," it means "I have acquired wealth."

If the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized when the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) abandons the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), such analytical cessation is termed both the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

If the uninterrupted path does not abandon the latent dispositions, and one realizes again at the time of attaining the fundamental state the analytical cessation previously realized, such analytical cessation is not the fruit of disjunction; it is solely the fruit of human effort.

This refers to the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) realized when one who has not yet entirely abandoned desire for the desire realm enters the path of seeing; at that time, the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) abandons ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya). Such analytical cessation is termed both the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyoga-phala) and the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala).

If one who has already completely abandoned the craving of the desire realm enters the path of seeing, the *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* (receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering) does not sever the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), yet it realizes the fundamental analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Such analytical cessation is not a fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*), because disjunction has already been attained previously;
rather, it is a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), because by the power of this receptivity, another acquisition (*prāpti*) arises, whereby it is realized once again.

If one who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), then regarding the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there are cases where some are abandoned by the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and others are not; and regarding the analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) realized therein, there are both new ones and those previously established. Correspondingly, there are two fruits or one fruit, and this continues in the same manner up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārge dharmajñānakṣānti*).

If one has not yet completely abandoned, has already partially abandoned, or has neither abandoned nor partially abandoned the craving of the desire realm, then regarding the eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there are cases where they are entirely severed or not severed, and cases where they are partially severed or not severed. Consequently, the *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through discernment) realized therein may be newly acquired, previously acquired, or both newly and previously acquired. Correspondingly, these constitute two fruits, one fruit, two fruits, or one fruit, as explained in detail in the preceding section.

If one who has not yet entirely abandoned the craving for the realms of form and formlessness enters the path of seeing, the analytical cessation realized through the patience of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), which abandons the eighteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the realms of form and formlessness—such analytical cessation is termed both a fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

If one who has already abandoned desire for the form and formless realms enters the path of seeing, then at the stage of the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*), there are eighteen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms that are either abandoned or not abandoned; the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized therein is either newly attained or previously established, corresponding respectively to two fruits or one fruit.

In this manner, up to the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*, for those who have either not yet abandoned or have partially abandoned the craving of the form and formless realms, there is likewise the total abandonment, partial abandonment, or non-abandonment of the fourteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms. The cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) thus realized may be newly attained or previously existing; according to their respective order, they also possess two fruits, two fruits, or one fruit, the meaning of which is as explained previously.

Regarding the various uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), each should be considered according to its specific meaning as illustrated by the preceding examples.
Having thus explained the characteristics of the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*), the characteristics of the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) shall now be explained.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), with the exception of those that have already arisen previously, are the dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*) of other conditioned phenomena; there is certainly no fruit whatsoever that arises prior to its cause.
What fault would there be if the fruit were to arise before its cause?
If a future dharma has already produced its fruit, then that which was to be done by the future would have been accomplished; since it would serve no further purpose, it should not arise again.
It is not the case that what has never arisen can undergo cessation; and because there would be neither arising nor cessation, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would be eternal.

If it is argued that this [conditioned formation] should be like dharmas that do not arise—wherein, although there is no arising or ceasing, the essence is nonetheless impermanent—this defense is untenable.
For one observes that within those same categories there are instances of arising and ceasing; thus, by analogy with such non-arising dharmas, one may indeed claim they are impermanent.
However, if formations were fundamentally devoid of both arising and ceasing, on what basis could one analogically assert that their essence is impermanent?
Therefore, this does not constitute a valid defense.
How should one understand the distinction between the two fruits—the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*)?

One should understand their distinction based on the difference regarding the agent and the recipient: the designation "fruit of human effort" applies exclusively to the agent, whereas the designation "dominant fruit" applies to both the agent and the recipient.

For example, with respect to farmers, crops such as rice and wheat are called "fruits of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) because they are produced by their power; they are also "dominant fruits" (*adhipati-phala*) because they are enjoyed by them.
With respect to those who merely enjoy [the fruit], it is only a dominant fruit, for it is not produced by their power, but is enjoyed by them.
Regarding that which is produced by a craftsman, one should understand that for both the craftsmen and those who are not craftsmen, there are two fruits and one fruit, as determined above.
All other cases are likewise.
Among the six types of causes explained above, at what stage does each cause take up its fruit and give forth its fruit?
The verse says:
Five [causes] take their fruit only in the present; two likewise give their fruit [only in the present].
Two causes give their fruit in both the past and the present; one gives its fruit only in the past.
The treatise states:
The five causes take their fruits only in the present; they certainly do not do so in the past, because those [causes] have already taken [their fruits];
nor do they do so in the future, because those [causes] lack efficacy.

To say that it "takes the fruit" means it has the sense of "drawing forth," namely, drawing forth the future so that it arises and so on. It acts as a seed for those of the same category; for those of a different category, by virtue of having the same fruit; for those that do not have a single fruit, by virtue of being of the same type; and for those of a different type, by virtue of possessing this continuity of its own aggregate.
Therefore, all [conditioned phenomena] are termed "projectors" (*ākṣepaka*); such projectors are said to "grasp the fruit" (*phalagrahaṇa*).
This function of grasping the fruit exists only in the present, not in the past or future; only this can be called the activity (*kāritra*) of the conditioned.
Among the six causes, which cause is excluded so that it may be said that five causes take their fruit only in the present?
That is to say, among the six causes, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is excluded.
For what reason is this efficient cause excluded?
Other masters say:

"This efficient cause (kāraṇahetu) has no fixed determination regarding the time of grasping the fruit (phalagrahaṇa) or the time of giving the fruit (phaladāna); therefore, it is not distinguished in either grasping or giving.
That statement is irrational.
Why is this so? Because this cause takes up its fruit, and there is nothing that is not present.
Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no sense of "giving" (bestowing) without taking up; how then can you say that time lacks determination?

However, as for the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), that which can take up a fruit is necessarily restricted to the present; it does not extend to the past or the future. This should be understood as being similar to the two causes—the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and the pervasive (*sarvatraga*)—yet it is not mentioned here because not all [efficient causes] possess or bestow a sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*). Thus, it is not discussed.

Is it not the case that the causal function of this [condition] to grasp its fruit also extends to the past? How then can it be said that that which grasps the fruit is necessarily and exclusively present?
Therefore, the Treatise states:
"Past dharmas, as equal-and-immediate conditions, can produce two types of mind."

If the mind emerging from the meditative attainments of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) were to take its fruit by means of the mind entering those attainments being present, then these two attainments would never manifest again.
Furthermore, there is no sense of "giving" [a result] without [the cause] taking [it]; therefore, the taking of the fruit must also extend to the past.
Such a thing does not exist; the mind entering the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) can only take as its object the attainment itself and the fruit of the emerging mind at the present moment.
However, since these two attainments are what is being sought, they must necessarily arise first.
Because of this obstruction, the mind emerging from concentration does not arise immediately after the mind entering it; this point shall be further analyzed later.
Therefore, as stated above, this cause takes its fruit only when it is present;
nor is there the sense of "giving" without taking. This principle is fully established.
Nevertheless, the *Vibhāṣā* contains the following statement:
As for the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu), it is claimed that its grasping of the fruit and its giving of the fruit both occur across the past and present;

however, this is logically untenable. For when a dharma abides in the present, it likewise—like the similar-cause (sabhāga-hetu) and the pervasive-cause (sarvatraga-hetu)—collectively grasps all future dharmas as its own fruits.

The same applies to the simultaneous (sahabhū) and associated (saṃprayukta) causes regarding the yielding of results; these two causes yield and give results only in the present, because for these two causes, the taking of the result and the giving of the result must necessarily occur at the same time.
As for the similar (sabhāga) and pervasive (sarvatraga) causes, they yield results throughout both the past and the present.
The same should be said regarding those things that possess fruits among the efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
However, since not all [causes] are capable of having a fruit, this is not discussed here.
Regarding the two causes—homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and pervasive (*sarvatraga*)—it may be so for the past; but how is it for the present?
Regarding the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*): because there is an immediate arising of the outflowing fruit.
That is to say, when these two causes have an outflowing fruit that arises immediately, they both grasp and give it while in the present state.
When this fruit has already arisen and its cause has ceased in the past, it is said that [the cause] has already taken and now gives.

If these two causes have ceased and reached the past, and their resultant flow (niṣyanda-phala) is just reaching the moment of arising, then these two causes first take and now give to the fruit that is currently arising.

Regarding "giving rise to a fruit," this means that these various causes properly provide the power for that [fruit] to arise and so forth; specifically, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) resides in the present.
Its dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) may already have arisen in the present, such as when the eye faculty acts as the efficient cause for the arising of visual consciousness and so forth.

There are various types of dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*) that arise without interval; for example, the "Highest Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) and others act as efficient causes (*kāraṇahetu*) to produce the "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and other such dominant fruits.

There is production across an interval, as when roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth act as efficient causes (*kāraṇahetu*) for the various sovereign fruits (*adhipatiphala*), such as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and others pertaining to the enlightenment of the three vehicles.
Regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), there are times when it takes up its fruit but does not give it; this should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first permutation refers to the final acquisition (*prāpti*) that is abandoned at the moment of severing the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Regarding the second phrase, it refers to the first acquisition obtained at the moment of reconnecting the roots of virtue.
On this point, the Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika) erroneously states:
"It should be said that what is reconnected at that time is the prior acquisition."
Examining that statement in detail now, it is logically untenable.

Why is this so? It is not only because the acquisition (*prāpti*) abandoned at the final moment of the state of cessation is a result of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*) equal to the acquisition first obtained at the time of reconnection; for even the acquisition already extinguished prior to that state of cessation is also a result of outflow equal to the acquisition at the time of reconnection.

How is it that while the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of many moments in preceding stages are all taken as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the present acquisition, at this present time only the acquisition of the very last moment is said to yield its fruit to the present acquisition?
Therefore, it is appropriate to follow the original text as the correct interpretation.
The third phrase refers to those who have not severed their roots of goodness during the remaining stages.
The fourth phrase refers to cases other than those previously described.
Furthermore, regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of unwholesome states, there are also four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first proposition refers to the acquisition (*prāpti*) that is finally relinquished at the time of becoming free from desire-attachment (*vairāgya*).
The second proposition refers to the acquisition that is initially obtained at the time of falling away (*parihāṇi*) from freedom from desire-attachment.
The Master of the Sūtra (*Sūtrakāra*) also states this regarding the present point:
"One should say that those who fall back at that time had previously attained [the fruit].
Examining his statement closely, it is likewise unreasonable, for it suffers from the same faults as previously mentioned.
The third phrase refers to those who have not yet abandoned desire and greed during all other remaining states.
The fourth phrase refers to cases excluding the aforementioned characteristics.

Within the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena, there are likewise four phrases; these should be explained according to reason regarding the time an Arhat attains [the state], the time they fall away from it, the time they have not yet attained it, and other instances.

Regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) that is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), there is a "consequent" clause: namely, at the time it gives its fruit (*phala-dāna*), it necessarily also takes its fruit (*phala-grahaṇa*).

Because the unobscured-neutral serves as a homogeneous cause and continues in a constant succession until *nirvāṇa*, there are instances where it takes its fruit but does not give its fruit; this refers to the final aggregates (*skandha*) of an Arhat, in terms of the distinction between moments that possess an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Regarding wholesome similar-cause conditions (*sabhāga-hetu*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established.
The first permutation refers to when a defiled or neutral mind arises immediately after a wholesome mind.
The second permutation refers to the opposite of the above.
The third phrase refers to when a wholesome mind arises immediately after another wholesome mind.
The fourth phrase refers to cases other than those previously mentioned.
For unwholesome minds and so forth, there are likewise four phrases as appropriate.

By way of illustration, it should be stated that maturation (*vipāka*) yields its fruit only in the past, because a maturation fruit is never simultaneous with its cause, nor does it arise immediately thereafter.
The masters of the West maintain that there are nine fruits; in addition to the five previously mentioned fruits, they establish four others:

first, the fruit of application (*prayoga-phala*), such as the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), which serves as the distant fruit of practices such as the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

Second is the establishment of results (*vyavasthāna-phala*): for example, the water-circle is the result of the wind-circle, and so on up to grass and other things being the results of the great earth. In this way, one should know that all such established phenomena are results of their respective establishing factors (*vyavasthāpaka*).

The fruit of the threefold conjunction refers, for example, to sprouts and the like being the fruits of time, earth, water, seeds, and so forth; and visual consciousness and the like being the fruits of the eye, visible form, light, and attention.
Fourth is the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*), such as the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) and so forth, which are the fruits of the dhyānas.
These four fruits are all subsumed under the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*); for this reason, it is said that there are only five fruits.
Having explained cause and effect, one should further investigate:
among these, which phenomena are produced by how many causes?
It should be understood that, in brief, there are four types of phenomena here: namely, defiled phenomena and phenomena born of maturation.
The first are the untainted dharmas; the remaining three are the other dharmas.
What are these "other dharmas"? They refer to all [dharmas] excluding those that are maturation.
The remaining indeterminate dharmas, with the exception of the first untainted [dharmas], and all other wholesome dharmas—
these four types of dharmas are summarized in the verse as follows:
Defiled, born of maturation, The remainder, and the first noble [dharmas], respectively.
Excluding the two—maturation and pervasive—and likewise excluding the homogeneous, other [causes] arise;
this refers to mind and mental factors. For others, exclude the associated cause.
The Treatise says:
All defiled dharmas arise from five causes, excluding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), because the dharmas produced by the ripening cause are not defiled.
Dharmas born of ripening arise from five causes, excluding the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), because the dharmas produced by the omnipresent cause are exclusively defiled.

Regarding the remaining three types of dharmas, excluding both the retributive and the universal causes, they arise from the other four causes; this is because these remaining dharmas are neither of the nature of retribution nor are they defiled.
Regarding the first untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, those of the same category (*sabhāga-hetu*) are excluded.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that the two causes—maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) and universal (*sarvatraga-hetu*)—are also excluded.
They arise from the remaining three causes because, for the first untainted dharmas, there are no previously arisen dharmas of the same category, and because they are wholesome (*kuśala*).
Other masters say:
"In this context, it should be stated that all defiled phenomena arise from only four causes. Why is this so?"
Since the essence of the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) is not distinct from that of the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu),
their statement is irrational. Why is this so?
If they do not mention the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*), they fail to explain the cause for the defilements of other categories.
If they do not mention the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), they fail to explain the causes for non-universal dharmas and the attainment of all defiled dharmas that are universal.

In reality, however, greed and the like have greed and the like as their causes, and acquisition arises by means of acquisition as its cause; therefore, it is logical to say that defiled phenomena arise from five causes, excluding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Regarding these four dharmas, what is being explained?
It should be understood that they are exclusively mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
If this is so, how many causes give rise to the remaining four categories of dharmas—the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and matter (*rūpa*)?
Just as with the mind and mental factors, one should know that other phenomena arise from four, three, or two remaining causes, excluding those [specific] causes.

That is to say, defiled matter and non-associated formations—excluding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) and excluding the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*)—arise from the remaining four causes, just like the mind and mental factors.

Matter born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arise from four causes, excluding the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), just like the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

As for the remaining three types of matter and formations dissociated from mind, they arise from three causes, excluding both the maturation and pervasive causes as well as the associated cause, just like the mind and mental factors.
Initial untainted matter and formations dissociated from mind arise from two causes, excluding the first three causes and excluding the cause of association, just as with the mind and mental factors.
There are no phenomena whatsoever that arise from only a single cause.
Now, one should reflect and discern:
among all phenomena (*dharma*), which phenomena can serve as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of how many causes?
That is to say, there may be some phenomena that fully possess the intrinsic nature of all six causes, and so on in sequence down to those that possess the intrinsic nature of only a single cause.
Among these, there are dharmas that fully possess the nature of being six causes; namely, all past and present unwholesome universal (*sarvatraga*) mind and mental factors.

There are dharmas that can function as five causes; namely, all past and present unwholesome non-universal mind and mental factors, or neutral universal mind and mental factors, or wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind and mental factors, or unwholesome non-universal non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

There are dharmas that can function as the nature of four causes: namely, all past and present unwholesome material dharmas; or wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) material dharmas and mental non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*); or unwholesome non-pervasive mental non-associated formations; or neutral pervasive mental non-associated formations; or neutral non-pervasive minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); or all untainted (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors; or all future unwholesome, wholesome, and out-flowing minds and mental factors.

There are dharmas that can function as the nature of three causes: namely, all past and present indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) matter-dharmas; or indeterminate non-pervasive mind-dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*); or untainted (*anāsrava*) matter and mind-dissociated formations; or future unwholesome (*akuśala*) and wholesome-tainted (*sāsrava-kuśala*) matter and mind-dissociated formations; or indeterminate and untainted mind and mental factor-dharmas (*citta-caitta*).

There are dharmas that can function as two types of causes; these are all future indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
There are dharmas that can function as a single type of cause; these are the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
There are phenomena that are not causes and phenomena that are not effects, namely space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, one should investigate whether these six causes, when compared in terms of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), are homogeneous or heterogeneous.
Furthermore, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) corresponds to the subsequent clause relative to the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*);

that is to say, while a co-existent cause is necessarily mixed with the efficient cause, there are efficient causes that are not co-existent causes, namely, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Furthermore, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) corresponds to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) according to the "subsequent clause" (*uttarapada*); that is, a homogeneous cause is necessarily a mixed efficient cause.
However, there are pure efficient causes that are not homogeneous causes, namely future phenomena (*anāgata-dharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Furthermore, the *kāraṇahetu* (efficient cause) corresponds to the *samprayuktakahetu* (associated cause) according to the latter part of the verse: that is, a *samprayuktakahetu* is necessarily a *sabhāga-kāraṇahetu* (a specific type of efficient cause).

However, there are pure *kāraṇahetus* that are not *samprayuktakahetus*, namely all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).

Furthermore, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) in relation to the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) also conforms to the latter part of the verse: that is, an omnipresent cause is necessarily a mixed efficient cause.
However, there are pure efficient causes that are not omnipresent causes, namely: future dharmas, past and present dharmas that are not omnipresent, and unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, when the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is contrasted with the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it also conforms to the latter clause: that is, a ripening cause is necessarily a mixed efficient cause.
However, there are pure efficient causes that are not ripening causes, namely, indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena and untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
If the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) is contrasted with the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it follows the latter clause;
that is to say, while a similar-type cause is necessarily mixed with the co-existent cause, there are purely co-existent causes that are not similar-type causes, namely, future dharmas.
Furthermore, regarding the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) in relation to the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), it also conforms to the latter clause:

that is, while an associated cause is necessarily mixed with the co-existent, there are purely co-existent causes that are not associated causes, namely all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, regarding the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) in relation to the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), it also follows the latter clause: that is, the pervasive cause is necessarily concomitant with the co-existent.
However, there are pure co-existent causes that are not pervasive causes, namely: future dharmas, and past and present dharmas that are not pervasive.
Furthermore, when comparing the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) with the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it also conforms to the latter part of the verse:

that is, a retributive cause is necessarily associated with the co-existent, whereas there are purely co-existent causes that are not retributive—namely, all neutral (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
If one compares the similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) with the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu), four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) should be established.
The first permutation refers to past and present matter (rūpa) and non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra).
The second phrase refers to the mind and mental factors of the future.
The third phrase refers to the mind and mental factors of the past and present.
The fourth phrase refers to matter, non-associated formations, and unconditioned phenomena of the future.

Furthermore, regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in relation to the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), it follows the latter part of the formal statement: that is, the pervasive cause is necessarily mixed with the homogeneous cause.
However, there are purely homogeneous causes that are not pervasive causes, namely those dharmas of the past and present that are not pervasive.
Furthermore, regarding the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) in contrast to the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu), one should formulate four propositions.
The first proposition refers to past and present indeterminate (avyākṛta) and untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
The second phrase refers to future unwholesome dharmas and wholesome dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The third phrase refers to past and present unwholesome dharmas and wholesome dharmas with outflows.
The fourth phrase refers to future indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena, as well as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
Regarding the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) in relation to the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first phrase refers to the minds and mental factors of the future, as well as those past and present minds and mental factors that are not pervasive.
The second phrase refers to the pervasive non-associated formations of the past and present.
The third phrase refers to all past and present mental states (citta) and mental factors (caitta).

The fourth phrase refers to all material phenomena (rūpa-dharma), all future non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra), past and present non-pervasive non-associated formations, and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Furthermore, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) also form four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first permutation refers to indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
The second permutation refers to unwholesome (*akuśala*), wholesome-tainted (*kuśala-sāsrava*) matter (*rūpa*), and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The third phrase refers to unwholesome and wholesome contaminated mental states and their associated mental factors.
The fourth phrase refers to indeterminate and uncontaminated matter, dissociated formations, and unconditioned phenomena.
Regarding the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) in relation to the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu), four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) should be established.
The first alternative refers to past and present indeterminate (avyākṛta) universal dharmas.

The second phrase refers to future unwholesome dharmas and wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas, as well as past and present wholesome contaminated and unwholesome non-universal (*avyāpaka*) dharmas.
The third phrase refers to past and present unwholesome universal dharmas.
The fourth phrase refers to future indeterminate and untainted dharmas, past and present untainted and indeterminate non-universal dharmas, and unconditioned dharmas.
Furthermore, one should reflect upon the distinctions among these six causes according to various categories, such as those that are material (*rūpa*) and those that are non-material (*arūpa*).

That is to say, among the six causes, the two causes of association (*samprayuktaka*) and universal concomitance (*sarvatraga*) are non-material; the remaining four causes pertain to both the material and the non-material.
It should be understood that the same applies to "with vision" and "without vision," as well as "with resistance" and "without resistance.
Furthermore, among the six causes, only the associated cause consists exclusively of associated phenomena, while the remaining causes pertain to both associated and dissociated phenomena.

It should be understood that the same applies to having a basis or being without a basis, having an awakening or being without an awakening, having a mode of activity or being without a mode of activity, and having an object of focus or being without an object of focus.

Furthermore, among the six causes, the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*); the remaining four causes pertain to both the with-outflows and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).

Moreover, among the six causes, the single efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) pertains to both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), while the remaining five causes are invariably conditioned.

Furthermore, among the six causes, the single pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*), while the remaining five causes pertain to both the defiled and the non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).
It should be understood that the same applies to what is culpable or blameless, black or white, obscured or unobscured, and conducive to regression or not conducive to regression.
Furthermore, among the six causes, the single cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) possesses only maturation; the remaining five causes admit both maturation and non-maturation.

Moreover, among the six causes, the single cause of efficient operation (*kāraṇa-hetu*) extends across the three time periods as well as the non-temporal; the three causes of coexistence (*sahabhū*), association (*samprayukta*), and maturation extend across all three time periods; while the two causes of similar type (*sabhāga*) and universal (*sarvatraga*) extend only through the past and the present.

Furthermore, among the six causes, the single pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is both unwholesome and neutral; the single ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) pertains to both wholesome and unwholesome; and the remaining four causes all pertain to all three natures.

Furthermore, among the six causes, the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) pertain to all three realms of existence; the remaining four causes pertain to all three realms as well as to that which is non-bound (*apratisaṃyukta*).

Moreover, among the six causes, the two causes—the pervasive and the retributive—are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*); the remaining four causes all pertain to all three types [of learners, non-learners, and those who are neither].

Furthermore, among the six causes, the single pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is abandoned only by insight (*darśana-heya*); the single retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is abandoned by both insight and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); and the remaining four causes are abandoned by both insight and cultivation, as well as being non-abandonable (*aheya*).

Furthermore, among the six causes, the single cause of efficient dominance (kāraṇa-hetu) is encompassed by all four truths as well as that which is not a truth; the two causes of pervasive association (sarvatraga-hetu) and retribution (vipāka-hetu) are encompassed only by the truths of suffering (duḥkha-satya) and origination (samudaya-satya); and the remaining three causes are encompassed by the three truths of suffering, origination, and the path (mārga-satya).

Furthermore, among the six causes: the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) are comprised solely within the four aggregates; the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—these three causes—are all comprised within the five aggregates; and the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)—this single cause—is comprised both within the five aggregates and that which is not comprised within the aggregates.

Furthermore, among the six causes, the associated cause (*samyuktahetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) are subsumed within the spheres of mind (*manāyatana*) and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). The single ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) is subsumed within four spheres: form (*rūpāyatana*), sound (*śabdāyatana*), mind (*manāyatana*), and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). The remaining three causes are subsumed within the twelve spheres (*dvādaśāyatana*).

Furthermore, among the six causes: the single pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is subsumed within the three realms of mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness; the single associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) is subsumed within the seven mind-realms and the dharma-realm; the single maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is subsumed within the realms of form and sound, as well as the seven mind-realms and the dharma-realm; and the remaining three causes are subsumed within all eighteen realms.

These various distinctions between cause and effect cannot be fully known by anyone other than an omniscient one; however, I have already extensively analyzed their characteristics within the context of the meaning of cause and effect, according to the scope of our own cognitive faculties.
In order to provide further clarification, one should investigate and discern the various conditions (*pratyaya*).
What are these various conditions?
The verse says:
It is taught that there are four kinds of conditions: The causal condition consists of the nature of the five causes;
The equal-and-immediate condition is not subsequent, Being the already-arisen states of mind and mental factors;
The objective condition consists of all phenomena; The dominant condition is simply the "acting cause."
The treatise says:
Where is this taught?
It is taught in the sūtras.

As stated in the sūtras, there are four types of conditions: namely, the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the nature of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the nature of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

In this context, the nature of conditions (*pratyayatā*) refers precisely to the four conditions. Just as the term "dwellings" implies the nature of dwelling, the word "nature" (*tā*) is used here to indicate their generic category.

While the intention is to discuss the various conditions—which possess infinite entities according to their specific distinctions—their essential meaning is subsumed within these four types; that is to say, no condition whatsoever exceeds this nature.
Among the six causes, with the exception of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the remaining five causes constitute the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
As stated in the treatise:
"What is meant by the causal condition?"
This refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Since the treatise does not state that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are also included, the five causes are established as having the nature of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Why, then, are unconditioned phenomena not established as causal conditions?
This is as explained previously: only non-obstructive presence constitutes the nature of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), and it is not subsumed under the other causes.
Its essence is all-pervasive in its inclusion of phenomena; yet, according to the diversity of specific instances, it is differentiated into many types.

For example, because they encompass a great many phenomena, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*), the dharma-base (*dharma-āyatana*), the dharma-jewel (*dharma-ratna*), the dharma-refuge (*dharma-śaraṇa*), the dharma-foundation of mindfulness (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*), and so forth, are each established as distinct general names.

In order to subsume the five causes and the meanings not included within the three conditions, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are established, as their essential natures are both extensive.
Furthermore, what are the distinctions among the characteristics of these various causes?
The distinctions among causes are briefly of two kinds:
first, the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*); second, the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*).
Furthermore, there are two other kinds:
First, determinate causes; second, indeterminate causes.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, common causes; second, uncommon causes.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, proximate causes; second, remote causes.
Again, there are two kinds:
First, the cause from a previous life; second, the simultaneous cause.
Furthermore, there are two types:
first, causes within the continuums of oneself and others; second, causes not belonging to the category of sentient beings.

Although the nature of all phenomena is inherently existent and not non-existent, the accomplishment of their functional efficacy must depend on causal power; just as the substance of derived matter is inherently not non-existent, yet the accomplishment of its functional efficacy must depend on the primary elements.
Among causes, the most excellent are only five types of causes.

For example, among the causes that produce derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), there are no more than these five; nor is there any conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that is established without depending on causes, just as a weak and sick person cannot rise up by themselves.
Based on this meaning, it is said in verse:
"Not a single thing is established without a cause; The Buddha has taught that all things arise from causes.
The causes of phenomena are manifold, subtle, and difficult to discern; The world, being deluded, claims they have no cause at all."

However, when the Elder speaks of "causal nature," he refers to the "ancient underlying element" (*pūrvānuśaya*), which is the capacity for the continuity of sentient beings to act as a cause through successive transmission.
He maintains that the Blessed One stated in a sutra:

"One should know that for such a person (*pudgala*), although wholesome dharmas have disappeared and unwholesome dharmas have appeared, there exists a concomitant root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) that has not been severed."
Because they have not been severed, there remains the possibility for further roots of goodness to arise from these roots of goodness.
Following along with these co-existent roots of goodness—that is, the original *anuvyañjana-dhātu* (concomitant element)—they continue in succession and function as the nature of a cause.
Categories such as these are called "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

This is likewise refuted by the same arguments used previously against the meaning of "seeds" (*bīja*) as maintained by the Master of the Sūtras (the Sautrāntika), for this "ancient realm of conformity" (*pūrvako 'nuśaya-dhātu*) is merely a different name for that very "seed."

Now, taking advantage of this context, we shall further refute [the opponent's view] by examining the distinctions between their asserted names and meanings. Upon observation, that "homogeneous realm" (sabhāga-dhātu) consists of nothing but empty words; when its substance is investigated and scrutinized, it is entirely unfindable. Therefore, one cannot maintain that this very [realm] constitutes a continuous succession capable of acting as a causal nature.
All things that exist as a continuous succession, acting as causes for one another, have a substantial entity that can be apprehended, such as form, sensation, and so forth.

If the "old latent dispositions" (*pūrvānuśaya*) were to exist as a continuous succession acting as a cause, they should likewise have a substantial entity that can be apprehended, just like form and the other aggregates.
What are its characteristics?
Its characteristic is the element (*dhātu*) formed by the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of these various phenomena.
Furthermore, it is difficult to know whether its essence is form (*rūpa*), or even consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The "homogeneous element" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) should be understood as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), for all conditioned phenomena are subsumed within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Therefore, if it exists, it must be one of the natures of the five aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Alternatively, they should be asked:
"How can there be a conditioned phenomenon that is not subsumed within the five aggregates, such as form and so forth?
Since its existence as a substantial entity must be admitted for the sake of logical consistency, [your position] is merely words without any actual reality."

Furthermore, the nature of the "ancient pervasive element" (*pūrvānuṣaṅga-dhātu*) cannot be known as a substantial entity, just like the "conjoined activity" (*sahabhū-caryā*) or "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).

This ancient pervasive element is inexpressible as a substance; it can only be described as the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), perfumed by karma and afflictions, which bring about the fruit of a future birth.
In this context, it is not merely that the entity is inexpressible; rather, to insist that it exists contradicts reason.
An inexpressible entity cannot be established as existing, for even conventional existents such as persons (*pudgala*) and jars can be said to lack a distinct entity.

If all real phenomena such as form, sensation, and so forth can each be said to possess a distinct substantial entity, the "ancient underlying element" (pūrvānuśaya-dhātu) cannot be so described; it is merely a provisional existence like a *pudgala* or a jar, and unlike real phenomena such as form, it does not exist substantially. Therefore, one should not maintain that this exists.
If this is so, how can you insist that it constitutes a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)?
Furthermore, the term "realm" (*dhātu*) is not taught in the Noble Teachings; it was merely established as such by the Sthaviras and others.
Moreover, according to their own position, which karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) perfume the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) to bring about the fruit of a future birth?

Does it mean that [the six sense bases] arise and perish simultaneously with karma and afflictions? Or that they arise subsequently in a continuous succession? Or that they arise immediately as the maturation (vipāka)?
If the six sense bases arising simultaneously with karma and afflictions were able to produce the fruit, then the subsequent six sense bases would have no capacity to produce the fruit.
The same should apply to both; how then could they induce a fruit?
Only karma and afflictions should possess the capacity to induce a fruit; why must one insist that the six sense bases induce the fruit of a future life?

Furthermore, one should not dogmatically maintain that the eyes and so forth are necessarily co-arising auxiliary causes for karma and afflictions; for even those who are blind and so forth, by relying solely on the conditions of karma and afflictions, still bring about the eyes, ears, and other faculties in subsequent births.
Furthermore, since it is admitted that cause and fruit can be established even when separated by time, what is the use of insisting on this as the "ancient pervasive element" (*pūrvānuśaya-dhātu*)?

If these six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) in their subsequent continuity are able to induce the fruit, yet they are entirely dissociated from karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), how could they be perfumed by those [karma and afflictions] to become a pervasive element?
It is not the case that existence and non-existence can have the sense of being associated.
[Objection: Is it not the case that cause and effect can possess association, since they become conditions by virtue of having identical characteristics?

[Response: That statement regarding "identical characteristics" is logically inconsistent; for when one speaks of "its characteristic," it refers to the characteristic of that [object], and one should say "this characteristic is identical to that characteristic. However, in this context, the term "this characteristic" has been omitted.
Since this karma and these afflictions differ in their nature and category from that subsequent continuity of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), how can these characteristics be identical to those?
How could they possibly correspond to become the condition (*pratyaya*) for them?

Alternatively, if it is their intention that when the six sense bases associated with karma and afflictions are about to cease, they act as conditions for the subsequent six sense bases because their characteristics are identical, this too is unreasonable. At the time when the preceding six sense bases are about to cease, the substance of the subsequent ones does not yet exist; since their substance does not yet exist, their characteristics do not exist either. How can there be an identity of characteristics that establishes the nature of being a condition?
Therefore, what they have said consists of nothing but empty words.

If their statement regarding the characteristic relies on that which is "to be," it would be like the worldly expressions "cooking rice" or "grinding flour," because those things will certainly exist in the future.
This analogy is irrational, for it fails to establish the same properties as the thesis to be proven.
Furthermore, there is a discrepancy regarding whether the analogy and the property (dharma) can or cannot exist conventionally.
First, one must carefully examine whether "cooking" and "grinding" in the ultimate sense possess an intrinsic nature or a distinct category.
Because [the subject] is ultimately non-existent, like a flower in the sky, the example and the thesis do not share the same meaning.
If one were to rely on conventional reality, where cooking and grinding are possible, one could say "cooking rice" or "grinding flour";
however, it is impossible for an existent phenomenon to be identical to a non-existent one. Therefore, this example lacks the power to prove the thesis.
However, this "rice-gruel" (odana) need not have a specific name, as rice and gruel are currently established as existing; considering this, one may say that Devadatta is identical to it.
The analogies of cooking rice and grinding flour are not applicable here, and thus they do not correspond.

Furthermore, once the rice has been cooked and the flour ground, the continuity of the original rice and flour still persists; in both cases, the similarity between the former and the latter can be perceived simultaneously.

When the subsequent moment of the six sense bases reaches the stage of having already arisen, the preceding moment of the six sense bases no longer exists; therefore, it cannot be said that they are identical to one another.
Since it cannot be said that this or that is identical in either the unarisen or the already-arisen state, the example established is not equivalent to the phenomenon [it illustrates].

Even if one grants that rice and flour possess a name, the analogy remains untenable. This is because the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) produced by a preceding moment are not identical to the six sense bases that arise together with karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). Since they arise with distinct characteristics due to karma and afflictions acting as simultaneous auxiliary conditions—and since these two are not in a cause-and-effect relationship—how could the former have the power to serve as the condition for the latter?

Therefore, it cannot be said that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) co-arising with karma and afflictions are superior to the preceding six sense bases, such that they share the same characteristics as the latter and thus constitute the nature of a condition (*pratyayatva*).

Consequently, if one were to say that the cessation of the preceding six sense bases gives rise again to subsequent six sense bases of their own kind, or that the cessation of karma and afflictions gives rise again to subsequent karma and afflictions of their own kind, then one could only speak of this in terms of "existence by way of future designation" (*bhaviṣyad-abhidhāna*), where the existence of the same characteristics serves as the basis for the meaning.

If the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) that coexist with karma and afflictions are no different from those mentioned previously, yet can serve as the causal condition for the production of subsequent bases with distinct characteristics, then one should not say that they possess the same characteristics as the subsequent six sense bases while serving as their causal condition.
Furthermore, for what reason would this cause it to become a condition for a subsequent [rebirth]?
Thus, what they have said is entirely devoid of real meaning.

If that which arises immediately [after death] were able to produce maturation (*vipāka*), and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) acting as the cause were able to induce the fruit, then there would be no karma to be experienced in a subsequent life, because only the immediate cause would produce maturation.
There is no such fault, because [karmic forces] can successively induce results through immediate proximity, just as seeds and the like can successively draw forth the production of fruits.
If that were so, it would incur an even more serious fault: karma to be experienced in the next life or in subsequent lives would become confused and intermingled.
In your own school’s tenet, it is admitted that a single karma perfumes the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), forming a continuous series (*saṃtati*) that draws forth a single fruit.
Furthermore, seeds, sprouts, and so forth are subsumed within a single continuum; thus, although the seed, sprout, and so on perish, a subsequent fruit can still arise.

Since the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) continue through karma and afflictions (kleśa), once those respective karmas and afflictions have ceased, how could the six sense bases subsequently continue in their own kind through successive transmission until the final moment, capable of producing that fruit?
Therefore, that dharma and its analogy are inconsistent in meaning.

Furthermore, since the six sense bases arise simultaneously with karma and afflictions, one should not admit that they are perfumed by karma and afflictions, lest one admit that cause and effect exist simultaneously.

How is it that from those six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) which have been perfumed by non-karmic afflictions, and without any other external conditions, there suddenly arises at a later time another set of six sense bases perfumed by both karma and afflictions?
Therefore, the principle you uphold is not well-established.

If you claim that it is like a seed being nourished by the elements of earth and manure to produce a sprout and so forth, this too is irrational, because it is something we ourselves accept, and furthermore, it does not prove your point.
That is to say, our school admits the existence of simultaneous causes, so this analogy can be established;
your school does not, so how could it be like the nourishing influence of seeds, manure, and soil?

Furthermore, in establishing the formal dharma and the analogy here, the seed should properly represent karma and the afflictions of the mind, while the six sense bases should be said to be like the manure and soil; thus, the category of karma and afflictions should be called the "concomitant element" (*anubandha-dhātu*).
How can the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) be said to be the "concordant realm" (*anurūpadhātu*)?

It is not because seeds are nourished and perfumed by dung and soil that they cause the arising of sprouts of the same class as the dung and soil; therefore, the seeds should be compared only to the six sense bases.
Because the six bases arise as the resultant maturation (*vipāka-phala*) perfumed by karma and afflictions, [it is argued that they are not distinct].
This defense is irrational, because it does not mean that the subsequent six bases are said to have the preceding six bases as their cause.
This means that the Sūtra states that karma and afflictions are the causes of the eyes and so forth, just as seeds are the causes for the production of sprouts and the like.
It is not the case that sprouts and the like take manure and such as their cause; therefore, the defense offered by them is not reasonable.
Furthermore, because the sūtras state that birth has karma as its cause, it is not the case that the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are [the cause].
Since the six sense bases serve as the seed, it cannot be maintained that karma and afflictions (kleśa) are the causes that produce birth, while the six sense bases are held to be their seeds.
Therefore, the five [faculties] beginning with the eye have no superior efficacy whatsoever in bringing about future birth;
whereas the mental base (manāyatana) may, in some cases, share the same fruit as karma and afflictions. Thus, the analogy you have established contradicts the actual nature of the phenomena.
Alternatively, the continuity of the seed and the continuity of the soil may simultaneously produce a distinct fruit.

Thus, although the continuities of karma and afflictions have long since ceased, one reckons that the continuity of the six sense bases acts as the cause, producing a distinct fruit drawn forth by karma and afflictions.
How can such a dharma and its illustration be said to be identical?
