Furthermore, since both the seed and the soil possess parts, two fruits could potentially arise in succession from within the sprout; how then can this be used as a parallel illustration for the claim that those without parts and those with parts equally produce a single fruit?

If one maintains that the manure, soil, and seed within the sprout are non-different from the substance of the fruit, then the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be identical to the thesis (*sādhya*), and both would be unestablished.

Furthermore, regarding their citation of scriptural authority to prove the existence of the "ancient pervasive element" (*pūrvānu-gata-bīja*), they quote the sacred word stating that there are "concomitant wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) that have not yet been severed."

This sūtra further proves that the "old pervasive element" (pūrvānuśaya-dhātu), which they falsely cling to, does not exist; for since the various roots of goodness have the nature of non-attachment and so forth, these do not manifest at this stage, yet because they have been attained and not yet abandoned, they are said to be "not severed."
This statement is made because of the impending severance of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Here, these roots of goodness consist solely of those acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*), for all those acquired through application (*prāyogika*) have already been severed.

Since the roots of goodness acquired at birth are obtained upon the reconnection of the roots of goodness according to the defiled mind, they are said to be "concomitant" (*sahagata*); that is, the nine grades of the accompanying factors are obtained instantaneously, and thus they are called "co-arising."
Alternatively, because these roots of goodness first arise and subsequently persist, they are called "concomitant" (*anuvartin*).
Because their actual manifestation does not conflict with or harm their acquisition (*prāpti*), they are called "co-existent" (*sahagata*).
This is the true meaning of this passage in this sutra.

For one whose roots of goodness have been severed, even those roots of goodness that arise concomitantly with [other states] are not currently present; therefore, this sutra says that at a later time, all of them are severed.
Since the concomitant roots of goodness are the same as the ancient "concomitant element" (anugata-dhātu), when these roots of goodness are absent, that concomitant element is likewise absent.
Since the "concomitant element" (anubandha-dhātu) does not exist, by what subsequent dharma could the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) continue to arise?
Furthermore, at the initial stage of reconnection, the roots of goodness are not presently manifest; thus, there should be no concomitant element.
Since the concomitant element does not exist, on what basis can it be called "reconnection," and how could subsequent roots of goodness arise?
Furthermore, by what cause?
For the Sūtra states:
"From this root of goodness, other roots of goodness will certainly arise again in the future."
Therefore, this further proves that the previously mentioned "accompanying element" (*anugata-dhātu*) does not exist.
Furthermore, they themselves state:
"The essence of this previously mentioned accompanying element cannot be described."
How can this be described as having the nature of roots of goodness and being the cause of roots of goodness?
Furthermore, since there is no internal differentiation within the essence of a single thought-moment or a single mind, how can it produce results that are desirable, undesirable, or neutral?
Because no cause for the differentiation of meditative concentration can be found.
Furthermore, wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral minds would have to arise simultaneously at all times; however, this cannot be admitted, as they are mutually contradictory.
That is to say, when a wholesome mind is actively manifesting, the realms of unwholesome and neutral minds constantly accompany it; they do not possess a separate substance from that wholesome mind.
By what reasoning can it be said that they are not manifesting?
In the state where the minds of the other two natures are currently manifesting, each should likewise be examined regarding its two natures; this should be understood as being the same here.
Furthermore, they should explain:

if multiple categories of mental elements (*citta-dhātu*) persist within a single moment of mind, for what reason does only one category of mind arise at a later time from these many persisting mental elements?

However, at one time, when the objective bases for all consciousnesses, as well as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), are all present, why do they not arise simultaneously?
Since each of those bases and so forth possesses the capacity to produce all consciousnesses at every single moment, what phenomenon acts as an obstruction?
At one time, multiple consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously from a single sense-faculty.
However, regarding this point, that Elder (Sthavira) asserts:
"There is a case where two consciousnesses arise together from a single sense-faculty in a single moment, as in the case of the *jīvañjīvaka* birds sharing a single body."
It is impossible for two sense organs (*indriya*) to arise in a single location; otherwise, it would contradict the nature of obstructive phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*).

This statement merely accords with the personal view of the Sthavira, for there is no principle that two sentient beings could share a single sense organ, as their mental continuities (*saṃtāna*) are distinct.

Furthermore, the two faculties such as those of the *jīvajīvaka* bird dwell in mutual proximity, just like the body and tongue faculties; therefore, two consciousnesses arise from these two faculties. It is not the case that two consciousnesses arise simultaneously upon a single faculty, nor do two sentient beings share a single faculty. This is logically how it ought to be.
That is to say, it is logically untenable for a single faculty to be the fruit of multiple karmas.

Furthermore, no faculty whatsoever is ever shared [among individuals]. Thus, O Sthavira, by what reasoning can you avoid the fault that multiple consciousnesses would arise simultaneously within a single continuum based upon one or more faculties?
Therefore, the claim that the "old" [condition] follows from the "limit of the realm" (*dhātu*) is not a sound teaching.

Furthermore, since the Sthaviras and others maintain that all phenomena arise only immediately following [their antecedents], would it not follow that the Great Master’s teaching on the nature of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) is rendered useless? For if the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is sufficient to bring about the arising of all phenomena, what need is there to laboriously posit a causal condition in addition to this?
Although that Śākya [opponent] says:

"The power of immediate succession (*samanantara-bala*) and the power of the cause of arising (*janana-hetu-bala*) differ in meaning, yet both function together in the production of phenomena," this lacks any real principle and consists of nothing but empty words.

This is because [the mind] abides immediately due to the power of the *anuvṛtti-dhātu* (the realm of conformity); apart from the mind and so forth, one cannot claim that there is a separate causal efficacy belonging to the power of immediate succession.

Furthermore, that Elder maintains that although the substantial entity (*dharmasvabhāva*) of a phenomenon may have been extinguished for kalpas, it continues through its own succession and persists as a causal nature.
Now, observing that such a phenomenon can only function as a condition (*pratyaya*), he gives rise to joy within his own mind and takes delight in this false conceptualization.
It cannot truly function as a cause for the arising of phenomena. Why is this?

If a dharma-entity, even though it has been extinguished for eons, could still act as a cause, then that very entity being the cause would be sufficient to produce the phenomenon; why then laboriously postulate the *anuvartaka-dhātu* (concomitant realm) as the cause?

Furthermore, if those phenomena, despite lacking an intrinsic nature, can act as causes to produce the phenomena they give rise to, then one must also admit that the sons of barren women could likewise act as causes to produce other offspring.

If it is claimed that the substance of the cause exists originally but is now absent—just as the son of a barren woman was originally non-existent—then that phenomenon would not constitute a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). This is because when the cause originally existed, the resultant phenomenon had not yet arisen; and by the time the result arises, the substance of the cause has already ceased to exist. Therefore, it must be said that causal conditions would necessarily be useless.

If the Elder [Vasubandhu] grants that only the arising within one's own continuum can definitively function as a cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), how can he further grant that wholesome and unwholesome dharmas function as cause-conditions to produce neutral maturation (*vipāka*)?
The indeterminate cannot arise with the non-virtuous or virtuous seeds as its cause, because their continuums are distinct.
If the indeterminate ripening were able to arise immediately after the virtuous or non-virtuous, why would this not be explained here?
How can the wholesome and unwholesome serve as causes for the arising of neutral (avyākṛta) maturation?

If it is argued that because the neutral perfumes the wholesome and unwholesome, the wholesome and unwholesome are thus the causes of the neutral, this too is unreasonable; for it has already been repeatedly demonstrated that the term "perfuming" (vāsanā) lacks any real meaning.
Furthermore, how can wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas become causes of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) through the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the indeterminate?
If it is argued that this is because they were previously perfumed by maturation, then maturation itself would have to be the cause of maturation.

If it is a maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) produced by wholesome or unwholesome dharmas as its cause, to claim that within this [fruit] there is no functioning of causal conditions and that it is subsumed solely under the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) is utterly unreasonable.
Why is this? Because wholesome and unwholesome states act as causes capable of drawing forth their respective effects; why, then, would these not be causes for those effects?
Furthermore, what they say contradicts the sacred teachings, as stated in the Sūtra:
By this cause and by this condition, those sentient beings are made to be born in the hells and other such realms.
Furthermore, it is said that the eyes and other faculties have karma as their cause.
Furthermore, it is said:
"All births have karma as their cause," and so forth.
Regarding this, the Sthavira offers the following explanation:
The claim that all dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) do not transcend the nature of causes is therefore logically established by what I have said.
This, however, is not reasonable, because the Sūtras separately state that there exists a dominant condition apart from the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, because this has never been stated in common with them elsewhere— meaning that no sūtra has ever declared that the nature of the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) is identical to the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*)—
the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* might offer such an interpretation, but the Dārṣṭāntikas could not make such a statement, for they do not accept the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*).
Furthermore, how could that Elder maintain that a single moment of mind possesses the perfumings of various elements (*dhātu*)?
For it is logically untenable for a single mind to contain multiple elements.
Nor does the Noble Teaching allow that ultimate phenomena (*paramārtha-dharma*) consist of a synthesis of a single essence and multiple essences.
If one says that although the substance of the mind is unitary, there are many elements (dhātus) within it,
then because these many elements are not different in substance from the mind, the elements should become one.
Since the mind and the multiple realms (dhātus) are not different in essence, the mind would necessarily become manifold.
Since the various realms, when compared with one another, are not different in essence, the essence of one and that of all would necessarily be intermingled.
This position is ultimately irrational; this should be examined in detail above.
However, following the term "bound" (*anuśaya*), one should say "pursued by faults," because it is pursued by immeasurable defects.
One should observe that they merely establish this name out of a desire to subvert the holy teachings and destroy correct reasoning.

Alternatively, because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profound and subtle, they are unable to endure it for long and become weary from hearing and contemplation; therefore, they have not yet attained thorough understanding of it.

However, among the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, there are none who, seeking renown through unskillful means, would falsely establish such a hollow reputation as a "conformable element" (*anuvartaka-dhātu*); therefore, one should explain the causal conditions by following the correct principles set forth in the Abhidharma.
Therefore, it is well said that the nature of dependent origination consists of five causes; this is an excellent teaching that cannot be shaken.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 18. *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 19.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eleven: The Eleventh Section of the Second Part, "Discriminating Differences. Having already explained the causes and conditions, [the following section begins].
What is the nature of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?

It consists of all previously arisen mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), with the exception of the final mental states and mental factors of an Arhat. All other previously arisen mental states and mental factors are exclusively the equal-and-immediate condition.
The term "already arisen" (*jāta*) is stated in order to exclude future phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
The terms "mind and mental factors" (*citta-caitta*) are stated in order to exclude all material phenomena (*rūpa*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Why is it that only mind and mental factors constitute the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
This corresponds to the meaning of the "equal and immediate condition" (samanantara-pratyaya).
Because these produced dharmas are equal and arise without interval, this term "equal and immediate" is established based on this meaning.
That is to say, within a single continuum, two dharmas of the same kind never arise simultaneously; therefore, it is called "equal."
This condition is called "immediate" (*ānantarya*) because there is no similar dharma intervening between it and its fruit.

If one were to define "immediate" as the uninterrupted succession of this fruit, then the mind and mental factors emerging from the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) and so forth would not be considered immediate in relation to what preceded them.

Alternatively, "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*) refers to the arising of equal factors in the interval; thus, there is no possibility for other equal factors to arise in the interval between these two.

Alternatively, the preceding co-arising collection of mind and mental factors acts as a condition for the immediately succeeding collection; it is not merely the similarity of type that constitutes "equal and immediate."
Those who maintain that only those of the same kind within a continuum [act as conditions] say:
"Only each individual mind and mental factor of its own class serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) for what follows it.
This contradicts what is stated in the *Mūla-śāstra*, which says:
What are the dharmas that arise immediately after the mind?
This refers to other minds and mental factors arising immediately after a mind, and so forth, as explained at length.
This [definition] also contradicts reason, for there are cases where a samādhi with vitarka and vicāra arises immediately after a samādhi without vitarka and vicāra, or vice versa.
Those vitarka and vicāra would not then be of the nature of an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);

furthermore, when a samādhi with vitarka and vicāra manifests immediately after a samādhi without vitarka and vicāra, those vitarka and vicāra would have no equal-and-immediate condition from which they arise.

He says: Although mind and mental factors arise as immediate antecedents (*samanantara*), they do not necessarily arise without an interval of a single moment. For example, when one passes away from the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), the mind and mental factors that ceased five hundred eons ago serve as the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the present mind and mental factors.

Furthermore, when the mind and mental factors emerge from the two meditative attainments, the mind and mental factors that entered [the attainment] serve as their equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This arises as an equal-and-immediate succession rather than a momentary succession; this case should be understood in the same way.

Since that person possesses the dharma of samādhi—both with and without applied and sustained thought, as well as without applied and sustained thought—which has long since ceased, it serves as the immediately preceding homogeneous condition (samanantarapratyaya) for the present [state]; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
That statement is unreasonable, because it is logically untenable for the past to serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the present.

If, at the stage of being in the process of ceasing, [a preceding mind] were already to take the subsequent minds and mental factors as its equal-and-immediate condition, would it not then follow that even those phenomena which are equal-and-immediate arise only after an interval of time?
Who establishes that the cause for a fixed state does not arise immediately [after its predecessor], but only arises after being separated by other stages?

Yet, since the non-conceptual heavens (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the two mindless absorptions (*acittaka-samāpatti*) possess periods of separation before their fixed causes are to arise, it follows that according to your own school, all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) in other conscious states would not be able to serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for what follows.

If you argue that this is like the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat, which, even if they do not serve as an equal-and-immediate condition for subsequent states, involve no fault—this too is unreasonable. For in the case of the Arhat, the subsequent mind and mental factors never arise again; whereas in the present case, there must be subsequent mind and mental factors capable of arising, yet none exist therein.
If similar types [of mind] intervene, why would they not constitute the substance of an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
Furthermore, since this mental complex is produced immediately after [a preceding one], on what grounds would it not be an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?

However, that which can accommodate subsequent minds and mental factors such that they necessarily arise is termed an equal-and-immediate condition; because the subsequent minds and mental factors of an Arhat cannot accommodate further arising, they do not fall under this category.
Regarding the contaminated (*sāsrava*) meditative absorptions, the reasoning is for the time being as previously stated;
however, within the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) absorptions, we shall further subject them to scrutiny and refutation.

That is to say, if one relies upon a meditative absorption involving vitarka and vicāra to attain entry into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and without generating a formal resolve (*cetanā*) to further attain a higher fruit, subsequently enters an uncontaminated absorption free of vitarka and vicāra—such that the previously relied-upon absorption no longer manifests—then that prior absorption ought not to possess the nature of an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Alternatively, if one attains entry into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the second dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, yet does not give rise to the aspiration for the attainment of arhatship, and subsequently enters the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna and so forth, then that subsequent concentration would necessarily lack an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This is because, according to the school that maintains the continuity of homogeneous types, there must necessarily exist a concentration with vitarka and vicāra that is to arise, as well as a concentration without vitarka and vicāra that has already ceased.
Furthermore, why labor so hard to further challenge and refute this?

For instance, the initial untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and others should not arise, because there would be no equivalent immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) to act as its apprehending cause.

If that were the case, liberation would ultimately be non-existent. Is it not just as when the initial untainted mind and others arise despite the absence of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) to apprehend them?

Even if there is no such thing as an equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) for grasping [the object], what prevents the initial moments of the untainted mind (anāsrava-citta) from arising?
This example is not equivalent, because the conditions must be fully present.

This means that although these [initial untainted minds] lack a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), they certainly possess a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) because there are other causes present; furthermore, the initial untainted mind and its associated mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) possess an object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Just as all other minds and mental factors are established as arising from four conditions, yet in your doctrine of homogeneous causality both [the preceding moment and the subsequent] are absent, how then can these minds and mental factors arise?

There are no universally established mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) arising from three conditions that could serve as a valid analogy; therefore, liberation must ultimately be non-existent.

If this were so, then these mental states and factors would arise solely through heterogeneous immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), just as [a result] is produced by heterogeneous causes alone when no homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) exists.

This is also unreasonable; for the principle of seeds establishes the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*) cannot serve as the seed for that which is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Therefore, it is not admitted that this [uncontaminated state] possesses a homogeneous cause or an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

By way of the principle of opening and making way, both similar and dissimilar types possess this capacity to provide a place for the arising [of a subsequent state], as there is no difference in their power.

All minds and mental factors, according to their respective natures, are able to induce [their successors] whether they are of a similar or dissimilar type; it is accepted that all are capable of acting as equivalent-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), and this involves no contradiction with either scripture or reasoning.

The analogies such as the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) do not correspond to the actual phenomena; that is to say, because they are dissociated (*viprayukta*) and are neither mind nor mental factors (*citta-caitta*), they cannot function as an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
However, the mind and mental factors at the time of emerging from [the state] can indeed take those mind and mental factors at the time of entering and arising as their causal origination.

In all other states involving consciousness, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is never momentarily absent from moment to moment; why then take the trouble to define it as an equal-and-immediate condition based on temporal separation?
Indeed, an equal-and-immediate condition is defined as that which provides the immediate occasion for the arising [of the subsequent mind].

Heterogeneous states of mind and the like share the same meaning as "drawing forth" (*ākṣepa*) a location, yet they are not equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*). What logic underlies this?

Furthermore, if greed and the like were to arise immediately from an equal-and-immediate condition of greed and so forth, then wholesome states of mind and the like would have no opportunity to arise;

likewise, if faith and the like were to arise immediately from an equal-and-immediate condition of faith and so forth, then defiled states of mind and the like would have no opportunity to arise. Such objections effectively refute the arguments of those who maintain that only homogeneous types of mind can succeed one another in a continuous stream.
For what reason do the single body and its mental states and mental factors not have two co-arising entities of the same kind?
Because there is no second immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Furthermore, for what reason is there no second immediately preceding condition?
Because each and every sentient being possesses only a single mind that evolves as a continuum.
Furthermore, by what evidence is it known that the minds of all sentient beings evolve as a single continuum for each individual?
This is because when the mind is actively distracted toward another object, it does not clearly cognize that other object;
furthermore, when the mind is in meditative concentration focused on a single object, a distracted mind directed toward another object cannot possibly arise.
Furthermore, there is currently the capacity to discipline the mind.
That is to say, if it were admitted that two minds arise simultaneously, what would prevent many more from arising together?
In that case, multiple minds would have to arise concurrently.
If it is difficult to subdue even a single mind within a single body, how much more so when there is one body with two minds, or one body with many minds?
Since there are those currently capable of subduing the mind, we know that within a single body, a single mind arises in continuous succession.
Furthermore, if multiple minds arise simultaneously within a single body, do they each have distinct objects or do they correspond to a common object?
If they correspond to a common object, then because that object and its characteristics would be without distinction, their simultaneous arising would be redundant.
If objects were distinct [for each individual], then defilement and purity, as well as good and evil, would arise simultaneously, and there would be no liberation.
Since this fault does not occur, it follows that for a single sentient being, there is only one mind that evolves as a continuous stream.
Furthermore, there is the supreme teaching that proves a single sentient being possesses only a single stream of consciousness that evolves; as the Sūtra says:
"When one experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time two feelings have both ceased."
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"The mind travels alone.
How, then, can one know that there is no arising of consciousness and so forth that does not depend upon the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
This is established by both scripture (*āgama*) and correct reasoning (*yukti*).
As for scripture, it is as stated in the Sūtra:
"And when the attention (*manasikāra*) that produces that [state] arises correctly."
According to correct reasoning, it is observed that cognitive awareness necessarily arises from a preceding state of cognitive awareness.
Otherwise, by what logic could one prevent the sudden emergence at this present time of sentient beings who previously did not exist?
For what reason are the final mind and mental factors of the various Arhats said not to be equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
It is because they lack the nature of being able to produce further dharmas; that is to say, they are incapable of drawing forth subsequent fruits.
Furthermore, for what reason does this lack the capacity to project a fruit?
It is because at that time, other conditions are deficient.

If that is so, and it is admitted that this [consciousness] possesses the function of projecting a subsequent fruit—such that the subsequent consciousness simply fails to arise due to the deficiency of other conditions—what fault is there in this?
This should not be accepted.

If it were accepted that [the mind] can project [the fruit], then it would necessarily possess both the capacity to grasp the fruit and the capacity to give the fruit; for in other states where the mind exists, the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) is never without these two functions.
Is it not the case that because other conditions are lacking, the two capacities are incomplete? In that case, one should say:
"Because other conditions are lacking, it cannot draw forth the fruit.
For this reason, it is said: "This [cause] is incapable of producing the nature of an existent phenomenon (bhāva-dharmin). Thus, the meaning of "cause" (hetu) is fully established.

Alternatively, that which is capable of drawing forth and providing the locus for the immediately succeeding mind and mental factors is called the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

That is to say, the mind and mental factors at the moment of ceasing are capable of drawing forth and providing the locus for those dharmas in the state of arising; this is termed the equal-and-immediate condition.

At the very moment when the final minds of all Arhats are in the process of ceasing, there exists no dharma that arises as their equal-and-immediate [condition]; therefore, it cannot be said that they possess an equal-and-immediate condition.

If that were so, then for the mind and mental factors immediately preceding the state of non-conception and the two meditative attainments—during their phases of actual cessation and actual arising—there would be no immediately preceding mind or mental factors to serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) in relation to the various minds and mental factors at the moments of emerging from those states; thus, one could not say they constitute an equal-and-immediate condition.
There is no such fault, because the mind of emergence (*vyutthāna-citta*) and so forth must necessarily arise.

When the mind of entry (*praveśa-citta*) and so forth is in the state of ceasing, it can serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for those [subsequent minds]; however, because they are separated by an interval of dissociation (*viprayukta*), the mind of emergence and so forth cannot arise immediately.
When that [subsequent state] arises, it is called "immediately antecedent"; therefore, this can be described as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

Alternatively, when this [preceding state] ceases, although that [subsequent state] has not yet arisen and there is an intervening gap, because it is grasped by the power of this equal-and-immediate condition, it is already meaningful to say that it arises immediately.
Other commentators explain:
because no further mind or mental factors arise in succession from them, the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat are not equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

However, this does not constitute a fault regarding the definition of the mental faculty (*manas*), for it is established that the mental faculty is defined by its role as a support (*āśraya*) for the subsequent arising of consciousness; since there is no subsequent moment of consciousness to follow this [final] mind, there is no deficiency in the definition of the mental faculty.

However, regarding the meaning of the final mind having a basis, because other conditions are lacking, the non-arising of subsequent consciousness is manifested by the function of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

If a dharma has already been taken as an effect by this condition, that dharma must necessarily arise immediately thereafter; thus, the cause [of non-arising] you have stated is entirely unreasonable.

If subsequent consciousness does not arise because other conditions are lacking, then it should follow that subsequent consciousness would necessarily arise whenever those other conditions are present.

Since this is not the case, one must say that this mind lacks the functional capacity of those conditions due to their absence; and because those conditions are absent, subsequent consciousness does not arise. Why, then, do you claim that it is not the essence of those conditions because no other minds or mental factors continue from this life to produce them?

If it is argued that even the final mind can take up a fruit, yet subsequent consciousness does not arise merely because of the deficiency of other conditions, then the basis [of that final mind] which receives the name "mind-element" (*manodhātu*) should likewise be said to be manifested by the equivalent-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the operation of that equivalent-immediate condition.
Since this [consciousness] possesses functional activity, why do the others not arise in succession?
For this reason, they ought to explain further principles;
therefore, the two previous explanations serve as reasons for their being faultless.
For what reason are future minds and mental factors not permitted at all to be established as equivalent-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?

Because the equivalent-immediate condition is manifested by the sequence of preceding and succeeding moments, and since such a sequence does not exist in the future, this condition is not established for them.

This means that previously arisen mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) can serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for subsequent mental states and mental factors that are currently in the state of arising; it is not the case that such a definite sequence of priority and posteriority is already established in the future.
If it were granted that such a thing exists, then the cultivation of correct application would be in vain;
for if a phenomenon is established immediately prior to this, then that phenomenon will necessarily arise immediately thereafter.
If one holds such a position, a virtuous mind would immediately be followed by all three types of minds—virtuous, defiled, and neutral.

However, the arising [of a subsequent mind] must depend upon correct application (*prayoga*) and so forth; just as a sprout from ashes can arise from a seed, it arises only by depending on the convergence of conditions. Therefore, the effort expended in cultivating correct application is not in vain.
This defense merely follows one's own inclinations and fails to resolve the difficulty.

This condition is established because [the result] arises with certainty; if, among the three types of minds, any single wholesome mind were to arise with certainty immediately following [the unwholesome], then the cultivation of correct preparatory application would be in vain.

If the three types of wholesome minds were not necessarily produced immediately after [their preceding moments], then this condition would not exist; since that which is not necessarily produced cannot be called an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), there is therefore no equal-and-immediate condition in the future.

If one maintains that there is a fixed sequence of before and after in the future—such as the case of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) in relation to the Patience regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and so forth—on what basis is such a fixed sequence asserted?

It is not possible for the sequence of before and after to be established for future phenomena; that is to say, it cannot be said that the Supreme Mundane Dharma is prior to or subsequent to the Patience regarding Suffering, because it is fundamentally comprised within a single temporal period.
The meaning of "prior" and "subsequent" is established only over the course of successive moments.

From the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) until its own arising, it is only upon the occurrence of the Receptivity to the Knowledge of Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) that it can be designated as "subsequent.
Therefore, the relationship of prior and subsequent does not exist in the future; for this reason, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) does not exist therein.

Furthermore, even if it were established that the future possesses a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority, one could still not establish the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). This is because, just as the arising of sprouts and so forth belongs to seeds and so forth, there may be a sequence of priority and posteriority without this specific condition existing between them.

If this phenomenon arises in dependence upon that phenomenon, such that it can only arise once that [condition] has already occurred, then the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is established only after [the preceding moment] has arisen.

If that were so, there would be no ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) in the future, because cause and effect must necessarily have a temporal sequence of before and after, whereas the future does not possess such a sequence of before and after.
There is no such fault, because although the sequence of cause and effect is fixed, this reason is not established in dependence upon that sequence.
That is to say, although a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) necessarily has a temporal priority and posteriority, the ripening cause is not established in reliance upon that priority and posteriority.
If that is so, how can this cause-and-effect relationship be established—namely, that such a karmic cause brings about such a ripened result (*vipāka*)?

This characteristic can indeed be described as existing even in the future; therefore, it may also be established with respect to the future. However, it is spoken of in advance in terms of the future by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

This cause arises prior and this effect arises posterior; since the condition of the cause having already arisen establishes the meaning of the effect being posterior, it is only at that time that "prior" and "posterior" can be called real. It is not the case that real priority and posteriority exist during the stage when [the cause] has not yet arisen.

Regarding those causes that can be said to exist in the future, such causes as the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) do not depend upon the passage of time to be established. Is it not the case, however, that the co-existent cause depends upon the intermediate period [of existence] to be established?
This criticism is unreasonable because it fails to understand the provisional meaning [of the term].
It is called the "simultaneous cause" (*sahabhū-hetu*) because they exist at the same time; this signifies the sense that they stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect.
If there were no equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) in the future, how could the Blessed One know the causes and effects of the future?

As stated in a sutra: "If one can make an offering to even a single part of eight of my bodily relics, one shall not fall into the evil destinies for thirteen kalpas, but will instead pass between the human and celestial realms, experiencing various sublime pleasures."
Such explanations as these are indeed numerous.
These matters are not within the domain of ordinary omniscience; even for one who possesses all-knowledge, it is impossible to measure or know their true reality. As the World-Honored One has said:
"The virtues, functions, and spheres of all Buddhas are inconceivable."
Therefore, one should not hold [the Buddha] accountable. Other masters say:

Just as the Buddha, regarding the past, exercises direct knowledge and vision concerning the future—meaning that when the Buddha wishes to know the causes and effects of sentient beings—because the duration of the present is brief, he observes the past and future more frequently.
It is not that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, desires to know the future limit; rather, he first contemplates the past limit and is then able to know it.

Unlike others who must rely on further conditions, because the cognition of past objects has become manifest to the Buddha, he is able to thoroughly penetrate the correspondence between karma and its fruit within the bodies of sentient beings in the past, [knowing] that "following this dharma, this dharma has arisen."

In this way, without depending on prior observation of the past limit, because the cognition of future objects manifests before one, one is able to definitively perceive within the bodies of sentient beings in future lives that the correspondence between karma and its fruit is such that immediately after this phenomenon, that phenomenon will arise.
Furthermore, other masters have stated:

Within the bodies of sentient beings, there currently exist the prior signs of future causes and effects, which are like reflections, being either material form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), or formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The Buddha knows the future simply by observing this; it is not necessary for him to currently engage in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) or supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, he does not know it by means of divining signs (*nimitta*), because he perceives the future through direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
It is not by means of divination that one can clearly perceive, realize, and discern what is being divined before one’s eyes.
Regarding such a dense forest of objective phenomena (*jñeya*), it is only when there is a rational basis that the Buddha can manifest the supreme skillful wisdom of unimpeded observation.

It is not that the Buddha, by virtue of being self-proclaimed as the Omniscient One, perceives objects such as form within the manifest field of experience through consciousness alone—without the prior apprehension of visual and other sensory consciousnesses—but rather that he constantly and clearly cognizes them solely by means of mental consciousness.
Furthermore, it is logically impossible for visual consciousness and the other sensory consciousnesses to function as mutual conditions for objects such as sound.
For what reason are all forms (*rūpa*) not equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
Because the meaning of "equal-and-immediate" is incompatible with them.
It is not that non-existent dharmas arise simultaneously as an interval; therefore, this [non-existence] lacks the condition of immediate antecedence (*samanantarapratyaya*).

That is to say, within a single body, while one stream of nutritive matter (*aupacayika-rūpa*) continues without interruption, a second stream of nutritive matter may arise without mutual contradiction or harm. For example, while a stream of matter nourished by food and so forth continues without interruption, another stream of matter nourished by food and so forth arises in succession.
Furthermore, there is one type of matter born of maturation (*vipākaja*) whose continuity remains uninterrupted, while another type of matter born of maturation arises as a new continuity.

Moreover, many homogeneous atoms (*paramāṇu*) of derived matter produced by the same four great elements arise simultaneously; therefore, it is impossible to establish [such cases] as having the condition of equal and immediate antecedent (*samanantarapratyaya*).
If a phenomenon arises immediately after another phenomenon such that it is equivalent, that [preceding] phenomenon may be established as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This refers to the currently active mind, whether it is bound by those [defilements] or not, along with the concomitant feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth.
Because it is identical in all these respects, it is called "equal" (*samanantara*).
Mental factors such as feeling and so forth arise simultaneously with two entities belonging to the same category; therefore, they are called "immediately preceding" (*anantara*).

Material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are not like this. That is to say, at the time of a single moment of mind, two types of matter—those bound to the desire realm and those bound to the form realm—may arise together, or matter bound to the desire realm and matter that is unbound may arise simultaneously. Therefore, material phenomena do not possess the condition of being an "equal and immediate antecedent" (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The Elder here falsely raises this objection:

"If one type of matter continues in an uninterrupted stream, and another type arises in a stream [simultaneously], then because of this, they would not be 'immediately preceding conditions' (samanantara-pratyaya). For what reason, then, do greed and other afflictions arise within that category which is associated with unique ignorance (āveṇika-avidyā)?"
One should counter-argue that Elder by asking:
"By what cause could greed and other afflictions co-arise with a mental state associated with non-common ignorance?
As long as the continuity of non-common ignorance has not been severed, there is certainly no possibility for greed and the like to arise simultaneously."

However, the claim that greed and the like arise simultaneously with non-specific ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) is merely intended to entice and deceive students of little learning, demonstrating one's own proficiency in the tenets of the Abhidharma school; yet, this principle is nowhere found in the root treatises or the words of the Noble Ones.
Furthermore, what is the intent revealed by that objection?

Is it to suggest that, just as the two types of nourished eye-faculties (*cakṣurindriya*) have no difference in their characteristics, so too the characteristics of greed (*rāga*) and the like, as well as non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*), are likewise without distinction?

Is it as with covetousness and so forth, where uncommon ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) differs in its characteristics, that one might take those two types as an analogy for the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) being nourished by them, such that their characteristics also differ?
Even if such an intention were held, one must state what benefit is gained by raising this objection regarding this point.
Could it be that because of this, sensation (*vedanā*) and the like, or greed (*lobha*) and the like, or faith (*śraddhā*) and the like, would thereby lack the status of being such conditions?
Therefore, the objection raised by him is verbally sound but logically baseless. Others further say:
Because material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) have no fixed certainty regarding the relative amount of their arising and ceasing, they do not constitute this condition (*pratyaya*).

That is to say, there are times when much gives rise to little, such as when a great heap of rice straw is burned to become ash, or when a body that once filled a large space transforms into one that is emaciated and small.

At other times, there is the arising of much from little, such as when a tiny seed produces a *nyagrodha* tree, whose roots, trunk, branches, and leaves gradually flourish and increase until its towering stem and spreading boughs cast a vast shade; likewise, the *kalala* and subsequent stages transform into a large body. Therefore, material phenomena certainly lack the nature of being an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Is it not the case that when mental factors arise in immediate succession, there are also instances where their categories are not equal—namely, among wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral minds, or those with vitarka and vicāra, or those in samādhi? While there are indeed such differences in quantity across different types, within the same category, there is no sense of inequality.
That is to say, it is not the case that a few sensations are immediately followed by many, nor that many are immediately followed by few;
the same applies to perception (*saṃjñā*) and the other mental factors. Thus, there is no fault of inequality.

Therefore, since the essence of the arising and ceasing of the mind and its mental factors is uniform, one may establish the principle of "equal and immediate antecedence" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) based upon them.

However, that Elder, in response to his own disciples, falsely raised an objection regarding this point, claiming that matter (*rūpa*) is also identical to mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) because each individual instance within its own class is distinct.

Although there are infinite forms within the composite aggregates of the various realms, each of those types possesses distinct differences when compared with one another; thus, such an objection is merely empty talk.
Since it is already admitted that there are similar types of matter (*sabhāga-rūpa*) existing simultaneously, the principle that similar types of matter arise together is established.

It is not the case that each individual thing possesses a distinct name such as "simultaneous similar type"; rather, since it is admitted that various aggregates (*saṃghāta*) differ from one another in their categories when compared reciprocally, the principle that within a single distinct aggregate there are multiple material entities belonging to the same category is thereby established.
Furthermore, if many atoms arise from the same set of primary elements (mahābhūta), how could the Venerable Elder maintain that their types are distinct?

Moreover, we observe that sesame, various beans, wheat, and so forth produce many fruits from a single kind of substance; since these many fruits are of the same type when compared to one another, how can you maintain that there is a difference in their types?
Furthermore, since he himself asserts that there is a plurality of homogeneous material forms (*rūpa*) in combination, why does he instead pose this as an objection?

That is to say, the Sthavira himself denies that material forms serve as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), yet he claims that multiple homogeneous and co-located material forms arise simultaneously;

whereas mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth do not arise simultaneously as homogeneous [entities]. Therefore, it is certain that material forms lack the status of being equal-and-immediate conditions.

Furthermore, as for what was said: although there is a distinction between matter and non-matter, they equally do not obstruct one another's acting as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and so forth;
likewise, those dharmas should also equally act as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Venerable sir, this objection is extremely confused; if it were so, one would also have to reckon that all material forms possess an object of cognition (*sālambana*).

Furthermore, just as you admit that among the co-existent and equal-and-immediate conditions (*sahabhū- and samanantara-pratyaya*) there are both those that are material and those that are non-material, so too should you admit that among the co-existent and homogeneous causes (*sahabhū- and sabhāga-hetu*) there are those that function as such conditions and those that do not.
For now, within this context, we provisionally grant their position in order to clarify that there is a distinction in meaning and to answer their inquiry.

However, in reality, it is not permissible to allow material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) to function as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), because their characteristics are incompatible.

If all dharmas such as material forms (rūpa) are associated with the characteristics of the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), they should naturally be established as such; why then is it necessary to cite examples such as the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu)?
This is because the meanings of "condition" (pratyaya) and "cause" (hetu) differ from one another.

If the various dharmas such as form are not associated with the characteristics of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), what benefit would there be in citing causes such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*)?
To cite those causes as examples for this condition when they offer no benefit to the argument is merely the hollow speech of the Venerable Elder, whose years have grown old.
Others further state:

Since all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) continue in a homogeneous succession, when one arises in a particular location, if another material phenomenon were to come and displace it from that location, there would be the possibility of it moving and arising in another place; therefore, it is not the case that the preceding matter arises simultaneously with its location.

Furthermore, when a mass of matter (*rūpa-kalāpa*) continues in an uninterrupted succession, other matter of a similar kind arises at its periphery; otherwise, the mass of matter would not undergo growth.
Since this principle does not apply to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), matter is not established as having an immediately preceding condition.

The Dārṣṭāntika masters assert that all material phenomena (rūpadharma) possess the condition of equal and immediate antecedence (samanantarapratyaya), just as mental states and their concomitants do. They observe that from milk, curdled milk, seeds, and flowers, there arise respectively, yogurt, vinegar, sprouts, and fruit; and just as mental states and their concomitants perish before they give rise to subsequent ones, they know that all material phenomena likewise possess this causal principle.

Furthermore, since no sūtra states that only mind and mental factors can serve as this condition, the claim that establishing this condition necessarily excludes matter is a false attachment; such a meaning does not exist.
The functions of various conditions possess infinite distinctions; they are summarized as fourfold.

This means that for all phenomena to arise, they depend upon the convergence of many conditions, and while the functional distinctions of these conditions are infinite, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has briefly explained them as four.

One should know that when effects such as curd, *arbuda*, or reflected consciousness arise from causes such as milk, the *kalala*, and so forth, and from conditions such as their forms and supports, they are subsumed within the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
On what basis is this known?

It has already been stated previously that when milk and so forth arise immediately after [the cessation of] curd and so forth, the preceding phenomenon is not the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the subsequent one.
What was stated previously?
This refers to what was stated previously: because the meaning of "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*) is inconsistent [with simultaneous arising].

We observe that it is universally established that when mental states and mental factors arise, they are necessarily dependent upon the equal and immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). All co-arising phenomena belong to distinct categories; those of the same category do not arise simultaneously. Therefore, since phenomena of the same kind are mutually exclusive, a subsequent moment can only arise once the preceding moment has ceased. It is on this basis—namely, the provision of a specific locus—that the equal and immediate condition is established.

When multiple atoms of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), such as milk—which are of the same category and produced from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—arise simultaneously without mutual obstruction, this state contradicts the definition of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Therefore, although the production of curd and so forth is dependent upon that [milk], it cannot be established as an equal-and-immediate condition.

The same explanation applies to the arising of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). That is to say, both homogeneous and heterogeneous types may arise together; they do not mutually obstruct one another at the same time. Although they may arise in succession, they do not serve as [simultaneous] conditions for one another.

Furthermore, as for the claim that no sūtra states that "mind-only" and so forth serve as this condition, the same applies to matter (*rūpa*); that is, there is no sūtra stating that various forms of matter also possess the capacity to serve as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for what follows. Therefore, the Dārṣṭāntikas' irrational and arbitrary insistence that matter also possesses an immediately preceding condition is untenable.
Furthermore, does the Dārṣṭāntika school admit that matter (*rūpa*) has an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
They say it does not. Is there any sūtra that clearly proves this point?
Although there is no such scriptural statement, the principle must necessarily be so; why then do they not likewise admit this for the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
Therefore, whatever that venerable one has said merely follows his own inclinations and lacks the foundation of true principle or scriptural teaching.
For what reason are the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) not established as having the condition of equal and immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
Because they arise in confusion;
that is to say, within a single body, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [states], as well as those bound to the three realms and those not so bound, arise simultaneously.
The *Vibhāṣā* states:

Mind and mental factors possess resistance in terms of their support (*āśraya*), object (*ālambana*), and mode of activity (*ākāra*); it is for this reason that they establish the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Matter (*rūpa*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) do not have such characteristics; therefore, they are not established as having this condition as their essence.
Venerable Sir, in this matter you have failed to apply yourself diligently to the training and have spoken erroneously.
This statement lacks any logical basis for proof; it merely demonstrates that the mind and its concomitants are distinct from form and its concomitants.

Examining what they have said, it appears they are not yet familiar with the underlying intent of their argument or the logical principles established herein: namely, that for a single basis, object, and mode of activity, there can never be two consciousnesses arising simultaneously; therefore, [a subsequent consciousness] must necessarily arise by depending on its preceding [moment] and its locus.
If the preceding [moment] acts as an obstruction, the subsequent one cannot arise.
From this it is proven that only the preceding mind and mental factors can serve as the equal-and-immediate condition for those that follow.
If this is so, since the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) does not arise simultaneously with two [other] states, why do you not allow it to rely upon the equal-and-immediate condition?

It might be argued that since this life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has characteristics similar to those of consciousness and other mental factors, it too should be established as an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This analogy is not valid, because both the life-faculty and the body are equally produced by the force of prior karma.

That is to say, this life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not projected by the power of a life-force that ceases without interval; rather, it must be projected by the power of karma performed in a prior state.
If that were so, the life-faculty should arise all at once in a single moment, because all [beings] would equally be projected by the power of karma from a single moment, based upon the same support.
The mind and mental factors induced by prior karma would arise without depending on the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Furthermore, there is no fault of all life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*) arising simultaneously, precisely because their arising is determined by the power of karma.
It is the natural law of cause and effect that a single moment of karma induces the arising of many moments of maturation (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, because it would serve no purpose, life does not arise all at once.

That is to say, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is induced to arise for the sake of sustaining the homogeneous group (*nikāyasabhāga*); a single continuity of life is sufficient to sustain it, and multiple instances would be redundant.

Although mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are projected by prior karma, they do not arise without depending on the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), for they must rely upon the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) to come into being.

Since they arise through the conjunction of the faculties and objects, even when many arise simultaneously, they are not without utility. Nevertheless, because there cannot be a second immediately preceding condition, two [identical] states of the same kind do not arise together.

Furthermore, the mind and mental factors are not produced solely by the force of prior karma, because they arise as both maturation and other types of heterogeneous occurrences; if they did not further rely upon the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), multiple factors would have to arise simultaneously within a single moment.

That is to say, the essence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is exclusively maturation (*vipāka*), being produced solely by the power of prior karma; thus it can be said that it arises determinately as a homogeneous succession.

Mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) do not possess such a quality: once maturation has ceased, there arises a flow-on (*niṣyanda*) state, and immediately following that flow-on, there may arise a momentary state, or a maturation state that is not necessarily homogeneous. Therefore, although mental states and mental factors are born of maturation, they cannot be said to be equivalent to the life-faculty and so forth.
Therefore, only those that arise constantly and without interval are called "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*).

Because this serves as the condition for that, it is termed the "equal and immediate condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*). But would it not be the case that within a homogeneous continuum of atoms, as each preceding moment ceases, the succeeding one arises, such that they are equal and immediate when viewed in relation to their own kind?
Because the subsequent [moment] can only arise after the preceding one has vacated its place, they do not contradict the definition of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This does not occur simultaneously because it would be purposeless; it is not due to the power of the equal-and-immediate condition that this is so.
This should be explained according to principle, following the previous discussion on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
However, since this [life-faculty] also possesses co-arising factors of the same kind (*sabhāga-sahaja*), it should not be said that it is subsumed under this condition (*pratyaya*).
Furthermore, if one were to establish this condition solely by way of making room for it, then even atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like could be said to be included within this condition.

However, this nature of the condition is established based on both the act of making way and the capacity to draw forth [a subsequent moment]. Therefore, although atoms and the like may precede and make way for what follows, they do not constitute this condition.
Since the mutual production of mental states and the like is both determinate and indeterminate, we know that this condition must also be established based on the power to draw forth [the effect].

We observe that a single mind continues in a sequence before and after; although the principle is the same whether the preceding [moment] avoids the succeeding one or not, there is a distinction between what arises and what does not, and between what is determinate and what is indeterminate. Regarding those cases where arising is determinate:

for instance, immediately following the mind of the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), the mind of "Patience regarding the Knowledge of the Dharma of Suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) necessarily arises. In this manner, up until the mind of the "Diamond-like Samādhi" (*vajropamasamādhi*), the mind belonging to the category of "Knowledge of Exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*) necessarily arises immediately thereafter. Furthermore, for one who still possesses afflictions (*kleśa*), an afflicted mind necessarily arises immediately following a determinate mind.

Regarding all such cases of non-arising in a fixed sequence: it is determined that immediately after a defiled state of mind, no untainted state of mind can arise; immediately after an untainted state of mind, no defiled state of mind can arise; immediately after any mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), no mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) can arise; immediately after a defiled mind of a lower stage, no defiled mind of a higher stage can arise; immediately after any resultant (*vipāka*) mind, no momentary category of mind can arise; and immediately after any momentary mind, no resultant category of mind can arise.

Regarding all such cases where arising is indeterminate: this means that immediately following a defiled mind of the desire realm, any of the four types of minds of its own level may arise; furthermore, immediately following a defiled mind of a higher level, a wholesome mind of a lower level may also arise.
All of these points will be further demonstrated later in the analysis of the characteristics of arising.

Since what has been stated shows that arising and non-arising are both determinate and indeterminate, we know that the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is not established merely by way of making room for the subsequent moment, but also based on the functional capacity to draw forth the production of a result.
Since such a functional capacity does not exist in atoms and the like, they are not established as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).
But would it not be the case that within the homogeneous continuity of the mind, there is likewise no such capacity to draw forth [the subsequent moment]?
It is not that this functional efficacy exists at one time and does not exist at another; for if it were absent at this time, it should likewise be non-existent later.

Since all minds and mental factors arise through the power of their own causes, what could the immediately preceding cessation possibly do? Why, then, do you claim that mind and its concomitants alone constitute this condition, while form and the dissociated factors do not possess the nature of such a condition?

Regarding the statement that "that which has ceased immediately prior has an efficacy": this means that although the sense faculties and their objects are currently in conjunction, if what precedes does not cease, what follows will necessarily not arise.

That is to say, even though many conditions may concur within a single body, consciousnesses of the same kind do not arise simultaneously; therefore, we know that at the moment when the preceding mind ceases without interval, it possesses the power to draw forth and cause the subsequent mind and its associates to arise.
Since such a thing does not exist for that which is non-associated with form (*rūpa*), it is not established as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
As it is said:
"What are the dharmas that are equal-and-immediate to the mind?"

This refers to the moments immediately following the mind, wherein other minds and mental factors have already arisen or are currently arising, as well as the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and so forth, as explained at length.
The term "already arisen" includes those of the past and present, while the term "currently arising" includes those at the moment of future birth.

If that were so, then the second moment of concentration and subsequent moments of the mind emerging from concentration would not be immediately preceded by the mind entering concentration, because those [subsequent moments] have not yet arisen.
Is it not the case that when those various dharmas subsequently arise in the present, they are termed "immediately preceding conditions" (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mind and so forth?
Therefore, there is no such fault.
How is it that there is no fault?

When that [mind] is arising, the preceding mind that had entered meditative absorption has long since ceased and passed away; thus, it cannot at this time be designated as the "immediately antecedent condition" (samanantarapratyaya). However, there is no such fault, because there is no other immediately antecedent condition intervening between them.
Other masters say:

although that dharma is distant, it can still be described as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) at the time of its actual arising, because once the fruit has been grasped, it is certain to arise.
If that were so, it would contradict the text within the *Skandhaka* on Views (*Dṛṣṭiskandha*), which asks:

"If a phenomenon serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for another phenomenon, is there ever a time when this phenomenon is not the equal-and-immediate condition for that one?"
He replied: "If this dharma has not yet reached the state of having already arisen, what contradiction or harm is there?

It is not contradictory that the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) must necessarily reach the state of having already arisen, for both interpretations are accepted as distinct [but valid] explanations."
If this dharma has not yet arisen, what would it mean for it to be "prior" or "subsequent"?

For example, when the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) gives rise to the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), does the Supreme Mundane Dharma fail to serve as the immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering while it has not yet reached the state of having arisen, or does it serve as the immediate antecedent once it has reached the state of having arisen?

When the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering has not yet arisen, it does not serve as the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the supreme mundane dharmas; once it has reached the stage of having already arisen, does it then serve as the immediate antecedent condition?
If one adheres to the former position, it may be so in the state of having a mind; however, how could it be so in the state of being without mind?

That is to say, when entering a mindless meditative absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*), the mind that has already arisen cannot serve as the equal-and-immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the second moment of that absorption or for the mind emerging from it.

If the mind entering meditative absorption were to become the equal-and-immediate condition for those various dharmas upon reaching the stage of having already arisen, then since the dharmas that are the fruits of the equal-and-immediate condition would be grasped and there would necessarily be nothing capable of obstructing their arising, all of them should arise simultaneously.
If the subsequent mind were to arise immediately after the mind that has entered [the meditative absorption], then these two absorptions would never arise again.

If one maintains the latter position, then as long as the "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) has not yet arisen, it should not serve as the immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya) for that "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma); however, one must necessarily admit that at the very moment the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering is in the process of arising, it is designated as the immediate antecedent of that supreme mundane dharma.

Among these, one class admits the previous position; however, they argue that since the *skandha* text speaks of "immediate succession" (*samanantara*) with reference to states possessing mind, there is no fault as previously stated.

Alternatively, they say that even if it were explained with reference to states devoid of mind, this fault would still not apply. That is to say, when the mind entering meditative absorption resides in the present state, it simultaneously grasps all the absorptions as well as the fruit of the emerging mind. Furthermore, at the very first moment, the absorption-fruit ceases and enters the past. Subsequently, as each of the later absorptions and the emerging minds arise one by one, they do not grasp a fruit because it has already been grasped.
Is it not the case that all equal-and-immediate conditions (samanantarapratyaya) take their fruit and give their fruit at no different times?
This objection is unreasonable; for while the taking of the fruit is necessarily instantaneous, the giving of the fruit occurs gradually, and thus there is no fault.
One should simply reprove [the opponent] by saying:

"Since they are both fruits of the same mind, for what reason do the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the mind emerging from attainment arise sequentially rather than simultaneously; and why is it that which is specifically sought must necessarily arise first?"
This means that because the mind entering meditative absorption seeks to conform to that absorption, the mind immediately preceding the state of absorption arises without interval.
If this is so, for what reason do the various moments of absorption arise in succession?
The simultaneous arising of multiple moments of meditative concentration (samādhi) would be purposeless; therefore, they do not arise simultaneously.

Because they are induced by the force of prior preparatory application (prayoga), multiple moments of concentration continue to arise over a long duration; it is not the case that multiple moments of concentration arise together at once.
Because that which cannot be accomplished by a single moment of concentration does not arise instantaneously, just like consciousness and other phenomena;
however, while these moments of concentration are indeed *samanantara* (immediately preceding), they cannot be said to function as a *samanantarapratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition).

If a phenomenon is produced by preceding moments of mind and so forth, it must not arise simultaneously with them; having arisen, it can further induce subsequent moments to arise, and may thus be termed "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) and "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*).

Although various meditative absorptions are induced by preceding minds of the same category and do not arise simultaneously, once they have arisen, they cannot induce subsequent states; thus, while they may be termed "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*), they are not "equal and immediate conditions" (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Therefore, there is no fault in establishing this analysis even for the state of non-mindfulness (*acittaka*).
Those who maintain this view say:

"The mind that enters the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) ceases and enters the past; only then is it able to gradually grasp the second moment and subsequent moments of the attainment, as well as the mind of emergence."
That mind entering meditative absorption should not be considered past.

That which has not yet taken its fruit is designated by the term "drawing forth" (ākṣepa); the capacity to draw forth a fruit is the activity (kāritra) of the formations (saṃskāra), and it is based on this activity of the formations that the distinctions between the three time periods are established.
If there were functional activity that was not present, would this not undermine the very basis for the distinction between the worlds?
Some commentators explain:
"The past eye and so forth lack the distinct functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and cognizing with respect to objects such as visible forms; therefore, they are not present."
That explanation by the Śākyas is not correct; we should examine and resolve this together:
Do the functions of the eye and so forth consist in the capacity for seeing and other such operations upon an object, or do they consist in the capacity to project a result?

If they consist in the capacity for seeing and so forth upon an object, then when the eye and other faculties are currently non-existent—either because they have not yet arisen or because they have already ceased in the darkness—what distinguishes them from those of the future and the past, such that you do not designate them as such?

Although the eyes and other faculties lack the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, and tasting in the dark, they all currently possess the capacity to project results, which may be termed "activity"; because they possess such function, they are all designated as "present."
The remaining functions, such as grasping an object or yielding a fruit, are not "actions" (*kāritra*) but rather "capacities" (*śakti*).
Such capacities can exist throughout the three times; this will be further examined in the section analyzing the three times.

Furthermore, the various minds and mental factors of past lives cannot act as obstacles to their respective bases and so forth; therefore, they cannot function as this condition (*pratyaya*) to grasp a fruit.
