Moreover, there is another class who permits the later position [of the Sautrāntikas]: "Is it not the case that when the *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti* is in the state of being about to arise (*utpadyamāna*), it serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the *laukikāgradharma*?"

In truth, it should indeed be so; however, since it is stated here that the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) is established only when [the subsequent state] has already arisen, there is no fault.
Thus, both of these interpretations regarding the term "not yet arisen" are entirely consistent with my own doctrinal position.
The correct principles regarding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) have already been extensively analyzed in the Abhidharma and other treatises.
Nevertheless, that Venerable Elder (Sthavira) further states:
"The immediately preceding condition refers to a previously arisen phenomenon [which causes] a subsequent phenomenon to obtain its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) without interval."
As the Blessed One has said:
"With the mind and mental objects as conditions, mental consciousness arises.
That is to say, with the mind as the cause and mental objects as the condition, mental consciousness is produced.
However, it is illogical for two consciousnesses to arise simultaneously at one time, because [such a state] would not be clear.

When matter and mind arise in immediate succession, both are caused by preceding births to acquire their own substance; how, then, can it be said that matter and mind act as one another’s equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?

However, one should not admit that they function as mutual conditions; for since the continuities of matter and mind are distinct, how could they serve as one another’s equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?

Furthermore, when a single mental state gives rise to multiple material effects, and no two consciousnesses arise in immediate succession from those multiple materials, how could they be considered equal-and-immediate conditions in relation to one another?
Therefore, one should not establish the "equal and immediate condition" (samanantara-pratyaya).
While it may be called "equal and immediate" in the case of mind and its associates arising individually,
how can this name apply when material form and other phenomena arise simultaneously?
Therefore, those who claim that matter (rūpa) serves as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) have failed to reflect carefully and have spoken erroneously.

Furthermore, for those whose school adheres to the theory of the "latent element" (*anuvyañjana-dhātu*), the two conditions—the equal-and-immediate and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)—should be identical, because there is no difference in the essential nature of the basis upon which the latent element relies.
If a wholesome state of mind arises immediately after an unwholesome one, one must explain which is the cause and which is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
for there is no difference in their essential nature.
The same challenge applies to other cases as well.
Therefore, the Sthavira school merely applies a deceptive web of permanence to the sacred teachings to delude the foolish.
Having already explained the nature of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), one should now state what the nature of the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) is.

This means that the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) consists of all phenomena (*dharmas*). Apart from the objects of perception belonging to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), no other phenomenon can be found as a determinate reality.
That is to say, all phenomena are what the mind and mental factors grasp and rely upon when they arise; therefore, they are called "objects" (*ālambana*).
Because this very object of focus (*ālambana*) serves as the condition for the arising of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it is called the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

"All phenomena" (*sarva-dharma*) refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*): namely, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness, along with their associated mental factors; these take, respectively, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharma*) as their respective objects of focus.
The six sense faculties are objects of perception solely for the mental consciousness.
By what reasoning is this known?
A sutra states:
Because the mental consciousness arises from many factors,
and because the sense organs such as the eye are not subsumed within the objects of the five [sensory] consciousnesses; thus,
according to the tenets of the Dārṣṭāntikas, the principle must necessarily be so.

The method of contemplation according to one's inclination is likewise for the five consciousnesses: that which is the object-condition is not the objective sphere, and that which is the objective sphere is not the object-condition.
Why is this so? Because they claim that if form and the other [objects] can serve as conditions to produce eye-consciousness and the rest, then such forms must necessarily have arisen previously.
If at the time when form exists, eye-consciousness has not yet arisen, then since consciousness does not yet exist, what could possibly act as the condition?
At times, when visual consciousness arises, the form may no longer exist; if the form does not exist, what could serve as its objective support?
Visual consciousness should not take a non-existent object as its support, because it is taught that the five consciousnesses take only the present as their object.

According to that school’s tenet, because the present is not non-existent, the form that is the present object-of-perception (*ālambana*) cannot be the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), since it arises simultaneously with the present visual consciousness;
this same challenge applies up to the tactile consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*). Thus, the five consciousnesses would lack the status of having an object-condition.

Regarding their school’s position that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the present as its object, it should be subjected to the same analysis and refutation as the five [sensory] consciousnesses.

If it were to take the past, future, or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its objects, there would certainly be no sense in which they could function as objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*), because they maintain that past, future, and unconditioned phenomena are all non-existent.
It is not the case that a non-existent entity can be established as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), for that would entail the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Regarding this, the Sthavira further states:
"The mental consciousness that takes the past and so forth as its objects does not lack an object; yet it does not take only what exists as its object."
For what reason is this so?
Because the five bodies of consciousness are said to be able to experience the various objects previously apprehended by the mind, as they arise in immediate succession from them.

In this way, the mental consciousness takes the mind as its cause; its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is precisely the objects of the five consciousnesses, because this [mental consciousness] arises only when those [five consciousnesses] have preceded it, and because the presence or absence of this follows the presence or absence of those.
However, this mental consciousness does not take existence alone as its object, because at that time the object has already ceased and perished;
nor is it without an object, because the presence or absence of this consciousness follows the presence or absence of that [object].

Furthermore, when one recollects an object that has long since ceased, because a present consciousness arises with that past object as its condition, this recollecting consciousness falls within a single continuum, arising through a process of successive transmission.
Although there may be other conditions for the arising of a recollective consciousness (*anusmṛti-vijñāna*), it must take that prior object as its condition in order to arise.

Such statements are entirely devoid of real meaning; they are like the speech uttered in dreams by those who are mute, which only foolish friends might blindly trust and rely upon. What person of wisdom could possibly accept them?

Since it is not admitted by him that the objects of the five consciousnesses arise simultaneously with the group of the five consciousnesses, then even the five consciousnesses would only arise after their respective objects have already ceased; how much more so could the mental consciousness arising immediately after them perceive those objects?
Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises in the third moment.

If the mental consciousness produced immediately after the five [sensory] consciousnesses were able to perceive the objects of those past five consciousnesses, and if you further maintain that its object is not non-existent, then you are clearly admitting that the object of mental consciousness, although termed "already ceased," exists to some small degree.

If, however, you hold that it is entirely non-existent, then you are clearly stating that the arising mental consciousness has no object at all; yet you further say: "Nevertheless, this mental consciousness does not perceive only what exists, because at that time the object has already perished and ceased, and thus it is not the case that it has no object."

To claim that "this [mental consciousness] exists or does not exist depending on whether that [object] exists or does not exist" is merely empty talk; a person possessed of shame and remorse should not use such a pretext to conceal the fault that this consciousness lacks an objective referent.
Furthermore, for what reason is it said that this mental consciousness does not take only existence as its object?
At that time, its object has already perished.
How could one admit that a dharma which has already perished is both existent and non-existent?

If that were so, one would simply be following the path frequented by the proponents of the *Nyāyapraveśa*, for the *Nyāyapraveśa* contains many avenues of meaning, as its functions, capacities, and essential natures differ.

However, past phenomena do not exist as they do now in terms of their functional activity, nor are they entirely non-existent like a flower in the sky in terms of their essential nature. If this were not admitted, what would be the purpose of saying that this mental consciousness does not take only what exists as its object?
One should say that this consciousness definitely takes non-existence as its object, or alternatively, one should say that it definitely takes existence as its object.
Furthermore, for what reason is it said that it is not without an object, given that the presence or absence of this [consciousness] follows the presence or absence of that [object]?
If consciousness and its object were established only by following the presence of the object, then the past would necessarily possess substantial existence.

If, however, there is present consciousness even when the past object is absent, then one should not say that [consciousness] exists or does not exist in accordance with that [object], nor should one say that it lacks an objective referent (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, since there is no object, it is called "having an object" (*sālambana*) only because the objective field exists; yet, if the substance of the object is non-existent, how can there be an object of cognition?

Moreover, when one recollects an object that has long since ceased, how could a previously arisen consciousness that took that object as its condition serve as a condition for the arising of the present consciousness?

The preceding consciousness exists at one time while the present consciousness does not yet exist; the present consciousness exists at another time while the preceding consciousness has already ceased. How, then, can it be said that the present consciousness arises because the long-elapsed object serves as its condition?

Non-existence (*abhāva*) and mere absence (*asat*) cannot possess the sense of being a condition (*pratyaya*). Nor can they serve as conditions merely by virtue of belonging to a single continuum. Why, then, would a rabbit’s horn not arise later after having not arisen previously?
For it is admitted that non-existence and non-existent things can function as conditions.

If it were argued that there exists a "concordant realm" (*anugata-dhātu*) distinct from those [objects], this is logically untenable; for within the preceding object, the consciousness concordant with it has never previously arisen. How, then, can it be said that the consciousness perceiving that object arises now because the preceding [object] acted as its condition?
It cannot be said that the *anuvṛtti-dhātu* (the conforming element) and consciousness perceive objects simultaneously, lest there be two moments at one time.

Furthermore, each consciousness would have its own distinct object, because the essence of the *anuvṛtti-dhātu* is identical to the present consciousness, and consciousness does not invariably take as its object a realm that has already ceased.
If it is claimed that the essence of the *anugata-dhātu* (concomitant element) is not the present consciousness, then two consciousnesses would have to arise simultaneously within a single continuum.
Furthermore, one should not say that consciousness arises from the *anugata-dhātu*, because [the latter] did not exist previously.
How can it be said that a present recollective consciousness arises because of an object that has long since ceased and served as its condition?

The argument that it functions as a condition because the presence or absence of the present follows the presence or absence of the prior is also unreasonable, for the presence and absence of the preceding and succeeding moments do not follow one another in such a manner.
However, they further state:

"Because of the past, which serves as a successive cause, and because of the future, which serves as a successive effect, cognitions and so forth arise; therefore, it cannot be definitively stated whether the objects of cognition exist or do not exist."
How extraordinary! In the East, even such treatises as these, which exhaustively address eloquent discourse, are still preserved in writing.

If one maintains that causes and effects in the past and future arise through a continuous succession, without observing that present cognition and so forth are produced, and furthermore maintains that the past and future are categorically non-existent, then cognition and the like must necessarily take non-existence as their object.

If one maintains that past and future causes and effects arise in succession, and yet observes that present cognition and so forth are produced, then a single mind would necessarily possess two types of deliberation (*vitarka*), because there is a distinction between the non-existent and the existent aspects.
Furthermore, regarding the successive progression of cause and effect, what is the referent of that term?
Since there is no temporal extension beyond the present moment, how can one establish the designation "successive progression" for the past and future?

Since "non-existence" and "existence" cannot be designated as mutually transforming, what they have asserted—that the knowledge of the mutual transformation of past and future causes and effects arises, and so forth—is merely sufficient for their own treatise and is entirely devoid of meaning.
Thus, the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) has been explained.

The nature of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is precisely the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); because the meaning of the efficient cause is subtle and boundless, it encompasses all phenomena.

If this [cause] does not obstruct that [effect] and allows it to arise, it possesses the meaning of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Among the meanings of the three conditions, this category is most prevalent and its functions are truly manifold; therefore, it is called "dominant" (*adhipati*).
Since this supreme encompassment of the Dharma is universally pervasive, how could it be further categorized as "threefold"?
When we speak of this supremacy, the name "supreme" is not established in opposition to the three entities themselves. Why is this so?
It is established based on its functional utility regarding three meanings.

While the functional utilities of various conditions do not interpenetrate one another, their essential natures are mutually intermingled; for instance, the categories of the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are immeasurable and its operations are vast and manifold, whereas this is not the case for the other three. Therefore, it alone is designated by the term "sovereign condition."
Other masters say:
"This dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is called 'dominant' because its nature and categories are the most numerous.
[Objection: Are not all phenomena objects of cognition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); why then is this condition alone designated as "dominant"?
The argument that co-existent dharmas are not object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but are instead dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
and therefore the objection is invalid, is unreasonable. Why is this so?
The objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) is established because it is not indeterminate.

That is to say, if a given phenomenon serves as the objective support (*ālambana*) for another, it remains the essence of an objective support even when it is not being perceived, because its nature as an objective field is stable.
Since all phenomena are objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), this condition alone should not be designated as "predominant" (*adhipati*);
this is certainly logical. Why is that?
Because it is not like the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

That is to say, if a given phenomenon serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for another, there is never a time when it is not a dominant condition with respect to that other; rather, at the very moment of its arising, it universally functions as a dominant condition.
The objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), however, is not like this; co-existent phenomena do not serve as objective conditions.

Why is this so? While their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are equal when considered generally, they differ in degree when viewed specifically; therefore, this single condition alone is designated as the "predominant" (*adhipati*).

The meaning here is that it is only the predominant condition whose categories (*jāti*) are universally numerous. This is not based solely on its essential nature, for while all categories of objects (*ālambana*) are predominant conditions, not all categories of predominant conditions are objects.
"Category" refers to the specific functional capacity regarding the result.
Other masters say: it is called the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) because that which is produced is extensive.
This means that all phenomena, with the sole exception of their own self-nature, are universally capable of giving rise to all conditioned things.
For example, at the moment an eye-consciousness arises, with the exception of its own intrinsic nature, it takes all phenomena as its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The same applies to other births.

For instance, within the self-continuum of a single moment of present visual consciousness, past consciousnesses serve as its seeds and future consciousnesses do not act as obstacles; they cause the already-acquired visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) to serve as its support. All past and future visual consciousnesses do not obstruct it and thus act as causes, enabling it to arise; furthermore, dharmas within the continua of others also serve as causes for it.

This means that when one perceives another's body, one’s own visual consciousness arises; or, when one takes pleasure in another's form, one’s own visual faculty is produced. Because these serve as successive conditions for the arising of one’s own visual consciousness, other dharmas belonging to others also function as conditions; they possess a predominant influence (*adhipati-bala*) with respect to the arising of one’s own consciousness.

All other material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) serve as causes for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), namely by acting as its object (*ālambana*) and by providing benefit or harm to its basis (*āśraya*); through these successive factors, visual consciousness has already arisen.
Sound also serves as a cause, insofar as one hears it;
through the impairment or benefit of its basis, it causes the increase or decrease of the eye-faculty, thereby producing either clear or dim visual consciousness.
Odors, tastes, and tangibles also benefit or harm their respective bases—the ears, nose, tongue, and body—and through this indirect succession, they become causes for visual consciousness.

Within the dharma-element, all conditioned phenomena serve as auxiliary companions, supporting causes, or as that which draws [the mind], or as supports; thus, through such indirect succession, they are all causes of visual consciousness.

As for the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) also being a cause: this refers to how sentient beings, through faith in or reviling of *nirvāṇa*, initiate karma that can bring about desirable or undesirable fruits; by means of this process, visual consciousness subsequently arises.

All conditioned phenomena possess non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); because those [conditioned] dharmas do not arise, they successively act as causes and also give rise to visual consciousness.
Space accommodates conditioned phenomena such as form; it also successively acts as a cause and gives rise to visual consciousness.
Therefore, all phenomena serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the arising of visual consciousness;
the same should apply to other cases.
Consequently, each and every phenomenon, in relation to others, functions as this causal nature for all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*).
In this way, all wholesome and unwholesome states should serve as successive dominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*) for one another.
That is to say, with the wholesome as the cause, one is born into a royal family and so forth, experiencing the fruits of wealth and happiness.
Relying on this, one frequently indulges in negligence and commits various unwholesome deeds.
With unwholesomeness as the cause, one encounters much suffering and oppression;
conditioned by this, one gives rise to world-weariness and extensively plants many roots of goodness.

Furthermore, internal and external phenomena also serve as mutual conditions for one another; that is to say, crops and the like arise because of farmers, and sentient beings grow and flourish because of food and drink.

One should know that all such things—whether animate or inanimate, possessing sense faculties or lacking them, having consciousness or lacking it, and being appropriated or unappropriated—mutually function as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
According to what is appropriate, this may be established by analogy.
In this way, one destination serves as the condition for the five destinations, because each one arises first and gives rise to all others.
Alternatively, one may rely on a single destination to give rise to all causes, because through these, one will experience their results in the future.

Furthermore, fearing the miserable realms, one cultivates various wholesome karmas and is born among humans or devas; yet, amidst those human and deva states, one may indulge in desires and commit offenses, leading to rebirth in the various miserable realms.
Since such categories are infinite, that which is produced by the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is the most extensive.
Since the entities produced by such a nature are vast, one should understand that this dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) has been described only in brief.

However, when the Sūtras speak of the three dominant factors of the white dharmas of the world, they establish the name "dominant" because these serve as the causes observed for ceasing unwholesome conduct and practicing wholesome conduct.
This means that when an object is present before one and afflictions are about to arise, one contemplates either one of them accordingly, thereby ceasing evil and practicing good;

because one attains predominance (*adhipatya*) within this cessation and practice, the sutra speaks of only three types of predominance and no others, as there is no sense of predominance in anything else.
Although the meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) applies both proximately and distantly, it is explained here according to its primary sense, just as one establishes the name "mother.
As stated in the Noble Teachings, craving is called the mother because it is that which gives birth to and nurtures all sentient beings.

It is not that other afflictions lack the capacity for growth and development; rather, because craving is superior, more prevalent, and binds the mind, craving is said to be the mother and no other affliction.
Furthermore, it is said that two dharmas can protect the world; this does not mean that others, such as compassion, lack the capacity to protect.
There are such categories as these, immeasurable and boundless; yet, speaking in terms of what is predominant, this case should also be understood accordingly.
However, the Venerable Elder (Sthavira) says:
"This dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) refers only to the arising of mind and mental factors based upon the sense faculties."
This position may be tenable, but that doctrine is not established. Why is this?

As has been repeatedly argued above, they do not admit the existence of simultaneous causes; thus, their assertion of the principle of antecedent causes cannot be sustained. Therefore, what they have said is nothing but empty words.

Furthermore, it is said that these conditions are not fully complete; for instance, when visual consciousness arises, its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) does not arise solely by depending on the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), but also has the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as its cause for transformation and its cause for growth and nourishment.
This means that various foods, drinks, karma, and afflictions serve as the causes for attraction.
This clarifies the cause of clarity and obscuration, namely the increase or decrease of the eye.
The head, feet, and bodily parts serve as the cause of sustenance; mental attention, light, and space act as auxiliary conditions to induce its arising.
Such categories as these are not discussed by him; therefore, he fails to explain that the conditions for these [cognitions] are incomplete.
As for the remaining ear-consciousnesses and so forth, they possess immeasurable conditions according to their respective requirements, yet these are not mentioned by him.
Therefore, the definition of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) as stated by him captures only a partial aspect; its meaning is not comprehensive.

Furthermore, since his own school also maintains that many factors serve as indirect causes for the arising of consciousness and so forth, why does he speak of this condition as consisting solely of the eye and other [sense organs]?
He further states:

"If a phenomenon can either produce or nourish another, it may be called a cause; for the meaning of 'cause' cannot exist without mutual dependence. Therefore, not all phenomena are capable of acting as causes or sovereign conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), because they do not depend upon one another."
That statement is irrational, because the various causes upon which phenomena rely when arising have no fixed limits.

That is to say, it cannot be said that when this phenomenon arises, it relies on only a certain number of factors as its causes; rather, just as external and internal phenomena must rely on time, space, various conditions, and seeds.

Whether dharma and adharma are conjoined or separated, and with other factors such as arising, abiding, and destruction, as well as the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) acting as distinct causes, sprouts and the body are then able to grow.
Therefore, when all phenomena arise and grow, the various conditions upon which they depend are not limited in number.
Thus, it is well said that all phenomena can serve as both efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, because they do not understand the meaning of the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*), they are unable to accept it here.
A cause that is itself the agent is called the "efficient cause"; its meaning is not contradictory to the sense of being that which brings about production.
There are reasons why something may be called a cause, and there are also reasons why it may be called a non-cause.

It can be termed a "productive cause" (kāraṇa-hetu) because it performs the two functions of producing; it can be called a "cause" because it does not contradict [the result]; and it can be called a "non-cause" because it does not depend [upon the result].
Therefore, the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) can encompass two meanings.
Furthermore, there are two types of non-contradiction regarding it: namely, that which can obstruct the produced phenomenon and that which cannot obstruct it.
That which is incapable of obstructing is equivalent in meaning to that which is capable of obstructing yet does not obstruct;
thus, this too possesses a partial characteristic of a cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), though it is not conventionally designated as such because its characteristic is not clearly manifest or unique.

Excluding the five types of predominant causes, such as the co-existent cause and so forth, all other causal meanings—whether proximate or remote—are designated as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Alternatively, that which acts as the cause for something else is called the efficient cause.
This refers to the sense that this and that serve as causes for one another; since such causal significance can be found within all phenomena, all phenomena are capable of acting as causes.

The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) has already been extensively analyzed; now, in order to explain the gateway of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the meaning of this term shall be briefly discussed once more.
However, the Venerable Sthavira says:
"In order to refute those who claim that all phenomena in future lives are the cause and condition for a single phenomenon, the Sūtra states that there are definitively four conditions."
Those words merely reveal his own lack of discernment; how could they contradict the causes and conditions explained in the Abhidharma?
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 19; *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 20.
Composed by the Venerable Saṃghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
Chapter Twelve: Differentiation of Distinctions, Part Two of Twelve. What are the distinctions among such causes and conditions?
In terms of their substantial reality, there is no distinction whatsoever.
One should explain how the causes and conditions mutually subsume one another.

As I have already stated previously, the nature of the five causes constitutes the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), while the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is simply the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); why, then, do you harbor further doubts?
Since the remaining two conditions have not yet been determined as being subsumed under the category of causes, doubt may still arise regarding them here.

Some say: "The similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)—each in a limited portion—are called the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because they are both indistinguishable [from one another] at the stage of having already arisen."
There is no such principle, because the results are distinct.
Is it not the case that all causes possess a result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*)?
For if a dharma possesses the power to produce something or to acquire something, that thing is the result of human effort of that dharma.
This is not so, because both causes are characterized by the meaning of being "outflow fruits" (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Furthermore, the distinctions and similarities—such as those between the wholesome and unwholesome, the contaminated and uncontaminated, and the various realms and stages—are all the "fruits of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The results of the two causes are based solely on their similarity in kind; therefore, they are not without distinction from this [homogeneous] condition.

Is it not the case that the outflowing results (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the two causes also include differences? For example, the outflowing results of the same category produced by the two causes associated with the desire realm—which are abandoned through the vision of suffering—may be either wholesome or neutral; these [results of the homogeneous cause] are likewise defiled, and thus their types are identical.

Because there are differences in terms of being with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*), as well as in terms of realm (*dhātu*) and stage (*bhūmi*), the two causes [the co-existent cause and the associated cause] necessarily do not exist [between them]; therefore, they are not without distinction.

If that were so, then since already-arisen mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are subsumed under the two causes—the associated cause and the co-existent cause—they should all fail to be established as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This is because the characteristics of this [equal-and-immediate condition] and those of the efficient fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of the two causes are each distinct.
This arises immediately after that and co-arises with it, because their fruits differ.
Is it not the case that the two causes [the co-existent and the associated causes] also produce the immediate *puruṣakāra-phala*?

There is no such principle; for the power of the mind and mental factors to produce an immediate *puruṣakāra-phala* should be understood as being precisely the *samanantarapratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition), and not the function of the co-existent or associated causes. These two causes possess only the power to obtain a *puruṣakāra-phala* that is co-nascent.

One should understand that the sense in which the mind and mental factors can induce their co-arising *puruṣakāra-phala* (human effort result) is precisely what is termed the simultaneous (*sahabhū*) and associated (*samprayukta*) causes; and the sense in which they induce the immediately succeeding *puruṣakāra-phala* is the equivalent-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Just as the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and the simultaneously arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) are established as two distinct causes based on their different meanings despite having no difference in their actual production of results, so too, although their substance is intermingled, their meanings differ.
One should understand that the relationship between these two causes and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is likewise the same in substance, though distinct in meaning.
Therefore, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is not identical to the various causes.
Is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) then identical to a cause?
Regarding this, some have said:
This refers precisely to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because its essence is similar to its fruit.
Is it not the case that the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) has the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) as its fruit?
Regarding this, some say:
The result of this object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is exclusively the sovereign result (adhipati-phala).
Alternatively, since the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) also possesses the virile result (puruṣakāra-phala), there is no fault.
If that were so, the two causes—the co-existent (sahabhū-hetu) and the associated (samprayuktaka-hetu)—should, like the object-condition, be subsumed under the efficient cause.
However, it is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), but rather a successive dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*);
nor is it a virile fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*), because it arises from an object-condition. Therefore, there is no sense of similarity between the substance and its fruit.

Therefore, there is an explanation regarding the distinction between causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*): that which is non-pervasive is a cause, while that which is pervasive is a condition, based on the principle of inclusion and non-inclusion, as in the case of a finger and its joints.

Consequently, one does not perceive that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) possess the quality of being included within a cause; that these differ from a cause is a matter that requires no further argument.
Only for the first and last two conditions (*pratyaya*) should one distinguish them from the cause (*hetu*).

Since there is already this distinction, the other two conditions must also have distinctions because their status as conditions is equivalent; therefore, there is a general statement explaining the difference between conditions and causes: namely, that the cause is that which produces, while the condition is that which nurtures, just like the distinction between the mother who gives birth and the mother who raises.

Furthermore, it is only through the assistance provided by conditions that a cause can produce [an effect]; once produced, it continues in succession, being nurtured by the power of conditions. Therefore, some say:
"The cause is singular, while conditions are manifold, just as a seed differs from manure, soil, and so forth."
Furthermore, they are distinguished by being "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) versus "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*); the shared refers to conditions (*pratyaya*), such as the eye and visible forms.

Moreover, that which performs its own specific function is called a cause (*hetu*), while that which performs the function of another is called a condition; this is just like the difference between a seed, manure, soil, and so forth.
Furthermore, that which can induce [an effect] is called the cause (*hetu*), while that which can sustain it is called the condition (*pratyaya*), like a flower and its stalk.
Moreover, what is proximate is called the cause, while what is remote is called the condition, like a gem and the sun.

Furthermore, the cause is that which can produce, while the condition is that which can bring about completion; it is just as when fresh butter is extracted from curd, this is brought about by the power of the person using the churning apparatus, for the apparatus and other such factors cannot cause butter to emerge from water, because the causal factor for butter is lacking within the water.
There are many such distinctions among these categories; therefore, distinct names and concepts are established for causes and conditions because there are differences in their functional power.

Furthermore, they are called "causes" (*hetu*) in the sense that they truly exist, and they are called "conditions" (*pratyaya*) because they are able to assist in manifesting [the result], just as the phonemes (*akṣara*) and the bases (*dhātu*) have distinct functions regarding meaning.

However, when the sūtras state that right view arises from two causes and two conditions, they refer to the arising of untainted right view through sounds, vocal expressions, and mental attention—both proximate and remote—and it is with reference to this meaning that the two terms "cause" and "condition" are revealed.

Furthermore, when a sūtra states that there is a cause (*hetu*), a condition (*pratyaya*), and a sequential order (*anukrama*), it reveals the distinctions in meaning among simultaneous causes, immediate causes, and remote causes.

Moreover, when a sūtra states that "eye-consciousness arises with the eye as its cause and visible forms as its condition," the intent is to show that eye-consciousness arises in dependence upon both the non-common faculty (*asādhāraṇendriya*) and the common object (*sādhāraṇaviṣaya*).
Furthermore, when a sūtra states, "this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the sequence," the intention here is to reveal the agent, the instrument, and other auxiliary conditions.
Sūtras such as these should be interpreted according to their respective meanings.

Having already extensively analyzed the various conditions (*pratyaya*) in accordance with reason and scripture, it has been shown that these conditions function to manifest the arising and ceasing of phenomena. It should now be explained: which condition exerts its activity upon which phenomenon at which stage?
The verse says:
Two causes exert their activity upon that which is ceasing; three causes, upon that which is arising;
the remaining two conditions act in the opposite manner.
The treatise states:
It was previously explained that five causes constitute the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and two causes exercise their function at the moment of "actual extinction.
The phrase "at the moment of actual extinction" indicates that the phenomenon is currently undergoing extinction as it manifests; thus, it is called the moment of actual extinction.
The two causes—the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*)—exercise their functional efficacy at the moment when a dharma is ceasing and manifesting.

Regarding the exercise of this efficacy by these two causes at that stage: it means that if even one factor among the co-arising group is missing, all functional activities cease, and the dharma is unable to apprehend its object.
Regarding their status in the present, although these two causes both simultaneously take up and give forth their fruits, here we refer only to the functional capacity of giving forth the fruit.

As for the statement that "three causes [operate] during the stage of arising," this means that when a future dharma is in the stage of arising—so called because it is currently being produced and brought into manifestation—it is termed the "time of arising."
The three types—homogeneous, pervasive, and retributive—exert their functional efficacy at the stage when the dharma is about to arise.
Therefore, some say:

"Regarding the two fruits of outflow and retribution, they are drawn forth by the power of the cause. In the case of the homogeneous and pervasive [causes], it is possible for an outflow fruit to arise immediately; thus, one may say that the cause exerts its activity at the very moment the fruit is about to arise."

The cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) and its fruit are necessarily separated by a long interval of time; the cause has long since ceased when the fruit finally arises. How, then, could the activity (*kāritra*) exist at the time the fruit arises?

Activity cannot exist in the past; this statement regarding "activity" intends to signify "functional capacity" (*śakti*), as has already been examined in the section on the distinction between the two characteristics.
Although the cause has ceased after an immeasurable period of time, it possesses a functional capacity that brings about its own effect.

Because this capacity is unique, even though the causal operation is absent at the moment the effect arises, the designation "operation" is applied to the capacity itself with respect to its own effect.

The Elder said: "It is difficult to say within a single moment that 'this is the time of arising' or 'this is the time of ceasing. It is not that dharmas arise first and then cease because of causes; rather, they are like a snake held by a staff with a lasso and drawn out of its hole by pulling it by the neck, only then having its life cut off. Yet, while their substance is fundamentally non-existent, they exist by virtue of causes."
That statement is merely a frivolous jest; it cites what is not our own tenet because it is a vulgar expression.

The Abhidharmikas do not maintain that a phenomenon is first produced and later destroyed by causes, as in the analogy of a coiled snake. Rather, it is simply due to the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that phenomena are so. This was said to instruct students regarding the functions of grasping and giving, demonstrating that the cause possesses the capacity to produce the effect.
Therefore, what he says merely increases frivolous play.
Furthermore, regarding his statement:
"It is difficult to say within a single moment whether this is the time of arising or the time of ceasing."

He constantly seeks out coarse and shallow heterodox doctrines; since he has already passed his prime and dwells in the period of senility, how could he possibly fathom the words of the Omniscient One—which have been contemplated and discerned from youth—which express the ultimate truth and represent the pinnacle of the systems traversed by perfected sublime wisdom?
Although it arises as a single moment, there is a sequence of beginning and end: the present moment of its actual arising is called the "time of birth";
immediately after having arisen, when it is precisely on the verge of passing away, it is called the "time of cessation."
Why is this difficult to explain?
Even if it is difficult to explain, it is not impossible to explain, for it can be explained through diligent application of skillful means.
How could you, by falling into exhaustion and being unable to explain it yourselves, cause others to abandon it as well?
Unsurpassed enlightenment is likewise difficult to attain; yet, because it is difficult to attain, should one abandon the pursuit of it?
Therefore, one should not, on account of having fallen into the stage of training and failing to understand its characteristics, dismissively declare that it does not exist.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that "the essence is originally non-existent and exists by virtue of causes," why trouble yourself with such words that contradict your own tenets?
If it were originally non-existent, how could you speak of an "essence"?
Since you can speak of an "essence," how can you say it was originally non-existent?
According to the Abhidharma school, one should state this:
future dharmas both exist and do not exist; that is to say, their activity (*kāritra*) is absent, yet their substance (*svabhāva*) is inherently present.

Because their substance—which was originally non-existent—now comes into being through various antecedent causes (*pūrvotpanna-hetu*) and simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), they are designated as the "future."
According to the school that maintains the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvavāda*), since that which has not yet arisen does not exist, how can one speak of its "nature"?
If you claim it can be called a "nature" because it will necessarily exist immediately thereafter, this entails the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Since the present must necessarily be non-existent in the immediate [future], it should be said to lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);

if that were so, everything would be non-existent. Furthermore, if you claim that the future possesses intrinsic nature because it is "to be," then why do you not say that the present lacks intrinsic nature because it was previously non-existent?
One might as well claim that the past exists substantially because it once existed;
if so, the temporal periods would become confounded.
Therefore, that position cannot withstand critical investigation, whereas the system of the Abhidharma remains unshakable in its reasoning.
The functions of the two conditions—cause and object—have already been explained as operating at two distinct times; the functions of the other two conditions operate in a manner contrary to this.

The immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) exerts its function at the moment a dharma arises, because at the time that dharma arises, the preceding mind and mental factors have induced its emergence by making way for it.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it exerts its function at the stage when the perceiving mind ceases, because the mind and mental factors must be in the present moment to apprehend an object.

As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it remains unobstructed throughout both the arising and ceasing stages of a phenomenon; therefore, its function is entirely unimpeded in accordance with every stage where there is no obstruction.
Now it should be considered:

since the simultaneous cause (sahabhū-hetu), the associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu), and the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) all exercise their functions only after a phenomenon has already arisen, why is it necessary to establish these two causes and one condition?

If one maintains that a cause and condition must possess an actual activity (*kāritra*) in order to be established as having the nature of a cause and condition, then there would be no causes and conditions in the future.
However, this should not be raised as an objection against our tenet.
If that is so, how can it be said that there is activity?
If these two causes and one condition were absent, then the various phenomena being drawn forth during the state of "presently ceasing" would lack both activity and the capacity to apprehend objects.

If that which lacks functional activity were also called a condition, then the final moments of consciousness of Arhats and the like would also have to be established as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This objection is unreasonable, as it has already been refuted previously.

It is not necessary for an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) to be established solely by virtue of having an active function; what relevance, then, is there in using that as an analogy for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
That condition must consist of making way and drawing forth [the subsequent moment]; therefore, it can only be properly established in the present, and it certainly does not exist in the future.
Because it once possessed causal activity at the time of the present, it can be established as such even though it is past.

As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is not restricted to the present alone; rather, anything that possesses substantial existence (*dravya-sat*) can function as a condition. It does not necessarily depend on causal activity for its establishment; the designation "causal activity" applies only to those few instances where a thing functions as a condition in a limited way, and not to all cases.
How is it known that an object must possess substantial existence (*dravya*) in order to function as a condition?
For if the substance of the object of cognition (*ālambana*) were non-existent, no awareness (*buddhi*) would arise. Other masters say:

Establishing causes and establishing conditions also has a distinct meaning; it does not necessarily require the capacity to produce [an effect]. Although they lack the function of actual production, they nonetheless constitute causes, just as one perceives the fixed causality within one's own continuum; this principle applies to the continua of others as well.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Two causes and two conditions give rise to right view.
This case should be understood in the same way: both that which is capable of producing and that which is not yet producing constitute the nature of a cause.

The capacity of coexistent dharmas to combine and draw forth a single effect from a distinct collection is termed "activity" (*kāritra*). Since within such a combined collection, if even a single dharma is missing, the rest become useless, these coexistent dharmas act as causes for one another.

As it is with the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu), so it is with the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu): because they possess reciprocal power to apprehend an object, it is not the case that only that which produces can constitute the nature of a cause.
If this is so, for what reason was it previously stated that they are called "causes" because they are relied upon by the arising of phenomena?

This statement is made because there is no sense in which a phenomenon that cannot be separated from its cause could possess the property of arising; it does not mean that only those things capable of producing an effect are designated as causes.
Since this is the case for the definition of a cause, it should likewise apply to conditions (*pratyaya*); therefore, once a phenomenon has arisen, its activity is not non-existent.
Having explained the various conditions, one should now state which phenomena arise from how many conditions.
The verse says:
Mind and mental factors arise from four; The two meditative attainments arise from only three.
The others arise from two conditions, because they are not produced by a creator god (*īśvara*) nor sequentially, and so forth.
The treatise says:
Here, the word "by" (*yena*) serves to clarify the meaning of "because," meaning that mind and mental factors arise due to four conditions.
As for the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it has no function other than to give rise to the mind and its concomitants.

That is to say, the six groups of consciousness and their associated mental factors take the five objects, such as form, and all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as their objective conditions, as appropriate.

The mind and its concomitants possess five causal natures as their conditions: they arise by opening up space for and inducing their own preceding class; this is called the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of the mind and its concomitants.
As for this dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it consists of all phenomena, each excluding its own self-nature, according to what is appropriate.
Is it not the case that the functioning of a single condition and two causes does not exist at the very moment that phenomenon arises?
Since mental states and the like arise by way of the four conditions, how can the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) possess the nature of all five causes?

Although its function is only established at the stage when the dharma ceases, it is not without efficacy at the time the dharma arises; for if this [efficacy] were absent, that dharma would necessarily not arise, since mind and mental factors must rely upon an object-condition and depend upon two causes in order to arise.

If a phenomenon serves as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for another phenomenon, it cannot serve as its cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), because there is no interval [of time] between them, and because this is not stated in the treatise.
Furthermore, the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) arise by way of three conditions; excluding the object-condition, because they are not capable of cognizing an object.
These causal conditions consist of only two types of causes:
first, the coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), which refers to the various characteristics such as arising and so forth associated with the two meditative attainments;
second, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), which refers to the previously arisen wholesome dharmas of one's own stage.
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to the mind entering meditative absorption and its associated mental factors (*caitta*).
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) is also produced by three conditions? Since it is the immediately preceding condition for minds and mental factors, should it not also be described as the "immediately preceding mind"?
However, because it is not produced by the application of mind and so forth, it is omitted and not mentioned here.
Alternatively, this "non-perception" (asaṃjñika) is indicated merely by its name, as it is not established in opposition to the two meditative attainments (samāpatti).

For what reason are the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) considered "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) the mind, yet not designated as "immediately preceding conditions" (*samanantarapratyaya*) for it?

It is because they are produced by the power of the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Just as the arising of minds and mental factors is necessarily bound to the cessation of the preceding mind, these attainments cannot coexist with other minds like material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), nor can they appear in a confused or simultaneous manner like acquisitions (*prāpti*), etc., nor are they associated with other companions like the [characteristics of] birth (*jāti*), etc. Thus, although they are immediately preceding, they are not called "immediately preceding conditions."
However, because it is induced by the mental application of skillful means (*upāya-prayoga*), it may be described as "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) the mind;

yet, because it is diametrically opposed to and destructive of that which arises simultaneously with the mind (*cittasahaja*), it is not the "equal-and-immediate condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mind.

Furthermore, this would contradict the logical nature of the causal conditions; that is to say, a practitioner enters a mindless absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*) out of aversion toward the currently active mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). If that mindless absorption were itself to induce the mind and mental factors as its own causal condition, then the practitioner would have no reason to take pleasure in entering such an absorption.
It is not logical that one enters a mindless absorption by abandoning the currently active mind and mental factors, yet subsequently gives rise to those same mind and mental factors.
Furthermore, there is authoritative scripture (*āgama*) that proves a mindless absorption is induced by the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the mind and mental factors, as it is said:
"Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one realizes the cessation of perception and feeling with the body and dwells in its fulfillment."
Therefore, we know that these two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are produced by the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

This is because they are realized through the manifestation of specific mental states (*citta-viśeṣa*). There is no authoritative scripture (*āgama*) proving that a mindless attainment can serve as the condition to induce the mind and mental factors; thus, they are not the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the mind and its associates.

Regarding the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), why is the relationship of equal and immediate antecedence (*samanantara-pratyaya*) not established between a preceding moment and a subsequent one?
It is because all moments are induced by a preceding mind; they cannot themselves induce what follows, as has already been explained.
Furthermore, since the final moment of thought ought to be without a result, what fault is there in taking the emerging mind as its result?

Has it not already been stated that this is not a mind-moment that functions as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)? How, then, can it be said that the final moment of thought necessarily has an emerging mind as its result?

Furthermore, because the mind emerging from meditative absorption arises based on the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the preceding mind and so forth, it cannot be said to be the result projected by the final moment of that absorption.

Since the mind entering absorption and its counterparts are not immediately extinguished relative to the mind emerging from absorption, how can the emerging mind be said to be its "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
Because there is an interval within the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), "immediate" (*anantara*) and "equal-and-immediate" (*samanantara*) differ in their respective meanings.
The power of a preceding mind and its associates draws forth the arising of subsequent dharmas; thus, those subsequent dharmas are called the "equal-and-immediate [condition] of the preceding."
Because there is no interval between moments, the term "immediate" (*ānantarya*) is established.
Therefore, the two terms have distinct meanings, and thus this statement was made.
If a phenomenon serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for a mind, is that phenomenon also immediately preceded by a mind?
This should be analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

The first proposition refers to the emergence of mind and mental factors from the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), as well as the moments of the second and subsequent moments of those various attainments.

The second proposition refers to the initial moments of those various attainments, as well as the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing (*jāti-sthiti-anyathātva-vyaya*) of the mind and mental factors during states possessed of mind (*sacittaka*).
The third phrase refers to the initial moments of the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), as well as the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) during states with consciousness.

The fourth phrase refers to the subsequent moments of the various meditative attainments, as well as the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the mind and mental factors upon emerging from a state without consciousness (*acittaka-samāpatti*).

If a phenomenon serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the mind, does it also serve as the immediate condition for a mindless absorption? This should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

That is to say, the former third and fourth permutations become the present first and second permutations, while the former first and second permutations become the present third and fourth permutations.

Other non-associated formations and all material phenomena are produced by both the causal and dominant conditions; how, then, is it known that all worldly phenomena arise solely from the causes and conditions as described above, and not from a single cause such as Īśvara, the Self (ātman), or Pradhāna?

By virtue of their sequential occurrence: if all things in the world were produced by a single cause, such as Īśvara and so forth, then they would all arise simultaneously rather than arising sequentially, since the cause is ever-present. What phenomenon could act as an obstruction to prevent them from arising together?
We observe that all phenomena arise in succession; therefore, we know they are not produced by a single cause alone.

If one maintains that the world does not arise instantaneously because it follows the sequential distinctions of Maheśvara’s will, then one must admit that it is not produced by a single cause, since one also admits that will is the cause for the arising of phenomena.
The principle that this desire undergoes differentiation through arising and ceasing at different times is also untenable, because its cause remains without distinction.
It is not the case that a result can possess differentiation while its cause lacks it;
for a result becomes distinct only by depending upon a distinct cause.
Alternatively, one must admit that distinct desires arise simultaneously, because their causes do not differ in terms of temporal sequence.
If this were so, all phenomena should likewise arise simultaneously; who could act as an obstacle to prevent them from arising all at once?

If Īśvara desires that things arise in a sequence of prior and posterior distinctions by further depending on other causes, then those causal factors would themselves have to depend on further causes, and thus the series of dependent causes would be infinite.

Because [the cause] is infinite, the sense of being "without beginning" is established; this does not deviate from the correct principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) within the Buddhist tradition (*śāsana*), yet it is merely a different name for asserting that Īśvara is the cause.

Furthermore, because it serves no purpose, one should not falsely cling to the view that all worldly phenomena have Īśvara as their cause. It is of little use for Īśvara to exert great effort to produce worldly phenomena; therefore, one should not claim that Īśvara is the cause.
If it is for the sake of producing one's own joy, then one should simply produce that joy; what need is there to produce anything else?
If joy does not arise apart from other means, then that joy is produced by those other means, and in this regard, it would not be autonomous. Thus, its autonomy would not be genuine autonomy.
As it is with joy, so it should be with the others as well, for no distinct cause or condition can be found.
Alternatively, one convenience should arise from another convenience; what need is there to postulate that they originate from Īśvara?
If joy were to arise through other means apart from those [specific] means, it would likewise not be produced by those means.
Or, if one were to produce joy for oneself by inflicting suffering upon sentient beings with instruments of torment, alas, what is the use of serving such a cruel and malevolent Īśvara?

Furthermore, if one believes that the world arises solely from the single cause of Īśvara, one then negates the manifest results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*)—namely, the various effects of good and evil seen in the world.

If it is argued that Īśvara requires the assistance of other causes and conditions to activate his functional capacity before becoming a cause, this is merely a statement out of partiality for Īśvara; for apart from those other causes and conditions, no distinct function [belonging to Īśvara alone] is observed.

At that time, various causes and conditions such as earth and water possess manifest efficacy in the production of sprouts and the like, because the existence or non-existence of the sprouts follows them.
Since no function other than their efficacy is observed in the production of sprouts and the like, one should not conceive that the arising of worldly phenomena has Īśvara as their cause.
Since this is the case for *īśvara*, the same principle should be applied to the "nature of the self" (*ātmatva*) and other such factors;

this should be investigated accordingly. Therefore, it is established by reason that no phenomenon arises from a single cause alone, but rather originates from the various causes and conditions as previously described.

Since it has been stated that material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are produced by the two conditions of cause and predominance (*adhipati*), and that what is derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is collectively termed "matter," how do these derived elements relate to one another as mutual causes and conditions when compared across self and other?
The verse says:
The primary elements are the two causes of the primary elements; they are the five kinds of causes for the derived [elements].
The derived [elements] are the three kinds of causes for the derived; they are the single cause for the primary elements.
The treatise says:

Regarding the initial statement that "the great elements act as two causes for the great elements," this refers to the fact that these primary elements (*mahābhūta*), when viewed in relation to one another, function solely as simultaneous (*sahabhū*) and homogeneous (*sabhāga*) causes. This is because they are distinguished by their respective modes of arising—either simultaneously or prior—and because if even one is missing, the others do not arise.

Mutually regarding one another, they possess the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); although their natures and categories differ, they share a single function and are mutually conducive, thus possessing the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
That which is greater [in magnitude] acts as five causes with respect to that which is produced (*nirmita*).

What are these five? They are distinguished as arising (*jāti*), dependence (*niśraya*), establishment (*pratisthā*), support (*dhṛti*), and nourishment (*anugraha*). Although they arise simultaneously, [the primary elements] function in accordance [with the derived matter].
Just as a sprout gives rise to a shadow, or a lamp’s flame produces light, the primary elements possess the causal status of being the cause for that which is derived from them.

These five causes are merely distinctions of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because it is logically untenable for the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) to serve as the other five causes in relation to derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
To begin with, the primary elements are not simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) in relation to derived matter, because they do not share a single fruit (*eka-phala*).

Is it not the case that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their characteristics, such as arising, do not share the same derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) as their fruit, yet they are not non-reciprocal co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*)?
Although they do not share the same derived fruit, there is nevertheless another sense in which they share a single fruit.

The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived characteristics (*bhautika*) can never have a single effect; therefore, the logic applied to [the relationship between] the primary elements and the characteristics such as "arising" (*jāti*) is certainly not uniform.

Furthermore, although the primary elements and the characteristics such as arising do not share a single effect when viewed in relation to one another, they do function as mutual effects for one another, and thus they may constitute simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) do not possess such a relationship.

Is it not the case that while the mind and its secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are not mutual effects, the mind and those characteristics are simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*)? If so, why should the primary elements and their derived matter not be likewise, and why are they not considered causes?

This example is not equivalent: although the mind and its secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) do not stand in a mutual relationship of being causes and effects toward one another, those secondary characteristics do indeed possess the property of being mutually causes and effects among themselves, and they certainly have the sense of being mutual causes and effects with the mind.

Furthermore, because the mental concomitants (citta-anuvartin-lakṣaṇas) share the same fruit as the mind, the mind acts as their simultaneous cause (sahabhū-hetu); however, such is not the case between the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), and thus the primary elements are not the simultaneous cause of the derived matter.

Furthermore, derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) may be either wholesome or unwholesome, whereas the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are invariably comprised within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature; thus, they do not constitute a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) based on such characteristics.
If that were the case, the primary elements would have to be a co-existent cause in relation to indeterminate derived matter.
It is not so, because the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral derived [matter] belong to the same category.

It is illogical for matter of the same category to have, in some parts, the primary elements as its cause and, in other parts, not have the primary elements as its cause; this is just as it is impossible for dharmas of the same category to be, in some parts, associated with the mind and, in other parts, not associated with the mind. Such a principle does not exist.

Furthermore, you admit that the primary elements (mahābhūta) exist in the past, while the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) extends across the past, future, and present; however, there is no such principle for a co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu).
Moreover, because their respective attainments (prāpti) differ, this [co-existent] cause does not exist.

That is to say, there are cases where one possesses derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) but not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), or cases where one possesses the great elements that act as the producers (*janaka-bhūta*) but not the derived matter; since the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) does not possess such characteristics, the great elements and the derived matter are not co-existent causes.
They are not associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) because they are non-associated (*viprayukta*).
Nor are they universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) or retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*), because the great elements are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) by nature.
It is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) because it arises simultaneously.

Even if it were to arise later, it would not be a homogeneous cause because its nature is different; for although they share the same status as being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), their specific types (*jāti*) differ. If you argue that—just as mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, though distinct in type, serve as homogeneous causes for one another—the same should apply to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), this reasoning is also incorrect.
Although sensations (*vedanā*) and so forth differ from the mind (*citta*) in their specific categories, they share the same result; therefore, they can serve as causes.
By this, one should understand the principle of the conditions (*pratyaya*).
Furthermore, there is textual evidence in the *Mūla-śāstra* stating that, generally speaking, derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) lacks the five kinds of causes.
As it is said: "There are instances where a form-base (rūpāyatana) is neither caused by that which is indeterminate (avyākṛta) nor itself indeterminate; namely, wholesome form-bases.

If the primary elements (mahābhūtas), when considered in relation to derived matter (upādāyarūpa), were to function as any one of the five causes, then the meaning of this statement would not be established.
If that were so, it would contradict the sūtras and śāstras.
As a sūtra states: "The aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is designated based upon the four great elements (mahābhūta)."
This treatise also states:

"The primary elements (mahābhūta) and their derivatives (upādāyarūpa) are not mutually contradictory in terms of being causes through predominance and so forth, because this statement is made with reference to productive causes (janakahetu) and the like.
That the primary elements act as the productive cause for their derivatives is because the latter arise from the former, just as a mother gives birth to a child.
It is the "cause as support" because it follows along with that [result], just as a minister relies upon a king;
it is the "cause as establishment" because it is able to sustain it, just as the earth supports things.
It is the sustaining cause (*dhāraṇa-hetu*) because, through its power of support, it prevents [the continuum] from being interrupted, just as food sustains life.
It is the nourishing cause (*puṣṭi-hetu*) because it is able to cause growth, just as the roots of a tree are moistened and nourished by water.
In this way, it is shown that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as the causes for the arising, transformation, maintenance, and growth of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Alternatively, they are "generative causes" (*janakahetu*), because all derived matter arises from the primary elements; there is no arising of derived matter apart from the various primary elements.

Once derived matter has arisen, during the stage in which it continues as a homogeneous succession without interruption, fire acts as the supporting cause (*āśraya-hetu*), for it enables it to remain dry and prevents it from decaying;
water acts as the establishing cause (*pratisthā-hetu*), for it provides moisture and prevents it from dispersing.
Earth serves as the supporting cause (*dhṛti-hetu*), for it can sustain those derived elements so that they do not fall.
Wind serves as the nourishing cause (*puṣṭi-hetu*), for it can induce their development and cause them to increase.

Thus, although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) lack the five types of causes—such as the coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)—in relation to the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), they possess five distinct causes such as "arising" (*jāti*). Therefore, there is no contradiction with the sūtras or śāstras.
Regarding this, the Elder has falsely claimed:
"The five causes, such as arising and so forth, are not taught in the Noble Teaching (ārya-śāsana); it is said that such names have never appeared in the Noble Teaching.
We do not yet know by what standard he defines the "Noble Teaching" in his own school.
Is this a verse composed by Kumāraśramaṇa, or a section of a treatise created by Vaṃśīdhara?
Furthermore, such designations exist within the Buddhist teachings; as it is said in the Sūtras:
"Craving gives rise to the person; craving gives rise to the self-entity."
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"Abiding by the precepts and dwelling in the precepts; name-and-form depend on consciousness, and consciousness depends on name-and-form," as the verse says: "The poet relies on his text.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
The four nutriments are established to sustain and benefit sentient beings who seek birth and those already born.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"Water supports the earth and so forth."
Furthermore, a sutra states:

"Hearing the true Dharma enables one to fulfill appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*)," and so forth, at length; "By means of faith, you have abandoned the household life to enter the homeless state; nurtured by faith, you have overcome the power of sleep," and so forth, at length.
The "ancient element of accompaniment" (*pūrvānu-bandha-dhātu*) as you maintain it is nowhere mentioned in any of the holy scriptures.

Among all derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*), when they are considered in relation to one another, there are only three causes: namely, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
According to the categories of conditioned phenomena, there are three types of causes, though not all [phenomena] possess them all.
