As for the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), this refers to the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—which follow the mind, as well as the seven branches [of the path], which serve as mutual causes for one another.
As for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), all preceding [moments] of the same category [serve as causes] for subsequent ones of that same category.

As for the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it refers to unwholesome actions and wholesome impure (*sāsrava*) actions of body and speech, which are capable of producing retributive fruits such as the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).

Derived matter acts as only one cause for the primary elements—namely, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—because the two types of karma, bodily and vocal, are able to summon the fruit of the primary elements as their ripening.

Having already explained how all phenomena arise through such conditions, we shall now, in accordance with our school's tenets, provide a detailed analysis of the meaning of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Although it was previously stated in general that all minds and mental factors that have already arisen—excluding the very last one—serve as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it has not yet been definitively specified which mind is immediately followed by how many types of minds arising.
Furthermore, from how many minds does it arise, and by what mind is it produced?
This shall now be definitively explained.
Since there are many kinds of minds, how can one provide a definitive explanation based upon them?
Furthermore, to speak briefly, there are twelve types of mind.
What are these twelve?
The verse says:
In the desire realm there are four types of mind: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral;
in the form and formless realms, the unwholesome is excluded; and in the untainted realm, there are two types of mind.
The commentary says:
Furthermore, within the desire realm there are four types of mind: namely, wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral.
Within the form and formless realms, there are three types of mind each; that is, excluding the unwholesome, the rest are as described above.
Thus, these ten types are said to be with outflows (*sāsrava*).
As for the mind without outflows (*anāsrava*), there are only two kinds, namely, that of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and that of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
Together, they constitute twelve.
Regarding how these twelve minds arise from one another, the verse says:
In the desire realm, the wholesome mind gives rise to nine; it, in turn, arises from eight.
The defiled arises from ten and gives rise to four; the remaining [neutral] arises from five and gives rise to seven.
Wholesome form-born consciousnesses give rise to eleven; these, in turn, arise from nine.
Obscured [neutral] arises from eight; this, in turn, gives rise to six.
Unobscured [neutral] arises from three; this, in turn, is able to give rise to six.
The wholesome of the formless realm arises from nine; it, in turn, arises from six.
The obscured-unspecified arises from seven; the unobscured-unspecified is explained as in the case of the form realm.
The learner’s mind arises from four and produces five; the others arise from five and produce four.
The treatise says:

Nine minds arise immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm; namely, the four minds of its own realm, and two minds of the form realm—wholesome and defiled—which arise respectively at the time of entering meditative absorption and at the stage of rebirth.
What kind of wholesome mind arises?
And by which stage (*bhūmi*) is it subsumed?

At this initial stage, an acquired wholesome mind (*prāyogika-citta*) arises; however, since at a later time one has attained the state of being free from desire (*vairāgya-prāpti*), and because [the mind] abides in accordance with that [attainment], there is no possibility for that innate wholesome mind (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*) to arise. This is because, while born in this intermediate state, one cannot cause that [innate wholesome mind] to manifest.
Some say that mind belongs to the stage of the "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya);
others say it is also included within the first dhyāna;
and some say it is also present in the intermediate dhyāna.
The Venerable Ghosaka stated as follows:
"It even occurs in the second dhyāna, just as when one arises from a different stage during the practice of leaping meditative attainments (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*). Others have stated:
A non-equipoised mind lacks the power to draw forth a mind of a different stage; therefore, that [opposing] argument is certainly illogical.

Furthermore, regarding the single case of the formless realm (*ārūpya*), at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*), a defiled mind of that realm—along with the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—arises immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because they are concordant with its abiding state. Consequently, immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, there definitely does not arise an obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind bound by the fetters of the form or formless realms, for all such minds are tied to their own respective stages.
Furthermore, wholesome states of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) certainly do not arise [in this context], because they are distant from these four types of distance:

first, distance of the basis (*āśraya-viprakarṣa*); second, distance of the aspect (*ākāra-viprakarṣa*); third, distance of the object (*ālambana-viprakarṣa*); and fourth, distance of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-viprakarṣa*).
This [desire-realm wholesome mind] in turn arises immediately after eight [minds], namely: the four [minds] of its own realm;

two minds of the form realm at the time of emerging from meditative absorption—arising from that wholesome mind when one emerges from it, and arising from that defiled mind of the first dhyāna when one is disturbed by it, as the desire-realm wholesome mind arises from that defiled mind because one seeks the lower wholesome state to prevent retrogression;
and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), which occur at the time of emerging from contemplation.

The defiled [minds] refer to the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified; each of these two arises immediately after ten [minds], namely the four of its own realm and the six of the form and formless realms.
At the stage of rebirth-linking, all six minds of the higher realms can terminate at death and give rise to the two types of defiled [minds] in the desire realm.

Since there is never the arising of a defiled mind from an untainted (anāsrava) mind, these [defiled minds] do not arise from the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Immediately following this, four minds can arise: namely, the four minds of its own realm. There is no possibility for others to arise;
it is absolutely impossible for a defiled mind of a lower stage to be immediately followed by the arising of a mind of a higher stage or an uncontaminated (anāsrava) mind.

The remainder refers to the unobscured-neutral states bound to the desire realm; this mind arises immediately after five [types of minds], namely the four of its own realm and the wholesome mind of the form realm, because the transformative mind of the desire realm arises from those.
Immediately following this, seven types of mind can arise: namely, the four of its own realm, as well as two from the form realm—the wholesome and the defiled.
At the time of entering meditative absorption, the transformation-mind of the desire realm further gives rise to that wholesome [mind].

At the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*), the unobscured-unspecified mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the desire realm produces that defiled mind of the formless realm, as well as one [type] of the formless realm itself.
At the moment of rebirth-linking, this unobscured-unspecified mind is capable of producing those defiled states.
Having thus analyzed the four minds of the desire realm and their definite capacity to arise immediately after one another, [we now consider] the wholesome mind of the form realm.
Immediately following it, eleven minds can arise; that is, excluding the non-obscured neutral mind of the formless realm, because the mind born of maturation belongs to its own respective realm.
This same [state] arises immediately after nine [states]: namely, excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm, and excluding the unobscured-neutral mind of the formless realm.
The obscured-neutral mind arises immediately after eight states: excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm, as well as the learner’s and non-learner’s minds.
Immediately following this, it can produce six types of minds: namely, the three of its own realm, as well as the wholesome, unwholesome, and obscured-unspecified minds of the desire realm.
The non-obscured [neutral mind] arises immediately after three [minds], namely only those of its own realm; for there is no possibility of it arising from any other.
Immediately following this, six minds can arise: namely, the three of its own realm, the defiled minds of the desire and formless realms.
Thus has been explained the mutual generation of the three minds of the form realm.
The wholesome [mind] of the formless realm arises immediately after nine; that is, excluding the wholesome of the desire realm and the unobscured-neutral of the desire and form realms.
This same [wholesome mind] arises immediately after six: namely, the three of its own realm, as well as the wholesome of the form realm, along with the learner’s and the non-learner’s minds.

The obscured-unspecified mind can arise immediately after seven minds: namely, the three of its own realm, as well as the wholesome mind of the form realm and the defiled minds of the desire and form realms.

This very mind also arises immediately after seven minds, namely, excluding the defiled minds of the desire and form realms, as well as the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The unobscured-neutral mind is as explained regarding form: it arises immediately after three [minds], namely the three of its own realm; all others are irrational.
This very mind can immediately give rise to six minds: the three of its own realm, as well as the defiled minds of the desire and form realms.

Having already explained the mutual arising of the three minds in the formless realm, the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) arises immediately after four minds: namely, the mind of one in training itself and the wholesome minds of the three realms.
Immediately following this, it can give rise to five minds: namely, the aforementioned four minds and the single mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
It is not defiled by the three realms, because it is mutually incompatible with them;
nor is it non-obscured-neutral, because it is not dull.

The remainder—namely, the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)—arises from five immediate [causes]: namely, the wholesome states of the three realms, as well as both the learner (śaikṣa) and the one beyond training.
Immediately following this, four types of mind can arise: namely, the wholesome minds of the three realms and the one [mind] of the Aśaikṣa.
A Śaikṣa mind does not arise, because it is not its fruit.
Nor do defiled or neutral-unobscured minds arise, for the reasons previously stated.
Having explained how the twelve minds arise from one another,
how are these divided into twenty minds?
The verse says:

The twelve become twenty when the wholesome minds of the three realms are divided into those acquired through application and those acquired by birth; furthermore, the non-obscured-unspecified minds of the desire realm are divided into four:
those of maturation, deportment, craftsmanship, and supernormal powers.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), excluding the mind of craftsmanship, the remaining numbers are as previously stated.
The treatise says:

The wholesome minds of the three realms are each divided into two types, namely those acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and those acquired by birth (*upapattilābhika*), due to their distinction.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), non-obscured (*anivṛta*) minds are divided into four types:
first, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*); second, those of deportment (*airyāpathika*); third, those of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*); and fourth, those of supernormal fruition (*nairmāṇika*).

In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), non-obscured minds are divided into three types, excluding those of craftsmanship, because in the higher realms there is no performance of various crafts and activities; furthermore, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are no such activities as walking or moving about.
Because there is no *airyāpathika* (posture) and no *samādhi* that encompasses the factors [of the path], there is also no supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*).
Some say this is because the formless realm does not take form and so forth as its object.

Since that realm lacks the two types of neutral minds, such as those pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*), one must admit that the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the Sphere of Infinite Space possesses deportment and the other such states.

If it is argued that there is no fault because that [consciousness] is necessarily fixed and this [consciousness] cannot possibly exist, then the former is not a valid reason; for even if it takes form and so forth as its object, the opponent also admits that this [consciousness] cannot possibly exist.

Based on this principle, there are eight types in the desire realm, six in the form realm, and four in the formless realm; together with the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), they total twenty.

Regarding these twenty [minds] that arise mutually: first, it is said that from the eight types of minds in the desire realm, ten arise immediately after the wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala*). That is to say, seven from its own realm—excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*), because a pure meditative absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*) arises immediately after a mind of its own class—and one wholesome mind of application from the form realm, as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This [state] in turn arises immediately after eight states: namely, four from its own realm—two wholesome and two defiled—as well as two from the form realm—the preparatory and the obscured—and finally, the states of one in training (śaikṣa) and one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

The wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*) arises immediately after nine minds: namely, seven of its own realm—excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*)—as well as the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) minds of the form and formless realms.

This same mind, in turn, arises from eleven minds: namely, seven of its own realm—excluding the mind of supernormal fruition—as well as two of the form realm—the preparatory (*prayoga*) and the obscured—and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The two defiled minds arise immediately after seven minds; that is, the seven minds of their own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).

These, in turn, arise from fourteen minds: namely, the seven minds of their own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition; the four minds of the form realm, excluding the preparatory wholesome (*prayoga-kuśala*) and the mind of supernormal fruition; and the three minds of the formless realm, excluding the preparatory wholesome.

The vipāka, airyāpathika, and ānantarya minds each give rise to eight [minds] immediately following them: namely, the six minds of their own realm—excluding the *prayoga-kuśala* and *abhijñā-phala* minds—as well as the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the form and formless realms.
This [mind] in turn arises immediately after seven minds: namely, the seven of its own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).

The mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*) gives rise to six minds immediately after it: namely, the six of its own realm, excluding the mind of preparatory virtue (*prayoga-kuśala*) and the mind of supernormal fruition.
This [resultant mind] in turn arises immediately after seven [minds], excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).

Immediately after the mind of supernormal fruition, two minds arise: one from its own realm, namely the mind of supernormal fruition itself, and one from the form realm, namely the wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala*).
This [state] also arises immediately after two [minds], namely, the two minds previously mentioned that pertain to its own form realm.
Having explained how the minds of the desire realm arise from one another, we now explain the six types of minds in the form realm.

From the wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala*), twelve minds arise immediately: the six of its own realm; three from the desire realm—the minds of application, of birth-acquisition (*upapatti-lābhika*), and the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*); and one from the formless realm—the wholesome mind of application—along with the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Furthermore, this [mind] arises immediately after ten [minds]: namely, four from its own realm—excluding those born of deportment and those born of maturation; two from the desire realm—the preparatory and the supernormal-attainment minds; and two from the formless realm—the preparatory and the obscured-unwholesome minds; as well as the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Immediately following a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*), eight minds arise: namely, five from its own realm—excluding the fruition-of-superknowledge mind (*abhijñā-phala-citta*)—as well as two from the desire realm—the unwholesome and the obscured-unneutral—and one from the form realm, which is the obscured-unneutral.

This very neutral mind arises immediately after nine minds: namely, the five of its own realm—excluding the result-of-communication mind—and four from the desire realm, consisting of two wholesome and two defiled minds.

This same mind, in turn, arises from eleven minds: namely, the five of its own realm—excluding the result-of-communication mind—and three from the desire realm, which are the innate wholesome, the functional (airyāpathika), and the resultant (vipākaja) minds; as well as three from the formless realm, excluding the preparatory wholesome mind.

The resultant (*vipāka*) and the deportment (*airyāpathika*) minds immediately give rise to seven types of mind: namely, the four of their own realm—excluding the preparatory wholesome (*prayoga-kuśala*) and the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*)—as well as two from the desire realm—the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)—and one from the formless realm, which is the obscured-unneutral.
This [resultant mind] in turn arises immediately after five [minds], namely the five of its own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).
Immediately after the mind of supernormal fruition, two minds arise: namely, the two of its own realm, the preparatory (*prayoga*) and the supernormal fruition.
This [uninterrupted mind] also arises immediately after two [minds]: namely, the two minds of its own realm previously mentioned.

Having explained how the minds of the form realm arise from one another, we now explain the four types of minds in the formless realm. Among them, the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala*) gives rise to seven immediately after: namely, the four of its own realm, the one preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm, as well as the learner’s (*śaikṣa*) and non-learner’s (*aśaikṣa*) minds.

This, in turn, arises immediately after six types of minds: namely, three from its own realm—excluding only the maturation mind—one preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm, as well as the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Immediately after a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*), seven minds arise: namely, the four of its own realm, one obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind of the form realm, and two minds of the desire realm—the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified.
This, in turn, arises immediately after four [minds], namely the four of its own realm.

The obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) mind gives rise to eight immediately after it: the four of its own realm, two from the form realm—the preparatory and the obscured—and two from the desire realm—the unwholesome and the obscured.

This, in turn, arises immediately after ten [minds]: namely, the four of its own realm, the three of the form realm—consisting of those acquired at birth, the matured, and the deportment—and the three of the desire realm; these are named as explained for the form realm.

The mind born of maturation (vipākaja) immediately gives rise to six [minds]: namely, three of its own realm—excluding the preparatory wholesome—and one from the form realm, which is the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), as well as two from the desire realm, which are the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified.
This [uncontaminated mind] in turn arises immediately after four [minds], namely the four of its own realm.
Having explained how the formless minds produce one another, we now explain the two types of uncontaminated minds:

from the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*), six minds arise immediately, namely the applied wholesome minds (*prāyogika-kuśala*) of all three realms, the innate wholesome mind of the desire realm, and the minds of those in training and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This [unlearned mind] in turn arises immediately after four: namely, the three preparatory minds and the learned mind.
Immediately after the unlearned mind, five arise; that is, among the six previously mentioned as arising from the learned mind, one—the learned mind itself—is excluded.

This [wholesome state] in turn arises immediately after five [states]: namely, the three types of preparatory effort (*prayoga*), as well as the states of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Furthermore, for what reason can maturation (*vipāka*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and deportment (*airyāpathika*) arise immediately after preparatory effort, yet the wholesome state of preparatory effort cannot arise immediately after them?

Furthermore, because that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is induced by the power of prior karma, its force is weak; since it is not induced by the exertion of effort, it cannot induce a mind of applied effort (*prāyogika-kuśala*). Therefore, it cannot give rise to a mind of applied effort.
Since the emerging mind does not function through effort, there is no contradiction in its arising immediately after a mind of applied effort.

Because the power of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) and deportment (*airyāpathika*) is weak—since they delight in exerting effort to produce craftsmanship and deportment—they cannot induce an applied (*prāyogika*) wholesome mind;
however, since the emerging mind (*vyutthānacitta*) proceeds without such effort, there is no contradiction in its arising immediately after the applied [wholesome] state.

If that were so, a defiled mind should not be immediately followed by an applied wholesome state, because it is contrary to the wholesome due to its attachment to objects and because its power is weak.
This is not a grave fault, for one who is weary of the afflictions appearing repeatedly may reflect:
"By what means can this mass of what is meaningless be brought to rest and prevented from arising?"
He then knows it as it truly is: that an object which gives rise to faults can also produce merit.
When he perceives that an affliction is about to arise within him, he immediately becomes aware of it and promptly applies wholesome protection.

By the power of this vow, one is able to initiate application; because of the repeated cultivation of defilements since beginningless time, their force is not weak, and thus wholesome application arises immediately after defilement.
The innate modes of activity (*ākāra*) in the desire realm are clear and sharp, yet they are not produced by superior effort.

Because they are clear and sharp, it is possible for minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as preparatory minds of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), to arise immediately after them;
however, because they are not produced by superior effort, those [higher] minds cannot be induced from this [desire-realm state].

Because the innate wholesome minds of the form and formless realms are not sharp and clear, and because they are not induced by superior effort, they do not arise immediately after the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) belonging to other realms; nor can those [wholesome] minds induce them.
Furthermore, because the innate [attainment] of the desire realm is clear and sharp, it can arise immediately after the defilements of the form realm and is capable of acting as a protection.
Because the innate [attainment] of the form realm is not clear and sharp, it does not arise immediately after the defilements of the formless realm.

There are three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), namely: those characterized by specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and those characterized by resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
What is called mental attention to specific characteristics?

It refers to mental attention associated with such contemplations as observing that all forms have the characteristic of being subject to transformation and resistance, up to and including observing that consciousness has the characteristic of discernment.
What is called attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*)?
It refers to attention associated with the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).
What is called attention through resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanasikāra*)?

This refers to the mental attention associated with such contemplations as the meditation on impurity, the four immeasurables, the form-sphere liberations, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality.

These three types of mental attention manifest immediately following the noble path, and immediately following the noble path, one is likewise able to fully arouse these three types of mental attention.
If one speaks in this way, it accords with this statement:
"One cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by the contemplation of impurity.
Other masters say:

Only from the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) does the noble path (*āryamārga*) manifest immediately thereafter; it is only after the noble path that one is able to fully give rise to the three types of attention.
If this is so, why does the Sūtra state: "One cultivates the factors of enlightenment, such as mindfulness, conjoined with the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhābhāvanā*)"?

Once the mind has been subdued through the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one is then able to give rise to the attention directed toward general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-manasikāra*); immediately following this, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) manifests.
It is based on this successive sequence of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) that [the teaching] was spoken, and thus there is no fault.
Others further state:

Only from the attention to common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra) does the Noble Path manifest immediately thereafter; and immediately after the Noble Path, one can likewise only give rise to the attention to common characteristics.
This statement is erroneous.

Why is this so? Because one may enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the three stages such as the *anāgamya*, and immediately thereafter give rise to the mental attention to common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-manaskāra*) of the desire realm; for the mental attention to common characteristics of the desire realm is not extremely remote from that noble path.

If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, what kind of attention (*manasikāra*) arises immediately after the noble path?
It is not the attention to general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-manasikāra*) of the desire realm, because it is extremely remote.

Furthermore, because it cannot exist in that stage, for one who has already attained the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*)—which is distinct from the previously attained aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)—the aids to penetration of the noble ones cannot manifest again; this is because once the fruit has been attained, the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) cannot be generated anew.
He should now explain what kind of attention to common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra) arises immediately after this noble path and manifests before him.
Is it not the case that, being connected to the levels conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), he also cultivates that same type of attention to common characteristics?

Just as one contemplates that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and contemplates that all dharmas are selfless and that nirvana is tranquil, the Noble Path induces them to manifest without interval.

This defense is unreasonable; because [the mental application] is connected to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and cultivated through effort, it cannot be brought into manifestation after the fruit has been attained, as it belongs to that same category.
It is logically sound to maintain, as previously stated, that immediately following the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), any of the three types of mental application may manifest.
If one attains the fruit of arhatship by relying on the *anāgamya* concentration, the mind that emerges from contemplation belongs either to that same stage or to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If one attains the fruit of arhatship by relying on the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the mind that emerges from contemplation belongs either to that same stage or to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
If one attains the fruit of Arhatship based on another stage, the mind that subsequently emerges from meditative absorption belongs only to that [same] stage and not to any other.
Within the desire realm, there are three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*):
first, that produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*); second, that produced by reflection (*cintāmaya*); and third, that acquired through birth (*upapattilābhika*).
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) also possesses three types of attention (*manasikāra*):
first, that produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*); second, that produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*); and third, that acquired through birth (*upapattilabdha*).
It lacks that produced by reflection (*cintāmaya*), because when one directs the mind toward reflection, one immediately enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
In the formless realm, there are only two types of attention (*manasikāra*):
first, that produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), and second, that acquired through birth (*upapatti-labdha*).

Immediately after the attention consisting of hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*) in the desire realm, the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*) manifests; immediately after the Noble Path, all three types of attention manifest together. This is because the arising of any Noble Path is necessarily connected to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).

The noble path does not manifest immediately after a naturally acquired wholesome mental attention (*manasikāra*), nor does it manifest immediately after a mental attention consisting of hearing or cultivation belonging to the form realm; likewise, immediately after the noble path, only those two types of mental attention arise.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), only the attention of cultivation (*bhāvanā-manasikāra*) arises immediately before the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) manifests, and immediately after the Noble Path, only the attention of cultivation arises;

it does not give rise to the attention of birth (*upapatti*) or acquisition (*pratilambha*). If one is born in the second dhyāna or above and gives rise to the three bodies of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) of the first dhyāna, then for those who have not yet abandoned the defilements (*kleśa*) of their own level, two types of consciousness manifest immediately after the wholesome, afflicted, or neutral attention of their own level; and immediately after these three types of consciousness, the three kinds of attention belonging to their own level arise again.

For those who have already become detached from the defilements of their own level, with the exception of the attention associated with detachment, only wholesome or neutral attentions arise immediately prior to the manifestation of the three consciousnesses; and immediately following the three consciousnesses, only these two types of attention likewise arise.
Regarding the twelve minds previously mentioned, when which mind manifests, how many minds can be obtained?
The verse says:
Within the defiled minds of the three realms, Six, six, and two kinds are obtained.
The wholesome [minds] of the form realm consist of three types of training; the four [types of training] are [attained] in the remaining [realms]. All others are obtained by themselves.
The Commentary says:
At the stage when defiled minds of the desire or form realms are manifesting, six minds are each obtained within the twelve minds.
In the state where an undefiled mind of the formless realm is currently manifest, one obtains only two minds from among the twelve.
Is this for a single moment?
One should say that it is not so.

Furthermore, when an afflicted mind of the desire realm arises—whether through falling back from a realm, reconnecting with the roots of virtue, or regressing from superior qualities—one obtains a total of six minds according to the possible number within these three stages.

When falling back from a realm, with the exception of one's own unobscured-neutral mind, one definitely acquires the three types of minds—wholesome and so forth—of that same realm. Furthermore, it is possible for a defiled mind of the form realm to continue the wholesome roots; in this state of restoring the wholesome roots, one acquires a wholesome mind of its own realm, because the wholesome roots are restored within a state of doubt.
When one falls from a state of superior virtue (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*), it is possible for any defiled mind of the three realms or any mind of a learner (*śaikṣa*) to arise.

If a defiled mind of the form realm arises—whether through falling back to a lower realm or through falling from a state of superior virtue—it is likewise possible for six minds to be obtained, according to the circumstances.
When falling back from a realm, one acquires three types of one's own [realm], as well as the non-obscured-neutral mind of the desire realm—namely, the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-citta*).
When falling away from a state of superior qualities, both the two defiled minds of the form and formless realms and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa-citta*) may all be acquired.
When a defiled mind of the formless realm arises, one simultaneously acquires two minds: namely, the mind of training (*śaikṣa*) and one's own defiled mind.

In this context, there is only the state of falling away from superior qualities and the state where a wholesome mind of the form realm is currently manifest; within these, one can acquire three minds: namely, one's own wholesome mind, as well as the non-obscured-neutral minds of the desire and form realms, due to the process of spiritual advancement.
Some say that when the fundamental dhyānas arise, three types of mind are acquired simultaneously, as previously stated.
While this general principle of acquisition is not without merit, at that specific time only the latter two are acquired, because the former type has already been obtained previously.
If it were not so, then the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) would also be obtainable in this state, and one should say that four [minds] are obtained.

When a mind of one in training is actually present, among the twelve minds, four are obtainable: namely, the mind of one in training, the non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the desire and form realms, and the wholesome (*kuśala*) mind of the formless realm.
If one first realizes and enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), at that time the mind of training (*śaikṣa-citta*) is said to be "attained.

If, by means of the noble path (*āryamārga*), one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), then at the moment the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises, one attains the non-obscured, neutral states (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) of the desire and form realms.
If one abandons the defilements of the form realm by means of the noble path, one attains the wholesome states of the formless realm.

Here, the term "abandonment" does not refer to ultimate abandonment, because the wholesome mind of the formless realm can already be attained even while the defilements of the form realm have not yet been entirely abandoned.
Some say that when one is completely detached from the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one attains the wholesome states of the fundamental stage of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

If that were so, one should also say that one attains the mind of training (*śaikṣacitta*); for at the time of becoming free from the defilements of desire, one also attains the wholesome states of the form realm. Thus, it would follow that one should say the mind of training attains five [types of minds].
"Others" refers to those minds other than the defiled ones and so forth previously mentioned;

that is, the three types of non-obscured-neutral minds of the three realms, as well as the wholesome minds of the desire and formless realms and the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). It should be understood that regarding these minds, one does not speak of attaining a specific variety of mind while they are currently manifest; rather, when these minds are currently manifest, they are to be attained only by themselves.

In the state where an unobscured-neutral mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is manifest, nothing at all can be acquired, because it has already been acquired previously; therefore, one should not say that "all [minds] are acquired by themselves.
Would it not be the case that when a mind of an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*) arises, four minds may also be acquired—namely, the wholesome minds of the three realms?

Since one cultivates [the path] in the future at the moment of the initial *kṣayajñāna*, it is not the case that what was previously obtained is being cultivated in the future; how then can it be said that this is "only self-obtained"?
Furthermore, when a wholesome mind of the formless realm (*ārūpya*) is currently manifesting, one also obtains the mind of a learner (*śaikṣacitta*); how could it then be "only self-obtained"?
What is now called "attainment" (prāpti) is not something previously established, as stated in the subsequent verse; therefore, this objection does not apply.

If it were otherwise, then for the wholesome acquisition of form (*rūpa-dharma*) there would be three [types of] attainment, and for the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa-citta*) there would be four, and one likewise could not say that other [attainments] are possible; thus, this point should be reflected upon.
Others say only that there are eleven types of mind, because the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are alike in being untainted (*anāsrava*).
Based on this meaning, the verse states in summary:
The wise say that when defiled dharmas arise, nine [types of acquisition] are obtained;
in a wholesome mind, six are obtained; in the indeterminate, only the indeterminate.

Regarding the defiled mind of the desire realm, at the stage of falling back from a higher realm, with the exception of its own unobscured-indeterminate [acquisition], it obtains the three types belonging to its own realm.

Regarding the defiled mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), at the stage of returning from a realm-reversal, one acquires its own wholesome and defiled minds, as well as the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and defiled minds of the desire and form realms.
Upon falling away from the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one acquires the defiled minds of its own realm as well as the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*).

This discussion regarding the number of minds acquired is based on the *dhātu* (realms), not on the *bhūmi* (stages); therefore, nine minds are acquired, as it is impossible for a wholesome mind of the formless realm (*ārūpya*) to be acquired [in this context].

Other masters state that ten minds are acquired, because when one falls from a higher stage and is reborn into a lower stage within the formless realm, a defiled mind arises at that moment and acquires its own wholesome mind.
Although it is said that one "attains" the mind, this is established in reference to the *dhātu* (realms).
For instance, one might also say that one attains the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind; why then is it not said that one attains the wholesome mind of a stage (*bhūmi*)?

When it is stated that among the wholesome minds one attains six types of mind, this refers to the time when one reconnects the roots of goodness through right view, and the time when one attains the wholesome [mind] of the desire realm while becoming free from the defilements of desire. It should be understood that at these moments, one simultaneously attains the non-obscured [neutral] minds of both the desire and form realms.
When first entering meditative absorption, one accordingly acquires the wholesome states of the form and formless realms.
When first entering the stage of separation from birth and realizing arhatship, one acquires the states of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
If that is so, why is it said that one attains six minds?

As the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) objects, one should say seven are attained; however, because the paths of training (śaikṣa) and no-more-training (aśaikṣa) are both untainted (anāsrava), they are collectively referred to as a single mind, and thus there is no error in saying six.
Other masters explain:

at the moment of attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one simultaneously attains six types of mind—namely, the wholesome minds of the three realms, the unobscured-neutral minds of the desire and form realms, and the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind.
Although it is possible to attain these six even across different times, this [text] speaks of this specific moment because it refers to their simultaneous attainment.
This general statement involves no contradiction, yet it is not the intended meaning of the present verse.
To encompass the preceding points, another verse is spoken:
"By means of rebirth, entering meditative absorption, as well as at the times of detachment from defilement and falling away,"
The mind attained upon returning to the state of wholesome roots is not something previously established.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 20. *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 21.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Three: Investigation of Dependent Origination (Pratyaya-vibhāga). Part One of Three. Having already established the acquisition of mind and so forth based on the three realms, one should now investigate what these three realms are.
How many distinct locations are there within each of these?
The verse says:
Hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, Humans, and the six classes of desire-realm devas.
The Desire Realm is said to have twenty locations, distinguished by the differences among the hells and continents.
Above this, seventeen places constitute the Form Realm;
therein, each of the first three dhyānas has three levels, while the fourth dhyāna has eight.
In the formless realm there are no locations; it is by way of birth that there are four types [of beings].
Relying upon the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), they cause the mind and its concomitants to continue in succession.
The treatise says:

The four lower destinies beginning with the hells in their entirety, a portion of the heavens, along with their retinues, intermediate states, and the receptacle world, are collectively termed the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As for the "portion of the heavens," this refers to the six heavens of the desire realm:
first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*); [and so forth].
2. The Heaven of the Thirty-three; 3. The Yāma Heaven; 4. the Tuṣita Heaven;
Fifth, the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations;
sixth, the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations.

Thus, including the hells and so forth within the realm of desire, along with the physical world (bhājana-loka), there are ten locations in total; when subdivided by the differences between the hells and the continents, they become twenty.
The eight great hells are distinguished as follows:

first, the Reviving Hell; second, the Black Rope Hell; third, the Crushing Hell; fourth, the Howling Hell; fifth, the Great Howling Hell; sixth, the Heating Hell; seventh, the Great Heating Hell; and eighth, the Uninterrupted Hell.
Regarding the distinction of the continents, it refers to the four great continents:
first, Jambudvīpa; second, Pūrvavideha; third, Aparagoyānī; and fourth, Uttarakuru.
Thus, these twelve, together with the six heavens of the desire realm, the animals, and the hungry ghosts, constitute twenty abodes.

Whether it be the realm of sentient beings, from the Heaven of Sovereign Power (*Īśvara*) down to the Avīci Hell, or the physical world, extending even to the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), all are subsumed within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Having already explained the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) along with its various locations, above this Desire Realm there are seventeen locations.

Specifically, each of the three dhyānas has three locations, while the fourth dhyāna alone has eight; the receptacle world (bhājana-loka) and the sentient beings therein are collectively termed the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
The first dhyāna stage consists of three [levels]: first, the Brahmakāyika Heaven; second, the Brahmapurohita Heaven;
and third, the Mahābrahmā Heaven. The second dhyāna stage consists of three [levels]: first, the Parīttābha Heaven; second, the Apramāṇābha Heaven; and third, the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
The third dhyāna stage consists of three levels: first, the Heaven of Limited Purity; second, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity; and third, the Heaven of Universal Purity.
The fourth dhyāna stage consists of eight levels: the Heaven Without Clouds, the Heaven of Merit-Born, and the Heaven of Vast Results, together with the five Pure Abodes, which constitute the eight.

The five Pure Abodes are: first, the Heaven of No Affliction; second, the Heaven of No Heat; third, the Heaven of Good Manifestation; fourth, the Heaven of Good Vision; and fifth, the Heaven of Ultimate Purity of Form.
Because it is produced from extensive virtue, it is called "Brahmā"; because this Brahmā is great, he is called "Mahābrahmā.

He is called "Great" because he has attained the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), because he was the first to be born, because he is the last to pass away, and because his majesty and other qualities are preeminent.
They are called the Brahma-pāriṣadyas (Retinue of Brahmā) because they are all those who are transformed by and subject to the governance of Mahābrahmā.
They are called the Brahma-purohitas (Ministers of Brahmā) because they stand in formation before Mahābrahmā to serve as his attendants.
They are called the Parīttābhās (Limited Light) because their intrinsic radiance is the least among the deities of that level.
Because its radiance is increasingly superior and its measure difficult to fathom, it is called Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābha*).
Because pure light universally illuminates its own level, it is called Utmost Pure Light (*Ābhāsvara*).
The experience of pleasure on the mental level is termed "pure"; since this purity is the most inferior within its own level, it is called Limited Purity (*Parīttaśubha*).
Because this purity increases to such an extent that its measure is difficult to fathom, it is called "Immeasurable Purity" (Apramāṇa-śubha).
Because this purity is all-pervasive, it is called "Universal Purity" (Śubha-kṛtsna); this intends to show that no other pleasure can surpass it.
Below this, the grounds where the gods dwell are like clouds closely joined together; therefore, they are called "Clouds" (Abhra).
Above these gods, there are no further grounds of cloud; as they reside at the head of the Cloudless realm, they are called "Cloudless" (Anabhraka).
Furthermore, because there are other places where ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may be reborn that possess superior merit, it is called "Merit-Born" (*Puṇyaprasava*).
As for its location, among the fruits of ordinary beings, this is the most excellent; therefore, it is named "Vast Fruit" (*Bṛhatphala*).
The noble ones who have abandoned desire wash away the stains of affliction with the water of the Noble Path; therefore, they are called "Pure" (*śuddha*).
Because these pure beings dwell therein, it is called the "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Alternatively, because they abide here until the very limit of saṃsāra—like having fully repaid one's debts—they are called "Pure"; and because it is the dwelling place of those who are pure, it is called the "Pure Abodes."
Alternatively, because there are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) mixed among these gods, and they are inhabited solely by noble ones (*ārya*), they are called the "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*).

"Proliferation" (*apraśānta*) refers to either confusion or vastness; because this [level] is the first among those free from confusion and is the lowest among the vast heavens, it is called "Non-proliferation" (*Avṛha*).
It is called "Without Seeking" because one does not seek entry into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Because one has already well subdued and eliminated the superior and middling obstacles to the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, and because one's mental disposition is pliant and free from all feverish afflictions, it is called "Without Heat."
Alternatively, "heat" (*uṣmagata*) refers to the afflictions that arise below; because one has now distanced oneself from these for the first time, it is called "Heatless" (*an-uṣmagata*).
Or again, "heat" signifies intense intensity; since one has not yet realized the superior cultivation of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and its fruit, it is therefore called "Heatless."

Having already attained the superior grade of the meditative absorption of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*), its resultant virtues are easily manifested; therefore, it is called "Good Vision" (*sudṛśa*).

Since the remaining grades of the obstacles to concentration have been thinned to an extreme degree through this mixed cultivation, one's vision is exceptionally clear and lucid; therefore, it is called "Good Vision."
There is no further place within the realm of form that can surpass this; thus it is called the Ultimate of Form and Name (*rūpa-nāma-akaniṣṭha*).
Alternatively, because this has reached the final limit of the body which is the basis for all suffering, it is called the Ultimate of Form and Name.
Some say that "form" refers to accumulated form; reaching its ultimate limit is called the "culmination of form.
These seventeen locations, comprising the receptacle world and all sentient beings, are collectively termed the "Form Realm" (*rūpadhātu*).

There are others who provide a different enumeration of seventeen bases (*sthāna*), establishing two bases collectively within the first dhyāna and separately mentioning the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñin*) in the fourth dhyāna.

That teacher should have stated that there are eighteen bases, because when compared with the Brahmakāyika devas, the Great Brahmā differs in terms of lifespan, physical size, lack of vitarka, and the nature of his experience.

Is it not the case that one does not aspire to the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva), because there are distinctions such as those among ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) and others? If so, should one not also say that there are eighteen places (sthāna)?
This objection is irrational, because those born in the Heaven of No-Thought are bound by the karmic fruits of the Heaven of Vast Results (bṛhatphala).
If that were so, the birth-body received by Mahābrahmā would also be the fruit of karma bound to the Brahmakāyika heaven, and thus it should not be mentioned as a separate celestial realm.

It is simply that superior-grade karma bound to the Brahmakāyika heaven brings about the fruit of Mahābrahmā; because this karma differs slightly from that [of the Brahmakāyikas], the lifespan and other attributes it brings about also differ slightly.

If the lifespan of Mahābrahmā were combined with that of the Brahmakāyika devas into a single unit despite their differences, then although the lifespans of the Parīttābha devas and others differ, they too would have to be combined into a single unit, which would lead to a great logical fallacy.
This example is not applicable, because Mahābrahmā is a single individual.
The designation of a celestial realm (*devasthāna*) must be established based on a commonality (*sabhāgatā*); a single Brahmā King cannot be called a "commonality.

Although his lifespan and other attributes differ from others, he does not constitute a "commonality" by virtue of being a single body; therefore, he is established as one celestial realm together with the Brahmapurohitas. Although their heights differ, they do not occupy distinct levels. This is contrary to the case of the Parīttābhas and other heavens, and thus they should not be cited as an analogy for this instance.
The Elder [Vasumitra] posits eighteen heavens within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), and thus makes this statement:
"The cultivation of each dhyāna consists of three grades—namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
According to these three grades of causes, one is born in three corresponding celestial abodes."

The Great Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna has a homogeneous nature (*sabhāgatā*) when compared with his own class, yet there is a distinction between him and those in the Brahma-purohita realm regarding their degree of excellence.
This is like the case of a village and a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*); although they are situated in close proximity, their locations are distinct.

It is argued that the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) constitute a fourth station within the fourth dhyāna because they differ from the Bṛhatphala gods; thus, there would be eighteen stations.

This is also incorrect, for then the first dhyāna stage would likewise have four stations, and the non-percipient beings would have to be established separately rather than being included within the Bṛhatphala realm.

If it is claimed that there are three distinct locations for each of the meditative stages (dhyāna-bhūmi) corresponding to the cultivation of the three grades [of concentration], then because the lifespan and other qualities of Mahābrahmā are superior, he must be distinguished from the first dhyāna by being produced by the karma of a superior intermediate concentration, rather than by the distinct causes of superior, middling, and inferior grades. Therefore, Mahābrahmā should be a fourth location, distinct from the three [levels] of the first dhyāna, as it is summoned by a separate karma.

Alternatively, Mahābrahmā would have no distinct cause [for his existence], because the lifespan and physical dimensions of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) are equal to and indistinguishable from those of the Bṛhatphala gods; thus, there would be no differentiating cause, and their location would not be the fourth dhyāna.
Therefore, the establishment of eighteen [levels] is logically untenable.
Furthermore, if it were necessarily so, the lifespan and body size at the Akaniṣṭha heaven would have to be thirty, twenty, or sixty-four [yojanas];

yet neither is permitted. Thus, one cannot establish distinct locations based on the differences between the three grades of meditative concentration (dhyāna) practiced; for although there are four causes, only three locations are established, and although there are three causes, four locations are established.

Furthermore, if there were three levels within the First Dhyāna, then the Great Brahmā King, when compared to the Brahma-purohita level, would have to be separated from it by a height and breadth as great as those between the upper and lower heavens; likewise, his lifespan and physical stature would have to be doubled accordingly. In that case, the entire system of established cosmology would be untenable.
However, the lifespan of the Brahmakāyika devas is half a kalpa, and their body size is also half a yojana; up to the Mahābrahmā heaven, the measurements are all halved.

If the station of Mahābrahmā were established as the third level, their lifespan and body size should increase to two [yojanas and kalpas]; consequently, all subsequent levels would likewise have to double, which renders all such establishments untenable.
Therefore, the great masters of Kaśmīra all maintain that the abode of Mahābrahmā is itself the Brahmakāyika level; for this reason, there are only sixteen levels in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).

What has been stated here is in perfect accord with the sūtras, for among the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), only the extremes are mentioned, as in the cases of the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens.
If it were otherwise, the sūtra would have spoken of them as being like the Mahābrahmā realm, rather than the Brahmakāyika heaven.
The lifespan and other factors of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) are no different from those of the Bṛhatphala heaven; how then can they be established as distinct?
He further explains:
it is not that there is no establishment of distinctions regarding lifespan and so forth in the first dhyāna, for in those three heavens, the lifespan increases by half [a kalpa] respectively.
If that were so, Mahābrahmā would also have to increase twofold, and thus the establishment of the higher heavens would all be destroyed.
There is no such fault, for it is accepted that even the Parīttābha gods increase by half in comparison to Mahābrahmā.
This is merely a false attachment, for it has not been established that there is a separate location for the gods of the Form Realm (rūpadeva) where [the lifespan] increases by half.
Furthermore, it violates correct reasoning. Why is this so?
Since it is already granted that three heavens are established based on the attainment of three grades of fruit from practicing the three grades of dhyāna,
by what reasoning is the middle heaven twice as large as the lower one?
Furthermore, since its upper region is only half as superior as the middle, what they say relies solely on false attachment.
Therefore, the establishment of the various heavens of the Form Realm is free from confusion only according to what my own teacher has taught.
Thus far, the Form Realm and its distinct locations have been explained.

In the Formless Realm, there are no locations at all; because formless phenomena have no spatial dimension, and because past, future, unmanifest, and formless phenomena do not abide in any location, this principle is certain.
However, regarding the distinctions of excellence and inferiority among those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), there are four types:

first, the sphere of infinite space; second, the sphere of infinite consciousness; third, the sphere of nothingness; and fourth, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These four are called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
These four [meditative attainments] do not differ in terms of superiority or inferiority due to their location, but rather because of the nature of their rebirth.
Furthermore, how is it known that they have no spatial location?
It is because those who attain these concentrations in a particular place are reborn in that very same place immediately after their death.
Furthermore, when one passes away from that state and is born into the desire or form realms, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises precisely at that location.
Although there are four different types of birth, there is no distinction of upper, lower, or spatial direction.
For what reason is the sequence of these four types as it is?
It is because one gradually abandons desire and gradually attains meditative concentration.
Alternatively, the sequence is such because of the order of their arising, according to the strength of the causes of arising and the resulting degree of fruitfulness.
Just as in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), all sentient beings must rely upon a body of form for the continuity of mind and so forth,
in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), what serves as the basis for the continuity of mind and so forth for sentient beings who take birth there?
For what reason does doubt suddenly arise again regarding this?

Because among all phenomena there is no self at all, and while the mind and mental factors can continue to evolve by relying upon the physical body within the realms of desire and form, in the formless realm there is no physical body;
therefore, it might seem that the mind and its concomitants could not possibly continue to evolve there—hence, doubt may arise once more in this regard.

It should be understood that those [phenomena] depend upon the continuity of the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*), life-force (*jīvitendriya*), mind (*citta*), and so forth; they do not have a self as their basis. Furthermore, the word "and" (*ca*) includes the other formations dissociated from mind (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), namely acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), birth (*jāti*), and the rest.
It is not that the existence of a substantial self-nature (*svabhāva*) for the *sabhāgatā* and so forth is being demonstrated here, as this has already been established previously;

rather, it is their function that is being demonstrated—namely, their capacity to act as conditions. A "condition" means acting as a basis (*āśraya*) that causes the mind and its concomitants to continue in succession.

Each of the four consciousnesses, beginning with the visual consciousness, takes as its support and as its nature of support both the immediately preceding ceased mind and its own physical sense-faculty. Furthermore, the primary elements upon which its own physical sense-faculty depends, as well as the body-faculty, the primary elements, the homogeneous faculty (*sabhāgatā*), the life-faculty, acquisition (*prāpti*), and the [conditioned characteristics] such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth, serve merely as its nature of support.

The body-consciousness takes both the mind and the body-faculty as its support (āśraya) and its nature of support (āśrayatva); however, it takes only the primary elements (mahābhūta), the homogeneous character (sabhāgatā), the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), acquisition (prāpti), and the [characteristics] such as arising (jāti) belonging to the body-faculty as its nature of support, but not as its support.

The mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes only the immediately preceding ceased mind as its support (āśraya) and its essential nature of support; the body faculty, the primary elements, the homogeneous character, the life faculty, acquisition (prāpti), and the [characteristics] such as arising (jāti) serve merely as its essential nature of support.

In this way, the minds and so forth of sentient beings in the realms of desire and form continue in dependence upon matter, the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and so on;

whereas for sentient beings in the formless realm, because they lack matter, their minds and so forth continue in dependence solely upon the homogeneous character and the life-faculty, yet it is not that they lack a basis.
Regarding the relationship between the support (*āśraya*) and that which is supported (*āśrita*), what is the distinction between their two characteristics?

Now, examining the essential tenet: the distinction between these two characteristics is that the former must exist for the latter to arise, whereas it does not arise in its absence; this constitutes the characteristic of the support.

It is established that there must be those characteristics and their corresponding transformations; these are called the support (*āśraya*) and the supported characteristic (*āśrita-lakṣaṇa*). [Objection:

Is it not the case that although there exist the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) of matter and so forth, at times the mind and its concomitants do not continue? How, then, can they be said to be the support of the mind and its concomitants?
This objection is not valid, because there exists a distinct dharma capable of obstructing the mind and its associates so that they do not continue.

Since the state of continuity of the mind and its associates necessarily depends upon that [distinct dharma], it is able to serve as the defining characteristic of the support for the mind and its associates.

It is directly observed that the mind and its associates do not arise at all within a dead body, whereas within a living body, the mind and mental factors necessarily arise; therefore, the characteristic of being a basis for those [mental factors]—namely, form and so forth—is thoroughly established.

From this it is known that visible forms, sounds, odors, and so forth cannot serve as the basis for the mind and mental factors. Although visible forms and sounds exist among external objects, the mind and mental factors never arise in dependence upon them. Therefore, the aforementioned "basis" (āśraya) is not universally present; for it is not the case that all minds and their concomitants undergo transformation in accordance with their respective bases.

Since the mind and its associates do not necessarily undergo transformation in accordance with the immediately preceding momentary cessation of the mental faculty (*manas*), how can they be said to have it as their support?
The mind and its associates necessarily undergo transformation in accordance with the mental faculty.
As for "conforming to change," this refers to causing a transformation.
At the very moment the immediately preceding mind is ceasing, it causes the subsequent mind and its associates to enter the stage of arising.
Once the mind-faculty has ceased and the subsequent mind and its associates have arisen, this constitutes the subsequent conforming to the change of the preceding.

Unlike the non-homogeneous [factors] which serve as the support for the mind and so forth—just as the eye and other faculties do not serve as the support for the immediately preceding ceased mind—the characteristic of being a support (āśraya-lakṣaṇa) is distinct from the characteristic of being supported (āśrita-lakṣaṇa); thus, throughout all supports, there is no fault of confusion between them.

In this way, for the minds of sentient beings in the realms of desire and form, all four aggregates arise simultaneously and serve as the nature of the support (*āśraya*), whereas only the single aggregate of form serves as the basis (*niśraya*).

The basis of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) should likewise include form, because it changes in accordance with form; we observe that when the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), wine, and so forth are disturbed, the mind is immediately altered.

It is impossible for the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) to have matter as its support (āśraya), for that which constitutes a support must necessarily produce transformations. However, the mental consciousness does not invariably arise following the transformations of the primary elements; even when the primary elements are absent, this [consciousness] still exists.
Therefore, in relation to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) can only function as its support (*āśraya*) and not as its objective basis (*ālambana*).
Consequently, within the desire and form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*), the six consciousnesses take the four aggregates (*skandha*) as their co-nascent support;
in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the mental consciousness lacks a further support in the form aggregate, so its co-nascent support consists only of the three [remaining] aggregates.
If that is so, why is it said that in the formless realm, the mind and its mental factors depend only upon the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*)?
This is stated because these two serve as a fixed and non-confused basis.
That is to say, although the mind and mental factors are mutually dependent, they are not a fixed and identical basis, because they do not depend upon themselves.
Nor is it non-confused, because when one is born in this stage (*bhūmi*), confusion arises from the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of both oneself and others.

Furthermore, the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*), life-force (*jīvitendriya*), and so forth have a common basis; moreover, since one born in this stage belongs only to this stage, even if a mind of a different stage should arise based upon these, they cause the mind of one's own stage to arise once again.
It is based solely on these two that this stage is said to arise, because the projecting karma arises without interruption; for this reason, they are described as having a common, non-confused basis.
Mental factors and so forth are not like this, and thus they are omitted and not mentioned.

If these two did not exist, then when the four aggregates of another stage were present, the sentient being at that time would have to be designated as belonging to that other stage rather than being subsumed under this stage, because the fruit projected by the prior karma of one's own stage would not be continuous.

However, this should not be accepted; therefore, it should be understood that just as the homogeneous body and life-force (*nikāya-sabhāga-jīvita*) in the desire and form realms serve as the basis for the mind and other factors, even though at times a mind belonging to a different level may arise, it nevertheless relies upon the body and so forth, and within this very birth, it will certainly later draw forth the arising of a mind belonging to its own level.

Thus, although there is no body in the formless realm (*ārūpya*), the mind and its associates necessarily depend upon the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*); therefore, the verse specifically mentions the homogeneous character and the life-faculty.

Since these are the maturation (*vipāka*) of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), they serve as the cause for the continued persistence of the remaining maturations, just as the roots and trunk of a tree provide the basis for its stability.

We observe that the leaves, branches, stems, and so forth of various trees, though produced from the same seed, abide by depending upon their roots; therefore, one should not claim that the eye-faculty and other faculties abide solely by depending on karma without having any other basis.
By this, it has already been explained that the mind and other factors born in the formless realm require a distinct basis; therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* does not state such a thing.

The transformation of the mind takes its associated mental factors as its basis, and it is precisely by virtue of this cause that acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and so forth are established. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to indicate in general that no specific name was mentioned, meaning that those [factors] are not produced solely by karma.
If it were produced by karma, it would not be a continuous succession; how then could that dharma serve as the support for the mind and its associates?
This is because, in its absence, the mind and its associates of that same level would necessarily not arise, just as with the body and so forth.
Alternatively, because that [homogeneous character] is the cause for non-confusion, one who has been born in a higher stage does not accomplish the wholesome [factors] of a lower stage.
Furthermore, there is no accomplishment of the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of a different stage;
therefore, it is established by reason that this [homogeneous character] serves as the basis for that [wholesome factor].
Other masters say:
Just as in the case of a pit or a trench, although there may be no wind or other such factors, the flame of a lamp will not arise;
so too, if those [physical] phenomena were absent, the mind and its associates would not arise. Therefore, we know that the mind and its associates take them as their support.
Perhaps some disciples might raise this objection:

"Since non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*)—just like the material body (*rūpakāya*)—should also be able to serve as a basis for the arising of mental consciousness and so forth, it is therefore taught that non-associated formations alone are the basis for the mind and its associates; it is not that the four co-emergent aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*) in the formless realm lack the sense of being a mutual basis."

However, within this context, the mind serves as the basis for feeling and the other mental factors, whereas those feelings and so forth do not serve as the basis for the mind, because they are not that which the mind follows.

It is only when the mind comprehends the general characteristics of an object that feeling and the others are then able to apprehend its specific characteristics; therefore, they follow the mind, and the mind does not follow them.
However, as for the statement that mind and mental factors are mutually dependent and mutually concomitant, this is because they share a single fruit.

For what reason is it not said that in the desire and form realms these two serve as the basis for the continuity of the mind and so forth, while it is only said that they depend upon the material body?

Although the body, the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and so forth, constantly continue as supports within the desire and form realms, the body is coarse and manifest; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.

Alternatively, this statement is made to establish that the homogeneous character and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) exist separately from the body. This is not because, in the formless realm or other stages, the mind and its mental factors produced by karma are not constantly present.
Alternatively, this statement is made because the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and so forth also function in dependence upon the body.
Although these factors and the body are mutually dependent, the body is predominant; therefore, it is specifically designated as their support.

Is it not the case that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is also a superior basis for the body? For if the life-faculty were absent, the faculties such as the body-faculty would all fail to function.

Although those [faculties] do not function in its absence, the body frequently encounters conditions such as calamities and misfortunes; thus, the life-faculty and others also undergo loss or benefit in accordance with the body. Therefore, the sense in which the body serves as their basis is preeminent.

Precisely for this reason, the masters of Abhidharma state that because there is no body in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*), life-force (*jīvita*), and other factors depend upon one another.
Here, the Sūtra Master (*Sūtrāntika*) assumes the role of an interlocutor and, erroneously adding to the correct meaning, raises this objection:
"If that is so, why do the mind and other factors of sentient beings with form (*rūpin*) not likewise depend solely on these two [homogeneous character and life-force] for their continuity?"
The Abhidharmikas explain as follows:
"Birth in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is [so designated] because these two [factors] are inferior there.
For what reason are these two causes stronger in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?"
Since those two realms arise from superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), their attainments (*samāpatti*) are able to suppress the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*).
If that is so, since the mental continuum and so forth in those realms depend solely upon superior concentration, what need is there for a separate basis?

Furthermore, it should now be explained: just as for sentient beings born in the form realm, the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) function in dependence upon form, what do these two depend upon in the formless realm?
These two revolve by depending upon one another.
Why do these two not depend [on each other] when there is form?
Because when born in the realm of form, these two are inferior.
Regarding these two [factors] in the formless realm, why are they so powerful?
Because those two in that realm arise from superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

It was previously stated that such concentration can suppress the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*); however, this would again entail the same difficulty regarding the continuity of the mind, or else it would imply that the mind and mental factors depend solely upon one another.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) must have received no instruction in the Abhidharma;
he has erroneously recorded these words, or perhaps, out of personal aversion toward the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma*), he fabricated this statement to confuse and subvert the orthodox tradition.
Who is there who possesses the subtle penetration of the characteristics of all phenomena that could provide such an answer to the previous question?
They establish their own position, asserting that the continuity of mind and so forth in the formless realm has no other support.
