That is to say, if there is a cause that has not yet abandoned craving for form, it gives rise to the mind and its concomitants; these induced minds and concomitants arise simultaneously with form and function in dependence upon form.

If, however, regarding form, the cause has already attained freedom from craving and has become averse to form, then the induced minds and concomitants do not arise simultaneously with form and do not function in dependence upon form.

This is also unreasonable; for if the power of the projecting cause were to cause that continuum of mind and so forth to proceed, then at the moment when a wholesome or defiled mind manifests, the continuum of mind and so forth would have no basis.

Furthermore, just as sentient beings in the desire and form realms—by the power of projecting causes—have a continuity of mind and so forth that arises together with matter and evolves in dependence upon matter;

likewise, sentient beings in the formless realm—by the power of projecting causes—have a continuity of mind and so forth that arises together with the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), evolving not in dependence on matter, but solely in dependence on the homogeneous character and the life-faculty.

Since it has already been granted that for sentient beings of the desire and form realms, the mind and its associates cannot possibly function without depending on the physical body, for what reason do the mind and its associates of sentient beings in the formless realm function despite having no basis whatsoever?

Furthermore, you yourself admit that in the desire and form realms, although the mental states of a single continuum are the fruit of one karma, they necessarily proceed in dependence upon other mental states;
why then do you not allow the same to be true for the formless realm?
Furthermore, one should not say that it is only in the case of form that mind and its concomitants—which have not yet abandoned the causes of craving—arise depending upon form;
for there currently exist mind and its concomitants, which have already abandoned the causes of craving for form, that arise simultaneously with form and depend upon form.
This is because those born in the desire or form realms, having already eliminated craving for form, manifest a mind of the formless realm.

Although such beings manifest a mind of the formless realm, they are not called "formless" (ārūpya) because they have not yet abandoned craving for form; rather, they rely upon the cause and effect of that craving as their basis, and thus this continuity of the formless mind proceeds.
Since the mind of the formless realm manifests in the lower realms while having a distinct basis, it should likewise be so in the higher realms.

Furthermore, when one born in the formless realm gives rise to a mind of another level or an untainted (anāsrava) mind, if there were no mental continuum based on even a slight factor of its own level, one would have to ask: to which level does this sentient being belong?
Such an investigation has already been repeatedly debated; therefore, the view held by the Sūtra-master is not excellent.

Regarding this matter, the Venerable Elder states that in the formless realm, the mind and mental factors depend upon one another for their existence, like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other, or like the mutual dependence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) in the lower realms.
One should challenge them as follows:
Just as in the desire and form realms, although the four aggregates are said to depend upon one another, it is admitted that their designations arise based specifically on matter;
likewise, although mental factors in the formless realm depend upon the mind, one must further admit that they have a distinct basis upon which they depend to maintain their continuity.
Therefore, to contradict the correct principles of the Abhidharma is necessarily incapable of establishing the reality of the meaning.
As stated in this treatise:
"What is the desire realm?"
This refers to those phenomena (*dharma*) in which sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) increases; the same applies to the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This statement is made to show that while these phenomena manifest within the three realms, they are not all necessarily bound (*paryāpanna*) to them.

Is it not the case that all dharmas are not subject to the increase of afflictions belonging to other realms or stages? One should indeed specify this by stating that they are subject to the increase of all afflictions belonging to their own realm.

While this is logically correct, only the predominant latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are mentioned to specify them, because for the majority of sentient beings, the latent disposition of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*) is what most frequently manifests.
Regarding "desire-attachment" (*kāmarāga*), this refers to attachment belonging to the desire realm; it is the same for attachment belonging to the form and formless realms.
Briefly stated, that which is induced by edible food and sexual intercourse may be designated by the name "desire," as a verse in a sutra says:
"The various exquisite objects of the world are not true desire; True desire is the greed of human conceptualization."
"The wondrous objects remain as they were in the world; / The wise have already removed desire from within them.
This verse is spoken to demonstrate that although the names for craving and desire differ, their substance is the same.

The realm to which desire belongs is called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); the realm to which form belongs is called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). This is stated by omitting the intermediate term, just as one says "pepper drink" or "diamond ring."
Because form (*rūpa*) does not exist within that realm, it is called "formless" (*ārūpya*).
What is termed "form" has the meaning of being subject to transformation and obstruction, or the meaning of manifesting.
Since its essence is not form, it is designated by the name "formless"; it is not the case that this [realm] takes the mere absence of form as its essence.
The realm to which the formless belongs is called the "formless realm" (*ārūpyadhātu*); this is a case of omitting the intermediate term, as explained previously.
Furthermore, the realm of desire is named the "desire realm" (*kāmadhātu*) because this realm is able to sustain desire; one should know that the same applies to the realms of form and the formless.
If a realm possesses form but lacks meditative concentration, it is called the desire realm;
if a realm possesses both form and meditative concentration, it is called the form realm;
if a realm is formless yet possesses meditative concentration, it is the formless realm.
If a realm possesses both form and the objects of desire, it is called the desire realm;
if a realm possesses form but lacks the objects of desire, it is called the form realm;
if a realm possesses neither, it is the formless realm.

If a realm possesses the maturation of the five aggregates, yet lacks the five aggregates acting as the maturation cause for the attainment of a single fruit, it is called the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
if a realm possesses both [the five aggregates and their maturation cause], it is called the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
if a realm possesses neither, it is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If a realm possesses most, though not all, forms, it is called the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
if a realm lacks all forms, it is called the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
if a realm is entirely devoid of all phenomena of form, it is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If a realm possesses form and also contains many destinies, it is called the desire realm;
if a realm possesses form but lacks many destinies, it is called the form realm;
if a realm is without form and also lacks many destinies, it is the formless realm.
There are countless other such varieties.
Are the three realms one, or are there many?
The three realms are boundless, equal in measure to space.

Therefore, although there are no sentient beings who first arise, and immeasurable, boundless Buddhas appear in the world, each one transforming and delivering countless sentient beings, causing them to realize the realm of nirvana without remainder, yet they are never exhausted, remaining like space.
How should it be said that the world abides?
It should be said to abide among animals (*tiryag-yoni*). Thus, the Sūtra says:
For example, it is like rain falling from the sky in drops as large as axle-trees, pouring down without interval or interruption;
in this same way, in the eastern direction, immeasurable worlds are either being destroyed or being formed without interval or interruption.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is likewise in the south, west, and north.
The zenith and nadir are not mentioned;
however, some say that there are also these two directions of zenith and nadir, because the sūtras of other schools speak of the ten directions.
Above the Akaniṣṭha Heaven there is again a desire realm, and below that desire realm there is an Akaniṣṭha Heaven; in this manner, worlds extend infinitely in succession.
If one becomes free from craving for even a single triple world, then craving for all triple worlds is extinguished and abandoned without exception.

When supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) arises based on the first dhyāna, the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) it produces can only reach the Brahma-world of the realm in which one has been born, and not elsewhere; it should be understood that the same applies to the remaining types of supernormal knowledge, so as to avoid the fault of over-extending their scope.
The three realms have already been explained.
What, then, are the destinies? In how many places do they exist, and of how many kinds are they?
The verse says:
Among these, the hells and so forth are called the five destinies by their own names;
they are exclusively non-obscured neutral, pertaining to sentient beings, and do not include the intermediate state.
The Treatise says:
Within the three realms, there are five destinies (gatis) as appropriate, which are made manifest by their own names.
That is to say, those previously mentioned—namely, hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas—are called the five destinies.

Only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are the four destinies (*gati*) complete; each of the three realms contains a portion of the celestial destiny (*devagati*). To demonstrate that there are realms not subsumed under the destinies, it is said that there are five destinies within the three realms.

Wholesome, defiled, and neutral states; sentient and insentient beings; as well as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and so forth—all these are of the nature of the realms (*dhātu*). However, the essence of the destinies (*gati*) comprises only the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and sentient beings, and does not include the intermediate state.

Regarding the statement that the substance of the destinies (*gati*) consists exclusively of the non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*): this is because only that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) constitutes the substance of a destiny.
By this, it is already explained that destinies pertain only to sentient beings, for that which is born of maturation does not exist among insentient things.
Among these, there are those that are not destinies (*gati*), which shall be discussed in detail later.
What authoritative scripture (*āgama*) can definitively establish that the essence of a destiny consists exclusively of the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)?
One might cite the *Saptabhava-sūtra* as a proof.

The Sūtras speak of seven types of existence (*bhava*): namely, existence as a hell-being, existence as an animal, existence as a hungry ghost, existence as a deva, existence as a human, karmic existence (*karmabhava*), and intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Among these, karmic existence (*karmabhava*) is the cause of the five destinies (*gati*); it is mentioned separately because it is distinguished from other causes of the destinies.
This sutra, in order to show that the essence of a destiny consists exclusively of the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), thus distinguishes it from other causes.

However, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) states that because they are mentioned separately, [the view] is certainly not subsumed under that [category], just as among the five corruptions (pañca kaṣāyāḥ), afflictions (kleśa) and views (dṛṣṭi) are mentioned separately as distinct corruptions;
since they are mentioned separately, those views are certainly not subsumed within the category of afflictions.

In this way, although karma and existence (*bhava*) are also "destinies" (*gati*), they are mentioned separately to clarify the causes of the destinies; thus, some claim that the essence of a destiny includes both the wholesome and the defiled.
That statement is irrational, for it is nowhere stated [in the scriptures].

In some places it is stated that "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is also an affliction (*kleśa*); although it is separately designated as a "turbidity" (*kaṣāya*) due to a specific cause, one knows from other explanations that it is indeed an affliction.
Nowhere, however, is it ever stated that [the turbidities] are the causes for rebirth in the various realms of existence (*gati*).

That karma is the very substance of the realms of rebirth (*gati*) can serve as a valid proof; for although it is spoken of separately as "existence" (*bhava*) because it has a cause, according to that same teaching, one knows that karma is the realm of rebirth.
How, then, is it definitively known that karma is the substance of the realm of rebirth?
Because there is a specific cause, there is a distinct designation for "existence" (bhava);

yet, while the substantial entity of karmic existence is not itself a destiny (gati), it is designated as "karmic existence" to reveal it as the cause of the destinies. Therefore, the analogy cited lacks the power to prove [your point].

Furthermore, what they have said involves an over-extension of the fault, for it would follow that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) must also be included within the destinies (*gati*). Yet they explain:

"Because it does not correspond to the meaning of a destiny, it is called the intermediate state because it exists between two destinies; if this were included within a destiny, it would not be the intermediate state."
This interpretation shall be further investigated later.
For the time being, the *Sūtra on the Five Corruptions* lacks the power to prove [your point], as it nowhere states that karma is itself a destination (*gati*).
Since the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) has been admitted, it is not the essence of a destination (*gati*) because it does not correspond to the meaning of a "destination";
the same must apply to karma as well, for since it too does not correspond to the meaning of a "destination," it certainly cannot be the essence of a destination.

If karma were the very substance of the destinies (*gati*), then the destinies would necessarily be intermingled, because within the body of a single destiny there exist the karmas of multiple destinies.

If the karma that is the cause of a destiny were itself the destiny, then a person who possesses hellish karma or for whom it is presently manifest would be both a human and a denizen of hell. Furthermore, one could not say that although the substance of the hell destiny is present, it is not yet hell; otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), for when the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) is actually manifest, it would not be hell, as there is no distinction [between the cause and the result].

However, since the sūtras state that once the maturation has arisen, it is called "hell" (*naraka*), it follows that karma is not itself a destiny (*gati*). Furthermore, the claim that karma is a destiny contradicts reason, because it is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is the cause of a destiny.

A "destiny" (*gati*) refers to that which is gone toward; the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) should not be considered a place to be gone toward, because it is by means of this [intermediate state] that one proceeds to the actual place of rebirth.

Therefore, it is not included within the destinies. Likewise, since it is accepted that karmic existence (*karmabhava*), being the cause of a destiny, is neither the place to be reached nor included within the destinies, it should be understood that the essential nature of a destiny comprises only the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). This principle is fully established.
Only that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) constitutes the substance of the various realms of existence (*gati*). By what means is this known?
Because it is stated in the *Sūtra*.
The *Sūtra* records that Śāriputra spoke these words:
Venerable one!

If, due to the manifestation of the outflows (*āsrava*) pertaining to hell, one performs and increases karma conducive to experience in hell, and because of the crookedness, impurity, and turbidity of that body, speech, and mind, one undergoes the maturation (*vipāka*) of the five aggregates within the hells (*naraka*); once this maturation has arisen, it is called "hell."
Apart from the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), that hell (*naraka*) cannot be found at all.

Since it is stated here that there is no separate hell apart from the five aggregates—such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth—which arise from maturation (*vipāka*), and since it is only after such maturation has arisen that one is designated a "hell-being," we know that the essential nature of the destinies (*gati*) consists solely of maturation.

Although that Śākya [the Buddha] spoke thus in order to negate the existence of a substantially real *pudgala* who transmigrates to various destinies—stating that apart from the phenomena of the five aggregates, that hell-being (*naraka*) is nowhere to be found—he did not speak these words in order to negate the remaining aggregates.

However, this is merely a false conceptualization of one's own mind; for the Sūtras state that it is only after the five aggregates of maturation (*vipāka*) have arisen that they are designated as *naraka* (hell).

Furthermore, it is said that apart from these factors of the aggregates of maturation, that *naraka* cannot be found. The phrase "factors other than the aggregates" is a general description, as it follows upon the prior arising of the five aggregates of maturation.

This statement also serves to exclude the existence of a substantially real *pudgala* who migrates to various realms, because it generally excludes anything other than the aggregates of maturation (*vipākaskandha*).

Furthermore, regarding their claim that "once maturation has arisen, one is called a hell-being," this means that one is designated a hell-being only when maturation has arisen; it does not mean that the hell-being is exclusively maturation itself.

This too is a false interpretation made according to one's own whims; for there is a subsequent statement that makes a specific distinction, namely: "Excluding the dharmas of the immediately preceding ripening aggregate (*vipāka-skandha*), those [other aggregates] are not found at all in that hell."
If the essence of the various realms of existence (*gati*) were not exclusively maturation (*vipāka*), why would it be necessary to state that they are only called "hell" once maturation has arisen?

It is not the case that the karma capable of summoning the existence (*bhava*) of hell already exists prior to the stage when the aggregates of maturation have first arisen; nor is it the case that it is already called "hell" at that time. Therefore, one knows that hell arises solely from maturation.

It is not that the karma capable of summoning those hells possesses any slight difference in its manifestation or its state of being accomplished—whether the maturation has already arisen or not; therefore, it is logically established that the essence of the destinies consists solely of what is born of maturation, and not of the wholesome, the defiled, or other such factors.
Other masters say that it also extends to the nourished (*aupacayika*).
This contradicts the sūtra and cannot be relied upon as authoritative.

Regarding the statement that "the outflows (*āsrava*) of the hells manifest," one should ask what the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the hells actually are, yet they are here referred to as the "outflows of the hells.

It is not the case that the afflictions of the various realms of existence (*gati*), such as the hells, are distinct according to their respective levels of attachment—such as the first dhyāna and so forth—just as it is with the karma of the various realms. Nevertheless, because the karma of the various realms is necessarily distinct, it is capable of giving rise to afflictions.

To say that the *gatis* (destinies) are not themselves the substance of karma, but are exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), would contradict the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*. That treatise states that all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with the five destinies; this statement was made because it refers to the minds capable of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhicitta*) belonging to the five categories (*pañca-varga*).

The destinies (*gati*) and the minds of beings are collectively termed "destinies"; there is no fault of contradiction here, just as a village and the vicinity of a village are both collectively called a "village.
For what reason is it known that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not a destiny?

Since the sūtras, śāstras, and reasoning serve as authoritative criteria (*pramāṇa*), first, regarding the sūtras: this refers to the *Saptabhavasūtra*, which specifically explains the causes and conditions for the five destinies (*gati*).
Regarding the śāstras, the *Prajñaptiśāstra* states:
The four modes of birth encompass the five destinies, but the five destinies do not encompass the four modes of birth.
What is it that is not so encompassed?
It is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The *Dharmaskandha-śāstra* states:
"What is the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*)?
It refers to translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) derived from the four great elements; it is the eye, the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), and the eye-element."
The realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods constitute the [five] destinies (*gati*), while the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is produced through cultivation.
As for the statement "by way of reasoning," a destiny refers to that which is gone toward; the intermediate state is not such, as has already been explained previously.
Furthermore, because one is born in the very same place where one dies, it is not a destination to which one travels; therefore, it does not constitute the essence of a *gati* (realm of rebirth).
However, an objection may be raised:
"If that were so, then the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) should also not be considered *gatis*, since birth is experienced in the very same place where death occurs."

That objection is unreasonable; for while death and birth occur at the very same location in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), and thus it constitutes the essence of a destination (*gati*), the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), although death and birth occur at the same location, involves movement to another place and therefore does not constitute the essence of a destination.
The Master of the Sūtra further states:
"If that is so, because the intermediate state (antarābhava) is named 'intermediate,' it should not be called a 'destination' (gati).
As for the claim that it is called the 'intermediate state' because it exists between two destinations, this is unreasonable, as the reason is unestablished."
If it were granted that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not established as a destination (*gati*), one could say:
"It is called the intermediate state because it exists between two destinations.
However, since the intermediate state is not established as a non-destination, how can it be said that it is called the intermediate state because it exists between two destinations?
Because it is called "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*), the [proposed] definition of its meaning is not established.

Even if one were to concede that intermediate existence is the substance of a realm of rebirth (*gati*), since the karma to be experienced accordingly must necessarily arise within the two existences of death and birth for one who has not yet abandoned craving, it is therefore named "intermediate existence. It is not called "intermediate existence" because it is said to exist between two realms of rebirth.

However, there is no such thing as "fundamental existence" (mūlabhava) that exists [independently]; to name it so would involve logical faults. This is because within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which exists between the stages of death and birth, there may be cases where one does not arise from fundamental existence.

That is to say, while it is possible for the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*) to manifest immediately after the existence of death (*maraṇabhava*) without first arising from fundamental existence, it is absolutely impossible for the existence of birth to manifest immediately after the existence of death while one remains in the intermediate state. Thus, there is no such thing as fundamental existence.
Therefore, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is so named so as not to be confused with other states of existence (*bhava*).

Although there are some who claim that not all beings in the desire and form realms necessarily possess an intermediate state, we shall establish its definite existence and refute their assertions during the subsequent investigation into the meaning of the intermediate state.
Alternatively, it may be called "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*) because it arises between two births of different classes;
it is not so called because it exists between two destinies (*gati*), as is the case with its "fundamental existence" (*pūrvakālabhava*) and others.
Such a thing does not exist.
Furthermore, when the Master of the Sūtras says:
"If this were included within the [five] destinies, it would not be 'intermediate'; therefore, it should not be called 'intermediate existence' (antarābhava)," this too is unreasonable.
Why is this so? If these were included among the destinies (*gati*), as previously explained, they would constitute the intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
since the intermediate state is not a destiny, the reasoning stated earlier is established, and the Master of the Sūtra’s later statement cannot serve as proof.
Regarding this, the Sthavira speaks as follows:

"If you admit that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not included within the destinies (*gati*), then you must explain that there exists a separate karma capable of producing the intermediate state, which is distinct from the five destinies."
There is no fault here, for this is what we accept.

That is to say, within our own school, it is accepted that the essence of the five destinies (*gati*) is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), whereas the karma that initiates existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), because it is wholesome with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*).
From this, one should know that apart from the five destinies (*gati*), there exists a separate karma capable of producing the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Furthermore, this intermediate state is itself the fruit of the karma of the destinies; that is to say, the karma that is able to summon the fruits of the various destinies is precisely what brings about the means of proceeding toward those destinies, and this means of proceeding is termed the intermediate state.

Just as it is accepted that both transformed and non-transformed births are the fruit of a single karma, so too should it be accepted that those included within the destinies and those not included within the destinies are summoned by a single karma; thus, parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state is established, because the karma to be experienced with certainty has already yielded its fruit.

If the karma that produces existence (*bhava*) and so forth—which is the fruit of distinct individual karma—has not yet yielded its result, it should be impossible for the noble path (*āryamārga*) that eternally abandons the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*) to manifest.
Yet, since the fetters that produce birth have already been abandoned, can such a noble path not manifest? As the Sūtra says:
"It should be known that such a person has already abandoned the fetters that produce birth, but has not yet abandoned the fetters that produce arising."
Therefore, it does not constitute a valid proof.
How is it that two fetters, though bound by the same stage (*bhūmi*), are severed sequentially without contradicting reason?
Thus, one should seek the intended meaning of that sūtra.
Now, as I investigate this matter with careful scrutiny, I perceive that the sūtra has such an underlying intention: namely, that these words were spoken in reference to two kinds of abandonment.
What are these two kinds of abandonment?
First is the abandonment through obtaining permanent counteraction; second is the abandonment through obtaining permanent non-occurrence.

Regarding these, the first abandonment refers to the arising of all fetters and a portion of the fetters of rebirth, because one has attained permanent detachment from craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), yet has not yet attained permanent detachment from craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If the second type of fetter is abandoned, it consists solely of the fetter of birth (*jāti-saṃyojana*).

For one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm or the form realm, there are two occasions when this fetter may manifest: namely, when abiding in the state of "prior existence" (*pūrvabhava*) at the time of projecting the karma that brings about a full existence, and when abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) at the time of linking to a new existence. While in the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), one creates the projecting karma that is capable of inducing the birth one is to undergo; however, because the power of its antidote suppresses its continuity and because one has realized the profound faults and perils of existence-in-birth (*upapattibhava*), [the fetter does not manifest].
While abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one is unable to manifest a karma that is fully capable of producing further existence; consequently, such karma will never arise.

Because there is no obstruction to the manifestation of the Noble Path while abiding in the intermediate state, one severs the remaining fetters before reaching the place of birth and attains parinirvāṇa.

Because there is no possibility for them to undergo rebirth-existence (*pratisandhi-bhava*), the fetters of a second birth never manifest again, as they have already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of those [fetters].
By this, it is established with absolute certainty that these various realms of existence (*gati*) and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are the fruit of a single karma.

Furthermore, this must necessarily be so; for, with the exception of those who attain parinirvāṇa within the intermediate state (antarābhava), there is no one who remains in the intermediate state without reaching the state of birth (upapattibhava) and then passing away.
If it were the result of distinct karma, it would have to be identical to the other distinct results of various karmas.
For what reason do those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) necessarily return to birth?

If other sentient beings, while in the intermediate state, have already yielded their results for karma pertaining to the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*) and so forth, why do they not die in the intermediate state—like those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*)—before reaching the place of birth?

This analogy is not uniform. This is because for one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) as a non-returner (anāgāmin), all fetters of birth (*upapattisaṃyojana*) have already been severed;

since this state is contrary to rebirth, the superior path of counteraction (*pratipakṣamārga*) has already become manifest, and the karma conducive to that [rebirth] has already yielded its fruit, such a person attains parinirvāṇa before reaching the existence of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).

Other sentient beings dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), whose fetters for rebirth have not yet been severed and who lack any superior path that counteracts rebirth, must necessarily experience the maturation (*vipāka*) of their birth-existence (*upapattibhava*), even though the karma conducive to such experience has already yielded its fruit; this is because the force of the maturation of such karma is both powerful and swift.

However, that Elder’s wisdom had declined; he falsely raised an objection regarding what was faultless, saying: "If the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not included within the destinies (*gati*), then one must say that there exists a separate karma capable of producing the intermediate state, distinct from the five destinies."
The Victorious One’s wisdom should not be gathered or extracted from among them.
Having thus provided a general explanation of the nature of the various destinies (*gati*), one should next explain the name of each individual destiny separately.
*Nara* means "human," and *ka* means "evil. Because humans frequently commit evil and fall headlong into it, it is therefore called the destiny of *naraka*.
Alternatively, it is called *naraka* because it is near humans, for those who commit grave offenses fall into it swiftly.
Or again, *ka* is a synonym for pleasure (*sukha*); *na* means "non-" and *ra* means "to give"; thus, that which is devoid of the granting of pleasure is called *naraka*.
Alternatively, *naraka* has the meaning of "rescue" (*nir-jāra*); that which cannot be rescued is called *naraka*.
Alternatively, *naraka* has the meaning of "delight" (*ramaṇīya*); that which is not delightful is called *naraka*.

Regarding the term "animals" (*tiryag-yoni*): they are so called because for the most part the bodies in that realm dwell horizontally; or because within that realm there may be a small portion that moves sideways.
Furthermore, they are named "animals" because their species are numerous and they are largely characterized by ignorance.
Regarding those called *preta* (hungry ghosts): it refers to those who, in other lifetimes, delighted in stealing the property of others and habitually practiced stinginess and greed.

Furthermore, they are mostly the ancestors to whom offerings are made; they mostly long for sustenance to survive; and they are mostly timid and weak, their forms emaciated and haggard, with minds and bodies that are flighty and restless; therefore, they are named hungry ghosts.
Some say that humans give rise to pride based on their celestial conditions, thinking:
"I am the most honored among these classes within the happy realms.
Alternatively, they are called "humans" because their own minds are characterized by excessive conceit (*adhimāna*) or excessive deliberation.
"Deva" (Heaven) refers to those who possess radiance and blazing majesty, who engage in play and discourse, and whose valor rivals one another.
Alternatively, they are called "devas" because they are honored and exalted, their spiritual powers are sovereign, and they are the objects of the prayers and petitions of the multitude.
Some say: "The asuras contend with and interact with the hosts of devas.
Since they were originally devas and their majestic power was superior, for these reasons they are included within the realm of the devas."

Because they lack the capacity for the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), because they resemble non-humans (*amanuṣya*), and because they are largely deceitful and crooked, they certainly do not belong to the heavenly realm (*devagati*), but are subsumed within the realm of hungry ghosts (*pretagati*).
Engaging in disputes and conflicts with the various classes of devas and so forth are all not valid reasons for proof, because they are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

To begin with, such conflict is not a valid reason for proving [the existence of] devas; we have heard that there were people who fought with rākṣasas, and we have also heard of rākṣasas fighting with monkeys, as well as King Māndhātṛ defeating the asuras—instances of this kind are truly numerous.

However, among the gods, the flavor of *sudhā* is supreme, while the daughters of the asuras possess beautiful and dignified countenances; because they thus encroach upon one another and frequently engage in conflict, they do not belong to the same realm (*gati*), and for that reason, they are not gods.

To claim that mutual intermingling also fails to constitute proof is incorrect; for we see even among the noble and the lowly that they intermingle with one another, and those who indulge in desire do not regard the caste of their consorts.
We have heard that the Great Kinnara King had a daughter of exquisite beauty named Manoharā, whom the Bodhisattva Sudhana took as his wife.

To claim that he was originally a deva does not constitute valid proof; it is merely words of praise spoken by Śakra, the Lord of Devas, regarding his father-in-law—words of eulogy that may be either true or false.
Since they were uttered out of a desire to please and as a form of flattery toward his father, how can they suffice as evidence?
Furthermore, although he originally resided on the summit of Mount Sumeru, he was forced by the gods to retreat and dwell below; thus, there is no fault in saying that he was originally a god.

Moreover, out of arrogance he claimed himself to be a god and repeatedly raised armies to wage war against the various devas; Śakra, seeking to stop him, skillfully consoled him with words suited to the time and place, making him joyful—even if these were false, there was no transgression.
Furthermore, superior majesty and power (*pratāpa*) are not a valid reason for proof, for it has been heard that King Mandhātṛ’s majesty and power surpassed those of the gods.
Although Nanda, Upananda, and others were animals (*tiryagyoni*), their majestic power and sovereignty exceeded that of the hosts of devas.
Therefore, the asuras are included solely within the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati).
Nor are they the sixth [realm], for it has never been so stated.

However, the reason they are not said to be subsumed under the miserable destinies (durgati) is out of fear that they might give rise to poisonous and malicious thoughts toward the Buddha, thereby undergoing various intense sufferings throughout the long night of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, based on its etymology, they are excluded from the category of devas. *Sura* means "deva," which signifies "sovereignty"; *asura* means "non-," signifying that they are not devas.
Because their sovereignty is diminished compared to the devas, they are called *asuras*.
Furthermore, *sukha* means "extremely desirable. Because the heavens are extremely desirable, they receive the name *sukha*.
Although those [heavens] also experience much pleasure, because they abound in deceit and crookedness, they are not "extremely desirable."

Some say: the various realms of existence (*gati*) may be intermingled in essence, because beings of different realms act as causes for one another to produce offspring; for instance, there are those with fish bodies and the Rishi Mṛgaśiras, of whom countless examples have been handed down from antiquity. Thus, because a single body may belong to two realms, they are said to be intermingled.
That argument is incorrect; for while the destinies of one's own karma are fixed, the conditions for birth therein are manifold.
When one observes that sentient beings arise within what is considered insentient, how could that single body be categorized as either sentient or insentient?

Just as the woman Āmrapālī was born from a tree, and the Gautama clan arose from the rays of the sun, these are cases of existence through mutual dependence; they do not serve as proof for a "mixed cause" (*miśra-hetu*).
It is further said that those of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*) may possess a fetal womb (*garbha*); if they already depend upon a fetal womb, how can they be called "miraculously born"?
Worldly discourse is largely hollow and should not be relied upon with faith.
Alternatively, even if they assume different forms, there is no logical contradiction;

for instance, the seer Mṛgāra and those who took the form of fish were actually human beings whose physical appearances differed due to the diversity of their *pūrṇakarma* (fulfilling karma). Thus, there is no confusion regarding their respective destinies (*gati*).
The remaining points concerning the differences in the causes and effects of rebirth shall be analyzed in detail within the investigation of karma.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 21; *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 22.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Part Two: Chapter Three, "Discriminating the Arising of Conditions," Second. Among the various realms and destinies previously described, there are seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) in their respective order.
What are these seven?
The verse says:
Diverse bodies and diverse perceptions; Diverse bodies and identical perception;
Reversing this, the perception of self-body is one, together with the three lower [realms] of the formless realm;
thus there are seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), while the remainder are not so because they involve impairment.
The treatise says:

To state it briefly: the humans and devas of the desire realm, together with those in the lower three dhyānas and the formless realms—these seven places of birth constitute the essence of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
If one were to analyze this in detail, it should follow the sūtras:
there are sentient beings with form whose bodies are diverse and whose appearances are diverse, such as humans and certain devas; this is the first station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
"One portion of gods" refers to the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those of the first dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*), excluding those who arise at the beginning of a kalpa.
"Sentient beings possessing form" means those who have accomplished a material body (*rūpakāya*).
Regarding "diversity of body" (*nānātva-kāya*): this refers to the various colors, forms, and physical features of their material bodies (*rūpa-kāya*).
Because they possess such diversity of body, or because some have different bodies, those sentient beings are said to have "diverse bodies."
Regarding the phrase "different perceptions" (*saṃjñā-nānātva*): this refers to the distinctions among their perceptions of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.

Because they differ in perception, they either possess diverse perceptions or cultivate diverse perceptions to constitute their nature; therefore, those sentient beings are called "those of different perceptions."
Now, one should reflect upon this:

Is it not the case that because of the statement regarding a "different body" in the context of future existence (*punarbhava*), the existence of form (*rūpa*) is already established, and thus the prior mention of "having form" would be redundant?
This objection is unreasonable, for we observe that the term "body" (*kāya*) is also used in reference to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

If it is argued that because there is a distinct mention of "perception" (saṃjñā) after the body, it is already established that the term "body" (kāya) refers exclusively to matter (rūpa), this too is unreasonable; for apart from perception, there would otherwise be no other matter, leading to confusion and ambiguity.

Alternatively, one might argue that because the term "subsequent existence" (paścādbhava) is used as it is by people, the term "prior body" (pūrvadeha) cannot be confused with it; however, this is also unreasonable, because the subsequent mention of the term "a certain class of devas" (ekadeśadeva) allows for the possibility of confusion.

If it is argued that the mention of "a portion of the gods" does not cause the term for their bodies to be confused with those in the formless realm—because it follows a specific sequence and because the terms for the various gods, such as the Brahmakāyikas, are subsequently mentioned—then [this objection is refuted].

This reasoning is also incorrect, because it is not a comprehensive statement; for it does not comprehensively state that all classes of devas are established within the other consciousness-abodes, lest doubt should arise.

Regarding the "one part of the heavens," this encompasses both the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the fourth dhyāna; therefore, it is said that they possess form and have different bodies. It is not that the Peak of Existence can be said to possess form, nor is it that the fourth dhyāna can be said to have different bodies.

Since the phrase "a portion of the gods" has already excluded those in the evil realms, and the remaining classes of humans and gods are each made manifest by their own names, the meaning of this statement regarding "a portion of the gods" is established as being subsumed as previously described.

Because the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the fourth dhyāna, and the various evil realms are not included among the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the term "possessing form" (*rūpin*) carries great significance and utility.
Alternatively, the statement "possessing form" serves to indicate a distinguishing cause; that is, the cause for the diversity of bodies (*kāyabheda*) is precisely "possessing form."
It is because there must be form that the body can possess difference;
and because the body possesses difference, the diversity of perception is established. Thus, the mention of "form" indicates its nature as the cause of difference.
This occurs through the manifestation of superior objects capable of causing benefit or harm.
When the body undergoes deterioration or improvement, the body itself undergoes transformation.
At the very moment such transformation occurs in the body, it causes food, drink, and so forth to also undergo transformation.

Because of that transformation, the differentiation of the body is established; from this, distinct perceptions such as pleasure arise. Therefore, the statement "there is form" (*rūpa*) is intended to manifest the cause of this differentiation.

If the statement that "there must be form" is intended to manifest that the bodies [of those beings] have different causes, then the bodies of the Ābhāsvara Heaven and others should also be different.
Furthermore, the Ābhāsvara Heaven should not have diverse perceptions, because the bodies therein are without difference.
Furthermore, the perceptions of the various Brahma-hosts would not be uniform, because the bodies among those gods differ.
For this reason, the explanation provided is not necessarily logical.
The principle is indeed necessary, as the causes for their difference are fixed.

This means that while the body has distinctions, these are caused by form (*rūpa*); it is not the case that non-form causes the body to be definitively distinct. Therefore, there is no fallacy of bodies becoming distinct in the Ābhāsvara heaven and elsewhere. This is just as visual consciousness and so forth arise with the eye and visible forms as their conditions.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises.
Although the eye and visible forms are present, visual consciousness does not arise; the same should apply to the others as well.
Furthermore, as a sutra states:
"When there is pliancy (praśrabdhi) in the body, one experiences pleasure.

The intent of this sutra is to show that for the experience of undefiled pleasure, meditative pliancy is the cause; it does not mean that physical pliancy necessarily produces the experience of pleasure.
This case should also be understood in the same way; therefore, this principle is necessarily so.
If it is argued that the eye and visible form are fixed as the conditions for visual consciousness, yet visual consciousness does not arise because other conditions are lacking:
As stated in the Sūtra:
"If the attention that gives rise [to consciousness] does not arise correctly, consciousness will not arise.
Since you admit that form serves as the cause for the differentiation of the body, by what further condition would you explain why the body does not differ?

Furthermore, the essence of the experience of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) is distinct from pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); although pliancy pervades all stages (*bhūmi*), there are stages where the experience of pleasure does not arise.
Since the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*) is likewise distinct [from pliancy], yet lacks a separate essence [of its own], all those possessing form would necessarily have a distinct body.
This is also not the case, for it is the same as the previous argument.

Although all things possessing form (*rūpa*) are causes for differences in the body, there are instances where other causes are lacking and thus the body does not differ. That is to say, within the desire realm and the first dhyāna, there are various differences in the causes that produce effects—namely, manifest action (*vijñapti*), non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), vitarka, vicāra, and multiple consciousnesses—and therefore those forms serve as causes for differences in the body.
However, because the Ābhāsvara deities and others lack such causes, although they possess the cause of form, their bodies are uniform.
One cannot claim that those [mental factors] are the cause for the body being distinct; for if one were to do so, one would not admit that the body is distinct because it possesses form.
Nor can one say that because attention (*manasikāra*) is able to produce visual consciousness, one must not admit that the eye and visible forms serve as its conditions.
Furthermore, one should not, on the grounds that the eye arises from karma, refuse to admit that the eye and so forth have causes such as the eye itself.
Nor should one, on the grounds that a sprout arises from a seed, refuse to admit that water, fertilizer, and so forth are its causes.
Therefore, one should not raise such an objection:
that because there is form, the bodies [of the gods] must differ, and thus the bodies of the Ābhāsvara gods and others would necessarily be different.

Furthermore, it is also illogical to claim that the Ābhāsvara gods must lack diverse perceptions simply because their bodies in that heaven do not differ; for the mind experiences both aversion and aspiration toward meditative concentration, just as it is said regarding the causes of pleasure.
Furthermore, the statement that perception is different is intended to dispel doubt.
Specifically, it means that if one asserts the body is one, then perception ought not to be different, because the mind follows the body.
To dispel the doubt within this context that perception follows the body, it is therefore stated that perception is different.
The meaning of this statement is to show that the minds of the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven do not follow their bodies, distinguishing them from other gods.

As for the remark that the perceptions (*saṃjñā*) of the various Brahmakāyika gods must be diverse because their bodies in that heaven are different—this is indeed logically correct; however, it is said that their perception is "one" (*ekasaṃjña*) in order to demonstrate that at the beginning of the kalpa, they all arose from a single cause and gave rise to a single conceptual grasping.
Therefore, the previous explanation regarding the term "a portion of the gods" (ekadeva) also includes the Brahmakāyika gods, with the sole exception of those who arise at the beginning of a kalpa.
The intent of this statement is to show that their perceptions are actually different; it is only from the perspective of their limited object of focus that they are said to have "one perception."
Because form (*rūpa*) is thus established as a distinct cause, the expression "possessing form" (*rūpin*) carries profound significance and utility.

Sentient beings possessing form who have diverse bodies but a single perception are like the Brahmakāyika devas; that is, those who first arise at the beginning of a kalpa, which constitutes the second station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Why is this so? Because at the beginning of the eon, when the Brahmakāyika devas first arose, they collectively conceived this thought:
"We have all been miraculously born as emanations of Mahābrahmā."
At that time, Mahābrahmā also gave rise to this thought:
"All these Brahmā-pariṣads were born through my transformation.
For what reason did the Brahmā-pariṣads collectively give rise to this thought?
This is because he perceives that the Brahmā King’s location, physical form, and supernormal powers are all superior;
furthermore, he observes that Mahābrahmā already existed previously, while the other gods were born only later.

He is unable to see those who have passed away from the higher realms; for although he develops the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives based on the first dhyāna, he cannot comprehend the objects belonging to the higher realms.
For what reason, then, does Mahābrahmā also give rise to this notion?
Because the assembly arises as soon as he first conceives the thought, they consider themselves his emanations.

This is not because they perish quickly; nor is it because they are ignorant of the principle of how karmic fruits are induced; nor is it because they perceive their own physical forms, stature, power, lifespan, majesty, and so forth, to be superior to those of the other members of the assembly. For these reasons, although the bodies of the Brahmā-paryanka and the Brahmā-rāja differ, they give rise to a single conception.
Do the Brahmā assembly not say:
"We were born from him"?
Yet the Great Brahmā King says:
"You say, 'I can produce them,' yet your perceptions differ; how then can you claim they are one?

This objection is unreasonable, because both the Brahmā-pariṣad and the Brahmā-rāja maintain that they were produced by a single cause, or because the perception regarding the created beings is identical for both.

Some say that in this context, the term "Brahma-parṣadya" (the assembly of Brahmā) refers solely to those who share a single perception, and not to the Great Brahmā King himself; for that sutra merely speaks of them as being "like the gods of the Brahma-parṣadya," and a single person, such as the King, cannot be designated as an "assembly."
Although those beings later attain wise awakening and give rise to different perceptions, their name was established based on their initial state; therefore, they are said to have "one perception.
Because the king followed the consensus of the multitude and acquired the name "One-Perception," that heaven may be collectively named "One-Perception."

Regarding the phrase "difference in body": it was previously stated that because those gods have manifest actions (*vijñapti*) and other causes that produce distinct results, sentient beings are established as having distinctions.
As the Sūtra says, the Brahmakāyika gods had this thought:
"We have previously seen such sentient beings living for a long time," and so on, until they formed a wish:
"How might we cause other sentient beings to be born into our own category?
When they correctly give rise to this aspiration, we are then born within that same category.
Where did the Brahmakāyika deities previously see the Brahmā King?
Other masters say:
they resided in the Ābhāsvara Heaven and, having passed away from that heaven, were reborn here.
Since they have passed away from that realm and been born here in this world, how is it that they can remember those past lives without having attained the second dhyāna?
Who says they have not attained the second dhyāna?

If they have attained it, they should have abandoned craving for the first dhyāna; how then could they still give rise to the view of rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) regarding the first dhyāna?
It arises only after they have regressed—what fault is there in this?
Is it not the case that there is no falling back (parihāṇi) in the realm of form (rūpadhātu)? Some say:
there is no obstacle to falling back for those who have just been born [there].
Other masters say: "While abiding in the intermediate state (antarābhava), one previously saw Brahmā.
This is not reasonable, for the Sūtra states that one sees him because he has long resided in the world.
Because those gods are currently undergoing birth within that heaven, and since the necessary conditions are not lacking, they cannot remain there for long.

It should be said that the Brahmakāyika gods reside in their own heaven and have previously seen the Brahmā King; this is because they saw him when he first took birth after passing away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

This refers to when the various Brahmā assemblies first descended to be born, they beheld the Great Brahmā King’s majestic radiance so intensely brilliant that, though they felt deep reverence and longing to approach him in person, they were unable to advance due to the pressure of his awesome spiritual power.
As time thus slipped away, a long period elapsed; later, exerting himself with single-minded devotion, he drew near to behold [the Buddha]. Upon arrival, they all together formed this thought:
"We have seen him before," and so forth, as described at length.

That is to say, when they see the Great Brahmā King from nearby, they are able to recollect and know the events they previously witnessed; furthermore, they can clearly understand that prior to the birth of the various subordinate beings, there was only the Brahmā King and his mental aspirations.
Alternatively, it may be that he previously saw the Brahmā King while in the Ābhāsvara Heaven and now, seeing him, remembers it.

That is to say, in the past, while in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, he saw the Brahmā King dwelling alone in a lower realm; knowing the King’s wish to dwell together with his assembly, he felt compassion and manifested a transformation-body of the first dhyāna, causing the manifested beings to attend upon the Brahmā King as companions. In the brief moment it took for this manifestation to arise, his own merit was exhausted; his life ended, and he was reborn in the first dhyāna heaven below.

The body and mind of Mahābrahmā, as well as the phenomena he emanated, were all objects of the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) of the first *dhyāna*; seeing them now, he immediately gave rise to the recollection of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*). Therefore, those Brahmā-hosts thought:
"We have seen this before," and so forth, as extensively described.
Other masters say:

The eye-consciousness that arises within the second dhyāna and takes the Brahma-world as its object is subsumed under the factors of the first dhyāna stage; therefore, one is now also able to recollect that consciousness through mindfulness.

Some say: Those gods of the Brahmakāyika realm do not undergo the suffering of the *marmaccheda* (the severance of the vital points) during gestation; because they thus possess mindfulness without forgetfulness, they remember such things as what they saw in their previous lives.
There are beings with form who have a single body but diverse perceptions, such as the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven; this is the third station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Here, by mentioning the latter, the former is included; one should know that this fully encompasses the second dhyāna.
If it were not so, under which consciousness-dwelling (*vijñānasthiti*) would the Parīttābha and Apramāṇābha heavens be subsumed?

Since those two possess the characteristics of a third consciousness-dwelling, there is no basis for saying they are not included within the consciousness-dwellings. Therefore, one should know that here the various consciousness-dwellings are explained by citing and manifesting the underlying principle; they are not merely as the literal words suggest.

In those heavens, there are no distinct bodily forms produced by causes such as manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*); therefore, it is said that their bodies are "one," meaning their physical forms and colors are identical.

This signifies that the deities dwelling in the same place have no difference in appearance. However, in the *Anuruddha-sūtra*, the Venerable Anuruddha stated that among the Ābhāsvara deities and others, differences in height and excellence or inferiority of body can be perceived.
This statement is made based on a specific location; it does not mean that there are physical differences among the bodies of the gods within a single heaven.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"In the Ābhāsvara Heaven, there are times when the gods gather together, and while their bodies differ, their radiance is identical."

This teaching states that the bodies of the various devas are distinct from one another; it does not say that their forms, colors, or features differ. Therefore, there is no contradiction with this sutra.
Some say: the term "Brahmapārisadya" (Assembly of Brahmā) refers to the Ābhāsvara Heaven, because its wondrous radiance surpasses that of the lower heavens.
In the second dhyāna, because the two perceptions of joy (*prīti*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) appear in a state of mutual confusion, it is said that "perception is diverse" (*saṃjñā-vicitratā*).

According to tradition, when the gods of that heaven grow weary of the faculty of joy belonging to the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*), they give rise to and manifest the faculty of equanimity belonging to the preparatory stage (*sāmantakabhūmi*); and having grown weary of the faculty of equanimity belonging to the preparatory stage, they give rise to and manifest the faculty of joy belonging to the fundamental stage.
For example, when people encounter various foods—whether plain or rich—their feelings of attraction and aversion increase alternately.

The Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) cites a sūtra to explain the meaning of "diversity of perception" (*saṃjñā-nānātva*): he states that among the gods newly born or long-established in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, there arises a mixture of two perceptions regarding the kalpa-fire—namely, fear and fearlessness—and it is for this reason they are called "those with diverse perceptions," not because of a mixture of the two perceptions of joy and equanimity.
If that were so, the third dhyāna should not be described as "having a single perception" (ekasaṃjñaka) on account of the perception of pleasure.

What is the distinct reasoning whereby the third dhyāna is called "having a single perception" due to the single perception of pleasure, while the second dhyāna is not called "having diverse perceptions" (nānātvasaṃjñaka) because of the intermingling of the two perceptions of joy and equanimity?
Therefore, what he has said may at first glance seem worthy of recording; yet upon careful examination, it is not sufficient to be relied upon as authoritative.
Regarding this point, the Elder (Sthavira) makes the following statement:
"In the third dhyāna, because there is no perception of fear at all times, it is said that the perception is one."

The scriptural citations he employs are the same as those of the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrāntika); however, upon careful examination, his words do not accord with the "abiding of consciousness" (*vijñāna-sthiti*).

Both this [interpretation] and the previous explanation are logically untenable; for if consciousness abides with joy and pleasure therein, it is established as an "abiding of consciousness"—how then can one say that the name "abiding of consciousness" is established based on a perception of fear?

On this very basis, it is taught that the various evil realms, the fourth dhyāna, and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are not included among the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*); the reasoning for why this must necessarily be so shall be explained hereafter.
The Elder also says:

"The various evil realms and so forth are not causes for the abiding of consciousness; that is to say, the term 'abode of consciousness' (vijñāna-sthiti) signifies where consciousness delights in dwelling.
As it is said:
Those places where they cause the minds of beings to dwell with pleasure are called stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*);
those that are not unwholesome places and the like, which do not cause the minds of beings to dwell with pleasure therein, are therefore not stations of consciousness.

Since it has already been stated that if consciousness does not find pleasure in abiding within them, they are not "stations of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*), then how could the perception of fear—which causes consciousness not to find pleasure in abiding—be called a station of consciousness?

If those perceptions of fear were established as stations of consciousness despite their ability to cause consciousness not to find pleasure in abiding, then your own argument that evil realms and the like are not causes for being stations of consciousness would suffer from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, because the perception of fear cannot possibly arise [there], the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven should not be said to have a single perception.
How is it known that such a perception does not arise for them?

It is because it has never been stated that they possess this perception; that is to say, there is nowhere it has ever been taught that the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven see the destruction by water below them and yet do not give rise to fear.

Perhaps they might argue that because the water does not rise upward, there is no concern regarding being swept away; thus, they have no fear. But if they fundamentally lacked any concern or anxiety, from what could their perception of fear possibly arise?
If one were to claim that there is even the slightest doubt regarding this, then the "Universal Purity" (*viśuddha*) would not be identical in name and conception.

Therefore, it is only by relying on the correct principles of the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma-yukti*) that the identity or difference of names and meanings is properly established; the logic of the Dārṣṭāntika school cannot be maintained. Thus, the wise should discern what is excellent and follow it.
There are sentient beings possessing form who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Universal Purity Heaven; this is the fourth station of consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "uniform in body," the explanation of its meaning is as previously stated.
Because there is only the perception of pleasure, it is called "one-perception.

The bliss of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven is tranquil and subtle; beings therein constantly experience delight and never give rise to weariness. Therefore, there is no basis for the intermingling of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), and thus the name "one-perception" is established based on this alone.
Is it not the case that there are also differences in perception among those in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven? As the Sūtra says:
"The devas of this Śubhakṛtsna Heaven experience a tranquil feeling of bliss, which is not like that of other Śubhakṛtsna devas."
This "difference in perception" (saṃjñā-viśeṣa) reveals that within pleasant feeling itself there are internal distinctions, as there is no separate feeling [apart from it].

While all conditioned phenomena differ from one another, even within a single category there are variations such as inferior grades; however, one cannot establish a difference in perception based on these.
Therefore, based solely on the single perception of pleasure, the establishment of "one-perception" (*ekasaṃjñā*) is logically unshakable.

Within the first dhyāna, it is said to have "one perception" because of its defiled perception; this is because one gives rise to the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) as a cause for that which is not a cause.

In the second dhyāna, it is said that "perception is diverse" because of the presence of two types of wholesome perception, and because the two feelings manifest in alternation through the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

In the third dhyāna, it is said that "perception is uniform" because of the presence of neutral perception, as only the single, uniform, and tranquil feeling of ripened pleasure (*vipāka-sukha*) manifests.
The lower three formless realms (ārūpya) are named individually as in the Sūtra; they are the three stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti).
These are called the seven.
What are the three formless realms?

It refers to those sentient beings who are formless; because they have transcended all perceptions of form, because all perceptions of resistance have vanished, and because they do not attend to perceptions of diversity, they enter the sphere of infinite space and dwell fully endowed with the base of infinite space, just like the gods of the Heaven of Infinite Space. This is the fifth station of consciousness.

As for the sentient beings of the formless realm, because they have completely transcended all the spheres of infinite space, they enter the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwell fully therein; like the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, this is the sixth abode of consciousness.

The formless sentient beings, having transcended the entirety of the sphere of infinite consciousness, enter into nothingness and dwell fully in the sphere of nothingness, just like the gods of the Sphere of Nothingness; this is the seventh station of consciousness.
Now, one should reflect:
Is the initial mention of "formless" (ārūpya) not indeed redundant?
For the purpose is already fulfilled by the statement that one has "transcended all perceptions of form" (rūpa-saṃjñā).
This criticism is not valid, for there is a distinct meaning [to be understood].

Sentient beings in the form realm (rūpadhātu), although free from the defilement of desire, still possess the ideation of desire; both its possession (*prāpti*) and its active manifestation (*samudācāra*) can be observed occurring simultaneously.
Do not give rise to such a doubt on this account:

that although non-material sentient beings lack material defilement, they must still possess the accomplishment and active manifestation of the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*). Therefore, it must be said that non-material sentient beings have completely transcended all perceptions of form; for the term "desire-perception" (*kāma-saṃjñā*) refers specifically to perceptions bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-saṃjñā*).
Is it not the case that by stating "one transcends all perceptions of form," both the state of being "formless" and the "transcending of perceptions of form" are accomplished?
This too is unreasonable. Some have said:
Since there is also form within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
the initial statement that it is "formless" is intended to demonstrate that there is absolutely no form within the formless realm;
the subsequent statement that one "transcends all perceptions of form" demonstrates that there are no perceptions of form whatsoever in that realm.
Since both of these statements possess their own specific meaning and function, one might ask:
"If those born in the formless realm also possess the perception of form, would not the statement 'transcending the perception of form' be meaningless?
This objection is unreasonable, because [the scope] has already been distinguished.
This means that because the preceding distinction specifies that perceptions bound to the desire realm are called "desire-perceptions," the same applies to form-perceptions;
since it is impossible for one born in the formless realm to also possess form-realm perceptions, this does not constitute a valid objection.
Alternatively, those perceptions of form may not manifest at all; even if one explains it in terms of taking form as an object, there is no contradiction in meaning.
As for "transcending all perceptions of form," this is because both the perceptions and the active manifestation of craving and defilement are transcended.

Regarding the term "perception of form" (rūpa-saṃjñā): it refers to the perception of the form realm (rūpadhātu), or specifically the perception belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna; because it takes the forms of its own or other levels as its object, it is called the perception of form.
"All resistant perceptions have vanished" means that all perceptions associated with the five consciousnesses have ceased.
Because the perceptions produced based on the resistant sense-faculties take only resistant objects as their domain, they are called "resistant perceptions."

When one attains freedom from desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), all conceptualizations involving sensory resistance (*sapratigha-saṃjñā*) associated with the two types of consciousness shall vanish, because there is no possibility for them to manifest again once one has been born in the higher realms.

When one attains freedom from attachment to the first dhyāna, although the various conceptualizations involving resistance associated with the three consciousnesses are indeed obscured, they do not cease entirely, for they may occasionally manifest again when one is born in a higher realm.
When one attains freedom from craving for the fourth dhyāna, all that was previously active shall become obscured, because in the formless realm there is no possibility for it to manifest again.
Regarding "not attending to diverse perceptions," this means one no longer attends to them so as to give rise to diverse perceptions.
The perception of distinct characteristics is called the notion of diversity; what does this mean?

It refers to a perception that operates with respect to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of its object, such as form (*rūpa*); because this acts as an obstruction to the abandonment of craving for form.
Now, by not attending [to them], one causes this perception of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) that is currently active to accord with the departure from desire.

Other masters say: "If a perception is able to take both the material (*rūpa*) and the immaterial (*arūpa*) as its objects in their entirety, it is called the 'perception of differentiation' (*nānātva-saṃjñā*)."

Now, by not attending to this perception and instead attending solely to the perception of the formless as its object, one transcends both the formless and all perceptions of form; thus, it is entirely reasonable that [the term "formless"] applies to both.
In this context, what dharmas are called "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*)?
They refer to the five aggregates (*skandha*) or four aggregates associated with those [realms], because consciousness delights in dwelling with attachment therein.
Other masters say:
Only those things categorized as sentient beings receive the designation "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*), for so it is stated in the Sūtras.
In order to clarify the objects upon which the various consciousnesses dwell and adhere, the Sūtras speak of the seven abodes of consciousness.

For this reason, other places are not included among the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), because in those places consciousness is subject to impairment; thus, consciousness does not delight in dwelling or adhering therein.
What are these other places?
This refers to the various evil realms, the fourth dhyāna, and the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
How is it that consciousness is subject to impairment therein?
It is because the factors that impair consciousness exist within those states.
What are the factors that impair consciousness? They are as follows:

in the various evil realms, there are intense painful sensations that can impair consciousness; in the fourth dhyāna, there is the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*); and in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there is the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), which can destroy consciousness so that its continuity is severed.

Furthermore, it is said that wherever sentient beings in other places delight in coming to dwell, and upon reaching which they no longer seek to depart, that is called a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
In the various evil realms, both of these conditions are absent.

In the fourth dhyāna, the mind constantly seeks an exit: ordinary beings seek to enter the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), while noble ones (*ārya*) take pleasure in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Since the gods of the Pure Abodes delight in realizing cessation (*nirvāṇa*), and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is dull and inferior, it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Some say: If consciousness is grasped by the power of craving and dwells therein, it is called a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
All evil realms, the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and so forth, are places where beings dwell through being grasped by the power of karma.

The non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) and those at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) maintain their abiding therein through the force of views and grasping; therefore, they are not included among the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Other masters say:
there are three kinds of sentient beings, namely: those who delight in sense objects, those who delight in pleasure, and those who delight in perception (*saṃjñā*).
Those who delight in and cling to objects are humans and the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Those who delight in and cling to pleasure are those in the lower three dhyānas.
Those who delight in and cling to perception (*saṃjñā*) are those in the lower three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The designation "abode of consciousness" (vijñānasthiti) is established only in these [seven] locations; since the others lack these three [factors], they are not abodes of consciousness.

As the masters of former generations have transmitted in their lineage: if a location possesses consciousness that is to be abandoned by seeing, abandoned by cultivation, and that which is not to be abandoned, it is designated as an "abode of consciousness"; otherwise, it is not subsumed under the category of an abode of consciousness.

Is it not the case that humans in the desire realm and the six heavens of the desire realm lack untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*), and thus should not be considered abodes of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*)?
