He [the opponent] claims that at a single location, both the color of the mirror and its reflection are seen appearing before one; however, two material forms (*rūpa*) cannot coexist in the same place because they depend upon different primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Furthermore, when the forms and shapes of objects on both banks of a narrow river appear as two reflections simultaneously in the same location, those standing on the two banks see them clearly from their respective positions; yet, never is there a case where two colors are seen together in one place. Thus, one should not claim that these two colors arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, shadow and light have never coexisted; yet we have seen a mirror suspended within a shadow, with the distinct image of light appearing clearly upon its surface. One should not, on this basis, claim that both arise simultaneously.

Some say that two things cannot coexist in one place; they claim that the mirror's surface and the reflection of the moon are considered two distinct entities because they are seen from different distances, just as when observing water in a well.
If they were indeed produced simultaneously, how could they be seen separately?
Therefore, one should know that these images do not exist in reality according to the principle;
yet, through the power of the conjunction of various causes and conditions, they are seen in this way, for the differentiation of the functional capacities of all phenomena is difficult to conceive.
Now, it is said that since those reasons cannot dispel the image, they are unable to resolve the objection concerning the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, as for their claim that two things cannot occupy the same location, this principle is incorrect, because both a wall and light can be perceived in the same place simultaneously.

Although the light on the wall differs in color from the large object upon which it depends, they can be perceived simultaneously in the same location; thus, one cannot deny that the light exists on the wall.
By this analogy, it is known that the mirror-image and its basis coexist; therefore, what [the opponent] has stated does not constitute a reason for negating the existence of the image.

If it is argued that there is no fault because light depends upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the solar disk, this is also logically untenable, because the tactile sensation of heat, like the light, can be perceived in close proximity.
Furthermore, the color of sunlight would then have no causal basis for its support, since you admit that the supported (the quality) can function apart from its support (the substance).

Thus, although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the basis for the two colors—the mirror and the reflection—are distinct, they can occupy the same location; therefore, the argument he advanced—that the two locations must be different because they rely on different primary elements—is rendered useless.
Furthermore, the locations of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) should be identical, because those [derived forms] have no separate basis apart from the diversity of the primary elements.

If it is argued that this fault does not apply because they possess resistance (*sapratigha*), then one should not use the difference in the supporting primary elements as proof that the mirror and the reflected color occupy different locations; for the resistance of both the primary elements and their derived forms is the same.
In principle, one should simply state that because both the mirror and the reflected image possess the quality of resistance (*sapratigha*), they cannot occupy the same location.
Since they do not occupy the same location, why say that the color of the mirror and the image are both seen appearing together in a single place?

If it is argued that because their locations are distinct they cannot be apprehended together, this is logically incorrect, as has already been stated previously; namely, that the color of a wall and its light occupy the same location and can thus be apprehended together.
However, because they possess resistance (*sapratigha*), in reality their locations are indeed different.
Although they occupy different locations, they can be perceived as identical, just as in the case of the principle of light and a wall;

the same applies to mirror images. For now, I shall explain to you the principle of their being perceived as identical: because the color of that image is extremely pure and subtle, it cannot obscure other colors. Since the mirror and the image are situated in immediate proximity, one gives rise to a conceit (*adhimāna*) and claims they are perceived in the same location. This is like the case of extremely pure and subtle substances such as mica (*abhrapaṭala*); when other intervening colors are in very close proximity, one likewise gives rise to a conceit and claims they are perceived in the same location.

Or, as previously stated, although the light-walls are distinct, they can be perceived at the same time and in the same location; according to that principle, this case should also be understood in the same way.

Furthermore, regarding the simultaneous and distinct perceptions of the reflected images of forms on both banks of a single body of water, such perceptions occur due to the differences in the conditions and causes.

This means that although multiple images do not arise upon a single body of water, their nature as clear and subtle is identical and thus does not obstruct one another; those for whom the conditions for seeing are assembled can perceive them, whereas if the conditions for seeing are lacking, they cannot be perceived.

Alternatively, there may be a single location where two visual cognitions converge; they observe the same form and image, and it is not the case that they do not see it together. This refers, for example, to an image seen by one person within a mirror, which others can likewise see at that very same spot.
If no distinct image arises within mirrors and the like that differs from other locations, what is the determining cause for why color and images are seen only within mirrors and such?
Or, when two sentient beings dwell separately yet observe the same object, why is it that one sees it while the other does not?

Just as when one draws patterns on a clean board using ash, after a long period of time has passed, even if one were to draw patterns anew upon a floor or wall, they would be visible or invisible depending on whether they face the light or are turned away from it.
It is not that two people cannot simultaneously observe a single color; rather, one uses this as an analogy to show that all other cases can likewise be seen together.
Do not conclude that because two people cannot simultaneously observe a single color, it follows by analogy that all other cases likewise lack common observation.
Therefore, what he has stated is not logically sound.

Furthermore, regarding his claim that light and shadow are mutually exclusive when occupying the same location, whereas the reflection of the moon and the surface of a mirror are seen in different places—this objection will be addressed concurrently within the subsequent refutation of the arguments established by the Venerable Rāma.

He asserts this: "The various images in mirrors and the like are not substantially existent; they have derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) as their nature. It is illogical for them to be produced either partially or universally.

That is to say, it is unreasonable to claim that the image-constituting derived matter is produced either by depending on a portion of the water, taking the lunar disc as its cause, or by depending on the water as a whole."
To rely on a portion of water is logically untenable, because there is no fixed cause and because it would follow universally;
yet to rely on it universally is also untenable, because it is perceived as having limited boundaries. Since both [positions] are irrational, it is not derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).

Furthermore, because shadow and light are mutually contradictory, it is said that if two mirrors are suspended within shadow and light, the two images of light and shadow will both appear simultaneously upon the mirror surfaces.
We clearly observe that light and shadow are mutually exclusive; if these two images were truly composed of derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*), they could not both be perceived in the same location.
Since both [the original object and its reflection] are simultaneously perceptible, it is not truly derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).

Furthermore, because their states differ and many [aspects] are perceived—namely, when the image of Devadatta appears in water or other media—it perceives various colors due to these differing states, such as blue, yellow, red, and white; if one were perceived, the others would not be. It is not possible for different colors to coexist in the same location.
If it were granted that they coexist, why would they not both be apprehended?
Therefore, we know that there is no distinct derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) therein.
Furthermore, there is no difference in their measurement, as movement is observed.
That is to say, when Devadatta turns his back and approaches a mirror, the reflection appears without any discrepancy [from the original], yet its functions of coming and going appear distinct.
Such a thing cannot possibly exist within a single derivative form (bhautika-rūpa);
yet since it is observed to exist, it is therefore not a derivative form.
Furthermore, it is because the locations of the images and their bases are seen to be distinct.
That is to say, when the image of the moon appears based on water and such, one perceives the image and its basis as being in different locations.
If the color of the image were produced upon the water itself, then one should not perceive the locations as being at varying distances.
However, because it perceives distance and proximity, it is not a derivative form (*bhautika-rūpa*). If that is so, what is it that is seen there?

Since visual consciousness arises conditioned by the primary object (*bimba*), just as visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms, so too does visual consciousness arise conditioned by the eye and mirrors or the like, with the primary object reflected in the mirror or similar surfaces serving as the cause. In reality, one sees the primary object, yet one speaks of seeing a distinct image.
Now, it is said that those various reasons cannot even dispel the image.

Furthermore, what they have asserted—that [the atoms] are neither partial nor pervasive—is irrational; for it is logically untenable that they are not produced from matter (*bhautika*), as the same principle applies to the others as well.

That is to say, if one asserts that eye-consciousness arises in relation to the eye and mirrors and so forth, directed toward the substance [of the face] reflected in the mirror and so forth, then these two types of critical inquiry apply equally, because neither a partial nor a pervasive [reflection] is logically tenable.
This means that seeing the original object again by relying on conditions such as a mirror—whether [the reflection] occupies one part [of the mirror] or the whole—is in both cases unreasonable.

First, it cannot be that one part of the mirror and so forth serves as the condition, because there is no fixed cause for this; rather, [the mirror] is able to manifest [the object] as a condition for seeing throughout all other locations.
Nor can mirrors and the like serve as universal conditions, because what is perceived therein is distinct and possesses spatial limitations.
Since both [theories] are irrational, they constitute erroneous attachments.

However, I do not maintain that the moon and so forth act as causes, nor that reflections arise based on a portion of the water and so forth; rather, when an object and its support face each other without interval, an image of the object arises within the support by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*).
How could a reflected image arise depending on only one part [of the reflecting surface]?
How is it known that the image arises pervading the entire basis?
It is observed that when many people stand side-by-side along the bank of a long canal, each sees the lunar reflection facing their own face.
If that is so, why does one not see many [reflections]?

It is because the conditions for such seeing are not assembled. Although moon-images arise in all places, they are seen only where the conditions for perception are present before one; thus, they are visible in one part and not elsewhere, as the lateral areas lack the condition of light and are obstructed by darkness.
Other masters explain:
The color of a reflected image is subtle; it can be clearly perceived when one is directly near it, but is difficult to see from a distance or at a tangent.
Alternatively, even as one moves gradually closer, one may perceive many [images]; therefore, one should not raise an objection regarding this matter.
If those [atoms] were many, then it would be impossible for a single [consciousness] to perceive many; thus, this cannot be raised as an objection.
If blue, yellow, and so forth could be perceived simultaneously, then these too would be identical to many-particled atoms (*paramāṇu*), because they would likewise be perceivable simultaneously.

However, as for the observation that the lunar image has spatial limitations, this is because its underlying substance (svabhāva) has limitations; the manifested image must necessarily conform to its supporting substance.
Alternatively, when a substance without limitations serves as the condition, an image without limitations arises upon the water, just as the reflection of the sky appears blue upon the water.
Therefore, because the primary object (svabhāva) has spatial limitations, there is no logical fault in the fact that although moon-images arise everywhere, they are perceived as having limitations.

Alternatively, as for the claim that one sees the characteristics of the primary object appearing before one by taking mirrors and the like as conditions, this is unreasonable whether [the mirror] acts as a condition partially or universally.
However, since we perceive the essential nature [of the reflection], one must certainly admit that mirrors and the like serve as its conditions.
The same applies to the production of the image; why then trouble yourself with such objections?

Furthermore, their claim that shadow and light are mutually contradictory and thus cannot coexist in the same location—by which they seek to prove that the image does not exist—is also unreasonable, for it is not what we accept.

This refers to the two images that appear when two mirrors are suspended within the light of a shadow; these are not real shadows or lights like material form (*rūpa*), because their tangibility cannot be apprehended.
If this is so, what is it that is clearly perceived?

This means that following two substances—a wall and so forth, and light and shadow—there arises within the surfaces of two mirrors a reflection of light and shadow that is not in contradiction with them; it is not, however, the actual color of the light or shadow.

Just as the body of a sentient being’s image is not itself a sentient being, so too the substance of the reflection of light and shadow is not itself light or shadow; thus, although they appear in the same location, they do not contradict one another.
Furthermore, according to their own tenets, a reflection is not a real entity; since it lacks substantial reality, what contradiction could there be?

It is impossible for that which has no substance to be said to be contradictory or harmful. Therefore, even regarding the meaning of "contradiction" as they conceive it, such a contradiction does not exist; thus, the reasons they have stated are neither accepted by either party, and their claim that light and shadow are mutually contradictory is untenable.
If there are things that should not occupy the same location, what is the meaning of this statement?
It means that if light and reflections were substantially real, they would necessarily be mutually exclusive and could not occupy the same location.
Since they do not exist in the same location, they should not be perceivable;
yet since both are indeed perceivable, it follows that the image is truly non-existent. Such is the meaning of what I previously stated.
Is it the case that only that which is truly non-existent is necessarily imperceptible?
Is there that which is non-existent yet can be apprehended, or that which is existent yet cannot be apprehended?

If that were so, then since it has already been stated that [the object] does not exist in the same location [as the cognition], it should be unapprehendable; what, then, is the use of this statement?
Even that which is non-existent in a particular location should be capable of being apprehended, because you maintain that even what is non-existent can be apprehended.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that not all non-existents are apprehendable, for there is no distinguishing cause [to differentiate them].
This means that because all things are signless and without distinction, it cannot be said whether they can or cannot be apprehended.

Furthermore, as for the claim that an image is not real because multiple [aspects] are apprehended due to differences in its states (*avasthā*), this statement is not contradictory even with respect to an image; for it is only regarding what exists that multiple forms can be apprehended through differences in state, whereas this is not possible regarding what does not exist.

Within the realm of objects that truly exist, there arise different cognitions of color—whether mistaken or correct—due to distinctions such as the clarity of the sense faculty, distance, and spatial location.

For example, when observing the truly existent colors of a spider’s web or a peacock’s tail-feather circle illuminated by sunlight, differences in spatial location and other factors result in distinct perceptions.
It is also like the perception of a whirling firebrand; therefore, one knows with certainty that the reflected color-form (pratibimba-rūpa) truly exists.
Because it is perceived as many distinct states, those [opponents'] reasons for denial are overturned and instead prove the existence of the reflection.

Alternatively, it is like the various colors appearing together in a lamp flame; because they occupy distinct locations that possess spatial obstruction, not every part of the visual field is perceived with total completeness.
Furthermore, it is like observing the curvature or straightness of an arrow; even if one perceives many such features, there is no fault in doing so.

Although there is not a single location where different colors coexist, when they are perceived, one speaks of them as being in the same place; this principle has already been fully discussed above, and therefore that logical objection regarding the reflection remains unrefuted.

Furthermore, as for their claim that the reflection is not real because it is observed to have movement without any difference in its dimensions, this reasoning is also incorrect, as has already been explained previously.

That is to say, although a distinct, real reflected color-form arises, the reflection necessarily conforms to its supporting substantial object; therefore, even though the dimensions are equal, in accordance with what is appropriate, three kinds of reflections—color, shape, and movement—arise upon the support in conformity with the substantial object itself.

Because the reflection conforms to its basis and its essential nature (*svabhāva*), although it lacks actual movement, it appears to come and go, and other movements and the three types of activity are perceived.

Such a characteristic of motion arises either because the essential nature is produced in uninterrupted succession as it moves toward another direction, or because the basis is shaken by the holder and others, or because the observer themselves is moving and perceives the reflection as shifting. Thus, these reflections do not exceed the dimensions or location of their basis; rather, they are seen to come and go and exhibit other signs of motion in accordance with the essential nature and other factors.
What contradiction is there in this regarding derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)?

To say that it is not derived matter because it is observed to exist [as such] is untenable; one cannot conclude that something is not derived matter simply because its characteristics differ from other derived matters. For example, although colors such as blue and yellow differ from one another, they are nonetheless derived matter.
Alternatively, because the characteristic of solidity would differ from heat and the other [elements], it would not be a primary element (*mahābhūta*); the same logic applies to other cases.

Just as the primary elements and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) are mutually distinct yet share the common nature of being "matter" (*rūpatva*), this [distinction] cannot negate the nature of derived matter.

Furthermore, the argument that what is seen—the image—and its basis are distinct, and therefore not derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), is also unreasonable; for the image of the moon in the sky arises in dependence upon the same water and other conditions as the actual moon.

That is to say, the sequential arrangement of the spatial element (*ākāśadhātu*) and that lunar disc, according to their respective proximities and distances, is the cause for the differentiation of the bases upon which the images appear.

It has already been established that the spatial element exists and is subsumed under the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*); therefore, it is capable of producing images respectively upon water and other surfaces together with the lunar disc.
Because the reflected image produced is identical to its substance, the perception and its locus appear to be distinct.
Alternatively, through such a conjunction of conditions for seeing, that which is neither distant nor near causes the perception to appear as distant or near.
It is like observing the patterns of painted brocades and embroideries; though there is no actual height, depth, or middle, one perceives such distinctions.
Because the moon is distant, the perception of its reflection is likewise so.
Just as with the full lunar disc, the reflection appears without any deficiency.
By this reasoning, those various arguments are refuted;
therefore, those arguments cannot dispel the image.
Nevertheless, following their own attachments, they speak to please the minds of the foolish, saying:
The essential nature serves as the condition for the arising of visual consciousness and so forth.
Such an intention is, in turn, refuted by the reasons previously stated by oneself;
namely, that it is illogical whether the mirror and other factors serve as conditions in part or universally.
Furthermore, what he has stated is merely based on deluded sentiment, for the original object does not exist within the mirror and such.
Since the object facing the mirror and so forth does not exist within the mirror and such, how could a phenomenon existing in one place be perceived in another?
The analogy is also illogical because it lacks the common property [of the subject].

That is to say, there has never been a case where a visible form resides in another location, yet produces visual consciousness by being perceived by the eye-faculty without being present before it; thus, it cannot serve as an analogy for how an original object might produce visual consciousness within a mirror or similar surface despite not existing therein.
If visual consciousness does not arise because its conditions are lacking, then it should not be cited as an analogy in this context.
How could there be such a case where that exists while this does not, such that it could be clearly apprehended here?
Furthermore, what he has stated merely expresses a deluded sentiment, because the reason (hetu) he establishes is not universally accepted (aprasiddha).
It is not universally accepted that visual consciousness arises based solely on the essential nature (svabhāva), the eye, and the mirror and so forth.
It is established by reason that visual consciousness arises only when the eye and visible forms serve as its conditions.
Since the image of the form appears clearly before one, it is known that what is apprehended is the image, not the essential nature itself.
Furthermore, this is logically necessary because the dimensions and color of the perceived image differ from those of the original object.
That is to say, in mirrors and the like, the dimensions of images such as mountains, rocks, ponds, walls, and forests are smaller than those of the original objects.

Furthermore, when holding a blade upright, one perceives the reflection of the face as long, whereas when held horizontally, it appears wide; thus, it differs from the substance of the original object.
Moreover, when observing the reflection of a face in oil or similar substances, the manifest color of the reflection differs from that of the original substance.
If the reflected image were identical to the original object, its shape and color should not differ from those of the object.
It is universally established in the world that whatever possesses a shape or color distinct from another is not that very thing.

I do not yet understand, Venerable One, what essential nature exists apart from shape and color, such that you maintain that although the reflected image’s shape and color are distinct, they are nonetheless identical in essence?

If you claim that this essence is neither identical to nor separate from the color and shape, yet is actually perceivable, then you are no different from the asura maiden who, through her skillful illusions, deceives the foolish.
If it is argued that although [the entity] is indeed that very same thing, it appears to be different due to being transformed by the power of conditions, this is also incorrect;
for the two [positions] are mutually contradictory and the reasoning is not established. Thus, it is not a sound explanation.
That is to say, if it were identical to that [prior state], it should not manifest as something different; yet since it does manifest as something different, it cannot be identical to that.

To claim identity while manifesting difference is mutually contradictory; furthermore, to assert identity while there is manifest difference is logically untenable, as it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

That is to say, one might as well maintain that the stages of old age and so forth are themselves the same as the earlier *kalala* and other embryonic states; for they appear differently due to the transformation brought about by the power of conditions.

Having exerted such effort [in argument], why not simply believe that a distinct image arises through the power of various conditions, rather than calculating that the conditions merely cause one to perceive the original substance again?

Therefore, the reasoning that asserts the essential nature [of the object] serves as the condition for the arising of visual consciousness and so forth is extremely weak and lacks the power to provide proof.

This is what the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) states here; thus, one should know that images do not exist in reality according to the principles of logic, yet the force of the conjunction of various causes and conditions causes them to be seen in such a manner.

Regarding the fact that the functional differentiation of the nature of all phenomena is inconceivable, why not say that the combined power of conditions such as a substance and a mirror can specifically produce an image? It is for this reason that it is seen thus.

Because the functional distinctions of the nature of dharmas as speech are inconceivable, and because the name "conjunction" is not a real dharma distinct from its constituents, how can one maintain that it possesses causal efficacy?
Furthermore, if one maintains that multiple conditions combine to form a single power, how can it be said that phenomena possess distinct functional capacities?

Therefore, just as there are distinctions in functional capacity, the eye, visible forms, and so forth act as conditions to separately induce distinct functional capacities, thereby causing visual consciousness to arise.

In this way, it is also due to a distinction in functional capacity that the substance, the mirror, and so forth act as conditions to specifically induce a distinct functional capacity, thereby causing the reflected image to arise.
From this, it is proven that reflections are substantially existent; otherwise, one would have to deny the existence of all phenomena altogether.
I have heard that there are those who categorically deny the existence of all phenomena; it appears that you, Venerable One, now share such a disposition.
If this is indeed the case, there is no need for us to engage in further discussion.
Furthermore, if that were the case, would those who deny the existence of a person in the intermediate state not also be able to say:

"The power of the conjunction of causes and conditions is inconceivable; although the interval between death and rebirth is vast and remote, it causes [existence] to arise in succession, because the functional distinctions of the capacities of various karmas are difficult to fathom."
Therefore, one should reflect carefully: if no image were produced upon a mirror or similar surface, how could it be clearly perceived as present before one, just like other real material forms?
Thus, the Abhidharmikas all maintain this view:

within the mirror and so forth, there exists a distinct image-form (*pratibimba-rūpa*), whose essence consists of a specific combination of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). This is because such an image arises in manifestation in relation to the particular object; it is just like the support for the original substance (*bimba*) from which this image is derived.

That is to say, within mirrors and the like, because the manifest substance (pratibimba) of the mirror and so forth serves as the supporting condition (ālambana-pratyaya), there arises an image that clearly resembles its supporting original substance and is distinctly visible; thus, the existence of the substantial object (ālambana-vastu) upon which the image depends is established as real.

With this image serving as the condition, images also arise clearly and perceptibly in other mirrors and such, following the substance upon which they depend; therefore, it is known that because the preceding image conditions the arising of the [subsequent] image, the thesis that it is substantially existent is established.
From this, one should know that all images truly exist; if these did not exist, what would serve as the objective condition for other images?

If it is argued that the original object (the *bimba*) which was the objective condition of the preceding image serves as that condition, this is also illogical, because the preceding object does not face the subsequent substratum (*āśraya*), and the subsequent image does not arise in accordance with the preceding object.

That is to say, the subsequent basis (the reflection) corresponds only to the preceding image and not to the preceding substance; how, then, can it be said that the preceding substance acts as its condition?

We do not observe that the substance of the mirror or other such objects ever turns away from the subsequent image while acting as a condition for the appearance of the image within the mirror and so forth. For this reason, it is established by logic that the subsequent image does not follow the preceding substance, but follows only the preceding image.

Therefore, the claim that the subsequent image reflected in a separate mirror or similar object merely takes the preceding substance as its condition and does not follow the preceding image, is nothing but a description of deluded sentiment.
Furthermore, how can it be known that the substance of the image actually exists?
Because an image does not transcend the characteristics of being substantially existent.
That is to say, whatever does not transcend the objective domain of visual consciousness and so forth is substantially existent, as will be established later.
Since an image can indeed be seen, we know it is substantially existent.
Furthermore, because it is obtained at certain times, if this [unconditioned] did not exist, it would either be invariably unobtainable at all times or always obtainable.

If you claim that its being obtainable or unobtainable at certain times is due to the presence or absence of the required conditions (*pratyaya*), then one must understand that other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are established as truly existing during the state when their conditions are assembled.

Furthermore, because it is the object of non-conceptual consciousness, it must be real; that is to say, while the objects of the five groups of sensory consciousness are universally established as being substantially real, since a reflection is also obtained by visual consciousness, one knows it to be substantially real.

Furthermore, it is like that which can obstruct the arising of other forms; that is to say, a reflected image can hinder the arising of another reflected image, because it obstructs the arising of others within its own location.
If a phenomenon possesses the aforementioned characteristics, one should know that the real existence of that phenomenon is fully established.
Since this image exists in this manner, we know it truly exists.
Did I not state previously that two images arise simultaneously in the same place upon a narrow stretch of water? How, then, can you say that one obstructs the arising of the other image?

Is it not as previously stated that, in cases such as light reflecting off a wall, although the locations are distinct, they are said to be the same location due to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and thus one should not hold them accountable?

Furthermore, because [the image] is apprehended in a separate location within the mirror—since within a single mirror and a single location two images cannot be perceived simultaneously—one apprehends the image differently according to the difference in conditions.
If it is argued that the principle of the nature of form (*rūpa*) is not established, this is also incorrect, because the principle is thoroughly established.
Furthermore, how is it known that the substance of the image definitely exists?
Because its mode of arising is similar to that of other existing phenomena (*bhāva*).

Just as it is universally established that dependently arisen phenomena such as consciousness and sprouts possess substantial existence, so too is this case; it is commonly perceived by the world to arise from a multitude of conditions. Therefore, one should know that the substance of the reflection definitely exists.
Just as other existent phenomena are established as definitely existing, arising from distinct conditions and possessing distinct characteristics, so too are reflections;
since they arise from distinct conditions and possess distinct characteristics, they must therefore definitely exist.
Because what has been stated here is similar to the arising of other existent phenomena (*dharmas*), its logic is fully established.
Furthermore, the claim that arising lacks a cause of its own is not tenable, as such a thing has never been observed.
As for the argument that a reflection is not an existent entity, this is also illogical, because I maintain that the arising of a reflection does have a cause of its own.
That is to say, I maintain that a reflection possesses a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), just as sprouts of consciousness and so forth arise from diverse conditions;

it is not that I maintain a reflection arises with a mirror and so forth as its cause, for I maintain that the arising of a reflection depends upon its own cause, while the mirror, water, light, and so forth merely act as the conditions for its apprehension.

For example, when one perceives motes of dust moving in a beam of light, this requires the interplay of light and shadow; yet neither the light nor the shadow is the cause of those motes, nor do those motes exist without a cause.
Alternatively, it cannot be said that what arises from different conditions is non-existent, because both similar and dissimilar forms of arising are equally perceived in experience.
For instance, how do we see fire and water produced from the sun, the moon, and a jewel? This case should be understood in the same way.
If it is argued that fire and water arise from their own seeds because both elements exist within the two gems, then fire and water should both arise from the two gems together.
Alternatively, the two gems should be able to produce wind and earth as well, since both elements are present therein, just as they produce fire and water.

If it is argued that because the two jewels increase in the two elements, they serve exclusively as the generative conditions for fire and water of their own kind, this reasoning is also incorrect; for both heat and moisture should be present in the two jewels, as they can be perceived therein.

If it is claimed that the two gems must be sustained by the light of the sun and moon so that the two elements increase and are then able to serve as conditions for the production of fire and water, then both kinds [of gems] should produce fire and water simultaneously, since both are equally sustained by the light.

If those two gem-spheres do not increase or decrease in their respective realms, for what reason does the condition of hot flames assist the sun-gem to produce fire, whereas the condition of cold flames does not cause the sun-gem to produce water?
One should likewise challenge the "moon-gem" (candrakānta) in this manner.
The principles of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are indeed difficult to realize, for when lime and water are combined, fire alone is produced.

That is to say, we observe in the world that stones are burned to ash, yet upon meeting water, they produce fire rather than water; this can only be described as the inconceivable nature of dependent origination. Aside from this, what faultless answer could there possibly be?
Furthermore, because the principle by which various color-aggregates such as rainbows arise from causes is extremely difficult to comprehend;
and because within a single color-aggregate, such as a diamond, various kinds of majestic spiritual powers are actually present.
Furthermore, because there are many extraordinary functions observed in activities such as healing humans, animals, and trees;

and because various types of entities undergo transformation upon encountering conditions such as heat, the sun, the moon, or incantations, they manifest as causes even though they do not combine with one another.
Therefore, the principle of dependent origination is in truth difficult to realize.

If one understands this correct principle of dependent origination, then one should not claim that arising occurs without its own cause; for since it has never been observed, a reflection certainly does not exist [as a substantial entity].

As for those who claim that while reflections may not be non-existent, they are nevertheless not derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*): such statements are coarse and superficial, and there is no need to labor over a rebuttal.

If they were not derived matter, they would not be objects of the eye; rather, one should simply say that reflections are not *exclusively* derived matter. Therefore, the existence of reflections as real entities is established by reason.

It is not logically established that one can thereby consistently establish the analogy of the discontinuous arising of a reflection for those who deny the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because it is accepted that a reflection arises from the uninterrupted continuity of a substance and its support with something intervening between them.

That is to say, the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the moon’s surface and so forth are by their very nature such that they can constantly produce pure and subtle primary elements; these reach everywhere without interval to the basis of perception, and wherever they are, they produce reflected images that resemble the original form.
If the basis is clear and limpid, the reflected image appears and is easily known;
if the basis is coarse and defiled, the image is hidden and difficult to discern.
Although the form of the image exists within the interval between the two, it manifests only where the basis is clear and subtle.
Just as sunlight and the like, though they arise everywhere, are visible only when appearing in dependence upon surfaces such as walls;
how then can it be known that a reflection arises in connection with its substance?
For where there is an intervening obstruction, no reflection arises.

That is to say, if a reflection could be produced in water and the like even when there is no continuity from the moon or other objects, then a reflection should also be produced when there is an intervening obstruction—just as your own tenet maintains that there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*), yet aggregates perish in one place and arise in another.

Furthermore, just as reflections manifest bending, stretching, bowing, looking up, coming, and going in accordance with their underlying substance, this proves that reflections arise in connection with that substance.

This cannot be cited as a metaphor to refute the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); for the metaphor is not invalid because the reflection does not exist, but rather because it lacks the same continuity as the substance upon which it depends.

If one were to claim that just as various reflected images perish according to their original substances, so too does birth-existence (upapattibhava) perish following the death-existence (maraṇabhava), then there would be the fault of a discontinuity in the continuum of sentient beings.

Furthermore, because the arising of reflected images resembles their original substances—since images of the moon and so forth are certainly similar to their originals—it would follow that from the death-existence of an ox or the like, only an ox or the like could be born.
Since this is not permitted, the analogy is therefore not equivalent.

Furthermore, because multiple images arise from a single substance: that is to say, when various images arise according to their respective substances and supports, it is possible for many images to be produced everywhere from a single substance in relation to numerous supports such as mirrors; however, it is not the case that from one continuum of aggregates at the moment of death, there arises a birth with multiple continua of aggregates existing simultaneously. Therefore, the image does not serve as an equivalent analogy in this context.

Furthermore, the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) do not constitute a continuum (*saṃtāna*), because the original object and its reflection do not belong to a single continuum; this is because the reflection and the original object exist simultaneously.
All things that constitute a continuum necessarily arise sequentially, whereas since the reflection and the original object arise together, they do not form a continuum.

Since the continuum of sentient beings proceeds without interruption from one moment to the next, dying in this place and being reborn in another, one should cite the growth of grain as the appropriate analogy; the reflection is not equivalent and thus cannot serve as a valid illustration.
Furthermore, because the manifested images arise from two factors—that is, because they are produced by two conditions—images come into being:
first, the original object; second, the mirror and so forth. This is clearly perceived in the world.
Birth-existence is not like this.
Why is that? Birth-existence is like a reflection, while death-existence is like the original object; what other dharma could there be that serves as the basis for the reflection?
Therefore, the examples cited are not equivalent to the phenomena [they illustrate].
Furthermore, the argument that semen, blood,
and so forth serve as the basis for the image is also illogical, because they are not sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding space and so forth, beings are suddenly born through transformation; what kind of basis could be grasped therein, such as that of a reflected image?

If it is argued that the continuity of the stream of consciousness alone accounts for the succession of death and birth, then what further purpose is served by postulating the continuity of material form?
This is not reasonable, because it is logically untenable that for those who have not yet attained freedom from craving for form, the mental continuum could continue to flow independently of form.

If the mind could continue to flow apart from form, then one undergoing rebirth would certainly not take up form; therefore, the mental continuum must necessarily be accompanied by form in order to be able to flow toward the place of rebirth.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"One is born bound and dies bound;
it is solely by being bound that one departs from this world for another."

The Noble One has taught that all those who have not yet abandoned craving for form are without exception bound by the fetters of form; therefore, there is no transmigration of the continuum of consciousness alone.

Furthermore, it cannot be reckoned that the original body of the previous existence itself continues on to the place of rebirth, for we clearly observe that at the place of death, the body perishes and is extinguished.
From this, it should be understood that there is a distinct form that travels; therefore, the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is established as a logical necessity.

If it is argued that one observes the mind functioning independently of form—such as when one dwelling here swiftly perceives the lunar disc, or when one dwelling in the capital city of Bāhlīka recollects the town of Pāṭaliputra—[this does not contradict our position].
The Blessed One also said:
"I do not see a single phenomenon that revolves as swiftly as the mind.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The mind travels far and wanders alone; bodiless, it slumbers in its cave.

In such passages as these, no distinct entity can be found existing in the interval. Likewise, although there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) at the juncture of death and birth, one nevertheless proceeds from this world to another world.

This is also unreasonable, because it has already been stated previously: that which grasps non-contiguous objects, and that which proceeds with equal speed [to its support], would mean—contrary to reason—that for one who has not yet abandoned desire for form, there is a mental flow alone, apart from form. As was said before, this is illogical.

Furthermore, the visual consciousness apprehends objects that are not in physical contact; while the mind abides here, it can apprehend the lunar disc from afar or think of another city at a distance, and there is no fault in this, for the mind does not travel to the place where the apprehended object or remembered object resides.
It has never been observed that [consciousness] arises apart from its basis, nor has there ever been an absence of fault in such a separation from its basis.
By this, the statement that "the mind travels far" and so forth is already explained.

Furthermore, it is the mind that swiftly revolves within its basis, object, and mode of activity; it is not the case that it merely moves toward the object and revolves with speed apart from its basis. Therefore, one should know that the mind does not flow and transmigrate toward the place of rebirth apart from the continuum of form (*rūpa*). From this, the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is established as a logical reality.

Thus, it has been clarified that a reflection arises in connection with its substance; therefore, the analogy [of the reflection] is not established because the places of death and rebirth are separated.
By this, the analogy of an echo is also refuted, because an echo is produced through a continuous transmission of sound across intervening objects, such as a mountain valley.

This refers to the primary great elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the original sound depends; these produce, in succession, subtle great elements that pervade the interior of the valley and so forth, and wherever they strike, they generate an echo resembling the original sound.
Although there is a continuous succession of sounds and echoes in the interval, it may not be heard because the particles are dispersed or too minute.
If, in the interval, one encounters mountains,
valleys, and the like, the sound can still be heard even when it has been accumulated.
How is this known to be so?
Because they are heard at different times.
That is to say, those who listen first hear the original sound, and only afterwards do they hear the echo produced by that sound.

If one were to claim that they are heard in uninterrupted moments, then because it would be difficult to discern the sequence between two such moments, one would likely give rise to overweening pride and claim they are heard simultaneously.
Yet this is not accepted as such; for one knows that within the continuity of sound there is a delay, and thus perceives it as being heard at a different time.

Since the continuity of sound proceeds in this manner through successive stages until it reaches a valley or similar location where an echo is produced, this further confirms that there must certainly exist an intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Is it not the case that your own school also certainly does not allow that the series of sounds successively enters the ear to be heard?
How then can you say that the series of sounds proceeds in succession, and only at a later time is the resonance produced upon meeting with conditions heard?
Your criticism is not valid, for I do not deny it.
That is to say, the continuous succession of sound is not what I deny;
rather, that it enters the ear and is heard is precisely what I do not allow.

Whenever there are primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as conditions for the production of sound, they all produce sound through mutual impact; however, sound can only be apprehended when it exists within the range of audibility.

Among these, one first apprehends the sound at the location of its original substance, and only subsequently hears the echo produced in a different location. Thus, there is no fault of [the sound] reaching the sense organ, as would be the case with the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

It is not that the sound-series itself continues and enters the ear to be heard; rather, because there was previously a sound at a substantial location that was heard, at a later time, when the substance has changed or is no longer in contact with the auditory faculty, one hears the resonance produced elsewhere.

If the ear could only apprehend sounds that arise in immediate proximity to it, one would not be able to hear sounds from distant locations; therefore, it is not the case that the sound-series enters the ear to be heard.

Nor is it the case that sounds do not proceed as a series, because sounds are heard from distinct locations at a distance, and because sounds are heard at different times and in different places. By this, the fact that there must necessarily be an intermediate [space] is established.
Other masters say:

Because there are differences in the conjunction of conditions such as wind, sound reaches [the ear] through successive transmission and, at the same time, does not depart from its substance; thus, both [types of sound] can be heard.
If this were so, the auditory faculty would be able to apprehend objects both proximate and non-proximate, which would result in the fault of contradicting your own tenet.
Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-three;
Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-four.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Four: The Analysis of Dependent Origination, Part Three, Section Four. Others further say:
Just as when one dies in the formless realm, there is no continuity [of matter] until matter arises in the desire or form realms.
Likewise, it should follow that when this death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) ceases, there would be no continuity, and that birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) would arise from nothing.

Thus, the analogy of the grain lacks the power to prove [the point]. Furthermore, this analogy contains an undesirable flaw (*aniṣṭa-doṣa*): namely, that the properties of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) ought to be identical. However, while seeds such as grain produce only sprouts of grain and the like, if this were so, a human being after death should only give rise to another human, and an ox after death should only give rise to another ox; therefore, the analogy possesses this undesirable flaw in this context.

Furthermore, since a sprout arises precisely where the seed perishes, it would follow that once consciousness and its associates have ceased within the eye-faculty, they would arise again in that very same location. Consequently, consciousness and its associates would be perpetually produced by a single faculty alone, rendering the ear and other faculties useless.

Furthermore, if within a single body consciousness and the other aggregates, having ceased, were to arise again in that very same place, then they would exist eternally, and the principle of death would be non-existent.

Likewise, if the *bhava* of death (maraṇabhava) were to cease in this location and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) were to arise in that very same location—such that each subsequent moment arises in the same place as each preceding one, until the cessation of the intermediate state occurs simultaneously with the arising of the next birth—then there would be no possibility of migrating to another life. In this way, the superior function of the intermediate state would be abruptly nullified here; thus, you have skillfully established such a metaphor that undermines your own school’s tenets.
All of this is unreasonable. Why is that?
Because for one who passes away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is born into the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is a continuity when the phenomena of form arise.

That is to say, when passing away from the formless realm and being born into the desire or form realms, it is precisely through the conjunction of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) at that location that the ripened form (*vipākavarṇa*) arises from karma to be experienced in subsequent lives; therefore, the arising of that form is not without continuity.

Alternatively, because the continuum as a whole proceeds without interruption—meaning that at the time of the final maturation in the formless realm, the four formless aggregates act as an uninterrupted and unbroken condition to trigger the arising of the aggregates that coexist with matter within the desire and form realms—the arising of that matter is not without continuity.

When one dies in the desire realm or the form realm and is reborn in the desire realm or the form realm, there is a vast spatial interval between the place of death and the place of birth; if there were no subtle entity to maintain continuity therein, how could death in the formless realm and subsequent rebirth serve as a valid analogy?

Furthermore, there is no fault of undesirability in this regard; for example, a single grain of rice serves as five causes—namely, the sprout, the husk, the cooked rice, and the ash—and likewise, a single continuum of a sentient being serves as five causes.
That is to say, a single grain of rice can serve as five causes; if it encounters favorable conditions, it then produces its own fruit.

Likewise, the continuum of sentient beings belonging to a single destiny (gati) possesses these five causes; if they encounter the convergence of such favorable conditions, they then produce their own fruit. Therefore, there is no fault of asserting that humans and others cease to exist [as individuals] and are merely born as members of their own respective classes.

Furthermore, there is no fault of seed and sprout arising and ceasing in the same location; for when the continuum of the seed gives rise to the sprout and so forth, although there is no interruption, it is not the case that there is no difference in location.
According to this principle, the same applies to internal phenomena; therefore, there is no fault of cause and effect being restricted to the same location.

This means that when the collection of seeds is in the process of disintegration, through the supportive gathering of conditions such as water, it can serve as the cause for the production of a gross and large mass of sprouts. At the moment the seed ceases, the sprout arises in another location; although the sprout grows and extends toward a distant place, there is no interruption in the continuous succession between them.

Just as external phenomena arise from seeds into sprouts through the principle of immediate succession rather than separation, so too do internal phenomena proceed in accordance with the continuity of the body and mind upon which they depend, without any logical inconsistency.

This means that at the time of death, the aggregate of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth, sustained by conditions such as the winds of karma, acts as the generative cause for the aggregate of primary elements that arises in the place immediately adjacent to death in the next birth. Karma alone cannot cause that aggregate of form to suddenly arise in a distant location without continuity; rather, that which is produced immediately adjacent to death is precisely the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). From this point, it proceeds successively toward birth in another region. In the interval between these stages, it neither remains identical to its prior state nor does it leap over it to reach the existence of rebirth (*upapattibhava*), just as sprouts and so forth gradually grow from seeds and so forth until they reach the fruit. Therefore, the citation of the analogy of grain does not contradict one's own tenet.

Furthermore, why labor so hard to forcibly deny the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? It has never been observed in the world that a collection of material forms (*rūpa-skandha*) arises in another location without continuity. We only observe things such as shadows, light, or flames arising in other places through an intervening continuity; therefore, it is not the case that the intermediate state lacks its superior function.
However, the power of the harmonious conditions for visual consciousness and the others does not transcend arising from distinct locations based on the body, as they possess no spatial location.
It is not the case that consciousness constantly arises and ceases while residing in a single sense organ within a single body; thus, the perpetual absence of death is already explained thereby.
Alternatively, since for one who dies the aggregates of the same class cease and the aggregates of a different class arise, there is no such fault.

Furthermore, in the case of a being born by transformation (*upapāduka*), the physical sense-faculties together with their bases—which are the results of karma performed in a previous life—suddenly cease at this location; immediately at this very location, other results of karma may suddenly arise. Thus, it is conceivable that the state of death is no different from what preceded it.

Regarding those who take birth in the remaining three realms: although the continuity of the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*)—which are the fruit of karma produced in previous lives—has ceased, one observes that their basis continues to evolve in a similar manner. This is because the subsequent material sense-faculties do not lack a basis, as they are the fruit of distinct karma; nor do they depend upon the previous ones.

From this it is proven that the faculties and their bases produced by other karma arise in a location adjacent to the basis where the preceding body’s faculties ceased; as these are obstructive phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*), they necessarily obstruct others in their own place of residence, preventing them from arising. Therefore, regarding this [state], there is no doubt that one will not die.
Others further say:

"Just as a measuring inchworm places its front leg and then moves its hind leg backward, so too, although the locations of death and birth are separated, one first grasps the next place and then relinquishes the former, thereby reaching another region; therefore, there is no need for an intermediate state (antarābhava) here."
The *Vibhāṣā* authors criticize this interpretation, stating:

"This explanation is utterly like the speech and meaning of common folk; for if it were so, there would be the fault that two sentient beings, two destinies, and two minds would proceed simultaneously."

Furthermore, the analogy of the inchworm does not establish the principle; for while that insect has no interruption within its body, it is possible for it to place its front part forward and move its rear part back as there is a spatial gap between them.

However, since there is an interval and separation between the bodies of the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) and the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), how could one possibly take hold of the body of the birth-existence?
Since birth has not yet been taken, how can death be relinquished?
It is not possible for the cessation of mind and mental factors to be established in a place where they do not exist, because the meaning of continuity is impossible apart from the body as its basis.
If it is claimed that there exists a form which serves as the basis for non-interruption, then the meaning of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is already established.
If it is claimed that one reaches the place of birth despite the interval between death and rebirth, then the analogy of the inchworm (*śalabhaka*) is inconsistent.
Others further claim: "Although the two states of existence—death and birth—are separated by an interval, they reach one another through a power similar to that of a mental impulse (*manojavitva*).
This too is not correct, because it is not what [our school] accepts.

If one were to pass away here and be reborn there as something other than this [continuum], with an interval of separation in between, it would follow that one must possess supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).
If that were so, this would have to be a specific variety of *saṃskāra*.
Indeed, it is so; however, because it is subtle, it is difficult to discern. One should not find it difficult to accept that this occurs within a single moment.

Therefore, the previous analogy of the grain is established as being free from error, because existence must arise through a continuous succession without interruption; thus, an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) definitely exists.
Furthermore, there is another reason why the intermediate state is not non-existent.
That which is observed to arise in immediate succession from moment to moment is so because it arises in immediate succession with respect to its location.
That is to say, as is commonly observed in the world, when appropriated matter arises in immediate succession from appropriated matter, it arises both momentarily and spatially without interval.

If birth-existence (upapattibhava) is material, and it is admitted that it arises immediately and without interval from the moment of death-existence (maraṇabhava), then its location must likewise be immediate and without interval.
However, such a principle does not exist; therefore, the doctrine of intermediate existence (antarābhava) is established.

If it is argued that just as when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the realm of form, the initial arising of form occurs by means of the former form being contiguous with its present location while having an interval of a moment, and thus continuity is achieved; then it should also follow that when dying and being reborn from a lower realm into the realm of form, there would be an interval of place despite the lack of an interval of moments.
This is also not the case, because it fails to understand the thesis.

That is to say, when one dies from the desire or form realms to be born in the formless realm, the place where the physical body ceases is not the same as the place where that very same physical body immediately induces the arising of a present physical body upon dying from the formless realm to be born in the desire or form realms; this is not our tenet. Therefore, in this instance, both the moment and the location are not proximate, and thus it should not be used as an analogy.
Furthermore, if moments arise in immediate succession, their spatial location is necessarily fixed; this is not due to the seed.

That is to say, those moments that arise without interval must necessarily arise in an uninterrupted spatial location; there is no such certainty for anything contrary to this. Therefore, the analogy proposed by the opponent is logically inconsistent.

Furthermore, the nature of being a cause is established only when other conditions conjoin, as this is what is observed in the present; thus, the doctrine of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is proven.
That is to say, it is commonly observed in the world that seeds can act as the cause for sprouts only when they conjoin with other auxiliary conditions.

Thus, when the seeds of consciousness produce a new existence with form, they must necessarily rely on external forms at the place of birth as conditions; therefore, consciousness is invariably conjoined with the forms of that place of birth.

It is not logical for a single consciousness to be simultaneously conjoined with both the body of the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) and the interrupted forms of the space between the places of death and birth; therefore, there exists an intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
If it is argued that there is no fault because that which is non-material has no place of abiding, this reasoning is also incorrect.

The statement regarding "no place of abiding" is based on the negation of the various consciousnesses abiding in their sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), just as one speaks of a person’s seat.

It is not that the principle of the conjunction of consciousness and form is entirely non-existent, for the sūtra speaks of the "consciousness-body," and another sūtra states that "consciousness is not separated from the body.

If it is argued that at death, the physical form acts as the direct cause [for the next life], just as the intermediate state (antarābhava) form gives rise to the form of the subsequent birth, this too is unreasonable.
Because the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) and the place of birth are separated, the former cannot function as a cause for the latter;

or rather, since external auxiliary conditions such as the physical elements of semen and blood would be separated from it, they could not provide any supportive efficacy. Therefore, there must be a distinct material cause of birth that unites with the semen and blood, and this is precisely the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, how is it known that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) definitely exists?
Because it can be perceived directly;
that is to say, the body of the intermediate state can be perceived before one's eyes by those with the pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Therefore, it is said that the bodies of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) can be seen only by those with the most pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Furthermore, the Venerable Aniruddha also said: "O Āyuṣmat!"
I observe that the manifestations of the Buddha are most numerous in their measure, unlike those of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Therefore, it is certain that the intermediate state is not non-existent.
Furthermore, because the holy teachings speak of the existence of the intermediate state; as the Sūtra says:
There are seven kinds of existence (*bhava*): namely, the five destinies of existence, karmic existence (*karmabhava*), and intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, because the sūtras speak of the *gandharva*, as the sūtra states:

"For one to enter the mother’s womb, three conditions must be simultaneously present: first, the mother’s body must be in a state of fitness at that time; second, there must be the union of the parents in sexual love; and third, the *gandharva* must be present."
Apart from the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*), what other distinct entity could be said to be "presently manifest" as a *gandharva*?

If you claim that these two sūtras are not accepted by me, it does not follow that they do not exist simply because you do not accept them; for there is no definitive reason that can serve as a valid proof such that whatever you do not accept must be non-existent in its essence.
Some say that the subsequent sutra should have stated:
"When *saṃkheda* (agitation) ceases, it manifests in the present.
However, the transmitters erroneously recited it as *gandharva*, because in this state there are no musical instruments.
This is not the meaning of the sūtra; for within this state, the preceding aggregates have already ceased, and thus there is no sense of "coming.
However, other sūtras state that the gandharva comes from the various directions—east, south, west, or north—as it is said in the *Aśvalāyanasūtra*:
"Do you know now?"
This gandharva appearing before us now—is he a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or a śūdra?
Has he come from the east, or from the south, west, or north?
Furthermore, it is said thus:
"Whichever clan [it belongs to], from whichever direction it comes, and as it now manifests—
since there can be no sense of 'coming' if the preceding aggregates have already ceased, what they say is based on their own speculative reckoning."
Furthermore, the worldly treatises state that the union of male and female is fully established through two causes and conditions:
first, the *gandharva*, and second, the *rākṣasa*.
Initially, it is because they naturally give rise to a craving for union; subsequently, it is because they are pressed by powerful external forces.
However, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) accords with the former sense; although that being lacks physical instruments [of pleasure], it is established as a *gandharva*.
Or perhaps these are merely conventional designations established according to worldly usage; why then trouble yourself with such stubborn attachment to them?

Even if that [other world] were not recited in this sutra, how could you still disbelieve such a scripture? For it says: "Whether you belong to this world, another world, or both, you shall be able to make an end of suffering within the intermediate state," and it further speaks of the time when one is about to die and about to be born.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"With my divine eye, I observe sentient beings as they are about to die and about to be born.

This expression "about to be born" refers precisely to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because [the being] has already passed away from this life but has not yet been born in that [future] one.

Some say that this statement refers to the ultimate state as being "distant," and thus uses the term "about to arise" with respect to that which has already arisen—just as one might say, "Where have you come from now, Great King?
One should likewise speak of "about to pass away" regarding that which has already passed away, because no distinguishing cause or condition can be found [to differentiate otherwise].

Furthermore, if that were the case, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would also be established, because it has already passed away from here but has not yet been born there; otherwise, to speak again of what has already been born would be redundant.

Moreover, the term "distant" is not used only in reference to the ultimate [end]; we observe that the term "distant" is also used for things that are merely remote, as when the Blessed One said to Śāriputra:
"Behold this boy who is now coming here."
By this definitive proof, it is established that the phrase "about to be born" does not refer to what has already been born, but rather designates the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, the *Sutra on Abiding* speaks of "mind-made" (*manomaya*) existence; for the Blessed One said to those who abide therein:
"At that time, when those sentient beings have already cast off this body and abide in the mind-made state, yet the subsequent class of bodies has not yet arisen."
I designate that at that time, one abides in a mind-made body (*manomaya*), possessing craving and grasping.
What is called "mind-made" refers precisely to the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*).
By this, it is proven that the intermediate state definitely exists.
There are those who, following their own arbitrary attachments, falsely interpret this sūtra, claiming that the term "mind-made" (*manomaya*) refers to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
They assert that when a friend who can dwell [in such a state] passes away, they transcend the realm of form and are reborn in the formless realm.

One might think that although they can be perceived by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), they cannot be seen; thus one asks the Blessed One about them, "If at that time those classes of sentient beings... and so forth, as explained at length.

As for the claim that "one class of bodies" refers to the bodies of the desire and form realms, while the term "mind-made" (*manomaya*) indicates their presence in the formless realm—this interpretation is irrational, as there is no definitive reason [to support it].
Furthermore, one should interrogate those who deny the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*):
this term "mind-made" (*manomaya*) refers to many meanings; how can you dogmatically insist that it signifies only the formless?
For at the beginning of the eon, this term was seen to apply to the realm of form, the formless realm, emanations, and the intermediate state alike.
I shall briefly demonstrate these points in their proper order.
As it is said, in that state there is a form-body produced by mind (*manomaya*), and all its limbs and members are fully complete.
Furthermore, it is said that such beings transcend the gods who subsist on coarse food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) and are born into a particular class of mind-made heavenly abodes.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said to Udāyin:
"Regarding the body of a mind-made deva, what do you think it is?
Do you not consider it to be called 'formless'?"
Furthermore, it is said that from this body, the mind arises separately, manifesting as another type of body that is material and mind-made (*manomaya*).
It is also said that immediately after this body has perished, such aggregates arise, which are material and mind-made.
Since "intentionally produced sound" (*abhisamcetayita-śabda*) refers to many meanings, how can it be definitively asserted that it denotes only the formless?
If you claim this is a statement from another source, the same objection applies; logically, it cannot be so.
This is because the Sūtras state that the former body has already been discarded and the subsequent one has not yet arisen.

Furthermore, their tenet is logically untenable; if they were to claim that the formless realm is "mind-made" (manomaya) for the sake of abiding there, then those beings should not be able to observe the desire and form realms by means of the supernormal power of the divine eye.

It is not possible for desire-realm or form-realm existence to arise apart from craving for form; if one were to observe the two realms with the supernormal power of the divine eye in order to seek those places of birth, one should not say that the formless realm is an "intentionally produced" abode, because such a place of birth cannot be definitively known.
This sūtra uses the expression "abiding in the mind-made body" (*manomayakāya*) specifically to demonstrate that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exists.
Furthermore, what sūtra serves as proof that the intermediate state is not non-existent?
It is because the sūtra speaks of the five types of non-returners (*pañca anāgāminaḥ*).
That is to say, the Blessed One taught:

there are five types of non-returners—first, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; second, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; third, those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion; fourth, those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion; and fifth, those who go upstream.
If the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) does not exist, how can it be called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state"?

If you claim that one is called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" because they attain parinirvāṇa between the two realms of desire and form, then since there is no intermediate state where one is born in those two realms, how could there be any sentient being who attains parinirvāṇa therein?

If it is claimed that there exists an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) among those [beings], this is logically impossible, as there is no authoritative scriptural statement (*āptavāda*) to support it.
That is to say, none of the schools possess a sūtra stating that an intermediate state exists; they rely solely on their own speculative calculations.

Furthermore, that position would entail the fault of over-extension; for it would follow that those born among the various heavens who attain parinirvāṇa while dwelling there should also be designated as "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadya-parinirvāyin) and so forth.

If you argue that just as one speaks of "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarābhava), one likewise accepts the establishment of both "intermediate existence" (antarā-bhava) and "existence upon birth" (upapatti-bhava), [we reply:]...

Although it is taught that there are those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra*) and so forth, one does not thereby admit the existence of a separate realm called "existence with exertion" (*sābhisaṃskārabhava*).
Likewise, although one admits the existence of a distinct intermediate state (*antarābhava*), how could this invalidate the name "heaven" (*deva*)?

To claim that [the intermediate state] does not lead to birth and so forth is also unreasonable; for while the three states such as "existence" (*bhava*) are established separately, there is no distinct function for [the intermediate state] apart from them.

It is not for the sake of abiding in those realms or attaining parinirvāṇa therein that these two—intermediate existence (*antarā-bhava*) and birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*)—are established with distinct functions.
