Furthermore, it is absolutely impossible to attain parinirvāṇa while abiding within the state of existence (bhava), because that state lasts for but a single moment.

It is not the case that establishing "existence-in-motion" (*gati-bhava*) and so forth as distinct categories serves any specific purpose for the system of the four existences; whereas the intermediate states such as birth (*jāti*) and so on are established as distinct names with their own specific functions within that system, the mere establishment of the four existences is sufficient for its utility. There is no need to laboriously posit other distinct names for existences.

If the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is established solely for the purpose of proceeding to rebirth (*upapatti-gamana*), why are birth (*jāti*) and the other [stages] not separately designated by the name "state" (*bhava*)?

If the intermediate state is established without reference to this specific function, yet you still grant it the separate designation of "state," then birth and the others should likewise be so designated, as there is no definitive reason for such a distinction.
What specific function does this intermediate state possess that justifies the designation "intermediate" (*antarābhava*), yet such a function is absent in birth and so forth?
Therefore, [the objection] is illogical.
Furthermore, since all established names correspond to their actual meaning, there is no room for arbitrarily establishing a different name here.
That is to say, one who attains parinirvāṇa through the diligent application of the path of preparation is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion" (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin);
if one attains parinirvāṇa without the path of preparation and without diligent application, they are called "one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion" (anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin).

It is impossible to establish another name for this; as for the "gods" (devas) you have established, they exist merely according to your own whim. Who would prevent you from arbitrarily establishing "gods of birth" (*upapattideva*) and so forth?
Therefore, this theory of false conceptualization cannot refute the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); thus, it is not non-existent.
Furthermore, how is it known that the intermediate state (antarābhava) definitely exists?
It is because the sūtra states:
"There are seven destinations for superior persons."

Regarding the aforementioned five types, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) are divided into three categories based on the distance of their location and the duration of time—namely, near, far, and intermediate.
For example, when a small spark from a piece of wood flies up, it is extinguished immediately upon arising; the first type of noble being (āryapudgala) is likewise.
For example, when a small spark of iron fire flies up and is extinguished upon reaching mid-air, such is the case with the second type of noble person.
For example, when a large spark of iron fire flies up and is extinguished before falling to the ground, such is the case with the third type of noble person.
If the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) did not exist, upon what would this [distinction] be established?
Since the separate intermediate state asserted by them does not possess these three categories of distinction regarding place, time, and type, their assertion is certainly irrational.

Some say that all those who sever the remaining afflictions during the interval of their lifespan are called "those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin). Because they attain parinirvāṇa upon reaching the stage of the realm (*dhātu*), or the stage of perception (*saṃjñā*), or the stage of vitarka, three categories are thus established.

This means that when one practices the preparatory application for abandonment while the afflictions remain in the state of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is called the "stage of the realm" (*dhātu-avasthā*).

Here, the intention is to show that the stage of the realm refers to one who possesses the seeds [of the afflictions] but they have not yet become active; this refers specifically to those of sharp faculties.
Once afflictions have arisen, one is able to diligently apply oneself to the preparatory practice for their abandonment; this is called the stage of perception (*saṃjñā*).
Here, the intention is to indicate that the initial activity of defiled perception is designated as the "stage of perception," which refers to those of medium faculties.
Having long been subject to the arising of afflictions, one is finally able to apply oneself with diligence to the preparatory practice for abandonment; this is called the stage of vitarka.

The intent here is to clarify that because the power of the afflictions causes the mind to seek variously toward its objects, it is termed the "stage of vitarka," which refers specifically to those of dull faculties.
The World-Honored One, based on this "path of the virtuous person" (satpuruṣagati), analyzed the intermediate parinirvāṇa into three types.
Although this is a skillful interpretation, the meaning is actually not so; for if that were the case, the "present-life parinirvāṇa" (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin) would not exist.
Furthermore, the stage of non-inquiry (*avitarka-bhūmi*) is also said to include those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), as stated in the Udāna verse:
“Gathering all the noble sages together: ten for each of the four dhyānas, seven for each of the three formless attainments, and only six for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”

In this verse, it is stated that those in the three stages from the second dhyāna upward also attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyī), because all who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state have severed the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni).

It cannot be said that one reaches the state of "with vitarka" from a stage that is "without vitarka," nor is there a deficiency of any of the noble destinies (*satpuruṣagati*) within the three higher realms.

Furthermore, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) would then have to include those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), because such individuals attain parinirvāṇa during the interval of their lifespan.

Furthermore, the Bhagavat, Śāriputra, and all others should be included within the category of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas in their final existence born in Tuṣita Heaven, and excluding those sentient beings born in Uttarakuru; for other sentient beings may indeed attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.

Furthermore, whatever else they may maintain is all inconsistent with the analogies of the parched grain, fire, and so forth; for if the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) were excluded, distinctions of distance—whether near, far, or intermediate—as well as temporal differences, would all fail to be established.

You merely give rise to this false attachment out of greed for your own views and aversion toward the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), rather than by relying on the correct principles of the holy teachings; therefore, it is established that the intermediate state truly exists.
Under which view is the denial of existence and non-existence in the intermediate state subsumed?

It is a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) arising primarily from delusion regarding the continuity of cause and effect; for various sūtras state that to deny the existence of beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*) is a false view.
Having already extensively established that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not non-existent, we should now further consider:
toward which realm of rebirth (*gati*) is it headed,
and what is the form of the intermediate state that arises?
What is the doubt here?
It is because [the self] would incur the fault of being either identical to or different from birth, and of having a single karmic fruit coexisting with them. Why is this so?

If birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) and intermediate existence (*antarā-bhava*) were the fruit of the same karma, it would contradict the sūtra which states in detail: "There is a person (*pudgala*) who has severed the fetters of birth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*) but has not yet severed the fetters of arising (*abhinirvṛtti-saṃyojana*)," and so forth; for all karmas necessarily arise from afflictions (*kleśa*).
Karma, like the afflictions, ought to have distinctions; thus, the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) should differ from that of the destination it is heading toward.

If the karma and its fruits for the intermediate existence and the birth existence were each distinct, by what cause would these two fruits necessarily arise in a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority?
Among these, there is karma not subsumed under categories such as that to be experienced in the present life; therefore, it must be exclusively indeterminate.
Furthermore, one observes that although the past karma of humans and others differs, their physical forms may be similar and without distinction;
likewise, there is karma that is identical yet yields different results. Thus, doubt may arise.
Is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the various realms of existence identical to or different from the form of the realm to which one is destined?
To dispel this doubt, the verse says:
Because it is projected by the same karma, It has the same form as its future original body.
"Original existence" refers to the period prior to death, situated after the moment of birth.
The treatise states:
There are two kinds of karma: first, projecting karma; second, completing karma.
In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), two types of existence arise: the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) is the same, while the completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*) is different.

Because the projecting karma is the same, the form of this intermediate existence resembles the state of the future primary existence (*mūlabhava*), just as the impression produced by a seal does not differ from the original image.

If that were so, within the belly of a single pig or similar creature, the intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of all five destinies could arise simultaneously, for it is possible for five children to die at the same time, each destined to be reborn in one of the five destinies.
Since the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of hell manifests before one, why does it not burn the mother’s womb?
There is no such fault, because the fires of hell burn only those sentient beings who possess transgressions, and not those who have not accumulated the karma that brings about rebirth there.
It is a settled principle that those who have not yet attained the fruit [of the path] may be incinerated by the fires of hell.
Furthermore, since that intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not constantly being burned, how could it be made to burn within the mother’s womb?

Even those who have already been born in hell are not constantly burned, as when they briefly visit the *ūrdhva-kalpa* (the intermediate hells); how much less so is this the case for those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? Some say:
"Even if it were granted that the intermediate state is constantly burned, it would be invisible and likewise intangible because the body is extremely subtle; therefore, the objection is irrational."
Although the intermediate beings (*antarābhava*) of the various destinies reside within a single womb, they do not touch or burn one another because they are shielded by karma.
Although the size of an intermediate being in the desire realm is like that of a child of five or six years of age, their sense faculties are clear and sharp.
Other masters say:
"The intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm is equal in size to that of a person in the prime of life at the time of their actual birth. Others say:
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a Bodhisattva is indeed such as this, but that of other sentient beings is not likewise.

The intermediate state of a Bodhisattva is like the time of his prime in years; his physical form is perfectly complete, endowed with all the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Therefore, when he dwells in the intermediate state and is about to enter the womb, he illuminates hundreds of millions (*koṭi*) of the four great continents and so forth. This is for the sake of auspicious omens favorable to the region, causing the Bodhisattva’s mother to see, within her dream, a white elephant calf entering her right side. Having already abandoned rebirth as an animal for ninety-one *kalpas*, how much more so in his final existence would he still appear as a white elephant?

Some say that all intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*) enter through the birth canal and do not enter the womb by breaking through the mother’s abdomen; therefore, among twins, the one born first is smaller and the one born later is larger.
In reality, however, the intermediate state being enters the womb according to its own inclination and does not necessarily require the birth canal, as there are no obstructions.

However, due to the power of karma, they are constrained within the womb; the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is complete in size like that of the actual birth-state. Yet, the body of the intermediate state of Akaniṣṭha is sixteen thousand *yojanas* in length, and there is no place in Jambudvīpa capable of containing it, for the great void is extremely vast.
The body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) has a color like that of a mani jewel or the light of a lamp, because it is without obstruction.
The intermediate state being of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is born together with clothing, because a sense of shame and modesty (*hrī-apatrāpya*) is predominant.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), for the most part there is no clothing because of a lack of shame (*ahrī*) and dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*); this is with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas and the nun Śvetā, due to the power of their original vows (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*).
Other masters say:

"With the sole exception of this nun, who gave monastic robes (*kaṣāya*) to the Saṃgha and made a supreme vow, from that time forth in every lifetime she possessed natural clothing that never left her body, changing according to the occasion; even until the time of her final parinirvāṇa, she wrapped her corpse in these very robes for cremation and burial, and when her remains were collected to erect a stūpa, the shape of the robes remained wrapped all around it."
All wholesome dharmas arising from a bodhisattva are exclusively dedicated toward unexcelled enlightenment.
We, who follow this school, maintain that both [theories] have their own explanations.
As for the "original existence" (prakṛtistha) to which it is likened, what is its essential nature?

This refers to the totality of the aggregates existing prior to the state of death (*cyuti-bhava*) and subsequent to the state of birth (*upapatti-bhava*), which is generally designated as "existence" (*bhava*). Although this encompasses the nature of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), it is analyzed into four distinct stages based on the preceding and succeeding phases of sentient beings:
first, the intermediate existence (*antarā-bhava*), the meaning of which has been explained previously;
second, the existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*), which refers to the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi-ksana*) within the various realms of existence.
Third is the existence of the fundamental state (*mūlabhava*), which refers to all positions prior to death, excluding the moment of birth;
fourth is the existence of death (*cyutibhava*), which refers to the final moment of consciousness.

If one has not yet attained freedom from craving for form, the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) will necessarily arise immediately following this [death] existence; thus, within the single stage of a lifetime, four distinct states are differentiated.

Is it not the case that, since the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is the very first among all states of existence, the name "fundamental existence" (*mūlabhava*) should refer to the intermediate state? It does not refer to the intermediate state because [the latter] immediately precedes [birth], and the three existences—birth and so forth—are not its effects.

If a state were to exist, it would necessarily arise without interval; thus, the intermediate states may be termed "prior existence" (*pūrvakālabhava*). This designation is established in relation to the various states of other births, not by establishing this name in reference to the three stages within a single birth.
Furthermore, this existence arises immediately from that existence; because it arises from that, it is established as having the name "fundamental" (*maula*) in relation to it.
Moreover, the name "fundamental" designates the primary destination, whereas the other three are not so, and thus do not receive this name.
The size and shape have already been explained; the remaining points shall now be analyzed.
The verse says:
Those of equal purity see with the divine eye; They possess supernormal power, speed, and complete faculties.
Without resistance and unalterable, they feed on fragrance and do not remain long;
with inverted minds, they pursue the realm of desire. Those born from moisture or by transformation are stained by their respective odors and locations;
the gods have their heads upward, while the three [lower classes] are horizontal, and those in hell have their heads turned downward.
The treatise says:
Within this context, what kind of eye perceives this intermediate state body?
Is it perceived by the eyes of its own kind, or by the pure divine eyes?

That is to say, the intermediate state body can be seen only by eyes of the same class and by the pure divine eye obtained through cultivation; it cannot be observed by those of a different class or by an impure divine eye, because it is extremely subtle. Even the divine eye acquired at birth cannot perceive it, let alone others being able to see it, for it is taught that only one possessing an extremely pure divine eye can see it.

Some say that the intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods each perceive themselves and those preceding them in their respective order, excluding those that follow.
Is it possible for anyone to obstruct the movement of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
Even the Buddhas, at their highest level, cannot obstruct it, because among all the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the power of karma is the swiftest.
Since the intermediate state possesses the most rapid power of karmic movement, the Sūtra says:
Among these, the power of karma is the most preeminent; no sentient being and no application of effort whatsoever can obstruct or suppress it.

To traverse space with mastery is the definition of *ṛddhi* (supernormal power). Because this power is derived from karma, it is called "karmic ṛddhi. Because the force and function of this power are swift, it is termed "expeditious."

Among these, there is one who possesses the most rapid power of karmic supernormal knowledge (*karmarddhi*), such that no other among the various supernormal powers can surpass its swiftness; it is on account of this that it is said to have the strongest karmic force.
Furthermore, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) possesses all the faculties (*indriya*) appropriate to the respective level (*bhūmi*).

Although it is said that the intermediate state (antarābhava) possesses a form similar to that of its future birth, because its initial maturation (*vipāka*) is most excellent and sublime, and because it seeks existence, it is never devoid of sense faculties.

It has been heard that when a glowing red iron ball is broken apart, one sees insects dwelling within it; thus, it is known that the non-obstructive nature (*apratighatva*) of the intermediate state is established.
"Resistance" (pratigha) refers to obstructive resistance; because this [intermediate state] cannot be obstructed even by such things as vajras, it is called "non-resistant" (apratigha).

This realm, destiny, and station cannot be altered: that is, one who is dying in the intermediate state of the form realm (*rūpāvacara-antarābhava*) will certainly not be reborn in the intermediate state of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-antarābhava*), nor can the reverse occur, because both this [intermediate state] and the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) are projected by a single karma.
It should be understood that the same applies to the non-reversal of the destination.
In this regard, does the intermediate state (antarābhava) body subsist on edible food?

For instance, in the desire realm, the intermediate being feeds on fragrance; according to whether its merit is great or small, the fragrance may be pleasant or foul. It is for this reason that it receives the name *gandharva*, as the meanings of verbal roots are not uniform.

Although this term *arbuda* correctly refers to the act of going (*gati*), it also carries the sense of "eating" therein; because they feed on fragrance (*gandha-bhakṣa*), they are called *gandharva*.
As for the short vowel in the pronunciation, it is like the cases of *śakuntaka* and *karkaṇṭaka*, where the elision of a syllable is not considered an error.
Some say that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) sustains its body by means of odors; because it moves seeking odors, it is called a *gandharva*.
For how long does such an intermediate state remain?
This intermediate body certainly does not remain for long.
"If the conditions for rebirth have not yet converged, how can it be that he will not remain long?
The Venerable One replied: "According to the common course of things, he will not remain long."
Those for whom the conditions have not yet converged may remain for a long time, because their life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not projected by a separate karma.
Other masters say:
this lasts only a short time, because within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one constantly seeks birth.
If one is fixed and immovable regarding both parents, then even if residing in a distant land, karma will cause a swift reunion with them.
If one is movable regarding either parent, then despite being extremely pure and virtuous and loathing desire, defiled conduct will arise toward another object.
Whenever one gives rise to a defiled meditative absorption, it causes it to arise even at an improper time;
or, it may arise within a similar class of other beings, such as when the body of a donkey resembles that of a horse.

It is not because there is a distinction in the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) upon which one relies that the single karma projected for birth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is lost; for although the conditions for birth may differ, that which is projected remains one.
Even if it were granted that one undergoes a subsequent birth of a similar type, there would be no fault, as even a slight similarity of type suffices.

Furthermore, if the realms, destinies, and locations do not undergo a complete transition, there is no fault even if there are slight differences in their characteristics; for while the karma that determines the realms, destinies, and locations does not shift, other external conditions for birth are observed to differ, as in the case of the *māṣa* and *yava* seeds. What fault is there in this?
Alternatively, the distinctions among the types of karma are infinite, such that only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to fully comprehend them.
With what kind of mind is the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) properly linked?
It is with a defiled mind, just as it is with the mind at birth (*upapattibhava*).
Regarding the process of linking existence (*pratisandhi-bhava*), what is the method?
While abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one rushes toward the place of birth due to mental inversion, hastening toward the objects of desire.

By the power of past karma, the faculty of sight (*cakṣur-indriya*) arises; although situated at a distance, it is able to see the parents at the place of birth engaged in union, thereby giving rise to an inverted mind.
If one is to be born as a male, he conceives affection for the mother and aversion toward the father; if a female, it is the reverse.
By reason of these causes and conditions, once the child has been born, he or she becomes partial toward either the mother or the father accordingly.
Therefore, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states as follows:
"At that time, the gandharva manifests one of two mental states, namely, either craving or aversion."

Due to the arising of these two kinds of perverted thoughts, he imagines that his own body has united with the beloved one; when the impurity of the hated one is discharged into the womb, he considers it his own and experiences joy and consolation. This state of generating joy is called "entering the mother's womb. Taking about two or three drops of the semen and blood left at the final moment, they form the *kalala*; the semen and blood support each other and abide without interval. Thus, the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) cease, and the aggregates of the birth-state (*upapattibhava*) arise.
If it is a male, he dwells in the womb leaning against the mother’s right flank, crouching with his face toward her back;

if it is a female, she dwells leaning against the mother’s left flank, facing her abdomen. This is because of their habitual engagement with left and right matters and the power of their past individual discernment.

In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are those who are neither female nor male, because the body of the intermediate state is not deficient in its sense faculties; yet after entering the mother’s womb, they may become non-males (*paṇḍaka*).
How can the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the rootless *kalala* serve as the basis for the arising of the various material sense faculties?
Who says that the sense-faculties depend upon those primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
The primary elements of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) depend upon the primary elements of the *kalala* as their support, and are able to produce the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*).

That is to say, the intermediate state and the primary elements of the *kalala* are mutually dependent; at the stage of final dissolution, the primary elements of the intermediate state take those [elements of the *kalala*] as conditions and causes to draw forth primary elements different from the previous ones. Those different primary elements can act as the support for the sense-faculties, just as a seed produces a sprout only by depending on the earth and so forth.
If that is so, for what reason does the sūtra state:
"The impurity of the mother and father produces the kalala; it arises depending on impurity"?
There is no fault of contradicting the sūtra, as other masters explain:
The great elements of semen and blood serve as the basis for the sense faculties during the stage of transformation;

that is to say, the preceding intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is devoid of faculties, ceases simultaneously with the arising of the subsequent state, which possesses faculties, in the same manner as the principles of the cessation of a seed and the arising of a sprout.
Their position—that when a material phenomenon arises, it does not arise as a continuity of material form from the intermediate state—is contrary to the principle of a sprout arising from a seed.
It is illogical for insentient matter to serve as the seed that gives rise to sentient beings, because their continuities are distinct.

When both sentient and insentient matter cease together, and subsequently sentient matter arises, it is illogical to claim that the insentient serves as its cause while the sentient does not; therefore, the previous explanation is superior in terms of reasoning.
This explains that among the four modes of birth in the desire realm, those born from a womb or an egg are defiled by the place of scent;

as for those born from moisture or by transformation, they are born because they are defiled by scent. That is to say, by smelling from afar the fragrance of their place of birth, they immediately give rise to craving and attachment, proceeding there to undergo rebirth. According to what is appropriate to their karma, the scents may be pure or foul.

As for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), they are born because of attachment to a place; that is to say, observing from afar the place where they are to be born, they immediately give rise to craving and attachment and go there to undergo birth. Depending on what corresponds to their karma, the place of existence may be pure or defiled.

Those who are born in the hells do so likewise by the power of karma. Some perceive their bodies encountering cold rain and freezing winds; others perceive their bodies beset by hot winds and fierce flames. As they suffer the unbearable agony of being tormented by heat or assailed by cold, they long for warmth or coolness in the hope of removing their distress. Seeing the blazing, intense flames of the hot hells or the whirling, driving cold winds within the cold hells, they immediately give rise to craving and attachment, rushing forward with their own bodies to throw themselves therein.
Other masters say:
By seeing one's own former companions at the time when that karma was first created which brings about rebirth there, a mind of longing arises and one rushes toward that place.
Regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) proceeding to whichever realm of existence, what is its appearance as it hastens to the place of birth?
Furthermore, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of those in the heavens moves upright, ascending like a person rising from a seat with their body straightened.
The intermediate states of humans and the other three realms of existence move horizontally, like a bird flying through the air toward another continent.
In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of hell, one falls head-first and feet-upward into its midst.
Thus a verse in the *Gāthā* says:
"Fallen into hell, Feet above and head directed downward."
"Because of slandering the sages, one delights in tranquility and practices asceticism.
Regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one should further investigate:
for what reason does the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) lack an intermediate state?
Because that karma cannot project an intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
For what reason is that karma incapable of doing so?
Because one is born there only after the fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been severed.

Karmic actions must be assisted by afflictions (*kleśa*) in order to project a fruit; karmic actions devoid of afflictions lack the power to project. This is because although Arhats possess various karmas, they cannot project a future existence (*bhava*).

Some say: If a stage possesses both coarse and subtle karma, one can have an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within that stage; however, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is the subtle but no coarse.
"Coarse and subtle karma" refers to material and non-material karma, or karma such as the body and so forth, or the ten paths of action (*karmapatha*).
This, moreover, should be further interrogated: for what reason is it that an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exists only when the realm possesses both coarse and subtle karma?

Herein, we perceive this intention: the intermediate state is subtle, whereas the realm of rebirth is coarse, because within the realm of rebirth, there is a greater abundance of completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*).

Furthermore, because the limits of the lifespan in the various realms of rebirth may be fixed, there are cases where one experiences the results of subtle *pūrṇa-karma* during the state of existence (*bhava*), and cases where one experiences the results of coarse *pūrṇa-karma* during the state of existence; since both types of karmic results are present within the Desire and Form Realms, there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
This is not the case for the Formless Realm.
Other masters say:
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is established in order to manifest the shape of the destination toward which one is heading;
however, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no place and no physical form.

If that were so, one would die and be reborn within one's own corpse at the very spot where the body-faculty (kāyendriya) ceases, without going to any other location; what, then, would be the use of an intermediate state (antarābhava)?
This [intermediate state] is established to represent the form toward which one proceeds, because either one of the two previously mentioned conditions must exist.
This defense is unreasonable, because the shape that indicates the destination has no superior efficacy within the birth-state to which it leads.

If the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) had already arisen, it could indicate the destination; however, since the shape would be useless [once the state has arisen], it does not arise—so how could it possibly indicate the destination?
Therefore, it is shown that the destination itself is not the cause for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
However, the Sthavira says:
"If one were to undergo rebirth at the very place where life ends, then the intermediate state would not exist."

That statement is not correct. It is not the case that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is only projected at the moment of death; how then can it be said that if one is born in the same place where one died, the intermediate state is not projected?

One has certainly already performed and accumulated karma that brings about the intermediate state during a previous time. Now, what could act as an obstacle to prevent the fruit of the intermediate state from arising and manifesting?

Alternatively, those born in the intermediate state (antarābhava) share the same karmic fruit; furthermore, the intermediate state is the very beginning of a single lifetime. If the intermediate state did not exist, birth would not continue, just as it is impossible for the *kalala* to arise without the *arbuda*, since the latter is the initial stage of that development.
If it is argued that birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) is the first moment while intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) is not, such a claim need not be cited;
for it is entirely devoid of meaning and consists of nothing but empty words, since both the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the process of arising (*abhinirvṛtti*) remain uninterrupted in that state.
You must also admit that for one who has not yet severed the fetters of birth (*jāti-saṃyojana*), existence (*bhava*) may or may not arise, because there is no differing cause.

It is not that the aggregates (*skandha*) arise through some separate function; rather, the arising of the aggregates necessarily depends on a cause—the non-abandonment of craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—and this is precisely the cause for the arising of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
If there were one destined to die within the womb, what need would there be for the arising of the sense faculties, except by the power of causes?

If it is argued that this case should be like those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarābhava), who lack karma for rebirth in a full existence, and thus those who are born at the very place of death likewise lack karma for an intermediate existence—this analogy is not equivalent. Just as the state of birth (upapattibhava) necessarily depends upon the intermediate state, the intermediate state does not depend upon the state of birth; therefore, the analogy is not equivalent.

Therefore, for all those who have not yet abandoned craving for the fourth dhyāna, if they have already performed the karma that fulfills the existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*), they will necessarily also be able to perform the karma that fulfills the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); this is established as a matter of course and need not be explicitly stated.

There may be those who are non-returners (anāgāmin) because, through the power of the antidote (pratipakṣa), their continuity is suppressed and thus the fetters (saṃyojana) do not manifest; these individuals can only produce the completing karma (pūrṇakarma) for the intermediate state (antarābhava).
If they lack the antidote and both [types of] dharmas fall away, they have no capacity to obstruct the manifestation of the two types of fetters.

Therefore, for one who has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*) must necessarily arise based upon the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).

Even if one were to undergo rebirth at the very place of death, one must certainly admit that the intermediate existence arises immediately after the existence of death (*mṛtyubhava*), and only then does the existence of birth arise immediately after the intermediate existence.

Furthermore, this intermediate state (*antarābhava*) possesses definitive characteristics: namely, there is no one who has not yet abandoned desire for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) who arises in existence without first passing through the intermediate state; nor is there an intermediate state that is not the fruit projected by the same karma as the birth-state (*upapattibhava*) it leads to; nor can an intermediate state enter a mindless state (*acittaka*) to become one who realizes liberation through both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) with the body, nor can it give rise to a mundane mind of a different category (*visabhāga*).

While abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there is no possibility of transforming one's faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), nor is there the capacity to abandon afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), nor to abandon the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the desire realm.
All such categories should be investigated and analyzed.
Do all intermediate state beings enter the mother’s womb with a perverted mind? No, they do not. Why is that?
The Sūtra states: "There are four ways of entering the womb.
What are these four?"
The verse says:
One is fully aware upon entering; Two or three are aware of both staying and exiting;
Four are aware throughout all stages; And those born from eggs are always without awareness.

The first three types of entry into the womb—namely those of the Wheel-turning King and the two kinds of Buddhas—occur because their karma and wisdom are both preeminent; the remaining four types of birth occur in the reverse order.
The Commentary says:

There are sentient beings who have extensively cultivated merit and wisdom; therefore, at the stages of death and birth, they are sustained by the power of mindfulness. Their mental conceptions are clear and distinct, and their correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*) remains undisturbed. Among them, some enter the womb with correct knowledge, some remain in the womb with correct knowledge as well as entering it, and some exit with correct knowledge as well as knowing both entry and remaining.
The use of the word "also" (兼) is intended to show that a subsequent state must necessarily be accompanied by the preceding one.

There are sentient beings whose merit and wisdom are both meager; they lack correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*) during the stages of entering, abiding, and emerging [from meditative absorption]. If they lack correct awareness in the preceding stage, they will certainly do so in the subsequent stage as well.

These four modes of entering the womb as described herein fully encompass all instances of entering the womb; this sequence follows the requirements of the verse, though the order in the Sūtras is not thus.
These four types have been explained thus far with reference to birth from a womb, which possesses distinctions between the states of being ignorant and non-ignorant.
As for those born from eggs, they are always devoid of consciousness throughout the stages such as entering the womb.
How can those born from eggs, having emerged from an egg, be said to "enter the womb"?
This designation is established with reference to what is to come, and thus there is no error; it is like the common worldly expressions "making bracelets" or "weaving clothes."
Alternatively, it may be said that those born from eggs and so forth have previously entered a womb; since this refers to the past based on the present, there is no fault.
One should understand that herein, based on whether perception (*saṃjñā*) and resolve (*adhimukti*) are inverted or non-inverted, one speaks of "correct" or "incorrect" awareness (*saṃprajanya*).

It refers to those sentient beings who possess perverted perceptions and understandings; among them, some have karma and cognition that are impaired. At the moment of entering the womb, they give rise to perverted perceptions and understandings, seeing great winds and rains, or scorching heat and bitter cold, or the clamor and intimidation of a vast army. Consequently, they see themselves entering dense grass, thick forests, leafy caves, or straw huts, or throwing themselves beneath trees and walls.

Among these, there may be cases where, although there is no error in the karma itself, an error arises through cognition such that one develops inverted perceptions and understandings while entering the womb; one perceives oneself entering a magnificent garden, ascending a flowered palace, or sitting and reclining upon various exquisite couches and seats.

While dwelling [in the womb], one perceives oneself as dwelling therein; upon emerging from that state, one perceives the body as exiting from this place. In these three stages, one lacks correct awareness (*asaṃprajanya*).

If sentient beings possess unerring perception and understanding, they know for themselves as they enter the womb that they are entering it; while dwelling and emerging from the womb, they know for themselves that they are dwelling and emerging. Thus, in these three stages, they are able to maintain correct awareness.
The *Catuḥprakāra-garbha-avakrānti-sūtra* should be explained according to this meaning.
For what reason is one who enters the womb without clear comprehension necessarily without clear comprehension during the stages of abiding and emerging?
It is logically impossible for one who is inferior in awakening to be superior in delusion;

there is no room for such a principle. This means that when one is about to enter [the meditative state], even if one’s limbs and sense faculties are complete and undiminished, and are strong, vigorous, and sharp, one still lacks correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*); how much more so when, at the time of abiding in or emerging from it, one’s limbs and faculties are impaired, deficient, weak, and dull—how could one possibly possess correct awareness? There is no logical possibility for this.
One who possesses correct awareness at the time of abiding is so because they are drawn by the single power of the superior cause of correct awareness at the time of entering the womb.
One who possesses correct awareness at the time of emerging is so because they are drawn by the dual power of the superior causes of correct awareness at the times of both entering and abiding.

Furthermore, there are three different ways of entering the womb, namely those of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*), and a great enlightened one (*mahābuddha*), in that order.
Regarding the first way of entering the womb, this refers to a wheel-turning monarch, who enters with full awareness, but neither remains nor exits with such awareness.

Regarding the two types of entry into the womb: the first refers to the Solitary Realizer (*pratyekabuddha*), who possesses correct awareness during the stages of entering and abiding, but not during the stage of emerging.
The third type of entry into the womb refers to the Unsurpassed Enlightened One (*anuttarabuddha*), who is able to maintain correct awareness throughout the stages of entering, abiding, and emerging.

These first three individuals are designated by their respective names; furthermore, one should understand that there are distinctions among them according to the following sequence, due to the superiority of three factors: karma, wisdom, and both.
The first is superior in terms of karma, because he had previously cultivated vast merit in past lives.
The second is superior in wisdom, because they have long practiced extensive learning and possess superior analytical discernment.
The third is superior in both, because they have cultivated superior merit and wisdom throughout vast eons.
Excluding these three types, all others born from the womb or from eggs are inferior in both merit and wisdom; these constitute the fourth category.
Some say that all four of these refer to Bodhisattvas: namely, his final existence was as the third [birth] in Tuṣita Heaven;
his previous birth was the second, when he encountered Kāśyapa Buddha.
The immediately preceding birth is the first;
all those prior to that are the fourth.

Alternatively, regarding the first, second, and third incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), they correspond respectively to the first three types of entry into the womb, while all periods prior to these are the fourth.
Is it not the case that the subsequent existence (*pratisandhi*) is necessarily a defiled mind? How, then, could one enter the mother’s womb with full awareness (*saṃprajānan*)?

Full awareness and mindfulness are said to constitute the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*); since the restraint of the sense faculties must certainly be wholesome (*kuśala*), there is no such fault.

All forms of correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*) are subsumed under the category of the wholesome, as this is what is accepted; otherwise, there would be no such thing as correct awareness in the case of deceptive speech.

Alternatively, the state of entering the womb is described in terms of the continuity of the stream, rather than referring solely to the single moment of the actual linking of existence (*pratisaṃdhi-bhava*).

In this state, wholesome minds arise frequently while defiled minds are few; therefore, it is said that there is "clear comprehension" (*saṃprajanya*), just as people in the world speak of a "heap of white beans.
Alternatively, it is designated as "clear comprehension" because it inspires reverence toward those [objects] and establishes non-delusion.
It means knowing things as they truly are: "This is my father; this is my mother. Therefore, it is called right knowledge (*saṃprajanya*).
How is it that the third type of Bodhisattva, who possesses clear understanding of the fruits of ethical discipline and so forth, experiences such events at the time of entering the womb?

It is not the case that there is a lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) during the stages of entering and remaining; rather, it is logical that there may be clear comprehension at the time of emerging.

As for this clear comprehension upon emerging, because it is induced by prior causes and due to the habitual cultivation of such worldly attachment (*saṃvṛti-tṛṣṇā*) since beginningless time, this fault does not arise.
It is observed in the world that by the power of habitual practice, beings possess attachment at the very moment of birth.
How, then, can one speak of four types of entry into the womb?

Since there are only two types of entry—namely, with full awareness and without full awareness—it is not the case that staying or departing from the womb can be called "entry. Therefore, one should not say that there are four kinds of entry into the womb.
Because his entry is superior, it is said that there are four absences of error.
This means that because there is a distinction regarding the time of entering the womb, he possesses correct awareness during the stages of abiding and emerging.

Since he does not enter the mother’s womb with incorrect awareness, he is able to maintain correct awareness during the stages of abiding or emerging; therefore, he possesses unerring perception and understanding regarding these stages.
One who is capable of self-awareness does so by virtue of the distinction of entry; therefore, the term "entry into the womb" (garbhāvakrānti) also includes the stages of abiding and exiting.
Thus, although there may be both correct awareness and lack of awareness during the stages of abiding and exiting, these do not constitute a separate category because entry is predominant.
Although there are three types, they differ in their commonalities and distinctions, yet they are collectively described as "entering.
This is because the account of the matter of entering the womb is completed through that many gateways.
Thus, there are two ways of entering the womb for those of different species; within those of the same species, there are likewise two, making four in total.
Herein it should be explained: who is it that goes to enter the womb? Why is this asked?
Because there is no self.

That is to say, if there were no self, who would it be that is said to depart from this world, mounting the intermediate state aggregates (*antarābhava-skandha*), and proceed toward another world to enter, dwell in, and emerge from the womb?
Therefore, there must be an internal agent (puruṣa) who, from this world, enters the womb and so forth.
To refute that [view], the verse says:
There is no self; there are only the aggregates, Which are produced by afflictions and karma.
Through the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one enters the womb like a flame;
like a drawn-out line, it increases in succession.
This continuity, driven by afflictions and karma, proceeds further toward another world; thus, the wheel of existence has no beginning.
The treatise says:
There is no real self that enters the womb. Why is this so?
Just as the intrinsic nature and functional activity of form, the eye, and so forth cannot be apprehended, so too,
at the stage when consciousness and the like arise in dependence upon their bases and objects, the distinct functions imputed [to them] do not establish a real self.
Since there is no distinct function and no self-nature that can be clearly apprehended—just like the horns of a rabbit—how can one insist on the existence of an internal agent (*puruṣa*)?
The Blessed One also refuted the grasped real self as being the doer, the experiencer, and the one who goes to future worlds; thus the Blessed One said:
"Karma exists and its maturation exists, but an agent cannot be found."
That is to say, it is that which can relinquish these aggregates and can continue other aggregates, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, how is it known that the substantially existent self, which you assert, is truly unfindable as an agent and so on?
Is it because its essence does not exist, or because its essence exists substantially?
It cannot be obtained due to the absence of a cause for existence, yet it can be obtained due to the presence of a cause for non-existence.
Our school definitively maintains that it is unobtainable precisely because the essence of the self does not exist, and not due to any other cause.

All instances of the arising of self-grasping do not exceed four types: first, grasping at a self that has the aggregates themselves as its nature; second, grasping at a self distinct from the aggregates that dwells within the aggregates; third, grasping at a self distinct from the aggregates that dwells in phenomena distinct from the aggregates; and fourth, grasping at a self distinct from the aggregates that dwells nowhere at all.
Thus, these four types of grasping at a self involve something real that cannot be found; all are irrational.
Furthermore, a self does not have the aggregates as its nature, for it is established neither as identical to them nor as distinct from them, nor as their totality.
Why is this so? Because it would not be subsumed under the specific characteristics of each [of the aggregates], and it would consequently have to be merely conventional.

Furthermore, it does not exist as something distinct from the aggregates while residing within them, because there would be the fault of its essence being both permanent and impermanent simultaneously.
If it were impermanent, then because each moment would be distinct, there would be no single self.
With death and birth occurring, the agent would lose [the results of their actions] while the non-agent would obtain them.
Furthermore, not even a fraction of a phenomenon characterized by arising and ceasing can be found apart from the aggregates; therefore, it is not impermanent.

If one were to claim that it is permanent, there should be no transformation, birth, aging, sickness, and death would all be impossible, and there would likewise be no possibility of migrating to other realms of existence.

Furthermore, when encountering objects that are either pleasant or unpleasant, I should not undergo transformation through suffering or happiness, nor should I be afflicted by the afflictions associated with suffering and happiness.

Since it is not that which causes affliction, one should not, on this basis, give rise to notions of dharma or non-dharma; thus, in future lives, since pleasant and unpleasant bodies would lack a cause, they should have no possibility of arising.

Thus, it cannot be said that although the essence of the self is eternal, the self undergoes transformation due to the changes of the body; for if this essence of the self does not transform in accordance with the birth, aging, sickness, and death of the body, nor with the suffering and pleasure of the various realms of existence, nor with afflictions, karma, and their fruits, then it must have been ultimately liberated from the very beginning.
Since this is not permitted, the self is therefore not permanent.
Apart from permanence and impermanence, one cannot separately maintain that there exists a third category to be reckoned as the self.

Just as unconditioned phenomena such as space, whose essence differs from the aggregates, do not abide within the aggregates, so too should this [self] be; it likewise should not abide within the aggregates.

Nor does it abide apart from the aggregates as a phenomenon distinct from the aggregates; since the defiled and pure phenomena of the aggregates do not rely upon one another, the self as you have conceived it becomes useless.
If it does not rely on the aggregates, what else could it rely upon? It would be nothing at all.

Because the self is not related to the aggregates, it cannot reside anywhere apart from them, for if it were entirely non-resident like unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the same faults as previously mentioned would apply.

Furthermore, it would follow that the self is eternally liberated from the outset; that is to say, since the grasped self has no place of residence, it would have no relation whatsoever to the physical body, feelings such as suffering and pleasure, perceptions such as small and large, formations such as good and evil, or consciousnesses such as form and sound. Consequently, it would be inherently separated from the five aggregates and naturally liberated without the need for effort.

Therefore, the grasped real self as an agent—which is said to abandon this [life] and continue into another—cannot be found because it does not exist; it is not substantially real. Since there is no cause for its existence and no cause for its apprehension, it cannot be found.
If that is so, upon what object do the non-Buddhists give rise to the grasping of a self?

Although there is no distinct nature of a self apart from the aggregates that serves as the object of such grasping, they nevertheless give rise to this grasping by taking only the aggregates themselves as its objective domain.
As stated in the Sūtras:
"Whatever [beings] perceive a self, all such perceptions arise solely with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Although there is no such truly existent nature of a self as asserted by those non-Buddhists, there is a conventional self spoken of in accordance with worldly usage within the Noble Teachings.
Since there is no real self (*ātman*), upon what basis is it metaphorically designated?
Although there is no real self, it is metaphorically designated as "self" in relation to the aggregates (*skandha*) in accordance with worldly convention.
For what reason do we know that this designation of "self" relies solely upon the aggregates and nothing else?
Because both defiled and purified phenomena are established solely in dependence upon the aggregates (*skandha*).

That is to say, a self does not truly exist; for all forms of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) depend merely upon the momentary continuity of the aggregates, which—impelled by the power of afflictions and karma—proceed through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and enter the mother’s womb.
Just as the flame of a lamp, through a continuous succession of moments, moves to another location, so too it is with the aggregates (*skandha*).

Furthermore, in the desire realm, for one who has not yet abandoned craving, conditioned by the internal and external bases (*āyatana*), improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) gives rise to afflictions such as craving; these arise together with inferior, middling, or superior volition (*cetanā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Once arisen, they are able to draw forth future undesirable fruits.
It also serves as the condition for the arising of the immediately succeeding consciousness and so forth; these immediately succeeding consciousnesses observe their own kind or different kinds.

When they arise based on the preceding co-nascent condition—whether they are wholesome, defiled, or indeterminate in nature—they are able, once arisen, to project their own future results and serve as the condition for the arising of the immediately succeeding consciousnesses and so forth.
Conditioned in this way, one should understand that the subsequent stages in succession are able to draw forth two fruits as appropriate.

This continuity of the aggregates receives the factors such as the lifespan projected by the afflictions and karma of previous lives; when the power of that maturation (*vipāka*) reaches its exhaustion, the death-consciousness, together with its support, arrives at the state of cessation and serves as the condition for the arising of the consciousness of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and so forth.

Within this intermediate state (antarābhava) exist the various aggregates (skandhas), which, through the continuity of prior afflictions and karma like an illusion, proceed to the place of birth and enter the mother’s womb; at the moment the intermediate state ceases, it further acts as a condition to produce the aggregates of the birth-existence (upapattibhava).
For example, although the flame of a lamp perishes moment by moment, it can proceed to another location through a continuous succession of causes and effects without interruption.
Therefore, even though there is no self and the aggregates perish moment by moment, the principle that one can travel to future lives is established.

These very aggregates, as projected by the power of prior afflictions and karma, gradually increase in succession; they continue in a serial stream throughout the duration of a single lifetime, and again, through afflictions and karma, they proceed toward another world.

It is directly observed that because causes differ, their effects vary; thus, the magnitude of the results of various projecting karmas (*ākṣepaka-karman*) is not equal. The length of the life-span resulting from these depends on the differences in karma, increasing or diminishing according to the strength or weakness of that karma. The projected life-span and the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), among others, are mutually dependent, gradually increasing through each successive stage, such as the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth.
What are those called the *kalala* and so forth?

They refer to the transformation and differentiation of the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha-santāna*), which gradually increase until the stage where the sense faculties (*indriya*) reach maturity.

Through the conditions of attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward internal and external bases (*āyatana*), and their conjunction, afflictions (*kleśa*) such as desire arise, leading to the performance and accumulation of various karmas.

Due to these afflictions and karmas, one continues through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as before and proceeds toward another world; it should be understood that this wheel of existence has no beginning.

That is to say: with afflictions as the cause, one is able to create various karmas; with karma as the cause, its power is able to draw forth birth; and with birth again as the cause, afflictions and karmas arise. From these afflictions and karmas, there is yet again birth. Thus, one knows that the wheel of existence revolves without beginning.
If one maintains that there is a beginning, then the beginning must be without a cause.
Since the beginning would be causeless, all other things should likewise arise spontaneously.
Because there would be no distinct causes, this would contradict what is empirically observed; therefore, it is certain that no phenomenon arises without a cause.
There is not even a single permanent phenomenon that can serve as a cause; this has already been extensively refuted in the critique of Īśvara.
Therefore, saṃsāra is definitely without beginning, like grains of rice and so forth, which continue in a successive succession.
However, there is an end, because the causes are exhausted; just as when seeds and the like are exhausted, sprouts and the like do not arise.

Since birth and death no longer exist, ultimate purity is attained. Therefore, defilement and purification depend solely upon the aggregates (*skandhas*). To cling to the existence of a real self (*ātman*) is thus rendered useless.
Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-four.
