Chapter Five: The Fifth Part of the Exposition on Dependent Origination. Having already explained the principles of the internal and external *kalala* and so forth, as well as the continuity of cause and effect, it should be understood that this is precisely what is termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Such dependent origination is not limited to twelve factors alone.
How is this known? As stated in the *Mūla-śāstra*:
What is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
It refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

However, in the sūtras where dependent origination is explained, it is sometimes described fully in terms of the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga*), as taught in such texts as the *Paramārthaśūnyatā-sūtra*.
In some cases, eleven [factors] are taught, as in the *Jñānaprasthāna* and other sūtras;
in others, only ten are taught, as in the *Nagaropama-sūtra* and others;
and in yet others, nine are taught, as in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*.
Some say there are eight, as stated in the Sūtra:
"There are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who do not know the nature of all phenomena as it truly is.
Such are the various distinctions that have been taught.
For what reason do the treatises differ from the sūtras?

The treatises follow the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), whereas the sūtras accord with the needs of those to be converted (*vineya*). Therefore, within the sūtras, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is analyzed and explained in various ways according to the differing capacities of those being taught.
In some cases, a treatise may discuss the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), while a sutra’s meaning is not definitive (*neyārtha*).

Or, while a treatise may speak generally of both sentient and non-sentient beings, a sutra speaks only in reference to those categorized as sentient; for it is by depending on sentient beings that defilement and purification can be established. It is precisely for the sake of revealing these two to sentient beings that the Buddha appears in the world.
Therefore, in the sūtras, dependent origination is explained in relation to sentient beings; it is analyzed in order to establish its great purpose and benefit.

Among the various members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), there are immeasurable distinctions in their categories and meanings. For now, I shall briefly explain how the twelve members exist as an uninterrupted succession through the stages of three lifetimes.
The verse says:
Such is dependent origination, consisting of twelve factors across three time periods;
two factors each belong to the prior and posterior limits, while eight belong to the middle, based on its full completion.

The treatise states: The twelve links are: first, ignorance; second, volitional formations; third, consciousness; fourth, name-and-form; fifth, the six sense bases; sixth, contact; seventh, sensation; eighth, craving; ninth, grasping; tenth, becoming; eleventh, birth; and twelfth, aging and death.
Regarding the "three time periods" (*traiyadhvika*): first, the past period; second, the future period; and third, the middle period—namely, the three lifetimes of the past, future, and present.
How are the twelve links established across these three periods?
This means that two branches are established for each of the prior and posterior limits, while eight branches constitute the middle limit; thus, there are twelve.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) belong to the prior limit, which refers to past existence;
birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) belong to the posterior limit, which refers to future existence.
The remaining eight [links] are situated in the middle period, namely the present life.
Of these, five fruits are those invited by the two causes of the prior period;
three causes are those upon which the two fruits of the subsequent period depend.
Not all who have taken birth in a single lifetime possess these eight; rather, it is said that there are eight branches based on those who are complete.
Who is "complete"? It refers to one whose factors are without deficiency.

Alternatively, it is summoned by the perfection of afflictions and karma; that is to say, it is induced by previously predominant afflictions and karma. Here, the term "individual" (pudgala) is intended.

One is called "perfected" because they have passed through all stages, which does not apply to those among the gods or in the form and formless realms, as they lack stages such as the kalala and so forth.

World-Honored One, you have spoken of twelve [links] only with reference to a limited portion of individuals within the desire realm, as stated in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, where the Buddha told Ānanda:
"If consciousness were not to enter the womb, would it be able to increase and expand?"
"No, World-Honored One! ...
[and so on, as extensively explained]."

Therefore, if there is a person who, in the immediately preceding life, produced ignorance and formations that fully summoned the five links beginning with consciousness in the present life, and further, in the present life, produced craving, grasping, and becoming that summon the two links beginning with birth in the subsequent life.
It should be understood that this sutra speaks based on that [principle].
If the various links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) were established based on all *pudgalas* indiscriminately, there would be confusion.

That is to say, some might possess the five present links, yet these would not be the results of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) from the immediately preceding life, nor would they be the links of birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) in the subsequent life; nor would they be the results of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) from the present life.
None of those [other views] clarify the intended meaning of this sutra. Do not see the cause and its fruit as being so far apart that you might doubt the capacity of the cause to evoke the fruit.

One should know that the branches of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) are, in brief, comprised of two parts belonging to the prior and subsequent limits—namely, seven branches and five branches respectively—because the fruits and causes are subsumed under the categories of effect and cause.
Alternatively, there are five branches for the cause and seven branches for the fruit, because causes are subsumed under causes and fruits are subsumed under fruits.

That is to say: present craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are the past ignorance (*avidyā*); the present branch of becoming (*bhava*) is the past volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); present consciousness (*vijñāna*) is future birth (*jāti*); and the remaining four present branches are future aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*). This is called the distinction between the two divisions of cause and fruit.
To what meaning does this term "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) refer?

Now, regarding the specific meanings found herein: *prati* has the sense of "presence," and the root *i* (from the class of roots ending in *u*) has the sense of "existence," because a single verbal root can possess multiple meanings.

By means of the prefix *pra*, the verbal root *√i* forms the sense of "conditioning" (*pratyaya*). The suffix *kta* signifies "that which has already occurred. The combination of these bases results in *pratītya*, where the root *√i* carries the meaning of "to go toward" or "to depend upon," and the prefix *pra* conveys the sense of "forth" or "toward. Furthermore, the prefix *sam* has the meaning of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), while the root *√pad* has the meaning of "existence" (*bhāva*). Thus, [the term *pratītyasamutpāda*] signifies "arising through conjunction with conditions."
With "ud" as the prefix, the root *pad* comes to mean "arising.
This is the general meaning: when conditions have already come together in the present, a phenomenon arises; this is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The statement that "present conditions" refers to a combination raises the question: what further function does this "combination" serve?
It is intended either to establish that even a non-existent phenomenon arises from a single condition, or to clarify the relationship between simultaneous and preceding conditions.

The phrase "conditioned by what is present" (pratyutpanna) clarifies the co-nascent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*); the phrase "conditioned by a combination of conditions" (*pratyayasāmagrī*) clarifies the previously arisen condition (*pūrvaja-pratyaya*).
This, then, clarifies the establishment of dependence: "when this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises"—this is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Furthermore, *pratī* signifies the sense of "to go toward" (*pratigamana*), *iti* signifies "an indestructible phenomenon" (*abhedyadharma*), and *sam* signifies "correctly assembled. This meaning collectively indicates that the cause for the manifestation of the world is termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

That is to say, when the element of cohesion (*ap-*) is preceded by the assistance of *pra-* (forth), it transforms into the condition (*ālambana*); and when [the element of] extension (*pṛthivī*) is preceded by the assistance of *ut-*, it causes the element of cohesion to transform into arising (*utthāna*).
Based on this meaning, the term "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) is established.

Regarding the explanation of its specific components provided by the Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtrakāra*) herein: *pra* has the sense of "reaching"; the root *i* has the sense of "going. Due to the influence of the preceding prefix, the meaning of the root undergoes a transformation; thus, "going" (utpāda) becomes "condition" (*pratyaya*) through the transformation of "reaching. *Sam* has the sense of "conjunction"; *ud* has the sense of "arising"; and the root *pad* has the sense of "existence."

To claim that there is a "reliance" (*pratītya*) which, through conjunction, transforms and arises—that is, that by means of this reliance, phenomena reach their conditions, conjoin, and then arise—is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Such an interpretation contradicts the tenets of your own school.

Furthermore, since that which exists arises through transformation by means of prior auxiliary conditions and is not something other than existence, what is ultimately established by once again manifesting the meaning of "existence"?
For according to their own tenets, there is nothing that is not arising; if there were no arising, then "non-existence" would likewise have no meaning.
After the Master of the Sūtras had established this meaning of the passage himself, he further raised the following objection:
"The meaning of this passage is logically untenable. Why is this so?"
If a single agent possesses two functions, there ought to be a term for "completion" regarding the prior function, just as when a person has finished bathing before eating.
There is no dharma of movement that exists prior to its arising and reaches the object first, only to arise at a later time; for there can be no function without an agent.
Therefore, it is said in verse:
"If [the effect] were to arise prior to reaching its conditions, It would be irrational for it to exist [then].
If they were simultaneous, the [condition's] status as a cause would be destroyed, For that [effect] ought to have been mentioned first."
Furthermore, he explains for himself:
"There is no such fault; rather, one should first counter-interrogate the masters of the science of grammar (śabdavādin):
At what time does a phenomenon arise?"
Does it exist in the present or in the future?
If so, what fault is there?
If arising were in the present, since arising has not yet occurred, how could it be established as being present?
If that which has already arisen is what is currently manifesting, how could it arise again?
If that which has already arisen were to arise once more, it would lead to an infinite regress.
If its arising occurs in the future, then at that time it does not yet exist; how, then, can it be the agent of arising?
Since the agent does not exist, how can there be an action?
Therefore, at the very moment of arising, it has already reached the conditions.
What is this "moment of arising"?
This means that when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the future are about to arise, they are said to "reach the conditions" even at the very moment of arising.

Such a statement cannot resolve the previous objection; for if the stage of arising is admitted to belong to the future, and according to that school the future lacks any substantial entity (*bhāva*), upon what could "reaching the conditions" and "arising" be established?

Therefore, the objection raised previously—that there exists no dharma of "slight activity" which, existing prior to its arising, first reaches the object and only subsequently arises—is not resolved by the claim that "there is no agent, yet there is the utility [of the action]"; this remains unexplained.
Furthermore, regarding the theory of sound (*śabdavāda*), the postulation of an agent and an action established through delusion is not logically tenable in reality.

While there is an agent who initiates an action, within this context no agent distinct from the arising of the action can be found as a real entity; therefore, these statements are unerring from the perspective of conventional truth.
This, too, is irrational.
Why? Because the agent and the action are not without distinction in meaning.
If there were no arising of activity based upon existence, then an agent would ultimately be non-existent.
Furthermore, even granting their claim that the agent and the action may be either different or identical, since the future lacks substantiality, it cannot constitute an agent.
Therefore, what he has stated does not avoid the aforementioned fault. The Venerable Rāma has said:
"One utters vocal sounds for the purpose of expressing meaning."

Terms such as "arising" and "ceasing" are all established based on the distinctions among the various states within the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); they attain their ultimate meaning only in relation to a multiplicity of factors, and not with respect to a single moment, because [the latter] is subtle and difficult to discern.
Once the establishment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) has been accomplished regarding the state of a continuum (*saṃtāna*), it may likewise be established by analogy for a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Such an assertion as yours is nothing but empty words.

Since you claim that sound (*śabda*) functions to express meaning, yet in your school the entities of birth (*jāti*) and so forth do not truly exist, the sounds "birth" and so on would have no meaning to express; for there is no non-existent dharma that can be designated as a meaning.

Furthermore, characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) are not established as states within the continuity of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), because this was already refuted previously when examining the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).

Only when established at the level of a single moment can these characteristics be validly applied to the continuity of formations, because a continuity is a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*) that is established by aggregating real entities.
Furthermore, upon what basis is that statement regarding "arising" (utpāda) made?

One cannot speak of a function when there is no functional utility, nor can one say something has a function if it is absolutely non-existent. Therefore, that [opponent's] attempt at a refutation is not a sound explanation; only the Abhidharma school’s position is free from fault, for both the act of arising and that which precedes arising can exist.

That is to say, when the Abhidharmikas state that at the time a phenomenon arises, its substance is substantially existent just as it is in the state of having already arisen, they may speak of an "agent" in accordance with conventional usage without error;
but how can there be no error in speaking of an agent when those who assert that the state of arising is absolutely non-existent?

If one maintains the theory of simultaneous arising of cause and effect, one cannot escape the faults already stated; for the aforementioned arguments apply to me regardless of whether one advances or retreats, since neither the agent nor time is fixed.

Although the expression "having already [done]" is spoken in reliance upon a single agent, we observe that the expression "having already [done]" may rely upon a different agent; for example, "Having already attained [it], you do not practice.
Although the expression "having already [done]" is spoken in reliance upon a prior time, it is also seen to rely upon a subsequent time; for example, "Having already opened his mouth, he sleeps."

Although it has already been stated that [the cause] is spoken of in reference to a different time, we also see cases where it is not so; for example, as people in the world say, "The lamp is extinguished when darkness arrives.

Therefore, for those who maintain the theory of simultaneous cause and effect, there is no fault in their reasoning regarding the principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); this alone is fully established as the meaning of the term "dependent origination."

For what reason did the Blessed One, when explaining dependent origination, first state, "Depending on this, that exists; because this arises, that arises," rather than simply stating "ignorance conditions [formations]" and so forth to explain the meaning of dependent origination?
Furthermore, the Elder stated:
"There are two kinds of dependent origination: first, that which pertains to sentient beings; second, that which pertains to non-sentient things.
The first two lines of the text encompass both types, as there is no distinction made in the wording."
The statement that "ignorance as a condition" and so forth refer exclusively to sentient beings is because sentient beings exist [in this context].
However, a direct disciple of that same Elder (Sthavira) has criticized this himself, saying:
"This explanation is irrational, for it does not correspond with the logic of the heading and its explanation."
The principle is that the preceding indicator and the subsequent explanation must necessarily correspond; why then do you indicate both [causes] at first, yet explain only one later?
Furthermore, external dependent origination should not have been indicated first in this sutra, as it would serve no purpose.
This criticism is unreasonable; for the explanations provided above do not contradict the headings and their respective expositions, as they are not without purpose.

That is to say, the subsequent explanations of ignorance and so forth do not exceed the scope of the "dependent origination of sentient beings" indicated by the heading; therefore, the logic of the headings and their explanations is not inconsistent.
Now, one establishes a prior heading in anticipation of a subsequent explanation;
since there is no subsequent explanation, what use is the prior heading?

Therefore, one should only establish headings for those things included within the category of sentient beings; to establish headings for non-sentient things would be inconsistent with the explanation.
Furthermore, if there were no separate headings, what fault would there be in not providing an explanation?
And if there is no separate explanation, what purpose is served by the general headings?

Herein, these general headings have a significant function: namely, to reveal the unmanifest internal dependent origination by means of the manifest external dependent origination of non-sentient things.

That seeds produce sprouts and so forth is what is commonly known in the world; however, that ignorance conditions volitional formations and so forth is not directly perceived by the world. The Blessed One has demonstrated this by showing that just as sprouts and so forth come to exist based on seeds and so forth, and because seeds and so forth arise, sprouts and so forth are produced.

Thus it should be understood: based on ignorance and so forth, volitional formations and so forth come to be; because ignorance and so forth arise, volitional formations and so forth arise. Therefore, the general designation [of the links] possesses great significance and function.
This collectively demonstrates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are such that not a single one does not arise from a multitude of conditions.
If this is so, why are non-sentient things (*asattva*) not explained here—just as sentient beings were first indicated and subsequently explained?
Non-sentient things are easy to understand and require only a general indication; however, the categories of sentient beings are difficult to comprehend and thus must be explained in detail.
Since most teachings on dependent origination are intended for those of sharp faculties, it is not necessary to provide a detailed explanation for every category mentioned.
Furthermore, because sentient beings are superior, they should be analyzed in detail.
External phenomena also take internal phenomena as their cause.
If that is so, why is there also extensive analysis of external dependent origination in other sūtras, such as the *Bījopama-sūtra* and others?

This interpretation is incorrect; thus, such a teacher and disciple have not acted with excellence. To take the tenets of a treatise composed by their own teacher through diligent reflection and then to frivolously disparage them merely to display their own prowess is something that those who skillfully expound the Dharma ought not to do.
In this regard, I have examined his interpretation in detail and found that it contradicts his own treatise in every respect.

That treatise asserts that all sūtras are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); yet, his current interpretation contradicts the tenets of that treatise because he fails to fully set forth the meaning indicated by the headings. Consequently, he must admit that this [sūtra] is not of definitive meaning; therefore, this is certainly not the intended meaning of the sūtra according to his own school’s tenets.
The Venerable Rāma, unable to accept his own teacher’s explanation, further explained it himself:
"If the twelve links are accepted as depending upon the three time periods, that constitutes a concise summary."
Regarding the teaching on dependent origination across the three time periods, it is stated that "depending on this, that exists" and "because this arises, that arises.
If one does not accept this, then these two phrases respectively demonstrate the direct and indirect causes.

This is also not the case; furthermore, one should examine in detail whether these two gates are taught to encompass the three time periods. Are the meanings of these two gates identical or different?

If their meanings were identical, then explaining only one gate would suffice for the full scope of the meaning, rendering the other useless; moreover, it would contradict the subsequent explanation which separately reveals two distinct causes.
These two statements are not repeated before and after for the purpose of making their intended meaning either identical or different.
If, according to the latter explanation, the two meanings were distinct, then these two statements would each have to be repeated in order to encompass the three time periods.
If it were otherwise and did not encompass all cases, then the title and its explanation would be inconsistent.
For how could the meaning be compatible when that which is not included within the title is extensively analyzed in the explanation?
Therefore, that [position] would again contradict the principle of the summary and its explanation.

Consequently, none of the direct transmissions contain redundant statements; rather, they merely follow one item from the summary, which would thus be inconsistent with the subsequent detailed explanation.

If it is claimed that these two [factors] pervasively belong to all the members—namely, that initial ignorance acts as a condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) either directly or indirectly, and that the same applies to volitional formations and so forth—this is merely a wishful thinking devoid of actual reasoning.
This is because no such distinction is stated later; thus, the headings and their explanations would fail to correspond.

Furthermore, according to the Dārṣṭāntika school, since the past and future lack substantial existence (*avastu*), how can the two types of causes—the immediate (*sākṣāt*) and the transmitted (*paramparā*)—be established?
Moreover, because a karmic action cannot produce its maturation (*vipāka*) without an interval, the action cannot be established as the immediate cause (*sākṣāt-hetu*) in relation to that maturation.
Nor is it a "transmitted cause" (*paramparā-hetu*), because there is no such thing as a transmitted meaning.
It is not that after an action has ceased, there remains some other cause by which the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is summoned through the power of the prior action;

rather, it is only when the primary cause has already ceased and another cause brings about the fruit that it is designated a "transmitted cause" by virtue of being distantly influenced by the power of the original cause.
All those who recklessly imagine such things as the "ancient pervasive element" (*pūrvānuśaya-dhātu*) have already been extensively refuted during the investigation of causes.

Even if one were to grant that such a transmission exists, it would still not constitute the two types of causes—distant and near—because there is no difference in their cessation; based on what, then, could one say that one is distant and this is near?

According to what has been said previously, this principle is also untenable; for when one [of two related things] exists, the other is absent, and it is impossible to speak of a transmission where no dharma exists.
By this, the argument based on what "will exist" is also refuted.
Although it exists in the present, because it does not exist in the future, it cannot be said that there is a transmission without something upon which it depends.

Therefore, one must certainly know that the proponents of the *Dṛṣṭāntika* school merely provide such explanations out of a desire to deceive and delude those who are confused by the true teachings and lack awakened wisdom.

Among the followers of the Elder (Sthavira), some explain these two phrases as refuting causelessness and eternal causes, while others explain them as revealing the abiding and arising of cause and effect.
Since the Master of the Sūtra (the *Śāstrakāra*) has already refuted these views, they shall not be further dispatched here.
The Elder spoke again:
"When this exists, that exists" means that when the effect exists, the cause has ceased.
"Because this arises, that arises" is said because there might be doubt that the effect could arise without a cause; therefore, he further stated:
Because it arises from a cause, the fruit can only come into being; it is not said to be without a cause.
The Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) raises an objection, saying: "If the meaning of the sūtra were thus, it should have been stated:
'Depending on this existing, that becomes non-existent.'"
Furthermore, one should first state:
"Because the cause arises, the effect arises"; only after that may one say that the effect exists and the cause has ceased.
Such a sequence alone constitutes a well-spoken exposition.
If it were otherwise, and one intended to explain dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), upon what sequence could one first speak of the cessation of causes?
Therefore, that interpretation does not accord with the meaning of this sūtra.

Thus, regarding whatever the Venerable Sthavira has said, even his own direct disciples and those of like view do not accept or believe it; how much less could those who follow the noble teachings and conform to correct reasoning possibly tolerate it?
The East values this, truly deeming it marvelous.
For what reason does the Master of the Sūtras merely state that those explanations do not accord with the meaning of this sūtra?
I shall now demonstrate that what the Venerable Upāli says is entirely devoid of reason, for he asserts that only that which has arisen previously serves as a cause, and that only the present exists.

For those who maintain the theory of substantial existence (satkāryavāda), it is never the case that a cause exists while its effect already exists and only then ceases, because at the time the effect exists, the cause has already ceased.
Since the cause may cease at the very moment the effect arises, the effect is still non-existent at the time the cause ceases.
If destruction exists only when the effect exists, then you must admit that the cause still exists at that time, which would undermine the doctrine of momentariness.

Furthermore, if you maintain that the cause is destroyed only when the effect exists, then the fault of cause and effect existing simultaneously follows; for while the effect exists, the cause has not yet ceased, and thus the effect itself would also possess destruction at that very moment.
Furthermore, if that were the case, one should not entertain the doubt that an effect arises without a cause, since both [cause and effect] are presently manifest.

That is to say, the cause perishes precisely when the effect exists; since the effect is currently seen to arise from that [cause], which has not yet ceased to exist, how could there be any doubt that the effect arises without a cause?
Then one should not further say that "because the cause arises, the effect arises.
If they offer this defense:

"My intention is not to say that the cause perishes only when the effect exists; rather, my intention is simply to say that it is only when the effect exists that the cause has its cessation. This means that at the time the effect exists, the cause has the sense of non-existence."
Even if one were to grant this, there should still be no doubt.

To say that the cause is non-existent only at the time when the effect exists already demonstrates that the cause was not non-existent prior to that; how, then, can one further doubt that the effect arises without a cause?
Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere:
"Depending on the existence of the seed and so forth, the sprout and so forth come to exist.
What is the meaning of this?
If that very meaning were present, one would forfeit one's own tenet.
If there is some other distinct meaning, for what reason do you insist that the future must be called "existent," while admitting it does not possess that [present] meaning?
Is it accepted that the past is "existent" (sat) in the same sense as that [present] entity?
Furthermore, a phenomenon lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should not be said to exist; this has already been fully refuted in the investigation of *nirvāṇa*.
Moreover, if the effect is yet to come into being, it ought to be established as "existent," because it would still be called "existent" despite its cause having already ceased to exist.
For this reason, the meaning of the statement "dependent on this being, that exists" would be indeterminate;
yet such is not admitted. Therefore, it should be understood that what the Venerable Elder (Sthavira) has said is entirely devoid of logical merit.

However, the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra), in making a specific denial, stated that this is not the meaning of the sūtra; it is no different from saying that the son of a barren woman is not extremely brave.

Furthermore, when the Master of the Sūtra recounted the interpretation of the two phrases given by his own preceptor (upādhyāya) to demonstrate his own benevolence and filial piety, he did not point out the faults therein, even though they existed.

The principle governing the relationship between teacher and disciple should indeed be such; however, as I have received no transmissions from that master, my critique does not detract from his great reputation, and thus I have here exposed his errors according to reality.
That is to say, those masters explain these two phrases to demonstrate the non-interruption and the arising of cause and effect:
namely, that dependent upon the non-interruption of ignorance, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are not interrupted; and precisely because ignorance arises, the formative forces come to arise.
In this manner, all subsequent links should likewise be explained in detail.

This interpretation is incorrect; if the meaning of the Sūtra were as you suggest, it would also have to state that "volitional formations (saṃskāra) are the condition for ignorance," and that "as long as volitional formations are not severed, ignorance is not severed," because volitional formations and ignorance share the same antidote.
It cannot be said that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is not yet severed at the stage where grasping (*upādāna*) is severed, because they share the same antidote (*pratipakṣa*).

If it is argued that this statement refers to the severance of active manifestation (*samudācāra*), then the mention of "arising" (*jāti*) would be redundant; for there has never been a case where ignorance (*avidyā*) was manifesting and yet was not called "arising"—so why state it again?
Thus we know that the masters from whom the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) received his teachings had not yet fully mastered the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

The masters of the Abhidharma explain these two phrases as follows: "The arising of all members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*) necessarily depends upon two causes, because there is a distinction between those that arise simultaneously and those that arise prior."

Some [conditioned phenomena] take mere existence as their cause, while others take the specific differentiation of existence as their cause; in order to first indicate these two types of causes, it is said: "When this exists, that exists" and "from the arising of this, that arises."
Subsequently, in order to explain these two kinds of causes, it is said: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise," and so on, up to "with birth as condition, aging and death arise.

Alternatively, although the meaning of these two phrases is not distinct, there are briefly two types of links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda): namely, the difference between cause and effect in the prior limit and the subsequent limit. To briefly indicate the prior limit, it is said, "When this exists, that comes to be"; to briefly indicate the subsequent limit, it is said, "Because this arises, that arises."

For this reason, regarding the past limit (*pūrvānta*), it is definitively stated that [the cause] has existed and [the effect] exists; that is, "dependent on the existence of this, that exists," because the cause and effect follow their respective order in the past and present.

Regarding the future limit (*aparānta*), it is definitively stated that [the effect] is currently arising or will arise; that is, "because this arises, that arises," because the cause and effect follow their respective order in the present and the future.
In the past limit (*pūrvānta*), the meaning of the existence of the fruit is already complete; therefore, it is said to "exist.

In the future limit (*aparānta*), the meaning of the existence of the fruit is not yet fulfilled; therefore, it is said to "arise. Since the fruit is that which is primarily sought, the explanation follows the fruit.
Alternatively, these two terms may be explained by means of the two truths.

The two truths are the conventional and the ultimate; based on the multiplicity [of factors], one name is established as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the establishment of the essential nature of the elements (*dhātu*) is termed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The former truth conforms to worldly conventional discourse; the latter truth conforms to the discourse of the noble ones.
Regarding the phenomena of conventional truth, there is what is called "arising" when they are acquired, and what is called "ceasing" when they are lost;
regarding the phenomena of ultimate truth, there is what is called "arising" when activity is initiated, and what is called "ceasing" when activity subsides.
Regarding the statement "existence is obtained," this means that based upon a collection of various conditions (*pratyaya*), a single existence is conventionally established as a designation.
Regarding the statement "the activity of arising," this means that when various substantial entities (*dravya*) combine with conditions, the activity of projecting a fruit arises.
The proponents of the theory that only the present exists must also necessarily admit these two kinds of existence as described; if they do not admit this, they should abandon the sūtra.
The statement "dependent on the existence of this, that comes to be" refers to the existence of the basis for designation, by virtue of which the designated entity can come to exist.
This means that the designation (*prajñapti*) exists but is not produced, for it is established based on the conjunction of its supports and conditions.
By what evidence is this known?
As stated in the Sūtra:

"Just as one gathers various parts together and conventionally speaks of them as a 'chariot,' so too, when one speaks of a 'sentient being' in the conventional sense, one should know that it is a gathering of the aggregates.
Afflictions such as craving mostly arise in dependence upon the conventional; only then can they act as the cause to produce consciousness for a future existence.
According to correct reasoning, it must necessarily be so.
As for the statement "because this arises, that arises," this refers to the arising of the actual realm (dharmadhātu); it signifies that the actual realm attains the state of arising.
This meaning explains the reality: through the power of various conditions, it is made to function; thus, this arising is not [an entity] that exists.
By what evidence is this known?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Two causes and two conditions can give rise to right view."
"Because this has arisen" means that it arises from past and present conditions.
"That will arise" refers to the arising of future results.
Although there is also the sense of "conditioning" (pratyaya) regarding the future, it is said to have "already arisen" only in reference to its specific stage (avasthā).
"Depending on this, that exists" means that based on the existence of a previously arisen cause, there is the sense of the existence of a presently arisen effect.
"With the arising of this, that arises" means that because the presently arisen effect arises, there is the sense of the arising of a subsequently arisen cause.
The intent here is to demonstrate that arising arises; thus, it excludes other antidotes as causes for the arising of subsequent existence.

Furthermore, based on the existence of the cause of present arising, the fruit of subsequent arising comes to exist; because the fruit of subsequent arising arises, each successive cause is able to arise.
In this way, the wheel of existence revolves without beginning.
Other masters explain that these two phrases are intended to ensure certainty regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
As stated elsewhere:
conditioned by ignorance, the formative forces come to be; the formative forces cannot exist apart from ignorance.
According to this principle, there are only four permutations; were it otherwise, there would be many more.
That is to say: based on the existence of this, that exists; yet that does not exist [independently].
Furthermore, because this arises, that arises; yet that does not arise [without this].
In this way, there are six distinct propositions.
It may be argued that just as when a lamp exists, there is light from the lamp and darkness does not exist;
and because the lamp arises, the light from the lamp arises while the darkness does not arise—this, however, cannot be so.
For when a lamp exists, darkness is extinguished, and there is no logical principle for a correspondence between cause and effect in such a case.

Because the principle of the correspondence between cause and effect is definitively absent in the position that "phenomena exist while the self does not," and because there was originally no deluded attachment [to such a view], these various phrases of the sūtra were spoken in order to reveal the principle of the correspondence between cause and effect; it is not that existence and non-existence possess the meaning of cause and effect.

In this way, the initial indication would be rendered useless; as will be explained separately later, there should have been a general indication at the outset. Since no such explanation follows, what is the purpose of the initial indication?
Therefore, it is better to follow the previous explanation, because this section only analyzes the characteristics of cause and effect.

The fourfold logical analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding this attachment is unreasonable; that is to say, it is not the case that darkness exists in dependence upon a lamp, nor is it the case that darkness exists because the lamp does not exist. What has been stated in this manner does not constitute the characteristic of cause and effect.

If this were necessarily the case, there should be eight lines, for only by that many could the arising and ceasing be fully and perfectly revealed; specifically, the first four lines would fully reveal arising, while the latter four lines would fully reveal ceasing.

If that were so, there would be only four distinct propositions: namely, "when this exists, that exists," and "when this does not exist, that does not exist," for these alone are sufficient to fully manifest the intended meaning.

It is not so; for while it has already been stated that "because this exists, that exists," with the intent of expressing only existence, it has not yet been stated that "because this arises, that arises.
This is because not all phenomena that exist necessarily undergo arising.
That what was previously non-existent now comes to be has already been refuted several times.
Therefore, as you have stated, it is certainly meaningless.
If you claim that this is taught in the *Paramārtha-śūnyatā-sūtra* by way of another interpretive approach, I shall provide a reconciliation of that point.
It was previously stated that the twelve links are established across the three time periods—namely, ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth, as explained at length.
Among these, what dharma is designated as "ignorance"?
And what dharma is designated as "old age and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*)?
The verse says:
Ignorance is the state of past afflictions; the various past karmas are called formations (*saṃskāra*);
consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the aggregates at the moment of linking birth; and prior to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

From the arising of the sense organs such as the eye, prior to the three conditions for the six sense bases, there is the differentiation of the causes of the three types of feeling; that which has not yet been fully understood is called contact (*sparśa*).
Prior to sensual craving (*kāmatṛṣṇā*) is feeling (*vedanā*); craving is the desire for the requisites of sensual pleasure.
Seeking everywhere for the sake of obtaining various objects is called "grasping" (*upādāna*);
"existence" (*bhava*) refers to the karma that truly creates and draws forth the fruit of future existence;
"birth" (*jāti*) is the linking of what is to be called future existence; and reaching the state of receiving [the results] is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
The treatise says:
From the stage of the various afflictions in past lives until the present ripening of the fruit, this is collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
Why is the term "ignorance" used to refer to the afflictions in general?
Because it is the definitive cause for drawing forth future existence (*punarbhava*).

Karma, being incited by afflictions (*kleśa*), is able to draw forth future existence; since there is no future existence where there is karma without afflictions, such karma does not draw forth future existence.

When the various formations arise, greed and the other afflictions all possess activity therein; since those formations necessarily depend upon ignorance at the stage of their origination, the term "ignorance" is used here as a general designation for the afflictions.
If that is so, why is it that only the afflictions of the preceding life are collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*), while those of this life are not?
It is because only the afflictions of the preceding life resemble ignorance.
When afflictions such as craving have not yet produced their fruit, their power remains unimpaired, and they are thus described as "clear and sharp."
If, after attaining the fruit, its acquisition, bestowal, and utilization are deficient, it is not called "clear and sharp.
Even if the power of ignorance has not yet been diminished, it is still not clear and sharp, because it is difficult to discern when that [ignorance] is manifesting.

The various afflictions (*kleśa*) from previous lives reach the present life with their power diminished because they have already produced their fruit; thus, their characteristics are not distinct and resemble the category of ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, only the afflictions of previous lives may be designated by the term "ignorance," and this should not be applied equally to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), for [the designation] is established as a conventional name and concept only within its own homogeneous class.
However, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) states: "Because they function simultaneously with ignorance, and because they manifest through the power of ignorance.
It is like saying 'the king travels,' which does not mean he is without attendants; yet, because the king is preeminent, one speaks generally of 'the king's travel.'"

One has not yet understood the meaning of "simultaneous operation" herein: do the various afflictions follow along with ignorance (*avidyā*), or is it said that ignorance follows along with the afflictions?

If one adopts the former interpretation, the principle is necessarily untenable; for when associated with other afflictions, ignorance is inferior, and it is logically impossible for the superior to follow along with the inferior.
If the latter meaning is adopted, the essence of ignorance should be named after that [condition], because it follows from it.
For something cannot be named after another unless it follows from it.

If it is argued that because this and that follow one another without distinction, they do not constitute a definitive cause and thus it is improper to establish a specific designation for them—how could such a claim bring about satisfaction?

Furthermore, regarding the statement "because they manifest through the power of ignorance," is this said with reference to the primary ignorance (*pravartaka-avidyā*) or with reference to the accompanying ignorance (*anuvartaka-avidyā*)?
Both of these two positions are irrational, because ignorance also functions in accordance with craving and the other afflictions;
since it is associated with others, it is not sovereign.
That which is not sovereign cannot be said to possess superior power.
One should simply say that ignorance arises through the power of craving and so forth, because within the associated category [of mental factors], the power of craving and so forth is predominant.
Just as one cannot say that the king is superior to his retinue, how can it be said that craving and so forth arise through the power of ignorance?
Therefore, both of these two reasons lack the power of proof;
the principle previously stated is superior.
From the stage of karma such as merit (*puṇya*) during a previous life until the ripening of the present fruit, the term "formation" (*saṃskāra*) is established as a collective designation.
The phrase "the stage of the first member" flows through to old age and death.
Regarding meritorious and other types of karma, they shall be extensively analyzed in the *Karmavarga* (Chapter on Karma) according to the intent of the Master’s treatise.
Here, it should be explained: for what reason is karma of such a kind from a previous birth alone designated as "formations" (*saṃskāra*)?
Because the name conforms to the meaning. What is that meaning?
It refers to that which has arisen based on the convergence of various conditions, or that which has been produced through the convergence of successive forces.

Furthermore, it can act as a condition that brings about the conjunction of effects, or, having already brought about this conjunction, it can serve as the condition for the effect; this is what is meant by the "actual meaning" (vastu-artha) that follows the designation "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
When the karma from a previous birth ripens as a fruit in the present, its formative characteristics (*ākāra*) are complete, and thus it alone receives the name "formations."
By this, karma that is to produce a future fruit has already been excluded, because the fruit of that karma has not yet matured.

Since its characteristics are not yet complete, it is not designated by the name "saṃskāra" (formative action). [Objection: Is it not the case that all [causes] which have already given their own fruits possess these characteristics as the essence of a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), and therefore should all of them be designated by the name "saṃskāra"?
What is the nature of this?
It refers to all that is non-karmic and to karma that has arisen prior [to the result].

Although it is logically possible for that which has already obtained its fruit to be so, it is explained in terms of what is predominant: karma is the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), because it is the most powerful in drawing forth the fruit.
Because karma that produces present fruits is coarse, manifest, and easy to know, one can thereby believe and understand the karma that produces past fruits;
for this reason, only this [present karma] is established as bearing the name "saṃskāra" (formative forces).

Although all causes that have already yielded their fruits should collectively be termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*), this [definition] refers specifically to those ripening causes (*vipāka-hetu*) capable of summoning future existence; therefore, there is no fault of the term "formation" being underinclusive.
Therefore, it is established that only those karmas experienced in a previous life which induce this present life are specifically termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*).

At the very moment of linking to rebirth within the mother’s womb and so forth, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) existing for a single moment are termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), because consciousness is predominant at that moment.
This is exclusively mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because within this state the conditions for the arising of the five sensory consciousnesses have not yet been fulfilled.
What is the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)? It refers to that which is capable of cognizing.

Regarding what was previously stated by other masters as a provisional explanation within the investigation into the nature of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), one should now further investigate this in order to refute the tenets held by the Sthavira and to clarify our own established position.
The Elder said: "That which is stated in the Sūtras—that consciousness is that which cognizes—is not from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), but is a conventional designation (saṃvṛti).
If that which cognizes were consciousness, then it would also have to be called non-consciousness."

That is to say, if that which is capable of discerning is designated as "consciousness," then at a time when it is incapable of discerning, it would follow that it is not consciousness; yet it is not appropriate to apply the name "consciousness" to what is not consciousness.
In this context, at what stage does the Venerable Elder claim that consciousness is incapable of discerning?

If one speaks of consciousness in the states of the unborn or the already ceased, it would be like a flower in the sky; yet according to your own tenet, consciousness exists in those states. How then can you say that if something is a cognizer, it is consciousness, while also saying it is non-consciousness?

Furthermore, it cannot be said that at the present time one possesses both a consciousness capable of cognizing and one incapable of cognizing, because a present consciousness necessarily cognizes its object. Since no fourth state of consciousness can be found, how could it be said that at the time of non-cognition it would follow that [consciousness] is not consciousness?

Furthermore, according to their own tenets, they do not describe consciousness as non-consciousness, nor do they describe non-consciousness as consciousness; for there is no phenomenon that is non-consciousness which they describe as consciousness, and they describe the present state of cognition as non-cognition.
As for the Elder’s statement that one should not apply the designation "consciousness" to that which is not consciousness, this results in a self-contradiction.

Those who assert that past and future consciousness exist substantially do not claim that it fails to be consciousness simply because it is not currently performing the function of cognition; rather, it is definitively capable of cognition, as its nature and category are identical to those of consciousness.
In this context, it is not said that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is designated as such only at the stage of cognizing;
rather, it is stated simply that when the various conditions converge, it is consciousness alone that is capable of cognizing.

One should explain it in this way: it is not necessary to grasp an image for it to be called perception (*saṃjñā*), nor is it necessary to investigate for it to be called wisdom (*prajñā*). Other instances should be understood accordingly.
Just as a worldly craftsman is called a "master" even when he is not currently making jars and such,
because when he encounters the necessary conditions, he alone is capable of producing objects like jars;
if one were to claim that the substance of the agent is entirely non-existent, then there would likewise be no such functions as cognition and so forth.
If it is claimed that there is also no functional capacity for cognition and so forth, then there would be no differentiation in the functions of consciousness and the rest.
If these were also non-existent, how could consciousness and the rest exist?
If consciousness and the rest did not exist, they would be indistinguishable from flowers in the sky.
There is no scriptural teaching stating that consciousness is not the cognizer; however, in order to refute the notion that "I" am the cognizer, the Blessed One told Potaliputra:
"I never say that there is a cognizer."

The statement here that [the self] is not taught does not mean it is not revealed; rather, its intent is to exclude the notion that there exists a self which is independent, lacks objects of perception, and is established without depending on anything else as the cognizer.
Therefore, that sutra says:
"Suppose someone were to come and ask, 'What is the object-condition of consciousness? and so forth, at length."
Regarding this question, for what does the "one who understands" serve as a condition?

If this sūtra were to pose such a point, why does it not directly state that he serves as a condition for that [birth], but instead says, "If I receive this question, I shall answer thus," and so on, up to "the arising of future renewed existence"?
In order to refute the notion that there exists a self which is the cognizer, consciousness is not explicitly stated to be its condition.
If it were stated that consciousness is its condition, one would conclude that the Blessed One was referring to the self by the name "consciousness."

Therefore, having first demonstrated that the essence of consciousness is birth, one subsequently states that birth necessarily conditions existence (*bhava*). Consequently, the next question asks what the condition for existence is, and the reply further states that it is precisely the future existence (*upapatti-bhava*).

This sutra does not state that the former serves as the cause for the present; rather, it states that the present cause is able to produce future existence (*bhava*). This is because by merely manifesting the latter, the former can be inferred accordingly.
It is like when one does not extensively manifest the distinctions of the subsequent fruit, but manifests only the preceding fruit, such that the subsequent can be inferred therefrom.
Why does the Blessed One mention birth (*jāti*) to illustrate consciousness (*vijñāna*)?

Because consciousness and birth share the same characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), when it is said that there is "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) by virtue of this shared characteristic, the meaning that "formations are the condition for consciousness" (*saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam*) is already fully established; therefore, he does not separately state the specific condition from which consciousness arises.
If this is so, how is there no fault in answering the question "What is the condition for the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*)?
by responding as follows? When one asks "by what condition," one is asking both from what [condition] it arises and what serves as its condition; thus, answering both ways incurs no error.
It is also like when one asks, "What is the condition for contact? and the answer to this question states: "Contact is conditioned by the six sense bases; contact, in turn, conditions feeling.
If this were a partial question, it should not have been answered with both [factors]. If a partial question is answered with both, then the question and the answer would be inconsistent.

Therefore, as for the question regarding the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), why is it identical to the question regarding contact (*sparśa*)? There is no fault in answering both together.
Thus, it is first stated that consciousness serves as a condition for others, and subsequently stated that consciousness arises with others as its conditions.

In this context, it is also stated that "old age and death have birth as their condition" and "birth has existence as its condition. This demonstrates that consciousness and birth, as well as the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*), do not differ in essence; therefore, there is no fault.

Alternatively, within this context, it is also correctly stated that consciousness itself functions as the causal condition (*pratyaya*), because of the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*). The term "up to and including" expresses the sense of a limit.
The intended meaning here is that "up to and including" refers to that which arises as future rebirth; this consciousness serves as its causal condition.
If that were so, it would again result in the fault of giving rise to doubt in others. It is not so;

rather, it should be explained that [existence] arises from conditions, as will be explained later. Regarding this condition for existence (*bhava*), the subsequent question asks: "What is the condition for existence? and the reply states: "Up to and including the very existence of future birth. Here, the term "existence" (*bhava*) signifies the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of consciousness.
Why, in this context, are only formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) indicated by the term "limit" (*maryādā*)?
This intention reveals that the projecting [of future existence] and the connecting [of future existence] both occur within a single moment.
This sutra does not deny that consciousness is the cognizer; it merely refutes the notion that a self is the cognizer. How is this known?
Because other sutras state:
What is called consciousness? It is that which is capable of cognizing.
Furthermore, because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, negated a distinct agent, we know that an agent is not entirely non-existent.
How does the Blessed One refute a distinct agent?
As the Blessed One has said:
"There is karma and there is its maturation, but an agent is not to be found."
This refers to that which is able to relinquish these aggregates and is able to continue other aggregates, with the sole exception of the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*).
Since this [negation] merely excludes a specific agent, one must therefore admit that other agents do not fail to exist.
To demonstrate that the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the continuity of cause and effect are themselves the agent, it is further stated:
"Depending on this, that exists; through the arising of this, that arises."
Although there may be an objection stating:
"Just as a single goldsmith can fashion a ring and a bracelet, such that their substance is one and the same whether they have not yet been made, have already been made, or are currently being made;
consciousness should also be like this, because it is the common agent."

This is also not the case; Devadatta’s essence is in fact not one throughout his earlier and later states, yet he falsely claims it is one. Thus, there is no single Devadatta whose essence is permanent.

Although in reality each preceding and succeeding moment is distinct, because the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are similar from beginning to end, their subtle differences are difficult to perceive; therefore, foolish worldlings falsely claim that they are one.

Just as when Yajñadatta acts in the same manner as Devadatta, one who does not perceive their distinction says, "Devadatta is acting"; therefore, in that objection, there is no example based on shared properties (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Thus, when the Sūtra speaks of consciousness as the "cognizer," it refers only to the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) and not according to conventional usage (*saṃvṛti*).
Yet the Elder said:
"This is not the ultimate truth (paramārtha), but a conventional expression (saṃvṛti-vyavahāra).
It is certainly unreasonable."
What is the distinction between the two conditions—volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—and consciousness (*vijñāna*)?
Where is it stated that these three are conditioned by consciousness?
Regarding "volitional formations as a condition for consciousness," this refers to what is taught in the Sūtras: "with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises."
Regarding "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form," as the Buddha told Ānanda in the *Mahānidāna Sūtra*:
"Would consciousness be able to abide without depending on name-and-form? "No, [it would not]."
World-Honored One!
Regarding consciousness having two conditions, as it is said in the Sūtra:
"Conditioned by two, consciousness arises."
What are these two? They are the eye and forms, up to the mind and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
There is consciousness conditioned by name-and-form that is not accompanied by formations; there is also consciousness conditioned by [name-and-form] that is accompanied by formations.

This means that it is specifically the consciousness at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) that is said to have volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) as its condition, because it is drawn forth by the power of those formations.

This consciousness of rebirth-linking lasts for only a single moment; it is also called "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), because it attains growth by depending upon name-and-form.
Furthermore, this is also called "consciousness conditioned by two conditions," because it arises with the mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*) as its conditions.

While the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and so forth involve only consciousness conditioned by these two conditions, would it not also be the case that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and consciousness conditioned by these two conditions likewise have formations (*saṃskāra*) as their condition? This is because all preceding karmic maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) or other forms of consciousness arise having formations as their condition.

Although this principle holds true, within the context of the arising of consciousness, only the predominant cause is designated as the "condition" (*pratyaya*); for example, although the arising of visual consciousness also depends on space and so forth, it is said that "consciousness arises depending on two [causes]."

This means that when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), it arises only by taking karma as its predominant cause; since one is drawn to this state by the power of prior karma, it is said that this [consciousness] has karma as its condition.
However, when reaching other states, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth can also serve as the predominant productive conditions for consciousness.
Is it not the case that the consciousness at the very first moment of rebirth also takes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as its predominant condition for arising?

This objection is not valid, because we observe that this consciousness of rebirth can arise even apart from an intermediate state; yet consciousness at other stages does not arise independently of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth. Therefore, it is said that volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the condition for consciousness only with respect to the initial moment of linking rebirth.
Other masters say:
"Consciousness conditioned by formations" refers to the time of initial grasping;
"consciousness conditioned by name-and-form" refers to the time of guarding after having grasped.
Regarding the second, "conditioned by contact, consciousness arises," this refers to the time when the protection [of the embryo] has already increased.
Some say that "conditioned by formations, consciousness arises" indicates past karma.
"Name-and-form as the condition for consciousness" indicates the sequential order.
"The two conditions for consciousness" indicate the objective basis.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Contact conditions consciousness" reveals the transformation of a single gateway;
"name-and-form conditions consciousness" reveals the transformation of two gateways, because at that stage, consciousness also transforms in dependence upon the gateway of the body-faculty.
The statement regarding "consciousness conditioned by two factors" reveals its operation through six gates.
There are many such distinctions of this kind.

Furthermore, the Bhagavān taught that there are two types of consciousness that serve as the condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): namely, consciousness at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), and consciousness during the period of existence (*bhava*).
Therefore, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"If consciousness were not to enter the mother's womb, would this name-and-form (nāmarūpa) become the kalala? No, it would not."
"World-Honored One!
... [as extensively explained] ...
" The World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda, saying:
"When consciousness enters the mother's womb, does it then abandon that name-and-form to give rise to a subsequent name-and-form? No,
World-Honored One."
...and so forth, as explained at length.

The meaning herein is this: if consciousness were not to enter the mother’s womb, then the name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that arises simultaneously with that consciousness would be unable to serve as the cause for the name-and-form of the kalala stage.

Even if one has already entered the mother’s womb and been conceived, if it is interrupted by obstructive conditions, the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) existing at the stage of the *kalala* will not lead to the subsequent name-and-form that follows the *kalala*; this is the meaning of the non-attainment of the member of name-and-form.
The Blessed One further addressed Ānanda, saying:
"If consciousness were to be severed and destroyed while one is in the stage of an infant or a youth, then name-and-form would certainly not grow, increase, or expand."

It is not possible for the state of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) to arise at a moment that is without interval [from consciousness] and yet be designated as the stage of an infant or a youth; therefore, this statement says that consciousness exists when [the body] is present.
Since these various terms for "consciousness" (vijñāna) are used without distinction, which stage of consciousness should be taken as the condition for name-and-form (nāmarūpa)?
To resolve this doubt, the verse states:
"The consciousness that is precisely the aggregates at the moment of linking rebirth [is so called] because it has volitional formations (saṃskāra) as its condition."

Although consciousness in its initial stage can serve as a condition for the name-and-form that arises simultaneously with it or arises immediately thereafter, this does not include the sense of being a condition for name-and-form that arises simultaneously; for in this context, dependent origination is explained solely in terms of sequential stages.
At the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) together with its accompanying factors are collectively termed "consciousness.
*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 25; *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 26.
