Chapter 3, Part 6: The Analysis of Dependent Origination (Pratītyasamutpāda-vibhaṅga), Section Six. From the moment after the consciousness that links rebirth until before the arising of the six sense bases, all intermediate stages are collectively termed *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form).
Is it not the case that since the two bases of body and mind have already arisen, one should say that these [other] four bases exist prior to their arising?
The Venerable Rāma explains according to his own view that the designation "base" (āyatana) is established only after name-and-form (nāmarūpa) has been transcended.

Although the substance of the mind (*manas*) is constant, there are instances where it is not designated as the "mind-base" (*manāyatana*); it must be a "sphere of contact" (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) to receive that name.

Within the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the mind-base is not destroyed; for this reason, it is admitted that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises. However, because other conditions are lacking, there is no contact (*sparśa*); therefore, it is not [designated as] "consciousness."
Within the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the two faculties of body and mind may be designated as "bases" (*āyatana*); therefore, it is said that name-and-form precedes the six bases.
To claim that the six bases arise with name-and-form as their condition is merely a groundless fabrication of false words, for it is entirely devoid of both correct reasoning and authentic scripture.
This means there is no logical teaching that can prove that mental consciousness arises with the mind and dharmas as its conditions;
furthermore, within such cases, there may be what is not termed the "conjunction of the three," or there may be the conjunction of the three without contact (*sparśa*).
If it is argued that in this state there is an inferior conjunction of the three, then contact (*sparśa*) must likewise exist; how then could it be entirely non-existent?
For that school admits that contact is precisely the conjunction of the three.

Furthermore, they also admit that there may be a sense-base without contact, since they themselves state that within the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the mental base (*manāyatana*) is not destroyed, yet contact does not exist.
If that is so, then within the stage of consciousness and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), what phenomenon could destroy the mind such that it is no longer the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*)?

Furthermore, according to their own tenet, apart from the triad of sense-faculty, object, and consciousness, what other distinct condition could directly produce contact (*sparśa*) such that they claim contact exists when these are deficient?
The Blessed Buddha never made such a statement; it is merely like the idle talk of a child playing in his own room.
Furthermore, because he stated that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is the condition for contact (sparśa), as he told Ānanda:
"If someone were to ask, 'Does contact have a condition?'"
One should answer, "It exists.
If he should further ask, "What is the condition for this contact?
one should correctly answer, "That which is called name-and-form (nāmarūpa)."

If that is so, would it not follow that since name-and-form (nāmarūpa) exists prior to the arising of the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), there must necessarily be contact (sparśa)? In that case, there would never be a time when the mind (manas) is not the mind-base (mana-āyatana).

If you argue that this is indeed the case—that name-and-form arises as contact before the six sense bases—then the stage of name-and-form would not be prior to the six sense bases. As the Blessed One told Ānanda:
"If consciousness were to be severed and destroyed while in the stage of infancy or childhood, name-and-form would certainly not grow or expand."
If this is so, how could name-and-form exist prior to the six sense bases?
Therefore, the claim that name-and-form itself is the condition for contact is also unreasonable, because consciousness is stated to be the condition.

That which serves as the condition for the arising of contact and name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the Blessed One has declared to be the consciousness at rebirth-linking (pratisandhi-vijñāna) acting as the condition; as it is said in the Sūtra:
"If consciousness were not to enter the mother's womb, would this name-and-form develop into the kalala?"
"No, World-Honored One! ...
[and so on] up to the full exposition."

Next, regarding the statement that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and contact (sparśa) serve as conditions for one another: since it is impossible within this stage [of embryonic development] to designate it as an "infant" and so forth, this defense is untenable.

Furthermore, what kind of form already exists within this stage to serve as a condition for the arising of contact, such that you claim that name-and-form serves as the condition for the arising of contact in this stage?
Some say that in this stage it is merely called "the arising of contact," yet in terms of the general state, it is said that "name-and-form" serves as the condition.

Others say that this refers to the complete stage of name-and-form; because bodily contact serves as the condition for the arising of bodily consciousness, it is said that name-and-form serves as the condition for contact.

Now, regarding the statement here that "name-and-form conditions contact," this is said in general terms according to their respective stages to possess two conditions; however, if explained specifically, the condition may be either name-and-form alone or both together.
Alternatively, since contact arises with the six sense bases as its condition, it is said that name-and-form serves as the condition for contact.
However, it is not the case that there is no contact (*sparśa*) at the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), for it is admitted that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) exists therein.

Nowhere has it been stated that contact has causes other than the sense faculties and their objects; therefore, to claim that consciousness exists here while contact does not is a statement without reason.
Furthermore, regarding what you have stated— that although the essence of the mind (manas) is eternal, there are instances where it is not the sense-base of mind (manāyatana)— what does this signify?
If it is indeed the essence of a sense-base yet is not designated as such, for what reason do you ultimately fail to state the cause?

Furthermore, it is said that the name "base" (āyatana) is established only when there is a locus of contact; if you admit this to be the essence of the base, then this statement [of yours] is undermined.
If it is not the essence of the base, then it contradicts the sūtra.
For "all phenomena" refers to the twelve bases, yet the Blessed One has demonstrated in various places that there is no phenomenon existing apart from the twelve bases.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that among all phenomena there exists an entity of "impropriety" (asthāna) that is nonetheless subsumed under the category of "locus" (sthāna).
Although a single atom (paramāṇu) cannot produce contact, there is no such thing as a single atom existing in the present.
That which is not the support or object of the five groups of consciousness is also the substance of a sense base (*āyatana*), because it possesses that characteristic.
Therefore, the claim that the substance of the mind (*manas*) exists eternally yet is not the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*) is an unreasonable statement.

If that is so, why does one not say: "The four bases prior to the arising [of the sense organs] are called name-and-form (nāmarūpa), because at the stage of consciousness and name-and-form, their functional capacity is diminished and inferior"?
That is to say, within these two stages, the substance of the internal bases has its function still diminished and inferior, and thus they are not established as "bases" (āyatana).
If, within this stage, the function of the bases (*āyatana*) is perfected and predominant, then the designation "base" may be applied to this very stage.
Alternatively, because the stages differ, their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are distinct.
That is to say, the mental body (*manas-kāya*) acquired at the stage of the six bases has a predominant function and a perfected essence, which was not the case for what was acquired prior to that.
Thus, regarding these six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), because name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) serves as their condition, it is said that "name-and-form conditions the arising of the six sense bases.

Alternatively, it is because in this stage they first attain full manifestation; that is to say, it is only when one reaches the stage of the differentiation of limbs that the male and female faculties (*puruṣendriya* and *strīndriya*) are obtained, at which time all the groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) are able to arise simultaneously.

Therefore, within the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it is only when the body and mind bases (*kāya- and mana-āyatana*) manifest in their essential nature and function that they attain their full status.
For this reason, it is said that the period prior to the arising of the six sense bases is the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
This explanation is excellent.
A detailed analysis of this branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) will be further demonstrated in the subsequent text.
That which arises with name-and-form as its condition, possessing the sense faculties such as the eye but before the three have come together, is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

This refers to the stage following name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) when the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have already arisen, yet before the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses have fully come together in combination; during this stage, they gradually increase through the sequence of weak, medium, and strong degrees, and are collectively termed the "six sense bases."
How could it be said that the three factors have not yet come together when, at this stage, the various consciousnesses do not arise?

Furthermore, there is no single stage where mental consciousness does not arise; even during the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), bodily consciousness arises—how much more so, then, can one say there is no "coming together of the three" at the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)?
The remaining groups of consciousness may also arise, yet they are neither constant nor predominant; therefore, the designation "triple-contact" (tri-saṃnipāta) has not been established for them.
Within this stage, the six sense bases (ṣaḍ-āyatana) alone are predominant; thus, the distinction of this stage is designated in terms of the six sense bases.

Since it is already admitted that name-and-form arises conditioned by the six sense bases, the six sense bases should be established immediately after a single moment of name-and-form, just as the member of name-and-form is established immediately after a single moment of consciousness.
This objection is not valid, because the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) must depend upon the maturation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) before they can arise.
What phenomenon is called the "maturation" of name-and-form?

There is no separate entity; rather, when name-and-form is in its lower or middle stages, it is unable to serve as a condition to project the arising of the six sense bases. Only when it reaches the superior stage can it serve as a condition to project the six sense bases; this very state is what is termed "maturation."

The six sense bases arise only when name-and-form has matured, just as a sprout can only emerge once the seed has undergone transformation; nor can the six sense bases arise apart from name-and-form, just as rain cannot fall except by depending upon clouds.
If that is so, the six sense bases do not arise from name-and-form; how then can it be said that "name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases"?
That which acts as a condition possesses an auxiliary capacity; it does not necessarily have to produce [the effect] directly in order to fulfill the definition of being a condition.
If, although drawn by projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), the completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*) were absent, the fruit would ultimately not arise.
Likewise, although the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are summoned by karma, they necessarily have no possibility of arising without the condition of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which are summoned by prior karma, arise only through the auxiliary condition of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), because they are drawn forth by the force of a single continuum.

Although matter and so forth also arise with name-and-form as their condition, these are produced from the moistening of the very first moment of consciousness; therefore, it is not said that they arise conditioned by name-and-form.

Furthermore, while those [factors] such as form (*rūpa*) pertain to both the animate and the inanimate, the present discussion clarifies only the dependent origination of sentient beings; therefore, it states only that "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) serves as the condition for the arising of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Alternatively, as previously established, when it was explained that "consciousness conditions name-and-form," this already constituted a general statement regarding the dependent origination of form and the other factors.
Now, after name-and-form, what further distinction is there between the form and so forth and those that preceded it?
Since their functional efficacy can be perceived, it is necessary to state that they arise from name-and-form; therefore, there is no error in what is stated in the original text.
In this context, because the Elder (Sthavira) wishes to maintain that the eye and so forth exist only as conventional designations for their functional aggregation, he makes this statement:
"The five faculties, beginning with the eye, exist only conventionally," and so on at length.
Such a desire is not consistent with reason.
Regarding the method for curing that [condition], as explained in the first chapter, there are slight differences which should now be further analyzed.
The Elder said:

"The consciousnesses produced by the five sense faculties perceive only that which exists conventionally, because they are devoid of conceptual discrimination, just as a clear mirror reflects various forms and images."
It is precisely for this reason that consciousness is not fit to serve as a basis.
As the Blessed One said:
"Rely on wisdom, do not rely on consciousness."

It is argued that because mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes both the conventional (saṃvṛti) and the ultimate (paramārtha) as its objects, its nature must comprise both that which is a support (āśraya) and that which is not a support.
This is also incorrect, for it would follow that wisdom (jñāna) would be the same.

If visual consciousness and the others, by virtue of taking the conventional as their object and being non-conceptual (nirvikalpa), were unfit to be supports, then wisdom should likewise be so; how could it be of a supportive nature alone?
That is to say, they claim that wisdom (*jñāna*) is a specific differentiation of volition (*cetanā*), and that wisdom also arises based on the doors of the five sense-faculties.
Because it takes conventional reality as its object and is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), it too—like consciousness (*vijñāna*)—should not be fit to serve as a support.
If it is claimed that wisdom arises having the ultimate as its object and possesses conceptualization, then consciousness should likewise be so;

that is, there would be mental consciousness capable of taking the ultimate as its object, and because it possesses conceptualization, it too could serve as a basis [for the realization of the ultimate].

If cognition were produced solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), one should not say that cognition alone is the support (*āśraya*); for it is admitted that mental consciousness takes both [the preceding moment of cognition and the sense organ] as its objects, and it is admitted that its substance simultaneously functions as both a support and a non-support.
Just as it is with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), wisdom (*jñāna*) also extends to that which is not based [on a physical organ]. Therefore, the mental consciousness should be like wisdom;

there must also be instances where it functions without a basis. Furthermore, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) should also be without a basis, because it operates in a single mode across many phenomena and is free from conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa*).
The Elder (Sthavira) accepts that such dharma-knowledge does not take the ultimate reality as its object; therefore, he says this very thing:

"The various knowledges arising in most sentient beings are cognitions of a single characteristic with respect to many phenomena—namely, they apprehend a unified characteristic within many phenomena—and it is difficult for such a cognition to arise by taking the ultimate reality as its object."

If it is argued that although this wisdom arises by taking many phenomena as its objects, it does not apprehend a synthetic whole (*ekapiṇḍa-saṃjñā*) among those phenomena, then the visual and other sensory consciousnesses should likewise be admitted to be so; for while they arise with many phenomena as their objective conditions, they do not apprehend a synthetic whole because they are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).

Thus, one must admit that the five consciousnesses depend solely upon the mental consciousness; they penetrate both the nature of having a basis and not having a basis, because they apprehend a unified composite appearance and take ultimate reality as their object.

Nowhere has it been stated that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) serves as a support (*āśraya*). Although the Sthavira occasionally speaks of it as having the nature of a support, this indicates that the Sthavira wavers and hesitates regarding the meaning of the sūtras, unable to definitively clarify it;
even if he were to provide such a clarification, it would contradict both reason and scripture. Therefore, the Sthavira’s intention cannot be accepted as a valid support.

The meaning of this sūtra will be analyzed separately in another section; fearing that the text would become overly cumbersome, I shall desist for now. One should simply reflect upon what is correctly elucidated here.

As for the Elder’s extensive employment of expedient means to establish the existence of consciousness without an object, this shall be refuted in detail in the fifth chapter, "On the Latent Dispositions" (*Anuśaya*).
It should be understood that within this analysis of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), one may likewise universally refute all those false conceptualizations.
The Blessed One said:
"When the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness comes together, it is termed contact (*sparśa*)."

This refers to the stage when one has not yet understood the distinct causes of the three types of feeling (*vedanā*), but merely possesses the conjunction of the three [bases]; this stage is called contact (*sparśa*).
The specific meanings of the various classifications of contact shall be discussed in detail later.

When one has already understood the distinguishing characteristics of the causes of the three types of feeling, but has not yet given rise to sensual craving (*kāmarāga*), this stage is called feeling (*vedanā*).

This means that when one has already been able to discern the conditions for suffering, pleasure, and so forth, yet sensual desire has not yet begun to operate, this stage is called the "position of feeling" (*vedanā-avasthā*).
The specific meanings of the various types of feeling shall be discussed extensively later.
When there is craving for exquisite requisites and sensual desire is currently active, but one has not yet engaged in extensive pursuit, this stage is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).
"Excellent requisites" refers to excellent material wealth; craving for these, as well as for sexual intercourse, is collectively termed "attachment.
A detailed analysis of the meaning of attachment is found in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa*.
Regarding this, the Sthavira further states:
Feeling (vedanā) is expected by craving (tṛṣṇā), but it is not its generative cause.
If that is so, how can it be said that "feeling is the condition for craving"?
Because feeling serves as the object, it is said to be the condition for craving.
This means that when various forms of craving arise, they take feeling (*vedanā*) as their object.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If one does not know feeling as it truly is—its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—one delights in feeling; this is called clinging (*upādāna*)."
How is this known? The Sūtra states that craving arises conditioned by feeling (*vedanā*).
Is it not the case that what was said—that one delights in feeling—has the very meaning of craving arising conditioned by feeling?
This is not a valid proof, for the seventh case (locative) can also be employed in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

That is to say, "from feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises through delight and attachment" means that craving arises based on feeling as its cause; it is for this reason that feeling is said to be the condition for craving.
If this were not the case, craving must already have arisen before there could be an object; craving that has not yet arisen cannot take feeling as its object because it lacks a substantial entity.
Since the entity of craving has already arisen through the power of other conditions, how can you further claim that "craving arises conditioned by feeling"?

If it were the case that when the substance of craving has already arisen through the power of other conditions, and feeling is its object, that feeling could also be called a "condition" [for that craving], then there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
That is to say, since feeling sometimes takes craving as its object, one would also have to say that feeling has craving as its condition.
Furthermore, since craving sometimes takes contact as its object, one should also say that craving arises with contact as its condition.
Moreover, since untainted wisdom also takes craving as its object, one should likewise say that this [wisdom] arises by taking craving as its condition.

Even if one were to grant that this sutra speaks of "delight in feeling" (*vedanāyām nandī*) with reference to the object conditioned by feeling, on what basis do you know that the statement "feeling conditions craving" (*vedanāpratyayā tṛṣṇā*) does not refer to a productive cause (*janakahetu*)?

For the position of the Sthavira also maintains that all explained dependent originations (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are based on productive causes; how then can the meaning of a productive cause be denied here?
Therefore, that treatise states:
"Dependent origination acts as a rope, binding sentient beings and causing them to dwell within birth and death.
If one can thoroughly know sensation, it is called 'severing the rope.'"
If one gives rise to [craving] by taking feeling as an object, it is called bondage.

It is said that feeling, which serves as the object, is for the purpose of thorough knowledge; yet, since craving is precisely what enables the thorough knowledge of feeling, why is it said that feeling is for the purpose of thorough knowledge?

It is not so. Why? It means that the feeling known by the wisdom of thorough knowledge (*parijñā-jñāna*)—namely, the feeling known by the wisdom regarding the origin of feeling and so forth—is precisely the object-condition (*ālambana*) of craving; there is no fixed cause [for its cessation].

The realization of the object of the antidote is precisely the objective support (*ālambana*) of that which is to be countered, namely craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth; therefore, one should not say that craving arises conditioned by feeling (*vedanā*).

When it is said that feeling as an objective support is for the sake of thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*), even if it is stated for the sake of thorough knowledge that feeling is the objective support of craving, what contradiction is there in principle to accepting that feeling as an objective support is the cause for the arising of craving?

Because of this denial, he negates the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), thereby denying the principle that consciousness arises with the mind-faculty (*manas*) as its cause by taking the mind as its object.

Furthermore, in various passages within his own treatise, that Elder (Vasumitra) states that craving arises conditioned by feeling (*vedanā*); that is, he asserts that there is feeling associated with ignorance (*avidyā*) which serves as a condition for craving, and that feeling produced by contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*) arises as a condition for craving.
Furthermore, it is said that craving is the fruit, which must necessarily have feeling as its cause, because the existence of a cause is known through the mention of the name of the fruit.
Moreover, it is said that ignorance assists feeling, thereby serving as the cause for the arising of craving.
Regarding what has been stated thus, the former contradicts the latter and the latter contradicts the former; these two preceding and succeeding statements are mutually inconsistent and subversive.
Because he speaks haphazardly without examining the underlying principles, his words cannot be relied upon or trusted.
The Venerable Vasubandhu provides this explanation:
"Craving and delight are themselves called 'clinging' (*upādāna*); since craving is subsumed within clinging, the Sūtra does not mention them separately."
The Elder here falsely dismisses this by claiming it is incorrect, arguing that the two categories of cause and effect must logically be distinct.
That is to say, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) differ in their causal nature, for grasping arises as the fruit with craving as its cause.
If, as that Venerable One says, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the cause that can again produce craving, what fault would there be?
This is logically impossible, because it describes them as having distinct characteristics.

That is to say, within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), causes and effects are described as having distinct characteristics in order to clarify the sequence of the continuity of birth and death; thus, one cannot claim that craving is subsumed within grasping (*upādāna*).
If craving arises again because of craving, then through such a succession it would lead to infinity; what could be fully known to cause craving to cease?
In that case, there would be no end to the cycle of birth and death.
What has been stated in this manner is entirely unreasonable.

Your own school admits that contact is itself the cause of contact because it possesses the nature of conjunction; yet you do not admit that contact and its cause possess distinct characteristics, or else you must admit that contact exists apart from its cause.

If it is accepted that contact (*sparśa*) and its cause, though lacking distinct characteristics, stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, then the same must apply to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*); how then can they be rejected?

If one argues that there is a difference between their conventional and ultimate characteristics, this is also unreasonable, for they do not possess distinct categories like those of feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.

That is to say, according to that school, contact and the cause of the separation from contact do not have distinct essential natures like feeling and so forth; how, then, can it be said that their characteristics differ?
Since no provisional phenomena possess a distinct characteristic or essence apart from their provisional basis, upon what could such a distinction be established?

Alternatively, just as the six sense bases serve as conditions for contact, it is not maintained that they function as conditions only in relation to their own kind; rather, they are accepted as conditions both in relation to their own kind and to other kinds. Nevertheless, within this context, there is no absence of cause and effect.

Thus, it should be admitted that craving and grasping function as conditions not only with respect to their own respective categories, but also with respect to both their own and other categories; yet within this process, there is no absence of cause and effect.
Furthermore, just as the six sense bases take name-and-form as their condition, they lack distinct characteristics yet possess cause and effect;

likewise, name-and-form takes consciousness as its condition, and the essence of consciousness is subsumed within name. Although there is no difference in characteristic between the preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness, it is not the case that consciousness and name-and-form lack cause and effect.

The same principle should apply to the category of grasping (*upādāna*) arising from craving (*tṛṣṇā*); therefore, although there is no difference in their characteristics within dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they still possess a cause-and-effect relationship. For this reason, there is no fault in stating that grasping is subsumed within craving.
The claim that the characteristics of cause and effect are necessarily distinct is a statement for which there is no logical proof.
In order to explain the sequential continuity of birth and death, one must state that cause and effect differ in their characteristics; it is not that their characteristics are without distinction.
What evidence is there for this?

If it is argued that the proof is not established because the beings to be converted would find it difficult to understand if cause and effect were non-distinct, why is that so? Because that argument also fails to constitute valid proof. Why? Because...
Because the meanings of "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) and "clinging" (*upādāna*) differ in their designations—

just as the designations and meanings of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and so forth are distinct from those of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth— it is not stated that craving itself is the cause of clinging.

How, then, can it be said that the distinction between the causes and effects of these two cravings is difficult to know, such that the sequence of the continuity of birth and death is difficult to discern?
It is clearly stated that craving can produce the fruit of grasping; how could such a distinction between cause and effect be difficult to understand?

Just as in your own tenets, it is not difficult to comprehend that name-and-form has consciousness as its cause, the six sense bases have name-and-form as their cause, and contact has the six sense bases as its cause.
Furthermore, because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has personally expounded this, as it is said in the Sūtra:
"If one takes delight in feeling, that is called 'clinging' (upādāna); clinging is the condition for existence," and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, the principle that [craving] is grasping is fully established.
The Sthavira further states:
"This sutra is not of definitive meaning (nītārtha), or else it has been misrecited by the reciter, because it speaks of a distinct antidote."

He [the opponent] maintains that this sūtra is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); rather, for the sake of causing rapid abandonment and cessation, the Blessed One metaphorically employs the term "clinging" (*upādāna*) with respect to the cause of clinging.
Alternatively, it should be recited as: "If one finds delight in sensation (*vedanā*), one is then able to give rise to clinging."
Why is this so? Because they are explained separately as antidotes in other places.
As the Sūtra says:
If one can extinguish this, then because joy (*nandī*) regarding all feelings is extinguished, grasping (*upādāna*) will also be extinguished accordingly.

Alas! In the Holy Teaching of the Eastern Land, there is no reliance; thus, failing to distinguish between the definitive (*nītārtha*) and the interpretable (*neyārtha*), they nevertheless judge various sūtras according to their own whims. To establish their own school, they speak of "grasping" as being conditioned by feeling and "clinging" (*tṛṣṇā*); they judge truly definitive sūtras to be non-definitive, and stubbornly cling to that which is actually reliable as being unreliable.
A sūtra that is not of definitive meaning (*neyārtha*) cannot be called definitive; let it not be that a sūtra of non-definitive meaning is termed a sūtra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
If this were so, there would be no authoritative scripture at all to rely upon, but only meaningless words that cannot be relied upon; thus, one would become a destroyer of the sublime Dharma.

If grasping (*upādāna*) is understood as being included within grasping because it is caused by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), just as the cause of the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) is included within the aggregates of grasping—then both the essence of grasping and its cause are spoken of using the term "grasping. This serves as an even more excellent condition for their swift abandonment; what contradiction is there in judging this to be of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)?

Furthermore, those original recitations should not be altered, for they have no superior utility within the meaning of the teaching; nor is there any deficiency in the meaning of the holy doctrine regarding what was originally recited—why then trouble oneself to change them at all?

Furthermore, the citation they have brought forward to prove that this sūtra is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is likewise no valid proof; for it states that when craving (*tṛṣṇā*) ceases, its fruit—craving and the rest—also cease accordingly.
The Bhagavān said:
"If one can extinguish this, then because craving and delight are extinguished, grasping also follows in being extinguished.
This is to demonstrate that a single cause can have multiple effects.
Furthermore, why do you not believe such a sūtra?
Because this sūtra states that delight (*nandī*) is itself called grasping (*upādāna*), another sūtra says:
"With the cessation of delight, grasping also ceases accordingly."
The World-Honored One made this statement in order to reveal that the delight comprised within grasping is itself the cause of grasping.
By making such a statement, it causes [grasping] to be severed more swiftly, because many faults are subsumed within grasping.

Furthermore, since other passages clearly state that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are distinct categories, one may conclude that this sūtra’s identification of delight as grasping is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
However, there is no such statement; rather, other sūtras judge that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is itself grasping (*upādāna*). As the Blessed One said:
"I shall teach you the phenomena conducive to grasping (*upādānīya-dharma*) and the essence of grasping (*upādāna-svabhāva*)," and so on at length, until: "What is the essence of grasping?"
Regarding the desire and greed herein,
the Elder himself stated:
"If the Blessed One himself both formulated and explained this, it is a sūtra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)."
It cannot be judged that this is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
Furthermore, the Bhagavān told the bhikṣus:
"Grasping (*upādāna*) is neither identical to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), nor is it separate from the five aggregates."

However, "clinging" (*upādāna*) is precisely the desire and greed within this context; therefore, this sutra states that "delight" is itself clinging. There is no room for judging this to be a sutra of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).

Furthermore, it is logically certain that clinging subsumes craving (*tṛṣṇā*), because all afflictions (*kleśa*) are causes of karma, just as all delusions regarding the past limit are termed ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"Taking (*upādāna*) conditions existence (*bhava*). This means that it is due to afflictions (*kleśa*) that various karmas are set in motion.

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the most preeminent cause for setting karma in motion; since it is subsumed within "taking" as its condition for producing existence, what logical flaw is there in not believing this dependence?

As in the case of dependent origination regarding the past limit (*pūrvānta*), it is said that "ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskārāḥ*). Since all afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of inciting karma, and because they are the cause of such karma, they are all termed "ignorance. Therefore, it is logically established that the delusions capable of inciting karma within the future limit (*aparānta*) are all subsumed under "grasping" (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, regarding what was said:
"Craving arises from craving; thus, through such a succession, it leads to infinity.
In truth, this is indeed infinite; what fault does this entail for our thesis?

That is to say, we admit that subsequent craving arises because of preceding craving, and that preceding craving, in turn, arises because of even earlier craving; since its cause is beginningless, it is in fact infinite in principle, and this is a merit rather than a fault in our own school.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated—that which is fully known causes craving to cease—it is because of the full knowledge of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the full knowledge of its cause that craving can be made to cease.
Briefly, there are two kinds of causes for craving:
first, those of a different class, namely sensation (*vedanā*); second, those of the same class, namely craving itself.

What evidence is there to prove that the cessation of craving occurs solely through the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the dissimilar cause, which is sensation (*vedanā*), rather than through the thorough knowledge of the similar cause, which is craving itself?

Even if one were to grant that the cessation of craving occurs solely through thorough knowledge, how could the thorough knowledge of the dissimilar cause, sensation, possibly contradict [the claim] that craving is subsumed within grasping (*upādāna*)?
Therefore, it is taught that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is also subsumed within grasping (*upādāna*); this principle is unshakeable.
Because one seeks everywhere to obtain various desirable objects, this stage is called grasping.

There are four kinds of grasping (*upādāna*), namely: the distinction between grasping at desire (*kāma*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the discourse on self (*ātmavāda*).
Because they grasp, they are called "graspings"; that is, the various afflictions (*kleśa*) perform the functions of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and karma (*karman*).
The afflictions and secondary afflictions bound to the desire realm, excluding views, are called "desire-grasping" (*kāma-upādāna*), like a chariot drawn by horses and so forth.
The four views belonging to the three realms are called "view-grasping" (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*).
That grasping at precepts and observances is called *śīlavrataparāmarśa*.
The afflictions and secondary afflictions associated with the realms of form and formlessness, excluding the five views, are called *ātmavādopādāna*.
Regarding such grasping through speech, it shall be analyzed in detail in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa* (Chapter on Latent Dispositions).
It is only in accordance with the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (Compendium of Ascertainment) that, in this context, ignorance (*avidyā*) is not established as a separate form of grasping;
for independent ignorance is neither sharp nor of a nature that understands [objects], whereas associated ignorance is capable of grasping only through the power of other afflictions.
For this reason, "clinging" (*upādāna*) is not established as a separate category.
Although the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is distinguished from other views, it is established separately because its power to accumulate karma is most predominant.

For this reason, it is said that the single view of clinging to precepts and observances possesses a power equal to the four [other] views in the gateway of accumulating karma; because this one view causes karma to blaze forth, opposing the Noble Path and distancing one from liberation, the clinging to precepts and observances is established as a distinct form of clinging.

The term "grasping" (*upādāna*) is used here to signify the sense of "relying upon and clinging to. Although all categories of afflictions involve relying upon and clinging to, these two types of grasping are preeminent in this sense; therefore, only these two are designated as "grasping," because they represent the most stubborn forms of attachment toward others.

However, between these two, the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is more powerful; because it functions with such intense obsession that it obscures [the truth], it is established as a separate "clinging" (*upādāna*) apart from the others.

Since all four views have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature, they possess a stronger sense of "grasping" (*parāmarśa*) than other afflictions; thus, these four are subsumed under and distinguished from the rest to be established as "view-clinging" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

The other two types of grasping are established because the remaining afflictions differ in terms of being in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*) or non-concentration (*asamāhita*), and because they differ in their causes—whether unwholesome (*akuśala*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*).
"Grasping at the discourse of self" (*ātmavādopādāna*) means grasping at the discourse concerning a self; it signifies the act of clinging to such discourse.
This "discourse on self" (ātmavāda) is called "discourse on self" because within it there is the meaning of discourse on self.
What is its essence?

It refers to the collection of phenomena belonging to the category of sentient beings; the attachment that arises toward this discourse on self is termed "clinging to discourse on self" (ātmavādopādāna).
If that were so, all afflictions should be termed "clinging to the doctrine of self" (*ātmavādopādāna*).
We accept this in our own school; thus, your objection is futile.
For what reason, then, is only a small portion designated as "clinging to the doctrine of self"?
In order to establish that all afflictions are forms of the grasping at the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*), distinct names are employed.

That is to say, the other three types of grasping are spoken of by their specific names to demonstrate that "grasping at the doctrine of self" is the general designation for them. This is seen frequently in the Noble Teachings, such as in the cases of the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the element (*dhātu*), or the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), and so forth.

In order to comprehensively encompass the remaining meanings that ought to be explained, a general name is established for a limited portion, as in the cases of the first power (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), and the constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, there is another method of explaining the grasping at the discourse of self (*ātmavādopādāna*): because one relies upon this, it is able to induce the utterance of "self"; this is precisely the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), which is termed "discourse of self."

The fetters of the form and formless realms, as well as greed, pride, doubt, and so forth, cause my view to increase, become firm, and multiply; because they act as companions to the doctrine of self (ātmavāda), they are called "clinging to the doctrine of self" (*ātmavādopādāna*), which means they enable the doctrine of self to be firmly adhered to.

Alternatively, it is taken as that which causes the "discourse on self" (*ātmavāda*) to flourish; it is not that desire-attachment (*rāga*) and so forth also receive this name. Only the afflictions of the meditative states (*samāhitabhūmi*) serve as the proximate cause for the extreme flourishing of the discourse on self, whereas the afflictions of the non-meditative states (*asamāhitabhūmi*) do not assist the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) to flourish in the same way as those of the meditative states.

Sentient beings of the desire realm mostly roam among external objects, causing their minds to become distracted; therefore, the afflictions of this stage do not cause the internal grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) to increase. For this reason, they are not termed "clinging to expressions of self" (*ātma-vādopādāna*).

Regarding these principles established in this Abhidharma, the Elder of limited learning has erroneously raised objections, claiming that such explanations are inconsistent with reason because they have never been so stated in the Noble Teachings.

That is to say, there has never been even a slight teaching in the Noble Doctrine that uses the expression "the word 'self'" to refer to the afflictions of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) bound to the two upper realms, nor does it use the expression "grasping" (*upādāna*) to refer to their other afflictions.
Furthermore, because what was stated previously contradicts what follows, it is said in the Abhidharma:
"For a long night, the non-Buddhist renunciants have clung to the notions of a self, a sentient being, a living soul, a creature, and a nourisher."
If that *pudgala* cannot even designate "selflessness," how much less could it establish the abandonment of the grasping at the doctrine of self?

Thus, the Elder is ultimately incapable of demonstrating that the Abhidharma school contradicts the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); he merely utters meaningless residual sounds like the final notes of a song.
Regarding the claim that "the holy teaching has never stated such a thing," we must first ask: what is this "holy teaching" of yours, O Elder?
Within the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka), we have never heard the Buddha state that the Dharma-seal or the Seal of Determination defines the extent of what constitutes the holy teaching.
If you claim that the holy teaching was spoken by the Buddha, how can you know for certain that these words were not spoken by the Buddha?
For we have never seen anyone who could definitively ascertain the limits of the Buddha’s speech.

That is to say, since it has never been seen that anyone can reach the limit of the Buddha’s word, how can one definitively state that the tenets of the Abhidharma school are not the teachings of the Noble One?

Regarding this, the Venerable [Vasumitra] might at first dismiss it by saying, "The principle thus explained contradicts the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)," but he should not categorically deny that it exists within the Noble Teachings.
The World-Honored One has often stated that whatever is taught must accord with the principle of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) to be capable of serving as a valid authority.
As it is said in the Sūtras: "That which accords with the Sūtras, elucidates the Vinaya, and does not contradict the nature of phenomena—only such teaching may be relied upon."

Since the Abhidharma is named as a comprehensive compendium that does not contradict any of the Buddha’s teachings, principles, or statements, the principles it explains do not violate the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Nevertheless, the Blessed One has also praised speech that, while not coinciding with his own intended meaning, nevertheless accords with correct reasoning (*yukti*), as stated in a Sūtra:
"Although what you have said is not my original intention, what you have spoken is entirely consistent with correct reasoning; therefore, it may all be accepted and upheld."

If it were argued that those points not explicitly stated in the Noble Teachings (āgama) are not valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this would entail an over-extension of the fault. For instance, where in the Noble Teachings is it clearly and definitively stated that trees and the like lack life-force (*jīva*); that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are definitively momentary; that jars and the like do not exist as separate substantial entities; that the past is definitively not a cause for the future; or that sentient beings (*sattva*) did not previously exist and have come into being now?

Furthermore, at what location did the Buddha, the World-Honored One, definitively explain the cryptic statements regarding the killing of one’s father and so forth—specifically, that tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*) is designated as "father" and so on?
Moreover, at what location did the Buddha ever speak of such things as the "ancient pervasive element" (*pūrvānuśaya-dhātu*), which you yourselves maintain?
If it is established as a proof by citing a similar teaching, since that does not explicitly manifest [the point], it may be interpreted otherwise.
Therefore, the claim that something does not exist simply because it is not mentioned in a sutra is not a definitive reason.

Furthermore, even Ānanda should not have asserted that such an explanation is entirely without basis; how much less, then, could that Elder, having mastered only a small portion of the Noble Teaching, be entitled to make such a definitive judgment?
Therefore, it is said in the Udraka Sūtra that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed Udraka, saying:

"I have now surveyed all the disciples of the Buddha within Jambudvīpa, and there is none capable of upholding such a Dharma-gate except for the Venerable One. Therefore, Venerable One, you should personally apply yourself with right diligence to uphold this Dharma-gate so as not to let it be lost, for the World-Honored One himself has spoken this Dharma-gate."
From this analogy, one may know that even now there is no one capable of fully receiving and upholding the Buddha’s holy teaching.

At the time of the Buddha’s initial parinirvāṇa and while he was still dwelling in the world, even those such as Ānanda—persons who were oceans of learning and retention—did not fully know the limits of the Buddha’s words; how much less could anyone today possibly know them all?

Therefore, the Elder says that there has never been even a slight portion of the Noble Teaching in which the term "self" (*ātman*) is used to refer to the higher realms and so forth; this [statement] merely seeks to display his own mastery of the limits of the Noble Teaching, yet it is an extreme exaggeration regarding what he himself knows.
However, the sūtra states:
"Grasping (upādāna) is the condition for existence (bhava).
Since all afflictions (kleśa) are capable of inciting karma, grasping should encompass all afflictions; the principle of this comprehensive inclusion has already been explained as before.
This does not contradict reason or scripture in the slightest; therefore, one knows that there must certainly be a scriptural passage stating this.

Thus, to harbor animosity toward and reject the eloquent expositions of other schools merely out of a desire to establish one's own tradition is not in accordance with the principles of the Noble Teachings. How can one who disparages others to exalt oneself be called a benevolent teacher?

Wise disciples all rely upon the Abhidharma to gather the sustenance of correct reasoning to increase their lives of wisdom; by drinking from and bathing in the clear stream of such well-spoken teachings, whatever they seek and desire shall be accomplished without fail.

Lacking pure faith and deficient in extensive learning, you have strayed from the path and slandered the True Dharma; by manifesting yourself as one who is indistinguishable from non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings, how can you claim that you are receiving the teachings of the Noble Ones? Your own conduct only serves to obscure them.
Does this interpretation not contradict the sacred teaching?
As the Blessed One told the bhikṣus:
"Did you formerly grasp my words as being a permanent, eternal, and unchanging phenomenon, thinking they were truly established?"
"It is truly so,
Blessed One," and so on,
as extensively explained.

The intention here is to say that among internal phenomena, grasping at them as a self is called "grasping at the discourse of self" (*ātmavādopādāna*); therefore, the Abhidharma commentary contradicts this sūtra.
This is not correct, however, because it misunderstands the meaning of the sūtra.

Furthermore, one should examine this carefully: when you questioned the bhikṣus based on the view of self, were you asking whether they formerly grasped my words as being eternal and so forth, or were you asking based on the objective referent of those grasped words, namely "self"?
Since my view lacks characteristics such as permanence or constancy, nor do I have any attachment asserting it to be permanent or constant,
why did the Blessed One ask the assembly of bhikṣus:
"Did you formerly grasp at the clinging to views regarding the self as being permanent, constant, and so forth, and consider it to be truly established?"
How could a bhikṣu truthfully reply, "It is so"?
Therefore, one should simply ask whether the object grasped as a basis is permanent and so forth.
This intention is that the term "clinging to the doctrine of self" (*ātmavādopādāna*) is used metaphorically for the doctrine of self (*ātmavāda*) which is itself the grasped object.
Alternatively, one should recite:
"Did you formerly, based on my words, grasp at [the self] as being eternal and so forth, and consider it to be truly abiding?
Or again, one should say:
"You formerly held that the substance of my teaching is eternal and permanent," and so forth, as explained at length.
Although this interpretation was offered, it is not what I intended; in truth, the meaning should simply be that which is grasped is called "grasping" (upādāna).
If it is argued that this explanation is logically untenable because the particle *luta* is frequently employed within the context of causal function (*kāritra*),
such reasoning is not necessarily conclusive, as the particle *luta* also occurs within the context of specific types of karma (*karmaviśeṣa*).
The meaning of this sūtra further clarifies the Abhidharma school’s interpretation of the term "clinging to the expression 'self'" (*ātmavādopādāna*).

That is to say, "the expression 'self'" refers to the statement "I"; because worldly convention commonly designates this [basis] as "self," it possesses the expression "self" and thus receives the name "clinging to the expression 'self'."
The expression "discourse on self" (ātmavāda) serves as the basis for grasping and attachment; therefore, it may also be called the "grasping at discourse on self.
What is its substance? It refers to the five aggregates of grasping (pañcopādānaskandhāḥ).
Because the world conceives notions of a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, and so forth, with respect to the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), the Sūtra says:
"Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas... and so on, as explained at length.
This passage states: "You formerly clung to the five aggregates of clinging as being permanent and eternal," and so forth, as explained at length.

Therefore, the meaning of "clinging" (*upādāna*) as taught in the cited sūtra cannot definitively prove the position they maintain, nor can it refute the definition of the "clinging to the doctrine of self" (*ātmavādopādāna*) as analyzed by the Abhidharmikas above.
However, that venerable one, by citing this sūtra, merely demonstrates that his own recitation of the text is confused regarding its meaning.

As for his claim that the preceding and succeeding statements contradict each other, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the preceding and succeeding parts of our school’s position; it is because he does not understand the intended meaning of the Abhidharma text that he follows his own erroneous interpretation and asserts that there is a contradiction.

Because those various classes of non-Buddhist renunciants do not understand the meaning of "clinging" (upādāna) and hear only the name, they merely follow that name and claim for themselves, "We teach the abandonment of three clingings, excluding only the fourth."

Why is this? Those non-Buddhists claim that the grasping at the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*) is precisely the self that is grasped; yet they conceive of this self as being permanent, eternal, unchanging, and of a nature that cannot be severed.

Furthermore, because they experience great fear regarding the annihilation of the self (*ātman*), the grasping to the doctrine of a self (*ātmavādopādāna*) is not established as something to be abandoned.
This means that if they truly and skillfully understood the meaning of "grasping," they would also have to establish the abandonment of at least a portion of the grasping to the doctrine of a self;

however, because they do not properly comprehend the meaning of grasping, but merely hear the term "grasping" and falsely infer it to have a real referent, the fourth [type of grasping] is excluded, and it is said that only three are abandoned.

Furthermore, it is like those who employ mere analogies in the present day: they do not establish what ought to be established, yet they forcibly establish what should not; within the very points that ought to be established, they instead fail to establish them.
Moreover, based on their own grasping at specific perspectives, they posit the abandonment of the three types of clinging to non-self-expressions.
However, the entities grasped by those [views] are not the same.
Within the grasping for sensual desires (*kāma-upādāna*), some say its entity consists of the objects of the various exquisite desires, while others say it is sexual craving.

In other schools, the observance of precepts and prohibitions is called the grasping for precepts and prohibitions (*śīla-vrata-upādāna*), and the various views of other schools are called the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*). Because one clings to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as being correct knowledge, the term "grasping for the doctrine of self" (*ātmavāda-upādāna*) is not established; therefore, it is said that three [types of grasping] are abandoned, but not the grasping for the doctrine of self.
Therefore, some among the non-Buddhists speak thus:
"Just as that Great Teacher is venerable and lovely, so too is my teacher;
just as that Great Teacher has reached the ultimate in the Dharma, so too has my teacher."
Just as those companions in the Dharma respect and love one another, so shall we do.
Just as they perfectly maintain and uphold the precepts, so shall we do.
Just as they have established the ability to sever all grasping, so shall we do.
What difference is there between him and us?
Therefore, our own tenets are consistent from beginning to end; how then does the Sthavira establish the various types of clinging (*upādāna*)?
Regarding what he calls "clinging to sensual desire" (*kāma-upādāna*), the Blessed One clearly and personally revealed it in the sūtras, as in the following inquiry:
"What is meant by 'desire'?
The World-Honored One replied:
"It refers to the five kinds of exquisite desires."
However, it is not that the exquisite sensual objects themselves constitute the essence of desire; rather, it is the craving for these objects that is here termed "desire.
Furthermore, the Blessed One exhorted reliance upon sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and such sūtras of definitive meaning should not be interpreted otherwise.

I now perceive this meaning herein: by the power of craving, desire and greed arise within the five exquisite objects of desire, whereby there is grasping; this is called "grasping at sense-pleasures" (*kāma-upādāna*).
The Sūtra is entirely inconsistent with that meaning; for within this Sūtra, the questions and answers are not based at all on the "desire-grasping" (*kāma-upādāna*) as it is conceived by them.

Furthermore, what the Sūtra teaches does not contradict the definition of desire (*kāma*) set forth in our own Abhidharma school, for we also maintain that the desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*) existing within the five objects of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*) is true desire.
Furthermore, what is ultimately established by this citation?
It is not because the Blessed One was here defining sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) as grasping (*upādāna*).

Moreover, this cited passage is not a sūtra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), for its underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) must be further examined. Specifically, the Blessed One himself negates it in the latter part of the sūtra, stating that "exquisite desires" (*kāmaguṇa*) are not themselves the essence of desire. What, then, is the hidden intent behind his direct answer to the question in the preceding part of the sūtra, where he says they are the "five exquisite desires"?

If there were some other underlying intention for a sūtra to be called "definitive" (*nītārtha*), yet no such further intention existed, then it would have to be called "non-definitive"; in that case, there would be no fixed establishment of what is definitive and what is non-definitive.

Furthermore, with what intention is it said that because sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) arises within the five objects of desire (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*), that which is grasped is called "grasping for sense-pleasures" (*kāmopādāna*)?
Is it the grasping of sensual desire itself, or is it the grasping of the objects of desire that is termed "grasping for sense-pleasures"?
If one were to form further attachments beyond these two types, there would be no basis for them.

Moreover, since their own tenet holds that "grasping" does not include "craving," it is illogical for the essence of "grasping at desire" (*kāma-upādāna*) to be "desire-greed" (*kāmarāga*); otherwise, their own preceding and succeeding statements would contradict and undermine one another.
If you maintain that the name "grasping for sensual desire" (*kāma-upādāna*) refers to exquisite desires themselves, would this not imply that afflictions can serve as the cause of karma?
Furthermore, grasping should not be held to arise conditioned by craving; rather, one should only admit that craving arises conditioned by grasping.
That Elder said: "Appropriation is not of two kinds;
rather, because desire and greed for the objects of sensual pleasure arise, one clings to them and does not relinquish them—this is called 'grasping at sense-pleasures' (*kāma-upādāna*).
He skillfully employed such deceptive terminology to delude the ignorant and credulous people of the East.
What is meant by "clinging" (upādāna)?
What is meant by "not relinquishing"?
Is it not the case that when sensual desire arises toward those five objects of pleasure, this is called clinging, and being addicted to them without discarding them is called not relinquishing?

Therefore, it was previously stated that their [erroneous] positions—which ought not to be established—are instead forcefully established, while those positions which ought to be established are inverted and not established; thus, the statement is proven to be without error.

Alternatively, one should analyze the characteristics of their adherence and refusal to relinquish [their views]; it is not the case that "desire-grasping" (*icchā-upādāna*) is simply identical to the two preceding types of grasping.
He says that "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consists precisely of the five views; that is, by the power of craving, one clings to them and does not relinquish them.
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"Because of the existence of that [craving], it should be known that these śramaṇas and brahmins have become unwise, fallen into the realm of ignorance, and their craving grows extensively."

He claims that various views are called "extensively flourishing" because they blaze forth in diverse ways through the power of craving; however, such an assertion contradicts what was said previously and fails to understand the meaning of the sūtra, so citing it is of no benefit.
How are their preceding and succeeding statements contradictory?

They claim that because it is capable of grasping, it is called "grasping," and that the substance of such grasping is precisely the five views; they further claim that because these are not abandoned, it is called "non-relinquishment. Thus, their subsequent statement contradicts what was said before.

That is to say, as previously stated, grasping at internal phenomena as a self is called "grasping at the discourse of self" (*ātmavādopādāna*), or simply "discourse-grasping. Since it is subsumed under "grasping at views" (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*) and possesses no separate nature, there should be only three types of grasping.
It is logically untenable to admit that their essential natures are intermingled; how then can it be said that they do not understand the meaning of the Sūtra?

For the Sūtra merely states that craving increases extensively (*prapañcayati*). How is it known that this "extensive increase" refers to its various intensifications through the power of craving, rather than the increase of craving through the power of views?
In this regard, I perceive the following meaning: craving increases extensively by the power of views.
As that sutra states:

"Certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, relying on attachments concerning the past, propound eternalist theories, asserting that both the self and the world are entirely eternal, and they engage in contentious debate regarding four matters."
Because that exists, it should be understood that these śramaṇas and brahmins have failed to achieve wisdom, have fallen into the realm of ignorance, and their craving grows extensively.
The intended meaning here is that craving grows extensively through the power of views, not that views arise from craving.
This scripture clearly states that craving increases extensively; how can it be inverted to claim that views increase?
How is this citation from the sutra of no benefit?
Even if one were to follow that interpretation, what would be established by citing it?
It is not by means of this that those views can be established as "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); how then could it possibly serve to prove them?

Apart from those various views, there is no grasping or non-abandonment; yet this very grasping and non-abandonment are themselves the views. Therefore, the cited sūtra provides no benefit for that [position].
He says that the "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) mentioned here is not subsumed under the clinging to precepts and observances among the five views.
What, then, is its essential nature?

It refers to certain non-Buddhists who, driven by the power of craving, undertake the precepts and observances of cows, deer, pigs, or dogs, vowing: "By the power of maintaining these precepts and observances, may I experience happiness, or may I achieve eternal liberation."
The views previously arisen through investigation are subsumed under the "clinging to precepts and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa) among the five views.
The precepts and observances previously undertaken through longing and desire are subsumed under the "clinging to precepts and observances" among the four clingings (upādāna).
Therefore, the essence of this [the view] and that [the grasping] are not the same.
In establishing it thus, there are two faults, because the essence of the grasping and the essence of the factors would both become confused.
Furthermore, there is no one who, merely desiring the fruit, undertakes the observance of precepts and prohibitions without being preceded by a [wrong] view.
Because one first regards [the object] as essential before hoping for it.

Even if you grant that the hope precedes it, yet the ascetic practices (śīlavrataparāmarśa) thus undertaken are not subsumed under the "clinging to rules and observances" among the five views, then you must certainly admit that the ascetic practices undertaken after first examining [them] are indeed subsumed under the "clinging to rules and observances" among the five views.
Regarding this grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) among the four graspings: is it the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) or the grasping at rules and observances?
Whichever one you accept, the graspings would become confused, or it would contradict your previous assertion.
He previously stated:

"The precepts and observances undertaken with desire as the primary motive are subsumed under the 'clinging to precepts and observances' (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) among the four types of clinging, not under the 'clinging to precepts and observances' among the five views. There is no such error, because the view that performs the grasping is subsumed under 'clinging to views' (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) among the four clingings, while the precepts and observances that are grasped are subsumed under 'clinging to precepts and observances' among the four clingings."
This defense is unreasonable, for the other four views should likewise be established in the same manner as the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

That is to say, the remaining four views should also be capable of grasping; they would then be subsumed under the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) among the four types of clinging, while the objects grasped by them would be established separately as other forms of clinging.

Furthermore, one should establish desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*) as the grasping for sense-desires (*kāmopādāna*), while establishing the objects of that attachment as separate forms of grasping; since there would be no fixed reason for distinguishing between these two, the number of graspings would consequently be indefinite.
Just as in the Abhidharma school, one view among the five views is established independently and named *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances);
so too in our own school, that which is predominant is established separately.
If this were the case, then only four views should be established as one, just as *śīlavrataparāmarśa* is.
Since desire and greed should be established as distinct types of grasping (*upādāna*), what reasoning could prevent this?
Therefore, the position held by that [opponent] does not constitute a sound definition of grasping.

Furthermore, the nature of the various links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) would become confused, because the link of grasping would contain the link of becoming (*bhava*). For the Sūtra states, addressing Ānanda:
One should know that those karmas capable of inducing future existence (*punarbhava*) are precisely this limb of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, karma is the cause of birth, as stated in other sūtras.

The upholder of the precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) argues that "existence" (*bhava*) is karma; since subsequent existence arises, it must be as in the previous limit (*pūrvānta*), and thus "birth-existence" (*upapattibhava*) should take "grasping" (*upādāna*) as its condition.
The Elder (*sthavira*) defends this by saying:
"That which arises subsequently is what is called 'existence,' and it takes grasping as its condition."
This defense is untenable; for if there is karma that is non-existent, yet this very type of karma is existent, one must inevitably be deluded by the heretics.
Furthermore, one should state that craving is the condition for existence (*bhava*), since they admit that the "observances and vows" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arise from hope.
From this, it is certain that one who transgresses the principles of the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma*) can never establish [the existence of] grasping (*upādāna*) without fault.
Now, one should investigate:
since all afflictions (*kleśa*) are conditions for grasping, as various delusions arise through mutual causality, why is it said that only craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the condition for grasping?

One cannot say that other afflictions serve as conditions for grasping (*upādāna*). Now, that which is called a "condition for grasping" is that which can act as a condition to cause the essence of grasping to arise and not abandon what is grasped.

Regarding craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in relation to grasping, it possesses both capacities; whereas other afflictions can only cause the essence of grasping to arise. Therefore, it is said that only craving can serve as the condition for grasping.
The Elder Śāriputra explained:
"The reason other afflictions are not mentioned is that they do not exist [in that capacity] according to principle.
That is to say, if craving is absent, the grasping of 'self-existence' (*ātma-vāda*) and so forth, which proceed in the present, will ultimately never occur."

It is not yet understood what intention underlies that statement; if it were intended to negate the arising of afflictions through their mutual influence, it would contradict both the sacred teachings and correct reasoning.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Craving arises from craving, and craving further gives rise to hatred."
Hatred arises from hatred, and hatred in turn gives rise to craving.
Thus it is also said that grasping is the condition for craving.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
Craving functions as the accumulation, the cause, the origin, and the category of ignorance;
since it has already been established that ignorance is grasping, one should also state that craving functions with grasping as its condition.
However, for the reasons previously stated, it is not mentioned; the principle should likewise apply here.

When pride arises, it is immediately followed by the encounter with conditions for the arising of anger; yet, instead of anger arising, attachment (rāga) arises in its place—what logic underlies this?
The conditions for the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and aversion (*pratigha*) are certainly distinct; by this, it is proven that craving also arises conditioned by other afflictions.

Therefore, it is not the case that grasping (*upādāna*) arises solely conditioned by craving. As for the reason why [craving] is mentioned specifically [as its condition], it is because craving possesses both capacities.

Venerable Sir, you have here provided a false interpretation of the sūtra’s meaning, claiming that [the afflictions] cannot manifest except by being separated from desire and hatred (*rāga* and *dveṣa*).
I do not yet understand what meaning this statement intends to convey.
Is it not the case that because desire and hatred do not arise simultaneously, they must necessarily manifest by being separated from one another?
If it is claimed that the meaning of this sutra is that the conduct of hatred must necessarily arise from prior craving, this is merely empty talk; for the sutra states:
"Hatred arises from hatred, and hatred in turn gives rise to craving."
Therefore, these are merely empty words.

Since the reasoning for what has been stated lacks any basis in reality, it follows that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) certainly does not arise dependent on other afflictions; thus, the principle that grasping (*upādāna*) arises solely from craving cannot be established.
Therefore, the principle that the *upādāna* (clinging) link taught in the *Abhidharma* subsumes all afflictions (*kleśa*) is sound.

Chapter Seven: The Seventh Section on the Analysis of Dependent Origination. Thus, because grasping (*upādāna*) has been established as a condition, when one rushes about in pursuit of various desirable objects, it inevitably draws forth and brings about karma that leads to future existence (*bhava*).

This means that when grasping (*upādāna*) becomes intensified through the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one pursues various objects, both wholesome and unwholesome; and in order to obtain them, one accumulates numerous pure and impure karmas capable of summoning future existence. This stage of the arising of such karma is collectively termed the "existence" (*bhava*) link.
It should be understood that herein, because something can produce a future fruit by means of this and depending upon this, it is established as having the name "existence" (*bhava*).
The Elder (*Sthavira*) explains, saying:
"Existence refers to the nature of existence (*bhāva*); therefore, the Blessed One said:"
Some claim that "existence" (bhava) refers to the arising of future rebirth;
they assert that the nature of existence is the sense of the arising of a fruit within the future life.
Such an interpretation contradicts both reason and scripture, because existence would then be indistinguishable from birth (jāti).
If the very entity that arises as the present fruit were itself the factor of "arising" (*jāti*), then the factors of dependent origination would necessarily be reduced in number.

Furthermore, it is unreasonable to claim that the present karma is designated by the name "existence" (*bhava*) merely because it possesses a cause; for the essence of karma is itself the state of being presently existent.
Karma exists as a present reality and can serve as the cause for future existence; therefore, one cannot simply say that something exists merely because it has a cause.
If its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is already existent, why would one need to establish a name for it?
Just as when karma exists as a cause it brings about a resultant existence (*vipākabhava*), this resultant existence does not require the name "existence as a cause" (*hetubhava*).

Even if one were to grant that such a name is established metaphorically, it would not be a loss for existence to have its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because both the capacity to produce and the thing produced possess the quality of co-existence (*sahabhū*).
To prove that point, one should not cite this sūtra, because there are variant recensions of its text.
What is the variant recension?
For example, some recite as follows:
Some say that it is that which causes future existence (*punarbhava*) to arise.
Even if one recites it in that way, there is no logical contradiction, because this is a case of applying the name of the effect to the cause.
Since its substantial nature (*dravya*) is the cause for the arising of future existence, it is metaphorically designated as the "arising of future existence."
To clarify this meaning, the Blessed One said:
"With grasping as condition, there is becoming.
Subsequently, in order to clarify that becoming is the condition for birth, he spoke this sutra.
Furthermore, because *bhava* (existence) is the most proximate cause for birth, the Sūtra states:
"Karma is the cause of birth.
To demonstrate that karma is indeed the proximate cause of birth, the name of the effect is metaphorically applied to the cause of *bhava*; this is necessarily so.
Therefore, the conclusion is summarized by stating that "appropriation conditions existence" because "existence conditions birth.
Furthermore, another sutra states that the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Karma that brings about future existence is here termed 'existence' (bhava)."
Therefore, the sūtra cited by the Elder (Sthavira) is incapable of serving as proof for his own interpretation;
