The Tathāgata merely taught the twelve links in order to eliminate such doubts, as has already been explained; that is to say, he did so regarding the past, future, and middle limits [of existence] in order to dispel the delusions and ignorance of others.

Now, examining this closely, it appears that the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrāntika), wishing to contravene the tenets of the *Vibhāṣā*, has abandoned his own laborious composition of verses that logically resolve doubts—namely, those stating that "from afflictions arise further afflictions and karma," and so forth.

One might claim that what has been said is able to avoid the objections of others; however, upon careful examination, that explanation does not actually avoid those objections. This is because, although one intends to dispel the delusions regarding the three time periods by teaching the doctrine of dependent origination, one fails to fully explain that old age and death have results and ignorance has causes. It is not that one lacks understanding of the meaning of the continuous succession of prior causes and subsequent effects; rather, it is called "having enabled those to be converted to dispel delusions regarding the prior and posterior limits" [only] when this is complete.

Regarding the sentient beings to be converted during the intermediate stages: if both cause and effect were absent—such as in the case of ignorance and old age/death—then the two views of annihilationism and eternalism would arise simultaneously. How then could they know that birth in the present life arises from the previous life, or understand that [existence] in future lives arises from the present life?

Since the Sūtra does not explicitly state that old age and death have results and ignorance has causes, continuing in an uninterrupted succession, those to be converted would certainly conclude that the other intermediate links likewise lack both cause and result, just like ignorance and old age and death. In that case, the teaching on dependent origination would merely suffice to fuel their doubts; how could it be said to eliminate the delusions regarding the three time periods?
Therefore, I have been utterly unable to resolve the objections raised; I have needlessly abandoned the labor of the verses I myself composed.
The refutation of the objections is now complete.
As the Blessed One said:
I shall now explain for you the phenomena of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the phenomena arisen through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
What is the difference between these two?
First, the *Śāstra* states:
What is dependent origination?
It refers to all conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, it is said:
What are produced phenomena?
They are those of the past and the present.
Since these produced phenomena must necessarily have conditions, it is known that only those of the past and present are called "dependently arisen phenomena."
By this same principle, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) also exists in the future, because that which abides in the future is a dharma that is about to arise.
Does not the fundamental treatise also state this, saying that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are called "dharmas arisen from conditions" (*pratītyasamutpannadharma*)?
There is no fault here, because the "aggregates arisen from conditions" (pratītyasamutpanna-skandha) include all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) of both the past and the present.
It is not logically tenable to designate a phenomenon that has not yet arisen as "already arisen," for such a definition would be contradictory.
Nevertheless, future dharmas may also be designated as "arising," because they are not dissociated from the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).

It is precisely for this reason that it was stated previously: because they are dharmas that arise, they are called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Therefore, future dharmas are not called "already arisen"; just as present and future [dharmas] are not called "already ceased," yet because they are dharmas that cease, they also receive the designation "ceasing."
Regarding this, some say:
according to the sense of "destined to exist," even dharmas that have not yet arisen are called "already arisen"; thus, people in the world say, "The cord is being made into a bracelet."
Non-Buddhist treatises also state:
"One seeks a son by sacrificing to the fire.
This contradicts both scripture and logic, as it is asked: "How can that which has already ceased not be a dharma?"
This refers to present and future phenomena, as well as all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
If future phenomena were designated as "already arisen" based on their future status, then the future and the present would have to be called "already ceased.

Just as present and future phenomena are subject to cessation and thus receive the designation "ceased" but are not called "already ceased," so too future phenomena are subject to arising and thus receive the designation "arising" but are not called "already arisen."
Only in this way can it be said that one does not contradict logical theory.

Furthermore, the doctrine of non-arising would be contradicted [by your position], because for those [dharmas] there is necessarily no principle of future arising; how then could one say, based on what is yet to come, that they are already "arisen"?

Furthermore, when that reasoning reaches its limit and one attempts to cite mundane examples as proof, there are nonetheless scriptural authorities and logical principles that establish this meaning. How could mundane speech serve as proof for the Dharma of the Noble Ones?
The Venerable Pūrṇāśa stated that within all phenomena there are those that are dependent origination but not dependently arisen; this should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first phrase refers to future dharmas.
The second phrase refers to all past and present dharmas at the stage of the final mind of an Arhat.
The third phrase refers to other past and present dharmas.
The fourth phrase refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If future phenomena were not "dependently arisen," would this not contradict what is stated in the Sūtra? As it is said:
"What are dependently arisen phenomena?"
This refers to the sequence from ignorance through birth to old age and death.
Since birth and old age and death exist in the future, why does the Sūtra describe them as "dharmas arisen from conditions"?

There is no contradiction here; rather, one should carefully understand that because all members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), each and every one is necessarily subsumed within the three time periods.
How can the members of ignorance and formations, as well as birth, aging, and death, be subsumed under the present?
This is because they are explained in terms of two future bodies of birth, based on the principle of their successive progression.
Present craving, grasping, and becoming receive the names of ignorance and formations when spoken of in relation to the two lifetimes of the past;
present consciousness through feeling receive the names of birth and old age and death.
Therefore, the four factors of the past and future can all be subsumed within the present.
However, that Venerable One further stated:
"If ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are in the present, then the remaining ten factors are in the future; eight are to arise immediately, and two are to arise later."

If birth and old age and death are both in the present, then the remaining ten members are in the past; eight have already ceased immediately [prior], and two—the third and the first—have already ceased.
By this principle, all twelve links of existence can be subsumed within the present world.

Therefore, birth, old age, and death are also called "already arisen" (*jāta*); by this, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra, for that which is in the state of not yet having arisen cannot be said to be "already arisen.

Now, examining the intended meaning of what the Venerable [Vasubandhu] has stated: if something arises from causes, it is called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*); if it serves as a cause for others, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena do not receive the designation "arising through conditions," because their causal characteristics are not complete.
What are these causal characteristics?
They are as previously stated: "When this exists, that exists; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not exist; with the cessation of this, that ceases."

Although the arising of all unconditioned phenomena occurs, one cannot say that because this arises, that arises; nor can it be said that because this ceases, that ceases. Furthermore, one cannot say that because this is absent, that is absent, for they are devoid of arising and ceasing, and their essence is eternally present.

All unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) abide without obstruction as objects of perception (*ālambana*). They function as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), yet they possess no power of appropriation or relinquishment regarding conditioned phenomena and thus lack the defining characteristics of a cause.
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"All causes and conditions that can produce consciousness are impermanent.
Other masters say:

Ignorance is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda), and volitional formations are called "dependently arisen" (pratītyasamutpanna). In this manner, proceeding successively, even birth is called "dependent origination," and old age and death are called "dependently arisen."

What has been stated thus does not accord with the meaning of the sūtras, for within the sūtras it is said that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors are all termed both "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*). Some say:

ignorance alone is called "dependent origination," while the final factor, old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), is called only "dependently arisen"; the ten intermediate links, however, apply to both meanings.
The stage of old age and death does not necessarily give rise to all afflictions; therefore, old age and death are designated only as "dependently arisen.
Ignorance, however, certainly initiates all formative activities (saṃskāras); therefore, the stage of ignorance is designated specifically as "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
The Abhidharmikas have stated:

"The two factors of the prior limit are called 'dependent origination' (pratītyasamutpāda) because these two are intended to be explained as having the nature of causes; the two stages of the posterior limit are called 'dependently arisen' (pratītyasamutpanna); and the eight factors of the intermediate limit encompass both meanings."
Both of these two explanations are inconsistent with the Sūtra, for the Sūtra states that all members [of dependent origination] apply to both [the past and the future].
Regarding the definitive meaning of these two phrases, the verse says:
The intended meaning here is correctly explained as: Causes refer to what has arisen; results refer to what has already been produced.
The treatise says:
The causal portions of the various members are called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Why is this so?

Because it serves as a condition for the arising of an effect, and because dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is explained in terms of the mutual dependence between cause and effect, this meaning of dependent origination is established solely by means of the term "condition" (*pratyaya*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"What is dependent origination?

It means that because this exists, that exists; and because this arises, that arises—namely, from ignorance as a condition, there is volitional formation, and so on, up to birth as a condition for aging and death."
Having spoken thus, he further said:
"In this context, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) up to its ultimate non-perversion is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
What is meant by 'the nature of phenomena' in this context?"

That is to say, within the mutual interdependence of cause and effect, the causal capacity is termed *dharmatā*; for it is only because there is a cause that cause and effect exist, being mutually interconnected rather than existing without a cause.
In this way, the term "nature" (*svabhāva*) signifies the sense of being able to produce; only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) obtain the name "nature.

Although in this sūtra it is not explicitly shown that the causal nature within the mutual connection of cause and effect is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the meaning of dependent origination is nevertheless revealed by the word "condition" (*pratyaya*). Therefore, it is known that the causal nature obtains the name "dependent origination," because the word "condition" functions only with respect to the sense of being able to reveal, and since the cause is able to reveal the fruit, it is designated as a "condition."
Therefore, the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat are not equivalent-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because they do not manifest any resulting fruit.

By this very principle, it is proven that the designation "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is established based on the mutual dependence of cause and effect; thus, in the *Paramārthaśūnyatā-sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"In this context, the conventional designation of phenomena refers to 'ignorance conditions volitional formations,' and so on, up to 'birth conditions aging and death.'"
Because it is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is established by means of conventional terminology (*prajñapti-śabda*).
This refers to the meaning of cause and effect being mutually interconnected; the resultant portions of the various members are called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*). Why is this so?

Because all these arise from conditions, because "result" (*phala*) is the designation for the accomplishment of phenomena, and because this meaning is established only when a phenomenon has already arisen;
likewise, the accomplishment of *nirvāṇa* occurs through its being attained as something already arisen, and thus it too is called a "result" by virtue of being already arisen.
Alternatively, this may be explained by way of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), wherein it is impossible for nirvāṇa to be raised as an objection.

If the meaning of "fruit" (*phala*) is determinate for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), that is what is clarified here; just as the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) and the fruits of past and present phenomena are determinate, they are called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
However, regarding phenomena in the future, the meaning of "fruit" is not determinate, and thus they are set aside and not mentioned.

This is the summary of the meaning: the arising of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*); the phenomena of the past and present are called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*), because the sense of being an effect is certain.

That is to say, within the mutual connection of cause and effect, that which is designated as the causal portion is called "dependent origination," while that which is fixed as the effect is called "dependently arisen."
Furthermore, that which is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) among these is so named because it is able to act as a condition for the arising of various effects.
Among these, those phenomena that are effects are called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*), because they do not arise apart from conditions in the past or present.
In this way, both meanings are established together, because all the members possess the nature of cause and effect.

Although they share the nature of cause and effect and their substantial entities are not distinct, the establishment of these meanings is by no means unproven, for there are differences in their respective points of reference.

That is to say, if one contemplates this as "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*), one does not thereby contemplate it as being further termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*); it is, for example, like the designations of cause and effect, or father and son.
However, this sutra contains an intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), whereas the Abhidharma speaks without such intentional meaning.
What is the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*) of this sūtra?
It is that the Bhagavat cryptically revealed that saṃsāra has no beginning but has an end by speaking these two phrases.

As for the term "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it reveals that the stream of saṃsāra revolves without interruption from time immemorial; therefore, he spoke of the arising of the various members in both forward and reverse order.

The expression "dependently arisen" is intended to show that if birth and death encounter their antidote, they have a limit and an end; that is to say, if there are conditions, they continue to arise subsequently, whereas if those conditions are lacking, they do not continue to arise. It is for this reason that the Sūtra speaks of "making an end to suffering."
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras:
"Dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is conventional, because its causes and effects are mutually dependent and lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva);
that which has arisen dependently (pratītyasamutpanna) is real in its essence, because it is the basis for those [causes and effects], just as a jar is the basis for its own parts."
The Abhidharma states that both are real, because the two entities of cause and effect both substantially exist.
Thus, it has been demonstrated that the Vaibhāṣika school does not contradict the principle of dependent origination as taught in the sūtras.

In detail, when the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) states that this contradicts the sūtra, it is because he has not received instruction from the Vaibhāṣika masters; or his teacher did not master the meaning of the Vaibhāṣika; or although he had perused the texts of the Vaibhāṣika, his mind was obscured by false attachments, and thus he failed to discern the correct principle.
Other masters of the Nikāya schools maintain that dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), because a sūtra states: "The Buddha told a mendicant:
'Such dependent origination was not made by me, nor was it made by another.'"
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, this nature of dependent origination remains eternally present; thus it is explained at length.
Based on this intention, the principle may also be so.
This means that such dependent origination has no separate agent; therefore, it is called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth always arise in dependence upon ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like, and not in dependence on other dharmas, nor without a cause.
Such a nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not created by a Buddha, nor is it created by anyone else; it is declared to be eternally abiding, and of this there is no doubt.
It is thus called "constant," for such is the necessary principle.

If one were to claim that a distinct phenomenon is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda)—such as analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and so forth, which are immutably eternal—this is certainly not the case; for it is logically untenable to assert that something is dependent origination while its essence is eternal.

Furthermore, regarding their tenet that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) constitute dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), is this [unconditioned nature] distinct from ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors, identical to them, or is it a synthesis of those factors?

These three positions are all illogical, because its intrinsic nature would be difficult to discern, because it would entail the fallacy of impermanence, and because its substance would necessarily be unreal.

Alternatively, if one were to grasp the meaning of the sūtras according to the literal expression, then one would have to admit that the four great elements are also permanent, because the Blessed One said:
"These four great elements may at times be made different," and so forth, as explained at length.
This sutra negates those conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
If one does not contemplate this underlying principle (*naya*), one would have to maintain that these are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, whether a Buddha appears in the world or not, the earth, water, and so forth always remain solid, moist, and so on; for what reason, then, do you not maintain that these are all permanent?
However, since there are points regarding that intermediate state which they accept and those they do not, it is clear that this is merely the product of a coarse mind.
Setting aside this matter for now, one should further provide a detailed explanation of the four links: ignorance, name-and-form, contact, and feeling.
Why is this? Because the formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) will be explained in detail in the chapter on the Latent Dispositions of Karma (*karmānuśaya*).
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have already been explained in detail in the chapter on the Fundamental Subjects (*vastu*).
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*), what are its characteristics?
Is it the absence of knowledge (*vidyā*), or is it subsumed under what is not knowledge?
If one adopts the former sense, then ignorance should be a non-entity.
If the latter meaning were adopted, then the eye and so forth would constitute its essence.
Thus, both of these positions are logically untenable.
Furthermore, the Sthavira says:
Because this exists, it causes clarity (*vidyā*) to be non-existent; this is what is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
It is unreasonable for that [opponent] to claim that such a thing can exist without a cause.

If it were the case that because this exists as an obstacle, clarity does not manifest, and thus the affliction is called ignorance because it lacks clarity, then all afflictions would necessarily be ignorance, since both [the presence of an obstacle and the absence of clarity] would be established whenever any one [affliction] occurs.

Furthermore, one should not maintain that ignorance can serve as the cause for the unconditioned state of clarity (*vidyā*), because the *Sūtras* do not state that existence and non-existence can function as causes for one another, and moreover, that which is non-existent cannot possess the nature of being an effect.
How can it be said that this thing cannot exist without a cause?
It is not that one can speak of existence regarding a non-entity; for that school admits the existence of only the present.

Furthermore, although that school’s tenet asserts that there is no ignorance (*avidyā*), it also admits that at times even clear knowledge (*vidyā*) does not exist; thus, one should not definitively state that ignorance obstructs clear knowledge.
If it is argued that they possess the "latent tendency of ignorance" (*avidyā-anuśaya-dhātu*), this is also unreasonable, because it is not an autonomous entity (*svabhāva*).
Even if such a latent tendency were admitted, its essence would still be ignorance.
Since this entity can sometimes give rise to clear knowledge (*vidyā*), one should not say that it obstructs clear knowledge.

If you argue that while this clear knowledge reaches the stage of being about to arise, the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) persists until the moment of its actual cessation—and thus ignorance is said to obstruct clear knowledge—then those dwelling on the path of training (*śaikṣa*) would have to be free from ignorance, or else clear knowledge would never arise at all, because the latent tendency of ignorance would never have been absent.

If you claim that it is like the acquisition (*prāpti*), then the same should apply to the realm (*dhātu*); that is to say, according to your own school, the acquisitions of various forms of ignorance (*avidyā*) are not themselves the essence of ignorance.
Nevertheless, there may be times when, although ignorance has been extinguished, clarity (*vidyā*) cannot arise because it is obstructed by the power of the acquisition of ignorance.
Furthermore, there may be times when, despite the presence of this [state of] attainment, luminosity can still arise through the power of application (*prayoga*).
Thus, in our school’s doctrine, the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of ignorance is not identical to the essence of ignorance itself.

However, it might be argued that even though ignorance (*avidyā*) has been extinguished at certain times, clear knowledge (*vidyā*) may fail to arise due to the obstruction of a latent disposition (*anuśaya-dhātu*), or it may arise at other times; what fault is there in this?
This defense is irrational because it contradicts your own statement, because it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and because it is not what we accept.
That is to say, he himself stated:
"Because this exists, that which is now clarified as non-existent is called ignorance (avidyā)";
yet now he speaks again:
The latent disposition (*anuśaya*) of ignorance is not the substance of ignorance itself, yet it is able to obstruct clarity.
Does this later statement not contradict your own previous assertion?

Furthermore, if the substance of ignorance were to arise again after having been extinguished for a long period, then ignorance should likewise arise again at a later time for one who is free from ignorance; for you admit that the substance of the latent disposition is not ignorance itself, and thus there would be no distinction between the two cases of being free from ignorance.
Furthermore, I do not accept that it is because the arising of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) is obstructed by the power obtained through ignorance (*avidyā*).
It is not the position of the Abhidharma school (*Abhidharmika*) that the function of this "acquisition" (*prāpti*) consists in obstructing other dharmas so that they cannot arise.
If that is so, what is the function it performs?
It serves as the cause by which ignorance is not lost.
What is meant by "not lost"?

Nor does it have a separate substantial entity; rather, it is by virtue of its functional activity that it allows the dharmas already acquired to arise again, and thus it is designated by the name "non-disappearance.
How could past ignorance possibly arise again?
Not so. If that were the case, what would be the purpose of this acquisition (*prāpti*)?

Although it cannot cause that which has been acquired to arise again, prior to the arising of the path of antidote (*pratipakṣa-mārga*), it ensures that [the defilement] constantly follows the continuum without interruption.
Is it not the case that this [ignorance] perishes simultaneously with nescience?

Although they perish together, it continues to arise subsequently; that is to say, at the moment of its cessation, by the power of its causal force, it draws forth another of its own kind to arise without interval, and that in turn draws forth another, continuing until the arising of the Path.

Alternatively, it may be that the function of this "acquisition" (prāpti) is to cause the acquired ignorance to yield its fruit; that is to say, once the acquisition has been severed, the fruit of this ignorance can no longer arise.

If the acquisition of ignorance were unable to yield its fruit even in the absence of ignorance itself, then ignorance would have to arise again even after clear knowledge (vidyā) has arisen, because past ignorance is not without substance.

Once [the fruit] has been obtained, even though the arising of the fruit of ignorance that was not yet severed continues, once it has been severed, that fruit no longer arises; therefore, this distinction is established by means of "attainment" (*prāpti*).
What has thus been stated does not deviate from the previously described characteristics.
That is to say, "acquisition" (*prāpti*) is so called because it acts as a cause for non-loss by ensuring that what has been obtained may arise again.
But is it not the case that there are dharmas which have acquisition yet do not arise? How, then, can acquisition be said to be the cause for the arising of a dharma?

Because the dharmas already obtained are free from acquisition (*prāpti*) and do not arise [anew], the cause for the arising of dharmas is designated as "acquisition. This is like how visual consciousness does not arise apart from the eye;
it is also like your own school’s "unmanifest latent tendency" (*avidyā-anuśaya-dhātu*), which, although it exists at all times, you do not admit that the fruit of ignorance arises constantly.
If you argue that my case is likewise and thus should not be subject to criticism, this analogy is unreasonable.

For in the Abhidharma school, although the acquisition (*prāpti*) of ignorance may be absent, ignorance can still arise; whereas in my school, ignorance cannot possibly arise apart from the pervasive realm (*anugata-dhātu*). Therefore, this pervasive realm is not the same as the *prāpti* of that [ignorance].
There is no such fault; for it is logically established that "acquisition" (*prāpti*) is cited as the cause for the attainment [of dharmas] according to their own school’s tenets.
That is to say, since a dharma that is acquired must necessarily arise, acquisition is established as the cause of arising by logical necessity.

Furthermore, since the *Anuśayanirdeśa* (Treatise on Latent Dispositions) establishes the same principle regarding acquisition, it follows that even in the absence of the *dharmānuśaya* (latent dispositions of dharmas), those dharmas can still arise.

That is to say, although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) lack the latent dispositions of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*), when they correctly cultivate the preparatory application (*prayoga*), the noble dharmas are capable of arising.

Furthermore, as previously stated, because of the use of the term "distinction," it means that by virtue of its function, the dharmas already acquired are permitted to arise again; thus, that which serves as the cause for non-loss is called "acquisition" (prāpti). How does this relate to the objection concerning what has already been lost or what has not yet been acquired? There is no connection.

Furthermore, since the principle of the "old latent realm" (*pūrvānuśaya*) has already been shown to be non-existent, according to that school’s tenet, one would have already attained permanent dissociation from ignorance during any state where ignorance is not manifest; how then could ignorance arise at a later time?
If one does not initiate the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the Noble Path, what factor acts as an obstruction to prevent clear knowledge (*vidyā*) from arising?
For this very reason, when Arhats are in a state where clear knowledge does not arise, they lose that clear knowledge; how, then, can clear knowledge arise again at a later time?
If it were not for the presence of heedlessness, the essence of ignorance would ultimately be non-existent; what dharma, then, could serve as its antidote so that ignorance does not arise?
Therefore, their claim that "because this exists, luminosity (vidyā) is absent, and this is called ignorance" is merely empty talk and entirely devoid of real meaning.
Only the Abhidharmikas might speak thus; those belonging to the school that refutes [the existence of] dharmas cannot maintain this.
The Sthavira further states: "Alternatively, such types of mind and mental factors are collectively termed ignorance."
If that were so, ignorance (*avidyā*) would not be substantially existent, because you admit it is a provisional construction based upon the mind and its associates.
Such an argument is also logically untenable, for it would follow that all minds and mental factors are ignorance.
That is to say, does this ignorance have as its essence the mind abiding in its own nature (*svabhāvastha-citta*) and so forth, or does it have something distinct?

If it were the mind abiding in its own nature, then all minds of various categories, such as the wholesome and so on, would necessarily be ignorance; yet it is not the case that all such minds are ignorance, nor is there any instance where ignorance is not present.
It arises with improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) as its cause, for the Sūtra states that this and that serve as causes.
It is not the case that non-defiled minds and mental factors can have improper mental attention as their cause.
If there were distinctions, that which performs the differentiation could be ignorance (*avidyā*), but not that which is differentiated.
Furthermore, one should explain the characteristics of these distinctions.

Since the essential natures and characteristics of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are each distinct, how could they collectively constitute a single characteristic of ignorance? How can it be said that the mind and mental factors as a whole are called ignorance?
Examining that mind’s wandering outside the Tathāgata’s teaching, the Elder further states:
"Alternatively, perverted clarity is itself called ignorance (*avidyā*), because the Blessed One has also spoken of wrong view as ignorance; as the Sūtra says:
'If one practices, cultivates, or frequently habituates oneself to wrong view, delusion (*moha*) becomes intense.'"
From this, it would follow that there are two kinds of ignorance: first, wrong knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), and second, darkness (*tamas*).
Their statement is unreasonable, because the distinction between the functioning of views (*dṛṣṭi-carita*) and the functioning of delusion (*moha-carita*) could not be established.

There is certainly a distinction between wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and darkness (*tamas*). If it were otherwise, these two would not exist as distinct types; for two things cannot be established as two types unless there is a distinction between them.

Since delusion (*moha*) becomes sharp through the practice, cultivation, or frequent cultivation of wrong view, then delusion likewise becomes sharp through the practice, cultivation, or frequent cultivation of darkness. This is because the Sūtra states that the cause of delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Is it not the case that, since there is no distinction between the two fruits, one must admit that the two causes are likewise without distinction?

If so, then the establishment of the distinctions between those whose conduct is dominated by views (*dṛṣṭicarita*) and those whose conduct is dominated by delusion (*mohacarita*) would be impossible.

However, there are distinct differences between those who practice through faith and those who practice through wisdom as they enter the gate of the Deathless; therefore, that Elder was confused regarding the meaning of the sutra.
If this is so, what then is the meaning of this sutra?

It is not that those who are not foolish possess perverted views; therefore, ignorance must necessarily coexist with wrong view. Consequently, when one habituates, cultivates, or repeatedly practices wrong view, delusion becomes intense; yet, wrong view itself is not identical to ignorance.
Why do ignorance (*avidyā*) and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) arise together?
Is it not said that delusion (*moha*) is more intense than wrong view?
This is not what is being clarified here; [the reason] exists but is not stated.
The intended meaning here is that greed, hatred, and delusion, when they manifest repeatedly and with intensity, constitute the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
This refers to a prior question:
"In what way do greed and the other [afflictions] become intense?"
He then replied: "If one practices, cultivates, or frequently cultivates covetousness, then covetousness becomes intense," and so on, as explained at length.
If that were the case, the two modes of activity established for views and delusion would become confused.
It is not so; there are three distinct types of views, and thus no confusion or error arises.
Namely, some views function solely as distortions (*viparyāsa*); others function through total superimposition (*samāropa*); and still others function through partial superimposition.

Among these three, because delusion (*moha*) is predominant in those who possess only inverted views, they are designated as "those whose conduct is characterized by delusion" (*mohacarita*). As for the other two, because their views are powerful, they are established as being manifest; thus, there is no fault of confusion in establishing these two types of conduct.
Although ignorance (*avidyā*) is present when greed and hatred arise together, it is not mentioned because it is weak;
thus, delusion (*moha*) is not particularly intense. Since these two afflictions function by taking objective entities as their objects, delusion is not predominant within this category.
To demonstrate that saṃsāra has no beginning, it is taught that the causes for the arising of afflictions may be of the same or different categories; as that sūtra states:
"All greed, hatred, and delusion arise without exception from ignorance."
Alternatively, it may be for the purpose of censuring and refuting incorrect views, stating that by practicing false views, delusion increases.
As that sutra says:
"One who is called wise is one who can extinguish ignorance."
Because this increases delusion, one is not called a wise person; this is explained at length.

Therefore, one should diligently seek the true meaning of the sūtras; one should not maintain the view that insight itself is ignorance, as this will be further refuted later in the commentary on the verse.
The Venerable Rāma spoke thus:

"It is not the case that the essence of wrong view is itself ignorance; rather, various forms of greed, hatred, and wrong view increase by means of three distinct roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—which belong to different categories."
This is also unreasonable: how can greed and hatred be termed "desire" and "ill-will" when they belong to different categories?
Furthermore, why is delusion only the root of false view, and not the root that increases desire and ill-will?
Why are greed and hatred not roots of wrong view?
However, they are unable to explain its intended meaning; therefore, what they have said does not accord with the meaning of the Sūtra. Some say:
The absence of wisdom is simply the non-existence of wisdom; therefore, ignorance (avidyā) is not of a conditioned nature (saṃskṛta).

If that were so, then with the exception of the Buddha, all others who have attained the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-phala) would possess ignorance, because they lack universal knowledge (sarvajñatā).

If it is argued that there is no such fault because ignorance is defined as the lack of knowledge regarding the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) and so forth when stated separately, this is not the case; for knowledge cannot be non-existent without distinction.
Now, when one speaks of "non-existence," both its nature (*svabhāva*) and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are absent; how, then, can it be said to belong to this or to that?

Alternatively, one should state that those two knowledges have no distinct characteristics; by what characteristic would one name them "knowledge of the past limit" and so forth, or "knowledge of non-arising" and "knowledge of non-interruption," and so forth?
Furthermore, by what characteristic are both [types of] wisdom negated?
One is ignorance (*avidyā*) and one is not ignorance; what logic is there for this?
Therefore, what they have said is also not the meaning of the sūtra.

Some say: Ignorance (avidyā) is the absence of knowledge regarding this object, just as people in the world speak of "saltless food" and so forth; furthermore, it cannot be ignorance simply because it is not separate from form (rūpa) and other such phenomena.

If it is argued that the absence of knowledge regarding all afflictions is designated as "ignorance" (*avidyā*), this is also unreasonable; for there exist separate designations such as "fetters," "bonds," and "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*) distinct from desire and greed, and because the aforementioned faults would still persist.
Furthermore, if ignorance (avidyā) were essentially identical to all afflictions (kleśa), then its essence would also have to be a view (dṛṣṭi). In that case, it would not be associated with views.
For this reason, it also cannot coexist with craving (rāga) and the other afflictions, because you maintain that the essence of ignorance is identical to craving and so forth.
It would follow that greed and the like could not be associated with greed and the like; thus, there would be no logical principle for afflictions to be mutually associated.
Furthermore, one would have to say that ignorance defiles the mind, because the essence of greed itself is ignorance.

If it is argued that this sūtra speaks according to specific distinctions, then it should likewise speak of the defilement of wisdom according to specific distinctions; thus, one must admit that there exists a distinct ignorance (*avidyā*) capable of defiling wisdom. One should not claim it refers to ignorance in general, for general ignorance does not possess a distinct nature.
Therefore, one must admit that ignorance exists as a distinct entity.
What is its meaning?
The verse says:

"Non-ignorance is that which is opposed to ignorance, just as 'non-friend' is [opposed to] a friend, or 'unreal' is [opposed to] the real, and so forth. The Commentary says: Just as among various kinsmen, one who stands in opposition to an enemy of those kinsmen is called a "non-kinsman" because he is contrary to a kinsman; it is not that there exists some other category of "non-kinsman" distinct from a kinsman, such as all other neutral persons. It is precisely because he is the opposite of a kinsman that he is termed a non-kinsman. The same applies here. Ignorance is defined as the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*); it is not a separate entity from knowledge, nor is it merely the absence of knowledge. Because it is the adversary of knowledge, it is designated as "non-knowledge" (*avidyā*). This is the meaning. Furthermore, the term "non-friend" (*amitra*) is used to indicate that which is hostile to a friend, not to indicate a mere lack of friendship. The same principle applies to terms such as "unreal" (*atattva*), "unwholesome" (*akuśala*), and "unpleasant" (*asukha*). Therefore, it is established that ignorance is the very opposite of knowledge. It is not that ignorance is simply the absence of knowledge. If ignorance were merely the absence of knowledge, then in states where knowledge is absent—such as in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) or during the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—ignorance would necessarily be present. However, this is not the case. Therefore, ignorance must be understood as a distinct entity that is the direct adversary of knowledge. Thus, it is definitively established that ignorance is not the mere absence of knowledge. Furthermore, if ignorance were merely the absence of knowledge, then since the absence of knowledge exists throughout the three realms, ignorance would likewise exist throughout the three realms. Consequently, the afflictions associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) would be absent in the form and formless realms. This contradicts the scriptural teachings. Therefore, ignorance is not the mere absence of knowledge. Moreover, if ignorance were merely the absence of knowledge, then when a person possesses knowledge, they would be devoid of ignorance. Since ignorance is the root of all afflictions, if one were devoid of ignorance, they would be devoid of all afflictions. If they were devoid of all afflictions, they would be liberated. Yet, it is observed that even those who possess knowledge can still be bound by the fetters of desire and so forth. Therefore, ignorance is not the mere absence of knowledge. Furthermore, if ignorance were merely the absence of knowledge, then because knowledge is absent in the state of the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantaryamārga*) prior to the realization of the truths, ignorance would be present at that time. If ignorance were present, the afflictions would arise, and if the afflictions arose, one would fall back into cyclic existence. Thus, there would be no liberation. Therefore, ignorance is not the mere absence of knowledge. Consequently, it is established that ignorance is a distinct entity that is the direct adversary of knowledge. It is not the mere absence of knowledge. This is the definitive conclusion. Therefore, ignorance is not the mere absence of knowledge. Consequently, it is established that ignorance is a distinct entity that is the direct adversary of knowledge. It is not the mere absence of knowledge. This is the definitive conclusion. Truthful speech is called "real"; its opposite, deceptive discourse, is called "unreal. This does not mean that everything else besides the real—such as all other categories like form, fragrance, and so forth—is unreal or non-existent.
The word "etc. (*ādi*) is used to indicate that they are not gods, not white, not Dharma, not beloved, and not beneficial things, and so forth.

Asuras and others receive names such as "non-gods" because they are the opposites of gods and the like; it is not that there exists some entity distinct from gods and the like that is called "non-god."
Thus, ignorance has a distinct, real essence; it is that which is counteracted by knowledge, being neither different from it nor non-existent.
How is this known? It is because, like consciousness and other phenomena, it is said to exist dependent on conditions and serves as a condition for others.
Furthermore, there is corroborating evidence, stated in verse:
Because it is described as a fetter and so forth, Because it is not a wrong view,
Because it is associated with views, And because it is said to defile wisdom.
The Treatise says:

The Sūtras explain ignorance (*avidyā*) as a fetter (*saṃyojana*), a bond (*bandhana*), a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), an outflow (*āsrava*), a yoke (*yoga*), and a flood (*ogha*). It cannot be said that these things—such as being a fetter or a bond—apply to the other sense organs like the eye, nor can they apply to a total non-existence. Therefore, there exists a distinct dharma called ignorance, just as one speaks of "having no wife" or "having no children" to refer to those who have bad wives or children.
In this way, such corrupted wisdom (*kuprajñā*) should be called ignorance (*avidyā*); however, it is not ignorance because it contains [wrong] view (*dṛṣṭi*).
All defiled wisdom is termed corrupted wisdom; since view exists within it, it is therefore not ignorance.
Since this [ignorance] is observed to involve investigation, vigor, wisdom, and decisive judgment, it cannot be said that it is called "delusion" (moha).
If that were the case, then ignorance would have to be a defiled wisdom (prajñā) that is not a view (dṛṣṭi).
This is also unreasonable, because it is admitted that ignorance is associated with views.
If ignorance were wisdom (*prajñā*), it would have to be dissociated from views, for two entities of wisdom cannot be associated together.

It cannot be said that seeing is not accompanied by ignorance, because seeing does not constitute a perversion unless it is characterized by delusion; furthermore, it is taught that ignorance can defile wisdom.
As the Sūtra says:
"Greed defiles the mind and prevents liberation; ignorance defiles wisdom and prevents its purification."

Wisdom cannot defile the essence of wisdom itself, just as craving—which belongs to a different category—can defile the mind; likewise, ignorance must also belong to a different category from wisdom in order to defile it.

Nor can it be said that ignorance defiles wisdom despite being non-associated with it, for while craving acts as a defilement, it must necessarily coexist with the mind; among the mind and mental factors, there is no "defilement by origination" (samutthāna-kleśa), but only "defilement by association with intrinsic nature" (svabhāva-samprayoga-kleśa).
A self-nature cannot be associated with itself; therefore, ignorance is certainly not unwholesome wisdom (*duṣprajñā*).
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtrakāra*) offers a provisional defense:
"Why do you not allow that defiled wisdom is interspersed with wholesome wisdom?"
That which causes impurity is called "defiling," just as greed defiles the mind and prevents liberation.
Must it necessarily be manifest and associated with the mind to be described as defiling?

However, because the power of craving damages and binds the mind, it prevents liberation; later, when those latencies (*vāsanā*) of craving are transformed and extinguished, the mind then becomes liberated.
In the same way, ignorance defiles wisdom (*prajñā*), rendering it impure; it is not that wisdom is associated with ignorance, but rather that wisdom is damaged and turbidified by ignorance.
Regarding such a distinction, what contradiction of principle does it entail?
Upon careful examination of that statement, it is not a sound analysis, because [defilements] cannot defile [the mind] apart from the category of association (*saṃprayukta*).
If greed is associated, it can defile the mind precisely because it is associated with the mind.
If it is argued that even greed dissociated from the mind can defile because it has not been abandoned, then an Arhat would necessarily possess no undefiled mind.
If one claims that such greed is both defiled and undefiled, this has never been observed.
Furthermore, this would result in the fallacy of it being unwholesome, because when the fetter of greed (*rāga-paryavasthāna*) is actually present, there would have to be a state of non-attachment.
Moreover, if the mere mutual intermingling of factors constitutes being "defiled," then even all untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) would be subject to defilement.

Furthermore, if non-afflicted wisdom were mixed with afflicted wisdom, it would follow that the afflicted must be transformed into the non-afflicted, because the power of the remedy is stronger than that which is to be remedied.

Moreover, when various wholesome wisdoms are actually functioning, afflictions certainly do not exist; and when various afflicted wisdoms are actually functioning, wholesomeness certainly does not exist. Thus, what could possibly be defiled?
Furthermore, with whom could there be defilement?
If that which exists and that which does not exist could mutually defile one another, then it would follow that liberation could never be attained.
If liberation occurs through the extinction of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), then since habitual perfuming is fundamentally non-existent, what further thing is there to be extinguished?
Even if there were such a thing as perfuming (*vāsanā*), it could not be that which defiles, nor could it be the essence of ignorance (*avidyā*), for this has already been explained previously.
What difference, then, would there be between the states of cessation and non-cessation?
Therefore, it is established by reason that ignorance is what defiles wisdom (*prajñā*), and that wisdom does not have [ignorance] as its intrinsic nature; thus, this principle remains unshakable.
If there were a distinct phenomenon called ignorance (*avidyā*), one should explain what its distinct nature consists of.
However, since there is indeed a distinct phenomenon—namely, non-comprehension (*apratisaṃkhyā*)—this itself is ignorance; why labor over further investigation?
One must first determine which phenomena constitute "non-comprehension" before they can be said to be the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Only the Blessed One possesses correct knowledge and correct teaching regarding all phenomena, both in their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);
others understand them only in a general sense. Why, then, labor so hard to press for a definitive definition?

However, regarding this, I perceive such a characteristic: there exists a distinct dharma capable of impairing the power of wisdom, which is the cause of inverted views, an obstacle to the virtues of contemplation, that which causes one to lack the desire to engage with objects of knowledge, and that which obscures the mind and mental factors; this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
How can it be definitively known that this is a distinct dharma?
Because it is spoken of as "permanent separation" in the same way as "craving" (*rāga*). As the Sūtra says:
"Through separation from craving, the mind is liberated; through separation from ignorance (*avidyā*), wisdom attains liberation."
Furthermore, this is because ignorance is stated to be the cause, as the sūtra says:
"With ignorance as cause, all defilements arise; with clarity as cause, one is free from all defilements."
Furthermore, it is said that because there is a direct antidote to wrong view; as the Sūtra states:
"The abandonment of all wrong views occurs through the arising of right view, and the separation from all ignorance occurs through the emergence of clear wisdom."
Furthermore, it is because a sūtra speaks of "one dharma. As the sūtra says:
"If there is a bhikṣu who is able to abandon one dharma, I truly declare that he has accomplished what was to be done; that [dharma] is none other than ignorance."
Furthermore, it is said that just as darkness has an antidote,
as a gāthā states: “Those who are able to sever ignorance, And are no longer deluded regarding what is to be deluded about,
They transform and extinguish ignorance and delusion, Just as the rising sun dispels the darkness.”
If it is claimed that the essence of darkness is not a distinct substantial entity, but rather has the absence of light as its essence, this is unreasonable, for the same would apply to light.

If it is further claimed that while the conditions for the arising of light can be perceived, those for darkness cannot, this is also illogical; for the conditions for their arising are distinct, just as they are with water and other such elements.
That is to say, some water-born [entities] arise without external collective conditions, while others arise depending on the power of external collective conditions.
This is not the case for earth and the other elements; as it applies to the rest accordingly, the conditions for the arising of phenomena each have their own distinctions.

Thus, the arising of light necessarily depends on other conditions, whereas darkness arises solely through adverse conditions; it does not come into being through the power of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) or a co-arising condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*).
What principle does this contradict?
Furthermore, since we observe that the substance of darkness possesses various grades, it is not the case that only light can lack such gradations.

If you argue that because there is a presence or absence of portions of light in a given place, darkness consequently becomes subtle or coarse, this too is unreasonable; for where there is no substantial entity, there is no possibility of establishing distinct categories of grade.
Furthermore, there is a distinction between darkness and shadow because they occupy different locations.

Moreover, since both darkness and shadow are objects of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), their substance must be truly existent, just like blue and other colors. As has already been demonstrated, the fivefold group of consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*) cannot take conceptual constructs (*prajñaptidharma*) as their objects.
Furthermore, because darkness is subsumed within the element of shadow, its status as a real entity is established.
Moreover, just as smoke and clouds obstruct other visible forms, so too should darkness; thus, its substance is not non-existent.

If it is argued that visual consciousness does not arise in the dark because light is absent—not because of an obstruction by darkness—this reasoning is also incorrect, for visual consciousness arises with respect to distant dark forms that are separated by light, yet other objects and colors within the darkness are not seen.

If it is argued that in a dark place other material objects are not grasped by ignorance because they are not obstructed by darkness, this reasoning is also incorrect, for those [objects] remain subject to doubt.
The underlying principle here has already been established as before.

Furthermore, this [object] is like the substance of fragrance, which is not non-existent; for it can be habitually cultivated and approached, its characteristics are not indistinct, and it serves as a cause for the benefit of the eye.

If one argues that the power and function of the eye are impaired by light, and that the eye is instead augmented when there is no such light, this is also illogical, because remaining within it for a long time and observing it can still act as a cause of impairment.

If it is argued that the essence of darkness is not a real entity because it does not coexist with light and lacks the characteristics of form (*rūpa*), this is also incorrect, for darkness is perceptible when mixed with light or when separated from light.
Is it not clear that where there is light, the substance of darkness must be absent? This applies to all things that possess resistance; why then should it be otherwise for light and darkness alone?
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"With darkness as a condition, the element of light can be discerned."
It is not the case that there is no existent phenomenon capable of acting as a condition for another; therefore, darkness possesses substantial reality.

Furthermore, since darkness can appear just as the sun does—for instance, when one says "the sun has set and darkness has appeared"—it is not logical for a non-existent thing to possess the quality of appearing.
Furthermore, it is said that because a shadow appears contingent upon a stump, and since the stump is a conventional designation, the shadow must not be real.
This objection is not valid, for as has already been established, although the belly is a conventional designation, it gives rise to actual hunger and thirst.
Furthermore, it can be experienced through touch just as feeling is.
Moreover, the Blessed One said to Vatsa:
"What do you think? Does a reflection not appear in dependence upon a tree stump?"
"If the root is severed, this phenomenon will not arise," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, it is not possible to speak of such a statement regarding a non-existent phenomenon.
Moreover, a sutra states:
It is like entering a sealed room and seeing it filled with darkness;
such a perception of being "filled" could not exist if there were no substantial entity.
Furthermore, a sūtra says:
By means of manifold radiances, all darknesses are destroyed.
If darkness were non-existent, its essence being fundamentally absent, why would it need to be destroyed?
Furthermore, a sūtra says:
"If one does not cut off the root, it will necessarily follow like a shadow," and so forth, as explained at length.
Through such numerous principles and scriptural teachings, we know that the substance of shadows and darkness truly exists.
Based on these statements, it is established by reason that ignorance (*avidyā*) is like darkness because it possesses an antidote;
therefore, ignorance is certainly a distinct dharma whose essence is non-knowledge, rather than being merely the absence of knowledge.
However, this ignorance is briefly of two kinds: namely, afflicted and non-afflicted.
How do these two differ?
Some say as follows:
If that which can obstruct wisdom is defiled ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*), then non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) is simply the absence of wisdom.

Now, let us examine the distinction between the characteristics of these two types of ignorance: that by virtue of which the difference between the ignorant and the wise is established is the characteristic of defiled ignorance;
whereas that by virtue of which, in certain objects, wisdom does not reach as far as ignorance does, is the second characteristic.
Furthermore, if after [defilements] have been severed, there is no distinction between the Buddha and those of the two vehicles, this is the first characteristic;

if after they have been severed, there is a difference between the Buddha and those of the two vehicles regarding whether [certain practices] are performed or not performed, this is the second characteristic.

Furthermore, if one is ignorant regarding the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, this is called the first characteristic of defiled ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*).

If one is unable to realize, as they truly are, the characteristics of phenomena—such as their flavor, potency, maturation, qualities, number, measure, location, time, and similarities or differences—this is non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
This non-afflicted ignorance is precisely what is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*).
An ancient master said:

"The term 'habitual tendency' refers to a specific category of non-afflicted mental factors (*caitta*) which is induced by the repeated cultivation of both afflicted and non-afflicted phenomena. It does not manifest within the continuum of an omniscient one; rather, it causes the mind and its mental factors to function without mastery. This is termed 'habitual tendency.'"
It is not merely that wisdom is absent, for there is no phenomenon capable of serving as a cause [for it].

Nor should one say that there exists a certain kind of mind and mental factors collectively termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), because non-afflicted ignorance has already been discussed previously. That is to say, does this ignorance have the mind abiding in its own nature (*svabhāvavihāra-citta*) and so forth as its essence, or is it something distinct?
If the essence consists of the mind abiding in its own nature and so forth, then even a Buddha would possess non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
If there were a distinction [between them], that which performs the differentiation could be ignorance, but not that which is differentiated.

When we observe the various categories of mental states and mental factors—such as the wholesome and so forth—we see that there must necessarily be distinct dharmas acting as their differentiators; it is not the case that everything is identical. For instance, within the category of the wholesome, there must necessarily be faith and so on; within the unwholesome category, there are shamelessness and so on; and within the defiled category, there are heedlessness and so on.
Within such categories of mind and mental factors, there must necessarily be a distinct dharma that acts as the differentiator.
Therefore, it is known that among these, there is also a distinct dharma capable of acting as a differentiator, which is non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).

Now, upon careful examination, that statement contains an excessive error: for the minds and mental factors of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not all truly perceive characteristics such as taste, potency, and maturation; yet, it is not observed that other mental factors arise [in their absence].

Furthermore, since those minds and mental factors arise with distinct characteristics in each and every moment of thought, there should be the arising of various distinct non-cognitive dharmas within each moment.

If you claim that it is a distinct characteristic [of the mind] that causes this non-cognitive differentiation, then this alone is sufficient to differentiate the categories of mind; why then must one separately postulate "non-defiled ignorance" (akliṣṭājñāna)?

Therefore, with respect to flavors, potencies, post-digestive effects, and so forth, a wisdom that does not strive for understanding acts as a cause—concomitant with factors of a different nature—to draw forth a subsequent wisdom of the same kind; this wisdom, again, without striving for understanding, further acts as a cause to draw forth a wisdom that does not strive for understanding. Thus, through such successive transmission from time immemorial, cause and effect follow one another until they become habitual and form a natural disposition.

Therefore, regarding those very objects such as tastes, the repeatedly practiced cognition that lacks the capacity for comprehension—the inferior cognition induced by this—is called non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
These very simultaneously arising mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are collectively termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*); this is logically certain.

Alternatively, when sentient beings are in a state possessed of afflictions (*kleśa*), their undefiled minds and their continuities are perfumed by the intermingling of those afflictions, thereby possessing a capacity to give rise to the constituent parts of afflictions. Consequently, the undefiled minds and their attendants arise with aspects resembling those [afflictions] due to the power of repeated practice, arising in succession. Therefore, even within a body free from faults, they are still said to possess habitual tendencies; however, for the Omniscient One, these are forever severed and do not manifest.

However, within the continuum of mind—whether defiled or undefiled—at the stage when what is to be abandoned by seeing has already been severed, there remains a residual propensity for the arising of afflictions; this is a vestige of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing. Among these, the defiled portion is termed "homogeneous nature" (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and all such factors are rendered non-manifest through the vajra-path.

If it is non-defiled, it is called the "habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions abandoned through seeing," and these are also severed by that same path; whether they function or not depends on the distinctions among the faculties (*indriya*).

If, during the stage where those [afflictions] abandoned through cultivation have already been severed, there remains within the continuum of a non-defiled mind a residual nature conducive to the arising of afflictions, this portion of the "fragrance" of afflictions abandoned through cultivation is called the "habitual tendencies of afflictions abandoned through cultivation."

Because these are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they have been abandoned by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); whether they manifest or not depends on the superiority or inferiority of their respective faculties.

Since the World-Honored One has attained mastery over all phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*), such [outflows] never manifest for him as they do for afflictions; therefore, the Buddha alone is called one whose mental continuum is perfectly pure (*suviśuddhasantāna*).
Precisely because of this, one acts without error and attains the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and so forth.
Furthermore, it is for this reason that, with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*), it is said that only a Buddha alone is called one who has attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*).
The Venerable Rāma spoke thus:
"There exists a non-defiled dharma called 'habitual tendency' (*vāsanā*), which is like the maturation (*vipāka*) produced by an unwholesome cause.

When the Blessed One was formerly in the stage of a Bodhisattva, throughout three incalculable eons he cultivated various preparatory practices; although he possessed afflictions, he was able to gradually eliminate the non-defiled habitual tendencies induced by those afflictions, while causing the habitual tendencies of the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) to gradually increase."

Later, at the time of attaining the permanent cessation of all outflows (*āsrava*), some of the previously accumulated habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are extinguished while others are not; because one has cultivated preparatory application (*prayoga*) over a long period, one realizes the unsurpassed and permanent exhaustion of all outflows.
However, the Buddha still possesses the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*), because it is said that such habitual tendencies may either be extinguished or not.
While this reasoning thus stated is also tenable, it cannot reveal the essential nature (*svabhāva*) [of those tendencies].
What is the essential nature of non-defiled habitual tendencies?
Is this not merely empty talk intended to produce a genuine understanding?
What is the essential nature of the "category-nature" (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) mentioned in the Sūtra?
Some say that its essence is the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
This contradicts the scriptural teaching, because within the *sūtra*, the nature of the aggregates (*skandha-prakṛti*) is taught as being distinct from the conceit "I am."
The Sūtra says:

"Now that I have thus known and thus seen, all cravings, all views, all categories of being, all attachments to 'I' and 'mine,' and the latent tendencies of the conceit of 'I am'—because these have been abandoned and fully understood—they are extinguished in shadowless quiescence."
Therefore, one should know that the nature of *mānātmaka* (pride-of-similarity) differs from *asmimāna* (the pride "I am").
Some say that other types of pride are subsumed under *mānātmaka*.

That assertion is incorrect, because all preceding terms flow into *asmimāna*; since *asmimāna*—through its inclusion of the term "clinging"—exhaustively encompasses all forms of pride, it should be understood as subsuming them all without exception, just as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and the others do. Nevertheless, within this context, those that are predominant are mentioned separately.

The grasping at "I" and "mine" is the root of all views; therefore, among the views, these two types are specifically distinguished. The term "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) is used to include doubt and hatred. Among the predominant afflictions, ignorance has not yet been mentioned; to distinguish it, the term "homogeneous nature" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is employed. It is called "homogeneous nature" because it accompanies all delusions universally and leads one universally to all realms of existence.
"Category" (jāti) is the meaning of "activity" (pravṛtti).
This is the essence of category, which receives the name "category-nature" (jātitva).

9. Chapter Three on Dependent Origination, Part Nine. Having already explained ignorance (*avidyā*), one should now explain name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Form has already been explained; what, then, is name?
The verse says:
It is called "name" (nāma) because it consists of the four formless aggregates (skandhas).
The treatise says:
The Buddha taught that the four formless aggregates are called "name."
Why is it called "name" (*nāman*)?
Because it is able to denote and summon; that is to say, it is able to denote and summon various objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
If this were so, it would not fully encompass the formless (*ārūpya*) and dissociated (*viprayukta*) phenomena, because they lack an object of cognition.
It is not so; the manifest [action] (*vijñapti*) exists only in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). As explained in the definition of "form" (*rūpa*), there is no error in what has been said.

The Buddha taught that it is called "form" because it is subject to transformation and resistance (*rūpaṇā*). Although past and future non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) and all atoms (*paramāṇu*) lack transformation and resistance, they are nonetheless named "form," because transformation and resistance do not exist within the formless realm.
That which is subject to transformation and resistance is designated as "form" (*rūpa*);

this is not unestablished. Likewise, since there may be that which indicates or designates within the formless (*ārūpya*) realms—which does not exist among those possessing form—there is no logical contradiction. Therefore, there is no fault in including [the non-manifest] within the category of the dissociated (*viprayukta*).
Furthermore, because it is subtle, it is established as a name according to its principle within various meanings and designated by the term "name" (nāman).
Unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) and so forth cannot be called "names," because their basis is apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, because it is able to seek out and reach all realms, stages, destinies, and births, it is given the name "name" (*nāman*).
It is not that the untainted and formless states cannot be called "name"; although they are not what is being explained here, they resemble it.

Furthermore, regarding the formless realm, according to the intention of those who explain it, "name" (nāma) is spoken of as a collective designation; there is no need for further inquiry or refutation.

The Elder’s intention is that because [the aggregates] accord with and establish the continuity of various sentient beings, they are called "name"; thus, they function as causes that accord with and establish that meaning.
If that were so, then material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) would also be "names" (*nāman*), since they too can serve as causes that conform to and establish them.
For the Buddha taught that earth and the other elements constitute the body of a sentient being, and the sutras state that a person (*pudgala*) consists of the six elements.

Furthermore, no sūtra states that the aggregates of formlessness alone constitute the body of a sentient being; rather, there are sūtras stating that the continuum of a sentient being arises dependent upon form and the other aggregates. Therefore, that [definition] for explaining the name has no scriptural basis.
Does not the Buddha speak this verse:
"Name can overshadow everything; there is nothing that surpasses name.
Therefore, this single dharma causes all things to follow its sovereign movement."
In this context, what is established by citing that [scripture]?
Is it to show that within those verses, the continuity of sentient beings is caused solely by formless phenomena (*arūpadharma*)?
To clarify whether the formless [aggregates] possess the power to strongly induce the material [aggregates], serving as the causal factor for the continuity of sentient beings:

if it is claimed that the continuity of all sentient beings is invariably caused by the formless, this is logically incorrect, because those who are mindless establish their continuity solely through the material [aggregates].
Sentient beings who lack consciousness have already been established as having non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) and so forth as their causal conditions.

Furthermore, since the aggregates (*skandha*) of the three realms constitute a single continuum for each individual sentient being, all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are likewise the causes for the continua of all sentient beings.
If it were not so, then one would obtain results without having performed the action, or lose them after having performed it, which would lead to an excessive absurdity.
If the matter-form (*rūpa*) throughout the various stages of a single sentient being’s continuum is not pervasive, the same applies to formless matter (*arūpa*).

Furthermore, one should carefully consider the meaning of this verse: does it state that the four aggregates—feeling and so forth—are called "name" (*nāman*), or does it state that the various distinct meanings signified by words are called "name"?

Just as the expression "the color of a cow" relies upon a name, here one should speak only of those names that signify all things, both material and immaterial; for it is only by the power of these that they can overshadow all phenomena. Since there is not a single phenomenon that is not signified by a name, what else could possibly overshadow all things?
Furthermore, the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are called "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*); how then could feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates outshine the twelve bases?

If it is claimed that all [phenomena] are the objects of perception for feeling and the rest, then in this context the term refers exclusively to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its associated factors (*samprayuktadharma*).

If it is argued that there is no such fault because the remaining factors are of the nature of "name" (*nāma*), then one should not cite this verse as proof that "name" acts as the cause for the continuity of sentient beings. That is to say, if only the mental consciousness and its associated factors were what this *gāthā* refers to as "name," then it would be improper to cite it as evidence for the meaning of "cause," because the five bodies of sensory consciousness and their associated factors also act as causes for the continuity of sentient beings.

Furthermore, as for how it is said that "names do not transcend," if one claims that names designate many aggregates (skandhas) yet do not transcend form (rūpa), then since form designates many elements (dhātus) and many bases (āyatanas), how could names possibly transcend those?
If it is claimed that "name" (nāma) applies universally even to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), then those things which do not so apply should not be called "name.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because what is non-universal is of the same category as what is universal, this reasoning is also incorrect, for the previous argument cannot be cited as proof.

As for those who lack supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they also act as causes for the continuity of sentient beings; since they are equal to those with such powers, apart from the names you have grasped, what other dharma could be said to exist such that all those dharmas proceed according to the will of a sovereign?
If it is claimed that this name follows form, that too is unreasonable, as it is not universally established.
For if one admits that name and form are mutually dependent, how can one say only that form follows the movement of name?
If it is argued that names pervade matter while matter cannot pervade names, this reasoning is also incorrect, because there are no such things as non-sentient [names].
Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that there exist sentient beings who are without mind.

Nor is there any phenomenon external to name-and-form that follows along with names; for the Sūtra states that all knowable phenomena are comprised of two categories—namely, name and form—and there is no third.
Furthermore, it is logically untenable for the four aggregates to be designated as "one.
Even if one were to grant that the term "one dharma" is used in contrast to form (*rūpa*), no fixed concomitant factor (*anuvartaka-dharma*) is observed;
for a self-essence cannot function as a concomitant to itself. Therefore, it is known that this name functions solely as a designator for perception (*saṃjñā*).
