If one interprets it in this way, there is no need for the laborious effort of explaining this verse, as its meaning is already clear;
however, to cite it as proof that the four aggregates are called "name" and constitute the body of a sentient being would certainly be unreasonable.
Regarding this, the Elder raises an objection:

"If the term 'name-and-form' (nāmarūpa) collectively subsumes the five aggregates, then since the Blessed One stated that consciousness depends upon name-and-form, consciousness itself would have to be twofold—namely, the support and that which is supported."
He then provides his own explanation:
"This objection is unreasonable, because consciousness has already been brought forth within the name (*nāman*).

That is to say, since consciousness has already been cited and designated as the 'supported' (*āśrita*), by analogy one understands that the 'basis of consciousness' (*vijñānāśraya*) refers only to the remaining factors of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)."

Now, upon careful examination, that objection is inherently untenable, because the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) necessarily depends on consciousness, as consciousness must depend on consciousness.

However, that Venerable Elder (Sthavira) does not admit the principle of mutual dependence between simultaneous consciousness and name-and-form (nāmarūpa), for his school does not allow for the existence of simultaneous cause and effect.
How can it be that consciousness does not arise simultaneously with two [factors], such that it would follow that consciousness has no basis and must instead rely upon consciousness itself?

Furthermore, even if one were to grant that there is a simultaneous mutual dependence, it could only be that consciousness serves as the basis for feeling and so forth, but feeling and so forth cannot serve as the basis for consciousness; how then could the basis of consciousness be taken as something other than name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)?
Therefore, those questions and answers are all unreasonable.

Now, within this context, one should further investigate: when the Buddha, in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra* (The Great Discourse on Dependent Origination) using the city analogy, explained that consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) serve as mutual conditions for one another, was this based on their temporal sequence, or did it refer to their simultaneous arising?

The statement that "consciousness conditions name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) is based on both temporal sequence and simultaneity, whereas the statement that "name-and-form conditions consciousness" refers only to simultaneity. Why is this so?

Because when consciousness enters the mother's womb and unites with the *kalala*, it constitutes the body of a sentient being; therefore, in the case of "consciousness conditions name-and-form," temporal sequence is also possible.

It is not that consciousness has already conjoined with name-and-form and then further binds the remaining consciousness; nor is it that consciousness, having not yet arisen, serves as the condition for name-and-form. Therefore, this refers exclusively to simultaneous arising.
There is name-and-form conditioned by consciousness, because the member of consciousness is singular.

Furthermore, because it occurs in a single moment—specifically, within the sequential explanation of the factors of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), where there is only the single factor of consciousness (vijñāna)—and this consists of a single thought-instant (ekakṣaṇa), how can one maintain that consciousness and name-and-form (nāmarūpa) are definitively explained as being mutually conditions for one another in terms of temporal sequence?
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"It is like a bundle of reeds.
That is, the sūtra says:
It is like two bundles of reeds standing in an open space, leaning one against the other for mutual support;
if one falls, the other also falls with it.
Thus it is, Venerable One!
These two factors are mutually dependent, namely: consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and name-and-form conditions consciousness.
If they were not co-arising and acting as reciprocal conditions, how would this be similar to the analogy of the bundle of reeds?
That is to say, at the stage of consciousness (*vijñāna*), the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) has not yet arisen;

and when the stage of name-and-form arises, the stage of consciousness has already ceased. Thus, there is certainly no sense of mutual dependence like that of a bundle of reeds; how much less could those who deny the existence of the past and future claim that these stages depend upon one another in such a manner?

Because one exists at times while the other does not, there can be no sense of mutual dependence between the non-existent and the existent, or between the existent and the non-existent; only between two existents can there be mutual dependence. Therefore, those who maintain that dependence must necessarily involve a temporal sequence of before and after are outside the sacred teaching; they do not belong to the school of the Buddha’s Dharma.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
ignorance and mental attention arise simultaneously, serving as mutual conditions for one another.

This refers to the teaching that ignorance has improper mental attention as its cause, and that improper mental attention is produced from delusion (moha), as well as the teaching that these two arise at the same time.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"With the eye and forms as conditions, there arises an attention that is defiled and produced by delusion (*moha*).
Herein, "delusion" is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*), and so forth, as explained at length.
The phrase "in this context" intends to clarify that it refers either to the very moment this attention (*manasikāra*) arises, or to the state of the conjunction of the designated conditions;
it does not refer to the sequential arising of factors belonging to the conditions themselves, because both arise simultaneously without obstruction.

Furthermore, just as a lamp and its light arise simultaneously yet possess the relationship of cause and effect—a point already fully demonstrated during the prior analysis of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)—the simultaneous arising of such cause and effect is thus established beyond doubt.
Yet, there may be a rescue argument stating:
"The lamp and its light are not different.
This is unreasonable, because the lamp and the light differ in their respective spheres of contact, their dimensions, their constituent matter, and their functions.
In the world, fire alone is spoken of as a lamp; thus it is said that the light of a lamp is the lamp and that the lamp can burn objects. The Āgama states:
"Clarity depends upon the lamp," just as the radiance of the sun and moon arises depending upon the solar and lunar disks.
Furthermore, just as the great earth depends upon the water-circle, it is only when water and earth arise together that they possess the sense of being a support for one another.
Thus, the distinct natures of the lamp and its light are established; herein, the principle that cause and effect arise simultaneously is made manifest.
Although light arises depending on its own primary elements (*mahābhūta*), at the time of its arising it is not separate from the lamp’s flame.

If it is argued that light and the flame arise from the same cause because the very cause of the flame is the cause of the light, this too is unreasonable, because there is a distinction between them.

It is not the case that a non-unitary effect arises from a single combination, nor does a non-unitary effect arise from a non-unitary combination; yet, when struck once, do not both fire and sound arise together?
How could it be that there is no single combination from which multiple effects are produced?
This reasoning is also incorrect, because they depend on distinct bases and because their respective homogeneous causes produce them separately.
Therefore, that defense is merely empty words; thus, the lamp and its illumination are distinct in their causal substance.
If consciousness and name-and-form serve as mutual conditions for one another, why does the Sūtra frequently state that "consciousness conditions name-and-form," emphasizing their reciprocal nature?
Although this principle holds true, the function of consciousness is particularly prominent; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.

Regarding the statement that consciousness has a stronger function: this means that because feeling and the other [mental factors] depend upon consciousness as their basis for their activity, and because consciousness depends upon them as its basis for its own transformation, consciousness has a superior function in sustaining the semen and blood to form the *kalala* and thereby forming the body of a sentient being.
Just as a king and his ministers, though mutually dependent, the king receives the name [of "ruler"] because he is the most preeminent;
so too should one understand the relationship between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Furthermore, that consciousness conditions name-and-form is based on its role as a condition in a prior existence.

The statement that they serve as conditions for one another refers exclusively to simultaneous arising; for while consciousness conditions name-and-form across both prior and subsequent moments as well as simultaneously, name-and-form conditions consciousness only through simultaneous arising, because the consciousness at the moment of rebirth-linking has no separate temporal stage.
Furthermore, when it is said that "consciousness conditions name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), this refers to name-and-form as a state (*avasthā*).
When it is said that they "mutually condition one another," this refers to name-and-form as moments (*kṣaṇa*).
The Venerable Rāma, following his own interpretation, states:

When one is reborn from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) of the intermediate state serves as the condition to give rise to the consciousness of the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*), which occurs without interval.

Upon the cessation of the name-and-form of the intermediate state, consciousness alone arises; this [consciousness] is then able to give rise to the name-and-form of the new existence (*upapattibhava*).

Such an investigation is not consistent with correct reasoning. Regarding the statement that the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) serves as the condition to draw forth the consciousness of the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) immediately thereafter: does the consciousness of the intermediate state itself also serve as the condition, or is it only the remaining "name" (*nāman*), excluding the consciousness of the intermediate state?

If the consciousness of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) also serves as a condition, by what reasoning do the final moments of mind, mental factors, and matter in the intermediate state serve as conditions only to draw forth the subsequent consciousness to arise, rather than the mental factors and matter?

If you claim that "conditions" (pratyaya) refers to everything except consciousness, by what logic would consciousness arising simultaneously [with its conditions] not possess the nature of a condition?

If you claim that at that stage there is no consciousness arising simultaneously [with the other factors], then the consciousness of rebirth-linking (pratisaṃdhi-vijñāna) would have nothing upon which to depend for its arising; furthermore, it would follow that mental factors (caitta) could not serve as the support (āśraya) for the mind (citta).

Furthermore, for what reason do the mental factors (*caitta*) at that stage act as the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*) only for consciousnesses of a different class, and cannot induce the arising of mental factors of the same class?

It is because it is impossible for consciousness to exist temporarily without depending on matter (*rūpa*) so long as one has not yet attained freedom from craving for matter. Therefore, the matter of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) certainly serves as a condition (*pratyaya*), drawing forth the matter that arises simultaneously with the mind at the time of rebirth.
How is it that consciousness alone arises in this state?

If you claim that although matter (rūpa) arises at this time, only consciousness is mentioned, then one should likewise mention mental factors (caitta) in this state, yet only the mind (citta) is mentioned.
Therefore, one should not again maintain this assertion:

that when the name-and-form (nāmarūpa) of the intermediate state (antarābhava) ceases, consciousness alone arises, and it is only this [consciousness] that is able to induce the name-and-form of the [new] birth.

Furthermore, this isolated consciousness cannot be the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) or the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*), because the intermediate existence has already ceased and the birth-existence has not yet arisen.
Since the state of the cessation of the intermediate existence is not itself the birth-existence, what they have said arises from their own false attachments.
Furthermore, regarding the theory that the mind and mental factors arise sequentially, how do you conceive of their arising in succession?

When, immediately following a visual consciousness, the feeling produced by eye-contact and other such factors arise, do they arise simultaneously with other consciousnesses, or do they arise independently as feeling and so forth?

If there are other consciousnesses, such as feeling (*vedanā*), that arise simultaneously [with the primary consciousness], does the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises take that very object as its condition, or do they arise as distinct other consciousnesses taking other objects as their conditions?

First, it is not the case that the mental consciousness that arises takes that very object as its condition; for since the feelings and so forth produced by eye-contact depend upon the eye-faculty, their temporal basis differs from that of this mental consciousness.

The sensations and so forth produced in dependence on the eye-faculty cannot have the past as their object; nor can the sensations and so forth produced by eye-contact arise with the mind and mental objects (*dharmas*) as conditions, because it is taught that mental consciousness and so forth arise with the mind and mental objects as conditions.

If [consciousness] were produced with mental phenomena (*dharma*) as its condition, it could not be said to be born from eye-contact, nor could it arise from other consciousnesses taking other objects as conditions.
If [various consciousnesses] could arise simultaneously based on different objects, then one should be able to apprehend all objects at once.

If the various consciousnesses did not arise together with sensation and the other mental factors, then subsequent consciousness would have no basis for arising; furthermore, that the stream of mental consciousness is interrupted and then resumes—something that has never occurred in the lower realms—is entirely disallowed by them.

Because that school admits that the continuum of consciousness arises without interruption even when entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and other such states, their claim that—after the final moment of mind in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)—consciousness alone arises immediately following name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and only subsequently induces the name-and-form of the next birth, is mere empty talk; for it contradicts both reason and scripture.
Regarding this, the Elder raises a hypothetical objection:
"The Sūtra should not state that consciousness conditions name-and-form, because [consciousness] arises only through the power of mutual succession.
He then provides his own explanation:
This objection is unreasonable, because there is a distinction in the conditions for arising and abiding.
That is to say, consciousness acts as the condition for the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), since it causes them to arise by entering the womb.

After that [name-and-form] has arisen, it serves as the basis for the abiding of consciousness; through successive conditions, consciousness attains stability. Therefore, it is also said that consciousness has name-and-form as its condition.

This is not so, because it contradicts both reason and scripture. For when the Buddha had not yet attained Great Enlightenment, he sought the conditions for the arising of consciousness and realized they were none other than name-and-form.
As stated in the Sūtra:

"The Bodhisattva seeks the conditions for old age and death, tracing them back through birth to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). He knows that from birth down to consciousness (*vijñāna*), each serves as a condition for the next; seeking the condition for the arising of consciousness, he realizes it is precisely name-and-form."
If that name-and-form were not the condition for the arising of consciousness, what the Bodhisattva knows would be erroneous.

Furthermore, as it has been stated, after its arising, name-and-form serves as the support for the abiding of consciousness; by acting successively as conditions, consciousness attains stability, and thus it is also said that consciousness has name-and-form as its condition.

To say there is a principle where there is no [logical] ground: this consciousness that has been explained as having name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as its condition is itself the consciousness produced by conditions from name-and-form; how then can it subsequently serve as the support for consciousness?
Furthermore, that sutra merely states that consciousness abides dependent upon name-and-form; thus the Sūtra says, addressing Ānanda:
"If consciousness were not to depend upon name-and-form, would it be able to abide?"
"No, World-Honored One!
This sutra does not say that name-and-form abide dependent upon consciousness; how then could they proceed in a reciprocal manner?"
Furthermore, since you do not admit that consciousness and name-and-form arise simultaneously, how can it be said that they abide by serving as mutual conditions for one another?
Moreover, as previously stated regarding the thesis that negates the past and future, when one exists, the other is absent.

It is not possible for non-existence and existence, or existence and non-existence, to have the sense of mutual dependence through reciprocal reliance; rather, it is only between existence and existence that such mutual dependence can occur.
How, then, can there be the sense of mutual dependence between two things that arise simultaneously?
If even one [of these conditions] were missing, the other could not be established.

Furthermore, in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, the Buddha did not explain the sequential causality of the limbs of existence (*bhavāṅga*), nor did he teach only the twelve limbs of existence; for in that sutra, he stated that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the condition for contact (*sparśa*).
Furthermore, the mention of "seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*) and so forth is for the sake of [establishing] the conditions for "attainment" (*prāpti*) and so on.

However, because the Buddha revealed the profound principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-naya*) to Ānanda regarding those [factors], the meaning of that sūtra—concerning the basis and the object—states only that consciousness dwells in dependence upon name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); and that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) dwells securely by relying solely upon the mind as its basis and phenomena (*dharma*) as its object.
The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, abide by having the eyes and so forth as their support (*āśraya*) and visible forms and so forth as their object (*ālambana*).
Likewise, for the mental consciousness, the support is singular while the objects are twofold; the five consciousnesses are the reverse of this.

Except for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), whose support (*āśraya*) must necessarily be of a different time, it is universally applicable that for the other [consciousnesses], their supports and objects of perception (*ālambana*) may exist simultaneously during the states of the various factors of existence.
Upon careful examination, the doctrine of the Sthavira school—which asserts that consciousness and name-and-form serve as mutual conditions—is logically untenable.
Nevertheless, the Sūtra states:
"When I contemplate dependent origination, I turn back at consciousness; beyond this point, my mind does not proceed further."
What is the meaning of this statement?

At that time, the bodhisattva retrospectively contemplates the conditions from which the various members of dependent origination arise in succession. First, he observes that the conditions for the arising of the [first] nine members are each distinct; finally, he observes that consciousness has no distinct condition for its arising. Therefore, upon reaching consciousness, it does not proceed further into other [members].

However, the consciousness at rebirth has two conditions for its arising: first, that which arises prior [to it], and second, that which arises simultaneously with it; for there is no difference in the sense that consciousness arises from formations (*saṃskāra*).

Having previously examined the link of birth (*jāti*), where the condition for birth was identified as existence (*bhava*), and having thus already examined the prior condition for consciousness as formations, one now examines name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as the simultaneous condition. Consequently, when one arrives at consciousness, the mind does not turn back further, because one has already fully examined both conditions for the arising of consciousness.

Since one observes that the consciousness at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*) in the present life arises through the power of two co-arising conditions from the preceding [moment], one should infer accordingly that the remaining factors (*aṅga*) are likewise in their respective cases; for each momentary arising possesses its own two conditions. Therefore, the contemplation of the two conditions is specifically and fully demonstrated only with respect to the factor of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
How is it that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) serves as the object-condition for consciousness?
Because within this [process], consciousness dwells and adheres to it.
As the Sūtra says regarding the stations of consciousness (vijñāna-sthiti): "With the exception of consciousness itself, the remaining factors are name-and-form."
Previously, the meaning of "abiding in consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*) was explained through the lens of attachment; therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Craving and delight moisten consciousness, causing it to increase and expand within the aggregates.
Furthermore, the *Mahānidāna-sūtra* also states:
"Does consciousness abide by depending on name-and-form?
No, World-Honored One."
...and so on, as explained at length.

This teaching states that consciousness dwells and adheres within the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that arises simultaneously with it; because it reveals the conditions that arise simultaneously with consciousness, the four stations of consciousness (*catasraḥ vijñānasthitayaḥ*) are taught.
Therefore, when the Bodhisattva reaches consciousness, he turns back.

Although the factor of old age and death is indeed identical to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth, the previous contemplation that old age and death have birth as their condition already demonstrated that the factor of consciousness conditions name-and-form; however, it was not established that all instances of old age and death have consciousness as their condition. Therefore, in order to definitively establish that consciousness conditions only name-and-form, one again contemplates that name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
Because that bodhisattva feels weary of and terrified by birth, he contemplates birth twice.
Due to the bodhisattva’s mind being weary of and terrified by cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), he does not examine all the members of cyclic existence in their entirety.

All branches of the process of transmigration have birth as their root; since one has already contemplated birth, one has thereby fully understood the branches of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), which are [respectively] craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*). Because one has already contemplated craving and the others, they are not contemplated again.
Because Bodhisattvas aspire to the door of cessation (*nirodha-mukha*), they thoroughly examine the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśa-bhavāṅga*).
Having already explained "name" (*nāman*), one should now explain "contact" (*sparśa*).
The verse says:
Contact arises from the conjunction of three.
The treatise says:
There are six kinds of contact, namely, eye-contact through to mind-contact.
What, then, is this? It is that which arises from the conjunction of the three; that is to say, because of the coming together of the three—organ, object, and consciousness—a distinct contact arises.
Although the sixth [consciousness] and its three [factors] belong to different time periods, their causal relationship is interconnected; thus, the meaning of "conjunction" is established.

Alternatively, "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*) has the sense of having a single result; although the faculty, object, and consciousness do not necessarily arise simultaneously, they are termed "conjoined" because their resultant contact (*sparśa*) is the same.
That the essence of contact exists as a distinct entity has already been established within the section on the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

Although [contact] arises from the conjunction of the three, it necessarily arises simultaneously with consciousness, because it is taught that it is produced by two conditions, just as consciousness is.
As the Sūtra says:
"With the internal body of consciousness and external name-and-form, these two pairs serve as conditions for the arising of all contacts," and so forth at length.
Is it not the case that this very point explains that contact arises from the conjunction of three factors?

That is to say, because there is the internal "body with consciousness," namely the six sense organs and the six consciousnesses, as well as the external "name-and-form," namely the six objects, contact arises from these two conditions; therefore, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is not established.
The meaning of the sutra is not otherwise, for the Buddha spoke of two [factors].
That is to say, this sutra states that "the two twos serve as conditions for the arising of all contacts," and does not speak of three.

Examining the meaning of this sutra, the phrase "body with consciousness" (vijñānakāya) reveals the six internal bases (ādhyātmikāyatana), while the term "external name-and-form" (bāhya nāmarūpa) reveals the six external bases (bāhyāyatana).
Other sūtras also state that [consciousness] arises from two conditions; thus a verse says:
"The eye, visible forms, and so forth," as has already been explained above.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that consciousness and contact both have name-and-form as their condition.
Since the conditions are identical, how could there be a temporal sequence?
When the conditions are complete, [the effect] must arise, for there is nothing capable of obstructing it.

From this, it is proven that the various phenomena such as the sensations produced by contact with the eye and other faculties arise simultaneously with the eye-consciousness and other cognitions, because they share the same causes for their arising as the eye-consciousness and so forth.
According to this scriptural passage:
"Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness—these dharmas are intermingled and inseparable.

Even for those who maintain that contact (*sparśa*) is merely a provisional designation, they must also admit that feeling and the other factors arise simultaneously with contact. This is because the sutra states that consciousness is intermingled with feeling and the rest, and because consciousness is a constituent part of contact.
Since there is no consciousness that is not intermingled with feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors], this proves that feeling and the rest are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
They argue as follows:
the meaning of "universal mental factor" does not necessarily require that it be concomitant with every state of mind.
If that is so, what is the meaning of "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmikadharma*)?

There are three sets of three levels, distinguished by the presence of vitarka and vicāra, the wholesome and so forth, and the stages of training and so forth. If a factor exists in all of these levels, it is called a universal mental factor; others are designated accordingly.
This is merely words, for it contradicts the preceding sutra;
as that [sutra] states, one should carefully examine the preceding sutra.
That sutra further says:
Whatever is felt is what is thought; whatever is thought is what is perceived; whatever is perceived is what is cognized.
Regarding this, is it in terms of the object of focus (*ālambana*) or in terms of the moment (*kṣaṇa*) that this is not yet understood?
What remains unclarified in this statement?
The former refers to moments (*kṣaṇa*), while the latter refers to the object of cognition (*ālambana*); the principle is thus certain.
How is it known that it is certain?
This is because other sūtras describe "intermingling" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) with reference to co-arising phenomena (*sahaja-dharma*). As a sūtra states:
"Vitality, warmth, and consciousness—these three phenomena are intermingled and inseparable."

In this context, the statement is not made with reference to non-simultaneous arising or with reference to the object of cognition (*ālambana*), because the three [mental factors] necessarily arise together and two [of them] lack an object of cognition.
Therefore, the aforementioned expression "the intermingling of sensation and so forth" must certainly refer to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), for it would otherwise be untenable.

That is to say, if one reckons that their arising immediately after one another constitutes "intermingling" (*saṃsarga*), then since the non-existence of one and the existence of the other cannot constitute intermingling—as has already been argued previously—it is also impossible to claim that they are called "intermingled" because they share the same object (*ālambana*).
Otherwise, it would follow that there is a sense of intermingling between mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), which is not the case.
Therefore, when consciousness arises in dependence upon a single object, there must necessarily be co-arising factors such as contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).

It is absolutely impossible for consciousness to arise apart from contact and the other factors, as has already been well established by the cited sūtra. How then can it be said that while these two factors—contact and feeling—arise together, contact is the condition for feeling, but feeling is not the condition for contact?
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"It is not that various contacts arise conditioned by various feelings; rather, various feelings arise conditioned by various contacts.

Furthermore, the Sūtra only states that eye-contact serves as the condition for the arising of feeling produced by eye-contact; there is no sūtra that ever states that eye-feeling serves as the condition for the arising of contact produced by eye-feeling.

Is it not clearly observed that although light and sprouts, as well as shadows and reflections, arise simultaneously, it is nonetheless due to the lamp and the sprout that the light and the shadow are produced? The same applies to contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).

This analogy is not equivalent, because [the latter] exists or does not exist according to the presence or absence of movement and stability; thus, there is no definitive cause to prove that contact and feeling, though arising together, [are related in that way].

Furthermore, while sensation is conditioned by contact, contact is not conditioned by sensation; although this does not manifest as a visible sign, it is logically necessary because sensation necessarily possesses distinctions that follow from those of contact.
If you still do not understand, I shall further provide an alternative method of exposition to facilitate your comprehension of this principle.
It is said that contact is twofold: first, the conventional; second, the real.
That which is called conventional refers to contact as the conjunction of the three, as stated in the Sūtra:
"The coming together and conjunction of these three factors is designated by the term 'contact'."
What is called "the real" refers to that which is touched by the mind, as stated in the Sūtra:
"The eye and form, these two conditions, give rise to eye-contact," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, a Sūtra says:
There is the internal body of consciousness and the external name-and-form; with these two pairs as conditions, various contacts arise.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Name-and-form is the condition for contact," and "The six sense bases are the condition for contact."

In all such immeasurable sūtras as these, it is taught that contact serves as the condition for the arising of sensation; it is not the case that sensation is the condition [for contact], because sensation does not arise from the conjunction of the three factors—sense faculty, object, and consciousness.
It is not that visual consciousness alone constitutes the essence of eye-contact; rather, all mental factors (caitta) are manifested by way of their supports.

Although consciousness is the predominant cause at the moment of the arising of sensation (vedanā), it is said that the arising of sensation and the other factors is also dependent upon the eye and visible form. Therefore, it is stated simply that "with eye-contact as condition, sensation produced by eye-contact arises."

It has never been said that eye-contact arises with eye-feeling as its condition; rather, since actual contact (*sparśa*) within this context is a mental factor (*caitta*), it can be said that feeling and contact serve as reciprocal conditions for one another.
Therefore, these two sūtras do not contradict one another.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction even when speaking from a distinct perspective: namely, that while feeling arises from contact by way of this door, contact does not arise from feeling by means of that same cause.
As the sūtra says:
"I do not see a single dharma that cuts off desire as effectively as the cultivation of mindfulness of the body.
This is stated by way of excluding all other dharmas through a specific perspective, rather than referring to all modes of counteraction (pratipakṣa) universally, for it continues later with:
Just as with the cultivation of mindfulness of the body, it is the same for mindfulness of breathing, mindfulness of the Buddha, the perception of death, and so forth.
The phrase "in this way" (evam) indicates the meaning of alternative formulations.
How is it known that feeling (*vedanā*) also has contact (*sparśa*) as its condition?
Other sūtras state that feeling is conditioned by contact (*sparśa*),
as a sūtra says: "Feeling arises from contact with the body."
This intention reveals that there is contact, which arises conditioned by bodily sensation.
Why is it that while the eye and other faculties are also conditions for sensation and so forth, one speaks of them only in relation to contact and not in relation to sensation and so forth?

Because the meaning of contact (*sparśa*) is manifested within the conjunction of entities, it is this conjunction of "this" and "that" that receives the name "contact," rather than the contact being named after its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The world establishes the term "contact" for such conjunctions; for example, when two pieces of wood meet, one says, "the woods are in contact."
Therefore, within the conjunction of the eye and so forth, one can only speak of contact (*sparśa*), not of sensation (*vedanā*) and the rest.
Furthermore, since the eye and so forth are not the causes that produce contact, why can you challenge this by saying:
"Since they are also causes of sensation and the rest, one should likewise speak of them in terms of sensation and the rest"?
If that were necessarily the case, one would have to admit that everything produced by the causes of contact is called "contact.

However, in reality, among all phenomena that are effects of contact, many distinct names are established according to specific conceptualizations, while others are given specific names based on general conceptualizations, such as the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana), the element of form (rūpadhātu), and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
By this, the statement found elsewhere—that all mental factors (*caitta*) are induced by contact (*sparśa*)—is well explained.
If that is so, since perception (*saṃjñā*) and the other factors all have contact as their condition, why is it said only that feeling (*vedanā*) has contact as its condition?
It is also taught that perception (*saṃjñā*) and the other [mental factors] take contact (*sparśa*) as their condition, as in the *Viniścaya-sūtra*; thus, one should not raise an objection.
Because the function of feeling (*vedanā*) is strongest in the stage following contact, the term "feeling" is used here to refer collectively to all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

However, regarding the cause of feeling (*vedanā*) as explained in the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), only actual contact (*sparśa*) is intended, not the conceptual construct of the "conjunction of the three" (*trikasannipāta*). Why is this so?
Because it specifies the basis (*āśraya*).

This means that only the actual contact (sparśa) is manifested in terms of its basis; it is not the case that among various conventionally existent things, one can discern their categories or measure their superiority or inferiority within a conventional basis, for if even one [factor] were lacking, such a thing could not exist.
From this, it is known that what is taught here is that actual contact conditions feeling.

Regarding the definition of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) taught herein: whenever, in whatever stage, whichever phenomenon is predominant, that is said to be the "condition"; it gives rise to the superior phenomenon of the immediately subsequent stage as its fruit. Therefore, there is no error.

Furthermore, regarding the great mass of future defilements, feeling (*vedanā*) serves as their proximate cause; therefore, within dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is taught in sequence that contact (*sparśa*) arises with feeling as its condition. By avoiding these conditions, feeling does not manifest, thereby severing its root.
Since all mental states and mental factors take the six sense bases as their condition, why is it said only that "the six sense bases condition contact"?
It is because contact is predominant at this stage; therefore, it is designated by the name "contact."
In truth, one should know that all minds and mental factors (citta-caitta) invariably take the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) as their conditions.

Furthermore, for what reason is it that, although actual contact (sparśa) occupies a superior state, it is said only to serve as a condition for that superior feeling (vedanā), and not said to serve as a condition for the arising of superior perception (saṃjñā) and so forth?
Although contact (*sparśa*) also arises simultaneously with those [mental factors], it is specifically mentioned because it is particularly conducive to feeling (*vedanā*).

For example, just as resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is particularly conducive to certainty, and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), diligence (*vīrya*), and so forth are particularly conducive to calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), such is the nature of their principles; one should not raise an objection against this.
Regarding the distinction between name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as the condition for contact (sparśa) and the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) as the condition for contact:
in which sūtra is it stated that name-and-form conditions contact? The *Mahānidāna-sūtra* states as follows:
Given that there are various modes of activity and various designations established by names,
if those modes of activity and those designations were absent, could the contact associated with designation (adhivacana-saṃsparśa) be known?
"No, Venerable Sir!
It is by means of various modes of activity and various designations that the form-body (rūpakāya) is conventionally established."
Without those modes of activity and without that designation, can it be known that there is contact with resistance?
No, Venerable Sir!
"If, in every respect, both the name-body and the form-body were non-existent, could one perceive contact or designate contact?
No, Venerable Sir."
Therefore, Ānanda! The source of contact, the cause of contact, the condition for contact, is what is called name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
What meaning does this cited sūtra intend to clarify?
It is explained that name (*nāman*) and form (*rūpa*) are the causes for the arising of contact.
"Name" refers to the sense bases of mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*); "form" refers to the sense bases from eye and visible objects up to body and tangible objects.
Among these, the collection of names is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-sparśa*); because it is called by means of names, it is termed "name-body-contact."
Thus, the form-body is called "contact with resistance" (*pratigha-sparśa*); because form constitutes the body, it receives the name "form-body.
This refers to its essential nature (*tattva*), meaning that form is its substantial entity.

Herein the intended meaning is this: that which has "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-sparśa*) as its cause is called "designation-contact," and that which has "contact with resistance" as its cause is called "contact with resistance."
It is not the substance of the two types of contact; for this reason it is said:
"Whatever has aspects and whatever has designations, these are designated as the group of names (nāmakāya) and the group of forms (rūpakāya)."

"Characteristics of activity" refers to the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*); because they are the objects of activity and possess the characteristics of being acted upon, they receive the name "characteristics of activity.

"Designation by indication" refers to the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*); it is because these indicate the names of the various contacts (*sparśa*) that they are called "eye-contact" through to "mind-contact."

This means that regarding all entities possessing name, there is the designation of "designation-contact" (adhivacana-saṃsparśa); regarding all entities possessing form, there is the designation of "resistance-contact" (pratigha-saṃsparśa).
Should any of these be lacking, the contact so designated cannot be established.

The above scriptural passage has provisionally analyzed conventional contact (*prajñapti-sparśa*); in order to analyze the actual contact (*dravya-sparśa*) that arises conditioned by this, it further states:
"If in every respect name-body (*nāma-kāya*) and form-body (*rūpa-kāya*) are all non-existent," and so forth, as explained at length.

The meaning of this passage is as follows: if, in every respect, a conventional contact does not exist, then it is difficult to discern the very name of that which the mind contacts throughout the three periods of time; because its substance does not arise, it cannot be known, and since it cannot be known, it also cannot be designated.
If one analyzes the meaning of the sūtra in this way, it would mean that "name-and-form conditions contact" refers to two things conditioning contact.
However, the state [of name-and-form] as a condition for contact is determinate; whereas if two things were to condition contact, their state would be indeterminate.

Although the stage of contact conditioned by the six sense bases is likewise fixed, it is presented specifically in terms of the support of sentient beings; whereas name-and-form as the condition for contact is presented in terms of both the support and the object. Therefore, there is a distinction between them.

Furthermore, there is another meaning: herein, "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacanasaṃsparśa*), which means that names serve as its basis, since it has the mental consciousness as its basis.

In this context, the "form body" (*rūpakāya*) is termed "contact with resistance" (*sapratigha-sparśa*), which signifies that form serves as its basis; this is because it takes the five sense faculties as its basis.

By virtue of the power of these bases upon which the various contacts depend, their names are distinguished individually—such as "eye-contact" (*cakṣuḥ-sparśa*) up to "mind-contact" (*manaḥ-sparśa*)—since consciousness and the mind (*manas*) have the same meaning.

If the six types of contact that depend upon name-and-form in every respect do not exist, then there certainly cannot be any other independent contact that can be cognized; since nothing can be cognized, it also cannot be designated.

The meaning of this statement is as follows: since there is no such thing as a conventional contact apart from the six bases and so forth, there is likewise no real contact existing apart from the substance of the six contacts.
If one interprets the meaning of the Sūtra in this way, then what is called "contact conditioned by the six sense-bases" is precisely "contact conditioned by name-and-form."

In this context, the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) itself is shown to be the differentiation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), in order to distinguish the various doctrinal gateways of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and to enable Ānanda to understand its profound meaning.
Other masters say: the statement that "name-and-form conditions contact" (*nāmarūpapratyayaḥ sparśaḥ*) reveals that [contact] arises from the coming together of the three.
To manifest the functions of the faculties and their objects, it is said that contact has two conditions;
to say that contact has the six sense bases as its condition manifests the function of the unique cause. Some say:
Regarding the three types based on the categories of elements, bases, and dependent origination, they correspond respectively to the aforementioned six contacts, which are further combined into two.
What are these two?
The verse says:
The five faculties should be considered "with resistance" (sapratigha), while the sixth is associated with the "designation" (adhivacana).
The treatise states:
The five contacts, such as that of the eye and so forth, are called "with resistance" because they have resistant faculties as their basis.
Because it has only the *dharmas* (phenomena) as its object, the sixth mental contact (*manas-sparśa*) is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacana*).
"Designation" refers to names; since names are the predominant objects of mental contact, this contact is specifically termed "designation-contact" based on that.
The mental consciousness takes both general names and meanings as its objects, whereas the five [sensory] consciousnesses do not take names as their objects; therefore, it is said to be "longer.

As it is said: the visual consciousness can only cognize blue, but cannot cognize that "this is blue"; the mental consciousness, however, cognizes blue and also cognizes that "this is blue," and so on, as explained at length.

Therefore, the name "contact with resistance" (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) is derived from its objective support (*ālambana*); the name "contact with designation" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*) is established in reference to the predominant object.
Some say: "Mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) is called 'designation' because it exercises sovereignty (*adhipatya*) over the production of speech."

Some say: "The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) functions toward its objects only when preceded by speech as its dominant condition (*adhipati*), whereas the five [sensory] consciousnesses are not so; therefore, the mental consciousness alone is termed 'discriminative' (*adhivacana*), and because it is associated with this, it is called 'discriminative contact' (*adhivacanasaṃsparśa*)."

Contact with resistance (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) is named after its objective support; contact with designation (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*) is established based on its predominant associated [mental factor].
These same six types of contact further constitute eight kinds according to their specific associations.
The verse says:
Knowledge, ignorance, and that which is neither; the untainted, the defiled, and the remainder;
associated with the two—craving and aversion; and corresponding to the three feelings such as pleasure.
The treatise says:

Contact associated with clarity (*vidyā*), lack of clarity (*avidyā*), and so forth, constitutes three types: first, contact associated with clarity; second, contact associated with lack of clarity; and third, contact associated with neither clarity nor lack of clarity.
These three should be understood, respectively, as contact associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*), the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), and the remaining [neither-tainted-nor-defiled] states.

The remainder refers to that which is other than the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), namely, the tainted wholesome (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

A portion of the contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*) arises frequently; based upon that, two further types of contact—those of craving (*rāga*) and aversion (*dveṣa*)—are established, because they are associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of craving and aversion.

Taken together, all [contacts] further constitute three types of contact: first, contact conducive to pleasant feeling; second, contact conducive to painful feeling; and third, contact conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is contact conducive to feeling (*vedanīya-sparśa*)?
It is called "conducive to feeling" because it is what is experienced by pleasant and other feelings, or because it serves as the basis for the activity of feeling.
How does contact serve as the basis for the activity of feeling such that it is experienced by feeling?
Its mode of activity (ākāra) is extremely similar to contact (sparśa), as it arises in dependence upon contact.
Furthermore, because it is associated with feelings such as pleasure, or because it can induce feelings such as pleasure, it is termed "conducive to feeling" (vedanīya).
Thus, there are sixteen types of contact in total.
Having analyzed contact, one should now analyze feeling.
The verse says:
From this, six types of feeling arise; five belong to the body, and the remaining one belongs to the mind.
The commentary states:
From the aforementioned six types of contact, six types of feeling arise—namely, feeling born of eye-contact, up to feeling born of mind-contact.
These combined constitute two types: first, bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*); second, mental sensation (*caitasikī vedanā*).
Among the six [types of contact], the first five are called bodily sensations because they depend on the physical sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*);
that which arises from mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja*) is called mental sensation because it depends solely on the mind.
The verse says:
These further become eighteen, due to the differences in the mental applications (*manopavicāra*).
The commentary says:
Regarding the aforementioned single-pointed experience of feeling, it is further divided into eighteen types based on the differences among the mental applications (*manopavicāra*).
What are these eighteen mental applications?
That is to say, there are six applications for each of joy, sorrow, and equanimity.
For what reason are these further established as eighteen?
Because the three types of feeling are associated only with the mental faculty (*manas*), and since there are differences among the six objects, they constitute eighteen.

It is not that there is a single body of sensation; rather, it is through association with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that objects become sixfold, because the modes of experiencing them differ.
What is the meaning of the term "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*)?
It refers to the fact that joy and the other [feelings] possess the power to act as proximate conditions, causing the mind to range repeatedly over its objects.

If it is said that because joy and so forth take the mind as their proximate condition and repeatedly engage with objects, they are called "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*), then perception (*saṃjñā*) and the other [mental factors] should also receive this name, since they are associated with the mind and proceed by means of the mind.
If mental applications (manopavicāra) occurred only on the level of the mind, would this not contradict the Sūtra? As the Sūtra says:
"Having seen a form with the eye, one gives rise to a mental application of joy toward a form that is conducive to joy," and so forth, as explained at length.

This is not contradictory; for example, although one may induce the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) based on visual consciousness, this contemplation of impurity is comprised solely within the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
Nevertheless, the Sūtra states:
"Having seen a form with the eye, one dwells fully established in the contemplation of its impurity accordingly."

This case is also like that; it is spoken of in this way because the mental applications (*manopavicāra*), such as joy (*prīti*) and so forth, are induced by the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) upon the mental level (*manobhūmi*).

Since that sutra states, "having seen forms with the eye," and so forth at length, one should not raise an objection that these mental applications are associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as induced by the five sensory consciousnesses.
For what reason are bodily sensations not mental applications (*manopavicāra*)?
Because they do not share the same nature as mental applications.
Since mental applications depend exclusively upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they are termed "applications" (*upavicāra*).
Because it discriminates the objects of the specific and general characteristics of the three periods of time and so forth, it is called "activity" (*saṃskāra*).
All bodily and mental sensations are contrary to this; therefore, they are neither "proximate to the mind" (*manopavicāra*) nor are they termed "activities."
Is it not the case that bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*) also possesses this characteristic?
Once bodily sensation has apprehended objects such as visible forms, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) follows along.
This is because, through the power of bodily sensation, the mental consciousness repeatedly ranges over those objects.
This is also not the case, because the characteristics [of sensation] have already been explained.
That is to say, the various bodily sensations do not depend upon the mental consciousness, because they are non-conceptual.
Since they are unable to discriminate between the merits and faults of an object, it is not by their power that the mind repeatedly ranges over objects.

Furthermore, because it is not fixed: that is to say, following a bodily sensation, a mental sensation is not necessarily present; however, when a mental consciousness arises in succession, a mental sensation is necessarily simultaneous with that mental consciousness. Therefore, only mental sensations are termed "mental applications" (manopavicāra).
Furthermore, since those such as those born blind possess mental engagement (*manopavicāra*) even though they lack visual perception up to tactile perception,
should the pleasure belonging to the mental level in the third dhyāna also be included among the mental engagements?
This objection is not valid, because it does not exist in the first realm (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, because it is stagnant, it is said that there is no pleasure of the mental level (*manobhūmika-sukha*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and although it exists in the third *dhyāna*, it is not established [as a faculty] there.

Furthermore, the pleasure of that stage is stagnant with respect to its object; whereas mental applications (*manopavicāra*) involve frequent shifts as they approach their objects, for it is only when one does not remain fixed upon a single condition that they are termed "applications.
Moreover, [the pleasure of that stage] lacks a corresponding counterpart, as it is a mental application subsumed under the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
If that were so, there would be no mental application of equanimity (*upekṣā-manopavicāra*), because there would be nothing for it to counteract.
This is not the case, because sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and joy (*saumanasya*) are themselves the counteracts to equanimity.
Furthermore, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) belonging to the mental level in the third dhyāna has no faculty of equanimity belonging to its own fundamental level to serve as its counteract.

However, there is no fault of [the mental applications] such as equanimity lacking their respective preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and so forth, because within the first realm (*kāmadhātu*), there exist counter-objects belonging to the same level.

Alternatively, it is because they may or may not exist: that is to say, mental equanimity and the like may have counter-factors belonging to the same level, whereas mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) certainly has no counter-factors belonging to the same level.
Therefore, there is no error.

However, among the eighteen [mental applications], the first fifteen—the applications directed toward form and so forth—are called "non-mixed objects" (*amiśrālambana*), because they each individually take objects such as form as their respective conditions.

The three modes of mental application (*manopavicāra*) all pertain to two types: if they take only the dharmas and the six internal bases as their objects, they are called "unmixed objects" (*asaṃsṛṣṭālambana*);
if they take these seven [bases] along with the five external bases—either individually or collectively—they are called "mixed objects" (*saṃsṛṣṭālambana*).
Even if they do not involve seeing and so forth, up to having touched [an object], the arising of joy, sorrow, or equanimity also constitutes mental application (*manopavicāra*).
Were it otherwise, those who have not yet abandoned desire and greed would lack mental applications directed toward the forms and other objects of the form realm.
Furthermore, in the form realm (rūpadhātu), there should be no mental applications (manopavicāra) that take the objects of smell, taste, and touch belonging to the desire realm as their conditions.
If this is so, why does the Sūtra state:
"Having seen a form with the eye, one gives rise to a mental application of joy toward a form conducive to joy," and so forth, at length?
There is no contradiction because this is stated according to what is clearly understood, or because it is easily distinguishable as being induced by the eye and so forth.

Furthermore, the various *upavicāras* (mental explorations) are established differently: having seen a form with the eye, one gives rise to mental explorations of sound and so forth; having known a phenomenon with the mind, one gives rise to mental explorations of form and so forth. The Sūtra speaks thus according to their lack of confusion, because within them the faculties and objects are fixed.

Regarding the arising of the mental application of joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*) toward objects conducive to joy, this citation of the present case serves to allow for an analogous understanding of the remaining cases.

At the moment of linking existence (*pratisandhi*) and at death, there is only the mental application of equanimity (*upekṣopavicāra*), not that of grief or joy; this is because equanimity is acquired spontaneously and because it is appropriate to those states.

Only the equanimity-based mental applications (*upekṣā-upavicāra*) that take various objects as their focus are able to correctly abandon defilement; because the mental applications (*manopavicāra*) are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is only equanimity—not the others—that can do so.

Furthermore, although joy-based mental applications (*prīti-upavicāra*) also exist within the preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*), they are not included within the immediate, the liberation, or the fundamental meditative absorptions (*anantarya-vimukti-maula-samādhi*).
In the final path of liberation, there may be the presence of the mental application of joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*).

Among all the mental applications (*manopavicāra*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)? Of the mental applications of the desire realm, how many have objects of perception (*ālambana*) within that same realm?
The same applies to the questions concerning the form and formless realms.
The verse says:
In the desire realm, eighteen [mental applications] take the desire realm as their object; In the form realm, twelve; in the higher [formless] realms, three.
Two take twelve objects of the desire realm; eight take their own [realm], two take the formless.
The latter two take six objects of the desire realm; four take their own [realm], one takes the upper.
The preliminary stage of the first formless takes four objects of the form realm, one takes the upper.
The four fundamental [minds] and the three derivative minds each take only their own respective objects as conditions.
The commentary states:
those bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) comprise all eighteen [types of mind].
The number is likewise for those that take the objects of the desire realm as their domain.
There are only twelve that take the objects of the form realm as their domain, excluding the six [cognitions] of odor and taste, because those [objects] do not exist there.
There are only three that take the objects of the formless realm as their domain, because the five objects, such as visible form and so forth, do not exist there.
The objects that are not bound [to any realm] likewise have only three types.
Having explained those bound to the desire realm, I shall now explain those bound to the form realm.
In the first and second dhyānas, there are only twelve, namely, excluding the six types of mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*).
If one speaks in terms of their objects of focus (*ālambana*), there are certainly no defiled [mental states] that can take a lower realm as their object.

Even wholesome states taking desire-realm objects possess all twelve; excluding the four related to odor and taste, the remaining eight take their own realm as objects, while two take the formless realm as objects—namely, the mental application to phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*).
The mental applications (*manopavicāra*) that take non-tied phenomena (*apratisaṃyukta-dharma*) as their object are likewise only of two kinds.
Those belonging to the third and fourth dhyānas consist of only six, namely the equanimity (*upekṣā*) applications.

Those wholesome applications that take the objects of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as their object also possess six; excluding the two [applications] of odor and taste, the remaining four take their own [realm] as objects, and one takes the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as its object—namely, the mental application of dharmas (*dharmopavicāra*).
The objects that are not bound [to any realm] are likewise only of one kind.
Having explained those bound to the form realm, those bound to the formless realm shall now be explained.

In the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space, there are only four kinds; that is to say, equanimity takes as its objects only visible forms, sounds, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
The fourth dhyāna also possesses four types [of mental applications], provided one accepts that there are distinct objects of observation.
If, however, one maintains that this stage observes only the lower realms in a collective manner, then there would be only the mental application of dharmas with mixed objects.
Regarding the objects of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only one, namely the object of dharmas (*dharmālambana*).
Unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are likewise of only one kind.

In the four fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*) and the three upper levels (*prāntakoṭika*), there is only one object, namely dharmas; these take only their own respective spheres as objects. This is because the fundamental stages of the formless realm do not take lower realms as objects, and those three upper levels do not take the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as objects.
It does not take lower objects as its conditions, as will be explained later.
This [mental application] that takes non-bondage as its condition is also only of one kind.
Do all these mental applications (manopavicāra) also include the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
The verse says:
"The eighteen [faculties] are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The commentary says:
There is no proximate application-attainment (upapattidhāraṇī) that is untainted (anāsrava). Why is this?
Because it increases existence (bhava).
The untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas are the opposite of this.
Some say that while "near-movements" (*upavicāra*) exist in all sentient beings, the untainted are not so; therefore, they are not near-movements.
Others say that because the Noble Path proceeds spontaneously, it accords with the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*).
Therefore, they are not of the nature of the mental applications (*manopavicāra*), because the nature of the mental applications is incompatible with this [nature].
Who accomplishes how many mental applications?

Those born in the desire realm who have not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm accomplish all those of the desire realm; eight of the first and second dhyānas; four of the third and fourth dhyānas; and one of the formless realm. Those accomplished in the higher realms do not take the lower realms as objects, because they are exclusively defiled.
If one has already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but has not yet abandoned desire-greed (*kāmarāga*), it accomplishes all [objects] of the desire realm.

In the first *dhyāna*, there are ten; in the state of equanimity (*upekṣā*), six types are complete, because the wholesome mind in the *anāgamya* stage can take fragrance and taste as its objects. Joy (*prīti*) possesses only four, because it is exclusively defiled and does not take lower levels as its objects.

Is it not the case that these mental applications (*upavicāra*) are induced by the visual and other sensory consciousnesses? Since those [beings] lack the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses, they should likewise lack the mental applications directed toward odors and tastes.

This objection is invalid; for if that were so, beings such as those born blind or deaf, as well as those who possess innate mindfulness or are in meditative absorption, would all lack the mental applications directed toward visible forms and so forth. Therefore, this does not apply to all cases.
The five consciousnesses induce the attainment of two dhyānas, making eight [mental states] in total; the third and fourth dhyānas and the formless attainments are as previously described.

One who has already abandoned desire and greed, yet has not yet acquired the wholesome mind of the second dhyāna, possesses twelve mental states of the desire realm and the first dhyāna—namely, excluding the six types of sorrow; the two higher dhyānas and so forth are all as previously explained.

If one has already attained the wholesome mind of the second dhyāna but has not yet attained detachment from craving for the first dhyāna, one possesses ten [mental factors] of the second dhyāna: namely, joy (*prīti*) consists of only four types because it is exclusively defiled; equanimity (*upekṣā*) possesses all six types because one has already attained the wholesome state of its preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*); the remainder is as previously explained.
By this principle, the remaining cases should be understood by analogy.

If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one accomplishes only one mental application of equanimity (*upekṣā-manopavicāra*) pertaining to the desire realm, namely that which is associated with the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-citta*).

In this context, the Master of the Sūtras provisionally offers an alternative explanation, stating that these various mental applications (*manopavicāra*) were established by the Vaibhāṣikas according to their own logic;
however, in my view, the meaning of the sūtra is different.

Why is this so? Because one who has already attained detachment from a particular stage cannot give rise to mental applications (*manopavicāra*) directed toward that object; therefore, the three—pleasurable, painful, and equanimous—*sāsrava* (contaminated) states are not all subsumed under "mental applications. Only those that are defiled (*kliṣṭa*), which repeatedly engage with their objects by drawing them in close association with the mind, are considered mental applications.
What is meant by "mental activity that is frequently accompanied by attraction, aversion, or indifferent equanimity based on lack of discernment"?

To counteract this, the six constant abidings are taught: having seen a form, one is neither glad nor sad, but the mind constantly abides in equanimity, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension; as explained at length, this applies likewise up to the cognition of mental phenomena.

It is not that non-Arhat lacks joy in wholesome phenomena conditioned by worldly objects; rather, this statement was made solely to exclude the near-operations (*upavicāra*) associated with defilement.

We do not yet understand what definition or meaning the Master of the Sūtras had in mind when he held within his heart that the tainted joy of an Arhat toward various wholesome phenomena is not a mental near-operation (*manopavicāra*).
It is not the case that non-Arhat possess mental applications (*manopavicāra*); this [position] slightly contradicts the correct principle and the Sūtras.
How is this known for certain?
It is because it is only toward objects that one feels either attachment, aversion, or equanimity through lack of discernment that these constitute mental applications.

This is not like what was previously stated regarding those who have abandoned desire or Arhats, for whom, although the contaminated factors have been completely severed, contaminated joy and so forth still manifest; why is it that these are not called "near-operations"? What is the reasoning behind this?

Furthermore, for what reason are only those forms of joy (*prīti*) and so forth that are associated with the afflictions (*saṃkleśa*)—such as greed—which are to be countered by the six constant abodes (*ṣaḍ-nityavihāra*) in their remote state, designated as "near-approaches" (*upavicāra*), and not other tainted wholesome joys and other feelings?
Furthermore, because he himself speaks of distinctions, it is established that the non-afflicted *upavicāras* definitely exist.
That is to say, he himself states:
"This was said merely to exclude the afflicted *upavicāras*."

Since it has already been granted that there are non-afflicted modes of mental application (*upavicāra*), and these are not what is specifically excluded by the six constant abidings (*ṣaḍ-āśraya-nityavihāra*), the *Upavicāra* described in the *Vibhāṣā* does not contradict correct reasoning or the sūtras.

Furthermore, all that is contaminated (*sāsrava*) is termed "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*); since it is admitted that all defilements are termed "near-operations" (*upavicāra*), how does this contradict the tenets of our own school?
Moreover, regarding what they have said: "However, the meaning of the sūtras as I see them is different."
It is exactly as you have said, because the meaning of the sūtra differs from what they perceive.

That is to say, that sūtra—intended to show that after one who has attained the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) has seen forms with the eye, they do not give rise to greed, hatred, or delusion as they did in the past—states that they are "not pleased" and so forth; it does not say that they do not give rise to mental applications (manopavicāra) after seeing forms.
Therefore, what is stated in the *Vibhāṣā* is correct.
How are these various "approaches" (*upavicāra*) acquired?

It is said that through the eight paths of uninterrupted transition (*anantarya-mārga*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) prior to the abandonment of desire and greed, one acquires the six approaches of equanimity within the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna. Within the ninth path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation, one acquires the approach of equanimity regarding phenomena (*dharma-upavicāra*) associated with the "result-of-liberation" mind (*vimukti-phala-citta*) of the desire realm, and one acquires the twelve approaches of the first dhyāna.

This mention of the "first dhyāna" includes its associated factors (*paryavasthāna*). Following this principle, one should consider the abandonment of the defilements of the higher stages accordingly.

However, there is a distinction: when abandoning the craving for the fourth *dhyāna*, during the ninth path of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one necessarily does not acquire the mental applications (*upavicāra*) of equanimity associated with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) belonging to one's own or lower stages.

When one becomes detached from the desire for the various stages beginning with the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), all the paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) involve the acquisition of only a single mental application of equanimity (*upekṣopavicāra*).

Upon attaining the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one acquires twelve applications of equanimity from the desire realm and the first two dhyānas; six applications of equanimity from the third and fourth dhyānas; four applications of equanimity from the sphere of infinite space; and one application of equanimity toward phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) from each of the higher stages.

At the stage of rebirth, when one passes away from a higher plane and is born into a lower plane, one acquires all the *anuparivartin* (near-attendant) mental applications belonging to that [new] plane.

Furthermore, when being born into the various *dhyānas*, one also simultaneously acquires the *upekṣā-dharma-anuparivartin* (mental applications associated with equanimity toward phenomena) belonging to the lower planes.

Furthermore, these same eighteen mental applications—consisting of joy and so forth—are taught by the Blessed One as the thirty-six "Teacher's Words" (*śāstṛpada*) based on the distinction between those that lead to attachment and those that lead to renunciation.
These distinct phrases are called "Teacher's Words" because they serve as a sign or seal indicating that the Great Teacher is indeed the Teacher.
These phrases can only be known and expounded by the Great Teacher, the Buddha, for no others possess such capacity.
Some say that this "feeling" (vedanā) should be called the "Trace of the Teacher," because it is the ground upon which the practices of all false teachers rely.

Some say: this sensation should be called the "Path of the Knife" or the "Path of the Enemy," because it serves as the locus where one is gripped by the knife of craving and the enemy of craving. Others say:
This feeling should be called the "wound of the sword," because the Sūtra states that the mind is the sword.
That which is based on attachment refers to all defiled feelings;
that which is based on renunciation refers to all wholesome feelings.
The unobscured-neutral [factors], because they accord with both the wholesome and the defiled, are included within the two [categories] as appropriate; they are not mentioned separately.
Regarding the determination of the realms and stages for these thirty-six [factors]: it means that all thirty-six are fully present within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In the first and second dhyānas, there are only twenty types: namely, eight based on attachment and twelve based on renunciation.
In the third and fourth dhyānas, there are only ten types: namely, four based on attachment and six based on renunciation.

Regarding the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), if it is admitted that there are distinct objects of focus, there are five types: namely, one based on attachment (*gardhāśrita*) and four based on renunciation (*naiṣkramyāśrita*).
If, however, one maintains that there is only a general object of focus, there are only two types: namely, one based on attachment and one based on renunciation.
In the fundamental dhyānas of the formless realm (*ārūpya*) and in each of the three higher stages, there are only two types each, as should be understood from what preceded.
This is according to the realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*).
Regarding the objects of focus (*ālambana*), when those in the desire realm take objects of the desire realm as their focus, there are thirty-six [types].
The objects of the form realm (rūpadhātu) consist of only twenty-four, excluding the six each based on odor and taste.
The objects of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) consist of only six types, namely the three each based on the mental-object application (dharmopavicāra).
The objects that are not bound [to any realm] are likewise only these six.
By this principle, the distinctions regarding the objects of perception in the form and formless realms should be understood accordingly.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

By relying upon the six types of equanimity-based applications of mindfulness toward the pleasant as a support and a basis for establishment, one is able to relinquish, abandon, and vomit out the six types of craving-based applications of mindfulness toward the pleasant; thus they are severed, and so forth, as explained at length.
The statement herein regarding the abandonment of the eighteen types of reliance on craving (*gardhāśrita*) indicates temporary abandonment, because [the mind] relies on joy (*prīti*) as its support.

The statement regarding the mental application of sorrow (*daurmanasyopavicāra*) indicates freedom from the defilement of desire, because [the mind] relies on equanimity (*upekṣā*) as its support, thereby abandoning reliance on renunciation (*naiṣkramyāśrita*).
