The term "pleasant mental application" (*prīti-saṃskāra*) indicates the departure from the defilements of the second dhyāna stage; because it relies upon equanimity (*upekṣā*) as its support, it abandons the various types [of sensation].

The term "supporting equanimity" indicates the departure from the defilements of the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*); because it does not rely upon that specific category [of sensation] as its support, it abandons the single type.
By the mention of "equanimity" as the basis of the nature [of feeling], it is shown that one has ultimately abandoned the defilements of the formless realm.
One should understand that within these explained factors of the dependent origination of feeling (*vedanā-aṅga*), there are immeasurable distinctions of meaning and categories.
For what reason are the remaining members of existence (*bhavāṅga*) not mentioned?
The verse says:
"The others have already been explained or will be explained."
The Commentary says:
As for the remaining members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), some have already been explained and some will be explained, as has been previously demonstrated.
If this is so, for what reason is this verse further presented?
The subsequent verse is intended to preclude doubts regarding the extensive explanation.
Since that later verse mentions "afflictions" (*kleśa*) and so forth, one should not harbor such a doubt as this:
"The meaning of the four members has already been extensively clarified; next, the remaining members of existence (*bhavāṅga*) ought to be explained in detail."

In order to clarify that the subsequent text relies upon afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and entities (*vastu*) to metaphorically illustrate the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as a whole, the Master (Ācārya) further offers this verse.
As previously stated, the twelve links of existence are briefly subsumed into only three categories—namely, affliction, karma, and entity—and these three have distinct functions.
What is the analogy?
The verse says:
In this context, the afflictions are said To be like seeds and also like nagas.
Like the roots of grass and the trunks of trees, and like rice enveloped in husks;
karma is like the rice with its husk, like medicinal herbs and like flowers.
All matters of ripened results (*vipākaphala*) are like cooked food and drink.
The treatise says:
In what way are these three things similar?
Just as sprouts, leaves, and so forth arise from a seed, so too do afflictions, karma, and entities arise from afflictions.

Just as a dragon dwelling in a pond ensures that the water never runs dry, so too do the afflictions dwell continuously within the pond of birth, causing the flow of deluded karma and its effects to be inexhaustible.

Just as when the roots of a plant have not been pulled out, the shoots will grow back again and again even if they are cut, so too, as long as the roots of the afflictions have not been uprooted by the Noble Path, the sprouts of rebirth will arise repeatedly even if they are severed. It is like branches, flowers, and fruits being produced incessantly from the trunk of a tree.
In this way, from afflictions arise further afflictions, karma, and their effects, just as rice grains encased in husks can produce sprouts and so forth.
It is not that [karma] alone can produce [results]; rather, it is karma enveloped by afflictions that is able to induce future existence (*punarbhava*).
It is not only that [karma] can induce [results], just as rice with its husk can produce sprouts;

karma accompanied by afflictions can summon maturation (*vipāka*). Just as for various medicinal herbs, the ripening of the fruit marks their end, once the fruit of karma has matured, it no longer summons further maturation.
Just as a flower is the proximate cause for the production of a fruit, so too is karma the proximate cause capable of producing a ripened result (*vipāka*).
Just as cooked food should only be consumed and cannot be transformed back into other food, [so too is the ripened result].
Once the matter of the ripening fruit has already matured, it can no longer project further ripening for another birth.
If these various ripened fruits were to again induce further births, and those in turn induce yet others, there would be no liberation.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-nine.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Thirty.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Ten: The Tenth Section of the Third Chapter on the Analysis of Dependent Origination.

Having already analyzed dependent origination, it is now divided into four types of existence (*bhava*) according to their positional distinctions—namely, intermediate existence, birth-existence, fundamental existence, and death-existence—as previously explained.
The distinctions among the wholesome and so forth, and their presence or absence within the three realms, shall now be briefly explained.
The verse says:
Among the four types of existence, the existence at birth is exclusively defiled.
By means of the afflictions of its own stage, [the birth-existence is defiled]; the other three [existences] belong to the three [realms].
The commentary states:
Among the four types of existence, the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) is exclusively defiled; it is definitely neither wholesome nor non-obscured neutral.
By which afflictions do all defilements arise?
Do the various defilements and stains give rise to the existence of birth? It is not so.
How so? It is solely by means of its own level; that is, when one is born in this level, it is only through all the afflictions (*kleśa*) within this level that birth becomes defiled.

Among the various afflictions, there is not a single one that lacks the capacity to moisten at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*). However, the linking of rebirth occurs solely through the power of the afflictions, and not through the secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) or impurities (*upakleśa*).

Why is this so? Because the fetters of remorse (*kaukṛtya*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), and so forth arise through the power of deliberate effort (*svabalavāhana*), requiring analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) to manifest.
However, in this state, the body and mind are dull and weak; thus, only those afflictions that operate spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*) can manifest.

Only the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), through the power of repeated cultivation, are predominant; thus, the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are able to manifest repeatedly and arise spontaneously at the time of linking existence (*pratisandhi*).

The various outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and impurities (*mala*), however, have weak power from repeated cultivation and do not manifest without deliberate reflection; therefore, the linking of existence is not brought about by the outbursts or the impurities.
Other masters say:

"The conceit of self (*asmimāna*) and self-love (*ātmasneha*) are frequently active among all classes of sentient beings; at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*), one or the other arises, their mode of activity being subtle and continuing without interruption. Therefore, these two alone are capable of defiling the existence of birth."

These two are not non-existent; however, they are not the only ones [to exist], because there are cases where the noble ones (ārya) undergo rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) without these two operating, and because there is also the arising of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*).

Since this pride (*māna*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are supported by the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), or because some may seek the annihilation of the self, these two do not both frequently manifest. By this it is established that the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is defiled solely by the power of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of its own level (*svabhūmi*). As for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the others, each is common to all three types—namely, they are all common to the wholesome (*kuśala*), the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
It should be understood that the very first moment of the linking of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) is necessarily defiled, just like the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*).
Regarding these four types of existence, to which realms do they belong?

The desire realm and the form realm possess all four; the formless realm possesses only three. It is not the case that karma of the formless realm produces the fruit of an intermediate existence, as has already been fully analyzed in the discussion of the intermediate existence.
By what do sentient beings subsist within these four kinds of existence?
The verse says:
Sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment; the substance of edible food in the desire realm consists of only three [types].
Non-material food cannot provide benefit, because it is liberated from its own sense-base.
The three foods—contact, volition, and consciousness—are with-outflows and pervade the three realms.
The mind-made, those seeking rebirth, those feeding on fragrance, and those in the intermediate state arise [from these].
The first two benefit this life, [namely] the basis and that which depends upon it;
the latter two [benefit] future existence, [namely] by way of projecting and actualizing, respectively.
The treatise says:

The Sūtra states that the Blessed One, having personally realized and perfectly awakened to a single dharma, correctly proclaimed it: namely, that all sentient beings subsist entirely through nutriment.
What are these nutriments?
There are four kinds of nutriment:
first, morsel food; second, contact; third, volition; and fourth, consciousness.
Morsel food is of two types: namely, subtle and coarse.
"Subtle" refers to the food of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because it feeds on odors;
and to the food of the gods and at the beginning of the eon, because it does not undergo transformation or impurity, like oil poured onto sand,
as it disperses and enters the limbs.
Or, that which is eaten by minute impure insects, infants, and the like, is called "subtle"; the opposite of this is "gross.

Such edible food exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because those born in the higher realms have abandoned craving for edible food; thus, the bodies in the higher realms do not depend on external conditions for their sustenance.

Although the great elements in the form realm possess the capacity to benefit [the body], they are not substantial food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), just as they are not "exquisite sensual pleasures" (*maithuna*).

For instance, although there exist subtle objects of form, sound, and touch within the form realm, they are not called "exquisite sensual pleasures" because they do not induce the arising of predominant craving.

Thus, although there exists a most excellent, subtle, and beneficial contact capable of sustaining life, it is ultimately devoid of segmentation and swallowing; therefore, it is not substantial food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Although it is not included within the category of substantial food, it does not lack the essential meaning of "food."
Although joy (*prīti*) is not included among the four types of nutriment, the Sūtra nonetheless describes it as a nutriment because it possesses the functional meaning of nutriment.
As the Sūtra says: "I feed on the nutriment of joy; by means of the nutriment of joy I abide for a long time, just like the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven."
If that were so, then in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as well, only that which is swallowed and consumed in morsels by the mouth should be called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

This is not the case; rather, in the desire realm, swallowing and consuming serve as the primary gateway, and because other [types of nutriment] can be associated with it, this name is established for them as well.

In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there is not even the slightest bit of swallowing or chewing that could cause the remaining types of contact (spraṣṭavya) to be named after it; therefore, the two realms do not suffer from the fault of lacking mutual correspondence.
Furthermore, if a person were born in Uttarakuru, where there is no swallowing of solid food, would their life-span (āyus) not be severed or destroyed?
Although they do not perish, their physical form and complexion are emaciated; how then can they survive?
If this is so, by what means do they subsist on food?

Fragrance and the like serve as their food without requiring ingestion; they invariably and constantly smell exquisite fragrances at will, or experience pleasant tactile sensations from agreeable winds and the like.
Furthermore, within those bodies there is that which can provide beneficial warmth.

It is not the case that all [beings] in the desire realm rely on edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), nor is it certain that edible food exists only in the desire realm; these statements are made from the perspective of what is most prevalent and predominant. Since the lower realms possess it while the upper realms lack it, this should not be raised as an objection.

However, although the substantial entities of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) are distinguished as thirteen, they are subsumed under three types according to their bases; that is, only the three of odor, flavor, and tangibility belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

All of these constitute the essential nature of edible food because they can be formed into morsels and swallowed; that is to say, they are received portion by portion through the mouth and nose. This statement is made by taking the majority for the sake of brevity.

Although it is not swallowed or chewed, that which benefits the body and enables it to endure for a long time is also subsumed under "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), just like shadows, light, heat, cold, ointments, or washes.
Furthermore, even the "earth-flavor" (*pṛthivī-rasa*) and other such foods at the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*) are called edible food, because they are consumed in distinct portions.
Furthermore, drinks and other such substances are also called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), because they are all consumed by being divided into morsels.
Other masters say:
among all types of food, this is the most excellent, because it is powerful and rapid in nourishing the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Is it not the case that seeking food is for the purpose of removing hunger and thirst? How then can hunger and thirst themselves be called "food"?
Because these two also serve to augment the sense faculties and the primary elements, just like massage and similar treatments.
Furthermore, because one lacks desire for food and drink, the body becomes emaciated; thus, these two are called "food.
Moreover, it is only when hunger and thirst are absent that one is termed "healthy"; therefore, these two constitute the essential nature of food and are superior to other types.
The sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) should be described as edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); it should not be said that it is so called because it is consumed bit by bit.
If this is so, why is it said that its substance consists of three bases?
It is because they are discussed in terms of food; therefore, only three are mentioned.
For what reason is the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) not called "nutriment"?
Because it does not reach the range of the faculties that grasp by contact.
As the Sūtra says:

Edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) cannot be considered food merely by being in one's hand or in a vessel; it must enter the nose and mouth, be chewed by the teeth, moistened by saliva, pass through the throat, descend into the stomach (*āmāśaya*), and be gradually digested. Only when its flavor, potency, and ripening qualities flow into the various channels to nourish the internal organisms is it called "food," for it is only at that time that it performs the function of sustaining life.

If the name is applied based on the vessel that holds it, as in the case of Devadatta being called "Naraka," then although that portion [of food] as a whole receives the name "food," at the time it becomes food, it consists only of odor, flavor, and tangibility; for at that time, these alone serve as the objects of the sense faculties.
If all things that constitute a physical portion were called "food," then sound, which is non-associated with matter, would also have to be food.

However, sound and similar entities do not exist within a physical portion in the same way that odors and so forth do; therefore, they cannot be called food. This is because they lack continuity and possess no physical form or segments.
An entity that lacks physical form or segments and is not continuous cannot sustain the body and thus cannot fulfill the function of food.
Furthermore, how is it known that the sense-field of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is not nutriment?

Because its function of sustaining and benefiting the faculties and the primary elements within the body is not perceived separately—just as with odors, tastes, and tangibles—and because at that time, consciousness of those objects does not arise.
Furthermore, it is universally established—without requiring further proof—that fragrance and taste function as nutriment (*āhāra*).
We observe that acts such as anointing and washing benefit the body, which demonstrates that tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*) possess this efficacy.

Indeed, nutriment necessarily depends upon flavor, potency, maturation, and virtue to either harm or benefit the body. Upon careful analysis, neither shape nor color possesses the nature of flavor, potency, maturation, or virtue; consequently, they lack the capacity to harm or benefit the body.

When [the food] is still within consciousness, it does not even benefit or harm its own sense-faculties or primary elements; how much less could it, once it has entered the body, produce its own consciousness and function as nutriment?
We observe that the disks of the sun and moon can benefit or harm the eye-faculty; this is the function of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*), not the power of shape or color (*saṃsthāna* and *varṇa*).

Is it not the case that suffering and pleasure arise simultaneously with consciousness, and because these two can cause harm or benefit, the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) likewise causes harm or benefit to the eye?
This reasoning is not tenable, for it would follow that the eye, along with light and so forth, would constitute nutriment (āhāra).
However, while those [objects] serve as the objective domain for contact that accords with suffering or pleasure and can thus function as food, the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is not so.

When one sees forms such as collyrium or a counting-stick, the eye is neither increased nor diminished; it is only when [the substance] reaches the eye that the eye is then increased or diminished. Therefore, edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) is certainly not the sense-base of form.
Furthermore, it possesses both common and uncommon characteristics when compared with universally established forms of edible food, such as incense and the like.

Moreover, all types of edible food must be taken into the mouth and chewed until crushed; only by destroying their original shape and increasing their fragrance, flavor, aroma, and tangibility do they become actual sustenance.

It is not that the increase of odor, flavor, and tangibility occurs without chewing; rather, they are clearly perceived as they are when already chewed. Therefore, only odor, flavor, and tangibility constitute the true substance of food, for it is solely for the sake of these three that labor is expended.
If that is so, why does the Sūtra praise edible food as possessing color, fragrance, and flavor?
It is for the sake of inspiring delight that it praises the auxiliary conditions as well; just as one might praise respectful giving, would respectful giving itself then be called edible food?
However, for a solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) to be established, it must possess both primary and auxiliary conditions.
This is like praising a grove of flowers as being endowed with blossoms, fruits, reflections, and water; would one then say that the reflections and the water are themselves the grove?
Alternatively, this sutra praises the sensation (*vedanā*) that is relinquished, rather than stating that the substance of the food consists of form, odor, and taste.
Furthermore, it has already been stated previously. What was stated previously?

It was that they are designated as "food" by virtue of their future function; at that time, they are not actually food. To praise these nominally designated foods for possessing color, fragrance, and flavor does not constitute a discussion of true food—what contradiction is there in this?
Furthermore, this praises the excellence of the food rather than analyzing its physical substance.
As stated in medical treatises:
there is desirable food and drink that possesses color, fragrance, flavor, and tangibility.
It is also obtained as non-substantiality.
Furthermore, by citing the characteristic of visible form (*rūpa*), it is indicated that odor, taste, and touch are likewise wonderful and worthy of delight; thus, this statement was made.
Why does the Sūtra not praise the touch associated with the requisites of food?

Since it has already been stated that contact (*spraṣṭavya*) is included among the praises of possessing color and so forth, there can be no unpleasant contact that possesses excellent color and so on; therefore, the existence of pleasant contact is established even without being explicitly mentioned.

Furthermore, the sphere of contact alone is the actual substance of nutriment (*āhāra*); since this substance of nutriment is praised as possessing color, fragrance, and taste, the Sūtra’s description of the substance of nutriment is complete and without deficiency.
However, the Elder says:
"The entire collection of things that are drunk or eaten constitutes the substance of nutriment (*āhāra*), as there is no separate teaching [to the contrary].

When these collections of things drunk or eaten undergo digestion and transformation, they are all capable of increasing the blood, flesh, and other bodily constituents, sustaining them so that their continuity is maintained and not severed or destroyed; therefore, everything is called nutriment."
That statement is unreasonable. Why is this so?
Because, although there is no separate explanation, they ought to be understood as distinct.
As the Sūtra says:
"Karma is the cause of birth.
Could this cause of birth apply to uncontaminated (anāsrava) karma as well?
Is it not the case that other non-karmic factors are likewise not causes of birth?
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:
"There is a karma that is neither black nor white, which is without ripening, and which can exhaust all karmas."
Can all such karmic actions exhaust all karma?
Are all karmas that which are exhausted?
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:

The arising, abiding, and originating of consciousness should be understood as having the meaning of the arising of suffering, the abiding of illness, and the originating of old age and death; it is not the case that this statement can be applied to untainted (anāsrava) consciousness.
There are numerous such examples in the sūtras; although they are not explicitly stated separately, they should be understood as distinct cases.

If, within a collection [of matter], there exists the characteristic of being edible and it is consumed, one should take only that as food and nothing else; therefore, this reason cannot prove that visible form (*rūpa*) is also food.

Furthermore, regarding what they have said—that when all that is drunk or eaten is digested and transformed, it can all increase the blood, flesh, and so forth, sustaining the continuum so that it does not break off or perish—[this is also untenable].
One should certainly know this and speak with sincerity:
since you have not stated the reason, how can it be known that form (*rūpa*) manifests during the state of digestion and transformation?

Just as odor, taste, and tangibility increase the blood, flesh, and so forth, and are able to sustain the body, therefore the substance of food consists only of odor, taste, and tangibility; visible form (*rūpa*) cannot benefit its own sense organ or [the mind] liberated from it.
Generally, that which is called "food" must first benefit one's own roots and primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and only thereafter reach others.
When consuming visible forms, they do not even benefit one's own roots and primary elements, let alone be able to reach others.

Because those sense faculties and their respective objects are distinct, when one experiences joy and pleasure upon seeing a form, it arises conditioned by the contact with that form; thus, it is nutriment, not the form itself.
This principle has already been fully explained above.

Furthermore, those who have attained the stage of non-returner and the arhat are liberated from craving for food; thus, even when they see exquisite food, no joy arises in them, as it provides no benefit.

Having already explained the realm-affiliation and the essential nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), the three types—contact (*sparśa*), volition (*manasikāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—shall now be demonstrated.

Contact (*sparśa*) refers to a mental factor (*caitta*) produced by the conjunction of the three—sense faculty, object, and consciousness—which has already been extensively analyzed within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Volition (*cetanā*) refers to mental action (*manaskarma*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) refers to the cognition of objects.
These three [types of nutriment] are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) and exist throughout all three realms.
Thus, the substance of these four nutriments consists of sixteen items in total.
The term "contaminated" is applied only to the final three nutriments to demonstrate that the three beginning with fragrance (*gandha*) do not overlap with the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
For what reason are untainted (*anāsrava*) contacts and so forth not considered nutriment?
Nutriment is defined as that which can attract and sustain the various forms of existence (*bhava*), serving as the locus for the growth of craving—which is itself loathsome and to be abandoned.

Although the untainted sustains the existence attracted by others, it lacks the inherent power to attract existence itself; nor is it a locus for the growth of craving that is loathsome and to be abandoned. Therefore, it is not established among the four nutriments.
For this very reason, in relation to other realms and stages, even though they are tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), they do not constitute the substance of nutriment (*āhāra*);

for although phenomena of other realms and stages can also act as causes that support what is presently existing, they cannot function as the cause that draws forth a future existence (*punarbhava*), and thus they are not called nutriment.

When various untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas manifest, although they can act as causes to support the faculties and the great elements (*mahābhūta*), they cannot function as the cause that draws forth a future existence (*punarbhava*).

Although they temporarily act as causes to support the faculties and the great elements, they do so solely for the purpose of establishing a superior basis for oneself, in order to swiftly proceed toward *nirvāṇa* and to eternally extinguish all forms of existence (*bhava*).
When the outflows (*āsrava*) belonging to one’s own level manifest, they sustain the present and cause it to increase, thereby being able to summon a future existence (*punarbhava*).
By this, the meaning of how edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) acts as a cause to summon a future existence has already been explained.
This means that when the nutriment of contact and so forth draws forth a future existence (*bhava*), it also draws forth internal dharmas such as odors of the future;

the present internal odors and so forth support the causes of contact and so forth, causing them to draw forth a future existence, and they themselves are also able to take future odors and so forth as their concordant results (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Therefore, because edible food shares the same result as the cause of future existence (*punarbhava-hetu*), it is also capable of drawing forth existence and is thus called "food.

Furthermore, the substance and category of smell, taste, and touch are threefold: namely, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those of equal outflow (*naiṣyandika*), and those of nourishment (*aupacayika*).

Because external odors and so forth awaken the internal tastes, smells, and tangibles within the body, thereby constituting the function of food, the principle of what has been taught as "food" is definitively established.

How so? One should understand that the foods of contact (*sparśa*), volition (*manasikāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) arise simultaneously, yet their functional activities differ. If one were to claim that these three have no distinction in their functional activity, the differentiation between the three types of food could not be established; for instance, just as when a single morsel contains the functions of taste, smell, and touch, their distinct functions are difficult to discern, it is therefore designated by the name "edible food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

The functions of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) and so forth are distinct and should not be treated like that [the element], because there is a difference between what is commonly known and what is not commonly known; for example, while the world commonly knows that odor, taste, and tangibility are of the same nature as food, tangibility and the others are not so.

Furthermore, contact (*sparśa*), volition (*cetanā*), and cognition (*vijñāna*) are distinguished as three because their essential natures and functions are subtle; this is not the case for odor and the other [objects].
Moreover, although they arise simultaneously, because one or another predominates, there is no lack of distinction when the result manifests.
Therefore, the distinction between the three natures is thoroughly established.
As it is said in a sutra:

"There are four kinds of nutriment that enable *bhūta* sentient beings to subsist and provide sustenance for those seeking birth. The term "*bhūta*" signifies the meaning of "already born"; all those who have been born within the various realms of existence (*gati*) are referred to as "already born."
Furthermore, when it is said that one seeks birth, what does this refer to?
It refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has spoken of the intermediate state by means of five names. What are these five?
First is the "mind-made" (*manomaya*), so called because it arises from the mind; this refers to the meaning of a fruit projected by propelling karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*).
If that were the case, there would be the fault of over-extension.
It is not so, however, because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) does not take up external conditions such as semen and blood to form a body.
Second is seeking birth, because one predominantly delights in searching for and examining the place of future rebirth;
"birth" refers to the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*), and during the intermediate state, there is much seeking to proceed toward that place of birth-existence.
Third is feeding on fragrance, because the body sustains itself by consuming fragrant food to reach the place of rebirth.
Fourth is the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), because it exists between the two existences of death and birth.

Fifth is called "arising" (*udbhava*), because immediately following the existence at death, the body arises instantaneously with its limbs complete; or alternatively, because it arises for a brief duration, determinedly directed toward the place of rebirth.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There is the arising of that which destroys its own substance; there is the birth of that which destroys the world.
"Arising" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"There is a person who has already severed the fetters that cause arising (*utpatti-saṃyojana*), but has not yet severed the fetters that cause birth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*).
For what reason is it said that there are only four kinds of nutriment?
All conditioned phenomena possess nutriment, for the Sūtras state that even Nirvāṇa has nutriment.
As a scriptural passage says:
"Nirvāṇa has nutriment, namely the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga)."
Although all conditioned phenomena possess the quality of being sustenance, this is explained in terms of their preeminence.
That is to say, for those to be converted, the Great Sage spoke of only four types of nutriment, as these are preeminent in terms of their function as support.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Two causes and two conditions can give rise to right view; pure ethical discipline and so forth have no causal function regarding the arising of right view.
What are the characteristics of the preeminent functions of the four nutriments?

That is to say, the first two nutriments benefit this body as the basis and that which depends upon it; the latter two nutriments draw forth future existence and give rise to future existence. Accordingly, they sustain and give rise to the two kinds of embodied existence—namely, the material and the immaterial—and thus four nutriments are established.
The basis refers to form, namely the body endowed with sense faculties;
the dependent refers to name, namely mind and mental factors.
Among these, edible food benefits the basis, because the body endowed with sense faculties subsists by means of it.
Among these, the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) benefits the dependent [mind], because the mind and mental factors are sustained by it.
Thus, these two nutriments possess the most preeminent capacity for sustaining an existence that has already arisen.
Volition acts as the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), and consciousness acts as the seed; together they project future existence.
This means that by virtue of karma, one is able to project the two types of existence—name and form—in the future.
Once the karma has projected [existence], craving moistens the seed of consciousness, enabling the arising of the body of name and form in the future.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Karma is the cause of birth; craving is the cause of origination.
These two types of nutriment possess the most preeminent power for initiating existence that has not yet arisen; thus, only these four are taught as nutriments.
Among these four nutriments, the latter two are like a birth mother, for they give rise to what has not yet arisen;
the former two are like a foster mother, for they nourish what has already arisen.

As for the difference in their sequence: by citing the distinction between the causes and effects of arising as perceived in the present, it is shown that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) exist without beginning; therefore, it is said that the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) cannot be known.

That is to say, in this present life, having already arisen, name-and-form serves as the basis for inducing karma that brings about future rebirth; because consciousness, moistened by craving, can act as the seed, it causes the fruit of name-and-form to arise in a future existence.

Thus, all name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in this present life arise because they depend on the name-and-form of the preceding life, are drawn forth by various karmas, and have the seed of consciousness moistened by craving as their cause.

That very name-and-form (nāmarūpa) which served as the basis in the preceding birth arises again by depending on the name-and-form of the previous life, with the various karmas drawn forth therein acting as the cause, moistened by craving (tṛṣṇā) and having consciousness (vijñāna) as the seed.
In this manner, each preceding factor serves as the basis for the subsequent one; therefore, both name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*) are beginningless.

Alternatively, sentient beings are distinguished by three types: first, those who predominantly delight in presently perceived agreeable objects; second, those who largely crave future agreeable objects; and third, those who maintain a state of equanimity toward all objects.

Edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) benefits all three types of sentient beings in general; contact-food (*sparśāhāra*) specifically benefits those who crave present objects; volition-food (*manahsañcetanāhāra*) specifically benefits those who long for future objects; and consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*) specifically benefits those who abide in equanimity. Therefore, only these four are taught as nutriments.

Some say: Feeling (*vedanā*) is the root of birth and death; edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is the object experienced by feeling; contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*) is the proximate cause apprehended by feeling; volition (*cetanā*) is the remote cause; and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the support. Therefore, only these four are taught as nutriments (*āhāra*).
Furthermore, edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) can increase craving for sense objects, because it nourishes the sense faculties (indriya) and the primary elements (mahābhūta).
Such craving for sense objects, in turn, can extensively cause the three factors to come together in contact (sparśa), thereby giving rise to contact.
Contact (*sparśa*) is able to induce feeling (*vedanā*), for it is that which is experienced.
Feeling, in turn, acts as the cause for the volition of longing (*prārthanā-cetanā*), because it gives rise to and constitutes the object of such longing.
The power of this volition of longing causes craving (*tṛṣṇā*) to expand, since through that volition one takes delight in false pleasure.
Craving can moisten consciousness so that it continues into the existence of rebirth, because only a defiled mind is capable of linking one birth to the next.
Consciousness can give rise to the sprout of name-and-form, because name-and-form grows by means of consciousness.

For this reason it is said: when one fully understands and abandons edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*), one also fully understands and abandons the defilement of the five types of exquisite sensual desire; when one fully understands and abandons the nutriment of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*), one also fully understands and abandons the three feelings, beginning with pleasure; when one fully understands and abandons the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsañcetanā-āhāra*), one also fully understands and abandons the three cravings, beginning with craving for sense-desire; and when one fully understands and abandons the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*), one also fully understands and abandons the two modes of existence, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Some say: Because these [four nutriments] counteract the four inversions, the four nutriments are taught.
By failing to observe the four types—edible food and so forth—one successively gives rise to the four inversions of purity, pleasure, permanence, and self.
The Sūtra states that the four nutriments (*āhāra*) enable *bhūta-sattvas* to abide and provide sustenance for those seeking birth.

This demonstrates that the four nutriments sustain beings dwelling within the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*), namely those abiding in the state of birth (*upapatti-bhava*), the fundamental state (*mūla-bhava*), and the intermediate state (*antarā-bhava*), respectively; excluding those abiding in the state of death (*maraṇa-bhava*), because nutriment lacks efficacy therein.
Regarding the term *bhūta*, it refers to that which dwells within the state of existence (*bhava*) and sustains that state of existence; therefore, it is said to "bring about stability.

This is intended to clarify that the state of existence lasts for only a single moment, and that it is only through the sustaining power of nutriment (*āhāra*) that it can subsequently draw forth the next moment.

Regarding the term "sentient beings" (*sattva*): it refers to those who abide in the state of prior existence (*pūrvabhava*). Because they abide within prior existence and are capable of verbal communication, they are distinguished from non-sentient things and thus called "sentient beings. They are said to be "caused to abide" because they are sustained by nutriment while in that prior existence. "Abiding" means the continuity of the state itself remains uninterrupted.

Regarding the term "seeking birth," this refers to abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Because one seeks birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) while abiding in the intermediate state, and because the food that sustains the intermediate state causes it to proceed toward the future birth without possibility of turning back, it is called "nourishing and benefiting."
Alternatively, there are briefly three types of sentient beings: first, those possessed of afflictions; second, those free from afflictions; and third, those with residual afflictions.
Those possessed of afflictions are called *bhūta*, because they are born repeatedly within the five destinies; since food can sustain them, it is said that it brings them peace.
Since correct contemplation is lacking, there is no aspiration to seek liberation, for one’s mind finds rest and contentment within the cycle of birth and death.
This is like a blind person who has no intention to move, remaining settled wherever they happen to be.

Those who are free from afflictions are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*); this is merely a conventional designation for those included within the category of sentient beings. Since food can sustain them, it is said to cause them to "abide.
Just as a broken cart may temporarily move toward another place by the power of various supporting conditions, it is therefore called "abiding."
The remaining afflictions are termed "seeking birth" (*upapatti-bhava*), for they may involve the aspiration for union with a future existence.
There is no difference in meaning between "union" (*saṃyoga*) and "birth-existence" (*upapatti-bhava*).

These remaining afflictions may involve aspiration until the exhaustion of the formations (*saṃskāra*) of the birth-existence; because nutriment can sustain them, it is said to "sustain and benefit" (*anugrāhaka*), meaning it sustains and benefits them until the stage where the formations are exhausted.
There are, in brief, two types of sentient beings: namely, those already born and those about to be born.
Those who are already born are called *pudgala* (sentient beings), while those who are about to be born are described solely as "those seeking birth."
Those who have already been born are further divided into two types:
first, those who experience the fruits of previously performed karma, called *bhūta*;
second, those who experience the fruits of present human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), called *sattva*.
Due to food from previous lives, physical form, strength, happiness, and eloquence are produced in the present body, and life is established therein.
Due to food in the present life, it merely causes the continuity of the present body to remain uninterrupted; therefore, it is called "subsistence."
To "cause to settle" means merely to prevent deterioration; to "cause to abide" means to bring about its specific causal efficiency (*kāritra*).
To "sustain that which is about to arise" means to cause it to proceed toward actual birth; therefore, it is said that [the sustenance] benefits those seeking birth.
Some say: since *bhūtas* (spirits) seek food individually, the term "sentient being" (*sattva*) is used for the sake of distinction, because it is taught that even non-sentient things consume food.
As stated in a sutra:
I have stated that the great ocean, the great rivers, and so forth all possess nutriment;
however, in order to distinguish them from those, it is clarified here that what is being explained is the nutriment of sentient beings, not that of the great ocean and the like.

If that were so, this statement would be rendered useless; for the purpose of exclusion has already been accomplished by the mention of "edible food" (kavaḍīkārāhāra) and so forth, since edible food and the like do not nourish the ocean and such things.
Since only the class of sentient beings possesses edible food and the rest, the term "sentient being" (sattva) serves no purpose as a qualifier.

This may be considered a brief explanation using the term *bhūta*; for within the term *bhūta*, the actual meaning is also revealed. This statement is made in order to refute the attachment to non-real sentient beings as being truly sentient beings.

That is to say, the various non-Buddhists, blinded by ignorance, maintain that all thickets possess volition and views, and for this reason they also call them sentient beings; these too must necessarily subsist on physical food and the like.
To exclude those [other entities], the word "real" (*satya*) must be stated; such a word "real" indicates a meaning that is universally established.

It refers to those sentient beings who are commonly accepted as possessing volition; it is only these universally accepted sentient beings who subsist on edible food and the like, not those who are not commonly accepted as sentient beings possessing volition.

Why does the Blessed One not merely state briefly that there are four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of sentient beings? What is the purpose of the two terms "bhūta" (already arisen) and "jijīviṣu" (desiring to live)?
Is it not already established? It is said that these terms are used to manifest the distinctions among those who have already been born, those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and so forth.
It is sufficient to state that sentient beings are sustained by nutriment; this meaning is already complete. Why labor further to explain it?
Regarding the distinctions among those already born and so forth, other sūtras have already stated:
"There are no sentient beings who exist without nutriment."

In this context, the distinction between *bhūta* (being) and *pretyabhava* (seeking rebirth) is taught in order to refute the denial of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and to demonstrate the proximate cause of birth.

Alternatively, it is taught so that one does not mistakenly think there is no difference in the nutriment consumed by Arhats, those in training (*śaikṣa*), and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); thus, the three phrases are stated to reveal the distinctions among nutriments.

That is to say, ordinary worldlings generally consume food and drink largely out of afflictions; Arhats consume food and drink solely for the sake of sustaining the body; and those in training (śaikṣas), though they mostly feel revulsion toward food and drink, still possess afflictions.

To demonstrate that although all types of nutriment equally sustain the body, some are to be consumed exclusively while others must also be abandoned, it is necessary to fully set forth these three propositions.
Regarding the statement "the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of edible food": although abandonment was previously mentioned, it was not yet understood what this refers to;

the subsequent mention of "thorough knowledge" clarifies that this is such an abandonment. Alternatively, the suppression of the afflictions that take that [food] as their object is termed "abandonment."
Because it uproots them forever, it is called "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
If that were so, one should not have made such a statement:

"When one thoroughly knows the abandonment of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), one also thoroughly knows the abandonment of the defilement of the five objects of sensory pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇa-rāga*)."
When the defilement of the five objects of sensory desire (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*) is permanently severed, it is by virtue of this that edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) may be said to be severed.

Although this principle holds true, the Buddha spoke thus in order to demonstrate that they are severed simultaneously; for at the moment the fetter of conditions regarding edible food is severed, the craving for the five objects of sensory desire is also severed in its very essence.

Although this principle holds, one should not say that when edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is abandoned, craving for the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) is also abandoned, because the two categories of form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) are not edible food.
This objection is not valid, because the two categories of form and sound share the same antidote as edible food in their essential nature.
Because those who practice meditation weary of edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) and universally renounce the desire realm, this statement is made.
Alternatively, what is taught here is that the defilement of the five exquisite objects of desire (pañca-kāmaguṇa) is not merely greed for the five objective spheres such as visible forms.
If that is so, what is this thing called "desire" (kāma) that is not the concern of the noble ones?

Greed that arises within this realm is called "desire-taint" (kāmarāga). The five objects of the senses—form and so forth—which are conducive to the increase of greed, are called the "five exquisite desires" (pañca kāmaguṇāḥ); the realm to which these five exquisite desires belong also receives this name.
The greed within this realm takes these five objects of exquisite desire as its basis and its object; therefore, it is called "defilement of the five objects of exquisite desire.
This means that if edible food is abandoned, all forms of greed in the desire realm are likewise abandoned, because the antidotes for both are the same.

It is not the case that when greed is abandoned, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is necessarily abandoned; rather, when edible food is abandoned, all forms of greed are necessarily abandoned. For this reason, the Sūtra speaks in this manner.

Some commentators explain that the mention of abandoning edible food refers exclusively to the abandonment of the defilements to be eliminated by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which is why it speaks of abandoning the defilement of the five objects of sensory pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*).

Such an explanation lacks profound reasoning; for here it is stated that the Noble Path is free from defilement, which already demonstrates that it only abandons what is to be abandoned through cultivation. Consequently, there is no possibility of the Noble Path simultaneously abandoning both what is to be abandoned through seeing and what is to be abandoned through cultivation within a single moment.

This means that when the Noble Path abandons the defilements to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), the craving for edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is certainly not yet abandoned; subsequently, at the time of correctly abandoning the craving for edible food, the craving to be abandoned by insight must have already been previously abandoned.

Therefore, although the statement "severing the defilement of the five exquisite desires" is not explicitly mentioned, it should nevertheless be understood as referring exclusively to the severance of those defilements abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, what is established by this further qualification?

Even if it is argued that what is called the "abandonment of edible food" (kavaḍīkārāhāra) also reveals the abandonment of craving abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya), if one understands it in this way, what fault is there?

Just as when it is said that contact (sparśa) and so forth are fully known through abandonment, other dharmas such as pleasure (sukha) are also fully known through abandonment; therefore, the previous explanation does not contradict reason.

Is it not the case that, as contact (*sparśa*) and the others are abandoned one after another, feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are all simultaneously abandoned? For what reason are they explained individually and in sequence?

It is because there are sentient beings who, while experiencing feeling and craving for future existence (*punarbhava*), perceive the faults of even a single factor among them; in order to enable them to quickly abandon these, the distinct causes such as contact are explained in their respective order.
Furthermore, although contact and the other [nutriments] arise simultaneously, their three natures are distinct because their effects differ.
Moreover, this is to clarify the meaning of the term "nutriment" (āhāra): it is called nutriment because it is that which can induce [sustenance].
By what is food induced?
It is induced by craving, for the Sūtra states that the four kinds of nutriment have craving as their condition.
What, then, can food induce?
Feeling, craving, and name-and-form—
this statement is made to clarify this meaning, namely, that when the cause is absent, the effect certainly does not exist.
Furthermore, how is contact said to be called "nutriment"?
Because contact possesses the function of providing benefit and support,
feeling is the essence of that benefit and support, whereas contact is not;
contact provides benefit and support, and it is also the essence of that benefit and support because it is the cause of benefit and support and is what is experienced by feeling.
Not all volitions constitute the nutriment of volition; only those that belong to longing, proceed in accordance with craving, and are associated with the mental consciousness are termed "nutriment.
Thus, in times of famine, ignorant children sustain their lives by hoping for a sand-bag suspended before them.
Furthermore, it is observed in the world that through the presence of hope, one's strength increases;
yet if hope is severed, strength declines and one’s undertakings fail.

However, when the sūtras speak of the nutriment of mental volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*), they reveal that it corresponds exclusively with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), or else they intend to exclude the notion that volition is a quality or function of a self.
When the sūtras state that the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) is the fourth, this is said solely in reference to those realms where edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) exists.
Consciousness can serve as nutriment; what are its characteristics?
It is that which, by cognizing desirable objects, is able to sustain the body.
If this is so, why was it previously stated that the nutriment of consciousness benefits those who abide in equanimity?
Since those [beings] also possess desirable objects such as the Noble Path to Nirvāṇa, and their contaminated discernment is capable of sustaining the body, there is no fault.
If it is so, what further purpose does the statement in the Sūtra regarding the four kinds of nutriment serve, specifically the mention of the second nutriment?
This is to refute the notion that there exists a consumer apart from the food, and to demonstrate that apart from the various types of food, no consumer exists.
For this reason, the Buddha told Potaliputra:
"I never say that there is a consumer."
The Buddha taught that the four nutriments are the causes and conditions of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). What is the meaning of "causes and conditions of craving"?
It is because the objects one longs for and craves constitute the essence of nutriment.
For what reason does longing and craving arise toward nutriment?

Because various pleasant feelings arise from this, and because pleasant feelings serve as the condition, various cravings come into being. Once these cravings have arisen, they grasp at things as requisites; for food is the proximate cause for the arising of craving.
If craving has already arisen, it further serves as the requisite for sustenance; therefore, it is said that food is the causal condition for craving.
But would it not also be the case that food as a condition gives rise to suffering? One should not say that it is exclusively the causal condition for craving, for as the Sūtra says:
"Of all that is suffering, there is none that does not arise because of food."
In truth, this is indeed so; yet, those of a foolish nature are shrouded by perversion, perceiving the cause of suffering as the cause of happiness and thus giving rise to craving for its conditions.

Alternatively, when oppressed by suffering, they give rise to craving for liberation from it. With this craving as the cause, they pursue food and drink; therefore, the Buddha taught that "food" is the causal condition of craving.

Alternatively, since the arising of results can constitute the function of nutriment (*āhāra*), and because the suffering that is the result of outflows (*sāsrava*) is said to have craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as its origin, it is therefore stated that the name "nutriment" refers to the causal condition of craving.
If this were so, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) would have no nutriment, because craving does not exist for those beyond training;
or else, all who possess nutriment would necessarily possess craving.
This objection is not valid, because [the text] has already made a specific distinction.

That is to say, it has already distinguished that those who seek existence in manifold ways are those possessed of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). For them, the four nutriments (*āhāra*) provide support and nourishment respectively; it is with reference to them that the name "nutriment" is said to have craving as its cause and condition. Therefore, there is no fault of implying that those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) possess craving while lacking nutriment.
Alternatively, there is no fault in calling the food of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) "conditioned by craving" (tṛṣṇā-pratyaya), as it was initially induced by the power of craving.
This is because, having been triggered by the force of prior craving, one still seeks food and drink even though one has now abandoned craving. Thus, a verse says:
"There is no life without food."
Furthermore, as it is said in the sutras:
"Enveloped by ignorance and bound by craving, both the fool and the wise alike obtain this body; yet for an Arhat, there is no longer the fault of ignorance and craving."
This case should be understood in the same way.
Although it is known that this [term] is designated as the "condition of craving" (tṛṣṇā-pratyaya), what further purpose does this statement serve?
It is intended to reveal that the various nutriments (āhāra) are capable of drawing forth future existence (punarbhava).

For those who possess craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), even edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) can serve as a causal condition for craving, because it draws one toward future existence (*punarbhava*).
This is because the Blessed One has taught that all four nutriments are the root of disease, abscesses, and arrows, and the conditions for old age and death.

Furthermore, this food is produced by being drawn forth by prior craving, and that prior craving is in turn induced by prior food; thus, through such successive cycles since beginningless time, the wheel of birth and death revolves without interruption.
These words were spoken in order to engender weary detachment [from it].

Furthermore, all arising suffering is caused by food; it is solely because food serves as the causal condition for craving that suffering arises. To eliminate the conditions for food so that suffering does not arise is like avoiding the conditions for illness when one wishes to cure it; thus, this statement is profoundly useful.
Having extensively analyzed the types of nutriment,
we should now investigate:
among the four intermediate states previously mentioned, during the two states of birth and death— which each last for only a single moment— what consciousness arises?
With which feeling (*vedanā*) is this consciousness associated?
Can death and birth occur in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita-citta*) or without mind (*acittaka*)?
In what kind of nature (*svabhāva*) of consciousness does one abide to enter *nirvāṇa*?
At the time of death, where does consciousness cease?
What is the nature of the "vital points" (*marmaccheda*) that are severed?
The verse says:
The severing and reconnecting of the roots of virtue, the falling away from detachment, and death and birth are held to occur only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Death and birth occur only in the state of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), not during meditative absorption or in the two mindless states; furthermore, these two [death and birth] are of the neutral (*avyākṛta*) nature, as is nirvāṇa.
Gradually dying, [the consciousness] ceases at the feet, the navel, or the heart; finally, the mental consciousness perishes.
For those not reborn in the lower realms, heavens, or human worlds, the vital points (*marmaccheda*)—such as water and so forth—are severed.
The Treatise says:

Regarding the six stages—the severing of the roots of goodness, the restoration of the roots of goodness, the departure from the defilements of a realm or level, the falling away from such detachment, death, and rebirth—it is held that only the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is operative in these states; for these are all exclusive functions of the mental consciousness, and the five sensory consciousnesses lack the capacity to perform them.

Is it not the case that at the very beginning, the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) is also comprised solely of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and that the term "birth" (*upapatti*) already includes that state? It is not that the stated [term] excludes it;

however, this specific term "birth" cannot encompass the intermediate existence of rebirth (*pratisandhy-antarābhava*), because the intermediate existence of rebirth is already subsumed under the category of "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*) itself, and because [the possibility of] birth within the intermediate existence has already been refuted.

The Sūtras state that there is a person (*pudgala*) who has already severed the fetters of birth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*) but has not yet severed the fetters of arising (*abhinirvṛtti-saṃyojana*), with four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) explained in detail.
This treatise also clarifies that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not [the same as] birth, [as it concerns one] who dies in the Desire Realm and is reborn again in the Desire Realm.

Regarding the statement that "desire-existence continues," this refers to passing away from the desire realm and subsequently receiving the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) of the desire realm.
Such textual passages appear to be in extreme contradiction.
However, there is no fault of contradiction, because the various sūtras and śāstras employ the term "birth" solely with reference to birth-existence.
Among these, although the first moment is also called "birth," it is not the existence of birth (upapattibhava); what contradiction or harm is there in this?
Furthermore, our own treatise also uses the term "birth" to describe the state of the intermediate existence (antarābhava) at the time of rebirth.

There are those who simultaneously acquire the two classes of fetters (saṃyojana) belonging to the desire realm—those to be abandoned by vision and those to be abandoned by cultivation. This refers to the time when one passes away from the upper realms and is reborn in the desire realm; for these beings, the term "birth" begins at that moment, as they suddenly acquire the desire realm immediately following the death-existence (maraṇabhava) of the form or formless realms.

How could the various fetters of the two categories not reside in that very moment of death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) such that one would obtain these fetters immediately? Furthermore, this establishes that the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) is also initially termed "birth" (*jāti*), thus validating its status as birth. However, since it is incorrect to say that those [fetters] are obtained in the death-existence itself, the term "birth" in the verse includes the intermediate existence by implication.

Although the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is associated with all three types of sensation (vedanā), at the time of death and birth there is only the sensation of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā). That which is in the process of dying is called "death," and that which is in the process of being born is called "birth," just as one speaks of "laughing" while in the very act of laughing.
The nature of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is not clear or sharp; whereas at the time of death and rebirth, the natures of both painful and pleasant feelings are extremely clear and sharp.
There is no sense of death and rebirth for a consciousness that is neither clear nor sharp, because at the time of death and rebirth, it must necessarily be dull and inferior.

For this reason it is said that in the lower three dhyānas, death and rebirth occur only through the mind of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*), because the fundamental stages lack the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Although it is said that death and rebirth occur within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they do not occur through the mind in meditative absorption, because death and rebirth do not take place across different realms or levels (*dhātu-bhūmi*).
Even if the realm and stage are identical, [the former] is extremely clear and sharp, and is induced by superior preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, because the mind in meditative absorption (*samāhita-citta*) is capable of providing benefit, death can only occur through harm.
Since all minds in meditative absorption are non-defiled, and one can only undergo rebirth through a defiled mind, there is no principle of death while in such states;
for a defiled mind of a different level also provides sustenance and arises through preparatory effort.
A defiled mind of a different stage must necessarily be subsumed under a superior stage; how, then, could it allow for the desire to go to a lower stage to undergo rebirth?
Therefore, such a mind also lacks the capacity for the process of rebirth.

All pure or neutral minds of different stages arise through preparatory effort (*prayoga*); thus, there is no principle for them to end life (death), and because they are not defiled, there is no principle for them to undergo rebirth.
Furthermore, it is not the case that there can be death in the absence of mind, for this would contradict logical principles.
There are two kinds of death: either being killed by another or dying naturally.
In a state of no-mind, one cannot be harmed by another, because there is a superior dharma that sustains the body.
One does not die spontaneously while in a state of mindlessness, because entering a meditative absorption of the mind can induce the emergence of the mind.

That is to say, when the mind enters [the absorption], it acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) to grasp the resultant phenomena, such as the body and so forth, which depend upon this mind; there is certainly no other distinct phenomenon capable of obstructing them so that they do not arise.

If the body that serves as the basis for existence is about to perish, death can only occur when the mind and body belonging to that very state necessarily arise once more; there is no other possibility.
Furthermore, a sūtra provides scriptural proof that one does not die while in a mindless state; thus, the sūtra says:
"The sentient beings in the realm of non-conception pass away from that place only after the arising of thought."

Birth cannot be attained in a state of mindlessness, because birth must necessarily be induced by the manifestation of a superior mind, because one undergoes birth while abiding in a state that is dull and inferior, and because there can be no undergoing of birth apart from the arousal of afflictions.
Furthermore, there is a sūtra that proves one is not reborn without consciousness; thus the sūtra says:
"If consciousness were not to enter the mother's womb, would name-and-form (nāmarūpa) be able to form the kalala?"
...and so on, as explained at length.

Although the mind at the moment of death can indeed be of any of the three natures, an Arhat necessarily lacks a defiled mind. Furthermore, although they may possess a wholesome mind or the two types of neutral (avyākṛta) minds, these are too powerful for them to enter nirvāṇa through them. The mind that enters nirvāṇa is exclusively one of the two types of neutral mind: namely, either the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
If it is asserted that there is a mind of equanimity that is a karmic maturation (vipāka) which enters nirvāṇa within the desire realm, it is categorized as both types of neutral (avyākṛta).
If it is asserted that there is no such mind of equanimity that is a karmic maturation entering nirvāṇa in the desire realm, it is exclusively the path of deportment (airyāpathika).
There can certainly be no mind existing independently, apart from feeling; this shall be examined in detail in the "Chapter on the Analysis of Karma.
Why do inferior wholesome states not enter nirvana?
Because those wholesome minds possess karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
This is because all Arhats, having become weary of and turned away from the various future fruits of maturation (*vipāka*), enter into nirvāṇa.
If that were so, one who abides in maturation would not enter into nirvāṇa.
It is not so; for it has already been specified that [the practitioner] is weary of and turns away from the future.
Why then would they not be weary of and turn away from the present maturation (*vipāka*)?
Because one knows that by relying on the present maturation, one can eternally sever all forms of existence (*bhava*).
Relying on the manifestation of the ripening result (*vipāka*) to realize the fruit of arhatship, one recognizes the debt of gratitude owed to it and thus does not speak of weariness toward it.

All Arhats, however, feel profound aversion toward future birth; therefore, at the time of death, they avoid those wholesome states that serve as its causes. Because only the two types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) states possess weak power, they accord with the faint and inferior mind that severs the continuity [of existence]; thus, entry into nirvana occurs through these two neutral states alone.

The various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, rely upon the material sense organs (*rūpindriya*) and yet have no spatial location; how much more so is this true for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Nevertheless, if one speaks in terms of the place where the body organ ceases: in the case of sudden death, the mental consciousness and the body organ cease abruptly and simultaneously, without there being any distinct location.
If one dies gradually, for those going downward to the human or celestial realms, consciousness ceases respectively at the feet, the navel, and the heart.
That is to say, falling into the evil destinies is called "going downward"; in that case, consciousness finally ceases in the two feet.
If one goes to the human realm, consciousness ceases at the navel.
If one goes among the devas, consciousness ceases at the heart.
The Arhats are called "unborn," and their final consciousness likewise ceases at the heart.
Other masters say: Its cessation occurs at the crown of the head.
At the moment of actual death, as the body-sense faculty ceases in the feet and other parts, the mental consciousness follows in its cessation.
At the time of death, the body-faculty gradually ceases; reaching the feet and other parts, it suddenly ceases entirely.
It is like placing a small amount of water on a hot stone: it diminishes and evaporates bit by bit until it is completely exhausted in one place.

It is certainly not the case that the continuity of the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*) acts as the cause capable of producing the subsequent existence (*punarbhava*) of the destination immediately thereafter.
Only for those who die gradually, at the moment of death, is there the occurrence of the painful sensations of the "vital points" (*marmaccheda*) which oppress them.

There is no separate entity called a *marmman*; rather, there are certain specific points within the body such that when they are touched, death immediately ensues—these are what are termed *marmmans*.

That is to say, there are distinct locations within the body where, when one is oppressed by the excesses of wind (*vāta*), heat (*pitta*), or phlegm (*kapha*), an extremely painful sensation arises and death follows instantly; thus, they receive the designation of *marmmans*.
As a verse says:
"There is a specific place within the body where contact causes the end of life,
just as when the filaments of a blue lotus are touched by something as minute as a speck of dust."

If the elements of water, fire, wind, and earth combine in disharmony and oppose one another—whether collectively or individually—and their respective powers intensify to injure the *marmans* (vital points), as if they were being severed limb by limb with a sharp blade, this will give rise to extreme painful sensations; from that moment, death shall certainly occur within a brief instant.
For this reason, they are called "vital points" (*marmaccheda*); it is not that they are called "severed" in the same sense as when one speaks of cutting wood.
Because they are severed without sensation, they receive the name "severed.

One who delights in uttering speech to mock and pierce others—whether true or false—inflicting deep wounds upon the human heart, shall thereby incur the suffering of the severance of the vital points.
For what reason are the vital points (*marmaccheda*) of the earth element not mentioned?
It is because there are no fourth internal calamities.
The three internal calamities are wind, heat, and phlegm; the increase of water, fire, and wind arises accordingly as appropriate.
Some say: This resembles the three calamities of the external vessel-world;
this severing of the vital points (*marmaccheda*) does not exist among the gods.
However, when these sons of the gods are about to die, five minor signs of decline first appear:
first, their clothing and ornaments cease to produce pleasing sounds;
second, the radiance of their own bodies suddenly becomes dim and inferior.
Third, while in the state of bathing, droplets of water cling to the body;
fourth, his nature was formerly restless and racing, yet now it is stilled within a single object;
fifth, his eyes were formerly fixed in stillness, yet now they blink and move repeatedly.
The manifestation of these five signs does not necessarily mean that one's life will end; for it is still possible to turn back [the process] by encountering superior and wholesome conditions.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of great signs of decay that manifest:

first, the clothes become stained with dust; second, the flower garlands wither; third, sweat breaks out from both armpits; fourth, a foul odor enters the body; and fifth, one finds no pleasure in one's own seat.
When these five signs appear, death is certain, for even if one encounters powerful external conditions, they cannot be averted.

It is not the case that all devas possess these five signs, nor do they necessarily possess each one individually; rather, it is said that there are five because they are spoken of as a collective set.
How is it known that not everything exists?
It is by means of scripture and reasoning. As for scripture, a sūtra states:

At times, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three assemble and sit in the Hall of Good Dharma to enjoy the bliss of the Dharma together. Among them, there may be a son of heaven whose merit and lifespan have both come to an end; he suddenly passes away right there in the midst of the celestial host without rising from his seat, and none perceive it at all.
The sūtras state that when the five signs of decline appear for the devas, they pass away after five days and nights; how could it be that they do not perceive them or fail to rise from their seats?
The principle is that these signs of decline are all the results of fully matured unwholesome karma; it is not the case that all devas have collectively accumulated such unwholesome karma.
The Blessed One establishes three groups among these sentient beings within the world of birth, abiding, and passing away.
What are these three groups?
The verse says:
The right, the wrong, and the indeterminate groups; the noble ones, those who have committed the immediate [sins], and the rest.
The commentary states:
first, the group of the fixed nature of the right; second, the group of the fixed nature of the wrong; and third, the group of the indeterminate nature.
What is called "right nature" (*samyaktva*)?
It is as the Blessed One said:

the complete and remainderless abandonment of greed, the complete and remainderless abandonment of hatred, and the complete and remainderless abandonment of delusion—the complete and remainderless abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*)—this is called right nature.
Why is it that only abandonment is designated as "rightness" (*samyaktva*)?
It is because this [abandonment] eternally exhausts all false and deceptive dharmas; furthermore, its essence is virtuous and constant, and it is certainly cherished by the wise.
The Blessed One also spoke of the Noble Path as "rightness," for the Sūtras state that one enters into "rightness and the departure from birth" (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
What is meant by "wrong nature" (*mithyātva*)?
It is said to be of three kinds:

first, wrongness of inclination; second, wrongness of action; and third, wrongness of view. These correspond respectively to the essential natures of the evil destinies, the five deeds of immediate retribution, and the five types of false views.

Regarding the two types of determination: for those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), the five deeds of immediate retribution lead, respectively, to the certainty of attaining dissociation from defilements and to the fruit of hell.

One who accomplishes this attains the designation of this collection and is thus called "noble" (*ārya*); because one who has committed an immediate transgression is correctly liberated from, or has already been liberated from, the bonds of affliction, they are said to be "noble."

"Ārya" (Noble) signifies the meaning of being sovereign and free from fetters; alternatively, it is called "Noble" because it is remote from all evils, as it has attained the ultimate attainment of freedom from fetters.
Alternatively, it is called "Noble" because it is the destination toward which the wholesome proceeds; it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) because there is no interval between them.
Because it serves as the cause for this [result], it is called "created" (*kṛta*).

Those that are fixed in either the right or the wrong path, and the remainder, are termed "indeterminate nature" (*aniyata-gotra*); because they can become either depending on two conditions and are not fixedly attached to one [outcome], they receive the name "indeterminate."
