Furthermore, that which is required for various different purposes—namely, that which causes the growth of the state of birth for sentient beings' homogeneous classes (nikāya-sabhāga) and so forth—is all termed "required.
Even if it is not something consumed as food, the meaning of being "required" is established.

If all the various distinctions between the internal and external worlds arise through the predominant influence of the karma of sentient beings, for what reason are the colors and fragrances of the *padma* and *utpala* flowers so exquisite?
They are not the bodies of sentient beings, because there are distinctions among the various fruits produced by the collective and individual karma of all sentient beings.
That is to say, when sentient beings perform collective pure karma, it produces exquisite forms, fragrances, and so forth, such as lotus flowers;
through collective impure karma, it produces things such as poisonous thorns.

Because the bodies of sentient beings are produced by non-common karma (*asādhāraṇa-karman*), and because they arise from a mixture of volitional actions, there exist both purity and impurity; thus, they cannot be analogized with lotuses and the like, for this principle must necessarily be so.
Because the various devas and others are moved by purely wholesome karma, both their internal bodies and external material conditions are equally exquisite and sublime.

However, those who are unworthy, seeing that in this world those who give generously suffer in poverty while the stingy enjoy wealth and happiness, increase their wrong views, claiming that there is no cause for the results [of action].

This is due to a lack of understanding regarding the distinctions among the results—ripened (*vipāka*), dominant (*adhipati*), and outflowing (*niṣyanda*)—obtained through repeated cultivation of the field and volition (*cetanā*).

That is to say, one may have planted the cause of giving in a superior field of merit in a previous life and thereby attracted wealth and happiness; yet, because one did not repeatedly cultivate the volition capable of relinquishing material things, one still harbors stinginess in this present life.
If one has repeatedly given gifts to unworthy recipients in previous lives, one will be poor in this present life yet delight in giving.
Why would anyone be deluded regarding such a principle?

Therefore, it is well established by reason that the various differentiated fruits of the world arise from two factors: the karmic force of sentient beings' past lives and their present human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
The proponents of the theory of evil causes (ahetu-vādin) raise this objection:
"How can it be known for certain that harming results in an undesirable fruit and non-harming results in a desirable fruit?
It is not the case that these two are contradictory; rather, both fruits should arise from each of the two causes, as explained previously."
What was the previous explanation?

It refers to what is commonly observed in the world: those who perform virtuous deeds are few, while those who commit evil deeds are many; yet, among sentient beings in the world, happiness is scarce and suffering is abundant. Thus, it can be seen that among the various classes of sentient beings in the world, most practice killing, while few observe the precept against killing.
If the fruit of craving were summoned by killing, then there would be more pleasure than suffering in the world;
since this is not the case, one can know with certainty that the cause of killing cannot summon the fruit of craving.
Furthermore, one observes that seeds of sweetness and bitterness serve as causes that respectively produce sweet and bitter fruits, for they are not contradictory.
Likewise, if one performs karma toward others that results in suffering or happiness, it should respectively bring about the fruits of suffering or happiness for oneself; these are not contradictory.

Is it not the case that in the world, although grass, reeds, horns, and rushes differ in their respective natures and species, they are seen to produce one another? In the same way, the karma of others should likewise be able to result in the fruits of pleasure or pain for oneself, corresponding respectively to those [experiences].
This analogy is not established, because it is not accepted [as such]; for one observes that fruits such as grain and barley resemble their causes.
That is to say, it is accepted that reeds grow from their own seeds, while hair and horns can only serve as auxiliary conditions for them.

Although grains such as rice and wheat arise from their own seeds, we nonetheless observe that they emerge from soil, water, and other conditions; therefore, the corroborative example (sapakṣa) cited by him is unestablished.
Furthermore, we see in the world that those who seek wealth and happiness must necessarily strive to benefit and bring joy to those possessed of virtue.

If, like the *pu-ṣu* grass, [the result] were produced from a different category [of cause], then those who seek future happiness should experience suffering rather than pleasure when directed toward virtuous beings;
yet, since they strive for their own happiness by diligently benefiting others, the cause of killing cannot bring about a pleasant fruit.

Furthermore, the claim that two fruits should each arise from two causes is logically untenable; for it has never been observed that causes lacking differentiation can separately produce desirable and undesirable fruits.

That is to say, one has never seen a cause that lacks differentiation yet can separately summon desirable and undesirable fruits; rather, one observes that from what is undifferentiated, only the undifferentiated arises.
Therefore, one should not maintain the view that pure and impure karma each separately summons two kinds of fruits.

If this were necessarily the case, since no other ripening cause would be observed and there would be no distinction between the fruits induced by pure and impure karma, it would follow that the karmic fruits of all sentient beings are without distinction;
however, such is not the case.
If you were to grant this, there would be no distinction between those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them; consequently, diligent cultivation and study would be rendered futile.
Yet, such a position must not be granted.

Furthermore, if that were the case, one would have to kill living beings, and one would simultaneously experience both the long and short lifespans—the two types of maturation—within the happy realms. The same difficulty would apply to those who abstain from killing. Likewise, for those who commit theft and those who abstain from it, they would both simultaneously experience wealth and poverty.

Furthermore, one should not maintain that although two fruits do not arise simultaneously, they are nevertheless experienced sequentially; for there is no distinction in the cause such that it would produce distinct fruits at different times.

Moreover, it has never been observed that once a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) has already produced its ripening fruit, it still possesses the functional power to summon a ripening fruit of a different category.

Furthermore, since it is observed that in some cases there is a determinacy regarding pleasant and unpleasant fruits, the length of life, and so forth—if two causes were combined to each produce two fruits that are experienced alternately, then there would be no determinacy regarding what is pleasant or unpleasant, the fixed length of life, or the distinct differences in experiencing suffering and happiness.

However, it is actually observed that there are those with fixed long lifespans or fixed short lifespans, and those with fixed abundance of pleasure or fixed abundance of suffering; therefore, it is impossible for two causes to alternate in producing two distinct results.

Is it not the case that all sentient beings cherish their own lives, and thus they should also cherish a long life even in hell? If this were so, it would result in a contradiction between cause and effect.

There is no such flaw, because at the time of creating karma one is capable of accomplishing many things; therefore, when the state of experiencing the fruit arises, various distinct fruits are likewise produced.

That is to say, when performing an action, those who kill cause others to suffer, sever their lives, terrify them, and destroy their majestic splendor; therefore, when experiencing the fruit, there are three corresponding aspects: because they caused suffering to others, they experience extremely heavy suffering within the hells as the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*);
because they severed the lives of others, they experience an extremely short lifespan within the happy realms as the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*);
and because they destroyed the majesty of others, they encounter external medicinal substances that all lack vitality and brilliance as the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Therefore, there is no fault of contradicting the established relationship between cause and effect.
If that were so, one would have to admit that the karma of killing produces a result in a happy realm;
but this is not the case, for it is not admitted that such karma produces a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) within a happy realm.
This refers to the lifespan in the happy realms, which is summoned by pure karma;
yet, that act of killing serves as a calamity for it, preventing it from fully attaining its own fruit. Therefore, it is said that killing can summon a short lifespan.

If there were evil karma that produced a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) within the happy realms, it would not be subsumed under "unpleasant fruits"; therefore, this too would not constitute a reversal of cause and effect.

Some maintain that when sacrificial rituals and incantations are preceded by the harming of sentient beings, they can summon pleasant fruits, and because this is not a case of random killing, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
If that were so, one would have to admit that killing—such as when a sorcery spell or an incantation causes someone to suffer from a fever until death—could produce a desirable result.

However, these spells and the like do not intend to bring benefit or happiness to the being being harmed; whereas the intent behind sacrificial mantras is to bring benefit and happiness to the sheep and other animals being sacrificed. Therefore, although those who perform such harm do indeed kill sentient beings, they do not incur a bitter result, just like a skilled physician.
Even for one who has escaped birth and death, if they harm insects or ants with a mind seeking their benefit and happiness, they should still incur a desirable fruit.

It is not the case that the fruits of killing sentient beings differ depending on whether it is done with a mystic spell or with a blade or staff, provided the intent to benefit and bring happiness remains the same.
Just as for the killer, merit or demerit is obtained based on the distinction between the goodness or evil of one's own mind;

likewise, the sheep, ants, and so forth that are killed should obtain merit or demerit through their own minds. It is not the case that by forcibly killing them, merit is produced in them such that it serves as a cause to invite desirable fruits.
Just as one who has escaped from birth and death harms other sentient beings, which serves as no cause for virtuous results but only invites evil ones;
so too, sacrificial rites preceded by incantations should likewise result only in what is undesirable.
In this regard, the skilled physician does not serve as a fitting analogy for the Dharma.

For a skilled physician, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to those who are ill, exerts himself in treatment to bring others peace and well-being; although the efficacy of his work may not be known by other physicians or bystanders in the present life or in future births, and although he may cause the patient temporary pain that touches their body, that skilled physician does not produce non-merit.
However, they themselves admit that sheep and other such animals are ignorant and incapable of discerning merit from non-merit.

Since they cannot endure the present suffering of being slaughtered, even if one says that they will obtain desirable results in the future, neither the killer nor those bystanders perceive this directly, nor is there any logical proof for it; therefore, the analogy cited is not consistent with the point at issue.
Although a bystander does not directly perceive the killer, they know it through the authority of the *āgama* (scriptures).
But how can one know that the *āgama* regarding sacrificial slaughter is an authoritative means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that it does not produce non-merit?
Because the essence of the sound of the vidyā-mantras is eternal;
that is to say, since the various vidyā-śāstras have no creator and the mantra words exist therein spontaneously, they alone can serve as authoritative criteria, and nothing else.
Is it asserted that only the sound of the *śāstra* (Vedic scripture) is eternal by nature, or is it admitted that all sounds are eternal?
If it is claimed that only the sound of the *śāstra* is eternal, there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove it, and thus the argument is necessarily untenable.
It is observed that other sounds, which are apprehended by the auditory faculty, are impermanent in nature;
since the various Vedic treatises are likewise apprehended by the auditory faculty, they too should be impermanent.

If all sounds were eternal, they would not constitute valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); for it is only the sound of the Vedas that is accepted as a valid means of knowledge because its sound is held to be eternal. To accept all sounds as valid means of knowledge would result in the loss of one's own fundamental tenet, namely that only the sound of the Vedas is subsumed under the category of valid means of knowledge.

Furthermore, sounds produced not by conscious intelligence can only be heard by the ear and lack definitive expression; since you admit that the *Vedāṅgas* (Explanatory Treatises) do not have conscious intelligence as their precursor, they too should not be included among the authoritative means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, if the essence of the sound of the *śāstra* were eternal, what would obstruct that sound so that it could not be perceived at all times?

It is the mutual striking and vibration of the chest, throat, and other locations that manifests the sound of the *śāstra*. Although this sound is eternal, it is not perceived constantly because the manifesting conditions are lacking.
This sound should not be manifested by conditions, because that which is capable of obscuring or obstructing it cannot be apprehended.

We observe in the case of jars and the like that when they are covered or obstructed by darkness or other things, they are only manifested once the covering or obstruction has been removed by means of light and so forth.

Prior to the sound being produced, the factors that could obstruct it are entirely non-existent; how, then, can it be said that sound is not constantly perceived because obstructions have not yet been removed?
Therefore, what they say relies solely on false conceptualization.
Furthermore, we observe in the world that although the manifesting causes may differ, the characteristics of the manifested object do not undergo any alteration.

However, the sound of speech is heard differently according to conditions; that is, as sounds are produced by the striking and vibration of the chest, throat, and so forth during the stages of youth, adulthood, or old age, each is heard distinctly. Therefore, it cannot be said that sound is merely manifested by those [organs].
Furthermore, sound is distinct from its manifestor because it can be perceived in a different location.

That is to say, sound can be apprehended in a location separate from the location of its manifestor; however, an object that is manifested cannot be apprehended in a location separate from the cause of its manifestation. Therefore, the chest, throat, and so forth are not the manifesting causes of the Vedas.
Furthermore, because there is no example based on commonality (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) here, one must ask: how could an object first be concealed and then by whom it would be manifested?
This cannot reasonably be the case—such as a jar being manifested by light—because it is not universally established (*aprasiddha*).
One should first examine this carefully:
Is it that the very same jar, previously obscured by darkness, is now made manifest?
Or is it that at the moment immediately following the cessation of the jar in darkness, a distinct jar-entity arises in conjunction with light?
Therefore, there is no commonly accepted similar instance (*sapakṣa*) here.

Even if one were to concede that the *Vaiśeṣika* treatise is manifested like a jar, it would follow that it is impermanent just as a jar is; for they themselves state that the jar is both manifested and impermanent, and this [treatise] should be the same.

Furthermore, pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth should likewise be subject to this same adherence. That is to say, while you maintain that this sound arises from its own cause, yet you adhere to the view that it does not arise but is merely manifested;
since the arousal of pleasure and so forth also proceeds from their own causes, why do you not likewise adhere to the view that they do not arise but are merely manifested?
Therefore, all sounds arise from their own causes; like musical instruments and the like, they should be understood as being produced rather than merely manifesting.

Consequently, the claim that the mantras within the *Vyākaraṇa* treatises have no creator, and thus are eternal in essence and constitute valid authority (*pramāṇa*), is a statement devoid of reality.

If that is so, it should be stated that the sounds of the *vidyā* treatises are subsumed under the "words of the authoritative teachers" (*āptavacana*), and are therefore a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

That is to say, when the *vidyā* treatises describe desirable fruits and the like, these are what have been perceived by the great sages and noble ones; because they are transmitted by them and are included within the words of the authoritative teachers, if one acts in accordance with them, one obtains all desirable fruits, whereas if one acts contrary to them, one immediately encounters undesirable retribution.

It is not so; the supreme sanctity realized by those sages whom you revere was not attained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor can it be known by inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, their oral tradition is not included among the authoritative teachings (*āptāgama*).

That which you revere—the Great Sages’ vision and the lovely fruits described in the treatises—has never been even slightly perceived by you yourselves; yet, based on this, you can verify that what they have taught is not false. By means of this inference, you know that their realization constitutes the state of a Most Noble One (Arhat), and you verify that the transmitted teachings are included within the category of the Ultimate Teaching (Āgama).
Therefore, what you have said is merely the speech of the ignorant; how could you possibly understand the characteristics of the truly ultimate teaching?

For instance, even the state of supreme holiness realized by the Great Master whom you revere is not something obtained through your own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet you nevertheless maintain that the teachings he proclaimed are included within the category of the ultimate teaching.
The same should apply to the others; why do you alone refuse to accept this?

This analogy is unreasonable. Our Great Teacher possesses the marks of a Supreme Sage, which can be verified in the present; by inference based on these characteristics, we know he has realized supreme sagehood, and thus we verify that the teachings he proclaimed are subsumed within the category of the Supreme Teaching.
What are the characteristics of one who has attained the state of an Arya?
When one is endowed with these characteristics, the nature of an Arya is established, and it is realized that what they say is subsumed within the "Ultimate Teaching" (āptāgama).
Now, false speech arises from greed, hatred, and delusion.

Our Great Teacher has perfectly realized and attained this; all faults such as attachment and aversion have been utterly exhausted. Because he has attained this exhaustion, he has become a Most Noble One (ārya), and therefore every word he utters is subsumed under the category of authoritative teaching (āptāgama).
How is it known by reason that the Teacher has transcended all faults?
Because he is able to perfectly teach the path to the transcendence of faults.
That is to say, our Great Teacher is able to perfectly teach the path to the transcendence of faults; by this inference, one knows that greed and all other faults have been utterly exhausted.
How is it known that this path can bring about the ultimate exhaustion of faults?
Because it causes one to temporarily and permanently depart from those factors that obstruct the attainment of liberation.

If a phenomenon can obstruct the attainment of the exhaustion of all suffering, then by means of the path as taught, one can temporarily and permanently depart from it; by departing from such phenomena, one is then able to realize the permanent exhaustion of all faults, such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
What is the nature of this obstructive dharma?
It is the grasping at a self, namely, the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

Since all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) assert the existence of a self, they are unable to achieve liberation from self-grasping; for apart from the vision of selflessness (*anātma-darśana*), there is absolutely nothing that can cause self-grasping to cease.
However, among all the sages outside the True Dharma, none are able to correctly teach non-self; because they lack this teaching, they do not abandon the grasping at a self.
Since they cannot abandon the grasping at a self, they are unable to realize the permanent exhaustion of craving and the other afflictions.
Since they have not realized the eternal extinction of suffering, it is possible that their words are false, for they have brought about those causes—greed, hatred, and delusion.
Therefore, the sages whom you revere are in truth neither Great Sages nor Supreme Holy Ones.
Because they are not the ultimate Sage, the sounds of the *Sāṃkhya-pravacana* and other treatises transmitted by them do not constitute the authority of the Buddha's word (*āptāgama*).
Since they are not authoritative, my previous argument—that within sacrificial rites, mantras that involve killing do not yield desirable fruits—is established as a matter of logic.
On this basis, their claim that sacrificial mantras benefit sheep and other animals— such that even though they harm sentient beings,
they are like a skilled physician and do not bring about bitter fruits— is logically untenable.
Since that [other view] is not established, it is only by the principle of karma as explained here that the distinctions among worlds are established.
Now, regarding the term "distinctions of worlds" (*loka-bheda*) in this verse, it may be understood according to the sixth case (genitive),
meaning "the distinction of the world," or according to the seventh case (locative), meaning "a distinction within the world."
What is the nature of this karma that is its basis?
It consists of what the mind intends (*cetanā*) and what is produced by that intention.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
There are two kinds of karma: first, the karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*); second, the karma after having willed (*cetayitvā-karma*).
Karma after having willed refers to that which is performed by volition; it has the meaning of being originated by volition.
One should know that volition (*cetanā*) is itself mental action (*manas-karman*), while that which is produced by volition consists of bodily and vocal actions.
These two types of action are taught by the Blessed One in the sūtras as three, namely: bodily, vocal, and mental action.
These three types of action are established according to their sequence by virtue of their basis (*āśraya*), their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and their motivation (*samutthāna*).

That is to say: because action has the body as its basis, it is called "bodily action" (*kāyakarman*); because the nature of the action is speech, it is called "vocal action" (*vākkarman*); and because this action has the mind as its basis, arises together with the mind, and motivates bodily and vocal actions, it is called "mental action" (*manaskarman*).
The intrinsic nature of mental action has already been explained herein; that is, it is volition (*cetanā*).
Volition has been analyzed as previously discussed. What, then, is the intrinsic nature of the two actions of body and speech?
The verse says:
These two types of action, bodily and vocal, are both of the nature of manifest and unmanifest.
The treatise says:
It should be understood that among all the actions thus described, both bodily and vocal actions possess the nature of both manifest and unmanifest.
Therefore, the root treatise states:
"What is bodily action?
It refers to all that is manifest and unmanifest belonging to the body."
What is vocal action? It refers to all that is manifest and unmanifest belonging to speech.
Furthermore, for what reason do only bodily and vocal actions possess the nature of manifest and unmanifest, while mental action does not?
Because that characteristic does not exist within mental action (*manas-karman*).
That which is capable of manifesting is called "manifest" (*vijñapti*), because it manifests one's own mind so that others may know it;
since volition (*cetanā*) lacks this quality, it is not called "manifest."
For this reason, it is said that only the two types of action—bodily and vocal—are capable of manifestation (*vijñapti*), whereas mental action is not.
Why, then, does the Sūtra state that "for those who possess craving, manifestation is itself mental action"?
This statement has a further meaning: it is intended to show that although the essence of mental action is non-material (*arūpa*), it becomes coarse through the influence of craving.

This refers to volition (*cetanā*) conjoined with craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Although its substance is not material (*arūpa*), its characteristic is coarse and manifest; thus, like bodily and vocal intimation (*kāya-vāk-vijñapti*), it can express its own mind and cause others to know it. In reality, it does not possess the nature of intimation, but it is metaphorically designated as such.
Therefore, the Sūtra merely states: "The intimation of those who crave is itself mental action (*manas-karman*)."
That which is driven by craving and clearly perceives the phenomena that move the mind is precisely the meaning of mental action (*manas-karman*).

If this sutra states that "craving" is the substance of mental action and is itself manifest (*vijñapti*), then one could cite this sutra to demonstrate that the function of mental action has manifestation as its nature.
Thus, it has been argued that mental action (manas-karman) is neither manifest (vijñapti) nor unmanifest (avijñapti).

Furthermore, because the initial arising of unmanifest action necessarily depends upon the primary elements (mahābhūta) that act as its generative cause, and because even after those generative causes have ceased, there must certainly exist similar primary elements serving as its basis for subsequent unmanifest action to continue arising in successive moments.

All mental actions (manas-karman) necessarily arise in dependence upon the mind; it is not the case that, at subsequent moments, a similar type of mind must necessarily arise in a continuous succession such that the agreeable non-informative matter (avijñapti) could rely upon that mind for a multi-moment continuity, because the mind’s states—such as being wholesome and so forth—differ from moment to moment.

If non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) were to arise as a continuous stream of the same type as the volition (*cetanā*), how could a mental action (*manas-karman*) based on a preceding mind proceed according to a subsequent moment of a different type?
Since there is no mental action that is dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta*), there is likewise no non-informative action within mental action.
Therefore, it is well established by reason that there are only two types of bodily and vocal karma, namely informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti).
Regarding this, the Sthavira states:
"How can it be said that a body which perishes moment by moment possesses movement or displacement called 'bodily karma'?"
If a phenomenon arises at a particular time and place, it ceases at that very same time and place without any movement or transition;
if this were not admitted, the principle of momentary destruction would be untenable.
The same applies to the difficulty regarding vocal karma.
The Abhidharma school does not accept that physical movement or activity is designated as bodily or vocal intimation (*vijñapti*). Why is this so?
The verse says:
Bodily intimation is admitted to be a distinct shape;
it does not have motion as its essence, because all conditioned phenomena perish in a single moment.
Because there can be no such thing as causelessness, the cause of arising must be capable of cessation.
Shape is not substantially existent, because it would have to be apprehended by two sense-faculties, and because there are no distinct atoms.
It is admitted that vocal intimation is the sound of speech.
The treatise says:

The collection of hair, body hair, and so forth is collectively termed the "body. Within this body, there is a distinction of shape and color that is the fruit of the four great elements produced by the mind; because it can represent the mind, it is called "bodily intimation" (kāyavijñapti).
Just as the nature of volition (*cetanā*), though perishing moment by moment, is established as mental action (*manas-karman*) without contradicting reason;
so too is bodily form established as bodily action (*kāya-karman*). Therefore, the objection raised does not apply to this system.
Furthermore, for what reason are visible form (*varṇa*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) not established as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)?
Because these are all exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) by nature.
Would it not follow that, just as they can produce the mind, they should also be established as having distinct natures such as wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth?
This criticism is unreasonable, because these [informative acts] arise independently of the agent's desire;
furthermore, they would arise even if separated from the mind, whereas informative acts necessarily depend upon the mind to arise.

If the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth were produced by a single mind, then just as there are distinctions in their substance, there would likewise have to be such distinctions in their phenomena; however, one cannot claim that what is produced by a single mind possesses distinct substances that constitute a nature of distinction.
Furthermore, how is it known that the two types of action—bodily and vocal—are both wholesome and unwholesome?
Because it is stated in the sūtras. As a sūtra says:
Regarding all defiled phenomena cognized by the eye and ear, it is not the case that the Venerable One possesses them;
the same applies to the explanation regarding all pure phenomena cognized by the eye and ear.
Furthermore, how is it known that the four great elements and so forth are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta)?
This is also established by what is taught in the sūtras. As a sūtra states:

There is a certain class [of beings] whose bodies remain for ten years, and so forth, as explained at length; it is said that the mind, mentation, and consciousness perish differently and arise differently.
Someone might raise this objection:
"The various types of manifest karma, such as the wholesome and so forth, possess distinct natures."
It is logically untenable that [the action] would be established as such, because there is a distinction among its own class, and thus it cannot be established by logic.

That is to say, although they are equally bodily actions (*kāyakarman*), depending on the motivating mind, they become either indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*), just as a child or others may grasp at their mother’s breast.
Therefore, bodily action cannot establish distinctions when viewed within its own category; it is exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) solely by virtue of the mind.
This [mind] possesses distinctions and is capable of differentiating [the action], whereby it can be established as wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth.
This objection is irrational, because the two are extremely similar; their distinct characteristics are difficult to discern, as in the case of the *āmra* (mango) species and others.

For instance, the color and shape of the *āmra* species are extremely similar to those of the *kṣīravṛkṣa* (milky-wood) species; yet, despite being extremely similar, they are not without distinction, for one observes differences in their fruits.
The same principle should apply to bodily and vocal informative actions (*vijñapti-karma*).

If one were to claim that while these differ as informative actions based on the motivating mind, they cannot be said to have distinctions such as being wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth, then volitional action (*cetanā-karma*) would likewise lack distinctions such as being wholesome; for volition too is designated as wholesome or unwholesome only when it coexists with faith, greed, and so forth.

If it were argued that [the distinction between] wholesome and so forth is established because they share a single fruit, this is also logically untenable, as they depend on others for their similarity.

For example, although volition (cetanā) shares the same nature of being a single fruit when associated with faith and other factors, it only achieves its specific wholesome or unwholesome character by depending on the power of faith and the rest.

Since such manifest karma (vijñapti-karman) is originated by wholesome and other types of mind and is a mental outflow (citta-nisyanda), it constitutes the distinction of being wholesome and so forth; its meaning is identical to that of volition (cetanā).

If the essence of bodily and vocal karma were itself wholesome and so forth, it would be the same as the argument of the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas, who claim that the nature of good and evil is like fire: because both volition and non-volition are equally capable of burning.
There is no such fault as that, because the manifestation of good and evil does not arise apart from the mind, just like the visual consciousness and so forth.
For example, although the visual consciousness and others have their distinctions, they can never arise if separated from the eye and other [faculties].

Thus, although manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) may be either wholesome or unwholesome, it cannot arise apart from the mind; therefore, there is no fault of equivalence with the Nirgranthas (Jains).
Furthermore, the ancient masters have already refuted the fire analogy established by the Nirgranthas, stating:

"When the people of the land of Bāhlika harbor feelings of wrath, while certain Nirgranthas give rise to a wholesome and pure mind, both might pull out the hair of a Nirgrantha with their hands. How could these two—sin and merit—possibly be equal?"

Thus, although the characteristics of these bodily and vocal actions are the same, there are distinctions between them as wholesome or unwholesome; therefore, they are not like fire, which lacks such differentiation.
Consequently, their argument is not consistent with correct reasoning, and thus our own school does not incur the same fault as theirs.
What is the bodily and vocal action established by that Elder? He says:

when a collection of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arises in a different location due to the power of other conditions, such that the subsequent effect follows immediately after the preceding cause, and is capable of providing benefit or causing harm—that very collection is called bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*).

That is to say, from the perspective of conventional truth, when a *pudgala* utters such speech that arises from conditions and produces such a result, it is termed "vocal informative action" (*vāgvijñapti-karman*).

From the perspective of ultimate truth, however, phenomena have no sovereign master; therefore, the name "informative" (*vijñapti*) is established based on the convergence of many real elements (*dhātu*), for a single entity cannot alone manifest [an intention], nor is there any other thing that can be called "informative."

Now, regarding the "informative action" (*vijñapti-karma*) established by that school: it is merely a fabrication of their own views outside the sacred teachings, for within the *Sūtras* it is stated only that the objects of the two consciousnesses—eye and ear—namely visible form and sound, possess defilement, purity, and mixture, whereas this is not the case for odors and the other [objects].

That school also maintains that all aggregates composed of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and that apart from bodily and vocal karma, no distinct defiled or pure matter or sound is observed.

Furthermore, the primary elements are not objects perceived by the eye; since it has already been thoroughly refuted that the five consciousnesses take the conventional as their object, what that school says merely expresses its own subjective preconceptions.

If it is argued that the aforementioned collective aggregate is not subject to the fault of being invariably indeterminate because it acquires distinctions according to its respective motivating causes (*samutthāna*) and because its effects are seen to be distinct, this reasoning is likewise untenable, as it is merely a matter of words.

According to that school’s own tenet, although the motivating causes (samutthāna) differ, there is no distinction among the aggregates of the primary elements (mahābhūta). Therefore, even though the motivating mind may be wholesome or otherwise, that which is motivated by it is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).

To concede that there are distinctions such as "wholesome" within a collection of great elements (*mahābhūta*) is an unreflective and reckless statement; for the substance of such a collection cannot be apprehended, and that which lacks substantiality cannot possess distinctions such as being wholesome.

Furthermore, one should not establish that within each of the bases of the aggregates there exist distinctions such as wholesome and so forth; for the primary elements are not objects of the eye, and the Sūtra states only that visible form and sound are defiled or pure.

Since the distinctions of being wholesome and so forth have already been refuted regarding visible color (*varṇa*) and other such phenomena, one should not maintain that the aggregates of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) possess distinctions such as being wholesome based on their respective concomitant motivations (*samutthāna*).

Even if one were to concede that visible color constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), this would entail admitting that bodily intimation exists substantially; and regarding what exists substantially, one must engage in debate.

Regarding the Abhidharmikas, they maintain that bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) refers to shape; they assert that manifest color (*varṇa*) is what constitutes bodily intimation. Thus, there is no great contradiction between our positions.
However, as previously stated, manifest color does not follow the movement of the motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*), and therefore it is not bodily intimation.

Furthermore, although the differentiation of effects involves benefit or harm, it must nonetheless be of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). This is because, despite the presence of benefit or harm in the differentiation of effects, one cannot say that the aggregate of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) possesses the distinctions of being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; for the same fault would apply to substances such as odors and so forth.

Yet the Sūtra merely states that the two [types of action] possess goodness and so forth; although there is no sovereign controller, because they are capable of producing results as if there were, they may also be said to possess the nature of being expressive.
Therefore, the bodily action established by the Venerable Sthavira is a mere fabrication of his own sentiments outside of the Noble Teaching.
By this, the linguistic karma proposed has already been refuted; that is to say, it is unreasonable for such conventional speech to be either virtuous or defiled.
Furthermore, it should not be said that the conventional arises from conditions, because conventional phenomena do not exist as real entities.
If phenomena were substantially existent, they could arise from conditions; otherwise, if they were not so produced from conditions, they would lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If that were the case, it would accord with the tenets of those who advocate the destruction of phenomena (*dharmavināśavādin*); therefore, one should not claim that such conventional expressions themselves arise from conditions.
If one provides this explanation according to the literal sequence of the text, such that conventional terminology applies only to the *pudgala*, then it would be unable to resolve two difficulties.
Namely, there is a prior objection raised by another treatise:
"How can a conventional phenomenon produce a result that is ultimately real?"
How can the existence of real indicative expression (vijñapti) constitute a subversion of the ultimate truth (paramārtha)?
First, it is shown that conventional reality arises from conditions and is therefore able to produce effects; this addresses the initial objection.
Next, it is raised that ultimate phenomena lack a governing subject and can only be expressed through synthesis; this serves to resolve subsequent objections.
If one were to argue that conventional reality does not belong to language, how could the preceding passage resolve the initial objection?

Furthermore, if you maintain that only conventional [phenomena] belong to the person (pudgala), then you must admit the existence of ultimate vocal karma; since this is precisely vocal intimation (vāgvijñapti), what reasoning could possibly preclude it?
Since you have already admitted that karma is established, you should likewise admit the existence of informative action (*vijñapti*).
Furthermore, that Sthavira himself has made this sincere declaration:
"It is not that I deny the real existence of speech; rather, I simply do not allow for a separate entity that, acting alone, can represent [an intention] and is thus called 'informative speech'."
I also do not admit that there is a distinct entity called "vocal intimation" (vāgvijñapti) apart from the sound of truthful speech; why, then, does the Venerable One not feel satisfaction with this?
For has it not already been stated that a single thing cannot manifest meaning on its own, and furthermore, that no other entity exists which could be termed "intimation"?
This lacks profound reasoning; for if the substance of speech is real, then the indicative [vocal sound] should likewise be so.
Just as there is no single word that can be uttered in isolation, there is likewise no principle by which it could independently produce auditory consciousness.
Nevertheless, speech possesses a real existence that does not undermine the ultimate truth; arising from conditions, it is called vocal karma (*vākkarman*).

Likewise, although there is no single substantially existent element capable of expressing meaning on its own, there exists a real expression that does not undermine the ultimate truth and arises from conditions; this is called vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
I establish it in this way; how could this be the same as your own school, which arbitrarily establishes the principle of *karma* outside of the sacred teachings?

It is not the case that visible color (*varṇa*) cannot be perceived because of its aggregation; for even when not aggregated, its substance exists, yet it is not seen because it is subtle, and thus it would not follow that it ceases to be visible color.
The same should apply to informative action (*vijñapti*); therefore, it is substantially existent.

Furthermore, they themselves admit that within the spheres of tangibles and phenomena (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu* and *dharma-dhātu*), there are many distinct entities; just as each individual entity separately receives the name "sphere" (*dhātu*), the collection as a whole is also a sphere. The same applies to the sphere of visible forms (*rūpa-dhātu*).
Just as a collection in its entirety, like its individual parts, receives the designation "form" (*rūpa*), so too should it be for informative action (*vijñapti*).
Therefore, the Abhidharmikas' establishment of the principle of karma is logically consistent.
Other schools, however, state:
Movement is bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
What phenomenon is designated as "movement"?
It refers to the activity of conditioned forces (*saṃskāra*).
How do the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) proceed?
It means they arise in other directions.
At times, conditioned phenomena act as the cause of production within their own original location to produce the resulting effects that are produced.
At times, when conditions converge, a phenomenon that is the fruit arises in a different location immediately following its preceding cause.
Therefore, when these conditioned forces (*saṃskāra*) arise in another location, they receive the name "bodily action" (*kāyakarman*) and are also called "bodily intimation" (*kāyavijñapti*).
Although this principle exists, it pertains only to the conventional (saṃvṛti); however, bodily informative action (kāya-vijñapti-karma) must be ultimate (paramārtha).
Yet, there is no actual movement in conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), because all conditioned dharmas are momentary (kṣaṇika).

Although this is the case in principle, one should not say that there is no real entity called "informative action" (*vijñapti-karman*) within the body. This is because it is taught that the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) constitutes action, and since the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena are themselves those very phenomena, what further principle is required to claim that an action must arise from elsewhere in order to be designated as such?
It does not abide at the very place where its cause is located.

If it were to abide at the very place where its cause is located, then whenever a phenomenon arises in any location, it would necessarily cease immediately at that very spot without proceeding to any other location.
Since action itself does not exist, how can there be a real manifestation?
Furthermore, since it has already been refuted that manifesting and so forth are actions, the position previously established is superior from a logical standpoint.
The Venerable Rāma stated as follows:

Since the very substance that is acquired through conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arises in a particular location, it is precisely in that same location that this substance ceases; therefore, there is no movement.

Although this principle holds true, while it may be possible for a substance to move and cease in a certain place, since you maintain that the substance of future phenomena does not yet exist, how can it be said that the very substance which is acquired arises in that location?
Furthermore, if its essence were already attained, it should not arise again;
yet since it must arise again, its essence was not already attained.
Therefore, what he has stated contradicts his own school’s tenets.

If it is argued that such a statement is made on the basis of what is yet to happen, this too is irrational; for in the world, one does not see anything that is non-existent being spoken of on the basis of what is yet to happen.
One only sees things that exist and may later change being spoken of on the basis of what is yet to happen.

As it is said in the world: "grinding flour," "cooking rice," or "weaving silk"; such expressions cannot be applied to that which lacks an essence. Therefore, what they have asserted is certainly not reasonable.
What is meant by a "kṣaṇa"?
It refers to the shortest possible duration, such that it can no longer be further analyzed into prior or subsequent parts.
Furthermore, what is meant by "time"?
This refers to the different states (avasthā) of the past, future, and present; it is by means of these that one numerically cognizes the distinctions among conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
Among these, the most minimal state of a conditioned phenomenon is called a *kṣaṇa*; therefore, it is said that because it is the most extreme brevity of time, it is named a *kṣaṇa*.
In this context, "moment" (kṣaṇa) refers only to the state in which dharmas possess functional activity, namely, the present alone.
Thus, a present dharma that possesses a duration of staying is said to have "moments," just as one speaks of a "moon-phase" (māsa).
Alternatively, it is called "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) because it is capable of destroying; this means it can act as the cause for the cessation of all phenomena.
That is to say, the characteristic of impermanence (*anityatā-lakṣaṇa*) is able to destroy all phenomena, and the factors that coexist with it are termed "possessing moments" (*sakṣaṇika*).

Alternatively, when it is said in worldly discourse that things possess "momentariness" (*kṣaṇika*), this has the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); that is to say, in their present state there is nothing capable of sustaining them so as to prevent their cessation, for they necessarily do not abide, and thus they are called "momentary."

Alternatively, when worldly discourse speaks of "no moment" (*akṣaṇa*), it carries the sense of "lack of leisure. That is to say, being attached to other matters and lacking the leisure to focus exclusively on one's own task is called "no moment.
Only at the present time is there necessarily a slight leisure, because one grasps its own result; therefore, it is called "having a moment" (*sakṣaṇa*).

However, within the various states of the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), there are temporal distinctions such as *lava* and so forth; among all these times, the *kṣaṇa* is the most brief. Since it is certain that this exists, it is called "possessing moments" (*sakṣaṇika*).
Yet the Master of the Sūtra says:
"What is meant by 'momentary' (kṣaṇika)?
When a dharma possesses the quality of perishing immediately after its acquisition, it is called 'momentary,' just as a person who possesses a staff is called 'one who has a staff.'"
That explanation by the Śākya is unreasonable, because it cannot be said that a staff is distinct from a person.

Since the analogy does not correspond to the dharma [it illustrates], and since there is no separate dharma distinct from the nature of the immediately preceding cessation of the entity itself, how can it be said that this possesses momentariness?
It is like a person with a staff;
nor can it be said that this is explained in terms of a continuum, for that which lacks an essence cannot possess an essence.

Alternatively, one would have to say that a non-existent dharma is called "existent" in its momentary state, yet there is no great fault in [the fact that] that which possesses an essence does not [itself] become a great fault.
Nor should it be claimed that the person with a staff (*dandī*) is cited as a homologous example (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*) for what appears to be a different statement;
otherwise, one would have to speak metaphorically of "possessing moments" (*kṣaṇika*), for such would be the logical consequence within the framework of this apparent mode of expression.
However, one should not admit that there is a metaphorical designation of "momentariness," because there is no universally established real momentariness.
That is to say, if one were to admit the existence of a real moment, one could then admit the existence of other things based on it through metaphorical designation;
but since the real object of comparison does not exist, the metaphorical designation cannot be established.
Therefore, the Abhidharma school’s assertion that conditioned phenomena possess the principle of momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) is uniquely free from fault.
One should not definitively state:
"That which perishes immediately after its acquisition (prāpti) is a momentary phenomenon; this is what is called 'momentariness'."
Furthermore, how is it known that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perish moment by moment and necessarily do not endure for long?
It is because all conditioned phenomena must eventually come to an end.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) offers the following explanation:
This means that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) perish without depending on a cause. Why is this so?
That which depends on a cause is a fruit; since there is nothing that is not a fruit, they perish without depending on a cause.
Since it does not depend on a cause, it ceases immediately upon arising.
If it did not cease at the beginning, it would likewise not cease later, because the subsequent [moment] is identical in nature to the initial one.

That explanation by the Śākya is unreasonable. Cessation (*kṣaya*) is itself extinction (*nirodha*); the Buddha taught that cessation and extinction are conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), and he taught that conditioned characteristics pertain to all phenomena (*dharma*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"All conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The arising of conditioned phenomena can be known; their cessation and their change while abiding can also be known.

If one were to claim that non-existence (*abhāva*), like form (*rūpa*) and other phenomena, can also act as a cause to produce consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth, then one must likewise admit that non-existence is an effect; for no distinguishing cause for such a difference can be found.
By what reasoning is a non-existent phenomenon (*abhāva*) a cause but not an effect?
Furthermore, it is observed that existent phenomena are preceded by [other] existents; this is universally established in the world as being an effect that has a cause.

In your own doctrine, cessation (*nirodha*) is likewise preceded by conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), for it must be preceded by conditioned phenomena before it can be non-existent. How then can you not admit that it is an effect which possesses a cause?
Furthermore, since phenomena have no cause, it must be admitted that they are eternal; if cessation were eternal, phenomena would never arise.
If you argue that since cessation is non-existent and thus lacks a substantial entity, how can it produce a result?
If it lacks an intrinsic nature, how could it serve as a cause to produce consciousness and so forth?
Furthermore, one should not deny that it possesses the characteristics of a conditioned phenomenon; just as you accept its existence [as a cause], you must likewise accept these characteristics.

Furthermore, the Dārṣṭāntikas are able to give rise to heterodox views and provide explanations of principles never before heard, asserting that the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are both arising and non-existence; if this were so, then the threefold enumeration would not be established.

That is to say, conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) receive the name "arising" (utpāda) when they acquire their own essence; whereas exhaustion (kṣaya) and change (anyathātva) both consist in the absence of that essence. It is not the case that there is some slight difference between a subsequent moment and the preceding one due to a cause, as has already been argued above.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arise in such a manner, for this would lead to the same [absurd] consequence and result in a great error.
That is to say, the arising of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) would likewise be without cause, because you maintain that all conditioned phenomena are exactly like this.

Therefore, since the principle that this "otherness" lacks intrinsic nature is established, it would follow that one should take non-existence as the characteristic of existence; however, since this cannot be admitted, destruction does not depend upon a cause.
Therefore, I provide this explanation herein:
there exists the cessation of phenomena that does not depend on adventitious causes.
Since it does not depend on adventitious causes, it ceases immediately upon arising.
If it did not cease at the beginning, it would likewise not cease at the end, because the primary causes for the later and the earlier moments are equal.
Since we observe that the later moments come to an end, we know that each preceding moment ceases moment by moment.
If one were to say this is not so, it is because it is observed in the world.

That is to say, we observe in the world that fuel and the like first exist, but when they subsequently encounter a contingent cause such as fire, they reach a state of extinction and non-existence, for they are no longer seen.
There is certainly no other means of valid cognition that surpasses direct perception; therefore, it is not the case that the cessation of all phenomena does not depend on adventitious causes.
Should this not be understood in the same way as the ringing of a bell or the flame of a lamp?

Just as with sound and flame, although they are separated from the wind of the hand, they perish moment by moment due to their primary causes; yet because the wind of the hand no longer conjoins with them, they do not arise again, and subsequently, the sound and flame can no longer be perceived.

In this way, fuel and the like are extinguished moment by moment due to a primary cause of cessation; subsequently, when they come into contact with fire, they do not require any further cause at the stage of extinction, because they no longer arise and can no longer be perceived.
Therefore, this meaning is established by inference (*anumāna*), not attained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
What is meant by inference?
It means that [the self] must arise [from causes], because there is no such thing as causelessness.

Regarding conditioned phenomena that do not arise without seeing or depending upon the two conditions of guest and host—namely, the *kalala*, the sprout, a wall, consciousness, and so forth—they necessarily depend on external conditions such as semen and blood, water and soil, or roots for assistance before they can arise.
If conditioned phenomena were to perish only by depending on external causes such as fuel, then they would all have to perish only after waiting for such external causes, just as they arise.

However, we observe in the world that cognitions, flames, and sounds perish through their own primary causes without depending on external causes; therefore, the cessation of all conditioned formations does not depend upon external causes.
Therefore, all conditioned phenomena perish as soon as they have arisen; because the cause of their destruction is ever-present, the principle of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhanga*) is established.

Some maintain that consciousness and sound perish after their causes have ceased; others maintain that even the extinction of a lamp’s flame persists due to an unconditioned cause; still others maintain that at the time of a flame's extinction, it is due to the power of merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*). All of these views are irrational.
Why is this? Because a dharma that has not yet arisen lacks functional capacity.
However, one should not say that it is because the two do not coexist, for such an objection would invite the censure of others who would say:
Although two things do not coexist, you admit that a preceding dharma serves as the cause for the arising of a subsequent one;
yet although two things do not occur simultaneously, why do you not admit that the preceding cause perishes after [the effect has arisen]?
A Proponent of Present Existence (Sattvavādin) ought to answer according to reason:
The preceding serves as the cause for the subsequent because it exists with a substantial entity;
since the future lacks a substantial entity, how could it serve as the cause for the cessation of the preceding?
Therefore, when establishing a cause, one should speak in this manner.
Furthermore, by what cause does final cessation occur? If it is argued that it abides due to the cause of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
this is also illogical, because a phenomenon lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot function as a cause.
Neither dharma nor adharma can be the cause of cessation, because one observes flames flickering within empty caves.

Furthermore, since one could conceive of such a cause existing within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), they would not need to depend further on fire or other causes for cessation; therefore, one should not maintain the position that this constitutes a causal principle.

Furthermore, if the destruction of fuel and so forth were caused by contact with fire, and if within the process of transformation through heating there were inferior, middling, and superior stages, then the very essence of the cause of production would necessarily become the cause of destruction.

Why is this so? It is because through contact with fire, wood and other substances undergo transformation through heating; as the middle and superior degrees of heating arise, the lower and middle degrees of heating perish. Thus, the very entity that serves as the cause of arising would have to become the cause of perishing.
However, it is not logically tenable that this phenomenon exists because of its counterpart, and then becomes non-existent because of that same counterpart.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because the flame arises without remaining stable, this is also illogical; for since their essential natures are not distinct, there is no definitive principle by which one could serve as the cause for both arising and cessation.
Furthermore, while one might reasonably assume a difference between the causes of production and cessation within the arising of distinct flames,

how can one conceive of a difference between the causes of production and cessation in the process where firewood and other substances undergo transformation through contact with ash, snow, vinegar, the sun, earth, or water?
If that is so, when we observe water boiling away until it is exhausted, what function does the conjunction with fire perform therein?

Through the conjunction with adventitious fire, the primary fire element increases; as the fire element gradually grows, it causes the mass of water to become the cause for increasingly inferior states of water in subsequent moments, because fire and the nature of water are mutually antagonistic.
Up until the final moment, it can no longer produce a subsequent [moment]; this is what is meant by fire performing its function within the process.
Therefore, the cessation of all phenomena does not depend on external conditions; rather, it occurs solely through the primary cause that brings about the cessation of those phenomena.
By means of such logical proofs, the principle of momentary destruction is established; therefore, it is known that the body certainly possesses no movement.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 33; *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 34.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Two of Chapter Four: Investigation of Karma. Within the True Dharma, there are those who speak as follows:
Since the body, mountains, and so forth endure for a long time without perishing, the Sūtra says:
"There is a certain class [of beings] whose bodies remain for ten years," and so on at length.
It further states that the *kalala* remains for seven days, and it also states that the earth-sustaining wind remains for one eon (*kalpa*).
From this, it is known that the body can endure for a long time; therefore, the principle that movement constitutes a manifest action (*vijñapti*) is established.

This argument is incorrect. Furthermore, since they themselves admit that all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇika*), this proves what they do not accept: the principle that the body, mountains, and so forth are also momentary. One should state it thus:
"The body is momentary, because its transformations are seen to follow those of the mind and its concomitants."

That is to say, when one perceives the characteristics of the body during the arising of suffering, pleasure, desire, hatred, and so forth, [the body] transforms in accordance with the mind and its associates; since the body undergoes transformation as it follows the mind and its associates—which are phenomena that perish moment by moment—the principle of momentary destruction is established.

Furthermore, because the body and the mind share the same security and peril: since the body is momentary and is appropriated by the mind, they must necessarily share the same security and peril; for as long as consciousness continues to abide within the body, it remains intact, but if consciousness departs from the body, it immediately decays and perishes.
Since it shares the same fate as the mind that perishes moment by moment, the body must likewise perish moment by moment, just like the mind.
Furthermore, the body is taught to be like consciousness; as the Sūtra says:
"This mind, intellect, and consciousness arise differently and cease differently from moment (kṣaṇa), lava, and muhūrta."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The body undergoes aging, decay, and exhaustion at each respective moment and stage.
Another sutra says:
"O Bhikṣus! All conditioned phenomena have no abiding; they swiftly return to destruction and cessation.
Furthermore, he said:
"O Bhikṣus! All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are like illusions; they increase or decrease, remaining only briefly before ceasing.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"O Māṇavaka! From the night of entering the womb until old age, all things perpetually and swiftly pass away; they neither abide nor turn back.
By such sūtras as these, it is established that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), and there is no principle for their long-term persistence.
As for the term "abiding," it is merely a conventional designation applied to the similar continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and thus there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, there are sūtras that state the mind abides, such as when it says:
"The mind abides and cannot be shifted."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The mind shifts from the first dhyāna into the second dhyāna, and so forth.
It also says:
When the mind is disciplined, it is able to abide in the higher [states].
Furthermore, because it is metaphorically designated as "feeling" (*vedanā*) while abiding for a long duration within the continuum after having arisen from suffering and so forth;

and although they admit that the lunar disk remains for an eon, it is still metaphorically designated as "new"—one must not, on account of such a metaphorical designation, insist that it exists as a substantial reality.
Furthermore, since characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are distinct, the principle that their substances (svabhāva) are different is established.

Characteristics cannot be distinct within a single substance, for we observe that characteristics are distinct only when substances are different, such as the dewlap found in an ox and the curling hair found in a horse.
Within a single continuum, since their characteristics are distinct, this proves that their essential natures must necessarily differ.
Although the manifest color of milk and curd may be identical, because they function differently, they must necessarily possess different essences.
That is to say, since two manifest colors and the tastes of sweet and sour coexist, their substances must necessarily be distinct at different times.

The body should be understood in the same way; since its characteristics differ between earlier and later stages, one can infer from this that the entire collection of elements constituting the body is distinct at each successive moment.
Therefore, the principle that [conditioned phenomena] perish moment by moment is thoroughly established.
Since all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) perish moment by moment, how is it that the principle of the ripening of karmic results (*karmaphala*) is established?
How is it not established?
Because they do not coincide.
That is to say, it has never been observed that a seed, once its substance has already perished, can still produce a sprout; nor is this even accepted [as a tenet].
However, it is not the case that all karmas, like a seed producing a sprout, bestow their maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) at the very moment of their own cessation.
Furthermore, that which is non-existent cannot function as a cause; therefore, there would be no ripening of the results of karma.
This is the fault of their school.
What is meant by "their school"?
This refers to the Dārṣṭāntika school.
Therefore, that school asserts:
"Just as the principle of the ripening and fruition of external seeds is established, so too should one understand the ripening and fruition of karma."

This means that just as an external seed, having encountered specific conditions, acts as a direct and transmitted cause to produce a fruit and then ceases; by virtue of this, various phenomena with distinct characteristics—such as roots, sprouts, stalks, branches, and leaves—subsequently arise. Although their substance does not persist, they continue in a succession until, at the final stage, they again encounter specific conditions and are then able to act as causes to produce their own fruit.

In this way, these various karmas, acting as direct and transmitted causes within the continuum, have already perished after producing their results. Consequently, within one's own subsequent continuum, there arises a phenomenon characterized by distinct states; although its substance does not endure, it evolves through the continuum, and only upon encountering specific conditions at the final stage is it able to act as a cause to produce its own result.

Although those external seeds do not directly act as the cause for the production of their own fruit, they do so through a successive series; likewise, these various karmas do not directly act as the cause for the production of their own fruit, yet they do so through the power of a successive series. Thus, the principle of the continuity of internal and external causes and effects is the same.

The "external" refers to seeds, roots, sprouts, and so forth; their non-interruption is called "continuity. As for the "internal" continuity of phenomena, it refers to the mind of preceding and succeeding moments being constantly uninterrupted; therefore, the fault criticized by the non-Buddhists does not apply.

Now, upon examining that explanation, everything may be accepted as plausible: namely, if one were to say only that [the self] exists in the present, the principle of its continuity and successive transition could be established.
However, since that principle is not established, it is merely words.
That [position] is not logically tenable, as has already been explained elsewhere.
Even if one were to grant that the principle of a successive continuum is established, it should not follow the logic of a seed and its fruit.
We observe that seeds and the like must produce their fruits through a continuous succession that is necessarily uninterrupted.
The mind can produce effects, yet its continuity is subject to interruption.

Therefore, the analogy of the seed and the fruit lacks the power of proof for the opponent's tenet regarding the actualization of karma and its results; this is because, as previously argued, when one enters the meditative attainments of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), the mind and its concomitants do not function.

Furthermore, it is said that because mental formations (*manasaḥ saṃskārāḥ*) cease therein, the single continuity of karma—which persists without interruption until the fruit is reached—does not exist.

That school admits only volition (*cetanā*) as real karma; however, this [volition] is merely the increase of functional capacity (*vṛddhi-śakti*), which has already been refuted elsewhere in the context of the theories of *anuśaya*, *vāsanā*, and *bīja*.
Therefore, the external opponent objects:
"The teaching of the ripening of karma by one who provides no analogy is like the principle of a seed producing its fruit; this constitutes a valid objection. [To this we reply:

It has already been established that within the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), the Abhidharma explains that the continuity of the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) is uninterrupted and that its substantial entity (*dravya*) truly exists.
Thus, this acquisition (*prāpti*) is said to constitute the substance of the continuum (*saṃtati*).

If it is argued that since the substance of acquisition is distinct from the fruit of karma, it should not be called the "continuum of karma," this objection is irrational; for [the acquisition] is the fruit of a single body, and "body" and "continuum" have the same meaning.
Furthermore, just as it is with the seeds of karma, so it is with the acquisition of karma; thus, the continuity of karma is without interruption.
Therefore, in our school, the way karmic fruits arise and respond is identical to that of seeds and their fruits, and there is no logical principle capable of obstructing this.

Although various karmas may undergo interruption, they are like seeds that have already perished: although their manifest activity has ceased, they possess a slight residual capacity to yield fruit, by virtue of which they are able to produce their own results at a later time.

Karma should also be understood in this same way; therefore, the Abhidharma school does not incur the fault of being identical to that [opposing] school. This will be established later: that which has already ceased still exists.

If it is argued that even so, there would still be the fault of one person performing an action and another receiving its fruit—since we do not admit a single agent who both acts and receives, as such a self-entity is held to be permanent—[we reply: [this is not the case].
This objection is not valid, because there are two kinds of difference.
Those who contemplate the principles state that difference is of two types: first, difference as distinct continuities; second, difference as distinct entities within a single continuity.
If the karmic cause produced by one distinct continuum must not have its fruit experienced by another continuum;
yet if the karmic cause is produced by a single continuum, what prevents its fruit from being experienced by that very same continuum?

How could it be otherwise? If distinct continua lack the capacity for performing actions and experiencing their results, then within a single continuum there would likewise be no such performance or experience.

If you argue that "distinct" refers to separate continua, whereas "different" refers to different entities within a single continuum—and that since these distinctions do not exist, the principle of one performing an action while another experiences its result does not apply—this too is unreasonable. This is because causes and effects may either be related or unrelated, just as a rice seed relates to a rice sprout but not to a barley sprout.

How could it be that because the two types—the rice seed and the sprouts of rice and barley—are distinct in essence and without differentiation, the rice seed is thereby made to be either equally related to or unrelated to both the rice and barley sprouts?
Although that rice seed is not distinct from the substance of the rice or barley sprout, it is causally connected to the rice sprout and not to the barley sprout.

In this same way, the principle of distinction between what is connected and what is not connected across the preceding and succeeding moments of one's own and others' continuums is established; therefore, within a single continuum, there is no fault of one person performing an action and another person experiencing its result.
Furthermore, the seed and its fruit are distinct; though the seed perishes long ago, it is observed to yield its fruit, which is not contradicted by reason.
The same applies to karma and its fruit: even though they are distinct, what fault is there in this?
Furthermore, it is accepted that within a single continuum, a cause at one time may produce an effect at another time without fault.

However, if there were different continua, such that a cause at one time produced an effect in a different continuum at another time, this would indeed entail a fault. Thus, is it not clear that there is a distinction between the presence or absence of cause and effect within a single or different continua?

Furthermore, it is like the succession of flames when a village is burned. For example, suppose someone wishes to set fire to another village; having taken fire, they burn a small portion of another's thatched hut, and as the flames continue in succession, they eventually burn everything until the houses of the entire village have all been reduced to ashes.
The villagers captured him and beat him, ordering him to pay restitution. He pleaded his innocence, saying:
"After I had burned a small portion of a house with a little fire, my fire was immediately extinguished; therefore, I should only have to pay for a handful of grass."
If he clears himself in this manner, how can he be established as being free from fault?

The wise should know that although the fire that burns an entire village arises through a continuous succession starting from the initial spark, the person is nonetheless guilty of the offense of burning the whole village.

Thus, one should understand that all fruits produced by the transformation of the continuity of these aggregates arise through a successive causal process originating from the initial aggregate. Therefore, although the karma and its supporting aggregates have long since ceased and passed away, there is no logical fault in the production of those fruits within subsequent aggregates.
It is observed that once the cause has ceased, the resultant phenomenon arises.
Why then do you not see this in the case of seeds and sprouts?
