For instance, one observes in the world that when the sourness of a citron undergoes a continuous transformation until the fruit ripens, although the causal sourness is no longer present, the resultant sourness arises. One should know that the principle governing karmic results is likewise the same.
The meaning of momentary destruction is established, as there is the experiencing of the fruition of karma; therefore, this is well-spoken.
Since all conditioned phenomena possess momentariness, there can be no actual movement. If this is so, why is it that in the world we perceive the movement of the body at times?

The power of conditions such as desire can cause the physical form to arise successively in different locations without interruption; those who do not investigate carefully give rise to overweening pride, claiming that there is a real entity present that can be perceived.

In actual observation, one does not perceive the rapid movement of the lunar disk; rather, at times, when clouds suddenly arise from another direction, one gives rise to overweening pride and claims to see the moon moving rapidly.
In this way, when the world perceives the body as rapidly turning, it means that all stationary objects appear to be rapidly revolving in the opposite direction.

Therefore, conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) possess no actual movement; because there is no movement, the principle that what is called "bodily intimation" (kāyavijñapti) is merely a distinction of shape is fully established.

This refers to a distinct type of shape produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that arise from an applied mind (*prayoga-citta*), which is non-abiding and not a result of a homogeneous flow (*nisyanda*); this shape does not depend on other visible colors (*varṇa*) as the cause for the arising of visual consciousness, and it is able to obscure the shapes produced by maturation (*vipākaja*) and those nurtured (*aupacayika*). Such a shape is called bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*).

It is not because of such qualities as being virtuous that the maturation-born [faculties] are severed when they are nourished; rather, it is like when the divine eye or ear manifests, the continuity of the other eye or ear faculties remains uninterrupted.

Others maintain that there arises a volitional mind (*prayoga-citta*) which, through a specific capacity within the aggregate of the body, acts as the cause for the body to arise in a different location immediately thereafter; this very cause of arising is termed "bodily intimation" (*kāya-vijñapti*).
If that were so, bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) would not be visible to the eye, because its specific force is nothing other than wind.
However, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) says:
"Shape is not substantially real; rather, when a collection of manifest colors (*varṇa*) arises predominantly in one direction, 'long color' is conventionally designated therein."

Based on this long color, one conventionally designates "short color" when it arises in small measure on one side of another aggregate of matter; one conventionally designates "square color" when it arises equally in great measure on all four sides; and one conventionally designates "circular color" when it arises pervasively in all directions. The remaining types of shape-color should be understood accordingly.

Just as when one sees a torch being moved rapidly and continuously in one direction, one calls it "long," and when seeing it move in a circle, one calls it a "circular" color; therefore, shape has no real existence as a distinct category of substantial matter.
If it were claimed that there exists a distinct category of shape-color as a real entity, then a single color would be apprehended by two sense organs.

That is to say, regarding the distinctions such as length within a collection of matter, both the eye seeing it and the body touching it could cognize it; consequently, this would entail the error of being apprehended by two sense organs.

It is logically impossible for the formless realm to be apprehended by two sense-faculties; however, just as one apprehends characteristics such as length based on the tangible, so too one might apprehend shape based on the manifest color. This reasoning is incorrect, because the characteristics perceived are distinct.
If on one hand only the manifestation of multiple births were [the basis], then there would be no distinction among the cognitions of their characteristics;
yet since there are distinct cognitions of "long" and "white," there must be a shape-color (saṃsthāna-rūpa) that exists separately from the manifestation itself.

It is observed that there are tangibles apprehended by the same sense organ which differ in their perceived characteristics; thus, they must differ in essence, as in the case of hardness and coldness, or warmth and hardness.
Likewise, although whiteness and length are apprehended by the same sense organ, they differ in their perceived characteristics; therefore, they must be distinct in essence.

Therefore, we know that as aggregated matter is analyzed and gradually diminished until it reaches a point where a perception of shape can still arise, there must necessarily be a cause for the arising of at least some degree of the perception of shape; it is logically certain that the atoms of shape-and-color (saṃsthāna-rūpa-paramāṇu) must still be present therein.

Because within a collection of matter (*rūpa-skandha*), only manifest color (*varṇa*) arises while shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) does not; therein, there is only the cognition of manifest color, not of shape.

It is like seeing colors such as light in the sky: if one were to claim that manifest color itself is what is called "shape," then the cognition of shape should also arise regarding manifest colors that lack spatial dimensions, since they are inseparable, just as heat is inseparable from the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*).
That analogy of the flame is incapable of proving [the point], because it can be figuratively applied elsewhere where it is already established.

That is to say, in other cases, when there are real causes such as length and roundness, which simultaneously and without interval are arranged in various directions and locations, the resulting material aggregate (rūpa-skandha) characterized by length and so forth is established as being conventionally recognized.

Therefore, regarding the colors of firebrands and the like, which shift uninterruptedly at different times and in different places, one conceptually posits "length," "roundness," and so forth as conventional designations; yet such things have never been observed. They are established neither in the conventional nor in the ultimate sense, and thus cannot be conventionally posited as objects apprehended by two sense faculties; this objection is also invalid, because length and the like are merely objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Since all conventional existents are merely objects perceived by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), as was previously established regarding their capacity to produce growth and so forth, the arrangement of atoms such as seeds is designated as "shape" (*saṃsthāna*).
This is apprehended by non-conceptual visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and cannot be apprehended by the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).

Such material forms are not understood in the same way that solidity, moisture, and so forth are perceived by relying on the body faculty; for the perception of length, shortness, and so forth does not occur in that manner.
This is because one cannot perceive characteristics such as length and shortness at the very moment solidity and moisture are perceived in the dark, nor can one do so immediately thereafter.

When many instances of contact arise in a single location, one must first discern the contact based on the gateway of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) before being able to infer the concomitance with contact.

This refers to the specific characteristics and distinctions of form-colors apprehended by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as it is drawn along by visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*); just as when seeing the color of fire or the fragrance of flowers, one is able to recollect the concomitant tactile sensation of fire or the color of the flower.

It is observed that visual consciousness, as the case may be, sometimes simultaneously cognizes both shape (*saṃsthāna*) and color (*varṇa*). Mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), however, distinguishes them sequentially without fixed simultaneity. Since color and shape are both objects of apprehension for a single visual consciousness, yet mental consciousness distinguishes them at different times and their perceived characteristics differ, their essences are not the same; furthermore, shape is not tactile.
How could the body-faculty (kāyendriya) possibly apprehend the object that is shape?
Therefore, one should not raise the objection that it must be apprehended by two faculties.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) further states:
In all cases where two dharmas are necessarily inseparable, one can, by apprehending one, recollect the other.
Since tangibility and shape are not necessarily inseparable, how could the apprehension of tangibility allow for the certain recollection of shape?
This is also illogical, for it is observed in the world that within various aggregates of tangibles there is a determinate shape.

That is to say, although shape is not invariably present in every tangible, when many tangibles arise on one side, there is necessarily the color-form of length; when tangibles arise pervasively across all sides, there is necessarily the color-form of roundness; such categories should be understood accordingly.

Therefore, while there is a determination regarding the tangible in relation to the shape, there is no such determination regarding the tangible in relation to the color-aspect as there is for the shape; for when one perceives the tangible, one can recollect the shape, yet there is no tangible arrangement corresponding to such a color-aspect that is determined in the same way as the shape.

Furthermore, one may also experience the tactile sensation of smoke within the eyes or throat, or sometimes smell its fragrance with the nose; by means of these, one cognizes the visible color (varṇa) within the smoke. Thus, it follows that the visible color is apprehended by two sense organs and cannot exist as a real entity.

Furthermore, this case should be consistent with that one; that is to say, just as there is no fixed relation between heat and color, nor between white and fragrance, so too form cannot be known by means of touch, nor can fire-touch or flower-color be recollected through the perception of fire-color or flower-fragrance. Therefore, this does not refute the position that form has a distinct substantial entity separate from manifest color.

Furthermore, there is inferential evidence that shape is not substantially existent: all resistant, substantial matter must necessarily consist of real, distinct types of atoms (*paramāṇu*); however, there are no atoms designated as "long" and so forth. Therefore, "long" and so on are merely conceptually established within the specific arrangement of many such substances.

Has it not already been stated that based on the arrangement of the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) themselves, the distinctions among accumulated forms perceived by visual consciousness are conventionally designated as "long" and so forth?
Although this has been said, it is merely partisan talk, for the ultimate atoms of shape (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) are not established as real.

That is to say, if the individual atoms (*paramāṇu*) of shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) possessed their own established intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that could be accumulated, then such an arrangement could constitute length and so forth; however, the individual atoms of shape-color do not possess such established intrinsic characteristics.
Just as with various manifest colors (*varṇa*), how could there be accumulation or spatial arrangement?
How can the Venerable One accept that [such a thing] is established?
Manifest-color atoms (*varṇaparamāṇu*) are not subtle parts of shape (*saṃsthāna*).
Just as with various manifest colors (*varṇa*), there is no principle for individual atoms (*paramāṇu*) to arise in isolation.
Even if they were to arise in isolation, because they are extremely subtle, they would not be apprehended by the eye; it is only when they are accumulated that they can be apprehended by the eye.

It is established through direct cognition that there are atoms of visible color (*varṇa-paramāṇu*); it should likewise be so for atoms of shape (*saṃsthāna-paramāṇu*). How can you alone refuse to admit what is established by its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-siddha*)?
In all places where resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*) is accumulated, atoms are invariably found to exist.

Since the cognition of shape arises within the production of a differentiated aggregate of matter, it does not depend upon color (varṇa); just as the cognition of another color arises without depending on other colors, there must therefore certainly exist distinct atoms of shape, such as length and so forth, which possess seeds capable of producing them.

The claim that because the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the visible forms possess resistance (*sapratigha*), they must be accumulated to provisionally establish [dimensions] such as length, is also irrational; for it would follow that the atoms of odor and so forth should likewise be accumulated to constitute length and the like. This is because those atoms of odor and so forth also possess resistance, since "resistance" is defined solely by the fact that they cannot occupy the same location simultaneously.

If it is argued that the atoms of odor and so forth do not possess the fault of being identical to those [visible objects] because they are not visible, then since the atoms of manifest color (varṇa) also do not possess shape, how could they constitute length and so forth?
How is it known that the subtle entity is not shape?
As previously stated, this is because its characteristics are different and because the cognition of shape arises without depending on the cognition of color.

Furthermore, since there are instances where a collection of colors is perceived without seeing shape, the entity itself cannot be shape; for when many atoms are accumulated without obstruction and one possesses sight, it may happen that the shape is not seen. Therefore, one should know that distinct from visible color, there are atoms of the form-aggregate (saṃsthāna-rūpa) subsumed under the sphere of form (rūpāyatana). From the aggregation of these, conventional forms such as length and so forth are produced; thus, the subtle divisions of shape are not unestablished.
How can that which has shape be without parts?
Since an atom (paramāṇu) is partless, its substance ought not to have shape.
If that were so, one should also doubt the case of manifest color (varṇa): how can it be admitted that the substance of manifest color is resistant (sapratigha) while possessing partless atoms?

Since one has never perceived names or manifestations in those partless phenomena such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, just as the manifesting characteristic of a manifest atom (*rūpa-paramāṇu*) does not exist, so too there may be atoms of shape (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) that lack the characteristic of shape; what contradiction would this entail with ultimate reason?
Now, as for "manifest form" (varṇa-saṃsthāna), it refers to that which can manifest properties such as blue or white.
It is not the case that atoms (paramāṇu) possess manifest form; therefore, there is no manifest form [inherent in atoms].
If shape were a real entity distinct from manifest color, it should be perceived as clearly distinct from blue, yellow, and so forth.

Although each exists substantially, such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) that they cannot be known as having distinct clarity, just as when shadows, light, and so forth are mixed with other colors.

This means that because shadows, light, and the like arise in consciousness in conjunction with the earth and other elements, their individual characteristics are difficult to discern; yet, in their actual substance, they are not without distinction.
At night, when there is a bright moon shining upon a plastered wall, the clarity of the moon and the whiteness of the wall assist one another, so that both are clearly manifest.
Since their natures are distinct, why is it that neither the wise nor the foolish can simultaneously and clearly discern the difference between their characteristics?
Just as it is with that principle, so it is with shape and color.
If color and shape are intermingled such that they are difficult to distinguish, one should diligently seek their distinct characteristics through correct reasoning.
Although they arise in mutual intermingling with visible color (*varṇa*), that which serves as a boundary and supports the visible color within its vicinity is called shape (*saṃsthāna*).

Therefore, when the blue sphere is broken, the manifest color remains while the shape is destroyed; this is because the circular shape resides only at its periphery, so that when the blue sphere is broken, the circular shape is immediately extinguished. However, since the manifest blue color pervades the entire sphere, the manifest blue color still persists even after the circular shape has been destroyed.

Alternatively, because the substance of shape-color (saṃsthāna-rūpa) is not the substance of manifest-color (varṇa-rūpa), its distinct characteristic is not as easily discerned as those of blue or yellow.
Furthermore, because all manifest-colors are the substance of manifest-color, their distinct characteristics are easily known in relation to one another.

Since such shape-color (saṃsthāna-rūpa) is a physical form, its distinct characteristic is easily discerned from other shape-colors; thus, the difference between shape and manifest color (varṇa) as self-characteristics is fully established.

Furthermore, although manifest color and shape are within the same aggregate, their essential characteristics are definitively distinct, because when one is destroyed, the other is not, due to the difference in their contradictory causes.
It is not that their substance is without difference; rather, there can be distinction and destruction or non-destruction due to contradictory causes.

Furthermore, since there are distinctions such as "wholesome" (*kuśala*) within the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), it should not be the case that visible color (*varṇa-rūpa*) possesses the nature of being wholesome and so forth, as has already been argued previously; therefore, there exists a distinct shape (*saṃsthāna*).

If it is argued that there is an inherent distinction within manifestation itself—namely, that it either arises dependent upon the mind or independent of the mind—then it is already fully established that bodily action (kāyakarman) is substantially real; there is merely some confusion regarding its designation and conceptualization.

However, there is a form-base (*rūpāyatana*) that arises through applied thought (*prayoga-citta*), which occurs pervasively at the periphery of a mass of matter and is capable of demarcating and distinguishing manifest color (*varṇa*). Because this is not of the same nature as manifest color, the Abhidharmikas establish it under the name of "shape" (*saṃsthāna*); this is what is called bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karma*).
Even if it is said that [bodily intimation] is merely manifest, or if it is called something else, it is nonetheless established as a real existent bodily intimation.

If it is argued that it is not real because its characteristic as an action is not established, this reasoning is also incorrect, because its characteristic as an action is established in the same way as volition (*cetanā*).

Furthermore, shape and color—like water, earth, and wind—are distinct in their characteristics and clearly differentiated in their defining marks; how could any reasoning prevent them from having separate essences?

Moreover, shape must necessarily differ from visible color, because, like visible color, it gives rise to a different kind of craving and is separately taught as an aspect of impurity for the purpose of serving as its antidote.
Furthermore, there is authoritative scripture that proves the existence of distinct forms, as stated in a verse:
"There are coarse and subtle, short and long, pure and impure, and so forth.
Moreover, a sūtra says:
The facial features are dignified and majestic: neither short nor long, neither coarse nor fine, neither white nor black, but radiant, smooth, and soft.
It is not that there is no distinct entity such that it could be described as distinct.
Furthermore, if you negate both motion and shape, what do you Sautrāntikas posit as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)?
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) explains that school's position:
"Bodily intimation is indeed shape, though it is conventional and not substantial."

The intended meaning of such statements is difficult to discern: does it mean that length and other shapes are merely conventional and not real, or does it mean that length and so forth—just as in the case of seeds and atoms—are designated as "shape" and are thus merely conventional and not real?
If shapes such as length and so forth are merely conventional and not substantial, there is no contradiction with what the Abhidharmikas teach.

However, it is unreasonable to claim that when atoms such as seeds aggregate into shapes like length, these are called "shape" and are thus merely conventional and not substantial; for according to their own tenets, shape is formed by color (varṇa), and color is not conventional.

If it is argued that [color] is not real because it is not distinct from manifestation (*varṇa*), then this would be equivalent to the Sautrāntika theory of the destruction of dharmas, and one could not engage in debate with such a position.

However, if the intention is to say that it is not real because its shape (*saṃsthāna*) is not different from its manifestation, then since heat is not distinct from the fire element (*tejodhātu*), heat itself should also be unreal.

If you grant that shape is not distinct from color, then just as you maintain that there is no separate shape apart from the real color, you should likewise maintain that there is no separate shape apart from the conventional color; for you hold that it is precisely the color itself that is established as being long and so forth.
In that case, the Sautrāntika school should establish that length and so forth are neither real nor nominal; how then can you say they are merely nominal?

Furthermore, if the Sautrāntika tenet maintains that shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) has a basis and is grasped as a substance consisting of real atoms (*paramāṇu*), then upon what basis does the dispute arise with the masters of the Abhidharma, who also speak in this way?
Is this intended to show that the atom itself is the real entity grasped as the conventional designations of "long" and so forth, or is it not so?
It is not so, because this has already been established previously.
Alternatively, because within a manifest aggregate one does not perceive distinct characteristics of shape such as long or short, the statement made [by the opponent] is rendered useless.
Furthermore, if they establish a conventional form as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), what other dharma do they establish as bodily action (*kāyakarman*)?

They state that action established in dependence upon the body is bodily action; that is to say, the volition (*cetanā*) capable of variously moving the body proceeds by way of the door of the body, and is therefore called bodily action.
It should be understood that the establishment of distinct names for vocal and mental karma is likewise according to their respective applications.
If this is so, why does the Sūtra speak of two kinds of karma: first, the karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*), and second, the karma after having willed (*cetayitvā-karma*)?
He offers this explanation: the volition of reflection that arises during the preceding preparatory stage— namely, the thought,
"I shall perform such and such an action that ought to be done"—
is called the karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*).

Having already engaged in reflection, one gives rise to the volition of purposeful action; performing the task in accordance with what was previously reflected upon by moving the body or initiating speech is called "action after reflection.
In this context, is this intended to encompass all karma exhaustively, or does it encompass only a specific portion of differentiated karma?
Some say: "This includes all karma.
Others state as follows:
The claim that it does not include the untainted (*anāsrava*) is not consistent with the meaning of the Sūtra, for intentionality (*manas-karman*) should not be excluded here.

Specifically, there is the volition of deliberation (*cetanā*) which initiates the two types of bodily and vocal action, and the volition of execution (*kriyā-cetanā*) which actually sets in motion the two types of bodily and vocal action; since both of these operate through the gateways of body and speech, they should both be included within bodily and vocal karma.
If this is so, what is it that is called "mental action" (manas-karman) here?

If you maintain that volition (cetanā) which operates through the two gateways of body and speech is also partially designated as mental action, then there would be the fault of confusion in the classification of actions.

Even if one were to grant that the volition (*cetanā*) which initiates bodily and vocal action for the sake of desire is of the nature of mental karma (*manaskarma*), it still does not encompass all forms of karma within this context. This is because there exist infinite outflowing (*sāsrava*) mental karmas that do not operate through the doors of body and speech, and none of these are included in this sutra.

Furthermore, it certainly does not include the various volitions (*cetanā*) arising from eye-contact and so forth, because those volitions are not subsumed under the two types of volition previously mentioned: that of reflection (*manasikāra*) and that of activity (*kṛtya*).

If it is claimed that the "volitional karma" (*cetanā-karman*) taught in this sutra exhaustively encompasses all mental karma (*manas-karman*), and that once volition has been mentioned, it is said to encompass all volitions proceeding through the two doors of body and speech, this is not the intended meaning of what this sutra should have taught.

Even granting that all these are indeed spoken of in this sutra, if one intends to incite the two types of volition—those arising from body and speech—under which category of karma would they be subsumed?
If they were subsumed under the category of mental karma (*cetanā-karma*), this would necessarily be logically untenable.

If it is accepted that volition (cetanā) is subsumed under the category of karma because it operates in dependence on body and speech when it is being contemplated, then the same should apply to the others as well; in that case, one should speak of only "one karma of volition. Furthermore, this would result in the fault of confusing the categories of karma, since mental karma (manas-karma) also operates in dependence on body and speech.

If it is argued that the volition which initiates bodily and vocal actions arises from the desire to move them, yet this volition does not depend on the body or speech for its operation, then the volition arising toward other objects would likewise not depend on those objects, as there is no difference in the underlying cause.
In that case, mental action (*manas-karman*) would not depend upon its object; however, this is not what is accepted, and thus the reasoning is untenable.

If it is argued that this is like [the case where] because it proceeds through the doors of body and speech, it is designated as "depending on body and speech" even though it is not the action of body or speech—this would result in a fault regarding mental action, for such a distinction could likewise be applied to it.

It is also illogical for [the action] subsequent to volition (*cetayitvā-karman*) to be subsumed under volition itself, because the term "subsequent to volition" is used only as a subsequent expression.
Furthermore, that which is the object of volition cannot be called "volition," because the meaning and the name do not correspond.
Furthermore, you Sautrāntikas claim that when various ṛṣis kill living beings out of mental indignation, under which category of karma does this fall?

Is it bodily karma or mental karma? However, in this case, there would be no distinction between the two types of volition (*cetanā*)—the volition that initiates the action and the volition that constitutes the action itself—since the very act of intending would be identical to the performance of the deed. Consequently, one could not avoid the fault of the confusion of karmic categories.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"For those who practice asceticism, there are distinct differences in the actions of body, speech, and mind.

Therefore, one must necessarily admit that within this [state], there exists an action of volition (*cetanā*) that operates by means of the body, because it simultaneously kills many beings through its association with that [volition].
Furthermore, since the act of killing is subsumed under bodily action (*kāyakarman*), the Blessed One should have stated that bodily action is the most grievous among all actions.
Therefore, the Sautrāntika school reflects upon and establishes the nature of all actions.

Furthermore, there is logical proof that karma is not merely volition (*cetanā*): for if one were to incur the immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) and other such offenses as soon as the volition arises with the desire to kill one's father and so forth, it would follow that the offense has already been committed at that very moment.

If it is argued that for an offense to be incurred one must move the body, and thus there is no fault because the body has not yet moved, then it follows that the principle of bodily action (*kāyakarman*) exists apart from volition (*cetanā*).
This is because bodily action—such as the offense of killing—is only established when there is movement of the body;
if the body does not move, even if an evil volition arises, the offense is not yet established.

Is this not like the school that maintains there is a distinct bodily karma (*kāyakarman*), according to which the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) and so forth are not established apart from an evil volition (*cetanā*)?
In the same way, although it is admitted that volition alone is karma, this offense is not established apart from the movement of the body.
This example is not equivalent.

Why is this so? Because in the Abhidharma school, both bodily and vocal karma constitute immediate retribution (ānantarya) only when produced by an evil volition (cetanā). If there is no evil volition, this karma does not arise; therefore, the sinful karma of the body depends upon an evil volition for its completion.

The school that maintains that karma consists solely of volition (cetanā) asserts that the arising of volitional karma does not depend on body or speech; rather, at the very moment volition arises, bodily karma is already established—so why wait for physical movement?

Furthermore, according to the Abhidharma school, because the motivating cause (hetu-samutthāna) possesses distinctions such as being wholesome and so forth, the bodily and vocal actions it initiates likewise possess the nature of being wholesome and so forth. Thus, one may say that it is necessarily due to the distinctions of volition that bodily karma becomes an immediate transgression (ānantarya-karma) or the like.

This is not the Sautrāntika position; for they maintain that when the karma of volition (*cetanā*) arises, it only becomes wholesome or unwholesome upon depending on body and speech, since they assert that body and speech are exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*). How, then, can it be said that the karma of volition must depend on moving the body in order to constitute an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*) and so forth?
Therefore, citing this example does not preclude that fault.

If it is argued that—just as in the thesis that the eye-faculty sees, where although the arising of the eye-faculty does not depend on the visual consciousness, the function of seeing form is only accomplished by depending on consciousness—likewise, the statement "only volition is karma" means that although the arising of unwholesome volition does not depend on the body, it nonetheless depends on the immediate preparation for bodily movement.
This, too, is not a valid analogy. Why is this so?

Because consciousness and the sense organ arise simultaneously, and it is admitted that the sense organ produces its superior function by means of consciousness; therefore, although the arising of the eye-organ does not depend on consciousness, the function of seeing visible forms is only established when it depends upon consciousness.

However, that evil volition must first arise before it can subsequently have the function of moving the body; it is not the case that at the moment the volition arises, a subsequent movement of the body causes even a slight differentiation in the operation of the preceding volition.
Furthermore, this attempted defense is logically untenable, because there is no phenomenon that can cause other phenomena to give rise to superior functional activity.
Moreover, there is authoritative scripture that refutes the Sautrāntika school’s formulation of the principles of karma, as stated in a sūtra:
"That which was sought after at night is manifested through bodily and vocal intimation during the day."

It is not the case that what is described here as "informative" (*vijñapti*) refers to volition (*cetanā*); for in other sūtras, informative action is said to be karma itself. Thus, another sūtra states:
"The informative action of those who crave is, in its essence, karma."
Furthermore, the Buddha instructed Rāhula, saying:
"If you perform actions through body or speech, regarding those very actions of body and speech that you have performed, you should diligently and repeatedly examine them with thorough scrutiny."
Since volition does not have the body and speech as its essence, how could it be said that "action created by volition" is called "action created by body and speech"?
Therefore, one should understand that the Sūtra itself states that the two manifest forms of body and speech constitute bodily and vocal action.

One should not interpret the meaning of this sūtra in such a way; when this sūtra states that "this karma is created by means of body and speech," it means that karma is created by volition (cetanā) based on the body and based on speech—it does not mean that there is such a thing as [intrinsic] karma in those [physical or vocal] forms themselves.
Why is this so? Because it has never been stated as such, nor has it been refuted.

That is to say, if there were a sūtra that had previously stated: "The various karmas produced by volition (cetanā) based on body and speech are called bodily and vocal karma, but they are not themselves the body or speech. [Yet no such sūtra exists.]

Furthermore, if there were a sūtra that negates the informative expressions (*vijñapti*) of body and speech as being the very nature of the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—it might be permissible to apply such undifferentiated language to this case and provide a differentiated interpretation based on that sūtra;
however, there has never been such a statement anywhere.

Furthermore, my citation of the sūtras does not contradict correct reasoning; therefore, their position is irrational. By frequently interpreting various sūtras according to their own personal biases, they cause them to deviate from their true meaning. Consequently, they should rightly be called "Masters of the School that Corrupts the Sūtras" (*Sūtrabheda-vādin*), for they do not take the definitive sūtras (*nītārtha-sūtra*) as the authoritative standard.
Furthermore, a verse in the Gāthās says:
"Due to coarseness and wickedness within the mind, One moves the body and utters speech externally;
Because of this, one can experience suffering, And by reversing this, one invites happiness."
In this context, it is explained that volition (*cetanā*) and the informative acts of body and speech (*kāya-vāk-vijñapti*) have the capacity to produce desirable or undesirable fruits.
Furthermore, another sutra states:

"Whatever bodily, verbal, and mental actions belong to those with wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), all of them can produce undesirable fruits; those that produce desirable fruits are the opposite of this."
From this it is proven that what is stated in the verse— namely,

that "due to the two manifest actions of body and speech, one experiences desirable and undesirable fruits"— is precisely what the Sūtra means when it says that bodily and vocal karma can produce desirable and undesirable fruits.

This interpretation is also untenable; for it is claimed that bodily and vocal intensions (*cetanā*) based on the body and speech are called bodily and vocal informative action (*vijñapti*), since he himself states that shape (*saṃsthāna*) constitutes bodily informative action, and as a designation, it is not substantial.
However, an intension ought not to be something that is merely a shape and lacks substantiality.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Rising to meet [the teacher], joining the palms, and performing respectful prostrations constitute bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti*).
Another sutra further says:
Manifest action (*vijñapti*) is itself karma.

By this it is proven that the specific shapes of the hands and other limbs, which are successively initiated by the intention to act (*cetanā*) and so forth, are called bodily manifest action (*kāya-vijñapti*), and are thus bodily karma (*kāya-karman*).
Therefore, the Abhidharma school establishes bodily and vocal karma; this accords with the teachings and conforms to reason, and is free from the fault of confusion.
By this, the logic of the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) explained here is established.
However, regarding this, there are differences among those who recite it; that is to say, some reciters make this recitation:
Alternatively, there are material aggregates that can be perceived solely by their visible color (*varṇa*).

These refer to things such as blue and so forth, or shadows and so forth—aggregates of derived matter produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)—because within them visible color predominates, while other qualities are not invariably apprehended; thus, only visible color can be perceived.

Regarding "the single manifestation in space": this refers to seeing Mount Sumeru within the sky as a purely uniform color. How could it be that while the colors of reflections and so forth possess various manifestations, one speaks of this [mountain] alone as having a single manifestation?

Not so. Why? Because colors such as reflections are mixed with the manifest colors of the earth and other elements to such an extent that they are difficult to distinguish and cannot be seen separately; it is on the basis of this sense of impurity that one says the color is not uniform.
This matter of the space-element has no distinct basis; because it is purely visible, it is called "one manifest color" (*ekavarṇa*).

Alternatively, there are material aggregates where only shape can be discerned—namely, the moving aggregate produced by the great elements co-arising with bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*). Because its nature as a continuous dharma is conceptually established through the apprehension of movement, its substance is not real.

However, within the aggregate of the body, the various distinctions of shape among the collection of real entities—which are produced by mental factors (*caitta*) as their outflow (*niṣyanda*) and consist of the great elements (*mahābhūta*)—are called bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*).

Alternatively, there are aggregates of matter where both [shape and color] are simultaneously discernible; that is to say, the aforementioned other aggregates of shape and color, because within such an aggregate, one cannot be perceived apart from the other.
Therefore, regarding this point, the objection raised by the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika)—as to how a single entity could possess two natures—is not established, for it is not what we accept.

Furthermore, shape and color are mutually dependent and associated, just as it is said that "a crane is not a banner" or "a banner is not a crow"; in these cases, both shape and color are equally perceptible.
Alternatively, there are material aggregates that are neither [visible nor tangible], such as odors, tastes, and so forth, as well as the aggregate of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Other reciters read it thus: "Alternatively, there are material aggregates consisting solely of visible form and so forth."
The first phrase refers to the collection of light and darkness; these very distinctions are designated as shadow and glare.
The second phrase is as previously explained.

The third phrase refers to the collection of visible forms not included within the two aforementioned phrases; for even the collection of colors such as blue and so forth possesses distinctions of shape and dimension, such as length and so on, which are perceptible to the eye.
The fourth phrase is also as previously explained. One might ask:
"Since shadows and the like also possess distinct dimensions and shapes that can be clearly perceived, should they not be termed 'coexistent'?

To this, it is said: within the aggregation of shadows and the like, there is no shape, because they are dispersed and insubstantial; thus, when other extremely obstructive objects enter into them, the shadows are not destroyed.
We observe in the world that when a mass of form possessing extreme resistance is assembled, other objects of extreme resistance entering into it cause it to be destroyed.
This is not the case for masses such as shadows; therefore, there is no form within them.
Furthermore, in those dense aggregates of matter characterized by extreme resistance, the material atoms (paramāṇu) are arranged in a surrounding configuration.
Because such an aggregate is maintained by its shape, there are consequently discernible boundaries and interstices.

It is not that within the collection of colors such as a shadow there is a formal grasping (saṃsthāna-parigraha) like that of a composite object, because no independent movement or oscillation is observed therein.
However, when dimensions such as length appear clearly and perceptibly, this is due to their conformity with the primary substance (mūla-dravya).
If that were so, there should be no images within mirrors and the like; for while a shadow has no form, its form can be perceived because it follows the nature of its source.
Likewise, these various images should have no manifest color (*varṇa*), yet manifest color should be perceivable because it follows the nature of its source.
Furthermore, reflections do not have shape-and-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) as their essence; although they appear to have height and depth, they are like paintings because they lack [substantiality].
Just as they follow their original substance and their support, shape-and-color, though non-existent, appears as if it were present.
Manifest color (*varṇa*) should likewise be so: appearing as if existent but actually non-existent.

Thus, a reflection is neither shape (*saṃsthāna*) nor does it have manifest color as its essence. A reflection is not a manifest color because, like a shadow, its shape is non-existent, and because the various reflections that follow [their causes] are not determinate; for a reflection follows both its material cause (*upādāna*) and its basis (*āśraya*).
That is to say, reflections manifest according to their shape and color; they appear either in accordance with their support (*āśraya*) or in accordance with their original object (*bimba*).

Shadows, however, never possess the principle of conforming to the original object, nor does shape possess the property of conforming to its support. That which serves as the locus of residence is called the "support"; therefore, there is no commonality between a reflection and a shadow.

If it is argued that because the reflection and the shadow share the same sense of "following," the reflection must lack substantial reality, this reasoning is also incorrect; for although the sense of "following" is the same, they are perceived as distinct.

This means that although reflections and shadows share the same form as their respective sources, a reflection also possesses height and depth according to its source, whereas a shadow merely possesses a coarse dimension according to its source. While they are similar in the sense of following the source regarding this coarse dimension, the dimension of the reflection is determined by the source, whereas the shadow is not necessarily identical in dimension to the source, for it may be larger, smaller, or even equal to it.

Although the meaning of "following" is the same for both the image and the reflection, it is only the reflection that lacks shape while the image does not lack color; for if color were also absent, there would be no following.

That is to say, the color of the reflection possesses its own manifestation (*prabhāsa*). Since this reflection takes manifested color as its essence, it is said that its shape follows the substance [of the original object], which is free from error.

If the substance of the reflection is neither shape nor manifest color, then since there would be no substance of the reflection, how could one say that the reflection conforms to its original object?

Alternatively, because it conforms to its support, the reflection must necessarily consist only of manifest color. This is because the boundaries of shape and form must depend on extreme resistance (impedance), whereas the boundaries of manifest color depend solely on the characteristics of manifest color. Therefore, reflections, paintings, and the like have no shape.

By this, the objection regarding the identity of the reflected image and its form is already refuted; for although their shapes correspond to the objects, they are like heights and depths which can be perceived as forms yet do not truly exist, since it was previously stated that visible shape (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) is also apprehended through inference (*anumāna*).
Among these, shape (saṃsthāna) is not as it is apprehended because its apprehension is indeterminate; thus, it may be said to be non-existent.
Regarding color (varṇa), its apprehension is not indeterminate in its non-existence, as its apprehension is the same as that of other colors; therefore, the reflection has only color as its essence.

If that were so, then just as with the color and shape of a reflected image—wherein the objects are distinct yet there is no equality of objects—it should likewise follow that the manifest color of the image and the shape of the shadow, though their objects are distinct, should also lack such equality of objects.
This analogy is not valid, as has already been stated.
That is to say, if the reflected image lacks manifest color (*varṇa*), then according to that principle, it should also lack [the quality of] conformity.

Furthermore, for what reason do you not accept this: just as the shadow and the reflection are identical in their conformity to the shape, yet there is no lack of distinction within that conformity, so too the manifest color of the reflection and the shape of the shadow, while identical in their conformity to the principle, are nonetheless distinct.
Should one not raise this objection here:
"Just as in shadows and the like, although there is no shape or color (*saṃsthāna-varṇa*), there is nonetheless a manifest dimension (*parimāṇa*) in the visible color (*varṇa*);
so too, in these dense agglomerations of matter that are extremely resistant, there should be only visible color without shape."
This objection is not valid. If even those dense aggregates of matter that are extremely obstructive were devoid of shape, then reflections would likewise lack any discernible dimensions.

When artisans such as painters use various manifest colors to intersperse with other manifest colors and imitate the shapes of elevations and depressions in an original object, there is in reality no such elevation or depression within the painting itself.

If all aggregated masses of matter that are extremely resistant were likewise devoid of actual shape and possessed only visible color, then—just as in the case of paintings where one visible color is juxtaposed with another to create the semblance of shape while actually lacking any elevation or depression therein—they would merely appear to have shape by depending on the arrangement of other visible colors.

However, in the case of dense material aggregates (*rūpa-skandha*) that possess extreme resistance, one can perceive actual dimensions such as height and so forth, which exist in themselves without depending on other manifest colors (*varṇa*) to distinguish them from intervening manifest colors. From this, it is proven that these dense aggregates possess a real shape (*saṃsthāna*) distinct from manifest colors; it is by virtue of this that reflections, paintings, and the like, though lacking shape-color, appear to possess shape.
Therefore, that statement does not constitute a valid objection.
Is it not the case that, just as a distinct image produced from a non-material substance—having a form as its essence—may appear and be perceived, yet lacks any real form?
In this way, reflections should arise from clusters of atoms that possess extreme resistance but lack shape as their substance;

they would have color but no shape, yet a shape could still be perceived. This, however, is irrational, because the image produced according to the shape of the original object appears as if it possessed shape, and the image arising from that [object] must likewise be perceivable as having a certain spatial dimension; this is necessarily so by principle.

The image that arises from that which lacks physical form manifests; the distinct image produced therein manifests only as being formless. Therefore, the image is formless, having manifestation alone as its essence.

By means of such analysis through question and answer, the thesis that the reflection is the essence of the image is already refuted, because the image and the reflection do not share the same characteristics.
While a reflection possesses various characteristics according to its original substance, an image does not; therefore, they are not analogous phenomena.
Furthermore, the arising of all images depends upon the obstruction of light; wherever there is light, there can be no image.
An image, however, is not so; therefore, it is not a similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
Furthermore, when one sees various images enter into water or a mirror, one does not see a shadow in the same way; thus, they are not similar instances.

Moreover, a shadow does not arise from a separate cause other than the shadow itself; rather, an image can act as a cause to produce a separate image. Therefore, an image and a shadow are certainly not similar instances.
Furthermore, a shadow does not vary in height according to the object it follows, whereas a reflection does; therefore, they are not of the same nature.
For this reason, one should not maintain that a reflection is identical to a shadow.
However, those who recite the initial [text] speak as follows:
It is not that shape (saṃsthāna) is absent within the collection of shadows and so forth; however, because color (varṇa) is predominant, only color is discernible.

Briefly stated, there are two kinds of shapes: first, those arranged all around the periphery of a collection of color that is highly resistant (pratigha); second, those arranged all around the periphery of a collection of color that is non-resistant.

It is merely the distinction of shape at the periphery of an aggregate of atoms that are in close conjunction and extremely obstructive; this is called bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*). Therefore, there is no fault in this position.
Having already analyzed bodily informative action, what is vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti*)?
That is to say, the sound of speech itself is called the informative action of speech (*vāg-vijñapti-karman*).

Why is it that the substance of the informative action of speech is the speech itself, while the informative action of the body and the mental action (*cetanā-karman*) are not identical to the body and the mind?

This is because there is no distinct sound capable of expressing [meaning] apart from speech; yet, apart from the body and the mind, there exist the informative action of matter (*rūpa-vijñapti*) and the mental action of volition (*cetanā*). Therefore, the name "bodily action" is established based on its substratum (*āśraya*), "verbal action" is designated according to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and "mental action" follows its origination (*samutthāna*). Consequently, there is no contradiction among these.
Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle 34; Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle 35.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Four, Part Three: Analysis of Karma (Karmavarga). Thus, the characteristics of the two types of manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) have been analyzed; the characteristics of non-manifest karma (*avijñapti-karman*) were already analyzed in the first chapter.
However, the Sautrāntikas say:

"This is also not real, because it is established merely by the prior vow of restraint; furthermore, that [non-informative matter] is designated based on past primary elements, yet the substance of past primary elements does not exist, and moreover, all non-informative matter lacks the characteristic of form."
All such arguments are unreasonable.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the mere non-performance [of an action] constitutes an unmanifest (avijñapti) karma, because unmanifest karma depends upon superior conditions.
This means that it is simply the non-performance [of the act]; for there is no difference between the time prior to making the vow and the time subsequent to making the vow.
Since the state of non-performance is already established even before the vow has been made, establishing a further limit through a vow would be redundant.
If it is claimed that the nature of restraint cannot be established unless one waits for superior conditions, then one must admit that a distinct dharma arises.
This is because we observe in the world that when superior conditions converge, there necessarily arises a distinct dharma possessing substantial existence.
If it is argued that the *āśaya* (intention) is obtained by virtue of making a vow, one must then inquire: what does the term *āśaya* refer to?
It refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) functioning in such a specific manner.
If that were so, one would lose the restraint during the state of non-breathing, and thus it would be necessary to repeatedly re-establish the vow of undertaking it.

If it is argued that such a mental disposition (*āśaya*) does not exist because there is never a time when breathing ceases entirely, that is indeed true; for such an entity simply does not exist, as it is impossible for a non-existent thing to arise or cease.

Furthermore, when one makes a solemn vow and establishes a commitment while dwelling alone in a quiet place, why would such an *āśaya* (intentional disposition) not be of the nature of restraint (*saṃvara*)?

Since it is granted that this nature must depend upon superior conditions, we know that there must necessarily arise a superior dharma; that is to say, there must necessarily exist a superior dharmic nature that arises only when such conditions converge. It is not the case that there is no superior dharmic nature at all, which could only be obtained through the application of the extensive teachings.
If it were otherwise, this would be identical to the various Brahmins and Nirgranthas, who employ grand, artificial expedients yet achieve nothing at all.

If you claim that such a vow must be established and undertaken—requiring one to manifest one's own aspiration before a multitude, as in the ritual for the confession of offenses (*pratideśanā*)—for it to be effective, then even without donning the Dharma robes, shaving the beard and hair, or carrying the alms bowl, one could simply make a solemn vow before a multitude:
"From this day forward, I shall certainly refrain from committing such evils."
One should call such a person "one who has gone forth and received full ordination.
Furthermore, as we observe in the world, when various sentient beings engage in diverse and superior applications of effort, various distinct phenomena accordingly arise.

Having seen one who has gone forth and received full ordination, one performs various kinds of superior preparatory practices; by inferring that a superior dharma will certainly arise [therefrom], this—in our school—is termed "unmanifest karma" (avijñapti-karman).
Even if you were to establish this as "āśaya" (intention), which persists continuously even when the mind is different or absent, there would be no logical fault in this designation.
However, if one were to establish this name for something that is entirely non-existent, it would constitute the grave offense of the fourth path of action.
Furthermore, as for what was said:

"That [past form] is also designated based on past primary elements (mahābhūta), yet the substance of past primary elements does not exist"—this reasoning is also incorrect. We must consider this together: only after determining whether the substance of past phenomena exists or does not exist can one raise such an objection.
Furthermore, it is not accepted that the great elements (mahābhūta), such as earth and so forth, could serve as the productive cause (*janakapratyaya*) in the past;

for they were once present and served as the productive cause for unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*), and thus there is no fault in the produced unmanifest form continuing to function even now, though those elements have passed away.

Furthermore, the claim that the unmanifest (avijñapti) lacks the characteristic of matter (rūpa-lakṣaṇa) is also logically untenable, as this has already been explained previously; specifically, this principle was established within the first chapter.

Since such characteristics do not exist among formless phenomena (arūpadharma), those [treatises] explain the general term "matter" by means of various distinctions of characteristics, such as susceptibility to transformation and destruction (vipariṇāma) and manifestation (vijñapti).

Since this characteristic does not exist among formless phenomena (*ārūpya-dharma*), although this meaning does not pervade all matter (*rūpa*), it constitutes a faultless etymological explanation of the term *rūpa*.
Alternatively, this same deficiency should also apply to consciousness (*vijñāna*), because not all forms of consciousness perform the function of discernment (*vijñapti*).
Since that [position] is free from fault, how could this one possibly have an error?
Furthermore, there are briefly three meanings for the explanation of all *rūpa*:
first, the meaning of manifesting spatial location; second, the meaning of being subject to contact and transformation; and third, the meaning of being designated based on matter (*rūpa*).
It is called "form" (rūpa) because there is that which is seen and can be pointed out as being in this or that location;
it is called "form" because all resistant forms (sapratigha-rūpa) can be affected and transformed through contact with hands and the like.
All forms that are invisible and non-obstructive are designated as "form" (rūpa) by way of their conventional designation as form;
they cannot be so designated apart from body and speech, because such a designation does not exist within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Alternatively, just as past and future forms (rūpa), though lacking transformation and decay, are nevertheless designated by the term "form," so too should this case be understood;
therefore, that objection is not valid.
Furthermore, one must certainly admit that all non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is substantially existent (*dravya-sat*). Why is this so?
The verse says:
It is said that there are three kinds of untainted form (*anāsravarūpa*), because [the Sūtra] speaks of "increase," "non-action," and so forth.
The treatise states:
According to the Sūtra, there are three types of form.

These three serve as the bases that encompass all forms: first, form that is visible and resistant; second, form that is invisible but resistant; and third, form that is both invisible and non-resistant.
Apart from non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), what else is further described here as the third kind of form that is invisible and non-resistant (*anidarśana-apratigha*)?
Here, the Venerable Sthavira, following his own arbitrary misconceptions, has altered the original text and recited it thus:
"The first is form that is visible and resistant; this refers to one sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), because it is not seen and because it is touched."
Second, there is matter that is visible and non-obstructive; this refers to one base, namely the base of form (*rūpāyatana*), because it is what is seen and not what is touched.

Third, there is matter that is invisible and non-obstructive; this refers to the remaining eight bases, because they are neither what is seen nor what is touched. There is certainly no matter that is both visible and obstructive.

If such an interpretation were based on faith and acceptance or upon sound reasoning, it might be permissible to cite it to refute the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) established by our own school.
However, since that interpretation does not avoid the faults already mentioned previously, and because no other sūtra has ever been cited in this manner, who could possibly accept it?
He says this: "In the sūtras recited by the masters of the Sautrāntika school, such [a passage] has indeed been seen; therefore, the masters of Abhidharma should study it with single-minded faith.

It is because the masters of Abhidharma, out of attachment to the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), have their minds deranged and have erroneously recited this sūtra that they do so; it is not that there is no sūtra recited in this manner."

The great masters of the Abhidharma truly exclaim: "How marvelous! Even those who are so stubborn as to stray from the path and a certain class who claim that only the sūtras are authoritative—how they can still be gathered in as fellow practitioners of the Dharma and occasionally engage in discussion with them regarding the profound principles and teachings!"

However, regarding what he recites, it has never been seen among the sacred words found within any of the scriptural collections; furthermore, the principles he explains contradict other sūtras. How could one possibly encourage a wise person to place exclusive faith in and study such a work?
The unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) of desire perfectly accords with this principle, for the Buddha himself accepted it within the sūtras.
That is to say, in the *Hastipadopama-sūtra*, it is stated that there exists form included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*). Thus, that sūtra says:
"O Venerable One!"

Among these, there are certain material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) that are exclusively objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); their essence is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), they are subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), and they are invisible and non-obstructive.
If one excludes the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), what other form could be said to be subsumed under the aggregate of form and the sphere of phenomena?
Why not allow that this is the form of the past and future?

[If you do not,] then the forms of the ten bases would not pertain to the three time periods, because you must allow that the past and future eyes and so forth are all subsumed under the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

Furthermore, this would contradict the *Sūtra on the Distinct Bases*, which states: "The 'dharma' refers to the external base; it consists of those phenomena not included within the eleven bases, being invisible and non-obstructive. This sūtra excludes the eyes and so forth from being subsumed under the base of mental objects.

Furthermore, those past and future eyes and so forth, according to their nature, possess visibility and resistance; therefore, they should not be subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Moreover, one should not admit that past and future eyes and so forth are "form" (*rūpa*), because at those times, the various characteristics of form—such as transformation and decay—are absent.
Thus, the previous objection and this explanation of the sūtra contradict each other; it is not a sound exposition.

Furthermore, matter belonging to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) must necessarily exist, because the sūtra on the distinct spheres speaks of the external *dharmāyatana*, and does not state that it is non-material as it does for the sphere of mental phenomena (*manāyatana*).

To maintain that within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) there definitely exists form and not the absence of form is profoundly consistent with reason, as has already been extensively analyzed in the "Chapter on the Fundamental Subjects" (*Maulī Kośasthāna*).
Thus, their recitation—which contradicts both scripture and logic—is merely the recitation of the ignorant Sautrāntikas.
Furthermore, his interpretation obstructs and excludes the sublime forms embraced within the teachings of the Blessed One.
If the masters of Abhidharma were to believe and study this, they would fail to benefit themselves or others; therefore, he should not encourage others to believe and study it.

Because certain individuals take no pleasure in the established principles of the noble teachings and, relying solely on their own views, falsely compose verses and commentaries that delude the ignorant, I shall from this time forward gradually abandon them.
Furthermore, what they recite not only contradicts the sūtras, but even when scrutinized in detail, it lacks any sound reasoning.
For what reason is it that only the single sense-base of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*) is called "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*), while other obstructive forms are not?
All material forms that possess resistance (*sapratigha*) obstruct the arising of other functions within their own respective locations; therefore, they are called "resistant" (*pratigha*).
That which possesses this resistance is given the name "possessing resistance.

It is observed that material forms, in their respective locations, act as obstructions when viewed in relation to one another; the same applies to the mutual obstruction between sound and so forth, and the eye and so forth.

Since they are currently manifest as mutually obstructing one another within their respective locations, yet claim to be "without resistance" (*apratigha*), their underlying intention is difficult to discern.
Therefore, the Venerable [Vasumitra] states that this position is entirely devoid of correct reasoning.

Furthermore, based on etymological analysis, the designation "appropriated aggregate of form" (*rūpôpādāna-skandha*) proves the existence of the term "resistant" (*sapratigha*); it does not refer solely to the sense of touch. This is because when it is touched or struck by hands and the like, it immediately undergoes transformation and decay.

The appropriated aggregates of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-upādānaskandha) are sufficient to establish that the spheres of form (rūpāyatana) and so forth are all characterized by resistance (sapratigha). Why is this?

It is not only the primary elements (mahābhūta) that are called the appropriated aggregates of name-and-form or designated as "hands" and so forth; rather, it is the sense that when these totalities—such as hands and the like—mutually touch one another, they undergo transformation and disintegration. This is the meaning here.
In the world, it is directly perceived that when one aggregate of matter comes into contact with another aggregate of matter, the latter undergoes transformation and disintegration.
Therefore, what they recite contradicts correct doctrine and reasoning.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrāntavādin) offers this explanation:

The various practitioners of yoga state this: the form of the meditative object produced by the power of concentration (*samādhi*) of one who cultivates dhyāna constitutes this third [type of form]; because it is not an object of the eye-faculty, it is called "invisible" (*anidarśana*); and because it does not obstruct space, it is called "non-obstructive" (*apratigha*).
This explanation is unreasonable, because all phenomena are objects of perception for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

For one dwelling in solitude, the mental consciousness takes as its meditative object those visible forms that possess visibility; these belong to a category of form distinct from other types of form, being produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arising from meditative concentration, unobstructed and transparent like the form of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*).
This principle has already been fully analyzed in the *Vastusamgrahanī* (Discrimination of the Bases) following the explanation of dream objects.
One should therefore challenge [the opponent] as follows:
How can a determinate object have the nature of color—such as blue—and shape—such as long?

Just as other forms (*rūpāyatana*) are not included among those that are visible (*sanidarśana*), [the form of the Buddha-body]—though produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arising upon emerging from meditative concentration and being exceedingly pure and sublime—is nonetheless not the object of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), because visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) does not exist during meditative concentration.
Just as with the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), although it possesses both color and shape, it cannot be seen by the eyes of those born [in the desire realm];
or as with the form of higher realms, which is not the object of the eyes of lower realms.

Since there already exist certain portions of the present sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) that do not serve as objects for certain portions of the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), why do you not allow that there may be certain portions of the sphere of form that do not serve as objects for all eye faculties?
Furthermore, regarding the objective sphere of form within a dream, it should be neither visible nor resistant, as it is solely the object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Therefore, based on the Sūtra’s statement that there are three kinds of form, the logical proof for the actual existence of unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*) is established.
Furthermore, it is stated in the sūtras that there is untainted form (*anāsrava-rūpa*). As the sūtra says:
"What are the untainted phenomena?
They are all forms—past, future, and present—with respect to which no craving or aversion arises; this applies likewise up to consciousness. These are called untainted phenomena."
Excluding non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), what phenomena are designated as "all untainted matter" (*anāsrava-rūpa*) in this sutra?
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtra (Sthiramati) also provides an explanation, stating:

"The practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*) say that among the forms produced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), those which depend upon untainted concentration are themselves called untainted."
I do not know at what place the Master of the Sūtras (Śāstrin) ever encountered which yogācāras, such that he has so frequently cited their words to harmonize them with the Noble Teachings?
Although we have heard that there were five hundred arhats who did not pass into parinirvāṇa until the True Dharma had endured, we have never heard that they made such a statement.
Even if such a statement were made, it would not contradict reason;
for it is illogical that all material forms (rūpa) co-arising with untainted meditative concentration (anāsrava-samādhi) should have shape and color as their essence.

If it is granted that these do not have shape or color as their essence, but are instead untainted matter (*anāsrava-rūpa*) arising in dependence upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*), then one should know that this is precisely non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).

The Dārṣṭāntikas say that all forms within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and within the external vessel-world are designated as "untainted" because they are not the basis for the outflows (*āsrava*).
However, a sūtra states:
"As for tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), they comprise all that exists as the eye," and so forth at length.

This designation of "tainted" does not arise because [the eye] is an antidote to the outflows; rather, it is used to refute their position and extensively generate polemical debate. As this has been fully examined within the analysis of the characteristics of the tainted (*sāsrava-lakṣaṇa-vicāra*), I shall not repeat the refutation here.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the eye-faculties and so forth are designated as "with outflows" (sāsrava) simply because they are not antidotes to the outflows; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that the various mundane paths of defilement would become "without outflows" (anāsrava).
This point will be established in detail later when the meaning is explained, [showing] that within the mundane path there is indeed the capacity to abandon defilement.
Furthermore, those [faculties] such as the eye are not like mental phenomena (*dharma*), because they are spoken of in relation to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
That is to say, within the context of the Buddha’s teaching on the characteristics of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it is stated:
"The mind belonging to the world, the phenomena belonging to the world, and the mental consciousness belonging to the world—these are called contaminated."
The supramundane mind, supramundane phenomena, and supramundane mental consciousness—these are called untainted (*anāsrava*).
Since such a statement is not made regarding the eyes and other [sense organs], it is known that those assertions merely recount erroneous conceptions.
However, since the sūtras speak of untainted (*anāsrava*) form, it is established that non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) exists as a reality.
Furthermore, the sūtras state that merit increases; as a sūtra says:

"Any faithful son or daughter of good family who accomplishes the seven bases of meritorious action with a physical basis—whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking—merit continually increases and merit perpetually arises at all times; the same applies to those without a physical basis."
Excluding non-informative action (*avijñapti-karma*), when one gives rise to another state of mind or is without mind, by virtue of what dharma is it said that the meritorious action increases?
Regarding this, the Sthavira says:

"Because the meritorious action increases due to the object given, it is stated thus: as long as the donated dwelling remains standing, it can cause the donor’s meritorious action to increase, arising in constant succession."
Furthermore, it is also stated in a verse:
"By giving gardens, groves, ponds, and wells, Bridges, boats, ladders, stairs, and houses—
Because of these deeds, for such a person, Merit constantly increases day and night."
The Elder’s citation of this passage is far from consistent with the sūtra; it merely serves his own school’s purpose of refuting the existence of unmanifest form (*avijñapti*).
For he was previously challenged: "If there were no unmanifest form during states such as those of a defiled mind, how could merit still persist?"
Yet the sūtras state that merit constantly increases; to claim that the increase of merit depends solely on the object given—how can this serve as a response to the objection raised by others?

In reality, while the increase of merit does depend on the object given, one must nevertheless distinguish which types of merit remain uninterrupted across states such as those involving defiled minds, and then explain them as "increasing."
The Elder has not yet presented his reasoning therein; thus, although he has made certain statements, they are rendered useless.
Furthermore, he himself raises a difficult objection, saying:
"If the gift does not abide within that [recipient], how can the three subsequent types of merit increase?"
He then offers his own explanation:
"Because the benefit produced by the food given continues to abide, it enables the donor's merit from giving to increase constantly.
This, too, shares the same faults as previously mentioned.
Furthermore, he states this again:
"Because the *āśaya* (intentional disposition) is not lost, merit constantly increases.

If that is so, then even when a donor is in a state of defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*) or the like, there may still exist a recollection of the gift; it is on account of this that it is said, "because it is not lost."
He says it is not so; what is this "non-forgetfulness"?
It refers to the *āśaya* (intentional disposition).
Apart from the mind, mental factors, and unmanifest karma (*avijñapti-karma*), what is the meaning of this term?
Is it not the case that, when examined through such reasoning and analysis, it becomes evident that the Buddha’s words are entirely devoid of meaning?
Furthermore, he himself asks:
"How can it be said, in the context of meritorious deeds that lack a physical basis, that merit increases by virtue of the object given?"
He then answered himself:
"This vehicle comes here because of the conventional usage of the phrase 'merit based on existence' recited previously.
In reality, however, there is no sense of an increase in merit within this context."

The Elder, for the most part, following his own deluded sentiments, arbitrarily established doctrinal tenets that contravene the teachings of the various sages; being unable to provide a coherent explanation, he then repudiated the sutras that were universally accepted as contradicting his views, claiming they lacked any real meaning.
How can one who slanders the Dharma in this way be called a virtuous person?
