If one does not understand the profound meaning of the sūtras, yet does not claim them to be superior, why would they suddenly reject and deny them?
Furthermore, it is said that because of the arousal of a thick and intense *āśaya* (resolute intention), merit also increases accordingly.
This is also unreasonable, as it has already been challenged previously; for this *āśaya* (intention) is not established by reason.

Furthermore, one would have to abandon the thesis previously established: that if merit increases even in the absence of a gift, then one should not have previously stated that merit constantly increases because the continuum of the gifted object persists for a long time.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) states:

"The former masters (pūrvācāryas) have explained it thus: by the power of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), meritorious karma increases; in whatever manner the donor bestows material goods, in that very same manner the recipient enjoys them."

Because there are differences in the benefits conferred by the merit of the recipients' enjoyment of the donated objects, even though the donor’s mind subsequently attends to other objects, a subtle continuum—perfumed by the volition (*cetanā*) directed toward the gift from the previous moment—gradually undergoes transformation and differentiation, whereby it is able to produce manifold fruits in the future.
Therefore, it is said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*) that meritorious karma constantly increases in its continuity and that meritorious karma arises in succession.
One should ask: what herein is called "continuity" (*prabandha*), and what is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*)?
What is meant by "differentiation"?
He replied: With volitional action (*cetanā-karman*) as the precursor, the successive arising of moments of mind is termed a "continuum" (*saṃtati*).
This very continuum, arising in distinct forms at successive moments, is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
When this [continuum], immediately following [the preceding moment], possesses a capacity to produce an effect that is superior to its prior state, it is called "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*).

If the consciousness with grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*) serves as the mind at the moment of death, then although there may have been various types of karma that project a future existence prior to this mind, at this time only that which is extremely heavy, or that which has been habitually practiced, or that which was performed proximately to death possesses the manifest power to project a result, and not any other.

Regarding all ripening causes (*vipāka-hetu*), the capacity to produce a result—which consists in a specific transformation within the continuity induced by that cause—ceases immediately after the ripening fruit has been bestowed.

Regarding all similar-type causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), the capacity to produce a result—which consists in a specific transformation within the continuity induced by that cause—ceases when, in the case of defiled states, one attains the ultimate path of antidote (*pratipakṣa-mārga*); at that point, the capacity to produce a concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) ceases.

That which is non-defiled follows the continuity of the mind until the state of parinirvāṇa without remainder; it is only then that the functional capacity for all its outflowing fruits (niṣyanda-phala) finally ceases.

What has been stated here is precisely that which I have repeatedly refuted previously, such as the "old pervasive element" (*pūrvānuśaya-dhātu*) and so forth; now, however, by means of different terminology—like a performer who artfully changes his costume—he seeks to provide a skillful interpretation of the cited sūtra.

However, as for what they say regarding subtle continuity, transformation, and differentiation, there is not the slightest logical principle that would allow a wise person to take it to heart; it is merely a fabrication of empty words and phrases, like the "conjunction," "quality," "sameness," "difference," and "inherence" postulated by the Vaiśeṣikas, which lack any distinct substantial entity.

Why is this so? As it is said that the continuity of mind possesses the sense of being defiled or purified, which refers precisely to the distinction between the prior and subsequent states of defilement and purification within the mind;
likewise, the distinction in the transformation of this continuity must also refer to the distinct meanings of the prior and subsequent states of the mind itself.

This mind, as a differentiated cause, attains its fruit; while this fruit may possess temporal distinctions of before and after, the various specific natures of the fruits thus obtained must necessarily stem from a corresponding variety in their causes. It is not possible for the essence of a single mind to possess such manifold diversity.
If it is argued that this is like the seed of a *padma* lotus, that too is unreasonable; for that seed is composed of many atoms (*paramāṇu*) and thus can possess distinctions.

Furthermore, within the various successions of seeds, sprouts, and so forth, there is no difference in their functional capacity when viewed sequentially from prior to subsequent stages. However, within the succession of a single mind, there are distinct differences in functional capacity—such as being wholesome or unwholesome—when viewed sequentially from prior to subsequent stages. It is not the case that a single momentary entity of consciousness could possess differing functional capacities, such as wholesomeness and so forth, without possessing subtle internal divisions.

Furthermore, within the Noble Teachings, it is accepted that a single body possesses karmic distinctions of states, such as karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), and so forth; by means of these as causes, one accordingly experiences the fruits of distinct states, such as those to be experienced in the present life, in their respective order. It is not possible for the substance of a single moment of mind to act as the cause for obtaining such distinct fruits of various states.

If it is argued that, just as the combined power of conditions for a seed may differ such that it either produces a sprout or produces ash, this too is irrational; for it would follow that both wholesome and unwholesome causes could equally bring about desirable and undesirable fruits. However, the Sūtra speaks of "impossibility" (asthāna) regarding such a claim.
Furthermore, although seeds and the like constitute a single continuum, when conditions converge, a sprout does not arise from a sprout itself.

The same should apply to the mind: although it is a single continuum, when conditions converge, an undesirable result does not arise from a virtuous mind, nor does an undesirable result arise from a non-virtuous mind. Therefore, you must admit that within a single mental continuum, at one and the same time, there are immeasurable minds arising simultaneously.
Alternatively, one must admit that the mind arises from the combination of infinite entities, like a blended fragrance or a mixed drink;
or one must admit that causes possess substantial existence in the past; or one must admit that effects arise without a cause. In such cases, one becomes like a person who has lost their way.
Furthermore, that which you have stated—that a single mental continuum arises as distinct instances in successive moments and this is called "transformation"—is certainly unreasonable.

For instance, if one performs a meritorious action and immediately thereafter performs a non-meritorious action, are these two of the same category undergoing transformation, or are they of different categories undergoing transformation?
If one says that this is a transformation of the same category, then there should be no distinction between demerit and merit.

If one says that it is a transformation of a different category, then one must explain what third mind exists, and based upon what characteristic could it be called the transformation of meritorious action?
Furthermore, what characteristics are said to constitute the transformation of unwholesome action?
Through such various investigations and analyses, all the conceived distinctions in the transformation of the continuum are inconsistent with the true principles of the Noble Teaching.
Furthermore, according to their own tenet that only the present exists, the continuity of dharmas cannot be established within a single moment.
Since continuity does not exist, what transformation can be spoken of?
Because there is no transformation, there is likewise no differentiation.
Therefore, those [opposing] statements are entirely devoid of real meaning.

Consequently, there exists a distinct dharma which, whether another mind has arisen or when one is without mind, continues to manifest in a constant succession and gradually increases; this is called "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*). Thus, the existence of unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*) as a substantial reality is established.

In this matter, the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) is utterly bewildered; failing to clearly comprehend the tenets of his own and others' schools, he seeks to equalize his own faults by attributing them to others. Inverting the opponent's censure, he offers this explanation:

"If it is asked how, through the specific excellence and benefit of one continuum, a transformation can be induced in the mind of another continuum such that it undergoes change despite having a different object of focus."

To resolve this doubt, it is the same as in the case of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). Furthermore, how could one continuum cause another continuum to produce a distinct, real dharma of unmanifest action through a specific excellence or benefit?

It is not so; because body and mind follow one another, due to the distinction in the donor’s meritorious intention, there arise such signs of informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) matter, which, together with their preceding derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), are born simultaneously.
Immediately after it has arisen, these four great elements and the derived matter perish simultaneously because they are co-nascent.

From this point, the subsequent unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) that arises inherits the preceding category and continues in a constant succession until it encounters conditions for its relinquishment.
Thus, although the donor’s mind may be directed toward other objects, the merit constantly increases due to the specific excellence of the recipient’s virtues; this is logically consistent.

However, the term "increase" indicates distinctions among the lower, middle, and superior grades [of merit], for it is the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) that they are sustained by external conditions.
Alternatively, this intention reveals that [the mind] continues to evolve for a long duration; therefore, it is stated next that meritorious karma arises in succession.
This is not the case in your school. Why is this so?
Once the distinctions in the donor’s meritorious thoughts have ceased, a defiled mind immediately arises in succession; at that time, the recipient’s qualities and benefits undergo a distinction.
Since the donor has increased [their demerit] due to that defiled mind, what use is there for such an increase in meritorious karma?

If it is claimed that there is a distinct non-defiled phenomenon that increases, what distinct phenomenon other than a defiled mind could be called "meritorious action" (puṇyakarman), such that its increase is spoken of?
One should carefully investigate and seek out its essential nature.
I have marked this at the head of my heart and shall reveal it gradually.

Now, I observe that you lack the capacity for such revelation; therefore, because you have not yet received instruction from a master who is profoundly learned in the sublime teachings and well-versed in correct reasoning, you harbor great desires in your hearts and arbitrarily establish your own conceptions of the Dharma. You falsely rely on yourselves to support the Sautrāntika school, holding onto the dust of your own attachments to defile the sublime teachings.

Furthermore, regarding the theory of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) propounded by them: since there is no informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) among meritorious acts not based on material things (*anupādāya-puṇya*), how could there be non-informative action?
This is also incorrect, because they certainly maintain that wholesome non-informative action exists therein.

This means that when one hears that a Tathāgata or his disciple currently resides in a certain place or region, one gives rise to joy; because of this, merit constantly increases. Such a person must possess superior faith, and by turning toward that direction from afar to respectfully offer prostrations and praise, they generate meritorious manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) and meritorious non-manifest action (*avijñapti*). Thus adorning themselves and aspiring to personally behold him, it is said that merit constantly increases based on that non-manifest action.
In the sūtras, the Blessed One spoke only of that which can initiate [the action], because this serves as the predominant cause for the arising of merit.

As previously established, apart from non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa), when other states of mind arise or when one is without mind, there is necessarily no continuity or increase of meritorious karma.

If one were to admit only that they possess a joyful mind, then they would possess only mental wholesome conduct (*manas-karma-sucarita*), which would arise momentarily and then cease; this would not accord with the principle of its constant increase.
Therefore, I definitively maintain that at such a time, they must also necessarily possess bodily and verbal wholesome conduct (*kāya-vāk-karma-sucarita*).

Furthermore, when an action is not performed by oneself but is instead commissioned to another, it would not constitute a course of action (*karmapatha*) if non-informative action (*avijñapti*) did not exist; for the informative act of commissioning another is not included within that person's own course of action, as this act has not yet directly performed what was to be done.
Once the task has been performed by the one sent, because this nature is without difference, the Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtrakāra*) offers this explanation: "It should be stated thus:

through the original preparatory effort, when the task is accomplished by the one sent according to the instruction, it is by the natural law (*dharmatā*) that it causes a subtle transformation of the continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*) to arise in the instructor; by means of this, many fruits will be experienced in the future."
When any action performed by oneself reaches completion, it should be understood that this is likewise due to such a principle.

One should know that this very subtle transformation and differentiation within the continuum is called the "path of action" (*karmapatha*); this is a case of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the effect, because it is the fruit induced by bodily and vocal actions.

That explanation is irrational; since the subtle transformation of the continuum through differentiation has already been refuted, there is no capacity for it to further resolve the objection. Therefore, to cite it again here would be useless.
Furthermore, he should explain that it is by means of the instructor who sends [the agent] to another place to harm another sentient being;

if at a later time the instructor comes to thoroughly understand the principle of the causal connection, he will thereby be able to give rise to deep regret and shame, or be able to initiate other superior wholesome states of mind.
At that time, when the messenger has completed the act of killing, he causes the path of action (karmapatha) of killing to arise within the mental continuum of the instigator.
Does this mental continuum result in a desirable fruit, an undesirable fruit, or both?

These arguments are all untenable: because at that time the karmic action of killing has reached its ultimate completion; because a wholesome mind cannot possibly bring about a fruit of suffering; and because it would result in the fallacy of confusing the timing of karma, such as karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and so forth.

If it is claimed that only the volition of manifest action (*vijñapti-karma-cetanā*) can draw forth undesirable fruits in the future, this would indeed be logically correct; however, what is this "transformation through continuity" (*saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*) that they maintain?
Since the mind of the instructor has already formed a wholesome continuity, what further dharma could he grasp that would produce many undesirable fruits in the future?
This is because within the subsequent continuity of the instructor, no distinct dharma arises that could produce such abundant results.
Such a position does not inspire confidence.

However, because the prior manifest action (*vijñapti*) and the motivating mind constitute the preliminary application (*prayoga*), even if the teacher subsequently gives rise to a virtuous mind that continues for a long duration, there still persists an unwholesome acquisition (*prāpti*) that continues to arise, thereby bringing the deed to completion. At that time, this [unwholesome acquisition] possesses the power to draw forth the production of such primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
The arising of this derived matter constitutes the fundamental course of action (*maula-karmapatha*).

That very prior manifest action (*vijñapti*) and the motivating mind, while existing in the present, act as causes capable of taking the presently produced derived matter as their outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*).
At the present moment when non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is arising, that [past action] existing in the past can produce its present fruit.

It is solely that volitional karma (*cetanā-karman*) previously arisen which acts as the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) for the undesirable fruit; subsequently, the arising of the path of action (*karmapatha*) acts as the completing cause (*paripūraṇa-hetu*), ensuring that the projected fruit will certainly arise.
Such a tenet may inspire joy.

It is not the case that the drawing power [of the action] itself causes the future results—whether pleasant or unpleasant—to arise with certainty; for apart from the informative volition (*vijñapti-cetanā*) produced by the instructor, if the continuum of a wholesome mind persists until the completion of the agent’s task, there would be no other distinct phenomenon (*dharma*) capable of bringing the unpleasant result to fulfillment were the non-informative (*avijñapti*) to be absent.
If the auxiliary causes could be obtained [independently], the result should not arise.

If the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) were itself able to ensure that the result necessarily arises without requiring the completion of the causal factors, then even if the executor sometimes does not carry out the act of killing, the undesirable result for the instructor would also necessarily arise.
Since this is not permitted, your Sautrāntika school establishes an extremely flawed principle regarding the relationship between karma and its fruit.

However, the Sthavira says: "When the person being instructed completes the preparatory act (*prayoga*) and the immediate sequence (*anantarya*), it causes the instructor to incur the immediate transgression (*ānantarya-āpatti*) arising from that preparation; for it is only when the matter dispatched by the messenger reaches completion that the fruit of the instructor's preparation is finally established."
In this regard, what is it that they maintain constitutes an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*)?
Is it the death of the mother and others, or is it the sin committed against them?
If you claim that the immediate transgression consists simply in the death of the mother and others, then one would incur an immediate transgression even if one were devoid of the intention to kill.

If it is claimed that the immediate [retribution] (*ānantarya*) is the sin produced [at the moment of death], then when the act commanded by the instigator has reached its completion, if the intention of the instigator is defiled, he may be touched by the grave sin of an immediate retribution;
however, if the instigator is precisely generating a wholesome intention at the time the one sent completes the act of killing, what sin could arise for that instigator?
How can one speak so without restraint as to claim that [an agent] is touched by the grave offense of an *ānantarya*? Therefore, one must certainly admit that there is a real *avijñapti*.
If one does not act oneself but merely dispatches another to do so, the transgression of a course of action (*karmapatha*) is produced through the arising of *avijñapti*.

Furthermore, if non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) did not exist, there would be no eightfold path of the noble ones (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), because speech and the other factors are absent during meditative absorption.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtrakāra*) raises the following objection:
"Moreover, he must explain how right speech, right action, and right livelihood can exist at the very moment one is on the Path."
Is it the case that in this state one utters right speech, performs right actions, or seeks clothing and so forth?

This objection is unreasonable, for the Buddha’s words are the same; thus, the masters of the Sautrāntika school should also be questioned: "While one is actually in the state of the Path, does one utter speech, perform actions, or seek clothing and so forth?"
How then can it be said that the Buddha’s words are subsumed under the factors of right speech, action, and livelihood?
Therefore, the critique should apply equally.
Nevertheless, he [the opponent] explains as follows:

Although there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), while in the state of the Path one attains such an intention and basis; therefore, after emerging from meditative absorption, by the force of that prior [attainment], one is able to give rise to the three right [aspects] and not give rise to the three wrong ones. Because the name of the effect is established upon the cause, it is possible to fully establish the eight branches of the Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
That explanation by the Śrāvakas is not correct, for it should apply equally to Right View and the other factors.

That is to say, one could likewise argue that although Right View and the others do not exist while one is in the state of the Path, one nevertheless attains such an intention and basis; therefore, after emerging from meditative absorption, Right View and the others arise through the force of the preceding [path], whereas Wrong View and the others do not. Since the name of the effect is established within the cause, the eight branches of the Noble Path can be fully established.
However, it is not the case that right view and the other factors do not exist within meditative observation; for if they did not exist, the Path itself would likewise not exist.

By this principle, the masters of the Abhidharma should establish the following analogy: just as right view and the others possess a real intrinsic nature while actually present in the Path, so too must right speech, right action, and right livelihood—the various untainted precepts—exist as real entities. This is because when one attains right view and the others during observation, after emerging from that observation, one does not give rise to wrong views and the like as an ordinary person does.
Having attained right speech and so forth through such contemplation, how is it that after emerging from contemplation one does not give rise to wrong speech and so forth as ordinary beings do?
How is it that what is produced differs from that of ordinary beings?

That is to say, although stream-enterers and others may give rise to defiled minds and engage in activities such as the pursuit of sensual desires, it cannot be said that they give rise to wrong thought (*mithyā-saṃkalpa*) or wrong speech (*mithyā-vāk*) and so forth.

Since they attain the antidotes for these within the context of their contemplation, why is it logically consistent to allow that there exists a distinct essence for right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) and so on, while not allowing one for right speech and the rest?
Furthermore, what reasoning allows for the conventional designation of "right speech" and so forth based upon "right view" and so forth?
This is not contradictory; otherwise, one would have to deny that these [factors] possess distinct entities. Therefore, the position held by those [opponents] is not well-established.

Furthermore, just as it is with concentration, so it should be with ethical discipline (*śīla*), because these are all said to pertain to both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). As a sūtra states:

"There is the ethical discipline of one in training, the ethical discipline of one beyond training; the concentration of one in training, the concentration of one beyond training; the wisdom of one in training, and the wisdom of one beyond training."

If it is claimed that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is merely a provisional designation for right view and so forth, then the separate mention of ethical discipline as pertaining to both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) would be rendered useless.

The Elder’s intention is that the capacity to refrain from unwholesome conduct of body and speech is what constitutes right speech and so forth; because the continuum is transformed by the power of the Noble Path, one possesses the capacity to refrain from these two types of misconduct. Therefore, right speech and the others do not possess a separate substantial entity.
If that were so, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) would also have to consist solely in the capacity not to intentionally engage in unwholesome conduct.

Why? Because when the mental continuum is transformed by the power of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), one possesses the capacity not to engage in unwholesome conduct; this very capacity is what is called right view, and it does not exist as a separate entity.
The Sūtra states:
"Wrong view is called an unwholesome mental action.
What distinction is there here in principle such that one [wrong view] is admitted to have substantial reality while the other [the others] is not?
Therefore, what they have said is entirely devoid of real meaning.
Furthermore, one should ask them:
"What is the nature of this dharma that is capable of non-action?"
As for his statement that it is "the virtuous and pure mental states and mental factors accompanied by a superior *āśaya* (intention)," this has already been refuted as before.
What is the refutation of the former position?

It means that if one were to give rise to a mind of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and so forth while in that state of cessation, one would lose the restraint (*saṃvara*), just as when one has not yet attained the [proper] stage. Furthermore, in the state of cessation, there is no dharma whatsoever—such as a superior intention (*āśaya*)—that persists as it did previously, which could be designated by the specific term "non-defiled mind" (*asaṃkliṣṭa-citta*) in the sense of a "special resolve of non-doing."
It may also be said that they are capable of not engaging in verbal misconduct and so forth; all the faults previously mentioned should be subsumed here.
Furthermore, regarding what they have stated—that *śīla* means "habitual practice"—therefore, *śīla* has no separate substantial entity.
That argument is incorrect; because it is taught as distinct despite sharing the same meaning of "habitual cultivation," it must necessarily have a separate substantial entity. As a sūtra says:
"If one has already well-cultivated the three—virtue, concentration, and wisdom."
"Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) means repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).

If "ethical discipline" (*śīla*) were defined solely as repeated practice, the Sūtra should not have separately mentioned the "cultivation of morality," for it would be illogical to speak of cultivating that which is already mere practice.
If the cultivation of concentration and wisdom were themselves called *śīla*, then one should not say that three things are cultivated.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Abiding in and relying upon *śīla*, one cultivates two dharmas."
How could it be said that one dwells upon and cultivates two dharmas?

Now, examining the conduct of the Venerable Bodhi, he relies solely on worldly treatises while obstructing the sacred teachings; therefore, the existence of unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is established as a reality.

Although they have many other groundless assertions, none of them transcend what has already been refuted above; fearing that the text would become overly cumbersome, I shall not refute them individually here, as the previous discussion regarding non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is sufficient to establish the point.
To what entity does this name "unmanifest" (avijñapti) refer?
It refers to the entity of abstention (virati).
Abstention, non-action, non-creation, and unmanifest are synonymous terms for one and the same entity.
It is not merely the negation of an action that is termed "non-informative" (*avijñapti*);

rather, it is like the common worldly expression "non-Brahmin," which is universally understood to designate a specific category distinct from Brahmins. Because karma is its cause, it is like the act of painting a picture.
This unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is also designated by the name "action" (*karman*), because it arises based on manifest action (*vijñapti*) and volition (*cetanā*).
Do all unmanifest forms arise from these two forces? No.

Why is this? Only the unmanifest (avijñapti) belonging to the desire realm can be produced by two powerful causes, because volition (cetanā) in the desire realm is not in a state of meditative equipoise (asamāhita).

Apart from bodily and vocal informative action (*vijñapti*), there is no capacity to produce non-informative action (*avijñapti*); however, because it is sustained by the power of concentration associated with meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), the volition (*cetanā*) therein possesses a superior capacity to produce non-informative action without depending on informative action.
For this reason, although the unmanifest (avijñapti) is not itself karma, it receives the name "karma" because it has karma as its cause.
It is not appropriate to designate feeling and so forth as karma, because the unmanifest karma is established based on the cessation of manifest karma (vijñapti-karman).

It is not the case that feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth are established as "action" (*karman*) merely by ceasing [other activities]; therefore, although feeling and so forth have action as their cause, there is no fault of them being identical to non-informative action (*avijñapti*), which is also termed "action.

Furthermore, while all non-informative actions have action as their cause, they do not themselves act as the cause for action; whereas feeling and so forth stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect with action. Thus, there is no error of identity with non-informative action.
Since non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) also takes that which is not action as its cause, for what reason is it not admitted to be called "non-action" as well?
It is indeed admitted to be non-action because it is not a performance; however, because it has action as its cause, it is also called "action."
The Blessed One has also stated that what is not produced is called "karma," as it is said:
"What is white karma with white maturation?
It refers to the five types of śīla and the seven types of śīla," and so forth, as explained at length.
Those learned in grammatical science (*śabdavidyā*) also employ the term "action" (*karman*) to refer to states such as sleeping and remaining, even when no action is being performed.

Furthermore, it is observed in the world that the designation "performing an action" is applied to a state where no action is actually being performed, provided there is something intended to be done.
For example, if one asks Devadatta,
"What karma have you performed?
he replies:
Since I am now either sleeping or remaining [in a state of composure],
there is no fault in using conventional expressions in this way. If that is so:

The first moment of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) in the desire realm should not be established as "informative action" (*vijñapti-karman*), because it is illogical for it to coexist with informative action while simultaneously ceasing that informative action.

This objection is unreasonable, because the initial non-informative (avijñapti) is of the same category as the cessation of informative (vijñapti) and non-informative [actions], and subsequent moments continue to evolve in accordance with the characteristics of that first moment.

That is to say, the non-informative action co-arising with the informative action at the first moment is of the same category as the subsequent non-informative actions that cease the informative; since it is admitted that they are of the same category when compared to one another, even though it arises simultaneously with the informative action, it can be established as having the substance of non-informative action, for it is produced entirely through the informative action.

Alternatively, virtuous non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) ceases evil karma, while non-virtuous non-informative matter ceases virtuous karma; therefore, although it arises simultaneously with informative matter (*vijñapti*) at the first moment, it may still be designated as "non-informative action."
If one explains the terms "detachment," "non-action," and "non-creation of karma" according to this same principle, there will be no error in any case.
Are the great elements that serve as the basis for both the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) and the manifest (*vijñapti*)—both of which are derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)—different or the same?
The verse says:
These primary elements that produce it are distinct from those upon which the manifest [action] relies.
The commentary says:

Although the unmanifest (avijñapti) and the manifest (vijñapti) arise simultaneously, their primary elements (mahābhūta) that serve as their generative causes are distinct; for the causes of two effects—one coarse and one subtle—must necessarily differ, and there is a distinction in the combination of their generative causes.

Most derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) arises simultaneously with its originating great elements (*mahābhūta*). Nevertheless, there are also some instances in the present and future that have past [great elements] as their cause.
What are these few instances?
The verse says:
The non-informative [matter] of the desire realm in subsequent moments arises based on past primary elements.
The commentary says:
Only after the first moment of that which is bound to the desire realm do all subsequent non-informative [forms] arise from past primary elements.
That is to say, the non-informative [form] of the first thought-moment bound to the desire realm arises simultaneously with the primary elements that produce it.
Once these primary elements have arisen, they serve as the cause for the production of all subsequent unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) within one's own continuum.

When these [elements] perish together with the unmanifest form of the first moment, and the unmanifest form of the second moment and thereafter arises, it is entirely produced by the preceding past primary elements.

These primary elements (mahābhūta) that follow [the initial moment] serve as the support for subsequent moments of non-informative matter (avijñapti), because they are capable of inducing it; therefore, they arise simultaneously with the subsequent moments of non-informative matter.
The primary elements within the body can only serve as its support, for if these primary elements were absent, the non-informative matter would not proceed.

In this way, the two sets of four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that coexist with the preceding [action] serve as the primary cause (*pravartaka-hetu*) and the secondary cause (*anuvartaka-hetu*) for all subsequent non-informative actions (*avijñapti*).
This is, for example, like the causes for the movement of a wheel: it depends on both the hand and the ground; the hand is able to initiate the motion, while the ground merely serves as its support.
It should be understood that the same applies to the primary elements (mahābhūta) that coexist with them.

Since the primary elements pertain to all five stages, so too do bodily and vocal actions. To which stage do the bodily and vocal actions of a particular stage belong, and by which primary elements of that same stage are they produced?
The verse says:
"The contaminated [attainments] depend on their own level; the uncontaminated [attainments] follow the place of birth.
The commentary says:
Bodily and vocal karma are, in brief, of two types: first, contaminated (*sāsrava*), and second, uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
If they are contaminated, they are bound to five levels.

Bodily and vocal karma bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are produced solely from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the desire realm; likewise, up to the bodily and vocal karma of the fourth dhyāna, these are produced solely from the primary elements of those respective levels.

If it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it relies upon the body of the five stages; as it arises in whichever stage it corresponds to, it should manifest there, being produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of that very stage. This is because untainted phenomena do not fall within the realms (*dhātu*); for there are certainly no primary elements that are themselves untainted, since the untainted arises only through the power of its support.
What is the nature of informative and non-informative karma?
Furthermore, by what kind of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are they produced?
The verse says:
The unmanifest (avijñapti) is non-appropriated (anupātta), and is also a derivative (naiṣyandika) belonging to the category of sentient beings.
That which arises from a state of distraction (vikṣipta) depends on derivative primary elements (bhūta) and is with appropriation (sopādāna), arising from distinct primary elements.
That which arises from meditative concentration (samāhita) depends on nurtured (aupacayika) primary elements, is without appropriation, and does not arise from distinct primary elements.
The [unmanifest] is exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*), and it belongs to the body as being appropriated (*upātta*).
The Commentary says:
In this verse, the unmanifest is first distinguished.
Non-informative karma (*avijñapti-karma*) is, in brief, of two types, distinguished by whether it pertains to the meditative state (*samāhita-bhūmi*) or the non-meditative state (*asamāhita-bhūmi*).
However, in their general characteristics, all such karma is without appropriation (*anupātta*), as it is diametrically opposed to that which possesses appropriation (*sopātta*).
Because it is exclusively wholesome or unwholesome, it is not born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Because there is no accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is not nurtured (*aupacayika*).
Because it has a cause of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*), it is a result of outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
This is also stated to reveal that [unmanifest form] possesses momentariness.
That is to say, the unmanifest form (avijñapti) co-arising with the first untainted [state] is included within the category of sentient beings because it arises dependent upon consciousness.

If one distinguishes its basis according to its specific differences, all unmanifest form within the non-concentrated states (asamāhita-bhūmi) arises from great elements (mahābhūta) that are outflowing (naiṣyandika), possessed of sensation (savyābādha), and distinct [from those of the concentrated state].
The statement "arising from different primary elements" indicates that the seven [types] of bodily and vocal [non-informative action] are each produced by their own distinct primary elements.

There are two distinctions regarding the non-informative action arising from meditative concentration (*samādhi*): namely, those of the dhyāna-restraints and the untainted restraints (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
Both of these are nurtured by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and are produced from primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that are without sensation and without differentiation.
The term "without differentiation" indicates that this unmanifest form (*avijñapti*)—the seven branches—is created by the same set of four primary elements.

It should be understood that informative [action] (*vijñapti*) is exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*). If this pertains to the body, it is appropriated (*upātta*); all other points are the same as those for non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) in the state of non-concentration.
That is to say, it belongs to the category of sentient beings, is based on outflow, is appropriated, and arises from distinct great elements (*mahābhūta*).

For what reason are the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that constitute the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) belonging to the realm of distraction (*vikṣiptabhūmi*) exclusively of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*)?

As for the non-informative matter produced by cultivation in the realm of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), it is because when a particularly distinguished mind is present, one is necessarily able to cultivate the great elements and the sense faculties. Therefore, that which co-exists with the concentrated mind must necessarily possess particularly distinguished cultivated great elements that can act as the generative cause (*janakahetu*) for the production of all the non-informative matter co-existing with that concentrated mind.

In the case of the non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) of the stage of scattering (*vikṣiptabhūmi*), because the motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*) does not exist simultaneously with it, and because it can arise even during states of mindlessness (*acittaka*), its basis—the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)—is exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*). This is because the motivating mind cannot nourish the primary elements that produce the non-informative matter.
If that is so, what is the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the primary elements upon which the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of the distracted state (*vikṣipta-bhūmi*) depends? Some say:

it is the outflow of the primary elements that have ceased immediately prior; these are the non-obstructive (*apratigha*) primary elements capable of producing [the unmanifest], and not the outflow of the obstructive (*sapratigha*) primary elements, because there is a distinction between the categories of subtle and coarse for the resulting fruit.

According to this explanation, there have existed from beginningless time determinate, non-obstructive derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) capable of acting as the creator; these previously ceased primary elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) capable of producing the present similar-flowing (*niṣyanda*) primary elements.

The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that produce manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) should likewise be the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of similar primary elements from beginningless time; they do not arise from dissimilar types. This is because the primary elements that serve as the basis for non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) are non-appropriated (*anupātta*), being the fruit of a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*); for there is certainly no affectionate mind that would appropriate these primary elements as its own present internal self.
Furthermore, because these primary elements (mahābhūta) lack any other characteristic of being appropriated (upātta), they are termed "unappropriated" (anupātta).

As for the primary elements upon which the unmanifest (avijñapti) of the non-concentrated stage depends, they are "appropriated" because they are the fruit of a distracted mind; that is, they are grasped as the present internal self by those possessing a mind of attachment.
Just as the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the basis for visible color and so forth are subject to destruction because they arise in dependence upon the physical body,
external objects likewise can produce suffering or pleasure when they come into contact with it.
For what reason is the unmanifest (avijñapti) produced by a concentrated mind generated from non-distinct primary elements (mahābhūta),
whereas the unmanifest produced in a distracted state depends on distinct primary elements?
The seven limbs, when compared with one another, arise through mutual force because they share a single fruit.
They arise solely from a single set of the four great elements; since their dispersion is contrary [to their cohesion], they rely on different great elements.

Some say: If those [unmanifest actions] share the same cause of arising, then upon the transgression of even one [limb], one should abandon all the unmanifest actions born of meditative concentration (*samāhita-avijñapti*).
Since the causes of arising for the seven limbs are identical when compared to one another, they must necessarily be abandoned simultaneously.

Is this not like the precept of abstaining from killing, which arises from a continuous stream directed toward all sentient beings? Although it is produced by the same set of great elements, one does not abandon it all at once in a single moment.
The principle that the seven limbs correspond to one another should likewise apply here.

However, this analogy does not hold; for although those [limbs] are each produced from a single set of primary elements (*mahābhūta*), the individual continuums (*saṃtāna*) of the sentient beings they correspond to are distinct.

If the sevenfold precepts do not differ from the great [vows], and since the mental continuum of the sentient being toward whom they are directed is one and the same, for what reason would violating one not constitute the abandonment of all?
Therefore, these two cases are not comparable as examples.
If that is so, this should follow the same principle as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Just as the essence of the life-faculty serves as the support for the possession of the body, it also serves as the support even when the body is incomplete.
Therefore, although the body may be deficient, as long as other faculties remain, the life-faculty is still able to sustain them, preventing their interruption or destruction.

In this way, a single set of great elements serves as the cause that can produce the fruits of restraint, whether complete or incomplete; therefore, even if some branches are lacking, as long as the remaining branches exist, the great elements are still able to sustain them so that they do not cease or perish.

This is not a valid analogy, because that life-faculty (jīvitendriya) first arises simultaneously with a deficient body, subsequently arises together with a complete body during the intermediate period, and later arises again together with it when the body becomes deficient; thus, it maintains each state—whether complete or deficient—separately.

The primary elements (mahābhūta) are not like this: a single set of primary elements serves as the cause for the arising of a single continuum of non-informative matter (avijñapti). If they were the cause for the arising of the seven branches [of the path], they would never, even for a moment, arise together with a deficient branch.
How is it that when one moment is missing, the remaining [vows] are maintained without being abandoned?

It is precisely by this principle that the precepts of abstaining from killing and so forth—which arise with non-greed and other [wholesome roots] as their cause—do not involve the abandonment of all [precepts] even if one transgresses against a single continuum of a sentient being at one particular time; for these are each the distinct results of their own primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Regarding the distinction of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*):

it is because the categories of their effects are distinct. Although many unmanifest forms (*avijñapti*) produced by non-attachment arise in relation to the diverse continuities of various sentient beings, they nonetheless have only a single set of primary elements as their cause, because there is no difference in the category of the effects produced.

Therefore, if with respect to the body of a single sentient being, a single set of seven factors shared the same cause of production, then by transgressing even one, one would have to abandon them all.
Such a proof could indeed be established logically; thus, the seven factors of restraint must depend upon distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
However, since it is not admitted that one may relinquish the vows separately, this proof is invalid; what was stated previously remains correct.
Just as when the divine eye arises, it does not destroy the original physical form, so too should it be understood when informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) arises.

Therefore, although bodily intimation arises within the body, there is no fault of a resultant form being interrupted and then resuming; nor is there the fault of two distinct shapes arising simultaneously within a single aggregate of primary elements (*mahābhūta*), because each bodily intimation has as its support newly arisen, similar-outflow (*niṣyanda*) primary elements.

When the manifest matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) arises in dependence upon a portion of the body, that portion of the body ought to be larger than before, because the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of both magnitude and shape have increased.
Yet, this is not perceived; how can this be logically explained?
Some explain this as follows:
because the informative [matter] (*vijñapti*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are subtle, it is like dyeing a limb; thus, no primary elements can be perceived. Others say:
Because there are cavities within the body, although [the elements] can be mutually accommodated, they do not become larger than their original size.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 35; *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 36.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.

Chapter Four: The Analysis of Karma, Part Four. It has already been explained that, in brief, there are two types of karma according to the distinction between volition (*cetanā*) and karma following volition (*cetayitvā-karman*).
Furthermore, there are three types, namely the distinctions among the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore, there are five types, namely the two categories of manifest and unmanifest action for both body and speech, as well as the distinction of the single category of mental action (cetanā).
Regarding these five types of karma, how are their nature (*svabhāva*), realm (*dhātu*), and level (*bhūmi*) established?
The verse says:
The unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is neutral; the other three are of three kinds. The unwholesome exists only in the desire realm.
Non-informative [action] (avijñapti) pervades both the desire and form realms; informative [action] (vijñapti) exists only in the two [realms] where there is sustained thought (savicāra).
There is no obscured (nivṛta) informative action in the desire realm, because it lacks a motivating cause (samutthāna).
The treatise says:
Non-informative action (avijñapti) pertains exclusively to the nature of the wholesome and the unwholesome;
it does not exist as indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Why is this? Because it is originated by powerful minds and mental factors.

The neutral mind is weak and lacks the functional capacity to act as a causal motivation (hetu-samutthāna) that draws forth a powerful karma, causing it to arise continuously throughout subsequent moments of other mental states and even during periods of non-consciousness.
As for what is called "the rest," it refers to the two types of manifest action (*vijñapti*) and volition (*cetanā*), which are threefold—namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.

Among these, the unwholesome exists only in the desire realm and not elsewhere, because [in the higher realms] there are no unwholesome roots, nor shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) or lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
Wholesome and neutral [unmanifest karma] exist in all three realms as appropriate, since there is no specific prohibition against them.

Both desire and form realms possess unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*), but it certainly does not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This is because in the formless realm, the perception of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*) has been suppressed; having become weary of and turned away from all forms, one enters the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and thus form cannot arise within those meditative states.
Alternatively, wherever there is the activity of body and speech, it is only in that place that there is bodily and vocal restraint (*kāya-vāg-saṃvara*).
Some say: because the great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) there.

That [absence of great elements] can only preclude contaminated (*sāsrava*) non-informative matter (*avijñapti*); there is no logical possibility for it to preclude uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) non-informative matter.

This is because, within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the great elements do not exist. Since contaminated discipline (*saṃvara*) belonging to a specific realm and level must necessarily be produced by the great elements of that very realm and level, there is no possibility for it to be produced by the great elements of a different realm or level; therefore, there is no uncontaminated discipline in the formless realm.

Since it has already been granted that [matter] can be produced by primary elements belonging to a different realm or a different level, what principle could possibly preclude this in the case of the formless realm?
Therefore, the previous statement is logically sound and free from error.
The Vaibhāṣika masters state as follows:
Śīla (ethical discipline) arises in order to counteract duḥśīla (immoral conduct).

Immoral conduct exists only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is distant from the desire realm by way of four types of distance: first, distance of the basis (*āśraya-viprakarṣa*); second, distance of the mode of activity (*ākāra-viprakarṣa*); third, distance of the object (*ālambana-viprakarṣa*); and fourth, distance of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-viprakarṣa*).

Regarding "remoteness of basis" (*āśraya-dūratā*): this refers to the fact that within the states of entering and emerging from meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*), there is no possibility for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) to serve as the substantial basis [for a desire-realm mind].

Regarding "remoteness of aspect" (*ākāra-dūratā*): this refers to the fact that a formless-realm mind ultimately lacks the capacity to produce aspects such as suffering or coarseness with respect to phenomena of the desire realm.

The meaning of "distance by object" (ālambana-dūratā) should be understood in this same way: because the mind of the formless realm can only take the contaminated phenomena of the fourth dhyāna or below as its objects through the mental aspects of suffering, coarseness, and so forth.

Regarding remoteness by way of antidote (*pratipakṣa-dūratā*): when one has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is absolutely impossible to give rise to the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), because these cannot serve as the two types of antidotes—namely, the antidote of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa*) and the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa*)—for unwholesome discipline (*duḥśīla*) and other such factors of the desire realm. It is not that they are unable to take those factors as objects; rather, they are simply incapable of producing revulsion toward them. Therefore, there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) in the formless realm.

Manifest form exists only in the two levels where there is investigation (*savicāra-bhūmi*), namely throughout the desire realm and the first dhyāna; it cannot be said that manifest form exists in the higher levels.
The mention of "with investigation" is intended to show that manifest karma exists everywhere within the first dhyāna.

If there were no bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti*) at all on the levels above [the desire realm], and since vocal informative action (*vāg-vijñapti*) is likewise absent, how could there be the sense-sphere of sound (*śabda-āyatana*)?
There is no fault here, for we do not deny external sound produced by external primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as its cause. Thus, there is no contradiction.
Other masters say:

"The three higher dhyānas also possess unobscured-neutral informative karma (*vijñapti-karma*); this must logically be so, for since there is no fault in the arising of the three bodies of consciousness (*vijñāna-kāya*) within those three higher stages, why would the mind that initiates informative karma not arise?"

However, from a virtuous or defiled mind of a higher level, no [virtuous or defiled] mind of a lower level arises, because the virtue and defilement of the lower levels are inferior and have been abandoned. Consequently, there is no manifestation of virtue or defilement arising from a higher level;
what was previously described as virtuous is so by virtue of this principle.
Why is this so? Although it manifests before one, it is not bound to that [level].
Manifest action (vijñapti) that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) is certainly non-existent in the desire realm; it can only be said to exist within the first dhyāna.
It has been heard that Mahābrahmā spoke words of deception and flattery, such as when, among his own assembly, he falsely praised himself in order to evade the questioning of Aśvajit.
Furthermore, for what reason is there no manifest action (vijñapti-karma) at all from the second dhyāna upward?

Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*), because there is no motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*) that initiates such action.
A mind accompanied by vitarka and vicāra can produce manifest karma, and such a mind is entirely absent from the two higher meditative attainments (*dhyāna*) upward.

Is it not true that we previously stated that when one is born in the three higher realms, one can likewise give rise to the three lower sets of consciousnesses? If so, why would the mind that expresses manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) not arise?
Has it not already been explained that although [the lower consciousnesses] may become present while relying on a body of a higher realm, they are not bound to that realm?
Some maintain this view:
based on a body belonging to another level (*bhūmi*), one cannot produce bodily or vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) by means of a mind belonging to a different level.

If that were so, how do we account for the sūtra which states that at one time the Blessed One ascended to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, where the hosts of devas there prostrated to, praised, and made offerings to the Blessed One?
Otherwise, this sūtra would result in being mere words devoid of meaning.
Furthermore, we hear it stated in the sūtras that the Śuddhāvāsa deities and others came to the Buddha’s presence to offer praise, prostration, and questions.
Therefore, there is no logical fault in asserting that one born in another stage can give rise to a mind of that other stage and produce bodily and vocal intimation.
However, as in the case of the *vijñānakāya* and so forth, [the manifesting mind] is not bound to that specific stage (*bhūmi*).

Furthermore, the mind that produces manifest action is abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because the afflictions abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) operate only within the internal domain.

Because within the desire realm there definitively exists no obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) affliction to be abandoned through cultivation, therefore informative action (vijñapti-karma) is entirely absent in the three higher stages, and there is no obscured-unspecified informative action within the desire realm.
Is it solely by virtue of their motivation (*samutthāna*) that phenomena come to possess qualities such as being wholesome or unwholesome? No. Why is this so?
The nature of wholesomeness and so forth is established by four causes: first, by ultimate reality; second, by intrinsic nature; third, by association; and fourth, by origination.
Which phenomena possess which nature, and by which cause is each established?
The verse says:
Ultimate goodness is liberation; intrinsic goodness consists of shame, dread, and the faculties;
associated goodness is that which is associated with them; and goodness by origination refers to form-karma and the like.
The opposite of this is called unwholesome; it surpasses the indeterminate and the two types of permanent [phenomena].
The treatise says:
"Ultimate wholesomeness" refers to true liberation, which is designated as "wholesome" in the sense of being secure and peaceful.

This means that within nirvāṇa, all sufferings are eternally stilled and it is supremely secure, just like being free from illness; this is established as "wholesome" by way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore, nirvāṇa is called "ultimately wholesome."

Alternatively, true liberation is "supreme" (*parama*) and is the "object" (*artha*); thus it receives the name "ultimate object" (*paramārtha*). "Supreme" means most venerable and peerless; "object" means that there exists a distinct, real essence. This indicates that because *nirvāṇa* is peerless and substantially existent, it is called the ultimate object. Such an ultimate object, being secure, is termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
Since such nirvāṇa is virtuous and eternal, its essence is the most sublime among all phenomena; therefore, it alone is designated as the "virtue of ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha-kuśala*).

As for "intrinsic virtue" (*svabhāva-kuśala*), this refers to the faculties of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), as well as the three roots of goodness—non-attachment and so forth—among conditioned phenomena. These are virtuous by their very nature, independent of association or other concomitant arisings, just like efficacious medicine.

Regarding "wholesomeness by association" (*saṃprayoga-kuśala*): this refers to that which is associated [with wholesome factors]. This is because the mind and mental factors must be associated with the wholesome roots of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) in order to constitute a wholesome nature; if they are not associated with those factors such as shame, their wholesome nature is not established, just like water mixed with medicinal herbs.

Regarding "wholesome by origination" (samutthāna-kuśala), this refers to bodily and vocal actions, the [four] characteristics such as birth, acquisitions (prāpti), and the two mindless attainments; they are designated as "origination" because they are originated by that which is wholesome by intrinsic nature (svabhāva-kuśala) and by association (saṃprayoga-kuśala), just as milk is produced from the essence of medicinal herbs.

Since acquisitions (*prāpti*) also arise due to minds of a different category—for instance, when a mind resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) is acquired because a superior neutral mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) has become manifest, or when various defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are acquired because a superior defiled mind has become manifest—how can these [acquisitions] be established as being of a virtuous nature (*kuśalatva*) and so forth?

This statement is made cryptically because [the mind] arises simultaneously with the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those dharmas; there is no fault, for it is not the case that minds of a different category do not function as conditions for arising.
Although minds of a different category also serve as conditions for arising, once they have become wholesome and so forth, they do not depend upon that [original] mind.

Alternatively, because those acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise in dependence upon them, they attain the nature of being wholesome and so forth by virtue of that dependence; thus, the distinction of the nature of being wholesome and so forth in acquisitions is established through their origination (*samutthāna*).
Just as it was stated that there are four distinctions of the nature of the wholesome, the four types of the unwholesome are the opposite of these.
How are they the opposite?
Ultimate unwholesomeness refers to the phenomena of saṃsāra; within saṃsāra, all phenomena have suffering as their intrinsic nature and are utterly unstable, like a chronic illness.

Intrinsic non-virtue refers to shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*). Among the tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena, only shamelessness, lack of dread, and the three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and so forth—are non-virtuous by their very nature, independent of association or other concomitant origination, just like a poisonous drug.

"Associated with the unwholesome" means that which is associated with them; for it is only when mental states (citta-caitta-dharma) are associated with shamelessness (āhrīkya), lack of dread (anapatrāpya), and the unwholesome roots (akuśala-mūla) that they constitute an unwholesome nature, whereas otherwise they do not, just as water mixed with poison [is not drinkable].

Unwholesome by origination refers to bodily and vocal actions, as well as birth and so forth, and acquisitions (*prāpti*), because they are originated by that which is unwholesome by nature and by association, like milk produced from a poisonous medicinal decoction.

If that were so, there would be no single contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomenon that is either neutral (*avyākṛta*) or wholesome (*kuśala*), because all such phenomena are subsumed within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); consequently, all of them would have to be subsumed under the unwholesome (*akuśala*).

Although this is indeed the case according to the ultimate principle, here we speak in terms of maturation (*vipāka*). Among all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), those that cannot be designated as having a maturation fruit are established by the name "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*); among these, those that can be designated as having a desirable maturation are called "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
Conditioned, indeterminate, and tainted wholesome dharmas, because they give rise to slight suffering—much like a minor illness—may also be termed "ultimately unwholesome" (*paramārthato 'kuśala*).
Just as there are ultimate wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas], are there also ultimately indeterminate (*paramārthato 'vyākṛta*) dharmas?
There are also [unconditioned phenomena]. How so?

It refers to two eternal phenomena: non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and great space (*ākāśa*). Since they have no other categories and are exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), they are established as the "ultimately indeterminate" (*paramārthāvyākṛta*) alone; they possess no distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor do they have associated or co-arising factors.
There is no single mental factor that is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta), because it is universally associated with an indeterminate mind.

Even if one were to establish three categories such as "self-nature" (svabhāva) and so forth through expedient means, they would still fail to encompass all [indeterminate factors], because indeterminate factors are numerous.
Thus, the indeterminate (avyākṛta) is of only two kinds: first, the ultimate (paramārtha), and second, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Conditioned indeterminate phenomena are subsumed under the category of intrinsic nature, because they are established as indeterminate without depending on any other distinct cause.
Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) indeterminate states are subsumed under the ultimate (*paramārtha*), because their nature is eternal and they lack any alternative modes of classification.

If the power of motivation (*samutthāna*) causes bodily and vocal actions to become wholesome or unwholesome, then the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the basis for those bodily and vocal actions should likewise be so; for both arise from the same single mind.
This objection is unreasonable, because the agent’s mind originally intends to initiate an action, and not the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
That is to say, there is no agent who, regarding the primary elements, gives rise to the desire:
"I shall bring forth such a kind of primary elements into manifestation."
Taking this as the gateway, wholesome and unwholesome minds arise.
Furthermore, it is observed in the world that the two types of action—bodily and vocal—arise dependent upon the mind; never has it been seen that bodily or vocal action arises apart from the mind.
However, the four great elements arise even apart from the mind; therefore, we know that those phenomena do not arise dependent upon the mind.
Furthermore, just as the eye and other faculties lack distinctions such as being wholesome or unwholesome when they do not depend on the mind for their arising,
so too the primary elements (mahābhūta), not depending on the mind for their arising, logically lack such distinctions as being wholesome or unwholesome.

If that were so, then acquisitions (*prāpti*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such as arising (*jāti*) would lack distinctions such as being "wholesome by origination" (*samutthāna-kuśala*), because they are not what the primary mind intends to bring about, and because they manifest even during states of non-consciousness (*acittaka*).
This objection is irrational, because the distinctions such as "wholesome" and so forth are established through the power of the dharmas themselves.
That is to say, the acquisition of the four characteristics is established in dependence upon the dharma; it does not exist independently of others like the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there is not a single phenomenon that does not depend upon the power of the mind to become wholesome or unwholesome. Therefore, it is well-established by reason that acquisitions (*prāpti*) and characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) must, like the phenomena to which they belong, attain their status as wholesome and so forth through the power of the mind.

Once it has arisen, although it continues to evolve as a mental stream apart from the mind, there is no logical fault; for it is induced to evolve by the power of the preceding mind. Likewise, it stands to reason that the non-informative (avijñapti) associated with meditative concentration arises through the power of that concentration and so forth.
The wholesome nature of the divine eye and divine ear should be subsumed under the category of the wholesome, because they are originated by a wholesome mind.

This objection is unreasonable, because those two [supernormal powers] are associated with the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which is neutral (*avyākṛta*), and because those two arise simultaneously with that path.
If this difficulty is thus resolved, why expend such great effort?
As stated above, bodily and vocal actions become wholesome or unwholesome through the power of their motivation (*samutthāna*). How many types of motivation are there?
What kind of motivating force causes bodily and vocal actions to become wholesome or unwholesome?
What are the distinctions between these motivating forces when they are compared with one another?
The verse says:
There are two kinds of origination: that which is causal and that which is momentary;
these should be understood respectively as "primary" (*pravartaka*) and "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*).
Consciousness abandoned through vision is exclusively primary; the five sensory consciousnesses are exclusively concomitant.
The mental application of cultivation and abandonment pertains to both [types of karma]; it is neither untainted nor maturation.
Regarding the nature of the primary [volition], such as being wholesome and so forth, the concomitant [volition] may each be of three types;
for a Muni, the wholesome is necessarily identical, while the neutral may be either [neutral or] wholesome.
The treatise says:

The motivating origins (*samutthāna*) of the two types of action—bodily and vocal—are twofold, namely, the causal origin (*hetu-samutthāna*) and the momentary origin (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*). This is because the former acts as the cause, while the latter exists at that very moment.
Respectively, the first is called "origination" (*pravartaka*) and the second is called "consequent origination" (*anuvartaka*).
This means that when the causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*) is about to perform an action, one reflects:
"I shall now perform such and such an action that ought to be done."
Because it is able to initiate [action], it is called "primary" (*pravartaka*).

At the moment when the action is being performed through its immediate arising, because it proceeds simultaneously with the karma initiated by the previously mentioned primary mind, it is called "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*).
If there were no *anuvartaka* (concomitant), then even though a prior cause exists as the initiator, the manifest (*vijñapti*) would not proceed—just as in the state of mindlessness or like a corpse.

The *anuvartaka* possesses the functional capacity to sustain the manifest; however, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) does not depend upon a concomitant to proceed, because the unmanifest continues to proceed even in states of mindlessness.
As stated above, because the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya-kleśa*) operate internally (*antarmukha-pravṛtta*), they cannot manifest external action.

If this is so, for what reason did the Blessed One say that from wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) arise wrong intention (*mithyāsaṃkalpa*), wrong speech (*mithyāvāk*), wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*), and wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*)?

This is not contradictory: consciousness abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) can only act as the *pravartaka* (initiator) for the manifestation of informative action (*vijñapti-karman*), because it serves as the necessary equipment (*sambhāra*) for the arising of vitarka and vicāra that produce informative action; it does not act as the *anuvartaka* (concomitant), because such [insight-abandoned] consciousness is absent at the time when the mind directed toward external objects (*bahir-mukha-citta*) is actually performing the action.

For this reason, it is said that a mind abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) serves as the causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*) for bodily and vocal actions, but it certainly cannot serve as the momentary motivation (*tatkṣaṇa-samutthāna*).

Although a consciousness abandoned by insight is capable of deliberation (*manasikāra*), it lacks the functional capacity to move the body or produce speech. Nevertheless, within the production of a single manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), it is possible for many moments of thought to deliberate and initiate it; however, only the final moment of thought proceeds simultaneously with the manifest action. Were this not the case, the manifest action would necessarily lack the nature of being momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

Although consciousness abandoned by seeing can act as the motivating force that initiates manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*), it is not itself manifest karma; for immediately following this consciousness, an inwardly directed mind (*antar-mukha-pravṛtti-citta*) arises without interval, which cannot give rise to the consciousness that accompanies bodily or vocal manifestation.

If it were otherwise, then the mind abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) would also have to serve as the momentary motivation (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*) for manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), because the applied mental consciousness (*prayoga-manovijñāna*) abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) can immediately induce the mind that co-exists with manifest action, and thus also serves as its momentary motivation in being co-existent with that manifestation.

Although that which is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) can serve as a cause to project various manifest actions (*vijñapti-karma*), apart from the motivating mind abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), a mind co-arising with manifestation cannot possibly arise; therefore, there is no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest action in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
However, in the Sūtras, based solely on the fact that [mental states] act as successive causes and motivators, it is stated cryptically:
"Due to wrong view, wrong speech and so forth arise.

In the Abhidharma, because those [wrong views] cannot immediately induce the consciousness that accompanies manifest action (*vijñapti*), it is said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*) that the mind abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya-citta*)—operating only within the internal sense-doors—cannot produce manifest action.
Therefore, the sūtras and śāstras do not contradict one another in principle.

Furthermore, if that which is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) were to manifest as derived form (*rūpa*), then this form would also have to be abandoned by insight; however, it has already been extensively established that form is not abandoned by insight.
If the five groups of consciousness function solely as concomitants, it is because they are devoid of conceptual discrimination and arise directed toward external objects.
The mental consciousness to be abandoned through cultivation admits of both types, because it possesses conceptual discrimination and arises directed toward external objects.
From this, a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established:
there is that which is the primary mover (*pravartaka*) but not the concomitant mover (*anuvartaka*), namely, the mind abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
There is that which is the concomitant mover but not the primary mover, namely, the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness.

There are those that are both the primary mover (*pravartaka*) and the concomitant mover (*anuvartaka*, i.e., the mental factors), namely, a portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
