There are those that are neither the primary mover nor the concomitant mover, namely, all other consciousnesses produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), because those produced by cultivation are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).

However, to say that untainted (*anāsrava*) states are not [of the nature of] maturation (*vipāka*) commits the faults of being too narrow and too broad, because tainted meditative minds (*samāhita-citta*) are likewise neither.

Furthermore, while various ripening consciousnesses (*vipākavijñāna*) may indeed be excluded from being "transformative" (*pravṛtti*), what reasoning could possibly preclude them from being "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*)?
However, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrāntavādin) states:

"Because it operates spontaneously rather than through volitional application (*prayoga*), the various ripening consciousnesses (*vipākavijñāna*) are neither the primary evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) nor its concomitants.
Others, moreover, say:
This [state] is induced solely by the force of prior karma and can only manifest when other mental activities have ceased; therefore, it is not of two kinds.

Even if this were able to give rise to informative actions of body and speech, what would its nature be: would it be born of maturation (*vipākaja*), a deportment (*airyāpathika*), or a craft (*śailpasthānika*)?
Furthermore, it is not produced by maturation (*vipākaja*), because it arises from present application (*prayoga*).
Nor is it the other two types [of mind], because it arises from a mind of maturation.

Such a principle can only serve to exclude the possibility that a mind produced by maturation acts as the causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*) for another mind that functions as the transformative agent (*pravartaka*) for the manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*).
Since the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja-citta*) operates toward external objects, how could it be logically contradictory for it to serve as the concomitant cause (*anuvartaka*)?

Furthermore, if one accepts that bodily intimation (*vijñapti-karma*) does not operate independently, but rather that its operation takes the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) as its concomitant cause, what fault is there in this?

Furthermore, one should state only that the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is not the motivating cause (*hetu-samutthāna*) because its force is weak; one should not say it is because it proceeds spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*) without application (*prayoga*). Otherwise, even the innate wholesome (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) would not function as the cause for initiating informative action (*vijñapti-karma*), since it too proceeds spontaneously without application.
Because of this, the Master of the Sūtra incurs the faults of deficiency and excess, and his reasons become non-reasons; the wise should understand this.
Are the primary consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the secondary consciousnesses (*anuvartaka-vijñāna*) necessarily identical in nature? No.

How so? It means that if the preceding evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is of a wholesome nature, the subsequent conforming evolving consciousness (*anuvartaka-vijñāna*) may be of any of the three natures—wholesome and so forth; the same applies when the evolving consciousness is unwholesome or indeterminate.
O Sole Honored Muni, the primary evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and its concomitant evolving consciousnesses are for the most part identical in nature, with only slight differences.

That is to say, if the primary evolving mind is wholesome, the concomitant evolving consciousness is also wholesome; if the primary evolving mind is neutral (*avyākṛta*), the concomitant is likewise so, because there is certainly no delusion regarding the continuity of moments.

While there may be occasions when the wholesome mind follows the transformation of the indeterminate, there is never a time when the indeterminate follows the transformation of the wholesome; for in the case of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, his mind never diminishes or falters during activities such as preaching the Dharma.
Other schools (nikāya) state:
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are always in meditative absorption (samādhi), their minds are exclusively wholesome (kuśala) and lack any indeterminate (avyākṛta) mind.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
“The nāga walks in concentration, the nāga stands in concentration,
the nāga sits in concentration, and the nāga lies down in concentration.
The Vaibhāṣika masters provide this explanation:
This demonstrates that the Buddha’s mind necessarily arises with full awareness, and there is no instance where his mind arises without being directed by his will.

Because he is undistracted regarding objects, he is designated as "one in meditative concentration" (*samāhita*); it is not the case that the Blessed Buddha lacks the deportment-mind (*airyāpathika*), the ripening-born consciousness (*vipākaja*), or the mind resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*). There is no logical fault in asserting that these various types of minds arise [in the Buddha].

Since it has already been stated that there are three types each for wholesome and so forth regarding both the primary (pravṛtti) and the concomitant (anuvartaka), this very heading and explanation serve as sufficient clear evidence: the various karmas produced become wholesome, unwholesome, and so on, by following the motivating cause (hetu-samutthāna) and not by following the momentary [state] (kṣaṇa-samutthāna).
Apart from this, since karma induced by a wholesome mental state coexists with unwholesome or neutral states of mind, by what principle could it be prevented from becoming unwholesome or neutral?
In that case, there would have to be the production of karma of a distinct nature from a cause consisting of a distinct volition.

Thus, for one who strives diligently with the desire to perform wholesome deeds, unwholesome or neutral karma may instead arise; or, conversely, if this occurs, it contradicts correct principle. Therefore, it is logically established that the establishment of karma as wholesome and so forth is determined by the power of the primary motivating force (*maulavṛtti*), and not by the power of the concomitant force (*anuvṛttivṛtti*).
However, the various non-informative actions (*avijñapti-karma*) that arise simultaneously with the concentrated mind share a single fruit with it;
thus, through the power of this concomitant transformation, they attain the nature of goodness, for they arise as being strictly subordinate to this mind.
In this context, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra), failing to clearly comprehend the underlying principles of the explanation, further raises this objection:

"Do all manifest actions (vijñapti-karma) constitute a virtuous nature and so forth in the same manner as the initiating mind (pravartaka-citta), or in the manner of the conforming mind (anuvartaka-citta)?"
If that were the case, what fault would there be?

If it were as you suggest—that [the view] acts as the "turner"—then within the desire realm there should be obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*), because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are capable of acting as the turner.

Alternatively, one must distinguish that not all minds abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) are capable of acting as the motivating cause (*pravartaka*); for if it were otherwise, then the informative action (*vijñapti*) of the Prātimokṣa vows, when conjoined with an evil or neutral mind that acts as a conforming cause (*anuvartaka*), would not be of a virtuous nature.
Regarding this objection, one ought to apply diligent effort; yet it is not clear with what underlying intention these words were spoken:
are they intended to encourage the great masters of the Abhidharma to apply diligent effort, or are they meant to encourage oneself?

If one were to urge the great masters of the Abhidharma, they have already applied diligent effort toward this matter, contemplating it well and explaining it skillfully; why, then, urge them further?

If [the author] urges himself in this way, it is clear that the Master of the Sūtras has not yet exerted himself regarding these principles; only now, as insight arises, can he reflect upon his own state, realizing he has not yet understood the tenets of the Abhidharma. May he, therefore, diligently seek the principles of the fundamental treatise and its commentaries.

Furthermore, it is said: if manifest karma (*vijñapti*) were not established as virtuous and so forth by the power of the concomitant mind (*anuvartaka-citta*), then one should not say that the aforementioned sutra refers only to the initial motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*) and not to the momentary [motivation], and thus there would certainly be no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest karma in the desire realm.
He [the opponent] says that this teaching establishes the determination of the nature of wholesome and so forth solely by the power of the simultaneous motivation (*sahabhū-samutthāna*).

Although the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) act as the antecedent motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*), there is absolutely no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) karma in the realm of desire.
This statement was made by the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) because he failed to understand the intended meaning of our own school’s position. The intent of this statement is as follows:

if the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) were to arise simultaneously with karma as its momentary co-arising cause (*sahabhū-samutthāna*), then it would be impossible for them to be separated from the mind that acts as the primary motivating cause (*hetu-samutthāna*) for the manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). If that were so, for what reason would there be no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) bodily or vocal manifest karma within the desire realm?

However, since even the afflictions abandoned through insight (darśana-heya-kleśa) cannot act as the cause that immediately induces the consciousness co-arising with karma, how could they possibly act as their own momentary origination (kṣaṇa-samutthāna)?
To say they cannot act as momentary origination is to indicate that they cannot act as the immediate origination (samanantara-samutthāna);
for whatever can act as immediate origination must necessarily be able to act as momentary origination.

Therefore, although the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and extreme views (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) act as remote causes that induce bodily and vocal informative action (vijñapti), they acquire the nature of unwholesomeness through the power of the proximate cause consisting in their abandonment through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya). For this reason, it is said that the aforementioned sūtra refers only to the motivating cause (samutthāna-hetu) in its prior state and not to the moment of actual occurrence; thus, within the desire realm, there is certainly no obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) informative action.

If this were not the case, one should not say that the sutra refers only to the preceding cause as the motivating factor (*samutthāna*), for the mention of "preceding" is intended to clarify the distinction between remote and proximate causes; it employs the term "preceding cause" specifically to exclude the proximate cause.
Therefore, the meaning of the words has not been fully understood by either party.

Having completed the ancillary discussion on the realms, spheres, and stages of informative action (*vijñapti*), we should now further clarify the characteristics of the preceding informative and non-informative actions (*avijñapti*).
The verse says:
"Non-manifest [action] consists of the three types of restraint, non-restraint, and that which is neither.
The treatise says:
It should be understood that, briefly stated, there are three kinds of non-manifest [action]: first, restraint; [second, non-restraint; and third, that which is neither].
The second is non-restraint;
the third is neither of the two, meaning it is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
It is called "restraint" (saṃvara) because it can obstruct and extinguish the continuity of immoral conduct.
How many distinctions are there in such restraint?
The verse says:
Restraint is distinguished as that of the Prātimokṣa, that born of dhyāna, and that born of the Path.
The treatise says:

Briefly, there are three types of distinction in discipline (*saṃvara*): first, the discipline of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*), which refers to the precepts of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
second, the discipline born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-ja-saṃvara*), which refers to the precepts of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The restraint born of the three paths refers to untainted morality (*anāsrava-śīla*).
What are the characteristics and distinctions of this initial restraint?
The verse says:
The initial types of restraint are eightfold, yet in actual substance there are only four;
because they differ in form and name, each is distinct and not mutually contradictory.
The treatise says:

There are eight distinct types of the prātimokṣa restraint: first, the bhikṣu restraint; second, the bhikṣuṇī restraint; third, the śikṣamāṇā restraint; fourth, the śrāmaṇera restraint; fifth, the śrāmaṇerī restraint; sixth, the upāsaka restraint; seventh, the upāsikā restraint; and eighth, the upavāsa restraint.
These eight distinct types of restraint are collectively termed the first, the Prātimokṣa restraint.

Among these, the first five types of restraint are established based on individuals (*pudgala*) who are capable of practicing the abandonment of unwholesome conduct and the abandonment of sensual conduct.
Because such a person, until the end of their life, is able to abstain from evil deeds such as killing and is able to remain far removed from unchaste conduct.

Next, based on the individual (pudgala) who is capable of practicing the avoidance of unwholesome conduct but not the practice of renunciation, the distinctions between the two lay assemblies (saṃgha) whose vows last for the duration of life are established.
Because such a person, until the end of their life, is able to abstain from evil deeds such as killing, yet is unable to remain far removed from unchaste conduct.
Therefore, this sutra states only: "One should abstain from sexual misconduct, not from non-celibacy.

Subsequently, based on the individual (pudgala) who is able to cultivate [restraint] but has not completely abandoned evil conduct and sensual desires, it establishes the distinction of the one-day, one-night restraint for laypeople.

Because such types of persons are unable to completely abandon unwholesome conduct and sensual desires, [the Buddha] establishes them in the practice of skillful means so that they may gradually train themselves to completely abandon unwholesome conduct and the pursuit of sensual desires.
Therefore, although there are eight names, the actual entities are only four:
first, the bhikṣu restraint; second, the śrāmaṇera restraint; third, the upāsaka restraint; and fourth, the upavāsa restraint.
Only these four types of distinct Pratimokṣa vows possess substantial reality, as their characteristics are each distinct.

Why is this so? Apart from the Bhikṣu vow, there is no separate Bhikṣuṇī vow; apart from the Śrāmaṇera vow, there is no separate Śikṣamāṇā or Śrāmaṇerī vow; and apart from the Upāsaka vow, there is no separate Upāsikā vow.
How is this known to be so?
Because while the substance itself undergoes no loss or acquisition, its designation changes due to the transformation of its form.
"Form" refers to physical appearance, specifically the male and female organs; it is by virtue of these two organs that the forms of males and females are distinguished.
It is solely through the transformation of the physical form that the various vows are designated as those of a *bhikṣu* or a *bhikṣuṇī*.
That is to say, at the stage of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya*), the original *bhikṣu* vow is termed a *bhikṣuṇī* vow, or the *bhikṣuṇī* vow is termed a *bhikṣu* vow.
It causes the śrāmaṇera vow to be called the śrāmaṇerī vow, or it causes the śrāmaṇerī and śikṣamāṇā vows to be called the śrāmaṇera vow.
The original upāsaka discipline may be termed the upāsikā discipline, or the upāsikā discipline may be termed the upāsaka discipline.

This is because at the stage of the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), there is no cause or condition for abandoning a previously obtained discipline or acquiring one not previously obtained; therefore, the four disciplines do not differ in substance from the three.

If one receives the *śrāmaṇera* vows from the *upāsaka* vows, and subsequently receives the *bhikṣu* vows from the *śrāmaṇera* vows, these three sets of vows are established with distinct names based on the progressive addition of methods for renunciation; they are not different in essence, just as a single coin and a pair of coins, or fifty and twenty [coins], are designated differently despite being the same substance.
When the three types of restraint are fully and simultaneously produced, their essences do not intermingle, and their characteristics are each distinct.

Within the simultaneous production of these three restraints, there are three instances of abstaining from killing; each instance of abstaining from killing has a distinct essence. It should be understood that the same applies to the others as appropriate; because the causes and conditions differ, their essences are not the same.

Just as one seeks to receive various types of training rules (*śikṣāpada*), so too, when one is able to abstain from various high and wide beds and seats, the drinking of intoxicants, and other bases for negligence and arrogance, one simultaneously abandons numerous conditions that give rise to killing and other unwholesome acts.
Since these various abstentions arise based on specific causes and conditions, there are distinctions among them according to those causes and conditions.
If this were not the case, then upon relinquishing the bhikṣu vows, one would have to relinquish all three sets of vows at that time, because the first two would be subsumed within the latter one.
Since this is not permitted, the three are distinct.

Nevertheless, these three types do not contradict one another; they operate simultaneously within a single body. It is not the case that one relinquishes the preceding restraint by receiving the subsequent one; otherwise, one would cease to be a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth upon relinquishing the bhikṣu vows, because one would have already relinquished those two previous restraints.
If there is one who diligently undertakes the lay devotee's (upāsaka) discipline, or a bhikṣu who undertakes the first two types of precepts, does he thereby acquire them? Some say:
"This should not be questioned."
If it already existed previously, there would be no principle for its further acquisition, as it would have already been obtained.

If it did not exist previously, then one would neither be a *śrāmaṇera* nor a *bhikṣu*; for since one had not previously received the lay (*upāsaka*) vows, there is certainly no principle by which one could receive and obtain the *śrāmaṇera* precepts.
If one has not previously received the śrāmaṇera vows, there is likewise no principle by which one could receive the bhikṣu precepts.
Thus, it would be impossible to establish those two names [of the ordination stages].
Inferring from this, it follows that [the bhikṣu ordination] should not be obtained.
Other masters say:
"There is also the principle that one may receive and obtain subsequent precepts even without having received the preceding discipline.
Therefore, those who uphold the Vinaya recite as follows:"
Although one did not previously receive the *śrāmaṇera* (novice) precepts, if one now receives only the full (*upasaṃpadā*) discipline, this is still called "properly receiving the full discipline.

By this principle, it is possible for a *śrāmaṇera* to receive the *upāsaka* (lay follower) discipline, and it is likewise possible for a *bhikṣu* (monk) to receive the *śrāmaṇera* and *upāsaka* precepts.

Is it not that one who has not diligently exerted himself should not claim for himself, "I pray you, bear witness that I am a lay follower (*upāsaka*)"? The same applies to a monk (*bhikṣu*); he should not claim for himself, "I pray you, bear witness that I am [a member of] the former two [orders]."
It is not the case that there is no principle for obtaining the precepts of an upāsaka or śrāmaṇera apart from such self-designating statements.
This objection is irrational, because both can indeed be designated.
That is to say, one may designate: "I am a śrāmaṇera and also an upāsaka; I pray that you bear witness to this."
The bhikṣu should also speak accordingly.
However, there is no fault in designating those two names based on their preeminent precepts.
If that were so, then śrāmaṇeras and bhikṣus would also have to receive the upavāsa restraint.
If one were permitted to become a lay follower (*upāsaka*), what fault would there be?
However, due to their inferiority, there are none who take joy in receiving it.

How are the four types of discipline—the lay follower (*upāsaka*), the one observing the fast-day vows (*upavāsastha*), the novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), and the fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*)—established?
The verse says: By undertaking the abstention from five, eight, ten, or all things that ought to be avoided, one is established as a lay follower (*upāsaka*),
one who observes the fast-day vows (*upavāsastha*), a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), or a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*).
The treatise says:
It should be understood that herein, according to their numerical sequence, four types of restraint (saṃvara) are established based on the four forms of renunciation.
That is to say, by undertaking the renunciation of the five things to be avoided, the first restraint—the lay follower's restraint (upāsaka-saṃvara)—is established.
What are the five dharmas that should be abandoned?
First, taking life; second, taking what is not given; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; and fifth, drinking various intoxicants.
If one undertakes the abstention from the eight things that ought to be avoided, the second restraint, the *upavāsa* (fasting) discipline, is established.
What are these eight things that ought to be avoided? First, killing; second, taking what is not given;

third, unchaste conduct; fourth, false speech; fifth, drinking various intoxicants; sixth, using perfumes, garlands, ointments, and attending performances of dance, song, and music; seventh, sleeping or sitting on high, broad, and luxurious beds or seats; and eighth, eating at improper times.
If one undertakes the abstention from the ten things that ought to be abandoned, the third *śrāmaṇera* restraint is established.
What are these ten things that ought to be abandoned?

They consist of the first eight [prohibitions], where the application of perfumes, garlands, dancing, singing, and watching performances is divided into two categories, with the addition of accepting and possessing gold, silver, and other precious objects as the tenth.

In order to encourage the many lay sentient beings who are fearful and timid toward the numerous rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), and to demonstrate that they are easy to uphold, the eight precepts combine two items into one; this is just as the Buddha briefly explained that there were three rules of training for the son of the Malla clan.
If one undertakes the abandonment of all bodily and vocal actions that ought to be abandoned, the fourth type of bhikṣu restraint is established.
Regarding the various distinctions among the names for the prātimokṣa restraint, the verse says:
It is called by the names *śīla*, Excellent conduct (*sucarita*), and restraint (*saṃvara*).
Only the initial moment of manifest and unmanifest [action] is called the distinct liberation and the path of action.
The treatise says:
It is named *śīla* because it is cooling.
In this context, *śīla* has the meaning of "leveling" or "smoothing. Thus, the *Śabdadhātunirdeśa* provides this explanation:
the verbal root *śī* is placed within the semantic field of leveling; since ethical discipline (*śīla*) can level out rugged karma, it is given the name *śīla*.
It is called "sublime conduct" (*sucarita*) because it is praised by the wise.
Alternatively, it is called "action" (*karman*) because one attains desirable fruits through its cultivation, and because it constitutes the very essence of what is performed.

Although the Sūtras state that all unmanifest forms (*avijñapti*) are neither created nor made—since those possessing a sense of shame and dread do not commit evil due to the power of having received the unmanifest—it is nonetheless designated as such.
The meaning of "volitional action" has already been explained above.
It is also called "restraint" (*saṃvara*), as previously interpreted.

Thus it should be understood that the name "Prātimokṣa-śīla" (Individual Liberation Precepts) applies without distinction to both the initial and subsequent stages; however, only the informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) [karma] of the first moment receive the names "Prātimokṣa" and "path of action" (*karmapatha*).

This means that at the time of receiving the precepts, because one individually abandons various evils through both manifest and unmanifest actions, it is established with the name "Prātimokṣa" (Individual Liberation) based on the sense of this initial, individual abandonment.
Alternatively, it is called *prātimokṣa* because it is what should be cultivated first;
or, it is called *prātimokṣa* because its initial arising is most capable of transcending [suffering], such as the prison-like and perilous miserable destinies (*durgati*).
The manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) actions of the very first moment may also be termed the "fundamental path of action" (*mūlakarmapatha*),
because at that initial moment they prevent misconduct of body and speech and give full expression to the karma of volition (*cetanā*).
From the second moment onward, until it is relinquished, they are not called "individual liberation" (*prātimokṣa*), but are termed the "individual liberation restraint" (*prātimokṣasaṃvara*).
These are not called courses of action (*karmapatha*), but are termed subsequent actions (*pṛṣṭha*).
Having already distinguished the different types of formal restraint (*saṃvara*), one should now distinguish the differences in the attainment of restraint.
Who attains which restraint?
The verse says:
Eight [factors] constitute the prātimokṣa; those who have attained dhyāna or are noble ones possess the dhyāna-born and path-born [restraints]; the latter two follow the mind.
The treatise says:
All eight classes of practitioners possess the prātimokṣa restraint, ranging from the bhikṣu down to the upavāsastha.
Do non-Buddhists not have any received precepts?
Although it exists, it is not called the *prātimokṣa* vow, because that which is undertaken lacks the capacity to bring about permanent liberation from all evils, as it is based on attachment.
That which arises from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) refers to this discipline because it arises from or depends upon meditative concentration.
If one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one will certainly achieve this discipline (*saṃvara*).
The "retinue" of meditative concentration is also termed meditative concentration.
The discipline born of the Path is accomplished by all Noble Ones (*ārya*); it is further divided into two types: that of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and that of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Among the three types of restraint previously mentioned, which restraints follow the mind?
Only the latter two: namely, that born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and that born of the Path (*mārga*).
The second is not the prātimokṣa.
Why is this? Because it continues to function constantly, whether the mind is different [from that of the vow] or even when there is no mind.
The two types of restraint—those of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and those that are untainted (*anāsrava*)—are also called the "restraint of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
Based on what stage are they established?
The verse says:
"Before reaching the nine uninterrupted paths, the two that arise together are called 'abandonment'.
The treatise says:

Within the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*), the meditative and untainted restraints (*dhyāna-śīla* and *anāsrava-śīla*) that arise simultaneously with the nine uninterrupted paths are called "restraints of abandonment" because they can permanently sever the unwholesome conduct of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as well as the afflictions that give rise to it; this is because only within the preparatory concentration does the "antidote of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*) exist.
By this, only the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) are included, because within these, ethical discipline (*śīla*) destroys unwholesome conduct.

Consequently, there may be the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) that is not the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*); thus, one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

The first phrase refers to the remaining contaminated dhyāna restraints (*dhyāna-saṃvara*), excluding the contaminated restraints of the nine paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
The second phrase refers to the uncontaminated restraints (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) based on the nine paths of immediate succession of the threshold concentration.

The third phrase refers to the contaminated restraint (*sāsrava-saṃvara*) associated with the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*anantarya-mārga*) of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*).
The fourth phrase refers to all remaining uncontaminated restraints (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), excluding those associated with the nine paths of uninterrupted transition of the threshold concentration.

In this way, there may be cases where there is untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) that is not restraint through abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*); one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That is to say, the aforementioned four permutations should be understood in reverse order.
If that is so, then regarding the brief precepts (*saṃkṣipta-śīla*) spoken by the Blessed One:
“Excellent is restraint of the body; excellent is restraint of speech;
excellent is restraint of the mind; excellent is universal restraint.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
One should well guard and well abide in the restraint of the eye faculty.
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this restraint of the mental faculty?
The intrinsic nature of these two is not non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
If that is so, what is it? The verse says:
The conjunction of clear comprehension and mindfulness Is called the restraint of the mental faculty.
The treatise says:

The restraint of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya-saṃvara*) consists of right awareness (*saṃprajanya*) and right mindfulness (*smṛti*), each acting individually yet combined as its own essence. Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"Having seen a form with the eye, one is neither glad nor sad, but always dwells in equanimity (*upekṣā*) with right awareness and right mindfulness."
In this manner, up until the mind has cognized dharmas, having enumerated the individual names, he again states the collective term.
"Prevention" refers to the two types of restraint; as listed in order, these two constitute its essence.
Now it should be investigated: regarding informative and non-informative [karma], who possesses what, and for how long?
First, let us distinguish the possession of non-informative [karma] in terms of restraint and non-restraint.
The verse says:
Abiding in the non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) of the Pratimokṣa, One always accomplishes the present [non-manifestation] as long as it has not been relinquished;
From the second moment onward, one accomplishes the past [non-manifestation]. The same applies to non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
One who attains the restraint of meditative concentration (dhyāna-saṃvara) always possesses it in both the past and the future;
for the noble one, at the first moment, the past is excluded; those abiding in meditative absorption or the Path possess the present.
The Commentary says:
For a person abiding in the prātimokṣa, from the first moment until they encounter conditions for relinquishing the precepts—such as abandoning the training—they always possess the present [precept].
This unmanifest (avijñapti) of the prātimokṣa restraint also becomes past after the first moment.
The preceding statement "as long as it has not been abandoned" applies universally to what follows.
Why then does the prātimokṣa restraint obtained in a previous life not become past at the very first moment of receiving the present ordination, just like the dhyāna restraint?
This objection is unreasonable, because this precept and the mind do not share the same fruit, whereas the mind free from defilement and so forth all share the same fruit.

If it were argued that this precept, like the mind, acquires past births, [we reply] that since the prātimokṣa has never been previously acquired, it should—like the superior dhyāna-restraint—not acquire past births in its first moment.
As it is said regarding one who abides in the prātimokṣa vows, it should be understood that the same applies to one who abides in non-restraint (asaṃvara).

That is to say, from the first moment until the conditions for abandoning the evil discipline—such as receiving the formal vows—have not yet passed, one constantly possesses the present non-informative (avijñapti) aspect of evil discipline; after the first moment, one also possesses the past [non-informative].
All those who have attained the dhyāna-restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara) constantly possess it in both the past and the future as long as they have not relinquished it;
for at the very first moment [of attainment], one necessarily reacquires that past dhyāna-restraint which was lost in previous lives.

In this regard, a distinction must be made in the explanation: the discipline (saṃvara) comprised within the levels conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) does not become past in its first moment; furthermore, that which is obtained in other lifetimes is relinquished at the time of death, for it is impossible to obtain it again in the present life.
Furthermore, it is not the case that all sentient beings have previously generated [this discipline], for it can only exist in those who possess the nature of attaining nirvāṇa.
All noble ones (ārya) constantly accomplish the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) of both the past and the future.
Regarding the distinctions: it means that at the first moment, one necessarily attains the future [path] but does not attain the past, because this type of noble path has not previously arisen.

That which was never previously attained and is now attained for the first time is called "initial. When one attains for the first time what was previously attained and then lost, one also attains the past.

That which has already arisen becomes past from the moment after its first instant until it is abandoned; furthermore, it remains constantly future until the state of the nirvana without remainder is attained.

If one is currently abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), that path successively constitutes the present *dhyāna-path restraint* (*dhyāna-mārga-saṃvara*). It does not constitute the present [restraint] at the time of emerging from contemplation.

Logically, it should only be said that when one is in the state of the path of concentration, one achieves the non-informative (*avijñapti*) of the present-world concentration-path; one should not say "abiding" as one does with the phrase "abiding in the fruit," for such a statement refers only to the achievement of the fruit, not to the actual manifestation of the fruit.
Now, since you merely say "abiding," how can it be known that the meditative path (*samāhita-mārga*) is actually manifest rather than merely accomplished?

Therefore, that statement still leaves room for doubt and cannot definitively clarify that the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is both accomplished and manifest; thus, one should simply say "in the meditative path. Although the word "abiding" is mentioned, it is laborious and useless.

Now, examining his intention in detail: the preceding passage has already explained the accomplishment of the past and future; this sentence specifically clarifies the accomplishment of the present. Thus, we know that the mention of "abiding" (sthiti) is intended to manifest "arising" (utpāda), not "accomplishment" (siddhi). This is because accomplishment alone does not constitute proof of the present, and because the non-informative (avijñapti) of the meditative concentrations and the Path necessarily follows the mind, whereas it can never be present when the mind is in a distracted state.
Having already explained those who abide in the wholesome and unwholesome restraints, how does one abide in the intermediate state?
The verse says:
Abiding in the intermediate state possesses non-informative action (*avijñapti*); At the first moment it is established as intermediate; thereafter, it is both.
The Commentary states:

Regarding those who abide in the intermediate state, this refers to those who possess neither restraint nor non-restraint; the unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*) produced by their actions does not necessarily exist in all cases.

If there is unmanifest [form] (*avijñapti*), it is comprised within the category of either virtuous restraint (*śīla*) or non-restraint (*aśīla*), or else it belongs to neither of these two categories.
In its initial moment, it exists only as "intermediate" (*madhya-kālika*), meaning it exists in the present; for this [present] is situated between the past and the future.
From the moment after the first instant until it is relinquished, one always possesses the non-informative (avijñapti) karma of both the past and present periods.
If one abides in either restraint (saṃvara) or non-restraint (asaṃvara), does one also possess unwholesome or wholesome non-informative karma?
If such a state were to exist, for how long would it endure?
The verse says:
Abiding in discipline or non-discipline, One gives rise to defiled or pure non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
The first is accomplished at the beginning; the middle and the latter two continue until the momentum of defilement or purity is exhausted.
The commentary states:

If one abides in restraint yet commits various unwholesome acts such as killing or binding due to predominant afflictions, non-informative (avijñapti) action of an unwholesome nature is thereby produced.

One who dwells in non-restraint may perform various superior wholesome deeds, such as prostrating to the Buddha, out of pure faith; by this, they also produce various wholesome unmanifest actions (*avijñapti*).

As long as these two types of mind have not been severed, the produced unmanifest action continues in a constant succession. However, its first moment constitutes only the present, while from the second moment onward, it constitutes both the past and the present.
Having already explained how the non-informative (*avijñapti*) is established, how is the informative (*vijñapti*) action established?
The verse says:
The informative is established as present while it is being performed; it is subsequently established as past, not as future.
"Both obscured and unobscured [informative action] are accomplished only in the present.
The commentary says:

All those who abide in discipline, non-discipline, or the intermediate state, as long as they are currently performing various manifest actions (*vijñapti-karman*), constantly accomplish present manifest action.

From the moment after the first instant until it is relinquished, one always possesses [the non-informative action] as past; there is never the possession of a future informative action, because its form is not concomitant with the mind and its force is extremely weak.
The same explanation applies to all non-informative (avijñapti) actions that are dispersed.

Regarding informative (vijñapti) actions that are either obscured-unneutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta) or unobscured-unneutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta), there is certainly no capacity to accomplish them in the past or future, because the power of their dharmas is inferior.
It can only induce the acquisition (*prāpti*) that arises simultaneously with the dharma; because the power of this acquisition is weak, it cannot induce a continuous succession of its own kind.

While it may be possible for a dharma to be said to be "accomplished" through a retrospective acquisition after it has already ceased, it likewise lacks the capacity to acquire a future dharma in anticipation.
Is it not the case that, just as this informative [action] (vijñapti) can give rise to a mind, it should likewise possess existence in the past and future?
This objection is unreasonable because the power of this informative action is weak; due to that weakness, the arising [of the action] is inferior to the mind that gives rise to it.

The reason for this is that while an indeterminate mind can manifest a manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), the manifest action it manifests does not give rise to an unmanifest action (*avijñapti*). Therefore, we know that the mind which initiates [the action] is inferior to the mind that gives rise to the unmanifest.
Just as there are distinctions among the names for restraint (*saṃvara*), are there also distinctions among the designations for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)? There are indeed. How so?
The verse says:
Evil conduct, evil discipline, and karma; these are the paths of action and non-restraint.
The commentary says:
These five synonyms, such as "misconduct" (duścarita) and so forth, are variations of the term "non-restraint" (asaṃvara).
They are designated as "misconduct" because they are censured and loathed by the wise, and because their results are undesirable.
It is called "unwholesome discipline" because it obstructs pure ethical conduct (*śīla*).
It is called "action" (*karman*) because it is produced by body and speech.

It is called an "action path" (*karmapatha*) because it is subsumed under the fundamental [actions], because it can fully express the volition of action, and because it is the path along which action travels.
The non-restraint of body and speech is called *asaṃvara*.
However, the name "path of action" (*karmapatha*) refers exclusively to the first moment, whereas the remaining four names are established by encompassing both the initial and subsequent stages.
Now, one should investigate: if one is possessed of a manifest action (*vijñapti*), is one also possessed of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*)?
One should formulate four propositions.
The verse says:
"One accomplishes informative action but not non-informative action, when one performs an act with weak volition while abiding in the intermediate state."
Having abandoned what has not yet arisen, the noble ones accomplish the non-informative (avijñapti) and not the informative (vijñapti).
The treatise says:
Those who accomplish only the informative and not the non-informative are those who abide in neither restraint nor non-restraint.

When inferior wholesome or unwholesome volitions perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds, the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—are capable of manifesting only manifest action (*vijñapti-karma*); they cannot even manifest non-manifest action (*avijñapti-karma*), let alone the manifest action produced by neutral (*avyākṛta*) volitions.

Excluding meritorious action based on material things and the completion of a path of action— because even those arising from inferior volition produce non-informative action (avijñapti), they consist solely of non-informative action and not informative action (vijñapti)—
this refers to ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) and noble individuals (ārya-pudgala) for whom informative action has not yet arisen or has already been abandoned after having previously arisen.

Is it not the case that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has already attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), even if they have not yet produced a manifest action (*vijñapti*) or have lost one previously produced, also accomplishes non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) rather than manifest action?
Why, then, does the verse specify only the noble ones (*ārya*)?
It is also logical that they are not ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Why, then, are ordinary beings specified in the commentary?
Both [interpretations] result in a negative construction; this should be reflected upon according to reason.
