If you think that just as there are cases where the wholesome vows (*saṃvara*) are incomplete in their branches, this [unwholesome vow] should be the same— meaning that just as one who undertakes the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a one-day observer (*upavāsa*), or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) may lack certain branches yet still obtain the discipline (*saṃvara*) comprised by those missing branches—
the same should also apply to the undertaking of non-discipline (*asaṃvara*).
This example is not equivalent, because there is a difference between restraint and non-restraint regarding whether they are acquired through effort or without effort.
That is to say, all virtuous precepts must rely upon effort and a virtuous intention (*āśaya*) to be received.
Because they are difficult to obtain, it follows by logical necessity that one does not receive all of them at once as a whole.

Conversely, if unwholesome precepts (*akuśala-śīla*) could be received without requiring effort—such that a negative intention (*akuśalāśaya*) alone suffices for their reception—then because they would not be difficult to obtain, it would follow by logical necessity that one would receive all of them at once as a whole whenever they are received.

Because in the desire realm the power of unwholesome states is strong, and evil *āśaya* (intentions) arise spontaneously, one commits various grave evils without requiring effort; furthermore, because wholesome *āśaya* is easily destroyed, by receiving even one [unwholesome] type, one simultaneously acquires all the others. This is not the case for the wholesome, and therefore the analogy is not equivalent.
We observe that weeds grow without effort, whereas fine grain only arises through diligent labor.
Furthermore, it is like a person who has undertaken an improper vow (*an-avadya-samvara*) and makes this formal commitment:
"For as long as I live, once every day or night, or once every fortnight, month, or so forth, I shall slaughter sheep and other animals."
One also acquires non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), because non-restraint is easily acquired.
Since the power of unwholesomeness is strong in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one acquires the evil precepts even if one does not constantly engage in them.
If those who wish to receive the monastic discipline (pravrajyā-saṃvara) make a formal commitment:
"For as long as I live, once every day, or night, or fortnight, or month, and so forth, I shall abstain from killing and other [unwholesome acts]," [they do not obtain the full discipline].
One cannot obtain the wholesome restraint (*kuśala-saṃvara*), because the wholesome restraint is difficult to receive and attain.

Since the power of wholesome dharmas is weak in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), if one does not maintain them constantly, one will not obtain the wholesome precepts; this case is likewise so, and thus the analogy is not uniform.

Therefore, while the Sautrāntika masters avoid the fault of [an act] being "unfounded," they instead fall into the fault of being "difficult to extricate. The wise should carefully examine this and correctly adopt or reject [the views].
Thus has been explained how non-discipline (asaṃvara) is acquired from them.
How one acquires non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and other types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)—the means by which this occurs has not yet been explained and shall now be stated.
The verse says:
The acquisition of all non-restraints Is through action and through formal undertaking.
One acquires the remaining types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) through the field, undertaking, or intense practice.
The Commentary says:

There are generally two kinds of persons who possess non-restraint (*asaṃvara*): first, those born into a family of non-restraint; and second, those born into other families who subsequently undertake this karma.
Those born into a family of non-restraint (aśubha-āsamvara) who initially engage in the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of killing and so forth acquire non-restraint through that very act.
Those born into other families who later take a vow, saying, "I shall perform such activities in order to seek wealth and sustain myself," [also acquire it].

At the very moment one makes the initial vow, one gives rise to an evil precept (*duḥśīla*); by virtue of this undertaking, one acquires non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). One acquires other types of non-manifest karma (*avijñapti*) through three causes.
These "other non-manifest karmas" refer to those that are neither restraint nor non-restraint, as they are subsumed under the intermediate category.

Regarding the three causes: first, by way of the field. That is to say, when one first gives a grove or similar gift to such a field of merit, wholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arises; this is as described regarding the various meritorious actions based on material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*).
Second, by way of undertaking (*samādāna*): this refers to making a personal vow,
saying, "From now on, if I do not make offerings to the Buddha and the Saṃgha,
I shall not eat first," or establishing a restrictive commitment to constantly give food and so forth during fasting days, half-months, or throughout the year.
From this, wholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) continues to arise.

Third, it arises through intense practice; that is, when one performs wholesome or unwholesome actions with such earnest attention—whether through pure faith or through intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*)—it can produce non-informative matter at the time of performing those wholesome or unwholesome deeds, which persists in a long-term succession until the power of that faith or the fetters is finally exhausted, as previously explained.
Having thus explained the acquisition of the vows and so forth, the relinquishment of the vows and so forth shall now be discussed.
First, how does one relinquish the vows of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*)?
The verse says:
The Prātimokṣa discipline is relinquished through intentional abandonment, death, the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs, the severance of the roots of virtue, and the passing of the night.
Some say it is relinquished by committing a grave offense; others say it is relinquished by the disappearance of the Dharma.
The Kashmiris say that committing the two [offenses] is like being in debt.
The Commentary states:
The term "vinaya" (discipline) is a synonym for "saṃvara" (restraint), because by means of it, the faculties are brought under control.

The Pratimokṣa discipline is relinquished through five conditions. First, by intentional relinquishment: this refers to the lack of aspiration for the discipline due to one's underlying intention (*āśaya*), whereby one performs a specific contradictory manifest action (*vijñapti-karma*) before a person capable of understanding, in order to abandon the training rules. It is not sufficient merely to give rise to the thought of abandoning the training rules, because that alone lacks the efficacy to effect such a change, just as it was with the mind that acquired the discipline.
Furthermore, because renunciation is not accomplished within a dream;
nor is it accomplished merely by the arising of a distinction in manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), since renunciation is not accomplished in states such as anger or insanity;
nor is it accomplished by both [manifest and non-manifest action] alone, since the arising of a mind and the manifestation of action toward animals and the like does not constitute renunciation.
Second, by the end of life, because the restraint is obtained through the predominant power of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Third, by the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), because when the body changes, the mind follows suit.
Furthermore, those with both sexual organs [do not receive the vows] because they lack predominance.
Fourth, it is due to the severance of the roots of goodness that serve as the cause; this refers to the severance of the mind that originates the manifest and unmanifest karma.

This is the meaning of the severance of the causes and conditions for this restraint. The lifelong precepts are relinquished through the four aforementioned conditions, while the one-day (upavāsa) restraint is also relinquished at the end of the night.
That is to say, the *upavāsa* (fasting) precepts are relinquished through the aforementioned four conditions, as well as by the end of the night, because the time limit has expired.
"The end of the night" refers to the moment when the dawn light appears.
Most masters of discipline generally agree that these five conditions constitute the relinquishment of the vows.
There are masters of other schools who maintain that by committing even a single offense entailing a grave downfall (*pārājika*), one abandons the monastic vows.

Others maintain that at the time when the True Dharma (*saddharma*) perishes, all forms of the Pratimokṣa discipline are abandoned without exception, because all the sacred teachings—including the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), the ritual boundaries (*sīmābandha*), and the formal acts (*karmavācanā*)—come to an end.
At that time, although there is no acquisition of previously unobtained discipline (*saṃvara*), there is no possibility of abandoning the discipline already obtained.
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīra, who have internalized the principles of the Abhidharma teachings in their hearts, state as follows:
"When one commits any one of the fundamental offenses (*mūlāpatti*), it does not follow that all discipline is abandoned."
However, one who has committed a grave offense has two designations: first, "one endowed with ethical discipline" (śīlavat), and second, "one who has violated the precepts.
If, regarding the offense committed, one should perform confession and purification, then by confessing and purifying it, they are designated solely as "one endowed with ethical discipline."

Just as one who possesses wealth but owes another a debt is called both a wealthy person and a debtor, whereas once the debt has been repaid, he is called only a wealthy person—this case should be understood in the same way; therefore, it does not constitute the forfeiture of the precepts.
By what reasoning and scriptural authority is this held in the mind?

To first distinguish the correct reasoning held in the mind: just as one does not obtain the vows of restraint in their entirety with respect to each individual [transgression], so too one would not, at every single moment, abandon them all in their entirety.
The restraint is acquired in relation to all sentient beings; therefore, one should not now abandon it all upon committing a single offense.

If you think that the monastic restraint necessarily lacks the sense of being acquired separately after being received separately, how can you say that it is like the case where restraint is acquired universally without being received separately—such that there would be no offense and no abandonment of it all by committing one? Thus, the analogy is not equivalent.

This objection is not valid, because it is something you yourself accept. That is to say, you also accept that for one in the householder’s discipline (*gṛhastha-saṃvara*), the entire discipline is not forfeited simply by committing a root offense; or, you yourself accept that for the *prātimokṣa* discipline, one regains exactly as much as was received at the time of each specific undertaking. In the same way, you should accept that when a transgression of the discipline occurs, it is forfeited only according to what was transgressed, rather than the entirety being forfeited.
Furthermore, the precepts one has received are established as such; they are not abandoned all at once upon a single transgression.
This principle applies equally to bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras: even when a grave offense is committed, there is no possibility that all [precepts] are abandoned.
Or perhaps this has already been stated.
What was stated previously?

It was said that if one who lacks the vows were still called a lay follower (*upāsaka*), then by the same logic, a monk (*bhikṣu*) or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) who lacked their vows would also be so designated; therefore, there is no such thing as a lay follower who lacks the vows.
Just as one who commits a specific offense does not forfeit the entirety [of the vows], the same principle should apply to bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras.
Or rather, what reasoning is there here that upon committing even one of the four pārājika offenses, the entire monastic discipline (*pravrajyā-vinaya*) is suddenly and completely relinquished?

It is not that one lacks a virtuous intention regarding these three types [of actions], nor does one wish to commit them even for the sake of saving one's own life; yet it is not that one abandons them entirely.

If, as your school asserts, one acquires non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) in this way, for what reason did the Blessed One say that one who commits the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*) is no longer called a bhikṣu, no longer called a śramaṇa, and is not a son of the Śākya? He said that such a person destroys the essence of a bhikṣu, harms the nature of a śramaṇa, is ruined, fallen, and is designated by the name of "defeated" (*parājita*).
This was said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) in reference to the ultimate (*paramārtha*) bhikṣu.
Now you should explain: for what reason does one who commits a grave offense (*pārājika*) immediately lose all [monastic status], whereas this is not the case for those who commit other offenses?

Because the remaining offenses are subject to confession and removal, if one has committed other offenses and has not yet confessed and removed them, one does not lose the nature of a bhikṣu; what benefit, then, would there be in confessing and removing them?
What further benefit would there be in seeking more?
This causes the nature of a bhikṣu to be without deficiency or leakage, imperishable and unmixed.
If it can bring about such a state, what merit is accomplished?
If it were so, one would thereby attain rebirth in heaven.

If that were the case, the gods should offer the utmost veneration to those who uphold the precepts, for such individuals, grasping at ethical discipline (*śīla*) without transgression, would be intent solely on seeking birth there.

However, the Noble Teaching does not exist solely for the sake of rebirth in heaven, as it causes bhikṣus and others to maintain the precepts with purity; thus, repentance is not intended exclusively for the sake of rebirth in heaven.

This being so, one should say that those who have not violated the precepts are unable to realize supramundane qualities in the present life; therefore, those who repent and eliminate [their transgressions] differ from those who do not repent and eliminate them.
Is it not the case that when a transgression against supramundane merit has been committed but not yet expiated, one is likewise not entirely deprived of the status of a bhikṣu?
For what reason, then, is it not permitted for a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense [to remain so]?

Because one has committed an irredeemable defeat (*pārājika*) offense, although one may still possess the remaining forms of discipline, one is ultimately not a vessel for supramundane qualities; therefore, the Blessed One stated that such a person is "not a bhikṣu," and so forth.
Furthermore, as long as the offense has not been expiated through confession, how could the nature of a bhikṣu still remain?

For that [offense] acts as an obstacle to entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), as well as to all other untainted (*anāsrava*) merits; it prevents the mind from even abiding on a single object during the cultivation of the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth, let alone achieving full accomplishment.

If there were such a thing as a "monk" in this category, one should personally take refuge in and pay homage to such a monk; what difference would there be between him and one who has committed a grave offense?

Therefore, it must be admitted that a monk who has committed a grave offense—just as one who cannot produce offspring is called "not a father," one who is useless to humans is called "not a human," and one who lacks male organs is called "not a man"—is incapable of accomplishing the function of a monk. Thus, despite possessing other forms of restraint (*saṃvara*), he is said to be "not a monk."
If the Buddha has spoken thus, how could this contradict the meaning?

It is not merely by being able to uphold the prātimokṣa vows that one achieves even a small measure of success in the Buddha’s holy teaching; for it is through this discipline (*saṃvara*) that one brings about its fruit.

However, the Buddhas’ intention abhors and turns away from the existence of karmic fruits; even observing the precepts without flaw does not yet meet with their approval, let alone one who commits a grave offense being able to satisfy the Buddha’s mind.

To contravene the Buddha’s intention is like a son disobeying his father; whatever deeds one performs will not accord with one's original aspiration. For this reason, it is said that such a person is "not a bhikṣu," and so forth.

This statement is not proof that it constitutes a cause for relinquishing the vows; the Vaibhāṣika masters, holding this principle in their hearts, have determined that this statement was made with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) in reference to a bhikṣu in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) states as follows:
"This statement is violent.
What is meant by 'violent'?"

This refers to interpreting the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*) spoken by the Blessed One according to a divergent meaning, thereby rendering them non-definitive (*neyārtha*), which serves as a condition for those with many afflictions to commit a grave offense.
How do we know that these words constitute a definitive teaching (*nītārtha*)?

According to the Vinaya’s own explanation, there are four kinds of bhikṣus: first, the bhikṣu by name and appearance; second, the bhikṣu by self-claim; third, the bhikṣu by mendicancy; and fourth, the bhikṣu who has broken the precepts.
Regarding the statement "not a bhikṣu" in this context, it refers to one who is not a bhikṣu who has received full ordination through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

It is not the case that this person was previously a bhikṣu in the ultimate sense and later became "not a bhikṣu" due to committing a grave offense; therefore, it should be understood that this statement is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Is it only a bhikṣu who has received full ordination through the formal procedure of the fourfold motion (jñapti-caturtha-karman) who commits a grave offense, while a bhikṣu who has received full ordination by reciting the Three Refuges three times does not also commit a grave offense?
What reasoning prevents these three refuges from conferring the precepts, such that one would not incur a grave offense and yet become a non-monk?

Even if it were granted that this statement is of definitive meaning—that only those who receive full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* incur the status of a non-monk upon committing a grave offense—nevertheless, because such a monk lacks the function of a monk regarding the arising of the noble dharmas, he is called a "non-monk. It is not that he loses the title of "monk" by abandoning the restraint (*saṃvara*).

Therefore, the authors of the extensive treatises make this determination, stating that this was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) with reference to a *bhikṣu* in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).

This is a sound explanation, for it employs the term "one who has committed a grave offense" as referring to one who has not yet produced the noble path (*āryamārga*). It is not by clinging to this as a definitive statement (*nītārtha*) that one can obstruct our own school’s settled intention.

If it were otherwise, for what reason would there be cases where, having committed the same transgression of the *śīla*, some lose their precepts while others do not, and some are no longer bhikṣus while others remain bhikṣus?

Therefore, apart from the Abhidharma school, there is no principle that can produce joy; yet, although such slander is made, it serves as a condition for those with many afflictions to commit a grave offense. Nevertheless, one should carefully examine who is most capable of creating the conditions for committing a grave offense.
Is it to say that although one has violated a single precept, there remain other precepts that one should diligently protect;
or is it to say that once one precept is violated, all remaining precepts are lost, and one may proceed to commit evil at will?

This definitive statement by the Abhidharmikas concerns the minor obstacles to rebirth in heaven and the attainment of liberation as a cherished fruit; it merely provides guidance to lead others to cultivate the necessary causes. How, then, can you slanderously claim that it encourages others to commit grave offenses?

This means that I have merely issued this admonition: when one precept is transgressed, the remaining precepts are not thereby forfeited; one should instead maintain them with diligent and focused effort. This is truly what is meant by "preventing others from committing grave offenses."
You claim that by committing a single offense, one abandons everything; does this not mean that the very act of committing it constitutes the condition for a grave transgression?
Therefore, the conditions for creating such sin lie with you, not with me.

Although you say this, it is not the case that this bhikṣu was previously a person of ultimate reality and later became a non-bhikṣu due to a grave transgression; such a statement is crude and superficial. Even if he had not previously realized the capacity to realize what was to be realized, if he later lacks that capacity, he is likewise said to have lost it.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Observe how this world and its devas, through negligence, fall away from noble wisdom.
Furthermore, this has already been explained previously.
What was meant by that previous statement?
It means that such a person is forever not a vessel for supramundane qualities; therefore, from the perspective of ultimate truth, they are said not to be a bhikṣu.
How do we know that the Great Master had this underlying intention?

Because it is stated therein that such a person is not a śramaṇa, and elsewhere it is said that there are four types of śramaṇas with no fifth, we know that in this context he is called "not a bhikṣu" solely from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), since that *pudgala* is termed a "śramaṇa who defiles the path."
"How can it be established that they first realized the Path and were later defiled?
The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) explains:
"Although this has been said, they possess only the remaining marks of a śramaṇa; therefore, they are called 'śramaṇas'."
Like scorched timber, a parrot’s beak made of straw, a dried-up pond, rotten seeds, a fire-wheel, or a corpse—these are mere words, for all the analogies cited are devoid of efficacy.
When pieces of timber have been slightly scorched by fire,
they are called "scorched timber" in the world;
it is not that which has become entirely charcoal that is called scorched timber.
If it is claimed that both the whole and a single part of what is being burned are equally admitted to be "burnt material," then there is uncertainty regarding both the analogy and the dharma.
The analogy lacks the merit of proving what it is meant to illustrate;
it is like a dried-up pond that may contain a small amount of water,
yet serves no function as a pond.
Therefore, the name "dry" is established.
Even if water were entirely absent, it would still be called "dry.
This remains as before a state of hesitation, which lacks the power to provide proof.

By this, the case of a dead person and a rotten seed has already been excluded; that is to say, although they may still possess a slight degree of causal capacity, the world likewise refers to them as "rotten seeds.
Alternatively, even if not rotten, if their capacity is impaired such that they no longer produce sprouts, they are also termed "rotten seeds."
There are those who share the nature of death and are thus called "dead people.
Therefore, the Sūtra states: "The heedless are always dead.
The two metaphors of the parrot’s beak and the whirling firebrand both contradict what is taught in the Sūtra.

There are four types of śramaṇas and no fifth; if one were to receive the name "śramaṇa" based solely on outward appearance, then there would be those in the world who, desiring the marks of a śramaṇa, deceitfully employ expedient means to assume the form of a śramaṇa—these should be called śramaṇas and designated as the fifth.
A false beak or a whirling fire-wheel cannot be designated as a "beak-wheel," for other characteristics are not real, and the beak-wheel is their primary cause.

Likewise, there ought to be a fifth [type of] person who, though not originally a śramaṇa, assumes the form of a śramaṇa; yet the Buddha spoke of only four and no fifth. This statement was intended to refute such attachments to the appearance of a śramaṇa. Therefore, none of the cited analogies possess the power of proof.

Furthermore, how does the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) know that the Buddha intended to say this, given that in other passages he states that such persons are not called bhikṣus, not called śramaṇas, and are not sons of the Śākya?
Have I not repeatedly exhorted you to investigate and reflect with care? Why then do you cling so stubbornly to a single passage?
Furthermore, I have already spoken on this before.
What was it that I said previously?
This is because such a śramaṇa is called "one who defiles the path.

It should be understood that this statement was made with the underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) of referring specifically to those who are bhikṣus in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), and not to all who are merely designated as bhikṣus and so forth.
Therefore, it is logically established that one does not cease to be a bhikṣu simply by suddenly abandoning all vows.

It is not the case that one is called a śramaṇa merely because he possesses the outward marks of other śramaṇas; for such a position would be logically untenable—like a charred log or a parrot’s beak—since the Blessed One stated that such a person should be called a "transgressor monk" (duḥśīla bhikṣu) or a "wicked monk" (pāpa bhikṣu).

If one were to suddenly abandon all vows of discipline (*saṃvara*), they should simply be called "one without morality" (*aśīla*) and so forth; why then designate them by the name "evil bhikṣu who has transgressed the precepts"?
In this regard, the Sthavira poses the following challenge:
"If you say they do not exist, what kind of morality would they lack?"

Since the term *śīla* (precept) also refers to the habitual practice of both wholesome and unwholesome ethical conduct, and since one also observes people speaking of "wholesome *śīla*" and "unwholesome *śīla*," what logical contradiction is there in making such a statement?
That person should most appropriately be said to lack *śīla*, for all beings possess the habituation of *śīla*.

However, since they are described as lacking *śīla*, it is understood that they are deficient in the *śīla* of pure ethical discipline; therefore, their objection that there is no profound underlying principle is unfounded.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) himself poses a question and answers it:
"If one who has committed a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) were no longer a bhikṣu, then there would be no such thing as a bhikṣu undergoing the training (*śikṣādattaka*).

It is not said that all those who commit a grave offense become persons who have committed a defeat (*pārājika*); rather, it is only said that those who have committed a defeat are certainly no longer bhikṣus. Should not the masters of the Abhidharma say this? Surely the Sautrāntikas are extremely arrogant people!
What is meant by "violent and arrogant"?

It refers to making such a claim as: "One who commits a grave offense does not incur *parājika* (defeat), because the Blessed One stated that one who has committed the four grave offenses is no longer called a bhikṣu," and so forth, as explained at length.

If it is argued that the Buddha declared them "not bhikṣus" and so forth because they abide in a mind of concealment, why then do you not allow that a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense lacks the superior capacity of a bhikṣu, rather than asserting he is "not a bhikṣu" due to the sudden abandonment of all vows?
The masters of our own school do not maintain this position; they assert that those who have committed a grave offense (*pārājika*) are not non-monks (*a-bhikṣu*). Rather, they say:

"Since one originally received the full restraint (*saṃvara*) with respect to all precepts, committing a single offense does not cause the remainder to be abandoned all at once, unlike your own school’s claim regarding the acquisition of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)."

In this context, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra), wishing to refute the correct reasoning, states that what [the opponent] has said—that one does not transgress a single aspect but must relinquish the entire vow—is in fact a challenge to the Great Teacher himself.

The Great Master establishes this analogy here: just as a *tāla* tree, once its head is severed, can never again grow or expand, so too when one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*), the remaining precepts cannot grow or expand; since the root of the precepts has been severed, it is logical that they are entirely abandoned.

That [opponent] does not correctly explain the meaning of the simile; for this simile merely excludes the growth of other [restraints]. Were it otherwise, the simile would fail to be established. However, I clearly perceive the meaning of this simile:

just as with branches and leaves, one may transgress other training rules (*śikṣāpada*) and yet still obtain the remaining restraint (*saṃvara*); whereas regarding the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*), if one commits even one, one will certainly no longer obtain the remaining restraints. Consequently, it is impossible to enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth. Therefore, the Sūtra states that only by abiding in ethical discipline (*śīla*) can one advance in the cultivation of sublime calm (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). If explained otherwise, the simile would not be established.

Furthermore, regarding the four grave training rules (*śikṣāpada*) which you uphold as your doctrine: do they collectively represent a single treetop, or does one treetop serve as a metaphor for one individual training rule?

If the four training rules were collectively represented by a single head, then violating one would not entail the forfeiture of all; it would be like cutting off a small portion of a treetop, where the remaining parts continue to grow without hindrance.

If one training rule is like the head of a tree, violating it at one time does not mean abandoning them all; for just as seeing the head of a tāla tree cut off does not prevent the remaining heads from continuing to grow.
As previously stated. What was stated previously?
It refers to the underlying principle herein: by what reasoning is the entire discipline (vinaya) forfeited all at once upon committing even one grave offense?
The other three [vows] are not protected; one does not abandon them all at once, just as when the crown of a *tāla* tree is severed, the rest remains.

Having observed that in the world, although one part of the crown of a *tāla* tree is cut off, the remaining parts still grow, one should know that the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*) are collectively like the crown of a *tāla* tree: committing one does not damage the other three.
Furthermore, when one head of a *tāla* tree is severed, it does not grow back, whereas other trees do not behave in this way;
yet you maintain that if one continuum of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is severed, all others are likewise severed. Therefore, your analogy is invalid.

By this, the analogy established by the Sthavira is also refuted; for he asserts that just as a great tree possesses roots, trunk, branches, and leaves, such that if the root is severed the whole tree withers and dries up, so too if even one root of morality is transgressed, the entire discipline is immediately destroyed.
Who among them says that the rest are not destroyed?
It has already been stated that when one [precept] is transgressed, the rest lack superior efficacy; that is, one will certainly be unable to enter the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth.

However, according to that analogy, there is no loss of the restraint (*saṃvara*), for it is seen in the world that a certain tree may have four roots that are equally deep and firm; it does not wither and die entirely at once when one is severed, but only when one part is damaged. The same should apply to the precepts.
Regarding the specific case, it should be explained in accordance with what was stated previously; therefore, that person’s proposed analogy is incapable of proving the point.
To this, the Master of the Sūtra (Sthiramati) further says:
"Since this is devoid of meaning, what is the use of such a feeble defense?"
If such a person still possesses the nature of a bhikṣu, one ought to take refuge in and pay homage to such a bhikṣu.

This statement would then be a slighting mockery of the Buddha, for the Buddha declared that even such a person is a śramaṇa, since despite having acquired the name "one who defiles the path," they still possess ethical discipline (śīla).
The Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtraprabhāva*) should state here:
"What is the point of laboriously defending such a meaningless position?

If one such as this still possesses the nature of a śramaṇa, then one should personally take refuge in and pay homage to śramaṇas of this kind. As for other types of śramaṇas, they have already been refuted previously; furthermore, the claim that those who are not bhikṣus and so forth [possess the nature of a śramaṇa] has also been explained away. By this reasoning, it is established that the various other scriptural authorities cited by him lack the power to serve as proof."
Furthermore, they are unable to provide even a slight explanation of correct reasoning to prove that by committing a single offense, one abandons all vows.

Moreover, they engage in futile investigation regarding what is meaningless; they insist that the actual existence of the restraint has been abandoned when it has not, and they encourage those who have already committed offenses to indulge their passions in creating evil. How can such people be called upholders of the Dharma who benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings?
If one who has committed a grave offense still possesses remaining precepts, for what reason should they be expelled from the community of bhikṣus?
What use is there for such a person of no power; it would be far better to expel them swiftly from among the pure assembly.

If one were to abandon the discipline (*saṃvara*) simply by committing a grave offense, it would follow that it could be abandoned just as when one is born with both sexual organs, because their natures are mutually contradictory, like darkness and light.

However, one who has not abandoned the discipline should be permitted to receive it again; for the lack of shame and dread of blame does not constitute a permanent obstruction to ethical conduct (*śīla*). Otherwise, such a person would never be able to receive the precepts.

Thus, we know that grave offenses can coexist with the precepts; however, because they defile the *śīla*, one is no longer permitted to receive them again. Since they lack superior efficacy, such individuals should be expelled.

Although the Elder has further arguments on this matter, they have already been generally refuted by the preceding reasoning and scriptural authority; fearing that the text would become overly prolix, I shall not refute them individually here.

Nevertheless, with his mind firmly entangled in afflictions, he composes texts and verses within his own treatise, uttering coarse and malicious speech to slander the sages and saints; thus, harming himself for no reason, he is truly to be pitied.

The afflictions and karma of the many sages of our land have already been eliminated; the Dharma teachings they have formulated rely upon the truth of reality. Yet those violent ones slander the Dharma and revile its exponents; having committed such grave transgressions, they shall surely invite intense suffering. How could I possibly respond to them with further words? I only pray that in the future their evil deeds may bear no fruit.
How are the two types of restraint—the dhyāna-restraint and the untainted (anāsrava) restraint—abandoned?
The verse says:
The abandonment of wholesome states born of meditative concentration occurs through changing levels, falling away, and so forth.
One abandons the noble [states] through attaining a fruit, refining the faculties, or falling away.
The treatise says:

wholesome dharmas associated with the various dhyāna stages are abandoned through two conditions: first, by changing the stage, which refers to being born in a higher or lower realm; [the second is through death].

Second, by way of falling away (*parihāṇi*): that is to say, when one falls away from a superior meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and relinquishes the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), or when one abandons "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the other stages at the time of becoming free from passion (*vairāgya*), as well as the concentration conducive to falling away (*hānabhāgīya-samādhi*).
To include these cases, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is further stated.

In the Master of the Sūtras’ commentary, the phrase "by detachment from defilement" (*vairāgya*) should be added. Just as the abandonment of wholesome states of the form realm occurs through three causes—changing levels, falling away, and detachment from defilement—the same applies to the formless realm.

The abandonment of untainted wholesome states occurs through three conditions: first, by attaining a fruit, whereby one completely abandons the preceding path; second, by refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), whereby one abandons the path of dull faculties; and third, by falling away (*parihāṇi*), whereby one abandons various superior paths. These [abandoned paths] are either the fruit itself or included within the superior fruit.

The Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) should here state two conditions, since the term "attaining the fruit" includes the term "refining the faculties. This is because at the stage of refining the faculties, one necessarily re-attains the fruit, as one abandons the path of the dull fruit for the superior fruit.

I shall provide a brief analysis of this point: if one relinquishes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), it should be understood that this occurs solely through attaining a fruit and not through falling away.
If one is an unshakable (*akopyadharman*) adept (*aśaikṣa*), they lack all other untainted [attainments] and may possess both types [of relinquishment].
Thus has been explained the relinquishing of all vows of discipline (*saṃvara*).
How is non-discipline (*asaṃvara*) relinquished?
The verse says:
One abandons the non-virtuous precepts through death, and acquires them through the arising of both sexual organs.
The commentary states:
All forms of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) are abandoned through three conditions; first, through death, because the physical basis is relinquished.

Second, by the acquisition of restraint: that is to say, if one receives and acquires the prātimokṣa discipline, or by obtaining the dhyāna discipline, the evil discipline is abandoned; because the power of the antidote is superior, the non-restraint is relinquished.
Third, by the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs within the continuum, for at that time the physical basis (āśraya) undergoes transformation.

One who dwells in immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*), even if at times relinquishes weapons, nets, and the like out of a virtuous intention, will never abandon that immorality so long as they have not obtained restraint (*saṃvara*). This is clearly seen in the fact that although one may avoid all conditions that provoke illness, the disease can hardly be cured unless one takes effective medicine.

When one who is unvirtuous (asamvara) undertakes the upavāsa precepts and relinquishes that discipline at the end of the night, does he become unvirtuous again, or is he designated as one who abides in the intermediate state?
Other masters say:
"One acquires non-restraint because the evil intention (*āśaya*) has not been permanently abandoned; it is like when hot iron is set aside: the red glow fades and the dark color arises.
Other masters say:
If one does not act again, there is no basis for causing that person to acquire non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), because non-restraint is acquired based on informative action (*vijñapti*).

What was stated previously is correct: since the underlying evil intention (*āśaya*) was not permanently abandoned at the time of first receiving the precepts, the evil discipline arises once more based on the previous informative action.
How is the intermediate non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) relinquished?
The verse says:
The intermediate is relinquished through the cessation of the vow, the force, the activity, the life-span, or the faculties.
The Treatise says:

The abandonment of the intermediate non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) occurs through six conditions. First, it is abandoned due to the interruption or destruction of the undertaking mind (*samādāna-citta*); that is to say, one previously vowed to always perform acts such as prostrating to a *caitya* and offering hymns of praise at a certain time, but now forms the thought, "I shall not do so again," whereby the underlying intention (*āśaya*) ceases from that point on, because one has discarded the original resolve.

Alternatively, when one performs a distinct action with intensified force that contradicts the activity previously being enacted, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) ceases because its original intention has subsided.

Second, it is abandoned through the destruction of its force; that is to say, the unmanifest induced by the force of pure faith or affliction is abandoned when the limit of that force is exhausted or destroyed, just like a released arrow or a potter’s wheel.
Therefore, the Master [Vasubandhu] has stated:

because it is projected by the power of the motivating impulse (*samutthāna*), even though one abandons the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and the underlying intention (*āśaya*), the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) may continue to persist for as long as life lasts; this should be understood to apply likewise even when striking birds and beasts with extremely intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
Alternatively, if a time limit was previously established for such a duration, the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is severed once that period has elapsed.

Third, it is relinquished due to the cessation or destruction of the performed action; that is to say, although one has not relinquished the fundamental mind of undertaking the vow, one no longer performs the actions undertaken, except for those instances where one fails to act due to forgetfulness. Since this non-informative action arises from the preparatory application (*prayoga*), when that application is cut off, the non-informative action is likewise relinquished.

Fourth, it is abandoned through the destruction of the object (*vastu*); that is to say, when the objects such as the monasteries, groves, and parks that were given as offerings, or the objects such as nets and snares that were provided for [hunting], are destroyed—the very things by which the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) was originally induced to arise—then the non-informative matter is abandoned.
Fifth, it is abandoned through the destruction of the life-span, meaning that the basis upon which it relies undergoes transformation.

Sixth, it is abandoned through the destruction of the sense-faculties upon which it relies; this refers to when one initiates the application of effort to sever wholesome or unwholesome roots, at which time one abandons the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) induced by those respective faculties. However, one does not abandon the intermediate wholesome or unwholesome non-informative matter until the point when the wholesome roots have been severed or when one attains meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), because such intermediate states are weak and inferior, and are thus abandoned as soon as the application of effort is initiated.
How are the non-manifest (avijñapti) states of intermediate virtue and non-virtue?
Regarding this point, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) states that the sixth condition is called "the severance of the roots of virtue" (*kuśalamūla-samuccheda*).

If one were to say this, then the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for severing the roots of virtue would also be called "severing the roots of virtue" and thus constitute the sixth condition; consequently, one would have to say that the preparatory stage of dhyāna is also called "dhyāna," which would result in seven conditions, because one abandons the non-manifest of evil during the preparatory stage of dhyāna.

It should be stated that "roots" refers to both wholesome and unwholesome roots; the term "abandonment" mentioned here refers to the preparatory stage of abandonment (*prayoga-prahāṇa*), because it relies on the abandonment by means of the roots as its sixth condition.
This interpretation of the verse is without fault in principle.
Regarding the non-material wholesome states of the desire realm and all other defiled non-material phenomena, how are they abandoned?
The verse says:
The non-material wholesome states of the desire realm are abandoned Through the severance of the faculties and through rebirth in a higher realm.
"Through the arising of the path of antidote, one abandons all non-material defilements.
The commentary states:

All non-material wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are abandoned through two conditions: first, the severing of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-samuccheda*); second, rebirth in a higher realm (*uparibhūmy-upapatti*).

It should be said that a small portion [of phenomena] is also relinquished through the abandonment of defilement (*vairāgya-prahāṇa*), such as the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) and other non-material wholesome dharmas.
All non-material defiled dharmas of the three realms are relinquished by a single condition: namely, the arising of the path of remedy (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).
If the path capable of abandoning a particular category of defilements arises, one abandons the delusions of that category along with their attendants.
Regarding which sentient beings possess virtuous or non-virtuous restraints (*saṃvara*),
the verse says:
Those with immoral discipline exclude those from the north, as well as the two types of eunuchs and hermaphrodites;
formal discipline also exists among the gods. Only humans possess all three types.
Those born in the desire realm, the heavens, and the form realm possess the discipline of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*).
The untainted [precepts] and those of the formless realm, excluding the intermediate dhyāna and the state of non-perception.
The commentary says:

Non-restraint exists only within the human realm; however, excluding the northern continent, it exists only in the other three directions. Within these three directions, it further excludes those who are *śaṇḍha*, *paṇḍaka*, or hermaphrodites. The same applies to restraint.
This means that since [the restraint] exists among humans—excluding those previously excluded—and also exists among gods, it can occur within two destinies (*gati*).
Furthermore, by what reason is it known that the mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) of eunuchs (*śaṇḍha*) and others does not possess the restraint?
This is because there is authentic evidence within the Sūtras and Vinaya.
Specifically, a sūtra records the Buddha telling Mahānāman:
"Any householder, a layman with male faculties," and so forth, as explained at length.
The Vinaya also states: "You should expel persons of this kind.
Thus, it is known that the discipline does not exist for such individuals.
Furthermore, by what reasoning does that [state] lack restraint?
Because the afflictions arising from two bases increase simultaneously within a single continuum, one lacks the capacity for correct discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*).
When they give rise to and continue in the practice of covetous desire, they are unable to subdue and eliminate it; therefore, they are not vessels for the precepts.

Furthermore, only those in whom intense shame and remorse are manifest can serve as a basis for the precepts; since such qualities are absent in them, they cannot be a basis for the discipline (*vinaya*).
If that is so, for what reason do they lack immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*)?
It is because the underlying disposition (*āśaya*) toward immorality within their mental continuum is inherently weak and not firmly established.
This is to say that, for eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*) and others, sexual desire is predominant, and they lack even a temporary path of remediation to suppress or eliminate it.

Those who do not give rise to intense craving toward various objects cannot give rise to an extremely fierce and malicious intention toward sentient beings such that it manifests before them; even if they were to produce it momentarily, it would not remain stable. Because their bodies lack capacity, their minds likewise lack capacity; therefore, such individuals also lack unwholesome discipline (*duḥśīla*).

Precisely for this reason, within that body, a virtuous *āśaya* is weak and does not endure firmly; it is only when there is a powerful and firmly enduring evil mind that unwholesome restraint (*akuśala-śīla*) exists, and only when there is a powerful and firmly enduring virtuous mind that wholesome restraint (*kuśala-śīla*) exists. Since both are absent in that case, neither of the two restraints is present.
However, the arising of both sexual organs causes one to lose both virtuous and non-virtuous precepts, because the two bases [of the organs] are characterized by an extreme increase in desire.
This does not apply to those who become *śaṇḍha* (eunuchs) and the like, for although they give rise to both bases, their desire is not extremely intense.

By this reasoning, the case of the Northern Continent has already been explained: because their two types of intention (*āśaya*) are not intense, and because they do not accord with the arising of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), those beings possess neither virtuous nor non-virtuous restraint (*saṃvara*).

In the miserable realms (durgati), there is no capacity to realize the correct principle, nor do they serve as a basis for intense shame (hrī) and dread of blame (apatrāpya). It is only when these are present, or when they have been impaired, that one can possess the wholesome or unwholesome restraints (saṃvara); therefore, there is neither wholesome nor unwholesome ethical discipline within the miserable realms.
Furthermore, those such as the *śaṇḍha* (eunuchs) are like saline wasteland; therefore, they cannot give rise to either virtuous or non-virtuous precepts.
As is seen in the world, various saline wastelands are unable to produce either fine grain or weeds.
If that is so, why does the Sūtra state:
"There are egg-born nāgas who, on the eighth day of each half-month, emerge from their palaces and come to the human world to seek to receive the eight-branch upavāsa fast."?
This constitutes the attainment of sublime conduct (*sucarita*), but not the attainment of restraint (*saṃvara*); therefore, restraint exists only among humans and devas.

Furthermore, only humans possess all three types of restraint, namely: that of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*), that of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).

If one is born among the gods of the desire realm or the form realm, it is possible for them to possess the dhyāna restraint; however, in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva), they can only be said to possess it through its accomplishment.
For those born in the formless realm, neither of these two exists; yet the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) also exists there in the formless realm.

This means that if one is born among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)—excluding those in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) and the non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñin*)—one may possess the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).

For those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it can only be accomplished [as a possession], because being formless, it necessarily does not manifest; yet, since one born in a higher realm can accomplish the lower, the untainted restraint is established there.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 39;
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 40.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter 8: Discerning Karma, Part Four, Section Eight. Having discerned that the natures and characteristics of various karmas differ, we shall now explain the various karmas designated within the sūtras.
Furthermore, the Sūtras state that there are three types of karma: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Karma that is stable, unstable, and neither is named Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
The treatise says:

All actions that bring about security are designated as "wholesome" (*kuśala*), because they can obtain desirable maturation (*vipāka*) and nirvāṇa, thereby rescuing sentient beings from suffering both temporarily and permanently.
Insecure karma is termed "unwholesome" (*akuśala*) because it can bring about undesirable maturation (*vipāka*) and because it most effectively obstructs progress toward *nirvāṇa*.

The other two types of karma are not designated as "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*), for they cannot be defined as either wholesome or unwholesome; this is the meaning of being neither secure nor insecure.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras that there are three kinds of karma: meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable. What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable; Wholesome karma of the desire realm is called "meritorious."
The unwholesome is called non-meritorious; the wholesome of the upper realms is immovable, because with respect to its own level and location, there is no movement regarding the fruit of the karma.
The treatise says:
Wholesome karma of the desire realm is called "merit" (*puṇya*); it is the opposite of non-merit because it brings about desirable results.
Unwholesome karma is called "non-merit" (*apuṇya*); it brings about undesirable results and is contrary to meritorious karma.
The wholesome states of the two upper realms are called "unshakable" (āniñjya).

Is it not the case that the Blessed One stated that the first three dhyānas are all "shakable," because the Noble Ones say that within them there is the movement of vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and vedanā?
Because the calamities such as vitarka and vicāra have not yet subsided in the three lower dhyānas, they are designated by the term "mobile" (*iñjita*).
As for "immobile" (*aniñjya*), it is so called in the sūtras because it can induce an immobile maturation (*vipāka*).
How can a meditative absorption that possesses movement produce an immovable maturation?

Although there is movement in the form of calamities within this absorption, the karma does not undergo the same shifting and transformation as it does in the desire realm with respect to its fruit; therefore, it is designated by the name "immovable."

This refers to the karma that completes one’s rebirth in other destinies or locations within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); by the power of specific conditions, it may be experienced in a different destiny or location. For instance, there may be karma capable of producing external or internal wealth, status, physical dimensions, complexion, strength, pleasure, and so forth, which was intended to ripen among the gods or similar beings; yet, due to being redirected by the power of specific conditions, this same karma instead ripens among humans or other beings.

Karma belonging to other stages or locations within the form and formless realms cannot be redirected to produce results in a different stage or location, because the locus of karmic fruition is immutable and because such karma is comprised within the states of meditative equipoise (samāhita-bhūmi), being free from distraction.
Based on this principle, the name "immovable" (*āniñjya*) is established.

It should be understood that herein, because of ignorance regarding the mutual dependence of cause and effect, one performs non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karman*); since non-meritorious karma is purely defiled, it necessarily depends upon the continuity of *dausthulya* (coarseness) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Due to this ignorance being present, one is unable to understand or believe in the causal connection between actions and their results; therefore, one initiates non-meritorious formations (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*).
Because of delusion regarding the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha-moha*), one performs meritorious and immovable (*āniñjya*) karma.
The meaning of reality refers to the Four Noble Truths.

When ordinary beings are deluded regarding these, even while in a state of virtuous mind, they occasionally give rise to [unwholesome states] through the force of which they fail to know, as it truly is, that the nature of the three realms is suffering; consequently, they produce meritorious and immovable karmic formations as causes for future existence.

For one who has already seen the Truths, such a thing does not occur; rather, as they gradually distance themselves from defilement through the power of prior practice, they are born successively in the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Furthermore, the Sūtras state that there are three types of karma, such as that conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanīya*); what are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Conducive to pleasure, suffering, and neither; Wholesome states up to the third dhyāna are conducive to pleasure;
All unwholesome states are conducive to suffering; Wholesome states of the higher realms are conducive to neither.

Others say that [the intermediate] also exists below, because it draws forth maturation from the middle [state], and because these three types of karma are admitted not to mature sequentially. There are five categories of karma conducive to feeling (*vedanīya*):
namely, those by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), by way of association (*samprayoga*), and so forth.
"And because of the difference in their objects, maturation, and manifestation.
The treatise says:
Among all wholesome karmas, those from the desire realm up to the third dhyāna are called "karmas conducive to pleasant experience," because pleasant feelings exist only up to that point.
All unwholesome karmas are called "conducive to painful feeling.

Wholesome karmas of the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms are said to be "conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling," because from this point upward there is no longer any experience of pain or pleasure.
It should be understood that these various karmas do not only result in the fruit of sensation (*vedanā*); they also bring about the provisions for those sensations.
Here, both the sensation and its provisions are termed "sensation," as the name "sensation" is established in general accordance with the inclinations of those to be converted.
Regarding the lower stages, is it admitted that there is karma conducive to neither [pain nor pleasure], or is it certain that there is none?
Other masters say:
"The lower stages also possess karma conducive to neither, because since there is neither suffering nor pleasure in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), there should likewise be no such karma."

Is it not the case that because the intermediate dhyāna and the first dhyāna share the same bond (*bandhana*), the karma of the intermediate dhyāna would produce the maturation (*vipāka*) of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) within the first dhyāna?
This is not logically tenable, as it contradicts the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*).
That is to say, the treatise asks:
"Is there any karma that produces a maturation of mental feeling but not bodily feeling?
It replies:
There is; namely, wholesome karma that is without vitarka (*avitarka*).

Since the karma of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is already without vitarka, if it were to induce the maturation (*vipāka*) of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) belonging to the fundamental dhyāna, it would follow that this karma without vitarka [induces] [a result].
If it were held that this karma brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) of both physical and mental feelings, it would contradict the root treatise.
Rather, this karma should be understood as bringing about only mental feeling, just as unwholesome karma brings about only physical feeling.
Even if it were granted that [karma] can induce [results] other than feeling, there would be no contradiction with the fundamental treatise (*mūla-śāstra*).

For the fundamental treatise should have stated that "wholesome [karma] is without investigation" (*avitarka*), or else that "not all karmas induce the result of feeling," since that [karma] should induce matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

However, among all actions that are without vitarka (*avitarka*), there are actions that can produce only the fruit of mental sensation (*citta-vedanā*); since this statement is made specifically with reference to those, there is no fault.

Therefore, while the action of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) produces maturation (*vipāka*), this does not prove that lower stages possess karma that is neither [pleasant nor unpleasant] (*aniyata*).
If that is so, there is further evidence for this point, namely, what the treatise states:
"Is it possible for three types of karma to experience their maturation neither before nor after one another?
It replies:
There is: namely, karma conducive to pleasant feeling is matter;
karma conducive to painful feeling is mind and mental factors;
karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is formations dissociated from mind, and so forth, as explained at length.
From this, it is proven that lower realms also possess karma that is neither [wholesome nor unwholesome].
It is not the case that these three types of karma exist apart from the desire realm, because they ripen simultaneously.
This, however, is not a valid proof, for the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the karma of the three realms corresponds to the three types of feeling.

However, it is not the case that karmas bound to the three realms can be experienced simultaneously; this [case] should likewise be so. As for the statement in the *Mūlaśāstra* that there are karmas of the three realms that ripen simultaneously, this was intended to test whether or not one understands the Abhidharma school’s position. Alternatively, it may be that the term "experiencing maturation" (*vipāka*) is used here to refer to the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*); because volition (*cetanā*) belonging to the form and formless realms sustains the maturation of lower realms, allowing it to endure for a long time, such a statement was made.

The textual passage concerning "karma conducive to the three feelings" can likewise be interpreted in this way; therefore, what he has cited is not a definitive proof. Why labor so hard to scrutinize his speculative assertions?
Upon examining those assertions, they contradict the *Prakaraṇapāda*, as it says:
"What is karma conducive to pleasant feeling?"
This refers to wholesome karma from that which is bound to the desire realm up to the third dhyāna.
There is no fault of contradicting that [scriptural passage], because there is no restrictive term [in the sūtra]; that is, it does not state that such karma leads exclusively to pleasant feeling.
However, although there are indeed actions conducive to neither-suffering-nor-pleasure in the lower realms, they are not explicitly mentioned in those texts because they are so few;
one must not, on this basis, conclude that the higher realms must likewise possess actions conducive to suffering and pleasure.
Because one is born there only after being free from the defilements of pleasure and pain.

For this reason, it is said that from the Bṛhatphala heaven up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana, there exists karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanīya-karman*); it is not said to exist in the lower stages, because in the higher stages there are no conflicting feelings, whereas in the lower stages there are conflicting feelings.

Because in the lower realms there may exist maturation that is neither painful nor pleasant, such karma cannot be definitively categorized as being bound to the three realms in the same manner; for this text allows for both the possibility and the actuality of experiencing [both types of feeling].
Is this karma wholesome or unwholesome? Some say:
it is wholesome, yet inferior.
Furthermore, it cannot be demonstrated individually, but may be stated collectively:

among various wholesome karmas, some classes are capable of producing pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and the requisites for feeling, while other classes are capable of producing that which is neither. It should be understood that karma which is conducive to benefiting pleasant feeling is called "conducive to pleasant feeling" (*sukha-vedanīya*), just as one speaks of a place "conducive to horses."
Alternatively, this karma that can experience pleasure is called "conducive to pleasant feeling" (*sukha-vedanīya*), just as bath-powder is conducive to bathing.
It should be understood that the same applies to karma conducive to other feelings.
Does karma conducive to pleasant feeling only produce the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of pleasant feeling?
Regarding those that ripen exclusively as the result of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya-vipāka*), all such cases are karma conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya-karman*).

However, there may be certain types of karma designated as "conducive to pleasant feeling" that do not ripen as the result of pleasant feeling; this refers to cases where such karma ripens as form (*rūpa*) or as factors dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta*).
It should be understood that the same applies to karma that is "conducive to other feelings.
This karma does not result in maturation solely as feeling; how then is it collectively designated as "karma conducive to feeling"?
Because all maturation produced by karma as its cause resembles feeling, it receives the name "feeling."
Why is this so? Because they all function according to their respective natures for the sake of benefiting, harming, or maintaining equilibrium within the body.
Just as water, fire, and so forth, accomplish the meanings of benefit, harm, or neutrality with respect to tree branches and the like.

Furthermore, there are many types of "conformity with experience" (*anubhava-anukūla*); briefly stated, there are five. First is conformity by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-anukūla*), which refers to the essence of feeling itself. As the Sūtra says:
"When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one understands as it truly is that one is experiencing a pleasant feeling," and so forth, as explained at length.
Second, the association with what is conducive to feeling (*anuloma-vedanīya-saṃprayoga*), which refers to all contacts (*sparśa*); as stated in the Sūtra:
"contacts conducive to pleasant feeling," and so forth, at length.
Third, the object of focus that is conducive to feeling (*ālambana-anuloma-vedanīya*), which refers to all objects (*viṣaya*); as stated in the Sūtra: [and so forth].
Having seen a form with the eye, one experiences only the form itself and does not experience craving for the form; this is explained at length.
This is because forms and so forth are the objects of feeling (*vedanā*).
There are four types of maturation that accord with feeling (*vipākavedanīya*), namely, karma that brings about maturation, as stated in the Sūtra:
"Karma conducive to pleasant experience," and so forth, as explained at length.
Fifth is "presently manifest karma conducive to experience," which refers to currently active feeling (*vedanā*). As stated in the Sūtra:
"When one experiences a pleasant feeling, the other two feelings cease," and so forth, as explained at length.

It is not that when this pleasant feeling is present, there is another feeling capable of feeling this pleasant feeling; rather, it is simply on the basis of the manifestation of the pleasant feeling itself that one says "one feels a pleasant feeling," because there are many kinds of things that accord with what is felt.
Although the maturation of karma is not in all cases feeling itself, it may nonetheless be designated collectively as "karma conducive to feeling.

This is because the form and non-associated formations produced by various wholesome karmas as their cause can give rise to pleasant feelings by serving as their objects, and because they are what those pleasant feelings experience and appropriate.

Because its desirable maturation is conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya*), it is also called "pleasant feeling. Consequently, although the various fruits summoned by this wholesome karma are not themselves pleasant feelings, because they are conducive to pleasant feeling, the karma that summons them is termed "karma conducive to pleasant feeling" (*sukha-vedanīya-karman*).
The same principle should also apply to [karma] that is conducive to suffering and that which is neither.
Thus, these three types of karma are both determinate and indeterminate; what are their characteristics?
The verse says:
This [karma] is either determinate or indeterminate; the determinate is of three types, such as that which ripens in the present life and so forth.

Some say there are five types of karma, while other masters speak of four categories. The treatise says: [The verse: This has both determinate and indeterminate aspects; The determinate consists of three, such as that which ripens in the present life and so forth. Some explain that there are five types of karma, While other teachers explain it in terms of four propositions. [The commentary says:]...

Regarding the aforementioned [karmas] conducive to pleasant feeling and so forth, one should know that each has the distinction of being either determinate or indeterminate; they are designated as "indeterminate" because their timing of experience is not fixed.

This means that karma conducive to pleasant [feeling] does not necessarily ripen; however, if it does ripen, one must necessarily experience its pleasant maturation. The same applies to the descriptions of the other two types of karma.
There are three types of determinate karma:
first, that to be experienced in the present life; second, that to be experienced in the next birth; and third, that to be experienced in subsequent births.
These three determinate karmas definitely produce their respective maturations (*vipāka*); together with the aforementioned indeterminate karma, they constitute four types in total.

Alternatively, there are those who maintain that indeterminate karma (aniyata-vedanīya-karma) is further divided into two types—namely, determinate and indeterminate with respect to its maturation (vipāka)—and thus, together with the three types of determinate karma, they constitute five types in total.
What is the nature of karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*)?
It refers to that which is performed and accumulated in this very life, such that its maturation (*vipāka*) is experienced only in this life and not in another.

The phrase "in this life" indicates the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*). The term "performed" (*kṛta*) is used to indicate the paths of action consisting of preliminary effort (*prayoga*) and the fundamental act (*maula-karmapatha*), while "accumulated" (*upacita*) is used to indicate the subsequent completion (*pṛṣṭha*).
Alternatively, "creating" (*karman*) indicates the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), while "increasing" (*upacaya*) indicates the completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*).
Alternatively, "creating" refers to acting impulsively (*sahasā*), while "increasing" refers to acting after deliberation (*cetayitvā*).
Alternatively, that which is regretted by the agent after the act is called "committed" (*kṛta*), while that which is welcomed with joy is called "increased" (*upacita*).

Or, when an action has a similar type as its companion, it is termed both "committed" and "increased"—as when a wholesome deed is accompanied by another wholesome one; conversely, [actions] contrary to this are termed only "committed."

There are those who, through firm attachment, perform an action; this is called both "performing" (*abhisamskāra*) and "increasing" (*upacaya*). Conversely, that which is contrary to this is called only "performing.
Alternatively, based on completeness, it is called "performing," whereas if it is by way of completeness, it is called "increasing."
There are many such approaches to explaining these meanings.
To say that "only this life experiences the ripening [of karma]" (*vipāka*) indicates the certainty of the timing.

However, some might argue that even if one performs and accumulates [karma] during a human birth, yet experiences its ripening in another life within that same human realm, it could still be termed "to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
To refute this attachment, it is further stated that "it is not others.

This demonstrates that regarding those who undergo death and rebirth, one may say that only these [factors] are intended, and they are not called "others"; thereby, it reveals that the timing of karma is indestructible, making it extremely clear and cutting through all webs of doubt.
How can it be determined from this statement that it is not other forms of sensation, simply by saying "not others"?
For the phrase "not others" could alternatively be explained as excluding non-humans, rather than excluding other bodies.
This interpretation is irrational, because the meaning that [the being] is not a human has already been established by the preceding statement "only this.
That is to say, since it was previously stated that "only this" is born, it has already definitively demonstrated that [the being] is certainly not a non-human.
Furthermore, the subsequent statement that "it is not others" is for the purpose of clearly excluding the possibility of other bodies; otherwise, what would be the point of stating it again?
Therefore, this karma is called "to be experienced in the present life," because "present life" (dṛṣṭadharma) signifies the current body.
What is the nature of karma to be experienced in the next life?
It refers to karma created in this life that is experienced in the immediately following birth.
The term "birth" here carries the sense of a place of rebirth; because it arises without interval after the creation of the karma, it is called "the next life."
This refers to the meaning of being experienced in the immediately subsequent birth; karma that accords with such birth is called "karma to be experienced in the next life" (*upapadyavedanīya*).
What is the nature of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives?
It refers to karma created in this life that is experienced in a birth following the immediate one.

What is called "subsequent" refers to the subsequent *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings) arising without interval; what is called "successive" indicates that [the karma] is experienced separately over many successive births.
The intent of this statement is to clarify that karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman*) is determined to sequentially induce each of these births individually.
To avoid the fault of excessive prolixity, a single name is established for multiple types of karma.
What is meant by "karma to be experienced indeterminately"?

It refers to a certain class of karma that the Blessed One perceives—whether through ethical discipline (*śīla*), or through right aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), or through the holy life (*brahmacarya*), or through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), or through the power of wisdom (*jñānabala*)—as being rendered entirely fruitless, or made slight, or shifted in its timing; all such cases are called indeterminate karma. To transform this karma, one should cultivate pure conduct.
Among all classes of sentient beings, this type of karma is most prevalent.
However, the Sūtra states:

"There may be certain karmas that are to be experienced in the present life, yet they instead ripen to be experienced in hell. This statement does not refer to karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) as defined here.

The meaning is that there is karma to be experienced in an indeterminate manner; if one is able to diligently cultivate the body, morality, mind, and wisdom, this karma created would be experienced among humans. However, because one does not diligently cultivate the body, morality, mind, and wisdom, one consequently falls into hell (*naraka*) by virtue of this very karma.
The Sūtra further states:

"There may be certain karmas that are destined to be experienced in hell, yet they are instead experienced among human beings. This also does not refer to karma fixed by time; rather, it speaks of what is indeterminate, and the interpretation of its meaning follows the previous explanation.

Alternatively, this explains the preceding sutra with the following intent: there may be karma that, although it is "created" (*kṛta*), is not "accumulated" (*upacita*). If its own power were allowed to take effect, it would be experienced in the present life; however, if one subsequently creates karma that induces rebirth in hell, this [new karma] assists and causes the former to increase, so that it is experienced in hell.
Therefore, a sutra states:

"There is karma that ought to be experienced among humans; however, because one subsequently creates karma that brings about rebirth in hell and causes it to increase, that [human karma] is diverted so that it is experienced within hell."
Therefore, it is known that they speak of indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karman*).
The Dārṣṭāntikas (Exemplifiers) say:
