"Karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and so forth may also receive its maturation (*vipāka*) in other lives; however, names such as 'to be experienced in the present' are established according to the stage of initial maturation. It is not the case that these names bring about only those specific results."

This means that his intended explanation is as follows: regarding all karmas performed, if they are able to act as the cause for yielding a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) from this very life, they are called "to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
If they are only able to act as the cause for yielding a ripened fruit from the immediately following life, they are called "to be experienced in the next life" (*upapadyavedanīya*).

If karma were to skip over intermediate births and yield its maturation only from the third birth onward, it would be called "to be experienced in a subsequent subsequent life" (*aparāparīya-vedanīya*).
For what reason do they hold such a view?
It is so that powerful karma does not have only a small amount of maturation.
That position is not tenable. Why is this so?

It is because it is logically impossible for the maturation (*vipāka*) of that karma to have already arisen at an earlier time, only to be interrupted and then arise again in the interim; this is like the case of a seed and its sprout.

If one were to claim that the subsequent body arises immediately [after death], there would be no distinction between the karma of dying and the karma of being born; or else, since the body would be no different, one would undergo death and birth repeatedly.
Furthermore, if a single karma were to bring about two or three births, would these various fruits be distinct or identical?

If the characteristics were different, they would be like the continuity produced by distinct karmas, where the fruit of one karma is not shared; or, if it were the fruit of a single karma, its characteristics should be identical. One must therefore explain by what cause the preceding and succeeding characteristics differ.

If it is argued that this is due to the auxiliary power of completing karma (*pūrṇakarma*), then there should be only a single birth (*ekajanman*) with distinctions occurring before and after; yet we observe that although there are many diverse fruits of completing karma within a single life projected by projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), because the projecting karma is one, it is designated as "a single birth."
This should also be the case, as there is no other cause [for the distinction].

If the characteristics were identical, they would have to arise as a single entity; yet it is not the case that what arises at the beginning and end of a single life are equal, for we can observe differences between earlier and later births.
This should also be the case, as it is the fruit of a single karma.

However, one cannot say that a single lifetime body is produced by many projecting karmas, because the projecting karmas themselves have distinctions; otherwise, there would either be death and birth within the state of *pūrvakālabhava* (the existence prior to death), or there would be no possibility of death or birth at all.
Furthermore, regarding the many births produced by a single karma: do they occur within a single realm of existence (*gati*), or across multiple realms?
If they were in a single realm, the fault would be as previously stated—that the preceding and succeeding [births] would have to be considered a single birth.
Alternatively, one might undergo numerous births and deaths within a single lifetime because there is no distinction in the fruit of a single karma.

However, if this were to occur across multiple realms of existence (*gati*), the principle would necessarily not hold, as the various realms are distinguished by superior, middling, and inferior grades; for it is logically untenable that a single karma created in a single moment could possess such superior, middling, and inferior qualities.
Furthermore, if that were the case, the destinies (*gati*) would become intermingled; however, as previously demonstrated, the destinies are not intermingled.

If it is argued that within a birth projected by other karma, there exists karma from a previous life that has already attained its fruit, yet the power to induce that fruit is not yet exhausted, such that one undergoes further maturation (*vipāka*) within this birth—therefore, although a single karma can project many births, there remain distinctions between the characteristics of death and birth fruits.
This is also unreasonable.
Why? Because it is impossible for karma that has already projected [a new existence] to simultaneously project and fulfill [its results] while depending on another birth to undergo those results.
That is to say: regarding the maturation experienced by depending on another birth, is it the "projected fruit" (*ākṣepaphala*) or the "fulfilled fruit" (*paripūraphala*)?
For now, one should not say that it is the projected fruit experienced by depending [on another], because the projected fruit of this life was projected by other karma.
A single fruit should not be projected again after it has already been projected; otherwise, the effort of one karma would be rendered futile, and subsequent karma would be utterly useless therein.

Furthermore, one should not claim that there are two projecting fruits within a single lifetime, lest there be the fault of multiple births and multiple destinies with simultaneous maturations being experienced within a single continuum of rebirth.

Furthermore, one should not say that the fruit of completion is received through entrustment; otherwise, there would be the fallacy that a projecting karma from a previous life, having already produced its projected fruit, would now produce the fruit of completion in this present life through its remaining projecting power.

This means that there is a certain class of karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) which, having already projected its primary fruit (*ākṣepaka-phala*) in the immediately following birth, now transforms within the birth projected by other karma into karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), projecting a ripening fruit of completion (*paripūraka-phala*). In this case, a single karma would both project and complete, resulting in the fault of confusion between projection and completion.

Furthermore, since all karmas mutually support one another, they would all become both performed and accumulated; thus, there should ultimately be no karma whatsoever that does not undergo maturation until the attainment of nirvana.

However, neither of these positions is accepted by either school; yet the fault lies more heavily with the Dārṣṭāntika, for in their system all karma—such as that to be experienced in the present life—is not determinate. Nevertheless, they must admit that various karmas mutually support one another, and thus it follows logically that all such karma constitutes both "created" (*kṛta*) and "accumulated" (*upacita*).
Regarding those who perform and further increase karma, the Blessed One has declared in the sūtras that such karma is determinate;
therefore, one should know that those who claim all karma is indeterminate are outsiders to the Buddha's teaching.

Furthermore, in this context, on what basis do they maintain that within the process of being projected by other karma, the remaining karma from a previous life—which had already projected the result—can act as an auxiliary cause for fulfillment, enabling it to endure for a long time?
It is not that what was previously projected by oneself can serve as a completing cause (*paripūri-hetu*) to sustain the continuity [of existence].

Furthermore, if there is karma conducive to rebirth in the heavens, and one dies from the heavenly realm and is born in hell, how could karma conducive to rebirth in heaven now produce a pleasant fruit in hell? Or how could one die from hell and be born in the heavens?
The same principle applies to the responsibility for karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*).

It is not possible for karma to be experienced upon rebirth in the heavens to yield its fruit in the Avīci Hell; nor is it possible for karma to be experienced in the Avīci Hell to yield its fruit within the intermediate state of the heavens.
If it is claimed that this karma can only produce its fruit heavily after transcending other destinies and within its own class of destiny, the fault of this has already been stated previously.
What was stated previously?

This means that it is logically impossible for a maturation to have already arisen from an action at an earlier time, and then, after being interrupted in the interim, for that maturation to arise again—just as in the case of a seed and its sprout.
Although they establish this reasoning to prove their own position, saying, "lest there be a small maturation fruit from a powerful action," [it remains untenable].
This, too, is not a proof.
Why? Because it is not the case that karma which results in many fruits is necessarily termed "powerful."
Karma to be experienced in the present life is termed "powerful" because it is able to yield its fruit swiftly; thus this name is established.

If many volitions and aspirations arise within a single action, and there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority among them—whether preceding or succeeding—they can induce both the maturation of the present life and that of future lives. Therefore, there is no error in saying that a single action may bring about multiple fruits.

Furthermore, if one maintains that an action must produce many results to be designated as "powerful," then the karma that produces the maturation of a Wheel-Turning King should be called more powerful than the karma that produces the maturation of a Buddha, because it produces more results.

If an action is called "powerful" because it brings about a sublime result pertaining to a Buddha, then there are many types of powerful karma, for the principle of powerful karma has many categories.
That is to say, some karma is called powerful because its result is proximate; others because their results are numerous, or because their results are sublime.
However, since the name "to-be-experienced-in-this-life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) is stronger due to its proximity, how could that strong name serve as proof for the production of multiple fruits?

Therefore, the Abhidharmikas maintain that among the various types of karma, each of the three—such as *dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya* and so forth—produces its own distinct fruit; that the fruits of karma are not intermingled is superior from the perspective of logical principle.
The Dārṣṭāntikas state that there are four categories of karma:

first, there is karma for which the timing is fixed but the maturation is not fixed; this refers to the three types of karma—such as karma to be experienced in the present life—that are not certain to yield maturation.
Second, there is karma for which the maturation is certain but the timing is uncertain; this refers to indeterminate karma that is certain to yield maturation.
Third, there is karma for which both are certain; this refers to karma such as that to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), which is certain to yield maturation.

Fourth, there are actions that are indeterminate with respect to both [the timing of their maturation and their certainty]. This refers to indeterminate actions (*aniyata-karman*) for which the maturation is not necessarily obtained.

They state that all such actions collectively constitute eight types: namely, actions to be experienced in the present life (*drstadharma-vedanīya*) are either determinate or indeterminate, and so on, up to indeterminate actions, which also have two types.
Regarding these explained distinctions of karma, the verse says:
Four wholesome [karmas] may be performed simultaneously; Only three can project a homogeneous life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*);
In all realms, four types are created; In the hells, wholesome [karma] excludes the present.
In the stage of detachment from passion, ordinary beings do not create karma for rebirth;
noble ones do not create karma for rebirth or subsequent existence; nor do those who have fallen away from the desire realm or the Peak of Existence.
The Commentary says:

In this context, it is solely to reveal that karma conducive to pleasure and so forth may be determinate or indeterminate with respect to its timing—such as the present life—and to explain the distinct characteristics of the four types of karma taught in the sūtras, such as that to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). Therefore, determinate karma is divided into three types, which, when combined with indeterminate karma, constitute the fourfold classification; this explanation is considered correct.

In principle, there can be no karma that is indefinite regarding its maturation (*vipāka*) yet definite regarding its timing, because a definite time is merely a specific stage within what is already definite regarding its maturation.
Since there is no temporal entity distinct from maturation itself, how could a definite time not be maturation?

In this context, the categories of "karma to be experienced in the present life" (saddṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) and so forth are established solely based on the distinctions in the timing of the attainment of results for karma that is determinate with respect to its maturation (vipāka-niyata).

If one were to claim that there is karma determinate with respect to time—meaning that its maturation must necessarily occur at this specific time and not another, and that if this time is bypassed, it will never be experienced at all—then such karma would be determinate with respect to time, but not determinate with respect to its maturation.
This [principle] should also apply determinately to maturation (*vipāka*), as the meaning is analogous. What is the analogy?

It means that just as there is "existence at a time" (*kāle bhavaḥ*) or it is designated by the name "time," and the temporal period (*kāla-bhāga*) is thus determined; so too, regarding existence through maturation (*pāke bhavaḥ*) or its designation as "maturation," it should be called "determined maturation" (*vipāka-niyata*), or else one must admit that both are undetermined.
Therefore, if an action is fixed in terms of its timing, it must also be determined in terms of its maturation;
if it is called indeterminate in terms of its maturation, it must also be indeterminate in terms of its timing.

For this reason, there are certainly not eight types of karma; since among the various karmas there is the sense of being indeterminate, they should all be collectively established as one "karma to be experienced indeterminately. Why is this so?
Because they are similar in meaning.

That is to say, just as karma that is determinate in its timing but indeterminate in its ripening is universally accepted as being "conducive to indeterminate experience" because its timing is not fixed, why is it not likewise accepted that karma determinate in its timing but indeterminate in its ripening is "conducive to indeterminate experience," since its ripening is not fixed?
Therefore, the Dārṣṭāntikas establish eight types of karma within this context, which is extremely confused.

Furthermore, the Dārṣṭāntikas assert that all karma—even that of the immediate retribution—is entirely reversible; if the karma of immediate retribution were irreversible, then no one would be able to transcend the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Now, observing that statement, there is this underlying intention: if one were to claim that among all karmas there is even a slight portion that cannot be averted, then the karma of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) must necessarily be its precursor. For among all karmas, the karma of the "existence of existence" (*bhava-bhava*) is the most subtle root of all birth and death; it possesses the power to encompass vast maturation (*vipāka*), and among sentient beings wandering in the stream of beginningless saṃsāra, none have ever been able to transcend it.
If it were possible to transform karma of such a kind, how could the karma of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma) not be transformable?

This too is merely a false and biased attachment; for while both the maturation (vipāka) and the state (avasthā) of the karma of immediate retribution are fixed, this is not the case for the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra). Therefore, the example cited lacks the power of proof.

If all karma pertaining to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) were irreversible and its arising necessarily produced its result, then it would be impossible, after having given rise to that meditative absorption, to realize the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣaphala*) and enter parinirvāṇa.
If all karma were capable of being transformed, the Blessed One would not have spoken of "fixed karma.
Is it possible for four types of karma to be performed simultaneously?
It is indeed possible.
How so? After dispatching the three messengers, one personally engages in sexual misconduct; these are all brought to completion simultaneously.
Among the four types of karma—such as that to be experienced in the present life and so forth—how many types of karma have the power to project a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?

Only three [types of karma] are capable of projecting [a new existence], excluding karma conducive to the present life; for karma conducive to the present life necessarily arises based on the homogeneous status (nikāyasabhāga) projected by prior karma, and thus it necessarily yields its fruit within the very same lifetime.
In which realms and destinies can how many types of karma be produced?
In all realms and destinies—whether virtuous or non-virtuous—all four types of karma may be produced as appropriate.

While this is the general rule, if one considers specific prohibitions: within the hells, virtuous karma excludes that which is to be experienced in the present life (*saddṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), because it lacks desirable fruit; all other types of karma may be produced there.
Other masters say:

"In the realms of form and formlessness, there is definitely no karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*), because karma to be experienced in the present life can only be established by depending upon a superior object and preparatory effort."

That is to say, regarding one's parents, the Buddha, arhats, and others who have cultivated their bodies through superior virtues, actions that cause them harm or benefit can produce immediate results.
Alternatively, initiating intense and persistent application of effort toward other objects also produces immediate results.
Karma of this kind does not exist at all in the higher realms; therefore, there is no karma to be experienced in the present life (*saddṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) within those two realms.
That [position] is unreasonable, because other types [of karma] can arise.

This means that even in the two higher realms, there exists superior karma whose power is so swift that it can produce results in the present life. Thus, although in the two higher realms there is no karma to be experienced in the present life—such as that which depends on encountering superior objects and so forth as previously described—there nonetheless exists superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) capable of producing results in the present life. This is because the categories of karma to be experienced in the present life are not limited to a single type.

For this reason, it is stated within the summary that the four types of karma—such as karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth—all belong to the desire realm, because they are all augmented by the pervasive and cultivated-abandonment latent dispositions (anuśaya) of both the form and formless realms.
In all places, these four types of formative karma are fully present.
That which is of a non-retrogressive nature is called "firm"; it exists in the stages free from defilement.
If one belongs to the class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), with the exception of karma to be experienced in the next life, they may perform the remaining three types.

The Noble Ones eliminate both types of karma to be experienced in the next life and in subsequent lives; they may, however, create the other two types. Since an ordinary person who has not fallen away from a state and has abandoned the defilements of that level cannot be reborn there immediately after death, such karma to be experienced in the next life must be excluded for them.
Nevertheless, because one who dies in a higher realm will necessarily be reborn in a lower one, it is possible for them to create karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.

Since a noble one does not regress, if they become free from those defilements, there is no possibility of being reborn in those realms again; therefore, for them, both the karma conducive to birth and the karma conducive to subsequent existence are eliminated.

In whatever realm they are born, they may perform karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), and there is no restriction anywhere regarding the performance of indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karman*).

However, when noble beings have already attained freedom from passion regarding the desire realm and the Peak of Existence, even though they may undergo retrogression, they do not create karma conducive to rebirth in those realms in future lives.
Because one who falls away from that [state] necessarily falls away from the fruit, and once the fruit has been lost, one does not die until the original fruit is regained.
Furthermore, does one also create karma while abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
It is also produced. How so?
The verse says:
In the intermediate state of desire, twenty-two kinds of karma can be produced;
all are subsumed under karma to be experienced in the present life, because their homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) is one.
The treatise says:
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one may be capable of creating twenty-two types of karma.
That is to say, there are five stages each for the intermediate state, the period within the womb, and the period after birth from the womb.
The five stages within the womb are: first, the kalala; second, the arbuda; third, the peśī; fourth, the ghana; and fifth, the praśākhā.
The five stages outside the womb are: first, infancy; second, childhood; third, youth; fourth, middle age; and fifth, old age.
These eleven stages are comprised within a single lifetime.

It should be understood that while abiding in the intermediate state (antarābhava), one can create karma for the intermediate state—both determinate and indeterminate—and likewise, up to the stage of old age, one can create two types of karma; this should be known to be the same in all cases.

It should be understood that the eleven types of determinate karma (*niyata-karman*) performed within this intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are all subsumed under "retribution in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), because there is no distinction in the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
That is to say, the state of the intermediate existence and its own ten [prior] states constitute a single homogeneous class, as they are projected by a single karma.

For this reason, karma conducive to existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not mentioned separately, as it is subsumed under karma conducive to birth (*upapadyavedanīya*) and so forth.

As for "homogeneous class" (*nikāyasabhāga*), it refers to classes such as humans; it is neither a realm of rebirth (*gati*) nor a mode of birth (*yoni*), because the homogeneous classes differ according to whether they pertain to a realm of rebirth or to existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhavabhava*).
What are the characteristics of those karmas that must necessarily be experienced?
The verse says:
"By means of intense affliction or a pure mind, and by what is habitually performed,"
Karma arising from a field of merit, as well as the karma of harming one's parents, is fixed.
The commentary states:
If an action is performed with intense affliction, or with a pure mind, or is done habitually, or is directed toward a superior field of merit, it is fixed.
The field of merit refers to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, or to superior individuals (pudgala) who have realized mundane or supramundane excellence.

Regarding such fields, even if one lacks intense afflictions or a pure mind, and even if it is not a habitual action, any karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that is produced therein, or if one commits an act of harm toward one's parents even with a minor degree of mental obsession (paryavasthāna), all such cases are subsumed under "definite karma" (niyata-karma).
Other masters say:

Actions performed with an intense intention, or those for which one feels joy after having committed them, or those repeatedly practiced at all times, or actions initiated through the power of a superior vow or the power of circumstances—all such actions are determinate.
What are the characteristics of karma that bears fruit in the present life?
The verse says:
Due to the excellence of the field and the intention, And because it is certain to bring about a specific maturation, [it bears fruit in this very life].
One attains permanent separation from the karma of that stage, which will certainly bring about results in the present life.
The commentary states:
Regarding the superiority of the field, it is heard that there was a bhikṣu who spoke of himself as a woman within the Saṃgha; in an instant, he was transformed into a woman.
There are many such accounts of this kind.
Regarding those of superior intention: it is heard that there was a eunuch who saved various oxen from becoming eunuchs; because of this, he was transformed into a man in an instant.
These accounts of such events are not limited to a single instance.

There are also cases where other karmic actions yield results in the present life; that is to say, when one is born in a particular realm and has permanently abandoned the defilements of that realm, all virtuous and non-virtuous karma pertaining to that realm must necessarily be experienced in the present, as rebirth in that realm will no longer occur.

For example, in the case of Arhats and Non-returners, they had already performed those karmas prior to their freedom from passion; because they have now become free from passion, those karmas become to be experienced in the present life.
What kind of karma is that?
This refers to karma fixed as to its maturation (*vipāka-niyata*). It should be understood that the karma described here is fixed as to its maturation but not fixed as to its timing (*akāla-niyata*).

If there were karma to be experienced with certainty in any other state, it would necessarily lack the possibility of permanently abandoning defilements; one would inevitably experience its maturation fruit in that other state.
If it were also indeterminate with respect to its maturation (*vipāka*), then because they are forever free from defilement, they would not experience such maturation.

This is because Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and Arhats, even if they were to fall away and give rise to defilement within the realm of desire or the three realms, would certainly not be reborn in the lower states, as they are destined for *nirvāṇa*.
Karmas that are determinate with regard to maturation (*vipāka-niyata-karman*) all become experienced in the present life; the others should be explained accordingly as appropriate.
By what kind of field (*kṣetra*) does one produce karma that is fixed for immediate experience?
The verse says:
Regarding the Sangha headed by the Buddha, as well as those who have emerged from the meditative attainment of cessation,
the state of non-contention, loving-kindness, or the path of seeing and cultivation— the karmas that cause harm or benefit toward them are experienced immediately.
The commentary states:
Within such fields of merit, wholesome and unwholesome karma will certainly yield its fruit immediately.

A field of merit refers primarily to the Saṃgha headed by the Buddha; with respect to the distinctions among individuals (*pudgala*), there are five types: first, one who has emerged from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This is because within this absorption the mind attains tranquility, and this absorption is tranquil because it is like *nirvāṇa*.

When the mind first arises from this meditative absorption, it is as if one who has entered nirvana were to emerge again; adorned with the ornaments of supreme tranquility and merit, it serves as the basis for the growth of a profound and pure mind.

Second, emerging from the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā*): this refers to having already permanently uprooted the continuity of all afflictions and calamities within this meditative state; it possesses an infinite superior intention directed toward all sentient beings as its object, and the merit of non-contention has been accumulated and infused into the body.

When emerging from this state, that mental continuum cannot be overcome by any worldly concentrated or unconcentrated mind; it is a field of excellence for the immediate fruition of both merit and demerit.

Third, emerging from the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*): that is to say, within this absorption, one accumulates and perfumes the body with the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) to benefit and bring happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, who serve as its object; when emerging from this absorption, the continuum of the body, perfumed by these immeasurable and most excellent conditioned merits, proceeds such that it is capable of producing superior karma.

Fourth, emerging from the path of vision (*darśanamārga*): this means that within this path, one is able to transcend a portion of the root of birth and death within the saṃsāra of the three realms—a root that has flowed on from beginningless time and cannot otherwise be transcended. Emerging from this path, there arises a succession of a superior, pure body capable of producing superior karma.

Fifth, those who have emerged from the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). This refers to those within this path who are able to transcend a portion of the root of birth and death; the rest is as previously explained.

From among these five types of individuals at the stage of initial emergence, because they ride upon the momentum of the superior merits previously cultivated, their minds still look back with focused mindfulness and do not abandon them; their faculties are tranquil and exceptionally distinct from the ordinary. Neither mundane nor supramundane, determinate nor indeterminate merit can surpass, subdue, outshine, or eclipse them. Therefore, these five are called "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*).
If one performs an action that causes harm or benefit toward such a person, this karma will certainly bring about its immediate fruit.

When emerging from other meditative absorptions or other fruits of the path, because the previously cultivated concentration was not particularly sublime and the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation have not been completely exhausted, their mental continuum does not constitute a superior field of merit.

Among the fruits of maturation (*vipākaphala*), feeling is the most preeminent. One should now investigate whether, among the various types of karma, there is any that brings about only mental feeling as its maturation, or perhaps brings about bodily feeling but not mental feeling.
There are also [those that are]. How so? The verse says:
It is maintained that wholesome karma devoid of vitarka produces only mental sensation, while unwholesome karma produces only bodily sensation;
this is the distinction between karma that results in sensation.
The commentary states:
Wholesome karma without vitarka refers to all wholesome karma from the intermediate dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Among these, that which brings about the maturation of feeling should be understood as inducing only mental feeling and not bodily feeling, because bodily feeling does not exist in those stages. Furthermore, bodily feeling is necessarily associated with vitarka; thus, karma without vitarka cannot produce a result associated with vitarka.

Regarding those unwholesome karmas that can be experienced, it should be understood that they produce only bodily sensation (*kāyika-vedanā*) and not mental sensation (*caitasika-vedanā*), because the fruit of an unwholesome cause is a painful sensation.

Painful sensation on the level of the mind is definitively termed "grief" (*daurmanasya*); since the sensation of grief is necessarily not included within the category of maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*), unwholesome karma produces only bodily sensation.

If one maintains that the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is definitively not a maturation (*vipāka*), then in which consciousness does the mental derangement produced by sentient beings reside, and by what cause is it induced?
Furthermore, upon what basis does it arise, and why is it not a maturation?
The verse says:
Mental derangement occurs only in the mental consciousness;
it arises from karmic maturation, as well as from fear, injury, or grief caused by adversity; excluding the Northern Continent, it exists within the desire realm.
The treatise states:

The mental derangement of sentient beings occurs only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); it can never occur in the five sensory consciousnesses, because the group of five consciousnesses is devoid of conceptual discrimination (*avikalpaka*).
For what reason do sentient beings become deranged in mind?
It arises from the karmic maturation of sentient beings.
From what kind of karmic maturation does it arise?

This refers to using medicinal substances or incantations to cause others' minds to go mad; or forcing others to drink what they do not desire, such as poison or alcohol; or manifesting a terrifying presence to frighten birds, beasts, and the like; or releasing fierce fires to burn mountains and marshes; or constructing pits and traps to cause sentient beings to fall into them; or performing other deeds that cause others to lose their mindfulness. Due to these karmic causes, in a future life, one brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) of discordant primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and by the power of those elements, the mind is driven to madness.

Because this mental derangement is not itself a result of maturation (*vipāka*), as both wholesome and unwholesome states of mind can be subject to derangement, it is therefore said to arise solely from the maturation of karma.

That is to say, unwholesome karma causes the production of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of unequal maturation; based upon these primary elements, the mind loses its mindfulness, and thus it is called "derangement."
Regarding such mental derangement (*citta-kṣipta*) in relation to mental distraction (*citta-vikṣepa*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That is to say, there is mental derangement that is not mental distraction, and so forth, as explained at length.
As for "deranged but not distracted," this refers to the non-defiled minds of those who are deranged.
"Distracted but not deranged" refers to the defiled minds of those who are not deranged.
"Both deranged and distracted" refers to the defiled minds of those who are deranged.
"Neither deranged nor distracted" refers to the non-defiled minds of those who are not deranged.
Is the derangement of the minds of sentient beings caused by this alone?
It is further caused by four other factors. What are these four?

First, due to terror: this refers to when non-humans and the like manifest terrifying forms and come to oppress one; upon seeing them, sentient beings consequently fall into madness. Second, due to injury:
this refers to when, because of one's actions, one annoys non-humans and the like; due to their anger, they wound one's limbs and joints, thereby causing one to fall into madness.
Within the bodies of sentient beings, there are distinct joints and members; if these are struck or touched, the mind immediately becomes deranged.

Third, it is due to disharmony: that is, when the internal elements of wind, heat, and phlegm mutually conflict, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) become unsuitable, thereby causing mental derangement.

Fourth, due to grief (*śoka*): that is to say, because of events such as the loss of loved ones, one is bound by the poison of sorrow within the heart, and the mind consequently becomes deranged, as in the case of Vāsiṣṭha and others.
Which classes of sentient beings possess this mental derangement?
Excluding those of Uttarakuru, all other sentient beings within the desire realm may experience mental derangement.
If even among the gods of the desire realm there are those whose minds are deranged, how much more so for humans and those in the miserable realms who might be free from such derangement?
In the hells, beings are perpetually insane because they are oppressed by manifold sufferings.

This means that those in the hells are constantly afflicted by various types of tortures that strike their vital points (*marmans*), being overwhelmed by intense and unbearable painful sensations; they do not even recognize themselves, much less discern right from wrong. Therefore, within the hells, they harbor resentment, lament with grief, and run about crying out in madness.

According to tradition, there is a text stating that among the noble ones (*ārya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), with the exception of the Buddhas, if the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are in disharmony, one may experience mental derangement (*cittavikṣepa*) without it being born of karmic maturation (*vipākaja*). If, however, there were determinate karma (*niyata-karma*), one would necessarily have to experience its results first before attaining the state of a noble one.
If it is not fixed karma, because one has attained the Noble Path, it can be rendered fruitless and cause no fear, for all Noble Ones have transcended the five fears.
Nor is there any harm, for Noble Ones have no cause for being detested or harmed by non-human beings and the like.
Furthermore, they are free from sorrow and anxiety because all noble ones have realized the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

The minds of all Tathāgatas are never deranged; they do not pass away gradually, nor do their voices ever falter. They are also free from such conditions as white hair or wrinkled faces, for they are born of the most pure and sublime karma.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras that there are three types of karma: crooked, defiled, and turbid. What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
The karma described as crooked, defiled, and turbid Arises from deceit, hatred, and greed.
The treatise says:

The three [paths of action] of body, speech, and mind each have three types—namely, crookedness (*vaṅka*), filthiness (*doṣa*), and turbidity (*kaṣāya*). These should be understood as arising, respectively, from deceit (*māyā*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and greed (*lobha*).
This refers to the actions of body, speech, and mind that arise based on guile (*śāṭhya*); these are called "crooked karma" (*kuṭilakarma*) because they belong to the category of crookedness.
Since actual crookedness refers to [wrong] views (*dṛṣṭi*), a sūtra states:
"What is actual crookedness?"
This refers to various wrong views; since *śāṭhya* (deceit) belongs to that same category, it receives the name "crooked.
Because the bodily, vocal, and mental actions arising from deceit have crookedness as their cause, the effect takes on the name of the cause; therefore, the Blessed One described them as crooked.
If bodily, vocal, or mental karma arises based on hatred (*dveṣa*), it is called "defiled action" (*kaṣāya-karman*), because it belongs to the category of the defilement of hatred.

Hatred is termed "defilement" because when it manifests, it is like a red-hot iron ball; wherever it is cast, it is capable of burning and harming the body and mind of both oneself and others. Since it is the most grievous among all afflictions (*kleśa*), the Bhagavān specifically established the name "defilement" for it, as it is the most extreme of all defilements.

Bodily, vocal, and mental karma arising from hatred is called "corrupt" because corruption serves as its cause; thus, the effect receives the name of the cause, and for this reason the Blessed One described it as corrupt.
If bodily, vocal, and mental karma arises based on attachment, it is termed "turbid" karma, because it belongs to the same category as turbid attachment.
Greed is called "turbid" because when greed manifests, it is defiled attachment toward its object; this is due to its nature as a defilement.
The arising [of karma] from that and so forth should be explained according to what preceded.
Furthermore, the truly straight path refers to the eightfold noble path; the three types of action that can obstruct its arising are called "crooked. True health refers to eternal nirvana.
That which obstructs the causes for realizing that [truth]—namely, the three types of karma—is called "impurity.
According to the views of non-Buddhists, that which obstructs pure faith within the Buddha's teaching is called "turbidity," because it is able to disturb and cloud pure faith.
The three types of action (karma) arising from that [view] are called "turbid.

Furthermore, because one falls into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism and thus deviates from the Middle Way, the actions of body, speech, and mind arising therefrom contradict the meaning of the straight path; therefore, they are designated as "crooked."

The various karmas arising from the view of negation (apavāda-dṛṣṭi) are designated as "corrupt" (kaṣāya) because they can defile pure dharmas; this designation of "corruption" necessarily relies on the sense of being extremely defiled.

The various karmas arising from the view of a self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) are designated as "turbid" (āvila) because they can obstruct the truly pure vision of non-self; this designation of "turbidity" relies on the sense of obstructing purity.

Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras that there are four kinds of karma: namely, there is karma that is black with black maturation; or again, there is karma that is white with white maturation; or again, there is karma that is black-and-white with black-and-white maturation; or again, there is karma that is neither black nor white.

There is no karma of non-retribution that can exhaust all other karmas; although the Sūtra briefly indicates this, it does not provide a detailed explanation. Now, this should be explained: what are its characteristics? The verse says: Based on the distinctions of "black-black" and so forth, The four types of karma as taught [in the Sūtra]— [The prose commentary: What is the meaning of these four types of karma? The verse says: The first three are established based on their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), While the last one is established based on its result (*vipāka*). (Verse 45) What is the meaning of this? Karma that is neither black nor white by nature and has neither black nor white maturation is called "neither-black-nor-white karma. This is because it is the karma that exhausts all other karmas. It is called "karma that exhausts karma" because it brings about the exhaustion of all other karmas. Why is this so? Because it is the antidote to all other karmas. Unwholesome [karma], desire-realm wholesome [karma], that which can exhaust those [defilements]— the outflow-free (anāsrava)—
should be known as black, white, both, and neither, respectively. The treatise says:
The Buddha, based on the different natures and categories of karmic results and the distinction between that which is to be remedied and its remedy, taught the four types beginning with "black-black.

All unwholesome karma is exclusively termed "black" because it possesses both the blackness of defilement and the blackness of being disagreeable; its maturation is also black because it is disagreeable.

Wholesome karma of the form realm is exclusively termed "white," because it is not intermingled with any unwholesome afflictions or unwholesome karma; its maturation is also white, because it is agreeable.
With what intention are the wholesome states of the formless realm excluded? Some say:

herein, by mentioning the first, the subsequent ones are implied; or, because within the form realm there are agreeable white states and clearly manifest white states that can be designated, the name "white" is established for it alone.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), although there is agreeable white, because there is no distinct white that can be designated as "clearly manifest," the name "white" is not established.

Alternatively, because within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) both the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of being born possess the two natures of whiteness, the name "white" is established independently. As a sūtra says:

"Whether male or female, having performed excellent conduct of the body... [and so on,] up to: after death, one attains a form-made existence (*manomaya*) with material form, like the radiance of a white garment or the brightness of a clear night."
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), one may possess all three types of action as well as the ten paths of action; this is not the case in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).

Yet, in the Sūtras it is said that dhyāna, the immeasurables (apramāṇa), and the formless attainments are all called "wholesome-white actions with white maturation" (śukla-śuklavipāka-karma); this is because they are designated as "white" based on their purely pure and desirable maturation.

However, that sūtra is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), because it employs the term "karma" to refer to all wholesome dharmas consisting of the four or five aggregates within the higher realms.

Since all causes of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) are manifested by karma, even those things that are not themselves karma are designated with the name "karma"; thus, one should know that the sūtra is not of definitive meaning.

The wholesome karma of the desire realm is said to be "black-and-white" because it is interspersed with the unwholesome; its maturation is likewise black-and-white because it is interspersed with undesirable results.
This designation "black-and-white" is established based on the continuum (*saṃtāna*), not according to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why is this so? Because there is no single karma or single maturation that is both black and white, as these are mutually contradictory.
If that were the case, then since the fruit of unwholesome karma is mixed with the fruit of wholesome karma, it too should be called "white-black."

This objection is unreasonable. Because within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the power of unwholesome states that frequently arise can suppress the wholesome, the fruit of suffering therein is mixed with the maturation (*vipāka*) of pleasure.

However, because the wholesome in the desire realm is weak and lacks the capacity to overwhelm the unwholesome, its fruit of pleasure likewise lacks the capacity to be mixed with the maturation of suffering; thus, the fruit of evil karma receives the name "pure black."
Other masters say:

"In the desire realm, wholesome karma arises through a mixture of intention (*āśaya*) and application (*prayoga*), which are black and white; it is for this reason that the two names 'black' and 'white' are established, not because a single karmic entity possesses both goodness and evil."

How is this so? For example, there is one who, desiring to deceive others and cause them to place their trust and allegiance in him, first feigns the practice of giving and even goes so far as to renounce the household life; such a person is said to have "black intentions but white preparatory actions."

Furthermore, there may be one who, toward their children or disciples, in order to prevent unbeneficial and non-peaceful matters and to cause them to abide in beneficial and peaceful matters, gives rise to coarse physical or verbal conduct out of a heart of compassion—such as beating, scolding, or pressuring sentient beings. This is called that which is black in its application but white in its intention.

If that were so, unwholesome karma should be called "white-black," because, as in the case of wholesome karma, it too may arise through a mixture of white and black intentions and applications as previously described.
However, this is not what is accepted; thus, there is no fault in the previous statement.

Those untainted (*anāsrava*) karmas that can eternally sever and exhaust the three preceding types of karma are called the fourth type of karma. Since this untainted karma is not defiled (*kliṣṭa*), it appropriately receives the designation "non-black" (*akṛṣṇa*); there is no logical error in this.
Because it does not fall within the realms and because it has severed the maturation [of karma], it is called "without maturation," and there is no error in this.
Since it is the ultimate white, why is it called "non-white"?
The Buddha also told Ānanda in that same *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra*:
"All dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are purely wholesome, purely white, and entirely without fault."
This treatise also states:
"What are the white dharmas?
They are all wholesome dharmas and non-obscured neutral dharmas."
This statement that it is "not white" was spoken with a hidden intention (*saṃdhāya*).
What is this hidden intention?

It means that herein, the fourth [type of action] is established as the antidote to the three preceding types of karma, so that those to be converted (*vineya*) do not give rise to such a doubt: [that there is no fourth type].
How can that which is white here serve as the antidote to what is white?

It is because the antidote is shown to be superior to its counter-agent; thus, it is designated by the name "non-white" with respect to the ripening it brings about, since it cannot bring about a white ripening.
Alternatively, because the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) can be found within a body that has transcended all defilement, they are designated as "pure white" (*avadāta*);
whereas the dharmas of one in training (*śaikṣa*) are not so designated as pure white, because they cannot be found within a body that has transcended all defilement.
Therefore, in that sutra, based on this meaning, the term "pure white" (*śukla*) is applied to the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
In the present sutra, however, because untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) does not accord with craving and cannot produce a white ripening (*vipāka*), it is described as "not white."
Do all untainted (anāsrava) karmas have the power to exhaust the three preceding types of karma? No. Why is this so?
The verse says:
The four dharmakṣāntis and the detachment from desire, Accompanying the first eight paths of immediate succession,
These twelve untainted volitions Exhaust only the purely black karma.

The ninth uninterrupted volition (*ānantarya-cetanā*) of the four dhyānas that transcend desire exhausts both the mixed and purely black [karma], while the four [volitions] cause the purely white [karma] to be exhausted.
The commentary says:

In the path of seeing, there are four moments of dharma-knowledge-acceptance (*dharmajñānakṣānti*); and in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), during the stage of abandoning the defilements of desire, there are eight preceding moments of uninterrupted noble path (*anantaryamārga*). The twelve volitions (*cetanā*) associated with these are exclusively for the exhaustion of purely black karma.

Accompanying the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the defilements of the desire realm, a single untainted volition (*anāsrava-cetanā*) simultaneously exhausts both the black-and-white and the purely black [karma]; for at this time, it completely severs the wholesome karma of the desire realm and also severs the ninth category of unwholesome karma.

The untainted volition (anāsravā cetanā) concomitant with the ninth path of uninterrupted liberation (ānantarya-mārga) that abandons the defilements of each stage within the four dhyānas causes only pure white karma (*śukla-karma*) to be exhausted.
As for the remaining types of karma, because they lack ripening (*vipāka*) and are not the subject under discussion here, they are not treated in this context.

Therefore, within this context, it is taught that only the noble volition (ārya-cetanā) concomitant with the seventeen paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) can eternally exhaust the three types of contaminated karma (*sāsrava-karman*).
Although the capacity to exhaust all such karma belongs to noble wisdom (*prajñā*), what is mentioned here is its specific "proximate antidote" (*pratipakṣa*).
Although bodily and vocal actions are also countered by these three [types of paths], they are not associated with wisdom; therefore, they are not mentioned here.
For what reason can only the final path, and no other, sever the contaminated wholesome karma of the various stages?
This is because wholesome dharmas are not abandoned by their own nature, for once they have been abandoned, there is the possibility of them manifesting again.

However, it is only when the afflictions that take those [wholesome dharmas] as their objects are exhausted that one says those wholesome dharmas are "abandoned," because at that time the wholesome dharmas attain dissociation from their fetters.

Consequently, as long as even a single grade of those afflictions remains as an object of condition, the meaning of "abandonment" is not established, because at that time wholesome dharmas are still bound.
The verse says:
Some say that karma experienced in the hells, as well as other desire-realm karma, is black or mixed.
Some say that the desire for cessation is [white], while other desires and karma are black.
The Commentary states:
Regarding the first and third [categories], there are differing explanations.
Other masters say:
"Karma that leads to experience in the hells, and karma that leads to other experiences within the desire realm, are respectively called 'pure black' and 'mixed' karma.
This means that because the maturation of the hells is induced solely by unwholesome karma, that which leads to such experience is called pure black karma."

Except for the hells, all other maturations (*vipāka*) within the desire realm are induced by both wholesome and unwholesome karma; therefore, they are termed "black-and-white" karma in accordance with their experience.
This explanation has already been refuted previously, because it is impossible for the wholesome to be mixed with the unwholesome.
Other masters say:
"The karma to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm, and all other karma within the desire realm, are respectively called 'pure black' and 'mixed' karma.

That is to say, because the karma to be abandoned by insight is not interspersed with the wholesome, it is called pure black karma; because the karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the desire realm includes both the wholesome and the unwholesome, it is called mixed karma."
This is also unreasonable, because among the two types of karma to be abandoned, co-existent karma cannot produce a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).

If it is argued that the three types of karma mentioned here are stated as having ripening based on their possession of ripening rather than being without ripening, then one should not have specified them as "to be abandoned by the desire realm and by vision."

Furthermore, it is logically impossible for karma of great strength to be intermingled with that of inferior strength; therefore, one should not say that unwholesome karmas abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) also receive the designation "intermingled."
Nor should it be said that in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) there is the power of the wholesome that surpasses the unwholesome, for it is not admitted that [the wholesome] can overwhelm evil karma.
Why is this? Because the wholesome in the desire realm is not practiced habitually (*asabhāga-carita*), and thus it lacks the capacity to induce a fruit lasting for an entire eon (*kalpa*).

Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras that there are three types of *muni*, and it is also stated in the Sūtras that there are three types of purity, all pertaining to body, speech, and mind. What are their respective characteristics?
The verse says:
The bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the mind itself, constitute the three types of *muni*.
The three purities should be known as the three sublime conducts (*tri-sucarita*).
The commentary states:

The bodily action of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is called the "sagehood of body" (*kāya-mauna*); the vocal action of one beyond training is called the "sagehood of speech" (*vāk-mauna*); and the mental action of one beyond training is called the "sagehood of mind" (*manas-mauna*). It is not the case that the sagehood of mind has mental action as its essence.
For what reason is it said that the Sage (muni) exists only within the aggregates of form and consciousness, and not in the other aggregates?
Other masters say:
by mentioning the last and the first, one indicates by analogy that this same principle applies to those in between as well.
According to the true meaning, the ultimate Muni has mind alone as its essence; thus, a sūtra says:
"Because the mind is tranquil, sentient beings are tranquil.

This mental Muni can be inferred through bodily and vocal actions because they are free from all evils; however, regarding mental action (*manas-karman*), there is no capacity for inference therein. It is only by combining that which is inferred with the object of inference that "Muni" is established.
Why is it that only the Muni is considered one who has nothing further to learn?
Because the Arhat is a true Muni, for all afflictions and verbal expressions have been eternally stilled.
The three types of excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind may be termed the three types of pure, untainted, and excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind.
Because they are eternally free from the defilements of misconduct and afflictions, they may be called pure.
However, since contaminated sublime conduct is still defiled by the stains of misconduct and afflictions, how can it be considered pure?

This is also termed "purification" because it can temporarily distance one from the defilements of misconduct; alternatively, the name "purification" is established because its power can induce the supreme, ultimate purification that is untainted (*anāsrava*).

If it is argued that this [uncontaminated state] should not be called "pure" because it can also induce the stains of affliction—namely, by acting as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for afflictions—this too is irrational.
When a wholesome mind arises, it does not do so by initiating the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of a defiled mind.

Consequently, an untainted (*anāsrava*) mind cannot arise immediately after a defiled one; however, a tainted wholesome mind can induce an untainted one. Thus, a tainted wholesome mind receives the name "pure" (*viśuddha*), because it accords with the untainted mind and is capable of removing impurities. These two are taught as such because they serve to pacify sentient beings' false notions of *mauna* (sagehood) and false notions of purity.

Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras that there are three types of unwholesome conduct (*duścarita*), and it is also stated in the Sūtras that there are three types of sublime conduct (*sucarita*), both pertaining to body, speech, and mind. What are their respective characteristics?
The verse says:
Unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind Are designated as the three types of unwholesome conduct.
As well as greed, hatred, and wrong view; the three types of sublime conduct are the opposites of these.
The commentary states:

All unwholesome karma of body and speech—including the preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*), the subsequent stages, and the fundamental acts—as well as unwholesome volition (*cetanā*), are respectively termed misconduct of body, speech, and mind.
However, there are three types of mental misconduct, namely: non-mental action consisting of greed, hatred, and wrong view.
Is it not the case that the sūtras also state that greed and so forth are called "mental action"? How can it be said now that greed, hatred, and wrong view are not mental action?
Because it is the provision (*sambhāra*) for karma, it is also called "karma," just as the provisions for the outflows (*āsrava*) are also called "outflows" and so forth.
How is it known that greed and the like are not mental karma?
It is known by means of both scripture (*āgama*) and correct reasoning (*yukti*).
Regarding the Āgama, it refers to the statement in the Sūtras:
"Greed, hatred, and wrong view are the accumulation of conditions for karma.
Therefore, one knows that greed and the like are not themselves the nature of karma.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"The various forms of craving are designated as mental action (manas-karman).
Therefore, we know that craving itself is not the essential substance of mental action.
Other examples should be understood accordingly; do not maintain the view that karma is identical to the accumulation of karma. Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"There is a distinction between craving and karma.
However, the Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika) says:
If you grant that afflictions are indeed mental karma, what fault is there in this?
Such a concession contradicts both the aforementioned sūtra and the subsequent correct reasoning; is this not a grave error?

If it is argued that just as it is said that greed can cause the mind to perform various evil deeds, this sutra—though stating that greed itself is the causal condition for the mental performance of evil deeds—does not fail to admit that greed is subsumed under mental misconduct.
Although it is thus stated that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the cause of karma, this craving itself should not be considered non-karma.
That analogy is not equivalent, for this sūtra does not state that craving can cause the mind to give rise to informative action (*vijñapti-karman*).

That is to say, as it was stated there that desire (*rāga*) can cause the mind to perform various unwholesome actions, this sutra does not state that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) causes the mind to give rise to manifest actions (*vijñapti-karman*). How, then, can that [previous statement] be cited as an analogy for this sutra to prove that the cause of manifest action—which is craving—is itself also karma?
As it is said in the sūtra, "all delusions are ignorance," this sūtra merely indicates that delusion is the essence of ignorance, demonstrating that what is not delusion is not ignorance.
Likewise, this sūtra states that "all seeking is craving," and all such cravings signify that they are mental karma (*manas-karman*).
The distinctions between the characteristics [of craving and attachment] have already been established in meaning.

If it were not characterized by seeking, it would not be craving; if it were not manifest, it would also not be mental action (*manas-karman*). Apart from being a mere conventional designation (*prajñapti*), there is no fault.
That mental karma is termed "manifest" has already been explained as before.
What is the correct reasoning?
It is that if affliction were itself karma, then the distinctions such as the twelve links of dependent origination and the three obstacles would not exist.
From this it is proven that greed and the like are not karma, because they are censured and loathed by the wise and because they can bring about undesirable results.
These courses of action are themselves evil, and are thus called "evil conduct" (*duścarita*); the three "sublime courses of action" (*sucarita*) should be understood as the opposite of these.

That is to say, all wholesome actions of body and speech—including their preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*), their fundamental stages (*maula*), and the corresponding wholesome volitions (*cetanā*)—are respectively termed "excellent conduct" (*sucarita*) of body, speech, and mind.

Furthermore, there are three types of excellent mental conduct that are not themselves karma: non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view. These are so designated because they are praised by the wise and because they bring about desirable results.
This course of action is itself sublime; therefore, it is called "sublime conduct" (*sucarita*).
Although right view and wrong view do not directly benefit or harm others, they serve as their basis; thus, they too constitute good and evil.
Furthermore, the Sūtras speak of ten courses of action (karmapatha), which may be either wholesome or unwholesome. What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
The ten courses of action as explained Are subsumed within the categories of misconduct and excellent conduct.
Its nature consists of the coarse categories, which are established as wholesome or unwholesome as appropriate.
The commentary states:
Among the previously mentioned unwholesome and sublime courses of action, those that are coarse, manifest, and easy to recognize are subsumed within the ten paths of action.

If wholesome conduct is subsumed under the [ten] paths of wholesome action as appropriate, and unwholesome conduct is subsumed under the paths of unwholesome action, what kinds of unwholesome or wholesome conduct are not so subsumed?
Preparatory and consecutive actions (*prayoga* and *pṛṣṭha*) and the like; for these are not coarse or manifest.

Furthermore, among the ten unwholesome courses of action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*), those bodily misdeeds that cause other sentient beings to lose their lives, their wealth, or their wives and concubines are designated as "courses of action" (*karmapatha*) for the purpose of causing them to be abandoned.
If verbal misconduct is particularly grave in its faults, it is designated as a path of action (*karmapatha*) so that one may abstain from it.
If mental misconduct, such as intense greed, hatred, and so forth, is grave, it is designated as a path of action so that one may abstain from it.
The preliminary application (*prayoga*), the subsequent action (*pṛṣṭha*), and other factors that are minor transgressions or unwholesome thoughts are all not paths of action (*karmapatha*).

Within the wholesome paths of action, the wholesome paths of bodily action do not encompass one portion of virtuous bodily conduct (*kāyasucarita*); namely, the preliminary application, the subsequent action, and other wholesome bodily actions, such as abstaining from intoxicants, giving alms, and so forth.
The verbal paths of wholesome action do not encompass one portion of verbal excellent conduct, namely, kind speech (*priyavāditā*) and so forth.
The mental paths of wholesome action do not encompass one portion of mental excellent conduct, namely, all wholesome volitions (*cetanā*).
Among the ten paths of action, do all seven of the first ones necessarily possess both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) aspects? Not so. Why is that?
The verse says:
The six unwholesome [paths] definitely possess non-informative [action]; those [two] performed by oneself and sexual misconduct possess both;
the seven wholesome [paths] arise from undertaking and possess two; those arising from meditative concentration possess only the non-informative.
The treatise states:

Among the seven unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-karmapatha*), six necessarily possess non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), namely killing and the others, with the exception of sexual misconduct.
This is because, in the case of these six, when one commissions another to perform them, informative matter (*vijñapti*) arises at the moment the fundamental act is completed.
If one personally commits those six courses of action (*karmapatha*), then all six possess both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).

This is because when the manifest action arises—whether the victim dies at that very moment or dies later—it is identical to the case of employing an agent; for at the moment the fundamental path of action is completed, there is only the unmanifest.

Only sexual misconduct necessarily possesses both [aspects], because it must be personally completed by oneself and cannot be accomplished by commanding another to act, as one experiences joy for oneself.

Regarding the seven wholesome paths of action, if they arise from formal undertaking (*samādāna*), they necessarily possess both—the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*)—because the morality (*śīla*) arising from such an undertaking necessarily depends upon the manifest.

The restraint comprised by dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) is called "born of meditative concentration" (samādhi-ja); this consists solely of non-informative matter (avijñapti), because it arises depending exclusively on the power of the mind.
Are the preparatory (prayoga) and subsequent (pṛṣṭha) actions like the fundamental (maula) action?
Not so. Why is this? The verse says:
The preparatory stage necessarily possesses informative [action], while non-informative [action] may or may not be present;
the subsequent stage is the opposite of this.
The treatise says:

The preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of a course of action (*karmapatha*) necessarily involves informative action (*vijñapti*); as for non-informative action (*avijñapti*) at this stage, it may or may not be present. If it arises from intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*) or a mind of pure intensity, then non-informative action exists; otherwise, it does not.

The subsequent action (*pṛṣṭha*) is the opposite of the preceding [action]; it necessarily possesses non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), whereas in this state, informative matter (*vijñapti-karman*) may or may not exist.
The second moment, beginning with the non-informative matter, is designated as the "subsequent" (*pṛṣṭha*); therefore, it necessarily possesses [non-informative matter].
If, at that time, one initiates an action following the preceding karma, then there is also informative matter; otherwise, there is none.
Within this context, how are the stages of preparation (*prayoga*), the fundamental act (*maula*), and the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*) established?

First, regarding the initial unwholesome action of killing: for example, when a butcher is about to slaughter a sheep, first he conceives the intent to kill; then he seeks out and negotiates the price for the sake of purchasing the sheep; he travels a long distance on foot with his own provisions to find the place where the sheep are kept; having arrived, he feels and examines the animal; he pays the price and leads it back, tethering and feeding it to make it fat; then, bringing it to the slaughterhouse, he takes up his knife and seeks a vulnerable spot, hacking and stabbing its body until life has not yet ended—all these are termed the stage of preparation.

When the victim dies as a result of this manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*), the manifest and unmanifest karma (*vijñapti-avijñapti-karman*) at that very moment is called the fundamental path of action (*mūla-karmapatha*) of killing.
Following that moment, the subsequent unmanifest karma of killing that continues without interruption is called the "subsequent arising" (*pṛṣṭha*) of killing.

Furthermore, when at a later time one skins, cuts, cleans, weighs, sells, and collects profits from them to support one's own kin, these manifest actions (*vijñapti-karman*) are also termed "subsequent" (*pṛṣṭha*).
Just as it is with the three parts for a sheep-slaughterer, so too should it be explained for the other forms of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) as appropriate.

Regarding the three stages of the karma of taking what is not given: for instance, when a thief is about to commit a theft, first he conceives the intent to steal; then he dispatches others or goes himself to scout the location of another's property, prepares food, drink, and clothing for the journey, and carries his tools of theft. He arrives secretly at the other's house, climbs over walls or ladders using various means to enter, and moves slowly with outstretched hands to feel for the wealth of others. All actions prior to the object actually leaving its place are termed the "preparatory stage" (*prayoga*).
When the object has been correctly separated [from its owner], the manifest and unmanifest karma within that very moment is called the "fundamental path of action" (*maula-karmapatha*).

Following that moment, all manifest karma—such as the unmanifest karma that continues, the carrying away of the property, its removal from storage, and its enjoyment—is called the "subsequent action" (*pṛṣṭha*).

Regarding the three stages of sexual misconduct, for instance, when a man first conceives a lustful desire for another's wife and intends to commit an impropriety, he commissions someone to scout her, acts as a matchmaker, engages in correspondence, adorns himself, approaches her, converses, and makes physical contact; all these actions prior to the completion of the act are termed the preliminary application (*prayoga*).
When the action is fully completed, the manifest and unmanifest karma within that very moment is called the "fundamental path of action" (*maula-karmapatha*).
Some say that completion refers to the entry into the wound-opening.
Other masters state:
This refers to the emission of impurity.

Following that moment, all manifest actions—including non-informative karma (*avijñapti-karma*), as well as other verbal expressions such as recounting, feeling shame, grasping, touching, or speaking—are termed "subsequent action" (*pṛṣṭha*).

Regarding the three stages of the karmic action of false speech: consider, for instance, a certain type of person who lives by the craft of deception in pursuit of wealth. Having first accepted a request to provide false testimony, he gives rise to a deceitful intention and goes before the assembly. There, he describes himself as being capable of providing honest evidence, saying: "I am neither an enemy nor a friend to that person; among all evils, I know none surpasses falsehood, and among all virtues, I know none surpasses truth. Since I have no personal interest in this matter, why would I unreasonably shoulder such a poisonous thorn? I only fear that an upright man might be unjustly subjected to punishment."
Prior to the actual accomplishment of the realization, all stages are termed "preparatory effort" (*prayoga*).

If one speaks while facing a crowd with the intention of speaking behind their back—deceiving those who do not see and so forth by falsely claiming that one does—the manifest and unmanifest karma (*vijñapti-avijñapti-karma*) within that moment is termed the "fundamental path of action" (*maula-karmapatha*).
Some say that [the act of deceiving] is only established when the deceived party gives their consent.

If this were so, there would be no possibility of deceiving the noble ones (ārya). However, since the fault of deceiving the noble ones is profound, one should know that the former explanation is superior.

After this moment, all subsequent non-informative karma (*avijñapti-karman*) and all informative karma (*vijñapti-karman*) performed to support one's own kin by means of acquiring wealth and profit are termed "subsequent" (*pṛṣṭha*).

Regarding the three stages of the karma of divisive speech (*paiśunya*): for instance, when a certain person intends to cause dissension in another’s mind, whether they dispatch a messenger to convey the message or go in person, feigning intimacy in the hope that their words will be trusted—all actions prior to the actual breach of the relationship are termed "preparatory effort" (*prayoga*).
The moment of manifest and non-manifest karma that arises from uttering divisive speech and is understood by the other party is called the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*).
Other masters say that it is only when the other party is actually divided that it is established.

If that were so, since the bonds between noble ones are profound and firm and difficult to break, there should be no offense of divisive speech against them; yet, because the offense incurred for breaking the bonds of noble ones is indeed grave, one should know that the previous explanation is correct.

After this moment, all manifest karma (vijñapti-karma) associated with the non-manifest karma (avijñapti-karma) and the mind that has not yet returned to its former state following the destruction [of the object], is termed "subsequent" (*pṛṣṭha*).

Regarding the three stages of the karma of harsh speech (*pāruṣya-vāk-karma*): for instance, when a certain person is about to utter harsh words, the arousal of a mind of resentment, the clenching of fists or stamping of feet, the raising of eyebrows, the glaring of eyes, the gnashing of teeth, and the movement of the lips—all prior to the actual utterance of the words—are termed the "preparatory stage" (*prayoga*).
The moment the verbal abuse is actually uttered and the other person perceives it, the manifest and unmanifest karma is termed the "fundamental path of action" (*maula-karmapatha*).
Other masters say that it is only when the other person is provoked to distress that it is fully established.

If that were so, then since a noble one endowed with the power of patience cannot be provoked or reviled, they would be without fault; yet, because one incurs profound guilt by reviling a worthy noble one, it should be known that the previous explanation is the correct one.

The manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*) that follows this moment—consisting of the non-manifest karma (*avijñapti-karma*), the act of returning the insult, and the repeated utterance of harsh words—is all termed "subsequent action" (*pṛṣṭha*).

Regarding the three stages of the karma of frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*): for instance, when a certain person, with a mind intent on jesting, first takes another's property, gathers various ornate discourses, and brings playthings to a crowd, the utterances made prior to the actual jest constitute the "preparatory effort" (*prayoga*).
The manifest and unmanifest karma produced at the very moment one initiates playful speech for the sake of entertaining others is called the "fundamental path of action" (*maula-karmapatha*).

Following that moment, all manifest karma involved in the subsequent acquisition, utilization, handling, or storing of the wealth obtained—concomitant with the unmanifest karma—is termed the "subsequent action" (*pṛṣṭha*).
Other masters say:
