If one dispatches an agent to commit one act, such as killing, while simultaneously completing another act, such as sexual misconduct, through one's own action, both are brought to completion at the same time.
If one performs two acts oneself, this should be considered according to the same principle.

If an evil karma was previously initiated through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), it reaches completion (*niṣṭhā*) in accordance with the three [factors] when other defilements such as greed or a non-defiled mind manifest.

If one gives rise to other defiled states of mind, such as greed and so forth, one spontaneously completes the karma of divisive speech, false speech, and so on; one should reflect accordingly on how these cause others to act and so forth.
Other masters say:
"When, after having dispatched two messengers, one personally commits sexual misconduct, all [three] reach completion simultaneously."

Furthermore, the claim that the two [paths of action] preceding speech arise simultaneously with it is also irrational, because greed is necessarily present at the moment of consummating sexual misconduct.
Since one of the three—greed and so forth—may be present when the path of action of speech is initiated, and because there would have to be a distinction even if another mind were to arise.

Regarding the fourfold simultaneous occurrence: this refers to when one intends to deceive another by uttering false speech or harsh words; in such a case, there is one path of mental action and three paths of vocal action.

This also applies when one sends two messengers while performing sexual misconduct oneself, or when an evil karma previously initiated through preparatory effort reaches its culmination upon the arising of greed and other afflictions, thereby completing all three [vocal paths].
Other categories of this kind should be considered by analogy.
Other masters say: "Both [the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Prakaraṇapāda*] speak of four types of speech."
This explanation is unreasonable, for it must be analyzed accordingly.
Thus, the cases of five, six, and seven [paths of action] should all be considered in accordance with reason.

Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of eight: this refers to one who, having previously engaged in preparatory effort for the six unwholesome courses of action, simultaneously brings them to completion while personally engaging in sexual misconduct.
Other cases should be considered accordingly.
Since the latter three [unwholesome paths] do not coexist, there are no [cases of] nine or ten paths.
For what reason must sexual misconduct be brought to completion by oneself, unlike killing and the others, which are accomplished even by commanding another?
Regarding killing and so forth, the commissioning of another necessarily involves a defiled mind;

that is to say, if one dispatches an agent to commit acts such as taking life, there is certainly a defiled mind. However, when commissioning another to engage in sexual misconduct, it is possible for the mind to be undefiled, as in the case of giving away a daughter in marriage and the like.

Furthermore, these types of afflictions must necessarily manifest before one; that is to say, when such afflictions arise, one personally commits acts such as killing and causes others to do likewise, whereas the affliction of inciting another to sexual misconduct does not necessarily function in the same way as one's own.
Furthermore, one must personally refrain from engaging in improper conduct; it is not called a personal transgression if one merely instructs another to do so.
That is to say, there may be cases where one refrains from improper conduct oneself, such as when giving a woman to her husband, which does not constitute a transgression on one's own part.

If one personally abstains from taking life regarding this object, yet incites another to kill, one is still called a killer; it has been heard that when a bodhisattva gave away his daughter as a gift to another, he immediately obtained the fruit of love.

However, this is not subsumed under non-celibacy or unwholesome karma; for if one causes another to commit an offense, it is the same as committing it oneself—how could one who abides in the preparatory application of an evil deed possibly bring about a fruit of merit?
Alternatively, certain bodhisattvas may commit misconduct.

Furthermore, abstaining from killing and so forth is established by relying on prohibited objects; because abstaining from sexual misconduct is for the sake of restraining one's own person, it does not follow that abstaining from killing all sentient beings constitutes a defeat (pārājika).
Rather, with respect to all [sentient beings], engaging in sexual intercourse in any instance whatsoever is termed a grave offense.

Furthermore, the principle must necessarily be so: for while a bhikṣu who merely dispatches another to kill commits a pārājika offense, one who acts as a matchmaker does not incur a grave transgression.
For what reason is it that by dispatching another to separate [a couple], one does not lose the precept against causing separation;
yet by merely dispatching another to take life, one incurs the sin of killing?

These two cases are not equivalent, because there is no instance of commissioning another to kill without the intention to kill, whereas there is an instance of commissioning another to abstain from killing without the intention to abstain from killing; thus, their meanings differ.

Furthermore, upholding the precepts is predominant in this context, whereas abandoning the violation of *śīla* is superior in another; thus, regarding the violation of precepts, there is the designation of "causing another to violate" as being "one's own violation," whereas regarding the upholding of precepts, there is no designation of "causing another to uphold" as being "one's own upholding."
Furthermore, it has already been stated previously.
What was stated previously?
It means that within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), evil is superior and good is inferior.
Furthermore, the phenomena of dependent origination possess various distinctions, so this cannot be raised as an objection.
For instance, visual consciousness does not abide within form, nor does it abide within the eye; it follows the increase or decrease of the eye, but does not follow that of form.

Furthermore, just as from the mind arise great elements such as visible form, which do not themselves become virtuous or non-virtuous by virtue of the mind’s power, yet their distinctions as virtuous and so forth do follow the mind;
likewise, the nature of sound in vocal karma follows the transformation of the mind, whereas the nature of sounds such as the snapping of fingers does not follow the mind.
Furthermore, the karmic act of killing is only completed once another has died; likewise, acts such as divisive speech are completed whether or not the other party is actually harmed.

Thus, regarding the precepts, there is no personal undertaking when one dispatches another to undertake them, yet there is personal transgression if one dispatches another to violate the precepts while oneself also violates them.

Among these, while commissioning another to kill constitutes the path of killing, commissioning another to engage in sexual misconduct does not constitute the path of sexual misconduct; thus it has been explained that there are differences in the number of unwholesome courses of action that arise simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*).

When the paths of wholesome action (*kuśala-karmapatha*) and volition (*cetanā*) are considered collectively, they may range up to ten; however, when distinguished according to their manifest characteristics, one, eight, or five are excluded.

Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of both: this refers to the time when the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are present, or when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) based on the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) are manifest. In these cases, the seven types of non-dispersed wholesome [paths] are absent, because the wisdom associated with them is not of the nature of vision (*dṛṣṭi*), and because there is no restraint (*saṃvara*) concomitant with the formless absorptions.

Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of three: this refers to when a mental consciousness associated with right view is present, provided that the seven types of material wholesome factors are absent.

Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of four: this refers to the state when an unwholesome or neutral mind is present, yet one attains the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a lay devotee (*upavāsa*), or a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*).
Sixfold simultaneous occurrence refers to when the five wholesome sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) manifest while one receives the three higher types of restraint (*saṃvara*).

Sevenfold simultaneous occurrence refers to when wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—which is associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and lacks accompanying matter (*rūpa*)—manifests while one receives the three higher types of restraint; or when an unwholesome or neutral mind manifests while one receives the bhikṣu precepts.

Regarding the ninefold simultaneous occurrence: this refers to when one acquires the bhikṣu precepts while the five wholesome consciousnesses are present, or when the mental consciousness associated with the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising—subsumed under dhyāna—is manifest, occurring at the time when the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are present in the formless realm.

The tenfold simultaneous occurrence refers to when the wholesome mental consciousness—associated with right view and accompanied by derivative matter—is present, such as when one obtains the bhikṣu precepts; or it refers to any other state where all [mental factors] associated with right view and accompanied by derivative matter are currently arising.

While such restrictions apply specifically to the manifest aspects, there are no such restrictions when considering both the hidden and the manifest; that is to say, apart from the formal vows (*saṃvara*), there are one, eight, or five [aspects of restraint].
Regarding the "one that functions simultaneously": this refers to obtaining the abstention from one branch when an unwholesome or neutral mind is present.

Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of five [factors]: this refers to when wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), accompanied by non-concomitant form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), manifests, one attains two factors and so forth.
Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of eight [factors]: this refers to when this same mental consciousness manifests, one attains five factors and so forth.
In which realms, destinies, and locations do the wholesome and unwholesome paths of action exist?
How many are merely possessed (*samanvāgata*),
and how many also manifest (*samudācāra*)?
The verse says:
In the unwholesome states and the hells, Coarseness, frivolity, and hatred pertain to both [types of existence].
Greed and false views are present as actualized; In the Northern Continent, the latter three are present as possessed.
Frivolous speech is present and acquired in all realms; the other ten [unwholesome paths] in the desire realm are both present and acquired.
Wholesome [paths] exist in all places; the latter three are present and acquired.
In the formless realm and the heaven of non-perception, the first seven are only acquired.
Excluding certain locations, they are present and established; excluding the hells and the northern continent.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, among the ten unwholesome paths of action, three exist in two ways within the hells—namely, harsh speech and frivolous speech—and all three exist both as manifest activity and as possession.

Because they are oppressed by suffering and revile one another, there is harsh speech; because they lament with resentment and wail in grief, there is frivolous speech; and because their bodies and minds are coarse, stubborn, perverse, and unbalanced due to mutual hatred, there is ill will.
Greed and wrong view exist but are not practiced, because there are no desirable objects and because they directly perceive the results of karma.
Since there are no methods of mutual harm, there is no killing; that is to say, beings die only when their karma is exhausted.
Because there are no women who possess property, there is neither theft nor sexual misconduct.
Because there is no purpose [for it], there is no false speech.
Alternatively, false speech causes another’s perception to become distorted; since their perceptions are always distorted [by nature], there is no deceptive speech.
Because they are constantly free from it, or because it would be useless, they have no divisive speech.

In Uttarakuru, greed, hatred, and wrong view are all invariably present in potential but do not manifest; this is because they do not grasp at "mine," because their bodies and minds are supple, because there are no causes for affliction or harm, and because they lack malicious intentions.
Only frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) is present there as a manifest action, because at times they sing with a defiled mind.
Because their lifespan is fixed, there is no killing.
Since they possess neither property nor women, there is no taking what is not given and no sexual misconduct.
Because there is no deceitful mind, there is no false speech.
Because there is no purpose [for it] or because they are always harmonious and conciliatory, there is no divisive speech.
Because their words are pure and beautiful, there is no harsh or abusive speech.
How do those people engage in unchaste conduct?

It is said that when a man and a woman give rise to mutual desire, they take each other’s hands and go beneath a tree; if the branches hang down and cover them, they know it is appropriate to proceed, but if the branches do not hang down, they depart from one another in mutual shame.
Excluding the aforementioned hells and the continent of Uttarakuru, the remaining realms within the desire realm all possess both [the paths of action as] actualized and as potentialities.

That is to say, among the gods, hungry ghosts, animals, and humans of the three continents within the desire realm, all ten unwholesome courses of action are common to both being actualized and existing as potentialities; however, there are distinctions.

That is to say, among gods, ghosts, and animals, the first seven courses of action are comprised solely of intermediate [neutral] states and lack non-restraint (*asaṃvara*); however, within the three continents of the human realm, both types exist.
Although the celestial hosts do not kill other gods, they may at times kill beings of other realms.
Other masters say: Devas also kill devas;

although their bodies may regrow after being severed, they do not regenerate once their heads are cut off or their torsos are split in half. Therefore, the path of action consisting of killing exists among the gods of the desire realm.
The unwholesome paths have already been explained.

Regarding the wholesome paths of action, the three beginning with non-attachment (alobha) pertain to both types—namely, possession (samanvāgama) and actual manifestation (samudācāra)—within all three realms and five destinies.
Regarding the seven branches of body and speech, although they may be accomplished in the formless realm where there is no perception, they certainly do not manifest.
This refers to noble beings born in the formless realm who accomplish past and future untainted restraints (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
Non-percipient beings necessarily possess the past and future dhyāna-restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara) of the fourth dhyāna.

However, whichever dhyāna stage a noble one has relied upon, the uncontaminated (anāsrava) morality that they have previously arisen and ceased becomes past when they are born in the formless realm; as for the future, it is possessed in all six stages.

Regarding the fact that there is no sense of manifest arising in either of these two locations: because those in the formless realm possess only the nature of the four aggregates, and sentient beings in the state of non-conception lack a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), the restraint (*saṃvara*)—which must rely upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)—does not manifest, as both the concentrated mind and the primary elements are mutually absent in these two locations.

In other realms and destinies—excluding the hells and the northern continent (*uttarakuru*)—all seven types of wholesome karma are both currently active (*samudācāra*) and possessed (*samanvāgama*), though there are distinctions among them.

Specifically, hungry ghosts and animals may possess the intermediate course of action (*madhyama-karmapatha*) apart from the formal restraint (*saṃvara*); in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is only the formal restraint; and in the three continents and the desire-realm heavens (*kāmadeva*), both types are present.
How do the paths of wholesome and unwholesome karma bring about their results?
The verse says:
All are able to summon the ripened result (vipākaphala), the result concordant with the cause (niṣyandaphala), and the dominant result (adhipatiphala).
"This causes others to suffer, severs their lives, and destroys their majesty.
The treatise says:
First, let us distinguish how each of the ten paths of unwholesome action brings about three types of results.
What are these three? They are distinguished as the maturation (*vipāka*), the outflow (*niṣyanda*), and the dominant (*adhipati*) results.

That is to say, if one habituates oneself to, cultivates, or frequently practices any of these ten types [of non-virtue], by the power of this, one is born in the hells; this is the maturation result.

Having departed from that [state], one is born here among the human *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) to experience the concordant results (*niṣyanda-phala*). That is to say: for the killer, the lifespan is short; for the thief, resources and wealth are meager; for the practitioner of sexual misconduct, the wife is unchaste; for the speaker of falsehoods, one frequently encounters slander; for the speaker of divisive speech, friends and kin fall into discord; for the speaker of harsh words, one constantly hears unpleasant sounds; for the speaker of frivolous chatter, one’s speech lacks authority and gravity; for the greedy, craving increases; for the hateful, anger intensifies; and for those with wrong views, delusion becomes predominant.
For what reason does wrong view cause delusion to increase further? One should not allow for the growth of that which is discordant through the practice of what is discordant.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) offers this explanation:
"Because delusion increases within that category."
Is it not the case that the ignorance associated with wrong view does not increase its activity through its characteristics, because it relies upon wrong view?
Now, when examining this meaning, at the time wrong view arises, it functions without a cognitive aspect (*ākāra*) toward the objective entity, thereby destroying the perceived reality.

This [ignorance] associated with attachment and aversion causes that delusion (*moha*) to increase, thereby making attachment and aversion toward objects of existence more intense as they proceed with specific modes of activity (*ākāra*).

Alternatively, for one who acts according to views, the power of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) causes true knowledge to become further and further removed; this is because when delusion increases, false views increase, and due to delusion, one proceeds to engage in inverted seeking.
When wrong views increase, delusion increases even further, because such views further obstruct true knowledge.
For this reason, it is said that false wisdom is the immediate enemy of right wisdom, as it acts as an ally to ignorance.
This is called the distinction regarding the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the paths of action.
How can a short lifespan be the outflow of killing?
Human lifespan must necessarily be the fruit of wholesome karma.
The Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) provides this explanation:

he does not say that human life itself is the fruit of the karma of killing; rather, he says that because the lifespan of humans is shortened by killing, one should understand that the karma of killing acts as an obstructive cause for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), preventing it from enduring long.

The meaning of what has been stated here is extremely difficult to comprehend. If killing as a cause can bring about a short lifespan, then of what phenomenon is "shortness" the designation, such that it is the fruit of killing rather than life itself?
For example, if a gold bar is short, that shortness is simply gold; life should be understood in the same way—how could shortness not be life?
How can it be said that lifespan is not the result of killing?

If you argue that because the karma of killing can induce calamities to life, killing is therefore the cause [of those calamities] and not the cause of lifespan itself, then one must clarify here: what is meant by "calamities to life"?
One should not say that it refers to things such as knives or poison, for knives and the like are merely the conditions for calamity.
Nor should it be said to be the outflow of killing and so forth, because those are the dominant results (*adhipatiphala*) of sentient beings.

"Obstruction of life" (*jīvitavipatti*) and "obstacle to life" (*jīvitāntarāya*) have the same meaning. Since it has been stated that the karma of killing acts as a cause for an obstacle to life, one should now investigate: what is meant by this "obstacle to life"?
If it is claimed that an obstacle to life is simply the non-arising of longevity (*āyus*), then one must further consider whether this [non-arising] is an existent or a non-existent.
If it does not exist, the essence of the fruit is not established; one who has not abided in the fundamental mind cannot claim that there is a fruit for what is non-existent.
If it does exist, this would not be distinct from life itself, which would contradict the teaching that life is not the fruit of killing.

One should explain that it is not said that human lifespan is the ripened result (*vipāka-phala*) of killing; rather, one should say it is the proximate dominant result (*adhipati-phala*) of the karma of killing.

This means that although human lifespan is summoned by wholesome karma, due to the dominant force of killing, that continuum lasts for only a short time. This is because in the desire realm, the unwholesome is superior to the wholesome, and possesses a dominant force capable of suppressing the wholesome.
If that is so, why is it called a "result of outflow" (*niṣyanda-phala*)?
It is because this term indicates that among the results of dominance (*adhipati-phala*), there is one that is most proximate.
If both were designated by the name "result of dominance," then the distinction between the proximity and distance of the results would not be made manifest.
If one were to say this is not so, how could it be that the unwholesome [karma] takes the non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) abandoned by cultivation as its outflow fruit (niṣyandaphala)?
There is no contradiction with reason; therefore, it can be said that a person’s short lifespan is precisely the outflow fruit induced by the karma of killing.

The sovereign results (*adhipati-phala*) produced by these ten [non-virtuous actions] are as follows: regarding all external means of subsistence, through killing, they lack luster; through taking what is not given, crops frequently suffer from frost and hail, and the yield is meager with fruits that are sparse and small; through sexual misconduct, there is much dust and grime; through false speech, there is much foul stench and impurity; through divisive speech, one’s dwelling place is rugged and crooked; through harsh speech, there is much unpleasant contact, and the fields abound with thorns, are stony and barren, or saline and alkaline; through idle chatter, the seasons are altered; through covetousness, the fruit is scant; through malice, the fruit is bitter; and through wrong view, the fruit is either scant or non-existent.
This is called the distinction regarding the dominant results (*adhipatiphala*) of the paths of action.
Does a single act of killing, after having caused rebirth in hell, further result in a short lifespan as an external adverse effect?
Other masters say:

Thus, for a single act of killing, there are three fruits: first, one experiences the ripening (*vipāka*) result; second, the proximate dominant (*adhipati*) result; and third, the remote dominant result.

In reality, at the moment of killing, it causes the victim to experience suffering, their life to be severed, and their majestic radiance to be lost. Because it inflicts suffering upon another, one is born in hell; because one has terminated another's life, one’s lifespan is short among humans. The former is the fruit of the preliminary application (*prayoga*), and the latter is the fruit of the fundamental act (*maula*).

When one kills while in both the fundamental and the preparatory stages, one destroys one's own majestic splendor and brings about adverse external conditions; thus, the karma of killing incurs three types of results.
The other paths of unwholesome action should be considered accordingly.
From this, one should understand by analogy the three fruits of the wholesome paths of action.

For instance, regarding the abstention from killing: if one practices, cultivates, or frequently performs it, then by the power of that, one is born among the gods and experiences the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
Having passed away from that state and been reborn among humans, they experience an extremely long lifespan as a proximate dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Furthermore, by means of this very [karma], they induce various external requisites as a distant dominant fruit characterized by great majestic radiance.
The three fruits of other wholesome [actions] should be explained by reversing those of the unwholesome.
Furthermore, a sutra states that among the eight factors of the wrong path (*mithyā-mārga*), bodily action is divided into three: namely, wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood.
What is the abandonment of wrong speech and wrong livelihood?
Although these are not distinct from that [abandonment of wrong action], they are explained separately. The verse says:
Bodily and vocal actions born of greed are called wrong livelihood, because they are difficult to eliminate.
The claim that these arise from greed for the necessities of life is irrational, as it contradicts the Sūtras.
The Treatise says:
The two types of karma—of speech and body—arising from hatred and delusion are, respectively, termed only "wrong speech" and "wrong action."

The two types of karma—bodily and vocal—arising from greed are called wrong speech and wrong action; they are also termed wrong livelihood, which is established separately from the other two because it is more difficult to eliminate.

Greed for subtle things can steal the minds of all sentient beings; even those of extreme intelligence find it difficult to restrain and guard against it. Therefore, among these two, it is the most difficult to eliminate.
For householders, wrong views are difficult to sever, because they frequently cling to false notions of auspiciousness and the like.
For those who have left the household life, wrong livelihood is difficult to eliminate, as all the conditions for their sustenance depend upon others.
Therefore, so that they may diligently cultivate right livelihood, the Buddha set it apart from the preceding items and taught it as a separate category.

Other masters maintain that only those bodily and vocal actions produced by craving for the requisites of life are termed "wrong livelihood," and not those produced by other forms of craving. Why is this so?
Performing songs, dances, and the like for one's own amusement does not support one's livelihood;
because this contradicts the sūtras, it is certainly not reasonable.

In the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*, the Blessed One also established activities such as watching elephant fights as wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*), because they involve the improper reception of external objects and the vain prolongation of life.

Therefore, it should be understood that not only is bodily and vocal action arising from craving for the requisites of life designated as "wrong livelihood," but right speech, right action, and right livelihood are to be understood as its opposites.
For what reason are body and speech presented first among the paths of action?
Within the eight factors of the path, speech is mentioned before bodily action because, among the paths of karma, they are described according to their relative coarseness or subtlety.
The sequence of the path factors follows their natural order of arising; thus, the Sūtra states:
"Having given rise to vitarka and vicāra, one utters speech."

Chapter Eleven: Discernment of Karma, Part Four, Section Eleven. As previously stated, there are five kinds of fruits; which karmas possess how many fruits?
The verse says:
Contaminated karma on the path of abandonment Possesses all five results;
Uncontaminated karma has four, Namely, excluding only the ripening result.
The remaining contaminated wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas] likewise consist of four [results], excluding the result of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*);
the remaining uncontaminated and neutral [dharmas] consist of three, excluding those previously excluded.
The treatise says:
The Path is able to realize abandonment and is able to sever afflictions; thus it receives the name "Path of Abandonment," which is precisely the Uninterrupted Path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
This path is of two kinds: namely, contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The karma of the path with outflows possesses five fruits:
the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) refers to subsequent states that are equal to or superior to the preceding ones among similar dharmas within its own stage.
The fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) refers to the desirable maturation summoned by the path of abandonment within its own stage.
The fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) refers to the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized through the power of this path in severing the afflictions.
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) refers to that which is drawn forth by the path, including its coexistent factors, its liberation, its cultivation, and its abandonment.
"Coexistent" refers to dharmas that arise simultaneously.
"Liberation" refers to that which arises immediately [after the path of seeing], namely the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
"That which is cultivated" refers to cultivation in the future.
Cessation refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which arises only through the power of the Path.

Regarding the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), there is this teaching: it consists of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) other than its own nature, excluding only those that have already arisen prior to it.
Some say: "The abandonment [of defilements] should also be the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) of the Path, because the dominant power of the Path is able to realize it.

If that were so, why does the *Vibhāṣā* state only that the abandonment of the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*) of the patience regarding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), and never says it is a dominant fruit?

It is not the case that something is not a result simply because it is not explicitly mentioned; for that very text states that the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the virile-result (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñānakṣānti*), and it never says that it is a sovereign-result (*adhipati-phala*).

However, although the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is indeed its dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), it is not explicitly mentioned because its meaning is already fully established.
This case should be understood similarly; for by mentioning the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), the principle of the dominant fruit is already implicitly included.

It is not only that which can arise that is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*); for non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is said to be the fruit of the mind, and there is no other sense of "fruit" apart from this.
Thus, among the paths of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), the karma of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) possesses only four fruits, namely, excluding the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).

Other contaminated wholesome and unwholesome karmas also have four fruits; that is, with the exception of the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*). They are termed "other" because they differ from the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*) mentioned previously.
The subsequent term "other" should be explained by analogy with this.

This refers to other untainted (*anāsrava*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) karmas, which have only three fruits; excluding those previously excluded—that is, excluding the previously excluded [fruits], namely, the ripened (*vipāka*) and the dissociated (*visamyoga*).

Having already provided a general analysis of how all karmas possess fruits, we shall next examine the characteristics of the fruits of karma through the gateway of their results. Within this, we first analyze the three types of karma—wholesome and so forth.
The verse says:
"Wholesome and so forth, with respect to wholesome and so forth; In the first [category], there are four, two, and three."
Among these, there are two, three, and four; subsequently, there are two, three, and three fruits.
The Commentary states:
The final statements all follow the sequence of the words "as appropriate" (*yathāyogam*), which clarifies that they apply universally to the preceding categories as required.

Furthermore, the three types of karma—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—each acting as a cause, produce results when correlated with the three dharmas (wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate) respectively.
One should understand that the enumeration of these results follows the same pattern as previously illustrated.
That is to say, a wholesome karma of the first [category] has four results consisting of wholesome dharmas, excluding the ripened result (*vipāka-phala*).
It has two results consisting of unwholesome dharmas, namely the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*).
It has three results consisting of neutral dharmas, excluding the outflowing result (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the result of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
Unwholesome karma in the intermediate [realm] has wholesome dharmas as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
It has unwholesome dharmas as three fruits, excluding the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
Taking the indeterminate as four fruits— excluding the fruit of disjunction—

the outflowing fruit refers to all unwholesome karma abandoned through the vision of suffering, as well as all pervasive unwholesome karma abandoned through the vision of origination, because these take the various indeterminate dharmas belonging to the category of the view of self-identity and extreme views within the desire realm as their outflowing fruit.
Subsequently, neutral karma has wholesome dharmas as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
It has unwholesome dharmas as three fruits, excluding the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).

Regarding the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*): this refers to the fact that the various neutral karmas belonging to the category of the view of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) have the unwholesome factors of the five categories as their outflow.
Neutral karma takes three fruits, just as unwholesome karma does.
Having already analyzed the three natures, one should now analyze the three time periods.
The verse says:
In the past, there are four for each of the three; in the present, it is likewise with respect to the future.
The present [karma] has two results in the present; the future [karma] has three results in the future.
The treatise says:
Each of the three types of karma—past, present, and future—acts as a cause, taking the past and so forth as its results according to what is appropriate.
As for the distinction: past karma takes the dharmas of the three time periods as its four fruits, excluding the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).

Karma of the present period takes future dharmas as its four fruits, as previously stated; it takes present dharmas as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding karma of the future, it has three fruits in the future, excluding the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
It is not said that subsequent karma has preceding fruits, because a preceding dharma is certainly not the fruit of subsequent karma.
Having already analyzed the three time periods, one should now analyze the various stages (*bhūmi*).
The verse says:
In the same stage, there are four fruits; in different stages, there are two or three.
The treatise says:
Within the various stages (*bhūmi*), whichever stage’s karma it may be, it takes dharmas of that same stage as its four fruits, excluding the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
If it is contaminated (*sāsrava*), it takes dharmas of a different stage as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

If it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it takes dharmas of a different stage as three fruits—excluding the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*)—because, not falling within the realms (*dhātu*), it does not preclude the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
Having already analyzed the various stages, one should now analyze those that are in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.
The verse says:
For those in training (*śaikṣa*), there are three [causes] each with three [fruits]; for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one, three, and two;
for those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), there are two, two, and five fruits respectively.
The treatise says:
Each of the three types of karma—those of training and so forth—acts as a cause, with each taking three dharmas as its result in their respective order.

Specifically, karma of training takes the dharmas of training as its three results, excluding the ripened and the disjoined; the same applies to its taking the dharmas beyond training as its three results.
Non-dual [actions] take three fruits as their result, excluding the maturation (vipāka) and the outflowing (niṣyanda).
Unlearned (aśaikṣa) karma takes learned (śaikṣa) dharmas as one fruit, namely the dominant (adhipati).
Logically, it should be said that there are two, namely adding the outflowing.
Taking the *aśaikṣa* as three fruits—excluding the ripening (*vipāka*) and the disconnection (*visamyoga*) fruits;
taking the "neither" as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Taking the "neither" karma with respect to *śaikṣa* dharmas as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort and the sovereign fruit.
The same applies to taking the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) as two [results].
Taking that which is neither [of these] results in five fruits.
Having already analyzed [the results] in relation to those in training and so forth, we shall now analyze those to be abandoned by vision and so forth.
The verse says:
Regarding karma to be abandoned by seeing and so forth, each one respectively has three [results];
for the first [category], there are three, four, and one; for the middle [category], there are two, four, and three results.
"Subsequently, there are one, two, and four; all should be understood according to their respective order.
The treatise says:
The three types of karma—those to be abandoned by seeing and so forth—act respectively as causes for each of the three categories, with each taking three dharmas as its fruit.

Regarding the distinctions: karma to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) takes phenomena to be abandoned by seeing as three fruits—excluding the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
It takes phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) as four fruits, excluding the fruit of disconnection.

Taking non-abandonable dharmas as one fruit—namely, the sovereign (adhipati) fruit—the karma to be abandoned by cultivation takes abandonable dharmas of the path of seeing as two fruits: namely, the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra) and the sovereign fruit.
Taking the factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) as the four fruits— excluding the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*)—
and taking the factors not to be abandoned (*aheya*) as the three fruits— excluding the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Regarding the final category, the karma not to be abandoned, it has the factors to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) as one fruit, namely, the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

Taking the factors to be abandoned by cultivation as two fruits—namely, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*)—and taking the factors not to be abandoned as four fruits, excluding the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
The phrase "all according to their respective order" means that these should be applied throughout all the preceding categories as appropriate; such is the nature of the abbreviated method.
In discussing various types of karma, one should further ask:

regarding the three kinds of karma described in the treatise—namely, karma that ought to be performed, karma that ought not to be performed, and karma that is neither to be performed nor not to be performed—what are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Defiled karma is that which should not be done; some say it is also that which violates proper decorum.
Karma that should be done is the opposite of this; the third category consists of that which is contrary to both.
The treatise says:
Some say that defiled actions of body, speech, and mind are called "unfit to be done" because they arise from improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
Other masters state:
All bodily, vocal, and mental actions that violate established norms (*vidhi*) should not be performed even if they are undefiled (*akliṣṭa*), because they are inconsistent with worldly conventions.

That is to say, any unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) bodily action—whether standing, walking, eating, drinking, or otherwise—that does not conform to the social etiquette of the world is termed a "bodily action that violates norms."

Any unobscured-neutral verbal karma that, at the time of speaking, destroys one's appearance or words, or involves the speaker and so forth, yet merely fails to accord with worldly etiquette, is all termed "violation of proper conduct" (dūṣaṇā).

The two preceding types of volition that motivate vocal karma and so forth are termed "intentional actions that violate proper decorum" (*akārya-karma*). These, along with defiled karma, are called "actions not to be performed.
Actions that are "to be performed" are the opposite of these; both of them contradict the former two and constitute the third type of karma.
If one relies on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), the latter [position] may also be correct;
however, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), what was stated previously is superior.

That is to say, only wholesome karma is called "to be performed" (*kārya*); only defiled karma is called "not to be performed" (*akārya*); and unobscured-neutral karma of body, speech, and mind is called "neither to be performed nor not to be performed."

However, not all actions that should not be performed are subsumed under "misconduct" (duścarita). Only those that are unwholesome (akuśala) by their very nature receive the name "misconduct. Furthermore, that which brings about desirable results is called "excellent conduct" (sucarita), while that which brings about undesirable results is called "misconduct."

Although that which is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) is something that should not be done, it is not subsumed under misconduct (duścarita), because what is performed through it is certainly incapable of producing either desirable or undesirable results.
Now, within this context, one should further investigate:
does a single karma project only a single birth, or does it project many births?
Furthermore, is a single birth projected by only one karma, or is it projected by many karmas?
The verse says:
One karma draws forth one birth; multiple karmas can bring it to completion.
The commentary says:
If one were to speak according to correct reasoning, it should be definitively stated that a single karma induces only a single birth.
This term "one birth" indicates the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class), for it is only upon obtaining such a homogeneous class that one is said to have "arisen."

If it is said that a single lifetime is projected by multiple karmas, or if it is said that a single karma can project multiple lifetimes—what fault is there in these two statements from the perspective of reason?

First, the former position contains a fault: since the fruit of a prior karma ends and the fruit of a subsequent karma arises within a single lifetime, and because these karmic fruits are distinct, there would have to be repeated deaths and births; or else, there would be no principle of death and birth across multiple lifetimes, because the ending and arising of karmic fruits would be identical to what occurs within a single lifetime.

Both positions entail faults: first, within a single existence (*bhava*), there would have to be numerous existences of death and birth; or else, until the attainment of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, there would never again be death or birth in the interval.

For what reason is it that within the confines of a single realm of rebirth (*gati*), there are cases where the arising of diverse karmic fruits constitutes both birth and death, while there are other cases where diverse karmic fruits arise without birth or death?
When one set of karmic fruits concludes and another set of karmic fruits arises, it is logically certain that one must establish the existence of both death and birth.

Furthermore, since it is asserted that a single lifetime is necessarily projected by various types of karma that have been performed and accumulated, it would follow that there must certainly be no such thing as premature death, or else one would never experience the results of those karmas and they would be eternally discarded.
However, this has already been explained.
What was explained previously?

It means that, as a matter of principle, there is no case where the maturation (*vipāka*) induced by karma fixed in terms of time should instead be experienced at another time; furthermore, as a matter of principle, there is no case where karma fixed in terms of time—provided it has been both performed and accumulated—would not necessarily result in the experience of its maturation.

If it is argued that birth is induced by various types of karma—both determinate and indeterminate—or that some births are induced solely by various determinate karmas, and therefore there are both premature deaths and lives lasting until the end of one's natural span, this is also incorrect; for there is no fixed certainty regarding whether the results of karma will be experienced at a specific time or not.

If there is a certain class of beings whose karma for results to be experienced during middle age or old age is fixed and must be undergone, while their karma for results to be experienced as infants, children, or youths is not fixed, how is that further explained?

In principle, it is impossible for a subsequent [moment] to exist apart from a preceding one; otherwise, the karma of the preceding state would necessarily be subject to fixed retribution, as its fruit would be destined to be experienced.

However, within this context, there is no definitive principle that causes the karma of the preceding state to have fixed retribution while causing the karma of the subsequent state to have indeterminate retribution. Therefore, a single birth is not projected by multiple karmas.
There is also a further fault: a single karma would then project multiple births, and thus karmas with fixed timing would become confused.
This lack of confusion has already been explained previously.
Therefore, no single karma can project multiple births.
If this is so, for what reason did the Venerable Aniruddha say of himself:

"I recall that once, through the maturation of a single gift of food given to a most excellent field of merit, from that point on I was reborn seven times in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, seven times among humans as a Wheel-turning Sage King, and finally I was born into the great Śākya clan, abundant in precious wealth and enjoying much happiness"?
The *Vibhāṣā* has already explained this statement:
"Based on a single gift of food, one gives rise to many superior volitions and aspirations, which can induce various distinct stages and produce many diverse maturations (*vipāka*)."
Therefore, this statement was made: "The maturation (*vipāka*) of a single gift of food.

It is not that a maturation can again produce a new birth; rather, it is said so in order to reveal the distinctions in the states of the maturations summoned by numerous volitions and aspirations arising with respect to the single object of a gift of food. Thus, this statement was made.

Alternatively, this statement was made to clarify the initial foundation: by means of a single karma, he experienced a life of great nobility and abundant wealth, as well as the knowledge of past lives; building upon this, he further created merit that induced other births, continuing in this succession until his final existence, when he was born into a wealthy and noble family and attained the ultimate fruit.

Suppose there is someone who possesses a single *kārsāpaṇa* and, through skillful means and diligent effort, seeks profit until it becomes a thousandfold, saying: "It was originally from this one *kārsāpaṇa* that I have now come to achieve such great wealth and status."
Therefore, a single karma induces only a single birth.
Although it is said that one birth is induced by a single karma, it is admitted that its completion is achieved through many karmas.
This is like a painter who first outlines the shape with a single color and subsequently fills it in with various hues.
Now, regarding the single form used as an analogy here: does it represent a single category of karma or a single moment?

If it represents a single category, it contradicts the principles of this school; for the statement that "a single [karma] projects a single birth" cannot be applied to a single category, since a category necessarily comprises many [moments], and it is illogical for many [moments] to project a single birth.
If one were to say that a single color represents a single moment, and that a single moment cannot constitute a shape, then the analogy established would be incapable of proving the point.
What we see here is that the analogy refers to a category of karma.
How can projecting karma be established in terms of its categories?
This is because the karma that projects a single realm of existence (*gati*) is manifold.

The intent of this statement is to clarify that within a single category of karma, only a single moment projects the *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous character); however, multiple moments of karma—whether of the same or different types—are capable of bringing it to completion, and thus they are described as being "many."
Therefore, it is as when one first sketches the outline of a form with a single color and subsequently fills it in with various hues; this statement accords with reason.

Consequently, although there are those who equally receive a human body, among them some possess the full complement of limbs, sense faculties, proportions, complexion, and strength, while others are deficient in many of these respects; this is because birth is projected and fulfilled solely by karma.

It is not so; all karma has a single fruit. Because the power of its dharma-force is strong, it both projects (*ākṣepa*) and completes (*paripūraṇa*) birth. Conversely, that which is contrary to this can complete but cannot project.
What is the essential nature of these two types?
The verse says:
The two mindless attainments and the acquisitions cannot induce other supernormal powers.
The commentary says:
Although the two mindless attainments possess maturation (*vipāka*), they lack the power to project a common destiny (*nikāyasabhāga*), because they do not coexist with karma.
Furthermore, all acquisitions (*prāpti*) of unwholesome states and impure wholesome states likewise lack the power to project a common destiny, because they do not share the same fruit as karma.
All other unwholesome and wholesome contaminated dharmas may pertain to both types: namely, those that project [a rebirth] and those that fulfill it.
The Bhagavān taught that there are three heavy obstructions: the obstruction of karma, the obstruction of afflictions, and the obstruction of maturation.
What is the nature of these three obstructions?
The verse says:
The three obstructions consist of the karma of immediate retribution, as well as the afflictions that are frequently practiced.
As well as all evil destinies, the northern continent, and the heaven of non-perception.
The treatise says:
The essence of karmic obstruction refers to the five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
First, killing one's mother; second, killing one's father; third, killing an arhat; fourth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha; and fifth, shedding the blood of a Buddha with a malicious mind.

Regarding the nature of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*): it refers to frequently occurring afflictions. Even if lower-grade afflictions occur frequently, although one may wish to suppress and eliminate them, they find no opportunity to do so; because these [afflictions] successively cause higher grades to arise, they are difficult to suppress and eliminate, and are therefore also called "hindrances."

If superior-grade afflictions (*kleśa*) do not manifest frequently, the path of antidotes (*pratipakṣamārga*) easily finds its opportunity; thus, although they may be extremely intense, they are not subsumed under the category of "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*).

Although all sentient beings dwelling in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who are bound by fetters equally possess all afflictions, their actualization (*samudācāra*) differs, resulting in distinct obstructions. Therefore, among the afflictions, only those that manifest frequently according to their superior or inferior grades are termed "affliction-obstructions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The essence of the obstruction to maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*) consists of the three evil destinies in their entirety, as well as a portion of the good destinies—namely, the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) and the Unconscious Heaven (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Why is it called an "obstruction"?
Because it obstructs the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), the provisions for that path (*mārgasaṃbhāra*), and the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).

It is not only the immediate [karmas] that constitute the essence of karmic obstruction; rather, all determinate karma capable of obstructing the vision of the Truths should be subsumed under karmic obstructions.

This refers to various karmas—both performed and accumulated—that can induce rebirth in the evil destinies, as well as birth from eggs or moisture, the female body, or the eighth existence among humans and gods; furthermore, it includes karma conducive to being experienced in a subsequent life that induces the status of Mahābrahmā, or a single or double birth in the form or formless realms. All such cases lack entry into the principle of the vision of the Truths.
For what reason is this not said to be subsumed under the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*)?
Because within this class of beings, there is no certainty;
that is to say, within such types of karmic categories, there are always powerful conditions capable of turning them back, as they do not obstruct the Noble Path or the provisions for the Path.

Within this context, although there may be minor karma that cannot be altered, it is not established as an "obstruction" (āvaraṇa), because only those types of karma belonging to the category of the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) are inherently unalterable; thus, it is only with respect to these that the designation "karmic obstruction" (*karmāvaraṇa*) is established.

The *Vibhāṣā* explains that these five causes and conditions—namely, the place, the destiny, the birth, the fruit, and the *pudgala*—are easily seen and easily known, and are therefore designated as "obstructions of karma" (*karmāvaraṇa*).
"Abodes" (sthāna) refers to these five destinies because they have mothers and so forth as their place of origin.
"Destinations" (gati) refers to these five destinies because they have the hells as their destination.
"Births" (upapatti) refers to these five destinies because they produce maturation (vipāka) immediately [after death].
"Result" refers to the fact that these five definitely bring about undesirable fruits.

"Person" (pudgala) refers to the person who, based on the performance of these five heinous acts with intense afflictions, is universally recognized as one capable of harming their mother and so forth.
Other karmas are not like this and are not established as obstructions.
One should understand that the establishment or exclusion of other obstructions follows the same principle.
Among these three obstructions, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are the most serious, because they give rise to karma, and karma brings about its results.
Other masters say:
Both the obstacles of afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma are most grave, because for one who possesses them, they cannot be remedied even in a second lifetime.
What is the meaning of "immediate" (*ānantarya*)?

Because this immediate karma (*ānantarya-karma*) must necessarily yield its fruit in the immediately succeeding birth, and because no other karma capable of yielding fruit can intervene, it is so called. Some say:

"A person (*pudgala*) who has committed an immediate transgression will, upon death from this life, certainly fall into hell; because there is no interval (*antara*), it is called 'immediate' (*ānantarya*)."

That which possesses immediate succession (ānantarya) receives the name "immediate"; it is called "immediate" because it is conjoined with immediate dharmas, just as one is called a "śramaṇa" because of being conjoined with the qualities of a śramaṇa.
One should know in which realms of existence these three obstacles are found.
The verse says:
The immediate [karmas] exist in the three continents, not among others such as the *śaṇḍhas* and so forth;
because they possess little gratitude and little shame. The obstruction [to the path] excludes these [immediate karmas], yet it pervades all five destinies.
The treatise says:

Not all obstructions exist in every realm of rebirth (*gati*). For instance, the immediate karmas (*ānantarya-karma*) exist only among humans in the three continents, not in Uttarakuru, nor in other realms or other destinies. Within those three continents, they exist only for women and men, not for eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*) and the like, just as there is no unwholesome discipline (*duḥśīla*) for them.
Some say: because parents bestow little kindness upon them, and they feel little shame toward their parents.
This refers to those whose parents give birth to them with incomplete bodies, yet still cherish and care for them.
Furthermore, because it is subtle, it is said that the gratitude [involved] is slight.

Their sense of shame and dread of blame (*hrī-apatrāpya*) toward their parents is also subtle; it is only when one destroys this profound shame and dread that one incurs an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*).
However, the Venerable Elder says:
If those such as Caṇḍāla and others were to harm their mothers or commit similar acts, they would also incur the immediate retribution (ānantarya).
Since these individuals of deluded nature perform actions that ought not to be done, how could it be permitted for them to ascend on account of this to the Tuṣita Heaven?
Not only does one who performs what should not be performed fail to be reborn in those celestial realms, but they will certainly be born in hell.
Therefore, although you have raised this objection, your words deviate from reason; devoid of any reflection, you have uttered these words in the dark.
Furthermore, he himself raises the objection:
"Since animals and others also kill their parents, why is this not an ānantarya [immediate] offense?
He then provides his own explanation:
This is because their awakening-wisdom (*buddhi*) is inferior, their perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are distorted, and their loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is thin.
But would these causes not also be possible in the case of eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*) and others? Therefore, there is no immediate [retribution] for them.

Even if one were to grant that such a person could incur the immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) for killing, this would not cause even a small amount of faith or understanding in the words of the Elder; therefore, my own position is superior in terms of reasoning.
Furthermore, if someone kills non-human parents, it does not constitute a transgression of immediate retribution, because the benefit [they provide] and the grounds for shame are minimal.
This means that the father does not possess toward the son the same kindness as a human being, and the son does not possess toward him the same sense of shame and dread of blame as a human being.
Having already established that karmic obstructions exist only among humans in the three continents, one should know that the remaining obstructions exist in all five destinies.
However, the afflictive hindrance (kleśāvaraṇa) pervades all places.

As for the maturational hindrance (vipākāvaraṇa), it encompasses the three evil destinies entirely; among humans, it exists only in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru); and among devas, it exists only in the realm of non-conception (asaṃjñisattva).

Is it not the case that those in the three continents who possess bodies such as those of the *śaṇḍha* (eunuchs) and others are not vessels for the Noble Path, and are therefore subsumed under the "obstruction of maturation" (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*)?

There is no such principle; for in those births, the continuity of the homogeneous group (*nikāya-sabhāga*) drawn by projecting karma can constitute male or other forms that serve as vessels for the Noble Path. It is only in the three evil destinies, the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), and the Northern Continent (*uttarakuru*) that there is absolutely no possibility of realizing the Noble Path; therefore, the obstruction of maturation is established only with respect to those states.

Some say that those [five] states belong exclusively to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while other states may be shared with noble ones (*ārya*); therefore, they are not said to be subsumed under the obstacle of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*).

Among the three types of obstacles previously analyzed, the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) were stated to constitute the essence of the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*). What is the essential nature of these five acts of immediate retribution?
Furthermore, the Venerable Elder states:
"The three types of action constitute the essence; bodily and vocal actions, each acting alone, are able to summon a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).

This is difficult to establish logically, because it is only through the deeds performed by mental action that the matter is weighty; thus, [the Elder] allows that it can induce a particularly distinguished ripened fruit. This is extremely far-fetched.
What is the meaning of "confused"?

You have already conceded that volition (cetanā) which operates in dependence on body and speech is designated as bodily and vocal karma; yet now you concede that mental karma constitutes the essence of the immediate transgression (ānantarya). If this were so, then the mere momentary arising of a volition intending to commit a transgression against a parent would immediately constitute that immediate transgression.

Furthermore, as for the claim that mental karma (*manas-karman*) performs weighty actions and is thus admitted to produce a distinguished ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*), this is merely a false admission, as it contradicts one’s own tenets.

For if a volition (*cetanā*) moves and initiates body or speech, that volition may indeed be said to perform a weighty action; however, it cannot be called "mental karma," because it functions by way of the two doors of body and speech.

If a volition cannot incite the body or speech, it is admitted by you to be mental action (*manas-karman*), yet its effect is not weighty; how then can you say that the effect of mental action is weighty?

If you argue that the two volitions which incite body and speech constitute mental action, and because the effect produced by such volition is weighty, it is said that the effect of mental action is weighty—this too is irrational, for the action itself is not weighty.

Volition alone does not constitute the two types of action—bodily and vocal; rather, it is the mental action that brings those matters to fruition with gravity. How could the gravity of the matter performed be established by volition alone?
The statement indicates that because it moves and initiates bodily and vocal actions, the "matter performed" is grave, and this does not apply to the volition of mental action.

If one considers that an action is heavy because the volition (*cetanā*) that produced it is heavy, and thus says that mental action (*manas-karman*) is heavy because the volition preceding the mental action can induce its fruit and the matter of that fruit is heavy, then there would be a great logical fallacy.

Furthermore, it is not the case that mental karma and the volition of body and speech share a common maturation simply because they stand in a cause-and-effect relationship; otherwise, that mental karma and its preceding volition would also stand in a cause-and-effect relationship and thus share the same maturation, which would lead to the undesirable consequence [of such an absurdity].

Furthermore, regarding that previous statement concerning the proof of this cause—namely, that it is difficult for bodily action (*kāyakarman*) and vocal action (*vākkarman*) alone to produce a maturation (*vipāka*)—what is the meaning of these words?
Does it mean that they produce maturation together with mental action (*manaskarman*), such that the nature and category of this [mental action] and those [two physical actions] are identical?

Furthermore, it is difficult to establish that volition (*cetanā*) alone can produce a ripened result (*vipāka*). Therefore, one must admit that the mind itself is the substance of the immediate [retribution], or that its substance is volition.
Moreover, one should investigate those who claim there is "mental action" (*manas-karman*) as the immediate [retribution]: by what power of volition does a matricide draw forth rebirth in hell?
Is it volition as reflection (*cetanā-manasikāra*) or volition as a path of action (*karmapatha-cetanā*)?
If it is volition as reflection, how could the mere fact of having not yet caused any harm to one's mother definitively lead to birth in hell?
If it is the volition (*cetanā*) of the path of action (*karmapatha*), how can one say that bodily and vocal actions alone are capable of producing the result?
This is because the fruit is not taken by the volition of the path of action through the power of prior deliberative volition (*vitarkacitta*).

Furthermore, since you yourself admit that there is first the deliberative volition and subsequently the volition of the path of action—whereby the former is mental action (*manaskarma*) and the latter is bodily or vocal action—their temporal characteristics differ when viewed in relation to one another; thus, there is no principle for them to have a single result. How, then, can it be said that bodily and vocal actions alone produce the maturation (*vipāka*)?
That reasoning is difficult to establish; therefore, what they have said lies outside of the sacred teaching.
However, as for the definitive meaning of our own school, the verse says:
Among these five acts of immediate retribution, Four are bodily actions and one is vocal action.
Three are killing; one is false speech; one is the preparatory stage of killing.
The Commentary says:
Among the five actions of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), four are bodily actions (*kāyakarman*) and one is vocal action (*vākkarman*).

Three are the fundamental paths of action of killing, one is the fundamental path of action of false speech, and one is the preliminary application of the path of action of killing, because the body of a Tathāgata cannot be harmed.
The immediate retribution of schism in the Saṃgha is a form of false speech; since it is false speech, for what reason is it called "schism in the Saṃgha"?
It receives its name from its cause, or because it is capable of causing a schism.
If that is so, what is the essential nature of a schism in the Saṃgha?
And by whom are the persons who cause the schism and those who are split accomplished?
The verse says:
The schism of the Saṃgha is a non-concordant mental formation (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra),
of an unobscured-neutral nature (anivṛtāvyākṛta-svabhāva), and is that which is accomplished by the schismatic Saṃgha.
The Treatise says:

The essence of the schism in the Saṃgha is the nature of disharmony; it is comprised within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha) and is non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta).

How, then, could it constitute an immediate retribution (ānantarya)? Since such a schism in the Saṃgha arises from the cause of deceptive speech (mṛṣāvāda), it is said that the schism in the Saṃgha is the fruit of an immediate retribution.
This schism is not accomplished by the schismatic; rather, it is accomplished solely by the monastic community being split.
What, then, does this schismatic person accomplish?
Where and for how long does the karmic maturation (*vipāka*) of causing a schism occur?
The verse says:
Only the one who causes the schism incurs this offense of false speech;
it ripens for one kalpa in the Avīci hell, and as the offense increases, so too does the suffering increase.
The treatise states:
One who is capable of causing a schism in the Saṃgha incurs the offense of *saṃghabheda*. This offense of *saṃghabheda* has the nature of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).

It consists of the vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) and non-intimation (*avijñapti*) that arise simultaneously with the schism of the Saṃgha. Such a person will necessarily undergo extremely heavy suffering for one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*) within the Avīci Hell; other heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) do not necessarily result in birth in Avīci.
However, this [Pratyekabuddha] does not pass through a full *mahākalpa*, because such a lifespan does not exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Nor is the duration of a single intermediate *kalpa* (*antarakalpa*) fulfilled,
for the Sūtra states that Devadatta came to be born among humans when the human lifespan was forty thousand years and realized the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha.
However, this does not contradict the statement that [the Buddha] lives for one *kalpa*, because the name "one *kalpa*" is applied to a small portion of a *kalpa*.
It is common to apply the name of the whole to a part; for example, one might say, "I have an obstacle on this day," or as it is said, "The bandits burned the village."
If one commits multiple *ānantarya* offenses, since the first alone already brings about rebirth in the Avīci Hell, the others would seemingly have no fruit.

However, there is no such fault of having no fruit; for while only one person who commits multiple *ānantarya* offenses can project [the birth], the others serve as auxiliaries to fulfill it, so that as their sins increase, the suffering increases even more intensely.

This means that by virtue of many grave offenses (*ānantarya*), one experiences a body of great softness and pliancy within the hells, encounters numerous fierce instruments of torment, and undergoes suffering two, four, five, or ten times more intense [than others].
Furthermore, since there is no premature death and one suffers for a long duration, how can it be said that other [grave offenses] must be without result?
The Elder provides this explanation regarding this point:
"Or one dies in hell and is reborn again.
If that were so, would it not then be karma to be experienced in a subsequent life?
In response to this objection, he replies by counter-interrogation:

"If one has previously committed other unwholesome karmas that have already projected rebirth in hell, and subsequently commits an immediate (ānantarya) offense, how then can this latter act constitute an immediate karma?"
Is there an intermediate state of existence (*antarābhava*)?

Surely [the fruit] must be experienced immediately following the preceding [moment]; for I have already explained that there is no principle by which karma whose timing is fixed (*niyata-kāla*) could be diverted to produce its maturation (*vipāka*) in another stage. Therefore, you should not raise such an objection.
Some say: One first creates other determinate evil karma that draws rebirth in the next hell, and subsequently does not create immediate (ānantarya) karma. Others say:

If one were to claim that only completing karma (*paripūri-karman*) is established—as when multiple immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) are committed, where the first acts as the projecting [cause] and the subsequent ones act as the completing causes—it would follow that not only the projecting cause is called an "immediate transgression. Therefore, their counter-objection is incapable of providing a valid answer.

However, as for their claim that there exists an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) between [death and rebirth], this is extremely crude; for it would be equally useless regarding the production of the next birth.

Just as when good karma for the heavenly realms intervenes, evil karma lacks the power to produce a birth in hell in the very next life, and is therefore termed "karma to be experienced in a subsequent life" (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman*).

Since the remaining karma from such hells intervenes, one lacks the power to induce birth in the next hell; how then is this not like being separated by the heavenly realms, which would cause subsequent heinous acts to become "favorable" and result in later retribution?

Therefore, there is no fault in the explanation provided by the Abhidharma school, for the Sūtras state that the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) result in retribution experienced in the very next life.
Who is capable of destroying whom, in what place, and at what time?
After how much time is it split?
The verse says:
When monks see pure conduct, They split [the Saṃgha] in another place, being fools.
When one endures a different teacher’s path, it is called a schism that does not last overnight.
The commentary says:
One who can cause a schism in the Saṃgha must be a *bhikṣu*; it cannot be a layperson, a *bhikṣuṇī*, or others, because their reliance lacks the necessary majestic authority (*vibhūti*).

Only those who act out of views and not out of craving can split the Saṃgha, because their malicious inclinations are extremely firm and deep, and because they are equally restless toward both the defiled and the purified categories.
It requires one who abides in pure conduct to be able to split the Saṃgha, for a person who has violated the precepts lacks the necessary majestic power.

It is precisely because of this proof that one who has committed another *ānantarya* offense cannot subsequently cause a schism in the Saṃgha; for there is no fixed certainty regarding the commission of other *ānantarya* offenses or the experience of their results.

In this context, we have first cited the case of pure conduct as an illustration; by analogy, this also applies to those who are handsome, possess perfect speech and faculties, and so forth, whereas those who are ugly, mute, or otherwise deficient lack the capacity to cause a schism.

One must refute [the opponent] in another location and not in the presence of the Great Master, because all Tathāgatas cannot be easily provoked or assailed; their speech is majestic and solemn, and no one would be able to withstand them face-to-face.
Furthermore, one refutes only ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and not noble ones (*ārya*), because others cannot induce [in the noble ones] the attainment of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*).
Some say that even those who have attained *kṣānti* (receptivity) cannot be split, because they possess the definitive receptivity spoken of by the Buddha.

The term "foolish person" (*bāla*) is used to encompass both meanings: namely, that the Saṃgha to be split must accept a teacher other than the Buddha, and that they must accept a path other than the Buddha’s teaching as being the remaining noble path (*āryamārga*).

It should be said that the schism of the Saṃgha occurs at such a time; this night it must necessarily be reconciled and cannot endure for a second night. This is called the "schism of the wheel-turning Saṃgha" (cakrabheda), because it can obstruct the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma and destroy the harmony of the Saṃgha.
This refers to when the Saṃgha is split and a false path prevails, whereby the Noble Path is obstructed and temporarily fails to function.
As for the "false path," Devadatta falsely proclaimed five practices as the way to liberation:
