first, one should not consume milk and the like; second, one should abstain from meat; third, one should abstain from salt; fourth, one should wear uncut garments; and fifth, one should reside in monasteries on the outskirts of inhabited areas.
When the assembly consents to what has been said, it is called the "breaking of the wheel of Dharma" (*cakrabheda*) and also the "schism of the Saṃgha" (*saṃghabheda*).
In which continent do how many people break the wheel of Dharma?
In which continent do how many people break the *karmasaṃgha*?
The verse says:
In Jambudvīpa, with nine or more [monks], one can only break the Saṃgha of the Wheel;
breaking the Saṃgha of Ritual occurs throughout the three continents with eight or more.
The treatise states:

Only among the people of Jambudvīpa—ranging from as few as nine or more—are those capable of destroying the Wheel of Dharma; this does not occur in other continents because there is no Buddha there, and it is only where a Buddha exists that a dissenting teacher can be established.

It requires eight bhikṣus divided into two groups to constitute the "schism" (bhedya), with the ninth being the one who effects the schism (bhedaka); therefore, even at the very minimum, nine persons are required.
The word "etc. (ādi) is used to clarify that beyond this number, there is no limit.
Only the suspension of the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) occurs throughout the three continents; it requires a minimum of eight persons and no maximum limit.
It is present in the three continents because there exists the holy teaching as well as a community of ordained disciples.

Since the Saṃgha within a single boundary must be divided into two factions to perform separate *karmas*, eight persons are required; because there is no restriction beyond this number, the term "etc.
(*ādi*) is also used. At what time can there be a schism of the Saṃgha or a schism of the *karma*?

Since the establishment of the boundary until the present day, there have also been instances [of schism] up until the Dharma has not yet ceased and the Saṃgha has not split over the Wheel of Dharma, excluding six specific periods. What are these six?
The verse says:
At the beginning and at the end, during the period before the pair of bubbles,
and while the Buddha has passed away but the boundaries have not yet been established— within these six stages, there is no schism of the Wheel-turning Sangha.
The treatise says:
The "former" refers to when the World-Honored One had not long attained Buddhahood; because sentient beings possessed virtuous *āśaya* (intentions) and evil *āśaya* had not yet arisen.

The "latter" refers to when the Sugata was about to enter parinirvāṇa; because the holy teaching was flourishing and well-established, the Buddha would only enter nirvāṇa once the Saṃgha was in harmony.
Other masters say:
Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fixed and because the entire assembly is filled with grief, there is no schism at the beginning or the end.

Within the Noble Teaching, a schism in the Saṃgha does not occur when the two "boils" (*gaṇḍa*)—of precept and view—have not yet arisen; it requires that the boil of views has first emerged before one dares to cause a schism.
Before the first pair of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* was established, it was natural that [the teaching] would quickly reunite through them;
however, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, others did not accept it because there was no true Buddha to serve as its adversary.
Before the boundary has been established, there is no single monastic community within a boundary that can be divided into two factions such as to be called a "schism in the Saṃgha.
Within these six stages, there is no breaking of the Wheel of Dharma; yet, all Buddhas have experienced such a schism in their Saṃgha.
Not so; it must have been due to past karma of having defeated others, for during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha in this Bhadrakalpa, Śākyamuni once defeated the assemblies of others.
Having concluded the digression, one should now analyze the conditions for the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*).
The verse says:
"Abandoning or destroying the fields of gratitude and virtue, Even through a change of gender, constitutes an immediate transgression."

The mother refers to her because of that blood; there is no [offense] for those who strike by mistake and so forth, or for one who strikes with the intent [to kill someone else], or for one who sheds the blood of a Buddha, or for one who harms a non-learner (aśaikṣa) after [the offense has already occurred]. The treatise says: [The verse: The mother refers to her because of that blood; There is no [offense] for those who strike by mistake and so forth, Or for one who strikes with the intent [to kill someone else], Or for one who sheds the blood of a Buddha, Or for one who harms a non-learner. [The commentary: Regarding "the mother refers to her because of that blood": this means that the basis for the offense is the shedding of the blood of one's own mother. Regarding "there is no [offense] for those who strike by mistake and so forth": this means that if one strikes with the intent to kill another person, or if one strikes by mistake, thinking it is someone else when it is actually the mother, there is no immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) karma. Regarding "or for one who strikes with the intent [to kill someone else]": this means that even if one strikes the mother with the intent to kill another person, there is no immediate retribution karma. Regarding "or for one who sheds the blood of a Buddha": this means that if one sheds the blood of a Buddha with the intent to kill someone else, there is no immediate retribution karma. Regarding "or for one who harms a non-learner": this means that if one harms a non-learner who is not one's mother, there is no immediate retribution karma. However, if one harms a non-learner who is one's mother, there is an immediate retribution karma. This is because the nature of the act is determined by both the object and the intent. Furthermore, if one harms a non-learner who is not one's mother, there is no immediate retribution karma because the object is not the mother. If one harms a mother who is not a non-learner, there is no immediate retribution karma because the object is not a non-learner. Only when both conditions—the object being the mother and the object being a non-learner—are met is there an immediate retribution karma. Thus, it is said: "The mother refers to her because of that blood; there is no [offense] for those who strike by mistake and so forth, or for one who strikes with the intent [to kill someone else], or for one who sheds the blood of a Buddha, or for one who harms a non-learner. This concludes the explanation.
For what reason do acts such as killing one's mother constitute an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), whereas other acts do not?
It is because they involve abandoning the field of gratitude and destroying the field of virtue.
That is to say, killing one's father or mother constitutes the abandonment of the field of gratitude.
In what way is there gratitude?
Because it is the source from which one's own body was born.
How could one abandon them? This refers to forsaking that field of merit characterized by such gratitude and virtue.

This means that because other Arhats and the like possess various supreme virtues and have the capacity to produce them, destroying the basis of those virtues constitutes a heinous crime (*ānantarya*).

If there are parents who, at the moment their child is first born, abandon it on a path frequented by jackals, wolves, and the like with the intent to kill, or who employ means to kill it while still in the womb, yet the child does not die due to the power of fixed karma (*niyata-karma*), what benefit did they receive such that abandoning it would constitute a heinous crime?
He certainly acted out of fear regarding his livelihood and so forth, and thus gave rise to a murderous intent toward his son in a moment of urgency;

yet, at the time of abandoning him, he must have harbored compassion, for his mind was repeatedly entangled by the attachment of parental love. If one abandons such a benefactor, one incurs the offense of *ānantarya* (immediate retribution) of the lowest degree. To demonstrate that this *ānantarya* offense has lower, middle, and upper grades, it is said that abandoning a benefactor constitutes an *ānantarya* offense in all cases.

Alternatively, it may be due to the natural law of the "field" (kṣetra), such as that of one's mother; even if she has been ungrateful, if one takes her life, one will necessarily be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
All wise people say this: the Blessed One has thoroughly realized the root and source of all phenomena, and his words should be accepted with deep faith.
When the physical forms of one's parents undergo transformation, does killing them constitute the crime of parricide?
It does indeed constitute the crime of parricide, because the basis [of the offense] remains the same. For this reason, it is asked:
Is there a case where one causes a male to lose his life-force, yet—though he is neither his father nor an Arhat—one incurs the immediate retribution (ānantarya) for that act?
Yes; this refers to the case of a mother who has undergone a change of gender.
The same question regarding a female is to be understood accordingly.

Suppose there is a woman whose *kalala* (embryonic mass) has fallen out, and another woman picks it up and places it within her own birth canal; when the child is killed, how does this constitute the causal basis for the parricide of matricide?
Because that blood is what gives rise to life, and it is only upon the entrusting of consciousness (*vijñāna*) to it that [the embryo] increases.

The second woman is merely like a foster mother; although all actions [concerning her] should be referred to her for decision, the harm [done to her] constitutes only a semblance of an *ānantarya* (immediate) offense.
Regarding this, the Elder (*sthavira*) spoke as follows:
"If the *kalala* possesses life, it does not perish; if it were to perish, it would necessarily have already ceased to live, for a sentient being certainly does not abide within filth."
Since such a case does not exist, the question is futile.
Even if it were so, killing [the father] after [the mother has been killed] would constitute a heinous crime (*ānantarya*), because one has abandoned a profound debt of gratitude;
however, killing [the father] before [the mother] is not so, because the profound debt of gratitude owed to the son does not pertain to him [the father].
The Elder is certainly unable to discern with precision the distinctions in the functional capacities within the courses of karma.
How is it that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) can penetrate even the diamond mountain, yet is constrained by the mother’s womb and does not go elsewhere?

Fire within a mother’s womb can dissolve metal and stone, yet the *kalala* grows therein; likewise, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) being of hell can manifest within a mother’s womb without burning her womb or its inhabitants. This too must be so, for the power of karma is inconceivable.
Even though this *kalala* falls from within one womb, what prevents it from being transferred to increase within another womb?

We have heard it said in the Sūtras that the Venerable Kumāra-Kāśyapa was born in such a manner; since he was placed at the birth canal and drawn up to the site of the womb, it cannot be said that he remained amidst filth and impurity.
Or there may be those who merely drink from the mouth into the abdomen, yet by the power of karma, they are transferred to the place of the womb.

The karmic activity of sentient beings is inconceivable; though they lack a desire for it, through the power of karma, [the embryo] is drawn into the abdomen and immediately becomes a fetal conception.
Although a stepmother possesses the kindness of nurturing and so forth, she is not the fundamental source from which the child’s body arises.

If harming such nurturing were to constitute a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense, then killing a foster mother would necessarily result in an immediate retribution; therefore, the position that one abandons a field of profound kindness is subject to the fallacies of being either unestablished or inconclusive.

Although a stepmother lacks the kindness of nurturing and so forth, she is the fundamental source of birth for her son; if one harms her without such nurturing, it does not constitute a parricide. As previously stated regarding those who harbor enmity toward their sons, if a son were to retaliate by harming them, there would logically be no immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
Therefore, what they have established is not related to that cause; it also suffers from the fallacies of being unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Thus, the superior condition for the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) in the human realm constitutes the matricide transgression, and this applies not only to the one who provides sustenance.
If one initiates the preparatory act of killing with intent toward one's parents but mistakenly kills another person, there is no immediate transgression (ānantarya).
Likewise, if one initiates the preparatory act of killing with intent toward someone who is not one's parent but mistakenly kills a parent, the immediate transgression is still not established.

If one performs a single preparatory act that harms both one's mother and another person, two non-informative (avijñapti) actions arise, whereas the informative (vijñapti) action constitutes only the immediate transgression (ānantarya), because the force of the immediate karma is predominant.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka states: "In this stage, there are also two informative actions, for an informative action is composed of an accumulation of atoms."

Now, observing that intention, it is expressed through multiple atoms (*paramāṇu*): some are subsumed under the immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*), while others are subsumed under other offenses.

If one harms an Arhat without the perception that he is an Arhat, yet also lacks the certain conviction that "this is not an Arhat," because there is no discrimination [between the two], the harm constitutes an immediate transgression.
This is not entirely the same as the case of one's parents; for while they are easy to recognize, even if one kills them without knowing it, the mind of gratitude is not abandoned.

An Arhat has no distinctive external marks; since it is difficult to recognize him as such, it is likewise difficult to know him as not being so. Therefore, even if one kills with a distracted mind, it constitutes an immediate transgression (ānantarya).
If one kills one’s father who is an arhat, one incurs a single ānantarya offense, because the basis [of the act] is one.
If that is so, how should the illustrative analogy be interpreted?
The Buddha told Śikhaṇḍin:
"You have already committed two heinous acts (ānantarya), namely, harming your father and killing an Arhat.
By revealing one heinous act as being accomplished through two conditions, or by means of two gateways, I reprove you for those offenses."
If one sheds blood from the Buddha with a malicious mind, does everyone incur the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)?

It is only when there is an intent to kill that the crime of parricide is established; if blood is shed with the intent merely to strike, there is no immediate retribution, because there is no definitive resolve to destroy the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).

If, during the stage of preparatory effort for killing, the victim has not yet become an Aśaikṣa, but attains the fruit of Arhatship just as they are about to die—does the one who kills them incur the offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya)? No;
because there is no preparatory effort for killing directed toward the person who is already an Aśaikṣa.

If one has initiated the preparatory action (*prayoga*) for an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), is it impossible to subsequently become free from passion (*vairāgya*) or attain the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*)?
The verse says:
In the fixed preparatory action for a transgression, there is no freedom from passion or attainment of the fruit.
The treatise states:

If the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) is certain to be completed, there can absolutely be no attainment of dispassion (*vairāgya*) or the fruit [of the path] in the interim.

Regarding the interim of the preparatory applications for other unwholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*), if the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) arises, the course of action does not arise; rather, one attains a transformation of the continuum (*saṃtati-parāvṛtti*), because it is necessarily in opposition to that [unwholesome action].
One who has not yet seen the Truths is touched by the offenses of the paths of action.
Since the preparatory acts for the immediate [offenses] can be turned back, why do you say that they cannot be turned back?
Some say: "None of these can be altered. Therefore, the *Mūlaśāstra* asks:
"Is there a case where, although one has not yet killed a living being and the act of killing has not yet ceased, this karma undergoes its maturation and one is certain to be born in hell?"
He said: "There is.
For example, one who dies during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of committing an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*).

Although Aṅgulimāla conceived the intention to kill his mother, he had not yet actually initiated the preparatory action of killing her; and although he harbored a harmful intent toward the Blessed One, he had not yet actually initiated the preparatory action of killing the Buddha. He formed this thought:"
It was only recently that he began to approach.
Because the Blessed One wished to obstruct his karmic hindrances, he did not allow him to draw near until he had developed faith.
Śrīgupta did not entirely harbor a disregard for the Bhagavān, as he spoke these words with a resolute intention:
"World-Honored One, if [the Buddha] is omniscient, he knows this because he has avoided it himself.
Other masters say:

"There are indeed cases where it can be turned back; the original treatise does not state that all preparatory applications (*prayoga*) for the immediate [offense] are irreversible, but rather says that if one dies without ceasing the preparatory application, they will certainly be reborn in hell."
The preparatory application (*prayoga*) that ceases is not what is being discussed here.
However, according to our own school, there are generally two types of uninterrupted preparatory application: first, the proximate, and second, the remote.
Among these, because the proximate cannot be diverted, the present treatise bases its questions and answers upon it.

This refers to one who initiates the preparatory act of harming his mother; as soon as he strikes her, before her life has ended, either the mother’s strength prevails and she kills him in turn, or he is captured and killed by the king or others, or his own lifespan is exhausted and he dies naturally. It is based on these cases that the *Mūlaśāstra* makes this statement.
Among these, those that are distant are still subject to reversal because they have not yet reached the stage from which there is no turning back;
were it otherwise, the Blessed One would have stated that even the preparatory application for an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*) constitutes an immediate offense.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"If even the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*) can still be diverted, how much more so their preliminary applications (*prayoga*)? Therefore, the Sūtra states:
'If there is a certain class of persons who perform and accumulate the five deeds of immediate retribution, they will necessarily fall into the Avīci hell immediately thereafter.'"
Based on this category of statement, we know that there is another category of persons who, although they commit an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), are not reborn in hell.
Otherwise, this specific category would be rendered purposeless.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"Sāḷha, you understand the meaning of what I have spoken, yet you lack the capacity to explain it.
Since this passage states that only the failure to understand the words constitutes a definitive obstruction, we know that the World-Honored One taught that all karma can be transformed.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One prophesied that all who circumambulate a caitya shall be reborn in the heavens.
Moreover, the World-Honored One prophesied that Devadatta, after severing his roots of goodness, would be incurable.
Furthermore, just as the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) can be transformed, so too can the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*).
Such statements are all non-establishing arguments (*asiddha*), for they do not properly comprehend either the scriptures or the underlying reasoning.

Furthermore, regarding the class of sūtras cited by him, their intent is to clarify that there are persons who, having committed all five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), will necessarily fall into the *naraka* hell immediately thereafter.

Alternatively, there may be those who commit even only one such crime; some may have committed many and further increased them through various doors, while others may have committed only one and not increased it further. All of these are born without interval (*ānantarya*) and fall into hell.

Furthermore, the term "a certain class" (*ekatyāḥ*) is used because it refers to the initial case; or rather, it indicates that there are those who, having committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*), will necessarily fall into hell (*naraka*).

It is said that "a certain class" [falls] because they may also commit other karmas; one should not say that because [the sūtra] mentions "a certain class," it implies that only those who have committed the cause of an immediate transgression are born there immediately.

The *Brahmajāla-sūtra* intends to show that those who commit the acts of immediate retribution do not understand the profound meaning spoken by the Tathāgata; because their karma constitutes an obstruction, they shall obtain such a result of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), and because the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) for contemplating the Truths have been impaired by its predominant power.
Furthermore, because some are afflicted by the distress of regret and anxiety, they are unable to deeply understand what the Buddha has taught.

If one adheres to the meaning of the sūtras merely according to the literal text, it would follow that there is absolutely no transition from the uninterrupted [state]. The term "uninterrupted" (ānantarya) is used to indicate the absence of any interval.
Furthermore, since Devadatta possessed only a superficial understanding of the Buddha’s words, for what reason would he necessarily be reborn in the Avīci Hell?
Thus, we know that this [statement] refers to "understanding" in the sense of deep comprehension.
The argument that his birth in heaven serves as proof [of the efficacy of the teaching] is also logically untenable, because the Buddha spoke with specific distinctions regarding that sūtra.
This refers to what that sutra states: that all those who rely upon others (*sāśraya-pudgala*) and circumambulate a *caitya* are reborn in heaven.
Those who possess skillful means (*upāya*) are called "those who rely upon others"; this signifies the logical principle that they are capable of being reborn in heaven.
However, the Dārṣṭāntikas briefly cite that sūtra and thereby open the door for sentient beings to commit many evil deeds;

for they maintain that one who has committed fierce and extremely grave evils can completely extinguish them by merely circumambulating a caitya for a brief moment while maintaining a weak wholesome mind or a neutral mind.

The logical proof for the severance of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) is likewise untenable; for even one who has severed the roots of goodness can still turn back from that state, and thus the Buddha should not have said that such a person is incurable.

Therefore, it is known that those words possess another meaning: namely, that Devadatta first gave rise to an evil desire, by which he should have already fallen into the evil destinies (*apāya*); subsequently, when he initiated the preparatory action (*prayoga*) intending to split the Saṃgha, by this he should have already fallen into hell; and finally, at the time he spoke a falsehood to destroy the Saṃgha, by this he incurred a lifespan in the Avīci hell for an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).

Once the roots of goodness have been severed by the subsequent arising of wrong views, it is certain that wholesome dharmas can no longer be made to manifest; therefore, it is said that this state is thereafter incurable, but this does not mean that one has definitively fallen into hell at that very moment.
However, at this stage, a doubt may arise as to why the Buddha did not treat Devadatta, even though he had reached such a state, unlike Ajātaśatru.

To dispel that doubt, the intention for not treating him is explained: "I do not see in Devadatta any white dharma (kuśala-dharma) capable of arising within his present existence; therefore, I have abandoned him and do not wish to provide medical treatment."

The few white dharmas—words expressing goodness, remorse, and shame—are intended here to show that the Buddha informed his kinsmen: "Devadatta has committed such grave evil karma; having severed all roots of goodness and being utterly devoid of a sense of shame, how can I possibly heal him?"

To say that something is "curable" means it can be transformed so that one gives rise to a wholesome mind of remorse and subdues the disease of evil conduct; if it has not yet increased, it is made not to increase, and if it has already increased, it is made gradually attenuated. It is not necessary to eradicate the root for it to be called "treatment," just as is the method of a skilled physician in treating diseases in the world.
The analogy for the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) also fails to establish [the point], because I do not admit that they can be transformed.
That is to say, when the afflictive obstructions arise, they determine the karma; thus, the maturation (*vipāka*) must necessarily be protected and cannot be altered.

Therefore, the Dārṣṭāntikas do not properly understand the sūtras or their underlying principles; with a mind burdened by a great mass of meaningless views, they falsely give rise to perverse arguments.
Among all evil deeds and immediate retributions (*ānantarya-karma*), which offense is the most grave?
Among all sublime practices and worldly wholesome karmas, which yields the greatest fruit?
The verse says:
"False speech that causes a schism in the Sangha is the greatest among transgressions."
The volition that causes one to fall into the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is the greatest fruit among worldly virtues.
The treatise says:
Of all evil deeds, this—uttering false speech for the purpose of causing a schism in the Saṃgha—is the gravest offense.
How is this offense subsumed under false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*)?
It is because the words spoken were based on a contrary perception (*anyathā-saṃjñā*).

That is to say, he perceived what is Dharma as Dharma, what is non-Dharma as non-Dharma, the Great Teacher as the Great Teacher, and himself as not being omniscient; yet, due to a deeply rooted and malignant intention (*paryavasthāna*), he concealed these perceptions and spoke otherwise.

If one were to cause a schism in the Saṃgha without harboring divergent views, one could not incur the grave karma of a kalpa-long lifespan; for what reason, then, is this offense the most wicked among all misdeeds?
It is because it injures the Dharma-body of the Buddha and obstructs the world from attaining the path to rebirth in heaven or liberation.

This means that as long as the Saṃgha remains split and has not yet been reunited, its power is able to obstruct ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) such that those who have not yet entered right concentration (*samyaktva-niyāma*) are prevented from entering it; those who have already entered right concentration are prevented from attaining further fruits; those who have already attained further fruits are prevented from becoming free from defilements (*vairāgya*); and those who have already become free from defilements are prevented from realizing the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*). Furthermore, activities such as practicing meditation, recitation, and reflection cease.

To state it briefly: because the Saṃgha has been split, the Wheel of Dharma does not turn in the great trichiliocosm, and the bodies and minds of devas, humans, nāgas, and others are thrown into turmoil.
Consequently, this necessarily brings about the ripening result of one kalpa in the Avīci Hell, whereas other misdeeds do not; therefore, among all misdeeds, this offense is the most grave.
If that is so, for what reason did the Blessed One at times state among all offenses that false view is the most serious, and further state that it is the greatest among the offenses of mental karma?

According to the five *ānantarya* crimes, the schism of the Saṃgha is said to be the most serious; according to the five deviant views, false view is said to be the most serious; and according to all karma, mental karma is said to be the greatest.
Alternatively, regarding the offenses abandoned through cultivation and through vision, they are described as most grave according to their respective order.
Or, based on the *Bṛhatphala* heaven, they are described as grave in sequence because they sever all roots of virtue and harm many sentient beings.

The volition that brings about the maturation fruit of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is the greatest among worldly virtues, because it can bring about the most ultimate and tranquil maturation; this statement is made with reference to its maturation fruit.

If one were to speak of this in terms of the five fruits generally, then one should say that the volition associated with the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) is able to attain a great fruit; namely, in addition to its ripened fruit (vipāka-phala), it can attain the four other conditioned and unconditioned fruits of arhatship.

Although the volitions of all untainted uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) produce four fruits—excluding the acquisition of maturation (*vipāka-prāpti*)—the fruit obtained here is the most preeminent, for it is the fruit through which all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are eternally severed.
To exclude these [other types of unwholesome karma], the term "worldly wholesome" (*laukika-kuśala*) is stated.
Are those who commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*) necessarily reborn in hell?

Those who commit acts similar to the immediate transgressions are also necessarily reborn there; however, they are not necessarily reborn immediately after death, as their acts do not constitute immediate karma.
What are the characteristics of the uninterrupted and similar [karmas]?
The verse says:
Polluting one’s mother, an Arhat nun; Killing a Bodhisattva established in the certainty [of enlightenment];
As well as for those noble ones still in training (*śaikṣa*), to deprive the Saṃgha of the conditions for its harmony,
or to destroy a stūpa— these are the "congeneric" (*sabhāga*) actions of the immediate (*ānantarya*) offenses.
The commentary says:
The term "similar" (sabhāga) means "resembling.
If one commits unchaste conduct with a mother who is an arhatī, it constitutes an extreme defilement and insult; this is called the first characteristic of similar karma.
If one kills a bodhisattva established in the fixed course, this is called the karmic characteristic similar to that of killing one's father.
If one kills a noble being who is still in training (śaikṣa), this is called the third karmic characteristic of a similar type.
If one seizes or robs the conditions for the harmony of the Saṃgha, this is called the karmic characteristic similar to that of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
If one destroys a Buddha stūpa, this is called the fifth karmic characteristic similar to that [of causing a schism].
There is a type of karma with ripening that is extremely capable of acting as an obstacle during three periods.
Regarding these three periods, the verse says:
"When about to attain *kṣānti*, the state of Non-returner, and Arhatship, karma acts as an obstacle."
The treatise says:

When one is about to attain the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) from the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), all karma that brings about rebirth in the miserable realms (*apāya*) becomes an extreme obstacle, because the stage of patience transcends those realms of karmic maturation (*vipākabhūmi*).
Just as when a person is about to leave their native country, all creditors become extreme obstacles;
so too, when one is about to attain the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), all karma bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) becomes an extreme obstacle.
When one is about to attain the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the karma of the form and formless realms acts as an extreme obstacle.
Regarding these latter two stages, the analogies are as previously explained.

However, within this context, one must exclude karma that ripens in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), karma with indefinite ripening (*aniyatavipāka*), indefinite karma (*aniyata-karman*), and among those with definite ripening, that which does not ripen in another location.
Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle 43 [and] Fascicle 44, composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter 12: The Twelfth Section of the Fourth Chapter on the Analysis of Karma. Regarding the bodhisattvas abiding in certainty as mentioned above, from what stage do they receive the name "abiding in certainty"?
Furthermore, with reference to what is it that they speak of "attaining meditative concentration"?
The verse says:
From the cultivation of the karma of the marks of excellence, The Bodhisattva attains the name of "one who has attained concentration."
"Born into a noble family in a happy realm, because he possesses a male body and firm mindfulness.
The Commentary says:

From the time he cultivates the karma that brings about the maturation of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the Bodhisattva is then able to be designated as "Abiding in Certainty," because from this point until his attainment of Buddhahood, he is constantly born in happy realms, noble families, and so forth.

"Rebirth in a happy destination" refers to birth among humans or devas; because one performs much wholesome conduct within these realms and they are excellent and praiseworthy, they are designated by the name "happy destination.
Within these happy destinations, one is constantly born into noble families, such as those of brahmins, kṣatriyas, or wealthy householders.

In the families of great brahmins, among those of noble lineage, there may be variations in the faculties—some being complete and others deficient—but that Bodhisattva always possesses superior faculties; he always receives a male body and never even becomes female, much less receiving the body of a *ṣaṇḍha* or other such forms.
In every successive birth, one is always able to recollect past lives, and in all virtuous deeds performed, one never experiences retreat or discouragement.
This means that in benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, at all times and by all means, the mind never grows weary; this is called being free from retreat and discouragement.
Because there is no regression or discouragement, it is called "firm. One might ask:

since the bodhicitta does not regress even during the stage prior to cultivating the karma for the marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*), should this stage not be designated by the name "Abiding" (*sthiti*)? Why is it necessary to reach the stage of cultivating the karma for the marks of excellence before a Bodhisattva receives the designation of the "Abiding" stage?
At that time, because humans and devas were for the first time able to know it together, previously it had been known only by the devas.
Alternatively, at that time, one enters the concentration of equal enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi-samādhi*); previously, it was exclusively determined as equal enlightenment and not anything else.
How should one understand the cultivation of karma that produces the marks of excellence?
The verse says:
In Jambudvīpa, a male, facing the Buddha, With a mind consisting of reflection upon the Buddha.
"Only after another hundred kalpas can one cultivate [them], each adorned with a hundred merits.
The Commentary says:

A bodhisattva must be within Jambudvīpa to be able to perform and cultivate the karma that leads to the marks of excellence, because the awakening-wisdom (*buddhi*) of this continent is the most clear and sharp.
It is exclusively a male body and not the body of a female or others, because at that time one has already transcended the status of being a female or otherwise.
This need not be stated, as the meaning of constantly receiving a male body has already been clarified in the preceding verse.

If it is argued that the previous statement—that after having performed this karma, one constantly receives a male body—was made to clarify that even at the initial performance of this karma, one is not a female or the like, and therefore there is a distinction between this and the former meaning.
This defense is unreasonable, for the meaning has already been established.

That is to say, it was previously stated that after one has performed this karma, one no longer possesses a female body or the like; it has already been shown that at the very time of performing it, one is likewise not female, because one who is not female transforms into another gender immediately upon performing this karma.

The karma that can bring about the sublime marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of a Sugata must necessarily depend upon a pure body to be initiated; therefore, this point has already been established by what was said previously.

When performing such karma, one must be in the direct presence of the Buddha—meaning, one must personally behold the Buddha’s uncommon physical body (*rūpakāya*), with its majestic major and minor marks and various extraordinary features—and possess the volition (*cetanā*) wishing to initiate the karma that brings about such results. This is because such a volition cannot arise in the absence of the Tathāgata.
These karmas that produce the excellent marks take only the thought of a Buddha as their object, because a Buddha is an object of qualities that inspire joy and accord with the mind.

The karma that produces these excellent marks consists solely of volition (*cetanā*) born of reflection (*cintāmayī*), not of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*), because it does not belong to the fixed realms.
Because this is the maturation (vipāka) experienced as being bound to this [realm], it is not produced by hearing (śrutamaya), for that is weak and inferior.
Nor is it innate (upapattilābhika), because it arises from application (prayoga).

That is to say, it can only be obtained within a body perfected through the cultivation of the perfections (pāramitā), such as generosity, over three incalculable eons; thus, it is exclusively a virtue of application, not an innate virtue.
Only the remaining hundred kalpas of cultivation were required, as it is the natural law for all Buddhas within their causal stage.
Only the Bhagavān Śākyamuni, through the perfection of his diligence, was able to transcend nine kalpas; thus, the karma for the marks of excellence was accomplished over ninety-one kalpas.
Therefore, the Tathāgata told the village headman:
"I recall that for ninety-one kalpas, I have not seen a single household that, by giving me food, suffered even the slightest harm, but instead achieved only great benefit."
From this point on, he naturally and constantly remembers his past lives; therefore, it is said that [this quality] extends up to this stage, not because he does not remember prior to it.
Each of the excellent marks is adorned by a hundred merits; herein, "a hundred merits" refers to a hundred volitions.

This means that when one is about to perform the karma for each individual mark of excellence, fifty volitions (*cetanā*) first arise to purify the vessel of the body; subsequently, one performs the karma that draws forth (*ākṣepaka-karman*) a single mark.
Thereafter, another fifty virtuous volitions arise to adorn the drawing karma, causing it to reach full perfection.
Regarding the fifty volitions (*cetanā*): based on the ten paths of action (*karmapatha*), five volitions arise for each individual path of action.

To take the first path of action, abstaining from killing, as an example, there are five volitions: (1) the volition of abstaining from killing; (2) the volition of exhorting others; (3) the volition of praising [abstinence]; (4) the volition of rejoicing; and (5) the volition of dedication—that is, dedicating what has been cultivated toward liberation.
The same applies up to right view, each having five grades.
Other masters say:

based on each of the ten paths of action, one gives rise to five grades of wholesome volition—mild and so forth—with the preceding and succeeding ones being likewise, just as in the cultivation of dhyāna.

Other masters say: Based on each of the ten paths of action, five types of volition arise: first, purity of the preliminary application; second, purity of the fundamental act; third, purity of the subsequent completion; fourth, freedom from harmful discursive thought; and fifth, maintenance through mindfulness.
Furthermore, there are teachers who say:
Each individual mark is produced by its own specific karma; the Buddha has never practiced [such] thoughts, yet all one hundred manifest simultaneously to serve as adornments.
What is the measure of each of these one hundred merits?

Some say: Because it is a body perfected through the accumulation of merit increased over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), it gives rise to such incomparable and innumerable, supreme merits, the measure of which is known only by a Buddha.

Some say: if, through the predominant power of karma, one attains the status of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) and exercises sovereign rule over the four continents, this constitutes a single unit of merit (*puṇya-pramāṇa*). Others say:

If, through the predominant power of karma, one attains the status of Śakra, king of the two classes of desire-realm devas and exercises sovereignty over them, this constitutes one unit of merit (*puṇya-pramāṇa*).

Some say that the meritorious karma cultivated by all sentient beings—excluding only those Bodhisattvas who are close to Buddhahood—that results in wealth and happiness, constitutes one unit of merit.
Other masters say:

"This measure is too small; one should say that when the world is about to be formed, the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings to produce the great chiliocosm is the measure of a single merit."
Now, during his former time as a bodhisattva, how many Buddhas did the Bhagavat make offerings to within each of the three incalculable eons?
The verse says:
During the three incalculable eons, He made offerings to seventy thousand [Buddhas] in each.
Furthermore, he successively made offerings to five thousand, six thousand, and seven thousand Buddhas.
The Commentary says:

During the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he made offerings to seventy-five thousand Buddhas; during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he made offerings to seventy-six thousand Buddhas; and during the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he made offerings to seventy-seven thousand Buddhas.

At the completion of each of the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), as well as at the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), which Buddha did he encounter?
The verse says:
At the completion of the three incalculable eons, He encountered, in reverse order, Vipaśyin, [Śikhin, and Viśvabhū];...
Dīpaṃkara, Ratnaśikhin, and Śākyamuni at the beginning. The commentary states:

Regarding the "reverse order," this means proceeding from the later toward the earlier. Specifically, the Buddha encountered and served at the completion of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa was named Abhibhū; the one encountered and served at the completion of the second kalpa was named Dīpaṃkara; the one encountered and served at the completion of the first kalpa was named Ratnaśikhin; and the one encountered at the very start of the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa was Śākyamuni.

It is said that when my Blessed One first resolved to attain enlightenment, he encountered a Bhagavān named Śākyamuni; at the time that Buddha appeared, it was precisely during the final kalpa, and after his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained for only one thousand years.

At that time, World-Honored One, I was a potter’s son; having conceived a profound and pure mind toward that Buddha, I anointed him with fragrant oil, bathed him with scented water, and after making these offerings, I made this great vow:
"May I become a Buddha, exactly as this World-Honored One is now."
Therefore, the Tathāgata now corresponds to each of them in this way.
In which stage and through which perfection (pāramitā) was I, as a Śākya Bodhisattva, perfected my cultivation?
The verse says:
But through universal giving out of compassion, remaining without anger even when his body was being dismembered,
praising Buddha Tiṣya, and [striving for] supreme enlightenment—
the six pāramitās; in these four stages, [he practiced].
"One and two, then again one and two; thus they are cultivated to perfection in sequence.
The Commentary says:

When a bodhisattva first practices generosity after having made the vow, they are not yet able to give all things to all sentient beings with universal compassion. However, through the power of subsequent habituation, their compassion becomes increasingly intense, enabling them to give all things to all sentient beings.

When a bodhisattva, out of compassion alone and not from a desire for any distinction in superior rebirth, is able to relinquish everything to all beings, to this extent the cultivation of the perfection of generosity is fulfilled.

Some say: When Bodhisattvas observe that all worldly beings are oppressed by poverty and the lack of material resources, they generate aspirations to seek superior births for themselves out of a desire to benefit them and out of compassion, because there is never a single moment when Bodhisattvas practice giving without exercising compassion.

When a bodhisattva has his limbs severed, even though he has not yet abandoned desire and greed, his mind harbors not the slightest anger; at this point, his cultivation of the perfections of ethical discipline and patience is complete.
The perfection of patience consists in having no anger toward those sentient beings.
The perfection of ethical discipline consists in not giving rise to physical or verbal karma that harms others.
Because there is no anger in the mind and no evil in body or speech, when one is free from anger, both ethical discipline and patience are perfected.
When the Bodhisattva, through courageous and diligent exertion, praised Tiṣya and thereby transcended nine kalpas, his cultivation of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) reached completion.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Tiṣya; that Buddha had two bodhisattva disciples:
one named Śākyamuni and the other named Maitreya.

The Buddha, observing the field of those he was to convert, clearly perceived that for these two disciples, Upatiṣya (Kāśyapa) was one whose own conversion would ripen first rather than his [the Buddha's], while Maitreya was one whose own conversion would ripen first rather than that of others.
Having understood this, he further reflected:
"It is relatively easy to bring a single body to swift maturity.

Thereupon, by means of skillful means, he entered a jeweled niche and sat in the full lotus posture; through the sublime meditative concentration unique to the Buddha-dharma, all [qualities] appeared before him.

Śāntamati encountered that Buddha, whose majestic radiance was exceptionally brilliant and extraordinary. Suddenly, with a pure mind, he grasped [the Buddha’s feet], supporting his entire body while standing on one leg for seven days and nights. He praised that Buddha with these sublime verses:
“In this world, within the realms of heaven and earth, in the abodes of the gods, or in the palaces of the departed—nowhere in the ten directions is there anyone equal to you.
O Great Śramaṇa, Bull among Men, though one searches the lands, mountains, and forests, none can be found as your peer.”
Having offered such praise, he transcended nine *kalpas* and was to realize the unsurpassed fruit before Maitreya.

At the time when the Bodhisattva sat upon the Vajrāsana, on the verge of ascending to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he dwelt in the *vajropama-samādhi* immediately prior to that supreme awakening; it was at this point that his cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhi-pāramitā*) and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) reached completion.

It is logical that this stage is fulfilled precisely at the moment when one immediately attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), for it is at this point that one reaches the further shore of perfect virtue through each distinct capacity.
These six are called *pāramitās*.
The Sūtra states that there are three types of meritorious actions (puṇyakriyāvastu):
first, meritorious action consisting of giving; second, meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline; and third, meritorious action consisting of cultivation.
How are these established as the bases of meritorious action?
The verse says:
Generosity, morality, and cultivation—these three classes, each according to what is appropriate.
They receive the names "meritorious action" (*puṇyakriyāvastu*), with distinctions as explained for the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
The treatise says:
All three categories are meritorious; they are either actions (*karman*) or bases (*vastu*), as appropriate, just as explained in the section on the paths of action.

That is to say, as in the analysis of the ten paths of action (*karmapatha*), there are actions that are also paths, and paths that are not actions; among these, there are things that are merit, action, and matter (*vastu*); those that are merit and action but not matter; those that are merit and matter but not action; and those that are merely merit, being neither action nor matter.

Furthermore, among the categories of giving (*dāna*), the two types of action—bodily and vocal—possess the threefold designation of "merit," "action," and "basis. Because they are wholesome, they are merit; because they are performed, they are also action; and because they serve as the doors through which the volition that initiates bodily and vocal actions operates, they are also called "bases" (*vastu*).

In those cases, volition (cetanā) alone is termed "meritorious action" (puṇya-karma), while the factors co-arising with volition receive the designation of "merit" (puṇya) alone. Since the category of morality (śīla) consists exclusively of the nature of bodily and vocal actions, it fully receives the designations of "merit," "action," and "basis" (vastu).
Among the types of cultivation, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is called merely a "meritorious matter" (*puṇya-vastu*), because it is a matter of karma.

Since the volition (*cetanā*) associated with loving-kindness is produced by taking loving-kindness as its gateway, the volition and the precepts (*śīla*) concomitant with loving-kindness are called merely "meritorious karma" (*puṇya-karman*).
Other co-existent dharmas receive the designation of "merit" alone.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) and so forth should all be analyzed in accordance with this.
Some say that "meritorious action" (*puṇyakarman*) reveals the sense of performing merit; that is, the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for merit.

The "bases" (vastu) clarify that which they depend upon; that is, giving, morality, and cultivation are the bases of meritorious action (*puṇyakarman*), because it is for the sake of accomplishing those three that one initiates the preparatory application of merit. Some say:
"Volition alone is true meritorious action; giving, morality, and cultivation are the bases of meritorious action, because meritorious action proceeds by means of these three."
What dharma is called "giving"?
What fruit does giving bring?
The verse says:
Because of this relinquishment, it is called "giving" (*dāna*);
that is to say, for the purpose of honoring or benefiting, [it consists of] body, speech, and their motivating factors. This brings about the fruit of great wealth.
The Commentary says:

Although both the object relinquished and the means by which it is relinquished may be termed "giving," the designation "giving" established here refers solely to the means of relinquishment; that is, because the act of relinquishing is accomplished by means of this instrument, the basis from which the relinquishing proceeds is the true essence of giving.

The object being measured cannot itself receive the name of "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*); rather, the name "means of valid cognition" is established based on the instrument that performs the measuring.

Alternatively, [one might engage in such acts] for the sake of victory, hoarding, or reputation, or by following others out of affection and attachment; through such motives, the act of giving is indeed accomplished, yet this is not what is intended here as the primary meaning. To distinguish it from those cases, the words "for the sake of offering" and "for the sake of benefit" are used: toward those already in *nirvāṇa*, it is solely for the sake of offering; toward others, it is also for the sake of benefit.
When those primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and sense faculties (*indriya*) perform an act of giving, they do so solely for the benefit of others. What is meant by "possessing" [these]?
It refers to bodily and vocal actions (*kāyavāk-karman*) and that which gives rise to them.
What is meant by "that which gives rise to them"?

That is to say, non-attachment (*alobha*) together with that which can give rise to this collection—namely, bodily and vocal actions, the mind that initiates them, and all factors concomitant therewith—is collectively termed the essence of giving (*dāna*).
As a verse says: "If a person, with a pure mind, relinquishes their own [possessions] to practice giving..."
"These wholesome aggregates of that very moment are collectively designated by the name 'giving.
One should know that such meritorious actions consisting of giving, when dedicated toward liberation, also result in the fruit of dissociation.
Furthermore, speaking in terms of what is determined proximately, it is said that this alone can attract the fruit of great wealth.
On what basis is the name "great wealth" established?
It is because such wealth is exquisite and vast, and cannot be taken away.
Generosity such as that of Viśvantara and others was wounded by the thorns of poison; although they practiced giving, they did not obtain the fruit of great wealth.
The statement that "generosity is a type of merit" clarifies that generosity constitutes its essential nature.
Just as in the cases of "clay-like vessels" or "wood-like pillars," the term "like" (*-jātīya*) is seen there not to indicate identity of essence;

likewise, since "knowledge like [subsequent] knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*) is not what is currently accepted [as a distinct entity], the terms "precept-like" (*śīla-jātīya*) and "cultivation-like" (*bhāvanā-jātīya*) should be explained accordingly.
For what benefit does one practice giving?
The verse says:
"For the benefit of oneself and others, one practices giving for neither of the two."
The treatise says:

When a donor gives, they contemplate two benefits: first, their own benefit in the form of the roots of goodness that bring about karmic results; second, the benefit for others in the form of the sense faculties and the great elements.
There are two kinds of donors:
first, those with afflictions; second, those without afflictions.
Those with afflictions are further divided into two types:
First, those who have not yet abandoned desire and greed; second, those who have already abandoned desire and greed.
Within each of these two categories, there are two types:
first, the noble ones (ārya); second, ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).

In this regard, when noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire and greed, as well as ordinary beings—whether they have or have not abandoned desire and greed—make offerings to a *caitya*, it serves solely for their own benefit.

That is to say, it increases two kinds of roots of goodness within themselves: first, those that bring about the fruit of great wealth; second, those that serve as the provisions for attaining the supreme goal.

When noble ones who have already abandoned desire and greed offer gifts to a *caitya*, these do not bring about great wealth—excluding those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life—because they have already attained the ultimate transcendence of that plane of maturation (*vipāka-bhūmi*).
However, since it can serve as a provision for attaining the higher meanings, it is also called "exclusively for one's own benefit.
It cannot benefit the sense faculties (*indriya*) or the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of others; therefore, it does not benefit others.

One who is free from afflictions gives to other sentient beings solely for the sake of benefiting others; that is, they are able to benefit the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of others, but do not increase the two kinds of roots of goodness within themselves, and thus it is not for their own benefit.
When one who possesses afflictions gives to other sentient beings, it benefits both parties.
When one who is free from afflictions makes an offering to a *caitya*, it does not benefit both, except for [karma] to be experienced in the present life.
There is a teacher who distinguishes the fruits of giving solely in terms of the attainment of great wealth. He asserts:

"In this context, when all ordinary beings—both those who have not yet abandoned desire and those who have abandoned desire—offer their own possessions as gifts to a *caitya*, this gift is said to be 'exclusively for one's own benefit,' because the recipient does not derive any benefit from it."

If noble ones who have already abandoned desire and greed bestow gifts upon sentient beings—excluding those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life—this gift is said to be "solely for the benefit of others," because they obtain benefit thereby, and not for their own benefit, as they have transcended the stages of fruition.

If those ordinary persons—both those who have not yet abandoned craving for sensual pleasures and those who have abandoned such craving—give away their own possessions to sentient beings, this giving is called "benefiting both."

If those noble ones, having already become free from sensual desire, make an offering to a shrine (caitya), this gift—excluding that which ripens in the present life—is called "not for the benefit of both," because it is performed solely as an act of veneration and gratitude.
Previously, it was explained in general that giving brings about great wealth; now, we shall specifically analyze the distinct causes for the results of giving.
The verse says:
Because of differences in the donor, the gift, and the field, The results of giving are distinguished.
The treatise states:

There are distinctions in giving due to three kinds of causes; that is to say, because there are distinctions in the donor, the gift, and the field, there are distinctions in the fruit resulting from the distinctions in giving.

Regarding the statement that there are distinctions among the donor (*dāyaka*), the gift (*deya*), and the field (*kṣetra*): this means that such categories of donors, gifts, and fields—whether superior or inferior—are distinct from other donors, gifts, and fields.
First, concerning the distinctions arising from the donor, the verse says:
The donor differs by virtue of faith and so forth, Practicing giving with respect and the like.
One attains respect and widespread affection, as well as timely and irremovable fruits.

The commentary states: There may be donors who have attained decisive conviction regarding cause and effect; there may be donors who harbor doubts regarding cause and effect; there may be donors who act impulsively according to their whims; there may be donors who possess pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), or those whose discipline is slightly deficient, or those who lack it entirely; and there may be donors who are extensively learned in the Buddha’s teachings, or those with little learning, or those with no learning at all, yet they practice giving.
Because the donor possesses distinct qualities such as faith, ethical discipline, and learning, they are said to be "different as donors.
Due to this difference in the donor, the gift becomes differentiated.
Due to differences in the manner of giving, there are differences in the fruits obtained.

When donors possess such virtues and are able to practice the four types of giving—respectful giving and so forth—in accordance with the Dharma, they will accordingly obtain the four fruits, beginning with being held in high esteem.
That is to say, if a donor practices giving with reverence, they will consequently experience being constantly respected by others.
If they give with their own hands, they will consequently experience the joyful enjoyment of vast wealth.
If one gives at the appropriate time, one will experience wealth that arrives at the appropriate time, because what is required is timely and not otherwise.
If one gives without harming others, one’s resources will not be plundered or destroyed by kings, fire, or other such calamities.
Regarding the distinctions based on the material objects given, the verse says:

The difference in wealth arises from color and so forth; One obtains a beautiful form, a good reputation, A body beloved by the multitude and supple, And sensations of pleasure that accord with the seasons.
The treatise states:

Depending on whether the material wealth offered is deficient or complete in terms of color, fragrance, taste, and texture, one accordingly obtains results that are either deficient or complete in terms of excellent form and so forth.
That is to say, because the color of the offered wealth is complete, one is reborn with an excellent form.
Because they are endowed with fragrance, they experience a good reputation, just as the scent of incense is pervasive in all directions.
Because they are endowed with flavor, they experience the love of the multitude, just as exquisite flavors are loved by many.
Because of the perfection of touch, one experiences a supple body and encounters tactile sensations that produce pleasant feelings at appropriate times.
If there is any deficiency, the corresponding result is diminished; likewise, because it possesses color, fragrance, and so forth, it is called a "difference in wealth."
Because the material objects differ, there are distinctions in both the essence of the gift and its fruit.
Regarding the distinctions based on the field of merit (*kṣetra*), the verse says:
"The field differs by way of the realm of rebirth (*gati*), suffering, And by way of the distinctions of kindness and virtue."
The treatise says:
Because the fields of giving differ according to their respective realms of rebirth (*gati*), suffering, kindness, and merit, they are called "distinct fields.
Due to these distinctions among the fields, there are differences in the fruits of giving.
Regarding the distinction based on the recipient:
as the Blessed One said, "If one gives to an animal, one receives a hundredfold fruit; if one gives to a person who has transgressed the precepts, one receives a thousandfold fruit.
What is the measure of these hundredfold and thousandfold fruits?

According to the field of merit to which the gift is given, the recipient’s lifespan and other qualities are increased by a certain measure through the acceptance of food and so forth; consequently, the donor, by virtue of this, will experience [rewards] among humans and devas that exceed those [benefits] by a hundredfold or a thousandfold.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"When a donor gives, they give five things—life and so forth—to the field of merit; by this, the donor shall in turn obtain the five fruits, such as life and so forth, among humans and devas."

Regarding the distinctions based on suffering: as stated among the seven meritorious actions based on material things (*aupadhika-puṇya-kriyā-vastu*), one should first give alms to guests, those traveling, the sick, and their attendants, as well as monasteries, regular meals, and clothing and medicine for cold winds and other seasonal needs.
Furthermore, it is said:
If there are men or women endowed with pure faith who accomplish these seven types of meritorious actions based on material things as described here, the merit they obtain cannot be measured.
Now, within this context, suffering differs due to the distinction of its conditions; and because the suffering of the experiencer is removed, there is a distinction in the result.

Regarding the distinction of kindness, this refers to parents, teachers, and others who have been kind, such as the various classes of beings who have shown kindness mentioned in the Jātaka tales, such as those concerning the bear and the deer.

When various evil karmas are committed toward those who have been kind, their results can be known from present experience; by this analogy, one may infer that the results of performing good deeds to repay kindness are likewise certain.
Regarding the distinction based on the recipient’s virtue, as stated in the Sūtra:
"The fruit of giving to one who upholds the precepts is a hundred-thousandfold, and so on, until the fruit of giving to a Buddha is most immeasurable."
Although all are immeasurable, there are still distinctions of small and great, like the difference between a drop of water from the Ganges River and the waters of the great ocean.
Just as the gift of Dharma is more honored than the gift of material wealth,
within the category of material gifts, which is the most excellent?
The verse says:
For one liberated giving to one liberated, the eighth gift is the most supreme.
The commentary says:
If one gives to a field that is already liberated, giving to a liberated recipient among all forms of material giving is the most supreme.

Furthermore, if Bodhisattvas, with a superior intention, desire to equally benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings and practice generosity for the sake of Great Enlightenment, although this is not the case of giving to a liberated recipient by one who is liberated, it is the most supreme among the merits of giving.
Beyond these, among the eight kinds of giving, the merit of the eighth kind of giving is also the most supreme. What are these eight? First, giving to those who arrive;

second, giving out of fear; third, giving in return for a favor received; fourth, giving with the expectation of a reward; fifth, giving as a habit inherited from one's ancestors; sixth, giving with the hope of attaining heaven; seventh, giving for the sake of reputation; and eighth, practicing generosity for the purpose of adorning the mind, supporting the mind, aiding yoga, and attaining the ultimate goal.
Giving according to circumstances refers to providing clothing and food as appropriate whenever sentient beings approach, without deep reverence.
Giving out of fear refers to practicing generosity upon seeing calamities and misfortunes, in order to cause them to subside.
Or, seeing that this object is manifesting signs of decay, one practices giving so that it may not perish; thus, one performs acts of generosity.
"Practicing the giving of predecessors" means practicing the tradition of giving established by one's ancestors and forefathers.
To adorn the mind means to practice generosity for the sake of eliciting the noble riches, such as faith and the rest.
To support the mind means to practice generosity with the desire to eliminate the defilement of stinginess.
The "requisite for yoga" refers to practicing generosity as a successive cause for attaining the bliss of meditative concentration.
That is to say, through giving, one becomes free from regret, and by this succession, one eventually reaches one-pointedness of mind.
Attaining the supreme goal means attaining *nirvāṇa*, because from the initial relinquishing of wealth up to the successive relinquishing of all *saṃsāra*, one is able to renounce everything.
Furthermore, the practice of giving is a cause for superior rebirth, as it serves as the basis for inducing and realizing the dharmas that lead to *nirvāṇa*.
Other forms of giving are easy to understand and therefore are not explained separately.
As the World-Honored One has said that the fruit of giving to the noble ones is immeasurable, is there perhaps any giving to those who are not noble whose fruit is likewise immeasurable?
The verse says:
To one's parents, the sick, and a Dharma teacher, as well as to a Bodhisattva in their final birth—
even if they have not yet realized the state of an Arya— the fruit of giving to them is likewise immeasurable.
The treatise says:
These five kinds of persons, even if they are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who give, can still bring about immeasurable fruit.
One who dwells in their final existence is called a "Dharma teacher in their last birth. Among the four fields of merit, to which field does such a person belong?
This is subsumed under the field of gratitude (*kṛtajña-kṣetra*). Why is this so?

Because the Dharma-preacher is able to show the gateway to the city of security to those who are about to fall into the various evil destinies, and reveals the path to rebirth in heaven and liberation; because he can cause those who have already engaged in unreasoned conduct to turn toward practice that accords with reason; because he is able to skillfully proclaim the intrinsic nature and the results of the dharmas of the black and white categories, as well as their antidotes; and because he can bestow the eye of wisdom upon those blinded by ignorance.
This is because, through the power of the teachings expounded by the Dharma-preacher, one can correctly discern the categories of affliction and purification.
To state it briefly, since a skillful Dharma-preacher can even perform the work of a Buddha, he alone is the supreme field of merit; thus, a donor will certainly reap immeasurable fruit.
Are all karmas capable of producing immeasurable fruits equal in their superior and inferior categories? No. Why is this so?
Due to six causes, all karma is rendered into categories of light and heavy.
What are these six?
The verse says:
The subsequent, the field, the root, the preparatory effort, volition, and the intention—
due to these being inferior or superior, karma becomes inferior or superior.
The treatise says:
The "subsequent" refers to that which is performed either immediately or repeatedly after having committed this action, following upon the preceding one.
The "field" refers to the basis upon which one performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds.
The "root" refers to the fundamental paths of action (*karmapatha*).
The preparatory action (*prayoga*) refers to that which induces the body and speech;
volition (*cetanā*) refers to that by which the course of action (*karmapatha*) is brought to completion;
and intention (*āśaya*) refers to the underlying disposition, namely: "I shall perform such and such an act."

If all six causes are of the highest degree, this karma is the most heavy; conversely, if they are otherwise, it is the lightest; apart from these, there are intermediate cases that are neither the lightest nor the heaviest.
That is to say, some karma may become a heavy category solely because it is embraced by a subsequent action (*pṛṣṭha*), since that action definitively establishes its ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).
It should be understood accordingly that, in some cases, [the result] arises solely through intention, or through two, three, or more [factors].
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Thoroughly reflecting upon the performance of action is called "formative activity" (*abhisamskāra*) and is also called "increase" (*upacaya*).
For what reason is action said to be "increase"?
It is due to five kinds of causes.
What are these five?
The verse says:
"By means of deliberate reflection and completion, and by the absence of regret and the presence of an antidote,"
Because it possesses both a companion and a maturation, this karma is called "increased" (*upacita*).
The commentary states:
"By reason of deliberate reflection" means that it is performed after careful deliberation; it is neither performed through a sudden impulse nor performed without any thought at all.

Regarding "by way of completion": this refers to the point at which karma, having reached its full measure, should cause one to fall into the miserable realms; such completed karma is termed "accumulated," whereas other karma is merely "performed."
For instance, there are some who fall into the evil destinies due to a single cause among their unwholesome deeds, while others do so even through three.
Among the ten paths of action, there are those who fall into the evil destinies due to one, or even up to all ten.
"Because there is no antidote for regret" means that there is no remorse and no counteractive action toward the karma.
"Because it has an associate" means that when one performs an unwholesome deed, the unwholesome itself serves as its assistant.
For example, stealing another's property, defiling another's wife, killing another's child, and so forth.
Regarding "due to maturation" (*vipāka*), this refers to indeterminate karma that has become determinate; it is the opposite of the superior [category] of wholesome maturation.
Apart from this, one should know that it is merely designated as "volitional action" (*abhisamskāra*).
As stated above, when those who have not yet abandoned desire and so forth make offerings to a *caitya*, it serves only their own benefit.
Since there is no recipient, how can the merit of the gift be established?
The verse says:
Merit consisting of the relinquishment of a *caitya* is like [the merit] of loving-kindness and so forth; it has no recipient.
The commentary says:
It is not that the merit of giving is established only when the recipient enjoys the material object that has been relinquished.
What, then, is the intended meaning?
Briefly stated, there are two types of merit from giving:
There are two types: first, that which consists of relinquishment;

second, that which consists of acceptance. Regarding merit consisting of relinquishment: it refers to the arising of the merit of giving simply by means of a virtuous mind that relinquishes material resources.
Regarding merit consisting of acceptance: it refers to the arising of the merit of giving only when the field of the gift makes use of the donated object.
Regarding the articles of offering presented at a *caitya*, although there is no category of "receiving" (*pratigraha*), there is the category of "renunciation" (*tyāga*) merit.

However, this merit of renunciation is established at the very moment one relinquishes the material wealth; for it acts as an antidote to greed, being originated by a volition (*cetanā*) associated with non-greed.
Once one has relinquished material wealth, whether the recipient-field actually uses the gift or not, the merit of the giving is not lost.

If it were otherwise, when one gives requisites for living to the Saṃgha or to an individual, and those items should perish before being used, the donor’s property would have been wasted in vain and the merit of the gift would not arise, as there would be no future fruit.
Since that [stūpa] has not yet been used, from what does merit arise?
Although there is no actual use of the merit, there is the experience of its fruit.
Since a caitya has no one to experience it, from what does merit arise?
Furthermore, by what reason is it proven that the arising of merit necessarily depends upon reception?
[The argument] that "because there is no benefit derived from them if they are not received" is not a definitive proof.
Why is this so? Because merit is likewise produced through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and other such practices.

That is to say, when one cultivates the meditative concentration of loving-kindness, one impartially gives rise to the intention to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings; although there is no recipient and no actual benefit conferred, much merit arises through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
The acquisition of merit through the cultivation of meditative absorptions such as compassion is likewise.
The same principle applies to the merit of giving to a *caitya*.

Even though there is no recipient and no benefit conferred upon others when one generates superior resolve toward a field of merit and offers worship with the utmost reverence to a *caitya*, much merit arises by the power of one's own volition; yet this does not mean that the action of giving and honoring is in vain.
This is because it is only through the arousal of an undertaking that a superior volition (*adhimokṣa*) arises, and it is only through superior volition that superior merit can be produced.

For example, there is a certain class of people who wish to harm an enemy; even after the enemy’s life has ended, they still harbor thoughts of enmity and initiate various unwholesome actions of body and speech, thereby producing much demerit (*apuṇya*), not merely by the arousal of the thought itself.

Thus, although the Great Master has already passed away, by subsequently expressing reverence and making offerings through the performance of physical and verbal actions, one generates abundant merit; it is not generated by the mere arousal of the mind alone.
An objection may be raised:
"If the seeds of the act of giving sown in a virtuous field produce desirable fruits, then those sown in an evil field should produce undesirable fruits."
This objection is unreasonable. Why is this so?
The verse says:
An evil field may yield desirable fruits, for there is no inversion between fruit and seed.
The treatise says:
We observe in the world that seeds and their fruits are never inverted; from a *tūṇaka* seed, a bitter fruit can never arise, nor does a sweet fruit ever grow from a *niṃba* seed.

It is not that the fruit produced by the seed undergoes inversion due to the power of the field; rather, it is because of a defect in the field that the seed planted therein produces either a meager fruit or no fruit at all.
