Since no authoritative scripture (āgama) specifically teaches that sound exists in the form and formless realms, it is difficult to rely upon or believe [this claim]."

However, since in various places throughout the holy teachings it is universally stated that "existence" (bhava) includes sound within the three realms, does one not also speak of "existence" with respect to objects? If so, why should the latent tendency of sensual desire (kāmarāgānuśaya) not be established separately?
This objection is irrational, because their modes of operation differ.
That is to say, various forms of sensual craving (*kāmarāga*) operate toward external objects, whereas that which operates toward internal objects is termed craving for existence (*bhavarāga*).
Furthermore, just as there is a difference between attachment to sense-objects and attachment to existence, so too is the distinction between the resulting latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Furthermore, because the objects of focus differ and their respective antidotes are distinct, body-attachment (*kāmarāga*) and existence-attachment (*bhavarāga*) are established as two separate categories.

Moreover, it is only when one has necessarily suppressed or subdued both sensual desire and aversion that an external ascetic (*bāhyaka-ṛṣi*) is able to enter the realms of form and formlessness; therefore, the essence of sensual desire is not identical to existence-attachment. This is because those sentient beings, focusing on their own mental continuum, are constantly pursued by self-love (*ātmasneha*), which never ceases.

The Elder has established the distinctions of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) most poorly here, because the term "desire-greed" (*kāmarāga*) could be said to include all greed belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Since the body born in the desire realm is also subsumed under the desire realm, how could the greed that takes that [body] as its object not be "desire-greed"?
As it is said that attachment to form (*rūparāga*) does not refer solely to that which takes form as its object, but generally refers to all attachment to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*);
so too, sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) does not refer solely to that which takes the realm of desire as its object, but generally refers to all attachment to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The sūtras upheld by the Elder also state:

"If, taking the desire realm as an object, one gives rise to defilement, gives rise to craving, gives rise to ālaya, gives rise to nyāna, and gives rise to various forms of attachment, these are the characteristics of sensual craving."
Therefore, to maintain that the possession of greed (*rāga-prāpti*) pervades all three realms is not a sound position.
Furthermore, it is not the Buddha’s teaching that only what pervades the three realms can be said to possess sound. Why is this so?
There are statements that refer to a portion of one realm, a portion of two realms, or a portion of three realms.
These should be interpreted accordingly, as in the *Saptabhavasūtra* regarding the "seven existences at most" and so forth.

Therefore, the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) mentioned here encompasses all forms of craving within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) without exception; the craving of the other two realms is collectively termed "craving for existence" (*bhavarāga*).
The reasons for establishing these names have already been explained previously.

If only that which takes internal objects as its condition and is characterized by greed were called "greed for existence" (*bhavarāga*), then within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the craving for visible forms, sounds, and tangibles—which arises without taking internal objects as its condition—would not be "greed for existence. Consequently, there would have to be eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) established.

Furthermore, when it is said that "existence" (bhava) exists, this does not refer solely to the birth-body (upapatti-deha), because the sūtras speak of karmic existence (karma-bhava) and intermediate existence (antarā-bhava); just as the term "desire-existence" (kāma-bhava) is used to include both the desire-realm itself and its objects.
Thus, the attachment to the body arising from conditions within the desire realm is also subsumed under the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*).
For this reason, all attachment bound to the desire realm is designated by the term "latent tendency of sensual desire."

Alternatively, one might argue that sound is also mentioned among the objects of desire (*kāmaguṇa*), and thus it would be redundant to speak of the latent tendency of sensual greed (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) separately because its meaning would already be included.
This reasoning is also incorrect, for since the term "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) is used, such an inclusion would be permissible.

This means that, according to the reasoning of the majority of cases, this may be so: for greed in the desire realm mostly functions toward external objects, whereas craving in the form and formless realms mostly functions toward internal objects. It is not that one must hold desire-greed arises only by taking external objects as its object, nor that only when it takes internal objects as its object is it called "existence-greed" (*bhavarāga*); rather, the two types of greed can be said to be distinct because their modes of operation differ.
Alternatively, they must admit that craving for the form and formless realms never functions by taking external objects as its objective support.
Furthermore, attachment to sense objects is itself attachment to existence (*bhava*), because all sense objects are also termed "existence."
Alternatively, those who are attached to existence (*bhava*) are precisely those attached to objects (*viṣaya*), because all forms of existence are also subsumed under the category of objects.
Therefore, the claim that attachment to objects and attachment to existence are distinct, as previously stated, is not a sound explanation.

Furthermore, regarding their statement that two [types of craving] are established separately due to differences in the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*) for craving toward objects and craving toward the body: does this term "counteractive measure" refer to specific ones or to general ones?

If it is claimed that this term refers to specific counteractive measures, then craving for objects should be divided into many types—namely, craving for objects such as forms, sounds, and so forth—because the counteractive measures for subduing each would differ.

If it is argued that this statement refers to general antidotes, and that these two types of antidotes have both differences and similarities, how can it be definitively stated that the antidotes are different?
Alternatively, since there are differences in the antidotes for the greed of the two realms—the form and formless realms—one should likewise divide them into two.

Furthermore, it is said that by suppressing and subduing sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*), external ascetics (*bāhyaka-ṛṣi*) are then able to enter the realms of form and formlessness; therefore, the essence of sensual desire is not identical to the craving for existence (*bhavarāga*). This is because those sentient beings, while taking their own mental continuum as an object, are constantly and without interruption pursued by self-love (*ātmasneha*).
This statement is utterly contrary to the principles of the noble teachings; it is only when [afflictions] do not manifest that they are said to be "suppressed.
Furthermore, the craving for the body produced by conditions and bound to the desire realm is called both "craving for existence" (*bhavarāga*) and "self-love" (*ātmasneha*).
If this self-love were to constantly manifest in its activity, it would certainly be impossible for them to enter the form and formless realms.

If external sages could enter the higher stages without having suppressed or subdued their craving for the bodies of lower births, then one should not say that only those who have subdued sensual desire and hatred are able to enter the form and formless realms.

If it is claimed that the manifest greed and hatred toward objects of desire can obstruct external sages from entering the realms of form and formlessness, whereas the greed for a body born of dependent origination bound to the desire realm cannot obstruct external sages—what logic is there in this?
Because one must first feel revulsion toward the lower body and environment before being born in the higher realms.
Although he further states:

"Is it not the case that even for those abiding in the desire realm who are candidates for arhatship (arhattvaphalapratipannaka), there is necessarily no self-conceit (*asmimāna*) or craving (*tṛṣṇā*) regarding the body of the desire realm?"—this cannot possibly be so.
Why not allow that this same situation also applies to the fruit of arhatship?

If one were to become free from the defilements of the desire realm without having severed the craving for the desire realm, then at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there would likewise be no principle of severance, because those [defilements] are not the antidotes to them.

Alternatively, all afflictions of the lower stages would have to be abandoned simultaneously with the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), rendering the cultivation of the preparatory path (the antidote) useless.
Or else, one must explain the specific causes and conditions for that distinction, as the abandonment of desire-realm greed occurs both gradually and instantaneously.
If it is argued that this proof is based on the *Sūtra on Peaceful Abiding* (*Kṣemaka-sūtra*), it is not so, for the meaning of that sūtra has not been understood.

That venerable one (Kṣemaka), having already seen the principles of the truths (*dṛṣṭadharman*), spoke those words—"I do not adhere to a self within form and so forth"—based upon the self-love (*ātmasneha*) and self-conceit (*asmimāna*) belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Nevertheless, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of self-conceit and self-love toward these five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) have not yet been severed.

This means that these afflictions function in accordance with the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); since the view of a self-entity has been abandoned, they do not manifest. Nevertheless, they have not yet been permanently severed, because their antidote has not yet been attained.
If one provides such an explanation, what contradiction arises?

There is indeed a contradiction, namely that the sutra states: when the Buddha taught this dharma-gate for him, the Venerable Kṣema attained arhatship, with all outflows forever extinguished and his mind well-liberated.
From this it is known that he was previously a non-returner who had already cultivated the path toward arhatship; at the moment of emerging from meditative absorption, he spoke these words:
"Within form and so forth... and so on, as explained at length, until the Buddha taught him the Dharma.
The Sūtra merely states that one "attains the fruit of arhatship" and does not mention other fruits;

therefore, this does not constitute a valid proof. That sūtra specifically cites only the most supreme fruit attained, as is explained in such texts as the *Tāla-phala-upama-sūtra* (the Sūtra on the Simile of Clapping Hands).
It is not that the noble ones engage in such deliberation as, "What am I like?
and so forth, as explained at length; rather, the Blessed One employed skillful means to awaken their minds.

The Sūtra merely states that they attained the fruit of Arhatship, meaning that the Sūtra says they understood what the Buddha had spoken and their minds became well-liberated as Arhats; it does not say that an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) hearing the Dharma suddenly realizes the fruit of Arhatship.
One who speaks thus cites the most prominent case; this [explanation] should likewise be understood.

Alternatively, that sūtra makes such a statement by way of the categories of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*); however, within these five aggregates of clinging, there remain unsevered latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of pride and craving regarding a self. In reality, there is only pride and craving for a self within the higher aggregates of clinging.

One who calls himself a son of the Śākyas must certainly not claim to have already abandoned desire and greed; for he still has not severed the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of pride and self-love (*ātmasneha*) belonging to the desire realm, let alone claim that these two constantly accompany his present mental activity.
Therefore, it is established by reason that *bhavarāga* (craving for existence) exists only in the form and formless realms, and not in the desire realm.

Since it has been stated that *bhavarāga* pertains to the two higher realms, it follows by implication that the craving of the desire realm is termed *kāmarāga* (craving for sensual pleasure); thus, it is not separately indicated in the verse.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle 45;
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle 46.

Chapter Five, Part Two: Analysis of the Latent Dispositions (Anuśaya). Regarding the six types of latent dispositions previously mentioned, they are further established as ten according to different categories.
How are these ten established?
The verse says:

The six become ten through the differentiation of views; "differentiation" refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), [the view of extremes, wrong view, adherence to views, and adherence to precepts and observances].
The view of extremes, false view, the grasping at views, and the grasping at precepts and observances.

The commentary states: Among the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), those that function as views are divided into five; the remaining ones that are not views constitute another five. When these are totaled, they form ten. Thus, among these ten, five are of the nature of views: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); third, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); fourth, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and fifth, the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Five are not of the nature of views: first, greed; second, hatred; third, pride; fourth, ignorance; and fifth, doubt.
These views and non-views together constitute ten types.
Furthermore, these same six types are established through different perspectives, resulting in ninety-eight types.
By what perspective are they established as ninety-eight?
The verse says:
Due to differences in aspect, category, and realm, they become ninety-eight:
those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and so forth in the desire realm are seventeen, seven, seven, and four respectively.
This means that, in order, they possess three, two, two, and one [of the views], as well as doubt.
In the form and formless realms, hatred is excluded; the rest are explained as in the case of the desire realm.
The commentary states:
The six types of latent proclivities (anuśaya), through the distinctions of their modes of activity, categories, realms, and gates, constitute ninety-eight.
That is to say, among these six, ten are established based on differences in their modes of operation (*ākāra*) and their functions (*carita*), as has already been explained previously.

These very ten types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have been discussed become ninety-eight through differences in category (*nikāya*) and realm (*dhātu*). "Category" refers to the five categories: those abandoned by seeing the four truths and those abandoned by cultivation; "realm" refers to the three realms: the desire, form, and formless realms.
Furthermore, within the five categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when multiplied by the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), they constitute thirty-six.

That is to say, from the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) up to that which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there are respectively seventeen, seven, seven, and eight.

Regarding the four [categories], these correspond to the five aforementioned classes [of afflictions] within the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); according to their respective order, they are fully comprised of the three views, two views, views, and doubt.
This means that those abandoned by the vision of the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) consist of ten [factors], as all of them are in opposition to the vision of the truth of suffering.

Those abandoned by the vision of the truths of origin (samudaya-satya) and cessation (nirodha-satya) each consist of seven, excluding the view of a self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), extreme views (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi), and adherence to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa).

There are eight [afflictions] abandoned through the vision of the Truth of the Path; these consist of the previous seven with the addition of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
There are four abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), excluding views and doubt.
Thus, they total thirty-six types.
The first thirty-two are called abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), because they are abandoned at the very moment the truths are seen.

The final four are called abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they are abandoned only after the four truths have been seen, through the repeated practice of the path in subsequent times.

By this, it has already been shown that among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) exists in only one category, namely, that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*);
the same applies to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

The clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) pertains to two categories, namely, those abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*).
Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) extends across four categories, namely those abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
the same applies to the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

The remaining four, beginning with craving (*rāga*), each extend across five categories, namely those abandoned through the vision of the four truths as well as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Thus, in summary, there are twelve [factors] categorized as views;
doubt is divided into four; and the remaining four each have five. Therefore, there are thirty-six [factors] in the desire realm.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) himself poses and answers the following question:
In this context, what characteristics constitute that which is abandoned through seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)? And so on, up to:

what characteristics constitute that which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)? If that which takes as its object what is abandoned through seeing [suffering] is called "abandoned through seeing," then whatever remains other than that is called "abandoned through cultivation."
This is not reasonable.

Why? Because universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) take all five categories as their objects, it would follow that the latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin must also be abandoned through the vision of the origin, suffering, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path that take non-abandonable phenomena as their objects, it should be asked: by what [vision] are they to be abandoned?
Therefore, their characterization as being "associated with what is to be abandoned" is not well-established.

If one perceives suffering as the object of one's vision, it is called "seeing suffering" (*duḥkha-darśana*). This is abandoned by these two: the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) regarding suffering. Taken collectively, these are termed "abandoned through seeing suffering. The same applies up to what is abandoned through seeing the path (*mārga-darśana*).
Cultivation (*bhāvanā*) refers to repeated practice; that is to say, for one who has seen the tracks [of the Truths], it is for the sake of attaining the higher goal.

The repeated perfuming of the knowledge regarding suffering and so forth is called cultivation; what is eliminated by this path is called "to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*). This is what is rightly established as the characteristic of that which is to be abandoned.
In the form and formless realms, the five categories each exclude hatred; the remainder are the same as in the desire realm, thus there are thirty-one in each.
Consequently, the masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* establish ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) by classifying the six according to their modes of activity, categories, realms, and gates.
Among the ninety-eight [defilements] thus explained, eighty-eight are abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), because they are destroyed by the Patiences (*kṣānti*).
Ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), because they are destroyed by the Knowledges (*jñāna*).
For what reason are the latent dispositions (anuśaya) established here according to the difference of realms (dhātu), rather than according to the difference of stages (bhūmi)?

Just as it is logical for latent dispositions belonging to different realms—such as the desire realm and the form realm—to increase together with respect to a single object, so too is it the case for those belonging to different stages within the first two dhyānas.

If it is argued that although the stages (bhūmi) differ, there is a common antidote (pratipakṣa), yet there is no such commonality between the antidotes for the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu), then one should not establish the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) as distinct, because the formless and the form realms share a common antidote.

If it is argued that because the antidotes to what is abandoned through cultivation arise gradually, form and formless realms should be established separately, then the same applies to the various stages (*bhūmi*); why are they not stated separately?
Therefore, there should be two hundred and eighty-four latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Even if one were to grant this, there would be no fault; for the ninety-eight [defilements] are established based on the distinction between the realms (*dhātu*).
This is because the analytical knowledges (*parijñā*) and the fruits of the śramaṇa are established by means of abandoning craving for the respective realms.

This means that these two are established based on the abandonment of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). Since this abandonment of latent dispositions pertains to the realms (*dhātu*) and not to the stages (*bhūmi*), the latent dispositions are not established according to the stages.
The ancient masters say:

"The Buddha, having clearly and thoroughly realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), is able to teach it to others; he must have clearly observed that the nature of the afflictions in the four dhyāna stages is similar enough that, although there are four stages, they are spoken of collectively as one."
The same applies to the combined discussion of the four formless realms (*ārūpya*), because the Sūtra speaks only of "attachment to form" (*rūparāga*) and "attachment to the formless" (*ārūpyarāga*).

For this reason, the masters of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (the *Nyāyānusārin*) establish that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are categorized according to the realms (*dhātu*) rather than the stages (*bhūmi*).
In what way are the natures of the fourth stage similar?
Some say it is because they are both stages that comprise the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
This explanation is unreasonable.
Why? Because afflictions arise within the various preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
Some say: because they are equally subsumed within the stage of Universal Illumination (Samantāloka-bhūmi). Others say:
Because these are afflictions of the same category as desire for form (*rūparāga*), I have stated that there is a slight similarity within them.

Only the Blessed One clearly and thoroughly understands this: it is only upon the permanent abandonment of the lowest-of-the-low grade (*mṛdumṛdu*) of the fourth dhyāna that one establishes "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*); this is not the case for lower stages. Therefore, we know that the four stages must necessarily possess some degree of similarity in their nature and category; it is not that the afflictions of a higher stage can take a lower stage as their object and bind it.
When one attains dissociation from the afflictions of the lower three dhyānas, why not establish a distinct entity for the "complete knowledge of abandonment" (prahāṇa-parijñā)?
It is certain that for a certain class of afflictions, even though they have already been dissociated, they remain similar to being bound because they have not yet been eliminated.

Since one can only be said to have attained ultimate dissociation when the corresponding category of afflictions is abandoned without remainder, it is logically superior to establish the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) solely by way of the realms (*dhātu*), rather than by way of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Other masters say:

It is like one who, having been imprisoned by an enemy in a dungeon, employs means to escape; yet as long as he has not reached a place dissimilar from the enemy’s city—such as a forest, a field, or an open space—he remains without complete security even though he has passed beyond the enemy’s prison.

Thus, when one has abandoned the craving for the three lower meditative absorptions (dhyāna), although one has not yet reached a state where that craving is dissimilar, and although one has only slightly reduced it rather than being fully established in tranquility, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are nonetheless established solely in terms of the realms (dhātu).
Other masters say:

"If one transcends the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one has already transcended many destinies (*gati*), many births, the great aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and immeasurable phenomena of suffering.
If one transcends the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one has already transcended the entirety of the *upādānaskandhas*, as well as many bases and many elements."
If one transcends the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one has thereby transcended all that is comprised within birth and death—the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

This is not the case for what is transcended by leaving the lower three meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*); therefore, the establishment of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is based on the realms (*dhātu*) and not on the stages (*bhūmi*).

However, the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* of old also maintained that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are established according to their respective stages (*bhūmi*). Therefore, they posed this hypothetical question and answer:
"Is there any ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who, having eternally abandoned all ninety-eight latent dispositions, possesses them all [simultaneously]?"
Yes; that is to say, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born in the desire realm who has attained the third dhyāna but has not yet abandoned craving for it.
Is there any ordinary person who has attained the third dhyāna but does not possess the complete abandonment of the ninety-eight types of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) previously mentioned?
Yes; that is to say, when those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have already passed away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Is it possible for one abiding in the stage of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) to fully accomplish the permanent abandonment of all ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)?
There is; namely, when those ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) enter into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Is it possible for a noble person (*ārya-pudgala*) to possess only four of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and yet achieve the permanent abandonment of eighty-two latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)?
There is; namely, when one who is bound by all fetters enters into the determination of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

At the time of abiding correctly in the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*), if the four dhyāna stages within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) were subject to the same bondage as the desire realm, what fault would there be?

This is consistent with establishing the thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) and the fruits of śrāmaṇya based on the abandonment of craving within a specific realm; furthermore, it accords with the root treatise’s statement that a universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) functions as a cause capable of producing defiled phenomena within its own realm.

This is not so, for it would contradict the principles of the sūtras and śāstras. To begin with, let us cite scriptural passages to prove that the four dhyānas do not share the same bond (*ekabandhana*).
As a sūtra states: "He forms this thought:
'I shall abide in the second dhyāna, which is tranquilized of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*')."
Although he forms this thought, he is unable to enter [the second dhyāna]. He then reflects further:
"By what cause and by what condition am I unable to enter my mind into this state? Having formed this reflection, he understands for himself:

"Because I have not yet recognized, mastered, seen, or known the faults of vitarka and vicāra; and because I have not yet cultivated or practiced extensively the merits of the meditative absorption free from vitarka and vicāra, I am unable to enter the mind of the second dhyāna. This is explained at length, up to: "I must now certainly abandon these faults—the various perceptions and mental engagements accompanied by the frequent arousal of vitarka and vicāra—which arise while I abide in this state," and so forth, as explained at length.

The meaning here is to clarify that just as one transcends the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), so too shall one transcend all perceptions (*saṃjñā*) and mental attentions (*manasikāra*) belonging to the lower stages, such as the dhyāna levels, which are capable of obstructing freedom from passion (*vairāgya*).
Furthermore, because it can cause retrogression, it is described as a fault rather than something belonging to its own stage; thus, one knows that the form realm is not a single bond.
Moreover, seeing these faults serves as the cause for revulsion, revulsion serves as the cause for detachment, and through detachment, there is liberation.
If they were bound by the same fetter, this [distinction] would be rendered futile.
Furthermore, it is taught that vitarka and so forth cease gradually; as the Sūtra states:
"When a yogācāra enters the second dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra cease," and so on at length, until: "Upon entering the Sphere of Infinite Space, the perception of form ceases."

If all the stages of the form realm were bound by a single fetter, then since practitioners of yoga lack the power to suddenly abandon vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and the perception of form—due to their minds being terrified by such an extremely heavy burden—they would ultimately never be able to abandon vitarka and the other factors.
Furthermore, it is said because of the statement regarding the departure from joy and the abandonment of pleasure; as the Sūtra says:
"The departure from joy and the abandonment of pleasure are not bound by the same bond.

In the various locations of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), even if one has not attained freedom from craving for an amount as small as a hair-tip, one may still be said to be "completely free from the bonds of desire" (*kāmabandhana*). This is the case except for those who have already abandoned the factors to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*); although they have not yet permanently abandoned the craving to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are called "free from bonds" because that [craving] is not their object.
If the various stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) were bound by the same bond, there would have to be other bonds, for liberation would not be possible through abandonment.
These [arguments] are called "contradictions with the sūtras.
Next, citing the treatise (*śāstra*) to prove that the four dhyānas are not of the same bond, as the treatise states:
Who accomplishes the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?
It is one born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, or one born in a lower realm, or a noble one (*ārya*) born in a higher realm.
Who does not accomplish it here?
This refers to the fact that when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is born into a higher realm, the dharmas of the lower realms do not arise.
Although it is said that these are not acquired upon being born into a higher realm, this does not occur because they have been severed by means of the same fetter (*bandhana*).

Within the Desire Realm and others, such a principle of definite acquisition is not observed; however, since the *Abhidharma-śāstra* states that the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is able to produce defiled dharmas of its own realm, this statement was made specifically for the purpose of defining the universal cause in terms of the establishment of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) according to their respective realms.
Furthermore, there are original texts that state [the afflictions] arise from their own level (*svabhūmi*).
Since these [positions] are called "contradictions with the treatises" (*śāstravirodha*),
how could a single bond (*bandhana*) be inconsistent with reason?

Furthermore, that which contradicts the principle of following the [respective] stages is as follows: one should not speak of the factor of "internal serenity" (*adhyātmasamprasāda*) in the two dhyānas, because they are still turbid with the afflictions associated with both *vitarka* and *vicāra*.
Furthermore, sentient beings born in the fourth dhyāna should also possess defiled vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha; yet the sūtra speaks of the cessation of vitarka and so forth.
Moreover, the sūtra states that they are "detached from prīti" and have "abandoned sukha."

Regarding that which contradicts the reasoning of the *Mūla-śāstra*: the *Mūla-śāstra* states that the second and subsequent dhyānas associated with relish (*āsvādana*) can act as only two conditions for the first dhyāna associated with relish—namely, the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

If the various stages of the form realm were bound by the same fetter, then craving for the higher stages would also be able to act as the cause and the object-condition for craving for the lower stages.
Furthermore, except at the time of rebirth, it would also function as the equal-and-immediate condition.
Furthermore, the craving for the first dhyāna should serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the greed of the fourth dhyāna;
likewise, from the immediate succession of the first "tasting" (*āsvādana*) dhyāna, up to the fourth "pure" (*śuddha*) dhyāna should manifest.
Furthermore, setting aside the case of rebirth, one should arise from the fourth pure absorption (śuddha-samādhi) immediately after [the fourth] defiled absorption (sāsrava-samādhi).
In this manner, regarding the equal-and-immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya) between the higher and lower levels, which arise in succession, many difficulties would have to be established.
Furthermore, one should not state within the context of the fourth type of karma that the four types of volition (*cetanā*) can sever white karma with white maturation;
nor should one say that the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher realms can sever the afflictions of the lower realms, because they are bound by the same fetters (*bandhana*).
Furthermore, the various Non-returners who have attained the first dhyāna would have to abandon [defilements] in the same manner as those who have attained the fourth dhyāna.

Therefore, one must certainly admit that the upper and lower stages differ—just as the realms, karma, afflictions, causes, and effects are distinct—because their principles are different, yet they are bound by the same fetter.
As previously stated, hatred is excluded from the higher realms; for what reason does hatred not exist there?

It is because the objective basis (*vastu*) for the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of hatred does not exist. That is to say, hatred increases in association with painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*), and since they lack painful feeling, hatred does not exist there.

Furthermore, because the latent tendency of aversion has the characteristic of dryness and coarseness—meaning that this affliction is characterized by dryness like a wind disorder—sentient beings whose mental continuums are moistened by *śamatha* do not possess that characteristic of dryness, which is aversion.

Furthermore, that [neutral state] is not the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) of hatred; for hatred necessarily brings about an undesirable ripening, whereas in the two higher realms there are no undesirable things—externally, there are no conditions such as poisonous thorns or *kāśa* grass ashes, and internally, there is no heat-wind, epilepsy, or similar afflictions.

Some say: Because it is free from the occurrence of affliction and harm, because it is the dwelling place of wholesome roots such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and because all forms of grasping are far removed.
Other masters say:
The nature of hatred is volatile and impetuous, and thus it can be swiftly abandoned; therefore, when a practitioner of yoga is free from sensual desire, they are able to suppress it immediately.
It is like dry, coarse grime that does not adhere to a hollow: with just a touch of washing and wiping, it is quickly removed.
The Vibhajyavādins maintain this position:
"There are no ninety-eight established latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), because the Sūtras state that there are only seven.
That is to say, the Sūtra declares:
If you wish to permanently sever the seven kinds of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), you should from this day forth diligently practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) under me.
From this it is known that the proponents of the *Nyāyānusāra* establish only ninety-eight latent dispositions based solely on their own conceptualizations.

If one were to establish [the existence of latent dispositions] based on one's own conjectures apart from the words of the Noble Ones, then one would have to admit an infinite number of latent dispositions, since they would be active within the bodies of infinite sentient beings.

Now, observing that the Venerable One is unable to examine the principles of the Noble Teaching with thorough and authentic scrutiny, he stubbornly denies the established number of latent dispositions according to both reason and scripture.

Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Seven Underlying Tendencies* cited by them does not definitively prove the fixed number [of afflictions], as it is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). For another sūtra states:

"If one wishes to become weary of, detached from, extinguish desire for, and be permanently liberated from form (*rūpa*), one should diligently practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) regarding 'what belongs to me' (*ātmīya*); this applies likewise up to consciousness (*vijñāna*)."

This sutra speaks only of desiring to sever the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), stating that one should diligently practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) within my domain; therefore, it is known that this sutra is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Furthermore, in other passages as well, there are instances where, based solely on the desire to abandon a portion of the defilement of a single realm or a single latent disposition, the statement "one should diligently practice the holy life within my domain" is made.
As a sutra states:
"If one wishes to permanently eradicate the latent tendency of craving for pleasant feeling, one should diligently cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) regarding what belongs to the self.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
If one wishes to eradicate the latent tendency of aversion toward painful feelings forever, one should diligently cultivate the holy life within my dispensation.
How could one, on the grounds that what is stated in that sutra is extremely brief, deny that it teaches seven latent tendencies?
Therefore, one should know that this scriptural passage, like the former, is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Now, it should be carefully analyzed: within this sūtra, the statement that one should practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) in order to sever the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) intends to indicate the number seven because the types of underlying tendencies differ.

As stated in the Sūtras, there are two kinds of phenomena (*dharma*), and there are no other phenomena apart from these two. How could this imply that one does not allow for the teaching of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*)?
However, since the remaining six elements are included within the category of the mind (*manas*), the [two] sets of twenty-eight [categories] do not contradict one another.

Furthermore, as it is said in the sūtras that there are five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), ignorance (*avidyā*) itself is not included among the hindrances, because the sūtra states that ignorance is "able to cover.
Moreover, those same five hindrances are spoken of as ten in other sūtras; as the Sūtra says:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the substance of the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) has two distinctions: first, internal; second, external," and so on at length.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra states that the great earth trembles due to four causes, it is not that there are no other causes.
Likewise, as the Sūtra says:
"There are three things in the world that ought to be brought forth."
However, some say there are four.
Furthermore, as a sutra states:
"Truth is only one; there is no second."
Nevertheless, for the sake of the brahmins, he taught that there are three truths as well as four [noble truths], and so forth.

Furthermore, as the sūtras state, there are two kinds of knowledge—namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)—but this does not mean that other forms of knowledge do not exist.
Furthermore, as it is said in the sutra:
"The mind is of two kinds, namely, wholesome and unwholesome;
it is not that there is no neutral [mind]."
There are immeasurable sūtras of this kind, each spoken by the Buddha according to the specific dispositions of his audience.

Those who fail to comprehend the underlying principles of the noble teachings, and instead consider only the refutation of other schools as a virtue—how could such people ever attain the fruit of eloquent exposition?
As the Blessed One told Udāyin:

"If one does not wish to seek the meaning within all things and all aspects as taught by the Tathāgata through various methods, you should know that such a person dwells in contention within the Noble Teaching," and so forth, as extensively explained.
Furthermore, according to what you have stated, one must admit that there are immeasurable latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
What fault is there in admitting this?
For, in terms of their distinct bases within the body, they are immeasurable in number.

However, when latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are distinguished according to their essential categories, they constitute only six types; these six, when differentiated by way of various classifications, become sixteen, or ten, or twenty-eight, or thirty-six, or seventy-four, or ninety-eight.

That is to say, the Buddha has displayed the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in various places through the distinctions of the gates of realms (*dhātu*), courses of action (*carita*), and groups (*nikāya*); following what the Buddha taught, the Master of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* establishes ninety-eight latent dispositions based on the differences of the realms and so forth.

Furthermore, there are six categories of underlying tendencies (anuśaya), namely: attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt; these distinct categories have already been explained as previously established.

Since the Blessed One stated in the sūtras that "craving" (tṛṣṇā) is the general designation for all greed within the three realms, we know that its essential nature consists solely of the six underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

It is precisely these six underlying tendencies, when categorized according to the distinctions of the realms, that the Blessed One provisionally described as two types of greed—namely, greed for the realm of desire (kāmarāga) and greed for existence (bhavarāga)—because their respective underlying tendencies differ.
The others may be understood by analogy through the distinctions of greed (*lobha*).
This statement is made to show that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), whether fixed or unfixed in their realms, each constitute two types.
However, only greed is mentioned as the distinction among the realms because greed is frequently taught as the primary factor.
This means that within the various established teachings on the afflictions (*kleśa*), greed is everywhere declared to be the foremost.

For example, it is taught in countless instances, such as the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*), the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the upper-tier three paths of action (*karmapatha*), the bonds (*bandhana*), and the accumulation of karma through conditions (*karmapratyayasamudaya*).
Since the sūtras state that the latent tendency of greed (*rāgānuśaya*) is the root of birth and death, they frequently mention it first in various contexts.
Now that it has been stated that this primary [tendency] is divided into two types, by this analogy it should be understood that the others are likewise so.

However, it cannot be said that hatred (*dveṣa*) is also divided into two categories according to the realms (*dhātu*), because the remaining distinctions are manifested through the presence of craving (*rāga*) in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
This is not the case for pride (*māna*) and the like, as they are said to exist even in the higher realms.

By means of this teaching, it has already been shown that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are determined according to their respective spheres—whether concentrated or distracted—and their specific realms.

Furthermore, in other passages, the Buddha employs another formulation regarding "possessing greed" (*sarāga*) to demonstrate that there are likewise distinctions among the latent dispositions within the realm of concentration.

This means that when the Blessed One taught among the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), he established craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*) and craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*) as two distinct categories; by this distinction in craving, the others may be understood by analogy.
This statement was made to demonstrate the difference between the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the various meditative realms of form and the formless.

However, since it is not among the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and is exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), it follows that the craving for the realm of existence (*bhavarāga*) is exclusively abandoned through cultivation; furthermore, because there are other afflictions abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) that share the same category as those abandoned through cultivation, they must also be distinct from one another.

Previously, the distinctions between what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as those pertaining to the concentrated (*samāhita*) and distracted (*asamāhita*) states and the various realms (*dhātu*), were shown in general. Now, the specific distinctions between what is abandoned by cultivation alone within the form (*rūpa*) and formless (*ārūpya*) realms are shown, because they are abandoned in this manner by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).

This means that the greed abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) regarding both the form and formless realms has a single antidote (*pratipakṣa*), whereas the greed abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) has distinct antidotes for each. Therefore, regarding the greed abandoned through seeing within the meditative states (*dhyāna-dhātu*), the distinction between the realms is not manifested; however, for the greed abandoned through cultivation, the distinction between the realms is manifested.
Thus, having separately cited two sūtras to demonstrate that craving has distinctions according to the three realms, it is shown that the others likewise have such distinctions.
Now, a single sūtra is further cited in total as evidence, as the sūtra says:
"There are three kinds of craving: first, craving for the realm of desire; second, craving for the realm of form; and third, craving for the formless realm."
The others may be understood by analogy through the distinctions of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
This was stated in order to demonstrate the distinctions among the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Thus, scriptural authority has been cited to prove that the latent dispositions are differentiated according to the realms.

There is also a difference in principle: namely, there is a certain class of *pudgala* who attains dissociation from all phenomena of the desire realm, but not from those of the form or formless realms; because they have abandoned these underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), they do not take birth in the desire realm.
These abandoned proclivities (anuśaya) should be understood as belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Those belonging to the form and formless realms (rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu) should be understood accordingly.
Therefore, by both scriptural authority and logical reasoning, there is a distinction between the realms; thus, the number of proclivities is established as sixteen.

The distinctions among the elements (*dhātu*) have already been clarified; how, then, are their modes of activity (*carita*) different? It is precisely through the difference in their modes of activity that the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are differentiated.

The Blessed One has stated in various places that there are five views, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, as previously enumerated. Thus, the six underlying tendencies, when categorized by their different modes of activity, expand and accumulate into ten, as has already been analyzed above.
When the courses of action (*carita*) and the elements (*dhātu*) are combined and divided, there are twenty-eight.
Having already manifested the distinctions among the courses of action, what are the differences among the groups (*nikāya*)?
"Group" refers to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) categorized according to their specific antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).

That is to say, there is a class [of afflictions] that is abandoned through the vision of suffering; likewise, there are those abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path; and there are those abandoned at a later time through the repeated cultivation and intensification of one of the knowledges.
If it were otherwise, the establishment of the vision of the Four Noble Truths and the subsequent knowledge of the fruit would be in vain.
However, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one must necessarily realize the Four Noble Truths gradually, as will be explained later.
These five categories are definitively distinguished, as the Buddha himself clearly demonstrated in the sūtras.
As the Blessed One said:
"In the past, I and you all traversed the long road of saṃsāra."
Because one cannot see the Four Noble Truths as they truly are,
If one can see the Four Truths, One will forever sever the bonds of existence;
Then birth and death will be utterly extinguished, And there will be no further states of existence.
In this context, the phrase "if one is able to see the four truths" reveals the severance of the four types of ignorance abandoned through the vision of the four truths.
Furthermore, the statement "permanently severing all bonds of existence" reveals the severance of the ignorance abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Is it not the case that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is spoken of here as the bond? How, then, can this be cited as proof for the five classes of ignorance (*avidyā*)?
For ignorance is not established as being explicitly mentioned here; indeed, there is nothing in the world bound by the fetter of craving that is not also characterized by ignorance.

Since it is already accepted that the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) exist among those things to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), why would it need further proof?
For craving does not arise in one who is not deluded.
Furthermore, there is another proof demonstrating the distinct categories of the various afflictions, as stated in the Sūtra:
There is ignorance regarding suffering, ignorance regarding its origin, ignorance regarding its cessation, and ignorance regarding the path.
Herein, the delusions concerning the past and so forth are subsumed collectively; four types of ignorance are established based on the objects of the Four Noble Truths.

It should be understood that in this context, the term "ignorance" (avidyā) reveals all latent dispositions (anuśaya), as explained in the section on dependent origination; thus, the various afflictions (kleśa) possess distinct categories.

However, it is not because ignorance has five categories that one may infer by analogy that all other afflictions likewise have five categories, for there are instances where other afflictions are explicitly stated to be excluded from such a classification.

This means that the Blessed One stated that by permanently severing views and doubt, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*). Using this as proof, it is established that views and doubt are not abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Furthermore, since the Sūtra states only that by severing the craving, hatred, delusion, and pride directed toward rebirth in evil destinies, one attains the fruit of stream-entry, it follows that the fruit of stream-entry is free from views and doubt, yet possesses craving, hatred, delusion, and pride that are abandoned through cultivation.
Based on this evidence, it is known that the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), when differentiated by their categories (*nikāya*), constitute twenty-eight;

when combined according to category and mode of activity (*paryavasthāna*), they constitute thirty-six; when combined according to category and realm (*dhātu*), they constitute seventy-four; and when categorized by way of category, mode of activity, and realm, the underlying tendencies are divided into ninety-eight, as has already been explained above.

Therefore, the Abhidharmikas, following the holy teachings of the Buddha and investigating through correct reasoning, have established ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) which cannot be shaken.
Yet that decayed and deluded Elder further claims:

"Although the Sūtras do not lack the names and characteristics they cite, there is nowhere it is stated that these latent dispositions are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), up to being abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)."

Now one should pose this challenge: when entering the Path of Seeing, although the Truth of Suffering has already been seen while the Truth of Origination and the others have not yet been seen, is it the case that the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing are still manifesting, such that one could say their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) have not yet been uprooted?
If this were not so, why trouble yourself with such a web of frivolous arguments?
Furthermore, according to your own position, afflictions are abandoned through their objects; yet, even without perceiving the object, they can be permanently severed.
In the same way, although these afflictions take the three truths as their objects, what prevents them from being severed all at once when the truth of suffering is perceived?
However, there is an objection:

"If one can suddenly sever the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) at the very moment of seeing suffering (*duḥkha*), then the subsequent seeing of the other three truths would be useless.

This is not logically so; for at this stage, one does not seek to see the origin (*samudaya*) and so forth, nor does one desire to abandon the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Nevertheless, due to the successive induction of prior cognitions, one naturally sees the origin and the others in their proper sequence.
If it were not so, then during the process of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), the minds seeking to see and so forth would necessarily be interspersed [with other thoughts].

Furthermore, there is no place where the Buddha has ever stated that there are ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); if there were such a statement, the Buddha would have spoken of it, and I would then accept it with faith.
The Elder’s interrogation of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in this manner—searching through them from the coarse to the subtle—does not strike the essential point.

This has already been clarified previously: the Buddha stated in the sūtras that the various latent dispositions are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and so forth. As the sūtra says:
"Those who have not seen the Four Truths wander for a long time in saṃsāra; upon seeing them, [the dispositions] are entirely extinguished."
How can it be said that the Buddha never stated anywhere that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) such as those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) exist?
Furthermore, since he taught that there are four types of ignorance regarding suffering and the other truths, how can these four ignorances be abandoned solely through the vision of suffering?
Thus, it is known that there are definitely five categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, they raise this objection:

"For one who has already seen the Truth of Suffering but has not yet seen the Truths of Origination and so forth, could there be the actual manifestation of afflictions abandoned by seeing [the truths], such that one would say their latent dispositions have not yet been uprooted?"

This is an excessively frivolous argument; for when one has not yet seen suffering, the afflictions abandoned by seeing suffering do not manifest either, and thus they should be said to have already been uprooted. If that were so, it would be incorrect to say that they are abandoned at the time of seeing suffering.
If one who has not yet seen suffering cannot eradicate all the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, the same should apply to the others as well.

One who has not yet seen the origin of suffering and so forth likewise cannot abandon the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of those [dispositions] to be abandoned, because the path that serves as their antidote has not yet arisen.

Alternatively, they ought to distinguish the cause for the difference between these two: why is it that while the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and so forth do not manifest, one [affliction] has not yet been uprooted while the others have already been uprooted?
Therefore, their objection is verbally consistent but lacks logical justification.
Furthermore, it is said:

"Just as your afflictions are conditionally related to their objects such that they are permanently severed without perceiving those objects, so too, although these afflictions take the three truths as their objects, they may be suddenly severed at the time of seeing the truth of suffering."

It is not our school’s position that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are permanently severed without perceiving their objects (*ālambana*). Although among the defilements to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) conditioned by the outflowing (*sāsrava*) are severed without perceiving their objects, those afflictions nevertheless arise based upon cessation and the path; this clarifies that the afflictions conditioned by the untainted (*anāsrava*) arise because they are nurtured by those [objects].

According to the explanation of the meaning, these are also said to be delusions regarding cessation and the path; therefore, they are eliminated by the power of that [path] which takes them as objects, rather than being latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take the other three truths as their objects.

Furthermore, when one conceives of suffering and so forth as pleasure and so forth, this ignorance arises based on the delusion regarding suffering; how could it be suddenly severed at the very moment suffering is seen?
Therefore, that citation does not apply as an analogy here, for the cases are not identical.

Furthermore, regarding what they say—that at this stage one does not seek to see the origin (*samudaya*) and so forth, nor does one desire to abandon the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), yet one sees the origin and so forth through the natural sequence induced by prior knowledge—[this is incorrect].

This is also irrational; for at that stage, one neither seeks to see suffering nor desires to abandon the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). Nevertheless, through the wisdom of the preceding stages such as *uṣmagata* and so forth, the vision of suffering is induced by the natural law (*dharmatā*) through successive transmission. At that time, one should not be abandoning the latent dispositions abandoned by the vision of suffering;
yet since these are being abandoned, it would follow that the same should apply to the others as well.

Furthermore, we do not say that at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one gives rise to a mind of applied effort (*prayoga-citta*) seeking to see or seek to abandon [the truths]. Rather, we also say that within the stage of clear realization, regarding the seeing of origination (*samudaya*) and so forth, there is no separate applied effort; it is simply through the successive induction of prior knowledge that, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), one sees origination and so forth in their proper order. Thus, at the very moment of seeing, there is both abandonment and realization.
This establishes profound utility, which is not comparable to your own school.

If you claim that there is definitely no vision of the afflictions to be abandoned by the other three truths, then the cultivation of the knowledge of those objects through the vision of the origin [of suffering] and so forth would be entirely useless; would the Great Master’s teaching of this then not be in vain?

By the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), one should naturally be able to perceive the origin and so forth; thus, the Buddha need only have taught that the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) is cultivated.

Furthermore, since the four noble truths differ in their characteristics, how could one understand that the abandonment of delusions regarding one truth occurs through [the cultivation of] another truth?
Therefore, it is not the case that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are abandoned all at once through the vision of suffering.
Furthermore, regarding what he said:
"Nowhere has the Buddha ever stated that there are ninety-eight latent dispositions; if there were such a statement, I would believe it because the Buddha has spoken it."

This is also not the case; I do not see in you any sign of faith in the Buddha’s teachings, for while I have previously established, based on the sacred scriptures and correct reasoning, that there are ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), you all lack any mind of acceptance or conviction.

Furthermore, you who possess auspicious qualities, from where have you now obtained this superior knowledge, by which you claim that the Buddha never stated anywhere that there are ninety-eight categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) distinguished by their modes, classes, and realms?
It is said that in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the teachings increase from one dharma up to a hundred dharmas.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the internal wisdom, mindfulness, and lifespan of sentient beings in this land will diminish day by day; the external medicinal herbs and so forth will gradually lose their flavor, potency, ripening, and virtue until their efficacy is scant; and as most people become entangled in evil deeds, how could they possibly uphold the Tathāgata’s holy teachings in their entirety?

Therefore, in the present *Ekottarika Āgama*, only those teachings ranging from one up to ten dharmas remain; even within these, much has already been lost, let alone anything beyond ten that could still be maintained.
Thus we know that within the sūtras, where the *anuśayas* (latent dispositions) are discussed, there must certainly exist a passage that fully enumerates the ninety-eight [types].

Such is the tradition, and the principle must necessarily be so; for this reason, the Buddha stated in the *Daśottara-sūtra* that profound sūtras will gradually disappear, until finally they vanish without remainder.

Furthermore, since time immemorial, the various sages who composed treatises have everywhere stated that there are ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); moreover, there are explicit texts providing rational exegesis. Therefore, we know that the fundamental Āgamas must certainly contain authentic passages designating this number.
Now, to further briefly cite various Āgamas as proof that many sūtras have now disappeared:

as the Buddha told Vāṣpa in that *Vāṣpa-sūtra*, "In the past, I proclaimed for the assembly of bhikṣus the Dharma of the youthful and noble horse; at that time, those like you were for the most part not truly present within this Dharma-gate."
That sūtra has now disappeared and is no longer extant.
Furthermore, in that *Duḥkhaskandha-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke to Mahānāman of the Śākya clan:

"In the past, at one time, I was staying in the great city of Rājagṛha, wandering on Mount Vaibhāra. There I saw the Nirgranthas all raising their arms high, seeking permanence through self-mortification. He then addressed them, and so forth, as explained at length.
That sūtra has now vanished and is no longer extant.
Furthermore, in the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra*, Ānanda spoke as follows:
"In the past, at one time, the Buddha was staying in the great city of the Śākyas, dwelling within a large guest house constructed there; at that time, he addressed me, saying:"
"Ānanda! Regarding this 'emptiness' in which I abide, do you wish to know it?
I shall inquire, and the Buddha will explain it for me; I shall then understand the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught."
That sūtra has also now disappeared.
Furthermore, in the Udāyin-sūtra, the Buddha spoke thus:
"In the past, I taught that there are four types of sensation (*vedanā*) that manifest in succession."
That sūtra has also now disappeared.
Furthermore, in another sūtra, the Bhagavān spoke as follows:

"In the past, at one time, I was staying in the great city of Rājagṛha, wandering among the mountains and valleys. At that time, a great number of renunciant non-Buddhists came to where I was and questioned me regarding the meaning of the Dharma," and so on, as extensively explained.
That sūtra has now also disappeared and is no longer extant.
Furthermore, in that *Rājāvavādaka-sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"Great King!..."
I recall that in the past I once said this:
"There are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas in the past, future, or present who can suddenly see and suddenly know all dharmas."
It is impossible that one could see and know [the truth] instantaneously; that sutra has now also vanished.
Furthermore, the non-Buddhist Vairāṭīputra said this regarding the *Gopaka Sūtra*:
I recall that in the past, I saw the Honored One, the Śākya Gautama, dwelling within the Kuñjika Grove at the city of Nādika, praising all the Dharma gates such as meditative concentration.
That sūtra has also now vanished and is no longer extant.
Furthermore, Ānanda stated in the *Pūrṇa-sūtra*:
"In my youth, I saw Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra extensively expounding profound Dharma-gates for the assembly."
That sutra has also now disappeared.
Furthermore, the Buddha spoke thus in that *Lambaka Sūtra*:
"In the past, at one time, I said to five bhikṣus:"

"Before I went forth, I constantly delighted in observing that the household life is cramped and fraught with many faults and afflictions; one should quickly cultivate weary detachment from it," and so on, as extensively explained.
That sutra has now also vanished and is no longer extant.
Furthermore, in that *Ārya-rāṣṭrapāla-sūtra*, it says:
"O Great King!
There are four paths of revulsion, which only the Bhagavat perceives correctly and knows correctly."

Although the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have extensively proclaimed [the Dharma], the people of the world are unable to diligently cultivate the practice of revulsion; one should know that they are certainly *tṛṣṇā-dāsa* (slaves to craving).
That sūtra has also now disappeared.
Furthermore, in the *Gati-sūtra*, Anāthapiṇḍada said:

"I have personally heard and received this Dharma discourse from the Bhagavān: if there are sentient beings who give gardens and so forth, by the power of this cause, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will be reborn among the devas and experience sublime happiness; [this is] explained at length, even unto the point that the giving of the Dharma serves as the cause."
That sūtra has also now vanished and is no longer extant.
Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, Ānanda said to Aniruddha:

"I have personally heard and received this Dharma-gate from the Buddha; the Buddha, the World-Honored One, attained parinirvāṇa with the clear eye while relying upon the immovable, tranquil fourth dhyāna."
That sūtra has also vanished at this time.
There are countless such sūtras that have all disappeared and are no longer extant today; for the most part, those originally compiled have fallen into decay.
Venerable Elder, how can you so hastily state that the Buddha never anywhere taught the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)?
Having already explained the principles regarding the distinctions among the underlying tendencies, the meaning originally intended [by the author] shall now be elucidated.
It was previously stated that there are eighty-eight [defilements] abandoned through vision and so forth; are these definitively abandoned through both vision and cultivation?
No. Why is this so?
The verse says:
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) destroyed by patience (kṣānti) at the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) are abandoned only through insight (darśana-prahātavya);
others are abandoned through both insight and cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya); those destroyed by knowledge (jñāna) are abandoned only through cultivation.
The Commentary states:

Among the latent dispositions (anuśaya) destroyed by the receptivities (kṣānti), those subsumed under the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) are abandoned solely through the path of seeing; for it is only the receptivity of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti) that is capable of abandoning them.
The remaining eight stages comprise both those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

This means that when noble ones (*ārya*) abandon them, it is only through seeing and not through cultivation, because they are abandoned accordingly by the patiences (*kṣānti*) of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
If ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abandon them, it is only through cultivation and not through seeing, because they are abandoned by the repeated practice of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) destroyed by wisdom are comprised within all stages and are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because both noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), as appropriate, abandon them by repeatedly practicing either untainted (*anāsrava*) or conventional (*saṃvṛti*) wisdom.
Regarding the verse’s statement that “the remainder is abandoned through both seeing and cultivation,” this is not explicitly stated; its meaning can be understood by implication. How is this known?
By means of what precedes and follows.

That is to say, since it was previously stated in detail that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by patience (*kṣānti*) at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are abandoned solely through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), and subsequently it was stated in general that those to be abandoned by knowledge (*jñāna*) are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), the remaining cases can be correctly understood by analogy; thus, there is no fault in this precise exposition, as it serves to clarify the meaning.
Other masters say:

The various sages among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are unable to suppress or sever the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*). As stated in the *Mahā-vibhaṅga-karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*, there are certain classes of non-Buddhists who have abandoned desire and greed, yet in whom wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) directed toward the desire realm still manifest.
Furthermore, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* also speaks of such types [of beings], stating that there are those for whom various views pertaining to the desire realm manifest.

That is to say, among those who engage in speculative theories regarding the past (*pūrvānta-vāda*), some maintain that all things are eternal, some maintain that a portion is eternal, and some maintain that all phenomena arise without cause. It is not the case that these afflictions belong to the form realm and arise by taking the desire realm as their object, because they have already abandoned craving toward the objects of the desire realm; therefore, it is certain that these various views belong to the desire realm and have not yet been abandoned.

This argument is incorrect, because both what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are capable of continuing rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Therefore, even if one portion is severed, the remaining portions should still continue rebirth within their own realm, just as in the case of stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and others.

However, it would certainly be unreasonable for those non-Buddhists who have even reached the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) to still have afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) manifesting within them.

Furthermore, by what reasoning could those non-Buddhist seers be called "those detached from desire" (*vītarāga*) simply because they have abandoned the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
It is not because one has not abandoned the afflictions to be abandoned by insight that one is also said to be "not free from desire.
Furthermore, this principle of interpretation was already demonstrated previously when explaining the *Sukhavihāra-sūtra*.
Therefore, the two types of sūtras cited by him contradict reason and are established as being of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
The Vaibhāṣikas explain those sūtras, saying:
"When he gives rise to [wrong] views, he temporarily regresses from his detachment from desire, just as Devadatta temporarily regressed and then regained it."
If there are only twenty-eight [defilements] that are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), for what reason do various sūtras speak of eighty-eight?
Those texts explain based on a sequential enumeration, whereas this [treatise] relies on the exhaustive principle; therefore, they are not contradictory.
Furthermore, that intention clarifies that the function of the Noble Path is preeminent.

Moreover, even if one has previously abandoned the craving of the lower eight stages, it is necessary to give rise to an untainted attainment (*anāsrava-prāpti*) by means of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because one thereby attains their analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); thus, there is no fault in this statement.
What are the distinct characteristics of those [afflictions] abandoned through seeing and those abandoned through cultivation?

If an affliction is abandoned solely by the wisdom of seeing, it is called "abandoned through seeing"; if an affliction is abandoned by the wisdom of both seeing and cultivation, it is called "abandoned through cultivation."

Thus, there are many such diverse characteristics: whether [defilements] are abandoned instantaneously by means of a single grade or gradually by means of nine grades; whether once abandoned by an Ārya they are never again subject to regression, or whether after being abandoned by an Ārya they may or may not regress; whether their abandonment allows for the realization of four, three, or two fruits, or whether their abandonment allows for the realization of three, two, or one fruit; and whether at the time of abandonment by an Ārya, that non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) must necessarily be realized prior to analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), or whether it is realized before, after, or simultaneously with it. Such categories of differences are numerous.
*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 46. *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 47.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter 5, Part 3: Analysis of the Latent Dispositions (Anuśaya). Regarding the six latent dispositions previously analyzed, the view is divided into five types due to differences in their modes of activity; these names have already been listed. What, then, is their essential nature?
The verse says: Self and what belongs to self, annihilationism and eternalism, Denial of reality, regarding the inferior as superior,
And falsely claiming what is not the cause or path to be so— These are the essential natures of the five views.
The treatise states:
