By the power of causes and teachings, there are foolish persons who, within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), grasp at a self and what belongs to a self; this view is called the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Because it exists, it is called *sat*; "body" (*kāya*) refers to an accumulation, meaning a composite aggregation.
When *kāya* is combined with *sat*, it is termed *satkāya*, which signifies that which is substantially existent and not singular.

This view clings to a self, yet the self truly does not exist; lest this view arise without an object of cognition (*ālambana*), the term "existent" (*sat*) is established for the object of that view.
Furthermore, fearing that one might cling to the existence of a self because of this, the term "body" (*kāya*) is established in turn to refute that clinging.

This refers to those who grasp at a self and conceive of a single self within either one continuum or multiple continua. None of these [conceptions] constitute the body, because the body is not a single entity.

Because such a view takes the *satkāya* (the "perishing collection") as its object, it is called *satkāyadṛṣṭi*; this means that it takes exclusively the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as its object.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world, all those who cling to a self—whatever they perceive and observe—arises solely with respect to the five aggregates of clinging."

For this reason, the Blessed One specifically designated the view of "self" and "what belongs to self" with the term *satkāya* (the existing body). This is so that one does not conclude, on the grounds that a self does not exist, that knowledge can take a non-existent object as its domain; nor that because knowledge takes an existent object, one must hold that the substance of a self is not non-existent. Otherwise, there would be no view directed toward contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena upon which the designation *satkāya* could not be established.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) provides this explanation here:

it is called *sat* because it perishes (*sīdati*); *kāya* means an aggregate (*caya*). Thus, it has the meaning of an impermanent, composite aggregate (*skandha*). Since *kāya* is [equivalent to] *sat*, it is termed *satkāya*.

This *satkāya* is precisely the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*). This name was established to exclude the notion of permanence and unity; for it is only preceded by this notion that one clings to a self.
If that is so, what is the purpose of designating it with the sound *sat*?
Since the term "kāya" (body/aggregate) alone is sufficient to exclude permanence, one should simply establish the name "satkāyadṛṣṭi" (view of a self-identity).
There is no dharma that is both permanent and capable of being aggregated; why, then, is the word "destruction" (*bhaṅga*) applied to the body?

Regarding the objects grasped as "self" and "what belongs to self," to grasp them as either annihilated or eternal is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), because one falsely adheres to the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism.
To give rise to a view that denies the existence of the truths of suffering and so forth, which possess real substance, is called false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

The five kinds of false views all function through inversion and should therefore be termed "false" (*mithyā*); yet, it is only the denial of existence that is specifically called "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), because its fault is most extreme.
This is as when one speaks of "stinking butter," "evil attachment," or "evil [views]," for this [denial] alone involves subtraction (*apavāda*), whereas the others involve addition (*samāropa*).
To regard that which is inferior as superior is called the "adherence to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

That which is contaminated (*sāsrava*) is termed "inferior" because it is to be abandoned by the noble ones (*ārya*); thus, the attachment to the inferior as superior is collectively named the adherence to views.

In reality, the term "adherence to views and so forth" (*dṛṣṭyādiparāmarśa*) should be established; however, for brevity, the word "and so forth" is omitted, and it is simply called the adherence to views.
Because it is the most prominent [of these views], only the term "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is mentioned; this is because "view" is taken as the primary element when grasping the other factors.
Regarding what is not a cause or a path, to view it as a cause or a path—all such instances are collectively termed the "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
That is to say, [some hold that] Maheśvara, time, primordial nature, or something else, are not actually the cause of suffering, yet they falsely give rise to the attachment that they are.
There are two kinds of paths:
first, the path of higher rebirth; second, the path of definitive excellence.
Practicing various wrong conducts such as throwing oneself into water or fire is not a cause for rebirth in heaven; yet to falsely cling to it as a cause is called the first path.

Solely upholding ascetic observances (*śīla-vrata*), the nature of the self (*puruṣa*), or intellectual knowledge (*jñāna*) is not a cause for liberation; yet to falsely cling to these as causes is called the second path.

Just as with the views regarding the past and so forth, or because of the preeminence of [erroneous] vows and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it is therefore established under the name "vows and observances.
One should know that the essential nature of the five views is thus.

If one regards Īśvara and others—which are not causes—as causes, such a view of vows and observances is deluded regarding the meaning of "cause. For what reason is this view not abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*)?
The verse says:
Regarding Maheśvara and others, to falsely cling to what is not a cause as a cause arises from the inversions of permanence and self; therefore, it is abandoned only by the vision of suffering.
The Commentary states:

To regard Īśvara and others as causes when they are not causes is necessarily an inability to observe the profound principle. Rather, one falsely asserts that the coarse resultant phenomena of the aggregates—such as Īśvara and so forth—are permanent, unitary, a self, and an agent; taking these as primary, one then clings to them as the cause. Therefore, this clinging is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

That is to say, the grasping at a self is the view of a personal body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); because one falsely clings to the meaning of the fruit of suffering as being a self, when suffering is realized through direct insight (*abhisamaya*), the view of self is immediately eliminated.

The wisdom of non-self arises not at a subsequent stage; for if the view of a personal body were to be abandoned upon the vision of the origin (*samudaya*) and so forth, then because the view of self would still persist within the continuum, the wisdom of non-self could not arise, since the view of self is extinguished precisely when one perceives only phenomena (*dharma*).

Although the view of self has been eliminated through the arising of the wisdom of non-self, there remains the view of a personal body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which conceives a single self within the continuous stream of phenomena such as the sovereign self; subsequently, one gives rise to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) regarding that same stream of phenomena, calculating it to be eternal.

From this, it should be understood that the two types of clinging—clinging to permanence and to a self—with respect to entities such as Īśvara and the like, are abandoned solely through the vision of suffering.
Thus, a verse says:
"As long as one has not seen suffering as it truly is, one will continue to see those [entities] as a self."
"If one sees suffering as it truly is, one does not see it as a self.

By this, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) has already been shown to be extinguished. For in the school that maintains the doctrine of non-self (*anātman*), the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is subsumed under right view; whereas for those who maintain the doctrine of a self (*ātman*), the view of annihilation is the view of extremes. Thus, it is known that both views are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), because when the various untainted practices (*anāsrava-dharma*) such as impermanence and so forth are seen during the vision of the truth of suffering, both views are extinguished.

Regarding the notion of Ishvara and other such entities as causes when they are not causes, this arises in conjunction with two views and ceases simultaneously with them; therefore, it is said that the adherence to these as causes is abandoned solely by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*).

However, among those who conceive of what is not the path as being the path, if the misconception contradicts the vision of the path and is particularly strong, it is abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga*).

Is it not just as when one reckons Īśvara and others to be the cause, yet adheres to suffering as the cause and allows only its abandonment through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), rather than through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya)? In the same way, when one reckons what is not the path to be the path and adheres to suffering as the path, one should likewise allow only its abandonment through the vision of suffering, rather than through the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya).
This objection is not valid, because viewing the Truth of Suffering as impermanent and so forth is not its antidote.
That is to say, if one holds that Īśvara or other such entities are the cause, one must first conceive of them as being without beginning or end.

This cause is held to be abandoned through the vision of suffering alone, because the perception of impermanence and so forth serves as the antidote to the perception of permanence and so forth. However, at the time of perceiving the truth of suffering as impermanent and so forth, one cannot yet counteract the attachment that conceives what is not the path to be the path; therefore, that attachment to the path is not abandoned through the vision of suffering.
By this, the [wrong views] abandoned through seeing the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) are also excluded, because seeing the cause and so forth is not the antidote to them.

That is to say, when one sees the cause and so forth regarding the origin, one cannot yet counteract the adherence that takes what is not the path to be the path; it is only when one sees the path and so forth regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) that one can counteract that adherence to what is not the path as being the path. Therefore, that adherence to the path should be abandoned through seeing the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).

If that is so, then this kind of adherence to what is not the path must logically also be understood as being abandoned through the vision of the truths of origin and cessation; for example, just as a false view denies the existence of the true path, one subsequently reckons that this very [denial] can lead to purification.
This adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is admitted to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Likewise, when wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) denies the existence of origination (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*), one subsequently regards them as capable of bringing about purification; therefore, those two forms of adherence to rules and observances should be abandoned by the path of seeing origination and cessation.

This objection is not valid, because its essential nature is not established. That is to say, the essential nature of the *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances) is twofold: first, regarding what is not a cause as a cause; second, regarding what is not a path as a path. If one were to hold the view that the false view which slanders the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-mithyādṛṣṭi*) can bring about purification, would this view not lack the function of abandoning origination? Consequently, it should not arise, for there is no mental conviction whatsoever that a cause exists.

Furthermore, since suffering and its origin are not distinct entities, the aggregates such as "sovereignty" (*īśvara*) and so forth should also be negated. If one holds the view that the false view which slanders cessation can lead to purification, would this view not fail to arise unless it possesses the function of realizing cessation?
How can one who denies the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya) later claim that the means for its attainment are not in vain?
Since such a person fails to establish the essential nature of the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) yet asserts that it must exist, their objection is invalid.
How can this be refuted?

It would also follow that the essence of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) could not be established, because after a view that denies the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), one immediately conceives of a path; thus, [the definition] would fail to apply.

This refers to wrong view or doubt directed toward the Truth of the Path—either denying it or doubting whether there is a path to liberation—and how one can then insist that this [denial] can achieve eternal purification.

The essence of this attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not non-existent; for it is admitted that there exists an attachment to the wrong view that slanders the Path, regarding it as the means to realize eternal purification, because that [view] is conceived by them as being understood correctly.
This means that one first retains within the mind another path of liberation, and subsequently clings to the false view that denies the true path as being a correct realization (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).

Regarding "correctly" (*yoniśaḥ*), they claim that their denial of the true path of liberation is non-erroneous; because they consider it correct, they cling to it as the cause of purification, thereby establishing the essence of the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Those other paths of liberation included within that mental aggregate are not the objects of the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because they take only the dharmas of their own category as their objects.
Since there are many types of paths, there is no logical inconsistency.
For this reason, the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) stated:

"If one denies the true path to liberation and falsely clings to some other cause for purification, then this clinging to something else as capable of attaining purification is not [itself] a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth; rather, it takes as its object those phenomena abandoned by the vision of the path (*darśanamārga*)."
This reasoning is also untenable; he has not yet fully understood the tenets of the Abhidharma school.

If that were so, then the essence of the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) would also have to be established, as it is identical in nature to [the clinging to rules and observances] to be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgasatya*).

This means that one first retains another basis for liberation within the mind, and subsequently clings to the false view that denies true liberation as being a correct realization; because it is considered a correct realization, one clings to it as the cause of purification, and its nature as the "clinging to rules and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa) should be established as before.

There is no such principle; for it is logically untenable to calculate that liberation as a whole is permanent and quiescent, and then to cling to the mind that slanders it as the cause of purification—just as it is illogical to calculate whether the essence of nirvāṇa is real or unreal.
That is to say, if one seeks the means for liberation, they must necessarily reckon that liberation exists.
For those who reckon that liberation definitely exists, they must necessarily admit that its essence is eternal and quiescent.
If this were not admitted, one should not seek [the truth].

For example, within the True Dharma, although there are differing views regarding the essence of nirvāṇa—some asserting it is real and others asserting it is unreal—they all equally agree that it is permanent and quiescent; therefore, both types of denial are seen as faults.

Thus, if one harbors other views regarding liberation within the mind, they will necessarily reckon nirvāṇa as eternally quiescent; because of this, they do not grasp the view that slanders liberation as being a correct understanding. Therefore, the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is certainly not to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).

Furthermore, just as Devadatta, while generally accepting the existence of the eternal and quiescent nirvāṇa, nevertheless reckons five separate dharmas as the path to liberation apart from the Eightfold Path;
so too must it be according to reason regarding the calculations of the non-Buddhists.

Therefore, while there may be those who, through the wrong view of slander, claim that the Noble Eightfold Path is "awakening according to reality," there are none who, through slander, claim that cessation (nirvāṇa) is such.

This is because the intrinsic nature and characteristics of ascetic practices and the like differ from the Noble Path; likewise, there is no one who claims that the nature and characteristics of nirvāṇa as eternal tranquility possess any differentiation [from the path]. Consequently, there is no sense in which cessation shares the same meaning as the path.
Other masters say:

There may be the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) based on the false view that takes what is not the path to be the path; however, this is not called the grasping at precepts and observances because it does not claim that "this is the path to their cessation.
Even if one were to hold the false view that takes what is not cessation to be cessation, the claim that "this is the path" would not constitute the grasping at precepts and observances.
To maintain that this is the path to be negated and extinguished is certainly unreasonable, because it is precisely what is being negated as non-existent.
If one maintains that this is the path to another nirvāṇa, then there must be two distinct capacities within a single entity, since seeing this would be the means to attain that [other].

Furthermore, there are no phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of cessation that take phenomena belonging to other categories as their objects; nevertheless, those non-Buddhists must necessarily conceptualize some specific form of suffering as liberation.

Now, one should investigate that which is a non-path yet conceived as a path—namely, the adherence to ascetic rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) as the cause of liberation, or the adherence to the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) as capable of realizing liberation: is this abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), or is it abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*)?

If one maintains that both [types of views] are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), then those to be abandoned through the path of vision (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*) would ultimately not exist at all.

Alternatively, one must state a distinct reason for why the view of what is not the path as being the path (*amārga-mārga-dṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the vision of suffering, while the remaining [views] are abandoned through the vision of the path. What is the basis for this distinction?
If one maintains that both are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one should explain why they are abandoned by the path of seeing;
for it is not at the time of the path of seeing that one can comprehend their object, or comprehend their intrinsic nature, or abandon their objective referent (*ālambana*).

Alternatively, one must acknowledge that the principle of establishing thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) would be undermined; for if the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) could take as their object those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana*), who could prevent the collapse of the established system of thorough knowledge?

For example, at the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, that which is to be abandoned by seeing suffering remains bound by the conditions of that which is to be abandoned by seeing origin; thus, although it has already been permanently abandoned, "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*) is not yet established for it.

In this way, up until the time when the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, that which is to be abandoned by seeing suffering remains bound by the conditions of that which is to be abandoned by the path of seeing; likewise, although it has been abandoned, "complete knowledge" (parijñā) should not yet be established.
However, this is not what is accepted; therefore, the underlying principle should be explained.
Our own school asserts that both [types of views] are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), as stated in the *Śāstra*:
"There are certain non-Buddhists who give rise to such views and establish such doctrines:"

If there were a person or individual who, by observing the cow-vow, the deer-vow, or the dog-vow, would thereby attain purity, liberation, and deliverance, forever transcending all suffering and pleasure and reaching the state beyond suffering and pleasure.

All such types of clinging to what is not a cause as being a cause should be understood as the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), as explained extensively therein.
Furthermore, for what reason are these abandoned through the vision of suffering?

Because [these views] are abandoned only by seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and take such things as the "cow-vow" (*go-yajña*) as their objects, they merely reckon coarse results to be their causes.

By this, the objection raised by the Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtrāntika*)—that there is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because of being deluded regarding the Truth of Suffering—is already refuted; for not all afflictions (*kleśa*) that take the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as their object are deluded regarding suffering, since not every affliction taking the contaminated as its object has the suffering of the result (*phala-duḥkha*) as its objective support (*ālambana*).
How could there be such an excessive error?

It is not that we grant both [the view of self as a real entity and the view of self as a collection] are abandoned through the vision of suffering; rather, it would follow that those abandoned through the vision of the path would be entirely non-existent. This is because there are two types of the "view of what is not the path as the path": first, that which takes upholding of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) as its object, and second, that which takes direct delusion regarding the path as its object.

Taking up precepts and prohibitions (*śīla-vrata*) as an object of focus contradicts the faith that realizes the Path; its power is not equal to that of taking up those who are directly deluded regarding the Path as an object of focus. This is because those who take up precepts and prohibitions have extremely coarse modes of activity, do not follow [the truth] closely, and lack firm intentionality; thus, with little exertion, their practice is immediately severed and extinguished.
The confusion regarding the path due to attachment to kin is the opposite of this.
From this, it should be understood that there are two categories of the "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which take what is not the path to be the path:
first, that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*); second, that which is abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
As previously stated, the view of permanence arises from the inversion of self;
however, are there only these two types of inversion? No, there are four inversions in total:

first, the inversion of grasping at the impermanent as permanent; second, the inversion of grasping at suffering as pleasure; third, the inversion of grasping at the impure as pure; and fourth, the inversion of grasping at the non-self as self.
What is the nature of these four inversions?
The verse says:
The intrinsic nature of the four inversions Is said to arise from three views.
"Because they are established solely by way of inverted reasoning and because perception and mind follow the power of views.

The commentary states: "The four inversions are established from among the three views. That is to say, from within the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), only the eternalist view is taken as the inversion of permanence; from among the views of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), those that conceive of pleasure and purity are taken as the inversions of pleasure and purity; and from within the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), only the view of self is taken as the inversion of self. This which has been explained is the tenet of one master."

However, according to the definitive meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*, when distinguishing among the twelve views by way of their categories, only two and a half views constitute the essence of perversion (*viparyāsa*).

These are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) in their entirety; and from the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the portion that clings to permanence. Since the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the views of eternalism and nihilism are mutually contradictory, it can be said that these two entities are distinct.
All those who propound theories of a self grasp at the notion that the self possesses sovereign power over those [aggregates]; this is the view of "mine," which thus functions through two doors.
Is it not the case that since all afflictions function as distortions, they should all be considered inversions (*viparyāsa*), rather than being limited to only four types?
Not so; for the characteristics of the perversions are established as distinct.
What are these characteristics of perversion?
They consist in possessing three causes.
What are the three causes? They are:
being consistently inverted, having the nature of conceptualization, and falsely superimposing [attributes].
The inclusion of the term "increase" (*adhi*) also indicates that the essence [of these views] is particularly predominant.

No other afflictions possess these three causes; that is to say, the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not exclusively a perverted conception, as it may involve the capacity to leave behind desire-taint (*kāmarāga*) and the like, and because one may attain purification during moments of slight discernment.

The view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) do not involve false superimposition (*samāropa*), because these two operate through the door of negating existing things; the "view-grasping" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) of other schools does not constitute a superior excellence; and the remaining afflictions do not involve inferential deliberation (*tarka*).
For this reason, there are only four inversions and no others.
But is it not stated in the Sūtras that inversions are collectively twelve in number? As the Sūtra says:
"Regarding the impermanent as permanent, there are inversions of perception, mind, and view."
The same applies to [the perversions] regarding suffering, impurity, and non-self.
It is not so, for perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) do not involve inferential deliberation (*tarka*).

Furthermore, they are designated as "perversions" by virtue of the power of the perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*), because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are identical to that of view with which they are associated.
However, sensations (*vedanā*) and the other [aggregates] cannot be designated as "perversions" in the same way that perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) can, because there is a distinct reason.

That is to say, when one gives rise to views such as permanence regarding what is impermanent, it must necessarily involve grasping the characteristic of permanence within the object; and that which grasps the characteristic is perception, and nothing else. Therefore, the designation "perversion" is applied to perception, but not to sensation and the others.

Furthermore, the term "perception" (saṃjñā) is also applied to the remediation of inverted wisdom; that is to say, within the mental applications such as impermanence, they are referred to as the "perception of impermanence" and so forth. This is because wisdom and perception mutually support one another in close proximity, and thus the name is established by following their association. This is not the case for feeling (vedanā) and the other [mental factors].
Due to the power of its basis, there is an increase in inverted reasoning; because it apprehends the characteristics of objects as established, the mind is called "inverted. As a sūtra says:
"The mind leads the world, causing it to drift and drown everywhere in the torrential flood of afflictions."
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
Only perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) can be designated as "perversions" (*viparyāsa*), because this is universally established in the world.

That is to say, the perversions of mind and perception are universally established in the world, whereas feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] are not; therefore, the Sūtra does not mention them.
Based on this, the designation "perversion" (*viparyāsa*) is established for perception and thought due to the power of the perversion of view, but not for feeling and the other aggregates.
Regarding this, the Venerable Sthavira asks:
"For what reason are there exactly three perversions, neither more nor less?"
There are only that many [factors] that can be established as perversions.

That is to say, these three perversions comprise: the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), which subsumes perception; the perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), which subsumes consciousness (*vijñāna*); and the perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*), which subsumes mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
It cannot be said that feeling (*vedanā*) is also subsumed under the perversions, because it arises with contact (*sparśa*) as its cause and is experienced according to its specific nature.
Is it not the case that there are other factors, such as mental attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth, within the aggregates?

Why would those not be erroneous? It is not so; rather, it is solely because of that [erroneous] inversion that the perception, thought, and view become the substance of inversion. Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"All immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas arise with irrational mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) as their root," and so on at length, until: "All are produced by mental attention, and contact (*sparśa*) is their origin."

From this it is proven that the inversions of perception, mind, and view are all produced by unwise attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*); because they are inverted by those [causes], they constitute the essence of inversion.
Now, observing that his previous and subsequent statements are contradictory, one must certainly know that this is not the meaning of the *sūtra*.
If you claim that the mind and its perceptions arise from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and the like, and because they are inverted, they constitute the essence of inversion;
yet, since feeling (*vedanā*) also arises from improper mental attention and the like, for what reason is it not itself an inversion?

If feeling arises from erroneous attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and so forth, yet is not itself erroneous, then the three—perception (*saṃjñā*), mind (*citta*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*)—should likewise not be of an erroneous nature, as there would be no distinct cause [for their being erroneous].

Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that feeling is also subsumed under the category of error, because it arises with contact (*sparśa*) as its cause and is experienced according to its specific character.

Is it not the case that perception (*saṃjñā*) would likewise fail to be established as inverted? For perception arises with contact (*sparśa*) as its cause, just as it should be according to [the nature of] perception.

Since it is taught that inversions of perception and so forth are produced by the contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*), does this not mean that because contact is the cause, and because one experiences [objects] accordingly, it serves all the more to prove that the essence of feeling (*vedanā*) is subsumed under inversion?
Since feeling (*vedanā*) is also produced by contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*),
what they have said— that only that many [factors] need to be established as perversions (*viparyāsa*), and thus there are exactly three perversions neither more nor less— is rendered meaningless.

Furthermore, if it were by the power of improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) that perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth become inverted, then improper mental attention itself should also be inverted; yet this has never been stated. Therefore, what they say arises from their own dogmatic attachments.

If one were to grant that their nature is inverted while yet not stating them to be the substance of inversion, then mental constructions (*saṃjñā*) and so forth would likewise not be called inversions; this would contradict the sūtra’s designation of the name "inversion."

If it is argued that, just as for you, because there is a distinct cause, although all minds and mental factors possess the quality of perversion by the power of [wrong] view, the Sūtra mentions only the perversions of perception and mind, and not those of feeling and the others.
My school’s position is likewise; for this very reason, it is certain that the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) and so forth are not erroneous.
Alternatively, if others were to claim they are erroneous, it would entail the fault of contradicting the sūtras.
This too is irrational, because [the cases] are not analogous.

That is to say, according to our school, although both the mind and mental factors possess the nature of perversion due to the power of views, it is only for the perception (*saṃjñā*) and the mind (*citta*) that the designation "perversion" is established because of specific causes, and not for feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [factors].

However, since the name "inverted" is correctly applied based on that which causes the perception, so too in your own school, because the power of attention (manasikāra) causes the mind and mental factors to possess the quality of being inverted, that attention itself should be designated as "inverted."

Furthermore, in our school, the intrinsic nature of perception and so forth is not erroneous; it is only through the power of [false] views that they are conventionally designated by the name "erroneous. The term "true error" refers to that which is produced by those views.

Your school should also be like this: by the power of mental attention (*manasikāra*), perception and so forth are in reality not erroneous, yet the name "error" is conventionally established for them.

Thus, the designation "inversion" is applied based on the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) that constitutes its basis; it should not be the case that the power of non-inverted phenomena causes other non-inverted phenomena to receive the name "inversion."
Furthermore, why not allow that the power of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) can cause mental attention (*manasikāra*) to become inverted in its nature?
It is only through the power of grasping signs (*nimittodgrahaṇa*) by means of conceptualization that innate (*sahaja*) irrational attention arises; therefore, the Sūtra says:
"By the power of grasping signs, it causes the arising of greed and other evil, unwholesome dharmas."
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"The mind becomes feverish due to the perversion of perception (saṃjñā-viparyāsa).
It does not say that the heat of the mind arises from improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manasikāra).

Furthermore, by the power of the predominance of the perversion, it stands to reason that the very essence of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) should also be called "perverted. It is not logical for attention (*manasikāra*) to be the predominant factor of perversion while perception and the others are subordinate; why then do you say only that perception and the others become perverted through the power of attention, rather than saying that the power of perception and the others can cause attention to become perverted?
Therefore, what they say relies solely on their own dogmatic attachments.

Furthermore, the Sūtras also state that desire (*chanda*) is the root of all phenomena, or that afflictions and ignorance (*avidyā*) are the roots; why then do they not say that by the power of those [afflictions], perception (*saṃjñā*) and the other [mental factors] also become inverted, but instead claim that inversion is established only through attention (*manasikāra*)?
Therefore, one should know that establishing the essence of the perversions (*viparyāsa*) based on the principles of the Abhidharma is most excellent.
As for what these various perversions are to be abandoned,
the proponents of the *Nyāyānusāra* state:

They are abandoned only by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), because the perversions such as the notion of permanence operate only with respect to suffering; because the cognitions of impermanence and so forth arise only by taking suffering as their object; and because one should not have to abandon the views of permanence, bliss, self, and purity only later at the time of seeing the origin, cessation, and path.
If that were so, it would contradict the correct principles of the sūtras and śāstras.
First, regarding the contradiction with the sūtras:

a sūtra states, "When a learned noble disciple perceives and knows the noble truth of suffering as it really is, and likewise perceives and knows the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as they really are, at that time that noble disciple has forever abandoned the inversion of perception, thought, and view that conceives the impermanent to be permanent," and so forth, as explained at length.

If all perversions were abandoned solely through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*), the Sūtra should not state that they are all permanently abandoned at the time one sees and knows the truths of origin (*samudaya*) and so forth as they truly are.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:

"If, having heard the Tathāgata teach the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—one is then able to permanently abandon the four perversions, such as [the view of] permanence and so forth."

It is not the case that all perversions are abandoned solely by the vision of suffering; for if they were, the Buddha would have taught that the other three [perversions]—those associated with the origin and so forth—are abandoned by the vision of the origin and so on, yet these are not their remedies.
Furthermore, Ānanda said to Prajñākūṭa:
"Because of the perversity of your perceptions, Your mind is consumed by feverish distress."
"Having distanced oneself from those perceptions, craving ceases and the mind becomes pure.
Regarding those who speak in contradiction to the treatise, as the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"Among these four perversions, how many have been abandoned and how many remain unabandoned by stream-enterers?"
One should say: "All have been abandoned.

If the four inversions were abandoned solely through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), then those who practice by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) would also have already abandoned them; why, then, is it said that only the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) has abandoned them?
Regarding those who contradict correct reasoning: if a noble one who has not yet abandoned desire were to abandon the perception of pleasure and purity, how could desire-attachment arise?
In our own school, there is no contradiction or harm regarding these three points.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the first sutra as I see it: when a noble disciple attains the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths, the four inversions accumulated since beginningless time are all permanently severed. However, one cannot thereby conclude that each and every inversion is abandoned through the vision of each of the Four Truths.

It has already been established that the two views of self and what belongs to self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) constitute the essence of the misconceptions of permanence and self; since these are subsumed within the view of self and what belongs to self, how could misconceptions of permanence and self regarding the origin [of suffering] and so forth be abandoned by seeing the origin?
However, in this sutra, it is stated that for one who has realized the truths (dṛṣṭasatya), [the defilements] are already "permanently abandoned" (*atyantaprahīṇa*).

What contradiction is there in this? As for the second sutra, there is no contradiction; it is not that the Blessed One taught the Dharma of the Four Truths solely for the purpose of abandonment. Rather, these four types of inversions (*viparyāsa*) are intended collectively for the ultimate cessation of all suffering. Nevertheless, there are those who, having heard [this teaching], permanently abandon the four inversions through the power of their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*). What contradiction is there in this?
In truth, this must be so; therefore, that sutra says:
"When the Buddha taught this Dharma for the sake of the eternal cessation of all suffering, those who heard it realized its reality: impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity."
The four inversions do not encompass all suffering; therefore, one should know that the meaning of that sūtra is as I have explained it.
Furthermore, that sūtra states:

"If sentient beings cause their minds to be inverted by these four kinds of inversion of perception, mind, and view, their minds will then become deluded with respect to this or that," and so on at length.
In this context, it may be said that the mind is deranged by the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) and the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*), because they are associated with the mind.
But how can an inversion of the mind itself cause the mind to be deranged?
Therefore, one should examine the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) of that sūtra; it must not be grasped as a definitive basis according to its literal expression.
The cited verse does not contradict the principles of the Abhidharma. Why is this so?
It is not our claim that perception is unconfused and non-perverted because it is obscured by sensual desire; rather, we say this:
Not all forms of confusion (*vyākula*) are termed "perversion" (*viparyāsa*).

This is because only those instances where confusion occurs in conjunction with a perverted view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*), such that perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) are likewise confused, are designated as "perversions.
If every form of confusion were to constitute a perversion, then all afflictions (*kleśa*) would necessarily be perversions.
When the Arhats travel along the streets, their minds become confused and deluded by the power of distorted perceptions (*viparyāsa*).

For instance, due to distorted perception, they may see a rope and mistake it for a snake; thus, within the category of distorted perception, only a small portion is established as "perversion" (*viparyāsa*). This is because the name "perversion" is applied only to that which is most predominant, and the most predominant causes and conditions have already been explained previously. Therefore, when a defiled perception (*kliṣṭa-saṃjñā*) manifests in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), why would it be contradictory or harmful to not designate it by the name "perversion"?

Furthermore, the fact that the sūtras do not state that those who possess mastery of eloquence (*pratibhāna-vaśitā*) are definitively established in the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*) does not constitute a valid proof [that they are non-returners].

When the treatise states that stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) have already abandoned the perversions (*viparyāsa*), it speaks thus for the purpose of removing doubt; it is so that those in the world who see a stream-enterer adorning their body with flowers, perfuming their robes with incense, hoarding precious wealth, indulging in lust, and relishing flavors, might not suspect that their perversions have not yet been entirely eliminated, [thinking] instead that such actions are performed because the mind is shrouded by ignorance.
To eliminate such doubts held by the world, it is said that the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) has already severed all perversions (*viparyāsa*).

Alternatively, while for the stream-enterer there is no distinction regarding what has been severed, among those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), some have severed them while others have not; because it is certain that [the stream-enterer] has severed them, he is designated as a "stream-enterer."
There is no contradiction with the *Nyāya*.

As explained in the *Gāthā*, there would otherwise be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): why not say that even for the noble ones (*ārya*), the notion of "I" (*ātma-saṃjñā*) still arises? For it is not the case that desire and greed (*kāmarāga*) arise toward women and so forth, or toward oneself, while one is free from the notion of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*).
One should not admit that a noble one possesses a mind characterized by the notion of a self (*ātman*), because knowledge of the mere dharmas has already arisen.
For this reason, such inversions are abandoned solely through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). The Vibhajyavādins speak as follows:
The inversions of permanence, self, pleasure, and purity—each consisting of three types—are eight inversions that are abandoned solely by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Four are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*, namely: the notions and cognitions of pleasure and purity.
This has been refuted according to the reasoning explained previously regarding the verse; therefore, what he says relies solely on false conceptualization.
That Sthavira states:

"For those who have attained the stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭiviparyāsa*) is entirely abandoned, while the inversions of thought and perception (*saṃjñā-cittaviparyāsa*) remain."
Afflictions cannot function for one who has not forgotten the perception of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity; therefore, the *Sukha-sūtra* states:
"The noble ones are at peace, and they speak thus:
'Among form and the other aggregates, I do not adhere to them as a self.'"

Nevertheless, because the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of pride and craving regarding these five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*) have not been severed, we know that noble ones (*ārya*) possess a mind that conceives of a self.
By analogy, it is certain that they likewise possess [the notions of] permanence, pleasure, and purity.
This statement by the Elder contradicts his own intended meaning, contradicts the sūtras, and contradicts reason; it is therefore not to be trusted or relied upon.

Regarding the claim that his explanation contradicts his own intended meaning: first, he himself explains the cause for the inversion of the sūtra, stating that it was "for the sake of those who are deluded regarding the principles of the sequence of saṃsāra and its cessation," desiring to enable them to understand it without error.

Therefore, it is said that for such a person who has not yet thoroughly understood the principle of the Four Noble Truths, who has already established a boundary regarding the various cycles of birth and death, and for whom only a very small remainder of afflictive obstructions remains—such that they are on the verge of attaining nirvāṇa as if it were held in the palm of their hand—if they possess such virtues, how could they be deluded regarding the sequence of the principles of saṃsāra and its cessation, or give rise to inverted views? For the illumination of noble wisdom dwells within them.
Furthermore, while he himself was debating the nature of the various perversions, he asked:
"What kind of view constitutes the essence of the perversion of views?
He then answered himself:
Furthermore, regarding suffering as pleasure and the impure as pure, its essence is false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
It further asks itself:
"Is it not the case that false view denies the existence of giving, and so forth," as explained at length.
He replied to himself:
"If one reckons saṃsāra as pleasant and pure, one must certainly deny the existence of true arhats who have attained right realization and right practice.

Does this statement not clearly show that since the noble ones harbor conceptions of pleasure and purity regarding saṃsāra, they must necessarily possess the active presence of false conceptions that deny the right realization and right practice of the arhats?"
If it is argued that noble ones lack wrong perception because they have abandoned wrong view, then noble ones should likewise lack perverted perception because they have abandoned perverted views.
As for the claim that this contradicts the sūtras, it refers to the statement in the *Sūtra*:
"Perverted perception, mind, and view are all abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*)."
Two sūtras prove this point, as fully cited previously.

If it is argued that these eight perceptions involve a perversion of mind, and that within the stage of cultivation they can only be permanently severed through the actual seeing and knowing of the Noble Truths—since there is no other means for permanent severance apart from this, and thus what has been stated here does not contradict the sūtras—then do you not see that the [wrong] views should likewise be subject to that same position? For they too are described as being abandoned by the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), just like these perceptions and minds.

If it is argued that because other sūtras exclude the view-erroneousness from being abandoned through cultivation, one must therefore maintain that only the two inversions of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) are abandoned through cultivation—how can you not admit that when the inversion of view is removed, the perception and mind are no longer inverted, given that other sūtras state that these three—perception, mind, and view—collectively possess the four inversions?
If it is argued that the Sūtra states that noble learners (*śaikṣa*) possess perverted perceptions (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), this has already been explained previously.
What was explained previously?

It was that not all perversions are termed "inversions" (*viparyāsa*), or that the aforementioned Sūtra does not intend to establish that those in the stage of learning (*śaikṣāvasthā*) necessarily possess mastery over discernment (*pratisaṃvid*).

Regarding the claim that this contradicts reason: when noble learners (*śaikṣa*) experience objects for the sake of seeking pleasure, although the truth of reality (*satya*)—namely, pleasure and purity—is absent within those objects, there exists a phenomenal pleasure and purity capable of inducing perceptions and thoughts of such pleasure and purity; thus, it is permissible for thoughts and minds of pleasure and purity to arise in these noble ones.
However, within the mass of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which entirely lack permanence and self, how could thoughts and minds of permanence and self possibly arise?
Do the inversions of pleasure and purity arise based on an existent entity or based on a non-existent entity?
As for the two inversions of permanence and self, they are subsumed under the ultimate truth because of the existence of pleasant feeling; this meaning is certain, as will be explained later.
Within contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), there is a small portion that is pure, because the *Sūtra* states that there are three types of pure karma.
Furthermore, the object of the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*) is taught in the *Sūtra*.
Moreover, pleasure and purity exist as real entities, as this is universally established in the world.

Within the aggregates of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), whether in terms of their factual substance or their underlying principle, no permanent self (*ātman*) or substantial entity can ever be found. Therefore, those who have not yet seen the Truth give rise to the perversions of mind and view by falsely conceiving of permanence and a self within these conditioned phenomena. Furthermore, by relying on even a slight degree of pleasure or purity among these phenomena, they invariably grasp them as being truly and substantially pleasant and pure; thus, the perversions of mind and view consisting of the notions of pleasure and purity are established.

Since those who have already seen the Truths perceive that within the aggregate of formations there is ultimately no permanence or self, they will certainly never again give rise to thoughts of permanence or self.

From this, it should be understood that the two perversions of permanence and self do not exist at all within the continuum of a Noble One (*ārya*). As for the notions and thoughts of pleasure and purity, because they rely upon existing entities, they may still manifest within the continuum of a Noble One; some of these are termed "confused" while others are not termed "perversion," because perversion arises solely from conceptual construction that is deluded regarding the principles [of reality].

However, the *Anvaya-sūtra* cited by him cannot prove that the noble ones possess a perverted mind regarding the notion of a permanent self; thus, it fails to establish the meaning of perversion as previously argued.

Upon such a detailed examination of the Sthavira’s assertions, they are found to be in no way inconsistent with the principles of the Noble Teaching; therefore, what he has said is not to be trusted or relied upon.
Having already explained the distinct characteristics of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) according to their views, one might ask: "Are there other distinctions as well?
Yes, there are. What are they?"
The verse says:
The seven types of pride and nine [afflictions] arise from the three [roots]; All are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation.
Just as with the fetters of killing and so forth, there are those abandoned through cultivation that do not manifest in the Noble Ones.
The treatise states:
There are those who, being deluded, first compare themselves with others regarding what exists and what does not exist; when their minds become uplifted as a result, this is termed pride (*māna*).
Based on their modes of operation, they are divided into seven types:
first, pride; second, excessive pride; third, pride beyond pride; fourth, the pride of "I am"; fifth, overweening pride; sixth, inferiority pride; and seventh, false pride.
Regarding those of inferior or equal lineage, social circle, and so forth, to consider oneself superior or equal is called pride (*māna*).
One might object: "Since these two [types of pride] operate in accordance with reality regarding their objects, they should not constitute pride."
To claim superiority when one is inferior, or equality when one is equal, is known through measurement and comparison; how could this constitute the pride of conceit (*māna*)?
When the mind gives rise to attachment toward an agreeable object, it functions in accordance with reality; how, then, could this constitute greed (*lobha*)?
Since this involves seeking after objects that are agreeable to one's mind and lacks any inversion, it should not be considered an affliction (*kleśa*).

However, because it arises from this [seeking] and is able to defile and distress the mind, and since it is admitted to constitute greed (*lobha*), which is of the nature of an affliction—likewise, although it actually arises in relation to superior or inferior objects, its ability to cause the mind to become haughty and defiled is termed the affliction of pride (*māna*); what logical flaw is there in this?
Therefore, the general characteristics of pride (*māna*) have been briefly explained above.

Pride can arise with respect to both existence (*bhava*) and non-existence (*vibhava*); this is just as anger (*dveṣa*) is designated by the same name whether it arises toward what is possible (*sthāna*) or what is impossible (*asthāna*).
To consider oneself superior or equal among others who are one's equals or superiors in terms of lineage, social circle, and so forth, is called *abhimāna* (conceit).
To consider oneself superior to others who are actually far more distinguished than oneself in terms of lineage, social circle, and so forth, is called *mānātimāna* (excessive conceit).
When one clings to the five aggregates of grasping as "I" and "mine," the mind becomes uplifted; this is called *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am").

From this it is proven that the two perversions of the notion of "I" and the mind can exist only when the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has not been diminished, and not when it has been diminished.
Regarding the superior attainments such as the paths, grounds, and abandonments that have not yet been realized, to claim they have already been realized is called "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).
What is the distinction between the terms "not having attained" and "having attained"?
Because there is no difference in meaning between "prior acquisition" and "subsequent acquisition," this statement is intended to clarify the acquisition of qualities not yet acquired.
Furthermore, it is accepted by our own school that there is an acquisition of acquisition.

When those, whether householders or renunciants, perceive themselves as slightly inferior to others who possess a great abundance of qualities such as craftsmanship or ethical discipline (*śīla*), yet give rise to a mind of haughtiness, this is called "inferior conceit" (*ūnamāna*).

In this context, one who is haughty toward oneself considers others to be mostly superior while considering oneself to be inferior; because it involves exalting oneself, it is also called "haughtiness" (*māna*).
Other masters state:
when one lacks confidence in one's own capacity and considers oneself inferior, it is termed "inferiority-pride" (*ūnamāna*).
Thus, what is called "inferiority" fails to achieve loftiness; therefore, one should know that what was previously explained is superior.
To claim for oneself virtues that one does not possess is termed "false pride" (*mithyāmāna*).

That which is called "lack of virtue" refers to various unwholesome actions; it is designated by the name "lack of virtue" because it contradicts virtuous qualities, just as [the term] "unwholesome" (akuśala) is used.

When one regards oneself as possessing such distinguished virtues while actually accomplishing these dharmas of lack of virtue, and thus becomes haughty and arrogant based on those evils, it is therefore called "false pride" (mithyāmāna).
If one claims that the term "lacking virtue" is a negation of "possessing virtue," yet asserts its existence within that which actually lacks virtue, this is called *mithyāmāna* (false pride).

In his explanation of the distinction between *adhimāna* (exaggerated pride) and *mithyāmāna*, he states that what is devoid of seeds is called *adhimāna*, whereas that which possesses seeds is called *mithyāmāna*.

Alternatively, if one were to claim that exaggerating [the qualities] in their entirety constitutes *adhimāna* (conceit), while exaggerating them only partially constitutes *mithyāmāna* (false conceit), such a distinction would logically be untenable; therefore, it should be understood that the previous explanation is superior.

Some say: With the exception of the views of self and what belongs to self (*ātma-ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*), that which is produced preceded by other wrong views and causes the mind to become uplifted is called "wrong pride" (*mithyāmāna*).
Other masters say:
To harbor a sense of superiority based on possessing actual accomplishments is called pride (*māna*).
To harbor a sense of superiority in one's mind based on possessing only minor accomplishments is called excessive pride (*atimāna*).
To harbor a sense of superiority in one's mind based on possessing no accomplishments at all is called pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*).

Preceded by self-love (*ātmasneha*) toward the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), the act of exalting oneself based on this sense of "I" is called the pride of "I-am-ness" (*asmimāna*).
To claim that one has realized many qualities when one has only realized a few, resulting in a state of mental exaltation, is called overweening pride (*abhimāna*).
To grasp at minor matters and consider them sufficient, then to rely on this and become arrogant, is called "inferior pride" (*ūnamāna*).
To be of truly base and evil nature yet to claim for oneself the possession of virtue, with the mind becoming uplifted and arrogant, is called "false pride" (*mithyāmāna*).

However, the root treatise states that there are nine types of pride (*māna*). "Type" (*prakāra*) here means category, referring to the specific distinctions of pride. What are these nine types? First, the type of pride thinking "I am superior";

second, the type of pride thinking "I am equal"; third, the type of pride thinking "I am inferior"; fourth, the type of pride thinking "There is someone superior to me"; fifth, the type of pride thinking "There is someone equal to me"; sixth, the type of pride thinking "There is someone inferior to me"; seventh, the type of pride thinking "There is no one superior to me"; eighth, the type of pride thinking "There is no one equal to me"; and ninth, the type of pride thinking "There is no one inferior to me."

These nine all arise based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). "I am superior" is a type of excessive pride (*atimāna*); "I am equal" is a type of pride (*māna*); "I am inferior" is a type of inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*). "There is one superior to me" is a type of inferiority pride; "there is one equal to me" is a type of pride; "there is one inferior to me" is a type of excessive pride. "There is no one superior to me" is a type of pride; "there is no one equal to me" is a type of excessive pride; "there is no one inferior to me" is a type of inferiority pride.

Therefore, these nine [types of pride] arise from three: namely, pride (*māna*), over-pride (*atimāna*), and inferiority-pride (*ūnamāna*). Due to differences in their modes of operation, they form three sets of three.
How can the class of "I-am-not-inferior" pride (*asmimāna*) be established as a form of exaltation?

This refers to one who, regarding a superior assembly of sentient beings whom they themselves desire, knows their own person to be extremely inferior, yet regards themselves with self-importance as if presenting an auspicious omen.

Or there may be a caṇḍāla; although he himself knows that he is universally despised by the world, when presenting auspicious signs or performing his duties, he becomes arrogant because he holds himself in high esteem.
Regarding these seven types of pride, by what are they abandoned?
Other masters state:

the pride of self (asmimāna) and false pride (mithyāmāna) are abandoned only through the path of seeing (darśana-heya), while the remaining ones are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
In reality, one should say that all seven [types of conceit] pertain to both [the past and the future]; therefore, one can safely state:
"I do not adhere to a self within form and the other aggregates.

Nevertheless, within these five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of self-conceit (*asmimāna*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) have not yet been abandoned; that is to say, as long as they have not been abandoned by the Noble One through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they are certain to manifest.

This is not fixed; that is to say, there are cases where [defilements] have already been abandoned yet can still manifest, such as the eye-faculty of one who has already become free from desire for sense-pleasures, or the latent tendencies toward suffering.

Conversely, there are cases where [defilements] have not yet been abandoned but certainly do not manifest, such as the fetter of killing in a noble one who has not yet become free from desire for sense-pleasures.
Regarding the "fetter of killing" (*vadhaparyavasthāna*): it refers to the intentional thought (*saṃcetanīya-citta*) that is initiated by this fetter to take the life of a living being.
The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes stealing and sexual misconduct.
The fetter of deception (*māyāparyavasthāna*) consists entirely of craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) and a portion of craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*).
What dharma is called "craving for non-existence" (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*)?
It refers to the craving for the impermanence of the three realms; this is termed craving for non-existence.
By this, craving for the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) impermanence is excluded, because that [uncontaminated state] is certainly not a basis for the satisfaction of craving.
There is one portion of craving, namely the wish to become the Great Nāga King Elāpattra and so forth.
The phrase "and so forth" is intended to include the Asura kings, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, the beings of the Unconscious Heaven, and others.
Although these fetters of killing (*vadhaparyavasthāna*) and so forth are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they certainly do not manifest in the noble ones (*ārya*).
To state that those abandoned through cultivation do not manifest would be redundant, because it will be explained later that while the noble ones possess them, they do not arise.
If there were the possibility for [defilements] to manifest within the body of an Arya, then the statement that they do not arise would be a purposeful one.
However, since there are no defilements to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) present in the body of an Arya that could possibly manifest, there is no need for further prohibition.
Since [the point] has already been established and the meanings of abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and non-occurrence are already known, why trouble oneself by stating it in advance?

If you argue that because pride was previously stated to pertain to both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation, the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) such as killing should likewise pertain to abandonment through seeing rather than cultivation, we reply: no. *Note: This translation assumes the context of Abhidharma scholasticism, specifically the classification of afflictions according to their mode of abandonment.*
This is also not the case, because the mention of the "fetters of killing" (*vadhakasaṃyojana*) and so forth already excludes those abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, the meaning can be understood from the subsequent explanation: for instance, the types of pride (*māna-jāti*) and so forth are increased by [the views].
Therefore, these words should apply only to the dharmas.
Furthermore, the commentary states:
"Because all these envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and cravings (*tṛṣṇā*) take as their objects only those things abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)."

The claim that [the object] is abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is not a definitive reason, because that which is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) can also take dharmas abandoned by cultivation as its object.
If one provides this interpretation—understanding that the term "only" (*kevala*) is implied—then this reason can serve as a definitive proof.
Is it not seen that what is abandoned by insight is also impermanent? Why, then, is craving abandoned only through cultivation?
In reality, it is also abandoned by insight; this is merely stated here in accordance with the Sūtra.

It refers to what is taught in the Sūtras regarding the three types of craving: craving for sensory existence (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).

In this sūtra, when craving for non-existence is said to take the impermanence of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) as its object, it is because one greedily seeks the cessation of the continuity of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
As a sutra states:
"A certain class of beings, oppressed by suffering, thinks thus:
'May I, after death, be annihilated and cease to exist; how wonderful it would be to be free from illness and suffering!'"
For now, based on this, it is said that [craving] is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and not through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
As previously stated, there is no craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*).

Regarding the types of pride (*māna*), the pride of self (*asmimāna*) is abandoned through cultivation; since noble ones (*ārya*) still possess it, its status as being abandoned through cultivation is established even without being explicitly stated.
For what reason do these [defilements] still exist in noble ones (*ārya*) yet not manifest?
The verse says:
The types of pride and the like, as well as self-pride (*asmimāna*), And the unwholesome among the regretful states (*kaukṛtya*).
The noble ones do not give rise [to existence], because they have eliminated the increase of doubt.
The commentary states:

The word "etc. is used to indicate the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) such as killing, the entirety of craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*), and a portion of craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*). This is because the noble ones have well-cultivated emptiness and correctly understand the principle that karma and its fruits are invariably connected.
These types of conceit, such as the conceit "I am equal," and bad regret, do not manifest even though they have not yet been abandoned by the noble ones;
furthermore, because these are closely augmented by views and doubt, they no longer manifest once views and doubt have been abandoned.

That is to say, the varieties of pride and the conceit "I am" are augmented by the view of a self-identity; the fetters such as killing are augmented by wrong view; all forms of craving for non-existence are augmented by the view of annihilationism; one portion of craving for existence is augmented by the view of eternalism; and unwholesome regret is augmented by doubt. Therefore, although these may not yet have been abandoned within the continuum of an Ārya, they are certainly never activated because they have been broken and overturned.
The Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle 47 [and] Fascicle 48, composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Five, Part Four: The Analysis of the Latent Dispositions (Anuśaya). Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions, how many are universal (sarvatraga) and how many are not universal?
The verse says:
Those associated with views and doubt, as well as the unique ignorance, which are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, are pervasive within their own realm and stage.
Among these, excluding two views, the remaining nine can take the higher realms as their object;
excluding acquisition (*prāpti*), the remaining concomitants (*anuvartin*) are also subsumed under the universal [factors].
The treatise says:
Only those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin have the power to function as universal; however, this does not apply to all of them.
Specifically, it refers only to the various views, doubt, and their associated or independent ignorance (*avidyā*), but not to others such as attachment (*rāga*).

There are seven views (*dṛṣṭi*) and two doubts (*vicikitsā*); the ignorance associated (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*) with them is subsumed under those, while there are two types of non-associated (*asādhāraṇa*) ignorance; thus, they constitute eleven.
These eleven are each able to function as universal (*sarvatraga*) throughout the five categories (*pañca-varga*) of their own respective realm and stage (*dhātu-bhūmi*).

This means that among the five categories of phenomena within one's own realm and stage, those which arise as defilement with universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) as their cause are designated by the name "universal" (*sarvatraga*).
To speak briefly in terms of the realms, thirty-three such factors are universal.
However, there is a teacher who says:
"Of the thirty-three [types of ignorance], twenty-seven are pervasive; the remaining six should be analyzed.

That teacher has exerted his efforts in vain here, for he fails to establish the principle of what is pervasive and what is non-pervasive regarding associated ignorance, just as it applies to the afflictions with which it is associated.

Therefore, the specific enumeration given here refers to the uncommon ignorance that arises through its own power; it does not include this ignorance which is abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin and is not universal. Consequently, it is stated that only thirty-three are universal.
This explanation is excellent.
Based on what meaning is this designation "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) established?
According to this explanation, that which is mixed is called "shared"; because it is not shared, the name "unshared" is established, which means that each [of the two] is distinct from the other.
As stated in the sūtra:
"The Buddha and the Saṃgha are not shared.
This reveals that the two jewels of the Buddha and the Saṃgha are distinct from one another.
Because it functions independently, it is called "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikī avidyā*); it is not so called because it is mixed with other latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Alternatively, the term "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*) means "universal" (*vyāpin*); since this [ignorance] is not shared, it is established by the name "unshared."

This "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) designation indicates that it is not common [to all]; that is to say, it does not pervade all afflictions, because it is not associated with the other latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Other masters state:
it is called "unshared" because it has no connection with other afflictions; that is to say, its meaning is being heavy (*styāna*) and immovable (*aniñjya*).
Because associated ignorance is conjoined with other afflictions, its characteristics involve agitation;

non-associated ignorance, however, arises by its own power and has no desire to engage in any activities, being heavy and unshakable like the *śaṇḍhasa* disease—therefore, it is called non-associated ignorance.

For what reason do only those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) possess universal pervasion (*sarvatraga*)?

It is because only these universally take all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as their object; since their underlying intention is undifferentiated and their power is firm, they are able to act as causes that universally produce [defilements] across all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*).

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path have as their objects only a portion of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas; because their objects are distinct and their force is not firm, they cannot serve as causes to universally produce [defilements] across all five categories.
Therefore, only the first two categories possess universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
By what means is this known?
Because defiled phenomena abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) have as their cause those universal [defilements] abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*).
How is it that this is not understood?
It is because we see in the world those who possess the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), and by the power of this view, craving for external objects increases;
whereas if the view of a self were absent, craving for external objects would be faint and slight.
Furthermore, it is established by the authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), as it is said:
"What are the phenomena that have abandonment through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) as their cause?
They are all defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*)."
It is further stated:
What are the phenomena that have the indeterminate as their cause?
They are unwholesome phenomena and conditioned indeterminate phenomena.
From these proofs, it is known that they serve as causes.

If the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) gives rise to defilements abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), what difference is there between those [defilements] already abandoned and those not yet abandoned?
For when they have been abandoned, the defilements abandoned through cultivation can still arise in the present, just as if they were not yet abandoned.

Furthermore, if all defilements abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) take those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) as their universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), then once that cause has been severed, since the defilements abandoned through cultivation would already be able to manifest, why is it that dharmas such as the types of pride (*māna*) do not necessarily manifest in noble ones (*ārya*)?

Furthermore, regarding the initial objection concerning the distinction between what has been severed and what has not been severed: there is indeed a significant difference. That is to say, in the state where [the defilements] have not yet been severed, they can act as pervasive causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) within one's own continuum by both grasping and giving results.
