In the subsequent state where they have already been severed, although they can still act as causes, they cannot grasp results; this is true except for those cases where a result was already grasped previously, which may still possess the sense of "giving" at present.

Furthermore, although those in the state of having already abandoned [the defilements] can still act as causes, they do not obstruct the Noble Path within their own continuum and can no longer induce the arising of their own acquisition (*prāpti*);
the opposite of this is the state of not yet having abandoned them.
As for the reason why dharmas such as the types of pride (*māna*) and so forth do not necessarily function in Noble Ones (*ārya*), the cause has already been stated previously.
Since they are identical in being abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), how could there be cases where they arise and cases where they do not?
This objection is irrational, because the causes [for their arising] have varying degrees of proximity and distance.
This means that among the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation, some have views and doubt as their proximate causes, arising in continuous succession from those views and doubts.
If those [views and doubts] are abandoned, these [defilements] will certainly not manifest.
Conversely, if they are contrary to those [views and doubts], there is the possibility for them to arise.

Furthermore, because there is a distinction between the acquisition and non-acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), there are cases where [the afflictions] manifest and cases where they do not.
By virtue of this explanation, both faults are avoided.
What is the meaning of the term "universal" (*sarvatraga*) as it is used here?
However, the meaning of "universal" (*sarvatraga*) is that they are able to take all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) as their objects in a comprehensive manner.

This refers to the thirty-three latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) mentioned above, each of which can take the five categories (*pañcavarga*) within its own realm and level as its object. Although some may give rise to a grasping at a self (*ātman*) specifically toward feeling (*vedanā*), this does not mean they take only one's own feelings as their object, because they also take other phenomena of that same category as their objects.

If one gives rise to wrong view, asserting that the wholesome and unwholesome actions one practices are all empty and without fruit, this is not merely a denial of the capacity of one's own karma to produce results, but a wholesale repudiation of the causal efficacy of all karma.
By this principle, one may infer the meaning of the remaining [afflictions] that do not have universal objects (*asarvatraga*).

Afflictions such as greed arise only by depending upon what has been seen or heard, and only when directed toward an object of reflection; for when greed arises toward a wife or similar object, one may take her manifest color as the object but not her shape, or take her shape as the object but not her manifest color. Therefore, it is known that greed and the other [afflictions] are not universally objective.
Furthermore, this statement was made by explaining the meaning of "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*) based on the sense that latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) can take all objects as their range.

However, if one explains the name "pervasive" based on the pervasive nature inherent in all phenomena within the same mental complex (*samprayukta*) as the latent dispositions, then these latent dispositions possess all three types of pervasiveness.
This refers to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that universally take the five categories as their object, as well as those that serve as causes for the universal production of defiled phenomena.
The associated factors possess both types of universality; that is, regarding the three meanings [of universality], they lack only the latent disposition.
Those co-existent dharmas possess the sense of being "universal" (sarvatraga) in one respect: namely, that they act as causes universally producing defiled dharmas.
Therefore, the previous explanation is not subject to the fault of deficiency.

Nevertheless, since there is not a single [defilement] capable of being universal in its latent tendency (*anuśaya*) toward its own self-substance and so forth, it would follow that there are no universal latent tendencies at all.

This objection is not valid. The name "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*) is established because these [defilements] operate without obstruction across the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*), not because they simultaneously underlie all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*).

Furthermore, the meaning of "pervasiveness" is also established because, within their own substantial entities and co-existent factors, these defilements underlie those factors of the same category belonging to the past and future.
For what reason is ignorance abandoned through cultivation designated solely as a delusion regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*), rather than being abandoned through insight?
It is because the objects of focus (*ālambana*) of this ignorance are few, and because the factors abandoned through insight do not serve as its objects.

Furthermore, because these [afflictions] arise only in accordance with craving and so forth, and because craving and so forth are exclusively afflictions of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa-kleśa), there exists a portion of ignorance abandoned by insight (dṛg-heya-avidyā) that is non-common; that [ignorance] functions exclusively within the bodies of ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).

When a practitioner of meditation cultivates contemplation during the stages of hearing and reflection, as they observe all conditioned phenomena through the aspects of suffering and so forth, their eye of wisdom is impaired by that ignorance, causing various kinds of perverted views to arise.
Therefore, one should employ an analogy to reveal that fault.
It is like this: when the sun has just set, a certain man sees an enemy from afar and thinks to himself, "That person is my enemy; I should not go there."

Having thus maintained right mindfulness, when evening arrived and the darkness of the night began to obscure his vision, he was unable to recall the appearance of the enemy; consequently, regarding that enemy, he perceived him as a tree stump, or thought he was not an enemy, or thought he was a friend.
In this way, one should understand unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).

Ignorance that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is not like this; rather, it arises with greed, hatred, and so forth as its primary factors due to the power of causes or the pressure of objects. It is able to obstruct the awareness of gratification, danger, and renunciation, and regarding the object with which it is confronted, it simply lacks knowledge.

It is not that desire does not function with respect to all objects, for it is like the śaṇḍhasa disease, which is heavy and immobile; thus, this ignorance is an affliction of its own specific characteristic.
If universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) can take the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* as their objects,
and arise by taking phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) or the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*) as their objects, by the vision of what are they abandoned?

If they were abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), then craving and the other [afflictions] would also be abandoned solely through the vision of suffering, because they too take all five categories as their objects.

Furthermore, just as the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) that takes as its object views to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, and which can take uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-viṣaya*) as its focus, is itself abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path—because it directly deludes regarding cessation and the path.
In this way, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is also a direct delusion regarding cessation and the path; therefore, it should be seen as abandoned [upon their realization].
Alternatively, one should explain the specific causes and conditions for this distinction.

Furthermore, just as the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is abandoned through the thorough knowledge of its objective referent (*ālambana*), so too should the case of the view of a self-identity be understood by analogy.

Furthermore, just as the object of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through full comprehension (*parijñā*), so too should it be the case for the view of grasping at extremes (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Since neither of these two positions is accepted by our school, the thesis you have established is not tenable from a logical standpoint.
The principle must necessarily be so, for there is a distinction in their meaning.

Furthermore, regarding the initial example—that craving and the like should also be abandoned through the vision of suffering alone because they take the five categories as their objects—or the counter-example cited here that the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) should likewise logically be included within all five categories: such examples are irrational, for it would then follow that craving and the like should also suddenly and simultaneously take the dharmas of all five categories as their objects in a single moment.

This means that within a single moment, the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) simultaneously takes the five categories of aggregates—from feeling up to consciousness—as "self" or "belonging to self. It is logically incorrect to say that the essence of the view of a self-body in one moment is divided into five parts, because craving and the other afflictions are all specifically characterized delusions (svalakṣaṇa-kleśa).
Since there is not even a single moment of thought that can simultaneously take two categories as its object, let alone five; therefore, the analogy is invalid.

As for the subsequent statement regarding the analogy—that just as the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, so too is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because both are direct delusions regarding cessation and the path, and thus should also be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path—[this is incorrect].
This is also unreasonable, because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) cannot praise that which it slanders;
furthermore, its objective referent has no limits.
The view of a self-identity does not first praise the views of cessation and the path before conceiving them as "self," nor does it take its object by delimiting it with boundaries.

The adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) necessarily involves praising [one's own view] and only then conceiving it as supreme through the false view that slanders the Path and Cessation; it functions as a "delimiting condition" (*pariccheda-pratyaya*) regarding its object. Since the underlying meanings are distinct, they cannot be treated as analogous cases.

However, when the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) perceives the Truth of Suffering, its objects of perception are thoroughly known and thus completely and permanently severed; this is not the case for the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), because there is a distinct cause for this difference: namely, that their objects of perception and their modes of cognitive engagement (*ākāra*) are either identical or dissimilar.

This means that just as the aggregates abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the three realms are selfless, so too is the characteristic of the aggregates abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); therefore, when suffering is seen, the view of selflessness arises, and all views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) regarding the perceived suffering are eliminated.
The estimation of superiority is not so [inherently false], because there are cases where one observes certain minor phenomena and estimates other minor phenomena to be superior.

Consequently, although the view-attachment (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) that accompanies the view of self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises by taking as its object phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, it is abandoned solely through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), just like the view of self-identity, because it is coarse.

Just as [views] arise taking as their object phenomena abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), so too do the view-grasping (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) that accompanies the views of negation regarding cessation and the path arise taking those same abandoned phenomena as their objects; yet, because these are far more subtle than the former and are not subsumed under the modes of conduct characterized by craving for pleasure or purity, they are excluded.

Because the false view induced by ignorance—which does not desire cessation and the path—is considered supreme, although one may possess universal knowledge of the object during the stage of seeing suffering, it is only when that object is permanently severed that [the affliction] is abandoned.

Therefore, the view of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is not like the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is completely and eternally severed at the very moment one sees suffering; thus, the principle regarding the distinctions in the severance of defilements as previously explained is established.

Alternatively, there are three types each for the view of holding to views that take as their objects those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and those to be abandoned by seeing the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*), because they are severed respectively upon the abandonment of any one of the views of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*), origin (*samudaya-darśana*), cessation (*nirodha-darśana*), or the path (*mārga-darśana*).

Regarding those [afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path: if one clings to the aspect of the fruit as predominant, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering; if one clings to the aspect of the cause as predominant, it is abandoned through the vision of origin.

If one clings only to that [object] as being truly realized, without specifically clinging to its causal or fruitional aspects, then whichever conditions arise, they are abandoned simultaneously with it; therefore, the grasping at views is not like the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Even so, one must explain the distinction between the views of dogmatic attachment (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*): why is it that they do not differ by way of their objects (*ālambana*) or their modes of activity (*ākāra*)?
For both take all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) as their object and both proceed with the mode of apprehension that grasps them as being "supreme."

Some say: "If [a universal cause] takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) or the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), then the vision is supreme, according to their respective order.
It is abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination, because it would otherwise overstep the established tenet that [such causes] are admitted to be universal (*sarvatraga*)."

If that were necessarily the case, one would have to admit that the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) could be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*), and that [the view of grasping at views] abandoned through the vision of the origin could be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
However, since this is not admitted, [your position] cannot be relied upon.

Now, to examine the distinction between these two: if they are produced through the power of views such as permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and one grasps at conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) therein as being supreme, this is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

If, by the power of a view that denies the cause for future existence, one is closely led toward it and grasps at conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being supreme, this is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Other masters say:

whatever grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) enters by way of the door of the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and grasps at conditioned phenomena as being supreme, this is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

If one enters through the gateway of karma and afflictions, grasping at various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being supreme, this is abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

If there is the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), or adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) that simultaneously take the five categories as their object, these are termed "universal" (*sarvatraga*). However, universal [afflictions] are not limited to just those; for wherever the view of a self operates, there necessarily arises self-love and self-conceit (*māna*).
If, in a certain case, there is the operation of views regarding purity and excellence, one must necessarily seek and exalt oneself in that case; thus, craving and pride should also be omnipresent.
This objection is not valid, because although they arise through the power of views, these two are restricted by their specific objects.

This means that although self-view and other such afflictions operate in a given instance, self-love and conceit must necessarily arise therein; yet it cannot be said that love and conceit take [the object] as their immediate condition, because it has already been stated that they are afflictions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*).
Therefore, there are only these eleven universal [factors]. Since the others are not [universal], they are not mentioned here; their non-universality is established by this very principle.

As for the previously stated eleven, each is able to function as a universal factor within its own realm and stage across the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) of those respective realms and stages. Is there, however, a universal factor belonging to another realm or another stage? To exclude such a possibility, it is specified that they are "of one's own realm and one's own stage."
Are there also [defilements] that are universal across other realms and other stages?

Among the eleven [types of universal defilements], excluding the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the remaining nine kinds are also able to take higher objects.

The term "higher" specifically clarifies the higher realms and higher stages, while also indicating that there are no underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take lower objects as their domain. If they were to take lower objects, the boundaries of the realms would have to be destroyed through thorough knowledge (*parijñā*); however, because higher objects are superior, taking them as objects does not entail this fault.

Furthermore, one wishes to see that the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) slanders the fruits of suffering in the form and formless realms as being non-existent; the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) clings to them therein as supreme; the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) reckons what is not a cause to be a cause; and doubt (*vicikitsā*) harbors hesitation regarding them. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the lack of clear understanding [of these]. This should be explained accordingly for the [false views] abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), such as "form conditions the formless," and it should be understood that this is the reverse of the aforementioned.
One should reflect upon the corresponding realms (*dhātu*) by way of their classification according to the levels (*bhūmi*).

However, regarding those realms and levels that are definitively distinct: from the Desire Realm up to the Fourth Dhyāna, there are universal [defilements] that take higher realms and higher levels as their objects; within the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), those taking higher realms as objects are absent; and in the single level of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), both types are entirely non-existent.

Although latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) may generally take both their own and higher stages as objects, it is logically impossible for them to take both simultaneously; this is because the various objective phenomena within one's own stage are both the objects of perception and the objects toward which the latent dispositions adhere.

If the various objective phenomena within a higher realm (*ūrdhvabhūmi*) are objects of perception (*ālambana*) but not the locus of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it would be impossible for a single moment of affliction to have a portion of its object where a latent tendency resides and another portion where it does not; this is because such a distinction should not apply to the associated mental factors (*samprayukta*) either.

Must one necessarily perceive the stages of the higher realms simultaneously? It is not necessary to perceive them simultaneously; rather, one may do so either individually or collectively. Therefore, the *Mūla-śāstra* states:

there are certain underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm that take the form realm as their object; there are certain underlying tendencies bound to the desire realm that take the formless realm as their object; there are certain underlying tendencies bound to the desire realm that take both the form and formless realms as their objects; and there are certain underlying tendencies bound to the form realm that take the formless realm as their object.
Regarding the classification by stage (*bhūmi*), it should be understood according to the [classification by] realm (*dhātu*).
For what reason do the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) not take the stages of higher realms as their objects?
Because it is logically untenable for them to grasp at those other realms as "self" or "mine," or to conceive of them in terms of annihilation or permanence.
This means that one does not give rise to the conception of a self within the aggregates of another realm or level; for it is logically untenable to maintain that there are two selves.
Since the conception of a self is untenable, the conception of "mine" is also untenable, because the object of such a conception must necessarily arise based upon the conception of a self.
Since the view of extremes arises following from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it likewise has no possibility of taking another realm or level as its object.
Therefore, it is established by reason that only nine [types of views] take what is above as their object. Other masters say:

Because it arises through the power of the two views and craving associated with one's own person, because it grasps what is appropriated as "mine," and because it takes presently perceived phenomena as its object, it certainly does not take higher realms as its object.
If one born within the desire realm gives rise to the view of a permanent sentient being by taking Mahābrahmā as an object, under which of the views is this subsumed?

In truth, it should be said that these two are not views; they are wrong cognitions induced by the view of self and the view of extremes. Having perceived a self and permanence within the aggregates through direct observation, one then infers that such is the case for those who are not directly perceived.

Suppose one first contemplates the appropriated aggregates (*upātta-skandha*) as being selfless, and subsequently, regarding those non-appropriated aggregates (*anupātta-skandha*), the knowledge of selflessness also arises, such that one knows every individual body is devoid of a self. If this were so, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) would not be universal (*sarvatraga*), because it would only conceive of the appropriated aggregates as the self, and not [the aggregates] belonging to other continuums which are not appropriated by oneself.
It is not so; for one also grasps the dharma that constitutes its category.
That is to say, when one conceives of feeling as "self," one does not say, "My feeling is my self and nothing else," but rather simply thinks:
"This feeling is my self."

The Great Brahmā does not incur this same fault, because there is no delusion that suddenly takes the higher stages as its object, and because the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is exclusively universal (*sarvatraga*) within its own realm and stage.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) raises this objection:
"For what reason are the other [afflictions] that take those [higher stages] as their object considered 'views,' while these [afflictions] which also take them as their object are not?"

Because those born in the desire realm do not form the attachment "I am Mahābrahmā," nor do they form the attachment that "Brahmā belongs to me," it is not the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Since the view of a self-identity is absent, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is also absent, for the view of extremes necessarily arises following the view of a self-identity. Furthermore, since no other view produces this mode of apprehension, this is a false wisdom induced by the view of a self-identity.

Some maintain that when one born in the desire realm perceives the Brahma-world as permanent, this is not an extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), but is instead subsumed under the "adherence to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) because it regards what is inferior as superior.
That explanation is irrational, for it contradicts the root treatise.
As stated in the original treatise:
"To perceive the impermanent as permanent is subsumed under the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), specifically the extreme of eternalism.

The Venerable [Vasumitra] should consider this view of the self as permanent to be subsumed under false view (mithyādṛṣṭi), just like the views of pleasure and purity; for the Venerable maintains that among the four inversions, the two inversions of pleasure and purity have false view as their essence. He himself explains:

If one conceives of saṃsāra as pleasant or pure, one is certainly denying the existence of true arhats who have attained right realization and right practice; therefore, to conceive of the objects of suffering and impurity as pleasant or pure is subsumed under wrong view.
Examining their explanation in detail, it stands to reason that this must also be admitted.
If one conceives of a self or permanence within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they certainly deny the existence of a true *arhat*.
Because there is no distinguishing cause, such a view should likewise be subsumed under false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
However, what they have stated is logically untenable, because it involves an increase or decrease regarding the actual state of things, which constitutes a distinct [false] view.
That is to say, all wrong views definitively deny that which actually exists, claiming it to be non-existent; how then could they maintain [the existence of] pleasure and purity?
The two views of pleasure (*sukha*) and purity (*śubha*) definitively grasp as existent that which is actually non-existent; how then could they not be false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)?
Therefore, the irrational and malevolent words of the Sthavira regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) should not be accepted or adopted.
The digression is concluded; we should now present the main argument.
Is the essence of the universal [defilements] solely the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)? It is not so.
How so? This includes the concomitant dharmas as well.

That is to say, the previously mentioned universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*), along with their concomitants—such as feeling (*vedanā*) and arising (*jāti*)—are all subsumed under the category of universals, because they share the same fruit.
However, within the category of "concomitants" (anuvartaka), only the various acquisitions (prāpti) are excluded, because the acquisition and that which is acquired do not share the same fruit.
Consequently, when the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) is contrasted with the latent dispositions (anuśaya), four distinct permutations (catuṣkoṭi) are fully established.
Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), how many take contaminated objects (*sāsrava*) as their object, and how many take uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava*) as their object?
The verse says:
Those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, which are associated with false view and doubt—
Including the unique ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*), six [of these] can take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Among those, that which takes cessation (*nirodha*) as its object takes only the cessation of its own level;
that which takes the path (*mārga*) as its object pertains to six or nine levels, because they serve as mutual remedies for one another.
Greed, hatred, pride, and the two types of grasping do not have uncontaminated objects as their conditions;
they should be abandoned because their objects are not hostile, and because [uncontaminated phenomena] possess the nature of tranquility, purity, and excellence.
The Commentary says:

Only the false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), doubts (*vicikitsā*), and their associated or independent (*asādhāraṇa*) ignorance (*avidyā*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*) and the path (*mārga-darśana*)—each consisting of three factors—constitute the six that can take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.

That is to say, the two false views and two doubts abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, along with the associated ignorance which is subsumed under them, and the two types of independent ignorance, together form these six.

Thus, among these six kinds of elements (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*), those that take cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as their objects are called "taking the untainted (*anāsrava*) as an object"; it goes without saying that the others take the tainted (*sāsrava*) as their objects. Some say:
because ignorance (*avidyā*) has no object, it does not take the untainted as its object.
On what basis is it known that this concentration has no object?

Because it is of the nature of non-cognition; that which is of the nature of non-cognition cannot be said to take an object as its sphere, just as, for example, external darkness—which is not cognition—is in the world.
This means that just as external darkness impairs the capacity for vision yet cannot be said to apprehend objects, so too is ignorance:
it obstructs the wisdom that understands objects and cannot be said to function simultaneously with wisdom.

Therefore, it is known that this [ignorance] has no object of perception (*ālambana*). If it were to have an object of perception, it would be associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*), as is the case with all mental factors.

Furthermore, it has already been established that ignorance exists as a real entity; if the essence of ignorance were not associated with the mind—just as external darkness obstructs the mind and its mental factors, preventing them from apprehending their objects—then the mind and its mental factors would never arise at all, because they would always be present within the continuum.

Just as in the case of the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) and the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*), one should not say that these are "deluded with respect to their objects.

External darkness does not obstruct the mind and mental factors such that they cannot arise in relation to all objects; rather, because it is an object of eye-consciousness included within the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), it merely impairs the capacity for vision regarding other objects.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise; it merely obstructs the arising of true vision regarding the principles of the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering, rather than obstructing the view of a self (*ātman*) with respect to the object itself.
Since it cannot obstruct the arising of all types of vision, we know that ignorance possesses an objective referent (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, the essence of sleep must have an object of cognition (*ālambana*). Just as sleep can only impair and obscure the functioning of wisdom (*jñāna*), it does not fail to operate simultaneously with wisdom regarding its objects, because sleep also possesses the function of apprehending objects; however, it causes the mind to become dull and indistinct with respect to those objects.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise; it is not without an object of perception (*ālambana*).

Why is it that [ignorance] which is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) or the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) has no object? Because the non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) abandoned through the vision of cessation or the path is already abandoned at the time of the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*).

This means that just as the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) operates with respect to all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) by way of the gates of cause and effect, such as [the notions of] pleasure and purity, so too this adherence to views can take as its object those things abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path.

Nevertheless, it is completely and eternally severed at the very moment one truly sees the truths of suffering and its origin, because the antidote arises that opposes the delusion regarding the principle of cause and effect.

Thus, this unique ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*), which obstructs the arising of the eight types of mental application (*ākāra*) regarding the Truths, is entirely severed because its antidote—the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of suffering and its origin—has arisen; apart from this, there is no other object for it to take.

Is it not the case that non-specific ignorance (asādhāraṇa-avidyā), which takes as its object those phenomena abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya-dharma), should be like that [view-grasping]? No, for it is not entirely like that, because its mode of activity (ākāra) is distinct.
This means that when the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) arises regarding contaminated phenomena, it functions through numerous modes of activity characterized by delusion and error.

When a practitioner of meditation perceives suffering and its origin, they regard those phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path as being suffering and so forth; thus, although they have already been able to counteract the delusions regarding cause and effect—such as conceiving them as pleasant or pure—they have not yet been able to counteract the view of grasping at views that regards [those phenomena] as meritorious qualities, nor the other supreme modes of activity associated with such grasping.

Therefore, although one has already attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the two truths of suffering and its origin, there still remains the view-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, which has not yet been eliminated.

Non-specific ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) has no distinct mode of activity; it consists solely of a state of heavy dullness and a lack of inclination toward mental engagement. It is a direct and specific delusion regarding each of the four noble truths, and apart from this, it possesses no other distinct mode of activity.
Since that which is abandoned through the vision [of the truths] is not deluded regarding suffering and its origin, why must one insistently seek out "unshared ignorance" (āveṇikī avidyā)?

Is there a distinct mode of activity that, by being abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, causes those things abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path to be identical to the grasping at views?

For what reason is it that all non-specific ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*) arising with respect to [the truths] abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), which takes those [truths] as its object, is entirely and permanently severed when one sees suffering and its origin?

Why is it not the case that all non-specific ignorance abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which does not take them as its object, is also entirely and permanently severed when one sees suffering and its origin?

One should not press for the specific conditions here; for if one admits that there is non-associated ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), one must necessarily admit that such non-associated ignorance can take only those phenomena abandoned by cultivation as its object.

It is not that one is deluded regarding the principles of the two Noble Truths of Suffering and Origin; for it would be logically untenable to say that this ignorance conditions factors abandoned through vision or untainted (anāsrava) factors.
Furthermore, one must necessarily admit that when a noble one contemplates dharmas, there exists an obstructive defilement consisting of attachment, aversion, and pride.
This means that when one practices the contemplation of the true Dharma, there may arise a state of delusion and disinclination to proceed, like the obscuration of the mind by the dullness of sleep.

Since this non-associated ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), we know that even though the noble one’s knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, there still exists a non-associated ignorance that takes as its object only those phenomena abandoned through cultivation, which obstructs reflection upon the true Dharma.
When suffering and its origin are being seen, why is this [ignorance] not abandoned?

Because this ignorance is to be destroyed by knowledge (*jñāna*); because the various patiences (*kṣānti*) are not the specific counteractive paths (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) for it; because one is not deluded regarding the principles of the two truths of suffering and origin; and because it does not take as its object those dharmas that are directly delusive regarding the principles of the truths.
Regarding the false view that slanders cessation: does it perceive cessation or not perceive cessation?
If it perceives cessation, how can one perceive cessation and yet slander it by saying "there is no cessation"?
If it does not perceive cessation, how can it take the outflow-free as its object?
Furthermore, how can it be said that this thing does not exist?
One should say that it is seen to cease; yet, by merely following the teaching and seeing [this], one slanders such a cessation as being non-existent.
Is it not the case that this vision directly takes cessation as its object; how then can one deny that this cessation exists?

For example, when one with sight sees a person standing at a distance in a place full of stumps and dismisses them as not being a person, although they are directly perceiving that person, this is still a denial.

Thus, there are cases where one perceives cessation and yet denies it as non-existent; however, not all wisdom that denies cessation or the path is abandoned by the vision of cessation or the vision of the path.

That is to say, if there is a wisdom that arises without analytical investigation, one will immediately give rise to slander upon hearing the teaching of cessation and the path; because this wisdom takes only names as its object, it does not perceive their abandonment.

If wisdom arises through the process of analytical investigation, deliberation, and inference regarding its object, and then definitively negates the taught cessation and path, only then does one perceive their abandonment.
As it is said for the sake of detachment:
"If one can know that the wind is suppressed by water, one will know that the arising of various views induced by vitarka and vicāra can be stilled," and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding these untainted objects, how many stages of cessation and the Path do they take as their respective objects within each stage?
Those that take cessation as their object take the cessation of their own stage as their object.

That is to say, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take cessation as their object while bound to the desire realm take only the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the formations of the desire realm as their object; likewise, up to the latent tendencies that take cessation as their object while at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they take only the analytical cessation of the formations of the Peak of Existence as their object.

Those who take the Path as their object take six or nine stages as their object. That is to say, the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that take the Path as their object while bound to the desire realm take only the Path belonging to the category of Dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣa) of six stages as their object; this is because whether it is the antidote to the desire realm or the antidote to other [realms], all categories of Dharma-knowledge are capable of taking them as objects.

Regarding the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take the path as their object within the eight stages of the form and formless realms, each one is able to universally take as its object the category of the knowledge of classes (*anvaya-jñāna-pakṣa*) across all nine stages—whether it be the path that counteracts its own stage or the path that counteracts other stages—because all categories of the knowledge of classes are capable of being taken as objects.

For what reason can the wrong views that deny suffering and deny the origin, when bound to the desire realm, take nine stages as their objects; those bound to the first dhyāna, eight stages; and so on, up to those at the Peak of Existence, which take only that stage as their object?
Regarding the false view that slanders cessation (*nirodha-mithyādṛṣṭi*), within each of the nine stages, it can only take the cessation of its own respective stage as its object.
There is a reason for this. Why is that?

That is to say, if there are dharmas that are moistened by craving for this stage, and which the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of this stage grasps as "self" or "mine," then those dharmas, upon their cessation, are abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering] belonging to this same stage.
This reason for [claiming that] wrong view does not take cessation as its object is incorrect, because it has not yet dispelled doubt.

That is to say: by what reasoning is it that wrong view takes cessation as its object, yet—unlike its taking suffering and origin as objects—it does not universally take both its own stage and other stages?
Alternatively, as for those wrong views that take suffering and its origin as their objects, why do they not—like those taking cessation as their object—take only their own level as their object?
Therefore, the reason this doubt was not previously dispelled is not because the doubt remains undispelled, but rather because the underlying intention was not yet understood.

However, the intention of the preceding [passage] is clear: if, among the various formations (*saṃskāra*), the craving for self and the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) operate within a particular stage, then because one is attached to the formations of that stage, upon hearing it said that those formations of that stage are subject to cessation, one gives rise to wrong views regarding that stage and denies them.
One who is not proceeding upward does not have attachment to a lower realm; how much less would one with a lower false view deny the cessation of that [higher realm]?
Although cause and effect are separated across different realms and stages, the suffering and origin of the nine stages mutually entangle one another.
Furthermore, the bases of birth rely on one another as causes because they serve as mutual causes for one another.

Within a single stage (*bhūmi*), false views may take many objects; however, there is no principle whereby the cessation [of suffering] and the signless [concentration] could mutually attract or act as causes for one another. Therefore, false views that slander cessation take only the cessation of their own specific stage as their object.

If that were so, when wholesome wisdom takes the Truth of Cessation as its object, it should take it with distinct limits, just like the view that denies cessation; for a single moment of wisdom should not suddenly take multiple stages of cessation as its object, since there is no logical distinction between the objects of these two.

Furthermore, while wholesome wisdom may take the cessation of a single stage as its object, there are cases where it takes the cessation of multiple stages simultaneously. This is because, according to the reasoning previously stated, such [wholesome wisdom] differs from false view. As it was said before: if one has an attachment toward certain formations, upon hearing of their cessation, one might give rise to a false view regarding that specific stage, denying its existence; however, since there is no attachment toward lower stages within higher formations, how could a false view of a lower stage deny the cessation of those higher ones?
Wholesome wisdom is not induced by attachment; since it takes the cessation of multiple stages as its object, what contradiction is there in principle?

Nevertheless, when wholesome wisdom arises, it contemplates the defects of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); having carefully contemplated these defects, it aspires for their cessation. Therefore, the wisdom of one stage takes the objects of multiple stages as its domain.

Furthermore, regarding [the aids to penetration] such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, one contemplates the faults of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) through their general characteristics and seeks their cessation.

One should not maintain that these are identical to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), for they possess a limited engagement with their objects of focus; since the principles of delusion and awakening are fundamentally different, the latter should not be used as an analogy for the former.

This means that when a practitioner of meditation observes how they are afflicted by the faults within their own stage and takes joy in the cessation of that stage, they are thereby able to observe the faults of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in other stages as well as the merit of renouncing them. Thus, as wholesome wisdom arises and awakens to its object, it is logically possible for it to simultaneously take as its object the cessation of the formations of multiple stages.

All false views arise from delusion regarding their objects; because they are obstructed by dogmatic adherence, they cannot take [all four truths] as a collective object. For what reason do false views that take suffering, origin, and cessation as their objects sometimes have a general scope and sometimes only a specific scope, while those taking the path as their object are not like this?
Because their antidotes differ and they are mutually dependent:

although the paths taken as objects of focus differ according to the various stages (*bhūmi*), they are interconnected and function as cause and effect for one another; therefore, these wrong views take all six and nine [stages] collectively as their objects.

If it is argued that the [knowledges of] cessation do not take one another as causes but only take their own stage as objects, does this not contradict the fact that the categories of the knowledges of dharma and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) also take one another as causes? Furthermore, should not false views of lower and higher stages both be able to take the categories of dharma and subsequent knowledge as their objects—just as they take suffering and origination as objects—without any restriction across the various stages?
This criticism is not valid, because [the path] is not an antidote.

If that were so, then the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*) in the six stages would not be the general object of the false views of the desire realm; for the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge in the five higher stages is not an antidote to the phenomena of the desire realm.
The stage of the Not-yet-attained (anāgamya) does not belong entirely to the higher stages, because it is not intended to counteract [the afflictions] of those stages.

Furthermore, that which counteracts the afflictions of the desire realm is not entirely [free from] wrong view, as it is specifically that which is countered by the Patience (kṣānti) [of the Path of Seeing].

The false view of slandering the Path in the form and formless realms should likewise be able to take as its object the category of the Path associated with the Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*), because the category of the Path associated with Dharma-knowledge serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) for the form and formless realms.

If it is argued that Dharma-knowledge does not entirely counteract those [defilements]—because the category of Dharma-knowledge regarding Suffering and Origin is not their antidote, and furthermore, it cannot entirely counteract the form and formless realms because it cannot counteract the defilements of those realms to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*)—then the first category of Dharma-knowledge cannot counteract the first category of those afflictions. Since it is not what is counteracted by this [first category], the category of Dharma-knowledge is not the object of those [false views].

In that case, one must admit that false views regarding form and the formless realms cannot collectively take the category of knowledge of classes (*anvaya-jñāna*) across the nine stages as their object, because the category of knowledge of classes does not collectively serve as the antidote to all afflictions within the two upper realms.

This means that the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the second dhyāna stage and so forth cannot serve as an antidote to the afflictions of the first dhyāna stage and so forth; nor is it the case that the first dhyāna and so forth are entirely incapable of doing so. The logical implications of these two points should be inferred as previously explained.

Furthermore, since the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms that take the Truth of the Path as their object are not counteracted by the receptivities (*kṣānti*) regarding suffering, origin, or cessation, it follows logically that the view of denigrating the Path cannot have the lower and upper realms as its collective object.

Regarding the six and nine stages of the path, such webs of [mutual] inclusion do not exist in reality; for dharmajñāna and anvayajñāna differ in their categories when compared to one another, yet within their respective groups—dharmajñāna-group and anvayajñāna-group—their antidotes are identical, they serve as mutual causes, and they serve as mutual objects of cognition.

That is to say, the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and the path are both of the same type as the antidotes for the delusions that take the Truth of the Path as their object within the desire realm; they share the same path of abandonment because they are mutually causal and mutually objective. Even if [the path] were not the antidote [for those specific delusions], it would still be the object of the afflictions in the desire realm that take the Path as their object.

Although the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and that belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) are mutually dependent, because they are distinguished by their types of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) and do not take one another as objects, the latter is not an object of the afflictions that take the path as their object within the desire realm.

By this same principle, the objection that afflictions taking the Path as their object in the Form and Formless Realms should likewise be able to take as their objects the categories of Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) which counteract the dharmas of the Form and Formless Realms is also refuted.

This is because, although within these [categories] there are some portions of the category of Dharma-knowledge that can counteract some portions of the afflictions of the higher realms and which also serve as mutual causes, they do not have the category of Subsequent Knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) as their object due to the distinction between types based on the mode of counteraction; therefore, they are not the objects of the afflictions that take the Path of the higher realms as their object.

Within the nine stages (*bhūmi*), the paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) act as causes for one another through their mutual relationship and serve as mutual objects of cognition; because their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) are of the same type, although they are not direct antidotes [to those specific afflictions], they can collectively serve as the objects of the afflictions that take the path as their object within the upper eight stages.
Therefore, the principle as stated in the verse is established.
Why is it that greed, hatred, pride, and the two types of grasping views are not abandoned by the untainted [path], and do not take the untainted as their object?

Because those who joyfully seek true liberation must certainly abandon the affliction of greed; if it were to take the untainted as its object—just as the desire for wholesome dharmas seeks after nirvāṇa and the noble path—then those seeking liberation would not be able to abandon greed.

Furthermore, the truths of cessation and the path would have to be objects to be abandoned, because the Buddha stated that an object from which craving is detached is called "abandoned. As a sutra says:
"If you can abandon craving for form, then form itself is also called 'abandoned'."

Furthermore, one can only become free from desire by perceiving faults in the objects of desire; if it were admitted that desire could take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object, then one would only become free from desire upon perceiving faults in Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*).
This view is not pure; how could it possibly exhaust all delusions?

Furthermore, greed arises only because one perceives merit within an object of greed. If you grant that greed can take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object, then when one contemplates the untainted through the mental applications of cessation (*nirodha*), tranquility (*śānta*), and so forth, greed should increase. How, then, could this lead to the exhaustion of all delusions?
Since both [greed and hatred] would fail to exhaust delusions, birth and death would be endless; therefore, we know that greed does not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.

Hatred arises only when there is an object of enmity or harm; since the untainted state is free from the characteristics of enmity and harm, hatred will certainly not arise when taking the untainted as its object.

Furthermore, the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣānuśaya*) is coarse and harsh in nature, whereas all untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) are most extremely subtle; therefore, there is no possibility for hatred to operate with respect to them.

Because the latent tendencies of pride (*mānānuśaya*) have the characteristic of loftiness, their nature is not tranquil; since all untainted phenomena are utterly tranquil, they do not give rise to loftiness.
Furthermore, one who gives rise to conceit thinks:
"I have attained this Dharma.
It is not the power of the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas that serves as the condition for giving rise to such conceit, because untainted dharmas are capable of counteracting conceit.

If the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) were able to take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, they would necessarily be identical to right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), because the untainted is the truly pure and supreme nature.
Since the two types of grasping are not erroneous, they should not be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*). Therefore, the two types of grasping do not have the untainted as their object.

If that were so, then for one who gives rise to the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣānuśaya*) toward wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the like that deny *nirvāṇa*, there would be no fault, as it conforms to its object; for it is appropriate to harbor a mind of aversion toward things that are faulty, since they ought to be abandoned. Consequently, hatred (*pratigha*) should not be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).
There is no such fault, because it is only toward those who slander that those who are deluded regarding the characteristic of cessation give rise to anger.

That is to say, having first clung to a notion of liberation elsewhere, one subsequently develops an intolerance toward the slander of true liberation; therefore, it is only those who are deluded regarding the true characteristic of cessation who give rise to extreme aversion toward wrong views that deny cessation and the like.

For those who see the cessation [of suffering] and abandon hatred, and who are not deluded regarding the true characteristic of cessation, any sense of aversion or repulsion toward wrong views that slander cessation is not the latent tendency of hatred; rather, it is subsumed under the wholesome root of non-attachment.

Furthermore, it is like one who has accumulated many ailments within their belly; although they may eat fine food for the sake of sustaining life, because it is mixed with disease, it all results in deterioration.
For one whose belly is free of illness, whatever they consume is entirely beneficial to the body and causes no harm.

Thus, if one falsely claims that what is not cessation is cessation and thereby gives rise to craving, because their mental continuum is defiled, the hatred and aversion they direct toward wrong views and the like are all said to be abandoned by seeing the cessation of suffering (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).

Regarding the aversion arising from factors such as wrong views: if one understands, in accordance with reality, that true cessation is indeed true cessation and is free from craving, then because the mental continuum is purified, there is no fault whatsoever in the resulting revulsion toward those wrong views and the like that slander true cessation.
If one gives rise to hatred toward the right view that there is nirvāṇa, by what [category of] view is it abandoned?
This need not be questioned; for hatred abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) cannot logically exist [in this case], because its object is a wholesome dharma.
This [craving] which has right view as its object is definitely abandoned through cultivation.
However, for one who has already seen the truths, this no longer arises, because craving directed toward the view that slanders cessation has been permanently severed.
How could one not believe that there exists an outflow-free (anāsrava) anger conditioned by [a specific] cause?
Is it not the case that this anger is known to exist in the world?
For instance, there are non-Buddhists (tīrthika) who say:
"In *nirvāṇa*, the sense faculties are forever extinguished; this is a great loss, therefore I certainly do not seek it with longing.
This is fundamentally not hatred, but rather a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); thus the *Mūla-śāstra* states:
"To conceive of pleasure as suffering is a false view subsumed under that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*)."
This must necessarily be so, because all suffering is only eternally extinguished upon reaching the state of ultimate bliss (*paramasukha*).
This state of ultimate bliss is none other than true *nirvāṇa*.
The term "ultimate bliss" here indicates bliss in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-sukha*).

Because they cannot discern the characteristics of this bliss, and because they do not understand the faults of birth and death, they become attached to the various realms of existence and find no joy in renunciation; thus, they give rise to wrong views and deny nirvana. How could they possibly grasp this as a condition for the cessation of hatred?

However, the Elder (Sthavira) says: "If one were to admit that wrong view, doubt, and the two types of ignorance take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, then both Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*) would consequently become tainted (*sāsrava*).

If it is argued that Cessation and the Path are not objects of delusion because only tainted things are objects of delusion, then [we reply]: even if there were something within those things that could be sought or attained such that afflictions could arise, there is certainly no fault of Cessation and the Path becoming tainted, for they do not possess the characteristics of being tainted."

Since the Buddha taught that outflows (*āsrava*) consist exclusively of the matters of craving and aversion, and since cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are not subsumed under these matters of craving and aversion, they cannot possibly incur the fault of becoming outflows even when conditioned by wrong views and the like.

If that were so, and you do not admit that the latent tendencies of greed and hatred are universal defilements—since not all objects are bound by greed and hatred—then it would follow as an error that even contaminated things could become uncontaminated.

He certainly does not understand the tenets of the Abhidharma, for he maintains that future afflictions (*kleśa*) with their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are definitely able to bind all contaminated things (*sāsrava-vastu*); however, since the truths of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the Path (*mārga-satya*) do not serve as the basis (*āśraya*) or the object (*ālambana*) for the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of greed and hatred throughout the three times, they cannot be treated as equivalent to those [contaminated] things.

Is it not the case that among the various classes of worldlings who are non-Buddhists, anger also arises even toward the untainted; that is to say, they are currently seen to harbor extreme hatred and aversion toward the true path to nirvana, such as right view, and toward nirvana itself?
In various places throughout the sūtras, one also sees extensive explanations concerning those who harbor hatred for and seek to destroy the Path.

Furthermore, when all afflictions are discussed according to their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), they are all subsumed within the two categories of greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dveṣa*).
As it is said that there are three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there are also said to be seven underlying tendencies.
Some speak of three fetters (*saṃyojana*), while others speak of nine fetters.
It is not the case that the seven underlying tendencies are not subsumed within the three, nor that the nine fetters are not subsumed within the three.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra states that there are three great diseases, how could the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth not be included among these great diseases?
If those categories are also designated as "great diseases," then the same applies to greed and hatred; there is no fault in including them collectively.

That is to say, greed can comprehensively subsume those afflictions associated with pleasure, while hatred can likewise comprehensively subsume those afflictions associated with suffering. Therefore, if it were admitted that the two—false view and doubt—and the two types of ignorance could take cessation and the path as their objects, then cessation and the path would also become tainted by way of being objects of hatred, which would be an error.
What has been stated in this manner is, in all cases, unreasonable.

First, regarding the claim that certain types of non-Buddhists manifest anger toward the untainted (*anāsrava*): because they do not understand the characteristics of the untainted, they merely lack a desire for it; it does not mean that they give rise to anger.

This means that because such a person’s deep mind is attached to birth and death and does not delight in renunciation, they give rise to wrong views; yet these do not constitute a denial of cessation or the path. How, then, could this be termed hatred?

Such a person may either negate [the existence of the noble truths] or claim they have faults; thus, regarding the untainted (anāsrava), they simply do not accept them. However, this mere lack of acceptance is not what is called hatred.

Just as the disciples of the Buddha do not tolerate the assertions of non-Buddhists regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the primal person (*puruṣa*), time (*kāla*), or the self (*ātman*), would this constitute hatred?

Furthermore, what those [non-Buddhists] say is stated in terms of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); for greed and hatred encompass all afflictions (*kleśa*), since wrong views and the like take cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as their objects.

The claim that cessation and the path should be included among the objects of aversion and thus constitute outflows (*sāsrava*) is also unreasonable, because it contradicts one's own position, because it entails the fault of over-extension, because it is indeterminate, and because it necessitates a different explanation.
That is to say, that Elder has stated in various places:
"The Blessed One should not have made such an erroneous statement.
If the Buddha intended to encompass all afflictions by mentioning only greed and hatred here, would this statement not be utterly erroneous?
If mentioning two [categories] were sufficient to encompass the rest, then the subsequent mention of the rest would be redundant.
Therefore, what they have stated contradicts their own intention.
How could their statement not entail an excessive fault?
It has already been explained that greed (*rāga*) and pride (*māna*), as well as the two types of grasping (*grāha*), do not take cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*) as their objects;

this principle is fully established. According to what you say, there must be an object [for these afflictions], because since false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is associated with pleasure (*sukha*), cessation and the path would also have to become objects of greed.

Alternatively, even if it is granted that these two categories encompass all afflictions, they cannot collectively take cessation and the path as their objects; thus, one should grant that only wrong views and the like take them as objects, but not hatred, because hatred is devoid of the characteristic of enmity.

Furthermore, from another perspective, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): one should say that there are only two major afflictions (*mahākleśa*), since it is admitted that greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) collectively subsume all delusions; likewise, the collection of causes and conditions for karma (*karmahetu-pratyaya-samudāya*) should not be threefold, and so forth—the number of such categories should all be reduced.

Regarding "indeterminacy": this refers to the claim that what was stated—namely, that greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) alone can encompass all afflictions—is like how latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth, though few, can encompass many.

This is not necessarily so; for in some places it is said that a few are encompassed only by their names and do not encompass others, while in other places it is said that a general term is permitted to encompass its particulars, as when the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that "craving (*tṛṣṇā*) conditions grasping (*upādāna*)."

That school maintains that craving alone is the condition for grasping (*upādāna*), and does not include other afflictions associated with pleasure; although the term "grasping" is general, they maintain that it refers exclusively to craving.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"I shall explain to you the various nets of craving."
In this context, because it speaks only of the characteristic of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it subsumes only "attachment" (*anunaya*) and nothing else.

Furthermore, other sūtras speak of the afflictions (*kleśa*) in general without including "views" (*dṛṣṭi*); for example, among the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), one may mention a specific name to subsume the afflictions in general, as the Sūtra says: "Ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*).
Furthermore, regarding the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and so forth within this context, it is also possible to say that they do not encompass all [defilements].

Those who would argue otherwise should state: if the Blessed One intended to explain the afflictions (*kleśa*) according to their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), he should not have mentioned greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) here, but should have mentioned only ignorance (*avidyā*). This is because, as in the formula "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations" (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*), ignorance is able to subsume all afflictions, as it functions in conjunction with all of them.

If it is said that greed and hatred can only be subsumed under what was previously stated, then what is the meaning of this statement regarding those matters in which one might seek something and thereby give rise to afflictions?

It is not our school’s teaching that afflictions arise only when one seeks to acquire something within an object; rather, afflictions—whether of aversion, seeking, or indifference—arise simply because one fails to understand the object.

If that were so, it would be more appropriate to say that one is "possessed by afflictions" in the sense that when afflictions gain mastery over an object, they are able to seize that object and cause it to arise in accordance with their increase;
it is not that at the moment an affliction arises, it seizes the object and places it at the forefront of the mind to be cherished like a treasure that is called being "possessed."
However, when afflictions attain mastery over an object, they seize it and cause it to conform to themselves, thereby attaining the sense of "increase.
If one is not possessed by them, although the afflictions arise by taking that object as their condition, they do not increase within that object.
Just as when a person raises their eyes to gaze at the orbs of the sun and moon, it can cause the faculty of the eye to either diminish or increase;
therefore, the principle that craving and other such afflictions do not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object is thoroughly established.
Although cessation and the path are objects of wrong view and other such afflictions, they are not *sāsrava* (with-outflows).
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 48; *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 49.

Chapter Five: The Exposition of the Latent Defilements (Anuśaya), Part Five of Five. To further clarify the preceding meaning, one should again investigate and discern: among the ninety-eight latent defilements (*anuśaya*), how many increase by way of their object (*ālambana*) and how many increase by way of association (*samprayoga*)?
The verse says:
As long as they have not been abandoned, the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase through their objects with respect to everything within their own stage;
those that are non-pervasive increase through their objects only with respect to their own category.
They are not untainted (*anāsrava*) nor do they take higher levels as their objects (*ūrdhvālambana*), because there is no inclusion [of such factors] and because it would involve contradiction;
rather, they increase in accordance with the associated dharmas (*saṃprayuktadharma*), for they increase by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).
The treatise says:

There are two distinctions of the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*): namely, those that are universal within their own realm and level (*sva-dhātu-bhūmi*), and those that are universal across other realms and levels (*para-dhātu-bhūmi*).
There are also two distinctions of the non-universal latent dispositions: namely, those that take contaminated (*sāsrava*) objects and those that take uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects.

Furthermore, among the universal [defilements], those that pertain to their own realm and level increase in accordance with their objects across all five categories of phenomena within their own realm and level.
Among the non-universal [defilements], those that take contaminated phenomena as their object increase in accordance with their objects only within their own category and their own realm and level.

Among those [defilements] that are not universal, those which take the untainted as their object, and among those that are universal, those which take objects belonging to other realms, lack the sense of "increasing" (anuśaya) with respect to their objective spheres. Why is this so?
Because that object of focus is neither grasped nor compatible [with them].

That is to say, if a phenomenon were grasped as "mine" by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) belonging to a particular stage, it would be possible for those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) existing within that stage to increase by taking that phenomenon as their object.

Regarding the term "increasing in accordance" (*anuśerate*), it means that the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abide within and increase in this dharma; that is to say, they bind in accordance with it and increase in their state of dull stagnation. This is like dust adhering to moist clothing, or like seeds growing in moist soil.

The untainted dharmas (*anāsrava*) and the dharmas of the higher stages are not grasped as "mine" by the views and craving of the lower stages; therefore, those lower afflictions do not increase with respect to them as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*), because they do not bind or increase through the intensification of delusion and stagnation.

If one born in a lower stage seeks a higher stage and so forth, this is a desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*) and not defiled; for such a desire arises in order to seek liberation from defilement.

Since the Noble Path, *nirvāṇa*, and the dharmas of the higher stages are incompatible with the lower-level afflictions that take them as objects, there is no logical basis for those two [the Path and *nirvāṇa*] to increase by way of their objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*).
Just as one’s foot does not remain upon a heated stone,
and as a goose does not grow within a flame,
these latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise primarily through their dependence on a basis; however, at the moment they actually arise, they also rely upon their respective objects.
Thus, having already explained how [defilements] increase with respect to their objects (*ālambana*), one might ask:
by what means does each respective latent disposition (*anuśaya*) increase with respect to its associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) through association?
Regarding this "increase" that has been discussed, it occurs until [the defilement] has been abandoned; therefore, the word "unabandoned" (*aprahīṇa*) is placed at the beginning of the first verse.

From this, it should be understood that for those conditions that are untainted (*anāsrava*) or belong to another realm or other afflictions, they increase only through association (*saṃprayoga*); whereas for those conditions that are tainted (*sāsrava*) and belong to one's own realm and level, they fully possess both objective support (*ālambana*) and association as modes of increase.
How do the latent dispositions (anuśaya) possess the sense of "increasing" with respect to associated dharmas and their objective supports?
The former masters of the Vinaya explained it thus:
It is like a heap of filth situated beside a city, composed of a mixture of excrement, soil, water, and so forth.

Within this mass, due to the defect of the excrement, even the earth, water, and so forth become impure; by the power of the water and other elements, the excrement increases further, and as they depend upon one another, all become utterly loathsome.

Thus, within this aggregate associated with afflictions, the mind and mental factors are defiled by the power of the afflictions; the afflictions, in turn, increase further through their influence, and as they rely upon one another, all become thoroughly defiled.
This accumulation, as it continues in succession, becomes increasingly defiled, and it also causes the associated factors such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth to become tainted.

It is like pigs, dogs, and the like dwelling amidst a heap of filth; they take extreme delight in it, sleeping and playing therein, becoming ever more unclean as they are smeared with excrement, while the heap of filth is further increased by the presence of the pigs and other animals.

Thus, the objects of focus belonging to one's own level are "with outflows" (sāsrava) by virtue of the power of the afflictions; furthermore, these [objects] possess the capacity to accord with the power of the afflictions, causing the three characteristics to increase progressively in succession.
Just as a clean person who has accidentally fallen into a heap of filth is not defiled by contact with that excrement, nor can anyone else further increase the filth of that heap,
so too, although uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas belonging to other realms or stages may be taken as objects by afflictions, they do not mutually increase one another.

Regarding these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states of a different level as their objects, they can only increase through association (*saṃprayoga*), for that is the logical principle.
Others further state on this point:
"Just as when alcohol is mixed with poison, its ferocity increases and the potency of the poison also increases, because their functional capacities are equal."
In this way, the outflows (*āsrava*) and the various afflictions (*kleśa*) mutually assist and increase together, as their functional capacities are equal.
It is like placing a potent medicine among various poisons; it causes the functional capacity of the poisons to be diminished rather than enhanced.
