Thus, although the untainted (anāsrava) is taken as an object by delusions, it only causes the functional capacity of those delusions to diminish and not to increase; therefore, while false views may arise taking the untainted as their object, they lack the power to sever the roots of goodness.

Furthermore, there is authoritative scripture that clarifies the principle that among the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), there are those with pure objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) that do not increase through association (*na-anuśerate*). As a sūtra states:
"Bhikṣus, you should know: what is it to eat with doubt?"
Regarding the so-called three periods of time: there are delusions and doubts concerning the past; the same applies to what is said regarding the present and the future.
Although the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is an object of the afflictions, it does not increase [the afflictions] through association; therefore, it is not mentioned here.
Since these untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) are not mentioned, by this same principle they should also not be objects of doubt.

Just as the Sūtra states in general that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" (*sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ*), in reality it refers only to tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), because it later describes their tranquility (*śānti*) as bliss (*sukha*).

Therefore, the root treatise also states that while afflictions increase in accordance with [the object] even when it is untainted (anāsrava), this occurs only through association (saṃprayoga) and not through the object (ālambana).

Regarding past and future latent dispositions (anuśaya), they possess "increase" (anuśayana); however, one should not say that they definitely exist [as entities], for they are capable of producing acquisitions (prāpti).
If it were otherwise, then ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in states of mind free from defilement would be liberated from their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
However, the Blessed One said:
"In infants, children, and those suffering from illness, although there is no defiled desire, the latent tendency of sensual craving (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) still increases."

Therefore, it is said that [latent dispositions] increase in accordance [with their objects] as long as they have not been abandoned; if they have already been abandoned, there is no increase of latent dispositions through either objective association or concomitant association. How could they still exist? For they would otherwise lose the defining characteristic of being a latent disposition.

This means that because their power has been destroyed by the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), they do not increase further; however, because the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have not been lost, it is said that they "still exist.

Alternatively, based on the fact that they previously had or will have this function, they are still termed "latent dispositions" even though they currently lack such function—just as a king who has lost his throne still retains the title of king, or a craftsman who has ceased working still bears the name of a craftsman.
The Elder (Sthavira) states herein as follows:

"Latent dispositions (anuśaya) possess neither the sense of 'concomitant increase' (samprayoga-anuśaya) nor 'object-increase' (ālambana-anuśaya); rather, they merely exist as a self-nature that binds the continuum without being relinquished."
"Is there a self-nature that follows along with the continuity of bondage, or is there the nature of existence without a self-nature?
He answered himself:
"There is only the nature of existence; it is only through this that the various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) can have association and an object of perception."
If that were so, one would also have to maintain that there is a self-nature (*ātmatva*) and a pot-nature (*ghaṭatva*), etc., distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*) and form (*rūpa*), etc.
Such a perverse attachment should be concealed by oneself.
Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
The verse says:

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the two higher realms, as well as the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm, along with their concomitant ignorance (*moha*), are neutral (*avyākṛta*); all others are unwholesome (*akuśala*).
The Treatise says:

All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms are subjugated by the four- and five-limbed meditative absorptions; because they lack the power to project a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*), they are all comprised within the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

If it is claimed that those [defiled states] can induce a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*), then there would have to be unpleasant feeling (*aniṣṭavedanā*) in the two higher realms; for it is not established that defilement induces pleasant feeling.
However, there is no fault of [the Path] becoming neutral (*avyākṛta*), because only contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) possess ripened fruit.
Only that which possesses no maturation (*vipāka*) within this category can be said to be of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
Is it not stated in the Sūtra:
"If any noble disciple (*ārya-śrāvaka*) is able to enter the fourth dhyāna, they are able to abandon the unwholesome and cultivate wholesome dharmas"?
What fault is there in this?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The noble disciples, having realized the immovable and well-liberated mind, possess the maṇi jewel; they are able to abandon unwholesome states and cultivate wholesome dharmas."
It is not that Arhats possess unwholesome states that must be abandoned.
Furthermore, since it is admitted that those who have already permanently severed all unwholesome states still diligently cultivate the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*),
one should understand that there is no error in speaking of these [efforts] in terms of the antidote of repudiation (*vidūṣaṇapratipakṣa*) and the antidote of distancing (*dūrībhāvapratipakṣa*).
How is this known to be so?
Because the sūtra states:
"Because one is free from all desires, evil, and unwholesome dharmas."
The Elder Śrīlāta explains that this is stated in reference to the fixed stage [of the dhyānas]; however, that explanation is irrational, for the same should apply to the desire realm as well.
Since there is also wholesome samādhi in the desire realm, one should likewise say that it is "separated from sensual desires and unwholesome states," as there is no distinction between them.
Furthermore, when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) enter the first dhyāna, it is also said that they are "detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states.

This is not your own tenet, for you maintain that the continuum of ordinary beings—though associated with outflows (*sāsrava*)—is free from all afflictions (*kleśa*), since you admit that even in those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) still persist.

Since the sūtra states that upon entering the first dhyāna one is "detached from all desires and unwholesome, evil dharmas," it follows that the two higher dhyānas are definitely devoid of unwholesome states.
Were it otherwise, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) currently enters the first dhyāna, they would—just as in the desire realm—not be detached from the unwholesome dharmas of their own level.

Furthermore, when one is born in this realm, the afflictions of the higher realms may also manifest; thus, even within the meditative equipoise of the [formless] attainments, there could exist karma—arisen from afflictions not separated from evil and unwholesome states—that is capable of summoning a future existence. Therefore, we know that while born here, one may give rise to those afflictions.
Since it has never been stated that those [afflictions] are not free from verbal expression, one can definitively know that this interpretation is irrational.
Furthermore, it is said that the afflictions of the higher realms should also produce undesirable results, just like the afflictions of the desire realm.

This means that although unwholesome afflictions of the desire realm assist acts such as giving in producing rebirth among humans or devas, they nonetheless do not fail to produce their own specific karmic maturation (*vipāka*). The same applies to the afflictions of the form and formless realms; because the functional capacities of afflictions differ, they are not capable of producing only the maturation of painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*).

This reasoning is also incorrect. This is because the intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm include the various evil destinies (*apāya*); because all locations are subject to the same underlying propensities (*anuśaya*); and because the afflictions of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven can also bring about the fruits of the evil destinies. Furthermore, it is not the case that in the form and formless realms there are distinct locations where one experiences the disagreeable maturation (*vipāka*) of afflictions; otherwise, one would have to maintain that there are causes for disagreeable maturation that lack their corresponding fruits, or one would have to maintain that there are places within the higher realms where one experiences disagreeable fruits.

Furthermore, within the human and celestial realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there exists the principle that unwholesome karma yields its full fruit; this is not the case for the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).

Moreover, according to your own school, although all afflictions (*kleśa*) are equally unwholesome, because their functional capacities differ, some have the power to induce painful feelings (*duḥkhavedanā*), while others lack such capacity.

In this way, one should also admit that although all afflictions equally involve a distorted perception of their objects, there are distinctions in their functional capacities; thus, some are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) while others are unwholesome (*akuśala*).

Furthermore, if those afflictions are of an unwholesome nature, and you do not admit that they bring about the maturation of painful feeling, do you then admit that they can produce the fruit of pleasant feeling? No.

If that were so, it would follow that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)—if it cannot bring about either desirable or undesirable results—is admitted by all to be of an indeterminate nature; why then do you alone claim it is not?

Furthermore, the claim that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not skillful by nature because it is subsumed under all afflictions (*kleśa*), and therefore all such states must necessarily be unwholesome (*akuśala*), is also illogical. Although they are all equally subsumed under the non-skillful nature of ignorance, we nevertheless admit that there are distinctions among them.
Just as you admit that although unwholesome natures are identical, they differ in being causes or non-causes of painful feeling;

likewise, those *śaikṣa* dharmas would also become unwholesome, because according to your own admission, those various *śaikṣa* dharmas are also said to be "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) with respect to the latent dispositions included within the category of lack of skill (*akauśalya*).

Furthermore, it should not be said that all afflictions are subsumed under unskillful ignorance, for the principle of their being so subsumed within a single self-entity is untenable; moreover, it is logically impossible for two volitions to arise simultaneously.
If it is claimed that "inducing" constitutes "appropriation," then all wholesome practices would become unwholesome, because they are induced to arise with ignorance as their condition.
Therefore, one cannot use that as a reason to prove that the afflictions of the form and formless realms are unwholesome.

The two views associated with the self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the delusion (moha) concomitant with them, when bound to the desire realm, are also of an indeterminate nature because they function as perversions; how then could they not be unwholesome?
Furthermore, since the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) accords with wholesome conduct and opposes the severing of the roots of goodness, it is certainly not unwholesome.

If it is argued that it should be classified as unwholesome because it can also accord with the unwholesome—since all afflictions may manifest following the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi)—it is therefore merely obscured-neutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta).

It is not that I claim something becomes of a wholesome nature simply because it accords with wholesome conduct; how then can you object by saying it becomes of an unwholesome nature because it accords with unwholesome conduct?
Just as wholesome states with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*), though they accord with both sides, do not lose their wholesome nature, so too should this be understood.
If it is argued that because the pursuit of heavenly bliss is a conforming meritorious action (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*), it should therefore be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), this analogy does not hold.

It is by the power of the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) that one generates a longing for heavenly bliss, thinking, "I shall experience heavenly bliss"; taking this very [view] as the gateway, one is able to produce meritorious action.
However, greed is said to be the predominant cause at the time of severing the roots of virtue; therefore, it is unwholesome.

Alternatively, it proceeds from the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and craving for heaven (*svarga-tṛṣṇā*); that is to say, one only gives rise to craving for those heavenly pleasures by seeing that "I shall experience heavenly bliss."

The conceit of self (*asmimāna*) also arises subsequent to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), causing the mind to become haughty and thus preventing one from conforming to the cultivation of wholesome karma.

Furthermore, it contradicts such practices as associating with virtuous friends; that is to say, because one exalts oneself and relies on such a conceited mind, it becomes difficult to successfully associate with virtuous friends and the like.

Among the views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), that which clings to the extreme of annihilation (*ucchedānta*) does not contradict *nirvāṇa* because it conceives of the cessation of rebirth; furthermore, as it accords with the gateway of revulsion and detachment, it is not unwholesome (*akuśala*).
As the Blessed One said:
"If this view arises, I do not tolerate it in any respect."
It should be understood that this view does not accord with craving but accords with non-craving, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:

"Among all the various speculative views of the non-Buddhists, this view is the most excellent: namely, 'I do not exist, nor do I belong to anything; I shall not exist, nor shall I belong to anything.'"
Furthermore, because this [state] does not fear the place of great terror, as it is said in a sutra:

"Among foolish ordinary beings who lack correct hearing, there may be one who is able not to fear the place of great terror—namely, 'I shall not exist, nor shall there be what belongs to me; I will not come to be, nor will there be what belongs to me'—and yet remains unstartled and unafraid."
Regarding this, the Elder spoke as follows:
"How could such a base and extreme view (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) be conducive to liberation?
For all the false views of sentient beings are subsumed within these."
However, I do not understand what intention there could be in holding this extreme view as being conducive to liberation?
This view is base; it is indeed as you say, for it is not a gateway to skillful means, as it clings to both arising and cessation.

Now, regarding this mode of practice, the Blessed One has at times spoken of it spontaneously to the bhikṣus without being asked; or there may be some who reflect thus: "I do not exist, nor does what belongs to me exist; I shall not exist, nor shall what belongs to me exist."
When one possesses such resolute conviction, one severs the lower fetters.
Therefore, it is known that this view is conducive to liberation; by this, one should understand that it is not of an unwholesome nature.

Furthermore, within such views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), there is no case of regarding what is not a means as a means, no case of regarding the inferior as superior, no case of denying that which truly exists, and no case of regarding what is non-self and impermanent as self and permanent. How, then, can it be said that all the false views of sentient beings are subsumed within these?
The adherence to the extreme view of eternalism arises in accordance with the view of self; this is of an indeterminate nature, as explained in the discussion on the view of self.

However, because they have not yet attained the wisdom that realizes ultimate truth, nor have they relied upon a teacher who has realized ultimate truth, they constantly give rise to the pride of thinking "I am capable," acting as a ladder for their conceit, and thus make such assertions themselves.
However, I do not understand what intention there could be in maintaining that these extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) accord with liberation, as you have truly stated.
Others further say:
since the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes are the root of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they ought to be unwholesome (*akuśala*).

That statement is incorrect, because there are three types of causes: first, the cause of origination; second, the cause of production; and third, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*). By means of the cause of origination, one does not transcend the realm or stage; by means of the cause of production, one brings about the attainment of birth; and by means of the ripening cause, one experiences the ripening result after having been born.
The two views associated with the self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) are the causes for the arising [of existence], not the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*); they are called the root of birth and death.
Therefore, the Treatise says:
"The view of a self can cause the continuity of the three realms of existence," and so forth, as explained at length.
However, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) says:
"The co-emergent view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is neutral (*avyākṛta*), as is the case when the view of a self manifests in birds, beasts, and the like.

If it were produced through discrimination (*vikalpa*), it would be unwholesome (*akuśala*); this is not reasonable, because it would be illogical to claim that it is subsumed under 'view' (*dṛṣṭi*) and abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*) if it cannot be discriminated."
This should not be said to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because it is directly contrary to the realization of non-self (*anātman*).
It should be understood as being abandoned only by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-heyā*), and is comprised within non-afflicted neutral wrong knowledge (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta-mithyājñāna*).
If this were not admitted, there would be the fault of over-extension.

That is to say, even animals and the like, who are unable to discern the prior limit and so forth, should also be subject to the manifestation of doubt and other such states, just as they possess the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Since the afflictions of discrimination also manifest in the form and formless realms, they ought to be unwholesome (*akuśala*).
However, the existence of unwholesomeness in those realms has already been refuted previously.

Therefore, within the desire realm, the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are subsumed solely under the category of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature.
All other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), being the opposite of those mentioned above, are all of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala*).

This refers to the desire realm; it is intended to show that among the factors of the desire realm, everything else not mentioned above is unwholesome. There is no need for further elaboration in the verse, as these remaining ones are all unwholesome.
Among the unwholesome afflictions mentioned above, how many function as the substance of the unwholesome roots?
The verse says:
The unwholesome roots in the desire realm Are greed, hatred, and unwholesome delusion.
The treatise states:
Only all greed, hatred, and unwholesome delusion bound to the desire realm are subsumed under the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).

In their respective order, the Blessed One has taught these as the three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion. Their nature is exclusively unwholesome; because they are afflictions that serve as the root of unwholesome phenomena, they are termed "unwholesome roots. Such is the established doctrine.
Is it not the case that all evil dharmas already arisen serve as causes for subsequent [rebirth], and are not merely of three kinds?
There is no principle that exceeds these three, because they are established by way of being the opposites of the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla).
For what reason are the wholesome roots such as non-conceit (*anabhimāna*) not established?
The Buddha knows [all things] within the Dharma and establishes them accordingly. Other masters say:
Within the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), there are no afflictions such as malice or pride that could serve as their opposites.

Furthermore, the designation of "unwholesome roots" (*akuśala-mūla*) is established based on five criteria: they must pertain to all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*), be present throughout all six consciousnesses, be of the nature of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), incite unwholesome bodily and verbal actions, and function as powerful preliminary efforts (*prayoga*) at the time of severing the roots of virtue.
Pride and the other [afflictions] are not like this; it is established by implication that they are not unwholesome roots, and therefore the verse does not mention them.
Just as there are unwholesome afflictions that constitute unwholesome roots, are there such roots among the neutral (avyākṛta) afflictions?
There is also. What is it? The verse says:
There are three roots of the indeterminate: indeterminate craving, delusion, and wisdom;
it is not others, because those two [pride and views] are elevated. The masters of the Western Regions establish four types:
craving, views, pride, and delusion, because all three meditative absorptions are characterized by delusion.
The treatise states:

The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīra maintain that there are likewise three types of neutral roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*), namely: neutral craving (*tṛṣṇā*), delusion (*moha*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). It should be understood that all such neutral factors are subsumed within these neutral roots.
The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) comprehensively includes both the obscured (*nivṛta*) and the unobscured (*anivṛta*).
Since "faculty" (*indriya*) has the meaning of "cause," and unobscured-neutral wisdom can also function as a cause, it is therefore included within the neutral faculties (*avyākṛtamūla*).
These three possess the power to give rise to all neutral states (*avyākṛta*).
For what reason are doubt (*vicikitsā*) and pride (*māna*) not considered neutral roots?
Because doubt operates by oscillating between two courses, whereas pride operates by being loftily elevated.
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) and indecision (*vimati*) are excluded from being established as faculties because they waver between two courses; for a faculty must be firm and stable.
Pride (*māna*), characterized by loftiness, turns upward; it is therefore not established as a faculty, as a faculty tends toward the downward direction.

The characteristics of roots as commonly perceived in the world are such that they are called "roots" because they are hidden beneath the earth; this signifies a substance that extends downward while producing sprouts above.
These three [faculties] are like those [roots], and therefore they are also called "roots."
Other latent afflictions lack superior functional efficacy; therefore, they are not established as neutral roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*).

The masters of the foreign regions establish four such roots, namely: neutral craving (*tṛṣṇā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and delusion (*moha*). The term "neutral" (*avyākṛta*) is used here to exclude both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
For what reason are these four established as the indeterminate roots (*avyākṛtamūla*)?

Because when foolish worldlings cultivate higher meditative absorptions, they do not go beyond relying upon the three—craving (*tṛṣṇā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and pride (*māna*). Since these three all function by depending on the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), these four are established as the indeterminate roots.

He says this: "Because the power of non-obscured-neutral wisdom is weak, it is not an indeterminate root (*avyākṛta-mūla*); for the meaning of a 'root' must be established upon that which is firm and stable.

Due to the power of pride (*māna*), practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*) fall away from hundreds of thousands of sublime qualities; therefore, the power of pride is superior, and it is established as an indeterminate root."
These four can give rise to indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) defiled dharmas. Regarding this, the Sthavira says:

"There are no indeterminate roots because there is no scriptural authority for them; moreover, the arising of wholesome and unwholesome states must necessarily depend on roots due to their intensity."
Since the indeterminate [afflictions] are weak and do not arise through effort but occur spontaneously, what need is there for them to depend upon the faculties?
Furthermore, it is unreasonable to claim that there is no scriptural authority [for their existence], because the existence of indeterminate afflictions is universally established.
By what cause is it that some defiled states arise depending on a homogeneous root (*sabhāga-hetu*), while others do not?
Defiled neutral phenomena (*avyākṛta-kliṣṭa-dharma*) possess a homogeneous root because they are defiled phenomena, just like unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*).
Furthermore, on what basis do you definitively maintain that this lacks scriptural authority?
Just because it was not heard by the ears of those Sthaviras does not mean it can be dismissed as not being the word of the Buddha.
Countless scriptures have already been lost; simply because the Sthaviras did not hear them, does that make them not the word of the Buddha?

Nevertheless, since the great masters of antiquity all extensively discussed the meaning of the "unmanifest faculty" (avijñapti-indriya), we know that there must have been explicit scriptural authority for it; it was designated by a general name without distinct sub-classifications, which is why these debates arose as to whether there are four or three [types].

Furthermore, throughout the Noble Teachings, it is stated in various places that there are both determinate (*vyākṛta*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas; moreover, in various places it is stated that determinate and indeterminate dharmas arise from roots.
In some instances, the designation "indeterminate root" is established through conventional means based upon determinate roots.
Therefore, one should not say that there is no scriptural authority for this.

Furthermore, the transformation of weak and inferior dharmas should be reckoned as arising from the power of the faculties rather than from those that are sharp; thus, the reasoning established by them cannot refute our position regarding the indeterminate roots (*avyākṛtamūla*).
In the various sūtras, fourteen "unanswered questions" (avyākṛta) are taught; are these the same as what is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) because they are neither wholesome nor unwholesome?
No. Why is this so?
Because it should be set aside, it is said that there are four types of discourse for answering questions. What are these four?
The verse says:
One should categorize [questions] as follows: those to be answered categorically, those to be answered by counter-question, and those to be set aside.
This applies to such matters as death and rebirth, excellence, and whether the self and the aggregates are identical or distinct.
The treatise says:
The word "etc. is used to include [other categories] based on different perspectives.

To briefly explain the four types of questions: first, those to be answered categorically; second, those to be answered analytically; third, those to be answered with a counter-question; and fourth, those to be set aside.
These four correspond respectively to cases where an interrogator asks about death and rebirth, superiority and inferiority, or identity and difference.
There are four types of responses because there are four ways of answering these questions.
For example, if one were to ask:
"Will all who are born necessarily die?
This should be answered categorically: "All who are born are certain to die.
If one were to ask this question:
"Will all who die be reborn? This should be answered with a distinction:
"Those with afflictions will be reborn after death; those without afflictions will not be reborn after death."
If one were to ask, "Are humans superior or inferior?
one should respond with a counter-question: "In comparison to what?"
Is he reborn among the gods of the four directions, or among the evil destinies?
If you say he is reborn among the gods of the four directions, you should declare that the person is inferior.
If you say he is reborn among the evil destinies, you should declare that the person is superior.
If one were to ask:
"Are the aggregates and the sentient being identical or distinct?

this should be set aside as an unanswerable question (*sthāpanīya*). Since the sentient being lacks substantial reality, the nature of identity or difference cannot be established, just as [attributes such as] sharpness or dullness cannot be predicated of a horse's horn.
Some maintain this view:
regarding that second question, one should not provide a differentiated answer, but rather a categorical response.
That is to say, if one asks, "Do all who die necessarily come to be born? [the answer is: No.]
This should be answered categorically; it is not otherwise.
Even if they were to ask again, "Who will be reborn?
one should answer categorically: "Those who possess afflictions."
Or if he were to ask again, "Who should not be born?
one should answer categorically: "Those who are free from afflictions.

That third question should not be answered with a counter-question; rather, it should be answered categorically. For instance, if one asks, "Is the human realm superior or inferior? [one should answer directly].
One should answer categorically that [the self] is both superior and inferior, because the respective points of reference differ.
For example, if one asks whether consciousness is an effect or a cause,
one should answer categorically that it is both an effect and a cause, because the respective points of reference differ.
Since that fourth question was not answered at all as to whether the aggregates and the sentient being are different or identical, it should not be called "answered.
Is this not like when the brahmin Jātiśroṇa asked the Blessed One: "O Gautama!"?
"I have a beloved who has already passed away; I now wish to offer him this food of faith. Will he receive this offered food?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This is not a certainty."
If your beloved has been reborn among such a class of hungry ghosts (preta), they may obtain this food.
Since you have admitted that this is the case, you should provide a specific answer.
Furthermore, in this context, it is asked: "Will all those who die be reborn?"
In this case as well, one should not give a categorical answer; rather, one should provide a discriminative answer: that those with afflictions are born, whereas those without afflictions are not.
Why is it that this is not a case where a discriminative answer should be given?
Since this is a question that requires a categorical answer rather than a non-categorical one,
and since its phrasing and meaning are identical to what is taught in the Sūtras, both should be termed "to be answered categorically" (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇīya*).
Alternatively, both should be termed "to be answered by way of analysis" (*vibhajyavyākaraṇīya*), as this is compelled by the underlying principle.
One must necessarily admit that, because these are questions concerning distinctions within the human realm itself, they should be answered with a distinction.
That is to say, suppose someone were to ask:
"Is the human realm superior?"
This should be countered with a question:
"To what do you compare it?
The same counter-question should also be applied when asking about something inferior.
If both were asked together, one should answer categorically that [the former] is both superior and inferior.

It is not that superiority and inferiority are being asked about simultaneously here; rather, the word "one" (*eka*) is used when asking about one thing to indicate that the questions are distinct—one asking whether it is superior and the other whether it is inferior. Therefore, this question constitutes a case for an answer by counter-interrogation (*paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇa*).
One must set aside the objection that the "to-be-set-aside" (sthāpanīya) response does not exist as a fixed category, because the four types of questions and answers are taught in the sūtras.
Otherwise, the sūtras would have mentioned only three types of responses.
If that were so, for what reason does the sūtra list four points, with the first three having answers and the fourth lacking one?
Regarding "not answering a question," this is because it is intended as a response to what was asked.
If that is so, why is it also designated by the name "answering"?
It is because it is explained here according to what is appropriate for each case.

This also refers to what is called "the speech that should be set aside"; among the types of questions, it should be stated as "should be set aside. If one were to provide an answer using any other mode of expression, it would not be valid.
How, then, can it be said here that there are four types of questions?
Who says that there are four types of questions here?

Since the question is but one and its characteristics are not distinct, it is merely by way of the four modes of answering that the differences among questions are revealed; therefore, they are called the "four types of questions to be answered."
What is meant by the "characteristic of inquiry"?
Some say that it is based on the two [aspects] being unobstructed; this is called the characteristic of inquiry.
This is not the characteristic of a question; rather, it is the characteristic of doubt as explained in the treatise composed by Vātsyāyana.
The actual characteristic of a question is as follows: whether there is a contradiction or no contradiction, one makes a formal inquiry out of a desire to comprehend a meaning not yet understood;
or, even if there is no such inquiry, one relies on two possible meanings and, through investigation, excludes one of them.
To have hesitation and be unable to reach a definitive resolution is called the characteristic of doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Based on the characteristics of actual questions held within the mind, the masters of the Abhidharma established the methods for answering them.
Regarding those who respond categorically: if someone asks, "Is conditioned existence impermanent?
one should answer categorically.
Regarding those who inquire with discrimination: if someone with a straightforward mind requests, saying,

"I pray that the Venerable One will preach the Dharma for me," one should explain that the Dharmas are manifold— namely, those of the past, future, and present— and ask, "Which of these do you wish to hear?"
If one says,
"Explain the past dharmas for me," one should further analyze that within the past dharmas there are also many kinds, from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
If one requests an explanation of form (rūpa), one should analyze it by saying:
"Within form there are three types: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
If one requests an explanation of the wholesome, one should analyze it by saying:
Within the wholesome, there are seven types, namely: abstaining from taking life, and so on, up to abstaining from frivolous speech.
If one is further requested to explain abstaining from taking life, one should distinguish it by saying:
"This is of three kinds, namely that which is produced by the three wholesome roots of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion."
If they request an explanation of that which is produced by non-attachment, one should distinguish it by saying:
"This is further twofold, namely, manifest (vijñapti) and unmanifest (avijñapti); which of these do you wish to hear?"
When such analysis reaches its ultimate conclusion, it enables the questioner to understand the meaning of what was asked; therefore, the characteristic of answering through analysis is established.
By this, the following objection is already refuted:
"Since there can be no further statement of an answer after the analysis, it should not constitute an answer, because the analysis itself is said to be the answer."

This means that at the time of analysis, the questioner clearly understands the meaning they wish to inquire about; because at the conclusion of the analysis, the meaning of the response has already been clearly manifested, the characteristic of "analytical explanation" (vibhajya-vyākaraṇa) is thereby established.
Before they have been analyzed, one cannot understand them; once they have been analyzed, they are understood, and thus they are called "determined" (*vyākṛta*).
This name "determined" is established with respect to that which is capable of being determined.
However, the inclusion of the *kṛt* suffix here serves solely to indicate that the latter does not deviate from the meaning of the former.

As it is said in the world that one "crosses the mountain and reaches the river," this does not clarify that the mountain is before and the river is after; rather, it is intended only to make understood that there is no sense of "reaching the river" apart from "crossing the mountain," and thus the suffix *ktvā* is employed.

Thus, in this context, it is only through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) that the meaning of "explanation" (*vyākaraṇa*) is established, not apart from discrimination; therefore, this is intended solely to show that the latter is not separate from the former, rather than to establish a distinct meaning between the preceding and the succeeding.
Regarding the method of cross-examining the questioner: if there is one who requests with a deceitful mind, saying,
"I pray that the Venerable One will preach the Dharma for me," one should cross-examine them as follows:
The dharmas are manifold; which of them do you wish to speak of?
One should not differentiate between past, future, present, and so forth. Why is this?

Because the questioner knows that the mind harbors deceit and seeks to find fault, one should not differentiate the various dharmas for their sake. Rather, one should respond with a counter-question to cause them to remain silent, or to make them provide their own answer, so that they have no opportunity to seek out faults.

Since at the conclusion of the counter-interrogation one is already able to illuminate the meaning of what was stated by means of its reflection, for this reason one must also admit that this counter-interrogation itself is called an "answer" (vyākaraṇa), because the questioner's inquiry is answered through the words of the counter-interrogation.
Some raise this objection:

"This response also does not constitute a valid refutation, because there is no possibility for any further explanatory statement to follow; thus, both the question and the response fail to correspond with one another."
To say, "I pray that the Venerable One will preach the Dharma for me," does not constitute a question; it should merely be called a request.

Regarding this, the previous objection should be refuted by the same means as before; however, there is a distinction between this case and the former one: namely, that if one employs a counter-interrogation such that a correct understanding arises spontaneously in the opponent, only then can it be called a "definitive response" (*vyākaraṇa*).
As stated in the Sūtra: "I shall question you in return; according to what you accept, you should answer truthfully."
Furthermore, as it is said in a sutra:
"What do you think? Is form impermanent, or is it permanent?

It is not that the Buddha here engages in analysis for his own sake; rather, he causes [the interlocutor] to understand through counter-questions. Would this not, in this context, be called the Buddha's "explanation" (*vyākaraṇa*)?
If one can remain silent without speaking when asked, thereby causing understanding to arise in others, this is called the "supreme answer" (*paramārtha-vyākaraṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the "answer by counter-interrogation" (*paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇa*) mentioned here, there are cases where counter-interrogation itself serves as the means of answering; thus, one should understand that the name "answer by counter-interrogation" is explained based on two meanings:
first, that the counter-interrogation itself constitutes the answer; and second, that after employing counter-interrogation as a skillful means, one subsequently provides the answer to the question.

As for the claim that the definition of a question does not correspond with what constitutes a question, this too is irrational; for we do not admit that the name "definition of a question" is obtained merely through the non-exclusion of two [other categories].
Although you may accept this, you thereby contradict your own tenets; when recounting their school’s position, I shall demonstrate how it contradicts reason.
There may be one who, though not relying on the two paths, merely desires to know the characteristics of the various paths and asks:
"Please explain the path for me.
Is this not, indeed, an inquiry regarding the characteristics of the path?
Based on what two words here would there be nothing to negate?
Therefore, what you have said merely reveals your own hatred for the eloquent discourse of others and your attachment to your own false imaginings; how could this possibly refute my position?
Furthermore, how does he establish his method of answering questions?
He too partially adopts the correct doctrine while simultaneously following his own inclinations, making such statements as follows.
If one asks:
"Are all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) permanent or impermanent?
To this, one should give a categorical response, stating that they are all of an impermanent nature.
Although the question admits of two directions—namely, permanence and impermanence—the response contains only one direction. In all such cases, it should be understood accordingly.
This is what is called that which should be answered categorically (ekāṃśavyākaraṇīya).
Regarding that which should be answered by way of analysis (vibhajyavyākaraṇīya), it is as when the brahmin Jātiśroṇa asked the Blessed One: "O Gautama!"
“I have a beloved who has already passed away; I now wish to offer him the food he trusted. Will he receive this offered food?
The World-Honored One replied:
“This is not a certainty. There are five destinies, distinguished as those of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, devas, and humans.”

If those you hold dear are born in the hells, at that time they can only consume the food of the hells; the food you have offered them cannot be received by them. To speak further, even if they are born among humans, at that time they can only consume the food of humans; the food you have offered them likewise cannot be received by them.
However, there is a place called the realm of hungry ghosts (preta); if those you hold dear are born within that realm, they will indeed be able to receive the food and drink you offer.
According to our own school, such a question should be answered through analytical explanation (vibhajya-vyākaraṇa), which is logically consistent and without contradiction.

However, according to your own school, such a question should be answered categorically (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*) rather than through analysis (*vibhajyavyākaraṇa*); the logical consequences of this, whether one advances or retreats, have already been demonstrated as before.
Regarding that which should be answered by counter-interrogation (*paripṛcchya-vyākaraṇa*), they say: if one asks, "Is the self permanent or impermanent? [one should respond by asking back].
One should counter-interrogate, saying:
"In dependence upon what self do you ask?
If it is in dependence upon a self consisting of form, or even a self consisting of consciousness, you should answer that it is impermanent."
If someone asks, "Do I exist?
Do I not exist? one should respond with a counter-question:
Based on what do you ask?
If you say you ask based on any one of those twelve bases (*āyatana*), the answer should be "it exists";
if you ask based on anything else, the answer should be "it does not exist."

Now, it is said that the counter-questions herein are unreasonable. To begin with, when asked, "Is the self permanent or impermanent? one should answer categorically that it is of an impermanent nature; for it is only within the aggregates (*skandha*) that the self is imputed, and all aggregates are exclusively of an impermanent nature.
As it is said in a sutra:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world, all those who cling to a self perceive it, upon close examination, as arising solely within the five aggregates of clinging."
Since there is no possibility for a second answer, one should provide a categorical response rather than a counter-interrogation.
Even if they were to reply:
"I do not rely on a self [identical to] form, nor even up to a self [identical to] consciousness."
How should this be answered?
Since there is no one who gives rise to the view of a self apart from the aggregates, your question is irrational; how should it be answered?

Because it is not to be declared whether [the self] is impermanent or permanent, nor can it be said that the self is of a permanent nature; for there are certainly no aggregates (*skandha*) of such a kind, and because the view of a self cannot arise apart from the aggregates.
Therefore, this must be answered categorically.
Regarding the second question—whether the self exists or does not exist—one likewise should not employ the method of counter-interrogation by asking:
"Upon what kind of self do you base your question?"

Since all views of a self necessarily arise with respect to one or another of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and because there is no possibility for a view of a self to exist apart from these, one should answer categorically that it does exist.
However, one may reasonably raise an objection here:
Regarding your previous question as to whether the self exists or not, do you ask about a permanent self or an impermanent one?
If you ask about the impermanent, the answer should be that it exists, because the term "self" is applied to the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*).
If one asks whether there is a permanent self, one should answer that there is not, because within all appropriated aggregates (upādāna-skandha) nothing is permanent.
This principle is revealed in the sacred teachings; thus, it is said in the *Tāḷasūtra*:

"A bhikṣu investigated and pondered, 'What is this self, what is this self? The Buddha, knowing his mind, extensively explained and defined the eighteen elements (dhātu), and then addressed the bhikṣu:"
If you were to say that this dharma is the self, you should say that this self is impermanent and non-eternal; [this should be] explained in detail up until: "O bhikṣus!
In your opinion, is this eye permanent or impermanent?"
He replied:
"Venerable Sir,
this is the nature of impermanence."
"Since it is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering?
He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
It is also of the nature of suffering.
Since it is impermanent and suffering, it is a phenomenon subject to change; would a learned noble disciple grasp at this as being "I" or "mine"?
The bhikṣu replied: "No, Venerable Sir!"
The meaning intended here is this: if one holds that impermanent phenomena constitute an impermanent self, one should say that the self exists;
if one holds that impermanent phenomena such as the eyes constitute a permanent self, one should say that the self does not exist.
Furthermore, apart from such phenomena as the eye and so forth, there exists no other subtle, permanent phenomenon that can be reckoned as a self; therefore, a permanent self does not exist.
For this reason, other sūtras also state:

"All conditioned formations (saṃskāra) are empty and impermanent; they are without constancy, without stability, and without unchangingness; moreover, they are empty of the nature of self and what belongs to a self (ātman-ātmīya)."
Furthermore, it was previously stated that the self is impermanent, non-eternal, unreliable, and subject to change; elsewhere, it is further said:
"O Bhikṣus! You are now being born and you are aging," and so forth, as explained at length.
This intention reveals that while the permanent self is empty, the impermanent is not empty; therefore, this statement was made.
As cited above from the sutra, the World-Honored One posed a counter-question:
"O Bhikṣus!"
"Do you think these elements, such as the eye and so forth, are impermanent or not?
Having asked this question, I shall later declare whether the permanent self exists or does not exist."
Furthermore, the *Yamaka-saṃyutta* and other sūtras also state by way of counter-question:
"O Bhikṣus! If one were asked whether the aggregates are permanent or impermanent, I declare that such a person does not exist."
Applying this principle by analogy, the same logic should apply here as well.
That is to say, regarding this matter, someone might ask:
"Does the self-entity exist, or does it not exist?"
One should respond with a counter-question:
"Regarding the 'self' you ask about, do you inquire about a permanent self or an impermanent one?
If you inquire about the impermanent, I should declare that it exists."
If one asks whether there is a permanent self, one should answer that there is none.
Therefore, what they have said is entirely unreasonable.
Regarding those matters that should be set aside, it refers to when a bhikṣu asked the Blessed One:
"Venerable One!
You should explain how many past kalpas there have been.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
The number of past kalpas is so vast that it cannot easily be described.
Because the bhikṣus therein did not know the number of kalpas, they questioned the Buddha; the World-Honored One replied to them that the number of past kalpas cannot be fully known.
It is designated as "to be set aside" because it is answered by being set aside; therefore, it is called "to be set aside.
In this case, how could there be a basis for a twofold non-refusal?
Yet you maintain that there is the characteristic of a question here. Since the Blessed One has not spoken [on this], what unspoken matter could be said to exist that might be considered a question?
Once the Blessed One has spoken, what is there to be excluded that could be called an "explanation"?

If a bhikṣu first asks a question and, due to total ignorance, still does not understand even after the Blessed One has spoken, then since both the act of questioning and the act of explaining are present here, do you also admit that this constitutes a "question and explanation"?
Furthermore, the sūtras state that there are four ways of answering questions; however, they themselves explain:
"It is precisely because of this reason that among the four types of answers listed, the first three are designated as 'answered,' while for the fourth alone, the term 'answered' is not employed."
If that is so, for what reason did you previously offer this interpretation—that one should provide a categorical answer as if setting the question aside?
Is it not the case that your earlier and later statements contradict one another?

If one provides a categorical answer by setting the question aside according to its requirements, then one must admit that the fourth type of response also possesses the quality of being "categorical" (*vyākarana*).

If it is argued that because this [category] has the characteristic of being indeterminate (avyākṛta), the word "determined" (vyākaraṇa) is not mentioned in the enumeration of its names, how can one then say that it is a "determination" consisting of setting aside according to the circumstances?
Therefore, this contradicts [your own] position.

Furthermore, one should not raise objections against another school; since you have not provided a definitive answer as to whether the aggregates and the sentient being are different or identical, it cannot be called a "definitive answer" (*vyākaraṇa*).
Therefore, that school’s formulation of the characteristics for answering questions is extremely flawed;
the previous explanation is what should be relied upon. *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 49.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 50.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Six: An Analysis of the Latent Defilements (Anuśaya), Part Five, Section Six. The analysis of the causes of the unwholesome and indeterminate latent defilements, along with its ancillary discussion, is now concluded.
Now it should be investigated: which underlying tendencies (anuśaya) bind to which objects?
What is meant by "object" (vastu)?
Although objects are not singular, we shall here define the objects to which [the defilements] are bound.
This, moreover, is twofold.
What are these two? They are explained in terms of their basis and conditions, as well as their categories.
Regarding those bound by way of object: the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that coexist with visual consciousness are bound to the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) solely as objects;
they are bound to their own associated mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta) through the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) and the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana) as associations.

In this manner, up to and including those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that coexist with body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna), they are bound to the sense-base of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana) solely as objects of perception;
with respect to their own associated mind and mental factors, they are bound to the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) and the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana) by way of association.

If there are any latent dispositions (anuśaya) concomitant with the mental consciousness, they constitute a bond by way of being an object (ālambana-bandhana) with respect to the twelve bases (āyatana);

with respect to their own associated minds and mental factors, they constitute a bond by way of association (saṃprayoga-bandhana) within the mind-base (manāyatana) and the phenomena-base (dharmāyatana).

Regarding their categories: the universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) constitute an object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*) with respect to the phenomena of the five categories, and a concomitant-condition (*samprayoga-bandhana*) with respect to their own associated minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

The non-universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) function as objects of attachment (*ālambana-bandhana*) only within their own category, and as associated attachments (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) toward the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are associated with them.
All such cases should be explained accordingly as appropriate.
To analyze this according to the three time periods: what kind of sentient beings possess which latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and by what means are they bound to what objects?
The verse says:
If, within this [object], greed, hatred, and conceit have not been abandoned, and have already arisen in the past or present, they will arise in the future as universal mental factors;
the five [sensory consciousnesses] will arise in their own respective realms; and even when they do not arise, they remain universal.
The others [the past and future] are pervasive; the present binds by way of actual engagement.
The commentary states:
When the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with a particular object within a given class of sentient beings, it is said that they are bound to that object.
That which is capable of binding must necessarily be unabandoned; therefore, at the initial stage of non-abandonment, [the afflictions] flow everywhere as appropriate.
Furthermore, there are generally two kinds of *anuśaya*s: first, those with specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), namely greed, hatred, and pride;
second, those with common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), namely views, doubt, and delusion.
Greed, hatred, and pride are afflictions of their own specific characteristics, as has already been demonstrated; clear textual evidence for this is found throughout the various holy teachings.
For instance, a sutra states that [the Buddha] addressed the mother of Kāṇḍārī:
"When your eye does not see a form, does that form serve as a condition for the arising of sensual desire?"
"Not so, Venerable Sir! ...
[and so on] up to the full exposition."
Furthermore, a sutra states that the Buddha told the Mother Mahāprajāpatī:

"What do you think? Regarding all forms whatsoever—those not seen by your eye, those not previously seen by you, those not yet to be seen by you, and those for which you have no desire to see them—do you, on account of these, give rise to desire, give rise to greed, give rise to intimacy, give rise to affection, give rise to *ālaya*, give rise to *nyanti*, or give rise to attachment?"
"It is not so, Venerable Sir!
and so forth, as explained at length.

Therefore, regarding this object, greed, hatred, and pride that arose in the past and have not yet been abandoned, as well as those that arise in the present, are able to bind one to this object; for greed, hatred, and pride are specific-characteristic afflictions (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*), and they do not necessarily arise universally in all sentient beings.

Is it not the case that if the meaning of "being bound" (*baddha*) were already severed, then [the term] would simply not exist? Since the word "bound" has already been stated, it clearly indicates that [the defilement] is not yet severed. For what reason, then, do you say that this [object] is "bound by what is not yet severed," and further state that it is "past, already arisen, and not yet severed"? In such a case, the term "not yet severed" would become redundant.
There is no fault of uselessness, for this statement "not yet abandoned" indicates that there are distinct categories which are abandoned gradually.

Indeed, in the subsequent passage of this very treatise, it is also stated that the future universal mental factors and so forth exist; that is to say, since those [afflictions] such as greed differ according to nine grades, when they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they are abandoned grade by grade. Regarding an object of this kind, even though the superior-grade latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have already arisen and already ceased, they have attained permanent abandonment.

Regarding this matter, there still remain future categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have not yet arisen or been extinguished; as long as these have not been permanently severed, they are still capable of acting as fetters. Therefore, although the *Mūla-śāstra* states in this context that one is bound by future craving and so forth, it employs the term "not yet severed" with respect to the past; thus, the expression "not yet severed" is profoundly purposeful.

However, when the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of this category belonging to the past are permanently severed, those of the future are also severed. Yet, it is possible that other categories of future latent dispositions remain capable of binding this object and have not yet been permanently severed; for the three—greed, hatred, and pride—associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in the future world universally take the three time periods as their objects. Thus, although they may or may not arise with respect to this particular object, as long as they have not been severed, they are all termed "capable of binding."
Regarding future greed and hatred associated with the five consciousnesses, if they have not been abandoned and are capable of arising, they bind only the future life.
By this, it has already been shown that the dormant afflictions (*anuśaya*) associated with the five consciousnesses that are capable of arising [bind only the future].
If it pertains to the past, it is bound only by the past; the same applies when it pertains to the present.

By extension of this principle, if a latent disposition (*anuśaya*) capable of arising is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and if it has not been abandoned in the past, present, or future, it may be bound by dharmas that do not belong to its own time period.

Not only do the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), when existing in the future, bind the three time periods; those latent dispositions associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*), if they are destined never to arise, likewise bind the three time periods.

That is to say, those objects may exist in the future, the present, or the past; although they have already attained ultimate non-arising, their temporal nature remains unsevered and continues to bind.

All remaining views, doubt, and ignorance that have not been abandoned in the past or future bind one universally across the three periods of time; for these three types are universal afflictions (*sāmānya-kleśa*), as they universally bind all sentient beings alike.
If, in the present, when correctly taking an object as its condition, [affliction] is able to bind that very thing according to what is appropriate,

by what evidence is it known that afflictions such as greed arise by taking objects of the three times— past and so forth— as their conditions, and that they are able to act as a bond within those very objects?
This is established by scriptural authority; thus, a sutra states:

"There are, in total, three kinds of phenomena that are objects of sensual desire: first, phenomena that are objects of sensual desire in the past; second, phenomena that are objects of sensual desire in the future; and third, phenomena that are objects of sensual desire in the present."

If desire and greed arise with respect to phenomena that were objects of desire and greed in the past, this arising of desire and greed should be said to be bound to those past phenomena, not dissociated from them; and so on, as explained at length.
Furthermore, a sutra states:

"If one gives rise to craving or aversion toward forms seen in the past, future, or present, it should be known that in this case the eye is not bound by form, nor is form bound by the eye; rather, it is desire and greed that truly act as the bond."
There are many such scriptural authorities of this kind.
Now, one must first deliberate upon whether the past and future exist as real entities or not, before one can discuss their bondage.

Regarding whether the past and future truly exist or not, masters of antiquity have harbored sectarian attachments, mutually criticizing and refuting one another while vying to promote their own systems of discourse; each has presented scriptural principles to establish their respective tenets.

Such debates were heard of everywhere: those who maintained that existence is real extensively cited principles and teachings, employing various skillful means to refute non-existence and establish existence;
while those who maintained that non-existence is real extensively cited principles and teachings, employing various skillful means to refute existence and establish non-existence.
Because this gives rise to a mass of co-arising great faults,
I shall now exert great right effort and reflect according to reason, establishing that the past and future exist as distinct from the present, rather than being absolutely non-existent.

That is to say, the establishment of the past and future is not like their existence as present phenomena, nor is it like the non-existence of things such as a horse's horns; rather, the essence of the past and future is established as being fully existent.
Only this accords with the true tenets of the Abhidharma school.

In this regard, one should first analyze the characteristics of existence; for once these characteristics of existence are held firmly in mind, one can then understand that the past and future definitely exist.
Because these analyzed characteristics are clear and easy to comprehend, even those who hold stubborn attachments will be able to accord with reality.
Regarding this, one group asserts:
"That which has already arisen but not yet ceased is the characteristic of existence (*sat-lakṣaṇa*).
This statement is incorrect, because "that which has already arisen but not yet ceased" is merely a specific designation for the present.
If it is asserted that the present exists as having characteristics (*sanimitta*), then by implication it has already been stated that the past and future are non-existent.
This principle must further be interrogated: for what reason do characteristics belong only to the present and not to the others?
Therefore, what they have argued does not constitute the characteristic of true existence. Regarding this, I say the following:

that which gives rise to cognition by way of being an object is the characteristic of true existence. This is twofold in total: first, substantial existence (*dravyasat*), and second, nominal existence (*prajñaptisat*), because these are established in accordance with the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and ultimate (*paramārtha*) truths.

If a cognition arises with respect to something without depending on anything else, that is the characteristic of substantial existence (*dravyasat*), such as form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth.

If a cognition arises with respect to something while depending on other things, that is the characteristic of conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*), such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), an army (*senā*), and so forth.
Others further establish a third type here, namely "existence through mutual dependence" (*apekṣā-sat*), such as "this shore" and "that shore.
This is already subsumed within the two previously mentioned types of existence; although the names differ, that which they refer to is no different.
Furthermore, what they maintain contradicts the sūtras, for the sūtras state only that there are two kinds of existence (*bhava*).
There are two types of real existence (*dravyasat*). What are these two?
First, there is that which possesses only its own essence;

second, there is that which possesses functional activity. This possession of functional activity is further divided into two types: first, that which possesses efficacy; second, that which lacks efficacy.
By this, the category of "possessing only its own essence" has already been explained.
Provisional existence is also twofold. What are these two?
First, that which relies on the real; second, that which relies on the provisional.
These two are, respectively, like a jar and like an army.
Within the various holy teachings, all the verbal instructions that speak of existence can be summarized into four types:
first, existence as a substantial entity; second, existence through the conjunction of conditions; third, existence as attainment; and fourth, existence as a causal nature.
As stated in a sutra:
"There is form that is impermanent; therein, I correctly know and see.
Furthermore, as another sutra states:
"That which does not exist in the world, that I know and see as being non-existent—such a thing is impossible.
Passages such as these speak of the existence of substantial entities (*dravyasat*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Only when there is a tree can there be a shadow.
O bhikṣus, if you are in harmony, there is no teacher equal to me.
Such passages speak of existence through the conjunction of conditions.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are wholesome roots that accompany [the mind] which have not yet been severed.
Furthermore, as another Sūtra says:
There is an internal fetter of the eye.
Furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra:
"Those two lack warmth."
Furthermore, as stated in the sutras:
"One who does not possess craving for existence is called a person with eyes.
Passages such as these speak of the accomplishment of existence (*bhava*).
As stated in the sūtra:
"When this exists, that exists; when this does not exist, that does not exist.
Passages such as these speak of the existence of causal nature (*hetutva*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"There is no mire like that of sensual desires; even if one were to attempt to describe such a thing, there would ultimately be no basis for doing so.
Such teachings state that [sensual desires] are absolutely non-existent.
Those who exclusively maintain that only the present exists are not capable of providing a correct analysis of the Buddha’s teaching on existence;
this principle will be fully elucidated later. This is what is called the characteristic of existence as analyzed by our own school.
The Dārṣṭāntika proponent speaks as follows:
"This [definition] is also not a truly existent characteristic, because it is admitted that even what is non-existent can serve as an object for the arising of cognition.

That is to say, one must necessarily admit that even what is non-existent can serve as an object for the arising of cognition; for when the two cognitions of a whirling fire-brand and a self arise, their objects do not exist."

Furthermore, because there is the mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) regarding the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth, if all cognitions possessed an objective referent (*ālambana*), then such mental attention of resolute conviction would be impossible.
Moreover, it is stated in the *Māyājāla* that one perceives what does not exist as an object.
Furthermore, a sutra states that one knows because [the object] does not exist. As a sutra says:
"Regarding desire for what is desireless, one is then able to understand it as non-existent, just as it truly is."
Furthermore, because objects do not exist in cases such as the world’s cognitions of a dream, a visual impairment, or multiple moons;
and since one apprehends what is non-existent as being "non-existent," what could serve as the objective referent (*ālambana*) for this cognition?
Furthermore, if sound were non-existent prior to its being perceived, what would this perceiving consciousness have as its object?
Therefore, one should know that both existence and non-existence can serve as objects for the arising of cognition; thus, what has been stated here is not the true characteristic of reality.
The masters of Abhidharma state as follows:

There is no cognition devoid of an object, because it is determined by two conditions; for the Sūtras declare that the six types of cognition are all invariably possessed of a support (*āśraya*) and an object (*ālambana*).

That is to say, visual cognition arises depending on the eye and conditioned by visible forms; this continues up to mental cognition arising depending on the mind and conditioned by mental objects (*dharma*). There is no seventh cognition that arises independently of an object which could be asserted as a cognition of non-existent objects.

If you grant that cognition can arise independently of its object, you must likewise grant that cognition can arise independently of its basis; consequently, those such as the congenitally blind would possess eyes and so forth, because no distinct causes and conditions for the arising of cognition could be found.

Furthermore, it is not the case that there exists no dharma which can be said to be subsumed under any one of these six objects; therefore, to maintain that cognition arises by taking non-existence as its object contradicts both reason and scripture, and is utterly crude and unsound.
Others raise this objection: "If one observes that some cognitions have an object of perception (*sālambana*), one concludes that all cognitions have an object of perception.
Since one observes that some cognitions take the past and future as their objects, it follows that cognitions such as those of the eye must also take the past and future as their objects."
If this is not admitted, one should likewise not admit that a cognition is established as having an object merely by seeing a portion of it.

That is to say, all cognitions have objects; therefore, one should not establish this inference, for if one were to do so, there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Thus, the existence of cognitions without external objects is truly established.

This is merely words and entirely devoid of logical consistency; for it is only by virtue of having distinct objects as their respective focal points (*ālambana*) that cognitions (*buddhi*) can differ, just like the cognitions of the eye and other senses.
That is to say, while cognitions such as those of the eye arise with respect to specific present objects, it is not the case that all [cognitions] take all present things as their objects.
In this way, while all cognitions arise with respect to distinct objects, it is not the case that all [cognitions] take all existing phenomena as their objects.

Furthermore, we observe that some cognitions have specific objects of perception (*ālambana*), which is universally established; by analogy with these cases, one should conclude that all other cognitions likewise possess objects, and thus there is no fault.

It is not observed that even a minimal portion of a cognition lacking an object of perception is established for both [parties]; how, then, could it be proven without fault that there is cognition without an object?
However, the Dārṣṭāntika previously stated:

"That both existence and non-existence can serve as objects to produce cognition is unreasonable, because cognition must have an object of cognition in relation to which the cognition itself is established."
This means that the designation "cognition" is established only when there is an object to be apprehended; if that which is apprehended does not exist, whose apprehension would it be?
Furthermore, the nature of consciousness is the act of cognizing an object; if that which is cognized does not exist, what would consciousness cognize?
Therefore, that consciousness which they assert to be without an object of cognition (*ālambana*) should not be called "consciousness," because it lacks anything to be cognized.

Now, to say something "does not exist" means its substance is entirely non-existent; since non-existence necessarily transcends both specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), how can it be termed an "object of awareness" or an "object of cognition"?
If it is claimed that non-existence itself is the object cognized by consciousness, this is not so; for consciousness must necessarily have an object.

That all mental states and mental factors take only specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as their objects, and do not arise with a total absence of phenomena as their object, has already been briefly demonstrated in the discussion on *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, if one maintains that a cognition arises taking a non-existent object as its condition, this cognition must be of a delusory nature.

That is to say, for one who maintains the theory that there is cognition without an object, the cognition they maintain which takes a non-existent object as its condition must necessarily be of a delusory nature.
As the Blessed One has said:
"If I were to contemplate that which does not exist in the world, I would surely become deranged.

It is not possible for the Bhagavān to be subject to derangement; therefore, one knows with certainty that there is no cognition that lacks an object as its condition. Logically, it should not be asserted that there could be even a slight portion of a mental state that arises where the Buddha does not take something as his cognitive object."
Furthermore, there is certainly no cognition that lacks an object-condition (*ālambana*) or an objective sphere (*viṣaya*), for it is said that what is unknowable and unobtainable does not exist.
As the Sūtra says: "The prior limit (*pūrvānta*) is unknowable."
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"An agent cannot be found.
This meaning reveals that awakening must necessarily have an object; because such an [independent] agent does not exist, it cannot be known or apprehended.

If it were admitted that cognition arises taking a non-existent object as its condition, then the prior limit [of existence] should be knowable and the agent should be obtainable, for there would be no obstruction within that which is non-existent.

Nor can it be said that within non-existence, one part is an object and another part is not an object; for it cannot be said that there is any distinction of superiority or inferiority between this non-existence and that non-existence.
Furthermore, it is said that there is definitely no such thing [as knowing or seeing what does not exist], because one cannot know or see what is non-existent. As a sūtra states:
"It is impossible for me to know or see that which does not exist in the world."
The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrāntika) explains the meaning of this sūtra as follows:

"It means that while others, harboring overweening pride (*adhimāna*), perceive even what does not exist as having manifest characteristics and thus claim it exists, I only regard what actually exists as existing."
If it were otherwise, then all cognitions would possess an object; for what reason, then, could there be doubt regarding an object, or could there be any distinction between them?

Such an explanation merely follows one's own whims; how can it be said that even a person of overweening pride perceives a manifestation of existence within that which does not exist? For there can be no manifest appearance of a characteristic within that which is non-existent.

If a sign were obtainable regarding that which does not exist, then it should be obtainable as a sign within a thirteenth locus; for such a sign of non-existence as described would transcend the twelvefold aggregate of the knowable.
