Although the objective entity does not exist at this stage, cognition is not non-existent; thus, there are two kinds of certainties.

All such statements by the Sthavira are like the dream-talking of a mute person. Having already extensively investigated and refuted [his views] in the section on the four conditions, one should follow that text as a precedent to refute this current assertion.
This explanation can only deceive the ignorant; when examined by the wise, it possesses no real meaning whatsoever.
Now, let us briefly reconsider this point once more. First, one should challenge their own resolution of the objection, which states:

"Within the continuum, there must necessarily exist a causal cognition and a resultant cognition; that which was previously produced, at the time the present cognition arises, also takes as its object the very same object previously apprehended by that [causal] cognition."
What is meant by the "knowledge of the cause" and the "knowledge of the fruit" regarding that which has already arisen, such that one says the present knowledge takes that as its object?
Is it the case that the present knowledge takes as its object that very same thing previously taken as an object, or is there yet another distinct knowledge that takes a different object?

If that which was previously apprehended is now the object of the present cognition, then since this object has already been taken as an object by a past cognition, how can it be called an "object never before apprehended"?

Conversely, if there were another cognition apprehending a different object, and you maintain that this other object is what is currently being apprehended, then how could the present cognition be said to have an object that has never been apprehended before?

That is to say, the cause and effect that were previously apprehended by the knowledge of the cause and the knowledge of the effect as their respective objects—since this object was already grasped by knowledge at an earlier time, how can it now be called an "object never before grasped"?
To claim that what was previously experienced is simultaneously not experienced is contrary to correct reasoning.

Furthermore, even if one were to grant that there exists an "old pervasive element" (*paurāṇa-anuśaya-dhātu*) which, through the power of its causal continuity, allows for the apprehension of objects long extinguished over many eons, there would still be no logical contradiction in such a case.
If there are objects that will exist after hundreds of thousands of kalpas in the future, how can they be apprehended now?

One cannot say that they can be apprehended due to the power of the successive continuity of cause and effect, because future entities do not exist—just like the horns of a horse—and because there is no "concomitant element" (*anugata-dhātu*) within the continuity [of the present].

Furthermore, if consciousness were to arise only within the range of objects previously grasped by tracing back through successive past causes, then there would necessarily be a distinction in the speed of apprehension regarding objects previously grasped that are near versus those that are distant.

It is not that the body currently residing in Pāṭaliputra recollects the events experienced in the past in the country of Bāhlika; rather, consciousness arises only through a gradual succession, for it is only when such a sequence has occurred that a consciousness taking those objects as its condition can suddenly arise.

Furthermore, immediately following auditory consciousness, there arises [a subsequent cognition] that takes as its object a consciousness previously apprehended at an earlier time. What serves as the cause for the arising of such a consciousness?
It cannot be caused by the seeds (anuśaya) present at that time, because auditory consciousness does not take those seeds as its objective domain.
Nor can it be because that consciousness was previously apprehended, for at that time, that which was previously apprehended no longer exists.
It is impossible for a non-entity to serve as a cause for the arising of another non-entity, lest even things such as horse-horns should likewise arise.
This has already been extensively examined and refuted in the discussion on the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*).

Therefore, in the school that maintains that there is only a single moment [of consciousness], it is absolutely impossible for a consciousness to arise with respect to past or future objects based on two determinate factors.
If one believes that the past and future truly exist, then these two definitive principles can be established.

Furthermore, because past actions have future results—meaning that previously performed wholesome or unwholesome actions await conditions to bring about future desirable or undesirable fruits—this has already been extensively established in the section analyzing karma.

It is not the case that the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) arises without a karma as its immediate cause, nor is it the case that the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) exists in the present at the time the fruit is arising.

If past dharmas were non-existent in their essence, there would either have to be the principle of a fruit arising without a cause, or else that fruit would never arise at all. Therefore, one should know that the past truly exists.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrāntavādin) states as follows:

"It is not the case that the Sautrāntika masters maintain that past karma can directly produce a future fruit. Rather, it is the transformation of a continuum—initiated by karma—that, through its specific differentiation, causes the future fruit to arise, just as, for example, a seed in the world produces a future fruit."
This means that just as a future fruit arises from a seed, the future fruit does not arise from a seed that has already perished.

Nor does the future fruit arise immediately after the seed; rather, it is the transformation of a continuity (saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa) induced by the seed as its precursor that is able to produce the future fruit.

This means that first there is the seed, followed by the successive arising of the sprout, the leaf, and so on up to the flower; it is from the flower, in due order, that the fruit subsequently arises.

Yet, when it is said that the production of the fruit comes from the seed, it is because the functional capacity—which was induced by the seed and transmitted through a series of transformations—residing within the flower gives rise to the fruit.
If a flower did not possess a capacity induced by its seed, it would be unable to produce such a kind of fruit.

Likewise, while a future fruit arises from karma, that future fruit does not arise from karma that has already perished, nor does the future fruit arise immediately after the karma; rather, a transformation within the continuum initiated by the karma—specifically a particular modification of that continuum—is able to produce the future fruit.

The continuity of karma (*karma-saṃtati*) refers to the successive arising of moments of mind, preceded by karma, which constitute a continuous stream. This very continuity, as it arises differently in each subsequent moment, is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). This transformation, at its final stage, possesses a superior capacity to produce a fruit immediately; because it differs from other transformations, it is termed "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*).
Such principles as these should be understood by analogy with what preceded.

This has already been refuted previously during the investigation of karma; now, taking this opportunity, those points where the reasoning was not yet exhaustive shall be further and extensively demolished.

Furthermore, the claim that karma is the preceding mind and its subsequent arising constitutes a "continuity of karma" is logically untenable, because there is a distinction between karma and the mind.
This distinction means that karma and the mind differ in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), category (*jāti*), and cause (*hetu*).
There is a difference in substance because their characteristics are distinct.
There is a difference in category because the categories of mind and mental factors are distinct.
There is a difference in cause because they arise from two causes or three causes.
Since there is this difference, how can it be said that the subsequent mind arises as a continuation of karma?
Furthermore, it has already been extensively established elsewhere in the discussion of simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) that the mind and karma arise at the same time.

Within the continuum of volition and the continuum of consciousness, one never observes the simultaneous arising of two similar types of continua; therefore, it is known that karma and the mind do not constitute a single continuum.
Furthermore, your school maintains that there is consciousness in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Yet the Buddha stated:
"In the attainment of cessation, all mental formations (*saṃskāra*) cease.
How, then, can the activity of the mind continue as a single continuum?

If it were admitted that karma and the mind belong to the same continuum, then just as the mind does not cease, the mental formations (*manasikāra*) would likewise not cease; and just as the mental formations cease, the mind would likewise cease.
However, it is established at length within the section on the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) that there is necessarily no mind in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Because the continuity of karma would be severed, subsequent results should not arise; yet there is no such principle as that which allows for the arising of subsequent results through the sequential continuity of seeds, sprouts, and so forth. Therefore, that [position] is nothing but a false conceptual construction.
Furthermore, the claim that the fruit arises from the flower is not logically established, for our own school maintains that the substance of seeds already destroyed still exists substantially.
Even if one were to grant its establishment as a continuum in that manner, the principle of this karma-continuum would still not be established, due to the specific reasoning previously demonstrated.

Furthermore, because the causes of desirable and undesirable fruits are fixed: that is to say, unwholesome actions are determined to be the cause that brings about undesirable fruits, whereas desirable fruits must necessarily have wholesome actions as their cause.

If one maintains that a flower is the transformation of the continuum of the seed—which, through its specific differentiation, is able to produce a fruit—then what established principle is there whereby distinct causes for excellent or evil conduct can each separately summon desirable or undesirable fruits?

Unwholesome conduct lacks the capacity to produce an agreeable result, and wholesome conduct lacks the capacity to produce a disagreeable result; neutral action lacks the capacity for either. What definitive principle should be stated regarding this?

Since all the functional capacities of these three types are not different in essence from the mind itself, one should not say that they differ in kind; nor can it be said that there is no distinct essence for what is not a separate kind, for such a thing has never been observed.

Furthermore, since the flower arises from a continuum such as the sprout, one might maintain that it possesses the functional capacity of a seed, because that capacity is not distinct in essence from the flower;
however, it is not the case that the wholesome and the unwholesome can lack a distinction in essence, lest there be a great error in this regard.

Furthermore, since the seed, sprout, and so forth constitute a single continuum, and you maintain that the flower possesses the functional capacity of the seed, the flower must likewise possess the functional capacities of the sprout and so on; for no distinction can be found between them. Thus, the sprout and its functions, as well as the seed and its functions, would all be non-different in essence from the flower.
Since the flower, as an auxiliary condition, is able to produce the fruit through its inherent functional capacity, sprouts and the like should likewise arise by virtue of this very same principle.
Yet, at that time, it produces only the fruit and not the sprouts; what is the cause for this?

It is not the case that within the flower there can be distinct capacities induced by the seeds and so forth residing separately; rather, at that time, it is only the capacity induced by the seed that, with the flower acting as a cooperative condition, is able to induce the arising of the fruit, and not a capacity induced by the sprout and so forth within the flower.

If it is argued that the functional capacity induced by the sprout and so forth, though residing within the flower, must await the fruit— or that the sprout and so forth must arise before the sprout and so forth can be produced— then,

just as the seed previously induced its own fruit and subsequently acts as the cause for the continuity of the seed-series within the subsequent sprout and so forth, so too should the functional capacity induced by prior karma, having produced the matured fruit (vipāka-phala) it attracted, subsequently act as the cause for the continuity of subsequent karma.

However, your school asserts that the final moment of maturation is caused by a distinct karmic action (*viśeṣa-karman*), which then draws forth the continuity of the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*); it is not the case that the seeds of a prior karma have the power to project a subsequent karma. Therefore, one should not use the continuity of seeds as an analogy for the continuity of karma’s ability to produce a fruit.

Furthermore, from time immemorial, each species of seeds, sprouts, and so forth has its own distinct continuum; it has never been heard that a rice seed or sprout, through a series of transformations, could eventually produce the fruit of a wild millet plant.

However, according to your own tenet that a single continuum of karma can induce both desirable and undesirable fruits, that [example] should not serve as a homologous illustration (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*).

Furthermore, if the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna*) were to carry the functional capacity of volition (*cetanā*), and the substance of volition were in turn to carry the functional capacity of consciousness, then since the capacity and the phenomenon would have no distinct substance, by what characteristic could this consciousness be distinguished from this volition?
Furthermore, if that were the case, karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth would become confused.

Such faults have been stated by me repeatedly in various passages; therefore, for those who harbor hatred toward and deny the existence of the past and future, the principle by which karmic results are brought about is certainly non-existent.

Therefore, for those ignorant ones who conceal and suppress the sūtras, the claim that there is a continuous transformation and differentiation capable of summoning a future fruit is logically untenable.
In this context, the Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika) further raises this objection:
"If one maintains that the past and future exist substantially, then the essence of the fruit would exist at all times; what functional efficacy, then, would karma have with respect to that fruit?"
When this objection arises, it shall be resolved according to reason.

For now, your argument that the fruition of karma is not established is refuted; rather, the past and future must certainly be substantially existent, because they are said to possess the characteristics of existence, just like the present.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Past and future form are already impermanent, how much more so is present [form].
Since impermanence is precisely the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), the actual existence of that characteristic in the present is established as a reality."

If one maintains that the past and future are not substantially existent, then they should not be said to possess conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) in the same way as the present; yet even that which is absolutely non-existent, such as a sky-flower or a horse’s horn, can still be said to possess impermanence. Therefore, it is known that the past and future are certainly substantially existent.
To claim that the existence of characteristics is asserted based on what has occurred or what will occur is also unreasonable, because there is no distinction in the statement itself.
It is not taught in the sūtras that past and future form was once impermanent or will be impermanent.
For this reason, that defense is merely a product of their own subjective sentiments.
Furthermore, what they say regarding "once" and so forth does not refer to past impermanence, but is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) for speaking of present impermanence;

that is, because they speak of the impermanence of the past, future, and present. If that were the case, since the present impermanence has already been stated, one should not further say, "how much more so the present."

Alternatively, one should speak only of the impermanence of the present; the impermanence of the past and future is already understood by this, as they are simply the states of having already ceased or not yet arisen in the present.

If the essence were to exist eternally at all times, then the nature of impermanence could not be established; this shall be explained according to reason when discussing the distinctions between the time-periods (*adhvan*).
Furthermore, one should not say that non-existence is impermanent; for the Elder provides this explanation here:
it is precisely because the entity itself does not exist that it is called "impermanent"; if the entity were not non-existent, there would be no principle for it to be impermanent.
If that were so, the present would have to be eternal in essence.
If the present is not non-existent and yet is impermanent, then one should not say it is impermanent because it does not exist.
He further objects, saying:
If [a phenomenon] were to abide eternally by its own nature throughout the three times, it should be described as permanent.

This objection is not valid; for what [phenomenon], such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, is universally accepted as being permanent while abiding eternally by its own nature throughout the three times, such that it could serve as a [counter-example]?
All things would be eternal and none would undergo worldly change.
Furthermore, one should not speak of the "constant abiding of nature," because it is admitted that there are differences in nature across the past, future, and present.
For this reason, the objection they have formulated is invalid.
Furthermore, regarding that interpretation of the sūtra which states that past and future matter (*rūpa*) are impermanent because they lack a present substance:

this interpretation is incorrect. This is because the subsequent passage asks, "How much more so for the present? implying that one must admit present matter is not impermanent, since it possesses a present substance.

Based on this as proof, it is universally established that the present is impermanent not because it lacks intrinsic nature, but because it possesses intrinsic nature while being impermanent; such must necessarily be the case according to reason.
Because the sūtras state that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing, the Buddha did not teach impermanence with respect to non-existent things.
Nevertheless, although the entities of the past and future truly exist, they can still be said to be subject to arising and ceasing; this principle I shall explain later.

Furthermore, it is logically established that even that which lacks intrinsic nature can be said to possess the characteristic of impermanence; therefore, one should know that the past and future truly exist.
Moreover, because the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states so, one knows that the past and future worlds definitely and truly exist.
That sutra states:

"This bhikṣu Pūrṇa, having seen a form with the eye, is able to cognize the form and cognize the craving for the form; he is able to know, as it truly is, the craving for forms cognized by the internal eye that exists within him, thinking, 'I have craving for forms cognized by the internal eye,' and so forth at length. It does not mean that seeing as it truly is arises simultaneously with craving.
To claim that there is a latent tendency (anuśaya) of attachment within the continuum of views is also irrational, because such a thing is not established.
Even if it were established, views themselves would not be established, for there is no essential difference between the substance of views and the substance of latent tendencies.
It is not admitted that cognition takes its own self as an object; how, then, can it be said that [cognition] perceives latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)?

If you argue that one believes in the existence of greed because one has not yet cultivated the antidote to greed, this reasoning is also incorrect, for you must explain in what state this greed resides.
That is to say, even if one were to grant that he believes and knows that greed exists, one should state at what stage he believes that greed exists.
If it is said that greed exists neither in the past, future, nor present, then one must explain how he can believe that greed exists.
That which is not a permanent phenomenon cannot be designated as "greed"; therefore, one must necessarily believe in the existence of the past and the future.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"One dwells observing internal feelings," and so forth, as explained at length.
There are many such authoritative teachings that can prove that the past and future definitely exist.

Furthermore, there is another reasoning that proves the existence of the past and future: if they did not exist, the principle of killing would be impossible; for in the present world, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) perishes at every moment through its own nature of cessation, even without the application of effort.
If the future world were non-existent in its essence, how could one explain the occurrence of the act of killing?
What dharma could it obstruct so that it would not exist?
Would it be a dharma already arisen, or one yet to arise?
Furthermore, a phenomenon that has already arisen cannot be obstructed, as previously explained.
That which is yet to arise also cannot be obstructed, because it does not exist at all.
Since the past has already ceased, the sense of "killing" is not established; therefore, there is no principle of killing regarding the past or the future.
Furthermore, the entities of the past and future worlds are not non-existent in reality, because the cognitions that take them as objects possess distinctions.

This is like the phenomena of form, sound, and so forth in the present world; since non-existent phenomena lack such distinctions, one cannot give rise to distinct cognitions by taking them as objects.

Only those among the laity and renunciants who believe in the three times as previously explained, and who acknowledge the existence of the three kinds of truly existent unconditioned phenomena, may rightly call themselves Sarvāstivādins.
Because they assert that only such phenomena as these exist, they are accepted as the Sarvāstivāda school; others are not so, because they involve either addition or subtraction.
Specifically, those who propound augmentation claim that there exists a real *pudgala* (person) as well as the aforementioned phenomena.
The Vibhajyavādins maintain that only present phenomena and past karma that has not yet yielded its fruit exist.
The Kṣaṇikavādins maintain that only the substance of the twelve bases (āyatana) existing within a single present moment exists.
The proponents of conventional existence (prajñaptisat) maintain that all phenomena existing in the present world are likewise merely conventionally existent.
The proponents of universal non-existence maintain that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) and are entirely like flowers in the sky.
None of these [positions] represent the teaching of Sarvāstivāda.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) levels the following censure:
"If one asserts that the past and future exist as real entities, this is not a sound exposition within the Noble Teaching."
If one wishes to explain "all that exists" correctly, one should do so as it is taught in the sūtras.
How does the sūtra teach this? As the sūtra says:
Brahmin, you should know that all that exists consists only of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), or only of the three periods of time; one speaks of "existence" according to what actually exists.
Does that sūtra state that only the substance of the present twelve bases exists, and not those of the past or future?
No, that is not so.
If that were the case, would there be clear teachings elsewhere that refute the existence of the past and future?
Do you not see and hear it stated in various sūtras that the two periods of the past and future also exist?
I have heard it said: for what reason is it a violation of the holy teachings to slander those who maintain that "existence" is not well-spoken?

Furthermore, you yourselves assert that among the twelve bases (*āyatana*) presently existing, some are substantially real while others are not; as in the position of the Sthaviras regarding form, sound, touch, and mental objects (*dharma*), how can this be called the Sarvāstivāda school?
There are others who, solely under the influence of afflictions, claim that all phenomena exist merely as designations; could they truly be proponents of the Sarvāstivāda school?

Furthermore, there are others who, under the influence of false views, claim that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature entirely, yet they also say that things appear as illusory existents; could such people, by speaking of existence while things are thus [illusory], also be called proponents of the Sarvāstivāda?

Therefore, in order to negate the existence of a *pudgala* and to generally open up the fact that there are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), the Buddha spoke this sutra to the brahmin; it was not for the purpose of establishing that there are only the twelve bases (*āyatana*) existing for a single moment in the present.

Therefore, those who detest [the idea that] the past and future truly exist should not call themselves Sarvāstivādins (*sarvāsti-vādin*), for their doctrine differs from that of the total non-existence school by only a single moment, and thus their views are not entirely identical.
The Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Volume Fifty-one [and] Volume Fifty-two,
composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.

Chapter 5, Part 8: The Exposition of the Latent Dispositions (Anuśaya). Regarding this Sarvāstivāda school as thus accepted, how many different lineages of masters have there been since antiquity?
Whose establishment of the world is most excellent and reliable?
The verse says:
Within this, there are four types: distinctions based on substance, characteristic, position, and relative dependence.
The third [position], which establishes the time periods based on activity (*kāritra*), is the most excellent.
The treatise says:
The Venerable Dharmatrāta spoke as follows:
Due to differences in category (*jāti*), there are distinctions among the three time periods.

This means that when phenomena proceed through the time periods, they differ by way of category but not by way of essence (*svabhāva*). It is like when a golden vessel is broken and fashioned into another object; although the shape differs, the essence remains unchanged.
Furthermore, just as when milk transforms into curd, it relinquishes its taste, potency, and so forth, yet does not relinquish its color;

likewise, when these dharmas proceed through the time periods—passing from the future to the present and from the present into the past—they relinquish and acquire their respective categories (*jāti*), yet they neither relinquish nor acquire their essential substance (*dravya*).
The Venerable Ghosaka stated as follows:
"The three time periods differ due to the distinction of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

He [Ghosaka] maintains that when phenomena proceed through the time periods, a past phenomenon is currently conjoined with its own past characteristic, yet it is not said to be separated from its present and future characteristics."
The future is currently conjoined with the future characteristic, yet it is not said to be separated from the characteristics of the past and present;
the present is currently conjoined with the present characteristic, yet it is not said to be separated from the characteristics of the past and future.
Just as when a person is currently attached to one wife, he is not said to be detached from his other concubines;
so too, the Venerable Vasumitra has stated that the three time periods differ due to their distinct states.

He [the opponent] maintains that when phenomena proceed through the time periods (*adhvan*), they receive different designations at each successive stage; these differences arise from the distinction between stages, not from a difference in their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
It is like moving a single counting-stick: placed in the units place it is called "one," in the hundreds place it is called "hundred," and in the thousands place it is called "thousand."
The Venerable Buddhadeva speaks thus:
"The distinctions among the three time periods arise from their mutual dependence.

He maintains that when dharmas proceed through the time periods, they are designated with different names based on their prior and posterior relations; it is not that there is any difference in their substance, category, or characteristics."
Just as a single woman is called a "daughter" when she is in relation to her predecessor and a "mother" when she is in relation to her successor according to their respective order,

so too, when these phenomena proceed through time, they are called "past" in relation to the present and future, "future" in relation to the past and present, and "present" in relation to the past and future.

Among these four schools that assert the existence of all things (*sarvāstivāda*), it is traditionally said that the first maintains that dharmas undergo transformation; therefore, they should be placed within the ranks of the Sāṃkhya.

Now, we say this is not so, for that Venerable One did not teach that the essence of conditioned dharmas is eternal, such that when they pass through the three periods of time, the dharma becomes hidden or manifest.
It is merely stated that when various phenomena proceed through time, although their essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) remain the same, their specific natures (*svabhāva*) differ.
This is consistent with the position of the Venerable Vasumitra; how can it be judged to be identical to the Sāṃkhya heretics?

The second and fourth [theories] establish the characteristics of the time periods as being intermingled; therefore, among these four, the third is the most excellent. This is because it establishes distinctions within the time periods based on the states of functional activity (*kāritra*), and it posits differences in the time periods due to these differing states. As I have argued, the real existence of the past and future does not contradict the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and is permitted by the Holy Teaching (*āgama*); to deny the past and future would contradict the nature of phenomena and constitute a slander of the Holy Teaching, involving many faults.
From this, one should know that the Venerable Vasumitra’s establishment of the real existence of the past and future accords with reason and conforms to the sūtras, such that it cannot be shaken.
For that Venerable One has stated:
"The Buddha, in the sūtras, spoke of the three time periods."
How are these three time periods established? They are established as distinct based on activity (*kāritra*).

That is to say, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are called "future" when their activity has not yet arisen; they are called "present" at the time their activity exists; and they are called "past" once their activity has ceased. There is no difference in their essential substance (*svabhāva*).
What is the referent of this term "activity" (*kāritra*)?
It refers to the capacity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) to project a fruit;
that is, it has the sense of being able to function as a causal nature at the time when other entities arise.

If one can establish the distinctions of the [three] times based on this, or can provide other faultless arguments for their differentiation, such a wise person should be recognized as one who discerns the principles.

If, however, out of delusion regarding the reasoning for establishing the distinctions of the times, one abandons the sacred word (āgama) for fear of others' objections, or rejects definitive sūtras (nītārtha) by claiming they are non-definitive (neyārtha), [one is not a knower of the principles].

To assert that the present exists while claiming the past and future do not; or to assert that only the present exists and it is merely a conventional designation (*prajñaptisat*); or to deny all three time periods altogether as being non-existent—all such views contradict the sacred teachings and correct reasoning. The wise should therefore reject those who hold such views as persons deluded regarding the principles of reality.
Those who slander the reality of the three times are smeared with immeasurable kinds of faults; though they exert great effort, it is difficult to bring them to liberation.

On the other hand, those masters who propound that the three times truly exist, even if they occasionally err slightly, are easily brought to liberation. Therefore, the wise should not slander [the Dharma] by saying it does not exist.

Nevertheless, for my part, I shall follow the Venerable Vasumitra in establishing the distinctions of the three time periods based on functional activity (*kāritra*), and I shall address various objections according to my own capacity.
Now, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) raises this objection:

"If the distinction between the three time periods is established based on functional activity, then what is the functional activity of the eye and other sense faculties when they are present but subsumed under their respective *sabhāga* [non-functional] states?"

If it is claimed that those [past causes] can both take up and give forth their fruit, then since past homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and so forth are already able to give forth their fruit, they would possess functional activity (*kāritra*)—or at least a partial activity—and thus the distinctions between the time-periods (*adhvan*) would become conflated.

This objection arises entirely from a failure to understand the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). All phenomena possess two kinds of power: first, "activity" (*kāritra*), and second, "capacity" (*śakti*).
That which draws forth a result through capacity is termed activity; however, activity does not encompass all capacities, for there are also capacities that differ from activity.
Furthermore, in darkness, the eye's capacity to perceive visible forms is obstructed by the darkness; it is not its functional activity that is obstructed.
That is to say, because the presence of darkness as an obstacle obstructs the capacity for seeing, the eye cannot see visible forms in the dark.
The activity that projects a fruit is not obstructed by darkness; therefore, the eye can also project its fruit even in the dark.
There is no deficiency in the activity during its present state, because the present is established solely on the basis of activity.

The cessation of various functional activities does not reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); rather, it serves as a causal nature for the arising of other natures. This is not a "functional activity" (*kāritra*) but merely a "capacity" (*śakti*), because only that which exists in the present time can project its fruit, whereas the unconditioned cannot project its own fruit; for only that which projects its own fruit is termed a "functional activity."
In this commentary cited by the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra), the capacity to yield a fruit is also considered an activity (*kāritra*).

This is clearly because he has not yet mastered the tenets of the Abhidharma; for although past causes can yield fruits, they lack activity, and thus the characteristics of the time periods do not become confused.

However, regarding this point, the Master of that Sūtra (Sautrāntika) harbors deep-seated deluded attachments and further raises extensive objections, claiming that the author of the *Vibhāṣā* (the Broad Treatise) is unable to provide a satisfactory explanation and thus fabricates a "reason-exhausted" interpretation for our own school.
The verse says:
What obstructs its activity, and what is that activity? If there were no difference [between past and future], time would be destroyed.
Who is it that has not yet arisen or ceased? This nature of phenomena is profoundly deep.
The treatise says:

He [the opponent] states that if a phenomenon exists eternally by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it should be able to exercise its function at all times. By what obstructing force could the function exercised by this phenomenon's intrinsic nature be such that it exists at some times and does not exist at others?

The intent of this objection is as follows: since the essential nature and characteristics of all phenomena are eternally non-distinct, by what obstructive force are they not of a single nature and category at all times?
This objection is irrational, because the absence of distinction between essential nature and characteristics does not constitute a valid reason for their being of a single nature and category.
That is to say, one cannot take the absence of distinction in essence and characteristic as a probative reason for the identity of nature and category.

As has already been argued, we observe in the world that while essence and characteristic may not differ, nature and category do differ—such as the case of the earth element and so forth, or sensation and so forth, or the eye and so forth.

Alternatively, one might object with the following intention: "In our school, it is held that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise from the combination of various conditions where they were originally non-existent. However, since those various conditions differ from one another, there are times when they combine and times when they do not; thus, phenomena do not arise constantly, and there can be no fault."

In your school, you maintain that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and their various conditions always possess an inherent nature at all times. Since you do not admit that phenomena are non-existent in the past and come into existence now, they ought to be eternally present; how then could they be obstructed?
This is also not the case, because the previous argument has already been established.

That is to say, it was previously stated that although their essential natures (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are the same, their categories (*jāti*) are distinct; this point has already been proven.

Now, you claim that the self-nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which arises from various conditions, is admitted to always possess its essence at all times. What obstacle could there be such that its activity (*kāritra*) is not constant, and why is it not always present at every moment?

If one understands the preceding meaning, this objection should not arise; for although their substance is the same, their natures are distinct, which is sufficient to establish that their activity is not constant. Therefore, such an objection should not be raised.
If you still persist in your position, you should be cross-examined as follows:

"In your own school, the various conditions and the formations produced by them likewise possess no difference in their essential nature or characteristics across time, yet you admit that they undergo gradual change from moment to moment."

Since the conditions for preceding and succeeding moments are no different, what obstacle prevents them from arising without distinction, yet you allow that each subsequent moment arises with increasing difference?

That is to say, when a preceding moment of volition arises together with its conditions, its essence and characteristics remain unimpaired as it perishes simultaneously with those conditions. Consequently, when the subsequent moment of the fruit arises through the power of this cause, it ought to be indistinguishable in category from its preceding cause. Since there is no difference between the two types of generative conditions—whether distinct or non-distinct—and since there is no distinction between the preceding and succeeding moments, by what cause would there be an obstacle such that the latter differs from the former?
If it is claimed that the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) must be thus, why do you not likewise admit that their functional activity (*kāritra*) is also so?

Furthermore, sensation (*vedanā*) should not be such that, despite having different objects, there is no distinction between its beneficial and harmful aspects; the same should apply by analogy to other minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Although there are differences in conditions such as firewood and chaff, we observe that the characteristic of heat in the fire remains no different.

Therefore, the nature and categories of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) follow many paths; one cannot demand that they all conform to a single uniform pattern, for their essential nature does not differ across all states.

Furthermore, the argument that because you admit the causal conditions (*pratyaya*) to be eternal, the activity produced by them must also be eternal, is likewise unreasonable. For although the conditions may be constantly conjoined, we observe that at times the effect of those conditions does not arise—just as in the case of your own "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), or like the eye and other sense organs.

That is to say, you do not admit that a fruit arises from a cause that has already ceased and is separated by an intervening period; rather, the specific seeds induced by multiple causes exist simultaneously within the continuum, yet those fruits do not always arise at the same time.
However, there may be seeds induced by certain causes that only produce their fruit after the passage of many kalpas.
Even if a fruit were to arise during the intervening period, both the time of its arising and the nature of the fruit itself would be indeterminate.

Since all causes exist at all times, what prevents all effects from arising simultaneously? Why is it that sometimes an effect arises from a certain cause at one time but not at another, or why is it that at one time an effect arises from this cause but not from that cause?

Furthermore, although the conditions such as the eye are constantly present, the visual consciousness and other such cognitions do not arise at all times; therefore, one should not raise such an objection.
Since you admit that the conditions are always present, their functional activity should likewise be constant.

If you claim that in our school the transformation of the continuum depends upon specific conditions to be able to produce an effect, then you must likewise admit that the same applies to causal activity (*kāritra*).
There are generally two types of conditions that induce an effect: first, those that arise simultaneously; second, those that arise prior [to the effect].

Within the co-nascent conditions (sahajātapratyaya), there are further two types: first, those arising within the same aggregate (samagrī-jāta); second, those arising within different aggregates (visamagrī-jāta).

Within the conditions arising within different aggregates, there are again two types: first, those belonging to the category of sentient beings (sattvasaṃkhyāta); second, those belonging to the category of non-sentient things (asattvasaṃkhyāta).
Within the conditions of prior births, there are also two kinds: first, those within the same continuum; second, those within different continua.

Conditions within different continua further comprise two kinds: first, those arising from an assemblage within the same continuum; second, those arising from an assemblage within a different continuum.

Furthermore, there are two types of arising from a collection of dissimilar continuities: first, those belonging to the category of sentient beings; second, those belonging to the category of insentient things.

It is by depending on the power of such concordant and discordant conditions within the continuities of self and others—whether simultaneous or otherwise—that phenomena possess the functional capacity to project their effects.

Such functional capacity is termed "activity" (*kāritra*); therefore, one should not say that because activity is admitted to have a permanent object, it must also exist at all times, for the various conditions cannot be in constant conjunction.
Furthermore, I do not yet understand what the Venerable One intends by the term "activity" (kāritra).
Now, you interrogate me regarding the past and the future; what obstacle prevents their activity from existing?
When the various conditions for a future phenomenon converge, a superior capacity arises, which is termed "activity" (*kāritra*).

That which possesses this activity is called "present"; that in which this activity has ceased is called "past. It is not that the substance (*svabhāva*) of that phenomenon differs before and after; how, then, can one object by asking: "By what obstructing force is the activity of the past and future worlds rendered non-existent?"

The meaning of this statement is as follows: when future dharmas reach the stage where various conditions converge, an activity arises; once the activity has arisen, they are no longer termed "future," because at that moment they are designated as "already come."
The stage when activity has ceased is not called "present," because at that time it has already passed away.
If the activity still persists and has not yet attained the designation of "past," this dharma is then called "present."
Since this distinction between the three time periods is established by way of activity (*kāritra*), their objection arises from a failure to understand our position.
Once our doctrine has been thus well-established, they still do not comprehend it and further challenge us, asking: "How can activity be said to belong to the past, the future, and the present?"

The intent of this objection is as follows: Dharmas can be established as past, future, or present by virtue of their activity (*kāritra*). By what, then, does activity itself possess these distinctions of the three times?
Can it be said that activity, in turn, possesses further activity?

If this activity is neither past, future, nor present, yet you still claim that activity exists, then because it would be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it should be eternally non-deficient; therefore, one should not say that activity has already ceased, nor that a phenomenon which does not yet exist is called "past" or "future."
Have the masters of the Abhidharma ever established that activity (*kāritra*) constitutes the past and future?
Yet, is your current criticism not without reason?

For it is precisely when the activity of a future dharma has already arisen that it is called "present," and when the activity of a present dharma has already ceased that it is called "past. How, then, can your objection against this be logically consistent?
It is not that I claim the past and future also possess functional activity; how then could you question whether functional activity exists in the past and future?
If you say that the past and future lack functional activity, you must explain that such activity was originally non-existent and now exists, or existed and has now ceased to exist.

As you have said, I definitively maintain that the activity (*kāritra*) of all phenomena is non-existent now and exists now, and having existed, returns to non-existence; for activity exists only in the present.
If that is so, since activity is a differentiation of dharmas, one must state whether it is different from or non-different from the dharma.

If it were different, it would follow that it possesses a separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), being previously non-existent and now existent, and having existed, returning to non-existence; in which case all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would likewise possess such activity.
If you say they are not different, you must explain how there can be distinctions while the essence of the dharma remains non-different.
Furthermore, it is more reasonable that activity—which was previously non-existent and now exists, and having existed, returns to non-existence—is distinct from the essence of that dharma.
I maintain that activity (*kāritra*) is a differentiation of the phenomenon (*dharma*), yet it cannot be said to be different from the essence of the phenomenon.
How can there be differentiation without being different?

Furthermore, how is it that in your own school, within a wholesome mind, there exist seeds and functional capacities for various distinct categories such as unwholesome states—which are differentiated by those factors—yet these are not different from the wholesome mind itself?
Furthermore, how could seeds not belong to the same category?
Moreover, as for that Sthavira, how can he claim there is a distinction between benefit and harm regarding the very substance of painful sensation?
Furthermore, although all sensations are identical in their function of experiencing, there is nonetheless no absence of distinctions such as pleasure and so forth within them.

Furthermore, as for you who abide in a continuum, although the characteristics of the dharmas in preceding and succeeding moments do not differ and external conditions are likewise the same, there is still difference between the preceding and succeeding moments.
If it were otherwise, such difference would not exist.

Just as objects produced by the conjunction of conditions such as fire, although their coarse state of abiding remains the same from one moment to the next, possess subtle differences in each of those moments;

so too it is in our school. Although the essence of a phenomenon (dharmatā) abides, when it encounters specific conditions or through its own inherent power (*dharmatā-bala*), a distinct function arises within that essence. Thus, what was previously non-existent now comes into being, and having existed, it returns to non-existence, while the essence of the phenomenon itself continues to abide eternally in its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as before.
What contradiction does this entail with respect to principle and scripture?

It has already been established that the essence (*tattva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not different; yet the nature and categories (*jāti*) of phenomena are not without distinction. Since essence, characteristics, nature, and categories are neither different nor identical, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena exists eternally, while their superior functional capacity (*śakti*) undergoes arising and ceasing.

If you claim that I admit the continuity of phenomena consists of moment-to-moment distinctions in their intrinsic characteristics— wherein they were previously non-existent and now exist, and having existed, they return to non-existence—

while you yourself maintain that the intrinsic characteristics of conditioned things remain constant, and only their specific differences are such that they were previously non-existent and now exist, and having existed, they return to non-existence, how can this possibly serve as an analogy?

If I also grant that intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are fundamentally non-existent, or if you likewise claim that intrinsic characteristics are fundamentally existent, the meaning would be identical; how then could this serve as an analogy?
An analogy requires that there be a difference between the two parties while sharing a commonality.

The analogy cited here is as follows: although the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a continuum of phenomena are identical, there is nonetheless no absence of distinction within it; yet, the essence of these distinct intrinsic characteristics is not different.

Furthermore, while the continuity of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is held to exist eternally regardless of whether the substance of a phenomenon (*dharmatā*) abides or does not abide, the distinctions therein arise in dependence upon conditions; therefore, it is not admitted that such distinctions exist at all times.

Although you admit that phenomena arise from being originally non-existent, you do not admit that distinct characteristics arise in each successive moment; how then can this not serve as a similar instance (*dṛṣṭānta*)?

Nevertheless, since you admit that although the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena are identical across preceding and succeeding moments, there is nonetheless differentiation, and I likewise admit that although the intrinsic characteristics of phenomena remain identical throughout their preceding and succeeding stages, there is nonetheless differentiation, it is therefore established by reason that they constitute a valid similar instance.

By this, it is established that although activity and substance are not different, this activity arises dependent upon conditions, whereas the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena does not arise dependent upon conditions. Therefore, [activity] is "previously non-existent and now existent," and having existed, it returns to non-existence. This also skillfully explains and reconciles the Sūtra’s statement that "what was previously non-existent is now existent," accords well with the Sūtra on the Existence of the Past and Future, and effectively dispels the objection regarding permanence; for while the substance of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) exists eternally, there are variations in the distinctions of their states (*avasthā*).

These distinct states arise from conditions and necessarily do not persist for even a single moment thereafter; therefore, the substance of these phenomena is also impermanent, as it is not distinct from the substance of their distinct states.

Transformation can only be established regarding existent phenomena; there can be no transformation within that which is non-existent. Thus, the definition of the time periods (*adhvan*) as you have formulated it is well-established.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) further states:

"If that were so, the definition of the time periods would be undermined. That is to say, if the activity (*kāritra*) is identical to the essence (*svabhāva*) of the phenomenon, and since the essence is eternally present, the activity should likewise be so. How, then, could there be times designated as 'past' or 'future'?"
Therefore, the definition of "time" established by them is untenable.
This has no bearing on our own position, for we do not assert that the activity is identical to the entity; how then could we be forced to admit that the activity and the entity both exist eternally?

Furthermore, I do not say that the substratum upon which [the temporal status] depends exists at all times and is therefore called "past" or "future"; how then could the established meaning of the time-periods (*adhvan*) be untenable? What is your position?

According to our school’s doctrine, the various differentiated functions of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are designated as "future" when they have not yet arisen; as soon as they have arisen, they are designated as "present"; and if they have already ceased, they are designated as "past."
The distinct function and its substratum cannot be said to be different, just as in the case of a dharma-series (*dharmasaṃtati*).
Just as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise uninterruptedly from moment to moment, this is called a "series."
This is not a different phenomenon, because it has no separate essence.
Nor is it identical to the phenomenon itself, lest there be continuity within a single moment.
It cannot be said to be non-existent, for one observes that activity occurs within the continuum.
Thus, these present differentiated activities are not different from the dharma, because they have no separate essence;
nor are they identical to the dharma, because while the essence exists, the activity may be absent;
yet they cannot be said to be non-existent, because once the activity has arisen, it is capable of drawing forth a result.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:
The continuum has no distinct entity, yet it is admitted that there is something produced;
The principle of activity is likewise so, and thus the worldly sense is established.

The causal relationship, mutual dependence, conjunction, and correspondence—along with the purity of the nature of the mind and so forth—all serve as analogies; therefore, although the essence and characteristics of the past, present, and future are identical, their specific natures and categories differ, and by this, the established doctrine of the three periods of time is proven.
In this context, the Master of the Sūtras further states:
He should also explain this: if the substance of dharmas exists as a reality in the same way as the present, then how could it be that some have not yet arisen and others have already ceased?
If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) exist substantially at all times, how can it be established that they are "not yet arisen" or "already ceased"?
What was previously lacking, such that their non-existence [at that time] is called "not yet arisen"?
Furthermore, what is it that subsequently becomes absent? Since that [future state] no longer exists, it is called "already ceased.

Therefore, if one does not admit that dharmas are non-existent now having previously existed, or that having existed they return to non-existence, then the doctrine of the three time periods would fail to be established in every respect.

How strange! That one with such meager merit should experience such a result; that the awakening-wisdom they have developed is so lacking in clarity that they cannot discern the numerous meaningless words.

Rather than applying diligent effort to contemplate and investigate the true meaning and the holy teachings, they harbor such stubbornness toward the true meaning that they even give rise to a spirit of defiance, repeatedly asserting their own fallacious reasoning while contradicting the established principles?
It has never been heard before, and now I shall once again raise my voice to address those who claim the sutras have been extinguished:
"Listen, O Venerable Ones!
It is not our own tenet that the past and future exist as substantially real in the same way as the present, for the three time periods possess distinct natures of substantial existence."
Venerable sir, you should not, according to your own limited understanding, slander those teachers who explain the Buddha’s teachings in accordance with reason.

The great sages of antiquity were all omniscient ones; the light they shed through their excellent exegesis of the sūtras dispelled the darkness of ignorance and caused the fame of their omniscience to be heard everywhere.

Venerable sir, for what reason do you form an evil alliance with those who are deluded regarding the sacred teachings and correct reasoning, thereby slandering such disciples of the Buddha—who possess supreme merit and transcendent wisdom—and causing immeasurable multitudes to fall into the pit of false views?
I pray that from this day forward you will utterly cease all meaningless speech.

If you do not so cease, it will cause profound harm, as it contravenes the principles of the Sage’s supreme teachings; consequently, you will certainly be unable to realize the true reality of all phenomena.

Furthermore, I do not yet understand how you interpret my meaning regarding the present; you claim that just as the substance (*dharmatā*) of present phenomena truly exists, so too do those of the past and future.

However, according to our school, those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) that are capable of projecting a fruit-position are termed "present. This projected fruit-position did not exist previously and will not exist later; it was on this basis that the distinctions between the three times were previously established. How, then, can you say that the past and future truly exist in the same manner as the present?

Furthermore, to speak briefly: just as the substantial entities (*dravya*) of various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are identical in nature yet differ in their functional capacities (*śakti*), so too the substantial entities of the three time periods are identical in nature, yet within them there is no absence of distinctions in activity (*kāritra*). Since there are immeasurable varieties of existential categories (*jāti*), this cannot be raised as a valid objection against our school.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:

"Just as form and so forth are all suffering, And many distinct natures of suffering are accepted, So too it is with existence in the three times; There is a distinction even regarding that which has not yet arisen."
Therefore, the three modes of existence—present, past, and future—are clearly distinct. How could the past and future be like the present?
It is by virtue of their existence that one can speak of "arising" and "ceasing"; it is with reference to what is non-existent that "non-arising" and "non-ceasing" are established.
This means that within the realm of existence (*bhava*), when a phenomenon first lacks functional activity because it has not yet come into being, it is called "not yet arisen.
When that same phenomenon later again lacks functional activity because it has already ceased to exist, it is called "already ceased."

Therefore, it is only because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exists prior to its arising and subsequent to its cessation that the principle of the three times is established; how could the three times be established if the intermediate state did not exist?
For if the past and future were entirely non-existent in essence, what would be "not yet arisen" and what would be "already ceased"?
Therefore, based on that [position], the establishment of the three time periods is untenable.

Furthermore, there would be no basis for verbal designation (*abhilāpa-āśraya*), yet the Sūtra states that all three time periods are bases for verbal designation; thus, we know that the past and future also possess real substantial entities.
He further derided those who uphold the Dharma, saying:
"To assert that the essence is eternally existent while claiming its nature is impermanent—such a statement has never before been heard.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:
"To maintain that the essence of phenomena is eternally existent, yet claim that their nature is impermanent,
while asserting that nature and essence are not distinct— this is truly the work of a capricious creator.
He spoke these words of derision regarding what is not a valid basis, for even the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, has spoken thus:
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, this nature of dependent origination remains eternally constant.

Yet the Buddha further states that dependent origination is impermanent; could it be that the World-Honored Buddha is to be lightly criticized for asserting that dharmas are eternally constant while simultaneously declaring them to be impermanent? Such a statement of meaning has never been heard before.
If, according to a specific sense, one speaks of permanence and impermanence, then one should not disparage or deride the Buddha;

for would it not also be the case in this instance? The essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) exists eternally, yet its nature undergoes transformation. This means that when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) proceed through the time periods, they do not abandon their own essence but manifest functions in accordance with conditions. Immediately thereafter, the manifested functions cease. For this reason, it is said that the essence of phenomena exists eternally but is not permanent, because its nature undergoes transformation.
How can this be ridiculed as the work of a capricious being?

The masters of Abhidharma might well offer such a critique: "To assert the existence of the three time periods while denying the reality of the past and future is a position never before encountered."

Although it is said that there is no basis for the existence of the past and future, this merely refers to a different perspective on the existence of the present, and does not concern the past and future, as has been explained previously.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:
"Though one admits the three time periods, One denies what has already ceased and what is yet to arise."
"There is becoming, yet there is no third; is this not a celestial delusion?
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras further states:
"Furthermore, it would clearly establish the heterodox arguments favored by the Vātsīputrīya heretics."
He asserts this: that which exists must always exist, and that which does not exist must always be non-existent;
that which is non-existent must never arise, and that which exists must never cease.
This, too, is not a case for applying words of censure or rejection.

It is explained by way of a different perspective that [past and future phenomena] have already ceased or have not yet arisen; for it is admitted by all that they both pertain to what exists and what does not exist.

That is to say, the various phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) in the past and future possess the nature of knowable phenomena (*jñeya-dharmatā*) characterized by arising and ceasing, and they possess the nature of being results co-arising with prior births; however, they lack the nature of being able to project a result (*ākṣepa-phala*) in the present.
That which possesses the function of projecting a fruit is called "present," whereas the past and future lack such a nature.

How can this not be identical to the position asserted by Vṛṣagaṇa? For those who maintain that only the present moment exists, it is impossible to avoid the same fault as his school: namely, asserting that the present world definitely exists while the two periods of past and future definitely do not. This is because they do not admit that the past and future may also exist, nor do they admit that the present may also be non-existent; thus, it is extremely difficult for them to escape the fault shared with that school.

If it is claimed that what is presently existing transforms into past non-existence, and what is non-existent in the future transforms into present existence, this too is irrational, because existence and non-existence are distinct.

Existence and non-existence cannot be transformed into one another; how could what is presently existing transform into past non-existence, and how could what is not yet existent in the future transform into present existence?

Your present existence is neither existent nor non-existent; your past and future are neither non-existent nor existent. The present is exclusively existent and the past and future are exclusively non-existent; since existence and non-existence are so strictly distinct, how could they ever transform into one another?
Therefore, you alone share our position regarding the various schools.
However, that which we maintain is definitively existent; that which is definitively non-existent can never arise, because a horse's horn cannot arise in the present.

If it is argued that a horse's horn cannot arise because it lacks a cause, this is also logically untenable; for the karma that brings about the result of a horse should be the cause of its horns, since you admit that both the horns and the body are fundamentally non-existent. There can be no distinction between non-existence and non-existence; by what reason, then, would one exist while the other does not?
In this context, the Master of the Sūtras further states:
"If one maintains that the past and future exist substantially, then the essence of the fruit would exist at all times; what function, then, would karma have with respect to that fruit?"
This is also not the case; for although its substance exists eternally, it possesses a specific functional capacity within each distinct state.

That is to say, karma has the capacity to cause a fruit to arise; this superior activity of drawing forth the fruit is the functional capacity of karma. Once this activity has arisen, it is designated as the "present" state. Therefore, karma possesses functional capacity specifically within these distinct states.

If karma can cause that which is non-existent to become existent, why would the karma that brings about the fruit of a horse not act as the cause for making the previously non-existent horns of a horse exist?
Based on this principle, there is a verse that says:
"If that which is non-existent could become existent, And that which is existent could become non-existent..."
If you allow that [a sensation] arises from this or that form, why not allow it to be received by a horse’s horn?
Just as a horse’s horn has no connection to the reception [of sensation],
so too there is no connection between a causal form and its resultant form.
The principle of their mutual connection is likewise non-existent;
you claim that matter produces matter, yet this is not the case for sensation or a horse’s horn—this is truly the work of a sovereign creator.
Therefore, for a phenomenon that lacks an inherent nature, there can be neither a cause nor a principle of production.
How can there be a school that denies the existence of the past and future while maintaining that cause and effect are interconnected through mutual response?
Furthermore, if the past and future were not substantially real, how could the relationship between the binder and the bound be established?
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) offers this explanation:
"Because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that produce them exist, it is said that there are past and future afflictions capable of binding;
because the latent dispositions of those [past and future] objects of cognition exist, it is said that there are past and future things to which one is bound."

The intent of this explanation is as follows: because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) produced by past afflictions exist in the present, it is said that there are past afflictions capable of binding;
because the latent dispositions that serve as the causes for future afflictions exist in the present, it is said that there are future afflictions capable of binding;
and because the latent dispositions of afflictions directed toward past and future objects exist in the present, it is said that there are objects bound by the past and future.

All such statements are meaningless, because it has already been demonstrated that, in reality, there are no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of present afflictions produced by past afflictions within the continuum; how then can one say that one possesses past afflictions capable of binding?
Even if it were granted that those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) exist in the present, how could one say that they are not "possessed" (*prāpta*) on account of the existence of a dharma?
For existence and non-existence are not mutually compatible.

Furthermore, if the possession of a cause is asserted based on the existence of its fruit, then the cause for the arising of a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) should also be possessed; yet you do not admit this, because according to your own tenet, the capacity—induced by various ripening causes—that is able to yield various ripened fruits has already ceased and no longer exists at the time the ripened fruit arises.
If it were not established because it is useless, then that [past affliction] should also be so; how then could it be established?

It should not be said that although past afflictions have already ceased to exist, they still have utility at the present time. That which has utility at the present time is merely the latent disposition (*anuśaya*); what utility, then, would past afflictions serve?

Even if one were to concede that there exist latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) which serve as the causes for present and future afflictions, one still should not say that one is "endowed with" (*samanvāgata*) future afflictions capable of binding; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa-doṣa*) resulting from this.

That is to say, if one asserts that a result is established based on the presence of a cause, then since it is admitted that there exists a cause capable of producing roots of virtue in those sentient beings who have already severed their roots of virtue, one should likewise assert that they possess those roots of virtue.
Since those roots of goodness are both established and severed, one must definitively state what kind of sentient being they are:
is it one who has severed the roots of goodness, or one who has not?
Furthermore, since there are causes for those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one should state that they have attained the fruit of arhatship.

Then one who is still in training (śaikṣa) ought to be an arhat; or, if one has attained the fruit of arhatship yet is not called an arhat, then even one who has attained the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) ought not to be called an arhat.
Alternatively, if an Arhat were to regress and fail to attain the fruit of Arhatship, there would be no distinction [between them].
In that case, all the sacred teachings and correct principles would be contradicted and subverted by what they have said.

Therefore, if one negates the past and future by asserting they are non-existent, it would certainly be impossible for afflictions of the past and future to be established; how then could one say that there are past and future [afflictions] capable of binding?

Furthermore, as for their claim that because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of those afflictions exist, one says there are objects of bondage in the past and future—this too contradicts the tenet they have established.
They maintain that the substance of the past and future is not substantially existent because their function is not established.
To claim that the past and future are non-existent yet still called "functions" (vastu)—such a meaning of words has never been heard before.

If it were granted that, within the present continuum, there exist latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of afflictions directed toward those objects, then these [dispositions] would necessarily be distinct from the afflictions themselves; for the afflictions that could have induced them have long since ceased, whereas the induced dispositions currently exist.

Since they are thus distinctly different, how can it be said that present latent dispositions (anuśaya) bind past and future objects, or that present latent dispositions take past and future objects as their conditions? For that which has never yet arisen cannot function as a binder.

Furthermore, the nature of present wholesome or neutral minds is not itself a fetter (saṃyojana); therefore, they should not be able to bind past or future objects that are subject to bondage. Apart from the mind, no latent disposition (anuśaya) can be found.
Therefore, what he has stated is entirely devoid of meaning.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrāntika) deceitfully sets forth a slanderous claim:
"The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that past and future entities exist in reality; however, they are unable to provide a coherent explanation for how these can exist therein."

Those who cherish themselves should understand this: the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profoundly deep and lies beyond the realm of discursive thought; how can you fail to provide an explanation and instead dismiss it as non-existent?
It is certain that you have secretly composed this treatise yourself and falsely attributed the title *Vibhāṣā* to it; for in the true *Vibhāṣā*, these words do not exist at all.

Furthermore, they do not act like those who, following their own whims, falsely claim that the past and future exist as truly present entities, asserting that the three times are substantially real with distinct natures.
One should examine their intent: they wish to bring ruin to the holy teachings by deceitfully fabricating false words to slander the correct doctrine.
How could such slanderous assertions possibly cause any impairment to our own philosophical system?

Could it be that among the great masters of our own school—those who have extensively studied and mastered the sacred teachings and correct reasoning, who possess all virtues and whose fame is widely renowned—there are none capable of providing a thorough explanation for even minor objections?

Therefore, you have deceitfully fabricated slanderous statements regarding what is not the case; having followed your own subjective sentiments to falsely establish your own tenets, it appears you have not yet perused the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā*.
I have already provided thorough explanations for the objections you raised; what further objection remains that cannot be resolved?

In what precedes, I have directly confronted the Master of the Sūtra (*sūtrapati*) regarding his determinations of the past and future; I have refuted him according to his own words to the full extent of my ability, while also briefly refuting the words of the Elder (*sthavira*). However, the reason I have not refuted him extensively point-by-point is that his assertions contain little that is coherent enough to be subjected to the same logical scrutiny as the preceding arguments, or because some are so extremely superficial as to be unfit for investigation, or because they consist merely of slanders against the Noble Ones and groundless self-aggrandizement.
If one were to respond to each of their statements point by point, what person of intelligence would not laugh at such things?
Even those who do not discern the truth might rely on that school's tenets, fabricating flowery rhetoric to falsely raise objections and challenges.

All you who possess discernment and delight in examining treatises, you should now scrutinize this matter with care and listen attentively: from this point forward, I shall return to our original school and respond to their arguments with free-flowing debate as they present them.
