Furthermore, there is a class of blind followers of discernment who claim that our own school holds the same tenets as the followers of the Yellow Sage (the Sāṃkhyas).

This is unreasonable, for the latter maintain that the cause transforms into the very essence of the effect, and the effect subsequently re-enters and merges into its own nature; thus, the substance of the past, future, and present is one and the same.

The temporal sequence established in our school is free from confusion; that is to say, functional activity exists only in the present moment, because at this stage it is certainly not subsumed under the two other time periods, because cause and effect are distinct and do not act upon one another, because once phenomena have ceased they do not arise again, because the effect does not dissolve into its own nature, because causes are beginningless and many causes produce a single effect, and because cause and effect are not sustained by a self.
Since such distinctions are infinite in this manner, how can it be claimed that our school shares the same tenets as the followers of Kapila?
Others further assert that there is definitely no past or future, because the sūtras speak of them as having "existed" and being "to be."
That is to say, the Blessed One said:
"When those who are wise harbor doubt regarding the past, one should resolve it by saying that it existed in the past;
when they harbor doubt regarding the future, one should resolve it by saying that it will exist in the future."
Since it has never been stated that those [past and future phenomena] truly exist, one might conclude that the past and future are certainly not real.
This, however, is irrational, because the terms "was" (past) and "will be" (future) are sometimes seen used to refer to the present; yet, one cannot say that the present itself does not exist.

Furthermore, since the superior capacity existed in the past but exerts its activity only in the present, the past should accordingly receive two names: it is "substantially existent" by virtue of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and it is "formerly possessed of activity" because that activity once existed.
By this same principle, the two names for the future [time] are explained accordingly.
The present should be called "substantially existent" (*dravyasat*) and "actually existing" (*vidyamāna*), because it possesses functional activity (*kāritra*) with respect to its substantial entity.

However, while the phenomena of all three times are bases for verbal designation (*abhilāpa-nimitta*), these terms are stated specifically regarding the past and future to express their unique meanings and to avoid confusion; how could this statement imply that they are not substantially existent?
Others further say:
"If the past and future exist as real entities, for what reason do you not allow that the two consciousnesses—the defiled and the pure—arise simultaneously?
For the causes of both these consciousnesses are equally real."
This too is unreasonable, because for various consciousnesses to arise, they must depend upon the conjunction of both a support (āśraya) and an object (ālambana).
Even if the supports and objects of all consciousnesses were simultaneously present, one should not admit that the visual and other consciousnesses arise at the same time.
As it is with that principle, so it is here as well.

Furthermore, since you too must face this same objection, why do defilement and purity—which are mutually contradictory—not arise simultaneously, given that your own school admits that what was originally non-existent can arise?
If one were to say: "That which has a cause arises," would this not contradict what was previously stated?

For it was said that since both are fundamentally non-existent, it is impossible to distinguish between having a cause and lacking a cause, as no such differentiated causes and conditions have ever been taught.

Furthermore, regarding those who argue that the past and future lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their position is subject to this severe critique: because the two causes—defilement and purification—such as the "ancient pervasive realm" (*pūrvānucita-dhātu*) and so forth, would have to exist simultaneously and perpetually within the present continuum.
Such difficulties are extremely acute for their school, whereas in our own school, these various causes do not exist as perpetual presences.

Some say: "The past is definitively and truly non-existent, because the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of present formations have already been abandoned. Were it not so, the essence of formations would be eternal; and by that consequence, there would be no possibility for liberation."

This is also unreasonable. If you claim that past formations (saṃskāra) have abandoned their own characteristics and thus are not subsumed under "formations," then since their essence no longer exists now, they could not be called "formations.

Since you admit they are indeed formations, you should not say they have abandoned their own characteristics; for apart from their own characteristics, there is no separate essence of formation that can be said to exist such that one might claim the characteristics have been abandoned while only the essence of formation remains.
Furthermore, it has already been stated previously. What was stated previously?

It is not the case that there is no impermanence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) because it lacks a substantial entity; for if the past lacked a substantial entity, it would follow that it is not impermanent. Why, then, would our own school have no principle of liberation?
The sūtra merely states:
"Present suffering has already ceased, and further suffering does not continue.

It does not say that one first attains nirvāṇa and then speaks of nirvāṇa; rather, it is when one relinquishes the characteristics of dharmas—without abandoning the characteristics of dharmas—that the cessation of formations is called nirvāṇa, as has already been explained.
Furthermore, it is said that if the past were substantially existent, there would be no nirvāṇa; for it is taught that when an arhat possesses the aggregates, there is no nirvāṇa.
Moreover, if past suffering were eternally present, then all sentient beings would have no liberation.

This is also unreasonable. If you claim that because past aggregates of suffering exist, there is no nirvāṇa, then since your own school asserts that the past and future lack substantial reality, the aggregates of suffering would not exist, and thus one should be in a state of constant nirvāṇa.
Alternatively, there may be sentient beings who are fundamentally destined for liberation because all past sufferings no longer exist.

If one were to claim that nirvana is defined merely by the cessation of present suffering and the non-continuation of future suffering, then one could not say that nirvana is impossible due to the existence of aggregates of past suffering.
Furthermore, it is said that the past and future are certainly not substantially existent because they lack functional characteristics (*ākāra*).
What are these functional characteristics?
They refer to the presence of a beginning and an end within the two periods of time, the past and the future.
It is argued that because each [of the three] is missing one, the aspect of activity (*ākāra*) does not exist.
This is also incorrect; for example, although birth and death (*saṃsāra*) lack a single type of aspect, they are nonetheless established.
Although the birth and death of sentient beings have no beginning, it cannot be said that they lack the aspect of activity.

Furthermore, the same fault should apply to the present as well; that is, for those who assert that the past and future do not truly exist, they must admit that the present they cling to has no beginning or end.
Moreover, my past possesses both a beginning and an end: the "beginning" of the past is when its activity has already arisen, and the time subsequent to this is called the "end."
The future also possesses both a beginning and an end; since it belongs to the same category as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it should not be considered a point of difficulty.

Furthermore, if the past and future were substantially existent (*dravyasat*), there would be no distinction between what has been abandoned and what has not been abandoned; this is not so, for if that were the case, the present would likewise have to be the same.
This means that since there would be no distinction between what has already been abandoned and what has not yet been abandoned in the present life, it would follow that they are non-existent.

However, regarding defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), it is not the case that they are not established once a portion of the undefiled has been abandoned; and although they are established when a portion of the undefiled has been abandoned, there remains the distinction of whether the delusive bondage has been severed or not. This is what constitutes the difference.

Furthermore, to claim that the past and future exist would contradict the scriptures. For the holy teachings state: "When this exists, that exists; when this does not exist, that does not exist. It is not reasonable that the present should exist because the future exists, nor that the present should be non-existent because the past is non-existent. Since you maintain that the essence of the past and future is eternally existent, it follows that only the present can be either existent or non-existent. Therefore, the past and future are certainly not substantially real.
Now one should examine this carefully. That scripture states:
"In order to manifest the existence of the entity and to manifest the meaning of the arising of existence.

If it were to manifest the existence of the entity, your own position would be flawed; for while the preceding scripture says "this exists because that exists," you maintain that while that [future] exists, this [past] does not, since you admit that formations have ceased and do not exist, while consciousness exists in the present.

Regarding the statement in later scriptures that "this being absent, that is absent," you maintain that while "that" has not yet ceased to exist, "this" currently exists; yet you concede that even when consciousness is manifesting, it is still non-existent.
Thus, your attempt to refute my school by citing this teaching is like a raised corpse that brings about its own destruction.

If it is argued that "existence" (asti) here signifies "arising" (utpāda)—meaning that because this cause exists, that effect subsequently arises—just as one says "this cause has that relic," then it does not indicate the existence of an entity, but merely indicates arising.
This poses no difficulty whatsoever for our own school; therefore, the existence of the past and future is established as a reality.

When the masters of the Abhidharma explain that [past and future] exist, they mean that because this exists, that comes to be; it is not that the cause can make the substance (*svabhāva*) of a dharma exist, but rather that it can cause the activity (*kāritra*) of the dharma to arise.

If it is argued that only that which is brought into existence by various conditions is the result, while the essence of the phenomenon (*dharmatā*) is not, this objection is invalid because there is no difference between their essences.
If that were so, both the essence and its function would have to be established by causes simultaneously.
This is also not the case, as has already been stated previously.
What was stated previously?
Although activity and essence have no distinct substance, they do possess differentiation.

This means that when various conditions combine, they cause the essence of a phenomenon (*dharmatā*) to arise with distinct states and differences; yet this arising of differences is not something other than the essence of the phenomenon itself. Therefore, the sense of "arising" is applied to the essence of that phenomenon only as a conventional designation.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:
"Existence arising from a multitude of conditions is conventional;
though its nature is no different when it arises, this existence is ultimate."
Furthermore, it is said that there is no exhaustion of future enjoyment; therefore, enjoyment in the future world cannot be exhausted.
This too is illogical, for it is universally established that the functioning of the phenomena of birth and death has no end.

There have been no sentient beings who were originally non-existent and then came into being, and countless sentient beings have long since attained parinirvāṇa; yet the phenomena of birth and death are inexhaustible in their experience.
By comparing the present with this, one knows that although there is no end to the future, it is not the case that they do not exist.

Furthermore, it is argued that past and future [forms] do not exist because they lack the characteristic [of matter], namely, that "form" (rūpa) is so called because it is subject to transformation and resistance;
since this is not the case for the past and future, they are not substantially existent.
This too is irrational, as it is based on only a partial definition; for it is not the case that all present forms possess transformation and resistance, yet they are not non-existent either.
Alternatively, one should admit that consciousness is substantially existent, as a sūtra states:
"Because it cognizes and cognizes, it is called consciousness.
What is it that is cognized?
This refers to the discernment of forms up to the discernment of mental phenomena (*dharma*).

According to your own tenet, consciousness does not discern past or future objects; nevertheless, you maintain that the substance of consciousness exists and is not non-existent, because it exists in the present.
For this reason, their refutation of existence is not established.
Furthermore, they claim that the substance of the past and future is not substantially real, because if it were substantially real, it would entail obstruction.

That is to say, material objects necessarily occupy space and mutually obstruct one another; if matter that has already ceased or has not yet arisen were substantially real, it would entail obstruction. Since there is no such obstruction, it should not be considered matter.
Because of this fault, one might conclude that [the entity] does not truly exist;
however, this too is unreasonable. According to your own tenet, things arise despite being non-existent, yet those factors [required for such arising] are absent.
As you have stated, that which arises does not exist [prior to arising]; only the future arises, and it certainly does not arise from the past.
Likewise, I say that dharmas possess obstruction; only the present has obstruction, certainly not the past or the future, because they possess distinct functions within the state of the present.
Other masters say:
Is the lamp of the future world already existent?
If it were already existent, it would be no different from a present lamp.
If it were otherwise, its substance would not be the lamp.
This objection is not valid, because there is only substance; that is to say, in the past and future, the substance exists as having function or lacking function.

This means that because past and future phenomena possess the nature of being objects of cognition and the nature of being cognizable, they are said to "exist"; it does not mean that past and future things possess functions such as burning.

Alternatively, one should admit that they are substantially existent just like consciousness. Just as you admit that there is a consciousness without an object of perception and without an act of discernment, yet its essence is not non-existent, so too is my future lamp: although it lacks the function of burning, its essence is not non-existent.
Furthermore, it is argued that because past and future [forms] are not apprehended by the eye, if past and future form were substantially existent, why would they not be apprehended by the eye?
This is also not the case, because the visual faculty takes as its object only those forms that possess superior functional efficacy (*sāmarthya*).

Although the essential nature and characteristics of all phenomena throughout the three periods of time are the same, their specific natures differ, as has already been argued previously. One cannot therefore suppress this point by objecting that because the eye and visible form serve as objects, one must necessarily apprehend all forms; for not even a single atom of form can be so apprehended.
Because this apprehends the present but does not apprehend the past and future, their distinct stages and differing functions should not be considered a difficulty.

Furthermore, it is said that they lack the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*); that is, the past and future lack the characteristics of the conditioned, and since they are also not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are not substantially existent.

This is also unreasonable, because those [dharmas] possess such a nature: namely, that future dharmas have the nature of being subject to cessation, present dharmas have the nature of being currently undergoing cessation, and past dharmas have the nature of having already ceased; therefore, none of them are devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
All phenomena that are subject to arising arise by the power of causes; the meaning of the arising of these phenomena has already been explained above.
Since all phenomena that do not arise belong to the same category as phenomena that do arise, they too receive the designation of "having the nature of being subject to arising."
That which does not arise is due to the deficiency of conditions;
the meaning of this deficiency of conditions has already been explained above.

Alternatively, one should take consciousness as a homologous example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*): just as you admit that there can be a consciousness whose object is non-existent, which lacks any object of discernment yet whose essence is not non-existent.
In this way, you claim that the past and future lack the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*); yet, what prevents them from existing?
Furthermore, your present [existence] ought not to have arisen, because its essence has already arisen.
There is no abiding or alteration, because it is admitted that immediately upon arising, there is cessation; nor is there any destruction.
For according to your own tenet, destruction is defined as non-existence, yet [the entity] is presently existent.
Furthermore, your own school maintains that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are established based on a continuum (*saṃtāna*) and not upon a single moment (*kṣaṇa*);
therefore, even your "moment" ought not to exist. *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 52; *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 53.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter 5, Part 9: The Exposition on the Latent Defilements (Anuśaya). Having concluded the ancillary discussion regarding how the latent defilements bind such objects at such stages, we shall now further investigate this matter:
If an object has not been abandoned, must it necessarily be bound?
Conversely, if an object is bound, must it necessarily be unabandoned?
If an object that is unabandoned must necessarily be bound, yet there are objects that are bound without being unabandoned—what is the characteristic of such binding that is not non-abandonment?
The verse says:
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of suffering, the remaining universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
as well as those of previous stages already abandoned, still bind one who is otherwise connected to them.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, at the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all objects (*vastu*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering have already been abandoned; however, if the pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of origin have not yet been permanently severed, those [tendencies] that can take this as their object remain bound to it.

Furthermore, at whichever stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) a particular path arises, among the nine grades of objects, those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have not yet been abandoned—which can take as their object those things already abandoned by the preceding grade—remain bound to them.

Furthermore, the word "and" (及) clarifies that while the preceding [stages] have already been abandoned, the succeeding [stages] have not yet been abandoned, yet all possess the sense of being able to bind.
Why, then, is it necessary here to state the phrase "conditioned by this"?
It is because the nine grades of what is abandoned through cultivation necessarily condition one another.
That which is not an object of cognition is sometimes not an object [of a particular cognition]; therefore, the statement that it "takes this as its object" would certainly be useless.

If you argue that there must be a separate mention because there are things that cannot be taken as objects, then one should likewise make a distinction among the universal [defilements], since there are universal defilements abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that do not take as their objects those things abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
With what intention does the Master of the *Śāstra* exclude this [category] and not that?
Now, it appears that the Master may have thought as follows:

"What is stated here—that 'the preceding category has already been abandoned'—is based on the mundane path (*laukikamārga*). Accordingly, the afflictions to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are generally divided into nine categories and eliminated gradually. Within the context of 'the preceding category having already been abandoned,' there remain other categories yet to be abandoned; the pervasive afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) are also capable of acting as a fetter in those cases."
If one were to exclude the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other stages as their objects, then the statement "taking this as an object" would be meaningful.
However, since the previously mentioned other universals lack the phrase "taking this as an object," their meaning is not established.
Alternatively, the subsequent explanation and the word "and" (*ca*) should also indicate that the preceding text includes the sense of being bound by these objects.

That is to say, regarding what was previously stated—that [afflictions] are abandoned upon seeing suffering—and regarding those matters of the preceding category that have already been abandoned, there remains something else; one is still bound by them as objects.
This text is disorganized; within the context of the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one or another of the remaining [specific] and universal [defilements] should be excluded.

However, this is an overly elaborate explanation that lacks the necessary conditions for such a statement; one should instead inquire into the intended meaning of the Venerable Maitreya’s own words: regarding what objects do how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase?
In this context, one need only analyze the characteristics of the objects of cognition (*ālambana*);

that is, by analyzing which phenomena are the objects of which consciousnesses, it will be easily understood that these bound entities necessarily possess such-and-such a number of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase in association with them.
Furthermore, how many categories of phenomena (*dharma*) and consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are there?
Although phenomena are numerous, they are briefly categorized as sixteen: those belonging to the five divisions within the three realms, plus the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The number of consciousnesses that can take these as objects is likewise the same.
Among these, which dharmas serve as the objects of how many consciousnesses?
The verse says:
Those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and those abandoned through cultivation, if they are bound to the desire realm, [are the objects of six consciousnesses].
The three [realms] of one's own sphere and one [realm] of the formless are the objects of untainted consciousness.
The three [realms] of each respective lower sphere and the pure [realm] above are the objects of the form-sphere consciousnesses.
The formless sphere pervades all three realms; each is the object of the three [types of] pure consciousnesses.
Those abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path all increase the objects of their own respective consciousnesses;
the untainted [dharmas] are the objects of the three final pure consciousnesses within the three realms.
The commentary says:

If one considers the phenomena associated with the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, and through cultivation, each is the object of five consciousnesses.
These consist of three from its own realm, as previously explained, and one from the form realm, which is that which is abandoned through cultivation.
The fifth category, the untainted (*anāsrava*), is included because it can serve as an object for all [consciousnesses].

To take the phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) as objects of the three consciousnesses of their own realm: these are (1) all [phenomena] abandoned through the vision of suffering; (2) the universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*); (3) the wholesome and neutral consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the desire realm; (4) the wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), but not others; and (5) within the untainted consciousnesses, only those belonging to the category of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna-pakṣa*).
The abandonment through cultivation regarding the origin [of suffering] should be understood accordingly.

As for those phenomena bound to the form realm previously mentioned, each of the three categories is the object of eight consciousnesses: namely, the three [categories] of its own and lower realms are all as previously stated; furthermore, one category from the higher realm—namely, that abandoned through cultivation—and the eighth, the untainted [consciousness], are all capable of taking them as objects.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that phenomena bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) are the objects of three consciousnesses of their own realm and one consciousness of the higher realms, this should be understood according to the previous explanation.

As for those that are the objects of three consciousnesses of the lower realm, these refer to: (1) the wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) associated with superior objects (*adhiālambana*) within the desire realm, which are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin; and (2) uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*), which consists solely of the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
The abandonment through cultivation by seeing the origin (*samudaya-darśana-bhāvanā-heya*) should be understood accordingly.

Regarding those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpya-pratisaṃyukta*), they are as previously stated: each of the three categories of phenomena is the object of ten consciousnesses. That is to say, the three [categories] of each of the three realms are as previously explained, and the tenth is the untainted (*anāsrava*), because all are capable of taking them as objects.

It should be understood that this is analogous to what was stated regarding those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the various phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*), it should be understood that for each one, its own respective consciousness increases as an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*). How is this so?

That is to say, those factors bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation serve as objects for six consciousnesses; the five [sensory] consciousnesses are as previously described, with the addition of the desire-realm consciousness abandoned through the vision of cessation.
The meaning regarding those to be abandoned through the vision of the path should be understood by analogy.

Regarding those factors bound to the realms of form and formlessness that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), they serve as objects for ninety-one consciousnesses according to their respective correspondences: eighty as previously stated, with each additionally including its own corresponding consciousness.

If they are untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena, they serve as objects for ten consciousnesses; namely, the three final categories within each of the three realms—specifically, the consciousnesses abandoned through the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)—plus the tenth, the untainted consciousness, all of which are capable of taking them as objects.
As for those points not explained in detail, they should be understood as appropriate.

One should keep in mind the sixteen dharmas briefly established above and contemplate the objects (*vastu*) upon which the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase; fearing that the text would become overly prolix, I have merely indicated the general direction.
Furthermore, suppose someone asks:
"In how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do the objects bound to the faculty of the fleshly eye increase?

One should observe that the faculty of the eye, taken as a whole, consists of only two types: namely, those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)."

These [defilements] increase in accordance with their respective objects, namely those to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire and form realms, as well as their universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
If one were to ask:
"How many kinds of latent dispositions increase in relation to the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object?"

One should observe that this consciousness consists generally of eight types: namely, three each in the desire and form realms—comprising those abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin (the pervasive and co-existent), together with those abandoned through cultivation, which total six; and one in the formless realm, which is abandoned through cultivation; and the eighth, the wholesome consciousness included in the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space, which is untainted (*anāsrava*). All of these take the eye faculty as their object.
Furthermore, one should understand that all untainted phenomena (anāsrava) are definitely not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya).

Regarding the [remaining] seven [categories], they correspondingly increase according to the three groups of each of the desire and form realms, while the universal latent dispositions of the formless realm increase through the abandonment by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

That is to say, regarding the consciousness associated with the desire realm that is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and is universal (*sarvatraga*), the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin (*samudaya*) increase therein.
One should understand that for the consciousness to be abandoned through the vision of origin, the reverse applies.

Regarding consciousnesses to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), those belonging to the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation, as well as all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), increase [in association].

By analogy with this, one should understand that the three types of consciousness in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the wholesome consciousness in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) can take the eye-faculty of the fourth dhyāna as their object; therein, the formless-realm factors to be abandoned by cultivation and their pervasive latent dispositions increase [in association].
Furthermore, if it is asked:
"In how many kinds of latent dispositions (anuśaya) does the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) increase?

One should observe that this consciousness is of thirteen kinds: namely, four types of consciousness for each of the three realms, totaling twelve when excluding those abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-heya), together with the untainted (anāsrava) consciousnesses that can take the eye-faculty as their object-condition.

According to what is appropriate for each case within the three realms and four categories, excluding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase through the vision of cessation, the consciousness associated with the universal [defilements] abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm can take the eye-faculty as its object. This consciousness may be a consciousness abandoned by the vision of suffering or the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), a universal [consciousness], a consciousness abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*)—whether wholesome or neutral—and furthermore, a wholesome consciousness abandoned by cultivation in the form realm, as well as untainted consciousness belonging to the category of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-pakṣya*).

Conditioned by these, the consciousnesses that take the eye-faculty as their object increase in accordance with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the path of cultivation, and the cultivation of form, as well as their universal [latent dispositions].
The remaining cases should be explained accordingly as appropriate.

Up to the case of an untainted consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object: this consciousness may be bound by the three realms; it may be an untainted consciousness abandoned by the path of seeing, or a wholesome or untainted consciousness abandoned by the path of cultivation. These various perceiving consciousnesses that take the eye-faculty as their object are, as the case may be, subject to the increase of the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned by the path of seeing or the path of cultivation within the three realms.

If one were to separately enumerate the twelve types mentioned above and specify how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in each, it should be stated that for the consciousnesses that take as their object those things to be abandoned by seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm, all underlying tendencies to be abandoned by seeing suffering and those to be abandoned by seeing the origin (*samudaya*)—as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) underlying tendencies—increase.

By reversing this, one should know that for consciousness abandoned through seeing the origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), consciousness abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm—as well as all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions—there is increase (*anuśayana*). For consciousness abandoned through seeing the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*), there is increase of the latent dispositions abandoned through seeing the path in the desire realm, as well as all pervasive latent dispositions.

However, regarding those with uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*), there is only binding through association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*); for the remainder, they merely increase [their influence] by way of being objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*).

Based on this, one should understand that there are distinctions between the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*). Regarding consciousnesses abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*), one should know that for the desire realm and the higher realms, respectively, there are objects belonging to the categories of *dharma-jñāna* and *anvaya-jñāna*. As for the consciousness perceiving the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), other instances of bound phenomena should be considered in the same manner as the example of the eye.
Now, within this context, one should further investigate:
if a mind is said to be "with latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) because of them, do those dispositions necessarily increase (*anuśerate*) with respect to that mind?
This is not certain; for it is said that those latent dispositions increase only when they have not been abandoned, not when they have already been abandoned.
As stated in the treatise:
"In relation to this mind, those [defilements] may either increase or not increase.
How do they increase?"
This refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are associated with this mind and have not yet been abandoned as objects of that mind;
how then could they not increase?
It means those latent dispositions that are associated with this mind have already been permanently severed.
What is called "a mind with latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya-citta*)?
On what basis is the term "with latent dispositions" established?
Furthermore, by virtue of what is it called "with latent dispositions"?

Furthermore, regarding what was previously stated—that the fifteen types of consciousness, five for each of the three realms, are called "minds with latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*)—each of these minds is of two kinds:

namely, universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal (*asarvatraga*). This distinction arises because there are differences between those that have outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*), and between those that take defiled objects and those that take undefiled objects.

The designation "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) is established based on two meanings: first, because [the state] is increased by the latent dispositions that follow it; second, because it takes the latent dispositions as its companions. It is called "possessing latent dispositions" by virtue of these latent dispositions.

The associated latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are both abandoned and unabandoned; however, only that which has an object (*ālambana*) that is unabandoned is said to be "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*).
How is it that the afflictions (*kleśa*) associated with the mind continue to increase within the mind until they are abandoned?
That is to say, these latent dispositions (anuśaya) are able to give rise to acquisitions (prāpti), which act as an obstruction within the mental continuum.

Furthermore, they serve as homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) for future lives, inducing the arising of the mental continuum’s outflow (niṣyanda). Therefore, as long as they have not been abandoned, it is said that they increase in accordance with the mind; once abandoned, this is no longer the case, as the sense of "increasing in accordance" no longer applies.

It is not because of their abandonment that they cause the mind to be separated from them; therefore, even though they have been abandoned, one is said to "possess" them, because their nature as auxiliary factors (*sahāya*) cannot be destroyed.

That is to say, the power of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) within the continuum can obstruct the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) so that they do not manifest, and it can also obstruct the acquisition (*prāpti*) induced by them, such that they no longer act as a constraint upon the mental continuum. Thus, it is said that for corresponding latent dispositions that have already been abandoned, there is no principle of further increase (*anuśayana*).

Because the power of the antidote cannot obstruct the nature of being a concomitant associate of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), the mind is said to "possess latent dispositions" even though they have already been abandoned.

Furthermore, as long as the latent dispositions that take the mind as their object have not been severed, they continue to increase within the mind—whether the mind itself has been severed or not—and thus constantly cause the mind to bear the designation of "possessing latent dispositions."

If the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with that object have already been abandoned, the mind is not said to "possess latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) on account of them, because the power of the Path causes the mind to be free from those dispositions.

Although they serve as companions and as objects—both of which are not things that can be separated from the mind by the power of the Path—their relationship to the companion and the object is more remote; therefore, this designation [of "possessing latent dispositions"] applies [only to the immediate factors].

This is based solely on the fact that [the afflictions] have not yet been abandoned; because their associated mental factors are of a proximate nature, they are also termed "possessing" (sānuśaya) even when [the primary affliction] has been abandoned.

In this context, the mind associated with the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is called "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) because the ignorance and the view of a self-body with which it is associated increase as its concomitants.

By virtue of being pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and abandoned through the vision of the remaining [truths] within their own category, and by virtue of the nature of increasing [the defilements], it is called "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*). The remainder are neither; therefore, they do not possess them.
The other minds abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin—whether pervasive or non-pervasive—should be considered accordingly.

The mind associated with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation is termed "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) because of the nature of its concomitant increase (*anuśayana*) through the ignorance and wrong view with which it is associated.

It is also termed "possessing latent dispositions" because, being comprised within its own category, it increases solely through the nature of concomitant increase regarding all objects that are tainted (*sāsrava*).
The remainder are neither, and therefore do not possess them.

As for the other [defilements] abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path—whether they take uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) or contaminated (*sāsrava*) objects—one should apply the same principles of analysis as appropriate.

A mind associated with craving that is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation is called "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) due to the nature of its concomitants—namely, the ignorance and craving that increase in association with it.
It is also called "possessing latent dispositions" by virtue of the nature of increase alone through other factors of its own category and all universal (*sarvatraga*) factors.
The remainder are neither, and therefore do not possess them.
The minds associated with the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) should be examined accordingly by analogy.

Non-defiled minds to be abandoned through cultivation are said to "possess latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) because the latent dispositions belonging to their own category and those that are universal merely increase in accordance with them.

All that has been discussed thus far refers to cases where [the underlying tendencies] have not yet been abandoned. If they have been abandoned and possess a concomitant nature (*sāhāya-bhāva*), then they are said to be "with underlying tendencies" solely by virtue of that concomitant nature.
Based on this interpretive framework, one should speak in this manner.
The verse says:
There are two types of minds with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*): namely, those that are defiled and those that are undefiled.
A defiled mind is associated with both [types of *anuśaya*], whereas an undefiled mind is restricted to those that increase (*anuśerate*).
The Treatise says:
There are two general types of minds accompanied by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*): those that are defiled and those that are undefiled, due to the distinctions among states of mind.

Among these, when a defiled mind is present, its associated latent dispositions possess both [types of] possession (*prāpti*) if they have not yet been abandoned; as for the object-condition (*ālambana*), it possesses only one.
When [the defilements] have already been abandoned, there is one [type of] possession through association, but none at all through the object.
Those afflictions belonging to an undefiled mind are said to possess *anuśaya* only during the stage when they have not yet been abandoned.
Once severed, they are entirely non-existent, as they are not concomitants.
These latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with objects that are undefiled are severed either prior to the mind or simultaneously with it.
Those associated with defiled objects are severed both before, after, and simultaneously; however, those that are associated with the mind itself must necessarily be severed simultaneously with it.

Therefore, those that are defiled are termed "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) across both categories, whereas those that are non-defiled are restricted to the single quality of having the nature of "increasing along with" (anuśayana).
As explained above regarding the ten types of latent dispositions, when they arise in succession, which ones precede and which follow?
The arising of the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) has no fixed sequence, as they may all arise after any other.
Nevertheless, there is a certain class of active afflictions (*kleśa-samudācāra*) that follow one another in succession, such that their order is not without sequence.

Now, to explain the sequence in relation to that [view]: there is a certain class of people who lack discernment; by the power of false hearing and the force of past habituation, within the practice of the selflessness (*anātman*) induced by causes and conditions, they suddenly give rise at the outset to the view of a self and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).

Next, regarding these aforementioned conceptualized formations, delusion concerning the cause is called "eternalism," while delusion concerning the result is called "annihilationism. Those who fall into the extreme of annihilation increase their false views; to grasp such views as supreme is the view of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

Those who fall into the extreme of eternalism do so because they seek for themselves the attainment of happiness and the departure from all suffering; thus, they serve Īśvara and others, cultivating the causes for superior rebirth and the path to liberation. Having given rise to the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), they perceive differences among various false teachers regarding causes and paths. Lacking a teacher to provide a definitive resolution, they consequently give rise to doubt:
"Among all these tenets, which is true and which is false?"

"Following" means that one becomes attached to a superior person, reckons them as one's own ally, and gives rise to pride based on that reliance; toward those seen as belonging to the opposing faction, one gives rise to hatred through contempt.

If, amidst these states, one cannot determine what is true or false, one is disturbed by doubt and finds weariness in contemplation. Giving rise to a mind of aversion and indolence, one then admonishes oneself to stop, thinking: "In the end, it will be difficult to reach a decision; what is the use of further observation? Only the Supreme Sages can understand this; it is not within my knowledge."

Having thus crushed his own diligent application of observation and resolve, he turns his back on observation and takes delight in ignorance; through this, he quiets his mind and rests within the chamber of ignorance. This constitutes the sequential order in which the ten types of underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of one class are drawn forth and manifest.

Furthermore, there is another class of people who are by nature dull-witted; unable to discern with precision the differences between superior and inferior among the teachings of various śramaṇas and brahmins, they consequently give rise to doubt:
"Who among these is superior?"

Therefore, one observes that those who fall into the view of self, by the power of that self-view, cling to the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism; desiring that they may obtain happiness and avoid suffering in the future, they falsely calculate and cling to inverted causes and effects.

If, when examining [phenomena], one falls into the view of selflessness, it is because one does not understand the true principle of selflessness; consequently, one negates the existence of cause and effect regarding giving and so forth. Within this view, one grasps it as supreme; through perceiving its excellence, one gives rise to craving for it; because of this, one gives rise to pride that looks down upon others; and toward other philosophical positions, one gives rise to hatred through aversion and rejection.

Due to such favorable and unfavorable circumstances, as well as joy and grief, they give rise to immeasurable afflictions and defilements; they distance themselves from the noble teachings spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One and sink into the ocean of suffering, making them difficult to rescue.
Furthermore, there is another sequential arrangement established for these [afflictions], stated in verse as follows:
Ignorance, doubt, false view, self-view, Extreme view, adherence to precepts and rituals, and views;
Greed, pride, and hatred follow in sequence, As each preceding one induces the arising of the subsequent.
The treatise says:

Regarding the successive arising of the various afflictions, first, due to ignorance (*avidyā*), one lacks clear understanding of the truths and has no desire to contemplate anything from the truth of suffering up to the truth of the path.

Because they lack understanding, they lack the capacity for discernment; having heard both sides, they harbor doubt as to whether it is suffering or not suffering, and so forth, as explained at length.
If they encounter false teachings, they give rise to wrong views, repudiating the Truth of Suffering, and so forth, as explained at length.
Since one negates suffering within the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises therefrom.

From this, one further clings to the notions of my existence being either annihilated or eternal; adhering to one extreme, one reckons it to be the means of purification. Regarding such a reckoning as supreme, one gives rise to craving by perceiving the perceived qualities therein. Thinking "this is superior to others," one gives rise to pride based on that reliance. Toward others who hold opposing views, one gives rise to hatred—just as those who cling to a self-group loathe the view of no-self.
Alternatively, during the process of accepting or rejecting one's own views, one must necessarily give rise to anger, hatred, and aversion toward that which is being rejected.

This explanation of the sequential order in which the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) manifest by drawing one another forth applies to a specific class of cases; in reality, the modes of activity of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are boundless. Because the conditions upon which they depend differ, there is no fixed sequence in which they arise.
Therefore, what has been discussed above is merely a brief indication of one or two points.
By how many common conditions (*sabhāga-pratyaya*) do the various afflictions arise?

There are many kinds of causes and conditions for their arising. One such cause is the "homogeneous character" (*nikāya-sabhāga*); that is, seeing that sentient beings, according to their respective homogeneous classes, necessarily manifest these specific types of afflictions—for instance, pigeons and mandarin ducks possess the most intense greed, while vipers, snakes, and scorpions possess the most vehement hatred—and so it should be stated for the remaining categories accordingly.

Alternatively, wealth and pleasure are the causes and conditions for this [attainment]. That is to say, many sentient beings possess wholesome aspirations and are capable of reaching excellence; however, by acquiring wealth and pleasure, they give rise to various afflictions and thus lose that capability. Only by relinquishing wealth and pleasure can they become capable of reaching excellence.

Alternatively, the specific region may be the causal condition for this arising; that is to say, those born in the south have greed that is predominantly intense, while those born in the north have hatred that is predominantly blazing; in this manner, it should be explained accordingly for the other regions as well.

Alternatively, false doctrines serve as the causes and conditions for these [afflictions] to arise: that is to say, by studying treatises on warfare, one increases hatred; by listening to licentious and dissolute discourses, one fosters sensual desire; and by studying the texts of non-Buddhist paths, delusion becomes even more prevalent. If one hears the True Dharma, afflictions do not arise, because through fear of birth and death, craving and the like are extinguished.

Alternatively, having little learning is the causal condition for this arising; that is to say, the afflictions of those who lack knowledge are intense, whereas the afflictions of those with much learning are slight, because they have suppressed their afflictions through the practice of extensive learning.
Excessive sleep is a causal condition for its arising, meaning that through excessive sleep, afflictions increase.
Alternatively, pleasure and so forth are causal conditions for its arising, meaning that pleasure increases greed, suffering increases hatred, and so on.
Alternatively, food and drink may be the causal condition for their arising, meaning that afflictions such as those from drinking alcohol become intensely active.
Alternatively, the stage of life may be the causal condition for their arising, meaning that the afflictions arising in youth, middle age, and old age differ from one another.
Either habitual practice is the cause and condition for its arising; that is to say, when one habituates oneself to this affliction, it subsequently increases and becomes more intense.

Or else, the objective field of the body is the cause and condition for its arising; that is to say, upon encountering an object that accords with the body, the corresponding type of affliction arises accordingly.

Sometimes the temporal period serves as the cause and condition for this arising; that is to say, there are sentient beings who, at such a time, give rise to this particular type of affliction according to their circumstances.
Although such causes and conditions are boundless, among them, only three are preeminent.
The verse says:
Because the latent dispositions have not been abandoned, because the corresponding objects appear,
and because improper mental attention arises— these are said to be the complete causes and conditions for the afflictions.
The treatise says:
All afflictions arise due to three causes and conditions.

For instance, when a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of sensual desire is about to arise, it does so because the latent tendency of sensual desire has not been abandoned or fully understood; because an object conducive to sensual desire has appeared before one; and because improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) directed toward that object has arisen.
The arising of other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) should be understood by analogy with this.

One for whom the latent disposition of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-anuśaya*) has not been abandoned and has not been fully known is said to have it "not abandoned and not fully known" due to three conditions: namely, because its acquisition (*prāpti*) has not been severed, because its antidote (*pratipakṣa*) has not yet arisen, and because the object (*ālambana*) has not been fully known.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of abandonment: first, abandonment with remainder; second, abandonment without remainder.

Therefore, the expression "not yet abandoned and not yet fully understood" is used. This explains that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise through the power of their causes when objects conducive to sensual desire appear before one.
Furthermore, one should inquire: what is this object?

If you claim that it is an object of attachment because it is bound by desire and greed (*rāga*), then it should also be called an object of hatred (*dveṣa*) since it is bound by hatred; thus, an object conducive to hatred would also be conducive to desire and greed. Since the objects of desire and greed would therefore lack any fixed nature, one should not say that a "conducive object" is present.
If it is argued that "agreeable" refers to objects conducive to greed, such agreeable objects are not definitive either, because an object that is beloved by one person may not be so for another.

If it is argued that this is not indeterminate because it is stated with reference to a single continuum, this too is unreasonable; for we observe that a single form may at one time be agreeable to a sentient being and at another time disagreeable.

However, one must necessarily admit that there exists a determinate object-field; it is by taking that as an object that desire and greed manifest. For this reason, it is said that "an object-field conducive to greed manifests.
The objections previously raised shall be explained later; for now, this has been stated to show that latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise through the power of the object-field.

"Arising conditioned by that irrational attention" means: when an object such as a piece of wood appears before one, and there arises an irrational attention like that of a fire-drill, the fire of sensual desire is produced by drilling that wooden object.
In this context, what is called "inappropriate mental attention" (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*)?

It refers to the mind that, regarding a woman manifested through exquisite clothing, flower garlands, ornaments, perfumes, cosmetics, and graceful gestures—as being merely a heap of excrement—gives rise to the perception of a sentient being; such a mind, sustained by these perceptions, is an inverted arousal of awareness, which is termed inappropriate mental attention.
This refers to the statement that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise through the power of application (prayoga).
If all arising latent dispositions possess these three causes and conditions, how can one admit the falling away (parihāṇi) of an Arhat?

It is not that one who is not an Arhat has not yet abandoned the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); nor is it necessarily the case that one must be designated as "fallen from Arhatship" only when afflictions (*kleśa*) are actually manifesting.
Alternatively, this statement is made with reference to what is immediately induced from preceding afflictions; thus, there is no fault in the explanation.
The arising of afflictions is, in general, of two kinds: first, that which is induced immediately following an affliction; second, that which arises from other states that are not afflictions.
If it were otherwise, afflictions would not be able to arise immediately following a wholesome or neutral state of mind.
In this context, it does not refer to subsequent births; therefore, one should not raise the objection regarding retrogression.
Alternatively, this is stated provisionally based on the presence of all causes and conditions, whereas in reality, there are cases that arise solely through the power of the object.
The masters of the Dārṣṭāntika school state as follows:
"Because suffering and pleasure arise through the power of conceptual construction, one knows that the essence of all objects is not established as real.
For the Buddha stated this in the *Māṇikarṣaka-sūtra*:"
For those suffering from leprosy, when they touch the fire of suffering, they perceive it as pleasure.
Furthermore, it is said that a single color is an "agreeable object" for one sentient being, but not for others.

Furthermore, because purity and impurity are not established as real— meaning that sentient beings belonging to the same class within a particular realm of rebirth perceive purity and impurity differently regarding the same object—
and since these characteristics of purity and impurity cannot be definitively apprehended, there are no truly established objects of either purity or impurity.
The proponents of the *Nyāyānusāra* state as follows:
"No object whatsoever fails to be established as real, for the Sūtras state that there is matter accompanied by pleasure, and they also state that one is attached to desirable forms."
Furthermore, it is said that there are desirable forms cognizable by the eye; moreover, because the objects of the mental applications (*manopavicāra*) are determinate.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"Within such forms, the aspect of purity and excellence disappears, and the aspect of disadvantage appears."
Nevertheless, in order to sever craving, he speaks of objects that are attractive, repulsive, or objects of delusion.
For one who should sever craving, this is based on understanding the pure realm through the contemplation of impurity.
Because the pure realm exists within these very things, he describes the various womankind as attractive objects.
Furthermore, because one who is free from craving does not observe those [objects].
Moreover, the Sūtra states:
"Within all aggregates of form, there are always the characteristics of gratification, disadvantage, and escape."
This principle should also apply here, for we observe that among various objects, the arising of the afflictions differs.
That is to say, although aversion may arise toward agreeable objects, it is not as intense as craving.
When those who have not yet abandoned craving encounter objects that are agreeable to their minds, craving arises spontaneously and aversion arises through conceptualization.

Since the causes and preliminary applications are without distinction, yet one observes a difference in the manifestation of the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is known that the intrinsic nature of these objects is not unreal.

If it is argued that the object is not established as real because it is differentiated by the power of the objective sphere—since one admits that desire and hatred arise toward a single thing—we say:
no, for within a single aggregate, two distinct objects can potentially exist.

This means that within an agreeable collection of things, there may be a slight aspect that is provocative to anger; it is like a fine garment slightly smeared with excrement, which causes all those who delight in purity to feel total aversion.
Or again, it is like one who loathes the scent of garlic, who also feels general disdain for its flavor and other qualities.
Among those tastes, there are those who give rise to craving; they likewise give rise to a general attachment toward those odors and so forth.

Thus we know that all phenomena arise together in a single collection: within one such collection, there exist factors such as those that are objects of craving. Therefore, within a single collection, greed, hatred, and delusion may all arise. It is not the case that when an object of greed arises, the other two necessarily arise; thus, no objective realm fails to be established as real.

If that were so, since there would already be a truly established mark of purity, the perception of purity upon observation would necessarily accord with reality; and by virtue of such a perception of reality, desire would not arise.

However, within objects there is no truly established mark of purity; it is through false conceptualization of them as pure that desire arises. Therefore, one knows that all objects are not truly established.
If it were not so, and one claimed that the object is not truly established, then taking up the perception of impurity would incur the same fault.
That is to say, within an impure aspect that is not truly established, whatever observation of impurity occurs would not be according to reality; how then could this possibly subdue the afflictions?

If one were to suppress the afflictions through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), then one should not hold such a view; for it is only by seeing things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*) that one can become free from desire, whereas the arising of desire necessarily results from not seeing things as they truly are.

However, although the objects of the environment do indeed possess a slight degree of pure aspect, one can suppress the afflictions by contemplating them as impure through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*);
likewise, although they do indeed possess a slight degree of impurity, greed arises toward them because of the mental exaggeration (*samāropa*) thereof.
Furthermore, if all phenomena lacked a truly established nature and arose solely through the power of conceptual construction, how could the Noble Teaching make such statements as:

"this thing is to be reviled, this thing is to be delighted in; this thing accords with the fetters, this does not accord with the fetters; this thing should be cultivated, this should not be cultivated"?

Furthermore, if you claim that because a single object may give rise to attachment, aversion, or delusion, the aspects of attractiveness and so forth within that object are not established as real, then surely you must have heard that the meaning of the verses composed by those harboring biased views should also be established as real?
As there is a verse in that treatise which says:
"Because regarding a single entity, One may see it as permanent, see it as impermanent, See both, or see neither; Therefore, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature."
If that were so, then cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*) would also fail to be established, because they consist in apprehending what is actually pure as being pure.

This is not the case; for in this context, one proceeds by way of mental construction (*manasikāra*) to superimpose [qualities] upon a slight seed of purity. That is to say, regarding objects that are either attractive or unattractive, one mentally constructs the characteristics of impurity or purity; based on this, aversion or attachment arises. It is not that the basis of the superimposition fails to be real; therefore, while proceeding by way of mental construction upon a slight seed, it is not the case that this is not a cognitive distortion.

Furthermore, because attachment and so forth, as well as pleasure and so forth, arise toward objects without certainty, it follows that even though the object is real, the nature of perversion is not unestablished.
If this were so, then even wholesome states of mind would have to be considered perverted, since there are cases where an object that is agreeable is taken to be disagreeable.
It is not so; since such attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is not erroneous.
If there is a wholesome attention that, through the power of resolute conviction, perceives only pure characteristics (*śubha-nimitta*) within its object, how could this not be erroneous?
It is not that this resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) possesses the power to sever the various afflictions (*kleśa*);

rather, because one observes for oneself whether or not desire has been severed and whether it still possesses power, although it proceeds by apprehending the aspect of purity in the object, it is not a distortion (*viparyāsa*).

Alternatively, if one now merely recollects, as before, the appearance of the object grasped by a defiled mind, in order to examine for oneself whether the fruit of cultivation attained has been realized or not, this is not a misconception because there is no further conceptual superimposition.
Alternatively, wholesome attention (*manasikāra*) regarding various objects is not inverted because it takes as its object only the signs of purity or impurity as appropriate;
whereas attention associated with greed and so forth regarding various objects takes them collectively as pure or impure as appropriate, and thus differs from the wholesome.

However, as for the claim that because suffering and pleasure arise through the power of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the object is not established as real, and that the *Māṇḍavya-sūtra* serves as proof for this—this is logically impossible. This is because we clearly observe that desire arises even toward objects that are not desired; otherwise, one would be denying the causal power of the objective field itself.

Furthermore, it is directly observed that due to defects in the sense faculties, one perceives sweet and other tastes erroneously; the same applies to cold, warmth, and so forth. It cannot be said that this occurs because the objects themselves are not established as real.

Furthermore, the argument that one knows objects are not established as real because a single form is called an "object of the agreeable" for one sentient being but not for others, is also unreasonable, as this has already been explained previously.

It was stated previously that a single aggregate can contain two objects; that is, within a single aggregate there may exist both agreeable and disagreeable seeds, which are then superimposed upon it, leading one to designate the whole as either agreeable or disagreeable.

Some say that the object becomes real in terms of its state and essence; that is to say, at this particular time, the object becomes agreeable and not disagreeable, whereas in other states it is the opposite.

Furthermore, they argue that because purity and impurity are not established as real, one knows there are no objects of pure or impure reality. This reasoning is also incorrect, for if that were so, the cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*) of perceiving purity within the impure would be impossible. That is to say, if there were absolutely no real impurity, even if one were to apprehend it as pure, how could it constitute the cognitive distortion of the notion of purity regarding the impure?
Since it is already admitted that a single object can be both pure and impure, what kind of conceptualization regarding it would be erroneous and what would not?
Furthermore, just as the perception of permanence within the impermanent constitutes an error, we know that the nature of impurity is definitively established as real.

Alternatively, if one were to grasp both permanence and impermanence regarding contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*), then the nature of impermanence itself would likewise fail to be established as real.
Or, just as with the nature of impermanence, so it is with the nature of impurity (*aśubhatā*).
Therefore, it is not the case that the pure and the impure are not established as real.

To say that sentient beings belonging to the same *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) within a different realm of rebirth perceive purity and impurity differently regarding a single object, and thus conclude that no truly established pure or impure object exists—this reasoning is also incorrect, because the previous explanation has already established that a single aggregate can contain two distinct objects.

To claim that the characteristics of purity and impurity cannot be definitively apprehended, and therefore no truly established objects of purity or impurity exist, is logically untenable, as it follows from what was stated previously.

That is to say, it is not the case that there is no nature of purity or impurity in the absence of characteristics; if such a nature did not exist, cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*) could not occur. Therefore, one should not assert that the non-apprehension of characteristics constitutes a reason for the non-establishment of purity and impurity as real entities.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, definitively establishes that contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) possess the nature of impurity.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that because contaminated phenomena are defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*), they are termed ultimately impure; thus, one knows that purity and defilement are not unreal.

If that were so, would it not follow that all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are impure? For there may be those who give rise to a perception of purity and excellence regarding them; since the object of such a perception is not established as real, the same logic should apply to other cases.

Although this [notion] augmented by cognition does not constitute reality, because the impure object is real, the meaning of the perversion—perceiving it as pure within that [object]—is established. When subsequent desire arises, it follows this perception of purity; therefore, although the augmented characteristic is not real, there is no fault of lacking an objective referent (*ālambana*), for it is not [absolutely] unreal.

Furthermore, as previously stated, within an impure aggregate there exists a small seed of purity; since the seed of purity and the nature of purity are not distinct entities, the pure object is not non-existent. It is merely that, by way of general exaggeration regarding it, one falls into perversion.
Furthermore, dharmas such as form possess a pure intrinsic nature; it is merely by virtue of being associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) that they are designated as "impure.
Therefore, no object whatsoever is not established as real.
Other masters say:

The objects of the afflictions arising based on the five consciousness-bodies are established as real, because two minds do not operate simultaneously upon a single object, because the five consciousnesses apprehend only present objects, and because the forms and other phenomena they apprehend are momentary in nature.

The objects of the remaining afflictions do not exist as real entities, because after apprehending form and so forth in a single moment, a subsequent continuum arises with different conceptualizations.

This [argument] should also be refuted by considering the aggregate as a whole: within a past agreeable aggregate, there may be an object capable of increasing hatred; first, one perceives the agreeable within the aggregate and generates greed, and later, recollecting the disagreeable within that same aggregate, one generates hatred. Therefore, the objects of the afflictions arising from the mental consciousness are not unreal.
The aforementioned latent dispositions (anuśaya), together with their attendants, the Buddha has described as outflows (āsrava), floods (ogha), yokes (yoga), and graspings (upādāna).
Regarding the outflows, there are three: first, the outflow of desire (kāma-āsrava); second, the outflow of existence (bhava-āsrava); and third, the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava).
Regarding the term "floods" (ogha), it refers to the four floods: first, the flood of sensual desire; second, the flood of existence; third, the flood of views; and fourth, the flood of ignorance.
The yokes refer to the four yokes, as explained in the section on the floods (*ogha*).

Appropriation refers to the four types of appropriation: first, appropriation of sensual desire; second, appropriation of views; third, appropriation of rules and observances; and fourth, appropriation of the doctrine of self.
What is the essential nature of these outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth?
The verse says:
The afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm together with their envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), excluding ignorance (*moha*), are called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
The outflows (*āsrava*) of the two upper realms consist solely of afflictions (*kleśa*), excluding ignorance (*moha*).
Because they are equally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), inwardly directed (*antarmukha*), and belong to the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*), they are combined into one.
Since ignorance is the root of all modes of existence (*bhava*), it is established as a separate outflow.

The floods (ogha) and yokes (yoga) are likewise; they are established separately because views are sharp and because views do not conform to abiding. They are not established as independent outflows (āsrava).
The yokes of desire and existence, together with delusion, have their view-portion divided into two and named "grasping" (upādāna).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is not established separately because it is not a grasping agent.
The treatise says:

The forty-one entities consisting of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm, excluding delusion (*moha*), are collectively termed the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*). That is to say, the thirty-one root afflictions bound to the desire realm together with the ten outbursts.

The afflictions of the form and formless realms, excluding delusion, consist of fifty-two entities collectively termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*); that is, the root afflictions of each of the two upper realms number twenty-six.

Although lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) also exist within the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*), these envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) should not be distinguished according to the realms; for in the higher realms, such envelopments are minimal and lack autonomy. Therefore, it is said that only the outflows (*āsrava*) constitute afflictions (*kleśa*).

If the *paryavasthānas* (outbursts) are also classified according to the realms (*dhātu*), then there are fifty-six entities that constitute outflows (*sāsrava*). Therefore, the *Prakaraṇapāda* states as follows:
"What are the outflows?"

This refers to the fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) belonging to the two realms of form and formlessness, excluding ignorance (*avidyā*).
For what reason are the afflictions of these two realms collectively designated as a single "outflow" (*āsrava*)?
