They are combined into one because they share three common characteristics: being of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), functioning within the internal door (*antarmukha-pravṛtta*), and arising from the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*).

Since the afflictions (*kleśa*) of that realm also function toward external objects—namely, the objects of visible form, sound, and tangibles—a second reason for their combination must be stated separately: namely, that those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have the same antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
If one relies on this interpretation, it does not violate the metrical verse; that is to say, it should be stated:
"For what reason are the afflictions of two realms spoken of together as a single outflow (āsrava)?
Because they are equally neutral, have the same antidote, and belong to the meditative stages (samāhita-bhūmi), they are combined into one."
For what reason do only these receive the name "outflow with outflows" (*sāsrava*)?

This is explained as being "possessing greed," as previously stated; by extension, the fifteen types of ignorance within the three realms constitute the substance of the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), and therefore the verse does not mention them separately.
For what reason is this alone established with the specific name "outflow" (*āsrava*)?
It is to demonstrate that the fault and affliction of ignorance (*avidyā*) are preeminent; that is to say, it alone can act as the root of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). As a sūtra says:
"With ignorance as the cause, greed and defilement arise," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, as a verse says:
"All the various evil destinies, Both in this world and in other worlds..."
"All have ignorance as their root, arising equally from craving.
Having already analyzed the three outflows (*āsrava*), one should further investigate them as stated in the *Mūla-śāstra*:

"The fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) constitute the first two outflows. If the name "outflow" is applied only when all five criteria are met, then the ten envelopments would not constitute the substance of the outflows.

If one were to receive the designation "outflow" (*āsrava*) merely by possessing any one of these [defilements], then afflicted volition, resentment, and so forth would also have to be called outflows; in that case, the enumeration of the objects previously established would be rendered futile.
Now, within this context, we rely solely on what is preeminent for the sake of clarity, and thus speak of the one hundred and eight delusions as outflows.

This means that non-defiled volitions (*cetanā*), resentment (*upanāha*), and so forth are not included among the outflows (*āsrava*). It is only these various afflictions (*kleśa*) that cause sentient beings to linger long in saṃsāra, or cause them to transmigrate within saṃsāra from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to the Avīci Hell. Because they are powerful and easily understood, they are specifically mentioned here.
The nature of the floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*) is the same as that of the outflows (*āsrava*); however, among them, views (*dṛṣṭi*) are established separately.

That is to say, the aforementioned outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is itself the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) and the yoke of desire (*kāma-yoga*); likewise, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) is itself the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) and the yoke of existence (*bhava-yoga*).

The reason for extracting the various views (*dṛṣṭi*) to establish them as the flood of views (*dṛṣṭy-ogha*) and the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭi-yoga*) is that they are particularly intense. This is because the meanings of "flood" (*ogha*), "yoke" (*yoga*), and "clinging" (*upādāna*) are established based on the sense of drifting away, binding together, and grasping.

Just as other afflictions—excluding ignorance (*avidyā*) alone—are able to drift, bind, and grasp through their mutual assistance as a whole, so too are the various views; yet, due to their intensity, they are able to drift, bind, and grasp even apart from the assistance of others. Therefore, they are also established separately as floods, yokes, and clingings.

Furthermore, all afflictions cause sentient beings to drift and sink into defiled phenomena; they lead them away from all wholesome qualities and toward wrong understanding. Like surging and overflowing waves, they violently toss sentient beings so that their distance from the wholesome increases further. For this reason, ignorance (*avidyā*) is established separately from [the other] views.
If that is so, why not establish "outflow of views" (dṛṣṭy-āsrava) as a separate category?
That which causes one to abide [in saṃsāra] is termed an "outflow," as will be explained later.
Views do not conform to that [definition], because their meaning is distinct.
They are called "outflows" (āsrava) because they cause both ordinary worldlings and noble ones alike to dwell within birth and death;
since various views lack this capacity to cause the noble ones to dwell [in saṃsāra], their meaning as "outflows" is incomplete, and thus they are not established separately.

Regarding the meaning of "drifting" (*plava*), there is a distinction between noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); therefore, in the latter three categories, "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is established separately.

This is because these various afflictions can cause ordinary beings to drift away from all wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*), potentially leading them to abandon them entirely; however, this cannot be said of noble ones.

Having caused them to drift, it brings all classes of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) into contact with various undesirable realms, destinies, and births; however, it cannot cause the noble ones (*ārya*) to be so joined.
Having brought them into contact, it causes all classes of ordinary beings to lack anything they do not rely upon or cling to; yet it does not cause the noble ones to be so.
Because ordinary beings and noble ones perceive superiority within these three gates, they are established separately.
Other masters say:

because their views are restless and sharp, they alone cannot accomplish the meaning of "abiding"; therefore, they are established in conjunction with other gates regarding the category of outflows (*āsrava*). When combined with others, they possess the capacity for abiding, just as when a young elephant is bound together with a king of elephants.

Thus, twenty-nine entities have been shown to constitute the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*): namely, five types each of greed, hatred, and pride; four types of doubt; and ten types of entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
Twenty-eight entities constitute the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*): namely, ten types each of greed and pride, and eight types of doubt.
The thirty-six factors are called the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*); that is, twelve views in each of the three realms.
The fifteen factors are called the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*); that is, five types of ignorance in each of the three realms.
It should be understood that the four yokes (*yoga*) are identical to the floods (*ogha*).
It should be understood that the four graspings (*upādāna*) are identical in substance to the four yokes; however, for the desire-yoke and the self-theory yoke, ignorance (*avidyā*) is added to each.

The view-yoke is divided into two, which differ from the previous yokes. Specifically, the desire-yoke together with the ignorance of desire—comprising thirty-four entities—is collectively termed the "grasping at desire" (*kāmopādāna*). These consist of greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance (five of each), doubt (four), and the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

That is to say, the previously mentioned yokes (*yoga*), together with the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the two realms, totaling thirty-eight entities, are collectively termed "clinging to the expression of self" (*ātma-vādopādāna*). This refers to ten instances each of craving (*rāga*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*), and eight instances of doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Within the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭi-yoga*), with the exception of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the remaining thirty entities are collectively termed the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

The six entities thus excluded are termed the clinging to precepts and observances; this is because it alone acts as an enemy to the Noble Path and because it deceives both the laity and the monastics alike.
For what reason is ignorance (*avidyā*) not established as a separate type of grasping (*upādāna*)?
The term "grasping" is established based on the sense of "actively grasping," yet various forms of ignorance are not of the nature of active grasping.
That which is defined as a lack of clear comprehension is called ignorance; it is not of the nature of active grasping because it is not sharp or intense.

They may, however, be established as "grasping" (upādāna) only by being combined with others; the establishment of grasping and its detailed determination should be understood accordingly, as in the section on dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
If the floods (ogha), yokes (yoga), and graspings were to subsume all afflictions (kleśa), they would contradict the sūtra, which asks:
"What is the yoke of desire (kāmayoga)?"

This refers to those who are foolish, namely unlearned worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), who do not know, as it truly is, the origin and cessation of sensual desires, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them, and so forth, as explained at length.

Regarding those various sensual desires, whatever desire-greed, desire-longing, desire-intimacy, desire-love, desire-delight, desire-oppression, desire-addiction, desire-relishing, desire-joy, desire-concealment, desire-pursuit, and desire-attachment there may be that bind and weigh down the mind—this is called the yoke of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*).
The yokes of existence (*bhavayoga*) and the yokes of views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*) should be understood in the same way.
These three names for "yokes" are stated with respect to the essence of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Furthermore, another sutra states that sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) is called "clinging" (*upādāna*); from this it is known that the sensual desire arising toward the four [objects]—sensual pleasure and so forth—is called "clinging to sensual pleasure" (*kāmopādāna*) and so on.
How can all afflictions be fully subsumed [within these]?
This is not contradictory, for the intent of the sūtra is distinct.
It is spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) according to the differences in the faculties and conduct of those to be converted, just like a torrential stream.
That is to say, a sutra states:
"There are four floods (ogha).
However, in another sutra, the Buddha, observing the differences in the dispositions and conduct of those to be converted, spoke these words:
If a bhikṣu can dwell extensively in this, he has already crossed over the five preceding floods and shall likewise be able to cross over the sixth flood.
How is it known that this is a statement of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*)?

It is not only craving that constitutes the essence of the three yokes; since the sūtras state that there are nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), and the categories of "fetter" and "yoke" are similar in meaning, we know that all afflictions possess the characteristic of being a yoke.
The Buddha observes the capacities and conduct of those to be converted and what they require; thus, from among many entities, he briefly cites only one.
Furthermore, as a sutra states:
"If you sever one dharma, I can guarantee that you will attain the fruit of non-returning; this 'one dharma' refers to the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)."
It is not merely by abandoning this that one attains the fruit of non-returning;
as it is further stated in the Sūtra:
"One should abandon malice and anger."
It is not that other afflictions should not be abandoned or eliminated.
Furthermore, as it is said that ignorance can shroud sentient beings, yet elsewhere it is stated that there are five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), so it is with this sutra as well:
because those to be converted are currently afflicted by craving within their own mental continuums, it is no fault to have taught craving in brief for their sake.
Regarding the two yokes of desire (*kāmayoga*), one may briefly mention craving (*tṛṣṇā*), because it subsumes them.
As for the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*),
since the natures of craving and the yoke of views are distinct, there is no fault in mentioning them separately.
Because the term "yoke of views" (*dṛṣṭi-yoga*) is understood through the method of etymological interpretation (*nirukti*) to encompass two meanings:
if "view" itself is the "yoke," it is called the "yoke of views," as in the case of the "yoke of ignorance" (*avidyā-yoga*);
if one is "bound by" the yoke of views, it is called the "yoke of views," just as in the case of being "bound by a yoke."

Because the Buddha intended for his disciples to understand these two meanings, although he also applies the name "yoke of views" (*dṛṣṭiyoga*) to craving, there is no contradiction with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Thus has the analysis of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) along with the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) been completed.
The Sūtras speak of them as outflows (*āsrava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and graspings (*upādāna*). What is the meaning of these names, such as "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*)?
The verse says:
Subtle, increasing in two ways, Persisting, and binding closely;
"Abiding, flowing, drifting, conjoining, and grasping—these are the meanings of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth.
The treatise says:
When the fundamental afflictions manifest, their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are difficult to discern; therefore, they are called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).
Therefore, the noble Ānanda said:
"I do not know now whether I have given rise to a mind of conceit toward my fellow practitioners of the holy life.

He did not say that such a state is entirely absent, for since the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the latent tendency of conceit (*mānānuśaya*) is so subtle, even he could not discern the presence or absence of such a mind; how much more so must this be the case for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), as other examples would suggest.
Some explain that even in a single moment and a single atom there is "increase" (anuśaya), and thus it is called "subtle.
As for the two types of increase: they are so called because [the afflictions] increase respectively with respect to their objects (*ālambana*) and their associated factors (*samprayukta*).
How do afflictions increase through their objects and through association?

As previously explained, or as when an enemy seeks out a vulnerability, and like the poison of a glance, one should understand that afflictions possess the sense of increasing within their own respective objects.

Just as a red-hot iron ball can cause water to heat up, and just as contact with poison [increases its effect], one should know that afflictions possess the sense of "concomitant increase" (*anuśaya*) within their own associated states.
Both are like a wet-nurse who causes an infant to grow: the nurse enables the infant to develop physically, and also allows his skills to accumulate gradually.
Through association with its object, it causes the various afflictions to continue, increase, and accumulate.
As for "pursuing," it means that from beginningless time, it has arisen within the continuum and persists in pursuit.
Regarding "concomitant bondage" (*anubandha*): it is so called because it is extremely difficult to sever, like a quartan fever or the poison of a rat.
Some say: concomitant bondage refers to that which is constantly followed by its acquisition (*prāpti*), just as the movement of the ocean follows the shadow moving through the sky.
For the reasons explained above, the ten types of afflictions are designated by the term *anuśaya*.

To explain this term through its etymological derivation (*nirukti*): that which "flows along" (*anu*) and "sleeps" (*śete*) within the continuum is called an *anuśaya*. This signifies that which conforms to the stream and dwells within the person, causing increased dullness and stagnation.

Alternatively, they are called *anuśaya* because they lie dormant (*anu-śī*) within the continuum of a superior being; that is, their meaning is that of delusion regarding the state of entering into reality as it is (*yathābhūta*).
Or, they are called *anuśaya* because they pursue and conceal sentient beings for a long time within the prison [of cyclic existence].
For what reason are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) only ten—namely, greed and the others—and not the others such as anger?
It is because only these ten types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are firm and stable, whereas those such as anger are not.

That is to say, only these ten have firm and stable habitual tendencies; once they arise, they are difficult to cease, being like a mountain being carried on one's shoulders, or like a fire, or like a grudge against an enemy. Therefore, they are called "latent dispositions."
If that were so, then resentment (*upanāha*) would have to be of the nature of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*).
It is not so; for while latent tendencies operate spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*), resentment only proceeds when effort is exerted.
Nevertheless, because the nature of latent tendencies is particularly grave, they proceed with firm persistence even without the application of effort.

Alternatively, it is because resentment (*upanāha*) acts in accordance with hatred (*dveṣa*). That is to say, the defilement of resentment is a derivative (*niṣyanda*) of hatred; it only functions as an active operation in accordance with what is done by hatred.

When one recollects various signs of anger, resentment is formed and not relinquished in accordance with what was done by hatred. Therefore, there is no fault of resentment failing to constitute a latent tendency (*anuśaya*). This is the etymological definition for establishing the latent tendencies.

They detain sentient beings, causing them to dwell long in saṃsāra, or cause them to transmigrate within saṃsāra from the Peak of Existence down to the Avīci Hell; because their continuity discharges faults inexhaustibly through the six wound-gates, they are called "outflows" (āsrava).
They are called "floods" (*ogha*) because they carry away the wholesome factors to the furthest extent.
They are called "yokes" (*yoga*) because they bind one to the realms, destinies, and births.
They are called "grasping" (*upādāna*) because they seize various individual existences.
In this context, the Master of the Sūtras further states:

"One who provides a correct explanation should say that because they flow, continue in succession, and leak through the various objects of perception without interruption, they are called 'outflows' (āsrava)."

If their force is predominant, they are called "floods" (*ogha*); that is to say, when sentient beings fall into them, they can only go along with them and have no power to resist, because they surge, overflow, and rush with such force that they are difficult to oppose.
When they are active, they are called "yokes" (yoga) not because they are extremely predominant, but because they cause sentient beings to be conjoined with various kinds of suffering;
alternatively, they are called "yokes" because they manifest repeatedly.
Because one grasps at desire and so forth, they are called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
What excellence is there in them?
Among the four names [of the aggregates], two are identical to "self," while two contradict reason.

That which they describe as "outflows" (āsrava) refers to the fact that within various objects of perception, there is a continuous flow and succession of leaking faults that never ceases; this is precisely what our own school explains as the outflows, because through that continuity, faults are discharged inexhaustibly from the six wound-like gates.

There is no separate continuity apart from the various outflows (*āsrava*); rather, it is by virtue of their power that faults are discharged toward objects. Thus, whether collectively or individually, the uninterrupted streaming of the afflictions (*kleśa*) receives the name "continuity" (*saṃtati*).
To speak of the six wounds (the sense organs) is precisely to speak of the six objects.
If their discourse is uninterrupted, then my [argument] is inexhaustible.
How does this differ from my own position? Why do you alone claim that theirs is superior?
When their force is predominant, they are called "floods" (*ogha*); this is what our own school means by saying they "completely sweep away the wholesome factors.
How does this differ from [the view that] they alone are wholesome?
When they manifest, because they are not extremely predominant, they are called "yokes" (*yoga*), for they cause one to be joined with various kinds of suffering.
This contradicts reason: if [the afflictions] are not predominant at the time they manifest, how could they cause one to be joined with various sufferings?
How, then, can that explanation be said to be correct?

Furthermore, if it is argued that wholesome dharmas, which frequently manifest, also cause sentient beings to be joined with manifold sufferings and thus should be designated as "yokes" (*yoga*) alongside the afflictions (*kleśa*), this objection is unreasonable.
My explanation does not share this fault, because I maintain that afflictions possess this capacity by way of their function in initiating karma (*karma-samutthāna*).

The interpretation of "clinging" (*upādāna*) as you have provided also contradicts reason. For if "clinging" were defined solely as craving (*tṛṣṇā*), how could the statement that "clinging conditions existence" (*upādānapratyayo bhavaḥ*) be established?
It would simply have to be stated that "craving conditions existence."

Furthermore, just as the karmic conditions of the past limit and the future limit should also encompass all afflictions— as was already extensively analyzed within the context of dependent origination—
the Vaibhāṣika masters do not maintain such a view, because that interpretation contradicts correct reasoning.
