subsequently, during the contemplation of suffering and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),

the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) characterized by the direct realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*) arises in succession; this is because everything thereafter arises spontaneously (*svarasena*) as previously described.

Alternatively, from beginningless time while in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one has repeatedly observed the suffering, origin, cessation, and path of the desire and form realms by means of mundane, deceptive cognition; therefore, although the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the two realms of desire and form have already been severed, one must again and thoroughly observe them by means of supramundane, non-deceptive cognition.

The Bodhisattva also cultivates those paths of counteraction; for those who have previously abandoned defilements as appropriate, once the path of seeing arises and they reach the stage of abiding in the fruit, since the obstacles to the path of superior fruit have already been eliminated beforehand, what fault could there be in attaining that path of superior fruit?
If this principle is accepted, it provides a sound resolution, and the exposition in the *Daśamukha-parivarta* is also well-established.
It would, however, be logically untenable for a Bodhisattva to achieve the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) resulting from the cultivation of the lower stages of abandonment.
Furthermore, the claim that one who abides in a fruit attains a path that is not a fruit contradicts the *Vibhāṣā*.
At the time of abiding in a fruit, one has not yet proceeded toward a subsequent fruit; therefore, the sense of having already attained a path that is not a fruit cannot possibly exist.
Furthermore, this is logically necessary: while the antidote that abandons [a specific defilement] is present, how could one obtain its future path of abandonment by means of it?

Moreover, when those bound by all fetters gradually attain the fruits [of the path], at the time they subsequently achieve the superior path of the fruit, the path subsumed under that fruit necessarily does not function.

Furthermore, when those who have previously abandoned defilements attain the fruit, if there were also the principle of attaining superior fruits, then the path subsumed within those fruits would never again function.

Moreover, it is not the case that while one abides in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) at the time of attaining the antidote for the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), there is also the attainment of the antidote for the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) pertaining to the Desire Realm.

Furthermore, when one attains the path of a superior fruit (*viśeṣa-phala-mārga*), one also accordingly attains the various mundane paths (*laukika-mārga*), because the mundane and supramundane paths are mutually interconnected.

If one has previously abandoned the defilements, then according to what is appropriate, the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) arises later; and upon reaching the stage of abiding in the fruit, one must necessarily also attain the path of a superior fruit. At the time of attaining the state of a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), one should cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), because it serves as an antidote to the same [defilements] and because it equally abandons the same obstacles.
For this reason, when I speak of attaining dissociation (*visamyoga*) and so forth, it is well-established as being consistent with the scriptures and in accord with reason.

That is to say, regarding these various dissociations, they receive their respective names according to the stage in which they are attained, for such designations are established in accordance with what is predominant.
There are two kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*): first, thorough knowledge as wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*), and second, thorough knowledge as abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
Thorough knowledge as wisdom has discernment (*prajñā*) as its essential nature.
Some say that this [analytical knowledge] is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Contaminated wisdom refers to all other mundane discernment of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), excluding that which is associated with the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*), which is capable of grasping the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; it includes the wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-mayī-prajñā*), as well as the wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) such as Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) refers to the wisdom of the supramundane paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

The aforementioned tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) is conducive to untainted knowledge; because it possesses the nature of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), it is also termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"When I engaged in such correct reflection, the realization of insight arose, and I knew that old age and death exist because of birth.
It further says:
If one has not attained or fully understood even a single dharma, I say that one cannot bring an end to suffering.

This is because it is not through untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) alone that all dharmas are fully understood; rather, the full understanding of knowledge (*jñānaparijñā*) also extends to tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*).
Only untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) constitutes the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñānaparijñā*); this is precisely what my school maintains as its orthodox position. As it is said:

"In order to bring about realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding dharmas not yet realized, one contemplates the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*). It is not by means of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtiprajñā*) derived from hearing and so forth that one can attain the fruits ranging from Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) to Arhat; for it is stated that the nine faculties (*indriya*) are acquired by those who have attained the fruit of Stream-enterer and the others.
Furthermore, the *Cakra-pravartana-sūtra* states:
"One thoroughly knows suffering and so forth by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
It should be understood that this is precisely the faculty of "that which is yet to be known" (*ājñātavya-indriya*).

However, when it is said that a Bodhisattva’s "realization" (abhisamaya) arises, this is a conventional designation of the term "realization" applied to worldly wisdom (*laukikī prajñā*), because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) functions in a manner similar to realization.

Regarding the statement "not having attained [knowledge] of even a single dharma" and so forth: if, with respect to a given dharma, one has not fully known (*parijñāta*) the obstacles to the exhaustion of suffering, there is no fault in speaking cryptically in this way; therefore, it is certain that only untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*) attains the name "full knowledge."
The essence of the full knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) is dissociation (*visamyoga*); because it is capable of fully knowing [the truth], it is termed "full knowledge.
How can this name for wisdom refer to abandonment?
Because it is the fruit of that wisdom, just as the fruit of karma is called "liberation" (*vimukti*).
This means that the sūtras refer to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as "action" (*karman*), because they are the fruit of action;
and they refer to the unconditioned state of fruition (*asaṃskṛta-phala*) as "liberation" (*vimukti*), because it is the fruit of liberation.
Thus, there is no error in designating thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) as "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*).
If that were so, the fruit of patience (*kṣānti*) would not be full knowledge (*parijñā*). The Vaibhāṣikas explain it thus:

because all patiences are attendants of wisdom (*jñāna*), the designation "wisdom's action" is applied to what is performed by patience, just as the actions performed by a minister are also called the king's actions.
Other masters explain:

The various paths of liberation also possess efficacy regarding the abandonment already attained, because they are able to maintain the acquisition of that abandonment and prevent the acquisition of the fetters from arising again; for this reason, that which is the fruit of patience also possesses the status of being the fruit of knowledge.

This explanation is incorrect, because it is taught that all abandonments (*prahāṇa*) are exclusively the *visamyoga-phala* (fruit of dissociation) and the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) of the various paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Alternatively, because the power of the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) associated with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is able to collectively gather all the untainted acquisitions of dissociation (*anāsrava-visamyoga-prāpti*) resulting from abandonment, the fruit of patience (*kṣānti*) at that time also becomes the fruit of wisdom (*jñāna-phala*), as well as the fruit of gradual attainment (*anupūrva-prāpti-phala*), and so forth.

Because the fruits of once-returning and non-returning are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as they have already become fruits of knowledge (*jñānaphala*); because it is accepted that the unconditioned state consisting in the permanent abandonment of the three lower fetters, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), is called a fruit of knowledge; and because it will be explained that the remaining three [fruits] are fruits of knowledge.

Is a single thorough knowledge established for each disconnection obtained through each individual path of abandonment, or is one comprehensive thorough knowledge established for all disconnections obtained through all paths of abandonment?
Neither of these two positions is tenable, as they both entail the faults of being excessively broad or excessively narrow.
If that is so, how [should it be understood]?
The verse says:

There are nine thorough knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*): One for the first two abandonments of the desire realm, two for each of the next two [abandonments], totaling three; the same applies to the three [abandonments] of the higher realms.
The remaining five concern the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), and there are three for the total abandonment of the form realm.
The treatise says:
All abandonments are collectively established as nine kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
Only nine conditions are established, as will be explained later.
What are called the nine kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)?

Briefly stated, six thorough knowledges are established based on the abandonment of the afflictions and so forth belonging to the three realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*). Specifically, the abandonment of the first two categories (*pakṣa*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) establishes one thorough knowledge; the phrase "first two categories" indicates those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*).

Next, one complete knowledge (*parijñā*) is established for each of the two classes [of afflictions] abandoned through seeing; the phrase "the next two classes" indicates those abandoned through seeing the truths of cessation and the path.

As it is with the three [classes] of the desire realm, so it is with the higher realms—that is, those bound to the two realms of form and formlessness. For each of these, there are likewise two [classes] abandoned through seeing and two abandoned through cultivation, making one for each, which together total three.

Regarding the abandonment of the remaining afflictions and so forth belonging to the other three realms that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), three types of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) are established. Specifically, the abandonment of the afflictions and so forth belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation is established as one universal knowledge; it should be understood that this is the universal knowledge of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīya-saṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā*), as it is established in conjunction with what preceded it.

The abandonment of the afflictions and so forth to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertaining to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is established as one thorough knowledge (*parijñā*); it should be understood that this is precisely the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūpatṛṣṇākṣaya-parijñā*).

The abandonment of the afflictions and so forth to be abandoned by the path of cultivation pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is established as one thorough knowledge, namely, the thorough knowledge of the permanent exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojanaparyādāna-parijñā*); this is because it is combined with the preceding [thorough knowledge] to establish a single [thorough knowledge].
These three, together with the preceding six, constitute nine universal knowledges (*parijñā*) in total.

Just as in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the attainment of the abandonment of afflictions and so forth that are abandoned solely by seeing is designated as "universal knowledge," so too in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is not the case that there is only one [universal knowledge] for what is abandoned by cultivation. Rather, two [of these nine] pertain to both seeing and cultivation, because they were established in combination with the preceding ones; furthermore, it is necessary to explain the universal knowledges of the collection at two distinct times. If this were otherwise, one could not speak of the five universal knowledges of the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*pañca-avarabhāgīya-kṣaya-parijñā*) and the universal knowledge of the exhaustion of all [fetters].

For what reason are the abandonments of the dharmas to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) in the form and formless realms established collectively as a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), whereas those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are each established separately?
It is because they are established according to the arising of their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).

That is to say, just as the aggregates of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are selfless, so too are the aggregates of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) selfless; for they are identical in being devoid of objective referents (*avastuka*) that are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), and because they do not coexist with the body, their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) are likewise identical.

Just as the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the formless realm are superior, those of the form realm are not so; because the objects to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) therein are distinct and their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) differ, they are established separately.
Regarding these nine kinds of thorough knowledge thus established, one should analyze how many among them are the fruits of the path.
The verse says:
Among them, six are the fruits of patience; The remaining three are the fruits of knowledge.
The fruit of the *anāgamya* stage comprises all [nine]; the fundamental [dhyānas] comprise five or eight;
the fruit of the final *ārūpya* stage comprises one; the same applies to the three fundamental [ārūpyas].
The worldly (*laukika*) fruit comprises two; the noble (*ārya*) fruit comprises nine. The *dharmajñāna* fruit comprises three; the *anvayajñāna* fruit comprises two.
The fruits of the category of dharma-knowledge are six; the fruits of the category of subsequent knowledge are five.
The treatise says:
Among these nine, one should first distinguish the differences between those that are the fruits of the paths of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).

The fruits of patience (*kṣānti*) are sixfold, namely the six types of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding the abandonment of the factors to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) bound to the three realms.

The fruits of knowledge (*jñāna*) are threefold, namely the universal knowledge of the exhaustion of the fetters conducive to the lower realm (*avarabhāgīya*), the universal knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*), and the universal knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-kṣaya*); these three universal knowledges are the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Having thus already explained the fruits of the paths of seeing and meditation, regarding the distinction of their fruits from those of the dhyāna stages: the fruit of the *anāgamya* (preliminary concentration) possesses all nine, because it serves as the basis for abandoning everything.

The fruits of the fundamental dhyānas are five or eight. Regarding the statement that they are five, the Vaibhāṣika masters say this because the fundamental dhyānas are not the antidotes for abandoning the afflictions of the desire realm.
Regarding the statement that there are eight: the Venerable Ghosaka says this is because the fundamental dhyānas also serve as antidotes for abandoning desire.

The thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) is excluded, because it is exclusively the fruit of the *anāgamya* stage and thus lacks the capacity to cultivate the antidote for abandoning those [fetters].
The intermediate dhyānas are as described for the fundamental [dhyānas].

Is it not the case that when one enters the vision of the truths (satyadarśana) by relying on a fundamental dhyāna, one also cultivates the future path of antidotes based on the *anāgamya* stage to abandon the afflictions of the desire realm? Since one obtains the antidote for abandonment, one should also realize the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) from those factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by vision; why then is it said that the fundamental [dhyānas] obtain only five fruits?

This criticism is not valid; for at that time, the cultivation of the antidote for abandonment based on the *anāgamya* stage is exclusively the antidote for abandonment in the form and formless realms.

Since the path of the fundamental stages cannot serve as the antidote for abandonment in the desire realm, how could it cultivate the path that is the antidote for abandoning the desire realm while it is currently manifest?
Because the "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*) cultivation practiced by them serves as an antidote that counteracts only the higher realms, its fruits are only five.
Furthermore, how is it known that once another antidote has arisen, one can no longer cultivate further paths of antidote?

Because this is what our school teaches; that is to say, regarding one who has previously abandoned attachment to form (*rūpa-rāga*) through investigation and enters the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), it is stated thus concerning whether or not the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of form is attained during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Some say that since it is stated that when one is detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one also cultivates the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the future stages;
how then can it be said that "one has not already cultivated other remedies for others"?
This objection is invalid, as it does not constitute a valid proof.

When it is said that one cultivates dhyāna while abandoning the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one cultivates only the future antidote to the formless realm, not the antidote to the realm of form; how could this serve as proof?
This, rather, proves that others do not cultivate other antidotes.
Some offer this explanation:

"This proof is not established for both [the path of seeing and the path of cultivation], because the characteristics of what is cultivated differ between the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.

That is to say, when the path of seeing manifests in the fourth dhyāna, one cultivates only the future path of seeing of the six stages; it is not so for what is cultivated when the path of cultivation arises."

Furthermore, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), a single uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) simultaneously abandons [the afflictions] of the eight stages, whereas this is not the case for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Moreover, the aspects (*ākāra*) of the knowledge cultivated therein differ according to whether they pertain to the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) or heterogeneous (*visabhāga*) categories; therefore, that which is cultivated in the path of seeing is distinct from that cultivated in the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are instances where while one antidote is present, another antidote is cultivated; for example, when abandoning desire, one cultivates the various subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*), and when abandoning the realms of form and formlessness, one cultivates the dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin. Therefore, it stands to reason that the same principle should apply to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, the fundamental dhyānas are also able to counteract the desire realm, as the Blessed One said:

"The six bases of renunciation, having joy as their cause, lead to dwelling and enable one to relinquish [the lower states]; the six bases of renunciation have sorrow [as their cause]," and so forth, as explained at length.

This equanimity is free from verbal expression and detached from the defilement of desire; it is not accepted as a faculty of joy in the peripheral regions of the tenets. Consequently, it is established that the fundamental dhyānas can counteract the desire realm; therefore, there are eight pervasive knowledges (*parijñā*) as the fruits of the stages of the fundamental dhyānas.
In this regard, others offer the following critique:

"It is not the case that the power of the path of abandonment and counteraction, by not manifesting [at the time of attainment], can induce the arising of the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) such that it is called 'attaining full knowledge' (*parijñā-lābha*), as is the case with the fruits of the religious life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*)."

Just as when one attains the two fruits [of stream-entry and once-returning] via the mundane path, although one cultivates the future untainted antidotes for abandonment, these are not called the attainment of the fruits of śrāmaṇya;

likewise, when the fundamental dhyānas are manifested, even if one cultivates the future paths that serve as antidotes for abandoning the desire realm, one does not thereby induce the acquisition of disjunction (visamyoga-prāpti). Therefore, the eight types of pervasive knowledge (parijñā) cannot be attained [at that time].

This lacks profound reasoning, because it is admitted that when one abandons all defilements through the mundane path during the stage of an Ārya, one obtains two types of acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*): both the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the mundane (*laukika*).
Since the mundane and untainted cognitions (*jñāna*) do not function simultaneously, the power of the future untainted path is able to induce the arising of the untainted acquisition of disjunction.

It is not that the fruits of śrāmaṇya are not established as realizations; for the principles governing the establishment of cause and effect, the attainment of the untainted (anāsrava), and the acquisition of disjunction (visamyoga) each differ.

When it is said that at the time of attaining two fruits via the mundane path (laukikamārga), they are not called fruits of śrāmaṇya, this refers to the meaning that these are present [attainments] and not future fruits. Because the attainment of disjunction from obstacles is untainted, at that time an untainted attainment of disjunction necessarily arises.
This untainted attainment (*anāsrava-prāpti*) is also induced by future untainted states; how is this proven?

Furthermore, when the two fruits are attained through the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), it is accepted that what is obtained is called a fruit of śramaṇaship (*śrāmaṇya-phala*), because future untainted paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and so forth are also designated as fruits of śramaṇaship.

This means that when one attains the two fruits by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), because the obstacles to the future untainted paths of liberation (*anāsravavimuktimārga*) and so forth are severed, all [the fruits] arise manifest.
What, then, are these fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*)?
This refers to the fruits of the śramaṇa in the present and future.

That is to say, when the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) manifests, there is an untainted [path] that receives the name "present path. That [untainted path] is the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of this [mundane] path, and it is also the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) of the future path; for the associated causes (*samprayuktakahetu*) and co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) pertain to all three time periods, and thus it takes the fruit of human effort as its own fruit.
Since all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) transcend the three periods of time, they are called the fruits of śrāmaṇya; what reasoning could possibly obstruct this?
Consequently, the position that the fundamental dhyānas are the fruits of the eight thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) is thereby established as logical.
However, this is not actually established, because that proof is invalid.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that when the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) of the fourth dhyāna manifests, one cultivates only the future Path of Seeing of the six stages, whereas when the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) arises, that which is cultivated is different—this does not constitute a valid proof.
This means that although the stages being cultivated are indeed different, they both exclusively cultivate the remedies for the higher realms.
Even though there is some slight difference in the stages being cultivated, by what logic would this necessitate cultivating other remedies?

When the path of cultivation that abandons the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) arises, although one cultivates future paths based on the nine stages, one cannot, merely because the cultivated paths are distinct, cause those [future paths] to function as the cultivation of other antidotes; otherwise, they would have to cultivate the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).

Furthermore, for this very reason, although one simultaneously abandons [the afflictions] of the eight stages in a single moment during the path of seeing, it is specifically the antidotes to those eight stages that are cultivated and no others; regardless of how few or many are abandoned, one always cultivates their corresponding antidotes.

Furthermore, because there is a difference in the characteristics of cultivation between the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and meditation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) due to the distinction between homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and heterogeneous (*visabhāga*) cultivation, it is well established by reason that one does not cultivate future antidotes other than those belonging to the path of seeing; for that which is cultivated in the path of seeing is exclusively homogeneous.

For example, when the patience regarding the origin (*samudaya-kṣānti*) manifests, although one has previously attained the patiences and knowledges regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth, one cannot cultivate them at this stage because they are not the antidotes for what is to be abandoned by seeing the origin. However, the paths of other stages can be cultivated here, because the path of this stage serves as a common antidote to them.

Alternatively, although one cultivates immeasurable future merits during the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one cultivates patience (*kṣānti*) specifically during the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) and nothing else, and during the stage of Knowledge (*jñāna*) one can cultivate only knowledge. Since even patience and knowledge do not mutually cultivate one another, how much less could the cultivation of other future remedial paths (*pratipakṣamārga*) be established as possible?
Furthermore, within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is certainly not the case that when one antidote is manifesting, there is the sense of cultivating another antidote.

Although various subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*) are cultivated at the time of abandoning desire, and the dharma-knowledges of suffering and origin are cultivated at the time of abandoning the realms of form and formlessness, these are not "antidotes of abandonment" (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*); they are cultivated because they are not [direct] antidotes.
For what reason is this cultivated?
It is because it is nourished by its causes; this shall be explained in detail within the section on the analysis of knowledge (*jñāna-vibhaṅga*).

Furthermore, there is no fault in the *Sūtra on Mental Application* (*manopavicāra*) cited there, for it speaks with reference to the observation within the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) that sorrow and joy serve as mutual antidotes.

Alternatively, for a practitioner who first perceives that sorrow based on attachment (*gardhāśrita-śoka*) can cause affliction, they subsequently infer by analogy that sorrow based on renunciation (*naiṣkramyāśrita-śoka*)—being of the same nature as the former—is likewise afflictive. Thereupon, they take delight in the sublime joy (*prīti*) manifesting in the First Dhyāna; because of this, they diligently cultivate the path of antidotes to abandon sorrow. Thus it is said that through joy one is able to relinquish sorrow.

Alternatively, immediately following the antidote that abandons the basis of renunciation through sorrow, the sublime joy of the first dhyāna may manifest; this is held within the mind and is thus cryptically said to be "present.
The basis of renunciation through sorrow and joy are closely related as mutual antidotes, intended to console those afflicted by the sorrow of renunciation so that they may find peace.

In no way whatsoever can the fundamental dhyānas serve as the antidote for abandoning [the afflictions] of the desire realm; for who would discard pleasant practice to rely on arduous exertion in order to realize the three fruits of śrāmaṇya?
Based on this reasoning, the Vaibhāṣika masters state that the fruits of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) resulting from the fundamental dhyānas are only five.
I am capable of providing a more extensive determination of this matter here, but fearing it would stray too far from the primary subject, I shall desist for now.

Regarding the distinction from the formless realms (*ārūpya-bhūmi*) as fruits: in the formless borderlands (*ārūpyāntara-bhūmi*), there is only one fruit; that is, by relying on the path of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one attains the fruit of the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā-kṣaya*).

The fruit of abandonment attained when a noble one, relying on the mundane path, becomes free from all defilements is also called "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*), because they have attained the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*).

Furthermore, the first three fundamental fruits are also only one; that is, by relying on the first three fundamental dhyānas of the formless realm, one attains the single fruit of the complete knowledge of the exhaustion of all [defilements].
Thus, by this, the distinctions regarding the number and variety of the fruits of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) obtained through the dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*) have been explained.

As for the distinction between their fruits and those of the mundane and noble paths: the fruits of the mundane path are two; that is, by the power of the mundane path, one can only obtain the fruits of thorough knowledge consisting in the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) and the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*).
There are nine fruits of the noble path, meaning that by the power of the noble path, one is able to transcend even the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Among these nine, it should be understood that two are common fruits,
while seven are uncommon fruits, as they are fruits exclusive to the noble ones (*ārya*).

Regarding the distinctions in the fruits of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*): the fruit of the knowledge of phenomena consists of three [results], because the power of the knowledge of phenomena is able to abandon what is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the three realms.
The fruit of the subsequent knowledge consists of two [results], because the power of the subsequent knowledge abandons what is to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms.

Regarding the distinctions between the results of the Dharma-knowledge category (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*) and the Subsequent-knowledge category (*anvayajñāna-pakṣa*): the results of the Dharma-knowledge category are six, namely the six results obtained by the aforementioned Dharma-knowledges and Dharma-patience (*dharmanirvedha*).
The results of the Subsequent-knowledge category are five, namely the five results obtained by the aforementioned Subsequent-knowledges and Subsequent-patience (*anvayanirvedha*).
The term "category" (*pakṣa*) here comprehensively includes both knowledge (*jñāna*) and receptivity (*kṣānti*).

Among the six categories of the Dharma, four are uncommon fruits: three belong to the receptivity to the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), and one belongs to the knowledge of the Dharma (*dharmajñāna*). Two are common fruits; that is, the final two pairs belong to both the two kinds of knowledge: the knowledge of the Dharma and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

Among the five categories of fruits, three uncommon fruits belong to the *anvaya-kṣānti*s (subsequent patiences), while two are common fruits—namely, the final two; their meaning has been explained as previously stated.
For what reason are the abandonments (*prahāṇa*) obtained through each individual path not each established individually as a single "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*)?
Because complete knowledge (*parijñā*) is spoken of at the time of permanent abandonment.
As it is said in a sutra:
"I shall now proclaim to you complete knowledge," and so forth, in detail. In this context, what is designated as "complete knowledge"?
This refers to the permanent abandonment of greed, the permanent abandonment of hatred, and the permanent abandonment of delusion, as explained at length.
The term "permanent abandonment" indicates the cessation that has been attained; only when there is no longer any residual bondage can it be termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
What is meant by "abandonment accompanied by residual bondage"?
What is meant by "abandonment without residual bondage"?
When abandonment is accomplished through three or four conditions, it is called "without residual bondage."

It is not called "possession" (prāpti) when it is incomplete. This means that in some cases, although a disjunction (*visamyoga*) has been attained through the severance [of defilements], because other acquisitions (*prāpti*) are lacking, it is possible for it to be abandoned again forever.

Alternatively, even if other acquisitions have arisen for a certain severance, they have not yet eliminated the firm foundation of saṃsāra; for although the defilements of the eight stages have been repeatedly abandoned, one has not yet eliminated their root, and thus falls back into the prison of the miserable destinies.

Furthermore, there may be an abandonment in which, although that [specific defilement] has been eliminated, other afflictive fetters have not yet been removed; thus, the sense of "permanent abandonment" is not yet perfected.

Alternatively, there may be an abandonment in which the remaining fetters have also been removed, yet one is still unable to transcend the realm to which they belong; because similar types of delusions have not been abandoned without remainder, the sense of "permanent abandonment" is likewise not yet perfected.
Such abandonments are termed "possessing residual bondage"; therefore, universal knowledge (*parijñā*) is not established for them.
Only within nine stages, where the three or four conditions are complete and abandonment is free from residual bondage, can universal knowledge be established.
What is meant by "possessing the conditions"?
The verse says:
One attains the acquisition of the abandonment of outflows, And the deficiency of the Peak of Existence.
"Because they extinguish both causes and transcend a realm, nine types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) are established.
The treatise says:

The abandonment of dharmas severed by insight (*darśana-heya*) is established as thorough knowledge when three conditions are fulfilled; the abandonment of dharmas severed by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is established as thorough knowledge only when four conditions are fulfilled.

Regarding the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and the abandonment of phenomena (*dharma-heya*), these possess three conditions: namely, the attainment of the untainted dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*), the deficiency of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and the extinction of the two causes.

In this context, although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may also be said to "extinguish the two causes" when they abandon the defilements of the eight stages, their abandonment does not constitute full knowledge (*parijñā*), because they lack the other two conditions.

Regarding the abandonments of the second and third moments within the stage of seeing the noble truths, although there exists an untainted acquisition of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*), universal knowledge (*parijñā*) is not yet established because the other two conditions are lacking.

In the fourth and fifth moments, although the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) has likewise been abandoned, the "universal knowledge" (*parijñā*) is not established because the dual causes have not yet been extinguished, as the causes to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*) remain unextinguished.

At the stage of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) during the accumulation [of the path], the abandonment of the two categories of afflictions pertaining to the desire realm is termed "universal knowledge" (*parijñā*) because it possesses three conditions.

In the subsequent five moments at the stage of the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the abandonment likewise possesses three conditions; therefore, all are termed "universal knowledge."
Regarding the abandonment of dharmas through cultivation, that which possesses four conditions consists of the three conditions mentioned above, with the fourth being the "transcending of the realm.
This means that when a noble one has not yet transcended a particular stage within the various realms, the abandonment attained therein possesses only two conditions.
If one has already transcended the stage but not yet transcended the realm, the abandonment attained therein still lacks one condition.
Only when transcending the realm are all four conditions fulfilled; accordingly, that abandonment is designated as "universal knowledge" (parijñā).
Should it not be that there are five conditions—namely, addition, separation, and the severance of both fetters?
Others say that since these are already included within the conditions of "extinguishing both causes" and "transcending the realm," they are not mentioned separately.
If that is so, one should likewise not establish "transcending the realm" as a condition, because transcending the realm also constitutes the cessation of both causes.

Although the dual causes and the dual fetters both rely upon a single object, their meanings differ: that which causes [the defilements] of the five categories to arise is called the "cause," while that which is able to bind within those very categories is called the "fetter."

Furthermore, when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, although these two categories lack the power to cause each other to arise directly, they do possess the nature of being indirect causes for one another. Consequently, while the sense of being bound by the defilements abandoned through the vision of origin remains as before, the sense of being bound by the defilements abandoned through the vision of suffering is entirely absent; therefore, the cessation of both causes does not itself constitute the dissociation from both fetters.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) is identical to "bondage" (*bandhana*), because afflictions (*kleśa*) that take uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) do not bind other aggregates.
For this reason, our own school explains both [aspects].
That they are not mentioned here can simply be stated as follows:
It is said that this and that are established by themselves, and it cannot be said that they are not distinct.

Because the meaning of "entity" (*tattva*) is broad, the two causes are spoken of together for now; although the two causes are extinguished in all stages of transcending the realms (*dhātu*), the time of extinguishing the two causes does not coincide with all instances of transcending the realms. Therefore, the condition of transcending the realms is established separately from the extinction of the two causes, because the universal knowledge (*parijñā*) has not yet been established when the two causes of the three stages are extinguished.
Who accomplishes how many types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)?
The verse says:
Those abiding in the stage of seeing the truths have none; Or they accomplish from one up to five.
The trainees accomplish six, one, or two; those beyond training accomplish only one.
The commentary states:
Although an ordinary person may be able to become free from defilement up to the eighth stage, they do not accomplish full knowledge (*parijñā*).

Among those in the noble stages who enter the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) based on the *anāgamya* concentration, there is no full knowledge (*parijñā*) from the beginning up through the stage of the *dharmakṣānti* regarding origination (*samudaya-dharmakṣānti*). Upon reaching the stage of the *dharmajñāna* regarding origination and the *anvayakṣānti* regarding origination, one achieves only one. Upon reaching the *anvayajñāna* regarding origination and the *dharmakṣānti* regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharmakṣānti*), one achieves two. Upon reaching the *dharmajñāna* regarding cessation and the *anvayakṣānti* regarding cessation, one achieves three. Upon reaching the *anvayajñāna* regarding cessation and the *dharmakṣānti* regarding the path (*mārga-dharmakṣānti*), one achieves four. Upon reaching the *dharmajñāna* regarding the path and the *anvayakṣānti* regarding the path, one achieves five.

For one who enters the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) by relying on the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*), there is likewise no thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) up until the stage of the patience regarding the subsequent cognition of origin (*samudayānvayakṣānti*); for subsequent stages, one should analyze accordingly as the principle dictates.

For one abiding in the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) who has not yet abandoned desire, from the initial stage of the subsequent cognition of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) until they have not yet attained complete detachment from the defilements of the desire realm or have even regressed from such detachment, they possess six [thorough knowledges].

Regarding those who have completely abandoned desire: starting from the ninth path of liberation of the abandonment of desire up to the final uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of abandoning the form realm, and for those who previously abandoned desire, from the knowledge of the category of the path (*mārga-jñāna-anvaya-jñāna*) until before the arising of the path of the exhaustion of the form realm, they possess only one thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), namely, the "exhaustion of the lower fetters" (*avarabhāgīya-kṣaya*).

Falling away from the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya*) and from the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) due to the arising of a fetter of the form realm is also exactly as described before.

For one who still possesses craving for the form realm, there is the exhaustion of lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-kṣaya*) upon the permanent exhaustion of craving for the form realm; for one who has previously detached from the form realm, there are two—namely, the exhaustion of lower-tier fetters and the exhaustion of craving for the form realm—from the moment the path that exhausts craving for the form realm arises until the point before they have completely detached from craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).

When one falls from the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) and gives rise to the fetters of the formless realm (ārūpya), two thorough knowledges (parijñā) are established; their names are as previously explained.
While abiding in the state of no-more-learning, one accomplishes only one, namely, the thorough knowledge of the permanent exhaustion of all fetters (sarvasaṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā).

If, at the time of entering the path of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the fundamental dhyāna (*mūla-dhyāna*), one also attains the designation "thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters" (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa-parijñā*) for all those abandonments [attained therein], how can you maintain that the fruit of the fundamental dhyāna possesses only five thorough knowledges?
Since the acquisition of the abandonment of those factors to be abandoned by insight in the realms of form and formlessness is designated as "universal knowledge," there is no fault.
For what reason is this alone also given that name?
Because the designation is established for this abandonment in the case of one who attains the fruit of non-returner through gradual stages.

Furthermore, those lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) which were previously abandoned by the mundane path are now rendered never-to-arise through the power of the noble path; therefore, that abandonment attained is metaphorically designated as this fruit. However, at present, one does not actually attain the "complete knowledge of abandonment" (*parijñā*) regarding desire.
Therefore, in this context, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That is to say: if one is about to attain abandonment (*prahāṇa*), is one also about to attain full knowledge (*parijñā*)?

There may be cases where one is about to attain abandonment but not about to attain full knowledge; namely, in various stages where one is about to attain what is to be abandoned, yet has not yet established full knowledge regarding that abandonment.

Alternatively, there may be cases where one is about to attain thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) but not about to attain abandonment (*prahāṇa*). This refers to one who has not yet abandoned desire and enters the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*): at the precise moment when the receptivity to the truth of origin (*samudayadharmanirvedhabhāgīya*) is ceasing, the abandonment of those dharmas of the desire realm to be eliminated by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) is about to attain thorough knowledge because all conditions are complete; however, it is not about to attain abandonment, because that [abandonment] has already been attained previously.

During the stage of the correct cessation of the "patience regarding the category of origin" (*samudaya-anvaya-kṣānti*), the dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering in the two realms are severed. For those who have previously abandoned desire and enter the vision of the truths based on the fundamental dhyānas, during the stage of the correct cessation of the latter three "patiences regarding the categories," the dharmas abandoned through the vision of the truths in the form and formless realms that were previously severed are likewise severed, as appropriate to each case.

Regarding the abandonment of those dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation that one wishes to see: at no stage is this an instance of "about to obtain abandonment," because it has already been obtained previously;
nor is it an instance of "about to obtain full knowledge" (*parijñā*), because this [abandonment] is not the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) for them.

If one enters the vision of the truths (satyadarśana) by relying on the threshold concentration (anāgamya), then during the stage when the three types of patience regarding phenomena and their categories (dharmajñānakṣānti and anvayajñānakṣānti) are in the process of ceasing, the previously abandoned defilements of the desire, form, and formless realms that are to be abandoned through vision are relinquished, as appropriate.

In the state of the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), while one is in the process of abandoning the defilements of the desire realm, there occurs the abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned through seeing in the three realms and the eight categories of dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.

In the state where the ninth uninterrupted path of the fourth dhyāna is currently ceasing, there is the abandonment of the nine grades of the first three stages and the eight grades of the fourth stage;
for one who has previously abandoned form, this constitutes the abandonment of the dharmas to be eliminated through cultivation across the four stages.
During the stage when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is in the process of ceasing, all the factors abandoned in preceding stages are abandoned.

Alternatively, one is about to attain abandonment and is also about to attain full knowledge (*parijñā*); that is to say, within these various stages, regarding the abandonment that is about to be attained, one is also about to establish full knowledge with respect to that abandonment.

These terms for the various stages indicate the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), signifying that one is about to attain the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the abandonment of the factors to be eliminated by each respective stage.

For example, when one who has not yet abandoned desire enters the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), at the precise moment the "patience regarding the origin of phenomena" (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*) is ceasing, the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of the origin are abandoned.

During the stage of the immediate cessation of the *dharmajñānakṣānti* regarding origination (*samudaya*), the factors to be abandoned through the vision of origination within the two realms are abandoned.

In this manner, it continues until, during the stage of the immediate cessation of the *mārgajñānakṣānti* regarding the path (*mārga*), the factors to be abandoned through the vision of the path within the two realms are abandoned.
Those who have previously abandoned defilement and enter the path of seeing should be considered accordingly.

Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), when one is free from the defilements of the desire realm, the fourth dhyāna, and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the dharmas to be abandoned by the ninth uninterrupted path (*anantaryamārga*) are severed.
Or there may be that which is about to be abandoned but not about to be fully known; this refers to cases other than those characteristics previously described.
For what reason are all the abandonments collectively established as a single full knowledge (*parijñā*) for both the Non-returner and the Arhat fruits?
The verse says:
Because of transcending realms and attaining fruits, there are two locations for the full comprehension of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
The commentary says:

Because two conditions are fulfilled, the abandonment that has been attained is collectively established as one "thorough knowledge" (parijñā): first, the transcendence of a realm; second, the attainment of a fruit.
The term "collectively" (saṃgraha) means the sense of being unified.
If, regarding the formless realm, one attains the fruit of stream-entry through partial separation from defilement, one attains arhatship through complete separation from defilement.
If, regarding the desire realm, one attains the fruit of once-returning through partial separation from defilement, one attains the fruit of non-returning through complete separation from defilement.
If one neither partially nor completely detaches from the form realm (rūpadhātu), one cannot attain the fruit;
it is only in two cases that both conditions are fully met, namely, at the time of attaining the fruit, which is simultaneously the transcendence of that realm.

For the Arhat and the Anāgāmin, the abandonments attained through cultivation are established as a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), because at that time a single-flavored attainment (*ekarasalābha*) arises in its totality.

At the time of the other two fruits [the Srotaāpanna and Sakṛdāgāmin], although the attainment is of a single flavor, one has not yet transcended the realm; and although one has transcended the realm at the time when desire for the form realm is exhausted, there is no single-flavored attainment. Therefore, the thorough knowledge is not accumulated at those stages, for it is only when both conditions are met that it is accumulated in its entirety.
Who abandons and who attains how many kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)?
The verse says:
One abandons one, two, five, or six; The attainment is likewise, except for five.
The treatise states:

Regarding the "abandonment of one," this refers to falling away from the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), or from the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya*), or from complete detachment from desire (*vairāgya*).

Regarding the "abandonment of two," this refers to those non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who fall away from the exhaustion of craving for the form realm due to the arising of the fetters of desire (*kāma-saṃyojana*), as well as at the moment they attain arhatship; and it refers to those who previously attained detachment from desire by relying on the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) and entered the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), specifically at the time of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*).
Regarding the statement "abandoning five," the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) explains:
"This refers to the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) when one has previously abandoned desire.

This should instead refer to the time of the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*), because at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path, those [five] have already been abandoned.
The statement regarding "attaining and abandoning" is based on what is about to be explained.

Furthermore, one should specify that this refers to those who enter the vision of the truths (darśana-mārga) by relying on the *anāgamya* concentration; for if one enters the vision of the truths by relying on the fundamental (*maula*) dhyānas, they do not obtain the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) regarding the abandonment of the desire realm. Consequently, they would not obtain the three types of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) concerning the abandonment of the factors abandoned through vision in the desire realm. Since it was not previously obtained, it cannot be said that it is "abandoned" now.
Regarding the statement "abandoning six," this refers to when noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire attain the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Regarding "attaining likewise," this means that some attain one, some attain two, and some attain six.

To say "one is acquired" refers to the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*), specifically within the nine stages beginning with the patience of the collection of categories (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), as well as when one falls back from the formless realm (*ārūpya*) due to the arising of fetters related to the form realm (*rūpa-saṃyojana*).
To say "two are acquired" refers to the time when one falls back from the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) due to the arising of various fetters belonging to the formless realm.
Regarding the statement "attaining six," this refers to the case of a non-returner (anāgāmin) who falls away.
There is no case of attaining five, as it is logically impossible.

This means that one who has previously abandoned desire by relying on the *anāgamya* concentration and enters the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) will, at the moment of the *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*, relinquish the five universal knowledges (*parijñā*) and attain the fruit of non-returning.

If one were to fall away from this fruit, one could obtain five types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*); since such a falling away does not exist here, there is no possibility of obtaining five. One might object:

"When one attains a superior fruit through spiritual progress (*viśeṣagamana*), does one not again give rise to a superior acquisition (*adhigama*) regarding the various unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*)? If it can be called 'acquisition' in that case, why should thorough knowledge not be relinquished [in this case]?"

Since they are actually abandoned and yet always remain accomplished [as latent dispositions], there is no fault in saying that within the context of the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*), when a new name is acquired, the original name is lost;
this is termed "abandonment" (*tyāga*). Furthermore, there is no error in this.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle 56;
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Fascicle 57.
