However, because one follows the teacher’s exposition of names, phrases, and syllables, a decisive wisdom arises regarding the distinctions of meaning; this wisdom is called "wisdom accomplished through hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
It is said to take only names as its object in terms of the preparatory means for entry, yet once the wisdom of hearing has been perfected, it functions to know the specific meanings.

Furthermore, by applying diligent effort and engaging in internal investigation and discernment—desiring that such discernment be free from error—one again recollects the teacher’s instructions regarding the sets of names, phrases, and syllables; through this, at a later time, a definitive wisdom arises concerning the distinctions among meanings, which is called "wisdom accomplished through reflection."

At this stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), because the power of reflecting upon the meaning induces mindfulness of names, it is said to take both [name and object] as its domain. Once reflection and wisdom have been perfected and meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) manifests, one realizes the distinctions among meanings without depending on names; this definitive wisdom is called "that produced by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-maya*).

The various practitioners of yoga establish an analogy for this: just as when a painter practices painting, he first respectfully receives a model from his teacher; he then scrutinizes its features and studies by copying it, practicing repeatedly until he can even scrape away the original.
Thereafter, one should turn away from the original count and repeatedly contemplate and practice the count, so that what has been practiced is free from error.

Furthermore, one should compare it with the model upon which one is copying, ensuring that one’s own work is equal to or superior to the model; otherwise, there would be no principle for progress in one's practice.
Consequently, at a later time, his practice becomes increasingly superior; without exertion, he contemplates the fundamental [nature] and accomplishes all according to his wish.
One should know that the cultivation of the three types of wisdom is likewise so.
The Vaibhāṣika masters further establish a separate analogy: it is like a certain class of people who attempt to float in deep, swift water; those who have never practiced cannot leave the shore.

Furthermore, when one who has previously studied but not yet mastered [the teachings] floats, they can temporarily relinquish their support and move away from it a short distance; fearing exhaustion or drowning, they may return again toward the shore.

Conversely, one who firmly grasps a support in which they have previously trained well can do so without fatigue or weariness, disregarding both the shore and the support; even after passing through extremely deep, perilous, and turbulent waters, they can avoid sinking and cross over freely by floating. In this way, one should understand the distinctions between the three types of wisdom.

The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) asserts that this [wisdom] consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*) is not established, arguing that since it takes both names (*nāman*) and meanings (*artha*) as its objects, it should respectively be considered wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī*) and wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*).

Now, upon careful examination, there is no fault in the three distinct characteristics: the superior wisdom produced by a practitioner based on hearing the authoritative teachings is called wisdom consisting of hearing; the superior wisdom produced based on correct reasoning through reflection is called wisdom consisting of reflection; and the superior wisdom produced based on the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of cultivation is called wisdom consisting of cultivation.

He speaks thus because he has not yet grasped the intent of the *Vibhāṣā*; however, when the *Vibhāṣā* distinguishes between the three characteristics, its meaning is not as [he claims]. That is to say:

if there is wisdom (*prajñā*) which, at the time of application (*prayoga*), draws forth an understanding of the meaning (*artha*) by the power of taking the name (*nāman*) as its object, this wisdom so drawn forth is called "consisting of what is heard" (*śrutamaya*).

If, at the time of application, one draws forth mindfulness (*smṛti*)—which is termed "understanding"—by the power of reflecting on the meaning, and from this subsequently produces a definitive wisdom, it is called "consisting of what is reflected upon" (*cintāmaya*).
If one does not rely on names but contemplates only the meaning, the wisdom that arises from internal realization is called "that produced by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).

As they maintain in their system when distinguishing these three types of wisdom, although they are all determinate and lack difference in their essential characteristics, there are distinctions among their three aspects due to the differing causes—namely, the authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), correct reasoning (*yukti*), and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Thus, in our school, we explain the meaning of the objects (*ālambana*) when these three types of wisdom are accomplished: although their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not distinct, they are designated as "object-condition" (*ālambanapratyaya*), "simultaneous object" (*sahālambana*), and "object-meaning" (*ālambanārtha*) respectively; because their preparatory applications (*prayoga*) differ, the three aspects are distinct.

Furthermore, that which is accomplished through reflection (*cintāmayī*) consists of reflecting upon correct principles; the definitive wisdom (*niścaya-jñāna*) produced thereby is its preparatory application (*prayoga*). Its power is firm and unerring.

Repeatedly recollecting the teacher’s instructions regarding the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*) constitutes the auxiliary companions to this preparatory application of reflection. While it is said to generally take both names and meanings as its objects in terms of its preparatory stage, this is not necessarily the case at the stage of full accomplishment.

Therefore, although there is no difference in the objects or aspects at the stage when the three types of decisive wisdom arise, because there are differences in their preparatory stages (*prayoga*), the Vaibhāṣikas distinguish them based on these differences.

This being so, it is not the case that the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is unestablished. Those who dwell in seclusion say that at the stage when the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is present, the light of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) has not yet pervaded the basis (*āśraya*), nor does it abide firmly.
At the stage of practicing the wisdom born of reflection, the light of pliancy has not yet pervaded the basis, though it attains a slight degree of firm abiding.

At the stage of practicing the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), because the superior primary elements (*mahābhūta*) induced by meditative concentration pervade the entire body, there arises a superior light of pliancy that fills the body, continuing in firm abiding. Consequently, the practitioner’s basis becomes extremely light, and their countenance is exceptionally radiant and distinct from its usual state.
The distinctions between the characteristics of these three types of wisdom are as follows.
Although other states that are not yet fixed also possess luminosity, they are not all subsumed under the wisdoms of hearing and reflection.
In this context, the two wisdoms are termed "accomplished" (*bhāvanā-maya*) in the sense that they are produced by the power of hearing and reflection.

Regarding the third type, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), which is termed "that which is accomplished" (*niṣpanna*): this means that cultivation itself constitutes its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is like saying a vessel is made of life, food, or jewels.
For those who wish to apply themselves diligently to cultivation, how can they purify the vessel of the body so that cultivation may be swiftly accomplished?
The verse says:
Both body and mind are secluded; there is no insufficiency or great desire regarding what has been obtained or not yet obtained; to seek much is what he does not possess.
The three [roots] counteract the discordant realms; they are untainted and have non-attachment as their nature.
The four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are likewise; the first three consist solely of contentment.
The first three concern the requisites of life, while the last concerns activity; they serve to counteract the arising of the four types of craving.
Because of the desire for "mine," "self," and "my affairs," [these] are temporarily stilled and permanently eliminated.
The commentary states:
The purification of the body-vessel is briefly due to three causes.
What are the three causes?
First, physical and mental seclusion; second, contentment and fewness of desires; third, abiding in the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
That is to say, if one wishes for cultivation to be swiftly accomplished, one must first diligently purify the vessel of the body and mind.
If one wishes to bring the vessel of the body to purity, one must first cultivate physical and mental seclusion.
Physical seclusion means staying far from evil companions;
mental seclusion means remaining free from unwholesome thoughts.
Because body and mind are freed from evil associates and discursive thoughts, the physical vessel becomes pure and the mind easily attains concentration.
As for how these two may be easily accomplished, it is through contentment with clothing and other necessities, as well as having few desires.
To speak of contentment means there is no lack of contentment.
To have few desires means there is no great desire.

Those who seek many requisites for life will associate with evil companions by day and give rise to evil discursive thoughts by night; consequently, there is no possibility for their minds to attain concentration.
What are the two distinctions regarding that which is absent?

They are as follows: when one has already obtained excellent and abundant clothing and so forth, yet does not wish for these to be twice as excellent and twice as abundant—because of the further longing and desire for what is more equal or superior within those very things—it is called *asamtuṣṭi* (lack of contentment).
If one seeks to obtain fine and abundant clothing and other such things when they have not yet been acquired, it is called "great desire" (*mahēcchā*).
The meaning here is that all existing possessions are sufficient to remedy suffering; if one seeks more than this, one transgresses the category of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-pakṣa*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"To whatever extent one attains physical ease and comfort, it makes the mind easy to concentrate and enables one to teach the Dharma.
Therefore, for those who seek objects that remedy suffering, this serves as an aid to the Path and is not a fault.
Therefore, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) says:
One should state it thus: to feel regret and lack of joy regarding what has already been obtained—whether it be of poor quality or insufficient—is called "lack of contentment" (*asamtuṣṭi*).
To seek out superior quality or greater quantity regarding things not yet obtained, such as clothing and so forth, is called "great desire" (*mahecchatā*).
This is not consistent with correct reasoning. Why is this so?

If one has already obtained an object that can alleviate suffering, yet remains anxious and unhappy because it has not yet been mastered; or if one has not yet obtained such an object at all and is longing for one that could alleviate suffering—such a state does not obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*). What fault, then, is there in this?
Furthermore, regarding the definition of non-contentment (*asantuṣṭi*) as explained in the Abhidharma, one might object:
"Does not further seeking also take as its object that which has not yet been obtained? If so, the distinction between these two [non-contentment and lack of excellence] would be untenable.

This is not logically sound. For the Abhidharmikas do not say that non-contentment consists in desiring other excellent and abundant garments or the like that have not yet been obtained while one already possesses excellent and abundant garments; how then can it be said that the distinction between the two is unestablished?
If that is so, what is the intended meaning of what was said?

It means that when one has already obtained sufficient clothing and other requisites that are capable of counteracting suffering and are excellent and abundant, yet one further manifests a desire for those very things to be equal or superior, and gives rise to longing for them—regretting not having previously obtained such clothing and other items that are twice as excellent and twice as abundant—this is called "lack of contentment" (*asamtuṣṭi*).

When one has already obtained that which is sufficient to counteract suffering, further excessive longing can indeed obstruct meditative concentration; however, when one has not yet obtained that which is sufficient to counteract suffering, further excessive longing does not obstruct concentration. Therefore, there is no error in what the Abhidharmikas have stated.
Alternatively, although there is no fault in further seeking even when one is not content, this differs from "great desire" (*mahēcchā*).

This means that while one already possesses all the requisites for life without deficiency, one still seeks more; because such seeking is produced by being led away from the lack of contentment with what has already been obtained, the effect receives the name of its cause and is termed "lack of contentment."
Regarding those means of subsistence not yet obtained, to have no regard for one's own condition and to seek them in excessive measure—such seeking is called "great desire.
Such are the characteristics of these two distinctions.
Contentment and fewness of desires are able to counteract these [faults]; therefore, one should know that their characteristics are distinct from those [faults] as they are their opposites.
That is to say, contentment is the characteristic that counteracts lack of contentment; it is the opposite of the characteristic of lack of contentment.
That which can counteract great desire and is diametrically opposed to it is the characteristic of fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*).
That which, regarding things already obtained that serve as antidotes to suffering, does not further long for more, is called contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*).
Not seeking in excess for objects that could remedy suffering when they have not yet been obtained is the meaning of having few desires (*alpecchatā*).
Contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and having few desires pertain to all three realms; furthermore, there are those that transcend the three realms and are subsumed under the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).

That is to say, contentment and fewness of desires associated with wholesome minds bound to the desire realm are themselves bound to the desire realm; the two types of untainted [contentment and fewness of desires] pertaining to the [upper] two realms should be explained by analogy with this.
What evidence is there to know that the two types of their opposites are exclusively bound to the desire realm?

In the form and formless realms, there are likewise those capable of counteracting [the opposites] through contentment and fewness of desires; for it is observed that when beings born in the desire realm arise from the form and formless realms and so forth, the two types of the countered states are distant from active manifestation, while the two types of the counteracting states increase in their active manifestation.

The specific characteristics of contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) have already been explained; their common characteristic is non-greed (*alobha*), because both are capable of counteracting greed.
The common characteristic of that which is to be countered is sensual greed (*kāmarāga*).

The noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) should be understood according to their antidotes; that is, they also pertain to all three realms, and as for the untainted ones, they consist of non-attachment (*alobha*).

Just as within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), although there is no object of enmity, the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adveṣa*) can still exist, so too, although clothing and such do not exist within the formless realm, the wholesome root of non-attachment can still exist. This is because, just as one does not crave the body there, one likewise does not crave the requisites of life.

The formless realm possesses all four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). Noble ones who experience sensual pleasures possess the underlying intention (*āśaya*) for the noble lineages, yet lack the actual application (*prayoga*); because they possess these various noble lineages, they are called "noble lineages."
Because the noble assembly is born from these four, they succeed one another in an uninterrupted succession; that the former serves as the seed for the latter is universally established in the world.

Since the *dharmakāya* of all the noble ones is produced by the power of contentment with clothing and so forth, this constitutes their noble lineage (*āryagotra*), and thus they receive the name "noble birth" (*āryajāti*).

Among the four [noble lineages], the first three consist solely of contentment; that is, one gives rise to contentment with whatever robes, food and drink, and bedding one obtains. These three forms of contentment are themselves the three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
The wholesome root of non-attachment has many varieties; among these, that which serves as the antidote to the greed for lack of contentment is called the first three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
The fourth noble lineage is the delight in abandonment and cultivation—namely, the cultivation of dissociation from fetters.

This refers to the joy of the noble path; it means having a deep longing and aspiration for that [joy]. It is called "delight in abandonment" (*prahāṇārāma*) because one delights in abandonment and cultivation.

Cultivation here signifies an aspiration for cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*); alternatively, it is called "delight in abandonment" because it is the cultivation of delight in abandonment.
"Cultivation" (bhāvanā) refers to the meaning of aspiring toward the path to cessation, because one cultivates the path for the sake of realizing the bliss of the cessation of afflictions.
Since this is able to counteract craving for existence and non-existence, it likewise has non-attachment as its essential nature.
Is it not the case that the fourth [root] is also able to counteract hatred and so forth, and thus should also have non-hatred (*adveṣa*) and so on as its intrinsic nature?

This is not incorrect; however, because the first three serve as its provisions, because those first three are exclusively of the nature of non-attachment (*alobha*), and because this one can also independently counteract attachment, it is described here in terms of its predominant function.
For what reason is contentment alone established as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*), and not fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*)?
This is because one who possesses few desires may still harbor longing for things such as robes;

that is to say, one whose disposition is inferior in aspiration does not dare to seek much regarding objects not yet obtained, yet even if they have already obtained much, their seeking may continue without ceasing.
One who sees contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) does not seek further even when they have obtained little, let alone when they have obtained much;
therefore, contentment alone is established as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).

Alternatively, it is to prevent the desire of those who practice asceticism that "fewness of desires" (*alpecchatā*) is not taught as a noble lineage; for such non-Buddhists do not possess superior desire, as their mental continuum is constantly permeated by inferior desire.

To feel a heart of joy according to what one has obtained, without further seeking with longing, is called "contentment" (*saṃtuṣṭi*). Among the various forms of pleasure, the abandonment of the pleasure of desire (*kāmasukha*) is the most supreme.

Sentient beings in the desire realm mostly delight in the pleasure of desire; this pleasure of desire contradicts the mind of renunciation, renders the mind dull and obscured regarding the separation from afflictions, and can obstruct the manifestation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Its fault is the deepest. Contentment can remedy this; therefore, contentment alone is established as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).

One does not experience joy in the mind when giving rise to a longing for robes and other requisites that one has not yet obtained, much less for those already possessed; therefore, because limited desire (*alpecchatā*) is not the most excellent among the remedies for the craving for pleasure, it is not established as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).
How can contentment arising from clothing and other such things be said to be untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Who says that such contentment is untainted?
If that were so, how could it be that all the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are universally categorized as untainted?

The noble path that arises through their predominance is named after them because it is induced by them; therefore, it is said that the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) all pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
It is not stated, however, that all contentment regarding robes and so forth pertains to the untainted.
The [terms] "having few desires" (*alpeccha*) and "without outflows" (*anāsrava*) should be explained according to this principle.
That is to say, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) that arises through their predominance is named after them because it is induced by them.
Since the Noble Path does not arise from conditions such as robes and other objects, for what reason did the Blessed One teach the four noble lineages (*catvāry āryavaṃśāni*)?

Because his disciples have abandoned worldly requisites and worldly occupations to go forth from the household life under the Buddha, he demonstrates to them that within the Buddha’s noble Dharma and Vinaya, there exist requisites and occupations capable of assisting the path.

This means that having developed revulsion for the household life of birth and death, one leaves home to seek liberation; possessing no worldly requisites, one feels profound contentment with whatever clothing and other items are obtained; and engaging in whatever activities are necessary, one takes deep delight in the abandonment [of afflictions] and the cultivation [of the path], for apart from this, there is nothing else capable of realizing *nirvāṇa*.
For what reason are there exactly four, neither more nor less?
Because up to this point, the causes for the arising of the noble ones are fully satisfied.
That is to say, there are briefly two kinds of causes for the arising of the noble ones:
First, the abandonment of faults; second, the cultivation of virtues.
These correspond respectively to the first three and the fourth [noble lineage]. Therefore, there are exactly four, neither more nor less.
Alternatively, all wholesome qualities produced through hearing, reflection, and meditation are noble lineages, for they are the basis for liberation.
Nevertheless, in order to counteract the arising of the four types of craving, the Blessed One has briefly explained these four.
Since the Sūtra states that there are four arisings of craving, the Sūtra says:

"Bhikṣus, listen attentively! Craving arises when it should arise, abides when it should abide, and is grasped when it should be grasped, due to clothing; likewise, it is said to be so with respect to food and drink, bedding and seats, and both existence and non-existence."
To counteract these four, only the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are taught.
Why is contentment with medicine not considered a noble lineage?
It is not so designated because craving arises toward it.

The Noble Lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are established for the purpose of treating the arising of craving; since the Sūtra states that there are only four types of the arising of craving, the Noble Lineage is not established with respect to medicine.

Alternatively, it is because medicine is already subsumed within the first three: some medicines are included among clothing, some among food and drink, and some among bedding and seats; therefore, contentment with medicine is not established as a separate Noble Lineage.
Alternatively, if one were to argue that pride and other such faults are induced by [the requisites] therein, the Noble Lineages (āryavaṃśa) are established as their antidote;
however, since no fault of inducing pride and so forth arises from medicine, there is no contentment with medicine among the Noble Lineages.
Alternatively, if all people were to make use of them, then contentment with those could be established as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*);
however, this is not the case for venerable individuals such as Bakula and others, who never suffered from illness and thus had no need to consume medicine.

Alternatively, those things that should be used at all times can be established as noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) based on contentment with them, because medicine is not something to be used at all times.

Furthermore, medical treatises also speak of contentment with medicine, whereas the Vinaya specifically speaks of contentment with robes and so forth; this is because the noble lineages exist only within the internal Dharma.
Some say that although there is contentment with medicine, it is not established as a noble lineage (āryavaṃśa) because various medicines can be conducive to the holy life (brahmacarya).
That is to say, it is observed in the world that for one who delights in training in the precepts, contentment with medicine acts as an obstacle to the holy life.

Alternatively, the Buddha taught the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) because he wished to temporarily pacify and permanently eliminate the desire for things belonging to the self (mamakāra) and the desire for the self itself (ātmakāra). Specifically, he taught the first three noble lineages to temporarily pacify the desire for things belonging to the self, and he taught the fourth noble lineage to permanently eradicate both the desire for things belonging to the self and the desire for the self itself.
The Master of the Sūtra himself provides this explanation:
"The objects of the self" refers to clothing and so forth;
"the object of the self" refers to one's own body, and the craving directed toward it is called desire.

If one were to provide this interpretation, the meaning would not differ from what was stated previously; thus, it should not have been formulated as a separate passage in the verse, for although the phrasing differs from the previous statement regarding the remedies for the four types of craving, there is no difference in their meaning.
For this reason, our own school, the Vaibhāṣikas, provides another interpretation of this passage from a different perspective: the grasping at "mine" (*mamakāra*) is designated by the term "desire.

Thus, in order to temporarily pacify the grasping at "mine," the Blessed One taught the first three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), which consist of contentment with robes and so forth, as well as the noble path induced by that [contentment] as its predominant influence.

In order to permanently eliminate the grasping at a self and its activities, the Blessed One taught the fourth noble lineage; that is, the delight in abandonment and cultivation, as well as the noble path induced by their predominance, are all termed "noble lineages."

The intent of this section is to reveal that the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are taught in order to cause the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) to temporarily cease and to be permanently eliminated.

Thus, having already explained what should be practiced when approaching the vision of the truths, as well as the practice itself, [this section now addresses] how to swiftly accomplish the purification of the vessel of the body for the sake of cultivation.
Having thus accumulated the provisions for the noble path, by what gateway does one enter into formal cultivation?
The verse says:
The essential gateways for entering cultivation are two: the meditation on impurity and mindfulness of breathing.
For those in whom desire and discursive thought predominate, one should practice accordingly in sequence.

The commentary states: The modes of conduct among sentient beings are manifold; therefore, the gateways for entering cultivation are likewise diverse. Nevertheless, most enter by means of two gateways: first, the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); second, mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*). Thus, these two alone are called the essential gateways.
Do all sentient beings enter [the path] by means of both? No;

rather, they do so according to whether craving or discursive thought predominates. That is to say, those for whom craving predominates enter by relying on the first gate (the mindfulness of the body), while those for whom discursive thought predominates enter by relying on mindfulness of breathing. This is because, as with a single disease that cannot be cured by a single medicine, one must apply the appropriate remedy.

Regarding the teaching on the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as a proximate remedy, it is capable of curing the disease of greed, though it is not incapable of treating other afflictions; one should know that mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) which cures discursive thought (*vitarka*) is likewise so.

However, because mindfulness of breathing takes a subtle object without differentiation and because its objective support is tied to one's own continuum, it is not like the contemplation of impurity, which takes many external objects and thereby can suppress distracted discursive thoughts.

Having already explained in general that greed and discursive thought increase, one enters cultivation according to the sequence of the two aforementioned gates. Among these, one should first analyze the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
What are the characteristics of such a meditation?
The verse says:
To serve as a universal remedy for the four types of craving, one first contemplates a chain of bones;
expanding this to include the ocean and then contracting it again is called the stage of initial practice.
From the feet up to the midpoint of the head is called "having already cultivated maturity";
binding the mind between the eyebrows is called "transcending the stage of mental attention.
The Commentary says:

The cultivation of the contemplation of impurity is specifically for the purpose of counteracting desire; however, there are briefly four types of desire: first, desire for color; second, desire for shape; third, desire for exquisite touch; and fourth, desire for service and offerings.

To counteract the four types of craving, one relies on two kinds of discernment: first, contemplating internal corpses; second, contemplating external corpses. Those with sharp faculties initially rely on the former, while those with dull faculties initially rely on the latter.

This means that those of sharp faculties first observe their own internal body—from the skin as the boundary, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head—thoroughly and completely, causing the mind to feel revulsion.

For one who wishes to subdue and treat greed for visible form (*varṇa-rāga*), they should single-mindedly attend to the transformed visible forms within the internal parts of the body, such as pus, blood, fat, semen, saliva, nasal mucus, marrow, brain, feces, and urine; and they should also attend to the transformed visible forms upon the skin of the internal body produced by various diseases—yellow, white, blue, or black, like clouds or smoke, mottled, sallow, dark, dull, and impure. By means of this, the mind becomes intensely revulsed, and one is thus able to subdue and treat greed conditioned by visible form.
By knowing that this body is of such a nature—that it is the locus for unattractive visible forms—one becomes free from attachment toward all things.

To subdue and remedy craving for beautiful form, one should specifically observe the various internal limbs of the body as being composed of a collection, arrangement, and combination of thirty-six substances, such as hair and so forth; apart from these, there is no such thing as "hair" or "form."

Furthermore, by means of resolute conviction, one divides the limbs of the body into two or more parts and scatters them upon the ground; various birds and beasts then vie with one another to devour them. As the flesh and bones fall apart and the limbs become separated, this causes the mind to give rise to extreme revulsion, whereby one is able to subdue and treat the craving for form and color.

For one who wishes to subdue and treat the craving for exquisite tactile sensations, they should employ superior discernment to strip away the skin and flesh and contemplate only the skeleton as coarse as gravel; by this means, the mind will develop extreme revulsion, thereby enabling the subduing and treatment of the craving that takes exquisite tactile sensations as its object.

To subdue and treat those who are attached to offerings, one should observe the internal body through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), seeing that it is like one who is asleep, intoxicated, fainted, or afflicted by epilepsy, unable to move its limbs at will; or like being in a state of old age or illness, whether already arrived or yet to come, such conditions having bound the body.

Furthermore, one contemplates the internal body as being devoid of self-mastery; it arises because it is not independent of various conditions. Within it, there is not even the slightest portion of a physical part that can serve as a basis for the deportment of making offerings. Yet, one falsely clings to it as the "offerer," as if there were a definitive entity capable of performing the act of offering.

Now, regarding the meaning indicated by the term "adornment" (*prasādhana*): it refers to those specific parts of the body which, acting as conditions, are determinately capable of performing the activities of deportment such as dancing, singing, laughing, gazing, weeping, and playing.

Contemplate that those activities have no fixed nature at all; like the melodies produced by instruments such as the *vīṇā*, they are all like the products of illusion. By means of this, one causes the mind to give rise to extreme weariness and aversion, thereby being able to subdue and remedy greed for offerings and service.

Those of sharp faculties who are beginners practice the wisdom arisen from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) by observing the internal body, thereby able to suppress the four types of craving so that they do not manifest.

As for those of dull faculties, because their faculties are dull, their afflictions (*kleśa*) are fierce and difficult to subdue; they can only be suppressed and treated by relying on the power of external conditions. Therefore, they first clearly observe external corpses to gradually cause the afflictions of their own minds to be subdued.
This means that when one first wishes to contemplate an external corpse, one should first arouse a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and proceed to the place where the body lies.
As the Blessed One said:

"A practitioner who first seeks the skillful means to quickly extinguish sensual desire should take the path of tranquility through a mind of loving-kindness and diligently cultivate contemplation," and so on at length.

Having reached that place, in order to subdue and treat the four kinds of craving, one should practice the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) according to the *Catuḥ-śubha-varga-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Four Paths of Renunciation). One contemplates the characteristics of external corpses to illustrate the internal body; since those characteristics are thus, this [internal body] must likewise be so. By means of this expedient, one gradually enables the mind to develop a profound sense of revulsion toward the internal body as well, whereby one is able to subdue and treat the four cravings previously mentioned.

Because one perceives the intrinsic nature of the internal body, in order to swiftly bring the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to fulfillment, one should cultivate eight perceptions (*saṃjñā*) to subdue and remedy the four types of craving.
To subdue and remedy craving for color (*varṇa-rāga*), one cultivates the perception of a livid corpse (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*) and the perception of a discolored corpse (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*).
In order to subdue and treat greed for visible forms and colors, one cultivates the perception of being devoured and the perception of dismemberment.
In order to subdue and treat greed for exquisite tactile sensations, one cultivates the perception of disintegration and the perception of skeletons.
In order to subdue and remedy the four types of craving related to food and offerings, one cultivates the perception of bloatedness and the perception of festering pus.

It is accepted that the meditation on impurity based on a skeleton (*asthi-śaṅkalā*) is capable of universally subduing and remedying these four types of craving; since a single skeleton possesses the objective conditions for being free from all four cravings, one should first explain the cultivation of the skeleton meditation.
However, when eliciting the various roots of virtue, there are three stages of the *pudgala* with respect to their practice: first, the beginner (*ādikarmika*);
second, the one who has already matured their cultivation (*kṛtaparicaya*); and third, the one who has transcended mental attention (*atikrāntamanasikāra*).

Furthermore, when a practitioner wishes to cultivate this meditation on impurity, they should first bind the mind to a part of their own body—whether it be the toes, the space between the eyebrows, the bridge of the nose, or the forehead—and focus intently without wavering on whichever place they prefer, in order to make their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) firm and stable.
From the moment one has entered [the practice], it is called "initial cultivation. The term "entry" is used to indicate the initial fixing of the mind.

One visualizes one's own body, beginning from the toes and so forth, down until one can see white bones the size of a coin; through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), this visualization gradually expands and increases until one sees the entire skeleton of the body.

This refers to the stage at which the various practitioners of yoga engage in imaginative contemplation (*parikalpa*), mentally visualizing that the skin and flesh rot and fall away, gradually purifying the bones until they are initially the size of a coin, and eventually until the entire body becomes white bone; at this stage, many such perceptions arise for them.

The phrase "the transformation of perception" (*saṃjñā-parāvṛtti*) indicates that one does not abandon the object of focus, but repeatedly generates further perceptions of superior resolve (*adhimukti*). Other masters say:

as long as the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is not yet perfected, mental attention (*manasikāra*) proceeds solely by the power of perception; once the practice of contemplation is perfected, it proceeds by the power of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Since this stage has not yet been established, it proceeds by means of perception (*saṃjñā*).

One should understand that the term "attention" (*manasikāra*) used here generally indicates that all mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*) proceed in a continuous stream through the power of perception.
Having seen the entire body, one again employs skillful means to enter the gateway of the meditation on the impurity of external white bones.

This is done in order to gradually increase one’s resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). One contemplates a skeleton situated near one’s own side, gradually extending it to fill a single bed, a single room, a single monastery, a single garden, a single village, a single field, and a single country, until it covers the entire earth bounded by the ocean; within this space, skeletons are completely filled, so that resolute conviction may further increase.

One gradually contracts the observation from the extensive object until one observes only the skeletal remains of one's own body; when the contemplation of impurity has been perfected through this gradual contraction, it is called the stage of the beginner practitioner (*ādikarmika*) for the yoga master.

In order to cause the increase of the superior resolve (*adhimokṣa*) through abbreviated observation, one further removes the bones of the feet from within one's own skeleton, contemplating the remaining bones while fixing the mind upon them. Gradually, until even half of the skull-bone is removed, one contemplates that half-bone while fixing the mind upon it. Up to this point, the abbreviated *aśubhabhāvanā* (contemplation of impurity) is perfected; this is called the stage where the practitioner of yoga has already mastered the cultivation.

To bring mastery over the resolve of brief contemplation, one removes half of the skull-bone and fixes the mind between the eyebrows; by focusing single-mindedly on this one object and abiding in profound stillness, the extremely brief contemplation of impurity is perfected, and the practitioner of yoga is said to have transcended the stage of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
It should be understood that at this point the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is accomplished, for all that was to be done has been brought to completion.
One dwelling in seclusion speaks thus:

"At this time, this contemplation possesses the characteristic of culmination; namely, a pure aspect suddenly appears before one. Because of this, either the inhalation of breath is diminished, or a mind of non-delight is aroused. This is because one realizes the culmination of the stage being cultivated, and because the arising of the pure form-aspect disturbs the mind."

It is like a person reciting aloud a text they have already mastered; furthermore, because they have attained what was previously unattained and have progressed to realize other superior roots of goodness, this state—like water overflowing and spreading throughout a field—is called the sign of the culmination of this contemplation.
Other masters say:

If at that time one does not apply the preparatory effort toward external dependent origination, this is called the culmination and perfection of the contemplation on impurity, characterized by mastery over the object of focus.
Whether small or large, one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) and reflect upon them according to reason.
Now, one should investigate:

since this contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) is comprised within the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika-manasikāra*), it should logically be termed "perverted attention" (*viparyasta-manasikāra*); thus, the essence of this contemplation would not be wholesome (*kuśala*).
Is it not a perversion to claim that the substance of this object of observation is entirely bone and to conceive of it all as bone?

Furthermore, it cannot be said that this contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is entirely subsumed under the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), because there are generally two types of contemplation of impurity:
first, that which relies on actual reality (*tattva*), and second, that which relies on resolute conviction.

Regarding "contemplation based on one's own reality": this refers to the power of wisdom associated with mental attention (*manasikāra*), by which one observes, as they truly are, all the impurities within one's own internal body—whether their shape or their manifest colors—such as the nine bones of a seer, two conch shells, or the hair, body hair, nails, and so forth found within the body, which are said to comprise thirty-six items in detail; these are called "contemplation based on one's own reality."
Because it is associated with attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*), it cannot permanently sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding that which relies on resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), this refers to the conceptual contemplation of various impure signs through the power of resolute conviction; this is not subsumed under distorted attention (*viparyāsamanasikāra*), because it is contrary in nature to the afflictions.
Now, that which is inverted is fundamentally unable to accomplish what one intends to do;
this [meditative object], however, can subdue the afflictions according to one's intent—how, then, could it be inverted?

If you argue that this object is not actually bone and yet one perceives it as all bone, and thus it must be inverted, this reasoning is also incorrect, for it should be understood in the following way.
That is to say, those who perceive a person in a tree stump do not entertain the understanding:
"I am now viewing this stump through the lens of the characteristics of a person; therefore, this is a perversion.
Now, the practitioner of meditation reflects in this way:

Although not all objects within the various spheres of perception are actually bone, I now, for the sake of subduing the afflictions (*kleśa*), should universally contemplate them as bone through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Since one can subdue the afflictions by resolving upon them according to one's desire and as appropriate, how could this be a perversion (*viparyāsa*)?
The power of this contemplation can suppress the afflictions so that they do not manifest for a time; since it possesses such skillful means, how could it not be wholesome?
Therefore, there is no loss as you have objected.

What is the nature of this contemplation of impurity? How many stages does it comprise? What object does it take as its focal point? In what place does it arise? What is its mode of activity? To which time period does its object belong?
Is it contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
Is it obtained through detachment from desire (*vairāgya-lābha*) or obtained through application (*prayoga-lābha*)?
The verse says:
Its nature is non-attachment; it exists in ten stages; it takes the beings of the desire and form realms as its object; it arises in humans.
The impure [attainments] have their own realm as their object; the outflowing ones are acquired through both [ways].
The commentary says:
This is answered in sequence according to what was previously asked.

This contemplation has non-attachment as its intrinsic nature; it is induced by a mental orientation that is contrary [to desire], characterized by aversion and rejection, and is the opposite of attachment. One should know that this is termed the "contemplation of impurity" (aśubha-bhāvanā).
To claim that what is called "contemplation of impurity" (aśubha-bhāvanā) must be wisdom (*prajñā*) is logically incorrect, because it conforms to [the nature of] contemplation (*bhāvanā*).

That is to say, because the contemplation of impurity can directly counteract greed (*lobha*), its essential nature should properly be non-greed (*alobha*); since greed arises from the perception of purity and is eliminated through the power of contemplation, non-greed is said to be what the contemplation conforms to.
All contemplations of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) are non-attachment (*alobha*), but not all non-attachment is the contemplation of impurity.
Only that which is capable of subduing and curing attachment to visible form (*varṇa-rāga*) and so forth is designated as the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of this contemplation.
This is stated with respect to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If associated factors (*anuvartaka*) are included, it possesses the four aggregates (*skandha*) or five aggregates as its nature.

It universally relies upon ten stages (*bhūmi*), namely: the four dhyānas, the four preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); for it is only in these many stages that this [state] can exist.

This contemplation takes only the objective sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) within the desire realm as its object, because the manifest colors and shapes of the desire realm constitute the objects of this contemplation.
If that is so, why does the Sūtra state:
"One who is protected by the restraint of the ear-faculty dwells in the contemplation of impurity," and so forth?

This statement is made for those who are overwhelmed by craving for visible forms (*rūpa-rāga*); for they are necessarily overwhelmed by craving for objects such as sounds (*śabda*) which serve as conditions.

One who wishes to overcome craving for visible forms that serve as conditions must first abide in the restraint of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya-saṃvara*), and only through this can one then abide in the meditation on the foul (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

Some say: This contemplation relies exclusively on the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), as it can induce the remaining modes of perception that counteract [unwholesome states]; therefore, whoever abides in the restraint of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya-saṃvara*) must necessarily first abide in the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
The power of this contemplation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is able to take as its object all forms (*rūpa-āyatana*) subsumed within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If it is argued that the Venerable Aniruddha was unable to perceive the celestial realms as impure, and that Śāriputra and others were likewise unable to perceive the physical body of the Buddha as impure, how then can this contemplation take all forms of the desire realm as its object?

This objection is not valid; for one who has attained mastery over non-perishing can contemplate the physical form of a deva as impure, and the Buddha can contemplate his own subtle and wondrous physical body as impure. Therefore, this contemplation certainly takes the entirety of the desire realm and the form realm as its object.
By this, it has already been shown that the object of focus is the meaning and not the name, and it has also been established that it universally takes all three natures as its object.
A beginner can generate this contemplation only by relying on the human realm, not the Uttarakuru continent;
for within the celestial realms, there is no bluish discoloration and so forth, and thus it cannot first arise there.
Having first arisen here, it subsequently manifests in that other place.

Although this aspect of the contemplative practice proceeds as impurity, its essential nature must be pure because it is virtuous; it is described as impure only with respect to its mode of operation.
This is subsumed under the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*); it is a preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and not fundamental (*maula*).

Although it is associated with the three faculties of joy, pleasure, and equanimity, it proceeds together with revulsion (*nirveda*), like the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-kṣānti-jñāna*). Depending on which time period [the practitioner] resides in, it takes as its object the realm of that same time period; however, if it is a dharma that has not yet arisen, it universally takes the three time periods as its object.
This aspect of contemplative practice is not subsumed under the sixteen aspects such as impermanence and so forth; therefore, it is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).

It is acquired both through preparatory application (*prayoga*) and through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*); at the time one abandons the defilements of a particular stage and attains the corresponding meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one simultaneously acquires this contemplation of that stage.
Once it has been acquired through the abandonment of passion (*vairāgya-lābha*), it may also be brought into manifestation at later times through application (*prayoga*).
For those who have not yet abandoned passion, it is acquired solely through application.

Among these, all noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in their final existence (*caramabhavika*) possess both types—those previously unacquired (*apūrva*) and those already acquired (*pūrva*); others possess only those already acquired.
*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Fifty-nine and Fascicle Sixty,
composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Six, Part Four: The Analysis of the Noble Ones and Sages (Caturtha Ārya-pudgala-viniścaya). Having already explained the distinctions in the characteristics of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one should next analyze mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
What are the characteristics of these distinctions?
The verse says:
Mindfulness of breathing is wisdom belonging to five stages; it takes wind as its object and relies upon a body in the desire realm.
The second [category] consists of those that exist externally but lack reality; there are six, namely number and so forth.
The treatise states:
"Mindfulness of breathing" refers to what is called *ānāpānasmṛti* in the sūtras.
"Āna" refers to the inhalation of breath, which has the meaning of drawing external wind into the body.
"Apāna" refers to the exhalation of breath, which has the meaning of drawing internal wind out of the body.
As stated in the Sūtra:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that one who holds the breath while inhaling draws in external air and causes it to enter the body; one who holds the breath while exhaling expels internal air and causes it to exit the body."
Wisdom observes this as its object through the power of mindfulness; therefore, it is called *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing).
Other masters say:

*āna* means "that which brings in," and *apāna* means "that which carries away. The intent of these terms is to show that inhalation and exhalation possess the sense of "bringing" and "carrying"; because wisdom observes this through mindfulness, it receives this name.
Regarding the winds associated with the body, there are briefly six types:

first, the wind of inhalation; second, the wind of exhalation; third, the wind that initiates speech; fourth, the wind of elimination; fifth, the wind of movement; and sixth, the wind that moves the body.

This refers to when sentient beings are in the state of being in the womb or within an egg, a karma-born wind first arises at the navel region, piercing the body to form a cavity like that of a lotus root or stem. First, a wind comes and enters the interior of the body; following this, other winds continue to enter through the mouth and nose. This initial wind and those that follow are called the winds of inhalation (*āśvāsa*).

When this wind of inhalation has just entered within the body, there arises a continuous wind called the wind of exhalation. It is like the natural entry of air when a goldsmith opens the mouth of a bellows; such is the inherent nature of wind that it necessarily flows into wherever there is an opening. Once it has entered, if one presses upon it, the wind emerges again; the sequence of inhalation and exhalation is likewise.

In reality, this wind has neither entry nor exit; it merely circulates in this manner, capable of benefiting or harming the body. Within the continuum of the stream [of existence], it is conventionally designated as "entry" and "exit.

At the stage when the inhalation circulates, it can drive out the putrid, filthy, and foul-smelling substances within the body, increasing the fire element and causing the body to become light and buoyant.
When exhalation occurs, it can dispel internal heat and dampness; by diminishing the fire element, it causes the body to become heavy.

As for the wind that initiates speech, there is a distinct wind preceded by desire, which is successively induced by the mind that intends to speak and is made to increase in strength. It arises from the region of the navel, flows upward to strike the throat, and impinges upon the great elements born of maturation (*vipākaja*), drawing forth those of the nature of natural outflow (*naiṣyandika*).

The wind element arises and vibrates the teeth, lips, tongue, and palate with specific distinctions; by this power, it brings forth the future intrinsic nature of the derived matter consisting of phonemes (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*). When this resides within the mouth, it is called "speech" (*vāk*) and also "karma"; when it flows out externally, it is simply called "speech."
The principle that the great elements arise from the mind is thoroughly established.
This is because we observe that those whose minds give rise to greed, hatred, or delusion exhibit facial expressions—whether moist, withered, or disordered—that are extraordinary.

Furthermore, it is traditionally reported that in one who harbors the poison of hatred, flames emerge from the mouth; this is because those lacking a compassionate heart give rise to the fire of greed, which burns the body and so forth.

Regarding the wind that expels: there is a specific wind that moves along the pathways of the excretory orifices and is able to clear away the two types of impurities. Because these impurities press upon the interior, painful sensations arise; because painful sensations arise, the desire to expel them is produced; from the desire to expel them, the mind directed toward the wind is induced; and this mind, giving rise to the wind, accomplishes the action of expulsion.
Furthermore, this wind-force brings stability and comfort to the body.
As for the *anuvartaka* wind, it refers to a distinct wind that circulates throughout all the pores of the bodily limbs; because of this, it receives the name *anuvartaka* (the "conforming" wind).

This does not depend on the mind but relies solely on the power of karma; it flows naturally through the pores and cavities of the body, thereby able to eliminate all putrid, filthy, and foul-smelling substances that reside within those pores and cavities.

Regarding the "wind that moves the body," this refers to a distinct wind capable of striking and moving the body to initiate manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*). It should be understood that this arises with the mind as its cause and is able to strike and move throughout all parts of the body.

Having explained the meaning of "wind" (*vāyu*) by way of discussing the six winds, this section primarily elucidates the two breaths (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), because the intention here is to define mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this mindfulness is wisdom (*prajñā*) and nothing else, for the Sūtra uses the term "clearly knowing" (*prajānāti*).

This chapter is given the name "Mindfulness" because mindfulness is predominant; it is so called because, through the power of mindfulness, one maintains awareness of the quantity of the inhalations and exhalations.
It is designated as "mindfulness" to demonstrate that the meditative concentration and wisdom which take the breath as their object are accomplished through the functional capacity of mindfulness.
Its concomitant nature should also be understood according to the preceding section.

The basis of this mindfulness extends only through five stages: namely, the desire realm, the intermediate dhyāna, and the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first, second, and third dhyānas. Consequently, it is associated only with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), because this mindfulness is cultivated as an antidote to discursive thought (*vitarka*).

Pleasurable and painful feelings and so forth can give rise to discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) concerning kinsmen and the like; therefore, for the antidote to such discursive thought, it must be present in its spontaneous state when feeling arises.
If this is so, why does the explanation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) speak of "discerning joy and bliss"?
This also involves no fault, because during the stage of cultivating mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), those formless mental images (*ārūpya-nimitta*) arise in the interim.

Although practitioners of yoga perceive these images, this does not constitute a deviation from the practice of mindfulness of breathing; it is with this in mind that the statement regarding the perception of joy and bliss is spoken cryptically. One must not, on this basis, maintain that mindfulness of breathing can also be associated with other feelings (*vedanā*).

In reality, one also perceives other phenomena herein, because it is stated that even during the stage of application for the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), one contemplates many sets of six phenomena.

That is to say, if one correctly observes the characteristics of those phenomena that are associated with the body, this is also called "dwelling in the contemplation of the body by following the body" (*kāye kāyānupaśyanā*).

Alternatively, that practitioner may shift his attention to the perception of wind and momentarily observe feelings of joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*); therefore, it is said that he "perceives joy" and "perceives pleasure.
For this reason, it is said that at that time, the noble disciple dwells in the contemplation of feelings with regard to feelings.
Is it not the case that at this stage one has emerged from mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*)?
No; for its preparatory application and intention have not ceased, and because the mindfulness directed toward the wind quickly arises once again.
If that is so, why does one perceive only joy and pleasure and not the other sensations?
It is because these two sensations possess the most powerful force as causes for the defilement of craving.
Since the practitioner desires to bring about the swift liberation of the mind from the defilement of craving, they specifically contemplate joy and pleasure.
Other masters say:

"This is not mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), but rather a merit produced by its preparatory application; therefore, because it realizes joy and bliss, it is given the name 'mindfulness of breathing. Others say:
In the three lower fundamental dhyānas, while one is actually in meditative equipoise, there is also the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
They say that this mindfulness (*smṛti*) relies upon all eight stages, because in the higher dhyānas, when they manifest, [the coarse mental activity] ceases and thus [this mindfulness] is absent.
This mindfulness takes only the wind of the breath as its object; it does not universally take as its object the six types of winds mentioned above.
This mindfulness first arises based on a body in the desire realm, occurring only within the human and celestial destinies, excluding Uttarakuru.

It is acquired solely through application (*prayoga*) and not through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*), because for one who has not yet abandoned the defilements, it necessarily manifests through application; furthermore, it is not comprised within a stage that is acquired through the abandonment of defilements.

It has already been stated that these are all subsumed under the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and not the fundamental stages (*maula*), because this mindfulness is induced solely by superior application (*prayoga*).
Therefore, one should not say that it is acquired through detachment from defilements (*vairāgya-lābhika*); it is associated exclusively with true mental attention (*tattvamanasikāra*).
Some say that it also extends to attention through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*), which can be cultivated only by sentient beings who possess the True Dharma;
non-Buddhists do not have it, because they lack a teacher and are unable to realize subtle dharmas.
Because this is utterly incompatible with the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), where that grasping at a self exists, this mindfulness does not.
It is complete by virtue of possessing six causes. What are these six?
First is counting, second is following, third is settling, fourth is observing, fifth is transforming, and sixth is purifying.

Counting means binding the mind to count the inhalations and exhalations from one to ten, neither decreasing nor increasing, for fear that the mind might become excessively agitated or distracted regarding its object.
However, within this context, there may be three types of errors:
first, the error of omission; second, the error of addition; and third, the error of confusion.
Regarding the error of omission, it consists of taking two as one.
The fault of increasing the count is to take what is one as two.
The fault of confusion is to take the five inhalations as exhalations and the five exhalations as inhalations; this means taking inhalation as exhalation and exhalation as inhalation.
To be free from these three faults is called correct counting (*saṃkhyāna*).
As for the three faults: first, the fault of excessive slowness; second, the fault of excessive haste; and third, the fault of distraction.

Regarding the fault of excessive slowness: it means that because the application (*prayoga*) is too lax, the mind becomes entangled with indolence and torpor, or else the mind is allowed to wander and disperse toward external objects.
"Excessive haste" refers to the fact that because the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is too hurried, it causes the body and mind to arise in a state of imbalance.

When one forcefully and repeatedly enters the inhalation and exhalation, the breath becomes oppressed; this then causes an unwholesome wind (*vāyu*) to arise within the body. Due to this wind, first the various channels (*nāḍī*) of the bodily limbs become swollen and frequent.
When this wind increases to an extreme degree, it can induce the arising of disease; because diseases arise in the limbs of the body, this is called "imbalances of the body.

Alternatively, by forceful and frequent inhalation and exhalation, the mind is oppressed and driven to distraction, or it is overwhelmed by heavy sorrow; such states are called "imbalances of the mind."
Therefore, it is said:
Among all exquisite foods and drinks that nourish the limbs of the body, none is like the breath-inhalation and breath-exhalation when regulated by skillful means;
among all thorns, swords, fire, or cauldrons of hot ashes that damage the limbs of the body, none is like the breath-inhalation and breath-exhalation when not regulated by skillful means.
Regarding the fault of distraction: this means that because the mind is distracted, it is overcome by all afflictions.

If the mind becomes distracted during the interval between [counting] ten, one should again count from one in successive order, starting over from the beginning until meditative concentration is attained.

When counting the breaths, one should first count the inhalations; since the inhalation occurs at the initial stage of birth and the exhalation is the last at the time of death, by thus observing the stages of birth and death, one will gradually be able to cultivate the perception of impermanence.
"Following" means binding the mind to the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, observing whether the breaths are short or long, and how far they extend before returning and turning back.
Furthermore, one contemplates the inhalation: does it pervade the entire body, or does it move through only a portion?
Following that inhalation as it enters, the mindfulness constantly tracks it as it proceeds through the throat, heart, navel, hips, thighs, knees, shins, ankles, and finally the toes.
Other masters say:

one should contemplate this inhalation as exiting from beneath the feet, piercing through the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanacakravāḷa*) and descending to the Wind Wheel (*vāyucakra*), before returning and turning back upward.

If one contemplates that the exhaled breath leaves the body and extends for the distance of one span (*vitasti*) or one fathom (*vyāma*), the mindfulness constantly follows it as it reaches its destination.
Other masters say: "The mindfulness follows the wind of the exhaled breath until it reaches the Vairambha wind, and then returns."
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) refutes that teacher’s statement:
"This mindfulness arises simultaneously with the attention of reality (*bhūtamanasikāra*); it should not be thought that the breath reaches as far as the wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*) and so forth.

That teacher says: "Although the root of this mindfulness of breathing is indeed associated with the attention of reality, there may be other instances where it arises in association with the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanasikāra*). This conceptualization is produced during the interval in order to cause the attention of reality to be quickly accomplished."
Nevertheless, there is no loss of mindfulness regarding the exhalation, because the application and the mental inclination toward mindfulness of breathing do not cease.

"Calm abiding" (śamatha) refers to binding the mindfulness [to a point], whether it be at the tip of the nose, between the eyebrows, or even down to the toes; one settles the mind upon whichever place is preferred, observing the breath as it dwells in the body like a thread through a pearl, whether it is cold or warm, and whether it is harmful or beneficial.

"Contemplation" means that after having observed this wind of breath, one simultaneously contemplates the derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) co-arising with the breath, as well as the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) that abide supported by that matter; thus, one takes all five aggregates (pañca-skandha) as the object of observation.

"Transformation" (*parivṛtti*) refers to shifting; it means directing the awareness of the breath-wind toward increasingly superior and wholesome roots, beginning with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). "Purification" (*viśuddhi*) refers to ascending and entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and beyond.
Other masters say:

that which begins with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and ends with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is called "transformation" (*parivṛtti*); only the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth are termed "purification" (*viśuddhi*).
How should the distinctions among the characteristics of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) be understood?
The verse says:
Inhalation and exhalation follow the body; they proceed based on two distinctions.
They belong to the category of sentient beings, are non-appropriated, are out-flowing, and do not take lower realms as their object.
The treatise says:
The breaths belong to the same level as the body in which they arise, because the breaths are comprised as a part of that body.
This inhalation and exhalation proceed based on the distinctions between body and mind; therefore, the root treatise states:
The breath turns in dependence on both the body and the mind, according to what is appropriate.

If inhalation and exhalation turned only in dependence on the body and not in dependence on the mind, then even when one has entered the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or is born in the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñika-deva*), the breath would still continue; however, as explained at length, the breath only functions when four conditions are present.
Based on this principle, the phrase "as appropriate" is stated to show that the cessation [of breath] necessarily depends on the specific conditions of body and mind.

Regarding the four conditions: first, the body which is the basis for inhalation and exhalation; second, the opening of the pores; third, the passage of the wind-channels being unobstructed; and fourth, the manifestation of a coarse state of mind belonging to the level of inhalation and exhalation.
Among these four, if any one is lacking, the breaths do not circulate; this is because in the state of mindlessness, the mind is absent.
When born in the formless realm, all four are absent, and thus the breaths do not circulate.

While dwelling within the ovum or embryo in the stages of the *kalala* and so forth, the breath does not circulate because the pores have not yet opened and the channels for the winds have not yet become permeable.

If inhalation and exhalation were to circulate while one is in the stage of the *kalala* within the ovum or embryo, there would be agitation; and because the body is so subtle and thin, it would consequently disintegrate.
In the stages such as the arbuda, although the body gradually thickens, it remains without cavities; therefore, the breath still does not circulate.
Upon entering the fourth dhyāna, the pores do not open and coarse mental activity is absent; therefore, the breath does not circulate.
For what reason is it said that they only enter meditative absorption and are not born there?
Has it not already been stated that they are born there, as in the case of the statement regarding being born in the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*)?

There are versions of the text that do not mention being born in the realm of non-perception; however, by merely stating that they enter absorption and are born there, it is already established. This is because the Sūtra speaks in this manner:
These [beings] first enter meditative absorption and only afterwards are born there. Other masters say:

when one is born in the fourth dhyāna, the breath also circulates at the moment the mind that manifests manifesting karma (*vijñapti-karman*) becomes present; since it is possible for breath to be present there, they do not mention birth [in that context].
The Vaibhāṣika masters do not accept this point. If that were so, how could one produce speech after being born there?
They also possess wind, yet it is not called "breath" because it lacks the fruit of either harm or benefit; therefore, there is no fault.

Regarding the statement "the faculties are matured" and "the faculties are fulfilled," these words do not refer to the eye and other such faculties, for it is observed that the breath continues even when those [faculties] are absent.

Rather, the terms "matured" and "fulfilled" are spoken with reference to the presence of the four conditions. Since the term "faculties" (*indriya*) signifies the sense of predominance (*ādhipatya*), and these four conditions possess a predominant power over the movement of the breath, there is no fault in metaphorically designating them as "faculties" in this treatise.

Regarding these faculties (*indriya*), those situated in states such as the egg-stage are called "immature," while those who have correctly entered the fourth dhyāna and so forth are called "incomplete.
It is said that when one enters the fourth dhyāna, the pores do not open; how then can there be a physical body without pores?
The pores refer to the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
How could there be a mass of form (*rūpakāya*) that is separate from the space element?

In principle, this is indeed the case; however, in this context, with respect to the general course of the breath, it is not an error to say that while there is a physical body, there are no [visible] pores.
For what reason does the body have no pores only when entering the fourth dhyāna, and not in other meditative concentrations?
Because that samādhi is extremely pure and thick, it draws forth the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the fourth dhyāna throughout the entire body.
For this very reason, the Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Upon entering that meditative absorption, the pores of the body close.

This principle is plausible if one enters the mundane fourth dhyāna, for that absorption can induce the subtle and dense primary elements (mahābhūta) belonging to that level, which fill the body so that no pores remain.
When one enters the untainted fourth dhyāna, how is it that this body likewise lacks pores?
It is because that state merely induces the manifestation of the primary elements (mahābhūta) corresponding to the place of birth to produce non-informative matter (avijñapti).

The great elements (mahābhūta) induced by that untainted concentration (anāsrava-samādhi), although included within the place of birth, are extremely subtle and dense; because they resemble those [great elements], there is no fault.
If one born in that stage has a body without pores, how can one born there produce speech?

The production of speech does not necessarily depend on the pores; rather, sound can also be produced by the movement of the jaw. For instance, how could the sound of a mechanical device arise from the pores?
Other masters state that for those born in those [higher] realms, there are also pores above the throat.
Some say: when the mind capable of producing speech manifests for one born there, the pores open momentarily.
These inhalations and exhalations are included within the category of sentient beings, because breath does not exist within a body devoid of awareness.
Although these arise from the external, they are connected to internal meaning.
This inhalation and exhalation are not possessed of appropriation (*anupātta*), because breath lacks the characteristics of appropriation.
Although there are winds within the body that are appropriated (*upātta*), these breath-winds are exclusively non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
The substance of these inhalations and exhalations is a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*), because they are fruits produced by causes of the same kind (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Although there are winds of nourishment (*puṣṭi*) and maturation (*vipāka*) within the body, these breath-winds are exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*).

This is because the breaths diminish when the body grows, and the breaths increase when the body diminishes; furthermore, that which is nourished does not continue as a succession after it has been severed.
It is not born of maturation (*vipākaja*), because other types of matter born of maturation do not possess these characteristics.
It is observed only by a mind of its own level or a higher level, as it is not an object of perception for a mind of a lower level.

That is to say, when one is born in the desire realm and gives rise to a mind of the desire realm, that body of the desire realm and the breath of the desire realm proceed in dependence upon that mind of the desire realm, and are thus observed by that very mind.

If one is born in the desire realm and gives rise to a mind of the first dhyāna, that body of the desire realm and the breath of the desire realm proceed in dependence upon that mind of the first dhyāna, and are thus observed by that very mind.
