If that were the case, one should rather say that this is the "subsequent knowledge of the type" (*anvayajñāna*), and because it is not a result of repeated cultivation (*asamucita*), it is included within the path of seeing.

This means that when one of dull faculties initiates the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it must arise through repeated practice; because this noble path arises through such repeated practice, it receives the name "path of cultivation.

However, this subsequent knowledge of the category (*anvayajñāna*) can be initiated instantaneously even by those of dull faculties without repeated practice, just like the moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the preceding stage; therefore, as before, it should be subsumed under the path of seeing.

This is also unreasonable, because for those of dull faculties, the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) likewise occurs only instantaneously, as it arises through the same single preparatory application (*prayoga*) as the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).
Alternatively, they should explain how the knowledge of exhaustion arises from repeated cultivation rather than the knowledge of the category of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

Just as that knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is admitted to be included within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) because its similar types manifest repeatedly, so too should this knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) be treated accordingly; it should not be classified as being included within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Other masters say: This Knowledge of the Path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) is subsumed under the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) because it is necessarily non-retrogressive.

That is to say, even for those of dull faculties, there is necessarily no retrogression from the Knowledge of the Path; since there is retrogression from the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), one must certainly admit that this [Knowledge of the Path] is subsumed under the Path of Seeing.
This is also not the case; because that which is abandoned by patience (kṣānti) can never arise again, there is no falling back from it.

That is to say, even if one were to admit the possibility of falling back from the Knowledge of the Path of Types (mārga-anvaya-jñāna), such a fall would necessarily be due to the manifestation of afflictions abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya).
If one possesses dull faculties and has already abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by seeing, they will certainly not arise again; therefore, there is no falling back from this state.

Furthermore, there is no falling back while abiding in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*); if one were to fall back from the knowledge of the category of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), one would necessarily have fallen back from the patience regarding the category of the path (*mārga-jñāna-kṣānti*).

However, it is accepted that there is necessarily no falling back from the *kṣānti* (patience) of clear realization; therefore, there is certainly no possibility of falling back from the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of the path).

Furthermore, because the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna* is able to sustain the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), even those of dull faculties do not fall back from it.

If it is argued that, for this reason, [the abandonment of the afflictions] must be included within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), this objection is not valid; for otherwise, the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) and others would also have to be included in the path of seeing in the same way.

That is to say, when one subsequently abandons the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) and reaches the paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) of the once-returner and so forth, one is likewise able to maintain the abandonment of the afflictions abandoned by seeing; therefore, those [abandonments] would also have to be included within the path of seeing.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because even in the subsequent stage one can maintain the abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation, this is also logically untenable, for [the abandonment] would then possess two natures.

Alternatively, one should not say that it is included within the Path of Seeing because it maintains the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing, for no distinct reason can be found to differentiate between the two.

What is the reasoning that would allow those in the stages of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and so forth to be able to maintain both types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*), yet be designated as belonging to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) rather than being subsumed under the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
Therefore, it is not possible to establish the distinction between the paths of seeing and cultivation based on their capacity to maintain the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśaprahāṇa*).

Alternatively, because one perceives that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) possesses various aspects, it is not the case that [the path] is subsumed under the "path of seeing" (*darśanamārga*) merely by virtue of being non-retrogressive.
This is because one observes that even among the noble ones (*ārya*), there are those who fall away; yet, it is not the case that all noble ones are subject to retrogression.
One observes that those of dull faculties may fall away, yet it is not the case that all of those with dull faculties fall away.
One observes that those of a nature prone to falling away (parihāṇadharman) may fall away, yet it is not the case that all of those of a nature prone to falling away fall away.
Although there may be retrogression from a path that is superior to its fruit, it is not the case that all such paths necessarily involve retrogression.

That is to say, those who regress gradually—and not by means of transcendence—do not undergo retrogression after having passed through a birth; yet among those who do not pass through a birth, some may be subject to retrogression while others are not. This should likewise be the case here; why then do you so stubbornly insist on a one-sided view?

This means that although one admits there is falling back from the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), this does not apply to all cases. With the exception of the first moment, at other times when one falls back from cultivation, it is not necessarily the case that one sees [the truths] again;

therefore, falling back is possible. However, if one falls back from the initial cultivation [of the path of seeing], one must necessarily see them again; thus, there is no principle of falling back [from the path of seeing], because there is certainly no falling back from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). It is not the case that it is not falling back; rather, it is subsumed under the path of seeing.
Other masters say:
This is subsumed under the path of seeing because it is accomplished through the preparation for the path of seeing.

That is to say, the knowledge of the type of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is accomplished precisely by the preparation for the path of seeing; therefore, like other [stages of] the path of seeing, it should not be said to be subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This is also unreasonable; for if one were to intend not to emerge from the seventeenth moment of mind and so forth, the same logic would apply.
If it is argued that this is because [the intention] is not fixed, that is also illogical; for even if it is not fixed, it is nonetheless subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

This refers to that which is produced by the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), yet is not included within the path of seeing itself; because it is established through this preparatory application for the path of seeing, it is not a definitive cause [for being included therein].

Furthermore, this reason would entail an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): since the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) is produced by the same single preparatory application as the path of seeing, it would consequently have to be included within the path of seeing.

Furthermore, since the various liberations (vimokṣa) and the uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga) arise from a single preparatory application (prayoga), they should be subsumed under the "uninterrupted" category.
Therefore, what they have established is not a definitive logical reason.
Other masters say:

There is another authoritative teaching that clarifies the knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) is included within the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), as the treatise states that there are nine groups of fetters (saṃyojana-kāya).

If the knowledge of the path were included within the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), then the fetters abandoned by it should be termed "abandoned through cultivation," and one should not further establish a separate group of fetters abandoned through cultivation.

Alternatively, the collection of fetters to be abandoned through seeing should consist of only seven; however, it is logically necessary that the eighth fetter must be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), because the path of liberation and the uninterrupted path perform the same function, as is stated regarding the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) by means of nine faculties.
This is also unreasonable, because the intent of the teaching is different.

For within the fundamental treatise (*mūla-śāstra*), it is stated that the fetters (*saṃyojana*) abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) are abandoned by the various patiences (*kṣānti*) and not abandoned by knowledge (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, this is proven by correct reasoning: the fetters directly abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) are not abandoned by insight. This is because the holy teachings speak of two aggregates of fetters: first, those abandoned by insight, and second, those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

However, untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) is of three types: first, that which is exclusively vision (*darśana*); second, that which is exclusively knowledge (*jñāna*); and third, that which pertains to both.

Among these three, that which is exclusively knowledge cannot sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*); that which severs them through vision alone is called "to be abandoned by vision" (*darśana-heya*); and that which severs them through both is called "to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*).

It is not so; otherwise, the establishment of the name would be devoid of meaning. Since the essence of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) comprises both knowledge (*jñāna*) and vision (*darśana*), that which is abandoned by it is not subsumed under what is abandoned by vision.

Nevertheless, the established designation of the "nine clusters of fetters" (*navasaṃyojananikāya*) is not entirely meaningless, as it is intended to show that the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) is comprised within the auxiliary factors of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
What is the purpose of demonstrating this?

It is to establish that the eighty-nine conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya (*saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*) taught in this treatise are indeed attained, because the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is itself śrāmaṇya, and it is by the power of this path that the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is induced.
If the bonds were not severed by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), there would be no possibility for the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) to arise.
It is like a king who can only dwell in sovereign security within a place where his ministers have already eliminated all enemies and bandits.
Alternatively, because there is a distinction between patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), the term "knowledge" is used in the treatise to refer to that which is abandoned by patience.
Or again, why labor over such a forced interpretation?
This passage should properly state that it is abandoned by the patience of the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti*); however, it does not say so because intermediate words have been omitted.

The meaning of attaining the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) by means of the nine faculties (*indriya*) has already been fully analyzed in the section on the faculties; therefore, one cannot prove from this that the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)—just like the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*)—is included within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Therefore, at the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are only fifteen moments of mind.

Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.

Chapter Six, Part Eight: Distinguishing the Noble and the Holy. Having already distinguished the differences in the arising of the paths of seeing and cultivation, one should now establish the various noble *pudgalas* (individuals) based on the distinctions between the stages of these paths.
Furthermore, regarding the establishment of distinctions among the noble ones based on the fifteen moments of mind during the path of seeing, the verse says:
They are named "Followers by Faith" and "Followers by Dharma," Due to the distinction between dull and sharp faculties;
Having abandoned from one up to five categories of afflictions, They are directed toward the first fruit.
"Having abandoned [the first three fetters], one is directed toward the second; having detached from the eight stages, one is directed toward the third.
The Commentary says:

Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are two types of noble ones (*ārya*): first, those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), and second, those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*). These two names are established based on the distinction between dull and sharp faculties (*indriya*).
Those of dull faculties are called followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), because they previously cultivated and accumulated the preparatory application through the power of faith and reverence.

Those of sharp faculties are called followers by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), because they previously cultivated and accumulated the preparatory application through delighting in analytical investigation.
The distinctions among the lineages of sentient beings have existed as such from the very beginning by the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

That is to say, if among the classes of sentient beings there are those who, from the outset, in all their activities and undertakings, do not delight in investigating what they can or cannot accomplish, but instead place their sole trust and respect in others and act in accordance with their words, then when they later cultivate and attain the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), they are called "followers by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) during the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*).
One who practices in accordance with faith is called a "follower by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*), because they previously practiced in accordance with the meaning as taught by others through faith.

Such a person possesses the state of practicing in accordance with faith and is thus termed a "follower by faith"; alternatively, they are so named because they have cultivated this practice of following faith until it has become their very nature. In them, faith is the primary factor, while wisdom functions as its attendant.
The practitioner who follows the Dharma (*dharmānusārī*) should be explained as the opposite of this.

That is to say, among the classes of sentient beings, those who, from the outset, in all their activities and undertakings, delight in carefully examining what is possible and what is impossible, and do not proceed according to the teachings out of faith in others, are called "followers of the Dharma" (*dharmānusārī*) when they subsequently attain the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) while in the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*).
One is called a "follower of the Dharma" (dharmānusārin) because they follow the meaning by first following the teachings;

thus, one who possesses such a practice of following the Dharma is termed a follower of the Dharma. Alternatively, one is called a follower of the Dharma because they have cultivated this practice of following the Dharma until it has become their very nature, for in them wisdom is primary and faith follows as its attendant.

Regarding these two types of noble ones (*ārya*), because there are differences in the extent to which they have abandoned the afflictions of the realm of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), they are established as three paths (*mārga*).

That is to say, if those two noble ones have not, from the outset, abandoned the afflictions of the realm of cultivation by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), they are termed "fully bound" (*sakalabandhana*).

Alternatively, if one has already abandoned from one to five grades of the desire realm, one is termed a "candidate for the first fruit" (*pratipannaka*) upon reaching this stage, because one is proceeding toward the first fruit.
What is called the "first fruit" refers to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), as it is necessarily the first to be attained among all the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).

If one has previously abandoned six, seven, or eight categories of afflictions of the desire realm, upon reaching this stage, one is called a candidate for the second fruit (*dvitīyaphalapratipannaka*), because one is proceeding toward the second fruit.
The second fruit refers to the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), as it is the second among all fruits that are fully attained.

If one has already abandoned the nine grades of the desire realm, or has already severed even one grade of the first dhyāna, up to having completely abandoned the sphere of nothingness, then upon reaching this stage, one is called a candidate for the third fruit, because one is proceeding toward the third fruit.
The third fruit refers to the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*); its enumeration follows the previous explanation.

Thus, for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), there are seventy-three distinct types each, based on the differences in the number of afflictions (*kleśa*) abandoned while still bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*).

This means that starting from one who is fully bound in the desire realm as the first, up to the abandonment of the nine grades as the tenth, and continuing in this manner through each stage up to the sphere of nothingness—with nine grades in each stage—there are seventy-three [stages].

Since those who are still bound by all fetters at the subsequent stages are the same as those previously described as having abandoned nine [categories of afflictions], there are no distinct "fully bound" individuals in the latter seven stages.
Next, regarding the establishment of distinctions among the noble ones based on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) at the time of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), the verse says:
Upon reaching the sixteenth mind, One abides in a fruit according to one of the three paths.
They are called *śraddhādhimukta* and *dṛṣṭiprāpta*, distinguished by their dull or sharp faculties.
The treatise says:

Those who were previously practitioners following faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or following the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind—the knowledge of the path-category (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*)—are said to "abide in the fruit" (*phalastha*) and are no longer called "candidates" (*pratipannaka*).

Following the three previous paths of approach, one now abides in the three fruits; that is, one who was previously on the path of approach to stream-entry now abides in the fruit of stream-entry, one who was previously on the path of approach to once-returning now abides in the fruit of once-returning, and one who was previously on the path of approach to non-returning now abides in the fruit of non-returning.

The fruit of Arhatship can never be attained for the first time [by one already on the path], because an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) cannot possibly be free from the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), and because the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) cannot possibly abandon the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

Upon reaching the stage of abiding in the fruit, one abandons two names and acquires two others: that is, one no longer bears the names of "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārin) or "follower by dharma" (dharmānusārin), but instead acquires the two names of "resolved through faith" (śraddhādhimukta) and "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

This is also due to the distinction between dull and sharp faculties: those with dull faculties, who were previously termed "followers by faith," are now termed "resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*), because their resolute conviction is manifested through the predominant power of faith;

those with sharp faculties, who were previously termed "followers by dharma," are now termed "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), because their right view is manifested through the predominant power of wisdom.

For what reason, when one has previously abandoned from one to five, or seven or eight categories (*prakāra*) of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm, or one category of the first dhyāna—and so on, up to the ninth category of afflictions in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)—yet at the sixteenth moment of mind, the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna*, is one designated only as a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or non-returner (*anāgāmin*), rather than as a candidate for once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship?
The verse says:

Among those who abide in the stages of attaining the fruits, because they have not yet attained the path to a superior fruit and thus have not yet given rise to that superior path, they are called "abiders in the fruit" and not "candidates."
The treatise says:

The establishment of the eight noble ones based on the attainment of the noble path has already been explained previously; therefore, at the time of attaining a fruit, one has certainly not yet attained the path of the superior fruit. This is because the mind that attains the fruit is not an antidote to the afflictions to be countered by the path of the superior fruit, and as previously explained, one does not attain the path that is the antidote to those [afflictions] at the very moment when that which is not their antidote is present.

Furthermore, it is not the case that at the very moment of attaining the fruit, there exists a path of superior fruit through which the acquisition of dissociation from the abandoned afflictions arises; for the *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti* cannot sever those acquisitions of bondage.

If the power of the path can sever the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those fetters, and this path induces the arising of the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*), one may say that this path can realize that cessation (*nirodha*).

Since at the time of attaining a prior fruit one has not yet attained the path of a superior fruit, those abiding in a fruit—so long as they have not yet given rise to the path of a superior fruit—are designated as "abiding in a fruit" (*phalastha*) even though they have previously severed one grade or more of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); they are not called "candidates for the subsequent [fruit]" (*uttara-pratipannaka*).
At what time thereafter does one obtain the untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*) of the disconnection from the previously abandoned afflictions of the stage of cultivation?
One obtains it at the time when the path of superior fruit (*viśeṣa-mārga*) manifests.

For those who have already abandoned those afflictions of the stage of cultivation and entered the state of "entry into the birthless" (*niyāmāvakrānti*), having obtained the preceding fruit, does the path of superior fruit necessarily arise in this very life?

This must necessarily be so, because the *Mūla-śāstra* states that those noble ones born in the fourth dhyāna or above definitely possess the untainted faculty of pleasure (*anāsrava-sukhendriya*). If this were not the case,

how could it be said that they definitely possess the faculty of pleasure when— having previously abandoned the defilements of the three lower dhyānas and subsequently entered the state of "entry into the stream" (*nyāma*) based on a lower stage— they are born in the fourth dhyāna or above after having attained the fruit?

It is not reasonable to say that only for those of such a class does this [path] necessarily give rise to the path of superior fruit, and not for others who have previously abandoned the afflictions of the lower stages; for no determining causes and conditions can be found [to restrict it], since those whose obstructions have been severed will certainly rejoice in that [fruit], and because the path whose obstructions have been severed easily manifests.

Having thus established the distinctions among the noble ones based on the sixteen moments of mind for those who enter the vision of the truths—whether they were previously endowed with double-detachment from desire or complete detachment—one should now explain the differences in the stages of the antidotal paths that arise gradually in relation to the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
The verse says:
In each stage, there are nine faults and virtues; three each for the lower, middle, and upper [levels].
The commentary says:
"Failure" refers to faults, which are the obstacles to be remedied; "virtue" refers to meritorious qualities, which are the paths that serve as remedies, as has already been explained.

One should know that when cultivating the abandonment of afflictions through the nine grades of distinction, this applies likewise to the four higher dhyānas and the four formless attainments, because there is no part of saṃsāra that is not subsumed within these nine stages.

Just as the obstacles to be remedied within each bhūmi are each divided into nine grades, so too are the remedial paths—the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and the liberative (*vimukti*)—each divided into nine grades.
How is it that these faults are each divided into nine grades?

This means that within the fundamental category there are inferior, middling, and superior levels; each of these three is further divided into inferior, middling, and superior distinctions. Consequently, the faults and virtues are each divided into nine grades: namely, the inferior-inferior, inferior-middling, inferior-superior, middling-inferior, middling-middling, middling-superior, superior-inferior, superior-middling, and superior-superior.

It should be understood that herein, the power of the lowest-of-the-low path is able to sever the highest-of-the-high obstacles; and so on, until the power of the highest-of-the-high path is able to sever the lowest-of-the-low obstacles. This is because the remedial qualities, such as the highest-of-the-high, do not yet exist at the beginning, whereas those faults, such as the highest-of-the-high, no longer exist once [the path] has arisen.
It should be understood that herein, although wisdom surpasses the afflictions, because it has not yet become fully developed, the path is designated as "inferior.
Furthermore, although the afflictions within the continuum are extremely difficult to sever, because they persist as subtle latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the path is designated as "inferior."
Based on this principle, one should establish an analogy: just as in the process of washing clothes, coarse stains are removed first, and subsequently, fine stains are gradually removed.
This means that those coarse stains do not adhere very firmly to the garment they inhabit; with little exertion of effort, they can be dispelled by washing with water.
It is not so with fine stains; because they adhere very firmly to the garment they inhabit, they can only be dispelled by using lye and the like, along with great effort.
Furthermore, just as coarse darkness can be dispelled by a small light, whereas subtle darkness requires a great light to be dispelled— meaning that coarse,
heavy darkness can be extinguished as soon as a small light is raised, while subtle, light darkness requires the raising of a great light to be extinguished.
The principle of the opposition between faults and virtues should likewise be so; it is on this basis that one may say the white is superior and the black is inferior.

If it were otherwise—such that only when the highest-of-the-high (adhimātra-adhimātra) path is present could it counteract the lowest-of-the-low (mṛdu-mṛdu) obstruction—how could one say that the power of the white dharma is superior and the power of the black dharma is inferior?

Furthermore, in a single moment, the path capable of counteracting [the afflictions] arises; having been successively augmented since beginningless time, it can forever uproot all firm delusions. For this reason, it is said that the white [virtue] is superior and the black [non-virtue] is inferior.
Just as various ailments accumulated over a long period can be cured instantaneously by taking a small amount of excellent medicine,
and just as the manifold darkness accumulated over a long time can be extinguished in a single moment by light.
Having already distinguished the nine grades of faults and defects, we shall next establish the distinctions among noble ones based upon them.

Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) for those in training (*śaikṣa*), they are generally termed "those resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) and "those who have attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). Furthermore, there are many specific subdivisions according to their respective stages; first, we shall establish the case of those who have not yet abandoned any [defilements].
The verse says:
Having not yet abandoned the faults to be abandoned by cultivation, one who abides in the fruit [of Stream-enterer] returns at most seven times.
The commentary says:

When those abiding in the fruit have not yet completely abandoned the faults to be abandoned through cultivation in all stages, they are called "stream-enterers" (srotāpanna), who are subject to rebirth for at most seven times.
The term "seven times" indicates seven cycles of returning and being born; this signifies the meaning of seven births each among gods and humans.

The use of the term "maximum" (parama) is intended to show that the number of rebirths is greatest; it does not mean that all stream-enterers (srotāpanna) are necessarily limited to exactly seven returns.

Therefore, when the Sūtra speaks of "at most seven returns," it means that seven returns is the maximum number of births for such a person; the meaning of this scriptural statement is no different from what has been explained here.
All untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) are collectively termed "flows" (*srotas*), because by taking these as their cause, one proceeds toward *nirvāṇa*.
The term "entering" (*pre*) is used to indicate the initial attainment; because one has entered that [stream], one is called a "Stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*).
What is the meaning designated by the term "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna)?
If the first attainment of the path is called "entering the stream," then the name "stream-enterer" should refer to the eighth person (the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry).

If the first attainment of the fruit is called "entering the stream," then those who have partially abandoned desire or completely abandoned desire would also have to be called "stream-enterers" upon reaching the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna).
This designation "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) refers to the initial attainment of the fruit.

However, those who have either partially or fully abandoned desire do not receive this name until they reach the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna), because that fruit is established based on the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
The stream-enterer (srotāpanna) necessarily relies on the universal attainment of the fruit because the name is established based on the first fruit attained.

The once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and non-returner (anāgāmin) are not necessarily attained for the first time; it is only this fruit [of the stream-enterer] that must necessarily be attained for the first time.
For what reason is this name not applied to the eighth [stage]?

Because one has not yet fully attained the untainted path of the candidate for the fruit; because one has not yet fully attained the untainted paths of seeing and cultivation; and because one has not yet universally attained the flow of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

The eight patiences and the eight knowledges are called the stream of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). At the moment of the knowledge of the path of types (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), one possesses the acquisition (*prāpti*) of all of them; therefore, the eighth [moment] is not called "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*). For this reason, the stream-enterer is exclusively the first fruit.
If one were to say that such a person would undergo seven births each among humans and devas thereafter, it should be stated as fourteen; why then is it said that they undergo at most seven births?
This objection is not valid, because the number seven is the same, just as in the cases of the "seven-leaf tree" (saptaparṇa) and the "virtue in seven places" (saptasthānakauśalya).

If it is argued that since the Sūtra states there is no possibility or occasion for one who has perfected vision to undergo an eighth existence, one should not say that such a person undergoes seven births each in the realms of humans and devas.
This is also not the case, for the sutra speaks with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) regarding a single destiny.
If one were to claim that this sutra is not spoken with intentional ambiguity, then one would likewise have to deny the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

If one were to undergo seven births combined within the realms of humans and gods, the Sūtra should simply state that one receives "seven [births] among humans and gods. For what reason does the Sūtra speak of "seven [births] as gods and humans"?
Since it uses the conjunction "and" (及), we know for certain that there are seven of each.
Furthermore, it must necessarily be so, for the Kāśyapīya Sūtra explicitly states that each receives seven [existences].

If this is explained according to the intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣya*) of a single realm of rebirth, then there is no contradiction with the scriptural statement that one who has perfected vision (*dṛṣṭisaṃpanna*) does not have an eighth existence.
How can there be one who undergoes universal exhaustion (*sarvacyuta*) among those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*)?
Since such a person experiences more than eight births in a single destiny (*ekāyanika*), there is no contradiction.
The mention of "not [experiencing] an eighth" is based on the stage of maximum seven existences (*saptabhava-parama*), and does not refer to the higher stages.

This means that when it is stated for a particular realm that noble beings undergo at most seven births, it is precisely within that realm that an eighth existence is precluded, not in the form or formless realms.
The scriptural statement regarding "seven returns" is not made without distinction across the three realms; how, then, could it be taken as a prohibition against an eighth existence [in general]?

This is stated in general terms regarding the lack of distinction among the three realms; therefore, this sutra’s negation of an eighth [existence] is like the expression "seven existences," which refers exclusively to the desire realm. Since it is spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), there is no fault of contradiction.
Others maintain that this interpretation is incorrect, because such a statement has never been made elsewhere, and because there are no signs of an intentional (abhisandhika) teaching here.

That is to say, nowhere has it been stated that the *ūrdhvasrotas* takes birth beyond seven existences; thus, this [passage] cannot be used as proof for the sūtra that restricts [the maximum number of births] to eight. Furthermore, the sūtra restricting [births] to eight does not refer exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), nor does it contradict other teachings. Since there is no separate intention behind those [other] teachings, they must possess a distinct intent; therefore, this [present] interpretation is judged to be an intentional teaching and is thus inconsistent with correct reasoning.
Does this not contradict and undermine the *Sūtra on the Eighth Existence*?
There is no contradiction, because the *Sūtra on the Upstreamer* speaks of the upstreamer in general and intends to include others as well.

This means that [the opponent] claims that only those who leap entirely (*aśakṣepaka*) or leap halfway (*ardhapluta*) are called "Upstreamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), because they do not undergo universal death (*aparihīṇa*).
Such an interpretation is certainly illogical, for it has never been stated elsewhere, nor has the definitive cause for the place of rebirth ever been explained in this way.

That is to say, nowhere has it been stated that those who ascend to the higher realms (*ūrdhvasrotas*) are of only two types and do not undergo universal dissolution (*sarvacyuta*); nor has it ever been stated that there is a fixed cause for their place of rebirth, such that one could say these ascenders will definitely be born in this specific location within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and not in that other location.

However, the Sūtra speaks of seven destinations for beings (*pudgala-gati*), employing numerous similes to demonstrate the successive rebirths of those who "stream upwards" (*ūrdhva-srotas*) through all the various levels of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).

Examining the intent of that Sūtra, since it states that those who stream upwards reach the limit of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and there attain cessation due to the absence of further conditions, it reveals that among those non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who are born in every location within the form realm, some exceed eight existences. Thus, we know that there must certainly be those who "stream upwards" after having passed through all [levels].

That is to say, in that sutra, six similes are taught for each of the six classes of *pudgala* (beings), while eleven similes are taught specifically for the seventh class, the "Upstreamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*). This demonstrates that this noble one is born successively in all the stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Thus, the sutra states: "Just as an upstreamer, upon reaching the edge of a road or the edge of water, ceases to exist because there is no further support," which indicates that when this noble one passes beyond these places, there being no place of rebirth, he attains parinirvāṇa.

Therefore, the *Urdhvasrotas-sūtra* has no other underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) than to negate the eighth teaching, which contradicts it; this is precisely the nature of the intentional terminology (*saṃdhābhāṣya*) of this sūtra.
Furthermore, one observes that when the sūtra employs expressions of non-distinction, there is within them no lack of an underlying intention of distinction.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There is no possibility, there is no occasion, for two wheel-turning monarchs (cakravartin) to appear simultaneously.
Although this sūtra does not contain explicit words of distinction, it is not the case that it refers solely to a single four-continent world system.
In this regard, one may also say:
since such a statement has never been made elsewhere, and because there is no indication here of an intentional (saṃdhāya) teaching, how can it be claimed that this interpretation is incorrect?
Therefore, you have needlessly given rise to dogmatic attachment regarding both [positions].

Furthermore, for what reason do the karmas that induce the eight existences (*bhava*) obstruct the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), while the karmas of the seven existences do not? If you claim that this is because a noble one (*ārya*) undergoes at most seven births within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and no eighth, this is likewise subject to doubt, as it lacks a valid basis.
If it is argued that their continuity must necessarily ripen at this time, this is also not the case, because there is no fixed cause.
For what determinate causal condition is there such that those whose faculties have not yet ripened for the exhaustion of all outflows in the seventh birth would reach the eighth birth?
Nor is the faculty for the exhaustion of all outflows matured.
If you argue that this is because the nature of the Noble Path is such, like being bitten by a seven-step viper, this analogy is incorrect;
for those whose lifespan is fixed can still proceed even beyond that limit.

Furthermore, if it is the nature of things that the category of the Noble Path (āryamārga) prevents the eighth existence (*aṣṭama-bhava*) from arising by its very production, how can one say that those karmas are able to obstruct the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*)?

One should simply say that the arising of the Noble Path prevents the eighth existence; one should not say that the karma which brings about the eighth existence is able to obstruct the vision of the truths.

If there exists karma for an eighth existence that has already been performed and accumulated, the Noble Path lacks the power to obstruct it; therefore, [the path] cannot arise. Furthermore, such karma should not be able to obstruct the vision of the Truths (darśana). What contradiction or harm is there in the correct principle that one attains parinirvāṇa only upon reaching the eighth existence?
Others offer this explanation:
because there remain seven other fetters for them—namely, the two lower-tier fetters and the five upper-tier fetters.

This [explanation] also lacks the power to prove that there are only seven existences (bhava) solely due to the fetters of greed and hatred, since it is these [seven fetters] that lead to the seven existences.

Furthermore, there is no sūtra stating that a non-returner (anāgāmin) undergoes at most seven existences, nor is there any sūtra stating that the five higher fetters (pañca-ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana) induce rebirth in the desire realm; therefore, what they have said lacks the power of proof.
However, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), one must undergo seven births at most; within this limit, one should not insistently apply further logical principles.

Although the Noble Path may manifest during the intervening lives, the force of residual karma prevents the realization of *parinirvāṇa*. Since the Pratimokṣa discipline exists only in dependence upon the appearance of a Buddha in the world, if one does not encounter the Buddha's Dharma during that seventh existence, one will attain the fruit of Arhatship while remaining a householder.
Having attained the fruit, he would certainly not remain at home; the majestic deportment of a bhikṣu would naturally be perfected in him.
Although he had not encountered what was previously taught by former Buddhas, he developed an intense sense of revulsion toward the remainder of his life and, before long, entered parinirvāṇa.
Some say: "He went forth as a renunciant in another [non-Buddhist] path.

This is logically untenable; for one who goes to another path does so through the power of wrong views and the activation of unwholesome karma—how, then, could such a person be said to possess the quality of being non-falling?

Because they do not produce karma leading to decline; because they oppose that which produces such karma and its fruit; because powerful roots of goodness suppress their bodies; and because both their preparatory application and their resolute intention are pure.

Since those who possess karma certain to lead to rebirth in the evil destinies cannot even give rise to the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), how much less can they attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*)? Thus, a verse says:
"Though small, a fool’s transgression leads to the evil destinies; Though great, a wise person’s transgression brings liberation from suffering."
"Just as a small lump of iron sinks in water, yet a large iron bowl can float.
When the Sūtra states that the Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) makes an end to suffering (*duḥkha*), by what meaning is the term "end of suffering" established?
Based on this [attainment], there is no further suffering thereafter; this is the meaning of making future suffering not continue.
Alternatively, the limit of suffering is what is called nirvāṇa.
How could nirvāṇa be something that is produced?
To eliminate those obstacles, the term "making" (kṛtvā) is used, as in the expression "making empty," which refers to the demolition of a palace or pavilion.

If one attains the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) within the human realm, they will undergo at most seven more births among humans; the same should be understood to apply to the heavenly realms.

Even non-Aryas may have a maximum of seven more births; through the continuity [of their practice], they mature and attain the state of nirvāṇa. However, this is not certain, and for that reason it is not mentioned.
It has already been explained that one who has not yet abandoned any of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation is called a Stream-enterer (srotāpanna), who has at most seven more births.

Now, one must distinguish the various noble ones according to their stages of abandonment. For the time being, we shall establish the candidates for and the fruits of the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
The verse says:
Having abandoned the third or fourth category of desire, One is a "Family-to-Family" (*kulaṃkula*) with three or two remaining births.
Having abandoned up to five [categories of afflictions], one is a candidate for the second fruit; having abandoned six, one attains the fruit of once-returning.
The treatise says:

That is to say, when a stream-enterer proceeds to abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, if three conditions are met, they are designated as a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner.

First, by means of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*): because one abandons three or four categories of the afflictions of the desire realm through cultivation; that is to say, these afflictions were abandoned previously while in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), or they are abandoned now during the stage of progressing toward the state of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

Second, by means of the accomplishment of the faculties (*indriya*), because one attains the untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) that serve as their antidote; that is to say, one has already accomplished those three or four grades of untainted faculties which constitute the path acting as their antidote.

Third, by way of rebirth: because one may undergo two or three further births in the desire realm. That is to say, if one abandons three grades [of afflictions], one undergoes three more births; if one abandons four grades, one undergoes two more births.

These three and two births result from the performance and accumulation of karma that induces those three and two births while one is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Noble ones (*ārya*), however, while in their noble state, cannot further create new karma that draws them toward future existence, because they have turned their backs on birth and death and are oriented toward *nirvāṇa*. For this reason, the Sūtra states that noble ones only experience previously created karma and no longer create new karma.
If any one, two, or all three of these conditions are missing, it is not called "one who goes from family to family" (kulaṃkula).
Why, then, is it established as a faculty (indriya)?

Since the verse does not mention the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala) but speaks of progressing to abandon the afflictions and thereby establishing the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) that serve as their antidote, this meaning is already established by implication; therefore, it is not stated in full.
If that were the case, one should not have mentioned "three or two births," because the meaning of abandoning three or four categories [of afflictions] would already be established.

That is to say, since it is certain that one who has already progressed to the point of abandoning three or four categories of afflictions has only three or two births remaining, the characteristics of a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) would be incomplete. Therefore, the word "etc. (*ādi*) should have been stated in the verse in order to fully encompass the three characteristics of a *kulaṃkula*.
Alternatively, one should not have spoken of "three or two births.

However, the reason the verse mentions "three or two births" is that there are those who progress further than the birth they have received—whether by being born fewer times, not at all, or exceeding this number.
Other masters say: There are also those who possess the three conditions for being a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) yet are not considered *kulaṃkula*.

This refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who, having previously abandoned three or four categories of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation, abides within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Because [this state] is manifested specifically by the birth of a *kulaṃkula*, and because it constitutes the stage of further progress (*viśeṣabhāgīya*) of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), whereas such a status does not apply to one abiding in the path of seeing, they are not called *kulaṃkula* despite possessing the three conditions.

Now, upon careful examination, that statement is certainly not reasonable. One who abides in the Path of Seeing does not possess those three conditions, because at that time they are unable to cultivate the antidotes to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Only when one attains the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) that serve as their antidote do they fulfill the definition of an "untainted faculty" among these three conditions; therefore, one abiding in the Path of Seeing does not possess all three conditions, and there is no one who possesses all three conditions who is not a *kulaṅkula* (one who goes from family to family).
It should be understood that there are, in general, two types of *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family):

first, the *deva-kulaṃkula*, which refers to one who attains parinirvāṇa after being born into two or three families within the celestial realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whether in one, two, or three celestial abodes.

The "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner is one who, having been born into two or three families within the human realm, realizes parinirvāṇa; this may occur in one, two, or three of the continents. Although there are seven births, they need not necessarily complete all seven, nor do they attain nirvāṇa in the interim before reaching the stage of "family-to-family."
To which category does this belong?

It is subsumed under the "seven births" (*sapta-janman*). The term "maximum" (*parama*) used here indicates the greatest number; by this, it is already implied that those who attain *parinirvāṇa* before their births are completed are also included therein.
Those with the most dull faculties may undergo up to seven births; however, those with sharp faculties do not necessarily complete all seven births.
Why, then, is one who has abandoned five [categories of] defilements also called a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family)?

Because when one abandons the fifth category, one must necessarily abandon the sixth; it is not the case that a single grade of delusion can obstruct the attainment of the fruit, just as one who has only one interval remaining has not yet transcended the realm.

One who is a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) proceeds to abandon from one grade up to five grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm; it should be understood that such a person is then designated as one "progressing toward the fruit of once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka).

If they abandon the sixth grade, they attain the fruit of once-returner. Having gone once to the heavenly realm and returned once to the human realm, they attain parinirvāṇa; this is called the fruit of once-returner because there is no further rebirth beyond this point.

By this very principle, it is established that among those who attain the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) stage, if one is a celestial family-to-family practitioner who undergoes three births, they undergo two births as a human and three births in the heavens.
If one undergoes two births, they undergo one birth as a human and two births in the heavens.

The case of the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) among humans should be explained by analogy with this. If one were to say otherwise, what difference would there be between that fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and that family-to-family who undergoes two more births?
Because that [once-returner] has only the inferior grades of greed, hatred, and delusion remaining, the fruit of once-returner is precisely termed "one whose greed, hatred, and delusion are thin."
Having already distinguished the stages of the candidate for and the fruit of the Once-returner, one should next establish the candidate for and the fruit of the Non-returner.
The verse says:
"Having abandoned seven or eight grades, One birth remaining is called 'One-interval' (ekavīcika)."
This is the third candidate, who abandons the nine [defilements] to attain the fruit of non-returner.
The treatise says:
When a once-returner proceeds to abandon the remaining afflictions, if three conditions are met, he is designated as an "ekavīcika" (one-intervener).
First, by the abandonment of afflictions, because one abandons seven or eight categories of afflictions of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation.

Second, by the attainment of faculties, because one acquires the untainted faculties of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) which serve as antidotes to those [afflictions].
Third, by way of rebirth, because one must undergo one further birth among the gods of the desire realm or among humans.
If any one of these three conditions is missing, or two are missing, or all are entirely absent, one is not called an "ekavīcika" (one-intervaller).

This is not mentioned in the verse concerning the attainment of the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), nor is it stated that one must further explain the cause for [attaining] a single birth; this should be explained accordingly by analogy with the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioner.

What is called "intermediate" (*antara*) is a synonym for "interval" (*chidra*); it means that because there is an interval within that state capable of admitting one more birth, one has not yet attained *nirvāṇa*.

Alternatively, "ekavicika" (one-intervener) refers here to the sense of being separated by an interval; that is, because at that stage there remains one more birth as an intervening period, one does not realize parinirvāṇa.
One who has this single interval is called an ekavicika.
How is it that having one remaining grade of afflictions to be abandoned can act as an obstacle, causing one to take birth in the desire realm, such that they are called "One-Interval" (Ekavīcika)?

If one has not yet attained the fruit of Non-returner (Anāgāmiphala), the abandonment of this final grade constitutes a transcendence of the ground of the two fruits—maturation (*vipāka*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*)—associated with the desire realm, which are produced by karma and afflictions. Since that [remaining grade] acts as an extreme obstacle, further rebirth is possible; however, when six grades have been abandoned, one has not yet transcended that ground. Therefore, there is no taking of birth in the intermediate state after abandoning five grades, nor can the fruit of Once-returner (Sakṛdāgāmiphala) be realized in the present body.

It should be understood that one who has abandoned seven or eight grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation is also called a candidate for the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmipratipannaka*).

If one who previously abandoned three, four, seven, or eight grades of afflictions entered the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), at the time they subsequently attain the fruit, would they be called a "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) or a "one-interval" (*ekavīcika*)?

This is not yet called "one who goes from family to family" (kulaṃkula) or "one with one interval" (ekavicika), because the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) that remedy those [defilements] have not yet been attained.
At the initial stage of attaining the fruit, the path of the fruit (phalamārga) is manifest; at that time, the path of superior fruit (viśeṣamārga) has not yet been cultivated.

It is only upon reaching the subsequent stage and giving rise to the path of superior fruit that one is designated as "one who goes from family to family" or "one with one interval," for it is only then that the untainted faculties which remedy those [defilements] are attained.

If the designations "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) and "one-interval" (*ekavicika*) were established only for those who have progressed to the stage of abandoning defilements as *srotāpannas* and *sakṛdāgāmins*, why does the Sugata state in the *Hastikakṣya-sūtra* that the seven-times-born and the once-returner abandon defilements in the same way as them?
As that sūtra states: "What is a 'family-to-family' (kulaṃkula) practitioner?

It refers to one who has eternally abandoned and fully understood the three fetters, beginning with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and will undergo rebirth at most seven times; it should be known that this is likewise [the case for others]."
What is the "one-interval" (ekavīcika)?

It refers to one who has eternally abandoned and fully understood the three fetters, beginning with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and has already attenuated sensual desire, hatred, and delusion.
The same applies to the "once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin); there is no contradiction, as it was not stated that [the abandonment] is exclusive.
As stated in the Sūtra:

regarding the Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), it is said that the Stream-enterer has eternally severed the three fetters (saṃyojana), yet he has not yet severed the remaining fetters.

It is further said that the Stream-enterer has eternally severed six factors: first, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi); second, the view of grasping at extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi); third, false view (mithyādṛṣṭi); fourth, craving conducive to the miserable destinies (apāya-gāmi-tṛṣṇā); fifth, hatred conducive to the miserable destinies; and sixth, delusion conducive to the miserable destinies.
Furthermore, it is said that a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) permanently abandons the three fetters and attenuates greed, hatred, and delusion, but it does not say they attenuate conceit.

Nor is it said that they abandon the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) and false views (mithyādṛṣṭi), as is the case with the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna); it is not that the fruit of once-returning fails to attenuate conceit or to abandon the view of extremes and false views.
However, since that sūtra does not state "only," and because it gives rise to the antidote for those [defilements], they must necessarily also be abandoned.

Thus, regarding what was said concerning the *kulaṅkula* (one who goes from family to family) and the *ekavīcika* (one with one interval), since it does not say "only," there is no fault in proceeding to abandon them further.
Furthermore, a sutra states:

"The number of their births is diminished. One can know with certainty that, compared to stream-enterers and once-returners, they have abandoned even more afflictions, because all afflictions are the causes of birth.
Precisely for this reason, it is known that, compared to the former, he has necessarily already produced a superior counteractive agent (*pratipakṣa*).

If that is so, why is it said that the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) and the *ekavīcika* (one who has one interval) have abandoned afflictions similar to those abandoned by the *saptakṛdbhava* (one who is reborn seven times at most) and the *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner)?

This is because it is intended to reveal that this [state] is a specific differentiation of that [state], or because the progress made toward abandoning the subtle [defilements] is difficult to perceive.

Alternatively, one should further seek the reasons for the commonality of their descriptions; one must not cite these fragments of esoteric teachings and thereby definitively conclude that the defilements abandoned by those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*) and those with one interval (*ekavīcika*) are similar to those abandoned by stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
The Elder’s intention was as follows:

the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) and the *ekavīcika* (one who has one interval remaining) differ from the *saptakṛtvaḥparama* (one who is reborn seven times at most) and the *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) only in terms of their faculties, which are exclusively sharp.

That is to say, those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who attain [the fruit] accordingly become *srotaāpanna* (stream-enterers); once they have become stream-enterers, they are further designated as "resolute through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*), and are also termed "those who are reborn at most seven times."

All those who follow the practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārin) upon attaining the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) are, if they have become stream-enterers, further designated as "those who have attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta). In this very stage, they are also called "those who go from family to family" (kulaṃkula), because such noble ones possess sharp and keen faculties; having been born into three or two more families, they then realize parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, among those who are "resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*), if one attains the state of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), they remain called "resolved through faith" as long as they are a once-returner; in this very stage, they undergo two more births.

Likewise, among those who are "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), if one attains the state of a once-returner, they remain called "attained through vision"; in this very stage, they are also termed a "single-interval" (*ekavīcika*). Because the faculties of such noble ones are sharp and keen, they experience only one interval of birth before realizing parinirvāṇa.
Such an establishment is not consistent with correct reasoning, because the term "maximum" (*parama*) indicates that birth is at its greatest number.

If one who attains parinirvāṇa after three or two births following the fruit of stream-entry were called a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family), how would this differ from one who has seven births at most (*saptakṛtparama*) and yet attains parinirvāṇa after only three or two births?

Furthermore, since it is asserted that one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and possesses sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*)—being a "family-to-family" (*kolopaka*) practitioner who is reborn in three or two families before attaining parinirvāṇa—is included among those who attain parinirvāṇa after seven births at most, and since it is also admitted that such a person may pass through three or two intermediate births before realizing final peace, how can you maintain that such a person is necessarily of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*)?
It is not the case that those of dull faculties cannot also be called "sharp" [in certain contexts]; therefore, what they have established does not accord with correct reasoning.

Furthermore, if one who is an *ekavīcika* (one-interval practitioner) attains parinirvāṇa after undergoing only one more existence solely because of being of sharp faculties, how can he be said to be identical to the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner)?
It is permitted that a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) is so called because they are born for a second time [in the desire realm].

Furthermore, that treatise states that it does not preclude the once-returner; rather, it is only regarding the heavenly realms that there is the principle of being born again, whereas for those who are "one-interval" (ekavicika), such a thing need not exist. This is not a case of being born again in a single realm, as they are not [simply] once-returners.

Furthermore, it would be impossible to establish the designation "one-interval" (ekavicika) on the grounds that it is separated by two births; for one should not say that a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) undergoes only two births exclusively within the celestial realm, since it is taught that such a person attains parinirvāṇa [in that very life].
If one were to undergo two births, how could one be called a "single-interval" (ekavīcika)?
Therefore, what they say—that such a thing might not exist—is untenable; this statement is logical.

Furthermore, for a "once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin), there can certainly be no possibility of taking two successive births within the heavenly realm (*devagati*), because otherwise there would be no distinction between them and those "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioners who are permitted by them [the opponents] to take two births within the heavenly realm.

If it is argued that, just as it is said "at most seven more existences," the term "seven times" is used based on the maximum limit while in reality there are those who do not complete this number, and likewise, the designation "Once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin) is established based on the maximum—meaning one attains parinirvāṇa after at most one return—while in reality there are also those who are reborn in the heavens and attain parinirvāṇa without returning to the human realm; this too is irrational, because the aforementioned fault persists.

Furthermore, what difference is there between that dull-facultied once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) whom you accept—who, after experiencing one birth among the gods, attains parinirvāṇa without returning to the human realm—and that "one-intervener" (ekavicika)?

There is no definitive principle that restricts those of dull faculties to necessarily attain parinirvāṇa only after returning to the human realm; if they do not return, they would instead become *ekavicika* (one-interval) beings.
Since it is not the case that those of dull faculties cannot also be called "noble ones" (*ārya*), what has been established [by the opponent] does not accord with correct reasoning.

Furthermore, what they assert contradicts the sūtras, for there are sūtras that speak of the nature of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), and state that if one attains superior roots of goodness, one is likewise called "sharp-facultied" (*tīkṣṇendriya*) and so forth.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If one possesses the five faculties that are superior, sharp, and perfectly complete, they are called an Arhat of 'liberation through both';
if one possesses the five faculties that are gradually inferior and dull, they are called 'liberated by wisdom' (prajñāvimukta)," and so on, as explained at length.
In this sutra, those who are liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) and have attained the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa) are also called those of sharp faculties;
if one has not yet attained the eight liberations, even if they are liberated at any time (asamayavimukta), they are called those of dull faculties.

If those of the lineage of faith-and-understanding (śraddhādhimukta) attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), they are also said to be of sharp faculties (tīkṣṇendriya) and bodily witnesses (kāyasākṣin);
if one has not yet attained the absorption of cessation, although they may be one who has reached through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), they are termed of dull faculties (mṛdvindriya).
Thus, one of the nature of faith-and-understanding who has attained a superior remedy is renamed "One-Interval" (ekābhisamaya);
however, if one has not yet obtained a superior remedy, they are merely called "Once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin), despite possessing the nature of "Vision-attainment" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

In this way, one should understand that the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) and "seven-times-at-most" (saptakṛtvaḥparama) [attainments] are likewise established. Therefore, the position that those designated as family-to-family and one-interval (ekavīcika) possess only sharp faculties is not logically sound.
Furthermore, the treatise of that school states as follows:
The classification of the abandonment of afflictions according to specific categories is not the true holy teaching.
The "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) and "one-interval" (*ekavicika*) stages established by that school consist only of those with sharp faculties;

how could these be the true holy teaching? It is not that the Sthavira himself admits his own person, nor do I admit him to be a truly great sage; how then can he claim his own words are subsumed under the holy teaching?
The Buddha has never stated such a thing anywhere.
Furthermore, what they say contradicts other authoritative scriptures (*āgama*), and thus they cannot claim it to be included within the authoritative scriptures themselves.

Nevertheless, the abandonment of afflictions through distinct stages is not contrary to the true authoritative scriptures, for the Blessed One taught that the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) involves the permanent abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion.

Lust, hatred, and delusion are not like pieces of wood that can be gradually thinned by cutting; rather, they can only be severed through successive stages of classification, where the remaining inferior grade is described as "thinned."
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"All non-returners have already abandoned desire and hatred without remainder.

Using this as evidence, we know that at the stage of once-returner, there still remain categories of desire and hatred that have not been abandoned; it is only upon reaching this present stage that they are abandoned without remainder.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"In the stage of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), one has already eternally severed all craving for the realms of existence and the evil destinies.
From this, it is proven that in the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and other stages, some categories [of afflictions] have been severed while others remain unremoved.

Furthermore, since it has already been demonstrated that one must attain superior remedies (*pratipakṣa*) before one can be established as a "house-to-house" (*kulaṃkula*) or "one-interval" (*ekavicika*) practitioner, and since one attains such superior remedies at those stages, it is known that the exhaustion of desire and other afflictions differs from what preceded; thus, the principle of abandoning afflictions through distinct categories is established, as has also been shown in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa*.
Furthermore, that treatise asks:

"By what cause and condition is it admitted that when abandoning afflictions, they are abandoned according to distinct categories, such that only nine categories are admitted and not ten or a thousand?
This objection is invalid, because only such ninefold distinctions of antidotes arise.

This means that at the stage of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), as the nine grades of the path arise within each respective level (*bhūmi*), one is able to permanently sever all the afflictions subsumed under that level; therefore, there is no need to laboriously establish [distinctions] such as ten or a thousand [grades].

Furthermore, because they are identical to those abandoned through seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*), that school admits that when abandoning afflictions (*kleśa*), there is also the sense of abandoning them in distinct categories; for they maintain that the various delusions abandoned through the paths of seeing and cultivation are severed sequentially upon entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
Since you have granted this, one may further challenge you:

For what reason do you allow for the abandonment of afflictions in distinct stages, yet establish only two categories—those abandoned through seeing and those abandoned through cultivation—rather than three or a thousand?
Since he has already granted that, this case should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, the Blessed One also spoke thus in the sūtras:
"The abandonment of afflictions occurs in nine grades."

As previously established based on that [scripture], the Buddha, having attained sovereign mastery and thorough penetration of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), spoke thus. This should be accepted as authoritative;

one ought not to subject it to frivolous questioning or interrogation. Therefore, it is only within the path of advancement (*viśeṣamārga*) toward the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) that the "One-interval" practitioner (*ekavīcika*) is established, and not while abiding in the fruit of Once-returner itself.

Furthermore, it is within the path of further advancement (viśeṣamārga) of the fruit of stream-entry that the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) stage is established, not while abiding in the fruit of stream-entry itself.
Such is the reasoning; this principle is necessarily so.

That is to say, when one who has already attained the fruit of once-returner exhausts all nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm, they relinquish the name "once-returner" and attain the fruit of non-returner, because they will certainly not again undergo birth within the desire realm.
This may be termed the "abandonment of the five lower fetters," as stated in the Sūtra:
"If one has eternally severed the five lower-fettering bonds, one is called a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

This statement is made with reference to the sequential abandonment [of the fetters]; for there is no possibility that the five fetters could be severed simultaneously, as two or three must have already been severed beforehand.
In truth, it should be stated:
within this stage, one abandons two or three [fetters] and attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 64.
