translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Nine: Distinguishing the Noble and Holy Ones, Part Six, Section Nine. Based on various sūtras concerning the stage of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), distinctions are established through diverse approaches; we shall now distinguish their specific characteristics.
The verse says:
Among these, there is one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion, one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion,
and those who stream upward through mixed cultivation, capable of proceeding to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
The leaper, the half-leaper, and the one who passes away completely; others can go to the Peak of Existence.
There are four types of those who practice the formless attainments; some attain parinirvāṇa while remaining here [in the desire realm].
The Commentary says:
These non-returners are generally said to be of seven types; specifically, there are five distinctions among those who proceed to the form realm:

first, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin); second, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin); third, those who attain parinirvāṇa through exertion (sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin); fourth, those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin); and fifth, those who go upstream (ūrdhvasrotas).
Because this one attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, it is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin).

One should understand accordingly that these are named "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin) and so forth because they attain parinirvāṇa after being born, or by means of effort (sābhisaṃskāra), or without effort (anabhisaṃskāra); and because this one is an "upper-streamer" (ūrdhvaṃsrotas), they are called "upper-streamers."

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*): this refers to a certain class of *pudgalas* who have already attained non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the fetters of birth, but not so regarding the fetters of arising.

When such a person encounters the conditions for affliction within the desire realm and is thus oppressed, they are able to exert themselves to cultivate the superior application (*prayoga*) for abandoning the remaining fetters. Before their application is complete, they encounter the conditions for death and pass away. By the power of the fetters of arising, they take up a form-realm intermediate existence (*rūpa-antarābhava*). Because they loathe the abundance of suffering, they rely on the path previously generated to advance and abandon the remaining fetters, thereby becoming an Arhat and attaining parinirvāṇa.

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*): this refers to a certain class of individuals (*pudgala*) who, because they previously possessed and cultivated karma conducive to arising and rebirth, pass away from the desire realm and take birth in the form realm. Due to possessing the path of swift progress through diligent cultivation, they become arhats not long after being born; they then enter parinirvāṇa only at the exhaustion of their lifespan.

One is said to attain parinirvāṇa upon birth (upapadya-parinirvāyin) with reference to the state where a remainder of the substrate of existence persists; it does not mean that one attains the nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa) immediately after being born, because such a person lacks mastery over the relinquishing of their lifespan.

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa through exertion (sābhisamskāra-parinirvāyin) and those who attain it without exertion (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin): this refers to a certain class of individuals who, after being born, only become arhats (aśaikṣas) after a long period. Among them, one is characterized by courageous diligence, while another is by nature slow and indolent; these are designated as "with exertion" and "without exertion," respectively.

This refers to a certain class of individuals who, while previously in the desire realm, by relying on the power of the samādhi of uninterrupted application, sever the five lower fetters and attain the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*). Later, having been reborn in the form realm after a long period of time, they are further able to cultivate the path of the same category and attain the fruit of arhatship; these are called those who attain parinirvāṇa through exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*).
Those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*) are the opposite of this.

Alternatively, having been born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) for a long time, one who attains liberation from the remaining fetters by relying on ascetic practices is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa through application" (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*), because they attain parinirvāṇa by practicing the path of effort;
that which is contrary to this is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa without application" (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*).

Is it not the case that since the modes of practice upon which those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), at birth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and upon manifestation (*abhisamskāraparinirvāyin*) rely also possess these [characteristics], one should establish for them the names "with effort" (*sābhisamskāra*) and "without effort" (*anabhisamskāra*)?
There is no such fault, because although this principle is equal, each of those [categories] possesses its own distinct stages.

This means that although those such as the "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin) also definitely rely on either painful or pleasant practice to liberate themselves from the remaining fetters, each of them has distinct stages of attainment; thus, in contrast to these, they are called "unshared distinctions.

Since this [attainment] lacks such distinct stages, its differences are manifested by way of the diversity of the paths. How, then, can this be used as an analogy for that [other case] to make them identical?
Therefore, there is no fault in what has been argued here.

Consequently, regarding those who claim there is a distinction between the two [types of nirvāṇa], it should be understood that because one attains nirvāṇa through the noble path conditioned by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) respectively, the same fault does not apply to them either.

The critique raised by the Master of the Sūtras (*sūtrakāra*) involves a great error; for while it is true that this principle has already been well explained—that although [the states] are equal, each possesses its own distinct stage—there are sūtras that state "non-application" (*apravṛtti*) comes first, and there are also sūtras in which "application" (*pravṛtti*) is mentioned first. Since there is no difference in time, there is no contradiction in whichever is spoken of; however, because "application" is worthy of esteem, I have mentioned it first.

Regarding the term "one who goes upstream" (ūrdhvasrotas): this refers to a certain class of individuals for whom the upward flow increases; they do not realize parinirvāṇa in the very place where they were first born.

That is to say, having passed away from the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and been reborn in the form realm (rūpadhātu), they do not realize parinirvāṇa therein, but must instead be reborn in a higher region before attaining parinirvāṇa.
There are two distinctions among these *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards), based on differences in their causes and their results.
Regarding the difference in causes: this is due to whether or not there has been mixed cultivation (*miśra-bhāvanā*) within the dhyānas.
Regarding the distinction of the fruit: because Akaniṣṭha Heaven and the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra) are the ultimate limits.

That is to say, if one has practiced the meditative cultivation of the dhyānas with intermingling, one can go to Akaniṣṭha and there attain parinirvāṇa, because such mixed cultivation is capable of inducing the fruit of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa).

This [attainment] further has three distinctions, based on the differences between "complete leaping over" (*atyantātyaya*), "half-leaping over" (*ardhapluta*), and "falling away everywhere" (*sarvasthānacyuta*).

Regarding "complete leaping over": this refers to one who, having previously cultivated the four dhyānas through mixed practice while still in a body within the desire realm, loses the upper three dhyānas due to encountering certain conditions. Taking the relish for the first dhyāna as a condition, they die and are reborn in the Brahmakāyika heaven. From there, they pass away from one place in the form realm and proceed directly to Akaniṣṭha.
Due to the force of habitual practice from previous lives, one is further able to practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna; passing away from that state, one is reborn in Akaniṣṭha.

Because one passes away in the first location among the sixteen locations of the form realm and is reborn in the final location, leaping over all the intermediate stages, this is the meaning of "complete transcendence" (sakalābhisambheda).

Regarding the term "half-leaping" (*ardhapluta*): it refers to those within the realm of form who, passing away gradually from the first heaven and so forth, descend as far as the intermediate heavens, and are able to leap over one station before proceeding to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; because they leap but not entirely, this is the meaning of "half-leaping."

Regarding the term "universal dissolution" (*sarvasthānacyuta*): it refers to one who, due to an abundance of craving for the flavors of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), is born in every location. Because such a person possesses inferior degrees of craving for each of the sixteen locations within the four dhyāna stages as the causal condition for rebirth, they pass away from each successive location—beginning from the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (*brahmakāyika*)—and only after reaching the Akaniṣṭha heaven do they finally attain parinirvāṇa; therefore, it is called "universal dissolution."
By this principle, it follows that the abode of Mahābrahmā within the First Dhyāna is not a separate realm, but is subsumed under the second Brahmakāyika heaven.
Were it otherwise, because the abode of Mahābrahmā is a place of heterodox views and has but a single leader, no noble ones (ārya) would ever take birth therein.
There would be no distinction between those who "die everywhere" (sarvacyuta) and those who "leap over half" (ardhapluta).

One should know that among these two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards), it is because they possess the cause of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) of the dhyānas that those who go to Akaniṣṭha attain parinirvāṇa there; whereas others, who lack the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas, are able to go only as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) before attaining parinirvāṇa.

This means that because they previously lacked the practice of meditative absorption through mixed cultivation (*miśra-bhāvanā*), and due to their attachment to the savoring of various concentrations as a condition, they pass away from here and are reborn throughout all the levels of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), except that they alone cannot go to the five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*).

Having passed away from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and having been born successively in the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), one subsequently attains parinirvāṇa in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Between these two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upward), the former is one of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-carita*) and the latter is one of meditative concentration practice (*samatha-carita*), due to the distinction between delighting in wisdom (*prajñā*) and delighting in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

It is not contrary to reason that those of the two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who stream upward) attain parinirvāṇa within the lower stages; however, the statement that they go to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven or the Bhavāgra Heaven is made based on their ultimate destination.

There is no non-returner who undergoes a second birth in the place where they have already been born, because such a person may seek further progress rather than equality or inferiority within that birth; thus, they pass away only from the desire realm and are reborn in the form realm.

There are those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). This does not refer to one who dies in the form realm and is reborn in the form realm, because there are no calamities within the form realm.

If, during the prior existence (*pūrvabhava*), one fails to attain nirvāṇa due to the presence of other obstructing conditions, the same applies to the intermediate state; for the intermediate state is inferior and not equivalent to the prior existence.
Furthermore, if such a person existed, they would have to be classified as one who attains parinirvāṇa in the upper realms (*ūrdhvasrotas*);

there would then be no distinction between one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) and one who attains it in the upper realms. That is to say, there is certainly no causal basis for making the claim that one who passes away in the desire realm and undergoes the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the form realm can then attain parinirvāṇa immediately.

One who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) does not do so after passing away from the form realm. For what reason is it that there is no learner (śaikṣa) who has not yet abandoned desire and greed who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state?

It is because the body upon which the intermediate existence (antarābhava) depends in the desire realm is weak and inferior, and thus lacks the capacity for the many tasks [required for such a transition].

While in the state of abiding in the prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*), one already finds it difficult to transcend the dharmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); how much more so in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) could one transcend the desire realm to attain the fruit of arhatship?

One who performs many tasks refers to one who transcends the three realms, eternally abandons the two types of afflictions (*kleśa*), and attains the realization of two or three fruits of the śramaṇa;
such capacity does not exist for one abiding in the state of intermediate existence.
Furthermore, because this [intermediate state] has not previously practiced the remedies for the nine grades of afflictions;

because the fruits such as that of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) are not attained by means of an intermediate body, being realized through the abandonment of predominant delusions; and because it is extremely difficult to become free from the defilements of the three realms, there is no one in the intermediate state of the desire realm who can attain parinirvāṇa.
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) differs from these in all respects; therefore, there are those who attain *nirvāṇa* within it.
Furthermore, those who attain *parinirvāṇa* in this intermediate state of the form realm give rise only to the noble path (*āryamārga*) belonging to that very intermediate state.

Among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state within the level of the first dhyāna, only the noble path of the fundamental dhyāna of that own level arises manifest; the preparatory (anāgamya) or intermediate (dhyānāntara) stages do not, because it is difficult to cause them to manifest.
In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because the physical basis is extremely weak, only those [attainments] that are easily aroused can manifest.
These five are called those who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

There are four distinctions regarding those who proceed to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): namely, having abandoned attachment to the form realm while in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they pass away from there and are reborn in the formless realm; within this, there are only four types of distinction, due to the differences such as "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*) and so forth.
Together with the five previously mentioned, these constitute six types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).

Furthermore, there are those who do not proceed to the realms of form or formlessness, but instead attain parinirvāṇa while remaining right here; they are called "those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*).
Together with the previous six, these constitute seven.

Alternatively, one should establish nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) in total; that is, those who attain nirvāṇa in the present life are divided into two kinds: first, those who were already well-versed in the noble intent during their prior stage; and second, those who are only able to become well-versed in it at the time of death.
Within the upward-streaming (ūrdhvasrotas) category, there are also two types: those who proceed to the form realm (rūpadhātu) and those who proceed to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Together with the previous four, these constitute eight; when combined with the "transformative birth" (parivṛtti-janman), they total nine.

Regarding the term "transitioning birth" (*saṃcārajanman*): it refers to one who, having already attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) or once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*) in a previous life, attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) only within this present life.

The term "attaining parinirvāṇa in the present existence" (*dṛṣṭadharmaparinirvāyin*) refers exclusively to those who first enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*) and reach nirvana within the present life.
Alternatively, the Non-returners are divided into nine types according to the distinctions of their faculties as appropriate.
Or, among the five types of Non-returners who proceed to the Form Realm, there is another classification that divides them into nine types.
The verse says:
There are nine types of those who practice in the form realm; that is, each of the three [categories] is divided into three.
Due to differences in karma, afflictions, and faculties, they thus constitute the distinction of three groups of nine.
The treatise says:

Regarding those who proceed to the form realm (rūpadhātu), the five types of non-returners (anāgāmin) are collectively established as three; each of these is further divided into three types, thus forming nine varieties.
What are these three?

Because there are distinctions among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain it upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and those who ascend to higher realms (*ūrdhvasrotas*). How is each of these three types further divided into three?

Regarding the division of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state into three: this is due to the distinction between attaining parinirvāṇa after first arising [in the intermediate state], after traveling a long distance, or after traveling a short distance before reaching the place of rebirth.

The *upapadya-parinirvāyin* (those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth) are divided into three types based on the differences between those who attain it immediately after birth (*sahasopapanna*), those who attain it with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*), and those who attain it without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Since all of these attain parinirvāṇa after having been born, they should all collectively be designated as *upapadya-parinirvāyins*.

Regarding the division of the *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards) into three types, this is due to the differences between the "complete leaper" (*pluta*), the "half-leaper" (*ardhapluta*), and the "one who dies everywhere" (*sarvasthānacyuta*).
Nevertheless, as all three types attain parinirvāṇa through either swift, non-swift, or prolonged means, they are further divided into nine types without any confusion.
Thus, these three types and nine types of non-returners, due to differences in karma, afflictions, and faculties, possess the distinctions of being swift, not swift, or taking a long time.

Furthermore, these are collectively established as three types because of the differences in the accumulated karma conducive to arising that produces subsequent existence; specifically, because there are distinctions in the manifestation of afflictions according to their sequence as inferior, middling, and superior, and because there are differences in the faculties as superior, middling, and inferior.

Each of these three [categories] likewise possesses its own distinctions according to their respective correspondences; because there are differences in karma, afflictions, and faculties, each has three further subdivisions, thus resulting in nine types in total.
This means that the first three [categories] each consist of three types due to differences in afflictions and faculties, rather than due to differences in karma.
The latter three also consist of three types because there are distinctions among the karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karma*).

Therefore, it is said that those who proceed by way of form (rūpaga) and are non-returners (anāgāmin) are divided into three groups of nine based on differences in their karma, afflictions (kleśa), and faculties (indriya).
If this is so, why do the various sūtras state that there are only seven destinations for noble beings (satpuruṣagati)?
The verse says:
Seven destinies of the noble persons are established because there is no distinction among those who go upstream;
because of the performance or non-performance of good and evil deeds; and because of going forth without returning.
The Treatise says:

There are three types each for those who attain nirvana in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) and those who attain nirvana upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*); those who "flow upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) constitute one.

Based on this, the Sūtra establishes the seven destinies of the noble persons (*satpuruṣagati*). Why are the first two each divided into three, while the third, the upward-flowing, is established as only one?
Because they proceed upward, they are called "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas); for this reason, despite their similarities, they are established as a single category.

Although the preceding two types are also similar in meaning, their internal specific characteristics are difficult to discern; therefore, each is divided into three for the sake of easy understanding.
In contrast, the Upstreamers have three distinct characteristics that are easily understood, so there is no need to establish further subdivisions among them.
Furthermore, the first two [types of non-returner] have only that many distinct varieties because they are easy to demonstrate; thus, each is divided into three.
The third, the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), has many types of distinct meanings that are difficult to demonstrate at once; therefore, it is established as one category in total.

That is to say, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon initial entry exist only while still in the process of being born; they are divided into three types due to differences in their faculties and the degree of their afflictions.
Those who attain parinirvāṇa after being born exist only once they have already been born; these too are divided into three types due to differences in their faculties and afflictions.

Regarding the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), there are those who are about to be born and those who have already been born. The "Upstreamer who is about to be born" is further divided into two types, namely: those who practice the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) in a mixed manner and those who practice them in an unmixed manner. The same division applies to the "Upstreamer who has already been born."

Furthermore, among these two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who stream upward), if there is no mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*), rebirth may occur in both realms; if there is mixed cultivation, rebirth occurs in only one realm.

Those who are reborn in a single realm are further divided into three types, distinguished by being "leapers" (*pluta*), "half-leapers" (*ardhapluta*), or "those who pass away everywhere" (*sarvasthānacyuta*).

Within the "half-leapers" (*ardhapluta*), there are many internal distinctions; because the specific characteristics of these various types of "upstreamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) would be too extensive to detail, and because it would be difficult to provide a complete explanation for each one individually, they are collectively established as "upstreamers" based on their common essential meaning.
Within the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), the distinctions in meaning are slight and easily discernible; therefore, it is divided into six.
Although each of these also possesses aspects of similarity, they are equal to the third [category].
Although there are differing interpretations regarding the *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards), it is equivalent to the previous two [types].
Because they are established to mutually illustrate one another, only seven are posited.

Since these alone have abandoned the unvirtuous qualities of desire-greed (*kāmarāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and so forth, and are extremely close to the fruit of a Great Virtuous Being (*mahāsatpurusa*) who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the Sūtra refers to them alone as the "destinations of virtuous beings" (*satpuruṣagati*).
It is not meant that stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*) cannot at all be called "noble persons" (*satpuruṣagati*); for the Buddha also spoke of them as noble persons.
As a sūtra says: "What is a noble person?"
This refers to being endowed with the right view of one in training (*śaikṣa*), up to and including being endowed with the right concentration of one in training.
"Ascending" (*ūrdhvaga*) means "tending toward," specifically tending toward higher fruits and tending toward higher rebirths; therefore, only seven [limbs] are mentioned.
Alternatively, it may be that only these seven are capable of practicing what is wholesome and refraining from what is unwholesome, whereas the others are not so;
furthermore, it may be that only these seven are born into the higher realms and do not return again, whereas the others are not thus.
Therefore, it is solely on this basis that the "destinations of the virtuous" (satpuruṣagati) are established.
Is there also such a distinction among those who, while in the state of a noble one (ārya), have already undergone rebirth? No.
How is this so? The verse says:
An Arya who has been born in the Desire Realm does not go to be born in another realm.
Regarding this and those born in the higher realms, there is neither the refinement of faculties nor falling away.
The treatise says:

If one is in the stage of an Arya and undergoes birth in the Desire Realm, they will certainly not be reborn in the Form or Formless Realms; for having realized the fruit of Non-returner (Anāgāmin), they are destined to attain parinirvāṇa in that very same body.

If a noble one (*ārya*) who has undergone births in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) were to be reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), that would be possible; however, when Śakra, Lord of the Devas, says, "I have heard there is a heaven named Akaniṣṭha, and when I eventually fall from here, I shall be born there," it is because he does not understand the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Abhidharma.
"Later than I" refers to the ultimate limit of the sovereign maturation of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
"Falling away" means that at a later time, one does not attain the fruit of arhatship.
"Those who would be born there" refers to those who vow to be born in Akaniṣṭha Heaven and not to be born in the desire realm.
Because Śakra, Lord of the Devas, experienced extreme sorrow and suffering due to the five signs of death, he came to take refuge in the World-Honored One;
once the signs of death had just been removed, he spoke these words for the sake of bringing about joy.
Furthermore, because obstructing them would yield little benefit, the Buddha did not prohibit it.

Thus, for those who have already undergone birth in the desire realm, as well as those who have already been reborn from here into the higher realms, noble ones (ārya) will certainly never undergo the refinement of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) nor experience regression.

For what reason is it not admitted that noble ones who have already taken birth in the desire realm or in higher realms possess the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) as well as retrogression?

Because they have previously been born within their own continuum and have accumulated the noble path until it is extremely firm, and because they have obtained a particularly excellent basis-body (*āśraya-kāya*), there is no logical possibility for them to refine their faculties or to undergo retrogression.

It was previously stated that the upward-streamer (*ūrdhvasrotas*), by taking the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas as a cause, is able to go to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Which dhyāna should one first mix-cultivate?
And by what stage is it known that the mixed cultivation has been accomplished?
Furthermore, for what reason does one practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna?
The verse says:
First, one mixes the fourth [dhyāna]; its accomplishment arises from a single moment of mixing.
"For the sake of receiving birth, manifesting pleasure, and preventing decline through afflictions.
The treatise says:

Those who practice the mixed cultivation of the four dhyānas must first practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna, because that meditative concentration is most capable and because it is the most excellent among all pleasant practices.

This means that when this dhyāna, which possesses the greatest capacity, manifests, it causes the power of the physical basis—the self-body—to increase and expand. Therefore, even if one relies on this mixed cultivation of dhyāna and subsequently falls away to be reborn among other devas, by virtue of the power of having previously cultivated that mixture, one is again able to rely upon that mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
It is for this reason that the fourth dhyāna is the most excellent among all practices of bliss, because its pliancy-bliss (*praśrabdhi-sukha*) is supremely sublime.
Who is it that can cultivate these dhyānas through a mixed practice?
Only the noble ones, comprising both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), [attain this].

Among those in training, it applies only to those who have attained faith through understanding (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have reached vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); among those beyond training, it applies to both those liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) and those not liberated by time (*asamayavimukta*).

One must first practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna within the three continents; even those who have regressed and been reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are also able to practice mixed cultivation.

But is it not the case that one who practices the mixed cultivation of the various dhyānas must have already abandoned desire for the [lower] three dhyānas? How, then, can it be said that the mixed cultivation of dhyāna applies to those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and yet become "stream-enterers bound for the upper realms" (*ūrdhvasrotas*)?

This means that one must first practice the mixed cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as a human being; subsequently, having regressed from the third dhyāna, one is born in the Brahmakāyika heaven. Therein, one must again become free from the defilements of the three dhyanas before being able to once more initiate the mixed cultivation of *dhyāna*. Only after passing away from there and being born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens is one designated an "Upstreamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

As previously stated, this principle does not apply to those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), because they necessarily do not regress from their freedom from passion; thus, such a fault does not arise, for it is not admitted that they have resided in the faculties of one who has attained vision since time immemorial.

That is to say, one who previously resided in the lineage of faith-understanding (śraddhādhimukta-gotra) practices the mixed cultivation of dhyāna and subsequently falls away; fearing that there will be further occasions of falling away in the future, they then cultivate the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) and achieve the nature of "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta-gotra).

Having passed away from the desire realm and been reborn in the form realm, one is able to further practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna based on previous attainment; therefore, all six types of spiritual lineages possess the "upward-streamer" (ūrdhvasrotas).
What skillful means are employed at the time of this mixed cultivation?

He must first enter the fourth dhyāna, wherein many moments of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states arise in succession; from this, he induces many moments of contaminated (*sāsrava*) states, after which again many moments of uncontaminated states manifest. Thus, as he cycles back, each subsequent stage gradually diminishes until finally, with two moments of uncontaminated states remaining, he induces two moments of contaminated states to manifest, followed immediately by the arising of two moments of uncontaminated states; this is called the completion of the preparatory application for the mixed cultivation of meditative concentration (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā-samādhi*).

From this point onward, without relying on deliberate effort, a single moment of outflow-free (anāsrava) consciousness spontaneously induces a single moment of outflowing (sāsrava) consciousness to manifest, which is immediately followed by the arising of another moment of outflow-free consciousness.

In this way, because the intermediate moment of the contaminated state is interspersed with the preceding and succeeding uncontaminated moments, it is called the fundamental perfection of the meditative absorption of mixed cultivation (*miśrabhāvanā*).
Having thus cultivated the fourth dhyāna through mixed cultivation, by the power of this, one is also able to cultivate the lower three dhyānas through mixed cultivation as appropriate.
The meditative cultivation of the dhyānas has the five aggregates as its substance.
Within this context, however, the various conventional knowledges (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) are cultivated in conjunction with the four *dharmajñānas*, the four *anvayajñānas*, and the eight knowledges.
Other masters say:

The various conventional knowledges (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) are mixed only with the subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*) of suffering and its origin, because those two [subsequent knowledges] are able to take these [conventional knowledges] as their objects.

If that were so, there would be no room for multiple untainted knowledges (*anāsravajñāna*) to manifest simultaneously through mixing; thus, one should not say that this [conventional knowledge] is mixed by virtue of being mixed with them. Consequently, the mastery of mixed meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) would not be fully accomplished. This is because it does not arise immediately after other [knowledges]—such as the dharma-subsequent knowledges (*dharmānvayajñāna*) of cessation and the path, or the dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*) of suffering and its origin—and because those various knowledges do not arise immediately after it.

There are briefly three conditions for the mixed cultivation of dhyāna: first, for the sake of rebirth; second, for the sake of present happiness; and third, for the sake of preventing the arising of afflictions and subsequent retrogression.

Among those non-returners who have attained "vision-arrival" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, they do so for the first two conditions: first, for the sake of rebirth, and second, for the sake of present happiness.
Is it for the sake of those seeking rebirth that they aspire for a superior birth— meaning they loathe common [rebirth] and delight in the uncommon—

or is it for the sake of those seeking present happiness that they delight in superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*)— meaning that mundane concentration (*laukika-samādhi*) is most capable of sustaining the body, thereby enabling them to dwell in happiness in the present life, with the preceding and succeeding untainted states (*anāsrava*) acting as its companions?

If those who possess faith and understanding serve as the two preceding conditions, they also act to prevent the arising of afflictions and regression; that is to say, for those of dull faculties who give rise to the two types of untainted states, they employ skillful means to guard pure meditative concentration (*samādhi*), causing the concentration associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) to recede further, and ensuring that the pure state does not serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for a defiled state.
Therefore, among Arhats, those who are not liberated at all times (asamayavimukta) cultivate dhyāna through mixed practice solely for the sake of present happiness.
Those who are liberated at times (samayavimukta), however, cultivate it both to seek present happiness and to prevent the arising of afflictions that would lead to regression.
If one practices the mixed cultivation of dhyāna in order to be born in the five Pure Abodes, for what reason are there only five such abodes?
The verse says:
"By means of the five grades of mixed cultivation, There are births in the five Pure Abodes."
The treatise says:
Because the fourth dhyāna is cultivated through a mixture [of the mundane and supramundane] in five grades, there are only five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).
What are these five grades?
This refers to the distinctions between the inferior, middling, superior, more superior, and extremely superior grades.

Among these, for the first grade, fulfillment is attained as soon as three moments of mind manifest: namely, the first is untainted (*anāsrava*), followed by the arising of a tainted (*sāsrava*) moment, and finally the arising of another untainted moment.
The second middling grade is perfected only when six moments of mind have manifested; that is, two contaminated moments are interspersed with four uncontaminated moments.
In the same manner, for the remaining grades, nine, twelve, or fifteen moments of mind must manifest as appropriate before they can be perfected, according to their respective order.
These five grades of mixed cultivation serve as the cause, sequentially bringing about the fruits of the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Thus, these fifteen types of contaminated and uncontaminated minds are all attained for the first time now, having never been attained previously.
Other masters say:

Of these, the first five untainted [minds] are those not previously attained that are now attained; the remaining ten are all minds already previously attained. This is because when the first five manifest, one has already cultivated them in the future. Regarding their completion through mixed cultivation, some do not require emerging from meditative absorption, while others must arise repeatedly before they can be fully perfected.
Other masters say:

Through the successive predominance of the five faculties beginning with faith, one brings about rebirth in the five Pure Abodes. That is to say, at times the faculty of faith predominates in the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, and at other times, up to the faculty of wisdom, predominates in the mixed cultivation of dhyāna; according to these distinctions, one brings about rebirth in the five Pure Abodes.
Is the rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens due to the power of karma or the power of the mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*)?
If it were due to the power of karma, then the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas would be rendered futile.
If it were due to the power of mixed cultivation, it would contradict what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
As that treatise states:

"All such places as those where one is born among the Śuddhāvāsa deities due to the practice of mixed dhyāna or due to karma are called 'dharmas not belonging to ordinary beings' (aśaikṣa-dharma). Some say:

The power of karma brings about rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; however, this does not render the mixed cultivation of dhyāna fruitless, because the volition for that practice manifests before one.
Other masters say:
"This is due to the power of mixed cultivation, and it does not contradict the text of the *Prakaraṇapāda*."
That treatise first mentions those who practice the mixed meditative absorption (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*) in order to show that they entered that absorption at an earlier time.

Subsequently, it further mentions those who are born in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) by means of karma, in order to show that at a later time they are born in the Pure Abodes precisely through the power of that [absorption].
In this regard, it is determined that both powers are required, because if either one is lacking, that [result] will not arise.
However, only contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma induces that maturation (*vipāka*), and not uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) power, because the latter turns its back on and abandons existence (*bhava*).
The Sūtra states that among the Non-returners (anāgāmin) there is one called "Body-witness" (kāyasākṣin). Based on what superior quality is this name "Body-witness" established?
The verse says:
A Non-returner who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) Is further designated as a Body-witness.
The treatise says:

One who possesses the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation is said to have "attained the absorption of cessation. That is to say, if a non-returner (anāgāmin) possesses the attainment of the absorption of cessation within their own body, they are further designated as a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin).
It is said that the non-returner (anāgāmin) is called "one who has realized through the body" (*kāyasākṣin*) because they have personally realized a state resembling nirvāṇa by means of the body.
How is it that they are designated merely as "realized through the body"?

It is because [the attainment] is without mind, because it arises in dependence upon the body, and because the power of the acquisition (*prāpti*) co-arises with the body; thus, even when that [attainment] has already ceased, one is still said to possess it.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) states:
"In truth, one should say that upon emerging from the attainment of cessation, one acquires what was previously unattained: a body with consciousness that is tranquil.
Thereupon, one thinks: 'This attainment of cessation is most tranquil; it closely resembles Nirvāṇa.'"
Thus, because one realizes the tranquility of the body, it is called "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*).
This is because one attains and realizes the tranquility of the body through the manifestation of attainment and gnosis.

Now, it is said that although one attains the tranquility of the conscious body—which was previously unattained—at the moment of arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the designation "bodily realization" is not applied to that state alone; for this name applies to both the preceding and succeeding moments.

Consequently, even if one lacks the knowledge of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because one has acquired its power, one is designated as "one who has realized through the body" (*kāyasākṣin*).
Therefore, the former explanation is superior in principle; since it refers to the final stage, it simply states:
"One who has attained the attainment of cessation and does not return [to this world] is called a 'realizer through the body'."

In reality, one who has realized through the body (kāyasākṣin) possesses all eight liberations without exception; this is attained by dwelling in realization through the body, entering the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) by means of the remaining liberations as its gateway.
The meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) must also necessarily result in the attainment of other liberations, as the Sūtra says:
"When entering the meditative attainment of cessation, one first ceases speech and action," and so forth, as explained at length.

For what reason does the Buddha state that those in training (*śaikṣa*) constitute the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), yet the Body-Witness (*kāyasākṣin*) who has not yet returned [to the world] is not included among their number?
It is because the World-Honored One told Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Householder, you should know that there are two kinds of fields of merit: first, those in training; second, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)."

There are eighteen types of those in training (*śaikṣa*), and only nine types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). What are the eighteen called "those in training"? They are: the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*), the fruit of stream-entry;

the candidate for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*), the fruit of once-returning; the candidate for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*), the fruit of non-returning; the candidate for arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*); the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*); the one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); the one attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); the one who goes from family to family (*kulaṃkula*); the one with only one interval (*ekavīcika*); the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*); the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*); the one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*); the one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*); and the one who flows upward (*ūrdhvasrotas*). These are called the eighteen.
What are the nine types of those beyond training (aśaikṣa)? They are:

the one of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman), the one of the nature of reflecting (cetayitadharman), the one of the nature of guarding (anurakṣaṇādharman), the one who abides securely (sthitākampya), the one capable of penetration (prativedhanādharman), the one of immovable nature (akopyadharman), the one of non-falling nature (aparihāṇadharman), the one liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta), and the one doubly liberated (ubhayatobhāgavimukta). These are the nine.

This principle should also be stated; yet it is not stated because the Buddha, observing that those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) possess distinctions based on their abandonments (*prahāṇa*) and faculties (*indriya*), recognizes that they can produce superior fruits and are thus called "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*).

However, because the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) attained by non-returners (anāgāmin) is still with outflows (sāsrava), it cannot be said that it is "pure" by virtue of being liberated by its own nature (svabhāva-vimukti).

Furthermore, because the physical body upon which it relies still possesses afflictions (kleśa) that have not been permanently severed, it cannot be said that it is "pure" by virtue of being liberated in its continuity (saṃtāna-vimukti).
Therefore, it is not restricted that only those established as being in the stage of training (śaikṣa) constitute the field of merit (puṇyakṣetra).

Although the contaminated virtues (sāsrava-guṇa) within the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) are not subsumed under liberation by intrinsic nature (svabhāva-vimukti), they are called "pure" because they are liberated through the continuity [of the mind]; for this reason, they too are able to produce extraordinary fruits.
Therefore, based on convention and the distinctions among the faculties, all nine fruits of arhatship are called "fields of merit.

Alternatively, because the basis (āśraya) and cause (hetu) for being established as a learner (śaikṣa) are absent, one who has attained realization through the body is not included within the category of learners.
What is meant by "establishing the basis for those in training" (*śaikṣa*)?

It refers to the three trainings and their fruits, which are untainted (*anāsrava*). Since the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is neither training nor the fruit of training, the distinctions of "those in training" are not established with reference to its accomplishment.
However, within this present stage of the Non-returner (anāgāmin), the "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin) is spoken of through a hidden teaching based on a non-differentiated perspective.

Were it otherwise, one should not say that only those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and do not fall back from the state of a Non-returner are designated as body-witnesses; this point shall be further analyzed later.

If one were to claim that the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) is defined by combining various alternative perspectives, then what was stated above would not constitute a satisfactory answer to the question, for the three formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*) also pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Having already analyzed the coarse distinctions of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), if one were to analyze them in detail, they would number in the thousands. Here, however, we shall provisionally rely on the five types of those who proceed to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-gāmī*), distinguishing them according to five categories such as the various stages (*bhūmi*).
That is to say, when categorized by stage (*bhūmi*), they number twenty, because there are five types within each of the four dhyāna stages.
When categorized by spiritual lineage (*gotra*), they number thirty, because there are five types within each of the six lineages.
Fifth, when categorized by birthplace, the number becomes eighty, because there are five types within each of the sixteen locations.

Fifth, when categorized by lineage and faculty, the number becomes ninety; that is to say, for the *parihāṇadharman* lineage, there are fifteen varieties due to the distinctions among the inferior, middling, and superior faculties, and this applies likewise up to the *akopyadharman* lineage.
Fifth, by way of the stages (*bhūmi*) and spiritual lineages (*gotra*), the number becomes one hundred and twenty; that is to say, because there are thirty [factors] for each of the four stages.
Fifth, by way of the stages, spiritual lineages, and faculties (*indriya*), the number becomes three hundred and sixty; that is to say, because there are ninety [factors] for each of the four stages.
Fifth, when categorized by birthplace and lineage (*gotra*), the number becomes four hundred and eighty, because there are thirty [types] for each of the sixteen birthplaces.

Fifth, when categorized by birthplace, lineage, and faculties (*indriya*), the number becomes one thousand four hundred and forty, because there are ninety [types] for each of the sixteen birthplaces.

Fifth, by calculating according to the stages of detachment (*vairāgya-sthāna*), spiritual lineages (*gotra*), and faculties (*indriya*), the total number of distinctions among non-returners (*anāgāmin*) amounts to ten thousand one thousand nine hundred and sixty.
This is calculated by multiplying the previous figure of one thousand four hundred and forty by the nine distinct grades of detachment.
Having already explained the distinctions between the third path and its fruit, one should now establish the fourth path and its fruit.
The verse says:
Among the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms, one abandons the first category of the first dhyāna.
Up to the eighth category of the Peak of Existence, one is entirely a candidate for Arhatship (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*).
The ninth path of non-obstruction is called the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropamasamādhi*);
with the attainment of exhaustion, there arises the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), whereby one becomes a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) who has attained the fruit of Arhatship (*arhattvaphala*).
The Commentary states:

That same Non-returner who proceeds to sever the afflictions abandoned through cultivation within the form realm and the formless realm—beginning from the severance of the first grade of the first dhyāna and ending with the severance of the eighth grade of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra)—should be known as being designated by the name "Candidate for Arhatship" (arhattvaphalapratipannaka).

Within this very context of the candidate for arhatship (*arhattvaprati-pannaka*), the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) that abandons the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is also called the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropamasamādhi*). This concentration is firm and sharp, being likened to a diamond because there is not a single latent tendency (*anuśaya*) that it cannot shatter.
Since that [previous category] has already been refuted, it does not refute all [defilements]; yet, in reality, there exists a functional capacity capable of refuting all of them.

Because this [present path] can destroy even the most subtle grade of afflictions, we know that among all the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), only this single moment is designated as the supreme grade; therefore, it is able to permanently sever all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Although within the Path of Seeing there is also an untainted antidote capable of severing the afflictions of the Peak of Existence, those nine grades of delusion can be severed in a single grade; this indicates that the power of those afflictions is weak and inferior.
Since the path of seeing serves as the antidote only for inferior afflictions, it is known not to be capable of destroying all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
If it possessed such power, what obstacle would prevent it from doing so?
Therefore, it cannot be designated by the name "diamond-like" (*vajropama*).

Furthermore, among the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), those that lack a substantial object (*avastuka*) are easily severed; since the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) counteracts them and they are not considered the most extreme or superior, the name "Vajra-like" is not established for it.

The Vajra-like Samādhi explained here, however, can counteract the final, most subtle, and most difficult-to-sever category among all the latent dispositions that possess a substantial object (*savastuka*); therefore, it is known to be capable of destroying all latent dispositions.
By the power of this, in a single kṣaṇa, one realizes the untainted attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) through the abandonment of all afflictions.
This aforementioned diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is associated with only one of the six knowledges (*jñāna*).

This refers to the four types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-dharma-jñāna*), which take the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of the Four Noble Truths as their objects. Since it is established by implication that these universally rely upon the nine stages (*bhūmi*), these distinctions are said to be manifold.

Furthermore, there are fifty-two types of "not-yet-attained" inclusion (*aprāpti-saṃgraha*): namely, when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) observe the suffering and origin of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) through the aspects (*ākāra*) of impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth, as well as cause (*hetu*) and so forth; these, in combination with their respective associated mental factors, constitute eight distinct categories.

The dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path (nirodha-mārga-dharma-jñāna) contemplates the cessation and the path of the desire realm through the aspects of "cessation," "tranquility," and so forth, as well as "path" and so forth; the distinctions associated with these are likewise eightfold.

The subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna) contemplates the cessation of each of the eight stages individually through four aspects; when associated with these, they constitute thirty-two.

The subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) takes all paths of the eight stages as its collective object and performs four aspects of mental application; when associated with those [aspects], it becomes fourfold in its distinctions. This is because the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge that counteracts the eight stages must necessarily take them collectively as its object, since factors of the same kind serve as causes for one another.
Cessation (*nirodha*) is conditioned solely by specific conditions, whereas the Path (*mārga*) is not; this has already been fully established in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa*.
Just as there are fifty-two [factors] included in the *anāgamya* stage, it should be known that the same applies to the intermediate dhyāna and the four dhyānas.

In the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana), there are twenty-eight [mental applications]. This is because one excludes the eight [applications] belonging to the category of the dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) regarding cessation and the path, as well as the sixteen [applications] associated with the four aspects of the truth of cessation for each of the four lower stages; this is because, in the formless realms, there is necessarily no dharma-knowledge, and because [the applications here] take the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) category of cessation of the lower stages as their object.
There is no logical obstruction to taking the stages of the lower paths as objects, for it has already been explained that the path necessarily takes all [stages] as its object.
Since the rest is as previously stated, there are twenty-eight; in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, there are twenty-four; and in the Sphere of Nothingness, there are only twenty.

This means that one further excludes from the preceding [count] the four and eight aspects of the objects of the Noble Truth of Cessation pertaining to the lower stages; these should be explained in sequence according to the previous method.
For those who maintain that the three formless stages possess knowledge of the cessation of the lower stages as their object, they state:
the Sphere of Infinite Space adds sixteen to the previous [count], the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness adds twenty, and the Sphere of Nothingness adds twenty-four.

Thus, in summary, there are seventy-two types of diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) based on the formless stages (*ārūpya-bhūmi*), or alternatively, it is said that there are one hundred and thirty-two.
Other masters state:

In the category of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna-pakṣa*), one also contemplates each of the eight stages of the path individually; therefore, there are eighty [aspects] for each of the first six stages, forty for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), thirty-two for the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and twenty-four for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Furthermore, there are those who wish to maintain that the knowledge of cessation regarding the category of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) involves both specific and general contemplations across the eight stages; thus, within the first six stages, there are respectively one hundred and sixty-four [moments], fifty-two for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), thirty-six for the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and twenty-four for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Both of those positions are unreasonable, because it has already been established that the Path necessarily takes [all objects] collectively as its object, whereas Cessation takes them only individually.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka states: "The Diamond-like Samādhi consists of thirteen moments in total;

that is, it comprises thirteen moments subsumed under the Uninterrupted Paths (ānantarya-mārga) for abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation at the Peak of Existence."
This is also not the case, because the eight uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) preceding the four types of patience (*kṣānti*) are not of the highest degree.

Since this concentration (*samādhi*) is capable of severing the ninth grade of afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and can bring about the exhaustion of these afflictions, it gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that occurs simultaneously with the attainment of that exhaustion; it causes the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) to arise. This knowledge of exhaustion is produced by the final uninterrupted path among those that sever afflictions, and it is the final path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) among those that sever afflictions. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of exhaustion induced by this concentration arises simultaneously with the attainment of the exhaustion of the ninth grade.

Alternatively, the term "exhaustion" (kṣaya) here indicates the exhaustion of all [defilements]; that is to say, because the ninth grade of defilement and all remaining afflictions have attained analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), it is called "exhaustion.

The diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) can induce the attainment of the exhaustion of all afflictions, which arises simultaneously with the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna). Because this [knowledge] arises for the first time together with the attainment of the exhaustion of all afflictions, it is named the "knowledge of exhaustion."
Other masters say: Because this [wisdom] arises for the first time within the body when all afflictions have been exhausted, it is called "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*).

When such knowledge of exhaustion has arisen, one then becomes an Arhat of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), because one has already attained the dharmas of the fruit of the worthy one of no-more-learning.
Because there is no further training to be undertaken for the sake of attaining a distinct fruit, one receives the name "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).
But is it not the case that those beyond training also aspire for a distinct fruit, since even those beyond training undergo the transformation of their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*)?
This objection is not valid, because it is unlike the case where one who has previously attained the stage of a learner (śaikṣa) seeks to obtain a different fruit;

that is not the case here. For example, just as one who is a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) is not [simply] a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), when he later attains the fruit of a once-returner, he relinquishes the name "stream-enterer" and receives the name "once-returner"; in all such cases, one relinquishes a specific previous fruit and acquires the designation of a different fruit.

This is not the case; for when one who has fallen back from the state of *parihāṇa* (regression) subsequently attains the state of *cetanādharma* (one subject to volition), although they abandon the name "one subject to regression" and acquire the name "one subject to volition," they do not abandon one distinct fruit to acquire the name of another distinct fruit, because both states are designated as "Arhat" throughout.

Only when one abandons the previous fruit and attains a distinct fruit does one abandon the designation of the former fruit and receive the name of the distinct fruit; since there is no further distinct fruit to be cultivated, it is called "no-more-learning" (aśaikṣa). Thus, the previous explanation is without fault.
This refers to those who are practicing toward [the goal] and abide in the stage prior to the fruit; for them to seek a distinct name for the fruit is meaningless.

Since it is stated that upon the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one becomes an Arhat of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), it follows by implication that as long as the knowledge of exhaustion has not yet arisen, the preceding seven noble ones are all called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*), because they are diligently practicing in order to attain a distinct fruit.
Why is one abiding in the state of the fundamental nature called "in training" (śaikṣa)?
Because the intention to train is not yet fulfilled, and because the attainment of training constantly follows [them].
Why is one beyond training (aśaikṣa) called an Arhat?
Having already completed the training in all practices for one's own benefit, one should now act solely for the sake of benefiting others.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"It is impossible for one who has not disciplined oneself to be able to discipline others."
There are three types of *pudgalas*: namely, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Although ordinary beings train in the three—ethics, concentration, and wisdom—they are still unable to see the truths as they truly are; since it is possible for them to abandon what is correct and practice what is erroneous, the designation "one in training" is not applied to them.
Those who have already been able to see the truths as they truly are, and who train correctly without falling back, receive the designation of "one in training" (*śaikṣa*).
For this reason, the Blessed One, in order to clarify the precise definition, repeated the word "training" with respect to those in training.
As the Buddha told Dāntika in a sūtra:
"One should train in what is to be trained;
one who trains in what is to be trained, I designate as a learner (*śaikṣa*)."
Those who have already trained well and no longer need to train further in the three—ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom—are designated as "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
Because they are worthy of being venerated by all those still in training (śaikṣa) and by ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), they are called "Fruits of Worthiness" (arhat).
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:
"If one has already well cultivated and studied The three— ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom—
Having ultimately abandoned sorrow and defilement, One is worthy of being a field of merit for the world."
What are the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*)?
They are the untainted conditioned dharmas (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*) of one in training.
What are the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
This refers to the uncontaminated conditioned dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Although all unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta*) are uncontaminated, they are not designated as "dharmas of those in training or beyond training" (*śaikṣāśaikṣadharma*), because they can be possessed by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and others who are neither; furthermore, if they are not possessed, they are entirely unrelated to the states of being in training or beyond training.

Thus, those who are in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) together constitute the eight noble persons (*āryapudgala*), because there are four each for those proceeding toward the fruits and those abiding in the fruits.

Although there are eight names, there are only five actual entities: namely, those abiding in the four fruits and those proceeding toward the first fruit; this is because the three subsequent paths of approach do not exist apart from their respective preceding fruits.
This is explained in reference to those who attain the fruits through gradual stages.

If one has partially abandoned desire or has completely abandoned desire, while abiding in the Path of Seeing, they are designated as being on the path toward the fruit of Once-returner or Non-returner; these are not included within the preceding fruits.
Why is it that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) belongs exclusively to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
For even those still in training (*śaikṣa*) know for themselves:
"I have forever exhausted [rebirth in] the hells and so forth."
This has been stated previously.
What was stated previously? It means that only when it is conjoined with the attainment of exhaustion (*kṣaya-prāpti*) is it designated as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).

Since those in the stages of stream-entry and so forth still possess residual afflictions, they lack both the attainment of exhaustion (*kṣayaprāpti*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); for this reason, the Sūtra states:
"All those in training (*śaikṣa*) are endowed with eight factors; if one is endowed with ten factors, he is called an Arhat."
If that is so, why did the Venerable Śāriputra say to the great householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"You have already fully accomplished right knowledge and right liberation"?

There is no fault of contradiction, because it was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) that, based on those [factors], one accomplishes the true path of antidote for the false wisdom and false liberation that lead to rebirth in the evil destinies.
If that is so, why is it not said that the learner (*śaikṣa*) accomplishes ten factors?
Because there are others who lack wisdom and whose minds have not yet attained full liberation.
If this is so, for what reason does the Sūtra state:

"All those who possess verified confidence in the Buddha are said to have already attained right view," and so on, up to "those who have already attained right liberation" and likewise for those "perfected in vision"?
Nor is there any contradiction. Why is this?
I do not say that those who are still in training (śaikṣa) lack right knowledge and right liberation; rather, I speak as follows:
He does not establish the factors [of dependent origination]. The reasons for not establishing these factors have already been explained as before.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 65.
