10. Chapter Six: Distinguishing the Noble and the Holy (Ārya), Part Ten. As stated above, there are two types of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*):
first, that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*);
second, that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Now, one should investigate:
by means of which path is detachment from which stage achieved within these two types?
The verse says:
The Peak of Existence is [abandoned] by the untainted; the others are [abandoned] by both for the sake of detachment.
The commentary says:

Regarding all afflictions within the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), only the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) can bring about their permanent abandonment; it is certainly not the tainted path (*sāsrava*).
Why is this so? Because only the power of this [untainted path] is capable of counteracting the higher stages.
Only within the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) immediately above can the mundane path (laukikamārga) arise to counteract the afflictions of the lower stages.
Since there is no higher stage for the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), there is no contaminated path capable of abandoning their defilements.
For what reason does the mundane path not cure the afflictions of its own level? Because it is that which is increased by those very latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
That which is increased by those latent dispositions should possess the power to cure them; however, [the mundane path] accords with and promotes the growth of those afflictions.

If there were a power capable of counteracting those [defilements], then this [path] would certainly not be subject to increase by them, because at that time, when it is being taken as an object, they are diminished.
For what reason, then, can the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) arising in a lower stage not counteract the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of a higher stage?

Because those [defilements] do not increase through the influence of those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and because they do not accord with the growth of those afflictions, one must admit that they can counteract the latent dispositions of the higher realms; for the higher realms are certainly not the objective referents (*ālambana*) for the path of abandonment consisting of the mundane practice of revulsion belonging to the lower realms.
One cannot become detached from the defilements of a higher stage by means of revulsion toward a lower stage, because the higher stage is infinitely more subtle than the lower.
From this it is proven that only the power of the untainted (anāsrava) can bring about detachment from the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra); thus, the principle is well-established.

Regarding the afflictions present in the remaining eight stages, they can all be permanently abandoned through two types of paths, as both mundane and supramundane paths are capable of abandoning them.
Since they are abandoned through both paths, how many kinds of acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) are there for each?
The verse says:
"The two noble [paths] and the eight [stages of] cultivation are each associated with two acquisitions of disjunction.
The commentary says:

When noble learners (*śaikṣa*) employ the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) to abandon the defilements to be eliminated through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the lower eight stages, they are able to fully produce two types of acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*): both contaminated and uncontaminated. This is because the functions performed by these two kinds of paths of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*)—contaminated and uncontaminated—are identical across the eight stages.
The same applies to becoming detached from those [stages] by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), as the function performed therein is identical.

Consequently, when a learner (*śaikṣa*) becomes detached from the eight stages to be abandoned through cultivation, whether the mundane or supramundane path is present, they cultivate both the mundane and supramundane paths in their future [attainment].

Since it has been stated that for the noble ones (*ārya*), both types of abandonment (*visamyoga*) arising from the cultivation of the eight stages each induce the acquisition of two types of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*), one may infer accordingly that when the noble ones abandon the cultivation of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), they employ the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) to induce only the acquisition of untainted disjunction; furthermore, they do not cultivate the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) in the future, because this is a matter distinct from the mundane path.

When an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) abandons the eight [levels of defilement] by means of the contaminated path (sāsravamārga), they only produce the acquisition of dissociation (visaṃyogaprāpti) that is itself contaminated; furthermore, they do not cultivate the uncontaminated path (anāsravamārga) in the future, as this is established as a matter of course because they have not yet entered the state of a noble one (ārya).
Other masters say:

When one abandons the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the lower eight stages by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), on what basis is it known that one also produces the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) which is tainted (*sāsrava*)?
Because if one were to relinquish the untainted acquisition, the afflictions would not be rendered non-existent.

This means that when a noble one in training (śaikṣa) becomes detached from those defilements by means of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), if they do not produce an acquired possession of dissociation (visamyoga-prāpti) that is tainted (sāsrava) and shares the same antidote (pratipakṣa), then, although they have already completely abandoned the [defilements] of the eight stages by means of the noble path, later, when they attain the transformation of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) based on dhyāna, they would suddenly discard all the previously held dull noble paths and obtain only the sharp fruit-noble paths of dhyāna. Consequently, the dissociation from the higher-level afflictions would fail to be established, and thus those afflictions would once again become manifest.

However, this is not what is accepted; therefore, it is certain that when noble learners (śaikṣas) abandon the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation belonging to the lower eight stages through the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), they likewise fully produce two acquisitions of disjunction (visaṃyoga-prāpti).
This proof is unreasonable.

Why is this so? Even if that noble one lacks the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the abandonment of outflows (*āsrava*), they likewise do not possess the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher stages. This is because, just as when one separates from the acquisition of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), or as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born in a higher stage does not possess afflictions, so it is here.

This means that, for example, when one has already separated from the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and subsequently attains the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) based on a dhyāna, the untainted acquisitions (*anāsrava-prāpti*) of abandonment have already been relinquished all at once; although there is no tainted acquisition (*sāsrava-prāpti*) for the dissociation (*visamyoga*) from that stage, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of that stage are nevertheless no longer possessed.

Furthermore, for example, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is born into the second dhyāna or higher levels, although they relinquish the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the abandonment of afflictions belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth, they do not remain possessed of those afflictions of the desire realm. This is because the acquisition of the disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) from the outflows (*sāsrava*) of the desire realm and other realms is subsumed under the first dhyāna and higher states, as these alone are their antidotes; moreover, if one is born into a higher level, this acquisition must necessarily be relinquished, since one who is born into a higher level necessarily relinquishes the wholesome states with outflows belonging to the lower levels.
Although these two do not possess the attainment (*prāpti*) of the abandonment of afflictions, because they are superior advancements, they prevent the arising of the attainment of delusions;
the same should apply to that [case] as well, and thus the proof is irrational. Therefore, one may only say this:

Because the function performed by the two paths within this context is identical, the manifestation of either one induces the arising of both acquisitions; it cannot be said that this is for the purpose of establishing abandonment.
Having already analyzed detachment from defilement according to the difference between the paths, we shall now analyze it according to the distinction of the stages (*bhūmi*).
By means of which path and stage is one detached from the defilements of which stage?
The verse says:
The untainted path of the *anāgamya* stage Is able to bring about detachment from all stages.
The remaining eight abandon their own and higher levels; the contaminated abandon the immediately lower level.
The treatise says:

All uncontaminated paths rely upon nine stages, namely the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

If the path included in the "not-yet-reached" (anāgamya) stage can abandon the defilements of the desire realm up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), the remaining eight stages likewise abandon their respective defilements as appropriate; each can abandon the defilements of its own level and those of higher levels, but cannot abandon those of lower levels, because when one has not yet abandoned the lower levels, the path of the higher levels necessarily does not manifest.

All contaminated paths (*sāsrava-mārga*) are capable only of abandoning the afflictions of the immediately lower stage, and not those of their own stage or higher stages; for [the latter] are augmented by the afflictions of their own stage, their power is inferior, and [the afflictions of the lower stage] have already been abandoned previously.
Regarding those [attainments] based on the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) that abandon the defilements of the lower levels:
while all uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) are subsumed under the preparatory stages, are all paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) likewise subsumed under the preparatory stages?
Not necessarily.
How so? The verse says:
The "near-separation" [attainment] abandons the defilements of the lower realm; It consists of the first three and the final liberation.
The fundamental or the preparatory [attainments], while for the higher stages there is only the fundamental.
The treatise says:
There are eight preparatory attainments that serve as the basis for the various paths, namely, the lower limits of the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments.

There are nine instances of abandonment: namely, the eight dhyānas and the first three preliminary concentrations (sāmantaka) abandon the defilements of the lower stages; and when the ninth liberation is present, one either enters the fundamental dhyāna or remains in the preliminary concentration itself.

Each of the five upper preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) is free from the defilements of the stage below; however, when the ninth liberation (*vimokṣa*) manifests, one necessarily enters the fundamental dhyāna (*maula*) and not the preparatory stage itself, because the preparatory and fundamental stages are equal in terms of their faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Because the faculties of feeling differ between the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental states (*maula*) of the lower three dhyānas, there are cases where one cannot enter them; furthermore, transitioning into a different type of feeling involves some slight difficulty.

Since one must necessarily aspire to the higher level when becoming free from the defilements of the lower level, if there were no difference in feeling, one would necessarily enter the fundamental state.

Regarding the paths of transcendence (*lokottara-mārga*), since it has already been stated that their uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and liberation (*vimukti*) paths take the four truths as their objects and consist of sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), this is established by implication.
What, however, are the objects and the aspects of the mundane paths (*laukika-mārga*)?
The verse says:
The worldly paths of immediate succession and liberation take the lower and upper realms as their objects, respectively;
they function as the three contemplations of coarseness, suffering, and obstruction, as well as the three contemplations of tranquility, excellence, and detachment.
The treatise states:

The worldly paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take the lower and higher stages as their respective objects, perceiving them respectively as coarse, suffering, and obstructive; and as calm, excellent, and detached.

This means that the various uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) take as their objects the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of their own level or the immediately lower level, and employ one of the three aspects (*ākāra*), such as "coarse" (*audārika*) or "suffering" (*duḥkha*).

If they are the various paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they take as their objects the contaminated phenomena of the immediately higher level, and employ one of the three aspects, such as "peaceful" (*śānta*) or "sublime" (*praṇīta*).

In terms of possibility, it may be said that each of the two paths possesses three aspects; however, it is not the case that every sentient being, at the stage of becoming free from defilement, necessarily possesses all three in both the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Within the lower stages, because they are characterized by excessive restlessness and their tranquility is weak and inferior, they are termed "coarse" (*audārika*).
Although great exertion may temporarily cause agitation, its force is weak and inferior; it still cannot induce the arising of sublime bliss, and is therefore called "suffering" (*duḥkha*).

Because it is constrained by many kinds of calamities and obstacles, and because it can obscure and hinder one’s capacity to perceive the way of transcendence, it is called an "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*).
In the various higher stages, because agitation (*auddhatya*) is subtle and weak due to the absence of effortful application, they are called "calm" (*śānta*).
Because one does not exert labor and agitation is subtle and weak, leading to the production of supreme bliss, they are called "sublime" (*praṇīta*).

Because one can definitively perceive all the calamities within the lower stages, such that the mind does not give rise to delight and is able to transcend them, it is called "detachment" (*vairāgya*).

It should be understood that this also implicitly demonstrates the three aspects of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the three aspects of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which arise in opposition to one another according to their respective order.

That is to say, in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the lower realm is perceived as coarse; in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the higher realm is perceived as calm. The remaining characteristics arise in reverse order accordingly, though their arising at the time of abandoning defilements is not fixed.

Since the mundane paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are able to abandon the nine grades of defilements of the lower realms and so forth, it should be understood that they likewise possess nine distinct grades.

Among these, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) abandons the defilements of the desire realm, during each of the nine paths of uninterrupted transition, one of the three aspects—coarseness (*audārika*), etc.—manifests, and in each case, one cultivates in the future all three aspects: coarseness, etc.

When any one of the three aspects—such as "calm" (*śānta*)—manifests in the eighth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), one cultivates in the future six aspects, such as "coarse" (*audārika*), for each.

In the subsequent path of deliverance (*vimokṣamārga*), what is cultivated in the present and future is as described for the eight paths of liberation; however, the difference from the former is that one further cultivates in the future the aspect of "limitless" (*apramāṇa*) subsumed under the first dhyāna.
In this manner, it should be understood that this applies up until the path of liberation immediately following the abandonment of the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

If noble ones abandon the defilements of the desire realm by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), then during each of the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*), one of the three modes of activity—coarseness (*audārikatā*) and so forth—is present before them, and in each case, they cultivate nineteen modes of activity in the future.

This refers to the three aspects such as "coarse" (*audārika*) and so forth, along with the sixteen noble practices (*āryākāra*), which are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

When any one of the three aspects—such as "calm" (*śānta*)—manifests in any of the eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), one cultivates twenty-two aspects in the future; that is, the previous nineteen plus the three aspects such as "calm. As for the subsequent paths of deliverance (*vimuktimārga*), those cultivated in the present and future are as previously described.
Regarding the eight paths of liberation that differ from the preceding [preparatory stages], one further cultivates nineteen aspects in the future, which are subsumed under the first dhyāna.

In each of the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) for abandoning the defilements of the first dhyāna, either one of the three aspects—coarseness (*audārika*), etc.—is present; in each case, one cultivates nineteen aspects in the future, namely: the three aspects beginning with coarseness, and the sixteen noble aspects (*āryākāra*) which are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
These sixteen modes of practice (*ākāra*) are subsumed under the lower stages (*adhobhūmi*), because the higher stages lack the noble modes of practice (*ārya-ākāra*).
One should understand that the subsequent cultivation of the noble modes follows this same principle.

In each of the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one of the three modes—calmness (*śānta*), etc.—manifests; for each, twenty-two modes are cultivated in the future, namely the previous nineteen plus the three beginning with calmness.
Regarding the subsequent paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), those cultivated in the present and future are as previously described.

As for what distinguishes the eight paths of liberation from the preceding ones: they further cultivate, in the future, the two meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) that encompass the infinite aspects (*anantya-ākāra*).
In this manner, it should be understood that this applies up to the path of liberation immediately following the detachment from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Other masters state:

within the paths of liberation immediately following the detachment from desire by both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*), one also cultivates the meditation on impurity (*aśubhā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and so forth; as for the cultivation of other higher stages, it is as previously described.

Because the roots of goodness at the limit of the first dhyāna are extensive, one cultivates such practices; because the roots of goodness at the limits of the higher meditative concentrations are few, what is cultivated is as previously described.

Furthermore, within the desire realm there are many afflictions, and for the sake of severing them, one cultivates many antidotes; this is not the case for the higher stages, and thus the cultivation of antidotes is slight.

Regarding the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) for becoming detached from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the three modes of cultivation—coarseness (*audārikatā*), etc.—that are cultivated in the future have as their object only the desire realm.

Regarding the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the three modes of cultivation—coarseness, etc.—that are cultivated in the future have as their object both the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
furthermore, the three modes of cultivation—tranquility (*śāntatā*), etc.—have the first dhyāna as their object.
Regarding the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—that are cultivated in the future by the subsequent path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they take all three realms as their object;
the three modes of practice—tranquility and so forth—take the first dhyāna as their object.

This continues up until the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) for abandoning the defilements of the first dhyāna through the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*); the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—cultivated in the future therein take the first dhyāna as their object.
Regarding the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—that are cultivated in the future by the eight paths of liberation, they take the first and second dhyānas as their objects.
The three modes of practice—tranquility and so forth—take the second dhyāna as their object.
Regarding the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—that are cultivated in the future by the subsequent path of liberation, they universally take the three realms as their objects.
The three modes of practice, beginning with tranquility (*śamatha*), take the second dhyāna as their object;

this continues up to the detachment from the defilements of the second and third dhyānas at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), all of which should be understood according to the preceding explanations as appropriate.

The three types of cultivation—coarseness (*audārika*) and so forth—practiced in the future during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*anantarya-mārga*) for the purpose of detaching from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna take the fourth dhyāna as their object.

The three types of cultivation—coarseness and so forth—practiced in the future during the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take both the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) as their objects; however, this does not occur in a single moment, because the realms (*dhātu*) are distinct.
The three modes of practice—serenity and so forth—take only the sphere of infinite space as their object.

Regarding the future cultivation of the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—and the three modes of practice—serenity and so forth—within the subsequent path of liberation, all take the sphere of infinite space as their object.

Up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*anantarya-mārga*) that abandon the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the three modes of conduct—coarseness (*audārikatā*), etc.—cultivated for the future have as their object only the Sphere of Infinite Space.

During the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the three modes of conduct—coarseness, etc.—cultivated for the future have as their object both the Sphere of Infinite Space and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
The three modes of practice—calmness and so forth—take only the sphere of consciousness as their object.

Regarding the future cultivation of the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—and the three modes of practice—calmness and so forth—within the subsequent path of liberation, both take the sphere of consciousness as their object.

This applies up to the detachment from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and the Sphere of Nothingness within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), all of which should be understood according to what was previously explained as appropriate.

For what reason, within the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), do the three modes of practice—coarseness (*audārikatā*) and so forth—which are cultivated for the future and subsumed under the dhyānas, take all three realms as their object, whereas those subsumed under the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) take only their own or higher levels as objects?

Among the various dhyānas, there is wisdom that takes all things as its object; however, the fundamental states of the formless realm (ārūpya) necessarily do not take lower levels as their objects. Therefore, the objects cultivated by these two differ.
Regarding this, a certain class of Dārṣṭāntika masters, wishing to clarify the tenets of the Vibhajyavādins, makes this statement:
"There is no ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who truly abandons the afflictions, because [such abandonment] can be lost."
That is to say, if one is truly able to eradicate the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there is necessarily no falling back;
if there is falling back, it is certain that the eradication was not real.

Since it is admitted that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) may fall back from the abandonment of the afflictions of the eight lower stages, it follows that an ordinary person does not truly eradicate the afflictions.
That explanation is irrational, for there would be faults whether one asserts that the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) have been suppressed or that they have not.
That is to say, regarding the afflictions of the Peak of Existence, do you assert that ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) have suppressed them, or do you assert that they have not?

If it is granted that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) can suppress the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), then just as they do not take birth in the lower realms once the afflictions of those lower levels have been suppressed, so too, having suppressed the afflictions of the Peak of Existence, they should not take birth in the Peak of Existence either; in that case, the ordinary person would have realized *parinirvāṇa*.

If one who has suppressed the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is still reborn there, whereas one who has not suppressed those of the lower stages is not reborn there, then one should not use the case of non-retrogression after the afflictions of the Peak of Existence have been severed as an analogy to claim that the same applies to the lower stages.

If it is granted that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cannot suppress the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), because the mundane path lacks the power to do so there and can only suppress the afflictions of the lower stages, then one should not use the case of non-retrogression after the afflictions of the Peak of Existence have been severed as an analogy to claim the same for the lower stages.
Thus, when scrutinized in this manner, both positions are flawed; therefore, one cannot say that those [defilements] are truly not subject to regression once severed.

However, as for their claim that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other afflictions subsumed under the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) do not regress once severed, this proves that all afflictions belonging to the lower stages should likewise not regress once severed.

Since it is observed that ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) may fall back even after they have abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower realms, one might conclude that they have not actually severed those afflictions of the lower realms.
This is not logical, because the nature of what has been severed is different [from what remains].

That is to say, it is not our position that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have the capacity to sever the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This is because, when those afflictions are severed, there would be no basis for the arising of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) at the Peak of Existence, and furthermore, because the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) arising therein would lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*). However, ordinary beings are able to sever the afflictions of the lower stages.

Since those who have already severed [the afflictions] differ between ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*), one must also admit the distinction between those who are subject to regression and those who are not. How then can you cite the principle that noble ones do not regress from what they have severed as an analogy to claim that ordinary beings likewise do not regress?
Furthermore, because it is not established— meaning that we do not admit that there is no falling back once the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) have been abandoned—
how can you use the principle of non-retrogression in that case as an analogy to force the same conclusion upon the lower realms?

Although there is no falling back once the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) included within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) has been abandoned, that [school] does not admit that such a state of suppression exists in that level as it does for the afflictions of the lower levels. Therefore, one cannot use the fact that there is no falling back from its abandonment as an analogy for the principle of no falling back from the abandonment of the afflictions of the lower levels. Since these two cases differ—namely, the absence of suppression versus the presence of suppression—one must likewise allow for a distinction between having falling back and not having falling back.

Furthermore, because the paths are different, it is said that it is not by this path that the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) included within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is abandoned; rather, it is by this very path that various types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abandon all afflictions belonging to the eight lower stages.

Since there are differences in the paths, one must admit that the abandonment of afflictions has two distinct varieties: that which is subject to regression and that which is not, for the abandonment of afflictions is the fruit of the path.
If it is argued that this point should give rise to doubt, such reasoning is incorrect, because it has been clearly stated.
That is to say, they might think:
"Since there are differences between these two paths of counteraction, doubt may arise.

However, one should not doubt whether ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) undergo retrogression or not; for the Blessed One has clearly and explicitly stated in various places that among ordinary beings, there are those who sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) and those who become free from defilement (*vītarāga*).
That is to say, the Sūtras state that among ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), there are those who abandon the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) and abandon both pleasure and pain. Furthermore,
the Sūtras state that Udāyī Rāmaputra was able to sever all desires.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"In the past, there was an external ascetic who served as a teacher for the world named Sunetra; he had already attained freedom from passion within the desire realm.
Moreover, in the section of the sutras analyzing karma, it is stated that there are external ascetics who have attained freedom from passion in the desire realm.

From this it is proven that because the paths differ, although ordinary beings may have truly severed the afflictions of the eight stages, there remains the possibility of regression; it is not the case that they cannot truly sever them simply because the paths differ. Therefore, one should not harbor doubts regarding this matter.
If it is argued that here "abandonment" and "separation from defilement" refer solely to non-manifestation, as the term "abandonment" and "separation from defilement" is used elsewhere,
this is also incorrect, because there is no definitive reason for it and it entails great logical faults.
That is to say, they may think as follows:

"Only the non-occurrence [of defilements] is called abandonment and detachment from passion; this is just as the term 'abandonment' is also used regarding the state of death, even though at the actual moment of death there is no real counteractive abandonment."
Furthermore, as it is said:

In a village or town, there may be young boys or girls who play by gathering sand and earth to build houses or cities; though they enjoy these things for a brief moment, they soon become detached from them.
The meaning of that statement is to show that craving no longer functions with respect to those objects; it does not mean that there is actual abandonment or separation.

Therefore, in this context, the designation "abandonment" and "separation from defilement" refers merely to their non-manifestation, and thus it cannot serve as proof [for the existence of a separate entity].
This is certainly not the case, as there is no definitive reason [for such a claim].

Regarding the statement here concerning the "severance of defilement," what definitive reason exists that could serve as valid proof to show that this merely indicates the temporary non-manifestation of afflictions, rather than establishing the attainment of the severance of all delusions?

If it is argued that because noble ones (ārya) necessarily do not regress once they have abandoned [defilements], whereas ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) do regress, one knows therefore that [the noble ones] have not yet abandoned them—this too is not correct, because it is not universally established (aprasiddha).
That noble ones do not regress is not something universally established; therefore, there is no definitive reason to prove this point.

Furthermore, regarding the terms "abandonment" and "detachment from defilements" mentioned here, if they were understood merely as non-occurrence [of the defilements], there would be the fault of over-extension; for in other places, the noble path itself is spoken of by the names "abandonment" and "detachment from defilements."
You should also consider that [the afflictions] merely do not manifest, as stated in other passages.
Therefore, that position is certainly irrational.

How is it known that this expression "abandonment through detachment from defilement" does not refer to the suppression of manifest entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), but rather to the abandonment of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions?
This is because they, like noble ones (*ārya*), also attain birth in the higher realms.

That is to say, it is accepted by both parties that a noble one in training (*śaikṣa*) must first abandon the afflictions of the lower realms to attain birth in the higher realms; since this class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) likewise attains birth in the higher realms, it should also be admitted that they abandon the afflictions of the lower realms.
If you claim that the paths are different because they are not the same, then this already demonstrates that ordinary beings undergo regression from abandonment.
Since the presence or absence of regression is sufficient to demonstrate the distinction between paths, why insist on abandonment and suppression as the means to reveal their difference?

Because the paths differ, there is a distinction between the suppression and the actual abandonment of the various afflictions; it is not because the paths differ that there is a distinction between falling away and not falling away from what has already been truly abandoned.
What reasoning serves as proof for this statement?

Furthermore, one who passes away with a wholesome or neutral state of mind should also be able to attain rebirth in a higher realm, even though the acquisition (*prāpti*) of afflictions has not yet been severed within their body. Why is this so?
Because they are separated from manifest entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).

That is to say, when a wholesome or neutral mind manifests in this state, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of one's own level necessarily do not manifest; thus it is called "separation. It is not because of this that the afflictions fail to function, as there is a slight difference [in this case] compared to when they are absent due to other conditions.

Furthermore, it is not because there is a distinction among separate dharmas that one may allow for a distinction within this [process]; for although they do not arise equally, there is nothing to be discarded.

That is to say, it is not the case that a separate dharma discards even a small portion within the continuum while others lack such power, such that one could claim that those [other] dharmas have something to discard; thus, although they do not function equally, there is a distinction in time.

If it is argued that one is born into a particular stage because one has attained the suppression of the opposing factors within that stage, then at the moment of death, when a wholesome or neutral mind is present, one is born into one's own stage and not a higher one; for the wholesome or neutral mind at the moment of death does not encompass the suppression of the opposing factors belonging to a higher stage.

This is also not the case; for those who, relying on a higher stage, suppress and subdue the afflictions of a lower stage, do they arise by the power of karma belonging to the higher stage, or by the power of the path that suppresses and subdues [those afflictions] belonging to the higher stage?

If one is born in a higher realm through the power of karma, one merely suppresses the afflictions of that lower realm; however, there must necessarily be karma that induces birth in this [higher] realm, and by the power of that karma, one must certainly be born here.

If one were to be born in a higher realm by the power of this path, then by relying on the path of this [lower] stage to suppress the afflictions of the desire realm, one would only be reborn in that very stage upon the end of life. Consequently, among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who die in the desire realm, there would be none who could be reborn as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); they would only be able to undergo birth in the First Dhyāna, because this path would certainly cause such a birth.

Because one who has not yet abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower stages lacks the capacity to be born in a higher stage, doubt may arise regarding the path taught by him, as it differs [from the established doctrine].
Since ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do indeed undergo retrogression, is this [retrogression] due to the severance or non-severance [of defilements]?

Such a doubt is certainly unreasonable; for this reason, it is established by what has been said—that because of the difference in the paths—that although ordinary beings have actually severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the eight stages, the principle of their retrogression is nonetheless valid.
Furthermore, other masters maintain that the mundane path has no definitive power to sever the afflictions; therefore, the Blessed One stated:
"It is only by attaining noble wisdom that one severs the afflictions, not those who are ordinary worldlings."
Once noble wisdom has been attained, how could it fail to sever the afflictions?
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"That which is superior to something else means that once it has surpassed that thing, it does not arise again; if it were to arise again, it would not be superior to that thing."
Although ordinary beings may sever their afflictions, those afflictions sometimes arise again; therefore, it is certain that they lack actual severance.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:

"When the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth have not been permanently severed, craving and other afflictions are likewise not severed; only when those [views] are severed do these [cravings] finally cease."
Furthermore, a sūtra states:

"As long as these three factors—view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—are not abandoned, one can never abandon greed, hatred, and delusion.
Since ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have not yet been able to abandon the view of a self-identity and the others, it is certain that they have not truly abandoned afflictions such as greed.
This is also not the case; for while praising the supreme one, it is spoken cryptically regarding the greed, hatred, and delusion of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

That is to say, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, praised the supreme one by stating that the abandonment of afflictions requires the attainment of noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*), because among all forms of wisdom for abandoning afflictions, noble wisdom is the most excellent in terms of correct contemplation (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
In the world, there are also expressions made from the perspective of excellence:
it is said that only a true king can protect a kingdom, and only a true virtuous person does not fall into deception or folly.

Therefore, this sutra speaks solely with the underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) regarding the path that ultimately abandons the afflictions; one must not, on this basis, be able to negate the function of various mundane paths in abandoning the afflictions.

By this, the superiority of this [sūtra] over that [other sūtra] has already been explained; for it is spoken with the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that the noble path which abandons the afflictions is never again lost or regressed, remaining without remainder.

This is just as in the world, where one says "having eaten this food, it will never again be vomited up" when one has eaten it, or "having burned this object, it will never again arise" when one has burned it.

It is not that what has already been transformed and expelled, or what arises subsequently, is neither food nor fire; rather, this is stated with reference to the ultimate absence of further transformation or arising.
This case should be understood in the same way. Otherwise, if the afflictions already severed were to arise again, then at the very moment they are severed, they could not be called "conquered."
Although it is not a permanent victory, a temporary victory is not non-existent; how can this be cited as proof that there is no actual abandonment?

As for the claim that when the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth have not been permanently abandoned, the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion must necessarily remain unabandoned—this does not contradict my own position, because this was spoken with the hidden intent (*saṃdhāya*) regarding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

This means that the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) belonging to the category of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) are first abandoned, and only at a later time are the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) abandoned.
This is stated with reference to the case where, after the afflictions of views have been abandoned without remainder, the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are subsequently abandoned.
Since it was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), it cannot serve as a definitive proof.
This sūtra is certainly spoken with intentional meaning, for within this very same passage it further states:
"If one has not yet abandoned these three dharmas, one will necessarily be unable to abandon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth."
What are the three factors?
First, improper mental attention; second, associating with wrong paths; and third, a debased state of mind—these are the three.

However, it is certainly impossible to first abandon these three factors and only later abandon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, because there is no antidote to those [three] prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is realized that this sūtra is a teaching of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*).

This refers to what was previously stated regarding the "sound of having abandoned": when the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) subsequently manifests, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth are actually abandoned.
The proponents of the *Nyāyānusāra* state as follows:
"One can also sever the afflictions by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), because there are clear scriptural and logical proofs for this.
First, regarding the scripture, it is said in a sūtra:"
If you are able to permanently sever a single dharma, I guarantee that you will attain the fruit of non-returning.
What is this one dharma? It is the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).

The intention of this sūtra is to state that one who has previously abandoned desire enters the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) and abandons the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); when this clear observation is perfected, they attain the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*). It is not the case that one who has not previously abandoned the greed of the desire realm attains the fruit of non-returner when their clear observation is perfected; therefore, the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) truly is capable of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*).

If his intention is that one gradually attains the realization of the fruit of non-returning after having already abandoned the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), then this statement is spoken cryptically based on such a meaning; it does not mean that the fruit of non-returning is attained at the very moment the view of a self-identity is abandoned.

This is also unreasonable; if it were based on this [interpretation], the Sūtra should also have stated that one "attains the fruit of arhatship," meaning that after abandoning the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one subsequently attains the fruit of arhatship through a gradual process.

However, since the sūtras do not state this, we know that it is only with reference to those who have previously abandoned desire that they enter the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) and, upon the completion of that clear observation, sever the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and attain the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*). Thus, even as an implicit statement, this [interpretation] can be established as a proof.

However, within the stage of the clear realization of the Noble Truths, there is no possibility of withdrawing without having attained the fruit; furthermore, it is impossible for them to attain any further fruit [beyond that]. Therefore, it is said:
"If you sever the view of a self-identity, I guarantee that you will certainly attain the state of Non-returning."
Since it is not attained without an interval, there is no fault.
This principle must necessarily be so, for in other sūtras the Blessed One has also stated that after attaining the fourth dhyāna,
one enters the clear realization (abhisamaya) and attains the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala).
As the Sūtra says:

"By means of such perfection of ethical discipline (śīla), he is able to abandon all desires and unwholesome, evil states," and so on at length, "until he fully dwells in the fourth dhyāna. By means of such perfection of meditative concentration (samādhi), he perceives and knows the Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is," and so on at length, "until he attains the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala)."

If it is argued: "Does this scripture not state that by seeing and knowing the Four Truths as they truly are, one is able to permanently sever the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*)?

If those fetters, such as sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), were already truly severed when one previously became free from the defilements of the desire realm, then it would be incorrect to say that for one who has previously become free from desire, those fetters are only severed now when the Noble Path arises. It is not the case that what was already severed can be severed again; therefore, the scriptural passage cited as proof is invalid."
This is also not the case, for the intent of this sutra is to reveal that at that time one attains only the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
That is to say, for those who attain the fruit of non-returning through gradual stages, they must, at that time, sever the five fetters (*saṃyojana*) without remainder.

In order to make it understood that one who has previously abandoned desire enters the clear observation of the truths (satyābhisamaya) and attains only the state of a Non-returner (anāgāmin), it is said that at that time one abandons the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni).
The intent of this statement is that [the fetters] can be completely severed; it does not mean that all five are severed simultaneously at this present moment.

This must necessarily be so, because the power of the path of seeing cannot eliminate the fetters of greed and hatred without remainder; it is only upon their complete elimination that one realizes the state of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*). From this, we know with certainty that those who have previously abandoned desire were already able to truly sever the two lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*); however, in order to demonstrate that such individuals realize only the state of a Non-returner through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), it is said that they now sever the five lower fetters.
Alternatively, this intention reveals that he is speaking cryptically regarding the severance of further rebirth at this present time.

That is to say, if one has not entered the clear realization of the Noble Truths, then even if such an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) should sever greed and hatred, they will inevitably fall back and lose them at a later time.
Alternatively, this may be a case where a term for "near" is used metaphorically for something distant, as in the expression, "From where does the king come now?

This means that although one has already previously severed the two fetters of greed and hatred, it is spoken of according to worldly convention as "severing them now," just as when a king arrives after having long since departed from his point of origin, one metaphorically says, "From where does he come now? and so forth.

Alternatively, when those three fetters enter the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), there is the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) and the acquisition of the untainted (*anāsrava-prāpti*); since the acquisitions of the two fetters of greed and hatred will never arise again, it is said that at that time five [fetters] are abandoned, without error.

If it is argued that although it is said that one attains the fourth dhyāna and subsequently enters the clear realization (abhisamaya) to obtain the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmiphala), it does not definitively state that the afflictions of the lower stages have been abandoned or suppressed, how can it be known for certain that those afflictions of the lower stages have actually been truly severed, rather than merely suppressed so that their active manifestations (paryavasthāna) no longer appear?
This should not be doubted, because this sūtra states that one attains the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
It cannot be said that this is attained gradually later on, for that has already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, it was already stated earlier that even ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have abandoned desire are born in the higher realms just like noble ones (*ārya*).
It is not universally established that one merely suppresses the afflictions of a lower stage and thereby arises in a higher stage;
rather, it is universally established that one arises in a higher stage only by truly severing the afflictions of a lower stage. Therefore, one should not entertain doubt regarding this matter.
Thus, because there is scriptural authority for this, it is known that the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) is also capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*).

As for the reasoning: the power of the afflictions is able to bind one’s own continuum, causing distinctions between realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*). Therefore, if the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) has not yet been truly severed, yet one were able to be reborn in the form or formless realms, then those afflictions would have no functional capacity to bind one to birth in specific realms and stages, thereby creating such distinctions.

If it is argued that the functional capacity [of a lower stage] is such that one who has not yet subdued the afflictions of a lower stage cannot necessarily give rise to a higher one, this is also incorrect; for even when the afflictions belonging to a particular stage have been subdued, one may still give rise to that stage. This is because there are those capable of subduing the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), yet they can still be reborn in the stage of the Peak of Existence.

Nevertheless, by relying on the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) of its own level, one can also subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*) of that same level; for instance, practices such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) likewise suppress the active afflictions of their own level and bring about the attainment of their abandonment.

One must attain the path of liberation from the various afflictions within this stage, subduing the afflictions so that they do not temporarily manifest; since even craftsmanship and deportment possess such power, how much more so must a wholesome mind have functional efficacy?
Just as one dwelling here is able to subdue all afflictions of the eighth stage so that they do not manifest, for what reason can one alone not subdue those at the Peak of Existence?
One must certainly admit such a principle.

If this were not admitted, how could those who have already abandoned the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), who have resolved their minds on non-arising, and who enter the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) to realize the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), fail to suppress the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) while the Noble Path that abandons them manifests?
Therefore, one who dwells in this realm must possess the skillful wisdom that subdues the afflictions pertaining to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Since it cannot be said that the non-arising of those afflictions in the Peak of Existence occurs merely by their suppression through the power of such wisdom without severing the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those afflictions, the same logic should apply to the eight lower stages. By this, it is definitively known that the mundane paths (*laukikamārga*) also sever afflictions; this principle is thoroughly established.

Furthermore, it would follow that all stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) could be born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because if one suppresses the afflictions of a lower stage, one would immediately attain rebirth in a higher stage.

There are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who first suppress the afflictions of the two realms (the desire and form realms) and later enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); when their clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is complete, they should attain the fruit of a stream-enterer rather than the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmī*). This is because it is admitted that such individuals remain bound by all the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) belonging to the three realms, and the path of seeing is not the specific antidote (*pratipakṣa*) for abandoning those [cultivation-afflictions].

If one dwelling in the stage of fruition should reach the end of life, it must be admitted that they will certainly be reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because the afflictions of the two lower realms have already been suppressed.
If, having been born there, they were to sever the afflictions of the desire realm and so forth to become an Arhat, this would contradict the Sūtra, which states:
"There are five noble ones who attain penetration here and reach finality here."
It is not that those noble ones possess a fixed cause necessitating their return to this very life before realizing parinirvāṇa.

If it is argued that because they are said to have "at most seven more births," they must certainly return to this life from there, this reasoning is also incorrect; for these words were spoken with the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) of referring specifically to the human and celestial realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
How do we know that "seven returns" refers specifically to the desire realm?

It is because the distinctions among the names such as "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) are established solely based on the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm.

That is to say, one is called a "non-returner" (*anāgāmin*) because of having abandoned five types of lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*); and one is called a "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*) because desire, hatred, and delusion have become thin within those same lower fetters.
The candidate for the fruit of non-returner is called "one-interval" (ekavīcika), and the candidate for the fruit of once-returner is called "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula).

Since these designations are established solely based on the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm, we know that the status of "seven-times-at-most" (*saptakṛtvah-parama*) is established only in dependence upon the stage where none of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm have yet been abandoned.

If the seven returns were established based on not having transcended the afflictions of this specific stage, then one would know that one undergoes seven existences only within that stage which has not been transcended; therefore, the seven returns do not pertain to the form or formless realms.

Furthermore, for one who has already abandoned the craving of the two realms, the designation "seven-times-at-most" (*saptakṛtvah-parama*) should not be established, because such a person is comprised solely within the category of those with sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), whereas being born at most seven times is a characteristic of those comprised within the category of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*).

Furthermore, what he has stated contradicts his own school’s scriptures; for those scriptures do not allow for seven rebirths, nor do they permit the possibility of undergoing an eighth birth. Since the places of birth in the form and formless realms are extremely numerous, it is impossible for there to be a maximum of only seven existences within them.
Furthermore, once one has completed seven births in that celestial realm, there is absolutely no possibility of returning to be born here; this would thus contradict the Sūtra.
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"There are five types of noble ones who have attained penetration in this place and reached the ultimate in this place."
Furthermore, being reborn seven times is not necessarily experienced [in full]; the term "maximum" (*parama*) refers only to the greatest possible number.

If a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) were to go there and attain parinirvāṇa after experiencing a second birth, they would also have reached the ultimate consummation in that place; this would certainly contradict the aforementioned sūtra. Therefore, it is absolutely impossible to attain rebirth in a higher realm merely by suppressing the afflictions belonging to the lower stages.
Since ordinary beings possess the capacity for higher rebirth, it is known that the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) is also capable of abandoning the defilements (*kleśa*).
Some maintain this position:

those who have previously detached from the craving of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) at the time they enter the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Although sensual desire and ill-will do not manifest [at that time], they possess those acquisitions which constantly follow and bind them.
Furthermore, they argue:

although one necessarily attains the realization of the fruit of stream-entry at the time of the clear observation of the Path, because that moment is extremely brief, the various sūtras do not state it in such terms.
One who has previously abandoned desire realizes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) at the stage of the clear observation of the path (*mārgābhisamaya*).

Furthermore, it is said that one who attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) simultaneously with the clear observation of the truths; here, the word "simultaneously" (*saha*) is established in reference to the immediate succession (*ānantarya*), as stated in the Sūtra:
"When sentient beings are born in the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), they subsequently perish from there as soon as perception arises together [with their birth]."
Furthermore, he says this:

"Because one attains the superior path at the stage of the clear realization of the Path, one immediately attains the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmiphala) at that very moment by becoming free from the craving of the desire realm.
All such [statements] are internally contradictory, like the words of a young child speaking in his own room.

That is to say, if it were claimed that one who has previously abandoned desire attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) at the time of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the path—on the grounds that although sensual desire and ill-will do not manifest, they still possess those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) which constantly bind them—then it would be incorrect to say that one attains the superior path at the stage of the clear realization of the path, such that by abandoning desire for the realm of sensuality, one immediately attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) at that very moment; for it is impossible to simultaneously attain both the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of non-returner during the clear realization of the path.

If the latter gate were correct, the former gate should be abandoned; if the former gate were correct, the latter gate should be abandoned, for it is impossible for both to be correct when they are mutually contradictory.

If their intention is that, just as when a path belonging to a higher stage manifests, one must necessarily cultivate the path subsumed under a lower stage—since a superior path, when manifesting, can cultivate that which is inferior—then this case should also be so: because one attains the superior path at the stage of the clear realization of the path (*mārgābhisamaya*), one becomes free from the craving of the desire realm, and thus at that time attains the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
This is not reasonable. Why?

Because that school does not establish the existence of the future; because they maintain that there is no "acquisition" (*prāpti*) distinct from the phenomenon itself; because it is logically untenable that a non-manifest path could sever the fetters of sensual desire and ill-will; because the path of seeing cannot abandon what is to be abandoned by cultivation; and because the two paths cannot coexist in a single moment of presence.
Furthermore, regarding that which is called "attaining the superior path" during the stage of the clear realization of the path taught by him—what is its essential nature?
At that time, there is no other superior path that can be correctly identified as what is attained.

Since they cannot describe the characteristics of the path attained, how can they claim that this path is capable of abandoning sensual desire, and thus assert that one attains the fruit of non-returning at that time?
Therefore, what they say is merely a product of their own subjective whims.

Furthermore, one should not claim that although the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) is necessarily attained at the time of the clear realization of the path (*mārgābhisamaya*), because that moment is extremely brief, the various sūtras do not state:
"One who has previously abandoned desire realizes the fruit of stream-entry at the stage of the clear realization of the path."

Furthermore, one should not say that a non-returner is attained simultaneously with the clear realization of the truths; for the term "simultaneous" is established here in reference to the uninterrupted path.
Why is this? Because the stage of once-returner is lacking.

Since one must necessarily realize the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*) immediately after the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), it is not the case that the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) is realized without interval from the fruit of stream-entry. Accordingly, the Sūtra should state:

"For one who has previously abandoned desire, at the stage of the clear realization of the path (*mārgābhisamaya*), the fruit of stream-entry is realized; simultaneously with the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), the fruit of once-returning is attained, and only from this immediately thereafter is the fruit of non-returning obtained."
Since he does not say so, it is unreasonable.

Therefore, that proponent stands with his back turned to the meaning of the True Dharma; he merely recounts his own sentiments through the scriptures and cannot be engaged in a deliberation of correct reasoning.
The digression is concluded; we should now analyze the primary subject.

The original discussion concerned the sequential arising of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) across various stages. Since it was previously stated that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) necessarily arises immediately after the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), what kind of knowledge arises immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion?
The verse says:
After the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) of the Immovable One, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) necessarily arises;
for others, it is either the knowledge of exhaustion or right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). These are present in all who have attained the fruit of arhatship.
The treatise says:

For those Arhats of the "unshakable dharma" type (*akopyadharman*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) arises immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). Since this knowledge was what they originally sought, it is necessarily attained simultaneously with the knowledge of exhaustion.
This means that they seek to attain what accords with their respective understandings; if this were absent, there would be an obstacle to entering nirvana.

When all Arhats simultaneously attain wisdom, they likewise aspire to seek the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*); however, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) ought logically to arise first, because it was what was previously sought during the stage of the cause.

Following the previously unshakable *vajra-samādhi*, one attains the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), yet it does not yet manifest; it only manifests immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).

With the exception of those who were previously unshakable, for other Arhats, the knowledge of exhaustion arises immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion, or it directly induces the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*); this is because, in the case of others, there is the possibility of falling back from the knowledge of non-arising.

This means that if one was previously of the nature of "one liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*), although they sought both types [of liberation] during the causal stage, because there is the possibility of falling away from the ultimate fruit, at the moment the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) is ceasing, one does not attain the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) but only attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Therefore, after the knowledge of exhaustion, either the knowledge of exhaustion manifests again, or it directly induces the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*).
First, for one of immovable dharma, after the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), either further knowledge of non-arising arises or the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi).

This view of one beyond training is common to all those who have attained the fruit of arhatship, just like the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna); therefore, at the very moment the diamond-like concentration (vajropamasamādhi) is ceasing, everyone attains the right view of one beyond training.

However, this right view is not what is primarily sought; therefore, immediately after the two knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), it may either arise at once or remain unmanifest.

Regarding the general meaning of this stage: if one was previously immovable, the initial arising of the knowledge of exhaustion lasts for only a single moment, and the subsequent knowledge of non-arising likewise lasts for a single moment or may continue in succession.
In the case of one liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimukta*), when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) first arises, it may occur for a single moment or as a continuous succession.

The unlearned right view (*aśaikṣī samyagdṛṣṭi*) arising from these two states lacks any fixed momentary or continuous character, because, as previously stated, such a person does not seek [the goal] correctly.
The Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Volume Sixty-Six;
The Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra, Volume Sixty-Seven.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.

Chapter Eleven: Distinguishing the Noble and the Holy, Part Six, Section Eleven. As it has been said regarding the śramaṇa and the fruits of the śramaṇa, what is meant by the nature of a śramaṇa?
What is the nature of this fruition?
How many distinct types of fruition stages are there in total?
The verse says:
The path of purification and the state of a śramaṇa, with their conditioned and unconditioned fruits—these consist of eighty-nine factors: the paths of liberation and cessation.
The treatise says:

One who is called a śramaṇa is so named because they are able to forever extinguish and eliminate the demons of birth and death within the various realms and destinies, or because they are able to diligently exert themselves to pacify all faults and bring them to eternal stillness; therefore, they are named a śramaṇa.
As the Bhagavān himself has explained:

because one is able to diligently exert effort to pacify and eliminate the various faults of defilement consisting of evil and unwholesome dharmas—and so forth at length—one is therefore called a śramaṇa.
That which belongs to a śramaṇa is called the nature of a śramaṇa; this is precisely the perfuming dharma cultivated by a śramaṇa.

"Perfuming" (vāsanā) has the meaning of expelling the foul-smelling afflictions; it takes the untainted noble path as its essence, rather than the mundane path, because it is able to bring all faults to ultimate rest without remainder.

Consequently, although an ordinary person may have already severed the defilements of the sphere of nothingness, they are not a true śramaṇa, because various faults still remain and their tranquility is merely temporary rather than ultimate.

Since the untainted path constitutes the nature of a śramaṇa, and it takes both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena as its fruits, the essence of the fruits of śramaṇaship thus encompasses both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The Buddha taught that these fruits comprise four types in total: namely, the first, stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), up to the last, arhatship (*arhat*).

The category of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) is called the conditioned essence of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*); the abandonment of the factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya-dharma-prahāṇa*) is called the unconditioned essence of the fruit of stream-entry.

Alternatively, the category of the subsequent knowledge of the path, or the category of the sixth untainted path of liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti-mārga*) for one who has become free from desire for the desire realm, is called the conditioned essence of the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*).

The abandonment of the factors to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and the first six categories of the factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) pertaining to the desire realm—this is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) essence of the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

The category of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) or the ninth untainted path of liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti-mārga*) for those free from desire in the desire realm—this is called the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) essence of the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

The abandonment of factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and the abandonment of factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) pertaining to the desire realm—this is called the unconditioned essence of the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the category of right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*)—this is called the conditioned essence of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*).
The abandonment of those dharmas of the three realms that are to be eliminated through seeing and cultivation is what constitutes the unconditioned essence of the fruit of arhatship.
Nevertheless, in the sūtras, the Blessed One speaks only of the unconditioned essence of the fruits of śrāmaṇya; as it is said:
"What is called the fruit of stream-entry?"
This refers to the abandonment of the three fetters, up to: "What is the fruit of arhatship?
It is that which has permanently abandoned greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth.
But has it not already been admitted that the fruit of non-returner involves the permanent abandonment of hatred?
This also involves no contradiction, as the explanations of the meanings differ.

The intention here is to state that "permanent abandonment" refers to the severance of all defilements of affliction; it does not mean that one who still possesses some remaining defilements of affliction can obtain the designation of "permanent abandonment" through a minor, partial severance.
However, it is stated elsewhere:
"What is full comprehension?
It is the permanent abandonment of craving," and so forth, as explained at length.
The intended meaning here is that if there is abandonment of every aspect (*sarvākāra*) and abandonment of everything (*sarva*), it is termed "permanent abandonment" (*atyantaprahāṇa*).

"Every aspect" refers to the abandonment of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) [of the defilements] and the abandonment of their objective supports (*ālambana*); this occurs specifically at the stage of abandoning those dharmas that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).

Regarding phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has already been abandoned, though the objective conditions (*ālambana*) that take them as objects have not yet been abandoned;

regarding phenomena abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), the objective conditions that take them as objects have already been abandoned, though their intrinsic nature has not yet been abandoned. Because these are not permanently severed, they are not yet termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
The term "all" refers to the permanent abandonment of any one category among the eleven afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and so forth.

By this, it is fully demonstrated that there are nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*), and it is also shown that the abandonments of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are not subsumed under thorough knowledge.
The Dārṣṭāntikas maintain that the essence of the fruits of śrāmaṇya is exclusively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), based on both scripture and reasoning.

The scriptural authority has been stated previously; now the reasoning shall be explained. Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are subject to destruction and thus cannot be relied upon, whereas the essence of the fruits of śrāmaṇya is worthy of reliance, it is therefore exclusively unconditioned.
Furthermore, this teaching is not so, for it accords with the previous explanation.

That is to say, as has been explained in various places previously, those *sūtras* cited by him—which possess further underlying intentions—cannot possibly establish the ultimate (*paramārtha*) principle.

Although the sūtra states that the essence of the fruit of stream-entry consists in the abandonment of the three fetters, it does not say "only. This is similar to the case of the concentration for dwelling in happiness in the present life among the four types of cultivated concentration.
While the sūtra describes this as the first dhyāna, the principle of this concentration actually extends to others as well; therefore, the word "only" was not used to indicate a specific intention.
This sūtra is also like this; one should not adhere to it dogmatically.

If it is argued that other sūtras state that dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) pertains to all four dhyānas, while this [sūtra] does not, such reasoning is also incorrect, for it is identical to those [other cases].
This means that other sūtras state that the permanent abandonment of six factors is called "stream-entry" (srotāpanna); how could it be limited to only the three fetters?
Furthermore, according to the principle, a stream-enterer should also actually have abandoned views of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), craving, and so forth.
This is not the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), as there is no separate cause for its realization; therefore, what has been stated does not bring about satisfaction.
Consequently, the sūtra cited here does not prove that only unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) constitute the fruits of śramaṇaship.
Principle is also not principle; for, in relation to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), non-erroneous wisdom is most worthy of being relied upon and trusted.

This means that when the wisdom of reality arises in a practitioner, they are able to know for themselves, "My births are exhausted," and so forth.
