The afflictions abandoned through seeing do not arise with a sense of relish; they can only be induced by the power of conceptual discrimination.
The afflictions abandoned through cultivation do arise with a sense of relish; they can be induced solely by the power of the objective sphere.
Alternatively, they must admit that even for Arhats who lack the seeds of past afflictions, there is still the possibility of regressing and giving rise to afflictions;
just as when wholesome roots have been severed without remainder, those roots can arise again even though their seeds no longer exist.
In reality, there are cases where the roots of goodness are severed without remainder, as it is said:

"In such a person, wholesome dharmas have vanished and unwholesome dharmas have appeared; although there remain some accompanying roots of goodness that have not yet been severed, at a later time, all of them will be completely severed."
This point has already been fully determined as previously explained.

However, it cannot be that afflictions arise without seeds, causing those who have attained the fruit of arhatship to all regress and give rise to afflictions; for this has already been thoroughly explained above.
For [afflictions] would only arise through regression if there were no constant application of effort or a firm path characterized by respect.

Furthermore, just as in your own school it is admitted that the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* arises in the continuum of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) despite the absence of untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), so too one must admit that afflictions (*kleśa*) can arise in an Arhat despite the absence of the seeds of affliction.
Regarding this, some say:
"The patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) can arise even though it lacks seeds.
This has already been thoroughly examined and refuted elsewhere.

To refute a certain class of views, one should further investigate that the seeds of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) within the continuum of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) entail faults whether they are considered tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*). First,

the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of an ordinary person cannot serve as the seed-nature for untainted phenomena, because they have not yet been induced by the capacity of the untainted, just like the seed-nature of afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth.
That is to say, as they conceive it: within the continuum, the capacity induced by afflictions is designated as the "seed of affliction," which serves as the productive cause for those afflictions.
If, within the continuum, that which is induced by wholesome states and so forth is designated as the "seed of the wholesome" and so forth, it serves as the cause for the wholesome and so forth.

It is not the case that the mental continua of ordinary beings already possess a capacity induced by the untainted (*anāsrava*), and therefore they should not be established as seeds for untainted phenomena.

If this capacity induced by the untainted were to be called the seed of those phenomena, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because everything would then become the seed of everything.

In this way, the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) would become seeds of affliction, and the various afflicted dharmas would become seeds of those beyond training; consequently, there would be no established distinction between the definitive characteristics of defilement and purification. Thus, according to their own tenet, just as external perfuming exists, the effort expended in perfuming by the wholesome and so forth would be rendered fruitless, because they assert that the mind and mental factors of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) are called "seeds of the outflow-free" (anāsrava-bīja) merely due to the presence of a capacity induced by outflow-free dharmas.

Furthermore, if the seeds of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) within the minds and mental factors of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) were themselves tainted (*sāsrava*), they would—due to their distinct nature—be incapable of being those seeds; how then could they act as the cause for the arising of the untainted?
A sweet fruit cannot be produced from seeds that are not bitter.

Only those things capable of acting as seeds can be called "causes of production"; therefore, from impure causes, only impure results should arise. How then can you insist that the impure serves as the seed for the pure?

If the seeds of untainted dharmas were themselves untainted, they would either not exist within the mental continuum of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), or the state of being an ordinary person would ultimately be non-existent, because all [ordinary persons] would have become possessed of untainted conditioned dharmas.
However, that treatise states:

"Although these minds and mental factors serve as the seeds for the untainted (*anāsrava*), their essence is not itself untainted, just as wood and the like are not themselves of the nature of fire and so forth.
This means that just as in the world wood is the seed of fire and earth is the seed of gold, yet one cannot say that wood is the nature of fire or that earth is the nature of gold."
Thus, although the minds and mental factors of ordinary beings possess uncontaminated seeds, their substance is not itself uncontaminated.
That assertion is irrational, because fire and other such elements already exist within wood and other materials as seeds of their own kind.
How is this known? By means of scripture and reasoning.
That is to say, a sutra states:
"In this mass of wood there are various elements (*dhātu*)," and so forth, as explained at length.

Furthermore, seeing that fire can arise from wood, those seeking fire take hold of the wood because the fire-element (*tejodhātu*) must necessarily exist within the mass of wood; therefore, wood is called the "fire-seed" (*tejodhātu*). This is because the fire-element is predominant within the wood, not because it was previously non-existent and only then acquired the name "fire-seed."
The principle that gold emerges from within the earth should likewise be understood as follows:

it is a specific differentiation within the earth from which gold emerges. If the earth were devoid of gold such that it could not serve as the seed for gold, then those seeking gold would simply take up any portion of the earth; they would not seek out a specific differentiation of the earth. Therefore, we know that there exists a distinct seed of gold within the earth, and it is not the case that one obtains the designation "seed of gold" while the earth lacks gold.

Therefore, their statement—that just as wood and the like do not have the nature of fire and so forth, so too the minds and mental factors of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), though possessing untainted seeds, are in essence not untainted—is logically untenable.

Furthermore, the treatise of that school states: "Because there is no heat prior to drilling. This means that when the wood being drilled has not yet been drilled, heat does not yet exist; therefore, one knows that at the stage before the wood is drilled, there are no fire atoms within it. The same applies to gold and other elements within earth and so forth.
To investigate in this manner contradicts both scripture and reasoning, for the Noble Ones have taught that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are inseparable.

This is also logically necessary, as the functions performed by the primary elements are observed within all material aggregates (*rūpa-kalāpa*). This has already been established at length in the discussion on the locus of the primary elements.
However, the fact that heat is not perceived before drilling is because that collection does not have an increase in the hot primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Furthermore, regarding what was said—

that it is granted that uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) take contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as their productive cause— this is consistent with both scripture and reasoning and incurs no contradiction.
This is also not the case, as it contradicts both scripture and reasoning.

For the Sūtra states that things of a similar kind take only those of a similar kind as their cause: "Because ignorance is the cause, defiled attachment arises; because clear knowledge is the cause, one becomes free from defiled attachment."
From this root of goodness, other roots of goodness arise; if one frequently engages in vitarka and vicāra regarding various objects, the mind will frequently enter into those very objects.
There are immeasurable sūtras such as these.
Since the categories of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are distinct, how can it be said that the former serves as the cause for the latter?
Furthermore, since the contaminated mind is the basis for afflictions, how could it possibly serve as the cause for phenomena that are pure by nature?
That it contradicts the teachings is already established.
As for its contradiction with reason: if contaminated phenomena were the cause of uncontaminated phenomena, then uncontaminated phenomena as causes would necessarily produce contaminated phenomena.
Even if this were granted, what fault would there be?
Just as the mind and mental factors of noble ones are produced by being drawn forth from the mind and mental factors of ordinary beings,
so too should the mind and mental factors of ordinary beings be produced by being drawn forth from the mind and mental factors of noble ones, for there is no difference in their causes.
If it is argued that the wholesome minds and mental factors of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) can serve as the productive cause for untainted phenomena (*anāsrava*) because they are both wholesome,
this fault is identical to the previous one.
What fault is there in the same [position] as before?

It would mean that because they are of the same class, they should mutually act as causes for one another. If this were so, then the mind and mental factors of an Ārya would produce the mind and mental factors of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), resulting in the absurdity of the noble and the ordinary acting as causes for one another.
The meaning of "receding from what is contended for" should be established by this, because both pure and defiled minds are equally outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*).
Consequently, the outflow-tainted pure mind of an Arhat should be termed a seed of the various outflows (*āsrava*), since the outflows themselves possess the nature of being outflow-tainted.
Thus, one would contradict what that treatise states:
"Because there are no seeds of affliction within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), there is ultimately no possibility of falling back from the afflictions already abandoned.
If an Arhat still possessed the seeds of affliction, he could not be called one who has exhausted the outflows (āsravakṣaya).
Furthermore, regarding what was said:

"Just as the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) takes uncontaminated phenomena (anāsravadharma) as its virile fruit (puruṣakāraphala), yet there is no loss of the ultimate non-arising [of those phenomena];
likewise, uncontaminated phenomena taking contaminated phenomena as their cause also entails no loss of the ultimate non-arising [of those phenomena]."

This is also unreasonable, because there is no fault in the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) being either of the same or a different category, as has already been extensively analyzed in the section on the four conditions.
However, since the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) differs from the equal-and-immediate condition in terms of its directness or indirectness, it cannot serve as a valid analogy.
If this were not admitted, the number of conditions would have to be reduced.
Furthermore, by such an analogy, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

That is to say, if one admits that [the preceding moment] acts as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), then it would also follow that it possesses the status of a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).

Just as when one dies from a defiled mind in the form realm and is born into the desire realm with a mind of rebirth, since it is already admitted that matter serves as an equal-and-immediate condition for the desire realm, one must likewise admit that it possesses the sense of being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

If it were admitted that the afflictions of the desire realm serve as the cause for the afflictions of the form realm, then noble ones who have abandoned desire-greed would still possess the seeds of desire-greed; consequently, their abandonment of afflictions through the noble paths would be subject to relapse.
This would contradict the teaching that because the seeds of affliction no longer exist, there is no relapse from the liberation that is the fruit of the untainted path.

Furthermore, one should not admit that among the afflictions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there exists the seed of desire-realm afflictions (*kāmadhātu-kleśa*) capable of serving as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for desire-realm afflictions, rather than [the seed of] form-realm afflictions themselves.

The reason for this is that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have already effectively severed the afflictions prior [to reaching the form realm], and because the seeds of those [severed] afflictions do not possess a distinct substantial entity (*bhinnasvabhāva*) from them.
If it is argued that this is like the perfuming of external phenomena, it is not so, because this and that are not analogous.

That is to say, in those external phenomena, both the perfumer and the perfumed exist as a continuous succession at the same time; there are distinct flavors and so forth that abide within the perfumed, persisting in succession for a long duration. Internal phenomena are not like this—how, then, could there be perfuming?
Therefore, the analogy for "the supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) established by him results in contradicting his own thesis.

Alternatively, it is like one who returns from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*): although they lack the seeds of form at that time, form arises because they have already become a worldling (*pṛthagjana*) who has truly abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*).
In the same way, why would it be logically contradictory for an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*), even if they lack the seeds of affliction, to fall back and give rise to afflictions?
However, as for what was said:

"Those who arise in the form realm from the formless realm—if they possess the seeds of the formless, they certainly should not return to birth in the form realm, because noble ones who have attained the formless do not return to birth in the form realm."
This too is unreasonable, because it is not analogous.

That is to say, those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have not yet been able to realize the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) included within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). It is not the case that there is a principle whereby one can realize the abandonment of afflictions to be abandoned by insight while remaining in that realm;

rather, one must first realize the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by insight before one can subsequently realize the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are necessarily unable to transcend the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), when the force of the karma that drew forth that maturation (*vipāka*) is exhausted, they must return to birth in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) even though the seeds of form no longer exist; therefore, when such ordinary beings are born in the formless realm, they have not yet realized the state of non-arising regarding form, because they will inevitably give rise to form again in the future.

When one is born as a noble being in the formless realm, they have necessarily already previously abandoned a portion of the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) that are to be abandoned by insight; furthermore, at the time of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation belonging to the formless stage, they have already abandoned the karma that definitely brings about form in that stage, and thus they are certain to realize the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation within the stage of the Peak of Existence.

When a noble one (*ārya*) passes from this realm to another realm, they have already realized the state of non-arising regarding form (*rūpa*), because form will certainly not arise for them hereafter.
It is by virtue of this that form does not arise for the noble one subsequently; it is not because the seeds of form within their body are non-existent.
Therefore, what they have said— that because form does not arise for noble ones who are formless, if the seed of form were absent, form should not arise— is certainly unreasonable. Consequently,
their statement that "if there were no difference between the abandonment of ordinary beings and that of noble ones, then what is attained should be the same" is also refuted.
This reasoning is also incorrect, because there is a difference in what has been abandoned.

That is to say, it was previously stated that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are unable to abandon the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and therefore they return from the formless attainments to be reborn below;
the noble ones (*ārya*) are the opposite of this—how could their abandonment not differ?

Furthermore, if an Arhat does not fall back because they lack the seeds of affliction, then a learner (śaikṣa), who possesses the seeds of affliction, would likewise fall back from the fruit attained by means of the untainted path; this is because the learner possesses the seeds of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation that are subsumed under their own realm and stage.
If this were not admitted, then one should not say that because those beyond training (aśaikṣa) lack the seeds of affliction, they are necessarily free from falling back.
This concludes the digression.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) further says:
Furthermore, the *Daśottara-sūtra* states as follows:
"One dharma should be cultivated, namely, liberation through love and time (*sāmayikī-kāntā-vimukti*).
One dharma should be realized, namely, immovable liberation (*akopyā-vimukti*)."

If the nature of the fruit of arhatship were designated as "liberation through occasional loving confidence" (samayika-kānta-vimukti), why would the fruit of arhatship be mentioned twice in this *Daśottara-sūtra*?

Furthermore, nowhere has it been stated that the fruit of arhatship is called "that which should be produced" (abhisamutthāpanīya); rather, it is only said to be "that which should be realized" (sākṣātkartavya).
This reasoning is also incorrect, because it is established by this very fact.
That is to say, since it has been stated that there are two kinds of liberation, it has already demonstrated that the fruit of arhatship (āsravakṣaya-phala) is subject to regression.
As the Sūtra says:
"I definitively declare that there is no cause or condition for one who has personally realized the liberation of the mind through immovability (*akopya-cetovimukti*) to fall away from it.
By implication, it is stated that for others, there is the possibility of falling away.
The Master of the Sūtras further states:

If it is claimed that there is falling away, and that this is because the Sūtra speaks of "occasional liberation through desire," I also grant this; however, one must examine whether that which falls away from occasional liberation through desire is of the nature of the fruit of arhatship, or rather of dhyāna and so forth.
However, because that fundamental dhyāna and samādhi must wait for the proper time to manifest, it is called "liberation by time" (samayavimukta).
Because he frequently desires its manifestation in order to attain the blissful dwelling in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra), it is called "craving" (tṛṣṇā).
At present, I have not yet fully understood their intention regarding whether dhyāna and samādhi are contaminated (sāsrava) or uncontaminated (anāsrava).

If they were uncontaminated, then all uncontaminated conditioned phenomena within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) would necessarily be of the nature of the fruit (phalatva); thus, it would already be admitted that the liberation through love at the proper time (kāla-vimukti) is of the nature of the fruit, which would establish this principle as being perfectly consistent [with their own tenets], thereby contradicting their own school’s position that there is no falling away from the state of one who has attained the fruit (phala-parihāṇi).
If it were impure (*sāsrava*), it would not be universally established.
If you argue that the fault is the same, this is not logically equivalent, because this is explained as being similar to the "unshakable" (*āneñjya*).

That is to say, when the Sūtra speaks of the "unshakable liberation," it is accepted as being the untainted (*anāsrava*) state within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); this principle is universally established.
Since the sūtra speaks of "liberation through time and through desire," it should also be fully established that this is the untainted [state] within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, because it is accomplished as non-periodic (akālika) and untainted, the sūtra states:
"There are arhats who are liberated non-periodically."
This is established for both parties: that non-timely liberation (akāla-vimukti) is the nature of the fruit of arhatship (arhattva-phala).

Since there is a sūtra stating that there are Arhats called "timely-liberated" (kāla-vimukta), it must likewise be established that this timely liberation is also the nature of the fruit of arhatship.
Furthermore, it is as with the "unshakable" (*āniñjya*), which is said to be "realized.

That is to say, just as regarding the unshakable, there is the statement that "it is realized by the body," so too the unshakable liberation is the nature of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*).

The Sūtra also speaks of "realization through the body" (*kāyasākṣitva*) at the time of "timely liberation with affection" (*sāmāyikī kāntā vimuktiḥ*), which likewise has the nature of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*). As the Sūtra says:

"If, by means of such characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-nimitta*), one has already realized liberation with affection through the body at the proper time, yet later cannot repeatedly reflect upon those same characteristics in accordance with reality, one then falls away from what was realized," and so forth, as explained at length.
If it is argued that one should be considered "with outflows" (sāsrava) because of this statement, rather than attaining arhatship through the characteristics of outflow-free (anāsrava) formations,
then the possibility of subsequent repeated reflection or non-reflection, as well as non-retrogression or retrogression, would be logically consistent.
This is also not the case, because it is spoken of in terms of categories.
That is to say, the Sūtra does not state that this is identical to that; rather, it speaks in terms of types, referring to the occurrence of repeated reflection or non-reflection at a later time.

The meaning here is that those in the stage of training and those in the stage beyond training alike contemplate the objects of the appropriated aggregates, such as form, through aspects such as impermanence; it is like the saying, "one should drink the same medicine one has previously taken."

Alternatively, because they share the same fault: that is to say, when one who has attained liberation through love (*sneha-vimukti*) realizes it by means of the characteristics of contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*), there is no subsequent repeated contemplation of those prior practices as having been previously cultivated for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*); rather, the preparatory application (*prayoga*) itself constitutes the very essence of the dwelling in happiness in the present life at a later time.

Therefore, what has been stated here does not prove that [the liberation] is contaminated (*sāsrava*); for this reason, one should not raise such an objection, but should instead examine those things from which it may regress and so forth.
Furthermore, as for their statement that "liberation through timely affection" (*samayikī-kāntā-vimukti*) is identical to the fundamental dhyānas and meditative absorptions (*samādhi*):
That principle is not established, because the sūtras state that the nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and liberation (*vimukti*) are distinct. As a sūtra says:
"Does concentration come first and liberation later, or does liberation come first and concentration later?"
...and so forth, as explained at length.

Although some claim that dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) is the very essence of liberation through love for the occasion (*samayikī kāntā vimuktiḥ*), this is not reasonable, because it has never been so stated; that is to say, no sūtra has ever made such a statement.

The "liberation through the destruction of craving" (*āsravakṣaya-vimukti*) is the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*); this is merely the statement of a youth living in his own room.

If it is argued that although there is no scriptural proof for what he says, there is nonetheless a definitive correct principle (*yukti*) upon which to rely—namely, that this [liberation] is like that [other liberation], because it is said to be subject to falling away (*parihāṇi*).

As it is said that there is a falling away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), it is likewise said that there is a falling away from the liberation cherished at the time of death (*samayavimukti*); therefore, one should know that these two differ in name but are identical in meaning.
Such an explanation is not logically sound, because it gives rise to many faults, such as establishing what is already accepted [by others].

That is to say, our school maintains that regarding the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), those of immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*) possess only the retrogression of enjoyment (*upabhogaparihāṇi*); as for those who are liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), there is also the retrogression of what has already been attained (*prāptaparihāṇi*).

It is not that those of immovable dharma also retrogress from their mastery (*vaśitā*); rather, they simply lack the leisure to manifest it due to other affairs. Although it does not manifest for a time, they do not lose their mastery.
If it were otherwise, the abiding in happiness in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra) would consist of both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava),
and since both would equally not be manifest due to their respective activities,
one would necessarily lose mastery over them both. Consequently, when seeking to realize mastery later on, there would have to be the possibility of falling away from what has not yet been attained.

However, the Buddha prohibited this [view] because he taught that there are two types of Arhats—those subject to regression and those not—based on whether they have attained what was previously unattained; furthermore, within the Noble Teaching, liberation alone is regarded as precious.

Since there is no falling away from this [state], one should say that there is only one type of arhat; yet the sūtras state that there are others who fall away from the bliss of the present life in other places and for other types, and it is also said that there are others who fall away from "liberation dependent on time" (samaya-vimukta) in other places and for other types. Therefore, we know that liberation dependent on time is not the dwelling in bliss of the present life.
Based on this reasoning, one should reject that assertion as merely the talk of a child staying in his own room.
Furthermore, he should be asked: when one withdraws from dhyāna, is there detachment from the various desires or not?

If one claims that there is such a thing as "falling away" from detachment, then to say that one falls away when there is actually no falling away from the state of desirelessness would surely contradict the experience of the joy and bliss born of detachment.
Furthermore, how could it be that Koṭikarna, knowing he had already fallen away six times, became so deeply despondent with himself that he took up a sharp blade and committed suicide?
If it is said that there is no abandonment [of defilements], then afflictions should arise; if afflictions do not arise, how could one ever regress from meditative absorption?
If you claim that while the antidote is lost, the fruit of abandonment is not, how then will you explain the *Udāyin-sūtra*?
Furthermore, the path is able to maintain the fruit of abandonment it has attained, because one must realize the path in order to realize abandonment.
Who would believe this statement that contradicts correct reasoning—that one abandons the path but not abandonment during the stage of superior progress?

Furthermore, within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the nature of mastery over concentration cannot be found apart from the absorptions themselves; therefore, it is only when afflictions arise that there is the possibility of falling away.
Alternatively, what distinction would there be in the nature of mastery itself?
Do not allow for the existence of a separate entity called the nature of sovereignty (*īśvaratva*).
Or, what does the term "nature of sovereignty" refer to?
If there were a distinct dharma named the nature of sovereignty, the aforementioned fault would ensue.
What is the fault of the former position?
It means that if [the state] were not manifest, one would have entirely lost mastery and would subsequently seek to realize it; this would contradict the sūtras.

Furthermore, if the nature of mastery were an entirely separate dharma, then there would be no principle for the loss of mastery, and consequently, there would be no such thing as a lineage characterized by the possibility of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).

Furthermore, just as Arhats of dull faculties must wait for the proper time for mundane fundamental dhyānas and samādhis to manifest before them, they are therefore called "liberated by time" (samayavimukta).
For what reason is it not likewise admitted that their untainted [attainments] are also so?
The untainted transformation must await the proper time before it arises, because it is something that has never been attained before.
It is precisely because there is regression from the fruit of arhatship that the *Daśottara-sūtra* speaks of two types of liberation.
However, as for the objection:

"Why is the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*) mentioned twice in this *Daśottara-sūtra*?"—I shall now explain that this repetition is precisely intended to demonstrate that there are two kinds of fruits of arhatship: those subject to regression and those not subject to regression.

However, the statement here that "the timely liberation (*samayikī vimukti*) should be cultivated and the immovable liberation (*āniñjyā vimukti*) should be realized" has a specific underlying reason.

That is to say, it is intended to make known that the timely liberation must be maintained through constant respect and application (*prayoga*); because one fears falling away from it, it should be frequently manifested before the mind, and thus it is said that it "should be cultivated."

There is no possibility of falling away from the immovable liberation (*akopya-vimukti*); rather, at the moment it is realized, it is called "having accomplished what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtya*). Therefore, the statement that it "should be realized" (*sākṣātkartavya*) is made only with respect to that [immovable liberation].
Furthermore, even the occasional liberation (*samaya-vimukta*) is said to "be realized," for the Sūtra states that one "bodily realizes" (*kāyena sākṣātkaroti*) it therein.

Furthermore, many sūtras state that the cessation of afflictions constitutes the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*), for all sūtras declare that this cessation is to be realized as the "fruit" (*phala*).
However, there is no place where the fruit of arhatship is called "that which is to be produced" (*utpādya*), because such a designation is not universal.
Furthermore, he asks himself:
"If occasional liberation (samaya-vimukti) is not the nature of an Arhat (arhat-phala), why does the Sūtra speak of an 'occasionally liberated Arhat'?
He then answers himself:

This means that because the faculties and nature of one who has attained the fruit of arhatship are dull, their meditative absorption only manifests when dependent upon time; if the opposite were the case, it would be called "liberation not dependent on time.
Such an answer does not establish the intended meaning, for it would follow that those still in training (śaikṣa) should also be described in this way.

That is to say, among those in training (*śaikṣa*), there is also a distinction between dull and sharp faculties; because their meditative attainments manifest either dependently or independently upon time, they receive the names "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*) and "not liberated by occasion" (*asamayavimukta*).
However, since this name does not exist, it is a perverse attachment.
If you argue that this name is not established because those in training (*śaikṣa*) have not yet attained liberation, then the principle is already established:

"love-liberation" (*rāga-vimukti*) is of the nature of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*), for it is accepted that one who has not yet attained liberation cannot possess the designation "liberation."
For this reason, that commentary on the *Cūḍāpanthaka-sūtra* states:

"In the past, while Cūḍāpanthaka was still in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), because he relished the state of occasional liberation (*samayavimukti*) to an extreme and because his faculties were dull, he repeatedly fell away from it. Deeply loathing and reproaching himself, he took up a blade and committed suicide."
Because he had no attachment or regret for his body or life, he attained arhatship at the moment of death and entered parinirvāṇa;
therefore, it is not the case that Ghoṭika fell away from the fruit of arhatship.

This is entirely inconsistent with the sacred teachings (*āgama*). If, while still in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), one were to experience the relishing (*āsvādana*) of occasional liberation (*samayavimukti*), then it would logically follow that one could be designated as "occasionally liberated" even while remaining in the stage of training; however, no such statement is found in the sacred teachings.

If, during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), one cannot be said to be "liberated by time" because one is not yet liberated, then since one is not yet liberated, it should not be said that the nature of being liberated by time has already been attained and experienced as a relish during that stage of training.
Therefore, that [commentator’s] interpretation of this *Cūḍāpanthaka-sūtra* also relies on a biased adherence.
However, that Sthavira, following his own dogmatic view, asserts:

"The liberation through love at specific times (*sāmaya-vimukti*) is attained by means of the mundane path; because it temporarily suppresses the afflictions and brings about a temporary dissociation of the mind from them, it is called 'liberation at specific times. This is because its nature is that of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*)."
Because afflictions exist, the designation "craving" is established; this refers to the sense of an object being defiled by greed.

As for the immovable liberation, through the untainted path one eternally severs the afflictions so that the mind becomes dissociated from them; because the continuum thus evolves, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are forever exhausted.
The Elder, relying on an inferior intention, places the fruit of arhatship in an extremely base position.

That is to say, he does not establish the fruit of arhatship as a "dwelling in happiness in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra) within the continuum of that Arhat’s body, despite the presence of other uncommon virtues; rather, he establishes it as merely a temporary liberation from bonds shared with those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Who would value those dharmas that are the objects and fruits of craving as a dwelling in happiness in the present life?

The skillful means for the temporary suppression and removal of afflictions within the body of one who has attained the fruit [of Arhatship] are cultivated to manifest as a dwelling in happiness in the present life; by this, it is well established that those not yet liberated have certainly not attained the nature of liberation-in-this-life.

Furthermore, it is only regarding the *phalastha* (those who have attained the fruit) that falling away (*parihāṇi*) is taught; for a sūtra states that five causes and five conditions lead to the falling away from the fruit of Arhatship of one who is "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*), whose nature is "liberation through desire" (*kāmarāga-vimukta*).

The holy teachings have never stated that there is such a thing as a "learner" (śaikṣa) named "one liberated by time" (samayavimukta), nor do they state that such a person would fall away from "liberation by time" upon encountering the causes and conditions for retrogression; therefore, no learner exists who is "liberated by time."
Or why would one not consider that there exists the liberation of immovability (*āniñjya-vimokṣa*)?

Furthermore, what they maintain is extremely crude and shallow; for in the Noble Teaching, liberation is held as supreme. Those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) have already fully perceived the truth and are well-versed in the unique, superior qualities of the Noble Teaching—how could they, for the sake of mundane, coarse, and fluctuating roots of virtue, initiate the preparatory action of suicide against a body capable of exhausting suffering?
Therefore, this position held [by some] is extremely unwholesome.

Some say: "One merely becomes weary of the active manifestation of the afflictions (*kleśa-samudācāra*), and then initiates the preparatory action (*prayoga*) of killing oneself; without having yet severed the root of existence (*bhava-mūla*), one takes up a blade and commits suicide."

This interpretation of the sūtra’s meaning lacks profound reasoning. It is said that the noble ones (ārya) are utterly terrified of future existence (*punarbhava*), as the afflictions (*kleśa*) serve as the proximate cause for it. Since the noble ones perceive the fierce and sharp faults of those [afflictions], they possess a path that abandons delusion and opposes future existence; if even a single temporary retreat prevents them from manifesting [that path], they would still rather crush their own bodies, let alone those who repeatedly retreat.

Knowing for himself that he must necessarily realize the fruit of arhatship through this [method], and seeing deeply the faults of the active defilements (*kleśa*), he longs for the previously relinquished fruit of arhatship; therefore, he takes his own life to attain arhatship.

If it is granted that even those in training (śaikṣa), who have not yet realized the sublime bliss of the fruit of arhatship, might still feel revulsion and fear toward the active manifestation of afflictions (kleśa) to the extent of taking up a blade to commit suicide, how much more so for an Arhat, whose transcendence of them is a thousandfold greater?

However, it is only in the case of one who has regressed from the fruit of arhatship that there is a sense of fearing the afflictions and taking one's own life, because such a person knows for themselves that afflictions will not arise again after death.

As for those still in training (śaikṣas), they know for themselves that at the end of their lives, afflictions will inevitably manifest, thereby inviting further existence and increasing the suffering of saṃsāra; how, then, could they possibly commit suicide?
If it were according to that interpretation, then Godhika would have been extremely dull-witted to commit suicide without cause.

However, the Māra sought his consciousness at the very spot where he was killed because he suspected that Godhika had died while still abiding in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) after having regressed.
Using the skillful means of Māra, he reviled the Buddha with these verses:
"How is it that the Honored One among Men, Whose disciple has transgressed the holy teaching,
Remaining in the stage of further training, Has not attained parinirvāṇa at the end of life?"

It is not the case that all noble disciples of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, pass away only upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa); how then could the celestial Māra alone mock the World-Honored One by suggesting that this noble one passed away while still in the stage of training (śaikṣa)?

Because Ghoṭika first attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and later regressed to the state of a learner (*śaikṣa*) before his death, that celestial Māra raised this as a reproach against the Buddha.
This must logically be so, for that Māra said:
"The disciples of the World-Honored One have transgressed the holy teaching."
What is meant by the "Noble Teaching"?
It refers to the severance of future existence.

The meaning of this verse is as follows: How could a Son of the Buddha, having attained the realm where future existence is severed and should enter parinirvāṇa, instead regress and fall back into a state of continued existence until his life comes to an end?
Thus, we know that Ghoṭaka did not merely regress from dhyāna.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* (Abhidharma-piṭaka) states:

"The latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) arises from three conditions: first, because the latent tendency of sensual desire has not been abandoned or fully known; second, because the phenomena conducive to its entanglement (*paryavasthāna*) are currently present; and third, because improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is directed toward them."
This is not contradictory to the meaning of "falling back" (parihāṇi), for it is spoken in reference to the immediate arising of afflictions from afflictions.
It is not the case that afflictions arise immediately only from afflictions; the meaning of such a statement has already been explained previously.
The arising of afflictions is generally of two kinds: first, from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), and second, from proper mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
This text speaks only of that which arises from the former; therefore, there is no fault.

All delusions that arise are preceded by improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*); let it not be thought that there is no beginning to this process, for if there were no initial loss of virtue, there would be no possibility for faults to arise.

Furthermore, whenever an affliction (*kleśa*) arises, there is necessarily concomitant improper mental attention; thus, at the moment an affliction arises, it can be said that the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) has not yet been abandoned.

This passage does not state that the arising of various afflictions must necessarily be preceded by the non-abandonment of greed and so forth; therefore, this passage does not serve as proof for that point.

Furthermore, regarding the citation of the mind of moral neutrality (*avyākṛta-citta*), the position that [afflictions] manifest through retrogression (*paryādāna*) does not constitute a contradiction or difficulty.
Regarding the school that maintains the retrogression of the manifestation of the category of defiled minds, there is no fault here, as this is based on the presence of all causes.

That is to say, if the causes and conditions for the arising of afflictions are complete, these three [factors] occur; however, even if any one among these three is lacking, there is still the possibility of their arising.
As it is said that one who accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas is born in hell, it is not the case that one fails to be born there if they accomplish even one among those ten.
Furthermore, as a sutra states:
"When three conditions are present, one can generate much merit."
It is not the case that only those with faith lack the generation of great merit;
there are numerous such examples.
Here, these three are collectively cited as conditions for the arising of afflictions, but this does not apply to all cases.

The meaning of this passage is to clarify that when afflictions arise, they do so due to the predominance of either the power of causes, the object, or preparatory application; thus it is said that sensual desire arises from these three bases.
If one maintains that all three must be present, then the statement would not be universally applicable.

That is to say, while it may be said that [a cognition] possesses all three when taking its own realm as an object, there is no logical possibility for it to possess all three when taking other phenomena as objects.
Therefore, the text of the Abhidharma does not contradict the meaning of non-retrogression.
Having reconciled that teaching, the author establishes the following reasoning:
"If an Arhat has produced the path of remedy that ensures afflictions will never arise again, then he should not be subject to retrogression by giving rise to afflictions."

If this path has not yet arisen for an arhat, they would not have exhausted their outflows (*āsrava*), because they have not yet been able to permanently uproot the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
If they have not exhausted their outflows, how can they be called an arhat?
This is not a fault, for it is what we accept.

That is to say, our school accepts that one who previously possessed the nature of a "one liable to fall back" (parihāṇadharman) has, due to inferiority in the power of wisdom, failed to realize the non-arising of defilements even though they have already abandoned them.
If that is so, for what reason is it called "abandonment"?

This has already been explained: when factors contrary to the afflictions arise, one abandons the acquisition of the fetters and acquires the acquisition of dissociation; this is what is called "abandonment."

Therefore, when it is said that [afflictions] are "abandoned," this occurs because the path of remedy arises and extracts the afflictions—along with their seeds—from within the continuum; it does not mean that the afflictions must never arise again, for they can arise once more in those whose power of wisdom is inferior.
However, there is no fault of not having attained the fruit of arhatship (āsravakṣaya-phala), because one has already obtained the acquisition of disjunction (visamyoga-prāpti) from all outflows.

Since it is granted that the abandoned afflictions still possess a substantial existence, what sound principle is contradicted by the claim that afflictions arise again when the path of their remedy is forgotten and the conditions for regression manifest?
Therefore, the reasoning set forth by that Master of the Sūtras has no power to prove the absence of falling away (*aparihāṇi*).
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 68; *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 69.
