Chapter Six, Part Thirteen: Distinguishing the Noble Ones (Ārya-varga). Having thus refuted the tenets of the Sūtra-master, [the discussion continues].
Other masters say:

Just as there is no possibility of falling away from the liberation attained through the abandonment of afflictions abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), because it is a fruit obtained by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*),

so too there is no possibility of falling away from the liberation attained through the abandonment of afflictions abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that are bound to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
That explanation is unreasonable, because the power of the paths differs and has already been explained previously.

Furthermore, it is observed that there is retrogression from the liberation attained through other untainted paths; that is to say, the functional efficacy of the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is distinct, because in the stage of the path of seeing, a single grade of the path abandons many grades of afflictions, whereas in the stage of the path of cultivation, many grades of the path abandon many grades of afflictions.

If it is argued that this difference arises from the power of the afflictions— namely, that the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) operate without a real basis (*avastuka*), whereas those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) have a real basis (*sāvastuka*)—
this is also not the case, because even when these afflictions are abandoned by the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), they likewise exist in many varieties.

Alternatively, one might argue that the reason there is no falling away from the abandonment of afflictions abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) based on their lack of objective reality (*avastuka*) is because such abandonment is the fruit obtained by the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).

If it is claimed that because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) can fall away even from the abandonment of afflictions lacking objective reality, this proves that the liberation from afflictions abandoned through vision by the noble ones (*ārya*) cannot be lost—on the grounds that it is the fruit obtained by the untainted path—then one should not say that although the afflictions are of many grades, they are abandoned by a single grade of the path simply because they lack objective reality.
Therefore, it is known that the meaning is established through the distinct power of the Path; for this reason, [the cases of] seeing and cultivation should not be used as analogies.
Furthermore, this was already stated previously.
What was stated previously?

This means that what is abandoned through seeing arises by the power of investigation, whereas the afflictions abandoned through cultivation arise by the power of the object; since noble ones do not give rise to even a trace of arbitrary conceptualization regarding their objects of perception, there is no falling away from liberation attained through the abandonment of what is seen.

Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) have not yet seen the truth; therefore, they may engage in arbitrary conceptualization regarding their objects of focus. Although they have already abandoned the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the lower eight stages, it is still possible for them to fall back from those.

Noble ones (*ārya*), having already seen the truth, can never fall back from what is abandoned by seeing; however, due to a lapse in mindfulness, they may grasp at signs such as "exquisite" and so forth regarding external objects, thereby proceeding with mental activity that is characterized by attachment, aversion, arrogance, or lack of clarity. By this principle, even noble ones may fall back from the liberation attained through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Therefore, what they say—that ordinary worldlings may regress even from the abandonment of non-substantial afflictions—is proven by the fact that there is no regression for the liberation attained through the vision of the noble ones; because this is the fruit obtained via the untainted path, their reasoning is certainly incorrect.

Furthermore, since other untainted fruits are also seen to be subject to regression, it must be that for those who hold this position, there is no fruit of the abandonment of afflictions by a noble one (ārya) that is obtained through the mundane path (laukika-mārga). This is because their own treatise states that the abandonment of afflictions by a noble one is a fruit of the mundane path, which is logically untenable.
The *Udāyin-sūtra* states:

There are noble ones who first attain the meditative absorption of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and subsequently are reborn in the Form Realm; for them, there is no possibility of falling back from that higher attainment or of being born in a lower realm once it has been severed.

That school does not admit that an Ārya suppresses afflictions (*kleśa*) through mundane paths (*laukikamārga*), nor does it admit that an Ārya gives rise to practices such as viewing [conditioned things] as peaceful (*śānta*). This is because, for them, an Ārya does not view conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as peaceful and so forth.

Furthermore, according to that school, no noble path (*āryamārga*) other than the vision of impermanence (*anityatā*) and so forth can truly sever afflictions. Since an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has severed afflictions reaches the stage of an Ārya, there is necessarily no possibility of regression, as they are stabilized by both paths. Therefore, afflictions are severed solely by means of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).

The Sūtra states that one who has previously attained the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling may later regress and be reborn in the form realm; therefore, it is fully established that there is also the possibility of regression regarding the fruits of abandonment obtained through other untainted paths.

Therefore, what he says is as follows: just as there is no falling away from the liberation attained by abandoning the afflictions through seeing (*darśana-heya*), so it is also with the liberation attained by abandoning the afflictions through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), because both are fruits obtained by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
This reasoning is certainly not correct.
The Sthavira also states in this regard:
"It is definitely impossible for an Arhat to fall away from the fruit of Arhatship."
Why is this so? It is because of both reasoning and scripture.
What constitutes the reasoning?
This is because an Arhat must necessarily be free from improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), otherwise the final mind of an Arhat would have to give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*).

That is to say, if it were admitted that an Arhat in a state of composure could fall back and give rise to afflictions while remaining in the state of equanimity (*upekṣā*), how could afflictions not arise at the time of death when the breaths are irregular and the faculties are disturbed?
If afflictions were to arise, they would lead to the continuation of future existence. What is the teaching?
It refers to what is stated in the Sūtra, where the Venerable Śuṇṭha spoke directly before the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
If there is a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted and who has become an arhat—expounding at length until—he is able not to forget the nature of liberation of mind."
If exquisite forms cognizable by the eye should appear before one, there is no need for exertion in guarding the liberation of mind that has been realized.
As stated in the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (The Sūtra on the Simile of Battle):
"When the noble disciples abide with a mind free from fear, at that time Māra cannot disturb them."
The *Lambaka Sūtra* also states:
"If one's outflows are exhausted and one has become an Arhat, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is no lack of peace and security. Why is this so?"
Because Māra cannot destroy it.
The *Salya-sūtra* (The Simile of the Poisoned Arrow) also states this:
the Buddha told Sunakṣatra, "For one who delights in nirvāṇa, all fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are at that time eternally severed and fully known."
Just as when the root of a tree is severed or the crown of a *tāla* tree is cut off, nothing remains such that it will not grow again;
so too do all the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* treatises state:

"If one dwells in close association with disciples, I say that because of this, one may fall away from any one of the four kinds of higher mental states (*adhicitta*) previously realized—the pleasant dwellings in the present life."

If, through dwelling in seclusion, solitude, and quietude, and by abiding with courageous diligence and without negligence, one realizes the unshakable liberation of mind through bodily witness, I declare definitively that there is no cause or condition for falling away from it.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"If there is a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted and who has become an arhat, I do not say that such an arhat need not be heedful."
Why is this so? Because that venerable one has already become diligent and can no longer engage in acts of negligence.
Such is the position held by that Elder; however, it is logically untenable, as improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) has already been refuted previously.
What was stated previously?
It was said that the arising of delusion is always preceded by irrational attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).

The treatise speaks here specifically of those [delusions] arising from defilement; if every arising of defilement were necessarily preceded by defilement, then minds of other natures would have no possibility of functioning.
Furthermore, the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) they have established is unestablished, because its category is identical to that of the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established.

That is to say, defiled attention (*kliṣṭa-manasikāra*) receives the designation "unreasonable" [only when it arises]; the reason they establish indicates that because an Arhat does not give rise to defilement, he does not produce afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus he is called an Arhat precisely because he lacks afflictions.
Now, one wishes to investigate whether an Arhat, whose mind is already free from afflictions, can still undergo retrogression and rebirth.
Their established thesis states:
"He certainly does not undergo retrogression and rebirth."
Furthermore, he establishes a reason, saying:
"Because there is no arising of defilement.
If this is so, is it not the case that their categories are identical?
This is not a valid reason, as determined by the wise.
Furthermore, what that [opponent] has stated contains no irrationality; for does he mean that [the effect] does not yet exist after having arisen, or that it does not exist while currently arising?
Both of these two alternatives are unestablished.
Alternatively, that intention may be that because there are no seeds of delusion, the various Arhats do not regress or give rise to delusion.
However, since the existence or non-existence of such seeds has already been extensively addressed above, the argument for their existence as a cause is flawed in every respect.
Because this has already eliminated non-inversion, and because inversion and the afflictions are not of a distinct nature,
the subsequent mind that gives rise to afflictions cannot serve as their cause. Why is this so?
Since the final mind of an Arhat is not an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), how could it have the capacity to induce a subsequent mind?
This is because it is directed toward parinirvāṇa without remainder, turns its back on the process of saṃsāric transmigration, and proceeds spontaneously and exclusively in a state of equipoise.
If one were to give rise to afflictions at this stage, it would obstruct the ultimate cessation of the aggregates;
therefore, within the state of an Arhat at the moment of death, it is certain that no afflictions can arise through regression.

Furthermore, abiding in this stage, one is extremely well-suited to a mind of renunciation; even those who previously possessed afflictions, upon reaching this stage, are able to sever them without remainder.
As the Sūtra says:
"In this present life, they extensively expound the noble intent."

Or even at the time of death—let alone when they have previously been free from afflictions and now have the mental attention directed toward entering nirvana without remainder manifest before them—how could they possibly give rise to delusion?
Therefore, there would be the fault that the final mind could give rise to afflictions.

Furthermore, the statement that an Arhat in the state of peaceful composure (praśrabdhi) might, while abiding in the characteristic of equanimity, be permitted to regress and give rise to afflictions is also unreasonable, as it is not what is accepted [by our school].

That is to say, I maintain that only when one is in a state of composure can a mind that is conducive to afflictions give rise to them; if one is in a state where one is actively engaged in firm faith and so forth—mental states that function as obstacles to the arising of afflictions—how could one possibly give rise to them?
Therefore, the reason they establish—that there is no principle for falling away from the fruit—cannot be proven.
Nor does scripture serve as proof that an Arhat cannot fall away.
Furthermore, the *Śuṇḍa-sūtra* does not contradict the position that falling away is possible at all, because this sutra was spoken based on the prohibition of receiving sensual pleasures.
It is said that while that venerable one was dwelling alone in seclusion, he suddenly thought to himself:
"My family is immensely wealthy and my kin are numerous; I ought to return home at once to enjoy sensual pleasures and practice giving to cultivate merit."

The Buddha, knowing his thought, dispatched a messenger to summon him; he then manifested supernatural powers for him, providing instruction and admonition that caused him to submit and awaken, whereby he attained the fruit of arhatship.
Having attained the fruit of arhatship, he reflected:
"I have come at the proper time to see the Sugata."
This intention was to show that having now received the summons to come, it was superior to his previous state of being free from improper mental attention (*vitarka*).

Having formed this thought, he again relied on another method to demonstrate that he and the various Arhats shared the common characteristic of not receiving further rebirths as a result of their fruit; thus he said:
"Venerable Sir!"

If there is a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted and who has become an arhat, at that time he abides in six states with his mind liberated: namely, he abides in renunciation, harmlessness, seclusion, the exhaustion of craving, the exhaustion of clinging, and the nature of non-forgetfulness of mental liberation.
Even if exceptionally exquisite forms cognizable by the eye were to appear before one, there would be no need for exertion or protection regarding the liberation of mind that has been realized.

This indicates that all those who have attained the fruit of arhatship, being sustained by the power of their antidotes, find it impossible and out of the question to experience the objects of sensual desire.
Therefore, the meaning here is that even if a sublime object appears before one, there is no need to laboriously guard the mind.
Alternatively, the Venerable [Vasubandhu] may rely on his own assertion and thus it should not be taken as a definitive proof; for not all Arhats possess the same faculty-nature as Śūṇa.
Alternatively, this [statement] refers collectively to all those who have attained the fruit of arhatship (*arhatphala*), because they themselves speak of specific distinctions, as when they say:
"Abiding in renunciation, harmlessness, and seclusion," and so forth, at length.
This demonstrates that if one can abide in renunciation and so forth, there is no need for strenuous protection; otherwise, it is not so.
Our own school also states that those who constantly respect and cultivate the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) will be able to avoid falling away.
This meaning is clearly demonstrated by the Blessed One in the *Salyasūtra* (The Simile of the Arrow); I shall provide a detailed analysis of it there later on.

Furthermore, the *Saṃgrāmasūtra* (The Simile of the Battle) does not constitute proof [for your position], as this is spoken in accordance with the negation of fear regarding future existence (*punarbhava*), for it is stated elsewhere that this is also the case here.

This means that when this sutra states "Māra cannot disturb [him]," its intended meaning is not to refer to the *kleśamāra* (the demon of afflictions), but rather to the gods of the desire realm and Maheśvara; for later in this sutra it says:
"At that time, that Māra suddenly vanished."

The meaning here is to clarify that if one has attained parinirvāṇa, Māra is unable to seek out one's consciousness. That is to say, when a disciple of the Buddha is about to pass away, many Māras come seeking their life-consciousness, thinking, "May his spirit-consciousness not transcend my domain."
As in other passages, the fear of future existence is also denied for one who has attained the fruit of arhatship, as the Sūtra says:
"The root of craving has been uprooted; being free from sorrow, what is there to fear?"
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"Just as when the roots of a tree have not been pulled out, the shoots grow back again and again even though they are cut;
so too, as long as the latent tendency of craving has not been uprooted, suffering arises again and again even though it is extinguished."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"If one has already seen the Noble Truths, the paths to existence are cut off;
once the root of birth and death is extinguished, one will no longer undergo future existence."
Furthermore, in all instances, the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*) is praised by saying:
"He has laid down all heavy burdens and exhausted all fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*).
As for why it is called "exhausting the fetters of existence," it means that the fetters which summon existence are termed "fetters of existence."

Because all Arhats are well-liberated in mind from the fetters of existence (*bhava-anuśaya*), they are said to have "exhausted" them; therefore, the sūtras cited by those [opponents] cannot refute our position that an Arhat may fall away from the fruit of arhatship.

By this, the *Lambaka Sūtra* has already been explained: they all know for themselves that they will not undergo further existence; although there may be fear and withdrawal from the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha*), there is nonetheless no lack of composure in their deportment (*īryāpatha*).
Therefore, when the knowledge regarding the dharmas arises in those who have attained the fruit of arhatship, they are able to know for themselves that they will not undergo further existence.
Since this was spoken with a specific intention in reference to the *Sūtra on the Simile of the Poisoned Arrow*, it cannot preclude the possibility of falling away from that state.

If an Arhat has attained the permanent abandonment and full knowledge of all fetters within the three realms—just as one cuts the root of a tree or severs the crown of a *tāla* palm so that nothing remains and they will not arise again—why is it that non-perception (*asaṃjñin*) alone is singled out for mention here?
Therefore, we know that this teaching was intended for a specific purpose.

We shall now clarify the reason for making this statement: in this sutra, the Buddha told Sunakṣatra, "To those who delight in worldly wealth and dwell in its presence, one should speak such corresponding discourse;

their minds will then abide within the meaning of what is taught, and they will also be able to practice in accordance with the Dharma therein," and so on at length, even including analogies to illustrate the point.
The Venerable Sunakṣatra addressed the Blessed One, saying:

"This person, in villages and other such places, has his mind bound by the fetter of sensual desire; [as explained at length] up to: when discourse associated with the immovable is spoken, he does not delight in hearing or receiving such extensive teaching."

Those who delight in the immovable do not take pleasure in hearing or receiving discourse associated with the sphere of nothingness; those who delight in the sphere of nothingness do not take pleasure in hearing or receiving discourse associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; those who delight in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception do not take pleasure in hearing or receiving discourse associated with parinirvāṇa; and those who delight in nirvāṇa likewise do not take pleasure in hearing or receiving discourse associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The Sūtra explains this in detail in such a sequence; it is not I who here speak these words:

"The Arhats delight in hearing discourses associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, their minds abide therein and they practice in accordance with the Dharma, whereby they become attached to and pursue that state."

How does this citation prove that an Arhat’s mind is not bound by the fetter of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*) regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)?
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke these two similes in order to preclude the possibility that one who has attained the fruit of arhatship might still harbor craving for rebirth in that state.
Our own school also accepts this principle; how then can you cite it to refute the possibility of falling away from the fruit of Arhatship?

This [text] must necessarily be interpreted as refuting the notion that an Arhat could create karmic formations (*saṃskāra*) that would summon a future existence in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). For it says therein:

"When that son of good family has attained right understanding and his mind is well-liberated, regarding the six sense bases—form and so forth—which are unsuitable, even after seeing them with the eye and so on, he does not remain bound by them. Extensively explained up to: within those objects, he does not dwell following after discursive thought (*vitarka*), nor is his mind corrupted by the fetter of greed (*rāga-saṃyojana*), nor does he accumulate evil, unwholesome dharmas that would induce a future birth, nor even accumulate old age and death for a future life. He is able to know this of himself as it truly is."

Now, to examine the intended meaning of what is stated here: it reveals that the Arhats (the fruits of application) are able to know, as it truly is, "I shall never again accumulate the provisions for future existence.

Nevertheless, one may say that in this sutra, the Buddha—relying on the parable of the poisoned arrow—reveals the possibility of falling away (*parihāṇi*). That is to say, the Buddha spoke these words therein:

"Suppose there were a skilled physician who, having extracted a poisoned arrow, first observes how deeply the arrow has penetrated; next, he devises a suitable method to pull it out; finally, he applies an excellent medicine so that no trace of poison remains, and only then says to the patient:"
"Alas, virtuous man!
I have already extracted the poisoned arrow for you, so that the toxic force within your body is entirely removed.
From this day forward, you should be careful regarding what is forbidden, eat what is suitable, and keep your wound clean at the proper times."
If one eats what is unsuitable, the wound will surely fester and leak.

What do you think, Sunakṣatra? If that man, having been treated by a skilled physician who extracted the arrow and removed the poison, were to avoid what is forbidden, eat only what is suitable, and regularly cleanse his wound, would he not certainly attain freedom from illness, peace and happiness, and an increase in physical strength?

By means of this analogy, it is shown that the Buddha, as a skilled physician, extracts the poisonous arrow from the beings he seeks to convert, causing their fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be drawn out until they are exhausted without remainder.

If, regarding the six sense bases such as forms—which are unsuitable—one dwells with attachment following upon seeing them with the eye, and so forth, up to dwelling in contemplation following upon the arising of discursive thought (*vitarka*) within those objects, then the outflow of afflictions (*kleśa*) arises because of this.
If this were not permitted, what fault would arise in the liberation of the mind such that it would be identical to a festering ulcer?

Furthermore, in this very sutra, the Buddha himself provides an analogy, stating: "It is possible for a certain class of persons who correctly understand that dependence is the root of suffering—like a disease, an abscess, a poison, or an arrow—to abide in the unsurpassed, non-dependent liberation of the mind through the exhaustion of dependence;
yet, once so abiding, it is impossible for them to harbor a grasping mind that clings to the phenomena of dependence which lead to further appropriation."
This sutra explains this meaning later, stating that "basis" refers to the body because it is the basis for suffering;
"conducive to grasping" refers to those factors that benefit grasping, because they serve as the objective supports for the various afflictions.

Regarding this, some say that "basis" (*āśraya*) is identical to "appropriation" (*upādāna*); however, according to the true meaning, the basis and appropriation are distinct. This means that, respectively, the body and the unsuitable objects are different.
To speak of "the body appropriating" refers to the sense organs, such as the eye, appropriating unsuitable objects.

Regarding the "clinging of the mind," this refers to the visual and other consciousnesses clinging to unsuitable objects. For one who delights in nirvana and frequently dwells in the mind-liberation of nirvana, it is impossible for them to cling to the body as a basis for grasping or to cling to the mind.

Now, to explain the intended meaning here in brief: it means that when those who have attained the fruit of arhatship dwell extensively within the six liberations of mind—such as renunciation and so forth—they do not remain bound by following after the six unfavorable conditions; just as when one is careful regarding what is to be avoided, afflictions do not arise.

If one does not dwell extensively in the six [factors] such as renunciation, one will remain bound to the six unsuitable objects; thus, although the poisonous arrows of future birth have already been permanently extracted, the outflows of afflictions still arise through the eyes and other faculties, like pus leaking from a wound caused by an injury to an unsuitable spot.
In this way, the Elder’s citation of this sūtra only harms his own school; how could it possibly contradict the tenets of others?

Furthermore, his claim that the *Sūtra on the Loss of Eloquence* speaks only of the loss of the higher mental states (*adhicitta*) and not of liberation (*vimukti*) is also incorrect, because other sūtras state that a time-liberated (*samayavimukta*) Arhat falls away due to five causes and conditions, without saying that he loses the higher mental states.

The *Cūḍāpanthaka-sūtra* also speaks of the falling away from the fruit of arhatship characterized by occasional liberation (*sāmayikī vimukti*); this should be understood as previously explained, as it serves to refute that erroneous attachment.
Furthermore, the *Aṅgārakāra-sūtra* also states that there is falling away from the fruit of arhatship, as will be established in the subsequent discussion.

The *Udāyi-sūtra* also states that there is falling away from the fruits of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga-phala*), and the *Śalya-upama-sūtra* likewise states that there is falling away, as has already been argued above.
The sūtra cited by him refers exclusively to the superior class of arhats; therefore, it does not constitute proof.
Some explain that this sūtra was spoken by the Buddha based on his own situation, stating that he dwells in association with his disciples;
however, since the *Apramāda-sūtra* has already been fully analyzed and resolved previously in response to the Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika), this too is not proof.
Therefore, the position of the Sthavira that there is no falling away from the fruit of arhatship lacks both logical reasoning and scriptural authority.
The Vibhajyavādins maintain this view:
"All noble paths are such that there is no falling away; consequently, the afflictions once abandoned will never arise again."
How is this known? It is by means of scripture and reasoning.
As for the scripture, it refers to the sūtra which says, addressing Kāśyapa:
If there are such numerous wholesome dharmas, I say that those wholesome dharmas have no abiding, much less any falling away.
Since Arhats possess such numerous wholesome dharmas, they do not fall away.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Such a fruit of arhatship is forever free from defilement and forever ultimate.
Ignorance is the cause that gives rise to all defiled attachments; because clarity (*vidyā*) is the cause, one is free from all defiled attachments."

All Arhats are entirely free from fault and transgression; because they have exhausted [the defilements], they create no new karma. Being detached and free from craving, they have already incinerated the seeds of existence so that the sprouts of the various realms of being no longer grow. This is like a lamp whose oil is exhausted and which is thus extinguished forever; this is what is meant by "instruction."
Furthermore, he establishes a logical argument:
"It is not reasonable for a seed that has been burned to produce a sprout.
All such cases are for the most part refuted in the same manner as before; only those few points where there is a slight difference shall now be specifically rejected.
Furthermore, that initial teaching cannot serve as proof, for it would imply that one in the stage of training (śaikṣa) must be admitted to possess the possibility of falling away.

It is not the case that those in the stage of training possess many wholesome dharmas identical to those of the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), since there are instances within the stage of training where unwholesome states arise, just as they do for ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana). Therefore, one must understand that the Sūtra made such a statement with a specific underlying intention, as other Sūtras speak of both the falling away and the non-falling away of those who have attained the fruit of arhatship.

If it is argued that the statement regarding falling back (*parihāṇi*) refers specifically to the conventional level (*saṃvṛti*), then one should likewise maintain that the statement regarding the absence of falling back is also made in reference to a specific distinction.

That is to say, while other sūtras state that there is no distinction [in the nature] of falling back, you nevertheless admit that the statement regarding falling back refers to a specific case and not others.
Although these words regarding "non-retrogression" appear to have no distinction, it is logically necessary to admit that they are spoken with reference to specific contexts.

However, the meaning taught in this sūtra is that the Blessed One praised the benefits obtained through constant cultivation and reverence for wholesome dharmas; or, his intention was to show that when one is correctly cultivating the wholesome, there is neither dwelling [in attachment] nor retrogression, rather than implying that this state persists at all times.

Alternatively, it may be that while all wholesome dharmas of those who have attained the fruit of arhatship are identical, there are distinctions such as between those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) and others; therefore, in this context, it is said that one who has accomplished numerous superior wholesome dharmas does not fall away, whereas for the opposite case, the principle that one falls away is beyond doubt.
"Permanently free from defilements (*malādi*) and so forth" has already been explained previously.
What was explained previously?

It was that there is no fault in speaking cryptically regarding the defilements (*kleśamala*) and so forth that arise in succession. Following this principle, one should explain the phrase "because they are exhausted" (*kṣayāt*) and so forth: because ignorance (*avidyā*) acts as the cause for the arising of attachment and the like, as explained before, there would otherwise be no retrogression, just as there is no [retrogression] when seeds are absent.
The reasoning established by him falls into the error of irrationality,
because it is admitted that a subsequent sprout will certainly not arise,
and because the reason is not established merely by setting forth an illustrative example.
Alternatively, one should interrogate the Vibhajyavādin:
"By what do you maintain that the various afflictions are incinerated?
He must certainly reply: "They are incinerated by the fire of wisdom."
One should further raise this objection:
"This is not logical; wisdom should depend upon afflictions, just as fire depends upon fuel.
Therefore, one should not say that untainted wisdom arises by taking the various afflictions as its basis."
Furthermore, at the stage where delusions are exhausted, wisdom should also perish, for just as fire is extinguished when the fuel is consumed.
Moreover, just as there must be residual ash when the fuel is exhausted, there should likewise be residual delusions within the body of an Arhat.
If you argue that the dharma and the example cannot be entirely identical, we reply: do not claim that there is absolutely no similarity between the dharma and the example.
Since this is so, why not accept it in this way:
although ignorance lacks the nature of burning, it possesses a slight resemblance to burning; therefore, one should not say that the dharma is entirely identical to the example.

If that is so, how can it be said that the abandonment of afflictions is like burning wood, in the sense that, just as a sprout does not grow again, a subsequent existence (*punarbhava*) is not produced?
For this reason, there is no logical principle that can prevent falling away (*parihāṇi*).
The proponents of the *Nyāyānusāra* speak as follows:

"Regarding the possibility of falling away from the abandonment of afflictions through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the scriptural authority and reasoning for this have been largely explained in the preceding sections of this treatise while refuting the positions of others. Now, in order to establish our own accepted position, we shall further demonstrate what was not previously stated."
This means that there is indeed the possibility of falling away even from the state of an Arhat (*arhatphala*), for it is clearly stated in the *Aṅgāra-upama-sūtra* (The Coal Simile Sūtra).

As it says: "When a learned noble disciple is walking or standing, there may be occasions and circumstances where, due to a lapse of mindfulness, unwholesome and evil thoughts arise, giving rise to greed, hatred, or delusion."
In this way, the well-learned noble disciple, though slow to lose right mindfulness, quickly recovers it again, causing whatever has regressed to be exhausted, submerged, extinguished, and abandoned.
What serves as proof of this?
Knowing that these learned noble disciples are Arhats, what need is there to labor over questioning them?
As this sutra states:
"The minds of those noble disciples have, for a long night, been in accordance with seclusion," as described in other sūtras.
Therefore, it is said within this sutra:

"When a well-heard noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka) is walking or staying, whether a king or a relative comes before him and requests his wealth and status—and so on at length—because that well-heard noble disciple’s mind has for a long night conformed to seclusion, is directed toward seclusion, and has entered into seclusion; because it has conformed to renunciation, is directed toward renunciation, and has entered into renunciation; because it has conformed to nirvāṇa, is directed toward nirvāṇa, and has entered into nirvāṇa; and because he delights in tranquility and delights in seclusion and renunciation—I declare that he has completely vomited out all phenomena conducive to the outflows (āsrava-dharma), and has attained coolness."
Furthermore, this sutra first states:

"He contemplates all sensual desires as being like a portion of glowing coals; by virtue of this contemplation, his mind is not defiled by desire for desires, craving for desires, intimacy with desires, affection for desires, attachment to desires, infatuation with desires, or clinging to desires."
Other sūtras state that arhats possess eight powers and so forth, which is the same as this sūtra.
That is to say, another sūtra says: "It was addressed to Śāriputra:
'Arhats possess eight kinds of power.'"
What are the eight? They are as follows:
the Arhat, whose outflows are exhausted, has for a long night had a mind that accords with seclusion and tends toward seclusion, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, that same sutra also states:
"He contemplates all sensual desires as being like a portion of charcoal," and so on at length,
just as in this sutra.
Again, he spoke these words:

"He has already cultivated and thoroughly mastered the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the factors of the path."

In the *Śuṇḍa-sūtra*, it is said that an arhat dwells in renunciation, harmlessness, seclusion, the exhaustion of craving, the exhaustion of clinging, and the nature of liberation of mind which is non-forgetful.
The *Sūtra of the Simile of the Poisoned Arrow* also states this.
The Buddha told Sunakṣatra:
"For one who delights in nirvāṇa, all fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are at that time forever severed and fully known."
From this it is proven that the statement in this sutra—that the noble disciples are arhats—is definitive in meaning and should not give rise to doubt.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) says:

"In truth, those mentioned later are indeed arhats; however, it is possible that while they are walking or standing, they have not yet fully mastered [their faculties], and thus such a state might occur."

This means that when a learner (śaikṣa) is walking or staying, they may give rise to afflictions due to a lapse of mindfulness; however, once they have subsequently become one beyond learning (aśaikṣa), there is no possibility for such arising. Since the preceding statement was made with reference to the stage of a learner, it is not erroneous.

Examining the intent of the sūtra, it is stated that within this sūtra the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) is taught first and the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is taught later; we must now carefully investigate whether this should be definitively accepted as the word of the Blessed One or merely the intent of the sūtra’s author.

However, within this sutra there is not the slightest ambiguity that could be cited to prove that the former refers to the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) while the latter passage is based on the stage of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*).

That is to say, in this sutra it is first stated that a disciple, by contemplating all desires as being like a portion of charcoal, has already caused his mind to be unstained by desire and the like; next, it is stated that at times he may lose mindfulness and give rise to afflictions; then it is further stated that he quickly regains his detachment; and subsequently it says that when he is walking or staying, even if kings and others come to invite him, he does not accept wealth or status, because throughout the long night he has conformed to seclusion and so forth, up until it says that he has already been able to permanently vomit out the phenomena conducive to the outflows (*āsrava*) and has attained coolness.

Throughout this sutra from beginning to end, we do not see the Buddha teaching any distinct dharma, nor do we see him teaching that by practicing a different path one attains a separate realization; by what, then, can it be known that those noble disciples first dwelt in the stage of training (śaikṣa) and later became those beyond training (aśaikṣa)?

Now, examining this sūtra in detail, its primary purpose is to refute such false speculations as those of the Sūtra Master and others. Therefore, it first states that the noble disciples, by contemplating all sensual desires as being like a portion of glowing embers, are able to prevent their minds from being stained by desire and the like; this demonstrates that they have already realized the fruit of arhatship.
Next, it is further stated that he loses mindfulness and gives rise to delusions; this already demonstrates that one who has attained the fruit of arhatship can fall away.
By this reasoning, it is known that both the initial and final passages of this sutra refer to those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, as for what was said:
"However, as long as one has not yet fully mastered [the practice] while walking or standing, such a thing might occur"—this reasoning is also incorrect.
For this sūtra states that those disciples, whether walking or standing, realize and penetrate [the truth], yet at times they forget and give rise to afflictions.
If it is argued that because the phrase "thoroughly realized" (*su-pratividdha*) is not mentioned [in this context], this is also incorrect, for the meaning has already been stated.
That is to say, this sutra states:

"When those noble disciples, whether walking or standing, have attained realization through subsequent cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), they may at times forget it; like ordinary worldly people, thoughts of greed, sorrow, and unwholesome, evil dharmas arise."
Is it not already stated that the term "thoroughly penetrating" (*su-pratividdha*) implies thorough penetration?
If the term "penetrating" (*pratividdha*) signifies thorough penetration, how could one who has thoroughly penetrated still give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*)?
This objection is invalid, for it has already been answered previously.
This means that because of a lapse in mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), various afflictions arise.
If this were so, it would follow that [the Buddha] has not yet fully mastered thorough penetration (*anabhisamaya*).
This is not the case, for the quality of being free from forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa*) belongs exclusively to the World-Honored One.
If that is so, why does a sutra state:
"The Venerable Śāriputra has accomplished the six modes of constant abiding"?

One should understand that this sutra’s intention is twofold: it either reveals that not all who have attained the fruit of Arhatship possess the six modes of constant abiding, or it reveals that although all may possess them, not all are able to dwell in them through actualization.

If it were otherwise, the Blessed One would not have used this as a gateway to reveal his excellence; for the community of bhikṣus would not know that Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom among the śrāvaka assembly, a great Dharma general capable of turning the wheel of Dharma, nor would they believe him to be an arhat, were it not for the Bhagavān praising and exhorting them by describing the qualities common to all those who have attained the fruit of arhatship.
Furthermore, it is stated in a sutra:
"An Arhat who is liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) is rare in the world.
It further states:
If there were a person who had accomplished the six constant abidings, it would be extremely rare in this world.

From this, it is proven that it is not the case that an Arhat, at all times when encountering unsuitable objects through seeing, hearing, and so forth, is able to have his mind abide in equanimity and constantly dwell in right mindfulness and clear comprehension. Therefore, Arhats may have lapses of mindfulness; for this reason, the statement that "there is no lack of thorough mastery" in this context is not well-founded.
Therefore, it is known that the preceding passage’s description of the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) does not accord with correct principle.
Furthermore, if this were necessarily the case, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

That is to say, the Sūtra states, "Birth for me has been exhausted," yet it does not say that [the exhaustion] is "wholesome" (*kuśala*); [if your logic held], one would have to conclude that such a person is still a trainee.
Furthermore, a sutra states that one has "already seen the noble truths," yet it does not say that one who "sees well" must be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Moreover, a sutra says that one causes the path to existence to be cut off, yet it does not say that one who "cuts it off well" must not be one who has attained the fruit of arhatship (*arhatphala*).
Since these [arguments] are not so, one knows that their explanation is incorrect.
Therefore, it is said that the meaning of "thorough penetration" (prativedha) must necessarily be virtuous.
Others, however, further insist with dogmatic adherence:
This *Aṅgāra-upama-sūtra* definitively teaches the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).
How is this known? Because the meaning serves as the basis.
Based on what meaning?

It is because it is admitted that those in training (śaikṣa) possess afflictions, whereas those beyond training (aśaikṣa) do not; and because those beyond training have already severed all inversions (viparyāsa), and since the seeds of delusion no longer exist, there is necessarily no possibility of falling back.

Furthermore, because it is subsumed under the fruit of the Noble Path, just as there is no principle for falling back from the abandonment of afflictions abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*), [you] should consider this.

That venerable one relies solely on his own adhered-to false meanings and has no desire at all to rely on the correct meaning of the Sūtras spoken by the Sugata; how can you, having long concealed your true intentions, constantly speak with such pretense?
I rely on the sūtras for my exposition and do not take the Abhidharma’s formal logic as my authority, because the tenets of the Abhidharma transcend the sūtras.
Now, however, you openly disregard the scriptural texts and arbitrarily establish doctrines according to your own deluded sentiments.
The proponents of the *Nyāya* (Right Reasoning) say this: "One is designated as being in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) based on reliance upon the meaning (*artha*).

Now, even if one grants that one relies upon the meaning, for one who acknowledges the Blessed One as their teacher, the established principles must not contradict the Sūtras; if they contradict the Sūtras, they are not right reasoning (*nyāya*). If they are not right reasoning, they cannot serve as proof. How can you then arbitrarily claim that because one relies upon the meaning, the statement that those in training possess afflictions (*kleśa*) does not conflict with the possibility of falling away from the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)?"

However, this sūtra does not mention those in training (śaikṣa), but speaks only of those beyond training (aśaikṣa); as has already been established through prior analysis, it is clear that the Arhat (saṃpannaphala) can experience a lapse due to loss of mindfulness.
The meaning set forth by the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) is most reliable; it is not a meaning falsely imagined according to your own personal whims.

If only those in training (śaikṣa) possess afflictions such that afflictions can arise for them but not for those beyond training (aśaikṣa), why did the Blessed One not state this specifically so that those to be converted might give rise to unerring knowledge, understanding that falling away due to loss of mindfulness occurs only in the stage of training and not otherwise?
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has transcended all faults; he does not utter confused or erroneous speech that would cause sentient beings to doubt.

Although this sūtra does not explicitly state that there is no distinction [between the stages], based on other sources we know that this refers to the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa). Therefore, what he said was spoken from his own perspective.

Furthermore, as for their claim that the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) has already severed all inversions (*viparyāsa*) and thus possesses the cause for realizing non-retrogression, this has already been refuted above; therefore, it lacks any probative function.
Consequently, the principle that those beyond training can still give rise to afflictions and undergo retrogression is thoroughly established and cannot be shaken.
Regarding this, the Elder again offers a mistaken explanation, saying:

"This *Aṅgārakalpa-sūtra* speaks of the stage of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), because for those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), the stains of afflictions have not yet been eliminated; thus, it is possible that they might encounter conditions and lose mindfulness, giving rise to afflictions. However, there is no logical possibility for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) to give rise to such afflictions."
Although the World-Honored One said:

"He has already been able to forever vomit up all dharmas conducive to outflows and has attained coolness," there is no fault in this statement because it speaks only of those "conducive to outflows" and does not explicitly mention the "outflows" themselves.
This does not constitute a valid explanation.
Why is that? Because the various outflows (*āsrava*) are also termed "dharmas conducive to the outflows" (*āsravasthānīya*).

That is to say, since the factors conducive to the outflows (*āsrava*) encompass all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), it would be logically inconsistent to claim that they do not encompass the outflows themselves.

To admit that this noble disciple has already been able to permanently vomit forth all contaminated things and has attained coolness (*śītībhūta*), yet to say he has not yet accomplished the fruit of Arhatship—such a teaching or principle for realization has never before been heard.

Alternatively, one would have to admit that the outflows (*āsrava*) are not factors conducive to the outflows (*āsravasthānīya-dharma*), which would contradict your own scriptural and philosophical tenets.

Furthermore, how could you maintain that a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) has already permanently vomited forth and attained the state of coolness regarding all factors conducive to the outflows within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)?
If the outflows (*āsrava*) within this stage have not been abandoned, one has certainly not attained dissociation from the factors conducive to outflows (*āsravasthānīya-dharma*) of this stage.

To assert that one has not attained dissociation from these factors, yet claim that one has already "permanently vomited them out" and "attained coolness" in this regard—such a statement reveals a marvelous wisdom, for the outflows and the factors conducive to outflows are abandoned simultaneously.

Since it has already been stated that [the mind] is compliant with the outflows (*āsrava*), vomited forth, and cooled, it is known through inference that those [beings] have exhausted all outflows; therefore, there is no room for interpreting this teaching as referring to a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Furthermore, regarding their claim that although this sutra speaks of the mind being "compliant with seclusion" and so forth throughout the long night, other sutras designate this as the power of a Fruit of Worthiness (*arhatphala*), yet one must possess eight factors to be called the power of an Arhat—therefore, they argue, there is no fault.
What proof is there that the power of the Arhat (the fruit of application) must necessarily possess eight names, rather than each being otherwise?
There is no scriptural authority or logical reasoning whatsoever to prove this; it is merely a matter of following one's own whims to embellish the terminology.
Furthermore, how can it be claimed that the power is established only when all eight directions are possessed collectively, rather than individually?

It is not the case that the various Arhats accepted by their own school admit that the eight kinds of powers manifest simultaneously; therefore, one should not say that the power is only accomplished through the totality of the directions.

Furthermore, when each of these individual factors is present before an Arhat, it is not the case that they lack the quality of power by being overwhelmed by various afflictions; how, then, can one calculate that each one is not powerful?
Therefore, what they have stated is certainly unreasonable.

Furthermore, even if one were to grant that the name "Power" (bala) is applied only to the aggregate as a whole, each individual [power] is nonetheless designated as the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*).
As it is said in the *Śūṇa-sūtra*:
An Arhat abides solely in detachment, harmlessness, renunciation, the exhaustion of craving, the exhaustion of clinging, and the nature of liberation through non-forgetfulness of mind.
The *Salyasūtra* (The Simile of the Arrow) states only this:
those who delight in Nirvāṇa permanently sever the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Is it not the case that because one’s examples are not exhaustive, they fail to establish the nature of an Arhat?
Now, observing all the statements he has made, they serve merely to let others know that he is capable of speaking.
Thus, for now, I have cited the *Aṅgāra-upama-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Simile of the Charcoal) as proof that there is such a thing as the falling away from the state of an Arhat.

Furthermore, it is said that there are two types of those who have attained the fruit (*phala*). As it is stated: "There are two kinds of Arhatship: first, the one subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*); second, the one not subject to falling away.

If you claim that this refers only to falling away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), this is logically untenable, because this sūtra speaks of two types of Arhats.

If one were to speak only of falling away from the happiness of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), there would have to be only one type of Arhat subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), because all [Arhats] possess the possibility of falling away from its actualization.
As the Sūtra says:

"I declare that regarding these four types of higher mental states (*adhicitta*) which constitute abidings in happiness in the present life, for whichever one there might be falling away, as for the unshakable liberation of mind (*akopyā cetovimukti*) which has been realized through bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*), I definitively declare that there is no cause or condition for falling away from it."

If it is argued that the term "one subject to falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*) is used in the sūtras solely with reference to the loss of mastery over meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and not to imply that all Arhats necessarily undergo such a fall—
meaning that one is called "subject to falling away" when they can lose their mastery while a dhyāna is currently manifest— then [the following applies].

If other affairs arise such that one is temporarily unable to manifest [the realization], yet one does not lose mastery even when it is not manifest, then although there is a regression in its actualization, it is still termed the "Dharma of Non-regression.
Therefore, the state of an Arhat is established through these two meanings.
This defense is untenable, because the sūtras state that there are two types of arhatship.
Furthermore, it was previously stated that one who has lost mastery over the dhyānas would give rise to afflictions regarding the desires if they were to abandon their detachment from them;
yet if they do not abandon them, since they have not regressed from their freedom from desire, to say that they have regressed from the joy and bliss born of seclusion is surely contradictory.
Therefore, if one loses mastery over meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it must logically follow that afflictions (*kleśa*) manifest.

If an Arhat were never to give rise to afflictions, then there would be no loss of mastery over concentration; consequently, all Arhats would possess only a single type of fruit, namely, the "non-retrogressive" (*aparihāṇadharman*) type.
If occasional liberation were of the nature of the fruit of arhatship, then the two types of fruits would not be distinct in essence.
Therefore, I maintain that because the Sūtra speaks of two kinds of fruits of arhatship, the principle of falling away from them is established.
Furthermore, it is said that this is because one knows the skillful means for ensuring that what is to be abandoned does not arise again. As stated in a sutra:

"I am like a skilled physician who, in accordance with reality, thoroughly understands the dharmas to be treated and abandoned, and certainly possesses the skillful means to ensure they do not arise hereafter."

By this analogy, one should understand that the afflictions to be abandoned possess the nature of arising again; therefore, with respect to the skillful knowledge of the means to prevent what has been abandoned from arising, I praise my own expertise, saying: "I am like a skilled physician."

If all those in the world were cured of their illnesses and never suffered a relapse, then one should not praise this excellent physician for his skill in knowing the means by which illness is cured and does not recur; therefore, we know that there is the possibility of falling back and generating afflictions once they have been severed.
If it is argued that this sutra speaks in reference to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is not so;
for it states that they possess the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). Specifically, it says:
"I have the internal factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-bodhyaṅga*); I know as it truly is that it exists," and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, we know that it is certainly not said [to apply] to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Furthermore, because it is stated that the fruit of arhatship possesses two types of knowledge—just as it is said that an Arhat possesses the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)—if all that has been abandoned were never to arise again, then the establishment of the knowledge of non-arising would be in vain.

If it is argued that the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is established based on its great benefit—because it demonstrates that the Arhat’s state of security is supreme by being severed from the arising of other distinct births—this is unreasonable.
For according to your own school, the mere arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) already constitutes the attainment of supreme security.
Furthermore, all Arhats know for themselves:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.
Being thus at peace, is this not the foremost?
Because although ordinary beings may attain the meditative absorption of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra-samāpatti*), they are subject to falling back and may even be reborn in the evil destinies;
only when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) has arisen can one know for oneself:
"I shall have no further rebirths, and there is nothing more to be done."
The meaning that the Arhat has attained the foremost peace and security has already been established; what need is there for the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)?

Although this foremost peace and security has been established, those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship further give rise to the knowledge of non-arising. The World-Honored One fully explained the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, stating that by this one definitively knows that although the afflictions of an Arhat have already been severed, he fears they might arise again in the future, and thus diligently seeks through skillful means the knowledge of their never arising again.
Therefore, the establishment of the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) is logically proven to be of great benefit.
From this it is demonstrated that the Arhat (argha-phala) is subject to regression.
*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Sixty-nine.

14. Chapter Sixteen: Distinguishing the Noble Ones, Part Fourteen. Furthermore, by what cause do all Arhats, having become free from the defilements of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), likewise not undergo further rebirth?
However, among them, there are those who have realized the state of non-arising with respect to the afflictions, yet this does not apply to all.
Some say this is due to differences in their faculties (*indriya*).

This explanation is irrational, because the sūtras state that those of the nature of falling away and those of the nature of non-falling away are identical in terms of their faculty-class; as it is said: "Because the five faculties are superior, sharp, and perfectly fulfilled, they are called 'liberated in both ways' (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)."

However, because there are those liberated through both parts who belong to a nature subject to regression, it is not due to the excellence of their faculties that they realize the non-arising of afflictions.
If this is so, by virtue of what difference in nature do these six types of lineages exist only for the Arhat, and not for others as well?
The cultivation for refining the faculties occurs exclusively in the stage of non-training (aśaikṣa), though it also exists in other stages.
The verse says:
"Those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) also have six; refining the faculties does not occur during the path of seeing (darśanamārga)."
The treatise states:

The lineages of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are likewise six, because the six types of fruition (*phala*) take these as their antecedents. Due to the distinctions among the lineages in which they abide, there is the subsequent arising or non-arising of the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).
At what time is one established in the state where the abandoned afflictions are no longer subject to arising?
It is at the time when one attains the sublime path capable of suppressing these types of afflictions.
If this is so, then this non-arising must be cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and not cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If it were non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), then non-analytical cessation would have to be the fruit of the Path; this would contradict the sacred teaching.
As it is said:
"What are the dharmas that are not fruits?"
This refers to non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and space (*ākāśa*).

There is no fault of failing to produce analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because the superior path arises for other purposes and not for this one; since it is not that which is being produced, it is not the fruit of the path.

This means that the transformation of the superior path is for the sake of realizing analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), not non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Therefore, when the path transforms, the non-arising that is realized is not called the fruit of the path.

It is like a person lighting a lamp: the original purpose is to dispel darkness, not to exhaust the oil. Although when the lamp is lit it not only dispels the darkness but also causes the oil to be exhausted, this exhaustion of the oil was not the original aim; therefore, it is not said to be the fruit of lighting the lamp.
This should also be understood in the same way; therefore, there is no fault.
Thus, when a superior lineage (*gotra*) and a superior path arise, one also realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*), yet this is not the fruit of the path.

Now, upon careful examination, the non-arising realized by means of the path certainly does not depend on the faculties (*indriya*), for if it did, it would follow that everyone would attain it. Rather, it is attained solely through the power of the distinguished lineage; therefore, for those who are immovable (*akopyadharman*), afflictions will necessarily not arise.

It was previously stated that there are three types of those who fall away from the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*): first, those who advance their faculties; second, those who fall back and abide as learners (*śaikṣa*); and third, those who abide in their own stage and enter parinirvāṇa.

For the four [types] beginning with the one who reflects (*cetanādharman*), there should be four, five, six, and seven [possibilities] respectively. It is not only those in the state of no-more-learning who can advance their faculties; learners and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) also possess this capacity. However, it is only those outside the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) who are able to cultivate the refinement of faculties (*indriyasaṃcaraṇa*), because in the state of the Path of Seeing, there is no room for the arousal of preparatory application (*prayoga*).

This means that because the stage of the path of seeing proceeds with such rapid momentum, there is no leisure therein to further cultivate other matters; one can only cultivate the refinement of the faculties while in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who possesses faith and understanding, just as in the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

As it is said that the "immovable" (akopya) [arhat] does not fall away from the bliss of the present life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra), how can it be admitted that even one of immovable nature (akopyadharman) is subject to falling away?
There is no contradiction here. Why is this so?
The verse says:
It should be known that there are three types of regression: from what has been attained, from what has not yet been attained, and from enjoyment.
The Buddha possesses only the last; among those of sharp faculties, there are the latter two, while for those of dull faculties, all three exist.
The treatise states:

It should be understood that there are, in total, three kinds of retrogression: first, retrogression from what has already been attained, which refers to falling away from superior qualities already acquired;
second, retrogression from what has not yet been attained, which refers to being unable to attain the qualities one ought to attain.
Third is the retrogression from enjoyment (*paribhoga-vihāni*), which refers to the non-manifestation of various already-attained superior qualities.
Among these three, the first two have non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) as their essence, while the third consists solely in their non-manifestation.

Among these three types of decline, the World-Honored One possesses only the decline regarding the enjoyment of requisites (*paribhoga-hāni*). This is because his mind is drawn toward his definitive tasks and activities; thus, although there exist other immeasurable and uncommon Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*), he finds no leisure to manifest them.
With the exception of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, those of immovable dharma possess both non-acquisition and enjoyment decline.
This means that because they have not yet attained superior qualities such as the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*) that ought to be attained, there is non-acquisition decline;
and because their minds are distracted by other activities, they lack the leisure to give rise to qualities already attained, there is enjoyment decline.
The other five types of lineage may possess all three [kinds of retrogression], as they are also susceptible to the loss of qualities already attained.

With respect to retrogression from enjoyment (*paribhoga-vihāni*), it is said that those of immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*) may retrogress from the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*); thus, there is no contradiction.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) states:
From the perspective of the school that maintains there is no falling away, one should not raise the objection:
"How can one who is immovable fall away from the happiness of the present life?"
This is not because it refers to whether one falls away from or does not fall away from meditative absorption (*dhyāna*);

for the Sūtra speaks of "shakable" and "unshakable" dharmas, stating that all Arhats possess untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*), which is termed "unshakable liberation of mind" (*akopya-cetovimukti*).

However, among those who have attained mastery over meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one who may fall away is called "one of the nature of falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*); one who cannot fall away is called "one of the nature of non-falling away" (*aparihāṇadharman*).
The same should be applied with due reflection to those of the nature of reflecting (*cetana-dharman*) and so forth.
If that is so, what is the distinction between the "non-retrogressive," the "abiding," and the "immovable"?
It is because there is no loss regarding mastery over meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) in all three cases.

One is termed "non-retrogressive" not merely by virtue of having refined one's faculties (*indriya*), whereas that which is obtained through the refinement of faculties is called "immovable. These two types of superior attainments (*samāpatti*) have the principle that even if they encounter conditions for retrogression, there is no possibility of falling away.
One who abides in the dharma merely does not fall away from the superior qualities already attained, but cannot further induce the arising of other superior qualities.

Even if they were to induce such arising, they could still fall away from them; thus, the distinctions among the three types—such as the non-falling [arhat] and so forth—and the establishment of the distinctions between falling and non-falling within the fruit of arhatship would be untenable.

Furthermore, regarding the loss of the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), the nature of mastery (*vaśitva*) is established as the basis for the "nature of falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*). As previously demonstrated through various logical investigations, this refutes the faults of confusion among the three types of non-falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*) and so forth.

Furthermore, according to that position, there is no distinction between the two noble ones—those who are non-regressive and those who abide [in their state]—with respect to their correspondence [to the fruit], because both are admitted not to have attained it through the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*); because both lack regression from the superior qualities already attained; and because both are capable of producing the superior qualities not yet attained.

Although it is said that there is the possibility of retrogression for one who abides in newly arisen superior qualities—distinguishing this from the state of non-retrogression—the designation "abiding" is not established in dependence upon that [retrogression]; rather, the name "abiding" is intended to manifest the state of being free from both progress and retrogression.
Furthermore, since that school admits [the existence of those] abiding in sharp faculties, how can it be said that there is a falling back from newly arisen superior qualities?
If one admits such falling back, they should be designated as "those subject to falling back" (*parihāṇadharman*).
According to that school, even those subject to falling back do not fall back entirely, for if they were to fall back entirely, they would necessarily give rise to afflictions.

The claim that "immovability" (akopya) is attained through the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) is also logically untenable, as it differs from the state of one who is non-retrogressive (anivartaka-dharman). This is because, according to their own tenets, one refines the faculties out of fear of losing mastery over the bliss of the present life (dṛṣṭadharma-sukha). Is the faculty obtained through such refinement subject to retrogression or not?

If it is admitted that there is falling away, one should be called "one subject to falling away" (parihāṇadharman), because they themselves state that if one loses mastery over meditative concentration, one is termed "one subject to falling away.

If it is admitted that there is no falling away, then just as the name "one subject to falling away" is established by the power of falling away, so too one should be named "one not subject to falling away" (aparihāṇadharman) by the power of not falling away.
In that case, "immovable" (akopya) and "non-retrogressive" (aparihāṇadharman) would be identical; how then can one firmly establish a distinction between them?

If it is argued that those whose innate nature is of sharp faculties are called "non-retrogressive," while those who later cultivate the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become sharp are called "immovable," and that these two names were established to manifest this difference—[this argument is untenable].

In that case, they would have to be identical to those who abide in the "capable-of-attaining" (*kandha*) state; for the latter are held to abide in naturally sharp faculties (*prakṛti-tīkṣṇendriya*) obtained without the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), being likewise without falling back.

Although it is said that one who does not fall back can newly evoke superior qualities—which differs from merely abiding—this is logically incorrect, because the status of "not falling back" is not established in reference to the new evocation of superior qualities.

That is to say, according to their own tenet, whether these spiritual lineages give rise to new, superior qualities or not, because they are by nature of sharp faculties, they do not lose their mastery over the happiness of the present life; this is the characteristic of non-retrogression.
The same applies to those who abide [in their state]; thus, there should be no distinction between them.

Because they are capable of reaching [the goal], they receive the name "capable of reaching" (*kāmada*). According to that school’s tenet, it is not said that from this lineage one further attains a different class of untainted liberation; rather, it must be admitted that by refining the tainted faculties, one transforms the practice of refining the faculties based on a previously existing "deteriorating" (*parihāṇadharman*) lineage, thereby becoming known as "capable of reaching. In this way, even the "capable of reaching" is established through the refinement of the faculties.
Are these attained faculties subject to regression or not?

If one allows for regression, they should be called "those subject to regression" (parihāṇadharman); if there is no loss, they should be called "immovable" (akopyadharman). This is because both are attained through the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) and are therefore non-regressive.

Furthermore, one should not say that when the cultivation of the out-flowing faculties (*sāsrava-indriya*) reaches its ultimate limit, it is called the "unshakable dharma" (*akopyadharman*). This is because this unshakable dharma is the nature of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*); it is not the case that an Arhat, for the sake of attaining mastery over a minor and inferior temporary experience of the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), initiates great application (*mahāprayoga*) to cultivate and refine the faculties, progressing through successive stages until reaching the unshakable dharma.
Therefore, the Master of the Sūtras merely expresses his own personal sentiments and cannot be relied upon.
To follow the principles of the Noble Teaching, one must rely solely on the correct reasoning of the Abhidharma to realize the distinctions regarding the regression of Arhats and so forth.

This means that based on the distinctions of superiority and inferiority among the untainted (*anāsrava*) qualities accomplished within the body of one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship, six distinct lineages (*gotra*) are established.

It is logically possible for various Arhats to exert great effort and undergo the training of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) in order to attain progressively more excellent and increased untainted qualities; however, this does not apply to the mere temporary manifestation of inferior, worldly qualities—such as those resembling a rotting corpse, which are easily destroyed and difficult to achieve—even if one were to exert great effort for their sake. Therefore, the doctrine they rely upon cannot be accepted as authoritative.
Since it is admitted that Arhats may fall away from their fruit, will they be born again?
Since they pass away while still possessed of afflictions at the stage of falling away, they ought to undergo further birth.
Furthermore, regarding the actions that one does not perform while abiding in the fruit, does one perform them at the time of falling away?
Once that delusion has arisen, there ought to be further occurrences that contradict its nature as a fruit.
There is no such fault. Why is this?
The verse says:
All who fall away from fruition Necessarily attain it again before they die;
What was not performed while abiding in fruition Is not performed again, as it was merely a temporary increase.
The treatise states:
There is no falling away from the fruit during the interval before death, because once one has fallen away, they will inevitably regain it immediately.
Furthermore, for those whose lifespan is about to expire, there is no possibility of falling away, as they lack the loss of mindfulness.
Only when there remains a portion of life does the possibility of falling away exist; once fallen, one will certainly realize the goal again before long.
As the Sūtra says:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that such well-learned noble disciples, though they may fall away from right mindfulness, quickly regain it, causing what has regressed to be exhausted, eliminated, extinguished, and transcended."
If one were to say otherwise, the fruit of practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) would not be a state of security that can be relied upon.

Furthermore, regarding those who abide in the stage of fruition, they should not engage in actions contrary to that fruition; for even though afflictions may manifest due to a temporary lapse in mindfulness caused by a momentary increase [in defilement], there is no logical possibility for them to act as they did while abiding in the fruition itself.
