It cannot lead to the attainment of bodhi, nor can it lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa; therefore, one should not cultivate this basis of supernormal power.

This is what should be sought through the Noble Eightfold Path; it is indeed logical that its purpose is solely to eliminate the obstacles to the fundamental dhyāna-concentrations that are to be realized.
Although concentration is identical to the divine (ṛddhi), this sutra states:
The term "divine" (*deva*) refers to the phenomena of the miraculous manifestations of divine fruits.

This statement was made in order to lead those who seek the coarse toward an awakening to the subtle, and furthermore, to demonstrate that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is its proximate cause; thus, there is no contradiction with the sūtras.
For what reason are faith and the others designated as "faculties" (*indriya*) and "powers" (*bala*)?
It is because they are predominant and because they are difficult to overcome.
For what reason are these five first called "faculties" and later termed "powers"?
Because these five dharmas are distinguished by priority based on their lower and superior grades,
and because they are distinguished by being susceptible to subjugation or not susceptible to subjugation:
since the power and function of lower-grade faith and so forth are weak, they are still subjugated by their counteractive factors and their own homogeneous types.
The superior grade is the opposite of this, and thus it receives the name "attainment" (*bala*).
What is the meaning of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) that have been explained?
Their meaning is "that which can awaken," and thus they are called factors of enlightenment.
If that were so, there would be only one factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

It is not so; mindfulness and the others are components of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), and they all conform to that investigation, being designated by their most prominent member.
Alternatively, the meaning of "factor of enlightenment" is that which is a limb (*aṅga*) of enlightenment.
If that were so, one would have to admit that there are only six factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

This is not the case; for the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is both awakening (*bodhi*) and a factor of enlightenment, whereas the remaining six are factors of enlightenment but not awakening itself.
What is the meaning of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)?
They are called factors of the path because they seek out the basis of the path.
If that were so, there would be only a single factor of the path.
That is not so; the other seven are factors of right view, and all are designated by their predominant characteristic as being "in accordance with right view.
Alternatively, the meaning of "limb of the path" (mārgāṅga) is that which is a limb of the path.
If that were the case, one would have to admit that there are only seven limbs of the path.
It is not so; right view is both the path and a factor of the path, while the remaining seven are factors of the path but not the path itself.
At which stage, then, should it be said that which awakening-factor increases?
The verse says: In the stages of the beginner, the aids to penetration, And the paths of cultivation and seeing,
One should know that the seven categories, Beginning with the foundations of mindfulness, increase in succession.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the stage of initial practice, it is said that the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) predominate. This means that in this stage, in order to eliminate distortions (*viparyāsa*), one is able to discern with precision the specific and general characteristics of objects such as the body through the power of mindfulness; thus, the function of wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant as it destroys the two kinds of delusion.

Regarding the stage of *uṣmagata* (Heat), it is said that the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) increase; that is to say, within this stage, one perceives the faults of saṃsāra and the virtues of nirvāṇa, thereby being able to rouse courageous diligence and vigor so as not to fall back into saṃsāra but to swiftly proceed toward nirvāṇa, because the application of effort is preeminent.

Regarding the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), it is said that the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) increase; this means that in this stage one is able to control the mind and consciousness, proceeding toward the stage of non-retrogression without ever becoming deficient, because the function of the wholesome roots such as faith and so forth, through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), is preeminent.

Regarding the stage of the dharma of patience (*kṣānti*), it is said that the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) increase; for in this stage, one eternally ceases rebirth in the evil destinies, never again falls back, and swiftly enters the state of certainty (*niyāma*). Thus, the sense of "predominance" (*ādhipatya*) is established, as the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) is preeminent here.

It is said that the five powers (*pañca-balāni*) predominate in the stage of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), because in this stage one is no longer overcome by the afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus the meaning of "power" is preeminent.
Although such a state may also be possible in the stage of "patience" (*kṣānti*), it is not certain; therefore, it is not so described.
Alternatively, because one is not overcome by any other dharmas of ordinary beings within this stage, the meaning of "power" (*bala*) is particularly predominant here.

In the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which is proximate to the state of enlightenment (*bodhi*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are said to increase because they specifically assist awakening.
Alternatively, because within this stage one abandons the nine grades of afflictions and repeatedly awakens, the meaning of "limb of awakening" (*bodhyaṅga*) increases.

Because all the meanings of the "path" (*mārga*) present in the stage of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) are fully possessed, the "limbs of the path" (*mārgāṅga*) increase; that is to say, it is called the "path" because it possesses both the sense of being the basis for seeking and the sense of proceeding toward the goal.

Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), two meanings are preeminent: first, because it is the stage where the noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*) first arises, and thus excels in seeking the principles of the truths (*satya*) as they truly are;

and second, because in this stage one does not give rise to anticipatory thoughts (*ākāṅkṣā-citta*), and thus excels in being able to proceed swiftly toward the goal, as the number [of moments] increases accordingly.
In the sūtras, the seven [foundations of mindfulness] are mentioned first and the eight [path factors] later;
this is not the sequence of their cultivation. Others establish a sequential argument here:

at the very beginning, by the power of wisdom, one understands the specific and general characteristics of objects such as the body as they truly are, thereby guiding the arising of all wholesome qualities—just as one with sight leads a group of blind people. Therefore, the four foundations of mindfulness are taught first.

Having established the objects of experience through the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one is able to initiate right effort (*samyakprahāṇa*) for abandoning evil and cultivating good; therefore, the four right efforts are taught in the second [section].

Through the power of right effort, faults are diminished and virtues are made to flourish within the mental continuum, whereby one is finally able to cultivate the sublime concentrations (*samādhi*); thus, the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are taught in the third [section].

With the supreme meditative concentration as their basis, they cause faith and the other faculties to serve as dominant conditions for supramundane dharmas; for this reason, these five faculties are designated as the fourth stage.

Once the meaning of "faculty" is established, they are able to resist and not be overcome by the evil karma and afflictions that lead to the miserable realms; for this reason, these five powers are designated as the fifth stage.

Since the meaning of the powers has already been established, and because one is now able to realize the objects of the Four Noble Truths as they truly are without doubt or hesitation, the seven factors of enlightenment are taught as the sixth stage.

Having realized the objects of the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, one develops weariness toward and relinquishment of saṃsāra while aspiring toward and proceeding toward nirvāṇa; therefore, the factors of the path are taught as the seventh stage.
Within this, each point shall be explained in its proper sequence; one should seek to understand them correctly as is done in the commentaries on the sūtras.
Since this treatise investigates the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there is no need for laborious elaboration regarding the logic of their sequence.
Now, within this context, one should analyze the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*): how many are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and how many are tainted (*sāsrava*)?
The verse says:
The seven factors of enlightenment and the eight branches of the path are exclusively untainted.
The four, three, five faculties, and powers are all common to both types.
The commentary states:

Among these, the seven factors of enlightenment and the eight branches of the noble path are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), because they are established only within the stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

This means that at the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) increase; being proximate to awakening (*bodhi*), they counteract the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Therefore, the essence of the factors of enlightenment is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). Although all factors conducive to awakening assist toward awakening, these alone are designated by the name "factors of enlightenment" because they are most proximate to the fruit of awakening.

According to this principle, it should be understood that the realization of the seven factors of enlightenment is taught solely in reference to the antidote for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); as these serve as the primary antidotes for the lower stages, the name "factors of enlightenment" is established exclusively for those that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
If this were not permitted, why would it not be accepted that both [the path and the fruit] are included?
Alternatively, among all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the designation "limbs of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*) is established based on proximity to enlightenment.

Within the path, the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is proximate to enlightenment by nature and is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); therefore, it is only the untainted path of cultivation that is designated as a limb of enlightenment.

Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are predominant; therefore, these are exclusively comprised within the nature of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Although right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and the others may also be associated with the tainted (*sāsrava*), they do not receive the name "factors of the noble path" (*āryamārgāṅga*), because the term "factors of the noble path" refers specifically to the untainted.

Furthermore, those who debate this matter concede that among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), those taught after the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are necessarily untainted (*anāsrava*); if they were taught prior to them, they would pertain to both types [tainted and untainted].
Since the limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are taught only after the limbs of enlightenment, the eight limbs of the path are exclusively untainted.
The remaining factors apply to both [stages], as is established by implication.

That is to say, among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), those that increase in the earlier stage also increase in their functional efficacy in the later stage, whereas those that increase in the later stage do not necessarily increase in the earlier stage.

Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "From the stage of initial application up to the attainment of exhaustion and non-arising, the foundations of mindfulness constantly increase," and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding these thirty-seven [factors], how many are present in each stage?
The verse says:
In the first dhyāna, all [factors] are present; in the *anāgamya*, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is excluded;
in the second dhyāna, vitarka is excluded; in the third, fourth, and intermediate [dhyānas], both [vitarka and vicāra] are excluded.
In the first three formless stages, the two preceding types [of factors] excluding the precepts are absent;
in the desire realm and the Peak of Existence, the factors of enlightenment and the path members are excluded.
The commentary says:

In the first dhyāna, all thirty-seven factors are present; however, in the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) is excluded because one still harbors doubt regarding the dharmas of the lower stages and has not yet attained firm confidence, and thus joy does not arise.

Furthermore, when the *anāgamya-samādhi* first manifests, one has not yet been able to abandon the afflictions of the lower stages; even though they have subsequently been abandoned, the situation remains the same as before. Therefore, at the time those [afflictions] arise, there is no joy whatsoever.
Some say: All stages of the *sāmantaka* (preparatory) paths proceed with effortful exertion; therefore, they lack the quality of joy (*prīti*).

In the second dhyāna, right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is excluded because vitarka has already ceased within that dhyāna; for it is stated in the Sūtra that that stage is without vitarka, as its higher levels of concentration proceed with tranquility.
Consequently, these two stages each have thirty-six factors.
In the third and fourth dhyānas, as well as the intermediate dhyāna, joy and vitarka are both eliminated, leaving thirty-five factors each.
In the first three formless attainments, the three branches of morality are excluded, along with joy and vitarka, leaving thirty-two factors each.

In the Desire Realm and at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), excluding the factors of enlightenment and the path factors, there are twenty-two each, because they lack the untainted (*anāsrava*) states.
Thus, across these various stages, the number of factors of enlightenment that manifest is indeterminate, varying according to what is appropriate for each.

This means that according to their respective stages, the subsequent necessarily includes the preceding; thus, while a single entity may be conceptually divided into multiple types, there is the sense that multiple types can arise simultaneously.

However, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) certainly do not arise together, because they are divided into four based on their objects of observation (*ālambana*). Since even two instances of wisdom (*prajñā*) cannot arise at the same time, how could all four wisdoms arise simultaneously?

A single wisdom cannot be divided into many based on its objects; for if it were subsumed under the mindfulness-establishment of dharmas through a general contemplation, there would necessarily never be a case where a single wisdom arises in a single moment with four objects and four aspects.
According to this principle, although the thirty-seven factors are present in their entirety within the first dhyāna taken as a whole,
at most only thirty-four can manifest simultaneously in a single moment.
Thus, at most, there can be thirty-three in the Not-yet-arrived [attainment] and the Second Dhyāna;
thirty-two at most in the Intermediate [Dhyāna] and the Third Dhyāna; and twenty-nine at most in the first three Formless [attainments].

In the desire realm and at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there are at most only nineteen [factors], because all [of them] exclude three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Those that are reduced therein should be considered according to their respective stages.
Why is the mind-king (*cittarāja*) not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Reason (*yukti*) is also subsumed within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, because they truly include all preparatory virtues (*prayoga-kuśala*).

However, it is not established as a separate factor like wisdom (*prajñā*) and the others because, regarding the categories of defilement and purification, the mind possesses an even and impartial functional power without partiality, whereas the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) possess an intensified functional power exclusively within the category of purification; therefore, it is not established [as a separate factor].
Other masters say:

"The factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) mostly take the common characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of all phenomena as their objects, whereas the mind-king (citta-rāja) mostly takes its own specific characteristics (sva-lakṣaṇa) as its object; for this reason, it is not established [as a factor of enlightenment].
Others further say:

The cultivation of the factors of enlightenment is fundamentally intended as an antidote to all afflictions; however, since the afflictions are mental factors (*caitta*) and not the mind itself (*citta*), the remedial dharmas are likewise not the mind but merely mental factors. This is because they are established through the mutual opposition between the obstacles and their remedies.
Some say: The factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) assist enlightenment (bodhi). Since enlightenment is a mental factor (caitta), its essence is wisdom (prajñā).

It is impossible for the mind-king (citta-rāja) to assist a mental factor, just as a king cannot be assisted by his ministers; therefore, the mind-king is not established as a factor of enlightenment.
Other masters say:

"The mind leads the world through the cycles of rebirth in the realms, destinies, and births without interruption; the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) serves to sever birth and death. For this reason, the sovereign mind (citta-rāja) is not established as a factor of enlightenment."

Other masters say: Since beginningless time, the mind has been defiled by numerous afflictions; it scatters among various objects and is stubborn and difficult to tame. To tame this mind, one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*); that which is to be tamed is not itself the tamer. Therefore, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is not established as a factor of enlightenment.
For what reason, among all the great mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), are only four established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?

In reality, they are subsumed within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, because those [foundations] truly encompass all the wholesome qualities of application (*prayoga-kuśala*).

However, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are established separately because these three possess a powerful efficacy that accords with the factors conducive to purification and can thus be established as limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); whereas perception, volition, contact, and desire possess a powerful efficacy within the defiled category, and therefore they are not established separately.

In the case of conceptual meditation (*parikalpita-bhāvanā*), resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) predominates; since the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) comprise only those elements conducive to the meditation on reality (*tattvārtha-bhāvanā*), this resolute conviction is not included among the factors of enlightenment.
Other masters say:
"Resolute conviction increases only upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)," because the Sūtra establishes it as a limb of no-more-learning alone.

The factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) increase during the stage of training (śaikṣa), because by the power of this cause they are able to bring forth the three types of enlightenment; therefore, resolute conviction (adhimukti) is not included among the factors of enlightenment.
The power of *manasikāra* (attention) can activate the mind, causing it to easily detach from its object and become unstable;

whereas the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) involve the careful and precise observation of an object, causing the mind to be single-pointed, which is contrary to that [function of attention]. Therefore, attention is not subsumed under the factors of enlightenment.
If that were so, why would one establish *vitarka* (applied thought) as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?

Although *vitarka* stimulates the mind toward its object, it is intended to cause the mind to investigate the ultimate principle, rather than to cause it to be flighty or easily distracted from the object. It possesses the capacity to stimulate the observation of the truths, for it is said that this power stimulates right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). For these reasons, *manasikāra* (attention) cannot be cited as an analogy for *vitarka*.
Other masters say:

At the initial stage of apprehending an object, whether it be defiled or pure, the power of *manasikāra* (attention) is predominant; thus, it is said to be "unreasonable" [to classify it as such]. However, when it reaches the stage of continuous engagement with the object (*prāptaviṣaya-saṃtati*), its force becomes subtle. Therefore, it is not established as a factor of affliction (*kleśa*) or a limb of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), because the factors of affliction and awakening only reach their full intensity during the stage of continuous engagement with the object.

Because its functional power increases within both the defiled and purified portions, *vedanā* (feeling) is established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); consequently, it is established as the member of feeling (*vedanāṅga*) among the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) regarding the process of transmigration, and as the factor of joy (*prītisambodhyaṅga*) among the factors of enlightenment regarding the process of cessation.
Other masters say:

Although feeling (*vedanā*) is predominant in relation to defilement (*saṃkleśa*), it also possesses the capacity to perform a beneficial function for the category of purity (*vyavadāna*). Just as the nature of a *caṇḍāla*, though base and inferior, can perform beneficial services for noble lineages, so too is feeling a limb of benefit (*anuśaṃsāṅga*) within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and is thus established under the name of a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) among the limbs of awakening (*bodhipakṣya*).

For what reason do all three feelings pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*), yet among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) only joy (*prīti*) is included and not the other two? It is because the mental aspects (*ākāra*) of the factors of enlightenment are sharp and intense, whereas the aspects of pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are dull and sluggish; therefore, they are not [included].
Other masters say:

"The two feelings of pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are obscured by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), and the equanimity of formations (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*); because their characteristics are not clearly manifest, they are not established [as factors of enlightenment].
For what reason are only four among the great wholesome mental factors established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?"

In reality, these are all subsumed within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, because those [foundations] collectively subsume all virtuous qualities of application (*prayoga-kuśala*).

Nevertheless, faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are established separately because these four are particularly conducive to awakening (*bodha-anukūla*).
How is it that these four have such strong application toward awakening?

Faith is the foremost in setting out for bodhi; faith is the primary foundation for practicing the various deeds; and faith is the root of the causes for pure fruits. Without faith, the practice of the path cannot be accomplished; therefore, the faculty of faith is established as a factor of awakening.
Other masters say:
Just as when a water-clearing jewel is placed in turbid water, the water immediately becomes clear and pure, enabling those with sight to discern various forms and images;

so too, by placing faith within the mental complex (*citta-pakṣa*), it can cause that co-arising mental complex to become limpid and pure. Through this, one is able to perceive the principles of the Four Noble Truths, which gradually increase until they constitute the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*). Therefore, faith most appropriately should be established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

Diligence is capable of universally stimulating all practices, causing them to swiftly proceed toward the enlightenment of the three vehicles; for if there were no right diligence, even if one had already set out, one would eventually become lax and abandon the path in the interim, resulting in nothing being accomplished. Therefore, diligence is established as a factor of enlightenment.
Other masters say:

The reason one has been unable to see the Four Noble Truths since beginningless time is entirely due to indolence and a lack of delight in hearing and correctly contemplating the principles of the Four Noble Truths. Because diligence can counteract that [indolence] by causing one to delight in hearing and correctly contemplating the principles of the Four Truths, one is able to see the Four Truths and swiftly realize Bodhi; therefore, diligence should also be established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).

By means of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), one causes the mind to become pliant; by means of equanimity (*upekṣā*), which is straightforward, one causes the mind to be balanced. Thus, one is able to increase all supramundane practices and cause them to swiftly proceed toward the enlightenment (*bodhi*) of the three vehicles; therefore, tranquility and equanimity are established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Other masters say:

Since beginningless time, a mind distracted by lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) has failed to perceive the principles of the truths; consequently, one does not realize the enlightenment (*bodhi*) of the three vehicles.

Lightness-and-ease (*praśrabdhi*) dispels lethargy, and equanimity of application (*vīrya-upekṣā*) halts restlessness; through these, one perceives the truths and swiftly proceeds toward enlightenment. Therefore, these too should be established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

If that were so, since shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*), being virtuous by nature, are included among the various categories of wholesome qualities and are termed "pure dharmas" (*śukla-dharma*), should they not also be established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?

They should not be so established, because shamelessness and lack of dread-of-blame are associated exclusively with all unwholesome minds; while they constitute a predominant obstacle to the ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), their obstructive power is weak regarding the realization of the principles of the Truths (*satyadarśana*).

That which is the opposite of those [two] is called *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (dread of blame); they are subsumed under the category of "virtuous by nature" (*svabhāva-kuśala*) and receive the designation of "white dharmas" (*avadāta-dharma*). Although they possess superior power regarding the virtue of ethical discipline (*śīla*) in the state of distraction, their contribution as auxiliary forces for the virtue of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is slight.

Among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), those that are favorable to meditative concentration and assist in awakening to the principles of the truths are taken up; therefore, those [other factors] are not established [as such].
If that were so, should non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*) not be established?
Since they are roots of goodness and are wholesome by their very nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*), they too should not be established [as separate factors].

Since various forms of greed and hatred associated with the six consciousnesses pervade all five categories as latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), they give rise to coarse and evil karma as their predominant preparatory application, severing the roots of goodness, obstructing the power of mundane wholesome states, and being inferior in their opposition to the vision of the truths. Because non-greed and non-hatred are established as the opposites of these, they receive the name "roots of goodness" and are subsumed under the category of intrinsic wholesomeness (*svabhāva-kuśala*).

Although the power of scattered wholesome karma is strong, its efficacy within the context of concentration-based wholesome states is weak; because the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) accord with concentration-based wholesome states and assist in awakening to the principles of the Truths, those [scattered wholesome states] are not established as such.

If that is so, then heedfulness (*apramāda*) should be established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), for it is through heedfulness that all practices are accomplished, and the Buddha repeatedly exhorts one to cultivate heedfulness.

Nor should it be established [as a hindrance] in the state of distraction; for in that distracted state, heedlessness causes the mind to run toward the five desires, which is capable of obstructing the wholesome activities of generosity and so forth with great force, whereas in the state of meditative concentration, the power of this hindrance is not predominant.

In contrast to those [factors], heedfulness (*apramāda*) is established; it merely protects the mind from the five desires so that it does not wander and can focus exclusively on practicing giving and other virtues. Thus, while its power and function are strong regarding scattered wholesome states (*vyākṣepa-kuśala*), its influence is weak within the context of meditative wholesome states (*samādhi-kuśala*). Since the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are selected for their conformity with meditative wholesome states and their assistance in awakening to the principles of the Truths, heedfulness is not established among them.

If that were so, non-harming (*ahiṃsā*) should also be established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), because harming (*hiṃsā*) afflicts immeasurable sentient beings and causes them to fall into the three evil destinies, and [non-harming] serves as its antidote.

Yet it should not be so established; for harming arises in dependence upon objects and causes affliction to various sentient beings, thereby obstructing the cultivation of mundane virtues (*vyavakīrṇakuśala*).

Non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) is the opposite of this; because it assists meditative concentration (*samādhi*) only slightly, it likewise should not be established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Other masters say:

among the great wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*), those whose opposites are powerful and whose intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are superior are established as factors of enlightenment, while others are not.
That which is "strong in counteracting" refers to those associated with all defiled states of mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*).
That which is "superior by nature" refers to those that assist the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), as previously explained.

Faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) possess both meanings; the six factors beginning with shame (*hrī*) and dread (*apatrāpya*) do not possess both.
Regarding the five factors such as shame (*hrī*) and so forth, both meanings [of being a factor of enlightenment] are absent.
As for the single factor of heedfulness (*apramāda*), it lacks only the excellence of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For what reason are delight (*abhinandanā*) and aversion (*vidveṣa*) not considered factors of enlightenment?
In reality, these are indeed subsumed under the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, as they collectively encompass all preparatory virtues (*prayoga-kuśala*).

However, they are not established separately as factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) because these two types have mutually contradictory aspects; neither universally takes the four noble truths as its object, neither can be constantly present at any single stage, and their mental states (*cittapakṣa*) are too narrow. For these reasons, they are not established [as such].
Other masters say:
"As for delight and aversion, they are induced by the power of the wisdom that contemplates objects; that is to say, they are conducive to the arising of awakening-wisdom.
Since their meaning is contradictory [to the factors of awakening], they should not be established as separate [factors]."

For what reason, while both vitarka and vicāra can be either cultivated wholesome states or untainted (anāsrava), is one [the former] included among the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) and the other [the latter] not? In reality, both are indeed common to all; the meaning is as previously explained.

However, while *vitarka* (applied thought) is established separately, *vicāra* (sustained thought) is not; this is because *vitarka* exerts a strong influence upon right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) within the Noble Path. Since its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is sharp and intense when it arises, it possesses the capacity to assist the vision by seeking the principles of truth (*satya*), and is therefore established as a constituent of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
Investigation (*vicāra*) is not like this, because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) arises as extremely weak.
Other masters say:

when both [vitarka and vicāra] operate together, the coarse mode of activity of vitarka overshadows that of vicāra; thus, only in the stage where vicāra alone arises does its mode of activity become subtle, and for this reason, vicāra is not established separately among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Since the arousal of right view inherently involves right effort, why establish vitarka (applied thought) separately as a factor of enlightenment?
Effort that arouses right view is distinct from vitarka; therefore, they should both be established together within the factors of the path.
This means that *vīrya* (diligence) exerts pressure upon them to cause rapid progress in cultivation; through the power of investigation, it urges them on to swiftly contemplate the Noble Truths.
For what reason is manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?

The factors of enlightenment are exclusively wholesome states conducive to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) co-arising with the mind possesses a superior capacity for such conduciveness, whereas manifest action does not; therefore, it is not established as one.
For what reason are the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?

Because they lack any distinct or superior capacity to assist in awakening and are dissociated [from the mind], unlike unmanifest form (*avijñapti*), which—though dissociated—serves as the hub for the wheel of the Path; therefore, they are not separately established among the factors of enlightenment.
Other masters say:

Because the two mindless absorptions (*acittaka-samāpatti*) can extinguish the mind, they are contrary to *vitarka*. Furthermore, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and possession (*prāpti*) possess the function of causing change and accomplishment in that which is characterized; these function equally toward both the defiled and the pure. Since the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) have a predominant function in accordance with the pure, [the characteristics and possession] are not established separately [as such].
For what reason is faith not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) or a factor of the path (*mārgāṅga*)?

At the time of first setting out on the path, faith is predominant; however, once one has entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), the factors of enlightenment and the path are established. At that time, the power and function of faith are weak and inferior; therefore, it is not included among the factors of enlightenment or the path.

For what reason are joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) established among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), yet not also established among the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)?
Because they are particularly conducive to enlightenment, whereas they are not conducive to the path.
What is conformity with awakening?

Furthermore, within the path of cultivation, one cultivates nine grades of superior awakening in each stage; as one repeatedly awakens to the truths in this manner, so too does one give rise to superior joy, and through the arising of that superior joy, one further comes to delight in contemplating the truths.

Just as a person who digs the earth and discovers treasure experiences joy, and because of that joy, delights in digging further, so too does joy increase the power that is conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya*).

It is only by means of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), which brings rest to all activities, and by means of equanimity (*upekṣā*), which renders the mind even, that one is able to discern objects with precise investigation; therefore, tranquility and equanimity are established among the factors of awakening.
Why are these three not in accord with the Path?
The meaning of the Noble Path is swift movement; these [three] slightly contradict such swift movement, as they all enable the mind to abide in tranquility.

For what reason are *vitarka* (applied thought) and *śīla* (ethical discipline) established as factors of the Path (*mārga*), yet not likewise established among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Because they are exclusively conducive to the Path and not conducive to enlightenment.
In what way are they conducive to the Path?
Furthermore, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), *vitarka* (investigation) urges the right view to swiftly observe the objects of the eight truths—both superior and inferior;

and *śīla* (ethical discipline) serves as the hub that completes the wheel of the path of seeing, enabling it to revolve swiftly through the truths. Therefore, both *vitarka* and *śīla* are established as factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
Furthermore, in what way does this [vitarka] not accord with *bodha* (awakening)?
First, vitarka functions without tranquility regarding the truths (*satya*), because its characteristic is the seeking of the principles of the Noble Truths.

Awakening, however, functions with tranquility once the truths have been seen; therefore, vitarka is somewhat contrary to awakening. Awakening is associated [with mental factors], possesses an object of cognition (*ālambana*), and has a mode of activity (*ākāra*) based upon that object.
The precepts are the opposite of this; therefore, they are not established among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
"Path" (*mārga*) is defined as that which leads universally, and thus it cannot be used as an analogy here.
For what reason are the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) not included within the factors of enlightenment?
The *Vibhajyavādins* accept that these are subsumed within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*); therefore, their school establishes forty-one factors of enlightenment.

As for my own position, I maintain that they are subsumed within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, yet are not established as separate factors of enlightenment because all factors of enlightenment can be practiced and are desired by both householders and renunciants alike; whereas the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are practiced and desired only by renunciants. Since householders may desire them but certainly do not practice them, they are not established separately.
Other masters say: If it is accepted that the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are, in their entirety, non-attachment (*alobha*), as has already been explained above;

and if it is accepted that the essence of the fourth lineage is diligence (*vīrya*), then there is no need for laborious questioning or objection regarding its inclusion among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
For what reason are the *avetyaprasādas* (clear realizations) not included among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*)?

In reality, they are indeed included within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth; yet they are not established as separate factors of enlightenment because the meaning of "progressive cultivation" predominates for the factors of enlightenment, such that one must practice them repeatedly before being able to realize *bodhi*.

The four kinds of clear realizations, however, emphasize the meaning of "attainment," as they are acquired—either gradually or instantaneously—at the time of seeing the Noble Truths. For this reason, the clear realizations are not subsumed under the factors of enlightenment.
Other masters say:
These are precisely faith and ethical discipline (*śīla*), which, as appropriate, are also subsumed within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).

16. Chapter Sixteen: Distinguishing the Noble Ones, Part Sixteen. When cultivating the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), one necessarily attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*). How many types of this are there, and in which stages are they attained?
What kind of phenomena constitute these entities? Are they contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
The verse says:
There are four kinds of verified purity (*avetyaprasāda*), namely: those regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts.
Upon seeing the three [truths], one attains the dharma-precepts; upon seeing the path, one also attains those of the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
"Dharma" refers to the entirety of the three truths and the paths of the Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Faith and precepts constitute their essence; all four are exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
The treatise states:

The Sūtra teaches that there are four types of verified purity (*avetyaprasāda*): first, verified purity regarding the Buddha; second, verified purity regarding the Dharma; third, verified purity regarding the Saṃgha; and fourth, verified purity regarding the noble precepts.

Furthermore, when one perceives the three truths during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), for each truth one attains only the verified confidence in the Dharma and the precepts (*dharma-śīla-prasāda*). Upon perceiving the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), one additionally attains verified confidence in the Buddha and the Sangha; that is to say, when perceiving the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), one attains the precepts beloved by the noble ones (*āryakānta-śīla*) as well as verified confidence in the Dharma.

Regarding which phenomena and in what manner does one attain the purification of faith in the Dharma? It means that by realizing within the Truth of Suffering alone that there is only the Dharma and no real sentient beings, one gives rise to decisive conviction.

Following this sequence, when seeing the Truth of Origination, one likewise attains the two purifications of faith as before, realizing that only the phenomena of origination can serve as the cause of suffering and that there is no internal agent (puruṣa), thereby giving rise to decisive conviction. Immediately thereafter, when seeing the Truth of Cessation, one likewise attains the two purifications of faith as before, realizing that only the phenomenon of cessation is true Nirvana and is truly worthy of pursuit, thereby giving rise to decisive conviction. Subsequently, when seeing the Truth of the Path, one simultaneously attains the two purifications of faith regarding the Buddha and the Saṅgha: one attains the purification of faith in the Buddha through the various dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) within the Buddha’s continuum; and one attains the purification of faith in the Saṅgha through the dharmas of both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training within the Saṅgha’s continuum.

The inclusion of the word "also" is intended to show that at the time of seeing the Truth of the Path, one also attains noble ethical discipline (*ārya-śīla*) and verified confidence in the Dharma (*dharma-prasāda*), realizing that the path alone is the cause for realizing cessation and is truly worthy of pursuit, thereby giving rise to resolute faith.

However, the dharmas that are objects of faith are briefly of two kinds: specific and general. The general category encompasses all four truths; the specific category comprises only three truths in their entirety.

Regarding the paths of the Bodhisattva and the Pratyekabuddha: the path of the Bodhisattva consists solely of dharmas of those still in training (*śaikṣa*), whereas the path of the Pratyekabuddha encompasses both those in training and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

If untainted faith arises by taking individual dharmas as its object, it is called "unmixed faith in the Dharma" (*dharme 'vetyaprasāda*); if untainted faith takes both the Buddha and the Saṃgha as its object, it is called "mixed faith in the Dharma. Therefore, when one perceives the three Truths, one attains only two types [of faith], whereas at the time of perceiving the Truth of the Path, one fully attains all four.
At the stage of seeing the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya), does one obtain the three kinds of verified confidence (avetyaprasāda) in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha as they manifest?
Not all are obtained as manifest; for at the time of seeing the Truth of the Path, what manifests is the general mental engagement with all the Truths of the Path.

It should be understood that in the present there is only a single dharma as the object of the clear confidence (*śraddhā-prasāda*), which takes various factors as its condition. By the power of this, one cultivates and attains multiple moments of faith in the future.

Among these, some take the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha individually as their objects, while others take two or three of the Jewels collectively. Those that take them individually are called the three types of clear confidence; those that take them collectively are subsumed under the clear confidence in the Dharma.
Because one cultivates eight knowledges at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), one also acquires two types [of restraint]:

the restraint of the Dharma and the restraint of the truths regarding the three truths. During the three moments beginning with the dharma-patience of the path (*mārgadharmakṣānti*), one cultivates in the future only the four types of the path-truth; although there are four names due to the distinctions among the objects of faith, it should be understood that in actual substance there are only two types.

That is to say, the three kinds of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*) regarding the Buddha and so forth have faith as their essence, while the verified confidence regarding noble ethical discipline has ethical discipline as its essence; therefore, there are only two [distinct entities].
If the sevenfold ethical discipline were in reality only one thing, how could there be eleven real entities among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?

There should be only ten types, or perhaps sixteen or more, because within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), the two karmas of body and speech are said to have distinctions and differences in their characteristics.
Although right livelihood (*samyagājīva*) is mentioned separately, it has no distinct essence or characteristic apart from the karmas of body and speech.
Based on their distinct characteristics, it was stated among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) that there are eleven actual entities (*vastu*).
Although the bodily and vocal actions are each manifold, they are established as one each because their types are identical, just like the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

The first three forms of verified purity consist of wisdom and faith; because they do not mix their objects but remain distinct according to their respective focal points, although there are many varieties, they are each established as one because they belong to the same category. This [case] should be understood in the same way.

Now, within the context of the "purity through realization" (avetyaprasāda), these are established as a single category because they depend upon the noble ethical discipline (ārya-śīla) associated with bodily and vocal actions, and because the sūtras likewise describe them collectively as being "without deficiency" (anupahata), "without breach" (acchidra), and so forth.

The classification of bodily and vocal karma follows two categories; since the noble precepts (ārya-śīla) are established as one due to their commonality, there is no fault of contradiction between the two and the one.
Based on what meaning is the name "clear realization" (*avetyaprasāda*) established?

Because one realizes the principle of the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, it is called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*); because one possesses correct faith in the Triple Gem and sublime ethical discipline, these together are called "purity" (*śuddhi*). Since this purity is attained through realization, it is designated by the term "realization-purity" (*avetyaprasāda*).

Right faith is subsumed under the characteristic of mental purity and may thus be called "pure"; however, since ethical discipline (*śīla*) is not subsumed under the characteristic of purity, how could it be established as having the name "pure"?
These four are all subsumed under the characteristic of purity because they are free from the defilement of lack of faith and the defilement of broken precepts.
Furthermore, because these four are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and are untainted by being free from defilement (*vimala-anāsrava*), they are designated by the name "pure" (*śuddha*).
For what reason is their sequence as it is?

Because the other three take the Buddha as their root, and because the Buddha possesses the functional capacity for correct teaching, the "pure confidence in the Buddha" (*buddha-prasāda*) is established at the very beginning.
The faculty of correct speech is established as the second purification of conviction (*avetyaprasāda*) because it arises from the realization of the Dharma;
the Sangha of the Noble Ones is established as the third purification of conviction because they alone constitute the realized treasury of the Dharma;
and the purification of conviction regarding noble ethical discipline is placed last because it is the basis upon which the realization of the Dharma-treasury depends.
Some say: The Buddha is the teacher who correctly expounds the Dharma; for this reason, the purity of conviction in the Buddha (buddha-saddhānusāra) is established first.
What does the Buddha teach?
The extinction of craving is nirvana; therefore, the second is established as the verified confidence in the Dharma.
For whom is the teaching intended?
It is for the Saṅgha of those progressing toward the fruits; therefore, the third is established as the verified confidence in the Saṅgha.
The Saṃgha is established by relying on the noble precepts; therefore, the fourth [refuge] is established as the purification of confidence in the precepts (śīla-prasāda). Some say:
these four are like a guide, a road, traveling companions, and the vehicle one rides; thus, the sequence of these four is as it is taught.
The Sūtra states:
"Those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) accomplish eight factors, while those in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa) fully accomplish ten.
Since those in the stage of training also achieve right liberation (samyag-vimukti) and right knowledge (samyag-jñāna), for what reason are these not established as factors (aṅga) in that [stage]?
What constitutes the essence of right liberation and right knowledge?
The verse says:
Because those in training still possess remaining fetters, they lack the factor of right liberation-knowledge.
Liberation is both conditioned and unconditioned; it refers to the destruction of the fetters and the destruction of delusion.
The conditioned factors of one beyond training are the two aggregates of liberation.
Right knowledge is as explained for enlightenment; it refers to the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
The Commentary states:
Because within the stage of training (śaikṣa) there still remain bonds that have not been liberated, there is no factor of liberation (vimukti-aṅga).

One cannot be called "liberated" while separated from even a few bonds; nor can the knowledge of liberation (vimukti-jñāna) be established in the absence of the essence of liberation. Therefore, these two factors are not established for one in the stage of training.

This means that the names of these factors are established based on their predominant auxiliary functions. Since those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) still possess remaining fetters, although they have liberation, it lacks the predominant auxiliary function; because they lack predominant liberation, their predominant wisdom is likewise absent. Therefore, these two factors do not exist in the stage of training.

Because those beyond training (aśaikṣa) have already been liberated from all fetters, two types of knowledge arise based on internal liberation; thus, there is a logical basis for establishing these as "limbs" due to their superior auxiliary function. Since this is not the case for those still in training (śaikṣa), they possess only eight [limbs].
The essence of liberation is twofold, namely conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Conditioned liberation has resolute confidence (*adhimukti*) as its essence; unconditioned liberation has the extinction of afflictions (*kleśa-nirodha*) as its essence.
Furthermore, it was previously stated that there are those who speak of the "learner" (śaikṣa) and the "one beyond learning" (aśaikṣa):
one is designated as a learner based on the ten bodies of the noble ones (ārya),
while the designation "beyond learning" is established based on the eighth noble stage.

Only within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) can the liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-vimukti*) be established as a factor of liberation (*vimukti-aṅga*), because the unconditioned cessation of afflictions (*kleśa-nirodha-asamskṛta*) lacks the functional utility of such factors.
Furthermore, there are two types of liberation included among these factors, distinguished by being "timely" (*sāmayikī*) or "untimely" (*asāmayikī*).
Some say: because there is a distinction between wisdom (*prajñā*) and mind (*citta*), one should know that these two constitute the aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*).
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Śrīlāta) intends to say the following:
It is not merely through resolute conviction that this aggregate receives its name. If so, what is it?
It is the power of true knowledge (*jñāna*) that can forever eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion; thus, the mind’s freedom from defilement is called the aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*).
What serves as proof?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"What is the most supreme purity of liberation?"

This refers to the mind being liberated from the defilement of greed, and liberated from the defilements of hatred and delusion; for the sake of fulfilling the aggregate of liberation that is not yet fulfilled, and for the sake of maintaining that which is already fulfilled, one cultivates desire, effort, and so forth.
What does this prove?
If the aggregate of liberation consisted solely of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), the Sūtra should not have stated:
"The mind is liberated from the defilement of greed, and liberated from the defilements of hatred and delusion," and so forth, up to the detailed exposition regarding the aggregate of liberation.
From this it is proven that the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*) is the mind itself when free from defilement, and not merely resolute confidence (*adhimukti*).
This does not constitute a valid proof, for the Sūtra also asks:
"What is called the most excellent purification of the mind?"

That is to say, having become detached from all sensual desires and unwholesome states, up to and including abiding in the fourth dhyāna, one cultivates desire, effort, and so forth, in order to fulfill the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*) that is not yet fulfilled, and to maintain that which is already fulfilled.
It is not that the mind’s freedom from defilement is itself termed meditative concentration (*samādhi*); this has already been established at length in the section on distinctions.

Just as various meditative concentrations arise and reach fulfillment through the functional power of diverse practices such as aspiration and so forth, the fulfillment of meditative concentration is called the purification of the mind. This is because meditative concentration causes the mind to be free from turbidity; it is not that the mind’s freedom from defilement is itself termed meditative concentration.

In this way, through the power of desire and so forth, the aggregate of liberation (vimukti-skandha) is brought to fulfillment and arises; the fulfillment of liberation is called "liberation of mind" (ceto-vimukti), because liberation causes the mind to be free from defilement. It is not that the mere absence of stains in the mind is itself termed liberation.
Therefore, what I have established does not contradict the sūtras.
Furthermore, just as a false resolve associated with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) is called "false liberation," yet one cannot say that this is simply the mind defiled by that overweening pride;
likewise, a right resolve dissociated from such pride is called "right liberation," yet one cannot say that this is simply the pure mind obtained through the abandonment of pride.

Furthermore, if it were the case here that the very mind free from defilement is called the aggregate of liberation (vimukti-skandha) and there is no separate liberation, then the Sūtra should not have previously stated that the purification of the mind is supreme; for there is no difference between the meanings of "purification" (viśuddhi) and "freedom from defilement" (vimala).

Furthermore, regarding this sūtra’s mention of the "aggregate of liberation" (vimukti-skandha), in reality it is not merely resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) alone; rather, the intention is to refer to resolute conviction together with its associated dharmas (samprayukta-dharma) collectively as the aggregate of liberation.
Therefore, my position that what they describe as the "aggregate of liberation" (vimukti-skandha) is not merely adhimokṣa (resolute confidence) does not contradict me.
Consequently, the principle that the essence of the two aggregates of liberation is indeed adhimokṣa is fully established.
Thus has been explained the essence of right liberation.
As for the essence of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), it refers to the manifestation of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
As previously stated regarding awakening (*bodhi*), it is the exhaustion of outflows and non-arising; what was previously termed "awakening" is here termed "right knowledge."
Regarding what is called "the mind-liberation of one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa-citta-vimukti*), at which stage is the mind truly liberated?
Is it in the future, the present, or the past?
The verse says:
"When the mind of one beyond training arises, it is precisely liberated from its obstructions.
The Commentary says:
As stated in the treatise, at the moment the initial mind of one beyond training is about to arise in the future, it is liberated from its obstructions.

Furthermore, one should reflect upon this passage from the *Mūla-śāstra*: the use of the term "future" would be redundant, as the meaning is already evident by the use of the term "at the time of arising.
This objection is not valid, because [the terms] are employed in accordance with the specific question being answered.
This means that the previous questioner asked at which time the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) attains liberation; therefore, the present answer states it occurs in the future.
Fearing that the questioner might think this refers to all things in the future, [the author] further specifies that it occurs "at the moment of arising."

Alternatively, one might simply say "liberation at the time of arising. However, some may claim that "the time of arising" refers to the present; to preclude this, it is specified as "future arising," because the present is what has already arisen and is therefore not the "time of arising."
If the designation "liberation" is established based on the continuum (*saṃtāna*), then all future [moments] would be called "perfect liberation.
If, however, the designation "liberation" is established based on the functioning of the momentary state (*kṣaṇa*), then only at the time of arising is it called "perfect liberation."
To specifically clarify these two meanings, the phrase "at the time of future arising" is stated.
Since all redundant expressions must necessarily reveal a specific meaning, one ought logically to investigate this; there is no room for denial.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:
"The phrasing is already sufficient for the meaning, yet further words are spoken;
it is not that there is phrasing without meaning—one should reflect and seek the distinct significance."

Although at this stage all the aggregates (*skandha*) attain liberation, it is only the mind (*citta*) that is mentioned; yet, this cannot be said to be a deficiency or an error, because mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth follow the mind, because among the defiled and pure phenomena the mind is primary, and because even though there is no self (*ātman*), one may metaphorically speak of "one who is bound" or "one who is liberated" with respect to the mind.
If the superior meaning has already been explained, the remaining meanings are implied.
Alternatively, within this context, just as when an example is cited, one should contemplate the rest by analogy through the citation of a single mental factor.

Although all minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) are also liberated from obstacles at the moment of their arising, the treatise speaks only of the liberation occurring when the first mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) arises; this is because it refers to liberation based on the realization of abandonment without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

Furthermore, because this refers exclusively to pure liberation (*vimukti*), there are cases here where the mind is liberated by its own nature (*svabhāva-vimukta*) but not liberated through its continuity (*saṃtāna-vimukta*). One should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the mundane (*laukika*) mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the untainted mind of one beyond training, and the remaining mundane minds; these should be understood as the distinctions between the four permutations in their respective order.

Although this passage mentions the moment of actual arising, in reality all [roots] in the future attain liberation, because they share the same nature as the obstacles to arising that the moment of actual arising possesses.
By the power of this, the mundane wholesome roots cultivated in the future also attain liberation, for they are able to arise based upon that purified continuum.
To further clarify that the first mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-citta*) is liberated from its obstructions at the moment it arises in the future, the treatise states again:

"When the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) has already ceased and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) has already arisen, at that time the mind of one beyond training is said to be liberated from its obstructions."

The path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*) refers to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) together with its associated mental factors. It is designated by the name of the present while it is in the state of approaching the past, because the designation "past" is subsequently applied to it. The term "having entered cessation" indicates that which is currently in the process of ceasing, for it must immediately enter the state of having already ceased.

The path of liberation refers to the initial *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion) together with its associated mental factors (*jñānaparivāra*). It is designated by the name "present" when it stands at the threshold of the present state; this is because the subsequent [moments] are then provisionally established as being "present. Furthermore, that which is "about to arise" is indicated as being "in the process of arising," because immediately thereafter it necessarily enters the state of having already arisen.

Regarding the phrase "at that time," it refers to the moment when [the mind] is in the process of ceasing and arising; the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) arises simultaneously with the first knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).

As for "liberation from obstructions," this does not refer solely to the obstruction of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa), because the karma that brings about rebirth in the form and formless realms is also an obstruction liberated at that very time.
This karma also obstructs the attainment of arhatship; for this reason, the great masters of old all said:
"Karma constitutes an extreme obstacle to the attainment of the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*)."
By providing this explanation of what was stated in the *Mūlaśāstra*, the meaning of "liberation of mind" (*cittavimukti*) as taught in the Sūtras has already been explained.
At which stage does the Path cause the abandonment of the obstacles to arising?
The verse says:
The Path exists only at the stage of being currently ceasing, and it is able to cause those obstacles to be severed.
The commentary states:

The word "only" is used to indicate that it is precisely at the stage of current cessation—not at any other—that this occurs. This is like the liberation simultaneous with the arising [of the Path] and the liberation simultaneous with the unarisen [Path]; it is not the case that both the already-ceased and the currently-ceasing [stages] cause the obstacles to be severed.
How can it be known that it is specifically at the stage of ceasing (*nirodha*) that the path is able to sever the hindrances, rather than at other stages?
This is because it is said that when the path is in the process of arising (*utpāda*), it is precisely then that one is liberated from the hindrances.

At the stage when the path has not yet arisen, liberation has not been attained; at the stage when the path has already arisen, liberation has already been attained. In neither of these cases can the designation "present liberation" (*sammukhībhūta-vimukti*) be established.
If the path were unable to sever the obstructions at the very moment it is ceasing, how could it be designated as "perfectly liberated" during the stage of its arising?
Therefore, the path is able to sever the obstructions precisely when it is ceasing; its function of severing is certainly non-existent in the preceding or succeeding stages.
How can that which has not yet arisen also be called "liberated"?
Because it is identical to that which is currently arising in its obstruction to birth.
This is as we see in the world: when a waterway is opened, both the near and distant waters are said to be "freed from obstructions."

Since one has thus seen that the path capable of severing the afflictions has already arisen within one’s continuum, it should likewise be said that both the proximate mind and the distant mind attain liberation.

Alternatively, just as the initial arising of the mind of an Arhat (aśaikṣa) is designated "presently liberated" because it has attained the state of being currently arising, so too can such future cultivated untainted minds and the like attain this designation.
Even those phenomena that are destined never to arise can still be said to have "rightly attained liberation," let alone those that are yet to arise.
The term "rightly liberated" used here indicates that the mind which has already been liberated is now rightly attaining liberation.
Is what has been stated here not contradictory?

The statement "already liberated" refers to liberation by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vimukti*), whereas the current statement "liberated" refers to liberation from hindrances (*āvaraṇa-vimukti*). Since the respective points of reference differ, how could there be any contradiction in meaning?

The statement "already liberated" refers to liberation as it originally exists, while the statement "liberated now" is spoken in reference to one currently abiding in the course of worldly existence; thus, there is no contradiction between these expressions.
Are all those who traverse the world liberated? No;
rather, it is those who diligently destroy the obstacles to birth.
Other masters say:
At the moment of perfect liberation, it is also designated as "the mind already liberated," because its nature has already abandoned the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

This must logically be so, because the path of liberation proceeds in dependence upon a mental continuum free from afflictions; having emerged from obstructions, it is called "already liberated," and being currently active in the world, it is called "presently liberated. Thus, what is stated here does not contradict one another.
The Sūtra states:
"The mind is now liberated from greed.
What is the meaning of this so-called "liberation"?
Is it that the mind is made to separate from greed, or is it that the nature of greed is no longer directed toward the mind?
As for the designation "mind with greed," is it because of association (*samprayoga*), because of being an object-condition (*ālambana*), or because of the persistence of acquisition (*prāpti*)?
If [liberation] were due to association, then only a defiled mind could be said to attain liberation; this would contradict your own school’s doctrine that a mind free from greed attains liberation.

Furthermore, if this dharma were associated with that [greed], there would necessarily be no possibility of making this [mind] separate from that [greed], and thus the mind would never be liberated from greed.

If [liberation] were due to the object of perception (*ālambana*), then even a defiled mind should attain liberation; it would be logically untenable to say that a mind associated with greed (*rāga*) is called "liberated.

Furthermore, if the nature of that greed takes this mind as its object, there would be no moment when it does not so take it, nor any possibility of it taking another object; how, then, could one say that the mind is liberated from that greed?

If it were because of being "concomitant" (*anugata*), then the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) should also be called "possessing greed," since it arises based on a continuum that has been made concomitant by the acquisition of greed.
The *Nyāyānusāra* masters state:
"Only the mind free from greed is now liberated."
What are the characteristics of the two types of mental states known as "with greed" and "free from greed"?

It is said that if a mind is associated with greed, it is called a mind with greed; if it is not associated [with greed] and does not act as a homogeneous cause for greed, it is called a mind free from greed.
The same applies to the presence of delusion (*moha*) and the departure from delusion.
Since it has been stated that the mind is liberated through the departure from greed (*rāga*), liberation is established as being exclusively the non-defiled mind (*akliṣṭa-citta*).

Furthermore, there are four types of non-defiled minds: within the contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are divided into the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); and within the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they are divided into those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the adept (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding the statement that "the mind free from craving is now liberated," there are two types of "now liberated": namely, the various contaminated minds (*sāsrava-citta*) that proceed through the continuum of worldly existence all possess liberation of the continuum; furthermore, it is also accepted that those attained through application (*prayoga-labdha*) likewise possess liberation of the proceeding [mind].

All untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) possess the liberation of active engagement (*vartamāna-vimukti*). It is also accepted that those comprised within the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) additionally possess the liberation of continuity (*prabandha-vimukti*).
As for those who say:
"If a mind enters into, becomes purified, abides in, and attains liberation," one should know that this refers to the discussion of the liberation of active engagement.
Regarding those who say that the mind is "rightly and well-liberated," one should understand that this explains liberation of the continuum (*saṃtāna-vimukti*).

Regarding those who say that the fruit of Arhatship consists of the attainment of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*), such as these are called the fulfillment of right liberation; one should understand that this explains liberation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vimukti*). Because the Arhat fulfills both types of liberation, it is said that his mind is "rightly and well-liberated."
It is said that all noble paths are termed the "right nature of liberation," and by depending upon them, one is called "rightly liberated.
Since all Arhats have realized this without deficiency, it is said that their minds are rightly and well-liberated.

Within these two types of liberation thus explained, no defiled mind can possibly exist; therefore, such a state cannot be called "attaining liberation. Regarding those who are externally free from defilement, both can be said to possess:

namely, right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*) and wrong liberation (*mithyā-vimukti*). However, it cannot be said that their minds are "rightly liberated," because the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*) is absent within their bodies.
Nor can it be said that the mind is not liberated, because it is fully endowed with detachment from the defilements of its own respective stage.

Furthermore, although one may grant that such a state exists as a "correct liberation," it is not designated as the "mind's correct liberation" because it does not proceed in accordance with reality as it does for the Noble Ones.
This means that when the noble ones correctly analyze the fetters of the five categories and sever them gradually, they are said to have "rightly liberated minds.

Those external worldlings who are free from defilement do not correctly analyze the fetters of the five categories; rather, they sever them all at once through the mundane path. Therefore, although they have severed the fetters, they cannot be said to have "rightly liberated minds."
Nevertheless, it is designated as "right liberation" because it truly functions to sever all false fetters.
As the Blessed One said:
"Because the mind is defiled by afflictions such as craving, one does not attain liberation."
From this it is proven that because greed and other afflictions have been severed, a non-defiled mind is called "attained liberation.
This is like when turbid water has subsided and water arises again; being free from turbidity and clear, it is called "pure water."

Thus, when the mind that functions in conjunction with defilements ceases, and the various minds of a pure continuum arise in its place, they are born free from bondage and are therefore called "liberated.

For one who has not yet abandoned defilement, the non-defiled mind arises within a body still possessed of defilement; it evolves as if undergoing transformation, like milk mixed with blood, and is thus not called liberated.

Although the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) are indeed untainted (anāsrava), because their mental continuity is not yet purified, they do not—unlike the minds of those beyond training (aśaikṣa)—bear the name "liberation through the continuity" (saṃtānavimukti).

Just as a dim consciousness arises based on diseased eyes, whereas when the eyes are free from disease, a clear and pure consciousness is manifested—yet there is no transference of an inherent nature of eye-consciousness—so too, although a virtuous and pure consciousness arises based upon a continuum impaired by afflictions, it functions without clarity or sharpness due to the power of those afflictions; when one is separated from afflictions, consciousness becomes clear and sharp.
Because that continuum arises in conformity with the afflictions, the mind that serves as its basis is not called "liberated";
however, if that continuum arises in opposition to the afflictions, this mind that serves as its basis is then called "liberated."

Therefore, within the continuum of the body of one who has abandoned defilement, the continuum upon which the non-defiled mind relies was previously impaired by greed and other afflictions; because it is now free from greed and the like, it is also called "present liberation."
Since a mind associated with greed and the like can never be liberated from greed and the like, the masters who rely on correct reasoning state:
"Only a mind free from greed attains liberation now."
The Vibhajyavādins speak thus:
"It is only the mind of greed that now attains liberation.
It is like a stained vessel from which the stain has later been removed, becoming like rock crystal; due to the difference in the color of the substrate, a different color arises."
In this way, when a pure mind is defiled by greed and so forth, it is said to be "possessing greed" and the like, though it later becomes liberated again.
The Noble Teachings also state that the nature of the mind is inherently pure, yet at times it is defiled by adventitious afflictions.
This is not reasonable, because it is unreasonable for a momentary phenomenon to be like the removal of dirt from a vessel.
