Although cessation is ever-present, it does not attain its nature [as an object]; only when that cessation is attained does this wisdom arise. It is only by virtue of the arising of cessation that it is designated as "possessing cessation," and it is at the stage of possessing cessation that this wisdom is produced.
Alternatively, the term "non-arising" may be derived from its attainment through cessation; just as the attainment of nirvāṇa is also called "nirvāṇa," as the Sūtra says:
"Because one places nirvāṇa within the mind."

When that [attainment] is reached, this knowledge arises; because this knowledge relies upon non-arising (*anutpāda*), it is called "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*). Others raise this objection:

"If it is called 'knowledge of non-arising' because it relies upon non-arising, then the knowledge of non-arising would have a non-ultimate reality (*asatyadharma*) as its object. This would contradict and undermine your own tenet."

Untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) arises taking only the Four Noble Truths as its object; he raises this objection without careful consideration, for I have already stated above that such analytical knowledge (*vikalpa-jñāna*) arises only after one has emerged from meditative absorption.

Alternatively, this [knowledge] relies upon sound as its seventh [object], rather than being a seventh [object] by virtue of being a non-object, as is the case with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Or, it may be permitted that this knowledge obtains its object through the non-arising (*anutpāda*), and is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) because it is not a non-truth.

Regarding the mutual inclusion of these ten knowledges: conventional knowledge includes one whole and a portion of one; dharma-knowledge and inferential knowledge each include one whole and portions of seven; the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation each include one whole and portions of four; path-knowledge includes one whole and portions of five; knowledge of others' minds includes one whole and portions of four; and the knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising each include one whole and portions of six.
For what reason are the two types of knowledge established as ten?
The verse says:
By way of intrinsic nature and antidote, And by way of aspect, aspect, and object.
The preliminary application accomplishes the perfection of the cause; therefore, ten knowledges are established.
The treatise says:
"By means of seven conditions, two are established as ten."
First, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is established by virtue of its intrinsic nature, because it has conventional knowledge as its very essence.

Second, dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are established by virtue of their function as antidotes, because they are fully capable of acting as antidotes for the desire realm and the higher realms, respectively.
The knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination are established by way of three aspects, because there is no difference in the essential substance of the objects of these two knowledges.
The knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path are established by way of four aspects and their respective objects, because both the aspects and the objects of these two are distinct.
The knowledge of others' minds is established on account of its preparatory application (*prayoga*); it is not that this [knowledge] fails to know the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) of others.

Although one originally cultivates the preparatory application for the purpose of knowing another's mind, and at the time of its perfection also knows the mental factors, it is nevertheless designated by the name "knowledge of others' minds" based upon its preparatory application.
The preparatory application (*prayoga*) has already been fully analyzed above.
Knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is established because the six tasks have been accomplished, as it first arises within a body in which those tasks are completed.
Knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is established because the causes are perfected, as it arises with all noble paths (*āryamārga*) as its cause.

This means that there is knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) which arises not because it has the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) as its cause, and there is knowledge of non-arising which does not arise with the knowledge of exhaustion as its cause.

As stated above, since it was said that both the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are fully capable of counteracting the phenomena of the desire realm and the higher realms respectively, is there a portion [of these knowledges] that counteracts the higher [realms] and the desire realm?
The verse says:
The dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path, Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), Also remedies the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms;
However, the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) lacks the power to remedy those in the desire realm.
The Commentary states:

The dharma-knowledges (dharma-jñāna) regarding cessation and the path, which are subsumed under the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), are also capable of counteracting the afflictions of the higher realms to be abandoned through cultivation.

In relation to the dharmas of the desire realm, these dharma-knowledges of the four truths are fully capable of counteracting the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya); furthermore, these dharma-knowledges also serve as the sustaining counteragent (dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa).

Both the antidotes and the objects to be abandoned receive their full names [when they pertain to their own respective realms]; when viewed in relation to the higher realms, both are deficient and are thus called "partial.
For what reason do only the Dharma-knowledges of Cessation and the Path simultaneously counteract the higher realms, whereas those of Suffering and Origin do not?
This is because their objects of focus (*ālambana*), tranquility, and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*) are identical.

That is to say, the cessation (*nirodha*) of the desire realm and higher realms, as well as the paths that serve as their antidotes (*pratipakṣa-mārga*), have no distinction when compared to one another.

This is because all analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are both wholesome and eternal, and all noble paths (*ārya-mārga*) are capable of leading to renunciation. However, their objects of focus—the suffering and origin [truths]—of the desire realm and higher realms are not the same, due to differences in quantity, subtlety, coarseness, and level (higher or lower).

Furthermore, the knowledge of suffering and its origin takes as its object that which is to be reviled; it is impossible to feel revulsion for that [object] while being free from craving for this [subject]. Logically, when one feels revulsion toward a particular stage, one abandons the afflictions of that very stage.
If you were to allow that revulsion and freedom from craving are distinct, then craving and freedom from craving would be distinct, and freedom from craving and liberation would likewise be distinct.

If it is admitted that one can become detached from the greed of the form and formless realms without being weary of those realms, then the principle of practicing weariness to abandon greed would be undermined.
Furthermore, there is no fault in the two knowledges of cessation and the path not taking objects of weariness as their domain, nor in their taking lower stages as objects to counteract higher ones.

Furthermore, it is like the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and the aspiration for nirvāṇa. That is to say, while the contemplation of impurity takes the objects of the desire realm as its focus and can only cause the mind to feel revulsion toward the desire realm;
when the aspiration for nirvāṇa manifests, it can universally cause the mind to feel revulsion toward all three realms.

In this way, when the knowledge of the origin and suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya-jñāna*) arises taking desire as its object, it can only cause the mind to become detached from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

When the knowledge of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*) arises taking the phenomena of the desire realm as its object, it is universally able to cause the mind to become detached from the defilements of all three realms; therefore, it is maintained that the category of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path increases until one attains the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).

Based on this, the Great Sage has perfectly and skillfully understood that the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are established according to the principle of complete antidotes; while a small portion of the knowledge of phenomena possesses the capacity to act as an antidote for higher realms, the subsequent knowledge certainly lacks the capacity to act as an antidote for the desire realm.

Only when one's own realm has been fully accomplished can one simultaneously act for the sake of other realms; it is not the case that when the tasks of one's own category have been completed while those of others remain unaccomplished, there is a necessity for assistance. Therefore, there is no subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) that remedies the phenomena of the desire realm.

Is it not the case that when the sixteenth moment, the Knowledge of Subsequent Realization (*anvaya-jñāna*), arises, one could, by virtue of this momentum, counteract the afflictions of the desire realm?

However, at the time of severing the afflictions of the desire realm, the Knowledge of Subsequent Realization does not function; even if one were to grant that it were currently active, because it would be constrained by the obstacles of its own realm, it would certainly lack the power to assist in accomplishing the work of the Knowledge of Dharmas (*dharma-jñāna*). Therefore, the Knowledge of Subsequent Realization is incapable of counteracting the afflictions of the desire realm.
Among these ten knowledges, which possess which aspects?
The verse says:
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) possess all sixteen aspects.
Regarding these and other worldly [knowledges], there are four types of knowledge for each of the Four Truths;
the untainted knowledge of others' minds consists of only four, namely those that take the Path as their object.
Tainted [knowledge of others' minds] takes specific characteristics as its object; both [types] take only a single thing as their object.
The fourteen [aspects] of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, excluding emptiness and non-self.
The treatise says:

Each of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) possesses the sixteen aspects, such as impermanence, suffering, and so forth; these sixteen aspects will be explained in detail later.
Worldly knowledge (*loka-jñāna*) consists of this and more; it is able to take as its objects the specific (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) characteristics of all phenomena.

That is to say, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) may sometimes fully exercise the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), as occurs during the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*).

Some are incomplete, such as the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), the "repeated concentration" (*samādhi*), and the "conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization" (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*).

Others function with characteristics that are not those of the noble ones (*ārya*), such as the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), and loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The aspects (*ākāra*) of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) are thus infinite.
Each of the four knowledges regarding suffering and so forth possesses four aspects, each taking its own respective truth as its object.

Within the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) possesses only the four aspects that take the Path (*mārga*) as its object, as this is subsumed under a portion of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
If it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it grasps its own objects—the mind and mental factors—as they are self-characterized (*svalakṣaṇa*) objects.
Just as the object is characterized by its own marks, so too is the mode of activity (*ākāra*); therefore, this is not included among the aforementioned sixteen modes of activity.
Thus, these two types [of consciousness] at all times, within a single moment, take only a single object as their objective condition (*ālambana*).

That is to say, when taking the mind (*citta*) as an object, they do not take mental factors (*caitta*) as an object; when taking feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth as objects, they do not take perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth as objects.
If that is so, why did the Blessed One say:
"One knows the mind possessed of lust as it truly is"?
It is not that lust and the mind are apprehended simultaneously, just as a garment and its stain are not apprehended simultaneously.

Regarding the three pairs of mental characteristics, such as the mind possessed of greed and so forth, the distinctions among them have already been explained in the context of the liberation of the mind. The Vaibhāṣika masters state:
"A concentrated mind refers to a wholesome mind, because it does not scatter toward its object."
A distracted mind refers to a defiled mind, because it arises in association with distraction and agitation.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) maintains that this does not accord with the sūtra, for the sūtra asks:
"How is this mind inwardly collected?"
This refers to when the mind functions together with torpor and drowsiness, or when it is internally associated with calm abiding (*śamatha*) but lacks insight (*vipaśyanā*).
What is external distraction?

It refers to when the mind wanders through the objects of the five kinds of sensory pleasures, scattering and flowing along with them, or when it is internally associated with insight but lacks calm abiding.
The Westerner’s interpretation follows the sūtras, asserting that what is associated with sleep is called "collected" (*saṃkṣipta*), while other defiled states are called "distracted" (*vikṣipta*).

However, this would entail the fallacy that a mind associated with non-defiled sleep would be both collected and distracted, since they do not admit that a defiled mind associated with sleep is termed "distracted."
It is not understood that the intent of the sūtra has been arbitrarily praised or disparaged, for the meanings of these two sūtras are each distinct.
In this sūtra, it is stated that there exist minds characterized by greed and so forth, in order to make known the distinction between the categories of defilement and purity within the mind.

This refers to the teaching that there are minds with attachment and minds free from attachment, in order to correctly understand the principles distinguishing the dark and bright categories of all states of mind.
That sutra speaks of concentrated and distracted minds for the purpose of making known the obstacles to the cultivation of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); as that sutra says:
"Examine your own mind: let it not be too sunken, nor too excited; let it not be inwardly withdrawn, nor outwardly distracted."

That is to say, when that practitioner cultivates the bases of psychic power, they should personally examine the obstacles to the cultivation of the bases of psychic power: "This mind is indolent; this mind is agitated; this mind is drowsy and lethargic; this is a distracted flow induced by improper mental attention toward forms and so forth."
Since the intended meaning of these two sutras differs, one cannot cite that sutra to negate or explain the characteristics described in this sutra.

That sutra merely states that when practicing the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the mind becomes excessively distracted or withdrawn regarding internal and external objects, and thus one does not wish to discern the characteristics of the mind’s defilement or purity.

What is taught in this sutra contradicts that [previous position]. Although all defiled minds possess indolence and the like, in order to manifest the specific distinctions among the faults of various defilements, states such as *laya* (sinking) are established according to their degree of predominance; one should know that states such as *pragraha* (exertion) are established by reversing this principle.
Therefore, our school’s interpretation accords with the sūtras and also skillfully distinguishes the various distinct characteristics of the minds.
This digression is now concluded; we should now state the primary meaning.
How is it that the knowledge of others' minds possesses both an aspect (*ākāra*) and an object (*ālambana*), yet it is said not to observe its own object or aspect?
This is because [the knowledge of others' minds] does not observe the objects or the modes of apprehension (*ākāra*) of another's mind.

That is to say, one only knows that the other has a defiled mind or the like, but does not know the colors and so forth that color that mind, nor does one know the mode of apprehension by which that mind takes its object. Otherwise, the knowledge of others' minds would also have to take objects such as form (*rūpa*), and furthermore, it would incur the fallacy of being able to take itself as its own object.

The untainted knowledge of others' minds should take suffering and other [truths] as its objects; it would then also have to be admitted as being associated with emptiness and signlessness. Since this is not admitted, we know that it does not contemplate these two.

The various types of knowledge of others' minds possess a definitive characteristic: they can only take as their objective referent the real, individual self-characteristics of present, homogeneous mental states and mental factors within the mental continua of others that are bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or are not so bound.

The [knowledge of] emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is not associated with the signless (*animitta*), and it is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

It does not exist within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) or the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), nor is it excluded by anything else; thus, as appropriate, the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising may be present. Excluding the aspects of emptiness and selflessness, each possesses the remaining fourteen aspects.
Because it is contrary to the mental state that emerges from meditative absorption, there are no two modes of activity while within the absorption.
That is to say, after emerging from the two types of knowledge, one necessarily realizes for oneself: "Birth has been exhausted," and so forth.

The intended meaning here is that although the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are ultimate truths, they involve the conventional because [the expressions] "my births are exhausted" and so forth are conventional; whereas emptiness and non-self are ultimate truths and must therefore involve the ultimate.

Following this contemplation, one definitively realizes that emptiness is not-self; therefore, by means of these two knowledges, one becomes free from [the notions of] emptiness and non-self, thereby attaining the untainted (anāsrava).
Beyond these sixteen aspects, are there further modes of activity (ākāra) included therein?
The verse says:
The pure [attainments] do not exceed sixteen; others say they do, because there is a treatise [to that effect].
The commentary says:

The masters of the Abhidharma maintain that there is one class of teachers who say that there are no more than sixteen uncontaminated aspects (*anāsrava-ākāra*), because nothing else can be found apart from these. [Objection:

Is it not the case that some say the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) necessarily involve self-awareness, such as "my births are exhausted" and so forth?
This is not contradictory, for it has already been stated previously.

That is to say, it was previously explained that after the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*), these modes of activity (*ākāra*) are performed within conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and not within untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

This mode of activity (ākāra) proceeds by eliciting conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) through the power of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); the merit is attributed to the fundamental [knowledge], and thus it is said that the latter "comprehends" [the former].

Therefore, it is accepted that this knowledge is free from [the notions of] emptiness and non-self; rather, the force of the original intention causes these two knowledges to subsequently necessarily elicit [the realization] that "my births are exhausted," and so forth. It is not the case that by contemplating internally within this mode of activity, one causes this mode of activity to arise at a later time.

Although these aspects of our practice do not exist when observed internally, because we are not deluded regarding self-realized liberation, it is said that at this stage there must necessarily be the forceful influence of aspects such as "the birth of the self has been exhausted. Since these are induced by prior conventional aspects and can induce subsequent conventional aspects, one is free from the fourteen [categories of] inexhaustibility and non-arising.

If it is argued that this should be stated as "the absence of sixteen," this is unreasonable; for, with the exception of fourteen, the remaining [categories] being "exhausted" or "non-arising" is not universally established (*aprasiddha*).

That is to say, one speaks of "leaving aside fourteen" based on a hidden intention (*saṃdhāya-vacana*), considering the notion that "my births are exhausted" and so forth to be the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*); it is in order to exclude that view that one says there is "the absence of fourteen. Since the others are not universally established, how could they possibly be the object of such an exclusion?
If that is so, since there exists uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), it should transcend the sixteen aspects of the uncontaminated.

This is because all knowledge of others' minds takes the real, individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, whereas the aspects such as the Path (*mārga*) take the collective, general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as their object. Since these two are distinct, one must conclude that there definitely exist uncontaminated aspects separate from the sixteen.
Because it is not definitively asserted, the objection is invalid.

That is to say, our own tenet does not definitively assert that the aspect of the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) merely takes a collection as its object, for we do assert the existence of two applications of mindfulness: those of feeling (vedanā) and mind (citta).

Just as when one contemplates a single instance of sensation (*vedanā*) as impermanent, it is universally established that at the moment this knowledge arises, it takes a single real particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object by means of a universal mode of activity (*sāmānyalakṣaṇākāra*).
Likewise, why not admit that untainted knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*) likewise takes a single real particular as its object by means of a universal mode of activity?
This means that knowing another's mind as being the true path and so forth takes as its object the single reality characterized by being the path and so on.

If one were to claim that, just as in the case of the mindfulness of feelings and the mindfulness of mind, one should take all feelings and minds of the three times as a collective object with the aspect of impermanence and other common characteristics, then the untainted knowledge of others' minds would also take all untainted minds of others across the three times collectively as its object with the aspect of being the path and so forth. This would contradict one's own school’s tenet that the arising of the knowledge of others' minds takes only the present, single, real specific characteristic as its object.
This is also not the case, because the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) differ.

The preparatory practice for this knowledge consists in the desire to know the specific states—such as the presence of greed—in the present minds of others; the preparatory practice for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) such as impermanence consists in the general revulsion toward all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). Since there is a distinction in the power of these preceding preparatory practices, when they reach the stage of perfection, the former manifests as a general cognition of particulars. Therefore, there is no fault of violating the principle of analogy.

If it is argued that because impermanence is not the intrinsic nature of feeling itself, one should not regard feeling as impermanent by taking its real, singular self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as an object, how then can this be cited as an analogy for the knowledge of others' minds?
Then he would have to admit that feeling is not impermanent, and thus one should not cultivate the contemplation of impermanence regarding feeling.
Just as feeling and mind are distinct in essence, it is certainly impossible to contemplate feeling as being the mind.

Although one contemplates feeling as impermanent, there is no fault of a single entity possessing multiple natures, because the impermanent nature of that which experiences [feeling] is not distinct [from the feeling itself].
Just as benefit, harm, and so forth are not separate from the act of experiencing, the same applies to the remaining aspects and other phenomena.
If that were so, it would contradict the authoritative teaching (*āptāgama*), as it is said:
"One dwelling in the contemplation of the body with respect to the body should speak of it as 'dharma-knowledge' (*dharmajñāna*)," and so forth, at length.
Furthermore, it is said:
Regarding the contemplation of aging and death, it should be said that these consist of four knowledges;

there is no contradiction between them. Furthermore, what was stated initially does not mean that the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and so forth abide in the mindfulness of the body apart from the sixteen aspects; rather, when contemplating the body as the body, one contemplates it only as it truly is—as impermanent and so forth.

I have already previously granted that the characteristics of mutual association also take the single real specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object; therefore, what they have stated does not contradict my position.

Furthermore, the term "old age and death" refers collectively to the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*); observing these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent and so forth is subsumed under the four knowledges (*jñāna*). What contradiction could there be?
If that is so, as it is said:
"When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is: 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.
How can this be subsumed under the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent-knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) paths?"
This should be examined: when feeling is present, it cannot be cognized, because it does not take itself as its object.
Nor can it be said that past and future feelings are cognized, for past and future are not designated as times when pleasure is being felt.

However, the *Sūtra* states that when one experiences a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling. Therefore, we know that this statement has a specific underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).

To explain this intention, it is like the cases of "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) and "non-arising" (*anutpāda*): these mental aspects (*ākāra*) arise only at a later time after emerging from meditative absorption; thus, there are no untainted (*anāsrava*) mental aspects outside of the sixteen.
There is a class of teachers who say:
"There are [factors] that transcend the sixteen, because the *Mūla-śāstra* states so.
As the *Mūla-śāstra* says:
Is there a mind that is not bound [to any realm] which can discern phenomena bound to the desire realm?
It is said:

it can discern them—namely, as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, as non-self, as cause, as origin, as production, and as condition. There is such a possibility; there is such a fact, discerned as induced by correct reasoning.
This proof is not established, for it misunderstands the intent of the treatise.

The treatise demonstrates that the aspects of the unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) are manifold; among these, there are those that take the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) as their object. It is with reference to this possibility that the expressions "there is such a case" (*asti sthānam*) and "there is such a thing" (*asti vastv iti*) are stated, which demonstrate the absence of error. For this very reason, these expressions are not applied to the others.
That is to say, that treatise further states:
"Is there a mind abandoned through vision that can discern phenomena associated with the desire realm?
It replies:

It is able to discern [objects] as: "I" and "mine"; as "annihilation" or "permanence"; as "causeless" or "effortless"; as "denial" (apavāda); as "venerable," "superior," "excellent," or "supreme"; as "purifying," "liberating," or "leading to deliverance"; and as "delusion," "doubt," "hesitation," "attachment," "aversion," "pride," or "ignorance."
It is a discernment induced by what is not in accordance with reason; apart from this, there is no room for any other aspect (ākāra). For this reason, it is not said that "this possibility exists.
Because they all function in a perverted manner, it is not said that "this fact exists. Therefore, the aspects of purity do not exceed sixteen.
Neither principle nor scripture contradict this; it cannot be shaken.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 73. *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 74.
Composed by the Venerable Saṃghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Part 2: Chapter Seven, "Discrimination of Knowledge," Section Two. Regarding the statement that there are sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), are these merely differences in name, or do they also differ in substance?
What are the aspects (*ākāra*) of the act of attending and that which is attended to?
The verse says:
The aspects are truly sixteen; their essence is exclusively wisdom (*prajñā*).
"The capacity to practice has an object, and that which is practiced consists of all phenomena.
The commentary states:

Some say that although there are sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) by name, there are only seven in actual substance (*dravya*). When taking the Truth of Suffering as their object to counteract the four inversions, both name and substance are four. When taking the other three Truths as their objects, there are four names but only one substance.
According to this explanation, there are indeed sixteen aspects, because the characteristics of that which is to be remedied and that which is practiced are distinct.
Regarding the statement that the characteristics of the objects to be remedied are distinct: one cultivates the aspect of impermanence to remedy the view of permanence;
one cultivates the aspect of suffering to remedy the attachment to all conditioned phenomena as pleasurable; and one cultivates the aspect of emptiness to remedy the view of "mine."

The aspect of "mark" (*nimitta*) is cultivated to counteract the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*); the aspect of "non-self" (*anātman*) is cultivated to counteract the theory of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*);
the aspect of "origination" (*samudaya*) is cultivated to counteract the theory of a single cause such as Īśvara;

the aspect of "arising" (*utpāda*) is cultivated to counteract the theories of transformation as the cause or a permanent cause; and [the aspect of "condition"] is cultivated to counteract the theory that knowledge precedes and is able to produce [phenomena].
Therefore, one cultivates the aspect of "conditioning" (*pratyaya*) to counteract the view that liberation consists in returning to a sovereign lord;

one cultivates the aspect of "cessation" (*nirodha*) to demonstrate that the eternal extinction of the aggregates (*skandhas*) is nirvāṇa; one cultivates the aspect of "calmness" (*śānta*) to counteract the false view that liberation is the possession of a self-essence characterized by afflictions and suffering;
and one cultivates [the aspect of "sublime"] to counteract the attachment to nirvāṇa as if it were...
One cultivates the aspect of wondrous conduct (*praṇīta-gati*) to counteract the view that curses lead to total destruction, which is a debased doctrine;

one cultivates the aspect of detachment (*niḥsaraṇa-gati*) to counteract the attachment to the view that one can regress from liberation; one cultivates the aspect of the path (*mārga-gati*) to counteract the attachment to the view that there is no path to liberation;
and one cultivates [the aspect of truth] to counteract the view that asceticism is the true path and the false doctrine that slanders the true path.

Just as with the aspect of practice (*pratipatti*), one cultivates the aspect of practice to counteract the notion that the cycle of birth and death is naturally pure and that worldly detachment from defilements is the true path;

and one cultivates the aspect of transcendence (*nairyāṇika*) to counteract the failure to respect the true noble path due to having been deceived by a path that does not lead to permanent freedom from defilement.

Regarding the statement that there are distinctions among the characteristics of the objects of practice: the Noble Truth of Suffering has four characteristics: first, impermanence; second, suffering; third, emptiness; and fourth, non-self.

Because it possesses arising and ceasing, it is impermanent; because its nature is oppressive and it contradicts the mind of the Noble Ones, it is suffering; because it lacks a sovereign master, it is empty; and because it contradicts the characteristic of a self, it is non-self.
The noble truth of origination has four characteristics: first, cause; second, origination; third, production; and fourth, condition.

It is called "cause" because it is capable of producing phenomena; "origination" because it consists of many varieties; "production" because it constantly brings forth and generates; and "condition" because each acts as a distinct auxiliary support.
The Noble Truth of Cessation has four characteristics: first, cessation; second, tranquility; third, excellence; and fourth, detachment.
It is "cessation" because it brings rest to all suffering; it is "tranquility" because the three fires of the three conditioned marks have been extinguished.
Other masters say:
It is "tranquil" because all suffering has ceased, as it is said:
"O Bhikṣus!"
All conditioned phenomena are suffering; only nirvāṇa is supremely tranquil.
It is virtuous, eternal, and sublime.
Because it is forever liberated from all calamities and afflictions, and because it is utterly secure, it is detachment.
The Noble Truth of the Path has four characteristics: first, the path; second, suchness; third, practice; and fourth, departure.
It is called the "path" because it enables one to thoroughly seek the nature and characteristics of all phenomena until reaching liberation.
It is "suchness" (tathatā) because it is non-erroneous;
it is "practice" (pratipatti) because it proceeds toward reality as it is. Other masters say:
Because it is capable of leading [to liberation], it is called "practice" (*caryā*);
as it is said: "This path can reach purification.
Other views necessarily lack the principle of reaching purification, because this [path] leads exclusively [toward it].

Because they are definitely able to reach [their objects], they are called "outgoing" (*niḥsaraṇa*). Thus, since there is a distinction between the aspects of the objects to be countered and the objects traversed, there are actually sixteen [aspects].
Since these aspects have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence, one might ask: are not all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) likewise said to possess aspects?
In this way, how can it be said that wisdom (prajñā) possesses an aspect (ākāra) while that which is associated with wisdom does not?

It is only the mind and its mental factors associated with wisdom that are called "possessing aspects," because these minds and mental factors have the sense of being able to apprehend (grāhaka) within the various categories of their objects (ālambana).

If the designation "having an aspect" (sākāra) were applied solely based on wisdom, then the other mental states and mental factors associated with wisdom would also be designated as "having an aspect" because they share the same name. This would be analogous to how they are designated as "with-outflows" (sāsrava) because they are equal to outflows, in the sense that they share the same antidote as the substance of the outflows.

In this way, the remaining mental states and mental factors likewise engage their objects through their respective modes of activity (*ākāra*); this means they function simultaneously without temporal sequence.

Alternatively, it may be that among the mind and mental factors, there are many that possess modes of activity, such as when the faculty of "having already known" (*ājñendriya*) is collectively designated as possessing a mode of activity.
Alternatively, it may be said that there is also an object (ālambana) based on the immediately preceding [moment], just as there is a support (āśraya). Thus, there is no fault.

That is to say, just as the mind and mental factors are all called "having a support," the mental factors associated with the mental consciousness arise simultaneously with their supporting consciousness; while the support of the consciousness is exclusively that which has just ceased, one should know that the principle regarding the existence of the aspect (ākāra) is likewise.
What capacity does wisdom that has just ceased possess with respect to the present?
It possesses a capacity toward the present, just as the mind that has just ceased does.
If that were so, then acquisition (*prāpti*) and the like should also receive the designation of "acquisition" and so forth.
Even granting this, there is no contradiction; however, it is not what is being debated here.
In this context, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati), relying on another school's tenet, states as follows:
"The various ways in which the mind and mental factors apprehend their objects are all termed 'aspects' (ākāra)."
This principle is not necessarily so; one should consider what constitutes the distinct categories of objects apprehended by the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

If it is claimed that all such categories of objective characteristics are capable of being reflected [in consciousness], this principle is certainly untenable, because objects possess a multitude of distinct characteristics, such as being wholesome or eternal.
Alternatively, all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) may also be subsumed under "aspects" (*ākāra*), because material phenomena are also capable of resembling other aspects.

If it is argued that [aspects] must be able to grasp the distinct characteristics of objects, then the aspects of the five consciousnesses would be untenable, as they cannot grasp the distinct characteristics of objects; for it is only a conceptualizing consciousness (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*) that is capable of grasping the distinct characteristics of objects, such as blue being non-yellow.
However, this is not what is accepted; therefore, the reasoning is not established. Consequently, the interpretation of our own school is superior. That is to say:

it is only those various forms of wisdom (*prajñā*) that operate by discerning within the aspects of an object that are termed "aspects" (*ākāra*). Since wisdom and all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) possess an object of cognition (*sālambana*), they are all "active agents" (*saṃcarin*); yet, this name "active agent" should apply exclusively to wisdom, because it is the very substance of the aspect.
Since the other mental states and mental factors are not themselves aspects, how could they possibly be active agents?

If it is argued that the remaining [mental factors] are called "active" because they arise in association with the characteristics of activity, then wisdom (*prajñā*) and the others, being associated with feeling (*vedanā*), should likewise be called "feeling."
Although this statement exists, the principle is not so.

That is to say, "aspect" (*ākāra*) is a synonym for wisdom (*prajñā*), while "that which can act" (*śakya-ākāraṇa*) is simply another name for the apprehension of an object; the term "that which can act" does not specifically denote wisdom alone.
If you argue that because the essence of sensation (*vedanā*) and the others is not the aspect of activity (*ākāra*),

they should not be considered "active" (*pravṛtti*), then consider this objection: Just as wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to discern within its object and is thus permitted to be called "active," and since perception (*saṃjñā*) can grasp images and consciousness (*vijñāna*) can cognize within their respective objects, why should these not also be considered "active"?
Therefore, the term "agent" (kāraka) generally refers to that which apprehends an object; thus, feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] should also be considered agents.
The term "object" (karman) generally refers to all existent phenomena (*dharmas*), whether substantial or nominal, as all such things are objects of cognition.

Due to these three gates, there is a difference in the breadth and narrowness of their essence: wisdom (prajñā) functions as both the aspect that acts and that which is acted upon; other mental states and mental factors function only as the agent and the object; and all other existent phenomena function solely as the object.
In the verse, the term "all that exists" (*sarvabhava*) should be reduced by one [instance], because the meaning is already established by mentioning even a single type.
As the Blessed One said:
"All phenomena (*sarvadharma*) refer to the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*); only these exist."
Therefore, when it is said that "all phenomena (dharmas) are the objects of activity," it has already been stated that these objects of activity are exclusively existent phenomena (saddharma).

Alternatively, when it is said that "existent phenomena are the objects of activity," it has already been stated that these objects of activity are all phenomena (sarvadharma); for all phenomena that exist as designations (prajñaptisaddharma) do not exist apart from their bases, and they are also subsumed within the respective locations according to those bases.
To include all that is exhaustible, there is no fault in explaining them together.
Having already analyzed the distinctions in the aspects and characteristics of the ten knowledges, one should now analyze their nature, inclusion, basis, and support.
The verse says:
The mundane [knowledges] are three; the nine wholesome ones; Regarding the stages, the mundane ones are all;
The knowledge of others' minds is only four; The dharma-knowledge is six; the others are seven or nine.
As for the physical basis upon which they arise: The knowledge of others' minds relies on the desire or form realms.
Dharma-knowledge relies solely on the desire realm; the remaining eight pertain to all three realms.
The treatise says:
Regarding the inclusion of these ten knowledges within the three moral natures, conventional knowledge pertains to all three natures, while the other nine knowledges are exclusively wholesome.

Regarding the distinction of their bases: conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) relies on all levels from the desire realm up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra); the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) relies only on the four fundamental dhyānas, not on the preparatory stages (sāmantaka), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), or the formless attainments, because the objects of this knowledge are extremely subtle.

This means that because the power of the path on those stages is weak and inferior, one cannot discern the subtle, present minds and mental factors within the continuums of others; furthermore, this application does not exist in the formless realms.
Furthermore, because it is universal in nature, the other stages are not its basis; rather, the five supernormal powers (abhijñā) rely upon calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).

The knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) universally relies upon six stages: namely, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara), and the four fundamental dhyānas. It does not rely on the other preparatory stages (sāmantaka), because those are exclusively contaminated (sāsrava).
Nor does it rely on the formless realms, because its object is the desire realm.
The remaining seven knowledges rely on nine stages, namely the three lower formless realms and the six stages previously mentioned.

This is the general explanation; however, there are distinctions. Specifically, among these seven types of knowledge (jñāna) mentioned, subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) definitely arises based on nine stages (bhūmi).

As for the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, the path, exhaustion, and non-arising: if they are subsumed under dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), they take six stages as their basis; if they are subsumed under subsequent knowledge, they universally take all nine stages as their basis.

Regarding the distinction based on the body: the knowledge of others' minds can manifest in both the desire and form realms, but it does not depend on the formless realm, because that [knowledge] does not exist there itself.
As for why the knowledge of others' minds belonging to a lower stage does not arise: this is because the matter (rūpa) that accompanies this knowledge cannot possibly arise in those [higher stages].

Dharma-knowledge arises based solely on a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and not on those of the two higher realms, because all contaminated minds that enter into and emerge from this knowledge exist only within the desire realm.
Furthermore, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the support for the matter (*rūpa*) concomitant with dharma-knowledge are bound exclusively to the desire realm.

Furthermore, this [knowledge] can counteract the afflictions that lead to the violation of precepts; since the violation of precepts pertains only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and not to the higher realms, it is so designated.
The remaining eight knowledges, when manifesting, universally rely on bodies belonging to all three realms.
Having already analyzed their nature, stage, and body, one should now analyze their inclusion within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The verse says:
All knowledges are subsumed under the foundations of mindfulness; the knowledge of cessation is only the last one;
the knowledge of others' minds consists of the last three; the remaining eight knowledges pertain to all four.
The treatise says:

The knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) is subsumed within the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*); the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) is subsumed within the last three applications of mindfulness; and the remaining eight are all common to all four.
Thus, regarding these ten knowledges in relation to one another, for each one it should be stated how many knowledges constitute its object.
The verse says:
The various knowledges take one another as objects: Dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge each have nine;
Knowledge of suffering and knowledge of origin each have two; All four have ten; knowledge of cessation has none.
The treatise states:
Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) can take nine knowledges as its object, excluding subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Subsequent knowledge can take nine knowledges as its object, excluding dharma-knowledge.
The knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) can take nine knowledges as its object, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), because the latter is not subsumed under the category of the path.

Each of the two knowledges of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) and origination (*samudayajñāna*) can take two knowledges as their respective objects: namely, conventional knowledge and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

The conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*) all take ten knowledges as their objects.
The knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) does not take them as its objects, because it takes only analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its object.
In total, how many dharmas are the objects of these ten knowledges?
What wisdom takes how many phenomena as its objects?
The verse says:
There are ten objects in total, namely those of the three realms and the untainted.
The unconditioned each has two; the conventional has ten objects, the dharma-knowledge five;
the knowledge of types seven, and that of suffering and origin six; the knowledge of cessation has one object, and that of the path two;
the knowledge of others' minds has three; and the knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising each have nine.
The Commentary states:

The objects of the ten knowledges comprise ten categories of phenomena in total. That is to say, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are divided into eight types, because those bound to the three realms and the untainted conditioned phenomena each have both associated (*samprayukta*) and dissociated (*viprayukta*) aspects.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is divided into two types, distinguished as wholesome (*kuśala*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) takes ten dharmas collectively as its object.
Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) takes five as its object: namely, the two [types] of the desire realm, the two [types] of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), and the wholesome unconditioned.

Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) takes seven objects as its cognitive domain: namely, the six [knowledges] pertaining to the form realm, the formless realm, and the untainted path, as well as the wholesome unconditioned (kuśala-asaṃskṛta).
The knowledges of suffering and origination each take the six [objects] bound to the three realms.
The knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) takes one object as its cognitive domain: namely, the wholesome unconditioned.
The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) takes two as its objects, namely, the untainted path (anāsravamārga).
The knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) takes as its objects the associated dharmas of the three realms: desire, form, and the untainted.
The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) take as their objects the eight conditioned [dharmas] and the wholesome unconditioned (kuśalāsaṃskṛta).
Is there perhaps a single moment of wisdom that takes all phenomena as its object?
No, it is not so. But is it not the case that the wisdom of the contemplation of non-self knows that all phenomena are non-self?
This, too, cannot take all phenomena as its object.
What phenomena does it not take as its object?
What is the nature of this [consciousness]?
The verse says:
Conventional wisdom, excluding its own category, takes all phenomena as its general object;
it functions through the aspect of "non-self" and is produced solely by hearing and reflection.
The treatise states:

When one contemplates all phenomena as non-self by means of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), one still excludes those belonging to its own category; "its own category" refers to the factors that are its own essence, its associated factors, and its co-existent factors.
Why do [dharmas] not take their own substance as an object?
The Abhidharmikas establish this reason, stating:
"Because no dharma ever depends upon its own substance."
The meaning of this statement is to clarify that when phenomena arise, they depend upon the nature of the four conditions as appropriate; if any [condition] is lacking, the phenomenon does not arise.

That which is not lacking and thus allows for arising is established as the nature of a condition. Since there is no time when phenomena lack their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is ultimately no sense of "non-arising due to deficiency. How, then, could it be established as a "condition to be depended upon"?
If it is argued that their essence should be like space and so forth, such that they can be established as conditions because they are unobstructed—this reasoning is also incorrect.

This is because, in relation to the phenomena produced, the other-nature (parabhāva) of space and so forth is fully established, and thus the principle that a phenomenon serves as a condition for another is fully established.

Furthermore, this is illustrated by present-day analogies to show that the arising of various cognitions necessarily cannot take themselves as their own objects: namely, one cannot see the edge of a blade, the tip of a finger, or one's own shoulder, because they cannot respectively cut themselves, touch themselves, or carry themselves.

Furthermore, there would be the fault that the establishment of wrong view, the knowledge of others' minds, the applications of mindfulness, the knowledge of suffering, and so forth, would all be untenable.

If it is argued that just as a lamp illuminates both itself and others, so too should cognition function, this is also illogical, because the very nature of a lamp’s illumination is not established as real.

That is to say, a specific collection of visible forms (*varṇa*) is designated as "lamp. It is called "illumination" because it is the cause for the arising of visual consciousness; it is said to be "destructive" because it is the opposite of darkness.
Because this [lamp] exists, obstructing causes such as jars can be perceived; thus, it is said to "illuminate jars and the like."
Apart from conventional designation, there is no real entity that possesses the capacity to illuminate its own self, just as salt and other such things function solely by means of their own nature.
Furthermore, if one grants that a lamp is an illuminator, then one must also grant that it illuminates itself as well as others;
likewise, one would have to grant that darkness, being an obstruction, has the power to obstruct itself as well as others, and that fire, being capable of burning, burns itself as well as others.
Since that is not the case, how could it be so for a lamp?

If you claim that the power of the lamp destroys the obstructing jar and that the lamp both destroys and perceives the jar because it dispels darkness, then both [the lamp and the cognition] should be called "illuminating."
This reasoning is also incorrect, because darkness either does or does not come into contact with the jar and the lamp.

That is to say, if darkness were to come into contact with the jar, one could say it obstructs the jar; however, although the jar is present, perception of it does not arise. For this reason, it is said that darkness can obstruct the perception of the jar.
When the lamp arises and darkness is extinguished, the jar becomes manifest and perception arises; therefore, the world says that the lamp has the function of illuminating the jar.

There has never been a time when darkness and a lamp coexist; lest one fall into the error of failing to acknowledge their mutual incompatibility and lack of counteraction, it cannot be said that darkness can obstruct a lamp.

Since there is no instance where a lamp fails to produce cognition, it likewise cannot be said that darkness acts as an obstruction to cognition. Therefore, although the arising of a lamp causes darkness to perish, one cannot say that the darkness is "illuminated" in the same manner as a jar.
Furthermore, what is the reason for maintaining that the function of cognition’s knowing is like the illumination of a lamp and not like the cutting of a sword?

That is to say, upon seeing what principle do you maintain that the dharma of cognition and the metaphor of the lamp are identical, while they are not so with the sword and other such things? Therefore, citing the metaphor of the lamp as proof lacks persuasive force.
Some may say: "Wisdom does not know its own self-nature; rather, it can know its specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
This reasoning is also incorrect, as it has already been established that a self-nature does not take itself as its object-condition (ālambana).

Since it is eternally impossible to apprehend its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it certainly cannot have itself as its object-condition (*ālambana*). Since it is not an object-condition, how could it apprehend a common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
Therefore, one should formulate the following inference regarding this:
"The specific characteristic must also be an object for its own essence, because it possesses the nature of its own essence, just like a common characteristic."

Alternatively, the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) ought not to be its own objective sphere, because it is the characteristic of itself, just like the particular characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, the principle that cognition takes the universal characteristic as its object is also untenable.

Furthermore, if wisdom manifesting before one were to take itself as its object, one would have to admit that the self-nature is also its own support (*āśraya*). If one admits both self-objectification and self-support, then the self-nature must be able to establish itself; since it establishes itself, one must admit it is eternal; and being eternal, it could not have the capacity to cognize other objects.
Furthermore, because there would otherwise be no distinction between the cognition and its object, there can certainly be no cognition that takes itself as its own object.

If it is argued that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) function respectively as the object and the subject of cognition, this is also logically untenable, as has already been stated previously.

As previously stated, since it does not take its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object—because that is its own essential nature—it likewise should not take a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

For this very reason, it does not take associated factors (*saṃprayukta*) as its objects, because it functions with respect to the same object as those associated factors; were one to admit that it takes associated factors as its objects, one would necessarily have to admit that it takes itself as its object.
Nor can it take coexistent phenomena as its object, because coexistent phenomena are too closely proximate.
Just as the eye does not see the matter that supports the visual faculty, the Sūtra also states that the wisdom of a single moment cannot simultaneously know all dharmas as objects.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who can see or know all phenomena instantaneously. By this principle, it is understood that [realization] occurs only gradually.
This wisdom is comprised solely within the desire and form realms; although this type exists within the formless realm, its objects are few and thus it is not what is being elucidated here.
This [wisdom] comprises the wisdoms produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as all are able to eliminate their respective categories while taking all phenomena as their objects.

However, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) states that [this knowledge] is not produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), because that which is produced by cultivation takes different levels (*bhūmi*) as its objects. If it were otherwise, one would have to abandon defilements all at once (*sakṛt*).
This is unreasonable, for the claim that what is produced by cultivation takes only different levels as its objects is not universally established (*asiddha*).

That is to say, our school maintains that the wisdom produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) subsumed within the dhyāna stages has the capacity to take [all] objects collectively, because it takes as its objects the realms from its own level upward according to the body upon which it relies; thus, by wearying of the lower and aspiring toward the upper, one is able to become free from defilement.

Since this [knowledge] takes [the object] as a whole and possesses only the aspect of aspiration, it lacks the capacity for the abandonment of defilements; therefore, what they have said is highly irrational.
Having already analyzed the objects of focus, one should further investigate:
who accomplishes how many knowledges?
The verse says:
For ordinary beings and noble ones on the path of seeing, in the first moment one definitely achieves one;
in the second moment one achieves three knowledges; thereafter, in each of the four moments, one knowledge is added respectively.

The path of cultivation definitely consists of seven [knowledges]; for one free from desire, the knowledge of others' minds is added. For those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), the dull-witted definitely possess nine, while the sharp-witted possess ten. The treatise says: The path of cultivation definitely consists of seven; For one free from desire, the knowledge of others' minds is added. For those in the stage of no-more-learning, the dull-witted definitely possess nine, While the sharp-witted possess ten.
The treatise says:

In the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and during the first moment of the noble path of seeing (darśanamārga), one definitely possesses one knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
In the second moment, one definitely possesses three knowledges, namely those [three] plus the knowledge of dharma (dharmajñāna) and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna).
In the fourth [moment], sixty-four moments occur; as for the subsequent stages, the respective types of knowledge—comprehension of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—are added one by one.

In all positions where these have not yet been added, the number of moments remains as previously established; therefore, throughout the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), seven knowledges are invariably accomplished.
If those in these various stages have already become free from desire, each increases by one.

That is to say, the knowledge of others' minds excludes only ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); however, during the stage of an ordinary being and within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one can only achieve conventional knowledge of others' minds.

At the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna), both types are fully accomplished; for at that moment, one first attains the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala), and simultaneously acquires the untainted (anāsrava) state to constitute the essence of that fruit.
In all other stages of cultivation, both types are likewise fully accomplished.
Those born in the formless realm abandon the conventional [knowledges].
Those liberated at all times (samayavimukta) definitely accomplish nine knowledges, namely, with the addition of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
Those liberated independent of time (asamayavimukta) definitely accomplish ten, namely, with the addition of the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
In which stage are how many knowledges cultivated simultaneously?
First, one should investigate:
what is meant by "cultivation"?
This means that by practicing wholesome conditioned phenomena, one brings them to fulfillment and mastery.
It is not defiled or neutral because it lacks superior desirable fruits;
it is not unconditioned wholesome because it does not exist within the continuum of personal existence.
Furthermore, because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has no fruit.
Having already explained the meaning of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the original question should now be answered.
Regarding the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the verse says:
When the patiences and knowledges of the path of seeing arise, they are cultivated in the future;

the three types of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are cultivated concurrently. The conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) does not arise from its own level or a lower level.
After the four [patiences] regarding suffering and origin, and after the [patience] regarding cessation:
Regarding the aspects and objects of their respective truths, these are obtained solely through application (*prayoga*).
The treatise says:

Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), whichever patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) arise, they all cultivate their own corresponding types in the future; however, they fully cultivate all the aspects (*ākāra*) and applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) pertaining to their respective truths.
For what reason is the path of seeing cultivated only as a homogeneous cultivation?
Because both its function and its object are definitively distinct. Some say:

Because this lineage has never been attained before, one can cultivate the conventional knowledge at the edge of clear realization (*abhisamaya-prānta-koṭika-saṃvṛti-jñāna*) only during the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, and cessation; since it can be cultivated only at the very end following the clear realization of each individual truth, it is given this name.
For this reason, in other stages one is unable to cultivate them concurrently, because what is to be accomplished regarding one's own respective truths has not yet been perfected.

Some say: "If these were cultivated at the stage of *dharmajñāna*, they should be called conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) within the context of clear realization (*abhisamaya*); the Sūtra would then not establish the designation 'at the edge of clear realization' (*abhisamayāntika*)."
Regarding the three stages, which is superior and which is inferior?
If judged by the continuity of the stream of being, each subsequent stage is superior to the preceding one, because they arise from the increase of the body.
If explained according to the realms (*dhātu*), those above are all superior to those below.

Therefore, that which was previously cultivated as belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) has a superior realm but an inferior body; that which is cultivated in the subsequent stage as belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) has an inferior realm but a superior body.
These constitute four permutations, which should be reflected upon according to reason.
Why is this not cultivated at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)?

This knowledge belongs exclusively to the retinue of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), whereas that [subsequent knowledge] is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); therefore, it cannot be cultivated.

This meaning is to say that because the cultivation of the "skill in the seven bases" (*saptasthānakauśalya*) serves as the seed, the path of seeing arises; thus, when the path of seeing arises, that [cultivation] is described as its retinue.

Alternatively, because conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) has, since beginningless time, already known, abandoned, and realized the three truths, it has never cultivated the path; therefore, it is not cultivated now.
Or, because one now perceives the true path, the false path is shunned with shame; thus, it is not that which is cultivated.

Alternatively, one might argue that this knowledge is cultivated at the stage of the culmination of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika*), but because the paths are infinite, it is not cultivated at this particular stage.

That is to say, regarding the clear realization of the facts (*vastv-abhisamaya*) within the context of the three truths, while a single practitioner may potentially attain the culmination of them all, there can never be anyone capable of universally cultivating all the paths; for one cannot cultivate the paths belonging to a different faculty or lineage (*gotra*).
Although it is possible for one to cultivate [the path] according to one's own faculties and nature, because not even one part in a hundred thousand arises;

and although at the stage of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) the accumulation of suffering has not been entirely abandoned nor its cessation fully realized, the task of abandoning accumulation and realizing cessation is already complete for that particular stage.

At the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), the afflictions deluded regarding the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) are not universally cultivated as their antidotes, because there are many grades of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and faculties (*indriya*).
For this reason, regarding the [remaining] three truths, the Blessed One spoke of them using the term "limit" (*anta*), as stated in the Sūtra:
"There is the limit of the suffering of the body, the limit of the origin of the body, and the limit of the cessation of the body."
No sūtra ever states that there is a "limit of the path of the body," for there is no one capable of cultivating the path to its ultimate limit.

This conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is a non-arising dharma (*anutpatti-dharma*), as it has no possibility of arising at any time; this is because the body upon which its arising depends will certainly never arise [again].

This means that while the bodies of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) may serve as a basis for inducing the arising of this knowledge, such [knowledge] cannot possibly arise during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Therefore, the body upon which it relies abides in a state where the dharma is not produced; because it does not produce it, it necessarily does not arise.
If that is so, on what basis is it said that there is the meaning of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*)?
It is called "cultivation" by virtue of "attainment-cultivation" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).

This means that at that time, one acquires mastery over [the dharma]; although its substance does not manifest due to the obstruction of other conditions, it is for this reason that it is called "attainment," because one realizes the acquisition of mastery over its arising.
There are certain dharmas that are attained and immediately manifest, such as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and others;
or there are certain dharmas that are first attained and later manifest, such as the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) and others.
There are certain phenomena that can never manifest, such as this very wisdom;
there are also certain phenomena that manifest despite not being attained, such as external forms and so forth.
Since no phenomenon belonging to the category of sentient beings can arise and manifest, there is indeed the sense of cultivation even though [the attainment] does not arise.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) poses the following challenge:
"If it cannot be produced, upon what does the meaning of 'attainment' depend?"
Therefore, the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) as you have defined it is not established; however, the meaning of cultivation can be established as explained by the ancient masters.
How do they explain it?

Through the power of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), one cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); subsequently, upon emerging from meditative absorption, a superior conventional knowledge regarding the truths manifests before one. Because one attains the basis for its arising, it is said that "one has attained this," just as obtaining gold ore is called "obtaining gold."
This is merely words, for it is subject to the same critique.
How can this wisdom not be present before one, yet be called "attained" based on the arising of its expression?
Furthermore, it cannot be called "present" based on its non-attainment, because the basis [of attainment] cannot be identical to the essence of that [wisdom].

If it is argued that there is a distinction because the capacity to see or not see exists in the subsequent state, this too is unreasonable; for it is admitted that the basis for arising does not endure for long.

Since this [capacity] is not present at the time when the basis for arising has already been relinquished, once the basis for arising has been relinquished, it certainly does not manifest; how then could one perceive its capacity to arise later?
If that which serves as the basis for arising must necessarily be manifest when it arises, how could it not be present during the state of its arising?
Since it is not manifest, how can there be a basis for arising?
Therefore, what they have said:
Since they cannot arise, upon what could the attainment of their objects depend?
This is an unreasonable objection, for you yourself admit that non-arising is also termed "attainment.
Whichever level the path of seeing manifests upon, one can cultivate [the dharmas] of that level and lower levels in the future.

That is to say, this conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) takes seven stages as its basis: namely, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara), the four dhyānas, and the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

If the path of seeing (darśanamārga) manifests based on the threshold concentration, one is able to cultivate, in the future, the path of seeing of one stage and the conventional knowledge of two stages.

Upon reaching the fourth [moment], when the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) manifests, one is able to cultivate the path of seeing of the six future stages and the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the seven stages.

That which is cultivated at the conclusion of the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) is subsumed under the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); that which is cultivated at the conclusion of cessation (*nirodha*) is exclusively the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Whichever truth’s conclusion it may be that is cultivated, one takes that very truth as its object by means of those specific mental aspects (*ākāra*).

That is to say, regarding the cultivation at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), one employs the four aspects (*ākāra*) that take suffering as their object: if it is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), it takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object; if it is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), it takes the truth of suffering of the higher realms as its object.

If one practices at the stage of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truth of origin (*samudayasatya*), one does so by means of the four aspects that take origin as their object; if it is bound to the desire realm and takes the origin of the desire realm as its object, those bound to the form realm take the truth of origin of the higher realms as their object.

If one practices at the stage of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truth of cessation, one does so by means of the four aspects that take cessation as their object; if it pertains to the desire realm, it takes the cessation of the desire realm as its object, and if it pertains to the form realm, it takes the cessation of the higher realms as its object.
This conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is acquired solely through application (*prayoga-pratilabdha*), because it is acquired through the application of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

That which is comprised within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is produced by reflection (*cintāmaya*), while that which is comprised within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*); it is not produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*), because the latter is too weak.
Because wisdom is predominant, it is designated by the name "wisdom.
If the accompanying factors are included, its intrinsic nature consists of the four aggregates of the desire realm and the five aggregates of the form realm.
Next, regarding the stage of detachment during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the verse says:
In the first moment of the path of cultivation, one cultivates six or seven knowledges;

during the uninterrupted paths that abandon the eight stages, as well as the remaining paths for those with desire and the eight liberations of the Peak of Existence, one cultivates seven knowledges in each case.
Above the Uninterrupted Path, one cultivates six and eight knowledges respectively.
The Commentary says:

At the first moment of the path of cultivation—namely, at the time of the sixteenth knowledge, the Knowledge of the Path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna)—one presently cultivates two knowledges: the Knowledge of the Path and the Subsequent Knowledge (anvaya-jñāna). These differ in name but not in essence.

Those who have not yet abandoned desire cultivate six future knowledges—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and those pertaining to suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

Those who have abandoned desire cultivate seven, adding the knowledge of others' minds; however, they do not cultivate conventional knowledge because it does not serve as an antidote to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

For those who have previously abandoned desire and entered the Noble Path, for what reason is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) not cultivated during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
Because the knowledge of others' minds is comprised within the virtues of contemplative observation (*vilokana*), it can only be cultivated based on a path of leisurely progression;
since the Path of Seeing involves the observation of the principles of the Truths (*satyārtha*) with extremely rapid preparatory application (*prayoga*), it is impossible to cultivate it therein.
The principle is the same for the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
