Now, at the time of the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), it is subsumed under the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); therefore, this knowledge is cultivated.

Regarding the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and eight paths of liberation that abandon the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm, as well as the four conventional knowledges and four dharma knowledges, they are cultivated in the present as appropriate to each case.

In the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) for abandoning the [defilements] of the upper seven stages, one currently cultivates, as appropriate, the four types of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

In the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) for abandoning [the defilements of] the desire realm, one currently cultivates, as appropriate, the conventional knowledge of the desire realm, the superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) with desire, and the four conventional knowledges and knowledges of the dharma (*dharma-jñāna*).

From this point upward, in the future, one cultivates all seven knowledges—namely, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of categories (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. When abandoning the first eight liberations of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one cultivates the four category-knowledges and two phenomenon-knowledges as appropriate for the present cultivation.
In the future as well, one cultivates only seven; however, excluding conventional knowledge, one adds the knowledge of others' minds.

Regarding the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) for abandoning the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), four types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and two dharma-knowledges (*dharma-jñāna*) are cultivated accordingly in the present. In the future, one cultivates six: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

In the ninth liberation of the path of cultivation for abandoning desire, one currently cultivates the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the four knowledges (*jñāna*), and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) as appropriate.

In the various paths of liberation for abandoning the seven higher stages, one currently cultivates the four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) as appropriate.

In the ninth path of superior progress for abandoning desire through cultivation, and in the various paths of preparation for abandoning the eight higher stages, one currently cultivates the conventional knowledge, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) as appropriate.

In the paths of superior progress for abandoning the seven higher stages and the eight categories of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one currently cultivates the conventional knowledge, the knowledge of phenomena, the subsequent knowledge, and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) as appropriate; this is because the paths previously cultivated may manifest at that time.

Above this, one cultivates all eight knowledges in the future; that is to say, the conventional, dharma, subsequent, four truths, and others' minds. Why is it that these four [knowledges]—the subsequent, which cannot sever the defilements of the desire realm, and the dharma-knowledges of suffering and origin, which are not the antidotes for the higher realms—arise as antidotes and are cultivated in the future?

If it were granted that one may cultivate [a mundane path] concurrently even when it is not an antidote, then one would have to cultivate the mundane path concurrently when abandoning the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and so forth.
This objection is unreasonable, because it is not accepted that only those [paths] which are identical in their function as antidotes are cultivated in the future.

This means that cultivation occurs because it is admitted that there is a connection [between the factors], as when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Alternatively, cultivation occurs through mutual support by the power of causes, as when the four categories [of noble truths] are cultivated concurrently at the time of abandoning desire, or when the dharmas of suffering and origin are cultivated during the stage of abandoning the defilements of the higher realms.

If one has severed the defilements of the desire realm but does not cultivate subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), or has severed the upper realms but does not cultivate the two dharmas of suffering and origin, then for one who attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) through gradual stages, there would be no possibility for subsequent knowledge to arise and become manifest.

An Arhat should not give rise to the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) or the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), because those previously acquired have already been relinquished, and those not previously acquired are not objects of cultivation.

This is because, by way of category, if something was previously acquired, it acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) whose power induces the arising of this knowledge as a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*).

Because it was previously induced by that wisdom, it can further serve as a cause for the same class of wisdom; therefore, the causal power of this arising wisdom supports that [future wisdom], and although they do not share the same antidote, it is cultivated in the future.
Next, the attainment of the stage of no-more-learning through the abandonment of defilements is explained.
The verse says:
"In the first moment of no-more-learning, one cultivates nine or ten [paths of action]."
Because of the distinction between dull and sharp faculties, the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) is likewise [divided].
The treatise says:

Regarding the first thought-moment of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), which consists of abandoning the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*): if it is the ninth liberation, one should practice, as appropriate, either the "comprehension of origin" (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) or the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*), because these take the Peak of Existence as their object.
Regarding the nine or ten [knowledges] for superior progress, one practices them as appropriate in the present; in the future, one practices nine or ten as appropriate.
This means that while those of dull faculties practice all except the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), those of sharp faculties also practice the knowledge of non-arising.
Next, the number of wisdoms cultivated in other stages is explained.
The verse says:
In the path of uninterrupted transition for refining the faculties, the learner cultivates six, and the non-learner seven.
The others train in six, seven, or eight; the *āpanna* trains in eight, nine, or all.
In the mixed cultivation and the uninterrupted paths, the learner trains in seven and the *āpanna* in eight or nine;
in the remaining paths, the learner trains in eight and the *āpanna* in nine or all.
The noble ones give rise to other virtues, as do ordinary beings in their various stages;
the extent of the wisdom they cultivate should all be considered in accordance with reason.
The treatise says:

Regarding the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) by one in training (*śaikṣa*): in all the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), one presently cultivates the four knowledges of dharma (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) as appropriate; in the future, one cultivates six—namely, the knowledges of dharma and subsequent knowledge regarding the four noble truths—because this resembles the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). One does not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) because it does not serve to sever the obstacles, nor does one cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) for the same reason. In all the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one presently cultivates the four knowledges of dharma and subsequent knowledge as appropriate.
Those who have not yet abandoned desire cultivate six future knowledges—the dharmajñāna, anvayajñāna, and those pertaining to the four truths.
Those who have already abandoned desire cultivate seven future knowledges, namely, with the addition of paracittajñāna.
Other masters say:

In the stage of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one also cultivates the mundane paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*); accordingly, the four mundane dharmas and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) are cultivated in the present.

For those who have not yet abandoned desire, seven [knowledges] are cultivated in the future; for those who have already abandoned desire, eight are cultivated, namely, with the addition of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).

Regarding the various paths of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*): if one has not yet abandoned desire, one presently cultivates four conventional knowledges and two knowledges of dharma and subsequent knowledge as appropriate, and seven are also cultivated in the future.

If one has already abandoned desire, one presently cultivates four conventional knowledges, two knowledges of dharma and subsequent knowledge, and the knowledge of others' minds as appropriate, and eight are also cultivated in the future.

When one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), in each of the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), they accordingly practice in the present four categories of knowledge and two types of dharma; in the future, they cultivate seven: the four truths, the dharma-knowledge, the subsequent knowledge, and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*). They do not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), as its cultivation is like that for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Therefore, in the five preceding paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they accordingly practice in the present eight categories of knowledge and two types of dharma; in the future, they cultivate eight: the four truths, the dharma-knowledge, the subsequent knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledge of exhaustion.

In the fourth [dhyāna], during the ninth liberation, one presently cultivates the path of suffering, origin, and the subsequent knowledge of exhaustion as appropriate; in the future, one cultivates nine.
In the final liberation, one presently cultivates the path of suffering, origin, and the subsequent knowledge of exhaustion as appropriate; in the future, one cultivates ten.
In all paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), one cultivates [the knowledges] currently as in the case of training; in the future, one cultivates nine.
In all paths of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*), for those of dull faculties, nine knowledges are cultivated currently as appropriate, and nine are also cultivated in the future.
Regarding the beneficial [roots], ten knowledges are cultivated in the present according to their application, and ten are also cultivated in the future.

In the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), during the various uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of mixed cultivation, four—the dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and worldly knowledge—are cultivated in the present according to their application, and seven are cultivated in the future.

In all paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), there are only four [knowledges]: the knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). In all paths of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*), there is additionally the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), which is cultivated according to circumstances; in all cases, eight knowledges are present in the future.

Regarding the various uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the mixed cultivation of the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the present cultivation is the same as that of the one in training (*śaikṣa*); as for future cultivation, it consists of eight for those of dull faculties and nine for those of sharp faculties.

Regarding the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), there are only four: the dharmas, the classes, the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*), and the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), which are cultivated in the present according to the circumstances; as for future cultivation, it consists of nine for those of dull faculties and ten for those of sharp faculties.

The various paths of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) are the same as those for the refinement of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*). During the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), when cultivating the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there are five paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*); in these, one presently cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and seven are cultivated in the future.

In the two paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) for the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) and the supernormal power of the divine eye (*ṛddhividhi*), and in the five paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*), one presently cultivates conventional knowledge. In the path of liberation for the supernormal power of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), one cultivates conventional knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledges of the path, dharma, and subsequent realization (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) as appropriate. For all paths of superior progress, one presently cultivates conventional knowledge, along with the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation as applicable.
From this point upward, in the future, one cultivates all eight knowledges.

For those beyond training (aśaikṣa) who cultivate the supernormal powers, in the five paths of immediate succession, they cultivate [knowledges] in the present as those in training do; regarding what is cultivated in the future, those of dull faculties cultivate eight, while those of sharp faculties cultivate nine.

The preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for liberation are cultivated in the present as they are studied; those cultivated in the future consist of nine types for those of dull faculties and ten types for those of sharp faculties.
The various paths of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) are identical to the path of refining the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).

Because the two paths of liberation regarding the divine eye and divine ear are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), they are not termed "cultivation"; the remaining noble [attainments], such as the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), are comprised within that which is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
When possessing outflow-tainted virtues (*sāsrava-guṇa*), one cultivates all present mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). Regarding the future:
for those still in training (*śaikṣa*), if they have not yet abandoned desire, they cultivate seven; if they have already abandoned desire, they cultivate eight.

For those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), those of dull faculties cultivate nine, while those of sharp faculties cultivate ten, excluding the *anuloma-viloma* mind, because this [mind] only cultivates mundane knowledge in the future.
If other untainted (*anāsrava*) merits arise that are subsumed under the dhyānas, one should accordingly cultivate the four dharmas and the knowledge of types (*jñāna*) in the present.

If they are subsumed under the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), one should cultivate only the four knowledges of types in the present; those cultivated for the future are the same as in the case of the tainted [cultivation] mentioned previously.

When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becomes free from passion, they cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) in the present as the ninth liberation (*vimokṣa*) for abandoning the passions of the first three dhyānas; furthermore, when they arise in the path of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*) based on the four fundamental dhyānas to become free from passion through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), they cultivate two knowledges in the future—namely, conventional knowledge and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). For all other cases in the future, they cultivate only conventional knowledge.

When cultivating the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated in the preparatory paths (*prayogamārga*) and two liberation paths (*vimuktimārga*); in one liberation path, conventional knowledge and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) are cultivated; and in all paths of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*), both are cultivated as appropriate. In the future, all [paths] cultivate both types.

In the five paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), both present and future cultivation consists solely of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). When cultivating other meritorious qualities based on the fundamental dhyānas, one always cultivates conventional knowledge in the present and both types [conventional and supramundane] in the future.

However, in the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), one necessarily does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), because these are the proximate attendants of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

When one cultivates other meritorious qualities based on the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of other stages, all such cultivation pertains exclusively to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and occurs in the present and future.
Regarding these various future cultivations, how many stages are cultivated?
And are all acquisitions (*prāpti*) that arise considered "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*)?
The verse says:
When one attains a path that relies upon a certain stage, one cultivates the impure factors of that stage;
when one arises from detachment from a certain stage, one cultivates the pure factors of that stage and those below it.
Only at the very beginning does one cultivate all [virtues] exhaustively;
the impure virtues of the nine stages are cultivated when arising in a higher stage, while those already attained in lower stages are not cultivated.
The treatise says:
When the various paths rely upon this stage and when they are attained in this stage, one is able to cultivate the contaminated (*sāsrava*) factors of this very stage for the future.

That is to say, when the mundane or supramundane path manifests while relying upon this stage, one cultivates only the contaminated factors of this stage for the future; this is because the attachment to contaminated factors is so firm that it is difficult to cultivate anything else.

Whichever stage one relies upon to become detached from the defilements of a lower stage, when the ninth liberation is present before them, they also cultivate it for the future; this is because the attained impure merits of the fundamental and preparatory stages of the higher stage necessarily result in the attainment of freedom from the bonds of the lower stage.

When a noble one is about to leave a stage or has attained it, and when the various paths within that stage manifest, they are all able to cultivate the untainted (*anāsrava*) [paths] of that stage and those below.

That is to say, whenever the contaminated (*sāsrava*) or untainted preparatory (*prayoga*) and other paths of any given stage are present before one, in order to abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) of that stage, one cultivates in the future the untainted paths of that stage and those below; for the lower [paths] are equally capable of acting as antidotes to the defilements of the higher stages.

Although there are antidotes capable of counteracting the afflictions of the higher stages when one eliminates those afflictions through the lower noble path (*āryamārga*), because the bonds of the contaminated states (*sāsrava*) to their respective stages are firm, one cannot cultivate those [antidotes] as long as one has not yet abandoned the lower stage.

Whichever stage one relies upon to become free from the defilements of the lower stages, at the moment the ninth liberation-dhyāna manifests, one also cultivates it for the future; furthermore, the untainted merits of the attained higher stage and all the lower stages arise in accordance with the current stage.
When the mundane noble path manifests, one cultivates all future untainted merits pertaining to this stage as well as those of the lower stages.

Only when the initial knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) manifests does its power enable the universal cultivation of immeasurable superior merits—such as the meditations on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) and those consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation—which are comprised within the mental sphere (*manobhūmi*) and pertain to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) states across the nine stages.

That is to say, whichever stage the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) manifests in, one universally cultivates [wholesome roots] of the future belonging to that stage, as well as those of the stages above and below it.
For what reason is it that at this initial moment of the knowledge of exhaustion, its power alone is able to universally cultivate all contaminated virtues?

Because it is able to utterly eradicate all afflictions and hostile roots of virtue that have existed since beginningless time, it is like when a common enemy of a nation is defeated and subdued; everyone comes together to rejoice, rely upon this, and praise it as excellent.
Furthermore, because the bonds of the afflictions have been severed without remainder, it is like the circulation of breath once the binding agent has been severed.
Moreover, as that sovereign mind ascends to the position of mastery, all wholesome dharmas arise and come to court.
For example, when a great king ascends the throne through the ritual of coronation, all territories come to pay tribute;

yet, once born in a higher state, one certainly does not cultivate the roots of goodness of lower states. That is to say, while one in the desire realm may attain arhatship by universally cultivating the roots of goodness of the nine stages across the three realms, upon being born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one cultivates the roots of goodness of only a single stage.

The term "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*) at the beginning indicates the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) in both the state of transcending the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the five stages of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), because in all these cases one abandons the previous path and newly attains the fruit.

Although one can also cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) pertaining to one's own level or lower levels during the three moments of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), this has already been discussed previously and will not be treated here again.
Regarding all that is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), only that which was previously unobtained and is now being aroused and obtained constitutes the object and the act of cultivation.
That is to say, if something was previously unobtained and is now obtained through the application of effort, it is truly what is cultivated;
however, if a dharma was previously obtained but then abandoned, even if it is recovered now, it is not "cultivated," because it was not realized through the exertion of labor.
If [a dharma] arises that was not previously attained, it can cultivate future qualities because its arising through extreme effort possesses superior power.

If, however, what was already previously attained now arises and manifests, it cannot cultivate future qualities; because it does not arise through great effort and its power is inferior, its cultivation has ceased, and thus it cannot cultivate the future.

If one who has previously attained [a quality] in the present were able to cultivate it for the future, then when the Bhagavān attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), he would not yet have fully cultivated all meritorious qualities; he would need to further practice in order to fully realize them, and thus his qualities would be incomplete, just like those of the two vehicles.
Is it only with respect to acquisition (*prāpti*) that one speaks of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*)? It is not so. Why is this?
There are four kinds of cultivation: first, cultivation by acquisition; second, cultivation by practice; third, cultivation as an antidote; and fourth, cultivation by elimination.
Upon what phenomena are these four types of cultivation established?
The verse says:
The cultivation of attainment and the cultivation of practice are established based on wholesome conditioned phenomena;
the cultivation of counteraction and the cultivation of elimination are established based on all contaminated phenomena.
The Commentary states:

When various previously unattained virtues manifest before one, and when the remaining future virtues are attained through new cultivation, these are all termed "cultivation by attainment" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
When previously unattained meritorious qualities arise for the first time, and because they are currently being cultivated, both are termed "cultivation through practice" (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*).
These two types of cultivation are established solely based on conditioned wholesome phenomena.

Regarding future phenomena, there is only "cultivation through acquisition" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*); however, regarding present phenomena, both types are fully present, because one acquires the counteracting remedies for the body and other such factors.

The body and so forth that are to be remedied are called "cultivation as antidote" (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*); therefore, when one attains the antidote for the body and so forth, it is said that one is cultivating the body and so forth. This should likewise apply to other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Because afflictions directed toward objects such as the body are abandoned, the cultivation of the factors such as the body is termed "removal" (*vibhāvanā*).

Thus, when afflictions directed toward the body and so forth are abandoned, it is also said that one is cultivating the body and so forth; this should likewise apply by analogy to all other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
These two [types of cultivation] are established based solely on contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena; therefore, wholesome contaminated phenomena possess all four types of cultivation.
Uncontaminated conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) and other contaminated phenomena each possess, respectively, the two types of cultivation—the former and the latter.

Within this context, with respect to the meaning of what ought to be cultivated (*bhāvanīya*), one distinguishes the various phenomena (*dharma*) according to how many of these [cultivations] they possess. Some phenomena possess all four and are termed "to be cultivated"; some possess three; some possess two; some possess one; and some possess none at all.

This means that when wholesome contaminated [dharmas] have not yet been permanently severed, they can be obtained and can arise, being complete in four ways: because they have not yet been permanently severed, they should be complete in the cultivation of counteraction and expulsion; because they can be obtained, they should be complete in the cultivation of acquisition; and because they can arise, they should be complete in the cultivation of practice.

That which has already been attained and is capable of arising possesses three [cultivations], excluding the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*); that which is capable of being attained but will not arise possesses three, excluding the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*); and that which has already been attained but will not arise, as well as that which cannot be attained and has already arisen, possess two, namely, the cultivation of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of expulsion (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*).
The same applies to defiled and neutral [dharmas] when they have not yet been abandoned.

If wholesome contaminated dharmas have been permanently abandoned, that which can be acquired and can arise possesses two types of acquisition: the acquisition of possession (*prāpti*) and the acquisition of cultivation (*vāsanā*). That which can be acquired but cannot arise possesses one, namely, the acquisition of possession; that which has already been acquired and can arise possesses one, namely, the acquisition of cultivation. It should be understood that the same applies to uncontaminated conditioned dharmas.

Excluding what was previously stated, all [other cases] are entirely non-existent—namely, those among the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) that have already been attained but do not arise, and so forth.

If it were the case that a dharma which does not arise within the body is called "cultivated" (*bhāvita*) merely by virtue of its attainment (*prāpti*), then one must admit that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is also called "cultivated," for there is no distinction [between them].
This objection is unreasonable, because those dharmas of the same class abide within the body.
That is to say, although dharmas that do not arise do not abide in the body, since dharmas of the same class do abide in the body, there is no fault in calling this "cultivation."

Furthermore, because they abide as a result of having attained [their non-arising], it means that wholesome dharmas of the future do not arise; by causing them to arise, this is expressed as abiding as a result. The intended meaning is that "we lack the necessary conditions and thus do not arise," not that we are currently not being drawn forth [into existence].
Pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha (cessation through deliberation) is different from this and cannot serve as an analogy.
Furthermore, while future dharmas do not arise as wholesome phenomena, they are nonetheless sustained and benefited by the power of their causes;
this is not the case for cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and therefore it lacks the sense of being "cultivated.

Moreover, because cessation through deliberation is exclusively a fruit—meaning that cultivation is fundamentally for the sake of attaining a superior fruit—it should not be cultivated, as cessation itself possesses no further fruit.

Furthermore, because analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is neither increased nor diminished, it cannot be cultivated. This is because those dharmas subject to cultivation proceed from the inferior to the intermediate, and from the intermediate to the superior; analytical cessation is not like this, and since it serves no purpose in cultivation, it cannot be cultivated.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Seventy-four.

Chapter Seven, Part Three: A Detailed Exposition of Knowledge (Jñāna). Having thus already distinguished the various types of knowledge, the virtues accomplished through that knowledge shall now be revealed.
Among these, we first discuss the Buddha’s unique qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*).
At the stage of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) upon his initial attainment of Buddhahood, he cultivates eighteen kinds of unique Buddha-dharmas.
What are these eighteen?
The verse says:
The eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) are the ten powers of the Buddha and so forth.
The commentary says:

The ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*): these combined are called the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*).
They are cultivated only at the time of a Buddha’s knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and since they do not exist in other noble ones (*ārya*), they are called "unique."
Furthermore, what are the distinctions among the Buddha’s ten powers?
The verse says:
The powers consist of ten [factors] regarding the possible and the impossible; eight [powers] concern karma, excluding cessation and the path.
The faculties, roots, inclinations, and elements are nine; the knowledge of the path leading everywhere is nine or ten.
The knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of death and rebirth are conventional; the knowledge of exhaustion consists of six or ten knowledges.
The knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of death and rebirth rely on the dhyānas; the remaining supernormal powers rely on all [four] dhyānas.
The male being of Jambudvīpa [perceives] the Buddha-body, because there is no obstruction regarding the object.
The commentary says:

Regarding the ten powers (*bala*) of a Buddha, the first is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), which has all ten types of Tathāgata-knowledge as its nature.
Based on what meaning is this name "power" established?
The Buddha himself stated in the sūtras:

"Bhikṣus, listen attentively! The Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, what is possible as possible; the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, what is impossible as impossible," and so forth, as explained at length.
To know that the intrinsic functional capacity and principle of all phenomena definitely exist is called the knowledge of the possible (*sthānajñāna*).
To know that the intrinsic functional capacity and principle of all phenomena definitely do not exist is called the knowledge of the impossible (*asthānajñāna*).

This wisdom universally takes as its object both sentient and non-sentient phenomena, and it is entirely non-contradictory with all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñā*). Fearing that this brief explanation might be difficult to realize due to its minimal effort, I have further extracted the remaining nine [categories] from within this context, just as the Blessed One extensively analyzed the meaning of the possible (*sthāna*) and the impossible (*asthāna*) in the *Bahudhātuka Sūtra*.

That unwholesome conduct of body and so forth will certainly result in undesirable fruits—this is a certainty; that it would result in desirable fruits is absolutely impossible—and so on, as explained at length.
Regarding those points not yet mentioned in that sutra, I shall provide a brief further analysis based on other teachings.

It is impossible that the Tathāgatas could still have errors or omissions; that they should provide categorical answers where distinctions ought to be made; or that they should lack the unique qualities (āveṇika-buddhadharma) such as the powers (bala), the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), and the three foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna). Such things can never occur.
It is impossible that the Noble Ones (ārya) would still give rise to afflictions abandoned through seeing, or commit transgressions leading to rebirth in the evil destinies.

It is impossible for one who has committed an immediate transgression (ānantarya) to perceive the Dharma in this very life, or for one who has fallen into wrong nature (mithyātva-niyata) to enter the right nature (samyaktva-niyata) in this very life. It is impossible for there to be true śramaṇas within the teachings of non-Buddhists; or for there to be those who undergo rebirth yet do not die; or for non-returners (anāgāmin) to be born again in the desire realm; or for Arhats to receive further existence; or for the two kinds of consciousness to continue manifesting while they have been relinquished; or for there to be thirteen bases (āyatana), nineteen elements (dhātu), a sixth aggregate (skandha), a fourth world-age (adhvan), or a fifth truth (satya). Such things are absolutely impossible.
It is impossible that anyone could obstruct the Tathāgata’s messengers;

as long as the World-Honored One’s mission is not yet completed, it is impossible for those who practice according to faith or the Dharma—while remaining in the meditative absorption of loving-kindness or the absorption of cessation—to be harmed, or for them to die and fall into the evil realms, or to meet with an untimely death. There is absolutely no such possibility.

It is impossible for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to be non-extinguished in *nirvāṇa* while being non-eternal; it is impossible for an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) to be able to sever the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); it is impossible for two minds to function simultaneously within a single continuum; it is impossible for an outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) to act as a cause that brings about a ripened result (*vipākaphala*); it is impossible for the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) to be associated with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); and it is absolutely impossible for there to be birth, death, the attainment of fruits, or falling away from them during the states of sleep or dreaming.

There are five groups of consciousness that are without vitarka and vicāra, which take as their objects names (nāma) belonging to the past or future and thus transcending the present; there are olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses that are obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta); and there are those born in the higher realms who enter into clear realization (abhisamaya)—that these should have auditory consciousness, see forms with the eyes, hear sounds with the ears, or smell odors with the tongue, is absolutely impossible.
Categories such as these receive the designation "impossible" (*asthāna*); those contrary to them are all designated "possible" (*sthāna*).

But surely, since the knowledge of the possible already knows the impossible, and the knowledge of the impossible already knows the possible, why is it necessary to mention both the names "possible" and "impossible"?

Although this is indeed the case in principle, the two terms are spoken together because the name "possible" (*sthāna*) is taught to refute the theory of causelessness, while the name "impossible" (*asthāna*) is taught to refute the theory of false causes; thus, there is no fault in speaking of both based on the single essence of wisdom.

How can one know that, within the power regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*), the remaining nine powers are implicitly included and difficult to discern separately, since all of them possess this sense of possibility and impossibility?
That is to say, it is impossible for unwholesome conduct to result in a desirable maturation (*vipāka*) or for wholesome conduct to result in an undesirable maturation;
conversely, it is certainly possible for the opposite to occur.

Furthermore, it is impossible that one who knows truly could attain superior qualities through a concentration conducive to decline, or fall into regression through a concentration conducive to advancement;
the opposite of this is certainly possible.

Furthermore, one knows as it truly is that if a faculty of this category can realize this fruit, yet this faculty is not perfected while having already realized it in this realm—such a case is absolutely impossible;
whereas the opposite is certainly possible.
Furthermore, it is impossible that one who possesses inferior resolve and delights in base and evil things could ever attain supreme excellence;
however, it is certainly possible for the opposite to be true.
Furthermore, it is impossible for sentient beings to know the distinct natures of their various realms as they truly are and yet have mutual affinity;
conversely, it is certainly possible for the opposite to occur.

Furthermore, it is impossible that one who truly knows the conduct leading to birth and death could realize nirvana, or that one who knows the conduct leading to nirvana could produce birth and death;
the opposite of this is certainly possible.
Furthermore, to truly know that there is a beginning to the prior limit [of existence] is necessarily impossible;
whereas the opposite—that there is no such beginning—is certainly possible.

Likewise, to truly know that one who has not severed the fetters of birth will not be reborn after death, or that one who has already been born will never die, or that one will not go to either a happy or an unhappy destination—this is necessarily impossible.
The opposite of this certainly has its place.
Furthermore, it is impossible that one could attain the exhaustion of outflows through improper attention;
the opposite of this certainly has its place.

Within each of these individual powers, I have briefly cited a mere indication to manifest the principles of what is possible and what is impossible; if one were to exhaustively detail their specific matters, the discourse would be endless. Therefore, they should all be termed the "power of the possible and the impossible" (*sthānāsthāna-bala*); however, fearing that such a brief explanation might be difficult to comprehend, I have established distinct names for them.

Second is the power of knowledge regarding the maturation of karma (*karmavipākajñānabala*). It has eight knowledges as its nature, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

That is to say, the unimpeded knowledge that correctly discriminates how such types of karma produce such types of various matured fruits is called the power of knowledge regarding the maturation of karma.

Or it is called the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*karmasvaka-jñānabala*); that is to say, skillfully discerning that such types of fruits are summoned by the power of the karma created by oneself, and cannot be given away or taken away by others, such as wives or children.

Karma of such a nature necessarily brings about its own fruit and cannot be exchanged; the unimpeded knowledge regarding this is called the power of the knowledge of one's own karma (*svakarmajñānabala*).
Furthermore, the Buddha himself spoke of the characteristics of this power, saying:

"Bhikṣus, listen attentively! Regarding all karmic dharmas and their experiences in the past, future, and present—their distinct locations, distinct causes, distinct events, and distinct fruits—the Buddha knows them all as they truly are," and so forth, as extensively explained.
There are three types of karma and four types of dharma-reception; because they are both karma and dharma-reception, they are termed "karma.
Alternatively, because dharma-reception is the nature of karma, it is called "karmic dharma" (*karmadharma*), which signifies the various categories of karma.

This demonstrates that the Tathāgata is able to know, exactly as they truly are, the various categories of past and other karmas—such as their locations and specific distinctions—as well as the fruits they receive.

In this context, "distinct location" (*sthāna*) means a distinct place; it refers to knowing that a certain karma was created in a particular place, and that this karma will ripen in a particular place.

This means knowing that this karma was created in a place such as the celestial realms, and that this karma will ripen in a place such as the human realm; this is called knowing the distinct locations as they truly are.

Regarding "distinct causes," this refers to the meaning of distinct conditions: knowing that such karma ripens upon encountering these conditions, or knowing that this karma was created by these conditions; this is called knowing the distinct causes as they truly are.

To speak of "distinct entities" means the sense of distinct things. It means knowing that when such karma reaches its time of maturation, it has the power to draw forth and produce distinct entities such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

Alternatively, it refers to knowing that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the karma is not the same [as other things], which is called "knowing distinct entities. That is to say, one knows that this karma has this thing as its nature, whereas others do not; this is called understanding distinct entities as they truly are.

Regarding the "distinction of results," this refers to the meaning of distinct maturation (*vipāka*). It means knowing that such karma will certainly produce a maturation result, while this other karma cannot necessarily produce one; that the maturation of this karma will occur after a certain period while that of another does not; and that the maturation of this karma may be with remainder while that of another is without remainder. To be able to discern such subtle distinctions in maturation—which are otherwise extremely difficult to comprehend—is called "knowing the distinct results as they truly are."

The third is the power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; the fourth is the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties; the fifth is the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations; and the sixth is the power of knowledge regarding the various elements. These four powers all consist of nine types of knowledge, excluding only the knowledge of cessation.

It means that knowing, as it truly is, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth is called "attainment" (*prāpti*); and the unimpeded knowledge (*jñāna*) that skillfully sustains the savoring, the pure, and the untainted states—namely, the factors conducive to decline, maintenance, progress, and penetration—is called the "power of the knowledge of the meditative absorptions and so forth."
Furthermore, the Buddha himself spoke regarding the characteristics of this power, saying:

"Bhikṣus, listen attentively! The Buddha knows, as they truly are, the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti), as well as their defilement, purification, and establishment," and so forth, as extensively explained.
The characteristics of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and so forth shall be explained in the section on concentration (*samādhi*).

"Defilement" refers to that which obstructs the realization of meditative absorption and so forth; "purity" refers to the purification of these very same phenomena. The abiding of all pure phenomena is termed "establishment."

The stage conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*) is termed "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*); the stages conducive to excellence (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*) and conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*) are termed "purity" (*vyavadāna*); and the stage conducive to maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*) is termed "establishment" (*vyavasthāna*).

If one knows, as they truly are, the distinctions among the categories of faculties (*indriya*) by which various classes of sentient beings attain superior qualities, this is called the "power of knowledge regarding the superiority and inferiority of the faculties" (*indriyaparāparajñānabala*).
Furthermore, the Buddha himself spoke regarding the characteristics of this power, saying:
"Bhikṣus, listen attentively! The Buddha knows, as they truly are, the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings," and so forth, as extensively explained.
This intent reveals that the Buddha’s knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings is without error.

Although there are those with middling faculties who depend upon the superior and inferior, they are not mentioned separately because they are subsumed within the categories of the inferior and the superior.
In this context, what phenomena are designated by the term "faculties" (*indriya*)?
They refer to faith and the other [wholesome faculties]. Even in the general continuum of one who has severed the roots of goodness, there still exist past and future wholesome dharmas such as faith.
Alternatively, regarding the eyes, the mind, and so forth:

if one possesses unimpeded knowledge that knows, as they truly are, the differences in the inclinations and pleasures of various sentient beings, this is called the power of knowing the diverse inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*).
Furthermore, the Buddha himself spoke regarding the characteristics of this power, saying:
"Bhikṣus, listen attentively! The Buddha knows, as they truly are, the various inclinations of sentient beings," and so forth, as explained at length.

This intent reveals that the Buddha knows the various distinctions among the categories of pleasure and inclination of all sentient beings, for "pleasure," "inclination," and "resolute belief" are termed "distinctions.

If one knows, in accordance with reality, the dispositions (*āśaya*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the natures of phenomena (*dharmatā*) formed through repeated practice since beginningless time within the classes of sentient beings—possessing unimpeded knowledge regarding these various distinctions—this is called the power of knowing the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñāna-bala*).
Furthermore, the Buddha himself spoke regarding the characteristics of this power, saying:
"Bhikṣus, listen attentively. The Buddha knows, as they truly are, the various elements (*dhātu*) in the world, which are not of a single nature," and so forth, as explained at length.
The "various realms" (nānā-dhātu) signify the sense of distinctness; the "not a single realm" signifies the sense of multiplicity.
It should be understood that within this context, "realm" (dhātu), "disposition" (āśaya), "latent tendencies" (anuśaya), and "dharma-nature" (dharmatā) are merely different names for the same thing.
Since these four powers likewise take conditioned phenomena as their object, they comprise only nine of the ten knowledges.

Regarding the seventh power, the knowledge of the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*), the word "or" indicates that there are two interpretations of its meaning. If it is held that this power takes only the various paths leading [to liberation] as its object, then nine knowledges are included, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
If it is claimed that this [power] also takes as its object the fruits toward which the Path leads, then its nature consists of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).

That is to say, the unimpeded knowledge that knows the causes and effects of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as they truly are, as well as the knowledge of the path to exhaustion (*kṣayamārga*), is called the power of knowing the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminīpratipad-jñānabala*).
Furthermore, the Buddha himself spoke regarding the characteristics of this power, saying:
"Bhikṣus, listen attentively! The Buddha knows, as it truly is, all paths leading everywhere; thus it is explained at length."
This meaning reveals that the Buddha is able to know, as they truly are, the courses leading toward saṃsāra and the courses leading toward nirvāṇa.
Within the courses leading toward saṃsāra, there are those leading to the hells up to those leading to the heavens; within each of these, there are again many varieties.

Regarding the courses leading toward nirvāṇa, there are the distinctions of the three vehicles, and within each of these, there are again many varieties. Based on this general description, the term "single course" (ekāyana) is established.

The eighth is the power of the knowledge of recollecting former abodes, and the ninth is the power of the knowledge of death and rebirth; both of these powers are of the nature of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), because there is a distinction between the characteristics of these two powers.
That is to say, the unimpeded knowledge that knows, as they truly are, the distinctions regarding the past lives of oneself and others is called the eighth power.
The unimpeded knowledge that knows, as they truly are, the continuity of rebirth in future existences for all classes of sentient beings is called the ninth power.
Furthermore, the Buddha himself spoke of these two characteristics, saying:
"Bhikṣus, listen attentively! Regarding the various past lives of the Buddha—whether one birth, two births, or as extensively explained as follows..."
The Buddha’s divine eye is pure and surpasses that of humans; he sees all sentient beings, and so forth, as explained at length.
These two are analyzed in detail as they appear among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*). Tenth is the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-bala*).

Alternatively, regarding the statement that "sound also reveals the meaning," there are two interpretations. If it is held that [the knowledge] takes only the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) as its object, then six knowledges are involved, excluding the knowledge of the path, suffering, origin, and the knowledge of others' minds.
If it is held that it also takes the means (*upāya*) for the exhaustion of outflows as its object, then ten knowledges constitute its nature.

This is indeed logical, for within the analysis of the characteristics [of the powers], it is stated that both the knowledge regarding exhaustion (*kṣaya*) and the unimpeded knowledge regarding the state of having exhausted (*kṣayāya*), are termed the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*).
Furthermore, the Buddha himself spoke of the characteristics of this power, saying:

"Bhikṣus, listen attentively! Because the Buddha has destroyed the outflows, he is liberated in mind and wisdom from all that is without outflow; he has personally realized, fully attained, and experienced this, being able to know correctly for himself: 'Birth for me has been exhausted,' and so forth, as extensively explained."

These latter three powers are identical to the three supernormal knowledges (*vidyā*). Because these three among the six supernormal knowledges are particularly distinguished, they are established as the "three illuminations" (*tisro vidyāḥ*) within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); when present in the body of a Tathāgata, they are also termed "powers."

Even if the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhiviṣaya*) and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) were present in the Buddha’s body, they would still lack great utility and thus are not designated as "powers" (*bala*).

For instance, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) can perceive the distinctions in the maturation (*vipāka*) of sentient beings within the happy and miserable realms; because it can thereby induce the arising of superior knowledge and correctly understand the karma that brings about those states, it is established under the name of the "knowledge of death and rebirth" (*cyutyupapādajñāna*).
The supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*) and the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) do not possess such great utility; therefore, those two are not established as powers (*bala*).

However, the reason the power of knowing others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*) is not mentioned separately is that its meaning is already subsumed within the powers of the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, because within the faculties and other factors of others, there exist both mind (*citta*) and mental concomitants (*caitta*).

Furthermore, the Bhagavat possesses all-encompassing wisdom and has attained mastery even in fields such as the arts and sciences; yet, since the work of a Buddha is fully accomplished by this [wisdom] alone, other forms of knowledge have no distinct or superior function therein. Therefore, although they exist, they are not mentioned separately.

This is because, by relying solely on the universal awakening to the ten kinds of objects of knowledge, all that the Buddha ought to do is fully perfected. What are these ten kinds of objects of knowledge? They are: the meaning of cause and non-cause among all phenomena;

the distinctions between the karma and its results across many dispersed states; the different categories of qualities within the meditative states; the differences in the faculties, inclinations, and elements of the sentient beings to be converted; the distinctions between the causes and effects of the remedial and the remediable; the different ways of traversing the past and future limits of time; and the distinct methods for the cessation of defilement and the non-continuation [of rebirth].

It is solely by awakening to this that the Buddha’s work is accomplished; whether other factors exist or not does not cause benefit or harm. Therefore, only these ten are designated as "powers" (*bala*).
Furthermore, when the Buddha observes the sentient beings to be converted, he requires only these ten knowledges (*jñāna*) to provide teachings that accord with their capacities.
That is to say, by means of the first wisdom, one observes the differences among those to be converted regarding their capacity or incapacity for the various vehicles;
by means of the second wisdom, one observes the distinctions in the karmic obstructions within the mental continuums of those to be converted.

By means of the third knowledge, one observes that those beings to be converted possess either attachment or non-attachment toward the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth, and the varying degrees of lightness or heaviness of their afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); by knowing these two causes, one also knows the ripening obstructions (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
By means of the fourth knowledge, one contemplates the distinctions in the functional capacities of the purified categories among those beings to be converted;
by means of the fifth knowledge, one contemplates the distinctions in the preparatory applications toward the categories of realization and purity among those beings to be converted.
By means of the sixth knowledge, one observes that the beings to be converted differ in their dispositions and inclinations regarding the categories of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*).

By means of the seventh knowledge, one observes the various distinctions among the beneficial and non-beneficial activities of those beings to be converted, and correctly contemplates while cultivating tranquility (*śamatha*).
By means of the eighth knowledge, one contemplates the distinctions among the various karmic accumulations gathered by those to be converted during their past lives;
by means of the ninth knowledge, one contemplates the distinctions regarding the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) for those to be converted in future lives.

Because the tenth wisdom observes that there are differences in the skillful means for liberating the beings to be converted, if any one of these ten wisdoms were lacking, one would not be fully equipped for the task of converting sentient beings; furthermore, having too many would be useless. Therefore, they are neither increased nor decreased.

The essential nature has already been explained. Regarding their distinction by way of the levels (*bhūmi*): the eighth and ninth [supernormal powers] depend on the four dhyānas; the remaining eight arise based on all eleven levels. These eleven levels consist of the desire realm, the four dhyānas, the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*). Such is the total number of levels upon which these various sublime qualities depend.
The basis in terms of the level has already been explained.
Regarding the distinction of the physical basis: all [ten knowledges] rely upon the male body of a Buddha in Jambudvīpa, for only this is capable of serving as the support for such power.
Since these ten knowledges also exist in the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), why is it that they receive the name "powers" (*bala*) only when residing in a Buddha?
Now, that which is designated as a "power" (bala) refers to unimpeded functioning; because the Buddha’s wisdom functions without impediment toward its objects, it is given the name "power.

This is not the case for others, for even the followers of the two vehicles cannot perceive the roots of goodness conducive to liberation within the mental continuums of sentient beings, much less can they know other profound and subtle matters.

For example, although Śāriputra abandoned his quest for liberation, he was unable to perceive the number of births of the pigeon being pursued by the hawk across its two temporal limits of past and future;
likewise, Mahāmaudgalyāyana could not perceive the distinctions among the various hungry ghosts led by the winds of karma.

Therefore, regarding the divine eye and other such supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the two vehicles, their observation of the distance and proximity of realms differs from that of the Buddha; because they are not unimpeded, they are not called "powers" (*bala*).
Since the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is the same for both the two vehicles and the Buddha, for what reason is it only the wisdom of the Buddha that is designated as a "power"?
Only the World-Honored One possesses the specific knowledge that universally penetrates the distinct characteristics of all outflows (āsrava) exhausted by sentient beings.

That is to say, the Bhagavat’s knowledge regarding the various categories and distinctions of the exhaustion of all outflows among sentient beings is unimpeded; this is not the case for the two vehicles. Therefore, the name "Power" belongs exclusively to the Buddha.
Furthermore, it is because the wisdom of the Buddhas alone is sharp and powerful.
In what way is it sharp and powerful?

Because the power of the Buddha’s wisdom can swiftly sever the afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). This is like individuals of strong or weak strength using sharp or dull knives to cut grass and other things.
Since the characteristics of the aggregates (skandha) are no different among all classes of sentient beings, how does the Buddha perceive various realms (dhātu)?
Although the characteristics of the aggregates are the same for all classes of sentient beings, there are nonetheless distinctions within them.

This means that although the essence of those aggregates is without distinction, there are immeasurable varieties of different categories; the Buddha knows them all exactly as they are without any obstruction, and thus the World-Honored One possesses the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*).

Alternatively, the names and reputations of the Tathāgatas are lofty and far-reaching, and their rarefied wisdom and wondrous functions are boundless; they can only be known by Buddhas and cannot be fathomed by others.
Since there are no distinct characteristics within that which is understood by others, what is so strange about the Tathāgata being able to know distinct characteristics?
Having already discussed the general principles regarding the power of the Buddhas' minds, we shall now discuss the physical power achieved by Bodhisattvas at that time.
The verse says:
The body possesses the strength of Nārāyaṇa, or else every joint possesses it as well.
The elephant and other [seven] multiples increase [in strength]; this has the sphere of tangibility as its nature.
The treatise says:
The physical power of the Buddha’s birth-body is equal to that of Nārāyaṇa.
Other masters say:
"Each and every limb and joint of the Buddha’s body possesses the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
In truth, however, the physical power of all Buddhas is boundless, just like their mental power, because it is capable of sustaining the great merit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

The Greatly Awakened One (Mahābuddha), the Solitary Realizer (Pratyekabuddha), and the Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) have their limbs and joints connected in successive order, resembling a coiled dragon or a linked chain with interlocking hooks; therefore, when these three are compared, there is a gradation in the superiority or inferiority of their strength.
What is the measure of the strength of Nārāyaṇa?
It is ten times greater at each successive stage than the seven types of elephants and so forth.

That is to say: the ordinary elephant, the fragrant elephant (*gandhahastin*), the mahānagna, the praskandin, the varāṅga, the cāṇūra, and Nārāyaṇa; each subsequent one possesses ten times the strength of the preceding one.
Some say: the first sixty [units] increase tenfold each time, equaling half the strength of Nārāyaṇa; one double that amount constitutes the full strength of Nārāyaṇa.
Other masters say:
The strength of this elephant king is equal to that of a thousand airāvaṇas.
What is the measure of the strength of this elephant king?

When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven were about to go to the pleasure groves, the elephant king, having perceived it, manifested various heads adorned in diverse ways and proceeded to the celestial palace.

The retinues of these devas number in the thousands; mounted upon them, they soar through the air as lightly as if holding a birch leaf, swiftly arriving at pleasure gardens to enjoy themselves as they wish.
Such is the power and majesty of the great celestial elephant kings; a thousand times this strength is equal to that of Nārāyaṇa.
Among these various explanations, only the former is largely consistent with reason.
Thus, bodily strength has the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) as its nature; this should, in its entirety, comprise all the varieties of tangibles. Some say:
It is merely a differentiation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Some say: "There is a derivative tangible (*upādāya-spraṣṭavya*) that exists apart from the [other] seven."
Some say: that which is heavy is strength, while that which is light is weakness.
This is what is called the physical body strength of the Buddha.
What are the specific characteristics of the four fearlessnesses of a Buddha?
The verse says:
The four fearlessnesses correspond, in order, to the first, the twelfth, and the seventh powers.
The treatise states:

The four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) of the Buddha are explained at length in the sūtras. First, the fearlessness of being perfectly awakened (*samyaksaṃbodhi-vaiśāradya*), which has the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) as its nature, is like the first power (*bala*).
Second, the fearlessness of having eternally exhausted all outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*), which has six knowledges as its nature, is like the tenth power.
The third, the fearlessness in proclaiming the obstructive dharmas, has eight knowledges as its nature, as in the second power.
The fourth, the fearlessness in proclaiming the path leading out [of suffering], has nine or ten knowledges as its nature, as in the seventh power.
For what reason are there only four fearlessnesses of the Buddhas?
It is solely because by this measure the perfection of both the self and others' virtues is revealed in the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

That is to say, the first fearlessness reveals the perfection of the Buddha's own wisdom-virtue, and the second fearlessness reveals the perfection of the Buddha's own abandonment-virtue; these two demonstrate that the Buddha's virtues for his own benefit are fulfilled. To further reveal the World-Honored One’s perfection of virtue in benefiting others, the latter two fearlessnesses are therefore taught.
The third fearlessness prevents one from following wrong paths, while the fourth fearlessness causes one to proceed toward the right path.

This means that in various places, the Buddha teaches his disciples the obstructing factors so that they may be abandoned; this is precisely what causes them to cultivate the skillful means for the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).

Furthermore, in various places he teaches the path leading out [of suffering] to his disciples so that they may practice correctly; this is precisely to cause them to cultivate the skillful means for the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).
These two manifest the perfection of the Buddha’s virtue of benefiting others.

However, it is solely because these four, as appropriate, manifest the Buddha’s perfected virtues of wisdom and abandonment—both for himself and for others—to their ultimate consummation that exactly four are established.
How can it be said that fearlessness is itself wisdom? One should rather say that fearlessness is that which is accomplished by wisdom.
In truth, this is indeed so; however, it is to demonstrate that fearlessness has wisdom as its proximate cause that the essence of fearlessness is derived from wisdom.
Now, fearlessness means the absence of timidity or dread; because one does not fear others due to the possession of wisdom, wisdom serves as the causal nature of fearlessness.

Only the four sublime knowledges of the Buddha are the causes of the four fearlessnesses; that is to say, the sublime knowledge regarding all phenomena and all their aspects possessed by the Tathāgatas is the cause of the first fearlessness.
The sublime wisdom of all Tathāgatas, which has severed all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), is the second cause of fearlessness.

Because our World-Honored One alone possesses this, he is neither saddened by insults nor delighted by offerings and praise; though constantly opposed and rejected, he always benefits others; though subjected to cutting and piercing, he feels deep compassion; though endowed with supreme assistants, supernatural powers, wisdom, and skills, he remains free from arrogance; he does not give rise to resentment when faced with rejection, nor does he harbor partial affection for those who delight in serving him.

Although he practices the means of attraction, he does not seek followers; although he practices reprimand, he does not wish for estrangement; although he temporarily expels them, he does not use harsh words; and although he permanently banishes them, he does not cause them to fall into error.

Though he is fearless, he is not coarse or fierce; though he is always affectionate, he does not give rise to craving; though he displays his own virtues, he does not pursue fame or profit; though he points out the faults of others, he does not do so to cause them shame; though he gathers disciples, he does not form a partisan faction; though he rebukes wrong companions, he does not destroy their friendships. Sentient beings of noble lineage and high repute frequently come to seek his intimacy, yet he shows them only the True Dharma and does not engage in worldly socializing. All of these qualities arise from the sublime wisdom of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*); therefore, this sublime wisdom constitutes the second cause.
If the Tathāgatas possess the sublime wisdom that knows whether the assembly of disciples will suffer loss or gain, this constitutes the cause for the latter two forms of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).

Alternatively, the essence of fearlessness is itself the fourfold sublime wisdom. "Fear" (*bhaya*) refers to timidity; it carries the sense of not fully comprehending the Dharma and harboring terror. Wisdom possesses the capacity to directly counteract this fear, and because it is the opposite of fear, it is called "fearlessness."
Is it not the case that the absence of wisdom (*ajñāna*) is itself the essence of fear? How then can it be said that the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*) is itself fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*)?
This objection is invalid, because wisdom serves as the direct antidote to many states, just as the absence of doubt (*niḥsaṃśaya*) does.

That is to say, just as wisdom (*jñāna*) can directly counteract ignorance (*ajñāna*), it also possesses the capacity to directly counteract fear; therefore, it receives the name "wisdom" and is also called "fearlessness.
Just as it counteracts ignorance, it can also counteract doubt; therefore, it receives the name "wisdom" and is also called "certainty" (*niścaya*).

Although the ignorance that is the object of antidote is not itself doubt, wisdom and the absence of doubt are said to be one in essence; likewise, although the absence of ignorance differs from fearlessness, the term "fearlessness" refers directly to the essence of wisdom, because a single wholesome factor is capable of severing many unwholesome states.
Some say: "Ignorance also subsumes the essence of fear.
Therefore, one should not raise an objection regarding this point.
What is the difference between the powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)?

There is no difference, for their essence is identical as both consist of wisdom (*jñāna*). Nevertheless, the term "power" is applied to the essence of wisdom based on one specific sense, while the name "fearlessness" is established based on another specific sense.
That which is the cause for not being defeated is called "power" (*bala*); that which is the cause for not being timid or fearful is called "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*).
Alternatively, the initial establishment [of the teaching] is called "power," while remaining unshakable once established is called "fearlessness."
Alternatively, the ability to subdue others is called "power" (*bala*), while the capacity to overcome the arguments of others is called "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*).
Other masters say:
for example, a skilled physician who has mastered all medical treatises is said to possess "power," while his excellence in curing various ailments is called "fearlessness."
Some say: "Vigor" (*bala*) refers to being robust and capable, while "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*) refers to being courageous and undaunted.

Thus, there is also a distinction between these two meanings: the sense of accomplishing tasks is the meaning of vigor, and the sense of being without timidity or apprehension is the meaning of fearlessness.
What are the specific characteristics of the Buddha’s three applications of mindfulness?
The verse says:
The three applications of mindfulness consist of mindfulness and wisdom, taking as their objects conditions that are favorable, unfavorable, or both.
The Treatise says:
The Buddha’s three foundations of mindfulness are explained at length in the Sūtra.

When the assembly of disciples is consistently respectful and able to correctly receive and practice [the teaching], the Tathāgata does not give rise to joy in dependence upon them; rather, he remains equanimous, dwelling in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension. This is called the Tathāgata’s first foundation of mindfulness.

If the assembly of disciples is merely disrespectful and does not correctly receive and practice [the teaching], the Tathāgata, conditioned by this, gives rise to no sorrow or distress; he relinquishes it and abides in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension. This is called the Tathāgata’s second application of mindfulness.

Among the assembly of disciples, some are respectful and able to correctly receive and practice [the teachings], while others are disrespectful and do not correctly receive and practice them; the Tathāgata, regarding this, gives rise to neither joy nor displeasure, but remains equanimous, dwelling in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension—this is called the third application of mindfulness of the Tathāgata.

Although those being transformed do not respectfully receive and practice [the teaching], the Buddha, the World-Honored One, nevertheless rains down the rain of Dharma; by means of this skillful expedient, they or other sentient beings may at a later time enter the True Dharma.

It is not that what was previously stated as four is now restated as three; rather, one may generally say there are seven applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), for these three are subsumed within the previous four.

That is to say, they are included within the application of mindfulness that takes external phenomena as its object; however, the substance (*svabhāva*) of these three types consists of both mindfulness and wisdom (*prajñā*).

This means that by abiding in right mindfulness and right situational awareness (*samprajanya*), one does not give rise to joy or sorrow regarding the three types of objects. One should not see that because certain great *śrāvakas* do not give rise to joy or sorrow regarding these three objects, these three qualities are therefore not the unique attributes of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). It is only the Buddha who has completely severed these along with their habitual tendencies, and who thoroughly understands the distinctions between the dispositions (*gotra*) of sentient beings.

If the assembly of disciples were subject to the Tathāgata, they would necessarily experience extreme joy when things accorded with him and grief when they opposed him; that the Buddha could remain unmoved by these is truly marvelous.
However, as he is not subject to the śrāvakas, his remaining unmoved is not extraordinary; therefore, this quality receives the name of "unshared" (*āveṇika*) only in reference to the Buddha.
How are the various aspects of the great compassion of all Buddhas distinguished?
The verse says:
Great compassion is exclusively conventional wisdom; It is distinguished by its equipment, its mode of activity, and its object.
Because it is impartial and of the highest degree, compassion differs [from great compassion] due to eight causes.
The treatise says:

The Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Tathāgata has conventional wisdom as its nature; it takes all sentient beings universally as its object and functions through the three modes of perception, such as the perception of suffering-as-suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
It is not that such a principle exists for untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*); upon what basis, then, is this name "Great Compassion" established?
It is established as "Great" based on five meanings.
First, it is great by way of its provisions (*sambhāra*), meaning it is accomplished through the vast provisions of merit and wisdom.
Second, it is great by way of its mode of activity (*ākāra*), meaning that this power is able to form mental images (*ākāra*) regarding the objects of the three types of suffering;
third, it is great by way of its object (*ālambana*), meaning that it takes all sentient beings of the three realms as its object;
fourth, it is great by way of its impartiality, meaning that it acts for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings with equanimity.
It is "great" (mahat) for five reasons due to its superior nature (*adhimātra*): first, because it is of the highest degree, such that no other compassion can equal it;

second, according to other masters, because it is realized through great application (*prayoga*); third, because it is accomplished only within the person of a Great Being (*mahāsattva*); fourth, because it is reckoned among the jewels of great merit; and fifth, because it is capable of uprooting the great suffering and affliction of sentient beings. For these reasons, it is designated by the name "Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*).
What is the difference between compassion (*karuṇā*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)?
These two differ by way of eight causes.
First, by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): because non-aversion (*avyāpāda*) and non-obstruction (*avihiṃsā*) are distinct in their intrinsic natures.
Second, by way of the physical basis (*āśraya*): they differ because the basis is either common to others or exclusive to the Buddha.
