Regarding the fruits of a single dhyāna bound to upper and lower stages, there is superiority or inferiority based on the levels of the supporting mental applications and so forth.

Regarding the fruits of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) bound to a single level or to higher and lower levels: although the levels are equal in terms of their basis, there is a distinction in the excellence or inferiority of their mental formations (saṃskāra). A fruit of a higher level may be bound to a lower level, and a fruit of a lower level may be bound to a higher level; this follows the respective inferiority or excellence of the levels and the excellence or inferiority of their bases and formations.
As it is with the attainment of dhyāna, so it is with the mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta), because the fruit and its basis are acquired simultaneously.

However, there are three general occasions for the attainment of dhyāna, distinguished by the differences between detachment from passion (vairāgya), rebirth (upapatti), and preparatory application (prayoga).
This means that when one abandons the defilements of a lower stage and attains a higher dhyāna, one also acquires the emanated minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) produced by that concentration.

Furthermore, when one dies from a higher stage and is reborn in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), or when one gives rise to superior qualities through application (*prayoga*), one newly acquires the dhyāna that serves as the basis, and simultaneously acquires the emanated minds produced by it.

When one attains the fruit of Arhatship based on a body in the desire realm, or when one attains the fruit of Arhatship during the stage of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*), all fourteen transformation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) are acquired simultaneously.

Even when one’s body is in the fourth dhyāna and attains the fruit of Arhatship, one acquires five transformation-minds; there is no principle whereby one could emerge directly from meditative absorption through a transformation-mind.

This [pure transformation-mind] arises from pure meditative absorption (*śuddha-samādhi*) and its own kind; it can immediately produce its own kind and pure meditative absorption. Therefore, it arises only from two [causes] and produces two [results], and not otherwise.
Only a transformation-mind of its own level gives rise to transformative activity of its own level; the speech produced by such transformation arises from a mind of its own level or a lower level.

This means that in the desire realm and the first dhyāna, the transformation-body and its speech arise solely from the mind of their own level. When a transformation-body in a higher level produces speech, it does so by means of a mind from the first dhyāna, because in those higher levels there is no mind capable of producing manifest action (vijñapti) of its own.
If one is born in the desire realm or the second dhyāna and above, how can manifest action be produced when a transformative event occurs?

It is not the case that the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) can arise based on a body belonging to a different realm, for they must necessarily rely upon a body belonging to their own realm.
This [position] is without fault, because they take as their support the manifestation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) subsumed under that [specific] realm.

This means that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are brought forth into manifestation and remain in close contact with the body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); based upon these, one gives rise to the mind capable of manifesting [action].
There is no mind of the non-concentrated stage (*asamāhitabhūmi*) that arises depending on a body of a scattered stage (*vyutthānabhūmi*).

Alternatively, there may arise a mind capable of manifesting expression based upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*), such as the visual and auditory consciousnesses produced by relying on concentration.
If a single emanator produces many emanated bodies, it is only when the emanator speaks that the emanated bodies speak; the articulation of their speech and sounds is entirely identical.
Therefore, a verse says: "When the one who transforms speaks, all those who are transformed speak;
when the one who transforms remains silent, all those who are transformed likewise remain silent."

This refers only to others; the Buddha is not like them. Because the power of concentration of all Buddhas is most sovereign, it is possible that his speech does not coincide with that of those he transforms, and what is expressed by his voice may also differ.

If, when one utters speech as a transformation in the three higher stages, the manifest mind of the first dhyāna arises to produce it, then at the moment this mind arises, the transformative mind has already ceased; thus there would be no transformation body, so how could the transformation body speak?

By the power of a prior vow, one retains the emanated body while subsequently giving rise to other mental states that produce the informative karma of speech; therefore, there is no fault of lacking a physical basis for the emanated speech.

It is not only during the lifetime of the emanator that one can retain an emanated body to cause it to remain for a long duration; one may also cause it to remain until after the end of life, just as the Venerable Mahākāśyapa retained his skeletal body until the time of Maitreya.
Only that which is of a solid and substantial nature can remain for a long duration; otherwise, Kāśyapa would have had to leave behind his flesh and other tissues.
Other masters say:

"The power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) to maintain the body cannot possibly cause it to persist beyond death; the skeletal remains of the noble Mahākāśyapa were maintained for a long time by the support of the devas."
A beginner, by means of many transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*), must rely upon a physical basis to produce a single transformative act.
One who has attained mastery, by means of a single transformation-mind, is able to produce numerous transformative acts without relying upon a physical basis.

In total, there are two types of transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*): first, those produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), and second, those acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*), etc.; the fruits of transformation they produce are likewise described as such.
Regarding the domains encompassed by transformations produced through cultivation, they are as previously stated, because one cannot transform them into the bodies of sentient beings.
Those obtained at birth and so forth are manifested as nine locations within the desire realm and seven in the form realm, based on their non-separation from the sense organs (*indriya*).

Regarding the statement that "nine [locations] and so forth are manifested," in principle there is no capacity to manifest actual sense organs; this applies to those who have attained the fruits of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*) when they are without mind. For others, manifestation is possible. When those who have attained the fruits of cultivation produce informative action (*vijñapti*), it arises through the mind of the one who manifests the transformation; for others, it may arise from their own mind, producing bodily or vocal informative action.
If the food and drink produced as a result of cultivation serves to sustain the body, it must necessarily be digested within the body of the emanator.

If it is swallowed for other purposes, such as precious metals or stones, it will either remain within that emanated body or be placed elsewhere as appropriate; the remaining emanated food and drink abide according to their respective supports.

The transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) resulting from cultivation is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); others, however, pertain to all three natures, namely the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth.
Just as the transformative minds of devas, nāgas, and others are capable of transformation, they are likewise able to manifest transformations of both their own bodies and those of others.
Regarding the terms "divine eye" and "divine ear," what do they signify?
Do they refer to the essence of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva*), or do they refer to the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*)?
If they refer to wisdom, they should not be called "divine eye" and "divine ear"; if they refer to the material sense organs, they should not be called "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*).
This has already been explained. What was previously stated?

It was said that within the four fundamental dhyānas, there exists a superior neutral wisdom associated with meditative concentration, which is termed the supernormal powers of the divine eye and the divine ear; the superior great elements produced by this [wisdom] are termed the divine eye and the divine ear.
What is their essential nature?
The verse says:
The divine eye and ear are faculties; They are pure matter belonging to the stage of meditative concentration.
Constantly of the same class and without deficiency, they apprehend what is obstructed, subtle, distant, and so forth.
The treatise says:
Their substance is precisely the divine eye and ear faculties, because they take sound and light as their preparatory practice (*prayoga*).

By relying on the four dhyānas, one brings forth the two faculties of the eye and ear—composed of the subtle primary elements (mahābhūta) of that stage and consisting of translucent matter (rūpaprasāda)—which see forms and hear sounds; these are called the divine eye and divine ear.
In this way, why are the eye and ear called "divine" (*deva*)?
Their very substance is divine because they are subsumed under the meditative stages (*samāpatti-bhūmi*) and are utterly pure; thus, they are designated by the name "divine.
As this sūtra states:
The divine eye and ear are devoid of skin, flesh, sinews, or blood; they consist solely of pure matter (*rūpa*) derived from the sublime primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Furthermore, there are three types of divine eyes and ears: first, those obtained through cultivation, as previously described;
second, those obtained by birth, which refers to those born among the gods.

Third, those that resemble the divine: this refers to beings born in other realms who, being produced by the influence of superior karma and so forth, possess the capacity for distant seeing and hearing similar to the divine eyes and ears—such as the *maṇi* (treasure-minister), bodhisattvas, wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), various nāgas, spirits, and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

The eyes and ears cultivated through practice are always of the same class (*sabhāga*) across past, present, and future births; because they must necessarily be accompanied by consciousness in the present in order to see and hear, their locations must be complete, unobstructed, and without defect.

For example, all sentient beings born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are able to perceive, as appropriate, forms and sounds that are obstructed, extremely subtle, distant, or located in various directions.
Therefore, regarding this, there is a verse:
"The fleshly eye, with respect to various directions, [Perceives] forms that are obstructed, subtle, or distant."
"There is no one capable of seeing its function; the divine eye sees it without omission.

Does this mean that while the previously mentioned mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) is acquired through cultivation and differs from others, the five [powers] beginning with the supernormal power of the base (*ṛddhiviṣaya*) each differ as well?
There are also [those who do]. How so? The verse says:
The five types of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) are produced through cultivation, birth, incantations, medicinal herbs, and karmic fruition;
the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) is produced through cultivation, birth, and incantations, with the addition of divination by signs (*nimitta*).
Three—cultivation, birth, and karmic fruition—are excluded from cultivation; all [the remaining] are of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).
Humans possess only that which is acquired through birth; those in the hells are able to know it from the very beginning. The commentary states:

There are five general types of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) belonging to the category of knowledge of the sphere of supernormal power: first, that acquired through cultivation; second, that acquired through birth; third, that accomplished through mantras; fourth, that accomplished through medicine; and fifth, that accomplished through karma. The supernormal powers of King Mandhātṛ, beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and others are subsumed under that which is accomplished through karma.
Other masters say:
There are four types of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), namely the three preceding ones and transformation (*nirmāṇa*) as one.
Regarding "transformation," as the Sūtra says:
"Dividing one into many," and so forth, as explained at length.

Regarding the category of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are four types in total; the first three are as described above, with the addition of that accomplished through signs (*nimitta*). Each of the remaining three [knowledges] has three types:

namely, those acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanāja*), those born of birth (*upapattija*), and those produced by karma (*karmaja*). With the exception of those obtained through cultivation, all are categorized as wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth; however, because they are not the fruits of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), they do not receive the designation "supernormal" (*abhijñā*).

Among humans, there is none who possesses [recollection] acquired at birth; all others may possess it, being comprised within what is innate, what arises through mindfulness, or what is produced by karma, as the case may be.
Humans are able to recollect the past due to their prior karma.

When first taking birth in the hell realm, one knows the minds of others and past lives solely through innate knowledge of others' minds (*upapatti-lābhika-paracitta-jñāna*) and the knowledge of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).
Once one is oppressed by painful sensations, there is no further capacity for cognition; how, then, can it be proven that they remember the past?
As stated in the sutra, they recollect for themselves:
"In the past, we heard others speak of the faults of sensual desires yet did not feel revulsion; therefore, at this present time, we undergo such intense suffering."
They can only remember their immediately preceding life.
In other realms, as appropriate, there is always the capacity for such knowledge; for example, animals such as conch-blowers and dogs possess knowledge of the past.
The spirits know the past, as a verse says:
"I formerly accumulated great wealth, By means of both dharma and adharma;
Now another enjoys that prosperity, While I alone endure poverty and suffering."
The devas know the past, as it is said in a verse:
“I have offered the Jetavana Grove, Wherein the Great Dharma King dwells;
As the noble Saṅgha makes use of it, My heart is filled with joy.”
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"All those born in the heavens must, upon their initial birth, give rise to three thoughts, saying:
'From where have I died?'"
Where was one born in this present life?
By virtue of what karma did one come to be born in this realm?
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 76.

Chapter 8: Discernment of Concentration (Samādhi-viniścaya), Part One. Having thus already discerned the distinctions among the various types of knowledge (*jñāna*), we shall next analyze the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) upon which that knowledge depends.
Only the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) can serve as a complete basis; therefore, the meditative absorptions are discussed first herein.

Alternatively, within the previously discussed common qualities, those qualities accomplished through wisdom—such as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*)—have already been explained. Now, the remaining qualities accomplished [by other means] shall be discussed; among these, the concentration that serves as their basis is discussed first.
Furthermore, regarding the dhyānas within the various concentrations, the verse says:
The dhyānas are four, each having two types; among these, those attained through birth have already been explained.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is defined as being virtuous and one-pointed; together with its attendants, it is of the nature of the five aggregates.
Initially, it possesses investigation (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*); subsequently, it gradually abandons these preceding factors.
The treatise says:
Since all meritorious qualities largely depend upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
one should first analyze the distinctions of meditative concentration.
There are four types in total.
This refers to the first, second, third, and fourth [dhyānas].
Yet, do not the various dhyānas possess unique names and designations such as "loving-kindness" (maitrī) and so forth?
Why, then, are they established with distinct names based solely on the enumeration of the first four?
In this context, it is not that there are no unique names or concepts;
however, there is no single name that universally encompasses all stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because each *dhyāna* has two distinct types.
This is because there is a distinction between meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and birth (*upapatti*).
Regarding the dhyānas of birth, they have already been explained previously:
namely, eight in the fourth [dhyāna], three in each of the first three.
There is no distinct name that collectively designates a single stage;
the general characteristics of these meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and dhyānas are without distinction.
That is to say, if one considers the essence of these four collectively:

All are subsumed under the nature of the wholesome (*kuśala-dharma*), because one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*) has wholesome meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If accompanied by its attendants, it has the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its nature.
Since these two are equally difficult to distinguish from one another,
although their characteristics are not different, their stages (bhūmi) are distinct.
To manifest this difference in stage, they are designated by name according to their numerical count.
Therefore, it is described as the first up to the fourth.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtra himself raises a question and provides an answer:
"What is meant by one-pointedness of mind?"
This means focusing exclusively on a single object.

That response is unreasonable; if the visual consciousness and the mental consciousness were to have the same object, they would have to be called "one-pointedness" (*ekāgratā*). Therefore, one must seek a different principle for this case.

That is to say, if one-pointedness of mind (ekāgratā) were defined as relying upon a single foundational faculty (indriya) and focusing exclusively upon a single object (ālambana), would it not follow that since there is no shifting of objects within a single moment of consciousness, one-pointedness would exist in all states of mind?
In reality, all [mental states] possess this quality, because each momentary mind and its associated mental factors (citta-caitta) operate upon a single object.

Nevertheless, not everything receives the designation "concentrated" (samāhita), for it is within this context that one-pointedness (ekāgratā) is discussed; this is merely to demonstrate that it is through superior meditative absorption (samādhi) that the continuum of wholesome minds and mental factors is made to proceed.

If that were so, then when the mind itself proceeds by means of a single sense faculty and induces the continuous arising of subsequent moments of mind directed toward their respective objects, this would be termed "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*); thus, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) would not exist as something distinct from the mind itself.

This objection is not valid, for it has already been explained previously. Specifically, in the extensive analysis of mental factors (*caitta*) presented earlier, it was already established that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) exists as something distinct from the mind itself.

For if the very substance of the mind were identical to *samādhi*, then the acts of making the mind "even" and so forth would likewise have no distinction, since no causal conditions for such differentiation could be found.
Such difficulties as these cannot be fully set forth here as they were previously; therefore, it is not the case that "mind" itself is designated as *samādhi*.
On what basis is the name "dhyāna" (meditative concentration) established?
It is because by relying on this tranquility (*śamatha*), one is then able to engage in careful investigation (*pravicaya*).
Investigation (*vitarka*) has the meaning of actual discernment; as it is said, when the mind is in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it can discern things as they truly are.

Because the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is established within the sense of investigation, this treatise maintains that investigation and concentration have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature.
According to the principles of etymological interpretation, this is "concentration" (samādhi).
It receives the name "meditative absorption" (dhyāna) because it is a state of contemplation regarding its object; it causes wisdom to arise and is free from turbidity and distraction. Some say:

This concentration is called *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) because it maintains excellence, possesses universal objectification, and involves reflection in accordance with reality (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).

The term "excellence" excludes the desire realm; "universal objectification" excludes the formless realm; and "reflection in accordance with reality" excludes that which is inverted. That which can maintain this concentration is the sublime samādhi (*samādhi*), and this sublime samādhi is termed *dhyāna*.
This statement indicates that only an undistorted meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in which calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) proceed in equilibrium is designated as "dhyāna.
If that is so, how can defiled states receive this name?
Because they too are capable of a perverted, deliberate reflection (*pravicaya*).
This name is also applied to similar states, just as people in the world speak of "rotten seeds" and so forth; therefore, there is no fault of [the term] "dhyāna" being applied to everything.

If one-pontedness of mind (cittaikāgratā) of a virtuous nature, together with its attendants, is established as the four dhyānas, by what characteristics are the first, second, third, and fourth established?

Established as being endowed with investigation (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*), it is designated as the first; that is to say, when a state of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is associated with vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha, such meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is called the first dhyāna.

In the verse, by stating only that it is associated with *vicāra* (investigation), the sense that it is also associated with *vitarka* (applied thought) is already revealed; for if there is *vicāra* coexisting with joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*), it necessarily cannot be dissociated from *vitarka*.

To clarify the second [dhyāna] as being established by the exclusion of *vicāra*, the verse states only that it "possesses *vicāra* but not *vitarka*"; otherwise, one would have to say it "possesses *vitarka*, joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*)".
Since the presence of *vitarka* implies the presence of *vicāra*, the latter need not be mentioned explicitly.

By gradually abandoning the preceding factors, one establishes the four [stages]: having abandoned *vitarka*, there are two; having abandoned both [*vitarka* and *vicāra*], there is joy (*sukha*); and having fully abandoned all three types [of factors], it is as follows in their respective order; thus, one-pointedness of mind is divided into four kinds.
The dhyānas have already been explained.
What about the formless attainments?
The verse says:

The formless [attainments] are likewise: the four aggregates, separated from the lower stages and including the three preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher levels, are collectively termed "removal of the perception of form.
The formless is so called because there is no form; subsequent forms arise from the mind.
The three beginning with Infinite Space are named according to their preparatory application (*prayoga*);
Non-ideation and Non-non-ideation are named because they are dull and inferior.
The Treatise says:
This is identical in number and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to the dhyānas.
That is to say, there are two of each; as for their arising, it is as previously explained—namely, that according to the *Lokanirdeśa* (World Chapter), there are four types based on birth.

As for the essential nature of the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), taken collectively, they are also comprised within the wholesome (*kuśala*) and consist of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). It is in reliance upon this that the statement "they are also thus" is made.
However, among the accompanying factors, this excludes the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), because in the formless realm there is no concomitant form (*anuvartaka-rūpa*).
Although there is no difference between one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) and its attendants, they are divided into four types because they arise separately from the lower stages.

That is to say: having already become detached from the fourth dhyāna, one establishes the sphere of infinite space; and so on, up to having already become detached from the sphere of nothingness, one establishes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is the meaning of "detachment" (*viveka*)?
It refers to the liberation from the afflictions of the lower stages by means of this path; thus, it signifies the detachment from lower defilements.

These four fundamental [dhyānas], together with the three preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher [formless attainments], are collectively termed the "removal of the perception of form" (*rūpa-saṃjñā-vyapagama*).

The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space does not yet receive this name because it gives rise to the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) by taking the forms of the lower stages as its object; it is not that the name "removal of form" could be established based on the perception of the forms of the lower stages.
If that is so, for what reason is it said in the *Mahābhūta-skandha* that the removal of the perception of form constitutes the fourth dhyāna?

Because one takes the various forms existing within one's own body in the desire realm as the object and gradually eliminates them, this perception cannot belong to the formless realm; since this is the preliminary practice (*prayoga*) preceding the elimination of the perception of form, there is no error in establishing the name for the fundamental state (*maula*).
By what meaning is the name "formless" (*ārūpya*) established?
The term *rūpa* signifies that which can be manifested or displayed; thus, it is called "form" (*rūpa*) based on the sense of being manifestable.

The prefix *ā-* signifies the sense of restraint or limitation. This is intended to show that even within the ocean of saṃsāra, there are places where form is temporarily restrained; therefore, based on the sense of restraint, it is called "non-" (*a-*). Thus, it is termed "formless."
Because within that realm, transformation and manifestation are restrained, it is called *ārūpya* based on the meaning of "formless" (*arūpa*).

Alternatively, the syllable *ā* here also conveys the sense of "extreme"; for although there are also phenomena that cannot be transformed or manifested in other realms, the formless realm is the extreme among those that cannot be so manifested, as it lacks any forms that serve as bases for being "here" or "there."

Alternatively, this term "a" (a-) also signifies existence; in order to preclude the notion that this realm consists solely of formlessness, the term "a" is used to indicate the existence of the formless.
That is to say, in the world there are instances where a negation functions as a mere exclusion, yet we also observe cases where a negation simultaneously expresses an affirmation.
How is it shown that this is not merely a negation? Therefore, it is said that the word "a" fully expresses both negation and affirmation.
If it were otherwise, one should have used the sound "aṅ".
Alternatively, since there is no form at all in this realm, it would logically follow that the name "aṅ-rūpa" should be established.
Now, regarding this term "ārūpya": the essence of rūpa is negated, hence it is called ārūpya; although the sounds [of *rūpa* and *arūpa*] differ in length, their meaning is no different.
Some say that because those forms (*rūpa*) are subtle, they are also called "non-existent," just as an object whose yellow color is faint is also called a "yellow-less" object.
What has been stated is merely empty talk, because physical characteristics cannot be predicated of them.
That is to say, it cannot be said that they possess bodily or vocal restraint (*saṃvara*); since the substance of body and speech does not exist, restraint cannot be established.
If you admit that there are bodies and speech in that realm, how can you then admit that the matter (rūpa) therein is subtle?

If you claim it is because the dimensions of the body in that realm are small, then the animal realm (tiryagyoni) should also include formless beings (ārūpya), for there are insects so minute that they are invisible.

If it is argued that those realms are called "formless" because their bodies are extremely subtle and refined, then the intermediate state and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) should also be named "formless.

If it is argued that the body in those realms is the most refined among all refined things, then only the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) should receive the name "formless," just as the bodies born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-ja-kāya*) are distinguished by degrees of superiority and inferiority.

Furthermore, regarding the material bodies produced in the dhyānas, due to the progressively superior power of meditative concentration, they become increasingly pure and sublime as one ascends from lower to higher stages; since they cannot be perceived by the sense faculties of the lower stages, how are they different from those [formless states], such that they are not called "formless"?

If one observes that there are names whose meanings do not correspond to their referents, and observes that there are names that apply to two distinct meanings, such that one cannot definitively adhere to a meaning based solely on the name, then regarding the claim that "there is form in the formless realm," one should carefully seek out scriptural authority and logical reasoning as proof.
Some maintain that that realm (the formless) definitely possesses form, because the Sūtra states:
"Life-force, warmth, and consciousness function in conjunction.
Since it is admitted that life-force and consciousness are not absent in that realm, it follows by logic that there must be warmth, and warmth is itself form.
Furthermore, it is said:
name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and consciousness (vijñāna) are mutually dependent, just as two bundles of reeds stand supporting one another.
Since you admit that the substance of consciousness exists in those realms, you must likewise admit that name-and-form exists there as well.
Furthermore, the Blessed One has said:
"Because of the four stations of consciousness.
Since it is admitted that there is consciousness capable of abiding in those realms, one must necessarily admit that there are forms and other objects upon which it abides.
As the Blessed One said:
"If one were to say that there is coming and going apart from form, up to and including apart from formations and consciousness, this would be mere words," and so forth at length.
Such is the teaching (*āgama*).
There is also sound reasoning: if there were no form whatsoever in that realm, from what would the form of one who dies there and is reborn below arise?

Alternatively, if the continuum of the aggregates of an Arhat were severed, one would have to admit that the aggregates resume their continuity at a later time; therefore, based on both scripture and reasoning, it is not the case that form is non-existent there.
This proof is not valid, because it is based on a lack of careful reflection.
Furthermore, the first two teachings, like other sūtras, were spoken with intentional ambiguity regarding the desire and form realms.
As it is said:
With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; these, along with the six spheres of contact, are called the "person" (pudgala).
How could that sutra be intended to apply universally to all three realms?
Rather, it was stated in this way based on what is possible [in certain cases].

If it is argued that because this sutra’s statement lacks qualification, it should not be interpreted differently, this reasoning is also incorrect; for although the statement lacks qualification, its meaning differs, just as in the two sutras cited previously.

Furthermore, external objects should possess life-force (*jīvitendriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), because they possess warmth (*uṣman*) and contact (*sparśa*), as well as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Although this sūtra statement makes no such distinction, it is nonetheless accepted that external warmth arises apart from life-force and consciousness, and that external name-and-form functions without depending upon consciousness.

Although this scriptural passage makes no such distinction, one must admit that in the formless realm, life-force and consciousness exist apart from heat; it is only name and consciousness that are mutually dependent.
Furthermore, the *Vijñānasthiti-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Abodes of Consciousness) also does not constitute proof [for your position].
The intent of this sutra is to state that it is impossible for there to be coming and going while being entirely separated from all four types of consciousness;
it does not mean that coming and going would cease upon being separated from even one type of consciousness.
Therefore, the *Vijñānasthiti-sūtra* expresses a general principle with specific intent, just as the Blessed One spoke in the *Pañcānantarya-sūtra*. As the sūtra states:
"One who commits the five acts of immediate retribution will, in the very next birth, necessarily fall into hell (*naraka*)."
How could one fail to fall into those [lower realms] by lacking even one of these?
Furthermore, it is said:
"The earth shakes due to four causes."
Although there is no explicit qualifying statement, one should understand it as making a distinction.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Sentient beings subsist by means of the four nutriments."
Could it be that those dwelling in the form and formless realms also subsist on edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*)?
According to those various sūtras, this teaching should be understood as applying universally.

If you argue that because the sūtra states there is a class of gods who have transcended edible food, and because it further states that those gods take joy (*prīti*) as their food, they lack edible food—and since the sūtra also speaks of sentient beings in the formless realm—one should not say that there is form (*rūpa*) in that realm.
If it is argued that a small amount of form receives the designation "formless," just as a small amount of salt is called "saltless," this is also unreasonable, because the Sūtra states:
"Because one has completely transcended all perceptions of form."
Therefore, those various Āgamas cited by him cannot prove that there is form (*rūpa*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The reasoning he establishes also fails as proof; for although there is no form whatsoever in that realm, when one subsequently passes away and is reborn below, form arises from mind. We observe in the world that even non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*) can arise through mutual dependence upon one another.

This means that because the mind differs, the differentiation of form arises; since there are distinctions among the material sense-faculties, the arising of consciousness differs accordingly. Therefore, when one is about to descend from the formless realm to be born below, a mental continuum that accords with the production of form persists, and by its power, it draws forth the arising of lower-level form.

However, it cannot be said that [matter] arises solely from that [mind], for it also takes as its conditions the continuity of the mind that previously coexisted with matter, and takes as its own seed matter that has long since ceased; thus, present matter now arises, as it is admitted that homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) operate across both the past and the present.
Once the various Arhats have entered parinirvāṇa, the continuity of the aggregates is severed without remainder.

Since there is currently not the slightest condition for the arising of the aggregates, this cannot be cited as a parallel to the case of passing away from the formless realm; therefore, the reason you have established as proof is unestablished.
Furthermore, the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is definitively devoid of form, for the sūtra states that it is the departure from form.
As the sūtra says:
"The departure from all forms is called the formless realm."
If there were still form within that realm, how could it be said that one can transcend it?
If it is argued that other sūtras state that some cannot transcend existence (*bhava*), and therefore this sūtra must certainly have another underlying intention, [we reply:]...
This is also unreasonable, because that sūtra speaks with the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) of negating [the existence of] pervasive and permanent emergence. Others offer this explanation:

"The intent of the sūtra on 'emergence from form' is to state that dharmas bound to the desire realm do not exist within the form realm, and dharmas bound to the form realm do not exist within the formless realm; it is not that there is absolutely no form within the formless realm, but rather that the word 'emergence' is used to negate [the presence of] the form realm."

Alternatively, the intention of this sutra may be stated as follows: by means of knowledge associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-jñāna*), one emerges from the afflictions associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kleśa*); by means of knowledge associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-jñāna*), one emerges from the afflictions associated with the form realm. It is not that there is no form at all within the formless realm; rather, the term "emergence" is used to indicate the cessation of the afflictions regarding form.

Furthermore, if a sutra states that "transcending all forms is called the formless realm," it would imply that there are no forms whatsoever in that realm. If this were so, since the formless transcends the realm of form by virtue of being non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*), that realm would likewise have to lack non-material phenomena as well.

Alternatively, just as there may be that which is non-material (*arūpa*), so too should there be material phenomena (*rūpadharma*). It is not the case that within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) there exists both matter bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-rūpa*) and that which is non-material.

However, since the Sūtra merely speaks of "emergence from form" (*rūpaviveka*), we know that the term "formless" is not applied based on a general emergence from the realm of form; rather, the term "formless" is spoken solely in reference to being free from [specific] form.

Furthermore, just as the form realm (rūpadhātu) is a departure from all desires, and no category of desire exists at all within the form realm, yet it is not that categories of form do not exist within the form realm;

so too, the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is a departure from all forms, and no category of form exists at all within the formless realm, yet it is not that categories of the formless do not exist within the formless realm.

Furthermore, just as the realm of cessation (nirodhadhātu) is a departure from the conditioned (saṃskṛta), and in that realm of cessation there are no conditioned phenomena whatsoever, so too, since the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) has already departed from all forms, it should likewise be entirely devoid of all forms in that realm.
Furthermore, within the formless realm (*ārūpya*), there is definitively no form, for the Sūtra states that those [beings] have "removed the perception of form" (*rūpa-saṃjñā*).
That is to say, because the Formless Realm abandons craving directed toward form, it is said to be called the "removal of the perception of form."

If it is admitted that there are still various forms (*rūpa*) in that realm, then since one has not yet abandoned craving for those forms, one should not say that the perception of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*) has been removed.
Although other schools (*nikāya*) speak thus,
saying that the statement "there is form" does not refer to a physical body (*rūpakāya*), because the Sūtra says:

When one becomes detached from the defilements of the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*), the mind has already attained detachment regarding the five elements (*dhātu*), yet it has not yet attained detachment regarding the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*).

Therefore, it is known that while the immaterial meditative absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*) lack a material body, they do possess untainted matter (*anāsrava-rūpa*) that evolves in accordance with the mind.
This is merely empty talk; for since those [uncontaminated factors] lack the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), there can be no derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) without primary elements.

The uncontaminated restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) takes as its generative cause the primary elements belonging to the specific place where the body is born; it is not so for contaminated derived matter, lest there be the fault of the intermixture of different realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*).
The untainted (*anāsrava*) is not like this; it follows the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the body. Since those [beings] lack a body, there is no untainted form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, the form that arises concomitantly with the mind (*anuvartaka-rūpa*) is definitely absent in those realms, because the Sūtra states:
"Therein exist the categories of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) up to the category of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)."
It does not say that there is form; for if there were form, it would have been stated thus:
"That which belongs to the category of form is like that within the dhyānas.
Furthermore, the formless realm is definitively without form, as the Sūtra says:
The formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*) are the most tranquil, as they transcend all forms (*rūpa*).

It is not that there is anything in the formless realm that does not transcend form; rather, the expression "transcending form" is used specifically to distinguish [the formless] from that [realm]. It is intended solely to demonstrate that even subtle form is definitively absent throughout all the formless stages; therefore, it is said that they transcend all forms.

If it is argued that the statement regarding "transcending all forms" was spoken with the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) of transcending coarse form, this is also unreasonable, because [the scripture] speaks of "all.
That is to say, the Sūtra states:
"Because sentient beings in the formless realm have transcended all perceptions of form," and so forth, as explained at length.

If it were claimed that there is truly matter within the formless realm, then the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of that matter would necessarily be perceptible; how then could one say that they have "transcended the perception of matter" and so forth?
Therefore, it is established by both scripture and reasoning that even subtle matter does not exist in the formless realm, and this conclusion is unshakable.
Thus has the general designation for the formless realms been explained.
Why are they specifically named "Infinite Space" and so forth?

Briefly, the names of the first three are derived from their preparatory stages (*prayoga*); for during the stage of cultivation, one contemplates infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness.
If it is accomplished through the preparatory application of contemplating infinite space by way of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

That is to say, there are certain phenomena which, although coexisting with form (*rūpa*), do not depend upon form in their essential nature; those who seek liberation from form must necessarily contemplate those phenomena first.
This means that although the essence of space coexists with form, it can only be clearly manifested by depending on the absence of form.

Since the characteristics of external phenomena subsumed under this category are boundless, it is easier to become detached from form when contemplating them; therefore, one contemplates space during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), and at the time of attainment, one may accordingly take other phenomena as objects. However, this name is established based solely on the preparatory application.
Other masters say:
"Because it first departs from the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) and thus initially opposes form, it is metaphorically designated by the name 'emptiness' (*ākāśa*).
Others further state:

Because practitioners who have attained liberation from form dwell extensively in the perception of emptiness regarding the aggregates of feeling and so forth within this very stage, it is based on this that the name "Infinite Space" is established.

If it is accomplished through the application of meditative cultivation consisting of the contemplation of infinite consciousness by way of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), it is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

That is to say, having correctly grasped the signs within the pure sixfold group of consciousnesses that are capable of discernment, one abides in resolute conviction; then, by the power of mental construction (*parikalpa*), one contemplates and examines the signs of infinite consciousness. Accomplished with this application as its precursor, it may also take other phenomena as its object as appropriate; however, this name is established solely based on the preliminary application.
Other masters say:

This name is established by way of both intention (*āśaya*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*). That is to say, when a practitioner of yoga is about to enter this meditative absorption, he first gives rise to an intention directed toward infinite consciousness. Upon emerging from this absorption, the appearance of this outflowing consciousness is most delightful; thus, both before entering and after emerging, one takes the object of consciousness as one's focus.
If, through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), one relinquishes all that is accomplished by application (*prayoga*), it is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

That is to say, seeing that the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of the infinite is coarse and agitated, one initiates this application with the desire to become weary of and abandon it; therefore, this sphere is called the "supreme relinquishment" (*parama-nyāsa*).
Because within this state one no longer delights in performing infinite mental formations, and the mind dwells in tranquility, having relinquished all engagement with its objects;

it is designated as the "Fourth" because perception (*saṃjñā*) therein is dull and inferior. Specifically, because perception in this stage is not clear or superior, it is called "Non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*), much like the realm of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*). Yet, because perception is not entirely absent, it is called "Neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); for there still exists a subtle and inferior perception in this stage.
These words indicate that the perception (*saṃjñā*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is unlike that of the seven lower stages, and thus it receives the name "Non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*);
yet, because it is not like the three mindless states (*acittaka*), it is called "Neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā*).
Is it not the case that practitioners of yoga in the preparatory stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) also think:

"All perceptions are like a disease, like an arrow, like an abscess; the Heaven of Non-perception is like delusion and darkness; only the Heaven of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception is the opposite of these, being tranquil and sublime"?
Why is it that this [attainment] is not designated by the name of its preparatory stage (*prayoga*)?
In truth, it should indeed be so, because a practitioner must first cultivate revulsion toward both perception (*saṃjñā*) and non-perception (*asaṃjñā*).
However, someone might ask:
For what reason does the practitioner form such a thought when practicing the preparatory application (*prayoga*)?
One must certainly cite this as the reason for answering the question; therefore, it is said that the establishment of the name is due to the dullness and inferiority of the perception (*saṃjñā*).
These four formless states are all called "stations" (*āyatana*) because they are the places where various forms of existence (*bhava*) arise and grow.

That is to say, these four stations serve as the basis for the arising and growth of various karmas and afflictions (*kleśa*)—whether pertaining to existence or non-existence—and because people falsely imagine them to be *nirvāṇa*, the Buddha taught that they are stations for the arising and growth of existence.
The formless attainments have already been explained.
What, then, are the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*)?
The verse says:

These fundamental attainments (*mauladhyāna*) are eight; the first seven each have three types—namely, the relishing (*āsvādana*), the pure (*śuddha*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*). The last has two types: the relishing and the pure.
"Relishing" refers to that which is associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*); "pure" refers to mundane wholesomeness (*laukika-kuśala*).
This is precisely that which is tasted and clung to; the untainted is called supramundane.
The treatise says:
The fundamental attainments (*samāpatti*) of dhyāna and the formless realm (*ārūpya*) discussed above comprise eight types in total.

Among these, the first seven each possess all three types; the attainment of the Peak of Existence possesses only two types, because this stage is dull and inferior and lacks the untainted (*anāsrava*).

The first, the attainment of relish (*āsvādanasamāpatti*), refers to that which is associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*); because craving is able to relish and cling, it is called "relish," and since it is associated with that craving, it receives the name "attainment of relish."

The statement "associated with craving" (*tṛṣṇā-saṃprayukta*) is spoken in terms of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), because this [attainment] has meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as its essential nature.

If one were to include the accompanying factors (*sahakārin*), one should say that the factors belonging to the category associated with craving are called "the attainment of relish" (*āsvādana-samāpatti*); however, here only the factors belonging to the single category of craving itself are taken.

The "pure" meditative attainments (*śuddha-samāpatti*) are termed "worldly wholesome concentration" because they are free from the defilement of afflictions and are associated with various pure dharmas such as non-attachment.
Because these are wholesome, they differ from those characterized by "tasting" (*āsvādana*); because they are contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are distinct from the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
This is precisely the object previously tasted and clung to; immediately upon its cessation, that tasting concentration arises.

One deeply generates attachment by taking the past pure state as an object; at that time, although one is said to have emerged from the concentration that was tasted, one is said to have entered the concentration that performs the tasting.

There are five general types of emergence from meditative concentration: first, emergence from the stage; second, emergence from the moment; third, emergence from the mental aspect; fourth, emergence from the object; and fifth, emergence from the category.
To enter from the first dhyāna into the second and so forth is called "exiting a stage" (*bhūmi*).

To proceed through a continuous succession of mental states within the same stage—where the aspect (*ākāra*) and the object (*ālambana*) remain constant, and one moment immediately follows the next—is called "exiting a moment" (*kṣaṇa*).
To enter from the aspect of impermanence into the aspect of suffering and so forth is called "emerging from the aspects.
To enter from taking the aggregate of form as an object into taking feeling and so forth as objects is called "emerging from the objects."

The transition from the contaminated (*sāsrava*) to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), or from the undefiled (*akliṣṭa*) to the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), and so forth, is termed "transcending the category" (*jātivyatikrama*).
Based on this transcending of categories, it is stated here that one enters the meditative absorption of the relisher (*āsvādaka*) by departing from that which is relished (*āsvādya*).
Is it not the case that these two statements contradict one another?

That which is capable of relishing is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), not the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) entered; that which is the absorption entered is not called "capable of relishing. How, then, can it be said that one enters an absorption that is capable of relishing?
There is no fault of contradiction, because it is observed that when one member of a pair is mentioned, the entire category is expressed;
just as when a householder is exhorted, brought to mind, or designated, both names are obtained due to their mutual intermingling.

Because meditative absorption (samādhi) associated with craving is termed "tasting" (āsvādana), and by the power of that absorption, craving itself receives the designation of "concentration," there is no contradiction between these two statements.

Some say that when craving continues in a series and manifests, each subsequent moment takes the preceding one as its object; thus, that which is tasted is the preceding moment that has already ceased, while the subsequently arising moment is called the "taster."

When this craving that experiences the tasted object manifests, it takes past objects as its objective support but does not take present factors—whether of its own nature, associated with it, or coexistent with it—as its support, because it necessarily does not observe its own nature and so forth.
It does not take the future as its object, because it has never been experienced before.

Concentration (*samādhi*) is defined as being focused on an object without wavering; since concentration associated with craving is likewise one-pointed toward its object, it also receives the name "concentration."

It is not so with association with other afflictions; that is to say, other defilements cannot cause the mind to focus intently upon its own object in the way that craving can. Therefore, when samādhi is accompanied by craving, its one-pointed concentration on an object resembles that of the wholesome states.
The untainted meditative attainments (*anāsrava-samādhi*) refer to supramundane attainments; because craving does not take them as its object, they are not objects of relish.

Among the eight attainments thus described, the factors (*aṅga*) are included within the dhyānas, but not within the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), because the formless attainments are extremely tranquil.
This means that when a practitioner of yoga delights in cultivating wholesome qualities, they diligently practice by establishing individual factors within a vast accumulation of merit.

However, because the formless realms are characterized by an increase in tranquility, the mind and mental factors function in a state of dullness and inferiority; therefore, no such factors are established therein.

Alternatively, it may be that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is predominant in those stages; however, a single predominance cannot establish a factor as a "limb" (*aṅga*), for a factor is designated as a limb only when many dharmas increase together.
For this reason, the dhyānas alone are established as having limbs, because in them concentration and wisdom proceed in equilibrium and many dharmas increase.

For this reason, the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are also not established as having constituent factors (*aṅga*), because in the preparatory stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), only wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant. Other masters say:
"Only when there is a distinct mental factor (*caitasika*) that is uniquely absent in a particular stage is that stage established as having [specific] constituent factors, and not otherwise."

In the first dhyāna, mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and physical pain (*duḥkha*) are abandoned; in the second dhyāna, applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) are eliminated without remainder; in the third, joy (*prīti*) is extinguished; and in the fourth, pleasure (*sukha*) is abandoned.
Although these are gradually extinguished in their entirety within the formless stages (*ārūpya-bhūmi*), there is no complete abandonment of them at each respective stage.
This explanation fails to dispel the doubts of others:
for what reason are the factors (*aṅga*) established only in this manner?
Therefore, the previous explanation should be accepted as correct.
How many factors (*aṅga*) are there in each of the four dhyānas?
The verse says:
The first dhyāna has five factors: vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and samādhi.
The second has four factors: internal clarity, joy, bliss, and concentration;
the third possesses five factors: equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, bliss, and concentration;
the fourth has four factors: equanimity, mindfulness, neutral sensation, and concentration.
The treatise says:

Among the four dhyānas that are exclusively pure and untainted, the first possesses five factors: first, vitarka; second, vicāra; third, prīti; fourth, sukha; and fifth, one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā).
One-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is a synonym for meditative concentration (*samādhi*); concentration and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) are identical in substance but differ in name.
Therefore, that which is called "concentration" is precisely superior meditative absorption, which is here described as one-pointedness of mind.
The second dhyāna has only four factors: first, internal serenity; second, joy; third, bliss; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind. The third dhyāna possesses five factors:
first, equanimity; second, right mindfulness; third, right discernment; fourth, the experience of bliss; and fifth, one-pointedness of mind.
The fourth dhyāna has only four factors: first, the purity of equanimity; second, the purity of mindfulness; third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind.
For what reason do the first and third [dhyānas] each possess five factors, while the second and fourth possess only four factors respectively?
It is because only that many factors are capable of being established as constituent parts.
Alternatively, it may be because the desire realm contains many unwholesome dharmas, and the five exquisite sensual pleasures are difficult to sever and difficult to relinquish.

In the second dhyāna, there is joy (*prīti*) belonging to a heavy stage; its characteristic is one of surging movement, the very pinnacle among forms of joy. It draws forth craving (*tṛṣṇā*) of five classes, which is difficult to relinquish and difficult to sever. To counteract this, why are there five factors (*aṅga*) in each of the first and third [dhyānas]?
The first three are not so; therefore, the remaining [attainments] each have four.

Alternatively, this is for the sake of conforming to the method of "leaping" (vyutkrāntaka) meditative attainments; that is to say, when first initiating a leaping attainment, it is difficult to enter a different category, whereas it is easy to enter the same category.

However, within the initial stages of arising from the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), one may enter the third from the first, or enter the fourth from the second; therefore, the second and fourth dhyānas each possess only four factors (*aṅga*).
The first and third dhyānas each possess five factors, while those that arise subsequently are easily established; therefore, there are no additional factors in the higher stages.
Since the names of the dhyāna factors total eighteen, how many distinct entities are there in total among them?
The verse says:
These are eleven real entities; the first two are bliss and pliancy;
inner serenity is the faculty of faith; and joy is the feeling of joy.
The treatise says:
In terms of actual entities, these factors consist of only eleven.
That is to say, the first five factors constitute five actual entities.
The three factors of the second dhyāna are as previously described; with the addition of the factor of internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), they total six.
The meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the third dhyāna is as previously described; with the addition of the remaining four factors, they total ten.
The three factors of the fourth dhyāna are as previously described; with the addition of the factor of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, they total eleven.
For what reason are the mind and other such factors not considered factors of dhyāna?
This should be understood according to the previous analysis of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). As for those points that differ from it, they will now be briefly distinguished.

Among the feelings (*vedanā*), three are established—excluding sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*)—because sorrow and suffering are comprised exclusively within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The three feelings (vedanā) are included as factors (aṅga) because they benefit each respective stage and their function in accordance with meditative concentration (samādhi) is powerful; thus, they are all subsumed under the factors.
For what reason is diligence (vīrya) not established as a factor of dhyāna?
Because the factors of dhyāna accord with the excellence of their own stage, whereas diligence accords with those above; therefore, it is not established as a factor.

Alternatively, while the factors of dhyāna are appropriately conducive to serenity and bliss, diligence in seeking excellence involves the exhaustion of strenuous exertion; thus, both vitarka and vicāra are established as factors, for they assist meditative concentration (samādhi) by restraining and directing the mind, causing it to abandon coarseness and subtlety, and counteracting desire and evil.
For what reason is non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) not considered a limb of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*)?
The limbs of meditative absorption assist the mind in abiding upon its object; since non-manifest action does not take an object, it is not established as a limb.

Thus, although there are eighteen limbs of meditative absorption according to the distinctions between the levels (*bhūmi*), when sought among the actual categories of entities (*dravya-jāti*), there should be only nine types. However, because the characteristics of feeling (*vedanā*) differ, they are divided into eleven.
For this reason, it is said that there are cases where something is the first factor but not the second factor;
one should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
The first permutation refers to vitarka and vicāra.
The second phrase refers to internal purity.
The third phrase refers to joy, bliss, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The fourth phrase refers to all other factors remaining after excluding those previously mentioned.
The remaining factors should be considered in relation to one another according to reason.
In this context, what is the meaning of the term "factor" (*aṅga*)?
It signifies the sense of "accomplishment."
What is being manifested and established?
It refers to manifesting and establishing that "this is the first dhyāna," up to "this is the fourth dhyāna.

Alternatively, these names for the factors (*aṅga*) follow their respective meanings, just as the citron and other fruits are called "drinking-factors" (*pānāṅga*); that is to say, each of the eighteen factors conforms to its own respective stage.

Alternatively, the meaning of "requisite" (upakaraṇa) is expressed by the term "limb" (aṅga), as in the case of the limbs of a sacrifice, such as cattle and horses; that is to say, vitarka, vicāra, and so forth, mutually support one another.
The Vaibhāṣika masters, wishing to manifest that samādhi is the most preeminent within the dhyāna stages, therefore state:
"Samādhi is both dhyāna and a limb of dhyāna; vitarka, vicāra, and so forth are limbs of dhyāna but not dhyāna itself."
How can one know that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the stages of dhyāna is supreme?
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "One should know that the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) exists within the four dhyānas."
However, because the meanings of mutual establishment and mutual protection are similar, it is said that they are "like a fourfold army.
There is no fault in this; for although the king and his retinue support one another, the king is preeminent among them.
Is it not the case that since the essential nature of the bliss in the three dhyānas is identical, there should not be eleven factors of meditative absorption?

The bliss of the third dhyāna has feeling as its essence, whereas the bliss of the first and second dhyānas is precisely pliancy; therefore, the factors of meditative absorption actually number eleven.

Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) pervade all four dhyānas; for what reason are only pliancy established in the first two, while only equanimity is established in the latter two stages?
It is because these [qualities] are particularly conducive to those respective states.

This means that in the desire realm there are various unwholesome dharmas, and in the stage of the first dhyāna there are vitarka and vicāra, which afflict the mind like poisoned arrows; because the first two [dhyānas] are free from these, pliancy increases.

In the second dhyāna, joy (*prīti*) is extremely agitated; in the third dhyāna, the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) is greatly increased. Both of these can serve as superior bases for the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); because these two [dhyānas] abandon them, equanimity (*upekṣā*) increases.

Alternatively, in the desire realm and the first dhyāna, the heaviness (*dausthulya*) induced by the sense-faculties and consciousnesses associated with form is more intense than in other stages; because the first two [stages] are free from that, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) increases.
In the third and fourth dhyānas, one is further removed from heaviness, and because tranquility becomes increasingly superior, equanimity (*upekṣā*) increases.

This means that pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is a bliss like first laying down a heavy burden; because it becomes increasingly subtle as one shifts through the stages, pliancy is established only in the first two stages.
In the third and fourth stages, it proceeds spontaneously and its tranquility becomes even more superior; therefore, equanimity (*upekṣā*) is established there.
Alternatively, the first and second dhyānas possess pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) as a condition, because joy (*prīti*) serves as a superior condition for pliancy.
As the Sūtra says: "Because of joy, there is pliancy."
In the third and fourth dhyānas, because there is no object for joy (*prīti*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is weak and thus not established as a factor (*aṅga*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) and pliancy mutually obscure one another; if one is present in a state, the second is absent.

Pliancy (praśrabdhi) counteracts sluggishness (laya), its characteristic being buoyancy; equanimity (upekṣā) counteracts restlessness (auddhatya), its characteristic being tranquility. Therefore, pliancy and equanimity mutually obscure one another.
What reasoning serves as proof that among the three factors of bliss, two are pliancy and the third is feeling (vedanā)?

It has already been stated that [the pleasure of the third dhyāna] is exclusively concordant with that [feeling], meaning that the pleasure of the third dhyāna is not pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and pliancy is not a factor (*aṅga*) of that [dhyāna].

This was explained previously: the pleasure of the first two dhyānas cannot possibly be the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), because it would be illogical for it to be either a mental or a bodily feeling.

This means that the pleasure of the first two dhyānas cannot possibly be bodily sensation (*kāyika-vedanā*), because while one is actually in meditative absorption, the five sensory consciousnesses are absent; nor can it be mental sensation (*caitasika-vedanā*), for it would then simply be joy (*prīti*).

Only when one is free from the craving for joy and the mind experiences a delight belonging to a different stage can it be established as a distinct "pleasure-sensation" (*sukha-vedanā*) differing from what preceded.
Joy (*prīti*) is the sensation of joy (*sukha-vedanā*); it is illogical for two sensations to coexist within a single moment of mind.

If one were to argue that there is no such fault because joy and bliss arise alternately, this reasoning is also incorrect, as [the sūtras] speak of being "endowed with five factors" (*pañcāṅga*) and "endowed with four factors" (*caturaṅga*).

If it is argued that the numbers four and five are stated in terms of what is possible and do not necessarily imply simultaneous occurrence, this is also unreasonable; for it would follow that there must exist a meditative concentration (samādhi) with vitarka but without vicāra.
However, the Sūtra speaks only of three types of meditative concentration, from "with vitarka and vicāra" up to the full exposition.
If the factors of dhyāna do not necessarily arise together, for what reason is it not stated that there is a concentration with vitarka and without vicāra?
Furthermore, the three samādhis should also be present within the desire realm and the first dhyāna; this would contradict what is stated in the sūtras.
In this context, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) provisionally cites the views of others, stating that there is certainly no mental faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
This is because what is described as the factor of pleasure (*sukha-aṅga*) within the [first] three dhyānas is exclusively pleasure comprised within bodily sensation (*kāyikī-vedanā*).
If that were so, it would contradict what is stated in the sūtra.
As the sūtra asks: "What is the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya)?"
This refers to the pleasant mental and physical sensations produced by the power of contact conducive to pleasure (*sukha-sparśa*).
In reality, there is no contradiction; however, others have added the word "mental" (*citta*) to this, because in the sūtras of other schools, it is mentioned as being only physical.

For what reason do you not claim that this refers to the sūtras of other schools, where others have deleted the word "mind" (citta), because those sūtras state that in the second dhyāna and above, there is no remaining consciousness and body and mind proceed as one?
If one insists that there is bodily sensation of pleasure (*kāyika-sukha-vedanā*) there, it contradicts reason, as will be explained later.

Although the factor of pleasure established in the third dhyāna is described in the sūtra as "pleasure experienced by the body," this cannot prove that the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in that stage is not subsumed under mental sensation; for it is also said that "joy born of seclusion is realized by the body. How, then, could one maintain on this basis that the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is not subsumed under mental sensation?
Furthermore, non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*) are also spoken of as "bodies," namely the six groups of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśakāya*) and the six groups of feeling (*ṣaṭ-vedanākāya*), and so forth.

If it were argued that only that which is formless is called a "body" because there is no term "body" applied prior to [the mention of] form, this is not certain; for within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the view of a body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is indeed spoken of.

Furthermore, it is because [the Buddha] spoke of the destruction of the body there; because he spoke of that body as being of inferior birth; and because we see the Sūtra state: "This is neither your body nor the body of another," referring to the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatana*).
Furthermore, because the physical body (*rūpakāya*) is also designated by a distinct name prior [to its specific classification], as stated in the Sūtra:
"Whatever physical bodies there are. Therefore, the existence or non-existence of a name preceding the physical body is not fixed.
Therefore, it should be understood that in this context, "mind" (*manas*) is designated as "body" (*kāya*).
What is the purpose of designating the mind by the name "body"?
It is to reveal that those pleasant feelings are personally realized within oneself.

This means that the bliss of that stage cannot be manifested by any supporting object or condition, but is realized solely through internal self-realization; this demonstrates the ultimate limit within that experience of pleasant feeling.

Furthermore, it is seen from his own statement using the terms "body" and "voice," as when he says, "one realizes the realm of ambrosia (amṛta-dhātu) by means of the body," which carries the meaning of realizing the realm of ambrosia through one's own self-realization.

Alternatively, it is to demonstrate that such pleasant feeling is similar to what was previously experienced by the body, and not similar to what is experienced by the mental factors of a lower stage;
for the purpose of distinguishing it from what is experienced by the mental factors of a lower mind, it is said that "it is pleasure experienced by the body."
Alternatively, it is to demonstrate that all faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) necessarily rely upon consciousness supported by the material body (*rūpakāya-vijñāna*).

By this, it is already shown that within the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*), there is also reliance upon consciousness that does not rely on matter; thus, it is said that such pleasure exists in all stages (*sarvabhūmi*).
By this principle, it is not explicitly stated in this sūtra that this is the pleasure experienced by the mental body (*manas-kāya*).
Furthermore, if the term "mental" (*mānasa*) were used, there would be the fault of including that which is not actually experienced.
That is to say, if it were said that "pleasure is experienced by the mind," one would take this pleasure to be "objective feeling" (*viṣayavedanā*).

However, this does not indicate that the pleasure of the third dhyāna is called "objective feeling" because it is an object of the mind; rather, it is intended to show that this [pleasure] is "essential feeling" (*svabhāvavedanā*), which is the very nature of the associated mental states that it experiences as they arise in contact with its own object. Therefore, the term "mind" (*manas*) is not mentioned here.

However, in order to dispel doubt, it is not explained in general terms; for if one were to speak only in general of the pleasure experienced, one would then wonder whether this pleasant feeling is the object or whether it is present before one.
If one were to specify the body [as the locus], this delusion would not arise; since it possesses this quality, the body should be mentioned.
Furthermore, there is a faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) that is subsumed under mental feeling, for the Sūtra says:
"I declare that one who enters and dwells fully in the third dhyāna cultivates pleasure."

Furthermore, it is taught that when one cultivates this pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), the underlying tendency of craving (*rāgānuśaya*) increases in accordance with that pleasure and is thereby abandoned.

It cannot be said that this is a bodily sensation of pleasure; therefore, it cannot be said that all the factors of pleasure (*sukha-aṅga*) within the three dhyānas are subsumed under bodily sensation. One must certainly believe that there exists a mental faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Furthermore, how is it known that the pleasure (*sukha*) of the first two dhyānas is the pleasure of bodily sensation (*kāyika-vedanā*) and not the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of the mind?
For although pliancy increases manifold in the fourth dhyāna, it is not said that it possesses the factor of pleasure (*sukha-aṅga*).
This has already been stated.
What was stated previously?
That pliancy (praśrabdhi) is not conducive to that state.

Furthermore, this pliancy (praśrabdhi) can give rise to bliss; just as an object of pleasure is also designated by the name "bliss," so too a place where there is bliss is designated as "blissful," whereas a place where there is no bliss cannot receive that designation.
If that were so, then the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of the third dhyāna should be called pleasure (*sukha*). It is not so;
for it has already been stated that [the pliancy of the third dhyāna] is not concordant [with the definition of pleasure].
Although the essence of the pliancy in the latter two dhyānas is superior to that of the preceding one, its characteristic is dull and inferior.
Due to the various causes and conditions previously explained, pliancy (praśrabdhi) is therefore not pleasure (sukha) in those [two stages].
If the pleasure of the first two dhyānas were indeed pliancy, it would entail the fault of contradicting the sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"If, at that time, the noble disciples realize with their bodies the joy born of seclusion and dwell in its fulfillment, at that time they have already abandoned five dharmas and have brought the cultivation of five dharmas to full perfection," and so on, as explained at length.
What are the five dharmas that are to be cultivated?
First, rapture (*prāmodya*); second, joy (*prīti*); third, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); fourth, bliss (*sukha*); and fifth, samādhi.
This sutra distinguishes pliancy from bliss; if pliancy were identical to bliss, how could there be five [dharmas]?
