These three types of meditative concentration (samādhi) take the preceding emptiness and so forth as their objects and apprehend the characteristics of emptiness and so forth; therefore, they are designated by names such as "emptiness-of-emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā).

The samādhi of emptiness-of-emptiness takes the previously mentioned non-learner’s (aśaikṣa) emptiness-trance (śūnya-samādhi) as its object and apprehends its characteristic of emptiness, because the characteristic of emptiness is more conducive to revulsion than the characteristic of non-self.

This means that one first gives rise to the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), contemplating the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Following this, one gives rise to a meditative concentration associated with superior roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*), which takes as its object the previously mentioned emptiness-trance of one beyond training and contemplates the characteristic of emptiness therein; because it apprehends emptiness within emptiness, it is called "emptiness-of-emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
Just as one turns a burning corpse with a staff, and once the corpse is consumed, the staff itself should also be burned;

so too, having burned away the afflictions through emptiness, one further gives rise to the concentration of emptiness to cultivate detachment from the preceding emptiness, namely the meditative absorption of "repeated emptiness" (*punar-śūnyatā-samādhi*).
After the aspect of emptiness arises, it immediately returns to being associated with the aspect of emptiness, for this alone is most conducive to the cultivation of wearying detachment (*vidūṣaṇā*).

The aspect of non-self (*anātman*) is not like this; one who perceives non-self develops a mind of wearying detachment toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), but not as effectively as one who perceives emptiness.

Those who have already realized that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*) yet still experience pleasure within existence do so because they have not clearly perceived emptiness (*śūnyatā*) amidst conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

Consequently, although this concentration on emptiness possesses both aspects (*ākāra*), it is designated only as "emptiness" and not as "non-self," because emptiness is extremely conducive to wearying detachment and relinquishment.
The "wishless-of-the-wishless" takes the aspect of impermanence as its object, namely the preceding wishless concentration (*asamāpatti*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This means that one first gives rise to the wishless concentration of one beyond training, contemplating the aspect of impermanence within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*). Subsequently, one gives rise to a concentration associated with superior roots of goodness, which takes that preceding wishless samādhi of one beyond training as its object and contemplates the aspect of impermanence; because one does not wish for even this wishless state, it is called the "wishless-of-the-wishless."
This should be understood through the illustration provided previously.

The subsequent arising of the concentration on wishlessness (*apranihita-samādhi*) following the aspect of impermanence (*anityākāra*) is such that it again becomes associated with the aspect of impermanence; for only this is capable of taking the path of revulsion as its object.
The aspect of suffering (*duḥkha*) cannot take the Noble Path as its object, because the Noble Path is not suffering; rather, it leads to the cessation of suffering.

Phenomena that are suffering themselves cannot lead to the quiescence of suffering. Furthermore, the four aspects—suffering and so forth—cannot take the Noble Path as their object, because the Noble Path does not cause suffering to continue.

Regarding the four aspects such as "not the path" (*amārga*) and so forth: because these involve wearying detachment from the path, the aspect of joyful aspiration (*abhinandanā*) cannot serve as the mode for wearying detachment. One might object:

"Is it not the case that, just as the 'wishless' (*apraṇihita*) does not aspire toward the noble path yet still employs the four aspects such as 'the path,' this [contemplation] should be understood in the same way?"

This example is not applicable. The wishless (*apraṇihita*) samādhi is primarily characterized by aversion toward existence (*bhava*), and because it also gives rise to a mind of non-aspiration toward the noble path (*āryamārga*), it is so called.
That is to say, while the preceding wishless samādhi is primarily averse to existence, the noble path relies upon existence; therefore, [the latter] is also characterized by non-aspiration.

Although the wishful intention (āśaya) expresses a lack of aspiration for the Path, it does not involve a genuine loathing of the Noble Path; therefore, it can also function as the four types [of aspects], such as the aspect of the Path.
Because the "wishless-of-the-wishless" (apraṇihitāpraṇihita) involves a genuine loathing of the Path, it contemplates the faults of the Path through the perspective of impermanence (anitya).
Since the aspect of the Path (mārga) and so forth does not allow for the path to be viewed with aversion, one does not apply those four aspects to it.
If the Path were subject to aversion because it is impermanent, then one would have to apply the aspect of suffering (duḥkha) to the Noble Path, as that aspect would be present there.
As a sutra states:
"All that is impermanent is suffering.
It is not the case that the noble paths possess the characteristic of suffering according to the principle of the established truths (*satya*), because their characteristics are distinct.

That is to say, the name "Truth of Suffering" is established based on specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); how then could the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) also possess the characteristic of suffering?
Furthermore, because it is distinguished and explained in the sūtras, as the sūtra says:
"In brief, all five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*) are suffering."
If the path possesses the characteristic of suffering because it is impermanent, then one should simply speak of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Since it is stated that only the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) are subsumed under suffering, this proves that the Noble Path is not suffering.

If it is argued that, for example, viewing origination (*samudaya*) as suffering is not a distorted view despite the difference in their respective characteristics of the truths—because the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) pertain to both suffering and origination—then one should know that viewing the path (*mārga*) as suffering is likewise not a distorted view despite the difference in their respective characteristics of the truths, because the untainted aggregates (*anāsravaskandha*) pertain to both suffering and the path; thus, the established principle of the truths remains unimpaired.

This is also unreasonable; furthermore, it must certainly not be held that viewing the origin as suffering is a non-perverted view, because the five aggregates of clinging are called "origin" by virtue of their causal nature and "suffering" by virtue of their resultant nature, and these natures are distinct from one another.
If one observes the cause as the effect, one must necessarily observe the effect as the cause, for no distinct causal conditions can be found.
This would then be a perverted view, not subsumed under the contemplation of the truths; how, then, could it not undermine the established principle of the truths?

In that case, there would be no distinction between the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of its origin (*samudaya-jñāna*); or else, the knowledge of the path regarding suffering should be established as a single "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) together with the knowledge of suffering and its origin, because their objects of focus (*ālambana*) are not distinct.

This is because it has been stated that suffering and its origin share the same essence; thus, viewing the origin as suffering is not a distorted view (*viparyāsa-darśana*), and since the two knowledges have the same object, they are not established as separate thorough knowledges.

Thus it should be said: since the path leading to suffering and the path of observation share the same substance, viewing the path as suffering is not a perverted view; because the objects of these two types of knowledge are identical, they are not established separately as distinct "thorough knowledges" (parijñā).
Since this is not permitted, how could the Path be suffering?
Furthermore, it is because the Path and suffering are distinct entities; as the Sūtra states:
"The five untainted faculties are able to sever all forms of suffering in the past, future, and present."
Furthermore, it is said that the path has birth as its primary object for severing suffering.
Moreover, a sutra states:
"The path should be cultivated; suffering should be permanently severed."
Therefore, the Path is not suffering.

If it is argued that because the Sūtra says "dharmas are like rafts," they too should be abandoned, this is logically incorrect; for the Sūtra does not state that dharmas are what is to be abandoned by means of the Path.

This refers to the dharmas of the noble path practiced at a previous time; since what was to be done has already been accomplished, they need not be cultivated further. It is in the sense of being "to be relinquished" that they are said to be "to be abandoned," and this is not the same as being abandoned through antidotes, as it differs from suffering.

Alternatively, in the sūtras, the term "dharmas" refers to the dharmas such as the sūtras themselves; the statement that they "should be abandoned" indicates that while one has realized the meaning, one must relinquish the verbal expression.

Or, when the sūtras state that even the dharmas [of the path] should be abandoned, this indicates that once the fruit has been attained, those causal dharmas which have served their purpose can be discarded—this is called "abandonment"—just like the *sthity-anukūla-bhāga* (the portion conducive to maintenance), and not because the nature of suffering or the path itself is to be abandoned.
Therefore, the essential natures of suffering and the Path are distinct.

Furthermore, if a sutra states that "all that is impermanent is suffering," it would imply that the Noble Path also possesses the characteristic of suffering. Moreover, since the sutra subsequently states that "all that is suffering is non-self," one would have to maintain that Nirvana is not of the nature of non-self, or else one must also admit that it is both suffering and impermanent. If this were admitted, it would necessarily follow that it is not the nature of Nirvana.

If you claim that it is only said that "whatever is suffering is not-self," but not that "whatever is not-self is suffering," why is it not also said that "whatever is suffering is impermanent," rather than saying "whatever is impermanent is suffering"?

If it is claimed that the very nature of impermanence is suffering, and that suffering is simply non-self with only the name being different, then emptiness and wishlessness would have no distinction, since you admit that non-self is identical to suffering and so forth.

If you claim that because the Sūtra states "suffering is precisely non-self," you accept that all suffering lacks the nature of self, then since this same Sūtra states that "the impermanent is precisely suffering," you should likewise accept that all impermanent things possess the nature of suffering.
The principle is indeed thus, because this sūtra speaks of impermanence (*anitya*) without explicitly stating "non-self" (*anātman*).
Based on what phenomenon is the term "impermanence" spoken?

It is spoken in order to destroy the four perversions (*viparyāsa*)—such as the grasping of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as permanent and so forth—which arise from the deluded worldlings. Thus, the term "impermanence" is spoken to refute that grasping.

Building upon this, it is further stated that "the impermanent is suffering. The intent of this statement is to reveal that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) impermanent phenomena possess the nature of suffering, and that what is suffering is not-self (*anātman*); it does not mean that everything impermanent is non-self.
This must necessarily be so, because in the sūtras, regarding objects conceived as permanent, it is stated that they are not permanent;
or rather, what is meant here by "not permanent" is not merely being subject to arising and ceasing, but specifically undergoing death and rebirth.

This means that because foolish worldlings conceive of the pleasures of humans and devas as [true happiness], the Sūtra—relying on those [pleasures] which are coarse and impermanent—declares them to be suffering, just like the three miserable realms.
What serves as proof that the terms "impermanence" and so forth in this Sūtra refer exclusively to the contaminated (*sāsrava*)?
Following this sutra, it further states:
"Because the various dharmas such as form and sensation are not-self, they are impermanent.
How could nirvana also be of the nature of impermanence?
Therefore, one should know that this sutra speaks only in terms of the four aspects of noble wisdom (*ārya-prajñā*) taking the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as its object.
If it is argued that the Noble Path must be suffering because it is impermanent (*anitya*), why not also accept that it is not suffering because it is untainted (*anāsrava*)?

If it is asked: "How can it be said that [the view] which conceives pleasure as suffering is abandoned only by the vision of cessation?"—it is because the error of regarding cessation as suffering is particularly grave.
To regard *nirvāṇa* as suffering greatly increases the mind that delights in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
this is not the case with the vision of the path. Therefore, it is mentioned specifically.
Just as a patient who loathes medicine can be easily treated, whereas one who loathes the cure for their illness is difficult to save;

so too, since the various noble paths proceed by relying upon suffering, the fault of viewing it as suffering is not considered particularly grave. For this reason, it is omitted in this treatise, and because there are other explanations, the meaning is not contradictory.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"If one knows joy and pleasure as they truly are, I definitively declare that such a person possesses the correct contemplation of the principles of the Four Noble Truths.

Thus, we know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are not entirely suffering. For this reason, regarding the Path (*mārga*), one may contemplate its impermanence (*anityatā*) to establish the profound state of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); one must certainly not contemplate it as suffering (*duḥkha*).

The signless-within-the-signless takes as its object the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the signless concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because there is no analytical cessation for untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
It grasps only the aspect of tranquility, not [the aspects of] cessation, excellence, or detachment.

This means that one first gives rise to an *asaikṣa* (non-learner) meditative concentration (*samādhi*), contemplating the aspect of tranquility within analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Following this, one gives rise to a meditative concentration associated with superior roots of goodness, which takes as its object the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the *asaikṣa* signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*), contemplating it as tranquil. Furthermore, regarding this signless cessation, one contemplates it as being signless; this is called the "signless-of-the-signless" (*animittānimitta*).
To illustrate this through an analogy, it should be understood as previously explained:

after the meditative equipoise of the "repeated absence of marks" (ānimitta-samādhi) has arisen with the aspect of tranquility (śānta-ākāra), one immediately returns to being associated with that same aspect of tranquility, for only this [equipoise] is capable of observing non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
It does not have the aspect of "sublime conduct" because its object is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
It does not have the aspect of "separation," because even though one has realized its non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), one remains bound by its latencies.
It does not have the aspect of "cessation," because non-analytical cessation is not the permanent liberation from all suffering.

Furthermore, because observing cessation prevents the confusion of it with impermanence, that which is called "tranquil" (śānta) manifests only the state of stillness; thus, analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) possesses the characteristic of tranquility.

Since one generates the perception of bliss within that state of rest after having undergone long-term toil in cultivating the Noble Path, one emphasizes the aspect of signlessness (animitta) by grasping tranquility rather than anything else.

The three types of "repeated concentration" (*anupūrva-samādhi*) are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), because they involve the cultivation of weariness toward and the relinquishment of the Noble Path; uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) meditative absorption does not cultivate weariness toward or relinquish the Noble Path.

While it is logically consistent to say that the two [concentrations] which take the Noble Path as their object and apprehend it as empty and impermanent constitute "weariness toward and relinquishment of the Noble Path," how can the "signless-of-the-signless" (*animittānimitta*) be called "weariness toward the path," given that it takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object and functions with the aspect of tranquility?
This is the cause for the non-arising of the joy associated with the signless meditative absorption (animitta-samādhi) of one beyond training; therefore, it is called "disgust for the path.
That is to say, when that concentration arises, its meaning is expressed as follows:
"The non-arising of the signless meditative absorption is virtuous."
Since this [state] delights in and praises the non-arising of the noble path, how can it not be called "disgust and relinquishment of the noble path"?
Furthermore, since the previous signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) is not the object of this [state], how is it designated as "signless-signless" (*animittānimitta*)?

Alternatively, one might concede that this meditative absorption does not take non-analytical cessation as its object, but rather takes the signless non-arising of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) as its object.
This is also not the case, for it follows the same explanation as before.
This refers to taking the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of signless concentration as its object;
since this non-analytical cessation is itself free from all signs, and because it takes the signless as its signless object, it receives the name "signless-signless."
Taking the signless object as its focal point, it functions with the aspect of tranquility; therefore, this meditative absorption is named after its object.

Only those born in the three continents can produce this absorption, and it is accessible to both men and women, because even by relying on a female body, one is able to freely prolong or shorten one's lifespan.
This applies only to those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), because those still in training (*śaikṣa*) merely delight in the Noble Path and have not yet attained disenchantment with it.
Even among them, this does not apply to all; it applies only to those liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*), because those liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) cherish the Noble Path.
It relies upon eleven stages, excluding the aforementioned seven upper levels, because those seven upper levels lack superior qualities.
If it occurs in the desire realm, it arises after the noble path subsumed under the *anāgamya* (threshold) stage;
if it occurs at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it is born after the noble path subsumed under the *ākiṃcanyāyatana* (sphere of nothingness).
The others all arise after the noble paths (*āryamārga*) of their own respective stages.

Speaking in terms of general categories, these [subsequent knowledges] arise immediately following the four knowledges of dharma (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), and cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).

However, speaking specifically: those included in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) do not arise after subsequent knowledge; those included in the higher realms do not arise after the knowledge of dharma; the first two do not arise after the knowledge of cessation; and the third does not arise after the knowledge of suffering, because this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) necessarily arises after the remaining aspects (*ākāra*).

Those who are to attain this all do so through the acquisition of dispassion at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); subsequently, it is only through application (*prayoga*) that it arises as a manifest presence.

Only our World-Honored One, without relying on application, brings this into manifest presence as he proceeds toward liberation; since he is even weary of the Path itself, how could he take delight in the various realms of existence?
Thereafter, the Noble Path also arises and manifests; however, because there is a sense of aversion toward the path itself, it does not arise immediately [following the previous state].

That which is comprised within the desire realm is produced through reflection (*cintā-maya*), while the others are produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) because they arise based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The sūtra further speaks of four types of cultivation of samādhi: first, the cultivation of samādhi for dwelling in happiness in the present life; second, the cultivation of samādhi for attaining superior knowledge and vision; third, the cultivation of samādhi for attaining analytical wisdom; and fourth, the cultivation of samādhi for the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (āsravas).
What are the distinctions between these four types?
The verse says:
To attain happiness in the present life, one cultivates the various wholesome meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
To attain superior knowledge and vision, one cultivates the supernormal power of the pure divine eye;
To attain discerning wisdom, one cultivates various preparatory virtues;
To attain the exhaustion of all outflows, one cultivates the diamond-like samādhi.
The Treatise says:

As stated in the Sūtra, there is the cultivation of samādhi—whether through practice, development, or frequent application—by which one attains abiding in happiness in the present life, and so forth, as explained at length.
The term "wholesome" comprehensively includes both the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Although one attains abiding in happiness in the present life by cultivating all wholesome dhyānas, the Sūtra mentions only the first dhyāna because the perception of pleasure (*sukha-saṃjñā*) is most predominant therein.
This means that because one has transcended the manifold faults of the desire realm, the perception of pleasure (*sukha-saṃjñā*) flourishes therein.
It is like a person traveling through a desert, exhausted by heat and thirst, who experiences a sense of superior joy even when first drinking turbid water.

Alternatively, it is because the Noble Path possesses this delight; that is to say, it is endowed with all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), and the nine thorough knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇaparijñā*) which serve as the remedies for the three realms.
Furthermore, these meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are the foremost of all concentrations and the cause of the bliss of all concentrations; therefore, they are specifically mentioned.
Is it not stated in the Sūtra:
"O Bhikṣus, it is thus!"?
Abiding here, one first experiences the joy and bliss born of seclusion; subsequently, when beings of the Brahma-realm are born, they experience a bliss identical to this.
Why, then, is it not said that one abides in the bliss of the subsequent dharma?

To examine this: the reason for speaking only of "bliss in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharmasukha) is to cause one to abandon the pursuit of sensual pleasures in the present, and by describing the bliss of present meditative concentration (samādhi), to inspire them toward it.

Alternatively, it may be manifested as dwelling in happiness, which is the basis for subsequent happiness; thus, by explaining both the support (*āśraya*) and that which is supported (*āśrita*), the point is already made clear. As a sūtra states:
"First, dwelling here in this world, one enters the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); only thereafter does one arise there."
Alternatively, while all three vehicles may abide in the happiness of the present life, their future happiness is not fixed;
therefore, it is not mentioned. This is because they may either fall back, be reborn in higher realms, or enter parinirvāṇa, and thus do not remain [in that state].

Although the various dhyānas are themselves the happiness of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*), they are spoken of as "attained" by way of their preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), because one attains the fundamental [dhyāna] through the power of cultivating the preparatory stage.
Alternatively, it is spoken of as "attained" by way of the happiness of the present itself, just as one speaks of the "substance of a pebble"; thus, there is no fault.

Some say that regarding this meditative absorption, the Buddha spoke based on his own experience; as it is said that while the Bodhisattva was dwelling in the Jambūvana grove, he first gave rise to a mundane concentration resembling the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), which could induce shared happiness for all sentient beings. For this reason, he did not speak of "dwelling in happiness in future lives" (*sukha-vihāra*) [in reference to that specific instance].
For this very reason, only the first is mentioned, because at that time the bodhisattva attains only the first.
If one cultivates the supernormal power of the divine eye based on the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), one is then able to obtain superior knowledge and vision.
On what basis is the designation "knowledge-and-vision" (jñāna-darśana) established?

Within the fundamental dhyānas, there is a wisdom of universal illumination; because it illuminates universally, it is designated by the term "vision" (darśana). Since the essence of vision is itself knowledge, it is called "knowledge-and-vision."
It is universally established in the world that the eye-faculty is called "seeing"; however, in order to distinguish it from that [ordinary seeing], it is designated as "knowing.
Alternatively, because this very seeing definitively determines its object, it is called "knowing," which is also termed "seeing."

This means that the fundamental dhyānas are paths of ease, because they manifest without much exertion; because they require no exertion, their substance is firm; because their substance is firm, their function is definitive; and because their function is definitive, they are established by the name "knowledge."
Because one perceives the object as previously described, it is called "knowledge and vision.

One cultivates this samādhi for the sake of knowing and seeing; that is, for the purpose of seeking definitive illumination of the object. This, too, was spoken by the Sugata based on his own experience.

This means that it is to manifest how the Buddha, through the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*), observes the perilous transitions of death and birth among sentient beings; only then does he initiate meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and other practices for their deliverance. Therefore, he cultivates the supernormal power of the divine eye for the sake of knowledge and vision.
Other masters say:

In order to overcome the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), one gives rise to superior knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*). This superior knowledge and vision cannot arise apart from the perception of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*). This perception of light induces the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*), and by means of the divine eye, one attains superior knowledge and vision.
If one cultivates the various preparatory virtues (*prayoga-kuśala*) of the three realms as well as untainted virtues (*anāsrava-kuśala*), one attains analytical wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-prajñā*).

That is to say, from the desire realm up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), all virtuous dharmas produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as all other untainted conditioned phenomena, are collectively termed "preparatory virtuous dharmas" (*prayoga-kuśala-dharma*).

Cultivating these wholesome dharmas can induce the arising of wisdom, which functions with differentiation regarding all objects; therefore, it is said that by cultivating these, one attains analytical wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyāna-prajñā*).

As it is said that the Sugata, abiding in two types of investigation (*vitarka*), is able to know the arising and so forth of all feelings as they truly are—this demonstrates that by cultivating the wholesome, one attains analytical wisdom.

The term "preparatory application" (*prayoga*) is used to distinguish it from that which is acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*); it does not refer to the cultivation of what is acquired by birth, because it involves the attainment of what was previously unattained.
If one cultivates the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), one then attains the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).

This means that if one cultivates the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) of the fourth dhyāna along with its accompanying dharmas, one will be able to attain the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
The Buddha himself declared that the fourth dhyāna is the basis for this, because unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*) is attained by relying upon it.
The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) realizes the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) instantaneously and induces the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*);
therefore, it is specifically mentioned. Some say that all antidotes for abandoning the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) within the fourth dhyāna are subsumed under this [concentration].

Regarding the distinctions in meaning between "practicing" (*abhyāsa*), "cultivating" (*bhāvanā*), and "frequently performing" (*bahulīkāra*) as taught in this sutra, they are intended to demonstrate that the objects to be countered (*vipakṣa*) become increasingly distant through practice, cultivation, and attainment, respectively.
Having thus already analyzed the meditative concentrations that serve as the basis, one should now analyze the virtues that arise based upon those concentrations.
Among all these virtues, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are analyzed first.
The verse says:
The immeasurables are of four kinds, serving as antidotes to hatred and the like.
Loving-kindness and compassion have non-hatred as their nature; sympathetic joy has joy, and equanimity has non-attachment.
Their respective mental aspects are, in order: bestowing happiness, removing suffering, giving joy, and remaining impartial.
Sympathetic joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) take sentient beings of the desire realm as their object.
Joy belongs to the first and second dhyānas; the remaining six [mental factors] belong to either five or ten [stages].
They cannot sever any of the afflictions (*kleśa*); when arising in humans, they constitute three [types of attainment].
The treatise states: There are four immeasurables: first, loving-kindness (*maitrī*); second, compassion (*karuṇā*); third, sympathetic joy (*muditā*); and fourth, equanimity (*upekṣā*).

They are called "immeasurable" because they take immeasurable sentient beings as their object; because these four can induce immeasurable merit; and because immeasurable fruits of affection have them as their cause.
Some say: Because these [four immeasurables] can oppose infinite conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), all afflictions such as greed are termed "conceptual proliferation.
For what reason are there no more or fewer than four immeasurables?
Because they serve as remedies for four types of predominant obstacles, as stated in the Sūtra:

"If one practices, cultivates, or frequently performs them—loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever hatred; compassion (*karuṇā*) can sever harmful intent; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) can sever lack of appreciation; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) can sever sensual desire and hatred. Therefore, there are only four.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) refers to the mind's desire to kill sentient beings.
The mental factor that desires to afflict sentient beings is called harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).
Non-congratulation (*anabhirati*) refers to the cause for not delighting in abiding in various categories of wholesome qualities due to attachment to sense objects.
The arising of defiled delight toward the objects of excellent sensual desires, characterized by a lack of satiety, is called "desire-greed" (*kāmarāga*).
In this context, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) have non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as their intrinsic nature. If that is so, what is the difference between these two?

Although their essential natures are not distinct, loving-kindness functions with the aspect of counteracting the anger toward sentient beings that leads to killing, while compassion functions with the aspect of counteracting the anger and resentment toward sentient beings that leads to harming; this is the distinction between them.
Just as with suffering and pleasure, although their nature as experience is the same, they differ in terms of harm and benefit; therefore, their essential natures are distinct.
That the natures of suffering and pleasure are distinct has already been explained above.
The distinction between the two types, compassion and loving-kindness, is likewise the same.
Some say: "Compassion (*karuṇā*) is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*), because it is the direct antidote to harming.
This is indeed the case in principle; however, harming resembles anger, and thus it is described by the name of that which it resembles.
The characteristic of compassion (*karuṇā*) is also similar to non-hatred (*adveṣa*), and thus it is designated by the name "non-hatred," though in reality it is non-harming (*ahiṃsā*).
The ancient masters state that joy (*muditā*) is simply the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*).
For what reason does the practitioner experience the feeling of joy at that time?
If its object were the conferring of happiness, it would be no different from loving-kindness (*maitrī*); if its object were the removal of suffering, it should be identical to compassion (*karuṇā*).
Furthermore, a sutra states:
Because of delight (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*) arises.
Joy is precisely the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*), as has already been explained previously.
Since the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of this joy is identical to that delight, what difference is there in meaning between "because of delight, joy arises" and "joy arises because of joy"?

If you claim that there is a difference in meaning between "lower" and "upper," then the same should apply to the meanings of *praśrabdhi* (tranquility) and *sukha* (pleasure), as no grounds for such a distinction can be found.
Furthermore, this would contradict the original treatise:
"What is called joy (*prīti*)?"
This refers to joy and the associated aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Herein, the intent is to reveal the factors belonging to the category co-arising with joy; because joy is predominant, they are collectively designated by the name "joy.
It is not that feeling is co-arising with feeling; this principle is certain.
If joy (*prīti*) is itself the feeling of joy (*prītivedanā*), why say it is "concomitant with feeling"?
If you claim that the Abhidharma takes reasoning as its authority, then you should recite the original treatise without error.

This is also not the case; for a treatise based on reasoning to be authoritative, it must have scriptural evidence to establish its textual formulations. If it contradicts the scriptures, the reasoning must necessarily be refuted; one should not arbitrarily alter the text of the treatise at will.
Therefore, this joy (*prīti*) is certainly not the feeling of joy (*prītivedanā*); it has gladness as its essence, or it is simply non-attachment (*alobha*).
This is because there exists a distinct defiled mental factor called attachment (*lobha*), which, regarding sentient beings, forms the thought:
"How might I ensure that whatever pleasure they possess cannot be obtained by them, but instead belongs entirely to me?"
Joy (*prīti*) is able to counteract that [craving], and is therefore non-greed (*alobha*), because it necessarily functions in conjunction with the faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*).

Just as remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and mental grief (*daurmanasya*) can be found in the three stages [of the form realm], joy is also a distinct characteristic of non-greed: it is the absence of attachment to the prosperity of others, and the profound sense of gratification and consolation felt upon knowing that others have attained success. Since joy is defined as the antidote to the fever of the mind (*cittatāpa*), one should know that this joy is also of the nature of non-greed.

The essence of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is solely non-attachment (*alobha*). The distinction between this and the third [immeasurable, sympathetic joy] is that it is free from the conceptualizations of affection and aversion toward sentient beings.
Just as one who has first entered a forest gives rise to the perception of trees, the cause for practicing impartiality is called equanimity.
If equanimity (*upekṣā*) can also counteract hatred (*dveṣa*), how does it differ from loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which is characterized solely by non-attachment (*alobha*)?
Furthermore, if you grant that this equanimity directly counteracts sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), what distinction is there between it and the meditation on the unattractive (*aśubhabhāvanā*)?

Furthermore, regarding the distinction between equanimity (*upekṣā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*): loving-kindness counteracts the hatred induced by hatred, and its essence is non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
Equanimity counteracts the hatred induced by attachment, and its essence is non-attachment (*alobha*).
Is it not the case that equanimity (*upekṣā*), which has non-attachment (*alobha*) as its intrinsic nature, can also counteract the hatred induced by attachment?
Likewise, if you grant that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as its intrinsic nature, it should likewise be able to counteract the attachment induced by hatred.
This objection is not valid, because its mode of operation (*ākāra*) is contradictory.

That is to say, the mode of equanimity (*upekṣā*) contradicts both greed and hatred simultaneously, because it abandons the distinct characteristics of distinguishing between those who are dear and those who are not; consequently, neither attachment nor aversion arises from it.
It is for this reason that equanimity (*upekṣā*) abandons only non-attachment (*alobha*); while it is primarily able to counteract attachment, it also incidentally counteracts aversion (*dveṣa*).
This is because the aspect of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is contrary to aversion rather than attachment, as it functions by bestowing happiness upon all sentient beings.

Thus, although both loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are equally opposed to hatred, loving-kindness accords with attachment while equanimity can oppose harmfulness; therefore, these two are fundamentally distinct.

Alternatively, one who cultivates equanimity remedies misplaced hatred, whereas loving-kindness remedies [misplaced] hatred toward those who are appropriate objects; hence, there is a distinction between them.
Impurity (aśubhā) and equanimity (upekṣā) serve as remedies for lustful craving and other types of craving, respectively; therefore, there is a distinction between them.
Since these four immeasurables do not cause harm or benefit to others, for what reason are they exclusively wholesome (kuśala) and not of an indeterminate (avyākṛta) nature?

Because they serve as direct antidotes to greed, hatred, and so forth; because they prevent the attraction of signs of the pleasant and the unpleasant; and because they possess the power to cause the mind to function with mastery—the essential characteristics of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others have thus been briefly analyzed.

Regarding the distinctions among these mental dispositions (*āśaya*): viewing sentient beings as like oneself is called loving-kindness (*maitrī*); wishing for sentient beings to be free from suffering is called compassion (*karuṇā*); rejoicing in the prosperity of others is called sympathetic joy (*muditā*); and not considering the distinction between friends and enemies is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Furthermore, not observing others as having either harm or benefit, but regarding all beings as friends is called loving-kindness (*maitrī*); feeling compassion for those who encounter suffering is called pity (*karuṇā*); through the power of resolute conviction, feeling gladness at the thought that sentient beings have obtained benefit and escaped harm is called joy (*muditā*); and regarding the equality of all sentient beings is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding the distinctions among these four aspects: how might one cause all classes of sentient beings to obtain such happiness?
Thinking thus, one enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
"How might I cause all classes of sentient beings to be free from such suffering?
Thinking thus, he enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of compassion (*karuṇā*).
"How wonderful it would be if all classes of sentient beings were to attain happiness and be free from suffering!"
Reflecting in this way, one enters the meditative attainment of joy (*muditā-samāpatti*).
Reflecting that all classes of sentient beings are equal and without distinction between friend and enemy, one enters the meditative attainment of equanimity (*upekṣā-samāpatti*).
If such aspirations ultimately fail to be realized, would they not be in vain?
Yet, can the power of cultivating meditative concentration—which is capable of subduing anger and other afflictions—be called in vain?
This must be a misconception; how could it possibly fail to subdue the defilements?
Is it a misconception to say that one wishes for sentient beings to obtain happiness and so forth?

This does not mean that one has already obtained happiness and so forth; rather, it is by means of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that one prays for all sentient beings to obtain happiness and so forth, thereby being able to suppress all afflictions. Therefore, the cultivation of these four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) is not in vain.
Within the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), four aspects (*ākāra*) are taught; how are they made equal?
This is as explained previously.

Regarding the statement that "one enters a certain meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) by reflecting in such a way," if this were understood in terms of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), then loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others would lack the capacity for immediate succession, because each is induced by a distinct act of reflection.
If it were co-emergent (*sahaja*), the term "entry" (*praveśa*) would be contradictory.

While in the stage of initial practice (*ādikarmika*) it is induced by distinct preparatory effort (*prayoga*), it also exists as co-emergent upon reaching the stage of perfection (*niṣpanna*). There is no fault in stating that one "enters" from the perspective of the initial [stage] according to the *Samādhi-skandha*.
Furthermore, what kind of happiness does one wish to obtain through immeasurable loving-kindness?
Some say one wishes to obtain the happiness of the third dhyāna, because among all types of experienced happiness, this is the most excellent.
If one has not yet realized it for oneself, one knows it by means of hearing.
Some say they wish to attain the wondrous bliss of *nirvāṇa*, because among all forms of bliss this is the most supreme.
Others say they wish to attain the bliss of an *arhat*, because this one has already been liberated from all afflictions (*kleśa*).

A beginner who has not yet realized this bliss cannot direct the mind toward it because it has not been directly realized; rather, they take as their object their own body and the bliss realized by others that is currently perceptible, wishing that all sentient beings may likewise realize this bliss. Thus, they take as their object the present, non-afflicted bliss born of correct reasoning and wish that others may experience it together with them.

If a bhikṣu who has already renounced what he received remains in a secluded place and experiences the joy of seclusion—even if he has not yet attained true antidotes—his power is able to eclipse the joy of the Lord of Devas and others, just as the five types of worldly pleasures do.

A verse states: Furthermore, for one who dwells in seclusion and diligently cultivates the wholesome, there will certainly be a continuous flow of wholesome attainment at every moment, like the waters of the great ocean that are pervasive and uninterrupted; from this, joy and the bliss of pliancy are induced.

With a mind free from stinginess, taking such happiness as an object, one should wish that all sentient beings may equally experience it—the superior happiness of those in training and those beyond training who possess the remainder.
How could one, by contemplating what is inferior and bestowing it upon others, fail to avoid inviting inferior results for oneself in the future?

If one were to claim that [the bodhisattva] does not wish to bestow this upon superior beings, it would contradict the fact that they universally take sentient beings as their object; for, due to the lack of stinginess regarding the merit that serves as the basis, they are truly unable to cause others to obtain happiness.

For example, if a poor person were to offer the coarse and inferior utensils they themselves use to a wealthy person, even though that wealthy person does not seek such a gift, the donor commits no fault; for this expresses their own heart of respect and lack of stinginess.
This case is likewise, and thus there is no error.
It is like planting a single small seed in fertile soil, from which the resulting fruit is both abundant and large, such as with the *bhaṇḍīra* tree or various types of melons and gourds.
Therefore, it is not the case that by observing an inferior object and teaching it to others, one will consequently invite an inferior result in the future.
Rather, all [immeasurables] take sentient beings of the desire realm as their object, for they are able to counteract obstacles such as hatred directed toward those objects.

This means that regarding sentient beings in the desire realm who fall into the three categories of enemies, kin, and neutral parties, one is able to give rise to anger and other afflictions; therein, by relinquishing the distinctions between enemy and kin, one is then able to suppress and eliminate afflictions such as anger.
Therefore, this object pertains exclusively to sentient beings of the desire realm and can certainly not take the form and formless realms as its cognitive object.
Great Compassion has non-delusion as its wholesome root; by the power of this, it is able to universally take all three realms as its object.
If the four immeasurables take only sentient beings as their object, why does the sutra state that one contemplates "one direction" and so forth?
This is because, through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one takes all sentient beings within the entire vessel-world as the object; thus, there is no fault.
These four [knowledges] pertain to both the desire realm and the form realm,
for the Sūtra states that they can bring about the superior fruits of being a Brahmā, Śakra, or a Wheel-Turning King. The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*,

relying on the knowledge produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya-jñāna*), states that seven knowledges cognize the objects to be abandoned through cultivation in the form realm, as well as the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase therein.

Other masters say: "The preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of these four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) pertain to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while their fundamental states (*maula*) exist only in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Regarding the distinction of the levels (*bhūmi*) upon which these four immeasurables rely: if 'joy' (*muditā*) is identical to the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*), it must be produced only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*). In that case, they should state that joy exists only in the first and second dhyānas, because the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) does not exist in other levels."

If joy (*prīti*) is distinct from the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), it would also be comprised within that which is produced by reflection (*cintā-maya*); in that case, one should state that joy pervades seven stages (*bhūmi*), because it is also associated with the feelings of pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Others say that joy (*muditā*) is associated exclusively with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*); if that were so, one should state that joy pertains to three stages, or else, as the verse states, it should pertain to only two and no others.

Compassion (*karuṇā*), joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) all pertain to six stages, namely: the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*).

Some maintain that these depend exclusively on five stages, namely excluding the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage, because this is a quality of composure that can only be produced by those who have already abandoned desire.
Others say that these four exist only in the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna, where they receive the name "immeasurables" (*apramāṇa*), whereas in other stages it is not so.

Because the sūtras speak of the immeasurables as the "brahma-abodes" (*brahmavihāra*), and because they speak of cultivating the immeasurables to be born in the Brahma-world, and because they speak of them as bringing about the fruits of being a Brahma-king, a Śakra, or a Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*).

Some say that, according to the circumstances, they generally rely upon all ten stages—that is, the desire realm, the four fundamental dhyānas, their preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
If compassion (*karuṇā*) also relies upon the lower three dhyānas, how can it be associated with joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*)?
This is because compassion functions with a mode of activity (*ākāra*) characterized by dejection, taking suffering sentient beings as its object.

It arises like the attention of renunciation (*nirvedha-manasikāra*) that is untainted (*anāsrava*); therefore, it universally relies upon the lower three dhyānas. Since that genuine attention (*bhūtamanasikāra*) is conducive to the arising of delight, there is no fault in its being associated with joy and bliss.
Since this attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) does not accord with the arising of joy, how can it be said to resemble that [joy]?
Since doubt (*vicikitsā*) is by nature dejection and does not accord with the arising of joy, how can you allow that doubt arises simultaneously with joy and bliss?

Adhimukti-manasikāra (attention through resolute conviction) should be similar to that [samyak-manasikāra]; however, this [adhimukti] is extremely conducive to joy and possesses the power to induce true attention (*bhūta-manasikāra*).
Doubt (*vicikitsā*), by contrast, is not so, as it is utterly contrary to the truth.
If that [joy] can still be associated with it, why should this not be admitted?

It follows logically that this attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) must be contrary to joy (*abhirati*), because there is a distinction in their modes of activity (*ākāra*) regarding the presence of gladness and dejection within the practice of the middle way.

Since compassion (*karuṇā*) functions with a mode of activity (*ākāra*) characterized by dejection, it should not be associated with joy (*saumanasya*) or pleasure (*sukha*), lest two modes of activity function simultaneously.
If that were so, one would have to deny its association with equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because equanimity functions with a mode of activity that dwells in the middle.

Since it is not denied that [these four] may be associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*), it must logically be admitted that they can coexist with joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*), lest they be entirely dissociated from feeling (*vedanā*).

Although it is said that these four can counteract hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth, they cannot sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), because they arise in association with attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika-manasikāra*); only attention consisting of reality (*tattvārtha-manasikāra*) is capable of severing the delusions.
Furthermore, because this [attention] takes only sentient beings as its object, one must attend to dharmas in order to be able to abandon the afflictions.

Moreover, because this [attention] takes only present objects as its object, one must attend to [objects] across the three times or to that which is non-temporal in order to be able to abandon the afflictions.
Furthermore, because the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) can be attained therein, it is only through the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) that afflictions (kleśa) can be abandoned.
Some state: "Because it is subsumed under the fundamental dhyānas with outflows (sāsrava)."

This reason is flawed; one should not say that [the three] rely on six stages, because [the factors] such as the threshold (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate (*dhyānāntara*) would then be absent from this [category].
Why does the Sūtra speak of the abandonment of hatred and so forth in this context?
Nor is there any contradiction, for there are two kinds of abandonment.

Alternatively, it is because this power induces the path of abandonment; that is to say, by suppressing anger and so forth, it induces the arising of the path of abandonment. Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of abandoning anger and the like.
If that is so, why does the Sūtra state:
"By well-cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one abides in the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*)"?
In this context, the noble path (*āryamārga*) is designated by the name "loving-kindness," just as in other instances the term "perception" (*saṃjñā*) and so forth are used [to designate the path].
Alternatively, it is said that one attains freedom from desire by first obtaining a mind of loving-kindness through the noble ones and subsequently practicing it repeatedly;
or it is said that one attains freedom from desire by diligently practicing in order to obtain the loving-kindness produced through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*).

Some say that these four reliances depend upon bodies of the desire and form realms, and do not take those of the formless realm as objects, because [the formless] lacks distinctions such as enemy or friend, and because one must first take those [lower realms] as objects when cultivating them.
According to the true meaning, they depend solely upon bodies of the desire realm; within the desire realm, they can only be generated by humans.
If *prīti* (joy) is not the feeling of joy (*sukha-vedanā*), then when it is established, it necessarily possesses four [factors].

If *prīti* is indeed the feeling of joy, then when it is established, one [factor] is certain and three are established; this is because in the third dhyāna and above, *prīti* alone is not established.
Based on what meaning does the Sūtra state:

"The cultivation of the four immeasurables reaches its limit in the Sphere of Universal Purity for loving-kindness (*maitrī*); it reaches its limit in the Sphere of Infinite Space for compassion (*karuṇā*); it reaches its limit in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness for sympathetic joy (*muditā*); and it reaches its limit in the Sphere of Nothingness for equanimity (*upekṣā*)?"
How can dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) produce a fruit in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?

Furthermore, since loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is not absent from any of the four dhyānas, for what reason does the cultivation of loving-kindness culminate only in the Sphere of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*)?
Others, weary of investigating this matter, defer to the Compassionate Honored One (*Maitreya*), who shall explain this meaning.
It is reported that the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra once questioned Śamathadeva on this very point; the venerable one reflected upon it and entered meditative absorption.
When the dawn broke and he was about to provide the explanation, Kātyāyanīputra again entered meditative absorption.
At that time, as they had not yet met and each entered parinirvāṇa, no one has been able to explain this from then until now.
The Vaibhāṣikas offer this explanation:

it should be understood that this sūtra speaks according to similarity; that is, the dharma of pleasant feeling is similar to loving-kindness (*maitrī*), because loving-kindness functions with the aspect of bestowing pleasure, and thus pleasure extends up to the Sphere of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*).
Since these [higher stages] are entirely devoid of them, it is said that the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) culminates at the stage of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*).
Seeking the dharma of liberation from suffering is similar to compassion (*karuṇā*), because compassion functions by taking the form of an activity that extracts suffering.
The form-body (*rūpakāya*) can act as the cause for the arising of coarse suffering, because as long as there is a body, there is the possibility of having one's head cut off and so forth.

Since the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) involves a state of weary detachment from the form-body, it is said that the cultivation of compassion reaches its limit at the sphere of infinite space.
The dharma of pliancy and bliss (*praśrabdhi-sukha*) resembles joy (*prīti*), because joy functions by taking the aspect of peaceful bliss.

In the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), pliancy and bliss increase, as it takes its own infinite consciousness as its gateway; since the aspect of infinite consciousness increases to the utmost degree of bliss, it is said that the cultivation of joy culminates at the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.
The ability to relinquish is similar to equanimity (*upekṣā*), because it functions with the mental aspect of performing the act of relinquishing.

In the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), equanimity is perfected through the relinquishing of the mental aspect of "boundlessness" during its preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*); therefore, it is said that one cultivates equanimity up to the sphere of nothingness.

Some say that this sutra is taught according to mutual conformity (*anuloma*): namely, arising from the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), one produces a flow of joy that conforms to the third dhyāna; arising from the third dhyāna, one produces a flow of desire that also conforms to the absorption of loving-kindness. In this manner, up to the point where, arising from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) through equanimity (*upekṣā*), one produces a flow of desire, these states conform to one another in succession.
This does not reveal the underlying principle and consists of nothing but empty words; one should perhaps seek a deeper significance therein.

Some say that this sutra speaks according to specific inclinations (*āśaya*), meaning that those who delight in loving-kindness (*maitrī*) delight in the third dhyāna, and so on, up to those who delight in equanimity (*upekṣā*) who delight in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
This too is irrational; by what means is it proven?
Therefore, the previous explanation is superior.

When first wishing to arouse the four immeasurables, one first divides sentient beings into three categories: namely, friends, neutral persons, and enemies. Each of these three is further divided into three—superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior friend refers to one who gives rise to the Dharma-body; because one relies on their profound kindness, it is difficult to remain [in this world] were they to depart.
The middling friend refers to one with whom wealth and Dharma are shared to the utmost degree of mutual affection.
The inferior type of friend refers to one with whom there is an association based solely on wealth, yet who is also mutually affectionate.
The superior type of neutral person refers to one whom one has never before seen or heard of.
The middling type of neutral person refers to one whom one has seen or heard of, but with whom one does not maintain a social relationship.
Regarding those of lower status who are neutral: although they associate with one, they remain free from both enmity and affection.
Regarding superior enemies: they are those who seize one's reputation, life, and close friends.
Regarding middling enemies: they are those who seize one's own life and the requisites for existence.
Regarding those who are enemies, it refers to those who have deprived one's relatives and friends of their lives, resources, and necessities.

Having categorized all sentient beings into these various groups, one who first cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) first generates a pure resolve (*adhimokṣa*) to bestow happiness toward those who are most closely related.

If, due to an evil disposition (*āśaya*) formed through habitual practice since beginningless time, the mind becomes rigid and one harbors deep resentment upon encountering even slight affliction, [the practice] will cease because of this.

Furthermore, one should exert effort in resolving to bring them happiness and contemplate their profound kindness; by generating the intention to grant them happiness once more, the sense of resentment will be forever eliminated through the power of repeated practice.

When the continuity of the resolute intention (*adhimokṣa*) to bestow happiness has become uninterrupted and unchanging, and this has been accomplished, one then gradually cultivates such a resolute intention toward those who are moderately or slightly dear.

Once equanimity has been attained toward these three grades of relatives, one next cultivates the mental disposition of wishing to bestow happiness sequentially toward neutral persons, those who are slightly hostile, those who are moderately hostile, and those who are intensely hostile. Finally, when one attains a mind of perfect equality toward even the most intensely hostile and the most dearly beloved, without any fluctuation whatsoever, this is called the fulfillment of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The cultivation of compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) should be explained by analogy with this.

That is to say, one observes that sentient beings are universally oppressed by the three types of suffering; one should not inflict further suffering upon them, but rather strive diligently to rescue and deliver them just as one would for oneself.

Gradually cultivating the intention to rescue and deliver others, until one regards enemies and kin with equal impartiality, free from fluctuation—this is called the perfected perception of the cultivation of compassion (*karuṇā*).

When one gives rise to profound joy and consolation regarding all sentient beings attaining happiness and being freed from suffering, no different from one's own experience—this is called the perfection of the cultivation of sympathetic joy (*muditā*).

Regarding the initial cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*): one first abandons those who are neutral, rather than abandoning enemies and kin first, because hatred and attachment are difficult to relinquish.

Furthermore, the power of equanimity increases when directed toward neutral parties. Within that category, as before, one first abandons the superior degree, then the middle and inferior degrees, as well as enemies and kin; proceeding from the inferior to the middle, and from the middle to the superior.
Regarding the initial relinquishing of enemies: because it is difficult to relinquish those who are dear, as the Sūtra says, "Greed is difficult to sever, not so hatred.

By practicing in this gradual sequence—from equanimity toward neutral persons, up to superior friends and so forth—one universally relinquishes all distinctions among sentient beings; reaching this point is called the fulfillment of the cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

If one seeks to find virtues in sentient beings, one will be able to swiftly cultivate and accomplish qualities such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), whereas this is not the case for one who seeks out faults in sentient beings.

This is because even those who have severed their roots of virtue possess merits that may be recorded, and even rhinoceros-like solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*) possess failings that may be noted; for the present fruits of their prior merit and demerit can be clearly perceived.
*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 79; *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 80.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eight, Part Four: The Analysis of Meditative Concentrations (Samādhi). Having already analyzed the immeasurables (apramāṇa), the liberations (vimokṣa) will now be analyzed.
The verse says:
There are eight kinds of liberation; the first three have non-attachment as their nature;
they are each fixed in two, two, and one dhyāna respectively; and the four formless absorptions are wholesome.

The liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception arises immediately after the *sūkṣma-sūkṣma* [state], by means of a pure mind of its own level or by emerging from the lower untainted [state].
Three objects are visible in the desire realm; four objects belong to the category of the *anvaya-jñāna* path.
"From the cessation of suffering, its origin, and its extinction, Non-analytical cessation, and space.

The commentary states: There are eight liberations (*vimokṣa*): first, the liberation of one who has the perception of internal forms while observing external forms; second, the liberation of one who lacks the perception of internal forms while observing external forms; third, the pure liberation, which is realized by bodily witness and dwelt in fully; fourth through seventh, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) as the four successive liberations; and eighth, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*).
Among these eight, the first three have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their essential nature, because they directly counteract attachment.

However, it is said in the Sūtras that they are "perception and contemplation" (*saṃjñā-vipaśyanā*) because perception and contemplation are predominant therein; this is like the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), which eliminates the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*).
Among these three, the first two function through impure aspects, because they take on the mental images of such things as the livid corpse and so forth.
The third liberation functions through pure aspects, because it takes on the mental image of being pure, radiant, and fresh.
The three [liberations], together with their associated factors, are all of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Each of the first two liberations relies upon either the first or the second dhyāna, as they are able to counteract the craving for visible forms (*rūpa-rāga*) within the desire realm and the first dhyāna, respectively.

The first two [immediate liberations] encompass both the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), because all five levels are capable of giving rise to the first two.

Since there is craving for visible forms (*varṇa-rāga*) in the desire realm and the first dhyāna—arising from the visual consciousness aggregate—the first two impure liberations (*aśubha-vimokṣa*) are established within the first and second dhyānas in order to achieve liberation from that craving.

Because visual consciousness is absent within the second and third dhyānas, and because there is no greed for manifest color (varṇa-rūpa) induced therein, the impure liberations (aśubha-vimokṣa) do not exist within the third and fourth dhyānas.

Although the wholesome roots similar to the first two liberations may also occur within the desire realm, they are intermingled with the greed of the desire realm; therefore, the designation of "liberation" is not established for them.

Although these [liberations] may also exist within the third and fourth dhyānas, they cannot be called the "third liberation" because they are distant from their respective objects of abandonment and thus possess weak power, and furthermore, they are suppressed by the perception of pleasure and purity.

Because the mind is pure and clear due to being free from the eight calamities based on the subsequent dhyāna, the name "subsequent dhyāna" is established for the fourth [dhyāna] as well as its preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*).

Although similar roots of virtue exist in the lower stages, they are not designated as "liberation" because they lack predominance. This is because in the desire realm, one is overwhelmed and intermingled with sensual craving; in the first and second dhyānas, impurity is suppressed; in the third dhyāna, one is deluded by pleasure; and furthermore, all these are disturbed by the eight calamities.

The subsequent four liberations, in their respective order, have the wholesome states of the four formless absorptions as their nature; they are neither neutral nor defiled, because those are not liberations, nor are they mundane wholesome states, because their nature is weak and inferior.
Regarding those [wholesome states] that are distracted (*vikṣipta*), they are like the mind at the moment of death.

Some say that there are also distracted wholesome states at other times, because these are exclusively innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika*) and lack those acquired through hearing or reflection (*śruta-cintā-maya*).

Furthermore, the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) belonging to the various preparatory stages (*sāmantaka-bhūmi*) are also not "liberation," because they do not turn away from the lower stages and because their objects are mixed with the paths of the lower levels.
Furthermore, because they have not yet completely abandoned the defilements of the lower stages, the Sūtra states that they have "transcended" those lower stages.
Some say that the various paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) belonging to the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are also called "liberation," because they turn their backs on the lower stages.
However, the reason other sources mention only the fundamental [attainments] is that within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), there is no complete liberation.

The eighth liberation is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); it is so called because one gives rise to this state by turning away from feeling and perception, or because one turns away from all objects of cognition in general.
However, the Elder says:
"The state within the continuum of sentient beings is what is called the attainment of cessation.
This too is irrational, as has already been extensively argued, because this attainment of cessation possesses a real substantial entity (*dravya*).

Furthermore, it cannot be said that this meditative absorption possesses a mind, for we have never seen a state where there is a mind yet no feeling, perception, or volition; thus, there is no possibility of proceeding by deviating from this path.

As it is said, "In this state, feeling, perception, and so forth are extinguished, being tranquil and blissful"; such a sublime liberation belongs only to Arhats and others. It is not possible to designate a mere continuity devoid of meaning or a mind as being "tranquil" or "blissful."
How can one conceive of the superior liberation of the Arhats and others?
There is a class of thought that has no object of cognition and proceeds free from mental aspects (*ākāra*).
Since that which possesses an object of cognition must necessarily involve contact (*sparśa*), if one admits the existence of contact, how could there not be the fruit of sensation (*vedanā*)?
One should ask: what is it that obstructs the non-arising of sensation and the other [mental factors]?
Therefore, there is no mental state within the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
It is not a case of being deluded regarding correct principles; with merely a brief glance at the scriptural text, one is able to comprehend the profound intent of the Noble Teaching.

Consciousness is not eternally extinguished, for it is said that it does not leave the body; just as when an illness has not been permanently cured, its temporary subsidence is still called "having [the illness].

Following the extremely subtle mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*), this meditative absorption manifests. Since the preceding state relative to the mind of perception was already termed "subtle," this is called "extremely subtle" because it is even more subtle than that; subsequently, with such a mind, one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

This means that the mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) consists of three grades: namely, the conceptual, the subtle, and the extremely subtle minds, distinguished by their superior, intermediate, and inferior qualities.
Since the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) must manifest immediately following the inferior grade, one enters the attainment of cessation next after the extremely subtle mind.

Upon emerging from the attainment of cessation, one either gives rise to a pure meditative mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) or immediately gives rise to an untainted (*anāsrava*) mind of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Thus, while the mind entering [the attainment] is exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*), the emergence from it may occur through either a tainted or an untainted mind.

Among these eight, the first three take only the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire realm as their object. As for their distinction: two take the aspect of impurity, while one takes the aspect of purity.
Since pure elements also exist among all forms, how could it not be subsumed under perversion (*viparyāsa*) to contemplate them collectively as impure?
Just as it constitutes a perversion to conceive of suffering phenomena as pleasant—

because even within conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) there is a mixture of suffering, yet one conceives of them as exclusively pleasant— the third [perversion], taking what is impure as pure, is likewise difficult to establish.
This is not a fault, for it is what we accept.
That is to say, we also accept that this is inverted reflection (*viparyasta-manasikāra*).
If so, how is its nature not unwholesome (*akuśala*)?
Since this is a fruit obtained through the departure from defilement, it does not accord with reality; how then could it oppose defilement?
It causes the attention that gives rise to craving to be distanced.

Just as one who has not yet abandoned desire can give rise to greed by contemplating the aspect of purity within the pure and impure, this [contemplation] does not involve perceiving an aspect of purity within that which is actually pure; because it is not a perversion, it may be subsumed under the category of wholesome states.

Thus, through detachment from desire, one contemplates the impure within the pure and is able to distance oneself from greed; it is not that one perceives the aspect of impurity within this very purity, for that would be an inversion and is therefore subsumed under the nature of unwholesomeness.
One should likewise explain the case of perceiving the impure as pure by analogy.

Alternatively, this does not refer to inverted contemplation; rather, all impure phenomena are generally of two kinds: first, those consisting of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and second, those consisting of admixture (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).

Because various pure phenomena are mixed with impure ones, they are also termed "impure"; this is universally established in the world, and therefore such contemplation is not called a perversion (*viparyāsa*).
By the same principle, the case where impure phenomena are mixed with pure ones should be understood accordingly.

However, when a practitioner first begins to cultivate contemplation, they do not apprehend the sign of impurity within a pure realm; rather, they apprehend the sign of impurity within an impure realm, causing the mind to revolve with signs of extreme aversion and contrariety. Subsequently, these signs of contrariety gradually expand and broaden, so that one gives rise to a general sense of weariness toward all objects of the sensual realm and the sphere of form, and no longer produces greedy attachment.
If, within the material aggregates of the pure realm— the form realm— one lacks the capacity for resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) to apprehend the aspect of impurity,

and since it is only within the material aggregates of the desire realm that resolute conviction can apprehend the aspect of impurity, one should know that the nature of the impure realm (*aśubhadhātu*) must certainly also exist within the material aggregates of the desire realm.
Since one perceives the impure as impure, how can it be said to be of a perverted nature?
The third [perception], which takes the pure as such, should be understood by this same analogy.
Since this operates upon its object in accordance with reality, how can it be called "attention consisting of resolute conviction" (adhimukti-manasikāra)?
Because this arises toward its object through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), it is called "attention consisting of resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣika-manasikāra*).
