For this very reason, it receives the name "liberation," since the meanings of "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*) and "liberation" (*vimukti*) are closely related.

Or, when one gradually increases the contemplation regarding a minor object through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), it is called "attention consisting of resolute conviction" (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
That is to say, when one gradually increases the contemplation regarding a small amount of purity, immeasurable defiled attachment arises because of this.
Once this has arisen, the mind becomes bound and constrained by its objects, losing its natural autonomy.
One gradually increases the contemplation of even a small amount of impurity, which—contrary to the previous state—augments all roots of goodness.

Just as one contemplates pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) as being of the nature of suffering through change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), viewing it as suffering because it is interspersed with the characteristics of suffering, and thus subdues the afflictions (*kleśa*) without being termed a perversion (*viparyāsa*);
so too, the pure realm (*viśuddhadhātu*) is interspersed with the impure, and one may likewise contemplate it as impure therein without it being termed a perversion.
One should know that this is also the case for distancing oneself from craving and attaining liberation through the perception of purity (*śubha-vimokṣa*).
When contemplation is not yet perfected, it is merely termed "attention through resolute belief" (*adhimokṣika-manasikāra*).
Once it is perfected, because it is the fruit of freedom from defilement and because it induces the Noble Path, it is also termed "attention to reality" (*bhūtamanasikāra*).
Having thus explained the objects of the first three liberations, we shall now discuss the objects of the subsequent four liberations:

each takes as its objective sphere the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation pertaining to its own level or higher levels, the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) across all stages, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and space (*ākāśa*).
The formless liberations (ārūpya-vimokṣas) turn their backs on the lower stages and therefore do not take them as objects.

Regarding the aspects (ākāra) of suffering and origin in the lower stages: the first two are impure, while the third is exclusively pure; neither of these constitutes the sixteen [aspects]. Since the formless liberations subsume the fundamental meditative concentrations (mauladhyāna), the aspects they perform are the sixteen.

Alternatively, regarding those not associated with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*) are associated with the foundation of mindfulness of the body; the subsequent four liberations are associated with all four foundations of mindfulness. Regarding their association with knowledge (*jñāna*):

the first three, the seventh, and the last one are associated exclusively with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); the fourth, fifth, sixth, and eighth are associated with the [other] knowledges.

Regarding their association with the faculties (*indriya*): the first two liberations are associated with joy (*prīti*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), while the subsequent five liberations are associated exclusively with equanimity.
Regarding their distinction by time (*adhvan*): they all pertain to the three periods of time.

Regarding the distinction of objects by time-period (*adhvan*): among the first three liberations, those already arisen and those yet to arise each take their own respective time-period as their object; those not yet arisen take all three time-periods as their object.
The subsequent four liberations take the three time-periods as their objects, but these are not [restricted to] specific time-periods.
Regarding their moral nature: all are exclusively wholesome.
Regarding their objects: the first three liberations take all three natures as their objects; the subsequent four liberations take the wholesome and the indeterminate as their objects.

Regarding the distinctions among those associated with the "to-be-learned" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth: the first three and the last two are exclusively neither [of the three categories], while the middle three liberations all pertain to all three types.
As for that which takes the "to-be-learned" and so forth as its object: the first three liberations take only the "neither" as their object, while the fourth takes all three types as its objects.

Regarding those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and so forth: the first three and the last two are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); the middle three are abandoned through cultivation if they are contaminated (*sāsrava*), otherwise they are not.

Regarding those that take as objects what is abandoned by seeing and so forth: the first three take what is abandoned by cultivation as their object; the subsequent four liberations each universally take all three as their objects.
Regarding "having oneself and others as objects": first, one takes both self and others as objects; next, two take others as objects; and the fourth takes all three types as objects.
Regarding the distinction in attainment: the eighth and third are attained only when previously unattained, while the remaining six are common to both [previously attained and unattained].
"Penetrating both" refers to the internal dharmas of noble ones and the external dharmas of ordinary beings; for ordinary beings, it is exclusively that which has been previously attained.
What is the meaning intended by the Sūtra’s statement: "One who possesses form perceives forms"?
It is not that one who has not yet eliminated the perception of form is able to penetrate the profound meaning of this sūtra as it truly is;
rather, the explanations transmitted by the former sages state that the inability to subdue and eliminate the perception of internal form constitutes the meaning of "possessing form."
How is this known to be so?
Because of the specific explanation regarding the second liberation.
That is to say, regarding the second [liberation], it is stated as follows:
Because one internally lacks the perception of form while observing external forms,
it is known that in the first liberation, the internal perception of form has not yet been eliminated.
For this reason, the commentators establish the first [liberation] as "the liberation consisting of the observation of external forms by one who internally possesses the perception of form."

This means that the practitioner, like one who has slain an enemy's corpse, although already free from sensual desire, further contemplates external forms through the aspect of impurity in order to make that freedom firm and stable.
Due to repeatedly observing external forms, a sense of revulsion also arises toward internal forms.
It is like one who cherishes purity and cleanliness but has a dog’s corpse tied around their neck; they feel extreme shame and profound loathing.
Having thus contemplated the signs of external impurity, one then perceives that the internal physical body is likewise impure.

Because the mind is pure, one sees that the interior of the body is filled with the thirty-six impure substances, viewing them as various objects within a casket; this is called the stage of the first liberation reaching full perfection.
In this stage of fulfillment, from what is one liberated?

It means that when the mind does not delight in, turns away from with aversion, reviles, loathes, and restrains desire and greed for form, it is liberated from that desire and greed; for its nature is non-attachment.
If it is argued that because it is described as "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*), it must be wisdom (*prajñā*), this is logically untenable; for its immediate antidote is sensual desire (*kāmarāga*).
If its essence were wisdom, it would have to be the immediate antidote to delusion (*moha*);
since it is the immediate antidote to desire, its nature is non-attachment (*alobha*).
From this point onward, the practitioner of meditation gradually eliminates the perception of internal forms.

That is to say, through the perception of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-saṃjñā*), he imagines his own death: his corpse is carried on a bier and placed in a charnel ground, where various birds and beasts vie with one another to devour it; in an instant, the body is entirely consumed, and he sees only the birds and beasts.
Or, at this place, one may burn it with fire until even the remaining ashes are scattered and driven by the wind; in an instant, the body is exhausted and only the realm of space is seen.
Or, one visualizes one's own body as being like ghee or salt, melting and dissolving away by fire, water, and so forth, until the body no longer exists and only the fire and other elements are seen.
This is called the liberation consisting of the perception of internal formlessness while observing external forms.
Because the power of this resolute conviction (adhimukti) eliminates the perception of form, although it arises in relation to the body, one does not perceive the body.
Since the perception of internal form has already been dispelled, the mental continuum proceeds without further activity; a state of supreme pliancy and bliss manifests spontaneously.

In this stage, by repeatedly practicing the mode of apprehension characterized by revulsion toward the objective sphere of visible forms, one achieves the fulfillment of the second liberation; this is also like the first liberation regarding sensual desire.

Although one may have previously cultivated the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) and thereby attained liberation from the desire and greed for external forms, the self-love (*ātmasneha*) accumulated since beginningless time is difficult to dispel; thus, if one contemplates the body as existing, there remains the fear of falling back into birth. Therefore, one subsequently cultivates the internal perception of formlessness (*adhyātma-arūpa-saṃjñā*), which, through its loathing of form, perceives purity even more clearly than before.

At that time, the practitioner, relying on the first dhyāna, attains these two contemplations and develops a deep attachment to them; desiring to cause these to further increase, he enters the second dhyāna and again cultivates the two liberations, and again cultivates the two dharmas in sequence as before.
For what reason can it be said that this state, which involves revulsion toward the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), is associated with the feeling of joy (*prīti-vedanā*)?
It is due to the power of the stage (*bhūmi-bala*), just as in the case of the knowledge of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-jñāna*).
Alternatively, it is because one perceives that the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*) previously cultivated have reached the point of fulfillment, and thus joy ought to arise.
Having already attained liberation from the perception of form, although one dwells in the contemplation of revulsion, it does not obstruct joy.

Next, one enters the third dhyāna; because one is deluded by its sublime bliss, the mind becomes indolent, whereby one is unable to cultivate the various liberations and instead gives rise only to roots of goodness that merely resemble liberation.
In this dhyāna, it is the natural state of the power of that stage that neither the contemplation of joy nor the contemplation of loathing can be fully accomplished.

Progressing from here to cultivate the fourth dhyāna, because the predominance [of those factors] has been relinquished, the mind gradually becomes clear and pure; since no further unwholesome perceptions arise with predominance, these are not called the first or second liberations, but may only be termed "similar roots of virtue."

Because that practitioner of yoga has long contemplated impurity, his mind becomes despondent due to the intensification of his revulsion. Desiring to stimulate it so that joy may briefly arise, or to momentarily relieve the fatigue of long-term cultivation, or to personally verify the efficacy of his contemplation of impurity, he again relies upon the fourth dhyāna to produce a resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the purity of forms in the desire realm. First taking up pure signs such as precious garments and flowers, he gradually expands his contemplation through the power of resolute conviction, producing the aspect of purity throughout the entire object of focus.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"At a later time, he should apprehend a small degree of the sign of purity and contemplate all forms as a whole.
Although this rouses the mind, it does not lead to agitation; although he contemplates the sign of purity, greed does not arise."

Having understood that the power of the roots of goodness has increased, one next further concentrates the mind upon the object, dwelling in the contemplation of purity within a single focal point; this stage is called the fulfillment of the liberation through purity (*śubha-vimokṣa*), because it is able to completely relinquish the perception of impurity.

This pure liberation is also like the second [liberation], wherein one, being internally percipient of no-form, perceives external forms; however, there is a distinction, namely, because of the difference in the level upon which it relies and the aspect of the practice to be remedied, as well as because it is common or uncommon to the bodies of those within and outside the Buddhist path.

These pertain to both what has been previously attained and what has not; however, because they pertain only to what has not been previously attained, they are acquired with little effort in some cases and with great effort in others.

Furthermore, regarding the pure liberation (*śuddha-vimokṣa*), one contemplates the signs concordant with craving yet craving does not arise; regarding the second liberation, one contemplates the signs discordant with craving and thus craving does not arise. The remaining five liberations should be understood as explained previously in the section on the formless bases (*ārūpyāyatana*) that are dissociated from thought.
For what reason is it said only that "one has no perception of internal form while removing the perception of internal form," but not mentioned regarding the external?
Because when the first dhyāna is attained, the perception of the external has already been removed.

This means that when one attains the first dhyāna, external perceptions of form have already been eliminated; within the fourth dhyāna, there is no further need for effortful removal, because all qualities of merit are attained progressively.
Furthermore, because the perception of external forms is easily eliminated, liberation is not established at the time of its removal.
Alternatively, since the perception of external forms is removed only upon reaching the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), it is said here that only internal [perception] is removed.
Regarding what is stated here—"having no perception of internal form"—does this merely exclude the perception of form, or does it specifically refer to other perceptions?

If one claims that this statement merely excludes the perception of form, then the statement is redundant, because the meaning—that one contemplates external forms while lacking the perception of internal form—is already established.
If it is claimed that this statement refers specifically to other types of perception (saṃjñā), one should explain what the object of this perception is.
This [statement] is not merely a negation, because it is stated as something distinct.
Of which phenomena does it take as its object?
If it were not that the aspect of practice revolves around the sphere of space (*ākāśadhātu*), how could it be called the second liberation?
There is no fault here, because it is so designated by way of its preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Regarding the statement here, "having no perception of internal form," this is the name for the second preparatory stage (*prayoga*). This second liberation (*vimokṣa*) receives the name "liberation" for several reasons:

because liberation arises only after this [preparatory stage] has been accomplished; because its power can induce liberation; because it possesses the nature of various liberations; and because it is conjoined with the resolute confidence (*adhimukti*) of liberation.
These various liberations depend upon the bodies of both men and women; they can be cultivated and realized by both noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Only the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) depends solely upon the body of a noble one, and within the class of noble ones, it is accessible to both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The Sūtra states that the attainment of cessation transcends all levels of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); how, then, can it be said that it also relies upon a body of one in training (*śaikṣa*)?
Although this [attainment] is subsumed under its own level, the Peak of Existence, it is nevertheless obtained by transcending other [levels], just like the dharmas of the higher stages.

Just as one transcends all craving for the fourth dhyāna before entering the fundamental sphere of infinite space, so too does one transcend all craving for nothingness before entering the fundamental sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In this way, only by transcending the craving for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) can one enter the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

That is to say, whether the craving for the Peak of Existence has been severed or not yet severed, one must first suppress it entirely before entering this attainment; therefore, although it belongs to its own level, it is termed "transcendence."

Alternatively, because those in training (*śaikṣa*) have already abandoned the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) by means of what is to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), it is called "transcending.

Furthermore, there are two general types of states at the Peak of Existence, distinguished by the difference between states with mind and states without mind; because one transcends the state with mind, it is called "transcending."
Alternatively, according to what is appropriate, it is said that there is no fault in transcending [the stages].
Only the third and eighth [liberations] are called "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*); this is stated by citing the two extremes to illustrate the remaining ones.

Among the form-sphere liberations, the "pure" (*śubha*) is the extreme; among the formless spheres, the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is the extreme. This is because each of these resides at the limit of its respective realm, or because only these two types are attained exclusively by those within our own tradition (the Buddhists), because they have never been attained before, because they are attained through great effort, and because they exhaust all derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) as well as the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

Some say that regarding the third [liberation], one first grasps the sign of purity within the physical form by the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*); subsequently, by gradually eliminating [the perception of impurity], liberation becomes perfected, and this constitutes the culmination of liberation from the body as its object.
Therefore, the designation "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*) is established specifically for this [attainment of cessation].
Since the mindless attainment of cessation abides solely in dependence upon the body, it is likewise designated as "bodily realization.
This is so because it is established according to what is predominant; however, in reality, both cases are the same, as there is a logical basis for applying the term to both.
A sūtra states: "What is called 'bodily realization' (kāyasākṣin)?
It refers to the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa)."
Regarding these eight liberations, what kind of sentient beings give rise to them?

Those who constantly seek antidotes toward their objects of focus, whose conduct is characterized by craving, and who delight in cultivating many paths—such sentient beings are able to give rise to the liberations.
For what purpose does the practitioner cultivate liberation and so forth?
It is to cause the afflictions to recede further away and to attain mastery over meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

Having attained such mastery, one is then able to evoke qualities such as the "absence of strife" (*araṇā*) and the noble supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); by means of these, one can transform various objects and perform diverse activities, such as prolonging or relinquishing life.
The liberations have already been explained; next, the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are explained.
The verse says:
There are eight kinds of spheres of mastery; two are like the first liberation.
The next two are like the second [base], and the final four are like the third.
The treatise says:

There are eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). The first is: possessing the perception of internal forms, one observes external forms that are few, whether beautiful or ugly; one knows these forms with mastery and sees them with mastery, maintaining such a perception—this is called the first.

Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as many; as explained at length, this is called the second [liberation]: having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as few.
As explained at length, this is called the third [liberation]: having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as many.

To speak at length, up to: this is called the fourth [liberation], wherein there is no internal perception of form, and one perceives external forms—forms that are blue, appearing blue, manifesting as blue light, like the *umakā* flower, or like deep-dyed blue cloth from Vārāṇasī; having superior knowledge and vision regarding these forms, one possesses such a perception. This is called the fifth [liberation], wherein there is no internal perception of form, and one perceives external forms.

Yellow, appearing yellow, manifesting yellow light—like a *karṇikāra* flower, or like a robe from Vārāṇasī dyed with deep yellow—and so forth, in detail, this is called the sixth [liberation]: having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms.

Red, manifesting red, appearing red, and emitting red light—like the *pāṇḍu-tībraka* flower, or like a deep crimson robe from Vārāṇasī; as explained at length, this is called the seventh [liberation]: internal non-perception of form while perceiving external forms.
It is white, appearing white, manifesting white light, like the star Uṣas, or like an exceptionally fresh white cloth from Vārāṇasī; as explained at length, this is called the eighth.
They are called "mastery-objects" (*abhibhvāyatana*) because they are able to subdue their objects;
that is to say, although all objective forms may be pure, radiant, and exquisitely complete, the power of one's roots of goodness is able to completely outshine them.
For example, although a servant may wear rare and precious garments, they are eclipsed by their master.

Because one can exercise mastery over these objects and does not give rise to afflictions in accordance with them, they are called "spheres of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*); they are established under the name "spheres of mastery" because they master the spheres.
Alternatively, these roots of goodness are themselves called "bases" (*āyatana*); because they are superior, they are designated by the name "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
"Limited" refers to the object of focus or the degree of mastery being small; the opposite of this is termed "vast."
The "attractive" and "unattractive" colors indicate inferior and superior forms respectively.
Some say they are called "mastery" (*abhibhava*) because one does not give rise to greed for the attractive and does not feel aversion toward the unattractive.
If that were so, the essential nature of mastery would have to consist of both non-greed and non-hatred; therefore, there is a distinct underlying intention here.

This means that by contemplating the general characteristics of impurity regarding both beautiful and ugly forms—just as one contemplates ugly forms, so too does one contemplate beautiful ones—one grasps impurity as a whole and the mind functions with mastery; why then labor further to contemplate the impurity of ugly forms?

Because various afflictions arise from having previously perceived purity—due to erroneous cognition regarding what was previously seen as pure—one now perceives things as they truly are to counteract former greed; thus, one contemplates even unattractive forms as impure.
The initial contemplation of this object is called "superior knowledge" (*jñāna*); when the subsequent contemplation is perfected, it is called "superior vision" (*darśana*).
To be able to personally realize, "I possess superior knowledge and superior vision regarding this," is what is termed "possessing such a perception."
These four bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are, by their intrinsic nature and so forth, respectively identical to the first two liberations (vimokṣa).

That is to say, the first two bases of mastery are the fruit of the first liberation, and the next two bases of mastery are the fruit of the second; for they serve as the provisions (sambhāra) through which one is able to enter these [liberations].

Having generally observed the impure to subdue oneself, one further observes the pure within this same object to effect subdual; that is, continuing from the previous state of being without internal perception of form, one separately contemplates the four types of manifest color, such as blue and so forth.
That which is called "blue" refers to the blue color of flowers and the like.
That which is called "manifestly blue" refers to the blue color of garments and the like.

The manifestation of blue and the manifestation of blue light reveal the blue characteristics inherent in these two types; they are purely deep and unmixed, unlike the blue shadows produced at the edges of blue objects or the blue of peacock feathers, diamonds, and so forth.
However, the term "blue light" indicates that the blue is fresh and pure; it does not mean that light is emitted externally as it is with the sun and so forth.

Alternatively, in order to demonstrate that the blue color is prominent, the metaphors of flowers and clothing are cited to show that during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one takes those as the gateway to enter the meditation on the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). This does not mean that within the actual meditation one perceives something resembling these colors.
Among flowers, the *umakā* flower is the most excellent blue; among those produced together with the blue, this is cited as the representative example.

Regarding the dyeing of Varanasi, which is skilled in blending colors, this is cited as the representative example within the blue category. These two are taken not merely because of their preparatory application (*prayoga*), but as representative cases.
Because they are not universally present, precious jewels are not mentioned.
If one dwells in a secluded place, one first takes up the sign of a flower; if one resides in a village, one first takes up the sign of blue cloth.
As it is with the perception of blue, so it is with yellow and the others as well.
However, during the night one should first take white stars, and during the day one should take [white] cloth; all else is as described above.
On a clear night, one should take the star Uṣas, for it is the most excellent among all white stars.

These four spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) should be understood as having the same intrinsic nature and so forth as the third liberation previously described; for the pure liberation serves as the cause for these four, acting as the requisite (sambhāra) by which one is able to enter them.

While the first three liberations merely grasp the general characteristics of impurity and purity among all forms, the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) now differentiate the distinct characteristics of blue and so forth, whether small or large, among all forms.

Therefore, while the preceding liberations merely involve turning away from sensual desire and the perception of impurity regarding form, the present eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are able to analyze and subdue the objects of focus, causing them to function in accordance with the mind.

From this it is proven that the third liberation is established as a single category because it grasps the sign of purity in its entirety, whereas the latter four of the eight spheres of mastery are divided into four types because they grasp the signs with differentiation.

If the pure liberations (*śubha-vimokṣa*) were also established as a single category despite having distinct objects of focus because they share the common nature of being pure, then the latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) should likewise be established as one, for no differentiating causes or conditions can be found [in their case].
Having explained the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), next the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are explained.
The verse says:
There are ten kinds of spheres of totality; eight are like the pure liberation (*śubhavimokṣa*).
The latter two pure [attainments] of the formless realm take the four aggregates of their own level as objects.
The commentary states:
There are ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), namely: observing earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, as well as the two boundless abodes of space and consciousness.

In these locations, it is said that there is a single perception; above, below, and across, there is no duality, only the immeasurable. Because one contemplates this everywhere, without interval or gap, pervading all places, they are called "totalities" (*kṛtsnāyatana*); they are established as "totalities" because they pervade every location.
Alternatively, these roots of goodness themselves are called "bases" (*kṛtsnāyatana*); they are designated as "totalities" because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are all-pervasive.
Herein, "earth" and so forth indicate the objects of focus (*ālambana*), while the term "totality" (*kṛtsna*) indicates the mode of activity.
Although their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are identical, their objects (*ālambana*) differ; therefore, the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are divided into ten types.
When the Sūtra speaks of "one," it indicates that in this meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), one contemplates a single type of objective aspect as appearing before the mind.
The term "perception" (*saṃjñā*) indicates that this is an act of attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*); were it otherwise, one should have said "a single cognition.
The terms "above," "below," and "sideways" indicate the movement of the mental stream.
The phrase "without a second" indicates the absence of any interval.

The term "immeasurable" indicates that resolve is boundless; by the power of polishing through superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it causes the practitioner’s mind to arise with mastery, enabling them to examine their object of focus exhaustively.
For what reason do only these ten receive the name "totality" (*kṛtsnāyatana*)?
Because beyond these, there are no further modes of universal activity (*sarvatraga-ākāra*).
Only in the fourth dhyāna, as well as in the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness, can one speak of the existence of such unlimited modes of activity.

The first eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are like the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*); their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is entirely the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*). If accompanied by their associated factors (*sānucara*), they consist of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The latter four spheres of mastery are produced through the application of effort (*prayoga*), and thus they are the same as those [first eight], being like the pure liberation.

Furthermore, just as the pure liberation (*śuddha-vimokṣa*) relies upon the fourth dhyāna and takes the visible forms (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire realm as its object, how is it that earth and so forth are also called "visible form bases"?
This is because there is a distinction between earth and the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), and so on.

Since it has already been stated previously that "earth" and so forth refer to manifest form (*rūpa*), when the "totalities" (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of earth and so forth are taught, they do not refer to the "earth element" (*pṛthivīdhātu*) and so forth; therefore, the first eight types take only the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) as their object.
Since wind and the wind-element are without distinction, how can it be said that [the first eight consciousnesses] also take the sense-field of form as their object?

This objection is irrational, because people in the world also speak of "black winds" and "whirlwinds"; therefore, the principle that the first eight [consciousnesses] take form as their object is established.

The latter two spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) correspond respectively to space and consciousness; their intrinsic nature consists of the two pure formless attainments (*śuddhārūpya*), each taking the four aggregates of its own level as its object.
By what means are the merits of these three gateways—liberation (*vimokṣa*) and so forth—attained?
In dependence upon which body does it arise?
The verse says:
As has been previously explained regarding the attainment of cessation, all others are obtained through both [types of acquisition].
The formless [attainments] rely upon the three realms; the others arise only in the human realm.
The treatise says:
The eighth liberation has already been explained previously, as it is identical to the aforementioned attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The remaining liberations and so forth are obtained through both means—that is, through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*) and through application (*prayoga*)—because there are those that have been previously practiced and those that have not.
When first cultivating the first eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), one always employs visual consciousness as the preliminary application.

The initial cultivation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is likewise; because at the outset it must take the matter of the space-element as its object, when it later reaches fulfillment through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), it takes all four aggregates of its own level as its object.

When first practicing the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-kṛtsnāyatana*), one employs only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), because at the outset it must take consciousness as its object. Through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), when it later reaches fulfillment, it likewise takes the four aggregates (*skandha*) of its own level as its object.

The four formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*) and the two formless totalities (*ārūpya-kṛtsnāyatana*) each arise based on bodies belonging to any of the three realms; however, their initial arising most often depends on a lower stage, while subsequent arising may depend upon either one's own stage or a lower stage.

Only the "nothingness" (ākiṃcanyāyatana) relies on the higher realms; all the remaining [attainments] rely on a body in the desire realm. They exist only among humans in the three continents, excluding the northern continent, because elsewhere the power of wisdom is inferior and the holy teachings are absent. Furthermore, because they serve as antidotes to sensual desire, they do not exist in the two upper realms.
Some say that its initial arising occurs only within the human realm, because it must be induced by the power of formal instruction; such instruction exists among humans but not among the gods.

Furthermore, those who are attached to pleasure are unable to initiate it at first; therefore, when one initially arises [in the formless realm] and subsequently falls back to be born in the desire realm heavens, there is the possibility of its subsequent arising due to the force of past habituation.
Furthermore, for what reason do the third dhyāna and the immeasurables (apramāṇa) possess the supernormal powers (abhijñā) and so forth, yet lack the liberations (vimokṣa)?
The reasons why there are no liberations have already been fully explained above.
Because liberation does not exist, the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) also do not exist, for one enters the spheres of mastery by means of liberation as the gateway.
Because the spheres of mastery do not exist, the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) also do not exist, for one enters the spheres of totality by means of the spheres of mastery as the gateway.

Furthermore, in the third dhyāna, one is attached to sublime pleasure; because this pleasure is superior within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one is unable to give rise to the three [qualities] beginning with liberation, as these three all involve turning one's back on *saṃsāra*.
Because the [four] immeasurables and so forth accord with bliss, one can also cultivate and give rise to them by relying on this meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the merits of these three gateways—namely, the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and so forth—if one attains any one of them, does one attain all of them?
This is not always the case.
What is the meaning? That which is attained later must necessarily have preceded it, but that which precedes it does not necessarily come later.
This means that one who attains the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality) necessarily attains all three; one who attains the *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery) necessarily attains *vimokṣa* (liberation).
As for the *kṛtsnāyatana*, it is not fixed—one may attain it or not.
If one attains *vimokṣa*, the other two are not fixed, because one enters the *kṛtsnāyatana* and *abhibhvāyatana* by way of *vimokṣa*, and enters the *abhibhvāyatana* by way of *vimokṣa*.
What are the distinctions between these liberations (*vimokṣa*) and so forth?

Merely being able to turn away from and abandon [objects] is called "liberation"; when this is combined with the analytical discernment of the focal object (*ālambana*), it is called a "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*); and when the realization of the infinite is added, it receives the name "totality" (*kṛtsnāyatana*). These three roots of goodness are cultivated in successive stages.
Other masters say:
These three roots of goodness differ by way of being inferior, middling, and superior.
That is to say, because they are able to abandon and overcome their objects of focus, and because their modes of activity (*ākāra*)—though boundless—possess degrees of inferiority and superiority.
Other masters say: "Liberation is exclusively a cause; the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are exclusively effects; and the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) pertain to both.
This now requires careful investigation.
Since there are no such exponents in the two higher realms, by what cause do they give rise to meditative absorption?
The verse says:
In the two realms, by means of causes and karma, one is able to give rise to the formless absorptions.
The arising of dhyāna in the form realm is also due to the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
The treatise says:
Birth in the two higher realms is generally brought about by three conditions, which enable one to further induce the production of the form and formless absorptions.
First, by the power of the cause (*hetubala*): this refers to having previously practiced [the meditation] both recently and repeatedly, which serves as the cause for its arising.

Second, by the power of karma (*karmabala*): this refers to having previously created karma that brings about rebirth in a higher realm and is to be experienced in a subsequent life; when the maturation (*vipāka*) of that karma is about to manifest, its force is able to cause one to further give rise to that meditative absorption (*samādhi*), because if one has not yet abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower realm, it is absolutely impossible to be born in a higher realm.

Third is the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā-bala*): when the receptacle world is about to be destroyed, sentient beings of the lower realms naturally (*dharmataḥ*) become able to give rise to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the higher realms, because at this stage all wholesome phenomena increase and flourish by the very power of their nature.

Those beings born in the two upper realms who give rise to formless meditative attainments do so through the power of causes and karma, not by the force of natural law; for the gods of the Cloudless Heaven and those above are not destroyed by the three calamities.
When one born in the form realm gives rise to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), it occurs through the two aforementioned conditions as well as the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
When one born in the desire realm gives rise to a higher concentration, one should understand that each instance additionally involves the power of instruction (*śāsana-bala*).
Regarding those [who uphold] by the power of the teaching, this refers to humans in the three continents.
Although the gods also hear the teaching, they are not mentioned because their capacity is subtle.
All the preceding analyses of various supreme dharma-gates were for the purpose of widely propagating and upholding the True Dharma of the World-Honored One.
What is the True Dharma?
For how long shall it endure?
The verse says:
The Buddha’s True Dharma is twofold: its essence consists of the teaching (*śāsana*) and the realization (*adhigama*).
As long as there are those who uphold, explain, and practice it, it shall remain in the world.
The treatise says:
The essence of the World-Honored One’s True Dharma is twofold: first, the teaching; second, the realization.
The teaching refers to the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma; the realization refers to all the untainted paths of the three vehicles.
If the realization of the True Dharma (saddharma-adhigama) abides in the world, then the teaching that is propagated and upheld will also abide.

This must necessarily be so, for we observe that while the realization of the Dharma has declined in the East and much of the teaching has disappeared there, the realization of the Dharma still flourishes in the North.

The authentic teachings of the World-Honored One still circulate extensively; for this reason, the realm of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed wisdom—the abode of the noble ones—and the unerring, true meaning of the Abhidharma flourish in this land, such that they cannot be transmitted or practiced in places like the East.

Of these two, the teaching of the Dharma (*deśanādharma*) mostly depends upon those who uphold and proclaim it for its persistence in the world; however, the realization of the true Dharma (*adhigamadharma*) depends solely upon the practitioner.
Yet, the practitioner is not the sole basis for the realization of the Dharma, for the teaching of the Dharma must also depend upon the practitioner.

This means that those who practice the Dharma without inversion are able to cause the realized Dharma (adhigama-dharma) to abide long in the world; when the realized Dharma abides, the taught Dharma (deśanā-dharma) also abides. Therefore, the endurance of the taught Dharma depends upon its being upheld through exposition and practice.
It is solely because practitioners cause the Dharma to abide that the Buddha’s True Dharma remains in the world for as long as it does, following these three types of persons.
This Abhidharma treatise is the basis upon which [the teachings] rely; it subsumes the essential, true meaning contained therein.
In that treatise, there are many ways of explaining its meaning; according to what principle does this present treatise explain it?
The verse says:
The principles established by the scholars of Kaśmīra— I have mostly relied upon them to explain the Abhidharma.
To offer even slight disparagement [of their views] would be my own fault; the determination of the correct principles of the Dharma rests with the Muni.
The commentary states:
The masters of the *Vibhāṣā* in the kingdom of Kaśmīra have well-established the reasoning of the Abhidharma; I have for the most part relied upon them to explain the tenets of the *Abhidharma*.

In this passage, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrapāla) sets forth his own original intention, stating: "Relying upon the Great Vibhāṣā, which expounds the principles of Abhidharma according to the consensus of the sons of the Sugata in this land, I have applied diligent effort and conducted a reasoned investigation. For the sake of causing the True Dharma to abide long in the world and for the benefit of sentient beings, I have composed this treatise; the frequent use of the term 'mostly' indicates that there are few divergent paths."
This refers to things such as physical forms, colors, and those belonging to the past and future.

However, the nature of all phenomena is vast and profoundly deep; one who can explain it according to reality is extremely difficult to encounter. Reflecting upon myself, my own awakening wisdom is exceedingly weak and inferior, and I have been unable to diligently seek out such a person who speaks according to reality. Therefore, it is my own fault if there is even a slight deprecation or misjudgment regarding the principles established in this extensive treatise.

The true principle of all phenomena is vast and profound; only those who have previously approached and cultivated the provisions for true wisdom under immeasurable Buddhas will be entirely free from doubt regarding the sphere of that wisdom.

Even the *ṛṣabha*, who is likened to a *pratyekabuddha*, is unable to definitively discern the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), let alone the *śrāvakas*, for the dharmas they realize are dependent upon the teachings of others.
Therefore, the definitive discernment of the correct principle of all phenomena resides solely with the Truly Great Muni.
Therefore, it is certain that the Abhidharma is truly the word of the Buddha; one should accept it with faith, practice it without error, and diligently seek liberation.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Eighty.
